1. ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME (ACS)

STEMI • NSTEMI • Unstable Angina
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Substernal chest pain/pressure >20 minutes, radiation to jaw/left arm/back, diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea. Pain not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.

Alternate Presentations:

  • Diabetics/Elderly/Women: Atypical symptoms - dyspnea alone, weakness, epigastric pain, syncope
  • Silent MI: No chest pain (30% of diabetics)
  • RV Infarction: Hypotension with clear lungs, JVD, Kussmaul sign
  • Posterior MI: Isolated ST depression V1-V3, need posterior leads (V7-V9)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Immediate: ECG within 10 minutes, troponin (repeat at 3 and 6 hours if initial negative for conventional troponin; 1h/2h rapid rule-out protocols available if high-sensitivity troponin [hs-cTn] is used — check institutional protocol), CBC, BMP, PT/INR, lipid panel, CXR

STEMI Criteria: New ST elevation at the J-point in ≥2 contiguous leads: ≥1 mm in all leads except V2-V3; in V2-V3, ≥2 mm in men ≥40 y, ≥2.5 mm in men <40 y, ≥1.5 mm in women. Posterior MI: isolated ST depression ≥0.5 mm in V1-V3 → obtain V7-V9 (≥0.5 mm elevation confirms). New/presumed-new LBBB is NOT diagnostic in isolation; use Sgarbossa criteria or strong clinical context (see pearl below) (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline; Fourth Universal Definition of MI)

Calculations: HEART Score, TIMI STEMI, TIMI NSTEMI, GRACE Score

🧮 HEART Score Calculator
Use: Risk stratification for chest pain patients to determine if safe for outpatient evaluation. Score 0-3 = low risk (outpatient), 4-6 = moderate risk (observe), 7-10 = high risk (admit).
🧮 TIMI Risk Score - STEMI
Use: Predicts 30-day mortality in STEMI patients. 30-day mortality by score: 0 = 0.8%, 1 = 1.6%, 2 = 2.2%, 3 = 4.4%, 4 = 7.3%, 5 = 12.4%, 6 = 16.1%, 7 = 23.4%, 8 = 26.8%, >8 = 35.9%. Check only one age box (if both are checked, ≥75 counts). Derived in fibrinolysis-era patients (InTIME II).
🧮 TIMI Risk Score - NSTEMI/UA
Use: Risk of death, MI, or urgent revascularization within 14 days. 14-day rate by score: 0-1 = 4.7%, 2 = 8.3%, 3 = 13.2%, 4 = 19.9%, 5 = 26.2%, 6-7 = 40.9%. Low 0-2, moderate 3-4, high 5-7 (Antman, JAMA 2000).
🧮 GRACE Score Calculator
Use: Estimates in-hospital and 6-month mortality in ACS. Low risk <109, intermediate 109-140, high >140. More accurate than TIMI for mortality prediction.
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Initial Management (MONA-BAH):

  • Morphine: 2-4mg IV PRN (use cautiously, may worsen outcomes)
  • Oxygen: Only if SpO2 <90%
  • Nitroglycerin: 0.4mg SL q5min × 3 (avoid if RV infarct, SBP <90, recent PDE5 inhibitor)
  • Aspirin: 162-325 mg PO chewed immediately (non-enteric-coated; give the load even if already on aspirin), then 75-100 mg PO daily (≤100 mg/day if on ticagrelor) (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline)
  • β-Blocker: Oral, start within 24 h (Class 1): metoprolol 25-50 mg PO. Hold if acute HF (Killip II-IV), low-output state or at risk for cardiogenic shock, PR >0.24 s, 2nd/3rd-degree AV block without a pacemaker, severe bradycardia, or active bronchospasm; reassess at 24 h and start once the contraindication resolves (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline)
  • Anticoagulation: Heparin bolus + infusion or enoxaparin
  • High-intensity statin: Atorvastatin 80mg

P2Y12 Inhibitor: PCI planned (STEMI or NSTE-ACS): prasugrel 60 mg load, then 10 mg daily (5 mg if <60 kg or age ≥75 y, use caution) OR ticagrelor 180 mg load, then 90 mg BID (keep aspirin ≤100 mg/day). NSTE-ACS with no invasive strategy planned: ticagrelor. Fibrinolysis: clopidogrel 300 mg load (75 mg if age >75 y), then 75 mg daily. Clopidogrel 300-600 mg load, then 75 mg daily, only if prasugrel/ticagrelor unavailable, not tolerated, or contraindicated. Prasugrel is CONTRAINDICATED with prior stroke/TIA. Hold before elective CABG: ticagrelor 3-5 d, clopidogrel 5 d, prasugrel 7 d (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline)

STEMI Specific: Symptom onset <12 h: primary PCI with first medical contact (FMC)-to-device ≤90 min (≤120 min if transfer needed); call cath lab immediately. Cardiogenic shock or hemodynamic instability: emergency revascularization regardless of time from onset. Onset 12-24 h: PCI reasonable. If anticipated FMC-to-device >120 min and no contraindication: give fibrinolysis (tenecteplase single IV bolus by weight: 30 mg <60 kg, 35 mg 60-69, 40 mg 70-79, 45 mg 80-89, 50 mg ≥90; or reteplase 10 U IV x2, 30 min apart; or alteplase 90-min weight-based infusion), then transfer: immediate rescue PCI if reperfusion fails, otherwise routine angiography within 2-24 h (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline)

NSTEMI Specific: Risk stratify with TIMI/GRACE. Refractory angina, hemodynamic or electrical instability → immediate invasive strategy. High risk (eg, GRACE >140) → early invasive, within 24 h. Intermediate/high risk and a revascularization candidate → invasive approach during hospitalization (Class 1); if not high risk, angiography before discharge. Low risk → routine invasive OR selective invasive (ischemia-guided, noninvasive testing first) approach, both Class 1 (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline)

Post-MI Arrhythmia Monitoring:

  • 48-Hour Standard: Continuous cardiac telemetry monitoring for minimum 48 hours is the standard post-MI observation period. Life-threatening arrhythmias (VF, VT, high-grade AV blocks) are most common in first 48 hours post-infarction, with peak risk in first 24 hours
  • Early Discharge Considerations: Hemodynamically stable, low-risk patients without complications may be considered for discharge after 24 hours. However, patients discharged before 48 hours remain at elevated risk for arrhythmias and require careful patient selection, thorough education about warning signs, and clear return precautions
  • Extended Monitoring (>48hr) indicated if: Arrhythmias detected, hemodynamic instability, large infarct, reduced EF (<40%), high-risk features, or persistent ischemia
  • Serial troponins: Peak at 12-24 hours, trend until downtrending
  • Daily ECG: Assess for evolution of infarct, new ischemia, conduction abnormalities
  • Echo before discharge: Assess LV function (EF), wall motion abnormalities, mechanical complications, LV thrombus
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • 48-hour arrhythmia window: Standard telemetry monitoring is 48 hours post-MI. Low-risk patients MAY be discharged at 24 hours if stable, but they remain at elevated arrhythmia risk until 48 hours. Early discharge requires careful patient selection and thorough education about warning signs (palpitations, syncope, chest pain)
  • Sgarbossa Criteria: Diagnose STEMI with LBBB: ST elevation ≥1mm concordant with QRS (5 points), ST depression ≥1mm V1-V3 (3 points), ST elevation ≥5mm discordant (2 points). Score ≥3 = STEMI
  • Wellens Syndrome: Biphasic or deep inverted T waves V2-V3 in pain-free patient = critical LAD stenosis, high risk of anterior STEMI. No stress test! Go to cath.
  • RV Infarction Pearl: If inferior STEMI with hypotension, always get right-sided leads (V4R). Treat with aggressive IVF, avoid nitrates/diuretics
  • Troponin timing: Can be negative first 2-4 hours. Serial troponins essential if high suspicion
  • Don't forget: Type 2 MI (supply-demand mismatch from anemia, sepsis, tachyarrhythmia) - treat underlying cause, not necessarily cath
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hemodynamic instability (SBP <90, shock)
  • Malignant arrhythmias (VT/VF, high-grade AV block)
  • Mechanical complications (papillary rupture, VSD, free wall rupture)
  • Acute heart failure/cardiogenic shock
  • Need for pressors or mechanical support (IABP, Impella)
  • Post-cardiac arrest
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable >24 hours (minimum for early discharge in low-risk patients; standard 48-hour telemetry monitoring preferred)
  • No recurrent chest pain or ischemic symptoms
  • No arrhythmias requiring intervention during monitoring period
  • LVEF assessed (echo)
  • Successful revascularization (if indicated)
  • On DAPT (aspirin 75-100 mg + P2Y12) for ≥12 months by default if not high bleeding risk; PPI if GI bleeding risk; if on long-term anticoagulation, stop aspirin 1-4 weeks after PCI and continue the P2Y12 (preferably clopidogrel). High-intensity statin. LDL-C goal (2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline): <70 mg/dL, or <55 mg/dL if very high risk (ACS within 12 months is a major ASCVD event; very high risk = 2 or more major events, or 1 plus 2 or more high-risk features such as age ≥65, PCI or CABG, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, HF); add ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 mAb on maximally tolerated statin to reach goal (very high risk: 1, A; see statin card). Oral β-blocker. ACE-I/ARB if LVEF ≤40%, HTN, DM, or anterior STEMI (reasonable in all others); MRA if LVEF ≤40% with HF symptoms or DM (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline)
  • Cardiac rehab referral arranged
  • Patient educated on arrhythmia warning signs if discharged <48 hours
  • Clear return precautions given
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Early (hours-days): Arrhythmias (VF, VT, bradycardia), cardiogenic shock, mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture), acute MR

Late (days-weeks): Heart failure, LV thrombus, pericarditis (early: Dressler's syndrome 2-10 weeks), recurrent ischemia

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Clopidogrel, 💊 Ticagrelor, 💊 Prasugrel, 💊 UFH, 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Atorvastatin, 💊 Metoprolol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 DIC Panel, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
↑ Back to Table of Contents

2. ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE

HFrEF • HFpEF • Acute Exacerbation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, lower extremity edema, weight gain. Physical exam: JVD, bibasilar rales, S3 gallop, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly.

Alternate Presentations:

  • Flash Pulmonary Edema: Acute onset, often with HTN emergency, minimal peripheral edema
  • High Output HF: Warm extremities, bounding pulses (thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula, severe anemia)
  • RV Failure: Isolated lower extremity edema, ascites, hepatic congestion without pulmonary edema
  • Elderly: Confusion, fatigue, decreased appetite may predominate over dyspnea
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: BNP/NT-proBNP (Class 1 to support or exclude HF; admission level also gives prognosis). Acute rule-out: BNP <100 or NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL makes acute HF unlikely. Rule-in: BNP >400; NT-proBNP by age (see pearl). Values in between are a gray zone; troponin (r/o ACS), BMP (assess renal function), CBC, Mg, TSH, LFTs

Imaging: CXR (cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, pleural effusions), Echo (assess EF, valves, wall motion)

ECG: Look for ischemia, LVH, arrhythmias

Calculations: NYHA Class, EF%, fluid balance (daily weights), creatinine clearance

Classify Hemodynamics: Warm vs cold (perfusion), wet vs dry (volume status)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Initial Management:

  • O2: Only for hypoxemia, SpO2 <90% or PaO2 <60 mmHg (ESC 2026 I C; AHA 2022 gives no target); avoid oxygen in non-hypoxemic patients. NIPPV (BiPAP/CPAP) for respiratory distress, RR >25 and SpO2 <90% (ESC 2026 IIa B2); caution with hypotension or RV failure
  • Diuresis (Wet): Start IV loop diuretic promptly (AHA 2022 Class 1; ESC 2026 I A). Loop-naive: furosemide 40 mg IV; on a home loop diuretic: IV dose 2× the daily oral dose; higher starting dose in CKD (ESC 2026 Fig 15); the DOSE high-dose arm used 2.5×. Adequate response: spot urine Na ≥70 mmol/L at 2 h or urine output ≥100 mL/h over the first 6 h; if not, double the dose. Repeat every 12 h until decongested; if 24 h diuresis is <3 L and congestion persists, escalate on day 2; usual max IV furosemide 600 mg/day, up to 1000 mg in severe kidney impairment (ESC 2026 Fig 15). Urinary Na-guided therapy may be considered (ESC 2026 IIb B1). Bolus and continuous infusion are equivalent (DOSE). Goal is resolution of congestion before discharge (Class 1), not a fixed daily net volume; BMP at least daily (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline; 2026 ESC HF guideline; DOSE, NEJM 2011)
  • Vasodilators (SBP >110, never if hypotensive): IV nitroglycerin as an adjunct to diuretics for dyspnea relief (Class 2b; no mortality or readmission benefit). Start 10-20 mcg/min (label: 5 mcg/min with non-PVC tubing), increase by 5-10 mcg/min every 3-5 min to symptom/BP response (label allows 10-20 mcg/min steps if no response at 20 mcg/min); usual max ~200 mcg/min. Mainly venodilator (preload) at low dose, arterial at higher dose; most useful in hypertensive or flash pulmonary edema; tolerance develops within ~24 h. Avoid with PDE5 inhibitor in past 24-48 h, severe aortic stenosis, or RV infarct (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline 2b B-NR; 2026 ESC HF guideline IIb C, as initial therapy when SBP >110; FDA label). High-dose nitroglycerin for hypertensive flash edema: see the acute pulmonary edema card
  • Sodium/Fluid Restriction: Avoid excessive sodium intake (Class 2a, low-quality evidence; no proven benefit from a strict numeric limit). Fluid restriction is not routine; its benefit is uncertain even in advanced HF with hyponatremia (Class 2b) and it corrects hyponatremia only modestly. Avoid restrictions severe enough to cause malnutrition (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline)
  • Daily weights: Essential for monitoring
  • VTE prophylaxis (Class 1): All hospitalized HF patients unless already anticoagulated or contraindicated: enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily (30 mg daily if CrCl <30), or UFH 5000 units SC q8-12h, or fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC daily (avoid if CrCl <30) (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline)

Cold & Wet (Low Output): Cardiogenic shock / end-organ hypoperfusion: IV inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) to maintain perfusion (Class 1); temporary MCS if end-organ function cannot be maintained (2a); shock-team management (2a); PA catheter may be considered (2b). Inotropes improve hemodynamics but not survival; long-term use outside bridge or palliation is harmful (Class 3) (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline). ESC 2026 is more restrictive on inotropes (SBP <90 with hypoperfusion unresponsive to standard treatment, IIb C); see the acute pulmonary edema card

Chronic HF Management (Initiate/Optimize):

  • HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%): Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), all four classes (each Class 1A)
  • ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) preferred if NYHA II-III; ACE-I if ARNI not feasible; ARB if ACE-I intolerant (cough/angioedema). No ARNI within 36 h of last ACE-I dose or with any history of angioedema
  • β-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol) - start low when stable
  • MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) if NYHA II-IV, eGFR >30 and K <5.0; monitor K and creatinine closely
  • SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) - proven mortality benefit; start in hospital once stable (AHA 2022 Class 1 for GDMT initiation; ESC 2026 I B1 for in-hospital SGLT2i)
  • HFmrEF (LVEF 41-49%): SGLT2i (Class 2a); HFrEF GDMT may be considered (2b), especially at the lower end of the range
  • HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%): Treat HTN to target, AF, ischemia. SGLT2i (Class 2a); MRA may be considered in selected patients (2b)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • BNP Pearls: Obesity lowers BNP. Renal failure raises it. Age-adjust NT-proBNP: <50yo: >450, 50-75yo: >900, >75yo: >1800
  • Diuretic Resistance: If poor response to IV loop diuretic: (1) Double the dose (switching bolus to infusion adds no benefit, DOSE). (2) Add a second diuretic (Class 2a): metolazone 2.5-5 mg PO 30-60 min before the loop dose, or acetazolamide 500 mg IV once daily with the loop dose for up to 3 days (ADVOR: more patients decongested by day 3; trial excluded patients on SGLT2i and eGFR <20). ESC 2026 (IIa B1) also lists oral hydrochlorothiazide with eGFR-based dosing: 25 mg daily if eGFR >50, 50 mg if 20-50, 100 mg if <20; acetazolamide may be preferable in advanced CKD (CLOROTIC: more weight loss, more worsening kidney function and hypokalemia). Check K, Mg, Na and creatinine at least daily on combination therapy (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline; 2026 ESC HF guideline; ADVOR, NEJM 2022)
  • Cardiorenal Syndrome: Cr bump with diuresis is often acceptable if congestion improving. Monitor BUN:Cr ratio (>20:1 suggests prerenal)
  • Don't stop GDMT: Continue and optimize home GDMT during admission unless contraindicated (eg, cardiogenic shock, symptomatic hypotension, hyperkalemia); a mild creatinine rise or asymptomatic BP drop is NOT a reason to stop diuresis or GDMT. Start GDMT in hospital once clinically stable; if anything had to be held, restart it as soon as possible (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline, Class 1)
  • B-type natriuretic peptide diuretics: Nesiritide (BNP analog) has no mortality benefit and increases hypotension - rarely used
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Cardiogenic shock (SBP <90, cool extremities, AMS, oliguria)
  • Need for inotropes or mechanical support
  • Acute respiratory failure requiring intubation
  • Refractory pulmonary edema
  • Malignant arrhythmias
  • ACS with hemodynamic instability
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Euvolemic (at or near dry weight)
  • No dyspnea at rest
  • Stable vital signs, O2 sat on room air
  • Transition to PO diuretics established, with a written diuretic adjustment plan based on weight and electrolytes (Class 1); safety labs scheduled after any GDMT start or dose increase (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline)
  • On optimized GDMT (HFrEF)
  • BMP stable, Cr at acceptable baseline
  • Patient education completed
  • Close follow-up arranged, generally within 7 days (AHA 2022 2a); rapid GDMT uptitration with frequent visits over the first 6 weeks (ESC 2026 I B2)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

During Admission: Cardiorenal syndrome (AKI), electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatremia), arrhythmias (AF most common), worsening renal function

Long-term: Recurrent admissions (risk highest in the early post-discharge period; early follow-up within 7 days is reasonable, Class 2a), progressive renal dysfunction, sudden cardiac death, need for advanced therapies (LVAD, transplant)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Carvedilol, 💊 Spironolactone, 💊 Empagliflozin, 💊 Dapagliflozin, 💊 Sacubitril-Valsartan, 💊 Metolazone, 💊 Eplerenone, 💊 Ivabradine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 NT-proBNP (Expanded), 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Low eGFR, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate

3. ATRIAL FIBRILLATION

RVR • New-Onset • Chronic AF Management
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Palpitations, irregular pulse, dyspnea, chest discomfort, fatigue, lightheadedness. Irregularly irregular rhythm on exam.

Alternate Presentations:

  • Asymptomatic: 30-40% discovered incidentally on exam or ECG
  • Embolic stroke: First presentation in some patients
  • Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy: Chronic RVR leading to heart failure
  • Hyperthyroid AF: Lone AF in young patient, check TSH
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: TSH (always), BMP, Mg, CBC, troponin (if chest pain), digoxin level (if on digoxin)

Imaging: ECG (confirm AF, assess rate, look for ischemia/WPW), CXR, TTE (assess for structural disease, valve disease, LV function, LA size)

TEE: Before cardioversion if AF >48hr or unknown duration (r/o LA thrombus), unless patient on therapeutic anticoagulation ≥3 weeks

Calculations:

  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc: Stroke risk (CHF, HTN, Age ≥75 [2pts], DM, Stroke/TIA [2pts], Vascular disease, Age 65-74, Sex [female]). Score ≥2 (♂) or ≥3 (♀) → anticoagulate
  • HAS-BLED: Bleeding risk (HTN, Abnormal renal/liver, Stroke, Bleeding, Labile INR, Elderly, Drugs/alcohol). Score ≥3 = high bleeding risk
🧮 CHA₂DS₂-VASc Calculator
Use: Stroke risk stratification in non-valvular AF. Anticoagulate if score ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women). Consider at ≥1/2 per 2023 ACC/AHA.
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Rate Control (First-line for most):

  • β-Blockers: Metoprolol 25-50mg PO q6h or 2.5-5mg IV, esmolol gtt (ICU). Goal resting HR <100-110, guided by symptoms (2a); strict control (<80) is not better (RACE II) (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)
  • Non-dihydropyridine CCB (only if LVEF >40%): Diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg actual body weight IV over 2 min (about 20 mg); if inadequate after 15 min, 0.35 mg/kg over 2 min (about 25 mg); then infusion 5-15 mg/hr (usual start 10 mg/hr; not studied above 15 mg/hr or beyond 24 h), OR 30-60 mg PO q6h. Contraindicated with 2nd/3rd-degree AV block without a pacemaker, severe hypotension or cardiogenic shock, or pre-excited AF (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline; FDA label)
  • Digoxin (2a; when β-blocker/CCB ineffective or contraindicated, alone or added): No negative inotropy, so useful with HF or hypotension. IV load 8-12 mcg/kg lean body weight total (about 0.6-1 mg for 70 kg): half first (eg, 0.5 mg), then one quarter every 6-8 h twice (eg, 0.25 mg x2), assessing response and toxicity before each dose; use a conservative load (6-10 mcg/kg) in renal impairment. Maintenance 0.125-0.25 mg daily adjusted for CrCl; level at least 6 h after a dose. Slower onset than β-blocker/CCB; weak rate control with exertion (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline; FDA label)
  • Avoid: IV diltiazem/verapamil with moderate or severe LV systolic dysfunction, with or without decompensated HF (Class 3: Harm). If β-blocker/CCB ineffective or contraindicated: digoxin, alone or combined (2a); IV magnesium as an add-on (2a); IV amiodarone in critically ill or decompensated HF (2b; may cardiovert, so weigh stroke risk). AV nodal blockers in pre-excited AF (WPW) can precipitate VF. β-blocker plus CCB is not prohibited; monitor for bradycardia, AV block, and hypotension (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)

Rhythm Control:

  • Indications: Hemodynamic instability (immediate cardioversion, Class 1). Reduced LV function with persistent or high-burden AF: trial of rhythm control to see if AF is causing the cardiomyopathy (Class 1). Symptomatic AF (2a); recent diagnosis <1 year, to reduce hospitalization, stroke and mortality (2a, EAST-AFNET 4); AF with HF (2a). Decide rate vs rhythm with the patient (shared decision-making, Class 1)
  • Cardioversion: Hemodynamic instability from AF → immediate synchronized cardioversion (Class 1). Elective, AF ≥48 h or unknown: ≥3 weeks uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation OR imaging (TEE) excluding thrombus first (Class 1). AF <48 h, not anticoagulated: consider TEE first if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (2b); if CHA₂DS₂-VASc 0-1 and AF <12 h, benefit of imaging/anticoagulation is uncertain (2b). Start therapeutic anticoagulation before cardioversion and continue ≥4 weeks after, uninterrupted (Class 1). If thrombus seen: anticoagulate 3-6 weeks, then re-image (Class 1)
  • Synchronized DC cardioversion (under sedation): confirm sync to QRS (Class 1); biphasic ≥200 J as initial energy improves first-shock success (2a); escalate energy or adjust electrode vector if unsuccessful (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)
  • Chemical (stable patients; reasonable alternative to electrical, 2a): Ibutilide (2a, A, without depressed LV function; best avoided with LVEF ≤40%) 1 mg IV over 10 min (0.01 mg/kg if <60 kg), may repeat once 10 min after the first infusion ends; correct K/Mg first, and a magnesium infusion just before may lower torsades risk; contraindicated if QTc >440 ms (2015 SVT Table 6); continuous ECG ≥4 h after or until QTc returns to baseline (torsades risk); no class Ia/III antiarrhythmic within 4 h. IV amiodarone (2a): usable with structural heart disease but slower (8-12 h). Flecainide 200 mg PO (<70 kg) or 300 mg (≥70 kg), or propafenone 450/600 mg: only with no structural heart disease, prior MI, or LV dysfunction (CAST boxed warning), and always with an AV nodal blocker (risk of 1:1 atrial flutter); outpatient pill-in-the-pocket only after a monitored test dose (2a). IV procainamide if others contraindicated or not preferred (2b) (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline; FDA label; Alboni NEJM 2004)
  • Antiarrhythmics (maintenance): HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%): dofetilide or amiodarone (2a). No prior MI or structural heart disease: flecainide or propafenone (2a); these are CONTRAINDICATED with prior MI, significant structural disease, or HFrEF (Class 3: Harm). Dronedarone (2a) but NOT with NYHA III-IV HF or decompensated HF in the past 4 weeks (Class 3: Harm). Dofetilide (2a) and sotalol (2b): start in hospital with renal dose selection and QT, K, Mg and creatinine monitoring. Low-dose amiodarone 100-200 mg/d (2a) only when other options fail, given its toxicity (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)

Anticoagulation:

  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (♂) or ≥3 (♀) (annual risk ≥2%): Anticoagulate (Class 1). Score 1 (♂) or 2 (♀) (risk 1-2%/yr): anticoagulation reasonable (2a). Aspirin, alone or with clopidogrel, is NOT an alternative to anticoagulation (Class 3: Harm); aspirin with no stroke risk factors has no benefit. Regardless of score: HCM, anticoagulate (2024 AHA/ACC HCM 1, B-NR; see HCM card); cardiac amyloidosis, anticoagulation is reasonable (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA 2a, C-LD; see cardiomyopathy card)
  • DOACs (preferred over warfarin, Class 1): Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran. Use warfarin instead with a mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)
  • Post-cardioversion: Anticoagulate ≥4 weeks without interruption (Class 1; thromboembolic risk peaks in the first 30 days, with atrial stunning and frequent early recurrence). After that, long-term anticoagulation follows the CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds above, which apply to AF generally, not to whether sinus rhythm is maintained (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • WPW + AF = Emergency: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia. DO NOT use AV nodal blockers (can precipitate VF). Cardiovert or procainamide
  • Rate vs Rhythm: AFFIRM/RACE trials showed no mortality difference with rate vs. rhythm control. However, EAST-AFNET 4 (NEJM 2020) showed early rhythm control reduces cardiovascular events (HR 0.79) in patients with AF ≤1 year — 2023 ACC/AHA guidelines give early rhythm control a Class IIa recommendation in symptomatic patients with recent-onset AF. Rate control remains reasonable for older, minimally symptomatic patients; consider early rhythm control in younger or more symptomatic patients.
  • Anticoagulation paradox: HAS-BLED ≥3 means high bleeding risk, but often same patients who need anticoagulation most. Don't withhold if CHA₂DS₂-VASc high
  • Holiday Heart: Alcohol-induced AF. Often converts spontaneously with abstinence
  • TEE before cardioversion: Even if on anticoagulation <3 weeks, consider TEE strategy to expedite cardioversion safely
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hemodynamic instability (SBP <90, shock)
  • Acute heart failure/pulmonary edema with RVR
  • Acute MI with RVR
  • Need for continuous IV rate control infusions
  • Post-cardioversion complications
  • RVR refractory to multiple agents
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Rate controlled (HR <110 at rest, <120 with activity)
  • Hemodynamically stable ≥24 hours
  • Transitioned to oral rate control meds
  • Anticoagulation started (if indicated)
  • No signs of heart failure
  • Follow-up arranged (cardiology if new-onset)
  • If cardioverted: Stable rhythm ≥24hr
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Stroke/TIA (most feared), hemodynamic compromise, heart failure, ACS (demand ischemia from RVR)

Chronic: Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (EF improves with rate/rhythm control), thromboembolism, bleeding (if anticoagulated)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Diltiazem, 💊 Digoxin, 💊 Amiodarone, 💊 Flecainide, 💊 Sotalol, 💊 Dofetilide, 💊 Apixaban, 💊 Rivaroxaban, 💊 Dabigatran, 💊 Warfarin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 Low TSH, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated D-dimer

4a. ESSENTIAL (CHRONIC) HYPERTENSION

Diagnosis • Staging • Long-Term Management
CLINICAL PRESENTATION / DEFINITION

Definition: Persistently elevated arterial BP without an identifiable secondary cause (~90-95% of adult HTN). Usually asymptomatic ("silent killer") - screen routinely

Diagnosis (2025 AHA/ACC, COR 1 / LOE A): Confirm with out-of-office BP - ABPM or HBPM. ABPM is the de facto reference standard; HBPM is often more practical and reproducible. Both endorsed for diagnostic confirmation. Do NOT diagnose on a single clinic reading; exclude white-coat and masked HTN

Staging (unchanged from 2017):

  • Normal: <120/<80
  • Elevated: 120-129/<80
  • Stage 1: 130-139 OR 80-89
  • Stage 2: ≥140 OR ≥90
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Confirm: Out-of-office BP (HBPM/ABPM)

Baseline labs: BMP (Na/K/Cr/eGFR), fasting glucose/A1c, lipid panel, TSH, UA with urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, CBC

Cardiac: 12-lead ECG (LVH, prior MI). Echo if HF/LVH suspected

Risk stratification: 10-yr CVD risk via PREVENT (replaces 2017 Pooled Cohort Equations). The 7.5% PREVENT threshold drives the stage-1 treatment decision (≈ Framingham ≥15%, the SPRINT inclusion criterion)

Secondary screen - primary aldosteronism (plasma aldosterone, renin activity, ARR):

  • COR 1 (recommended): resistant HTN (regardless of K+), spontaneous/diuretic-induced hypokalemia, OSA, adrenal incidentaloma, family history of early-onset HTN, or stroke at age <40
  • COR 2b (may be considered): all adults with stage 2 HTN (PA prevalence 11-22%, similar to resistant HTN)
  • Practical: most antihypertensives EXCEPT MRAs can be continued during screening
TREATMENT - BP TARGET (2025)

Universal target: <130/80 mmHg (COR 1 / LOE A); reduce SBP toward <120 mmHg when tolerated (SPRINT, BPROAD)

Individualized (less intensive) targets: shared decision-making for limited life expectancy, institutionalized/frail patients, or treatment intolerance. No fixed relaxed numeric target - clinical judgment

When to start drug therapy:

  • Stage 2 (≥140/90): start meds + lifestyle now
  • Stage 1 (130-139/80-89) WITH clinical CVD, diabetes, CKD, or 10-yr PREVENT ≥7.5%: start meds + lifestyle
  • Stage 1, low risk (PREVENT <7.5%, no CVD/DM/CKD): lifestyle 3-6 months, then meds if still ≥130/80
  • Elevated (120-129): lifestyle only

Lifestyle (all): DASH diet, Na <1.5-2.3 g/d, weight loss, ≥150 min/wk aerobic activity, limit alcohol, K-rich diet if no CKD/hyperK

TREATMENT - DRUG SELECTION

First-line classes (3; COR 1 / LOE A): thiazide-type diuretic, long-acting dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine), and ACEi OR ARB (not together). Beta-blockers are NOT routine first-line - reserved for compelling indications (less effective for stroke prevention)

Thiazide note: HCTZ, chlorthalidone, indapamide grouped as "thiazide-type"; acceptable to choose among them for routine HTN (DCP trial: switching HCTZ→chlorthalidone did not lower MACE overall). Chlorthalidone/indapamide preferred specifically for RESISTANT HTN (greater efficacy)

Initial therapy:

  • Stage 2: start TWO first-line agents, ideally as a single-pill combination (COR 1 / LOE B-R) - applies to all stage 2, not only those ≥20/10 above goal
  • Stage 1: monotherapy with sequential addition is reasonable (COR 2a)

Compelling indications:

  • CKD with albuminuria / Diabetes: ACEi or ARB first-line (COR 1). Add SGLT2i (slows kidney decline, ↓CVD); GLP-1 RA and finerenone beneficial in CKD+T2DM with albuminuria (adjuncts, not primary antihypertensives)
  • HFrEF: ARNI (preferred) / ACEi / ARB + evidence-based beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) + MRA + SGLT2i. Avoid non-DHP CCB (diltiazem/verapamil contraindicated)
  • Post-MI / angina: beta-blocker ± ACEi/ARB
  • Black adults without HF/CKD: thiazide or CCB first-line (± initial combination); ACEi/ARB if albuminuric CKD/DM
  • Pregnancy: labetalol or extended-release nifedipine preferred (COR 1 / LOE A); methyldopa a secondary option. CONTRAINDICATED (COR 3: Harm): ACEi, ARB, direct renin inhibitors, atenolol, MRAs, nitroprusside

Combination rationale: ACEi/ARB + thiazide OR CCB is synergistic. Do NOT combine ACEi + ARB ± renin inhibitor (COR 3: Harm - ↑CVD, kidney injury, hyperkalemia)

RESISTANT HYPERTENSION

Definition: BP above goal on ≥3 optimally dosed agents (incl. a diuretic), OR controlled requiring ≥4

Optimal regimen: ACEi or ARB + CCB + thiazide-LIKE diuretic (chlorthalidone or indapamide)

Workup: confirm adherence + technique, exclude white-coat (ABPM), review interfering agents (NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, OCPs, alcohol), screen secondary causes - primary aldosteronism, RAS, OSA, pheo, Cushing, thyroid

4th agent: spironolactone preferred (COR 1 / LOE B-R; PATHWAY-2 - superior to doxazosin/bisoprolol). Amiloride 10-20 mg if MRA not tolerated; eplerenone an alternative (weaker evidence). Aprocitentan (endothelin antagonist, FDA-approved for resistant HTN) newly available

Renal denervation: COR 2b - "may be reasonable" in carefully selected patients (office SBP 140-180, DBP ≥90, eGFR ≥40) after optimal therapy; requires multidisciplinary evaluation (COR 1). Only ~60-70% achieve ≥5 mmHg SBP reduction

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Confirm out-of-office: use HBPM/ABPM before labeling chronic HTN - avoids overtreating white-coat
  • Target: <130/80, push toward <120 SBP when tolerated
  • Risk tool: 2025 uses PREVENT ≥7.5% (not PCE ≥10%) for the stage-1 treatment decision
  • Thiazides: interchangeable for routine HTN; reserve chlorthalidone/indapamide for RESISTANT HTN
  • Stage 2: start with a single-pill TWO-drug combo
  • Avoid: ACEi + ARB together; in pregnancy also avoid atenolol and MRAs
  • Screen: stage 2 / resistant HTN for primary aldosteronism (commonly missed); continue most agents except MRAs during screening
⚠️ ESCALATE / REFER IF:
  • Resistant HTN
  • Suspected secondary cause
  • BP >180/120 (assess emergency vs urgency)
  • Pregnancy
  • Age <30 onset
  • Rapid renal decline
✓ OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP
  • Recheck 1 month after starting/changing therapy until at goal
  • Then q3-6 months once controlled
  • Reinforce HBPM
  • Recheck BMP (K+/Cr) after starting ACEi/ARB/diuretic/MRA
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Stroke, CAD/MI, heart failure, CKD progression, LVH, retinopathy, aortic disease, atrial fibrillation

4. HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCY

End-Organ Damage • ICU Management
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Severe hypertension (typically SBP >180 or DBP >120) WITH acute end-organ damage

Classic: Severe headache, visual changes, chest pain, dyspnea, altered mental status, focal neurologic deficits

Alternate Presentations:

  • Neurologic: Hypertensive encephalopathy (HA, confusion, seizures), stroke (ischemic/hemorrhagic), PRES
  • Cardiac: Acute MI, acute pulmonary edema, aortic dissection
  • Renal: Acute kidney injury, hematuria, proteinuria
  • Microangiopathic: Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia

Severe Hypertension (formerly "hypertensive urgency"): BP >180/120 WITHOUT acute target organ damage. No IV drugs and no aggressive short-term lowering; restart or intensify oral therapy, preferably outpatient, with close follow-up. Hospitalized patients: no as-needed IV or extra oral doses to acutely lower BP (Class 3: Harm) (2025 AHA/ACC HBP guideline)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: BMP, troponin, CBC, UA, peripheral smear if hemolysis suspected, BNP if APE concern

Imaging: ECG, CXR, Head CT if neuro symptoms, CT chest if dissection suspected

Fundoscopic: Look for papilledema, hemorrhages, exudates

Calculate Target BP: No compelling condition: lower BP no more than 25% in the first hour (a more conservative 10-20% MAP reduction is also widely used); if stable, to <160/100 over the next 2-6 h; then cautiously to 130-140 systolic over 24-48 h (Class 1, C-LD; no RCT compares strategies). Compelling condition: SBP <140 in the first hour for most; <120 in aortic dissection (Class 1). Ischemic stroke, ICH and pregnancy have their own targets (see Specific Scenarios). Severe HTN (>180/120) WITHOUT acute organ damage in inpatients: do NOT give as-needed IV or extra oral doses to acutely lower BP (Class 3: Harm; BP falls spontaneously in 40-50%) (2025 AHA/ACC High Blood Pressure guideline)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

General: ICU admission, continuous BP monitoring (arterial line often needed), IV antihypertensives

IV Agents:

  • Nicardipine: 5 mg/hr, increase by 2.5 mg/hr every 5 min (max 15 mg/hr). First-line. No negative inotropy; avoid in advanced aortic stenosis
  • Labetalol: 0.3-1 mg/kg (max 20 mg) slow IV every 10 min, OR infusion 0.4-1 mg/kg/hr up to 3 mg/kg/hr; MAX cumulative 300 mg/24 h. Avoid in reactive airway disease/COPD, 2nd/3rd-degree heart block, bradycardia, decompensated HF
  • Clevidipine: 1-2 mg/hr, double every 90 sec until near target, then smaller increases every 5-10 min (max 21 mg/hr, max 72 h). Short-acting. Contraindicated with soy or egg allergy or defective lipid metabolism (eg, pancreatitis)
  • Esmolol: β-blocker for dissection. 500-1000 mcg/kg over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min; re-bolus and increase by 50 mcg/kg/min as needed (max 300 mcg/kg/min). Avoid with bradycardia, decompensated HF, or concurrent β-blocker therapy
  • Nitroprusside: 0.3-0.5 mcg/kg/min, increase by 0.5 mcg/kg/min every 5 min (max 10 mcg/kg/min), shortest possible duration, arterial line recommended. Option for acute pulmonary edema. Cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity risk at ≥3 mcg/kg/min and/or ≥3 days, higher with renal or hepatic dysfunction: stop and give sodium thiosulfate or hydroxocobalamin. Avoid in acute cerebrovascular disease (2025 AHA/ACC HBP guideline, Table 26)

Specific Scenarios:

  • Aortic Dissection: Arterial line, ICU. Target SBP <120 (or the lowest BP that keeps end-organ perfusion) within 20 min-1 h, AND heart rate 60-80 bpm (Class 1). IV β-blocker FIRST (esmolol or labetalol; Class 1); if β-blocker contraindicated, IV diltiazem/verapamil for rate (2a). Add a vasodilator (nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroprusside) only after β-blockade if BP remains high, to avoid reflex tachycardia (Class 1). Treat pain (2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease guideline; 2025 AHA/ACC HBP guideline)
  • Ischemic Stroke: Permissive HTN. Thrombolysis candidate: lower to <185/110 before lytic, then keep <180/105 for at least 24 h (Class 1). After endovascular therapy: ≤180/105 during and for 24 h (2a). No reperfusion therapy: if ≥220/120, lowering ~15% in the first 24 h might be reasonable (2b). Correct hypotension and hypovolemia (Class 1)
  • Hemorrhagic Stroke (ICH): SBP 150-220 at presentation: lower promptly to 130 to <140 and maintain for at least 7 days; stop antihypertensives if SBP <130 (2a). Keep control smooth, avoiding peaks and large variability (2a). SBP >220: do NOT lower below 130 (Class 3: Harm); cautious, modest lowering to about 160-180 may be reasonable (2025 AHA/ACC HBP guideline, sec 5.3.9.1; 2022 AHA/ASA ICH guideline)
  • Preeclampsia/Eclampsia: SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 confirmed within 15 min → lower to <160/<110 within 30-60 min (Class 1). Labetalol 10-20 mg IV, then 20-80 mg every 10-30 min (max cumulative 300 mg) or 1-3 mg/min; OR hydralazine 5 mg IV/IM, then 5-10 mg every 20-40 min (max cumulative 20 mg); OR nifedipine IR 10-20 mg PO, repeat in 20 min, then 10-20 mg every 2-6 h (max 180 mg/day). Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis/treatment: 4-6 g IV over 20-30 min, then 1-2 g/h, continued 24 h after delivery or last seizure (monitor reflexes, respirations, urine output). ACE-I, ARB, and nitroprusside contraindicated. Definitive treatment is delivery; involve OB immediately (2025 AHA/ACC HBP guideline Table 23; ACOG PB 222)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Urgency vs Emergency: Only EMERGENCY needs ICU/IV meds. Urgency = oral meds over hours-days
  • Don't drop too fast: Cerebral autoregulation reset in chronic HTN. Rapid drop → stroke/MI
  • Ischemic stroke exception: Brain needs perfusion! Only lower if SBP >220 or giving tPA
  • PRES: Headache, confusion, seizures, vision loss + posterior white matter edema. Usually reversible
  • Transition to PO: Start long-acting oral agents before stopping IV to prevent rebound
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL hypertensive emergencies require ICU
  • Need for continuous IV infusion
  • Acute end-organ damage
  • Altered mental status
  • Arterial line needed
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • BP controlled on oral regimen ≥24hr
  • End-organ damage stabilized
  • Off IV medications
  • Patient educated on compliance
  • Close follow-up arranged (within 1 week)
  • Secondary causes evaluated if indicated
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

From Hypertension: Stroke, MI, aortic dissection, acute renal failure, retinopathy, heart failure

From Treatment: Hypotension, stroke from rapid BP drop, rebound HTN, cyanide toxicity (nitroprusside)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Nicardipine, 💊 Clevidipine, 💊 Labetalol, 💊 Esmolol, 💊 Hydralazine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Low eGFR, 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Urinalysis, 🔬 Anemia

5. COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA (CAP)

Outpatient • Inpatient • ICU Management
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Fever, cough (productive/dry), dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain. Exam: Tachypnea, rales/crackles, bronchial breath sounds, dullness, egophony

Alternate Presentations:

  • Elderly: Minimal fever, confusion/delirium, weakness, falls. May lack respiratory symptoms
  • Atypical Organisms: Dry cough, headache, myalgias, diarrhea (Legionella, Mycoplasma)
  • Aspiration: Witnessed event, right lower lobe/posterior segments, foul sputum
  • Immunocompromised: PCP, CMV, TB, fungi. The ATS/IDSA CAP guidelines (2019, 2025) exclude immunocompromised hosts (e.g., chemotherapy, transplant, advanced HIV, immunosuppressive drugs)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging: Chest imaging is required to confirm CAP. CXR (PA and lateral); lung ultrasound is an acceptable alternative where operators are trained and protocols are documented (ATS 2025; conditional, low). Practical: CT if CXR is negative and suspicion remains high

Cultures (2019 ATS/IDSA): Pretreatment blood cultures and sputum Gram stain/culture only if severe CAP (strong), empiric MRSA or P. aeruginosa coverage (strong), prior MRSA or P. aeruginosa infection (conditional), or hospitalization with IV antibiotics in the last 90 days (conditional). Not routine for nonsevere inpatients (conditional) or outpatients (strong). Intubated: send an endotracheal aspirate promptly.

Procalcitonin: Start antibiotics for clinically suspected, radiographically confirmed CAP regardless of the level (2019; strong, moderate).

Labs (Practical): CBC, BMP; ABG if hypoxic.

Urinary Antigens (2019): Pneumococcal and Legionella antigens only in severe CAP; Legionella also with an outbreak or recent travel (conditional, low). Severe CAP: also Legionella culture or NAAT of lower respiratory secretions (conditional, low).

Viral Testing: Influenza: rapid molecular test (NAAT, preferred over an antigen test) when influenza is circulating (2019; strong, moderate). Noninfluenza viral panels are not routine (ATS 2021, as summarized in ATS 2025); use judgment. MRSA nasal PCR when MRSA coverage is started or considered. Practical: SARS-CoV-2 testing; HIV screening.

Site of Care (2019 Q6): Use a validated rule plus clinical judgment; PSI preferred (strong, moderate) over CURB-65 (conditional, low).

  • PSI/PORT: Classes I-II: outpatient; III: outpatient or brief observation; IV-V: admit (Fine MJ et al, NEJM 1997;336:243-250). Admit regardless of score for inability to maintain oral intake, substance use, cognitive impairment, severe comorbidity, or impaired function (2019)
  • CURB-65: Confusion, BUN >19 mg/dL (urea >7 mmol/L), RR ≥30, SBP <90 or DBP ≤60, age ≥65. 30-day mortality: 0-1, 1.5%; 2, 9.2%; ≥3, 22% (Lim WS et al, Thorax 2003;58:377-382). 0-1: outpatient candidate; 2: consider admission; ≥3: admit. Not a tool for ICU triage
  • Severe CAP (2007 IDSA/ATS criteria, used by 2019 and 2025): 1 major criterion (septic shock needing vasopressors; respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation) OR ≥3 minor: RR ≥30, PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, BUN ≥20 mg/dL, WBC <4,000 (from infection), platelets <100,000, temp <36°C, hypotension needing aggressive fluids
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Outpatient (2019 Q8, Table 3; no MRSA or P. aeruginosa risk):

  • No comorbidities: Amoxicillin 1 g PO TID (strong, moderate) OR doxycycline 100 mg PO BID (conditional, low) OR, only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%, azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg daily or clarithromycin 500 mg BID (conditional, moderate)
  • Comorbidities (chronic heart, lung, liver, or renal disease; diabetes; alcoholism; malignancy; asplenia): amoxicillin-clavulanate (500/125 mg TID, 875/125 mg BID, or 2,000/125 mg BID) or cefpodoxime 200 mg BID or cefuroxime 500 mg BID, PLUS azithromycin or clarithromycin (strong, moderate) or doxycycline 100 mg BID (conditional, low); OR levofloxacin 750 mg daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily alone (strong, moderate)
  • Recent use of one class: choose another class. Weigh QT risk (macrolides), FDA fluoroquinolone warnings, and C. difficile history

Inpatient, Nonsevere (2019 Rec 9.1, Table 4; no MRSA or P. aeruginosa risk):

  • Standard (strong, high): β-lactam (ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5-3 g IV q6h, cefotaxime 1-2 g IV q8h, ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily, or ceftaroline 600 mg IV q12h) PLUS azithromycin 500 mg daily (IV or PO) or clarithromycin 500 mg PO BID
  • Alternative (strong, high): Levofloxacin 750 mg daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily alone. Practical: give PO when the patient can take it (high oral bioavailability)
  • Macrolide and fluoroquinolone both contraindicated: β-lactam PLUS doxycycline 100 mg BID (conditional, low). β-lactam monotherapy is not routine
  • Suspected aspiration: Do not routinely add anaerobic coverage unless lung abscess or empyema is suspected (conditional, very low)

Severe CAP (2019 Rec 9.2 and Q11, Table 4):

  • Standard: β-lactam (as above, e.g., ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily) PLUS azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (strong, moderate) OR β-lactam PLUS levofloxacin 750 mg or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily (strong, low). Fluoroquinolone monotherapy and β-lactam plus doxycycline are not recommended in severe CAP
  • MRSA coverage (prior respiratory MRSA isolation in the past year; or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics plus locally validated risk factors): add vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h, adjusted to levels, or linezolid 600 mg q12h (IV or PO). Send cultures and MRSA nasal PCR; a negative nasal PCR generally allows withholding or stopping MRSA coverage, especially in nonsevere CAP
  • P. aeruginosa coverage (prior respiratory isolation in the past year; or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics plus locally validated risk factors): add piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h, cefepime 2 g IV q8h, ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h, meropenem 1 g IV q8h, imipenem 500 mg IV q6h, or aztreonam 2 g IV q8h. Practical: the antipseudomonal agent replaces the standard β-lactam
  • Nonsevere CAP with only recent hospitalization and IV antibiotics: Culture (and nasal PCR) but withhold MRSA and P. aeruginosa coverage unless results are positive. Prior respiratory isolation: cover even if nonsevere
  • De-escalate at 48 h if cultures are negative and the patient is improving. Do not use the HCAP category (strong, moderate)

Duration: Treat until clinical stability (see pearl). 2019 ATS/IDSA: at least 5 days total (strong, moderate). ATS 2025, with IDSA agreement: outpatients and nonsevere inpatients who reach stability, <5 days with a 3-day minimum effective duration (conditional, low); severe CAP, ≥5 days (strong, low). Suspected or proven MRSA or P. aeruginosa: 7 days (2019). Longer for meningitis, endocarditis, empyema, abscess, or other deep-seated infection. Not stable by day 5: look for a resistant pathogen, a complication, or another diagnosis. IV to PO: same agent or same class (2019).

Corticosteroids: Nonsevere CAP: do not give (ATS 2025 strong; 2019 strong). Severe CAP without influenza: systemic corticosteroids suggested (ATS 2025; conditional, low); SCCM 2024 recommends them for severe bacterial CAP (strong, moderate). Best started within 24 h of meeting severe criteria. Regimen in the trial with the strongest results (CAPE COD, per ATS 2025): hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV for 4 or 7 days, then taper to 8 or 14 days total. Avoid with influenza, Aspergillus, uncontrolled diabetes, or recent GI bleeding. Refractory septic shock: follow Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

Influenza or Other Virus Positive: Influenza: oseltamivir for inpatients regardless of symptom duration (2019; strong, moderate); suggested for outpatients (conditional, low). Antibacterials: give in severe CAP (ATS 2025; IDSA agrees). Outpatients without comorbidities: suggest withholding (ATS 2025; IDSA agrees). Outpatients with comorbidities and nonsevere inpatients: ATS 2025 suggests empiric antibiotics; IDSA did not endorse these two recommendations and favors individualized decisions, including brief withholding in nonsevere illness. Influenza with no bacterial evidence (including low procalcitonin) and early stability: consider stopping antibiotics at 48-72 h (2019).

Supportive (Practical): O₂ to SpO₂ ≥90%, IV fluids for sepsis, VTE prophylaxis

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Legionella clues: Hyponatremia, elevated LFTs, GI symptoms, relative bradycardia. Test with urinary antigen, plus culture or NAAT of respiratory secretions in severe CAP (2019). No ATS/IDSA fixed duration; ATS 2025 lists suspected Legionella as a reason to avoid courses shorter than 5 days
  • PCP Pneumonia: Subacute, dry cough, exertional dyspnea in HIV. Bilateral interstitial infiltrates; LDH often elevated (nonspecific). TMP-SMX for 21 days; add prednisone 40 mg BID days 1-5, 40 mg daily days 6-10, 20 mg daily days 11-21 if room-air PaO₂ <70 mmHg or A-a gradient ≥35 mmHg, ideally within 72 h (HHS adult OI guidelines). See PCP card
  • Clinical stability (ATS 2025 Table 6): Temp ≤37.8°C, HR <100, RR <24, SBP ≥90, SpO₂ ≥90% or PaO₂ ≥60 mmHg on room air or baseline O₂, normal mentation; plus able to eat (2019). Guides IV-to-PO switch, discharge, and duration
  • Macrolide resistance: US S. pneumoniae macrolide resistance >30%, mostly high-level (2019). Outpatient macrolide monotherapy only where local resistance is <25%; never macrolide monotherapy for inpatients (pair with a β-lactam, or use a respiratory fluoroquinolone)
  • Vaccines (CDC, page updated Feb 25, 2026): PCV-naive adults ≥50 or unknown history: PCV20 or PCV21 alone, OR PCV15 followed by PPSV23 1 year later (8 weeks may be considered with immunocompromise, cochlear implant, or CSF leak). ACIP lowered the routine age from 65 to 50 in October 2024. Adults 19-49 with risk conditions: CDC risk-based schedule
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Septic shock needing vasopressors or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation: direct ICU admission (2019; strong, low)
  • Otherwise ≥3 minor criteria (see Severe CAP) plus clinical judgment for ICU, step-down, or telemetry (2019; conditional, low)
  • Do not set level of care by CURB-65 or PSI (built for mortality and site of care, not ICU need)
  • Ward patients who deteriorate: ward-to-ICU transfer carries higher mortality than direct ICU admission (2019)
  • Practical: rising O₂ need, high-flow nasal cannula, or NIV
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Clinically stable by ATS 2025 Table 6 criteria (see pearl)
  • Able to eat and take oral antibiotics; IV to PO with the same agent or class (2019)
  • Remaining antibiotic days completed at home (see Duration)
  • Reliable follow-up and a return plan, especially with short courses (ATS 2025)
  • Vaccination addressed (see Vaccines)
  • No routine follow-up chest imaging if symptoms resolve within 5-7 days (2019; conditional, low); check lung cancer screening eligibility
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Early: Respiratory failure, sepsis/septic shock, parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess

Late: Organizing pneumonia, fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia (consider malignancy)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Azithromycin, 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Levofloxacin, 💊 Amoxicillin, 💊 Amoxicillin-Clavulanate, 💊 Doxycycline, 💊 Linezolid, 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Cefepime, 💊 Oseltamivir, 💊 Hydrocortisone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated A-a Gradient, 🔬 Blood Cultures

6. COPD EXACERBATION

AECOPD • Acute on Chronic
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Increased dyspnea, cough, sputum production/purulence beyond baseline. Wheezing, accessory muscle use, pursed-lip breathing

Definition (GOLD 2027): Worsening dyspnea and/or cough and sputum over up to 14 days, which may come with tachypnea and/or tachycardia

Severity, Rome classification (GOLD 2027 Figure 4.2): Moderate = at least 3 of 5: dyspnea VAS ≥5 (0-10 scale), respiratory rate ≥24/min, heart rate ≥95/min, resting SaO2 <92% on usual oxygen and/or a fall of >3%, CRP ≥10 mg/L. Mild = below these thresholds. Severe = moderate plus, on ABG, PaO2 ≤60 mmHg and/or hypercapnic acidosis (PaCO2 >45 mmHg and pH <7.35)

Alternate Presentations:

  • Hypercapnic Encephalopathy: Confusion, asterixis, somnolence from CO2 retention
  • Right Heart Failure: Peripheral edema, JVD from cor pulmonale
  • Elderly: Fatigue, decreased functional status, falls
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: ABG in more severe cases; a venous gas can help in less severe ones (GOLD 2027). CBC with eosinophil count, BMP, CRP (part of the Rome severity score; GOLD 2027). Troponin and BNP: GOLD 2027 suggests they may be checked routinely (weak evidence), because cardiovascular events rise during and after exacerbations; abnormal values need a cardiac workup. Sputum culture with frequent exacerbations, severe airflow obstruction, or mechanical ventilation (GOLD 2027). Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic protocols: not recommended (GOLD 2027; conflicting data). Vitamin D: check hospitalized patients for severe deficiency (<10 ng/mL) and replace if found (GOLD 2027)

Imaging: CXR (r/o pneumonia, PTX, CHF), consider CT if recurrent or PE concern

ECG: Evaluate for MI, arrhythmia, right heart strain

Calculations: A-a gradient, FiO2 requirements

Triggers (GOLD 2027): Mainly respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, RSV); also bacteria and environmental exposures (air pollution, heat or cold, wildfire smoke). Practical: inhaler nonadherence

Mimics or aggravators to exclude (GOLD 2027): Pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, acute heart failure, myocardial infarction or arrhythmia, pneumothorax

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Bronchodilators:

  • Initial (GOLD 2027, Evidence C): Short-acting beta-agonist with or without a short-acting anticholinergic (albuterol with or without ipratropium). Nebulizer: one dose every hour for 2-3 doses, then every 2-4 hours by response (pMDI: 1-2 puffs on the same schedule). Avoid high SABA doses; use air-driven, not oxygen-driven, nebulizers
  • Doses: Albuterol 2.5 mg and ipratropium 0.5 mg per nebulized dose, or one albuterol-ipratropium vial (2.5 mg + 0.5 mg). That vial's label: 4 times daily plus up to 2 extra doses per day; GOLD's hourly start can exceed this, so step down to every 2-4 hours as soon as the response allows (Practical)
  • Long-acting bronchodilators: Continue during the exacerbation, or start as soon as possible before discharge (GOLD 2027)
  • Not recommended: IV methylxanthines (theophylline, aminophylline): side effects (GOLD 2027)

Systemic Corticosteroids:

  • Dose: Prednisone 40 mg PO daily for 5 days (GOLD 2027; Evidence A). Oral is as effective as IV. If unable to take PO: IV methylprednisolone at an equivalent dose (Practical: methylprednisolone 32 mg = prednisone 40 mg; 40 mg IV daily is within the Solu-Medrol label's 10-40 mg initial range). Nebulized budesonide may be an alternative in some patients (GOLD 2027)
  • Harms: Even short bursts are linked to pneumonia, sepsis and death, and longer courses to more pneumonia and mortality (observational); give only for significant exacerbations (GOLD 2027). Withholding steroids when eosinophils are low (STARR2) was tested in primary care and is not validated in hospitalized patients (GOLD 2027)

Antibiotics (GOLD 2027, Evidence A): Give if (1) sputum purulence is increased plus at least one of more dyspnea, fever, or more sputum volume; (2) a prior exacerbation had a positive sputum culture; or (3) the patient is on NIV or invasive ventilation

  • Choice (GOLD 2027): By local resistance: amoxicillin-clavulanate, a macrolide, or a tetracycline; a quinolone in selected patients. Oral or IV by the patient's condition and the drug's pharmacokinetics. Duration 5 days (GOLD 2027 Figure 4.7, Evidence B; the text also gives 5-7 days)
  • Doses (labels): Azithromycin 500 mg PO daily for 3 days, OR 500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg daily on days 2-5 (Zithromax label, acute bacterial exacerbation of COPD). Doxycycline 100 mg PO every 12 hours (label: 200 mg on day 1, given as 100 mg every 12 hours)
  • Pseudomonas or resistant organisms: With frequent exacerbations, severe airflow obstruction, or mechanical ventilation, culture sputum or airway samples, because gram-negative organisms such as Pseudomonas may not respond to the usual agents (GOLD 2027). If covering Pseudomonas, use an antipseudomonal agent chosen by culture and local antibiogram; ceftriaxone is not one (Practical)

Oxygen Therapy: Controlled oxygen if hypoxemic (GOLD 2027). Target SpO2 88-92% (BTS 2017, non-US; GOLD 2027 gives no number); recheck blood gases after changes. When to aim higher, and delivery devices: Condition 50. SpO2 is less accurate in darker skin (GOLD 2027)

Ventilatory Support:

  • Order (GOLD 2027 Figure 4.7, Evidence A): High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNT) first for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure; NIV for hypercapnic respiratory failure or when HFNT fails, unless absolutely contraindicated
  • NIV: Recommended over standard oxygen for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (ATS 2026, strong, moderate certainty). Start if at least one (GOLD 2027 Figure 4.9): PaCO2 ≥45 mmHg with pH ≤7.35; severe dyspnea with signs of muscle fatigue or more work of breathing; persistent hypoxemia despite oxygen. Hypercapnia without acidosis: NIV not suggested (ERS/ATS 2017, conditional). No lower pH limit for a trial, but failure is likelier as pH falls (ERS/ATS 2017). Stop without weaning once 4 hours of unassisted breathing are tolerated (GOLD 2027). Settings and the HFNC option in mild acidemia (ATS 2026): Condition 50
  • Intubation (GOLD 2027 Figure 4.10): NIV failure or intolerance of HFNT and/or NIV; persistent life-threatening hypoxemia despite HFNT or NIV; after respiratory or cardiac arrest; reduced consciousness or agitation not controlled by sedation; massive aspiration or persistent vomiting; inability to clear secretions; severe hemodynamic instability despite fluids and vasoactive drugs; severe ventricular or supraventricular arrhythmias. Respiratory stimulants: not recommended (GOLD 2027)

Adjuncts (GOLD 2027): VTE prophylaxis for hospitalized patients (subcutaneous heparin or LMWH; Condition 295); fluid balance, with diuretics if indicated; treat heart failure, arrhythmia or PE if present; N-acetylcysteine may help patients who cannot clear secretions; smoking cessation

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • O2-induced hypercapnia: High O2 in COPD → worsens V/Q mismatch and Haldane effect → CO2 retention. Keep SpO2 88-92% (BTS 2017, non-US)
  • NIV works: Success in 80-85% in RCTs; reduces intubation and mortality (GOLD 2027). Pooled vs standard oxygen in acute hypercapnic failure, 42 RCTs, mostly COPD: mortality RR 0.47, intubation RR 0.43 (ATS 2026). Start early
  • Steroid duration: REDUCE trial showed 5 days = 14 days for outcomes. Don't give longer courses
  • Antibiotics: Strongest benefit in exacerbations needing ICU care; less clear on the ward and in outpatients. Started in the first 2 hospital days, they were linked to better outcomes (retrospective) (GOLD 2027)
  • Home oxygen (GOLD 2027): PaO2 ≤55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤88%, confirmed twice over 3 weeks; or PaO2 55-60 mmHg or SaO2 88% with pulmonary hypertension, edema suggesting heart failure, or hematocrit >55%. Reassess after recovery: gases at later follow-up predict long-term need better than values at discharge
  • Cardiovascular risk (new in GOLD 2027): MI, heart failure, arrhythmia and stroke become more likely during an exacerbation and stay elevated for up to 1 year. No routine preventive drug (e.g., aspirin); beta-blockers and statins per their cardiovascular indication
  • Prevention (GOLD 2027): Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, RSV), smoking cessation, LABA+LAMA+ICS when indicated, pulmonary rehabilitation. Test once for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency if never tested (GOLD 2027; A1F 2016): Condition 256
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Persistent or worsening hypoxemia and/or hypercapnia despite ventilatory support (GOLD 2027 Figure 4.4)
  • Worsening mental status: confusion, lethargy, coma (GOLD 2027)
  • Need for invasive mechanical ventilation (GOLD 2027)
  • Hemodynamic instability needing vasopressors; cardiac arrhythmias (GOLD 2027)
  • Starting NIV: ICU or intermediate care unit with rapid access to intubation (ATS 2026; Condition 50)
  • Life-threatening comorbidity, e.g., MI or sepsis (Practical)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Full review of clinical and laboratory data (GOLD 2027 Figure 4.11)
  • Maintenance: long-acting bronchodilators; LABA+LAMA+ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300/µL, or ≥100/µL if already on LABA+LAMA (GOLD 2027 Figures 3.9, 4.11)
  • Inhaler technique rechecked; patient knows how steroids and antibiotics will stop (GOLD 2027)
  • Need for continuing oxygen assessed; written management plan (GOLD 2027)
  • Follow-up: early, within 4 weeks; late, at 12-16 weeks; comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease followed up (GOLD 2027). Pulmonary rehabilitation started within 4 weeks of discharge (GOLD 2027)
  • Practical: back to baseline dyspnea and function; SABA needed no more than every 4 hours; SpO2 at goal on room air or home oxygen; pH normal if acidotic on admission
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Respiratory failure requiring intubation, pneumothorax (bullous disease), pneumonia, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, heart failure, stroke (GOLD 2027), venous thromboembolism (PE in up to 5.9% of hospitalized patients; GOLD 2027)

Chronic: Cor pulmonale, progressive lung function decline, long-term oxygen need, recurrent exacerbations

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Albuterol, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Azithromycin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated PaCO2, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
