7. ASTHMA EXACERBATION

Acute Bronchospasm • Status Asthmaticus
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Dyspnea, wheezing, chest tightness, cough, accessory muscle use, prolonged expiration

Alternate Presentations:

  • Silent Chest: Severe obstruction with minimal air movement; life-threatening
  • Poor Perceivers: Some patients (especially after near-fatal asthma; more often men) feel little dyspnea despite a large fall in lung function. Measure PEF or FEV1 (GINA 2026)
  • Cough-Predominant: Consider pertussis when cough dominates an atypical exacerbation (GINA 2026)
  • Children: May present with only cough or difficulty feeding

Red Flags for Fatal or Near-Fatal Asthma (GINA 2026 Box 9-1): Prior intubation for asthma; hospitalization or multiple ED visits in the past year; current or recent OCS; not using ICS; poor ICS adherence or no written action plan; SABA over-use (average >1 canister per month) or nebulized SABA; psychiatric disease or psychosocial problems; food allergy or anaphylaxis; poor perception of airflow limitation; comorbid pneumonia, diabetes, or arrhythmia

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Immediate: SpO2, RR, pulse, ability to speak, accessory muscle use, air entry, mental status; ask about anaphylaxis features, red flags (above), and treatment already taken. Measure PEF or FEV1 before treatment if this does not delay it, then at 1 hour and until a plateau (GINA 2026: strongly recommended, except in life-threatening presentations)

Exclude Mimics and Complications: Pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, pneumonia, anaphylaxis, inducible laryngeal obstruction, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, inhaled foreign body, DKA (GINA 2026)

Blood Gas (not routine): If PEF or FEV1 <50% predicted, no response to initial treatment, or deteriorating; keep controlled O2 on while sampling. PaCO2 is usually <40 mmHg; PaO2 <60 mmHg with normal or rising PaCO2 (especially >45 mmHg) means respiratory failure (GINA 2026). Practical: a VBG is acceptable to screen PCO2

Chest X-ray (not routine): If a complicating or alternative process is suspected (especially in older patients), or if not responding and a pneumothorax could be missed clinically (GINA 2026)

Severity (GINA 2026 Box 9-6; adults and children ≥6 y):

  • Mild (all of): Talks in sentences, can lie down; RR normal or mildly increased; no or mild accessory muscle use and expiratory wheeze; SpO2 (room air) ≥94%; PEF or FEV1 >70% personal best or predicted
  • Moderate: Talks in phrases, prefers sitting, not agitated; RR increased; accessory muscle use; expiratory wheeze; reduced air entry; SpO2 (room air) ≥92%; PEF or FEV1 50-70%
  • Severe (any of): Unable to speak, drink, or lie down; SpO2 (room air) <92%; RR >30/min; accessory muscle use; silent or quiet chest; PEF or FEV1 <50%
  • Life-threatening: Drowsiness, confusion, cyanosis, or silent chest. Practical: bradycardia or hypotension signals impending arrest
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Anaphylaxis Features: Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM, anterolateral thigh, FIRST, then bronchodilators (GINA 2026). Label: max 0.5 mg per injection; may repeat every 5-10 min (Adrenalin label)

Bronchodilators (GINA 2026 Box 9-6; albuterol 100 mcg/puff, ipratropium 20 mcg/puff; shake before each puff):

  • Mild: Albuterol 4 puffs by pMDI + spacer; reassess, repeat once after 30-60 min if needed. GINA alternative: budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg 2 puffs (US: off-label; the Symbicort label says it is not for relief of acute symptoms)
  • Moderate: Albuterol 4-6 puffs + ipratropium 4 puffs by pMDI + spacer, OR albuterol 2.5 mg + ipratropium 0.25 mg nebulized. If needed, up to 3 times, 20-30 min apart
  • Severe: Albuterol 6-10 puffs + ipratropium 4 puffs by pMDI + spacer, OR albuterol 5 mg + ipratropium 0.25 mg nebulized. If needed, up to 3 times, 20-30 min apart. Life-threatening: nebulized
  • Delivery: pMDI + spacer works as well as a nebulizer (Evidence A; life-threatening asthma not studied) and avoids aerosol spread of viral infection
  • SABA toxicity: Tachycardia, tremor, hypokalemia, arrhythmias, lactic acidosis and compensatory hyperventilation can mimic worsening asthma and prompt still more SABA. Reassess before each extra dose (GINA 2026)
  • Dose note: GINA 2026 doses are more conservative than older regimens because of evidence of over-treatment; trials of continuous vs intermittent nebulization conflict

Systemic Corticosteroids (all but the mildest; within 1 hour of arrival; GINA 2026, Evidence A):

  • Prednisone or prednisolone: 40-50 mg PO once daily (morning) for 5-7 days total (GINA 2026 Box 9-7). 5- and 7-day courses work as well as 10- and 14-day courses (Evidence B). PO is as effective as IV and is preferred
  • IV only if too dyspneic to swallow, vomiting, or on NIV or intubated: methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily (about prednisone 50 mg; within the label's 10-40 mg initial range) or hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV in divided doses (GINA 2026). IM offers no benefit over PO
  • No taper needed for courses under 2 weeks (GINA 2026 Box 9-2; Evidence B)

Oxygen: Give if SpO2 <92%; titrate by oximetry to SpO2 92-95%, no higher than 96% in adults (GINA 2026). Controlled O2 is associated with lower mortality than 100% O2 in hospitalized patients (Evidence A). Life-threatening: start 100% by non-rebreather, then titrate. Do not withhold O2 if oximetry is unavailable. Oximetry may overestimate SpO2 in dark skin; targets are lower at altitude

Severe, Not Responding to Initial Treatment:

  • Magnesium sulfate: 2 g IV over 20 min, single dose, if no response to initial treatment and persistent hypoxemia; reduces admissions (Evidence A). Not routine; nebulized magnesium gives no benefit (GINA 2026)
  • Terbutaline: 0.25 mg SC (lateral deltoid); may repeat once after 15-30 min; max 0.5 mg in 4 h (FDA label; age ≥12; boxed warning against prolonged tocolysis). GINA 2026 does not address SC terbutaline; it does not support routine IV beta2-agonists (Evidence A)
  • Epinephrine: Only for concurrent anaphylaxis (above); not routinely indicated otherwise (GINA 2026)
  • Heliox: No role in routine care (Evidence B); may be considered if not responding to standard therapy (GINA 2026)
  • NIV: Weak evidence; GINA makes no recommendation. If tried, monitor closely; not in agitated patients; never sedate to allow NIV (Evidence D)
  • If intubated: Ventilator settings for obstructive disease (lower respiratory rate and shorter inspiratory time to lengthen expiration; measure auto-PEEP and plateau pressure; hypotension after intubation may be from hyperinflation): Condition 50 (Practical)

Do NOT Give: Sedatives (must be avoided; linked to avoidable asthma deaths); antibiotics unless strong evidence of lung infection (e.g., fever or purulent sputum, or radiographic pneumonia); IV aminophylline or theophylline (poor efficacy and safety) (GINA 2026)

Pregnancy: Treat exacerbations aggressively with SABA, oxygen, and early systemic corticosteroids to avoid fetal hypoxia (GINA 2026)

Consider Admission (GINA 2026 Box 9-6): Not improving, or any of: SpO2 <92% on room air; SABA still needed more often than every 1-2 h; dyspnea persisting 4-6 h after systemic corticosteroids; factors affecting adherence or follow-up; red flags (above). Clinical status and lung function at 1 hour predict admission better than status on arrival

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Silent chest = BAD: Means severe obstruction with minimal air movement. This is life-threatening!
  • Ipratropium in asthma: Add to SABA for moderate-severe exacerbations only, in the first 1-2 hours (fewer admissions, Evidence A); no benefit after that (GINA 2026)
  • Magnesium: Calcium antagonism relaxes airway smooth muscle (Practical). One 2 g IV dose for nonresponders with persistent hypoxemia reduces admissions, including adults with FEV1 <25-30% (GINA 2026, Evidence A)
  • Normal PCO2 is concerning: PaCO2 is usually <40 mmHg in an exacerbation. Normal or high CO2 = respiratory fatigue
  • Steroid timing: OCS need at least 4 hours to work. Give within 1 hour of arrival (GINA 2026)
  • SABA can look like asthma: Lactic acidosis from high-dose SABA drives hyperventilation that is easily read as worsening asthma (GINA 2026)
  • Discharge medication: Never SABA alone. Every patient leaves on ICS-containing treatment, preferably MART with budesonide-formoterol (see Discharge Criteria)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Life-threatening features: drowsiness, confusion, cyanosis, silent chest (GINA 2026)
  • Deteriorating despite intensive bronchodilator and corticosteroid treatment (GINA 2026)
  • Respiratory failure: PaO2 <60 mmHg with normal or rising PaCO2 (especially >45 mmHg) (GINA 2026)
  • Need for intubation, or an NIV trial (Practical)
  • Hemodynamic instability or arrhythmia (Practical)
  • Ongoing need for continuous or near-continuous nebulization (Practical)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Symptoms and signs meet "mild" criteria for at least 1-2 hours after the last albuterol dose (GINA 2026 Box 9-6)
  • SpO2 ≥92% on room air
  • PEF or FEV1 >70% personal best or predicted
  • Adequate resources at home; no barrier to adherence or follow-up
  • ICS for all (SABA-only is not recommended). Preferred: MART with budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, 2 inhalations twice daily plus 1 as needed, max 12 inhalations/day (Step 4; GINA 2026 Box 4-8A, Box 9-7). On ICS or ICS-LABA with SABA reliever: increase the ICS dose for 2-4 weeks. Budesonide-formoterol as reliever is off-label in the US (Symbicort label)
  • Prednisone or prednisolone 40-50 mg daily to complete 5-7 days
  • Inhaler technique and adherence checked; written asthma action plan given
  • Follow-up in 2-7 days. Refer for expert advice if ICU was needed, or if ≥1 exacerbation needing OCS or urgent care in the past 12 months (GINA 2026 Box 9-7)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Status asthmaticus, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, cardiac arrest

Iatrogenic: SABA toxicity (hypokalemia, tremor, tachycardia, arrhythmias, lactic acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation); systemic corticosteroids (hyperglycemia, sleep disturbance, mood change; increased risk of sepsis and thromboembolism even after a short course) (GINA 2026)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Albuterol, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Magnesium, 💊 Ipratropium, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Hydrocortisone, 💊 Epinephrine, 💊 Budesonide-Formoterol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated PaCO2, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Hypokalemia, 🔬 Hypomagnesemia
↑ Back to Table of Contents

8. PULMONARY EMBOLISM (PE)

VTE • AHA/ACC Acute PE Clinical Categories A-E (2026 guideline)
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, hemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling

Severity: AHA/ACC Acute PE Clinical Categories (2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline, Figure 2; replaces massive/submassive):

  • A, subclinical: Incidental and asymptomatic (e.g., found on a staging CT)
  • B, symptomatic, low severity score (PESI ≤85, sPESI 0, or Bova ≤4): B1 subsegmental (single or multiple); B2 non-subsegmental
  • C, symptomatic, elevated severity score (PESI >85, sPESI ≥1, or Bova >4): C1 normal RV and normal biomarkers; C2 abnormal RV or ≥1 abnormal biomarker; C3 abnormal RV and ≥1 abnormal biomarker
  • D, incipient cardiopulmonary failure: D1 transient hypotension (SBP <90 or drop >40 mmHg lasting <15 min or responding to IV fluids); D2 normotensive shock (any of: lactate >2 mmol/L, AKI, urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h, mental status change, cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m², MAP <60 mmHg, increased SCAI stage or CPES score)
  • E, cardiopulmonary failure: E1 recurrent or persistent hypotension with cardiogenic shock; E2 refractory cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest
  • Respiratory modifier R (e.g., C3R): with C, SpO₂ <90%, RR ≥30, or any supplemental O₂; with D, >6 L nasal cannula or nonrebreather; with E, hypoxemic respiratory or ventilatory failure
  • Chronic course: Progressive dyspnea months after PE suggests post-PE CTEPD; may be misdiagnosed as heart failure
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Calculate Pre-test Probability: Wells score (calculator below), revised Geneva, or gestalt, after a targeted history and exam for risk factors (COR 1, LOE A). PERC only when gestalt probability is <15% (e.g., Wells <2); all 8 criteria negative means no further testing (2026 AHA/ACC PE, Table 3)

D-dimer (low or intermediate probability, <50%, only): Valid only if not already anticoagulated. Age-adjusted threshold (age × 10 µg/L FEU, validated for age >50) excludes PE without imaging (COR 2a, LOE B-R). Alternative: YEARS algorithm, threshold 1000 µg/L if no YEARS item, 500 µg/L if ≥1 (clinical signs of DVT, hemoptysis, PE most likely diagnosis) (COR 2a, LOE B-R). Pregnancy: pregnancy-adapted YEARS (COR 2b, LOE B-NR). Image if probability is high (>50%) or D-dimer exceeds the threshold (COR 1, LOE A).

Risk Labs After Diagnosis: Troponin and/or BNP in Category C (COR 1, LOE B-NR); lactate in Categories C-E (COR 1, LOE B-NR). Practical: ABG if hypoxemic (hypoxemia, widened A-a gradient).

Imaging:

  • CTPA (CT Pulmonary Angiography): Preferred over V/Q to confirm PE (COR 1, LOE B-R). A positive CTPA or high-probability V/Q is diagnostic (COR 1, LOE A). Report the numerical RV/LV ratio (COR 1, LOE B-R)
  • V/Q Scan: If CTPA is not possible (e.g., contrast contraindication), V/Q over MR angiography (COR 2a, LOE B-R); SPECT over planar (COR 2a, LOE B-R)
  • Pregnancy: With symptoms, YEARS findings suggesting PE, and a normal chest x-ray, low-dose CTPA is reasonable over low-dose perfusion scan (COR 2a, LOE B-NR)
  • Lower Extremity Duplex US: Only if signs of DVT or the result will change management (COR 2b, LOE B-NR); not useful after a negative CTPA (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE B-NR)
  • Echo: Not for confirming or excluding PE (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE B-NR). Use for RV risk stratification in Categories C-D (COR 1, LOE A), preferred over CT (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). Report RV/LV end-diastolic ratio, RV end-diastolic diameter, TAPSE (<1.7 cm abnormal), RV systolic pressure, McConnell's sign (RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing), tricuspid velocity, septal motion, IVC collapse (COR 1, LOE B-NR)

ECG (Practical; not addressed by the 2026 AHA/ACC guideline): Sinus tachycardia most common. Classic S1Q3T3 pattern uncommon. Right heart strain pattern may be present

Risk Stratification After Diagnosis (2026 AHA/ACC PE, Section 3.2): Assign Category A-E (see above). Categories A-B: Hestia, PESI, or sPESI to confirm low risk (COR 1, LOE B-R). Hemodynamically stable C-D: a validated PE-specific score (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). RV imaging in C-D (COR 1, LOE A). D2: evaluate for normotensive shock (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). C3 with MAP <80 mmHg may need escalation (COR 2a, LOE B-NR).

sPESI (1 point each; 0 = low risk):

  • Age >80 years
  • Cancer
  • Chronic cardiopulmonary disease (HF or chronic lung disease)
  • HR ≥110 bpm
  • SBP <100 mmHg
  • SaO₂ <90%

Hestia (any "yes" = not suitable for outpatient care): Hemodynamically unstable; thrombolysis or embolectomy needed; active bleeding or high bleeding risk; O₂ needed >24 h to keep SpO₂ >90%; PE diagnosed on anticoagulation; IV pain medication needed >24 h; medical or social reason for admission >24 h; CrCl <30 mL/min; severe liver impairment; pregnancy; history of HIT.

Outpatient treatment is reasonable for selected Category A-B patients identified with a decision tool such as Hestia or sPESI (COR 2a, LOE B-R), with immediate access to the anticoagulant and rapid, reliable follow-up (COR 2a, LOE B-R). Individual-patient meta-analysis of outpatient care: 30-day mortality 0.30%, recurrent VTE 0.57%, major bleeding 0.45%.

🧮 Wells Score for PE
Use: Pre-test probability of PE. Score ≤4 = PE unlikely (consider D-dimer), >4 = PE likely (proceed to CTPA).
🧮 PERC Rule (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria)
Use: Only when gestalt pretest probability is <15% (e.g., Wells <2). If ALL criteria are ABSENT (unchecked), PE is ruled out without D-dimer (2026 AHA/ACC PE, Table 3).

Check if ANY of these are PRESENT:

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Anticoagulation (2026 AHA/ACC PE, Section 4.2.1): Start in all patients without an absolute contraindication (COR 1, LOE B-R); if Category C2 or higher is suspected and bleeding risk is low, start while awaiting imaging (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). Categories A-B: DOAC (COR 1). C1-E1 needing parenteral therapy: LMWH over UFH (COR 1, LOE B-R). E2: LMWH or UFH (COR 1). Oral therapy: DOAC over VKA (COR 1, LOE B-R).

  • Enoxaparin (LMWH): 1 mg/kg subQ q12h or 1.5 mg/kg subQ once daily; CrCl <30: 1 mg/kg subQ once daily (FDA label). CrCl <30: anti-Xa monitoring is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE C-LD); when monitored, draw a peak level 3-5 h after a dose once ≥3 doses are given (COR 1, LOE C-LD). Routine anti-Xa monitoring is not indicated (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE A). BMI >40: a reduced dose may be reasonable (COR 2b, LOE B-NR). Preferred over UFH when an endovascular procedure is likely (COR 2a, LOE C-LD)
  • Unfractionated Heparin: FDA label: 5,000 units IV bolus, then 20,000-40,000 units/24 h continuous infusion, adjusted to coagulation tests. Common practice: weight-based nomogram, 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/h, titrated to aPTT or anti-Xa (Raschke RA et al, Ann Intern Med 1993;119:874-881). Practical: chosen when rapid reversal may be needed
  • Fondaparinux: SubQ once daily: <50 kg 5 mg; 50-100 kg 7.5 mg; >100 kg 10 mg. Contraindicated if CrCl <30 (FDA label)
  • DOACs: Rivaroxaban or apixaban can be started immediately without a parenteral lead-in. Dabigatran and edoxaban start only after 5-10 days of parenteral anticoagulation (FDA labels)
    • Rivaroxaban: 15 mg PO BID with food × 21 days, then 20 mg PO daily with food; avoid if CrCl <15 (FDA label)
    • Apixaban: 10 mg PO BID × 7 days, then 5 mg PO BID (FDA label)
    • ⚠️ The initial high-dose phase is mandatory; starting at the maintenance dose is inadequate

Special Populations (Section 4.2.1):

  • Pregnancy: LMWH or UFH (COR 1, LOE C-LD). DOACs and warfarin are potentially harmful (COR 3: Harm, LOE C-LD)
  • Breastfeeding: LMWH, UFH, or warfarin over a DOAC (COR 1, LOE C-LD)
  • Thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome: VKA over DOAC (COR 1, LOE A)
  • CKD: Stage 2-3: DOAC over VKA (COR 1, LOE A). Stage 4-5 or hemodialysis: whether apixaban is better than VKA is uncertain (COR 2b, LOE B-NR)
  • Chronic liver disease: DOAC over VKA is reasonable in Child-Pugh A (COR 2a, LOE C-LD), may be reasonable in B (COR 2b, LOE C-LD), and is not recommended in C (COR 3: Harm, LOE C-LD)
  • Obesity (BMI >30): DOAC over VKA is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-NR)

Systemic Thrombolysis by Category (2026 AHA/ACC PE, Section 4.4.1, Table 7):

  • E1-E2 with acceptable bleeding risk: reasonable (COR 2a, LOE C-LD)
  • D1-D2: may be considered (COR 2b, LOE C-LD). C3: benefit uncertain (COR 2b, LOE C-LD)
  • A1-C2: do not use; increases major bleeding and ICH (COR 3: Harm, LOE B-R)
  • Alteplase (tPA): 100 mg IV over 2 hours (FDA label). Lower dose (25-50 mg) may be considered to reduce bleeding (COR 2b, LOE C-LD). Start parenteral anticoagulation near the end of or right after the infusion, once aPTT or thrombin time is ≤2× normal (FDA label). Tenecteplase is not FDA approved for PE
  • Contraindications (FDA label): Active internal bleeding; recent stroke; intracranial or intraspinal surgery or serious head trauma within 3 months; intracranial conditions that raise bleeding risk (some neoplasms, AVMs, aneurysms); bleeding diathesis; current severe uncontrolled hypertension
  • Risk: Severe bleeding about 9.9% and ICH about 1.7% with systemic thrombolysis (meta-analysis cited in the 2026 AHA/ACC guideline)

Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis (CDL), Mechanical Thrombectomy (MT), Surgery (Sections 4.4.2-4.4.4, Table 7): E1: CDL (COR 2a, LOE C-LD) or MT (COR 2a, LOE B-NR) reasonable. D1-D2: CDL or MT may be considered (COR 2b, LOE B-NR). C2-C3: benefit unclear (COR 2b, LOE C-LD). A-C1: no benefit (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE C-EO). CDL vs MT in C2-D2: neither preferred (COR 2b, LOE B-R). D1-E1: CDL (COR 2b, LOE C-LD) or MT (COR 2b, LOE B-NR) may be considered over systemic thrombolysis to reduce major bleeding. CDL alteplase below 5 mg per pulmonary artery is not recommended over 5-10 mg (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE B-NR). Surgical embolectomy: E1 reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-NR); D1-D2 may be considered (COR 2b, LOE C-LD); not for A-C3 (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE C-EO) or for E2 not on mechanical circulatory support (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE B-NR). Clot-in-transit in C3-E2: advanced therapy over anticoagulation alone is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). VA-ECMO for E2 (COR 2a, LOE B-NR); continue anticoagulation on VA-ECMO (COR 1, LOE B-NR). PE response team (PERT) for Categories C-E (COR 1, LOE B-NR).

IVC Filter (Section 4.3): Use when anticoagulation cannot be tolerated (COR 2a, LOE B-R); retrievable over permanent (COR 1, LOE B-R); retrieve as soon as PE risk has fallen and anticoagulation is tolerated (COR 1, LOE C-LD), with a structured follow-up program (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). Recurrent PE despite optimal anticoagulation: may be considered (COR 2b, LOE C-LD). Routine filter in anticoagulated patients: harmful (COR 3: Harm, LOE A).

Hemodynamic and Respiratory Support (Sections 4.2.2-4.2.3): Shock (D2-E2): vasopressors and/or inotropes (COR 1, LOE C-LD). Norepinephrine first; at higher norepinephrine doses add a second vasopressor (vasopressin or phenylephrine) rather than escalating further; add dobutamine for persistently low output; dobutamine may be the first agent in D2 normotensive shock. Fluids: only if reduced preload is suspected in D1-D2 (COR 2b, LOE C-LD), as small boluses (≤500 mL); larger volumes can worsen RV function. Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators may be considered in C2-E (COR 2b, LOE B-R). Moderate-severe hypoxia: heated high-flow nasal cannula over standard nasal cannula (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). Avoid deep sedation and intubation unless clinically indicated (COR 3: Harm, LOE C-LD); have vasopressors, inotropes, and VA-ECMO ready before induction (COR 1, LOE C-LD).

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • PERC Rule: Apply only when gestalt pretest probability is <15% (e.g., Wells <2). If all 8 criteria are negative (age <50, HR <100, SpO2 ≥95%, no hemoptysis, no estrogen, no prior VTE, no surgery or trauma requiring hospitalization within 4 weeks, no unilateral leg swelling) → PE excluded, no D-dimer needed
  • D-dimer pitfalls: Elevated in many conditions (infection, cancer, pregnancy, older age). Use only to rule OUT PE when pretest probability is low or intermediate (<50%) and the patient is not anticoagulated, with an age-adjusted or YEARS threshold
  • Massive/submassive retired: The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline replaces the 2011 AHA massive/submassive and 2019 ESC risk tiers with Categories A-E (+R). Treatment intensity follows the category: systemic thrombolysis is harmful in A1-C2 and reasonable only in E1-E2
  • Anticoagulation duration (Section 5.2, Table 9): Major reversible risk factor (surgery with general anesthesia ≥30 min, hospitalization ≥72 h confined to bed, cesarean section, lower limb fracture): stop after 3-6 months (COR 1, LOE B-NR). No major reversible risk factor: continue into the extended phase without a stop date (COR 1, LOE A). Persistent risk factor (active cancer, autoimmune disease, IBD, chronic immobility): extended phase is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). Minor reversible risk factor (e.g., estrogen, peripartum, hospitalization <72 h, trauma with reduced mobility ≥72 h): shared decision (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). Extended phase: DOAC over VKA (COR 1, LOE A); reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily (COR 1, LOE A; FDA labels: after ≥6 months of treatment); cancer: DOAC or LMWH over VKA (COR 1, LOE A); reassess risk and benefit periodically (COR 1, LOE B-NR)
  • Don't give IVF blindly: With RV dysfunction, fluid helps only if preload is low; give small boluses (≤500 mL) and stop if there is no response. Larger volumes worsen RV function
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Category D or E: transient hypotension, normotensive shock, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest (Practical; 362 hospitalizes C-E and calls for PERT)
  • Any thrombolysis, systemic or catheter-directed: ICU or intermediate care unit (COR 1, LOE C-EO)
  • Practical: respiratory modifier D-R or E-R (>6 L nasal cannula, nonrebreather, or respiratory failure)
  • Category C3 with MAP <80 mmHg (COR 2a, LOE B-NR); Practical: C3 with worsening vital signs, lactate, or O₂ need
  • Stable after mechanical thrombectomy: telemetry unit is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-R)
  • Activate PERT for C-E (COR 1, LOE B-NR). C3-D: transfer for advanced therapy may be considered (COR 2b, LOE C-LD). Category E: stabilize before any transfer (COR 3: Harm, LOE C-EO)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Category A: may go home from the ED; Category B: early discharge generally recommended (2026 AHA/ACC key messages)
  • Low risk by Hestia (all "no"), sPESI 0, or PESI class I-II
  • Immediate access to the anticoagulant and rapid, reliable follow-up (COR 2a, LOE B-R)
  • Practical, Categories C-E after admission: hemodynamically stable, SpO₂ >90% on room air or at baseline, pain controlled with oral agents, on a stable discharge regimen
  • Clinic follow-up within 1 week of discharge (COR 1, LOE C-LD)
  • Visit at or before 3 months to set duration and screen for persistent symptoms (COR 1, LOE C-EO)
  • Encourage early ambulation over bed rest (COR 2a, LOE A)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: RV failure, cardiac arrest, recurrent PE, bleeding (from anticoagulation)

Chronic: Post-PE chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD); CTEPD with pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) follows about 3% of PEs (CTEPH workup and treatment: Condition 334). Post-thrombotic syndrome if DVT. Dyspnea or functional limitation after ≥3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation: evaluate for CTEPD (COR 1, LOE B-NR) with TTE plus lung perfusion scan (COR 2a, LOE B-NR) or CPET (COR 2a, LOE B-NR); continue anticoagulation until the evaluation is complete (COR 1, LOE B-NR). Asymptomatic: no routine follow-up CTPA or perfusion scan (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE B-NR).

Follow-up (Section 5.1): Ask about PE symptoms and function at every visit for at least 1 year (COR 1, LOE C-LD). PE without identifiable risk factors: history, exam, and age-appropriate cancer screening (COR 1, LOE A); no routine CT or PET-CT for occult cancer (COR 3: No Benefit, LOE A). Recurrent PE on anticoagulation: confirm with imaging (CTPA preferred), check adherence and dosing, consider switching drug class (Section 5.2.1).

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Unfractionated Heparin, 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Apixaban, 💊 Rivaroxaban, 💊 Fondaparinux, 💊 tPA
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated D-dimer, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated A-a Gradient, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated PTT
↑ Back to Table of Contents

9. SEPSIS/SEPTIC SHOCK

Life-Threatening Organ Dysfunction • Sepsis-3 • SSC 2021
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Sepsis Definition (Sepsis-3): Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Operationalized as suspected infection + acute SOFA score increase ≥2 points.

Septic Shock Definition (Sepsis-3): Sepsis + vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg + serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Hospital mortality >40%.

Classic: Fever/hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypotension

Alternate Presentations:

  • Elderly: May lack fever; present with confusion or falls only
  • Immunocompromised: Blunted fever response, rapid progression
  • Cryptic Shock: Normal BP but lactate >2 mmol/L — tissue hypoperfusion without overt hypotension. Treat as septic shock.
  • Cold Sepsis: Hypothermia, cool extremities (late presentation, poor prognosis)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP
🧫 ABX COMPANION Cunha Empiric Framework
→ Sepsis — Unknown Source

Labs: Blood cultures ×2 (different sites, before antibiotics), CBC, CMP, lactate (repeat q2–4h if >2 mmol/L), procalcitonin, coagulation studies (PT/INR, fibrinogen), LFTs

Source Identification: UA/urine culture, CXR, wound cultures, consider CT abdomen/pelvis if source unclear

Calculate: qSOFA (screening), SOFA score (diagnosis/severity), lactate clearance at 2–4h

Lactate Interpretation:

  • <2 mmol/L: Low risk — reassess clinical picture
  • 2–3.9 mmol/L: Elevated — initiate resuscitation, remeasure q2–4h
  • ≥4 mmol/L: High risk — treat as septic shock regardless of BP (cryptic shock)
🧮 qSOFA Calculator
Use: Quick screening for sepsis outside ICU. Score ≥2 suggests high risk for poor outcomes. NOT diagnostic — prompts full SOFA evaluation and escalation.
TREATMENT PROTOCOL — HOUR-1 BUNDLE (SSC 2021)

⚠️ The 3-hour and 6-hour bundles have been replaced by a single Hour-1 Bundle. Goal: begin all elements immediately. Antibiotic timing is stratified by severity (see below).

1. Measure Lactate: If initial lactate >2 mmol/L → remeasure at 2–4 hours to assess resuscitation response. Lactate ≥4 mmol/L = high-risk; treat as septic shock even if normotensive.

2. Blood Cultures ×2 Before Antibiotics: Two separate sites (aerobic + anaerobic). Do not delay antibiotics >45 minutes waiting for cultures.

3. Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics — Timing Stratified by Severity:

  • Septic shock or high-likelihood sepsis → within 1 hour of recognition
  • Possible sepsis without shock → rapid assessment first; administer within 3 hours if infection still suspected
  • No source identified (community-acquired): Vancomycin + cefepime OR vancomycin + pip-tazo
  • No source identified (healthcare-associated / high MDR risk): Vancomycin + meropenem
  • Pulmonary source: Cefepime + vancomycin (add pip-tazo if aspiration concern)
  • Abdominal source: Pip-tazo OR meropenem (if severe or ESBL risk)
  • Urinary source: Ceftriaxone (low ESBL risk) OR ertapenem/meropenem (ESBL risk or prior MDR organism)
  • Skin/soft tissue: Vancomycin + pip-tazo
  • Immunocompromised / febrile neutropenia: Add micafungin if Candida risk factors; consider antiviral coverage

De-escalation: Reassess at 48–72 hours with culture data. Narrow spectrum based on sensitivities. Use procalcitonin trends to guide duration — target ≤7 days for most sources if clinically improving.

4. IV Fluid Resuscitation — 30 mL/kg Balanced Crystalloid:

  • Indicated for hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L
  • Preferred fluid: Lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte A — suggested over normal saline (SSC 2021). SMART trial (NEJM 2018) showed reduced 30-day mortality in sepsis subgroup (26.3% vs 31.2%, aOR 0.74) with balanced crystalloids.
  • Avoid normal saline in large volumes — causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, may worsen renal outcomes. Reserve NS for specific indications (hypochloremic alkalosis, hyponatremia correction).
  • 30 mL/kg is a starting point, not a mandate — reassess after initial bolus. Use dynamic markers of fluid responsiveness (pulse pressure variation, passive leg raise, point-of-care echo) before giving additional fluid. Avoid reflexive boluses in non-fluid-responsive patients.
  • No hetastarch / gelatin — increased AKI and mortality. Albumin not first-line; may consider as adjunct after large crystalloid volumes.

5. Vasopressors if MAP <65 During or After Fluid Resuscitation:

  • Norepinephrine (first-line): Start 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP ≥65 mmHg
  • Vasopressin (add-on): 0.03–0.04 units/min (fixed dose, do not titrate) when NE ≥0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min — may reduce NE requirements (VASST trial)
  • Epinephrine: Second-line adjunct if NE + vasopressin insufficient
  • Phenylephrine: Avoid — reduces cardiac output. Use only if severe tachyarrhythmia precludes norepinephrine.
  • Dopamine: Avoid in septic shock — SOAP II (NEJM 2010) showed significantly higher arrhythmia rate vs norepinephrine with no mortality benefit

Do not wait to "finish" the 30 mL/kg bolus before starting vasopressors if patient remains hypotensive — start concurrently.

Source Control: Drain abscesses, remove infected devices, decompress biliary obstruction, debride necrotic tissue — target within 6–12 hours of recognition.

Additional Management:

  • Stress-dose steroids: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV (continuous infusion or 50 mg q6h) if refractory shock despite adequate fluids and vasopressors (NE ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min). Do not use for sepsis without shock.
  • Glucose control: Initiate insulin when glucose ≥180 mg/dL. Target 144–180 mg/dL (8–10 mmol/L). Avoid tight control (<110) — increased hypoglycemia without mortality benefit (NICE-SUGAR).
  • Sodium bicarbonate: Do NOT use to improve hemodynamics or reduce vasopressor requirements. May consider if pH ≤7.2 with concurrent AKI (AKIN stage 2–3).
  • Vitamin C: SSC 2021 recommends against IV vitamin C (CITRIS-ALI, VITAMINS trials — no mortality benefit).
  • VTE prophylaxis: LMWH preferred over UFH unless CrCl <30 (use UFH). Mechanical prophylaxis if anticoagulation contraindicated.
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis: For patients on mechanical ventilation or with coagulopathy. Avoid routine use in all ICU patients (PEPTIC trial — no mortality difference; PPI may increase C. diff risk).
  • Nutrition: Early enteral nutrition within 72 hours if able to be fed enterally. Avoid parenteral nutrition in first 7 days unless enteral not feasible.
  • Goals of care: Address within 72 hours of ICU admission. Integrate palliative principles early.
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Sepsis-3 vs old criteria: No more SIRS. Organ dysfunction = SOFA ≥2. qSOFA is a bedside screening tool — not diagnostic.
  • Time is tissue: Every hour delay in antibiotics in septic shock increases mortality. Door-to-antibiotic <1 hour for shock; <3 hours for possible sepsis without shock (SSC 2021 — new nuanced timing).
  • Cryptic shock: Lactate ≥4 mmol/L = septic shock even with normal BP. Treat aggressively.
  • Lactate clearance: ≥10% reduction at 2–4 hours associated with improved survival. Trend it, don't just check it once.
  • Balanced crystalloids over NS: SMART trial sepsis subgroup showed aOR 0.74 for 30-day mortality with LR vs NS. BaSICS and PLUS trials showed consistent directional benefit. SSC 2021 formally suggests balanced crystalloids.
  • 30 mL/kg is a starting point: Reassess fluid responsiveness dynamically — not all patients tolerate or benefit from full resuscitation volumes.
  • Dopamine is out: SOAP II showed higher arrhythmia rates vs norepinephrine. No role in septic shock.
  • Vasopressin timing: Add at NE 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min rather than continuing to escalate NE alone.
  • Procalcitonin: <0.5 mcg/L = low likelihood of bacterial infection. Serial values guide de-escalation — target 7 days or less for most sources.
  • Vitamin C and bicarb: Both recommended against in SSC 2021 (no mortality benefit, potential harm).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL septic shock (vasopressors required)
  • Lactate ≥4 mmol/L
  • Respiratory failure requiring ventilation
  • Acute mental status changes
  • Oliguria/anuria despite fluids
  • Multiorgan dysfunction
  • Target: ICU admission within 6 hours of recognition (SSC 2021)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Afebrile ×24–48 hours
  • Hemodynamically stable off pressors ≥24h
  • Lactate normalized
  • Source identified and controlled
  • Mental status at baseline
  • Tolerating PO, able to complete antibiotic course
  • No new organ dysfunction
  • Close follow-up arranged
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: ARDS, AKI requiring dialysis, DIC, multiorgan failure, cardiac dysfunction, death (mortality 10–40%; septic shock >40%)

Long-term: Post-sepsis syndrome (cognitive impairment, weakness, PTSD), recurrent infections, chronic organ dysfunction. Consider post-hospital rehabilitation referral for ICU stays >72h or mechanical ventilation >48h (SSC 2021).

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Cefepime, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Vasopressin, 💊 Hydrocortisone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR, 🔬 Elevated PTT, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hyponatremia

10. ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (AKI)

Prerenal • Intrinsic • Postrenal
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Increase in Cr ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48hr OR increase to ≥1.5× baseline OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6hr

Classic: Oliguria, fluid overload, edema, uremic symptoms (N/V, confusion, asterixis, pericarditis)

Alternate Presentations:

  • Non-oliguric AKI: Cr rising but urine output preserved (often ATN from nephrotoxins)
  • Hyperkalemia: May be presenting sign, can be life-threatening. See Hyperkalemia management
  • Metabolic Acidosis: High anion gap from uremia
  • Elderly: Minimal symptoms despite significant Cr elevation
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: BMP (Cr, BUN, K+), baseline Cr for comparison, UA with microscopy, urine electrolytes (Na+, Cr, osmolality)

Imaging: Renal US (assess for obstruction, kidney size, hydronephrosis)

Consider: Renal biopsy if diagnosis unclear or concern for glomerulonephritis

Categorize AKI:

  • Prerenal (60-70%): Decreased renal perfusion - volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis, NSAIDs
  • Intrinsic (25-40%): Acute tubular necrosis (ischemia, nephrotoxins), acute interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis
  • Postrenal (5-10%): Obstruction - BPH, kidney stones, malignancy, neurogenic bladder
🧮 FENa Calculator
Use: Differentiate prerenal AKI (<1%) from ATN (>2%). FENa 1-2% is indeterminate. If on diuretics, use FEUrea instead.
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

General Principles:

  • Treat underlying cause
  • Stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE-I/ARB if AKI severe, aminoglycosides, contrast)
  • Adjust all medication doses for GFR
  • Avoid further insults (hypotension, contrast, nephrotoxic drugs)

Prerenal AKI:

  • Volume Depletion: IV fluids (LR or NS), correct hypotension
  • Cardiorenal: Diuresis if volume overloaded, optimize cardiac output
  • Hepatorenal: Albumin + midodrine + octreotide, or terlipressin

Intrinsic AKI:

  • ATN: Supportive care, avoid nephrotoxins, optimize hemodynamics. Usually resolves in 1-3 weeks
  • AIN (Acute Interstitial Nephritis): Stop offending drug, consider steroids if severe/not improving
  • Glomerulonephritis: Nephrology consult, may need steroids/immunosuppression ± plasmapheresis

Postrenal AKI:

  • Relieve Obstruction: Foley catheter (if bladder outlet obstruction), nephrostomy tubes, ureteral stents
  • Watch for post-obstructive diuresis - may need aggressive fluid replacement

Indications for Dialysis (AEIOU):

  • Acidosis - severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1) refractory to medical management
  • Electrolytes - hyperkalemia refractory to medical therapy
  • Ingestions - toxic alcohols, lithium, salicylates
  • Overload - volume overload refractory to diuretics, pulmonary edema
  • Uremia - uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • FENa limitations: Not valid if on diuretics (falsely elevated), chronic kidney disease, or contrast nephropathy. Use FEUrea if on diuretics (prerenal <35%)
  • BUN:Cr ratio: >20:1 suggests prerenal (BUN reabsorbed more than Cr). <15:1 suggests intrinsic renal disease
  • Muddy brown casts: Pathognomonic for ATN on urine microscopy
  • Triple whammy: ACE-I/ARB + diuretic + NSAID = high risk for AKI. Avoid this combination!
  • Contrast-induced AKI: Peak Cr at 3-5 days. Prevent with IV fluids before/after contrast. No evidence for NAC or bicarb
  • Post-obstructive diuresis: Can lose massive amounts of fluid after obstruction relieved. Replace half of UOP with 0.45% NS
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hyperkalemia >6.5 with ECG changes
  • Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2)
  • Volume overload with respiratory failure
  • Uremic encephalopathy/pericarditis
  • Need for emergent dialysis
  • Hemodynamic instability
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Cr downtrending or stable
  • No dialysis-requiring complications
  • Electrolytes controlled (K+ <5.5)
  • Volume status optimized
  • Cause identified and addressed
  • Nephrotoxins stopped
  • Close nephrology follow-up if Cr not at baseline
  • Patient educated on medication adjustments
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, uremia, need for dialysis, death

Chronic: Chronic kidney disease, progression to ESRD, recurrent AKI episodes

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Sodium Bicarbonate, 💊 Calcium Gluconate, 💊 Dextrose D50/D10, 💊 Regular Insulin, 💊 Patiromer
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated BUN, 🔬 Low eGFR, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Low Bicarbonate, 🔬 Urine Sodium/FENa, 🔬 Urinalysis, 🔬 Elevated Lactate

11. HYPERKALEMIA

K+ >5.5 mEq/L • Life-Threatening Arrhythmias
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Often asymptomatic until severe. Weakness, paresthesias, palpitations

ECG Changes (Progressive):

  • Mild (5.5-6.5): Peaked T waves (tall, narrow, symmetric)
  • Moderate (6.5-8): PR prolongation, P wave flattening/loss, QRS widening
  • Severe (>8): Sine wave pattern, ventricular fibrillation, asystole

Alternate Presentations:

  • Pseudohyperkalemia: Hemolysis during blood draw, severe leukocytosis/thrombocytosis, fist clenching
  • Acute on Chronic: Patients on ACE-I/ARB with CKD who take NSAIDs or get dehydrated
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: Repeat K+ to confirm (rule out pseudohyperkalemia), BMP, Mg, Ca, VBG, consider digoxin level if on digoxin

ECG: CRITICAL - assess for cardiotoxicity. ECG changes indicate true emergency

Identify Cause:

  • Increased Intake: K+ supplements, salt substitutes, IV K+
  • Transcellular Shift: Acidosis, insulin deficiency, β-blocker, digoxin toxicity, succinylcholine, tumor lysis
  • Decreased Excretion: AKI/CKD, hypoaldosteronism, ACE-I/ARB, K+-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, heparin, TMP-SMX
TREATMENT PROTOCOL (Sequence Matters!)

Step 1: Cardiac Membrane Stabilization (if ECG changes or K >6.5):

  • Calcium Gluconate: 1-2 amps (10-20 mL of 10% solution) IV over 2-3 min
  • OR Calcium Chloride: 0.5-1g (5-10 mL of 10%) IV via central line (more potent, sclerosing)
  • Effect: Immediate (1-3 min), duration 30-60 min
  • Does NOT lower K+, only protects heart
  • Can repeat dose if persistent ECG changes

Step 2: Shift K+ Intracellularly (Temporary):

  • Insulin + Dextrose: Regular insulin 10 units IV + D50 50mL (25g dextrose) IV push
    • Consider reduced dose (5 units, or weight-based 0.1 units/kg) especially in renal impairment, lower body weight, or other hypoglycemia risk factors — studies show significantly less hypoglycemia (e.g., 19.5% vs 28.6% in one renal-impairment cohort) with comparable or only modestly less K+-lowering effect; 10 units remains standard/acceptable, this is an evolving practice area
    • If glucose >250: give insulin alone, no dextrose
    • Effect: 15-30 min, duration 4-6 hours
    • Lowers K+ by 0.5-1.5 mEq/L
    • Check glucose in 1hr (risk hypoglycemia)
  • Albuterol: 10-20mg nebulized (or 0.5mg IV)
    • Effect: 30 min, duration 2-4 hours
    • Lowers K+ by 0.5-1 mEq/L
    • Additive with insulin
  • Sodium Bicarbonate: 50-100 mEq (1-2 amps) IV over 5 min (only if concurrent metabolic acidosis)
    • Controversial efficacy if pH normal

Step 3: Remove K+ from Body (Definitive):

  • Loop Diuretic: Furosemide 40-80mg IV (if adequate renal function)
  • Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate): 15-30g PO/PR
    • Effect: Hours, lowers K+ by 0.5-1 mEq/L
    • Avoid if ileus (risk colonic necrosis)
  • Patiromer or Sodium Zirconium: Newer K+ binders, better tolerated but slower onset
  • Hemodialysis: Most effective. Indications:
    • K+ >6.5 with ECG changes refractory to medical management
    • Severe AKI/ESRD
    • Ongoing tissue breakdown (rhabdo, tumor lysis)

Step 4: Stop Exacerbating Factors: Hold ACE-I/ARB, K+-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, K+ supplements

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • ECG trumps K+ level: If ECG shows changes, treat aggressively regardless of exact K+ value. ECG changes = cardiac emergency!
  • Calcium first! If ECG changes, give calcium before anything else. Protects heart immediately while you arrange other therapies
  • Insulin hypoglycemia: Very common! Check glucose 30min and 1hr after insulin. Have D50 ready. Consider dextrose infusion
  • Kayexalate controversy: Limited evidence for efficacy, risk of colonic necrosis esp with sorbitol. Consider newer agents
  • Repeat K+ frequently: Check K+ q2-4h during acute management. Temporizing measures wear off!
  • Chronic management: Low K+ diet, loop diuretics, K+ binders. Avoid "hyperkalemia cocktail" (ACE-I + spironolactone + NSAIDs)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • K+ >6.5 with ECG changes
  • Hemodynamically significant arrhythmias
  • Need for emergent dialysis
  • Rapidly rising K+ despite treatment
  • Cardiac arrest from hyperkalemia
  • Requires continuous cardiac monitoring
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • K+ <5.5 mEq/L and downtrending
  • ECG normalized (no peaked T waves)
  • Cause identified and addressed
  • K+-raising medications stopped/adjusted
  • Patient educated on low K+ diet
  • Close follow-up with repeat K+ within 2-3 days
  • If CKD: nephrology follow-up arranged
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Cardiac: Ventricular arrhythmias (VT, VF), heart block, asystole, sudden cardiac death

From Treatment: Hypoglycemia (insulin), hypokalemia rebound, volume overload (from IVF), GI complications (kayexalate)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Calcium Gluconate Chloride, 💊 Regular Insulin, 💊 Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Low Bicarbonate, 🔬 Urinalysis

12. HYPONATREMIA

Na+ <135 mEq/L • Osmotic Demyelination Risk
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Nausea, headache, confusion, lethargy, seizures (if severe/acute)

Severity by Symptoms:

  • Mild (Na 130-135): Often asymptomatic or mild nausea
  • Moderate (125-129): Nausea, confusion, headache
  • Severe (<125): Vomiting, seizures, coma, respiratory arrest

Alternate Presentations:

  • Elderly: Falls, gait instability, cognitive impairment
  • Athletes: Exercise-associated hyponatremia from excessive free water intake
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Step 1 - Check Serum Osmolality:

  • Isotonic (280-295): Pseudohyponatremia (hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperproteinemia)
  • Hypertonic (>295): Hyperglycemia, mannitol
  • Hypotonic (<280): True hyponatremia - proceed to step 2

Step 2 - Assess Volume Status:

  • Hypovolemic: Dry mucous membranes, ↓skin turgor, orthostatic hypotension
    • Urine Na <20: GI losses, third-spacing, skin losses
    • Urine Na >40: Diuretics, salt-wasting nephropathy, adrenal insufficiency
  • Euvolemic: Normal volume status
    • SIADH (most common), hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, psychogenic polydipsia
  • Hypervolemic: Edema, elevated JVP, ascites
    • CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, advanced CKD

Labs: Serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine Na, BMP, TSH, cortisol if indicated

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

⚠️ CRITICAL: Correct slowly! Target 6-8 mEq/L in first 24 hours (do not exceed 8 mEq/L standard-risk, 6 mEq/L high-risk — see below). Faster correction → osmotic demyelination syndrome

Acute Symptomatic (<48hr onset with seizures/coma):

  • 3% Hypertonic Saline: 100 mL IV bolus over 10 min, can repeat × 2 if needed
  • Goal: Raise Na by 4-6 mEq/L (enough to stop seizures), then slow correction
  • Check Na q2-4h

Chronic or Asymptomatic:

  • Hypovolemic: NS at 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr. Na will auto-correct with volume repletion
  • Euvolemic (SIADH):
    • Fluid restriction (800-1000 mL/day)
    • Treat underlying cause
    • Salt tabs + loop diuretic if needed
    • Tolvaptan (vasopressin antagonist) for refractory cases
  • Hypervolemic: Fluid + sodium restriction, diuretics, treat underlying (CHF, cirrhosis)

Correction Rate Calculation:

  • Target: 6-8 mEq/L in 24 hours, 12-14 mEq/L in 48 hours
  • High-risk patients (chronic, malnourished, cirrhosis, K+ <3): Limit to 6 mEq/L in 24hr
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Osmotic demyelination (ODS): From overly rapid correction. Presents 2-6 days later with dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriplegia, locked-in syndrome. PREVENT by slow correction!
  • SIADH criteria: Hyponatremia + low serum osm (<280) + inappropriately concentrated urine (>100) + euvolemic + normal thyroid/adrenal
  • Beer potomania: Hyponatremia from excessive beer intake with poor solute intake. Na can rise dangerously fast when solute repleted!
  • Tea and toast diet: Similar to beer potomania - inadequate solute intake in elderly
  • Exercise-associated: From drinking too much water during endurance events. Treat with hypertonic saline, NOT more water!
  • Hyperglycemia correction: For every 100 mg/dL glucose >100, add 1.6 mEq/L to measured Na to get "true" Na
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Seizures or coma
  • Na <120 mEq/L
  • Acute symptomatic hyponatremia
  • Need for 3% hypertonic saline
  • Rapid changes requiring q2h monitoring
  • Respiratory compromise
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Na >125 mEq/L and stable/improving
  • Asymptomatic or symptoms resolved
  • Underlying cause identified/treated
  • Can comply with fluid restriction if needed
  • Follow-up arranged with Na check in 2-3 days
  • Patient educated on risks
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

From Hyponatremia: Seizures, cerebral edema, respiratory arrest, death

From Overcorrection: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (irreversible neurologic damage)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 KCl, 💊 Magnesium, 💊 Sodium Bicarbonate, 💊 Calcium Gluconate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Serum Osmolality, 🔬 Urine Osmolality, 🔬 Osmolar Gap, 🔬 Urine Sodium/FENa
↑ Back to Table of Contents

13. DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS (DKA)

Hyperglycemia • Acidosis • Ketones
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad: (1) Hyperglycemia (glucose ≥200 mg/dL) or known diabetes, (2) Ketosis, (3) Metabolic acidosis (2024 consensus)

Classic Symptoms: Polyuria, polydipsia, N/V, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid), fruity breath odor, altered mental status

Precipitants: insulin omission and infection are the most frequent causes (2024 consensus). US admissions: insulin omission 41-60%, new-onset diabetes 17-24%, infection 14-16% (2024 consensus Table 1).

  • Insulin: Omission or inadequate dosing
  • Infection: UTI, pneumonia
  • New-onset diabetes
  • Drugs: SGLT2 inhibitors (also euglycemic DKA), glucocorticoids, antipsychotics, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Ischemia: MI, stroke
  • Intoxication: Alcohol, drugs
  • Pregnancy
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

DKA Criteria (all 3; 2024 consensus; ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1):

  • D: Glucose ≥200 mg/dL OR prior history of diabetes (any glucose)
  • K: β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip 2+ or greater
  • A: pH <7.3 and/or HCO3 <18 mmol/L (venous blood gas)

Euglycemic DKA: about 10% of DKA presents with glucose <200 mg/dL; SGLT2 inhibitors now account for most cases (2024 consensus). See Euglycemic DKA.

Labs: VBG (pH, HCO3), BMP, anion gap, blood β-hydroxybutyrate (preferred over urine ketones for diagnosis and monitoring), phosphate, Mg, CBC, ECG, blood cultures, UA/CXR if infection suspected

Monitoring (2024 consensus): capillary glucose every 1-2 h; electrolytes, phosphate, creatinine, β-hydroxybutyrate and venous pH every 4 h until resolution

Calculate: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3). Normal 8-12. Also calculate osmolality if altered mental status. The anion gap is not a diagnostic criterion and should not be used to define resolution (saline-induced hyperchloremia; 2024 consensus)

Other causes of high ketones: starvation ketosis, alcoholic ketoacidosis, ketosis of pregnancy or hyperemesis (2024 consensus)

Severity and level of care (2024 consensus Table 2; not all variables needed):

  • Mild: pH >7.25 to <7.30 or HCO3 15-18; β-hydroxybutyrate 3.0-6.0; alert. Regular or observation unit
  • Moderate: pH 7.0-7.25; HCO3 10 to <15; β-hydroxybutyrate 3.0-6.0; alert or drowsy. Step-down or intermediate care
  • Severe: pH <7.0; HCO3 <10; β-hydroxybutyrate >6.0; stupor or coma. ICU
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Fluids (2024 consensus):

  • Initial: 0.9% saline or balanced crystalloid (lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte) 500-1,000 mL/h for the first 2-4 h (1 L/h if severely hypovolemic), if no cardiac or renal compromise
  • Balanced crystalloid: faster DKA resolution and less hyperchloremic acidosis than saline in prospective and observational studies and meta-analyses
  • Then: rate guided by BP, HR, intake-output and Na; replace about 50% of the estimated deficit in 8-12 h and correct the deficit within 24-48 h
  • Older adults, heart failure, ESKD on dialysis: smaller boluses (e.g., 250 mL) with frequent hemodynamic reassessment
  • Once glucose <250: add 5% or 10% dextrose to the 0.9% saline or crystalloid and continue insulin
  • Euglycemic DKA (glucose <200): start dextrose with the saline when insulin starts
  • Hypotonic 0.45% saline only if osmolality is not falling despite adequate fluid balance and insulin; a rise in Na as glucose falls is not by itself an indication (2024 consensus, HHS section)

2. Insulin (2024 consensus):

  • Moderate or severe DKA: regular insulin IV, fixed rate 0.1 units/kg/h. Bolus 0.1 units/kg IV only if starting the infusion is delayed
  • Mild, uncomplicated DKA (consensus text also allows uncomplicated moderate DKA): rapid-acting analog SC 0.1 units/kg, then 0.1 units/kg every 1 h or 0.2 units/kg every 2 h, in the ED or a step-down unit. Not for severe or complicated DKA
  • Glucose <250: reduce IV insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h (SC: 0.05 units/kg every 1 h or 0.1 units/kg every 2 h) and add dextrose; keep glucose 150-200 until resolution
  • Do NOT stop insulin when glucose falls: glucose usually reaches <250 within 4-8 h, before the ketoacidosis resolves. Continue until DKA resolution criteria are met (see Pearls)
  • Nurse-driven variable-rate protocol: rate no less than 1 unit/h (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Basal insulin: a home basal regimen can be continued at the usual dose. Early basal insulin 0.15-0.3 units/kg SC during the infusion shortened time to resolution and prevented rebound hyperglycemia in several studies; some clinicians avoid it because of hypoglycemia or hypokalemia risk
  • Transition: after resolution and when eating, start basal-bolus SC insulin 1-2 h before stopping the infusion (2024 consensus; ADA SOC 2026 text: basal insulin 2-4 h before)
  • SC dose: home regimen, or 0.5-0.6 units/kg/day (0.3 units/kg/day if frail or CKD), or the sum of stable hourly IV needs (may overestimate); 40-60% as basal, the rest as 3 mealtime doses

3. Potassium (CRITICAL; 2024 consensus): confirm urine output (about 0.5 mL/kg/h)

  • If K+ <3.5: Hold insulin. KCl 10-20 mEq/h until K >3.5; faster replacement needs central venous access. US KCl label: usually no more than 10 mEq/h when K is above 2.5; up to 40 mEq/h only for K <2.0 with ECG changes or paralysis, on continuous ECG monitoring
  • If K+ 3.5-5.0: add KCl to each liter of IV fluid to keep K 4-5 mEq/L (20-30 mEq/L suffices for most; Fig. 4 gives 10-20 mEq/L)
  • If K+ >5.0: start insulin, give no K, recheck K every 2 h
  • Check K 2 h after starting insulin, then every 4 h until resolution. K of 2.5 or less during treatment is linked to about 3-fold mortality

4. Phosphate (not routine): only with muscle weakness, respiratory or cardiac compromise and phosphate <1.0 mg/dL (0.32 mmol/L) (ADA SOC 2026 Fig. 16.1; symptomatic hypophosphatemia usually does not occur above this level, Bakerman's ABC's). Then add 20-30 mmol potassium phosphate to replacement fluids; rapid replacement can cause hypocalcemia (2024 consensus). The 2024 consensus prints <1.0 mmol/L, which is 3.1 mg/dL, at or near the lower limit of normal.

5. Bicarbonate (not routine; consider only if pH <7.0): sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol (8.4%) in 400 mL sterile water every 2 h until pH >7.0. Risks: hypokalemia, lower tissue oxygen uptake, cerebral edema (2024 consensus)

6. Treat Precipitant: Antibiotics if infection, adjust insulin regimen, etc. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors on admission (2024 consensus)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • DKA resolution (2024 consensus): blood β-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L AND venous pH ≥7.3 or HCO3 ≥18; ideally glucose <200. Do not use the anion gap or urine ketones to define resolution. Don't stop insulin just because glucose normalized!
  • Two-bag system (Practical): Run two IV bags (one NS, one D5-NS) through Y-connector. Adjust ratio to maintain glucose 150-200 while continuing insulin
  • Euglycemic DKA: about 10% of DKA; most cases are SGLT2 inhibitor related. Check ketones even if glucose is normal, and start dextrose with insulin. See Euglycemic DKA
  • K+ shifts: Total body K+ depleted despite normal/high initial K+. With insulin, K+ shifts into cells → life-threatening hypokalemia. Monitor closely!
  • Cerebral edema (2024 consensus): rare in adults (<0.1%) with about 30% mortality; cause unclear (osmotic shifts, hypoperfusion, inflammation). Low threshold for brain imaging with any change in mental status; mannitol and mechanical ventilation are suggested
  • Ketone tests: urine nitroprusside tests detect acetoacetate, not β-hydroxybutyrate. They can understate ketosis early and overstate it during recovery, as β-hydroxybutyrate converts to acetoacetate; captopril and valproate can give false positives. Monitor blood β-hydroxybutyrate (2024 consensus)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe DKA: pH <7.0, HCO3 <10, β-hydroxybutyrate >6.0, or stupor/coma (2024 consensus Table 2)
  • Altered mental status
  • Critical illness as the precipitant: MI, GI bleeding, sepsis (2024 consensus)
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Severe electrolyte derangements (Practical)
  • Cerebral edema concern
  • Moderate DKA: step-down or intermediate care; mild DKA: regular or observation unit (2024 consensus; level of care stays a clinical decision)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • DKA resolved: β-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH ≥7.3 or HCO3 ≥18 (2024 consensus: use judgment; do not delay discharge if not all are met)
  • Tolerating PO intake
  • Transitioned to subQ insulin with 24-h coverage (basal-bolus preferred)
  • Precipitant identified and treated
  • SGLT2 inhibitor: not recommended in T1D; after DKA in T2D, restarting is not routinely recommended (2024 consensus)
  • Patient educated on recognition, prevention and sick day management (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.17)
  • Diabetes follow-up arranged
  • No ongoing complications
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Cerebral edema (<0.1% of adults; 2024 consensus), ARDS, thrombosis (prophylactic-dose LMWH unless thrombosis is suspected; 2024 consensus), mucormycosis

From Treatment (2024 consensus Table 3): hypoglycemia (16-28%; check glucose every 1-2 h), hypokalemia (about 55%; K <2.5 in 16%), hyperchloremic non-gap acidosis (less with balanced crystalloids), volume overload, acute kidney injury

14. HYPEROSMOLAR HYPERGLYCEMIC STATE (HHS)

Extreme Hyperglycemia • Hyperosmolarity • Mostly Type 2 DM
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Key Differences from DKA: glucose ≥600, high osmolality, no significant ketoacidosis, more profound dehydration; develops over days to a week; change in cognitive state common (2024 consensus)

Classic: Altered mental status, severe dehydration, hypotension. Often insidious onset over days to a week

Typical Patient: most often a middle-aged or older adult with T2D (US: 88% of HHS events in T2D), but HHS occurs at any age and in T1D. Most frequent precipitants: infection (UTI, pneumonia) and insulin omission (2024 consensus)

Mixed DKA/HHS: about 1/3 of hyperglycemic emergencies (US admissions: 27%); highest mortality of the three (2024 consensus). Manage ketoacidosis as in DKA

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

HHS Criteria (all 4; 2024 consensus Fig. 2B; ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1):

  • Glucose ≥600 mg/dL
  • Effective osmolality >300 mOsm/kg OR total osmolality >320 mOsm/kg
  • No significant ketonemia: β-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip less than 2+
  • No acidosis: pH ≥7.3 and HCO3 ≥15 mmol/L

Calculate (conventional units): Effective osmolality = 2(Na) + glucose/18 (no urea). Total osmolality = 2(Na) + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8. Normal 280-295. As glucose falls, Na rises about 1.6 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL (2024 consensus)

Mixed DKA/HHS: β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0, pH <7.30 or HCO3 <18 with HHS features; insulin as for DKA (2024 consensus)

Labs: Same as DKA (VBG, BMP, β-hydroxybutyrate, phosphate, Mg, ECG); identify precipitant. Glucose every 1-2 h; electrolytes, creatinine and serum osmolality every 4 h (2024 consensus)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Fluids (2024 consensus):

  • Initial: 0.9% saline or balanced crystalloid 500-1,000 mL/h for the first 2-4 h (1 L/h if severely hypovolemic), if no cardiac or renal compromise
  • Then: replace about 50% of the estimated deficit in 8-12 h and correct the deficit within 24-48 h; guide by BP, HR, intake-output, Na and osmolality
  • Older adults, heart failure, ESKD on dialysis: smaller boluses (e.g., 250 mL) with frequent hemodynamic reassessment
  • Rising Na as glucose falls is not by itself a reason for hypotonic fluid; use 0.45% saline only if osmolality is not falling despite adequate positive fluid balance and insulin
  • Glucose <250: add 5% or 10% dextrose; keep glucose 200-250 until resolution

2. Insulin (2024 consensus):

  • HHS without significant ketonemia: regular insulin IV, fixed rate 0.05 units/kg/h
  • Mixed DKA/HHS (β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0, pH <7.30 or HCO3 <18): 0.1 units/kg/h, as for DKA
  • Some recommend withholding insulin until glucose stops falling with fluids alone, to limit the fall in osmolality; few studies have assessed the best HHS insulin regimen
  • Home basal insulin can be continued at the usual dose
  • Glucose goal: correct over about 8-10 h; the fall should not exceed 90-120 mg/dL/h. At glucose <250, add dextrose and keep glucose 200-250 until resolution; continue insulin
  • SC rapid-acting insulin regimens are not recommended for HHS
  • Transition: as for DKA (SC insulin 1-2 h before stopping the infusion)

3. Potassium and phosphate: same protocol as DKA (hold insulin if K <3.5; KCl in fluids at K 3.5-5.0; none above 5.0). Phosphate only if <1.0 mg/dL with muscle weakness or respiratory or cardiac compromise (2024 consensus: same approach as DKA)

4. Correct Slowly (2024 consensus): osmolality should fall no faster than 3.0-8.0 mOsm/kg/h; Na by no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h; glucose by no more than 90-120 mg/dL/h (cerebral edema, osmotic demyelination)

5. Complications (2024 consensus Table 3): thrombosis (HHS especially prothrombotic; prophylactic-dose LMWH unless thrombosis is suspected); cerebral edema (rare); osmotic demyelination (relative hyponatremia; correct with 0.9% saline); hypoglycemia; hypokalemia; acute kidney injury

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • HHS vs DKA: both occur at any age in T1D and T2D; DKA is more common in young people with T1D, HHS in older adults with T2D; about 1/3 are mixed (2024 consensus)
  • Why little ketosis? Residual insulin secretion minimizes ketosis but does not control hyperglycemia (2024 consensus)
  • Mortality higher: 5- to 10-fold higher than DKA (DKA <1%). One US study: inpatient mortality 5% for HHS, 8% for mixed DKA/HHS, 3% for DKA (2024 consensus)
  • Fluids first: fluids alone lower glucose (about 50-70 mg/dL/h in DKA, often more in HHS), so recheck glucose before and after starting insulin (2024 consensus)
  • Slower correction: Osmolality built up over a longer time; correct slowly to avoid cerebral edema and osmotic demyelination (2024 consensus)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • HHS: ICU care is recommended (2024 consensus)
  • Altered mental status/coma
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Critical illness as the precipitant: MI, GI bleeding, sepsis (2024 consensus)
  • Severe electrolyte abnormalities
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • HHS resolved (2024 consensus): calculated osmolality <300, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h, cognition improved, glucose <250
  • Mental status at baseline
  • Taking PO
  • On SC insulin with 24-h coverage, or another appropriate diabetes regimen
  • Precipitant treated
  • Patient educated on recognition and prevention of hyperglycemic crises (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.17)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Regular Insulin, 💊 Potassium Chloride, 💊 Insulin Glargine, 💊 Enoxaparin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperglycemia, 🔬 Serum Osmolality, 🔬 Osmolar Gap, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

15. UPPER GI BLEED

Hematemesis • Melena • Variceal vs Non-Variceal
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Hematemesis (bright red or coffee-ground), melena (black tarry stool), syncope, hemodynamic instability

Common Causes:

  • Non-Variceal (90%): PUD (H. pylori, NSAIDs), erosive gastritis/esophagitis, Mallory-Weiss tear, Dieulafoy lesion
  • Variceal (10%): Esophageal or gastric varices (cirrhosis, portal hypertension)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Immediate: Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type & cross (4 units), BMP, coags, LFTs

Risk Stratification: Glasgow-Blatchford Score 0-1 = very low risk, may be discharged from the ED with outpatient follow-up (ACG 2021, conditional). Score ≥2: admit or observe

EGD: Within 24 hours of presentation, after resuscitation (ACG 2021, conditional). Nonvariceal high-risk: ACG 2021 no longer suggests earlier than 12 hours. Suspected variceal: within 12 hours (AASLD 2024)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Resuscitation:

  • Transfusion: Transfuse at Hgb <7 g/dL (ACG 2021, conditional). Threshold 8 g/dL reasonable with pre-existing cardiovascular disease; hypotensive patients may be transfused before Hgb reaches 7. ACS: evidence insufficient for a threshold. Variceal: target Hgb ~7 g/dL (AASLD 2024)
  • Fluids: Crystalloids for volume resuscitation
  • Antithrombotics (ACG-CAG 2022, all conditional): Warfarin: no FFP, no vitamin K; if reversal needed, PCC over FFP (consider for life-threatening bleed, INR far above range, or when massive transfusion is undesirable). Dabigatran: no routine idarucizumab (selective use if life-threatening and dabigatran taken within 24 h). Rivaroxaban/apixaban: no andexanet. DOACs: no PCC. Antiplatelets: no platelet transfusion. Cardiac ASA for secondary prevention: do not hold; if held, resume the day hemostasis is confirmed. Cirrhosis: no FFP or platelets to INR or platelet-count targets (AASLD 2024)

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Pre-EGD erythromycin: 250 mg IV over 20-30 min, given 20-90 min before endoscopy (ACG 2021, conditional). Reduces repeat endoscopy and length of stay; not shown to reduce rebleeding or mortality. Caution with baseline QT prolongation or QT-prolonging drugs
  • PPI (after endoscopic hemostasis of a high-risk ulcer): High-dose PPI × 3 days (ACG 2021, strong). Continuous: pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus, then 8 mg/hr. Intermittent: 40 mg 2-4 times daily, PO if awake without nausea, vomiting, or dysphagia; an initial 80 mg bolus may be appropriate. No outcome difference continuous vs intermittent. Then PPI BID until 2 weeks after EGD (ACG 2021, conditional)
  • Vasoactive (known or suspected cirrhosis, start on presentation): Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus, then 25-50 mcg/hr. Continue 2-5 days if portal hypertensive bleeding is confirmed at EGD (AASLD 2024)
  • Antibiotics (known or suspected cirrhosis, any GI bleed): Start IV on presentation (AASLD 2024). Ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h until stable for discharge or 5 days, whichever is shorter; stop once bleeding is controlled if no active infection

Endoscopic Management:

  • PUD: Epinephrine injection + thermal coagulation ± clips
  • Varices: Band ligation (preferred) or sclerotherapy
  • If refractory variceal bleeding: Balloon tamponade (Blakemore tube), TIPS
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Don't over-transfuse: Restrictive threshold Hgb 7 g/dL (8 g/dL with pre-existing CVD). Liberal transfusion worsens outcomes (increased rebleeding)
  • Rockall score: Post-EGD risk score. Predicts rebleeding and mortality
  • PPI timing: Pre-EGD PPI doesn't reduce mortality but may reduce stigmata of recent hemorrhage
  • Mallory-Weiss: Longitudinal tear at GE junction from forceful vomiting. Usually self-limited
  • NG tube controversial: Not routinely needed. Doesn't improve outcomes, uncomfortable for patient
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation
  • Massive transfusion (>4 units in 24hr)
  • Variceal bleeding
  • Rebleeding after endoscopic intervention
  • Need for airway protection
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable × 24hr
  • Hgb stable (no transfusion need)
  • Post-EGD with low-risk lesion
  • Tolerating PO
  • On PPI BID × 2 weeks, then daily
  • H. pylori testing sent/treated
  • GI follow-up arranged
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pantoprazole, 💊 Octreotide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Lactate

16. CIRRHOSIS WITH ASCITES

Portal Hypertension • Decompensated Cirrhosis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Abdominal distension, weight gain, peripheral edema, early satiety, dyspnea from diaphragm elevation

Physical Exam: Shifting dullness, fluid wave, bulging flanks. Stigmata of chronic liver disease: jaundice, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, caput medusae, asterixis

Alternate Presentations:

  • SBP: Fever, abdominal pain/tenderness, altered mental status without obvious peritonitis
  • Hepatic Hydrothorax: Right-sided pleural effusion (usually) without cardiopulmonary disease
  • Tense Ascites: Respiratory compromise, severe discomfort, umbilical/inguinal hernias
  • Hepatorenal Syndrome: Progressive AKI despite volume resuscitation
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging: Abdominal Doppler ultrasound in the initial evaluation (AASLD 2021); detects mild (grade 1) ascites not apparent on exam; evaluates liver texture and portal vein. CT abdomen if unclear etiology or concern for HCC

Diagnostic Paracentesis (as soon as possible: new-onset ascites, every emergent admission even without signs of infection, or any clinical deterioration; AASLD 2021, AGA 2025 BPA 2):

  • Cell count with differential: PMN >250 = SBP
  • Albumin: For SAAG calculation
  • Total protein: <1g/dL = high SBP risk
  • Gram stain and culture: Inoculate blood culture bottles at bedside (improves yield)
  • Consider: Glucose, LDH, cytology (if malignancy suspected), TB studies, amylase (if pancreatitis concern)

SAAG (Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient):

  • Calculate: Serum albumin - Ascitic fluid albumin
  • ≥1.1 g/dL: Portal hypertension (97% accuracy) - cirrhosis, cardiac ascites, Budd-Chiari syndrome, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
  • <1.1 g/dL: Non-portal causes - peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB peritonitis, pancreatic ascites, nephrotic syndrome, serositis

Labs: CBC, CMP, albumin, PT/INR, hepatitis panel (HBsAg, anti-HCV), AFP (HCC screening), lipid panel

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Sodium Restriction: <2g/day (88 mEq/day). This is THE most important intervention! Effective in 10-20% as monotherapy

Diuretic Therapy:

  • Initial regimen: Spironolactone 100 mg PO daily, with or without furosemide 40 mg PO daily (AASLD 2021). First episode: spironolactone alone is often adequate; long-standing ascites responds better to the combination
  • Titration: Increase stepwise, at least 72 h between dose changes, to maximum spironolactone 400 mg and furosemide 160 mg/day (AASLD 2021). Practical: keep the 100:40 ratio to maintain normokalemia
    • Step 2: Spironolactone 200mg + Furosemide 80mg
    • Step 3: Spironolactone 300mg + Furosemide 120mg
    • Maximum: Spironolactone 400mg + Furosemide 160mg
  • Goal weight loss: 0.5kg/day if ascites alone, 1kg/day if peripheral edema present
  • Inpatient volume overload: Escalate or trial IV loop diuretic (furosemide or bumetanide) as bolus 2-3 times daily or continuous infusion; escalate cautiously every 2-3 days, monitoring volume status, kidney function, daily weights, and symptoms (AGA 2025 BPA 12). Refractory anasarca: coordinate with nephrology (acetazolamide, metolazone, or ultrafiltration; AGA 2025 BPA 13)
  • Monitoring: Daily weights, BMP at least 2×/week initially (watch Na, K, Cr)
  • Stop diuretics if (AASLD 2021): AKI (creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, or ≥50% within the prior 7 days); Na 120-125 (stop diuretics, water restriction 1 L/day) or lower; K <3 or >6; hepatic encephalopathy; hypovolemia

Large Volume Paracentesis (LVP):

  • Indications: Tense/refractory ascites, respiratory compromise, severe discomfort, new-onset ascites for diagnosis
  • Volume per session: No fixed limit if albumin is given, but PPCD risk may increase with >8 L in a single session (AASLD 2021). Practical: limit to 8 L per session
  • Albumin replacement: 6-8 g IV per liter removed, as 20-25% albumin, if >5 L removed, to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction (AASLD 2021, expert opinion; AGA 2024 BPA 4; AGA 2025 BPA 6). ACLF: 6-8 g/L regardless of volume removed (AGA 2024). Smaller volumes otherwise: strongly consider albumin if systolic BP <90 mmHg, Na <130, or AKI (AASLD 2021); AGA 2025 BPA 6 adds hypotension, renal insufficiency, or electrolyte abnormalities

Refractory Ascites:

  • Definition: Unresponsive to maximum diuretics + sodium restriction OR development of diuretic-induced complications
  • Management options:
    • Serial large volume paracentesis q2-4 weeks + albumin
    • TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt): refer well-selected patients with refractory ascites, hepatic hydrothorax, volume overload, or hyponatremia (AGA 2025 BPA 7). MELD ≥18 are poor candidates; small-diameter (<10 mm) coated stent preferred to reduce post-TIPS encephalopathy (AASLD 2021). Practical: avoid with active hepatic encephalopathy
    • Liver transplant evaluation, regardless of MELD score (AGA 2025 BPA 4)

Fluid Restriction: Not needed for ascites unless moderate or severe hyponatremia (Na ≤125): 1,000 mL/day for Na 120-125; stricter restriction plus albumin for Na <120 (AASLD 2021)

Hyponatremia (inpatient, severe or symptomatic): Sodium and water restriction; reduce or stop diuretics and laxatives; IV albumin based on volume assessment or oral vasoconstrictor (AGA 2025 BPA 10). Hypertonic saline only short term for symptomatic or severe hyponatremia or imminent transplant; vaptans with caution, 30 days or less. Correction goal 4-6 mEq/L per 24 h, not to exceed 8 mEq/L per 24 h, to limit osmotic demyelination risk (AASLD 2021). Recurrent or refractory: multidisciplinary, including transplant team (AGA 2025 BPA 11)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • 100:40 ratio maintains normokalemia: Spironolactone (K-sparing) + furosemide (K-wasting) balance each other
  • SAAG: ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension with about 97% accuracy; <1.1 suggests other causes. Ascitic protein >2.5 g/dL supports a cardiac source (AASLD 2021)
  • Paracentesis is safe: Elevated INR or thrombocytopenia is not a contraindication; do not give FFP or platelets beforehand (AASLD 2021). In a study of patients with INR >1.5 and platelets <50k, 1% had minimal cutaneous bleeding. Possible exceptions: DIC; uremia with thrombocytopenia (consider desmopressin)
  • SBP prophylaxis (AASLD 2021): Secondary (recovered from SBP): long-term daily norfloxacin; oral ciprofloxacin if norfloxacin unavailable. GI hemorrhage: IV ceftriaxone 1 g/24 h (up to 5 days per AASLD 2024). Primary: can be considered in selected patients with ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL plus renal dysfunction (Cr >1.2, BUN >25, or Na <130) or liver failure (Child-Pugh score >9 and bilirubin >3)
  • Medications to AVOID: NSAIDs (precipitate HRS, worsen ascites), ACE-I/ARBs (hypotension, HRS), aminoglycosides (nephrotoxic)
  • Nonselective beta-blockers (AASLD 2021): Not necessarily contraindicated in refractory ascites; use with caution if hypotension, hyponatremia, or AKI. Hold temporarily in SBP with MAP <65 mmHg or AKI; consider holding in any AKI, especially if hypotensive
  • TIPS considerations: Reduces ascites and variceal bleeding but increases hepatic encephalopathy. Best for refractory ascites with MELD <18
  • Hepatorenal syndrome triggers: SBP, GI bleeding, large volume paracentesis without albumin, overdiuresis
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hemodynamic instability/shock
  • Respiratory failure from tense ascites
  • HRS-AKI (formerly type 1 HRS; AASLD 2021)
  • Grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy
  • Variceal bleeding
  • Severe SBP with sepsis
  • Need for mechanical ventilation
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Ascites improved/controlled on oral diuretics
  • No evidence of SBP (if tapped)
  • Renal function stable (Cr not rising)
  • Electrolytes acceptable (Na >125, K 3.5-5.5)
  • Encephalopathy grade 0-1
  • Patient/family educated on 2g sodium diet
  • Daily weight monitoring arranged
  • Hepatology follow-up within 1-2 weeks
  • Liver transplant referral considered: grade 2 or 3 ascites (AASLD 2021); refractory ascites or hepatic hydrothorax regardless of MELD (AGA 2025 BPA 4)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

From Disease: SBP, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatic hydrothorax, umbilical/inguinal hernia rupture, respiratory compromise, hepatic encephalopathy

From Treatment: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, AKI, muscle cramps, gynecomastia (spironolactone), metabolic alkalosis

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Spironolactone, 💊 Lactulose
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Bilirubin, 🔬 Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated Ammonia, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 Ascitic Fluid Analysis
