17. SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS (SBP)

Infected Ascites • Cirrhotic Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad: Fever, abdominal pain/tenderness, altered mental status in patient with ascites. BUT symptoms may be very subtle!

High Index of Suspicion: Any cirrhotic patient with ascites who clinically deteriorates (worsening encephalopathy, AKI, ileus, hypothermia, unexplained acidosis)

Alternate Presentations:

  • Asymptomatic or atypical SBP: Up to one-third of spontaneous infections are entirely asymptomatic or present only with encephalopathy and/or AKI. Detected by diagnostic paracentesis, indicated on every emergent admission of a patient with cirrhosis and ascites even without signs of infection (AASLD 2021)
  • Hypothermia: Temperature <36°C. Fever or hypothermia should raise suspicion of infection in cirrhosis; no SBP-specific mortality figure is established. In cirrhosis with septic shock, mortality rises about 10% for every hour antibiotics are delayed (AASLD 2021)
  • Isolated Worsening Encephalopathy: May be the ONLY presenting sign
  • Acute Kidney Injury: SBP frequently triggers hepatorenal syndrome
  • Ileus/Decreased Bowel Sounds: Without obvious mechanical obstruction
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Diagnostic Paracentesis: MANDATORY with low threshold! Any clinical suspicion warrants immediate tap

Ascitic Fluid Interpretation (AASLD 2021):

  • PMN >250 cells/mm³: Diagnostic of SBP regardless of culture result (AASLD 2021). Start antibiotics immediately
  • PMN >250 with negative culture: Still SBP; treat the same. Diagnosis rests on the PMN count, not the culture
  • Bacterascites (PMN <250, positive culture): Without signs of infection, no antibiotics (usually self-resolves or is a contaminant); repeat diagnostic paracentesis to look for progression to SBP. AASLD 2021 withholds antibiotics only when signs of infection are absent

Ascitic Fluid Studies:

  • Cell count with differential (STAT): PMN is the key number
  • Gram stain: Usually negative in SBP: organisms seen in 7% of spontaneous vs 40% of secondary peritonitis (Akriviadis and Runyon 1990). Part of initial ascitic fluid testing (AGA 2025 BPA 2)
  • Culture: At bedside, before the first antibiotic dose, inoculate at least 10 mL into aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles; raises culture sensitivity to >90% (AASLD 2021). Send blood cultures at the same time
  • Albumin: For SAAG if new ascites
  • Total protein: <1.5 g/dL predisposes to SBP; 1-year SBP probability 20-60% depending on severity of liver and kidney dysfunction (AASLD 2021). Guides primary prophylaxis; does not diagnose SBP
  • Glucose and LDH: Help distinguish primary from secondary peritonitis

Blood Studies: CBC, CMP, blood cultures × 2, lactate

Common Organisms:

  • Usually monomicrobial; about 60% gram-negative; fungi <5% (AASLD 2021)
  • Most common: E. coli, then Klebsiella pneumoniae, S. aureus, Enterococcus faecalis and E. faecium (AASLD 2021)
  • Series of 1,333 patients (Sanford): gram-negative 55% (E. coli 33%), gram-positive 43% (streptococci 15%, staphylococci 13%, enterococci 9%)
  • Shift toward gram-positive and multidrug-resistant organisms, especially in nosocomial and healthcare-associated SBP (AASLD 2021)

Secondary Bacterial Peritonitis (Gut Perforation): In neutrocytic ascites, suspect perforation if at least 2 of 3 are present (Runyon and Hoefs 1984; Akriviadis and Runyon 1990):

  • Total protein >1 g/dL
  • Glucose <50 mg/dL
  • LDH > upper limit of normal for serum
  • Prospective validation: 100% sensitive but only 45% specific for perforation
  • Organisms on Gram stain in 40% of secondary vs 7% of spontaneous peritonitis
  • Nonperforation secondary peritonitis: ascitic PMN not below baseline after 48 h of antibiotics (fell in all spontaneous but only two-thirds of secondary episodes)
  • If suspected: surgical consult (AASLD 2021). Practical: urgent CT abdomen/pelvis

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Empiric Antibiotics (start IMMEDIATELY if PMN >250):

  • First-line (community-acquired, low MDRO risk): Third-generation cephalosporin (AASLD 2021): ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h (Sanford) or cefotaxime 2 g IV q12h (AASLD 2021; Sanford lists q8h)
  • Nosocomial, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, or sepsis/septic shock: Piperacillin-tazobactam (AASLD 2021; 4.5 g IV q8h extended infusion per Sanford); add vancomycin if prior MRSA or positive MRSA screen; add daptomycin if prior VRE or VRE colonization. Recent piperacillin-tazobactam exposure or known MDR gram-negative: meropenem (1 g IV q8h per Sanford) with or without vancomycin (AASLD 2021)
  • Beta-lactam allergy: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h (Sanford); quinolone resistance is increasing, so discuss with ID
  • Duration: 5-7 days (AASLD 2021). A small study found shorter courses when antibiotics were stopped once ascitic PMN fell below 250

Albumin Infusion (with antibiotics):

  • Day 1: 1.5 g/kg IV at diagnosis
  • Day 3: 1.0 g/kg IV
  • Example: 70kg patient → 105g on day 1, 70g on day 3
  • Mechanism: Prevents hepatorenal syndrome and improves circulatory function
  • Evidence: RCT of 105 patients: AKI 10% vs 33% and death 10% vs 29% with albumin plus antibiotics vs antibiotics alone. Greatest benefit with renal dysfunction (BUN >30 or Cr >1.0) or bilirubin >5 (AASLD 2021). AASLD 2021: give albumin; AGA 2024 BPA 5: may be considered

Follow-up Paracentesis:

  • Response may be assessed by repeat diagnostic paracentesis 2 days after starting antibiotics (AASLD 2021)
  • PMN decrease of less than 25% from baseline indicates lack of response
  • If no response: broaden antibiotic coverage and evaluate for secondary bacterial peritonitis (AASLD 2021)
  • Nonselective beta-blockers: Continue unless hypotensive; hold temporarily if MAP <65 mmHg or AKI develops; restarting may be considered as blood pressure recovers (AASLD 2021)

Secondary Prophylaxis (After SBP Episode Resolves):

  • Duration: Long-term (AASLD 2021): until transplant, or until liver function recovers to a compensated state with resolution of ascites (Sanford)
  • Options:
    • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO daily: reasonable alternative to norfloxacin, though direct evidence is lacking (AASLD 2021; Sanford)
    • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: high-quality data lacking, some experts advocate it (AASLD 2021). Practical: 1 DS tablet PO daily
    • Norfloxacin 400 mg PO daily (Sanford) was the agent of choice but was withdrawn from the US market in 2014 (AASLD 2021)
  • Landmark RCT: 1-year recurrence 20% with norfloxacin vs 68% with placebo (AASLD 2021). Cochrane 2020 network meta-analysis: very low-certainty evidence; benefit of prophylaxis uncertain

Primary Prophylaxis (Never Had SBP):

  • Low-protein ascites (AASLD 2021): Can be considered in selected patients with ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL plus renal dysfunction (Cr >1.2, BUN >25, or Na <130) or liver failure (Child-Pugh score >9 and bilirubin >3). Agent individualized; ciprofloxacin a reasonable choice (consider FDA fluoroquinolone warnings)
  • GI hemorrhage in cirrhosis: IV ceftriaxone 1 g q24h regardless of ascitic protein, until discharge or 5 days, whichever is shorter (AASLD 2024; AASLD 2021 maximum 7 days)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • PMN >250 = Treat NOW: Don't wait for culture; 30-40% of SBP is culture-negative with standard technique (Sanford)
  • Albumin in SBP: 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1 g/kg day 3 with antibiotics (AASLD 2021). Not for infections other than SBP unless AKI is present (AGA 2024)
  • Low threshold to tap: When in doubt, tap. Bleeding is rare even with coagulopathy (1% minimal cutaneous bleeding with INR >1.5 and platelets <50k; AASLD 2021). Missing SBP is worse than an "unnecessary" paracentesis
  • Bedside inoculation: At least 10 mL of ascitic fluid into blood culture bottles at the bedside raises culture sensitivity to >90% (AASLD 2021)
  • Secondary peritonitis clues: In neutrocytic ascites, at least 2 of protein >1 g/dL, glucose <50 mg/dL, LDH > serum ULN suggests gut perforation; sensitive, not specific. Surgical consult and urgent imaging
  • Recurrence: 68% at 1 year with placebo vs 20% with norfloxacin in the landmark RCT (AASLD 2021). Continue secondary prophylaxis long-term
  • No prophylaxis for everyone: Primary prophylaxis only for very high risk (protein <1.5 + advanced disease or GI bleed)
  • Quinolone prophylaxis and encephalopathy: Don't withhold indicated prophylaxis over encephalopathy concern; Cochrane 2020 found no difference in serious adverse events vs no prophylaxis (very low certainty). But ciprofloxacin labeling warns of confusion, delirium, disorientation, and seizures, with renal dysfunction as a seizure risk factor (FDA label 5.4): in refractory or atypical encephalopathy, consider drug neurotoxicity after the usual precipitants, and dose ciprofloxacin for renal function
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Septic shock requiring vasopressors
  • Respiratory failure needing intubation
  • Severe hepatic encephalopathy (grade 3-4)
  • Rapidly progressive AKI/HRS
  • Hypothermia or severe sepsis
  • No clinical improvement despite 48hr treatment
  • Suspected secondary peritonitis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Completed minimum 5 days antibiotics
  • Afebrile × 24-48 hours
  • Clinical symptoms resolved
  • Renal function stable or improving
  • Repeat paracentesis (if done) with PMN <250
  • Started on secondary prophylaxis
  • Close hepatology follow-up arranged
  • Transplant evaluation if not already listed
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: AKI/HRS-AKI (AKI 33% with antibiotics alone vs 10% with albumin in the pivotal RCT, AGA 2024; AKI is the main predictor of in-hospital death, AASLD 2021), septic shock, paralytic ileus, worsening hepatic encephalopathy, death (short-term mortality about 15-40%, Cochrane 2020)

Recurrence: 68% at 1 year without prophylaxis vs 20% with norfloxacin (landmark RCT, AASLD 2021)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Albumin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Ascitic Fluid Analysis, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
🧫 ABX COMPANION Cunha Empiric Framework
→ Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

18. HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY

Altered Mental Status in Cirrhosis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

West Haven Grading (ACG 2026, Figure 7):

  • Grade 0: Abnormal psychometric/neuropsychological tests without clinical manifestations
  • Grade 1: Impaired attention/computations/sleep; euphoria/anxiety; oriented to time/space
  • Grade 2: Disoriented to time/space; inappropriate behavior; personality changes; dyspraxia; asterixis; apathy
  • Grade 3: Somnolence/semistupor; gross disorientation; confusion; bizarre behavior; responsive to stimuli
  • Grade 4: Coma
  • Minimal (grade 0) or grade 1 = covert HE (CHE); grade 2 or higher = overt HE (OHE) (ACG 2026 key concept 1)

Physical Exam Findings:

  • Asterixis: Flapping tremor of the hands with wrists hyperextended; a West Haven grade 2 feature that can also be elicited in lower grades, including CHE (ACG 2026). Isolated asterixis without changes in behavior or alertness does not diagnose OHE (ACG 2026 key concept 2)
  • Hyperreflexia: Increased deep tendon reflexes (HESA grade 2); clonus, rigidity, Babinski sign, or nystagmus (HESA grade 3) (ACG 2026, Figure 7)
  • Stigmata of chronic liver disease: Spider angioma, palmar erythema, splenomegaly, abdominal wall collaterals (AASLD 2021 ascites guidance); signs of decompensation such as ascites or jaundice (ACG 2026)

Alternate Presentations:

  • Acute Change: Sudden worsening in a previously stable patient; evaluate for bleeding, infection, sedating medications, and toxic and metabolic abnormalities (ACG 2026 key concept 10)
  • Post-TIPS: HE occurs in 30-40% of patients after TIPS (ACG 2026)
  • Covert HE (CHE): Subtle cognitive or behavioral changes reported by the patient or caregivers and/or identified by an experienced clinician; consider testing with work difficulties, traffic violations, motor vehicle accidents, or unprovoked falls (ACG 2026)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Diagnosis of Exclusion: Rule out other causes of altered mental status first!

Essential Studies:

  • Labs: CBC, CMP, venous pH/lactate. Ammonia not needed to guide treatment (ACG 2026 rec 5, conditional); if checked and normal, look for other causes (ACG 2026 key concept 11)
  • Infection workup: Blood and urine cultures in all patients; diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid culture if ascites present (rule out SBP); stool and sputum cultures if clinically suspected (ACG 2026). If no response to lactulose with or without rifaximin within 48 h, search for infection with pan-culture, paracentesis, and chest x-ray (ACG 2026). Practical: urinalysis and chest x-ray on admission
  • Toxicology screen: Urine drug screen to verify the history of central-acting medications or recreational drugs; intoxication or withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opiates, other drugs) is in the differential (ACG 2026)
  • Brain imaging (CT or MRI): Not routine in cirrhosis with confusion and no new focal neurologic deficits (ACG 2026 rec 6, conditional, very low certainty); it does not diagnose HE. Image, with neurology consult, if new focal deficits; consider with seizures, recent head trauma or falls, or no response to HE treatment, to look for subdural hematoma, subarachnoid bleed, stroke, or brain lesion (ACG 2026)

Identify Precipitants (ACG 2026):

  • Infection: Most common cause of hospital admission in cirrhosis and a common HE precipitant; include skin and oral cavity in the search
  • GI bleeding
  • Constipation: Including ileus or small bowel obstruction
  • Dehydration: Including diuretic overdose and diarrhea from lactulose overuse
  • AKI and electrolyte disorders: Hyponatremia; hypokalemia (including from lactulose overuse)
  • Medications: CNS depressants: benzodiazepines, opioids (also slow gut motility, increasing ammonia absorption), gabapentin and related GABAergic drugs, zolpidem. Also proton pump inhibitors
  • Lactulose nonadherence: With dehydration, a common cause of breakthrough HE on lactulose
  • Portosystemic shunting: TIPS or spontaneous portosystemic shunts (SPSS)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Identify and Treat Precipitant (MOST IMPORTANT!):

  • Tap ascites (rule out SBP)
  • Check for GI bleeding
  • Treat infections
  • Review medication list - stop sedatives/opioids
  • Correct electrolyte abnormalities

2. Lactulose (First-line Therapy; ACG 2026, strong):

  • Initial dose: 10-20 g (15-30 mL) PO every 2 hours until 2 soft bowel movements (ACG 2026)
  • Maintenance: Reduce to 2-4 times daily, titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026)
  • Goal: Acidify colon, decrease ammonia production/absorption
  • If cannot take PO (grade 3-4 or aspiration risk): Nasogastric tube at oral dosing, or retention enema if anal sphincter tone preserved: 300 mL lactulose solution in 700 mL water or normal saline, retain 30-60 min, repeat every 4-6 h until mental status improves (ACG 2026)
  • Alternative: High-volume (e.g., 4 L) polyethylene glycol 3350, PO or by NG tube (ACG 2026, conditional); consider with abdominal distension, ileus, or lactulose intolerance
  • Watch for: Overuse causes perianal skin irritation or infection, ileus, aspiration, dehydration, hypernatremia, and hypokalemia, which can precipitate HE recurrence (ACG 2026)

3. Rifaximin (add to lactulose; ACG 2026):

  • Dose: 550 mg PO BID (FDA-approved dose for reducing OHE recurrence)
  • Mechanism: Non-absorbable antibiotic, reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria
  • Evidence: RCT of 299 patients with 2 or more OHE episodes in 6 months (91% on lactulose): 58% risk reduction in breakthrough OHE (NNT 4) and 50% in HE hospitalization (NNT 9). Acute OHE: one RCT of rifaximin plus lactulose showed higher complete reversal, shorter stay, and lower mortality; acute role less defined
  • Practical: often requires prior authorization; start the process before discharge
  • Indications: Recurrent OHE on lactulose (strong, high certainty); acute OHE, added to lactulose (conditional, low); outpatient prevention after OHE (conditional, low)

4. Zinc (adjunct in selected patients; ACG 2026):

  • Indication: Persistent symptoms despite lactulose and rifaximin, with low blood zinc (ACG 2026 rec 14, conditional, very low certainty). Practical: zinc sulfate 220 mg PO daily (dose not specified in ACG 2026)
  • Efficacy data conflicting; appears safe as an adjunct and may improve cognition when added to lactulose (ACG 2026)
  • Zinc deficiency reduces urea cycle efficiency (ACG 2026)

5. Recurrent or Refractory HE Despite Optimized Therapy (ACG 2026):

  • Imaging: CT or MRI to look for spontaneous portosystemic shunts (SPSS) if HE recurs or persists despite adequate medical treatment (ACG 2026)
  • Shunt embolization: Suggested for refractory HE on optimized medical therapy with adequate hepatic function and no contraindications (ACG 2026 rec 16, conditional, very low certainty). Best candidates: MELD usually under 15, shunts 8 mm or larger (ACG 2026)
  • After embolization: Reassess HE symptoms, labs, and liver Doppler at 1 month (thrombosis, new ascites); EGD at 6 months (new or worse varices); cross-sectional imaging at 1 year (new SPSS) (ACG 2026)

6. Supportive Care:

  • Airway protection if grade 3-4 (consider intubation)
  • Avoid or discontinue sedatives (ACG 2026, Figure 8); avoid benzodiazepines; prefer short-acting agents and short boluses over infusions. If sedation is needed in hospitalized ACLF (e.g., intubated), dexmedetomidine is suggested (ACG 2022 ACLF, conditional). Practical: if an antipsychotic is needed for dangerous agitation, use the lowest dose with QTc monitoring
  • Nutrition: Do not restrict protein (ACG 2026 rec 20, conditional). Target 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day (rec 17, strong); critically ill up to 2 g/kg/day (key concept 22); BCAA supplement if needs not met by food (rec 18, strong); late-night snack (rec 19, conditional)

What NOT to Do:

  • Do NOT restrict protein: Increases muscle breakdown and does not shorten HE (ACG 2026 rec 20)
  • Neomycin: Not addressed in ACG 2026. FDA-labeled as adjunctive therapy in hepatic coma, but carries a boxed warning: systemic absorption after oral dosing, with neurotoxicity (including ototoxicity), nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade; higher risk with advanced age, dehydration, or impaired renal function (FDA label, Teva, rev. 10/2022). Practical: avoid; rifaximin preferred
  • Ammonia level: Don't use to guide treatment or follow serially; venous levels do not correlate with HE severity (ACG 2026)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Always find the precipitant: HE rarely occurs without a trigger. Treat the cause, not just the symptom
  • Ammonia: No diagnostic threshold; levels don't track severity, and sample handling and protein intake affect values. A low or normal level has negative predictive value for HE as the cause of altered mentation and should prompt evaluation for other causes (ACG 2026)
  • Protein restriction is wrong: Target 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day (ACG 2026 rec 17, strong); up to 2 g/kg/day if critically ill
  • Vegetable protein: Small studies (10 patients or fewer) suggest benefit; substituting one meat meal lowered postprandial ammonia (ACG 2026). Practical: don't eliminate meat entirely
  • Lactulose goals: 2-3 soft BMs/day (Bristol 3-4), avoiding diarrhea and hypernatremia (ACG 2026, Figure 8). Too much: dehydration, hypernatremia, hypokalemia; too little: constipation, an HE precipitant (ACG 2026)
  • Rifaximin timing: ACG 2026 suggests adding rifaximin to lactulose in acute OHE (conditional) and recommends it for recurrence on lactulose (strong)
  • Post-TIPS HE: Occurs in 30-40%; refractory in 3-7%, mostly when the portosystemic gradient falls by more than 60% (ACG 2026). Prevention: start rifaximin 14 days before elective TIPS and continue at least 6 months in decompensated cirrhosis (ACG 2026 rec 22, strong); embolize extrahepatic collaterals at TIPS (rec 23, conditional). Refractory cases: the TIPS may require closure, and patients with HE should be referred for transplant evaluation (ACG 2026). Practical: TIPS diameter reduction is an alternative to closure
  • Asterixis is NOT specific: Also seen in other metabolic encephalopathies, such as uremia (ACG 2026)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • West Haven grade 3-4 HE: step-down unit or MICU; grade 2: floor (ACG 2026 key concept 9, Figure 8). Monitor with GCS when consciousness is significantly impaired (ACG 2026)
  • Inability to protect airway or need for intubation (ACG 2026)
  • Practical: rapidly progressive deterioration, hemodynamic instability, or severe concurrent illness (sepsis, GI bleeding)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: mental status at baseline (grade 0-1)
  • Precipitant identified and treated (ACG 2026 key concept 10)
  • Lactulose dose established, titrated to 2-3 soft BMs/day (Bristol 3-4) (ACG 2026)
  • Rifaximin added for recurrent HE (ACG 2026, strong); consider after a first episode (conditional)
  • Patient and caregivers educated on HE signs and lactulose use, with HE educational materials (ACG 2026 key concept 18)
  • Oral and written advice to avoid driving after overt HE within the past 3 months, given to patient and caregivers (ACG 2026 key concept 17)
  • Nutrition plan and physical therapy (ACG 2026, Figure 8)
  • Practical: hepatology follow-up within 1 week
  • Refer for transplant evaluation if not listed (ACG 2026); consider early evaluation with high MELD 3.0, grade 3-4 HE, or frequent episodes (ACG 2026 key concept 28)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Aspiration pneumonia, falls/trauma, pressure ulcers, malnutrition, inability to take medications

Chronic: Recurrent HE (about 40-60% have a second episode within 1 year; ACG 2026), cognitive decline, poor quality of life, increased mortality

From Treatment: Lactulose overuse: perianal skin irritation or infection, ileus, aspiration, dehydration, hypernatremia, hypokalemia. Other lactulose adverse effects are generally mild: nausea, bloating, flatulence, diarrhea (ACG 2026)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lactulose, 💊 Rifaximin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Ammonia, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hypokalemia

19. ACUTE PANCREATITIS

Gallstones • Alcohol • Hypertriglyceridemia
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Epigastric or left upper quadrant pain, usually constant, radiating to the back, chest, or flanks; intensity and location do not correlate with severity. Dull, colicky, or lower abdominal pain suggests another diagnosis. Vomiting and reduced intake add to hypovolemia (ACG 2024)

Physical Exam: Assess for SIRS, signs of hypovolemia, altered mental status, and pleural effusion, which are risk factors for severe disease (ACG 2024, Table 4). Bowel sounds should be present before early oral feeding (ACG 2024)

Causes (ACG 2024):

  • Gallstones: 40-70%; transabdominal ultrasound in all patients, repeat if inconclusive (rec 1, conditional, very low)
  • Alcohol: 25-35%; requires more than 5 years of moderate or heavy use; only up to 5% of heavy drinkers develop AP
  • Hypertriglyceridemia: About 5% of cases (up to 56% in pregnancy); TG should exceed 1,000 mg/dL to be considered the cause (KC 2). Serum is lactescent in up to 20%, so recheck fasting TG 1 month after discharge
  • Post-ERCP pancreatitis
  • Pancreatobiliary tumor: Consider if older than 40 with no other cause (KC 3); 5-14% of patients with these tumors present with idiopathic AP
  • Drugs: Azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, and didanosine clearly cause AP; data are limited for most other drugs
  • Rare and often falsely attributed: Other medications, infections, hypercalcemia
  • Idiopathic: No cause after labs (including TG and calcium) and imaging. Repeat ultrasound, MRI, and/or EUS (rec 2, conditional, very low); avoid routine ERCP. Cholecystectomy after a second idiopathic episode if fit for surgery (KC 4)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Diagnosis Requires 2 of 3 (ACG 2024):

  • 1. Characteristic abdominal pain
  • 2. Serum lipase (preferred) or amylase >3× upper limit of normal; amylase alone is unreliable, and lipase stays elevated longer
  • 3. Characteristic imaging findings (contrast CT: over 90% sensitivity and specificity)

Labs:

  • Lipase: Do not repeat once the diagnosis is made; levels do not track severity or prognosis and should not guide refeeding or discharge (ACG 2024)
  • CBC, CMP (calcium, creatinine), triglycerides, LFTs (ACG 2024). BUN and hematocrit at baseline and serially: elevated or rising values predict severe disease (KC 9)

Imaging:

  • Transabdominal ultrasound: All patients, for gallstones; repeat if inconclusive (ACG 2024 rec 1)
  • CT or MRI: Not routine at admission to assess severity; reserve for unclear diagnosis or no improvement after 48-72 h (KC 1). Necrosis is usually absent on admission and may develop after 24-48 h. CT and MRI are comparable; MRI if contrast allergy or renal insufficiency, and better for CBD stones (ACG 2024)
  • MRCP or EUS: See ERCP below. Routine preoperative MRCP is unnecessary in mild AP with normal bilirubin (ACG 2024)

Severity (Revised Atlanta definitions, per ACG 2024):

  • Mild: No organ failure and no local complications; usually interstitial (edematous) pancreatitis
  • Moderately severe: Transient organ failure (resolves within 48 h) and/or local complications (fluid collections, necrotic collections, pseudocyst, walled-off necrosis)
  • Severe: Persistent organ failure (more than 48 h)
  • Organ failure: Shock (SBP under 90), PaO2 under 60, creatinine over 2 mg/dL after rehydration, GI bleeding over 500 mL/24 h, or modified Marshall score 2 or more
  • Predicting severity: Scoring systems and imaging alone are not accurate (KC 7). Ranson and APACHE II are cumbersome and need 48 h; BISAP (includes BUN and SIRS) performs better but may be no more accurate than monitoring BUN and SIRS. SIRS in the first 24 h: sensitivity 85% for organ failure, specificity 41% for severe disease
  • Risk factors for severe disease (Table 4, KC 9): Age over 55, BMI over 30, altered mental status, comorbidity, SIRS, BUN over 20 or rising, hematocrit over 44 or rising, elevated creatinine, pleural effusions or infiltrates
  • Even in mild disease, watch for severe disease and organ failure during the first 48 h (KC 8)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Fluid Resuscitation (ACG 2024):

  • Volume: Moderately aggressive IV fluids (rec 3, conditional, low). Without hypovolemia, no more than 1.5 mL/kg/h initially; with hypovolemia, 10 mL/kg bolus, with more boluses as needed. Most patients need about 3-4 L in the first 24 h, depending on BMI
  • Fluid: Lactated Ringer's over normal saline (rec 4, conditional, low)
  • Timing: Fluids matter most in the first 24 h (KC 11). After 24 h, or once severe disease develops, aggressive hydration may be harmful
  • Monitoring: Heart rate, blood pressure, urine output; aim for falling BUN and hematocrit. Reassess within 6 h (latest by 6-8 h after admission) and over the next 24-48 h (KC 12)
  • Caution: Older patients and those with cardiac or renal disease: monitor for volume overload, pulmonary edema, and abdominal compartment syndrome (KC 10)
  • WATERFALL RCT (de-Madaria, NEJM 2022): Moderate hydration over the first 24-48 h was as effective as aggressive hydration, with less volume overload (as summarized in ACG 2024)

Nutrition (ACG 2024):

  • Mild AP: Early oral feeding within 24-48 h as tolerated, instead of NPO (rec 10, conditional, low); start with a low-fat solid diet, no clear-liquid step (rec 11, conditional, low). Meta-analyses also support early oral feeding in moderately severe and severe AP
  • Before feeding: Bowel sounds present and no significant nausea, vomiting, or ileus
  • Cannot eat: Enteral nutrition, nasogastric preferred over nasojejunal (KC 20), continuous rather than bolus; it seems to prevent infection in moderately severe or severe AP (KC 18). Avoid parenteral nutrition unless enteral is not possible, not tolerated, or not meeting needs (KC 19)
  • Predicted severe AP: Tube feeding started within 24 h did not reduce infection or mortality compared with on-demand feeding (ACG 2024)

Pain Control:

  • Practical: IV opioids as needed (morphine, hydromorphone). ACG 2024 does not address analgesia
  • Opioids vs other analgesics: no difference in pancreatitis complications or clinically serious adverse events, and opioids may reduce the need for supplementary analgesia (Cochrane 2013, 5 RCTs, 227 patients)

ERCP (ACG 2024):

  • Cholangitis: ERCP within 24 h; decreases morbidity and mortality (KC 13)
  • Biliary AP without cholangitis: Medical therapy over early ERCP within 72 h (rec 5, conditional, low). Urgent ERCP only for cholangitis or progressive cholestasis (rising bilirubin, over 3-5 mg/dL) in moderately severe or severe AP
  • Suspected CBD stone without cholangitis or jaundice: MRCP or EUS first; avoid diagnostic ERCP (KC 14)
  • Unfit for cholecystectomy: Biliary sphincterotomy prevents recurrent biliary AP

Antibiotics (ACG 2024):

  • No prophylactic antibiotics, including in severe AP (rec 8, conditional, very low); none for sterile necrosis (KC 15)
  • Suspected infection: Start antibiotics while the source is confirmed; stop if cultures are negative and no source is found. Early SIRS can mimic sepsis
  • Infected necrosis: Confirmed by blood or other cultures or by gas in the necrosis; FNA not suggested (rec 9, conditional, very low). Use agents that penetrate necrosis: carbapenems, quinolones, cephalosporins, metronidazole. No routine antifungals (KC 17)
  • Goal in infected necrosis: Delay drainage beyond 4 weeks; some patients avoid drainage entirely (KC 16)

Cholecystectomy (Biliary AP; ACG 2024):

  • Mild biliary AP: Cholecystectomy early, preferably before discharge (KC 21)
  • Without same-admission cholecystectomy, 18% were readmitted for recurrent biliary events (8% recurrent biliary pancreatitis) vs 0% with early cholecystectomy
  • Necrotizing biliary AP: Cholecystectomy is typically delayed; joint surgical and GI decision
  • After biliary sphincterotomy: Still refer for cholecystectomy, depending on age and comorbidity
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • LR over NS: Suggested (ACG 2024 rec 4, conditional, low); in RCTs, less SIRS, and fewer ICU admissions with shorter stays
  • Early feeding is safe: Low-fat solid diet within 24-48 h in mild AP (ACG 2024 recs 10, 11)
  • No prophylactic antibiotics: Better-designed trials show no benefit (ACG 2024 rec 8). Treat suspected infection; stop if cultures are negative
  • CT timing: Necrosis is usually absent on admission and may develop after 24-48 h; image only for unclear diagnosis or no improvement after 48-72 h (ACG 2024 KC 1)
  • Lipase over amylase: Lipase preferred; amylase alone is unreliable and may be normal in alcohol- or TG-induced AP (ACG 2024)
  • Hypertriglyceridemia: TG over 1,000 mg/dL to be the cause (ACG 2024 KC 2). Practical: insulin infusion acutely. Long term: dietitian referral for TG 1,000 or more is recommended; fibrate or prescription omega-3 is reasonable for TG 500 or more, especially 1,000 or more, despite diet (ACC/AHA 2026 dyslipidemia)
  • Sterile vs infected necrosis: Can look identical (fever, leukocytosis, organ failure); gas in the necrosis or positive cultures confirm infection. Stable infected necrosis: antibiotics, and delay any intervention, preferably 4 weeks; minimally invasive approach preferred (ACG 2024 KC 16, 22, 23). Intervene sooner if unstable or not responding. Sterile necrosis: no antibiotics (KC 15)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • SIRS: monitored bed; organ failure: ICU (ACG 2024 KC 6)
  • Assess hemodynamic status and risk early to triage to a nonmonitored, monitored, or ICU bed (KC 5)
  • In one study, organ failure, SIRS, or BISAP 3 or more prompted ICU consideration (ACG 2024)
  • Practical: hemodynamic instability; infected necrosis with clinical deterioration
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Tolerating oral diet without persistent nausea; persistent nausea at discharge risks readmission (ACG 2024)
  • Do not use the lipase trend to decide refeeding or discharge (ACG 2024)
  • Practical: pain controlled on oral medications; no organ dysfunction
  • Mild biliary AP: cholecystectomy before discharge (ACG 2024 KC 21)
  • Alcohol-related AP: treat alcohol use, which reduces recurrence and progression to chronic pancreatitis (ACG 2024)
  • Suspected hypertriglyceridemia: fasting TG 1 month after discharge (ACG 2024)
  • Idiopathic AP: outpatient repeat ultrasound and TG; consider tumor if older than 40 (ACG 2024 KC 3)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Early: About 20% develop moderately severe or severe AP: organ failure (shock, respiratory, renal), pancreatic necrosis (sterile or infected; infected necrosis mortality averages 30%), acute fluid collections; from fluids, volume overload and abdominal compartment syndrome (ACG 2024). Practical: hypocalcemia

Late: Walled-off necrosis (wall forms after about 4 weeks), pseudocyst, recurrent AP (20-29%), chronic pancreatitis (ACG 2024). Practical: splenic or portal vein thrombosis, diabetes, exocrine insufficiency

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Morphine, 💊 Hydromorphone, 💊 Ketorolac, 💊 Ondansetron
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Lipase, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Hypercalcemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Low Albumin

20. CELLULITIS

Skin/Soft Tissue Infection
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Acute onset of erythema, warmth, edema, and tenderness in affected area. Usually unilateral lower extremity. Pain typically present. Systemic symptoms: fever, chills, malaise in 40-60% of hospitalized patients

Physical Exam: Ill-defined borders spreading centrifugally (vs erysipelas which has raised sharp borders), no fluctuance (vs abscess), lymphangitic streaking in 15-20%, regional lymphadenopathy. Measure and mark borders with pen. Look for portal of entry (trauma, tinea pedis, fissures)

Common Organisms: β-hemolytic Streptococcus (Group A Strep, most common in non-purulent), Staphylococcus aureus (especially MRSA if purulent/abscess present)

Risk Factors: Obesity, diabetes mellitus, venous insufficiency, chronic lymphedema, tinea pedis (toe web intertrigo), immunosuppression, prior cellulitis (20-30% recurrence rate), skin barrier disruption

Alternate Presentations:

  • Erysipelas: Superficial cellulitis with sharply demarcated, raised, indurated borders. "Orange peel" appearance. Almost always Group A Strep. Face and legs most common
  • Periorbital Cellulitis: Eyelid edema, erythema WITHOUT vision changes or pain with eye movement (vs orbital cellulitis which needs emergent CT/ENT). Can progress to orbital cellulitis
  • Facial Cellulitis: Consider dental source (odontogenic), sinusitis. Higher risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis if near nasolabial triangle
  • Diabetic Patients: More likely polymicrobial, higher risk of progression to necrotizing infection. Check for gas on imaging
  • Immunocompromised: Consider atypical organisms (fungi, mycobacteria, Pseudomonas). May lack fever/leukocytosis despite severe infection
  • Post-Surgical: If within 48 hours, consider Group A Strep (rapidly progressive, very painful). If days later, S. aureus more likely
  • Water Exposure: Vibrio vulnificus (salt water), Aeromonas (fresh water) - both can cause necrotizing fasciitis. Ask about water exposure!
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis: Based on appearance - culture/biopsy rarely needed for typical cellulitis. Positive predictive value of clinical diagnosis >70% by experienced clinicians

Labs (Obtain if systemic symptoms or severe):

  • CBC: Leukocytosis common (WBC >12k in 50%), left shift. Leukopenia concerning for overwhelming sepsis
  • Blood Cultures: Low yield (<5% positive) but obtain if: fever >38.5°C, hypotension, immunocompromised, suspected bacteremia, failed outpatient therapy
  • ESR/CRP: Elevated but non-specific. Can be useful if diagnosis uncertain or to follow treatment response
  • BMP: If systemic toxicity (assess renal function before vancomycin/aminoglycosides)
  • Lactate: If concern for sepsis or necrotizing infection

Imaging (NOT routinely needed):

  • Ultrasound: Can differentiate cellulitis from abscess. "Cobblestoning" of subcutaneous tissue seen in cellulitis. Can identify fluid collections needing drainage
  • CT with IV contrast: If necrotizing fasciitis suspected (gas in tissues, fascial involvement), deep abscess, osteomyelitis concern
  • MRI: Gold standard for osteomyelitis, deep space infections, necrotizing fasciitis. Use if diagnosis unclear and high clinical suspicion
  • X-ray: Can identify foreign body, subcutaneous gas (necrotizing infection), osteomyelitis (after 2 weeks)

Culture/Biopsy (Consider if):

  • Purulent drainage present → Send for culture & sensitivity (guides antibiotic de-escalation)
  • Failed initial therapy
  • Immunocompromised (atypical organisms)
  • Penetrating trauma or water exposure (atypical organisms)
  • Punch biopsy/aspiration: Low yield (20-40% positive), painful, generally not recommended for uncomplicated cellulitis

Mark Borders: Draw around erythema with marker, date/time. Essential for tracking progression/regression. Take photo for documentation

Differential Diagnosis to Consider:

  • Stasis Dermatitis: Bilateral, chronic, hyperpigmentation, varicose veins. Often misdiagnosed as cellulitis
  • DVT: Asymmetric edema but typically no erythema. Get duplex if uncertain
  • Contact Dermatitis: Pruritic, vesicular, bilateral distribution, exposure history
  • Necrotizing Fasciitis: Pain out of proportion, hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, systemic toxicity, rapid progression
  • Gout/Pseudogout: Acute monoarticular arthritis, usually joint-based
  • Lipodermatosclerosis: Chronic, indurated, inverted champagne bottle appearance of lower leg
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Key Decision: Purulent vs Non-Purulent

  • Non-Purulent: No drainable abscess, no purulent discharge → Target Streptococcus, NO MRSA coverage needed
  • Purulent: Abscess, furuncle, carbuncle, purulent drainage → MUST cover MRSA

Non-Purulent Cellulitis (No Abscess/Furuncle) - Streptococcal Coverage:

  • Mild (Outpatient):
    • Cephalexin 500mg PO QID × 5-10 days (first-line)
    • Dicloxacillin 500mg PO QID × 5-10 days
    • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg BID × 5-10 days
  • Moderate (Inpatient/Observation):
    • Cefazolin 1-2g IV q8h (excellent Strep/MSSA coverage)
    • Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV q24h (good for once-daily dosing)
  • PCN Allergy (Non-anaphylaxis):
    • Cephalosporins safe if non-IgE mediated reaction (~98% safe)
  • Severe PCN Allergy (Anaphylaxis):
    • Clindamycin 600mg IV q8h OR 300-450mg PO TID (covers Strep/MSSA, not MRSA reliably)
    • Doxycycline 100mg PO/IV BID
    • Levofloxacin 750mg PO/IV daily (avoid if other options available)

Purulent Cellulitis (WITH Abscess/Drainage) - MRSA Coverage Required:

  • Mild (Outpatient):
    • TMP-SMX DS 1-2 tabs PO BID × 5-10 days (excellent MRSA coverage)
    • Doxycycline 100mg PO BID × 5-10 days
    • Clindamycin 300-450mg PO TID × 5-10 days (if local resistance <10%)
  • Moderate-Severe (Inpatient):
    • Vancomycin 15-20mg/kg IV q8-12h (goal trough 15-20 for complicated infections)
    • Daptomycin 4mg/kg IV q24h (skin infections, not if pulmonary involvement)
    • Linezolid 600mg PO/IV BID (excellent bioavailability, reserve for VRE risk)
  • I&D (Incision & Drainage): Drain abscess if present. Send purulent material for culture & sensitivity. I&D alone may be sufficient for small abscesses <5cm without surrounding cellulitis

Severe/Complicated Cellulitis:

  • Septic/Toxic appearance: Vancomycin 15-20mg/kg IV q8-12h + Pip-tazo 3.375g IV q6h
  • Necrotizing Fasciitis Concern: Vancomycin + Pip-tazo + Clindamycin 900mg IV q8h (clindamycin inhibits toxin production). IMMEDIATE surgical consultation
  • Immunocompromised: Broader coverage - consider Vancomycin + Cefepime or Vancomycin + Meropenem
  • Water Exposure:
    • Salt water (Vibrio): Doxycycline 100mg IV BID + Ceftriaxone 1g IV q24h
    • Fresh water (Aeromonas): Ceftriaxone + Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h

Special Populations:

  • Diabetes: Lower threshold to admit. Check for gas on imaging. Consider broader coverage if severe or neuropathy present
  • Cirrhosis: Higher risk of Vibrio if shellfish exposure. Consider ceftriaxone + doxycycline
  • Neutropenic: Cefepime or meropenem + vancomycin. Consider antifungal if not improving
  • Bite Wounds:
    • Human/Animal: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg BID OR Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV q6h
    • PCN allergic: Doxycycline + Metronidazole OR Moxifloxacin

Adjunct Measures:

  • Elevation: Keep affected limb elevated above heart level. CRITICAL for reducing edema and speeding recovery
  • Analgesia: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600mg q6h) or acetaminophen 1g q6h. NSAIDs have anti-inflammatory benefit
  • Treat Underlying Conditions:
    • Tinea pedis: Topical antifungal (terbinafine cream BID × 2 weeks)
    • Venous insufficiency: Compression stockings after acute infection resolves
    • Edema: Diuretics if appropriate, elevation, compression
  • Wound Care: Keep clean and dry. Gentle cleansing with soap and water. No need for topical antibiotics

Duration of Therapy:

  • Standard: 5-10 days typical. Minimum 5 days if rapidly improving
  • Severe: 10-14 days if slow response, extensive disease, or immunocompromised
  • Transition to PO: When afebrile >24hr, improving cellulitis, tolerating PO, stable vitals
  • Response Time: Expect improvement within 48-72 hours. Erythema may initially expand first 24-48hr despite appropriate antibiotics (inflammatory response). If not improving by 72hr, re-evaluate

Recurrent Cellulitis Prevention:

  • ≥2 episodes/year or ≥3 lifetime: Consider prophylaxis
  • Penicillin VK 250mg PO BID OR Erythromycin 250mg PO BID (indefinitely or seasonally)
  • Address predisposing factors: Treat tinea pedis aggressively, compression for lymphedema/venous insufficiency, good skin hygiene
  • Patient education: Early recognition and treatment at first sign reduces hospitalizations
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • MRSA coverage ONLY if purulent: Overuse of vancomycin drives resistance. Non-purulent cellulitis = β-lactam monotherapy. Don't reflexively add vanc!
  • Mark borders religiously: Date and time your marking. Simple intervention that objectively tracks progression/regression and improves clinical decision-making
  • Elevation is NOT optional: Elevating the affected limb above heart level significantly speeds recovery by reducing venous congestion and edema. It's as important as antibiotics!
  • Recurrent cellulitis screening questions: Ask about tinea pedis (toe web maceration = portal of entry), lymphedema, venous insufficiency. Treating these reduces recurrence dramatically
  • Purpura = NOT cellulitis: If non-blanching purpura present, think necrotizing fasciitis, meningococcemia, septic emboli, vasculitis. Blanching erythema = cellulitis
  • Pain out of proportion = Surgical Emergency: If pain is much worse than exam findings suggest, think necrotizing fasciitis. Also: hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, "wooden" induration, rapid progression, systemic toxicity → STAT surgical consult + broad antibiotics + clindamycin
  • Initial expansion doesn't mean failure: Cellulitis commonly gets worse in first 24-48 hours despite appropriate antibiotics due to inflammatory response. Don't panic and broaden coverage unless systemic symptoms worsen
  • Stasis dermatitis masquerader: #1 cellulitis mimic. Clues: Bilateral (cellulitis usually unilateral), chronic course, hyperpigmentation, varicose veins, hemosiderin deposition, pruritus > pain. Don't treat with antibiotics!
  • LRINEC score for necrotizing fasciitis: CRP, WBC, Hgb, Na, Cr, glucose. Score ≥6 → 50% PPV for NF. Score ≥8 → 75% PPV. But don't wait for lab results if clinical suspicion high!
  • Blood cultures low yield: Only 5% positive in cellulitis, but still obtain if fever >38.5°C or concern for bacteremia. Don't withhold antibiotics waiting for culture results
  • Prophylaxis pearls: For recurrent cellulitis (≥2/year), continuous penicillin prophylaxis reduces recurrence by 50%. But address underlying causes first (tinea pedis treatment, compression, lymphedema therapy)
  • Failed therapy checklist: Wrong diagnosis (stasis dermatitis, DVT)? Inadequate coverage (MRSA not covered)? Abscess needing drainage? Underlying osteomyelitis? Deep space infection? Non-infectious cause?
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Necrotizing fasciitis suspected or confirmed (pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, "wooden" feel)
  • Septic shock (SBP <90 despite fluids, lactate >4)
  • Rapidly progressive cellulitis despite IV antibiotics (expanding >5cm/hr)
  • Compartment syndrome (tense compartment, pain with passive stretch, paresthesias, pulselessness)
  • Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (hypotension + multi-organ dysfunction)
  • Airway compromise (facial/neck cellulitis, Ludwig's angina)
  • Need for vasopressors or aggressive resuscitation
  • Hemodynamic instability with failed floor management
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Afebrile × 24 hours (Temp <38°C)
  • Hemodynamically stable (SBP >90, HR <110)
  • Erythema/edema clearly improving (borders regressing)
  • Pain controlled on oral analgesics
  • Tolerating PO intake and oral antibiotics
  • No evidence of abscess requiring drainage
  • No concern for necrotizing infection
  • Adequate home support for elevation/wound care
  • Close follow-up arranged within 2-3 days
  • Patient educated on: limb elevation, signs of worsening, medication adherence
  • If diabetes: glucose controlled, good perfusion to affected area
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Local Complications: Abscess formation (fluctuance, purulent drainage - needs I&D), necrotizing fasciitis (pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, rapid progression), compartment syndrome (increased pressure in fascial compartment - surgical emergency), lymphangitis (red streaking), chronic lymphedema (after repeated episodes), post-infectious scarring/hyperpigmentation

Systemic Complications: Bacteremia/sepsis (5-10% of hospitalized patients), septic shock, endocarditis (especially MRSA bacteremia), osteomyelitis (if bone involvement), septic arthritis (if joint nearby), glomerulonephritis (post-Streptococcal), toxic shock syndrome (Strep or Staph toxins)

Treatment-Related: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, C. difficile infection, drug allergy/rash, nephrotoxicity (vancomycin, aminoglycosides), red man syndrome (vancomycin infusion reaction), thrombophlebitis (IV site)

Recurrence: 20-30% recurrence rate, higher with lymphedema. Monitor for: inadequately treated portal of entry (tinea pedis), unaddressed edema/venous insufficiency, immunosuppression

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Cefazolin, 💊 Cephalexin, 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Doxycycline, 💊 TMP-SMX, 💊 Clindamycin, 💊 Nafcillin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Blood Cultures

21. URINARY TRACT INFECTION / PYELONEPHRITIS

Cystitis • Pyelonephritis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Cystitis (Lower UTI): Acute onset of dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain/pressure, hematuria (gross or microscopic). NO fever (Temp <38°C) or flank pain. Symptoms typically develop over hours to 1-2 days

Pyelonephritis (Upper UTI): Fever >38.5°C, rigors, unilateral flank/back pain, costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness on exam, nausea/vomiting. Often accompanied by dysuria and frequency. Can progress to sepsis

Complicated UTI Definition: Structural/functional abnormality of GU tract, instrumentation, immunosuppression, pregnancy, males, indwelling catheter, recent antimicrobial use, diabetes, renal transplant, hospital-acquired. Higher risk of treatment failure and complications

Alternate Presentations:

  • Elderly Patients: May present with altered mental status, confusion, falls, functional decline, or generalized weakness WITHOUT classic UTI symptoms. Fever often absent or blunted. Dysuria may not be reported. High index of suspicion needed
  • Diabetic Patients: Higher risk of emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas-forming infection - E. coli, Klebsiella), papillary necrosis, perinephric abscess. Worse outcomes, longer treatment needed. May have poor glucose control as only manifestation
  • Pregnancy: 20-30% of untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria progresses to pyelonephritis. Pyelonephritis can trigger preterm labor, low birth weight. Must screen ALL pregnant women and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria. Higher risk of recurrence during pregnancy
  • Men (Any Age): Almost always complicated UTI. Assume prostatic involvement until proven otherwise. Need 7-14 days of treatment. Evaluate for structural abnormalities, BPH, prostatitis. First UTI in young man = red flag for anatomic defect
  • Catheter-Associated (CAUTI): New fever, flank pain, suprapubic pain, altered mental status in catheterized patient. Often polymicrobial. Pyuria alone is NOT diagnostic (50% of catheterized patients have asymptomatic pyuria). Need symptoms to treat
  • Perinephric/Renal Abscess: Persistent fever despite 48-72 hours appropriate antibiotics. Unilateral flank pain, palpable flank mass. Risk factors: diabetes, IV drug use, renal stones, obstruction. CT diagnostic. May need percutaneous or surgical drainage
  • Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis: Rare chronic infection causing granulomatous destruction of kidney. Mimics renal mass on imaging. Presents with persistent flank pain, fever, weight loss. Kidney non-functional, requires nephrectomy
  • Emphysematous Pyelonephritis: Life-threatening gas-forming infection. 90% diabetics. Presents with severe sepsis, CVA tenderness. CT shows gas in renal parenchyma. High mortality (20-40%). Requires IV antibiotics + possible nephrectomy
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Urinalysis (Essential for ALL):

  • Pyuria: >10 WBC/hpf highly suggestive. >5 WBC/hpf = abnormal. Absence of pyuria makes UTI unlikely (95% NPV)
  • Bacteriuria: Any bacteria on unspun urine microscopy = ≥10^5 CFU/mL
  • Leukocyte Esterase: Sensitive (75-96%) but less specific. Produced by WBCs. Can be false positive with contamination
  • Nitrites: Highly specific (90-100%) but only 50% sensitive. Many uropathogens (Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus, Pseudomonas) don't produce nitrites. Requires bacteria in bladder ≥4 hours
  • Hematuria: Present in 40-60% of UTIs but non-specific
  • WBC Casts: Pathognomonic for pyelonephritis (indicates renal parenchymal involvement). Differentiates from cystitis

Urine Culture & Sensitivity (When to Send):

  • ALWAYS send before antibiotics if: Pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, pregnant, recent antibiotic use, healthcare-associated, symptoms >7 days, recurrent UTI, immunocompromised
  • NOT needed for: Uncomplicated cystitis in young women (treat empirically)
  • Collection: Mid-stream clean catch (not catheter unless catheter present <2 hours). First morning void best
  • Interpretation:
    • ≥10^3 CFU/mL = diagnostic for cystitis (2010 IDSA consensus; lower than the older 10^5 "Kass criterion," which missed up to 50% of true symptomatic infections)
    • ≥10^4 CFU/mL = diagnostic for pyelonephritis
    • ≥10^2 CFU/mL = diagnostic if catheter specimen
    • Multiple organisms = contamination (repeat culture)
  • Common Organisms: E. coli (75-95%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (5-10%), Proteus mirabilis (5%), Enterococcus (5%), Staphylococcus saprophyticus (5-15% in young women)

Blood Cultures:

  • Obtain if: Pyelonephritis with sepsis/hemodynamic instability, immunocompromised, persistent fever despite 48-72hr of antibiotics, concern for bacteremia
  • Positive in 15-25% of hospitalized pyelonephritis patients
  • Usually same organism as urine culture

Additional Labs:

  • CBC: Leukocytosis common in pyelonephritis (WBC often 12-20k with left shift). Leukopenia suggests severe sepsis
  • BMP: Assess renal function (baseline Cr), check for AKI. Evaluate electrolytes
  • Pregnancy test: ALL women of childbearing age (ectopic can present as flank pain, UTI changes management in pregnancy)
  • Lactate: If sepsis suspected (goal <2, elevated suggests tissue hypoperfusion)

Imaging (NOT routine, but obtain if):

  • CT Abdomen/Pelvis WITH IV Contrast (Test of Choice):
    • No clinical improvement after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
    • Sepsis/septic shock
    • Immunocompromised (evaluate for abscess)
    • Concern for urinary obstruction (hydronephrosis, stones)
    • Recurrent pyelonephritis (>2 episodes)
    • Men with pyelonephritis (evaluate for anatomic abnormality)
    • Suspected emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in tissues)
    • Suspected perinephric/renal abscess
  • Renal Ultrasound: First-line if pregnant or contraindication to IV contrast. Can detect hydronephrosis (obstruction) but less sensitive for abscess than CT. Good for assessing kidney size/echogenicity
  • KUB X-ray: Limited utility. Can identify radiopaque stones (calcium) but misses 10-20% of stones

Special Diagnostic Considerations:

  • Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB): Positive culture (≥10^5 CFU/mL) WITHOUT symptoms. Very common in elderly, catheterized patients. DO NOT TREAT except in pregnancy or before urologic procedures. Treatment causes antibiotic resistance without benefit
  • Sterile Pyuria: WBCs in urine but negative culture. Differential: TB (send AFB culture × 3), fungal infection, interstitial nephritis, appendicitis, recent antibiotic use, urethritis (chlamydia, gonorrhea), kidney stones
  • Catheter-Associated UTI Diagnosis: Catheterized patient with fever (>38°C) OR new onset suprapubic pain OR flank pain OR altered mental status WITHOUT other source PLUS positive culture ≥10^3 CFU/mL. Pyuria alone is NOT diagnostic
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Uncomplicated Cystitis (Healthy Non-Pregnant Women):

  • First-Line Options:
    • Nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100mg PO BID × 5 days (preferred)
    • TMP-SMX DS (160/800mg) PO BID × 3 days (only if local E. coli resistance <20%)
  • Second-Line Options:
    • Fosfomycin 3g PO × single dose (convenient but slightly lower cure rate ~90%)
    • Pivmecillinam 400mg PO TID × 3-5 days (not available in US)
  • When β-lactams Necessary:
    • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg PO BID × 5-7 days
    • Cefpodoxime 100mg PO BID × 5-7 days
    • Less effective than nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX - use only if alternatives unavailable
  • AVOID Fluoroquinolones: Reserve for pyelonephritis due to serious adverse effects (C. diff, tendon rupture, neuropathy) and resistance concerns
  • Contraindications:
    • Nitrofurantoin: CrCl <30 mL/min, pregnancy at term (risk of hemolytic anemia in newborn), G6PD deficiency
    • TMP-SMX: Pregnancy (especially 1st trimester - neural tube defects), severe sulfa allergy, CrCl <15

Acute Pyelonephritis - Outpatient (Mild, Tolerates PO, Reliable):

  • Fluoroquinolone (if local resistance <10%):
    • Ciprofloxacin 500mg PO BID × 7 days OR 1000mg XR daily × 7 days
    • Levofloxacin 750mg PO daily × 5 days
    • Can give single dose ceftriaxone 1g IM in ED before starting oral quinolone
  • If Fluoroquinolone Resistance or Contraindicated:
    • Ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV × 1 dose, THEN oral step-down based on culture susceptibility
    • If susceptible: TMP-SMX DS BID × 14 days OR Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg BID × 10-14 days
    • Cefpodoxime 200mg PO BID × 10-14 days (if susceptible)
  • Duration: 7-14 days depending on agent and clinical response. Fluoroquinolones 5-7 days, β-lactams 10-14 days

Acute Pyelonephritis - Inpatient (Toxic, Septic, Unable to Tolerate PO):

  • Moderate Severity:
    • Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV q24h (excellent E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus coverage)
    • Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h OR Levofloxacin 750mg IV q24h
  • Severe/Septic/Complicated:
    • Cefepime 2g IV q8h (broader than ceftriaxone, covers Pseudomonas)
    • Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375g IV q6h or 4.5g IV q8h
  • If Gram-Positive Cocci on Culture: Add Ampicillin 2g IV q4h (for Enterococcus - VRE risk if amp-resistant)
  • ESBL Risk Factors Present: Previous ESBL infection, recent hospitalization, healthcare exposure, international travel, chronic care facility resident
    • Ertapenem 1g IV q24h OR Meropenem 1g IV q8h
    • Avoid cephalosporins/fluoroquinolones if ESBL confirmed
  • Transition to Oral: When afebrile × 24 hours, improved symptoms, tolerating PO, hemodynamically stable
    • Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID or Levofloxacin 750mg daily
    • TMP-SMX DS BID (if susceptible)
    • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg BID (if susceptible)
  • Total Duration: 7-14 days
    • 7 days if uncomplicated, rapid response to treatment
    • 10-14 days if complicated, bacteremia, slow response, immunocompromised, male

Complicated UTI/Urosepsis:

  • Broad-Spectrum Initial Coverage:
    • Pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h OR Cefepime 2g IV q8h
    • If MRSA suspected (skin breakdown, recent healthcare): ADD Vancomycin 15-20mg/kg IV q8-12h
    • If critically ill: Meropenem 1g IV q8h (covers ESBL, Pseudomonas)
  • De-escalate Based on Cultures: Narrow to organism-specific therapy once susceptibilities available
  • Duration: 10-14 days minimum. Extend if slow response, abscess, obstruction
  • Source Control: Remove catheters if possible. Drain abscesses. Relieve obstruction (nephrostomy, stent)

Special Populations:

  • Pregnancy:
    • Screen ALL pregnant women for ASB at 12-16 weeks (treat if positive)
    • Cystitis: Nitrofurantoin 100mg BID × 5-7 days (avoid at term) OR Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg BID × 5-7 days OR Cephalexin 500mg QID × 5-7 days
    • Pyelonephritis: ADMIT - Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV q24h until afebrile × 24-48hr, then Cephalexin 500mg QID × 10-14 days total
    • AVOID: Fluoroquinolones (cartilage toxicity), TMP in 1st trimester (neural tube defects), nitrofurantoin at term
  • Men (Always Complicated):
    • Assume prostatic involvement
    • Fluoroquinolone × 10-14 days (penetrates prostate): Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID or Levofloxacin 750mg daily
    • Alternative: TMP-SMX DS BID × 14 days (if susceptible)
    • If severe: Start IV (ceftriaxone, cefepime), transition to PO quinolone
    • Urology referral for: recurrent UTI, first UTI in young man, concern for obstruction
  • Catheter-Associated UTI (CAUTI):
    • Remove or replace catheter if possible before starting antibiotics
    • Often polymicrobial, resistant organisms (Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Candida)
    • Empiric: Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily OR Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h
    • If severe: Cefepime or Pip-tazo (Pseudomonas coverage)
    • Duration: 7 days if catheter removed, 10-14 days if catheter remains in place
    • De-escalate based on cultures
  • Renal Impairment:
    • Avoid nitrofurantoin if CrCl <30 (inadequate levels)
    • Dose-adjust fluoroquinolones, β-lactams based on CrCl
    • TMP-SMX: Avoid if CrCl <15
  • Elderly/Nursing Home:
    • Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria
    • If symptomatic: Consider atypical presentations (AMS, falls)
    • Higher resistance rates - obtain culture before treating
    • Lower threshold to admit (dehydration, frailty, poor PO intake)

Recurrent UTI Management (≥2 in 6 months or ≥3 in 12 months):

  • Non-Antibiotic Strategies:
    • Increase fluid intake (2-3 L/day)
    • Void after intercourse
    • Avoid spermicides, diaphragms
    • Cranberry products (modest benefit - 500-1500mg proanthocyanidins daily)
    • D-mannose 2g daily (prevents E. coli adhesion)
    • Vaginal estrogen cream (post-menopausal women) - Estradiol 0.5g intravaginally 2x/week
  • Antibiotic Prophylaxis:
    • Continuous: TMP-SMX SS (40/200mg) daily OR Nitrofurantoin 50-100mg daily at bedtime
    • Post-coital: Single dose TMP-SMX SS or nitrofurantoin 50-100mg within 2 hours of intercourse
    • Self-start therapy: Patient-initiated 3-day course at first symptom if reliable patient
  • Further Workup: Consider urologic evaluation (cystoscopy, renal US) if: recurrent pyelonephritis, hematuria, men, young children, suspicion of anatomic abnormality
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Pyuria alone is NOT infection: 30-50% of catheterized patients have asymptomatic pyuria. Need SYMPTOMS to diagnose and treat CAUTI. Don't treat labs, treat patients!
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria - DON'T treat (with 2 exceptions): Treating ASB in elderly, catheterized, or diabetic patients drives resistance without benefit. ONLY treat in pregnancy or before urologic procedures. This is one of the most common antibiotic stewardship errors
  • E. coli is the usual suspect: Causes 75-95% of community-acquired UTIs. Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus are next. If unusual organism (Pseudomonas, Staph aureus), think catheter, recent healthcare exposure, or structural abnormality
  • Men = complicated until proven otherwise: Almost all UTIs in men involve prostate. Need 10-14 days treatment (vs 3-5 days women). First UTI in young man = red flag for anatomic abnormality (posterior urethral valves, etc) - needs urologic workup
  • Nitrofurantoin doesn't work for pyelonephritis: Doesn't achieve therapeutic levels in renal parenchyma or blood. Excellent for cystitis only. Using for pyelo = treatment failure
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis = life-threatening: Gas in kidney on CT. 90% in diabetics. E. coli or Klebsiella ferment glucose → gas production. High mortality (20-40%). Needs IV antibiotics ± nephrectomy if refractory. Never miss this on imaging!
  • WBC casts are pathognomonic for pyelonephritis: If WBC casts on UA = renal parenchymal involvement (vs cystitis which is bladder only). This finding confirms pyelonephritis diagnosis
  • Post-treatment UA not needed: If symptoms resolve, don't recheck UA/culture. Pyuria can persist for weeks after successful treatment. Only reculture if persistent symptoms. "Test of cure" is symptom resolution, not negative UA
  • Pregnancy ASB MUST be treated: 30% of untreated ASB in pregnancy progresses to pyelonephritis → preterm labor. Screen ALL pregnant women at 12-16 weeks and treat positive cultures even if asymptomatic. This is the ONLY population where ASB treatment is indicated
  • Fluoroquinolone resistance is rising: E. coli resistance now 20-30% in many areas. Check local antibiogram. If resistance >10%, avoid empiric quinolones for pyelonephritis - use ceftriaxone instead
  • Perinephric abscess if fever persists despite antibiotics: Still febrile after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics? Get CT - look for abscess. Abscess >3cm usually needs percutaneous drainage. Antibiotics alone often insufficient
  • Recurrent UTI red flags needing urologic evaluation: Recurrent pyelonephritis, men, young children, painless hematuria, suspicion of stones/obstruction/anatomic defect. These need cystoscopy and/or imaging to find underlying cause
  • Sterile pyuria differential: WBCs but negative culture = TB (get AFB culture × 3), partially treated UTI, urethritis (STI - test for chlamydia/gonorrhea), interstitial nephritis (NSAIDs, antibiotics), kidney stones, appendicitis, fungal infection (Candida in catheterized/diabetics)
  • Nitrites are specific but not sensitive: If positive = infection. But 50% of UTIs are nitrite-negative because many organisms (Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) don't convert nitrate to nitrite. Don't rule out UTI based on negative nitrites alone
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Urosepsis with septic shock (SBP <90 despite fluids, lactate >4, requiring pressors)
  • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
  • Severe sepsis with multi-organ dysfunction (AKI, AMS, coagulopathy)
  • Obstructive uropathy with sepsis (needs emergent decompression)
  • Perinephric or renal abscess with hemodynamic instability
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis with shock (may need nephrectomy)
  • Papillary necrosis with obstruction and sepsis
  • Fournier's gangrene (necrotizing perineal infection - surgical emergency)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Afebrile × 24-48 hours (temperature <38°C)
  • Hemodynamically stable (SBP >100, HR <100)
  • Tolerating PO intake without nausea/vomiting
  • Pain controlled on oral analgesics
  • Able to take oral antibiotics and reliable for adherence
  • Improving leukocytosis (if initially elevated, downtrending WBC)
  • Stable or improving renal function (if AKI, Cr trending toward baseline)
  • No evidence of obstruction requiring intervention (if imaging done)
  • No abscess, or abscess drained and improving
  • Urine culture results available and organism susceptible to oral agent
  • Patient educated on: completing full antibiotic course, adequate hydration (2-3 L/day), return precautions
  • PCP follow-up arranged within 1 week (urology if recurrent, male, or anatomic concern)
  • Plan for repeat culture if: pregnant, recurrent infection, initial blood culture positive
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Early Complications (Hours-Days): Sepsis/septic shock (15-25% of hospitalized pyelonephritis), bacteremia with metastatic seeding (endocarditis, vertebral osteomyelitis, septic arthritis), acute kidney injury (from sepsis, obstruction, or bilateral pyelonephritis), urinary retention (from UTI-induced detrusor dysfunction), severe hematuria (can cause clot retention requiring continuous bladder irrigation)

Late Complications (Days-Weeks): Perinephric abscess (persistent fever >72hr despite antibiotics, needs CT diagnosis and drainage), intrarenal abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis (diabetics - gas-forming infection, 20-40% mortality, may need nephrectomy), renal papillary necrosis (diabetics, sickle cell disease, analgesic abuse - presents with flank pain, hematuria, AKI), chronic pyelonephritis with renal scarring (recurrent infections → CKD), xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (rare chronic granulomatous destruction of kidney)

Treatment-Related Complications: C. difficile infection (fluoroquinolones highest risk), antibiotic-associated diarrhea, allergic reactions (rash, anaphylaxis), tendon rupture (fluoroquinolones - Achilles tendon), peripheral neuropathy (fluoroquinolones - can be irreversible), QT prolongation (fluoroquinolones, especially if other QT drugs), photosensitivity (fluoroquinolones), pulmonary fibrosis (nitrofurantoin with chronic use >6 months), hemolytic anemia (nitrofurantoin in G6PD deficiency)

Pregnancy-Related: Preterm labor and delivery (pyelonephritis), low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, maternal sepsis, respiratory failure (ARDS from pyelonephritis in pregnancy)

Recurrence: 25-30% recurrence within 6 months if underlying factors not addressed (kidney stones, obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, anatomic abnormality, poor hygiene, sexual activity with spermicide use, post-menopausal atrophic vaginitis, BPH in men, neurogenic bladder, immunosuppression)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Nitrofurantoin
