27. ANEMIA

Microcytic • Normocytic • Macrocytic
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

General Symptoms (severity depends on acuity and degree): Fatigue, weakness, dyspnea on exertion, dizziness, headache, tinnitus, palpitations, chest pain (angina if severe anemia + CAD). Pallor (conjunctivae, palmar creases), tachycardia, systolic flow murmur, orthostatic hypotension if acute blood loss

Alternate Presentations by Etiology:

  • Iron Deficiency: Koilonychia (spoon nails), glossitis, angular cheilitis, pica (ice chips/starch/dirt craving), restless leg syndrome, dysphagia (Plummer-Vinson syndrome with esophageal webs)
  • B12 Deficiency: Neurologic symptoms - paresthesias (glove-stocking), ataxia, decreased proprioception/vibratory sense, dementia, psychiatric changes. Glossitis (beefy red tongue). Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (dorsal columns + lateral corticospinal tracts)
  • Folate Deficiency: Similar to B12 but NO neurologic symptoms. Glossitis, diarrhea. Often in alcoholics, malnutrition
  • Hemolysis: Jaundice (↑unconjugated bilirubin), dark urine (hemoglobinuria), splenomegaly. If intravascular: hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria. If extravascular: splenomegaly, gallstones (pigmented)
  • Acute Blood Loss: Tachycardia, hypotension, orthostatic changes, melena/hematochezia (GI bleed), hematemesis, vaginal bleeding. Hgb may be normal initially (takes hours for equilibration)
  • Anemia of Chronic Disease: Underlying inflammatory condition (RA, IBD, malignancy, CKD). Usually mild-moderate anemia (Hgb 9-11)
  • Thalassemia: Mild microcytic anemia often asymptomatic. Family history Mediterranean/Asian descent. Splenomegaly if thalassemia major
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Labs: CBC with differential, reticulocyte count (assess bone marrow response), peripheral smear, iron studies, B12/folate, LDH/haptoglobin/bilirubin (if hemolysis suspected)

Approach by MCV (Mean Corpuscular Volume):

MICROCYTIC (MCV <80 fL) - "TAILS":

  • Thalassemia: Hgb electrophoresis (↑HbA2 in β-thal trait), family hx, ethnicity. MCV often <75, RBC count elevated despite low Hgb (RBC >5 million). RDW normal. Mentzer index (MCV/RBC count) <13 suggests thalassemia
  • Anemia of chronic disease: Ferritin elevated (>100) or normal, TIBC low, transferrin saturation low-normal. Inflammatory markers elevated (CRP, ESR). Look for underlying chronic condition
  • Iron deficiency: Ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific). Serum iron low, TIBC elevated, transferrin saturation <20%. RDW elevated. Peripheral smear: hypochromic microcytic cells, pencil cells. Investigate source of blood loss (GI workup if no obvious source)
  • Lead poisoning: Basophilic stippling on smear, elevated blood lead level. Occupational exposure, pica
  • Sideroblastic anemia: Ring sideroblasts on bone marrow. Elevated ferritin, normal/high iron. Causes: alcohol, isoniazid, lead, copper deficiency, myelodysplasia

NORMOCYTIC (MCV 80-100 fL):

  • Check reticulocyte count to distinguish:
  • Elevated reticulocyte count (>2-3%) = Appropriate Response:
    • Acute blood loss: Obvious source (GI bleed, trauma, surgery, menorrhagia). Hgb may be normal initially
    • Hemolysis: Elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, elevated indirect bilirubin, +/- hemoglobinuria. Smear: schistocytes (TTP, HUS, DIC, mechanical valves), spherocytes (autoimmune, hereditary spherocytosis), sickle cells, bite cells (G6PD). Coombs test for autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  • Low reticulocyte count (<2%) = Inadequate Response:
    • Anemia of chronic disease/inflammation: Ferritin normal/high, low TIBC. Underlying chronic illness (CKD, cancer, infection, autoimmune)
    • CKD: Low EPO production. Cr elevated, usually Hgb 9-11. Start EPO if Hgb <10
    • Bone marrow failure: Pancytopenia (↓WBC, ↓platelets, ↓RBC). Aplastic anemia, myelodysplasia, leukemia, myelofibrosis. Needs bone marrow biopsy
    • Early iron/B12/folate deficiency: May be normocytic before becoming micro/macrocytic. Check iron studies, B12, folate

MACROCYTIC (MCV >100 fL):

  • B12 deficiency: B12 <200 pg/mL (or <300 if high clinical suspicion). Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine (more sensitive). Hypersegmented neutrophils on smear. Causes: pernicious anemia (anti-IF antibodies), malabsorption (Crohn's, celiac, gastric bypass), strict vegan diet, metformin
  • Folate deficiency: Folate <2 ng/mL. Elevated homocysteine but normal methylmalonic acid. No neurologic symptoms (vs B12). Causes: poor diet (alcoholics, elderly), malabsorption, medications (methotrexate, phenytoin, TMP-SMX), pregnancy/lactation (increased demand)
  • Alcohol: Direct marrow suppression. Often with folate deficiency. MCV 100-110. Elevated GGT, AST>ALT
  • Hypothyroidism: Check TSH. MCV usually 100-110
  • Medications: Hydroxyurea, zidovudine (AZT), azathioprine, 5-FU, methotrexate
  • Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): Elderly, refractory anemia, dysplastic cells on smear, cytopenias. Bone marrow biopsy shows dysplasia. Risk of transformation to AML
  • Reticulocytosis: Young RBCs are larger. If brisk hemolysis/blood loss with appropriate reticulocyte response, MCV may be elevated

Additional Workup for Specific Situations:

  • GI workup if iron deficiency with no obvious source: EGD + colonoscopy to evaluate for occult GI bleeding (gastritis, ulcer, colon cancer, AVM). Celiac serologies. H. pylori testing
  • Hemolysis workup: Coombs (direct antiglobulin test) for autoimmune hemolytic anemia. G6PD level (if bite cells, acute hemolysis after oxidative stress). Osmotic fragility (hereditary spherocytosis). PNH flow cytometry if intravascular hemolysis
  • Bone marrow biopsy if: Pancytopenia, suspected malignancy (leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma), unexplained anemia, MDS suspected
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Transfusion Thresholds:

  • Stable, no CAD: Transfuse if Hgb <7 g/dL (restrictive strategy)
  • CAD or high cardiac risk: Transfuse if Hgb <8 g/dL
  • Acute MI/ACS: Transfuse if Hgb <10 g/dL (some say <8, controversial - individualize)
  • Symptomatic (dyspnea, angina, orthostasis): Transfuse regardless of Hgb if symptomatic
  • Chronic anemia: Often tolerate lower Hgb (compensatory mechanisms). Treat underlying cause, transfuse only if symptomatic or Hgb <7
  • Each unit pRBC raises Hgb by ~1 g/dL (or Hct by ~3%)

Specific Treatments by Etiology:

Iron Deficiency:

  • Oral iron (first-line): Ferrous sulfate 325mg PO TID (65mg elemental iron per tablet). Take on empty stomach with vitamin C (enhances absorption). Common SE: constipation, dark stools, nausea. Response in 2-4 weeks (↑reticulocytes), full repletion 3-6 months. Continue 3 months after Hgb normalized to replete stores
  • IV iron (if oral intolerance, malabsorption, CKD, need rapid repletion): Iron sucrose 200mg IV × 5 doses or Ferric carboxymaltose 750mg IV × 2 doses or Iron dextran (test dose required). Risk: anaphylaxis (rare with newer formulations), hypophosphatemia. Ferric carboxymaltose: FDA boxed warning (September 2026) for symptomatic hypophosphatemia (weakness, fatigue, confusion, arrhythmias; osteomalacia and fractures if chronic). Correct low phosphate before dosing; check phosphate in patients at risk and before any repeat course within 3 months; consider stopping permanently for severe symptomatic or persistent hypophosphatemia (FDA)
  • Treat underlying cause: GI bleeding (PPI for ulcer, colonoscopy for polyp/cancer removal), menorrhagia (NSAIDs, OCPs, IUD, ablation)

B12 Deficiency:

  • Cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg IM daily × 7 days, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong (if pernicious anemia or malabsorption)
  • Oral B12 1000-2000 mcg daily: Alternative if dietary deficiency or mild malabsorption (compliance issue - less reliable)
  • Neurologic symptoms may be irreversible if prolonged deficiency: Treat urgently
  • NEVER give folate without B12 in macrocytic anemia - can worsen B12 neuropathy!

Folate Deficiency:

  • Folic acid 1mg PO daily × 1-4 months until replete
  • Treat underlying cause: Alcohol cessation, improve diet
  • Pregnancy: All women of childbearing age should take 400-800 mcg daily (prevent neural tube defects)

Anemia of Chronic Disease:

  • Treat underlying condition (control inflammation, treat cancer, manage CKD)
  • If concurrent iron deficiency (ferritin <100 in setting of inflammation): IV iron (oral poorly absorbed)
  • EPO (erythropoietin): If CKD with Hgb <10, or cancer-related anemia. Epoetin alfa 50-100 units/kg SC 3×/week. Target Hgb 10-11 (don't overcorrect - ↑thrombosis risk). Requires adequate iron stores

Hemolytic Anemia:

  • Autoimmune (warm AIHA): Prednisone 1mg/kg daily, taper over weeks-months. If refractory: Rituximab, IVIG, splenectomy. Folic acid 1mg daily (increased RBC turnover)
  • Cold agglutinin disease: Avoid cold exposure. Rituximab. Don't transfuse unless life-threatening (can worsen hemolysis)
  • G6PD deficiency: Avoid oxidative triggers (sulfa drugs, dapsone, antimalarials, fava beans). Supportive care, transfuse if severe
  • TTP: URGENT plasmapheresis (see TTP section)

Thalassemia:

  • Trait (minor): No treatment needed. Avoid unnecessary iron supplementation. Genetic counseling
  • Major: Chronic transfusions (maintain Hgb >9-10), iron chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox) to prevent iron overload. Splenectomy if hypersplenism. Bone marrow transplant curative
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • MCV is your roadmap: Microcytic → think iron/thalassemia/chronic disease. Normocytic → check retic count (high = bleeding/hemolysis, low = bone marrow problem). Macrocytic → B12/folate/alcohol/hypothyroid
  • Ferritin <30 = iron deficiency: Most specific test. But ferritin is acute phase reactant - may be falsely normal/elevated with inflammation. If ferritin 30-100 with chronic disease, still suspect iron deficiency
  • RDW helps distinguish: High RDW = iron deficiency (mixed cell sizes). Normal RDW = thalassemia, chronic disease (uniform small cells)
  • Thalassemia has HIGH RBC count: Despite low Hgb/MCV, RBC count often >5 million (vs iron deficiency with low RBC count). Mentzer index <13 suggests thalassemia
  • B12 deficiency causes neuro symptoms, folate doesn't: Paresthesias, ataxia, dementia = B12. Never give folate without checking B12 first in macrocytic anemia - can worsen neuropathy!
  • Acute blood loss: Hgb lags: Initial Hgb may be normal because both RBCs and plasma lost equally. Takes hours for equilibration. Treat based on clinical status (hypotension, tachycardia)
  • Hemolysis triad: Elevated LDH + low haptoglobin + elevated indirect bilirubin. If all three present, hemolysis confirmed. Then figure out cause (Coombs, smear)
  • Restrictive transfusion saves lives: Transfuse <7 in stable patients (or <8 if CAD). Overtransfusion increases mortality, volume overload, immunosuppression
  • Each unit pRBC raises Hgb ~1 g/dL: Don't transfuse more than needed. Reassess after each unit
  • Iron pills cause constipation/GI upset: Take with food if intolerant (absorption slightly decreased but better than not taking). Try every-other-day dosing (absorption actually better). Black stools are expected
⚠️ ICU TRANSFER CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia unresponsive to fluids/transfusion)
  • Active massive hemorrhage requiring massive transfusion protocol
  • Severe symptomatic anemia (Hgb <5-6) with angina, AMS, respiratory distress
  • TTP/HUS with neurologic changes or renal failure
  • Severe autoimmune hemolytic anemia with rapid decompensation
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Hgb stable or improving
  • No active bleeding
  • Tolerating PO intake (including iron/B12 if applicable)
  • Underlying cause identified and treated (or plan in place)
  • Appropriate outpatient follow-up arranged (PCP, hematology, GI)
  • Patient educated on medications, dietary recommendations
  • Transfusion reactions ruled out if transfused
  • Safe for discharge from functional standpoint
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute Complications: High-output heart failure (severe chronic anemia - Hgb <6-7 with inadequate compensation), angina/MI (demand ischemia from anemia in patient with CAD), syncope, falls (orthostasis, weakness), transfusion reactions (see transfusion section)

From Iron Deficiency: Restless leg syndrome (improves with iron repletion), cognitive impairment (especially children), increased risk infection (impaired immune function), pica complications (lead poisoning from paint chips, bowel obstruction)

From B12 Deficiency: Irreversible neurologic damage (subacute combined degeneration - ataxia, spasticity, paresthesias), dementia, depression, increased homocysteine → thrombosis risk

From Treatment: Iron overload (chronic transfusions - hemochromatosis, cardiac/liver damage, requires chelation), transfusion reactions, infection from immunosuppression (rituximab, steroids for AIHA)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Iron, 💊 Erythropoietin, 💊 Folic Acid, 💊 Vitamin B12, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 IVIG

28. NEUTROPENIC FEVER

Oncologic Emergency • Empiric Antibiotics Within 1 Hour
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Single oral temperature ≥38.3°C (101°F) OR temperature ≥38°C (100.4°F) for ≥1 hour WITH absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <500 cells/µL OR ANC expected to decline to <500 within 48 hours

Calculation: ANC = WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands) / 100

Typical Presentation: Fever may be ONLY sign of infection (neutropenic patients lack inflammatory response - no pus, minimal symptoms). Subtle findings: mild hypotension, tachycardia, confusion. Absence of fever does NOT rule out infection

Common Sources (often no clear source found 50-60%):

  • GI tract (most common): Oral mucositis, esophagitis, typhlitis (cecal inflammation), C. diff, perirectal abscess
  • Lungs: Pneumonia (bacterial, fungal - Aspergillus, PCP)
  • Skin/soft tissue: Cellulitis, catheter site infection, perirectal abscess
  • Bloodstream: Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI - coag-neg Staph, S. aureus)
  • Urinary tract: Less common (neutrophils needed for pyuria - may have negative UA despite UTI)
  • Sinusitis: Especially if prolonged neutropenia (fungal - Mucor, Aspergillus)

Alternate/High-Risk Presentations:

  • Septic shock: Hypotension, tachycardia, AMS, lactate elevation. Requires urgent resuscitation + antibiotics
  • Typhlitis (neutropenic enterocolitis): RLQ pain, diarrhea, distension. CT shows bowel wall thickening cecum/ascending colon. High mortality if perforation. Needs surgical consult
  • Perirectal abscess: Severe perianal pain, tenderness. Often NO fluctuance (neutropenic - can't form pus). Needs exam under anesthesia + drainage + antibiotics
  • Invasive fungal infection (if prolonged neutropenia >7-10 days): Persistent fever despite antibiotics. Aspergillus (pulmonary nodules, halo sign on CT), Candida (bloodstream, hepatosplenic candidiasis), Mucormycosis (sinusitis, black eschar)
  • Atypical pneumonia: PCP (HIV/lymphoma), CMV, viral (RSV, influenza)
  • CNS infection: Headache, AMS, focal deficits. Listeria, Aspergillus, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs (STAT):

  • CBC with differential: Confirm ANC. Trend daily. Platelets (thrombocytopenia common)
  • Blood cultures × 2 sets: One from EACH lumen of central line (if present) + peripheral. Label which lumen. Positive in 20-30%
  • CMP: Renal function (for antibiotic dosing), electrolytes, LFTs
  • Lactate: If concern for sepsis
  • UA with culture: Even if UA negative (neutropenia → may not have WBCs in urine despite UTI)
  • Stool culture, C. diff if diarrhea
  • Procalcitonin: May help distinguish bacterial vs non-bacterial (not routinely recommended)
  • Fungal markers if prolonged fever (>4-7 days) or high risk: Serum (1→3)-β-D-glucan (Candida, Aspergillus, PCP), Galactomannan (Aspergillus), Cryptococcal antigen

Imaging:

  • Chest X-ray: All patients. But CXR may be normal early (neutropenia → no infiltrate). If negative but respiratory symptoms, get CT chest
  • CT Chest (if respiratory symptoms, hypoxia, or persistent fever): More sensitive for pneumonia, fungal nodules. Look for: infiltrates, nodules, halo sign (Aspergillus), cavitation
  • CT Abdomen/Pelvis (if abdominal pain or no clear source): Evaluate for typhlitis, abscess, colitis
  • CT Sinuses (if sinus symptoms, especially prolonged neutropenia): Rule out invasive fungal sinusitis

Other Studies:

  • Respiratory viral panel (if respiratory symptoms): Influenza, RSV, COVID
  • Lumbar puncture (if CNS symptoms): After platelets >50k. CSF for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture, Crypto Ag, fungal culture
  • Skin biopsy (if skin lesions): Culture and histology. Rule out disseminated fungal (Fusarium, Mucor)

Risk Stratification (MASCC Score - guides inpatient vs outpatient, intensity):

  • MASCC Score ≥21: Low risk (mortality <5%). May consider outpatient management in select patients
  • MASCC Score <21: High risk (mortality >20%). Requires inpatient management + aggressive treatment
  • High-risk features: Prolonged neutropenia (>7 days expected), ANC <100, hemodynamic instability, pneumonia, mucositis grade 3-4, neurologic changes, abdominal pain, renal/liver dysfunction, age >60
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

EMPIRIC ANTIBIOTICS (START WITHIN 1 HOUR):

Initial Monotherapy (Preferred):

  • Cefepime 2g IV q8h (antipseudomonal cephalosporin, preferred)
  • OR Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h (broader spectrum)
  • OR Meropenem 1g IV q8h (if PCN allergy or resistant organisms suspected)
  • Monotherapy covers: Pseudomonas, E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus, Staph (not MRSA), Strep

ADD Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h if:

  • Central line/catheter infection suspected (erythema, tenderness at site)
  • Severe mucositis (oral, esophageal, GI - ↑Strep viridans, Enterococcus risk)
  • Hemodynamic instability/septic shock
  • Skin/soft tissue infection
  • Known MRSA colonization
  • Pneumonia (cover MRSA)

ADD Antifungal Coverage if:

  • Persistent fever >4-7 days despite broad-spectrum antibiotics (empiric antifungal)
  • Clinical/radiographic evidence of invasive fungal infection: Pulmonary nodules, halo sign, sinusitis
  • Positive fungal markers: β-D-glucan, galactomannan
  • Options: Micafungin 100mg IV daily (Candida), Voriconazole 6mg/kg q12h × 2 then 4mg/kg q12h (Aspergillus), Liposomal Amphotericin B 3-5mg/kg IV daily (broad spectrum, if refractory)

Special Situations:

  • Perirectal abscess/typhlitis: Pip-tazo + Vancomycin (or Meropenem + Vanc). Metronidazole 500mg IV q8h if extensive bowel involvement. Surgical consult
  • PCP suspected (HIV, lymphoma): TMP-SMX 5mg/kg IV q8h. Prednisone if severe (PaO2 <70 or A-a gradient >35)
  • Viral respiratory infection (influenza): Oseltamivir 75mg PO BID × 5d if within 48hr symptom onset (or longer if immunocompromised)
  • HSV/VZV (mucositis, vesicular rash): Acyclovir 5-10mg/kg IV q8h

Duration of Antibiotics:

  • If source identified: Treat for appropriate duration (7-14 days typical)
  • If NO source, clinically improving, afebrile >48hr: Continue until ANC >500 (at least 7 days total)
  • If persistent fever but stable: Continue antibiotics until ANC >500 or until fungal workup complete
  • Do NOT stop antibiotics just because fever persists - fever may persist due to tumor, drugs, blood products, non-bacterial causes

Supportive Care:

  • G-CSF (filgrastim 5 mcg/kg SC daily): Consider if high-risk (MASCC <21, pneumonia, septic shock, invasive fungal, prolonged neutropenia expected >7-10 days). Shortens duration neutropenia. NOT needed routinely low-risk patients
  • Fluid resuscitation: NS boluses if hypotensive. Early aggressive hydration improves outcomes
  • Avoid rectal temps/exams, suppositories, enemas: Risk of bacteremia from mucosal trauma
  • Transfusion support: pRBCs if Hgb <7-8, platelets if <10k (or <50k if bleeding/procedure)
  • Oral care: Chlorhexidine or salt/soda rinses QID. Pain control (opiates if severe mucositis)
  • Isolate patient: Private room, hand hygiene, avoid fresh flowers/plants (fungal spores), low-microbial diet controversial
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Door-to-antibiotic <1 hour saves lives: Mortality increases 18% for each hour delay. Don't wait for cultures - empiric antibiotics immediately
  • Fever may be only sign: Neutropenic patients can't mount inflammatory response. No pus, minimal symptoms despite severe infection. Low threshold to treat
  • ANC <100 is very high risk: "Profound neutropenia." Mortality >20%. Need aggressive treatment, GCSF, close monitoring
  • Persistent fever >4-7 days → add antifungal: Empiric coverage for invasive fungal (Aspergillus, Candida). Don't wait for positive cultures/markers
  • Don't forget perirectal exam: But be gentle! Perirectal abscess common, may not have fluctuance. Severe tenderness = likely abscess. Needs drainage
  • CXR can be falsely negative: Neutropenia → no infiltrate despite pneumonia. If respiratory symptoms, get CT chest even if CXR normal
  • Mucositis = add vancomycin: Oral/GI mucositis ↑risk Strep viridans bacteremia. Must add vancomycin to empiric regimen
  • Typhlitis is surgical emergency: RLQ pain + fever + neutropenia = typhlitis until proven otherwise. CT shows cecal wall thickening. High mortality if perforation. Surgical consult urgently
  • Don't remove central line unless CRBSI confirmed: Lines are precious in chemo patients. Can treat through line unless Staph aureus, Candida, or persistent bacteremia
  • GCSF shortens duration: Use if high-risk (MASCC <21). Shortens neutropenia by ~2-3 days, reduces infection complications. NOT needed routinely
⚠️ ICU TRANSFER CRITERIA
  • Septic shock requiring vasopressors
  • Respiratory failure requiring intubation
  • Multi-organ dysfunction (renal failure, hepatic failure)
  • Hemodynamic instability despite fluid resuscitation
  • Profound neutropenia (ANC <100) with sepsis
  • Typhlitis with concern for perforation
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Afebrile >24-48 hours off antibiotics (or on PO antibiotics if continued)
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • ANC recovering (>200-500 and rising)
  • No evidence of active infection requiring IV therapy
  • Able to tolerate PO intake
  • Close outpatient follow-up arranged (oncology within 48-72hr)
  • Patient education on infection precautions, when to return
  • Low-risk by MASCC score if outpatient management planned
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Infectious Complications: Septic shock (mortality 30-50%), invasive fungal infection (Aspergillus pneumonia, disseminated candidiasis - high mortality), typhlitis with perforation (requires surgery, high mortality), perirectal abscess with necrotizing fasciitis, catheter-related bloodstream infection (S. aureus, Candida - may require line removal), PCP pneumonia with respiratory failure

Non-Infectious: Tumor lysis syndrome (especially with treatment of hematologic malignancies), mucositis (severe pain, inability to eat/swallow, TPN required), bleeding (thrombocytopenia), VTE (hypercoagulable from cancer), drug toxicity (nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity from antibiotics/antifungals)

Mortality: Overall 5-20% depending on risk factors. Low-risk (MASCC ≥21) <5%, High-risk (MASCC <21) >20%. Mortality higher if: ANC <100, septic shock, pneumonia, invasive fungal infection, age >60

🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukopenia/Neutropenia, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

29. ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL

CIWA-Ar Protocol • Delirium Tremens • Thiamine BEFORE Glucose
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Timeline of Symptoms:

  • Minor withdrawal (6-12 hours after last drink): Tremor, anxiety, agitation, diaphoresis, nausea/vomiting, headache, insomnia, mild tachycard ia, mild hypertension
  • Withdrawal seizures (12-48 hours): Generalized tonic-clonic, typically brief (<2 min), single or clustered (2-4 seizures), self-limited. If prolonged or focal → think other cause (structural lesion, infection)
  • Alcoholic hallucinosis (12-24 hours): Visual, auditory, or tactile hallucinations WITH intact orientation (patient knows hallucinations aren't real). No autonomic instability. Benign, self-limited
  • Delirium Tremens/DTs (48-72 hours, can be up to 7-10 days): Life-threatening. Severe autonomic instability (tachycardia >120, hypertension, hyperthermia >38.5°C, profound diaphoresis), delirium (disoriented, agitated, hallucinations), tremor. Mortality 5-15% if untreated, <1-5% with treatment

Risk Factors for Severe Withdrawal/DTs: History of DTs/severe withdrawal, concurrent illness (pneumonia, pancreatitis, trauma), advanced age, multiple prior detoxifications (kindling phenomenon), prolonged heavy drinking, abrupt cessation, metabolic abnormalities (↓K, ↓Mg, ↓PO4)

Alternate/Complicated Presentations:

  • Occult withdrawal in hospitalized patients: Admitted for other reason (trauma, surgery, infection), develops withdrawal 24-72hr into admission. High suspicion if unexplained tachycardia, hypertension, agitation
  • Concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy: Acute thiamine deficiency. Triad: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus, gaze palsy). Often only 1-2 of triad present. Needs urgent IV thiamine BEFORE glucose
  • Co-ingestion: Benzodiazepines (may mask withdrawal initially then rebound), opioids (can have concurrent withdrawal), stimulants (confound tachycardia/hypertension assessment)
  • Hepatic encephalopathy mimicking DTs: Both have AMS, but HE has asterixis, elevated ammonia, slower onset. Can coexist
  • Seizure complications: Status epilepticus (rare but life-threatening), aspiration pneumonia, traumatic injury from fall
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis: Based on history, timeline, CIWA-Ar score. No specific diagnostic test

CIWA-Ar Score (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol, revised):

10-item scale, max score 67. Assess q1-2h initially:

  • Nausea/vomiting (0-7)
  • Tremor (0-7)
  • Paroxysmal sweats (0-7)
  • Anxiety (0-7)
  • Agitation (0-7)
  • Tactile disturbances (0-7)
  • Auditory disturbances (0-7)
  • Visual disturbances (0-7)
  • Headache (0-7)
  • Orientation/clouding of sensorium (0-4)

Interpretation: <8 = minimal withdrawal, 8-15 = moderate, >15 = severe, >20 = very severe (high DT risk)

Labs:

  • BMP: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia common. Anion gap metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis). Renal function
  • CBC: Macrocytosis (MCV >100), thrombocytopenia. Leukocytosis if infection
  • LFTs: Elevated AST>ALT (2:1 ratio), GGT elevated. Assess for cirrhosis, hepatitis
  • Albumin, INR: Synthetic liver function (low albumin, elevated INR = advanced liver disease)
  • Magnesium, phosphate: Correct deficiencies (affect seizure threshold, cardiac arrhythmias)
  • Thiamine level: Usually not sent (takes days, unreliable). Just give empiric thiamine
  • Ethanol level: Helpful to know if still intoxicated vs pure withdrawal. But low/negative ethanol doesn't rule out withdrawal
  • Lipase, troponin if abdominal pain/chest pain: Pancreatitis and ACS common in alcoholics
  • Ammonia if concern for hepatic encephalopathy
  • Blood cultures if fever: Rule out infection (pneumonia, SBP, bacteremia)

Imaging:

  • CT Head (if first seizure, focal seizure, persistent AMS, focal neurologic deficit, head trauma): Rule out ICH, subdural, stroke, mass
  • CXR: Aspiration pneumonia common (especially post-seizure), eval for other pulmonary pathology
  • EEG (if prolonged seizure or concern for non-convulsive status): Withdrawal seizures are brief, self-limited. If prolonged → other etiology
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Benzodiazepines (Cornerstone of Treatment):

CIWA-Ar Protocol (Symptom-Triggered):

  • Assess CIWA-Ar q1-2h (or q4h if stable/asleep)
  • If CIWA ≥8: Lorazepam 2-4mg IV/PO OR Diazepam 10-20mg IV/PO OR Chlordiazepoxide 50-100mg PO
  • Reassess 1 hour after dose, repeat if CIWA still ≥8
  • Goal: CIWA <8, patient calm but arousable
  • IV preferred if severe withdrawal, NPO, vomiting, or poor absorption

Fixed-Dose Protocol (if CIWA not feasible - ICU, intubated):

  • Lorazepam 2mg IV q6h scheduled + 2mg q1h PRN breakthrough
  • OR Diazepam 10mg IV q6h scheduled + 10mg q1h PRN
  • Taper over 3-5 days once stable

Choice of Benzodiazepine:

  • Lorazepam (Ativan): Intermediate-acting. No active metabolites. Safe in liver disease. Predictable IM absorption. PREFERRED if: liver disease, elderly, need IM route
  • Diazepam (Valium): Long-acting, active metabolites (smoother withdrawal, less breakthrough). Preferred by some for DTs. Accumulates in liver disease. PREFERRED if: normal liver function, severe withdrawal/DTs
  • Chlordiazepoxide (Librium): Long-acting, PO only. Good for mild-moderate withdrawal outpatient. NOT for severe/DTs

Delirium Tremens (DTs) - Aggressive Management:

  • ICU admission
  • High-dose benzodiazepines: Lorazepam 2-4mg IV q10-15min or Diazepam 10-20mg IV q10-15min until symptoms controlled. May need 100s of mg/day
  • Phenobarbital (if refractory to benzos): Phenobarbital 130-260mg IV q15-20min (max 10-15 mg/kg loading dose) then 30-60mg IV q6-8h maintenance. Synergistic with benzos, works on different GABA receptor
  • Propofol/dexmedetomidine infusion (if refractory, intubated): Propofol 20-80 mcg/kg/min, Dexmedetomidine 0.2-1.5 mcg/kg/hr. Adjuncts, not replacements for benzos
  • Avoid antipsychotics (haloperidol) as monotherapy: Lower seizure threshold, don't treat withdrawal. Can use low-dose as adjunct for hallucinations if needed (haloperidol 0.5-2mg)
  • Aggressive supportive care: IVF, cooling for hyperthermia, electrolyte repletion

Thiamine & Nutritional Repletion (CRITICAL):

  • Thiamine 100mg IV daily × 3-5 days, then 100mg PO daily
  • MUST give thiamine BEFORE glucose (glucose depletes thiamine, can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy)
  • If concern for Wernicke: Thiamine 500mg IV TID × 3 days (higher dose)
  • Folic acid 1mg PO daily
  • Multivitamin daily
  • Magnesium repletion: Mag sulfate 2-4g IV (or Mag oxide 400-800mg PO TID). Recheck and replete until >2 mg/dL. Hypomagnesemia ↓efficacy of benzos, ↑seizure risk
  • Phosphate repletion: K-phos or NaPhos based on K level. Goal >2.5 mg/dL
  • Potassium repletion: 40-80 mEq IV (if <3.5). Recheck q4-6h until >3.5

Seizure Management:

  • Acute seizure: Lorazepam 2-4mg IV (treat seizure + withdrawal). Usually self-limited
  • NO prophylactic AEDs: Benzodiazepines prevent seizures. AEDs (phenytoin, levetiracetam) don't prevent withdrawal seizures
  • If status epilepticus or prolonged seizure: Standard status protocol (lorazepam, then phenytoin/fosphenytoin or levetiracetam loading)
  • Replete magnesium aggressively (low Mg lowers seizure threshold)

Supportive Care:

  • Hydration: NS 100-150 mL/hr (many patients volume depleted). Monitor for volume overload if cirrhosis/cardiomyopathy
  • Cooling for hyperthermia: Ice packs, cooling blanket. Acetaminophen (avoid NSAIDs if cirrhosis/varices)
  • Aspiration precautions: NPO if AMS, HOB elevated, monitor for pneumonia
  • Restraints only if necessary: Can worsen agitation, rhabdomyolysis. Verbal de-escalation, sitter, adequate sedation preferred
  • Treat concurrent conditions: Pancreatitis, pneumonia, GI bleed common
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Thiamine BEFORE glucose: Glucose depletes thiamine stores, can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy (irreversible). Always give thiamine first in alcoholic patients
  • Withdrawal seizures are 12-48hr, self-limited: If seizure <12hr (still intoxicated?) or >48hr (other cause?), broaden differential. No need for AED prophylaxis - benzos prevent withdrawal seizures
  • DTs peak 48-72hr: Life-threatening. Autonomic storm (tachy, HTN, fever, diaphoresis) + delirium. Needs ICU, massive doses of benzos. Mortality 5-15% if untreated
  • Magnesium is key: Hypomagnesemia lowers seizure threshold, reduces benzo efficacy. Aggressively replete Mg until >2 mg/dL
  • CIWA doesn't work if intubated/ICU: Need fixed-dose protocol. CIWA requires patient cooperation
  • Phenobarbital for refractory DTs: If benzos failing (which is rare), add phenobarbital. Different GABA receptor, synergistic. Works when benzos don't
  • Don't confuse with hepatic encephalopathy: Both have AMS in alcoholic. HE has asterixis, elevated ammonia, responds to lactulose/rifaximin. Can coexist. If unsure, treat both
  • Occult withdrawal in hospital: Patient admitted for trauma/surgery/infection, becomes unexplained tachy/HTN/agitated 24-72hr later. Think withdrawal, check alcohol history
  • Restraints worsen outcomes: Increase agitation, rhabdomyolysis, aspiration. Use adequate sedation instead. Chemical > physical restraint
  • Can't oversedatewith benzos in withdrawal: Respiratory drive preserved until massive doses. Goal is calm but arousable. Don't underdose - prevents DTs
⚠️ ICU TRANSFER CRITERIA
  • Delirium tremens (autonomic instability + delirium)
  • Refractory withdrawal requiring high-dose benzos or phenobarbital
  • Seizures (especially if recurrent or status epilepticus)
  • Severe agitation requiring intubation for airway protection
  • Hemodynamic instability, severe hypertension
  • Concurrent critical illness (sepsis, GI bleed, pancreatitis)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • CIWA <8-10 for >24 hours
  • Stable vital signs off benzodiazepines
  • No seizure activity
  • Tolerating PO intake
  • Ambulating safely
  • Completed thiamine/vitamin repletion (or on PO regimen)
  • Substance use treatment/counseling initiated or arranged
  • Outpatient follow-up arranged (PCP, addiction medicine)
  • Safe discharge environment
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute Complications: Delirium tremens (mortality 5-15% if untreated), seizures (aspiration, trauma, status epilepticus), Wernicke encephalopathy (irreversible if not treated - ataxia, confusion, ophthalmoplegia → Korsakoff syndrome with permanent memory impairment), aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis (from agitation, seizures, restraints - can cause AKI)

Cardiovascular: Arrhythmias (especially if hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia), cardiomyopathy exacerbation (alcoholic CMP), hypertensive crisis, MI (demand ischemia from tachycardia)

From Underlying Alcoholism: GI bleed (varices, gastritis, Mallory-Weiss), pancreatitis, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, coagulopathy (low platelets, elevated INR), infections (pneumonia, SBP)

From Treatment: Over-sedation with respiratory depression (rare with benzos alone), paradoxical agitation, delirium from benzodiazepines

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lorazepam, 💊 Diazepam, 💊 Chlordiazepoxide, 💊 Phenobarbital, 💊 Thiamine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Ethanol Level, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hypomagnesemia, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Elevated INR

30. DELIRIUM

Acute Confusional State • CAM Criteria • Treat Underlying Cause
CLINICAL PRESENTATION & DIAGNOSIS

CAM Criteria (Confusion Assessment Method) - ALL required:

  • (1) Acute onset + fluctuating course: Symptoms developed acutely (hours-days), wax/wane throughout day
  • (2) Inattention: Difficulty focusing, easily distracted, can't follow conversation
  • PLUS EITHER: (3) Disorganized thinking (rambling, illogical) OR (4) Altered level of consciousness (hyperalert, lethargic, stuporous)

Types: Hyperactive (25% - agitated, combative, hallucinations), Hypoactive (25% - lethargic, withdrawn, often missed), Mixed (50%)

Common Causes - "I WATCH DEATH": Infections, Withdrawal, Acute metabolic, Trauma/CNS, Hypoxia, Deficiencies (B12, thiamine), Endocrine, Acute vascular, Toxins/drugs, Heavy metals

High-Risk Medications (Avoid): Anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, TCAs), benzodiazepines (paradoxical), opioids, H2 blockers, corticosteroids, dopamine agonists

WORKUP & TREATMENT

Labs: CBC, CMP, UA/culture, blood cultures if fever, TSH, B12, drug screen, ammonia if liver disease, ABG if hypoxia

Imaging: CT head if focal signs, fall, anticoagulated, new-onset

LP if: Fever + AMS with no clear source (meningitis/encephalitis)

Non-Pharmacologic (FIRST-LINE):

  • Reorient frequently (clocks, calendars, familiar objects)
  • Normalize sleep-wake cycle (lights on during day, dark/quiet at night)
  • Early mobilization (PT/OT daily)
  • Sensory aids (glasses, hearing aids)
  • Avoid restraints (worsen delirium)
  • Family/sitter presence

Pharmacologic (ONLY if severe agitation, danger to self/others):

  • Haloperidol 0.5-2mg IV/PO q4-6h PRN (low-dose). Avoid if QTc >500, Parkinson's, Lewy body dementia
  • Quetiapine 25-50mg PO q12h (if hyperactive, sundowning). Better for elderly
  • Avoid benzodiazepines (except alcohol/benzo withdrawal)
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Delirium vs Dementia: Delirium = acute onset (hours-days), fluctuating, inattention. Dementia = chronic (months-years), stable throughout day, memory loss predominates
  • Hypoactive delirium often missed: Quiet, withdrawn, "pleasantly confused." Worse outcomes than hyperactive. Screen all elderly admissions with CAM
  • Anticholinergics are enemy #1: Diphenhydramine, TCAs, scopolamine, first-gen antihistamines. Avoid in elderly
  • Restraints worsen delirium: Increase agitation, prolong delirium, cause injury. Use sitters, reorientation instead
  • Every delirious patient needs infection workup: UTI, pneumonia, bacteremia most common. Even if afebrile
⚠️ ICU TRANSFER CRITERIA
  • Severe agitation refractory to medications
  • Respiratory compromise requiring intubation for airway protection
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Concern for life-threatening cause (meningitis, severe sepsis)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Delirium resolved or significantly improved
  • Underlying cause identified and treated
  • Safe functional status (ambulation, ADLs)
  • Medication reconciliation (d/c deliriogenic meds)
  • Adequate support at discharge (may need rehab/SNF)
COMPLICATIONS

Acute: Falls, aspiration, pressure ulcers, prolonged hospitalization (↑LOS by 5-10 days), functional decline

Long-term: Persistent cognitive impairment (30-40%), increased mortality (11% at 1 month), institutionalization, progression to dementia

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Haloperidol, 💊 Quetiapine, 💊 Lorazepam, 💊 Melatonin, 💊 Dexmedetomidine, 💊 Thiamine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hyperglycemia, 🔬 Urinalysis, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 Elevated Lactate

31. HYPERTHYROIDISM / THYROID STORM

Graves • Toxic Adenoma • Storm = Emergency

Presentation: Weight loss despite ↑appetite, tremor, palpitations/AFib, heat intolerance, diarrhea, anxiety, proximal weakness. Graves: exophthalmos, pretibial myxedema, diffuse goiter

Storm (Life-Threatening): Fever >40°C (104°F), severe tachycardia (>140), AMS, agitation/psychosis, heart failure, vomiting/diarrhea. Diagnosis is clinical, in a severely thyrotoxic patient with systemic decompensation, aided by the scale (ATA 2016 Rec 34). Burch-Wartofsky (BWPS) ≥45 = storm, treat aggressively; 25-44 = impending storm: decide on aggressive therapy by clinical judgment and observe closely. Mortality 8-25% in modern series (ATA 2016)

Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (Diagnose at the Bedside):

Parameter Finding Points

Score ≥45 = thyroid storm | 25-44 = impending storm | <25 = unlikely≥45

Scale source: ATA 2016 Table 6 (Burch and Wartofsky). The Celsius bands are as ATA prints them and overlap at 38.3 and 39.4; the Fahrenheit bands do not. ATA's table lists the precipitant points reversed; its text counts an identified precipitant, as above

Common Precipitants: abrupt stopping of antithyroid drugs; thyroidectomy, or other surgery with unrecognized or undertreated thyrotoxicosis; acute illnesses; occasionally radioiodine (ATA 2016). Also infection, trauma, parturition, iodine load (contrast, amiodarone), DKA (Practical). Prevent by keeping patients euthyroid before elective surgery and delivery (ATA 2016)

Labs: TSH suppressed (usually undetectable); free T4 and/or T3 above the reference range. In mild disease only T3 may be high (T3-toxicosis); total T3 is often preferred to free T3 (ATA 2016). Find the cause if not clinically apparent: TRAb, radioiodine uptake, or thyroid blood flow on ultrasound; scan if toxic adenoma or multinodular goiter is suspected (Rec 1). Before an antithyroid drug: CBC with differential and liver profile (Rec 15). Also check glucose and cortisol (consider coexisting adrenal insufficiency) (Practical)

Storm Treatment (ATA 2016; start all promptly):

  • Antithyroid drug now: PTU 500-1000 mg load, then 250 mg every 4 h (preferred in storm: also blocks T4→T3 conversion), or methimazole 60-80 mg/day (ATA 2016 Table 7)
  • β-blocker: propranolol 60-80 mg every 4 h (blocks T4→T3 conversion at high doses); IV alternative: esmolol infusion 50-100 mcg/kg/min. Consider invasive monitoring in heart failure (ATA 2016 Tables 4 and 7)
  • Iodine, at least 1 h after the antithyroid drug: SSKI 5 drops (0.25 mL, 250 mg) PO every 6 h; alternative Lugol's solution (ATA 2016 Table 7), 10 drops every 8 h (Practical)
  • Hydrocortisone 300 mg IV load, then 100 mg every 8 h (prophylaxis against relative adrenal insufficiency; may block T4→T3 conversion); alternative dexamethasone (ATA 2016 Table 7)
  • Supportive: cooling with acetaminophen and cooling blankets, volume resuscitation, nutritional support, respiratory care and ICU monitoring as needed (ATA 2016 Rec 35); avoid aspirin (Practical); treat the precipitant
  • Refractory: plasmapheresis/plasma exchange or emergency thyroidectomy (ATA 2016)

Outpatient Hyperthyroidism: β-blocker for symptomatic thyrotoxicosis, especially older patients, resting HR >90 or cardiovascular disease (ATA 2016 Rec 2); propranolol 10-40 mg 3-4 times daily (Table 4). Graves: radioiodine, antithyroid drug (about 12-18 months, Rec 22) or thyroidectomy (Rec 3). Toxic adenoma or multinodular goiter: radioiodine or surgery (Rec 37)

Antithyroid drugs: methimazole for nearly everyone, except first-trimester pregnancy (PTU), thyroid storm, and minor methimazole reactions in patients refusing radioiodine or surgery (Rec 13). Starting methimazole by free T4: 5-10 mg/day if 1-1.5 times the upper limit, 10-20 mg if 1.5-2 times, 30-40 mg if 2-3 times. PTU 50-150 mg three times daily. Because of PTU hepatotoxicity, the FDA advises reserving PTU for the first trimester or methimazole intolerance. Warn patients to stop and call for fever, sore throat, rash, jaundice, dark urine (Rec 14). Recheck free T4 and total T3 2-6 weeks after starting; TSH can stay suppressed for months (ATA 2016)

⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky ≥45)
  • Hemodynamic instability or arrhythmias (AFib with RVR, VT)
  • Altered mental status, seizures
  • High-output heart failure
  • Hyperthermia not responding to treatment
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Heart rate controlled (<100 at rest)
  • Afebrile, mentating normally
  • Tolerating oral medications
  • On appropriate thionamide dose with β-blocker
  • Endocrinology follow-up arranged within 1-2 weeks
  • Free T4 and total T3 rechecked 2-6 weeks after starting the antithyroid drug (ATA 2016)
💎 PEARLS
  • Only one sequencing rule in storm: iodine at least 1 h after the antithyroid drug (ATA 2016 Table 7). Give the antithyroid drug, β-blocker and hydrocortisone promptly; do not delay the antithyroid drug
  • Iodine without an antithyroid drug = bad: it can feed new hormone synthesis (Practical). Iodine lowers hormone release and inhibits its own organification (Wolff-Chaikoff), but escape occurs (ATA 2016)
  • Pregnancy (ATA 2026): switch methimazole to PTU when planning pregnancy; PTU may be used when starting treatment before 16 weeks, and a switch from methimazole to PTU may be considered until 16 weeks (about 1:20, e.g. methimazole 5 mg daily = PTU 50 mg twice daily). After 16 weeks it is unclear whether to continue PTU or switch to methimazole. Methimazole exposure is linked to more severe malformations (e.g. aplasia cutis, omphalocele). Lactation: methimazole preferred
  • Apathetic hyperthyroidism (elderly): presents with fatigue, weight loss, AF and weakness without classic sympathetic symptoms (no tremor, no anxiety). TSH suppressed; easy to miss if not checked (Practical)
  • Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT): type 1 (underlying nodules or Graves): methimazole, about 40 mg daily. Type 2 (destructive thyroiditis): prednisone 40 mg daily for 2-4 weeks, then taper over 2-3 months. Unstable, unclear type or no response to one agent: both. No response to both: thyroidectomy. Whether to stop amiodarone is decided case by case with the cardiologist (ATA 2016 Rec 112-116)
  • Aspirin in storm: avoid; salicylates can raise free thyroid hormone. Use acetaminophen and cooling blankets (Practical; ATA 2016 Rec 35 names acetaminophen)
  • Cholestyramine as adjunct: binds thyroid hormone in the gut; ATA lists it for rapid preparation before urgent surgery (ATA 2016)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Methimazole/PTU, 💊 Esmolol, 💊 Hydrocortisone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low TSH, 🔬 Free T4/Free T3, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Troponin

32. HYPOTHYROIDISM / MYXEDEMA COMA

Severe Hypothyroidism • Rare but Lethal

Chronic Hypothyroidism: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, hair loss, dry skin, bradycardia, delayed DTRs, periorbital edema. Labs: overt = TSH above the reference range with low free T4; high TSH with normal free T4 = subclinical (card 237); low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH suggests central hypothyroidism (Practical)

Treatment Outpatient: Levothyroxine full replacement about 1.6 mcg/kg/day when TSH is markedly elevated; lower doses (e.g. 25-50 mcg) in milder disease (ATA 2014). Older patients: start low and titrate slowly; normal TSH runs higher over 65, so higher targets may fit (ATA 2014). Known coronary disease: start 12.5-25 mcg/day (ATA 2014). Check TSH 4-6 weeks after any dose change; adjust by 12.5-25 mcg/day (ATA 2014). Take 60 min before breakfast or at bedtime (3 h or more after the evening meal); separate from calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate (4 h traditional) (ATA 2014). Avoid overtreatment, especially TSH <0.1 in older people and postmenopausal women (atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis) (ATA 2014). Pregnancy: raise the dose about 25% at a positive pregnancy test; TSH every 4 weeks to midgestation (ATA 2026)

Myxedema Coma (Emergency; high mortality, ATA 2014):

  • Presentation: Profound hypothermia (<95°F), severe bradycardia (<50), hypoventilation (↓CO2 drive, respiratory failure), hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, AMS→coma, non-pitting edema, pericardial/pleural effusions
  • Precipitants: Infection, MI, stroke, hypothermia, sedatives/narcotics, surgery
  • Diagnosis: clinical. Start treatment on clinical suspicion; do not wait for results. TSH may not reflect severity (wide range, lower rises in older patients, inappropriately normal or low in central hypothyroidism); free T4 low. Draw cortisol before steroids (ATA 2014)

Myxedema Coma Treatment:

  • Glucocorticoid first: stress-dose IV glucocorticoid before levothyroxine (ATA 2014 Rec 21b); IV levothyroxine is contraindicated with uncorrected adrenal insufficiency (US label). Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, then 200 mg/24 h as on card 33; stop once adrenal insufficiency is excluded (Practical)
  • Levothyroxine IV: ATA 2014: 200-400 mcg load (lower for smaller or older patients and those with coronary disease or arrhythmia), then 1.6 mcg/kg/day reduced to 75% while IV. US label: 300-500 mcg load, then 50-100 mcg IV daily, lower in older or cardiac patients; boluses >500 mcg are linked to cardiac complications. Switch to oral or enteral once improving
  • Liothyronine IV (optional, ATA weak recommendation): 5-20 mcg load, then 2.5-10 mcg every 8 h, lower for smaller or older patients and coronary disease or arrhythmia; avoid high doses, since high T3 during treatment is linked to mortality; continue until clearly recovering (ATA 2014). US label (Triostat): 25-50 mcg initially (10-20 mcg with cardiovascular disease); case reports linked ≥65 mcg/day in the first days with lower mortality; little experience above 100 mcg/day. Label and guideline differ; ATA is the more cautious
  • Endpoints: mental status, cardiac and pulmonary function; T4 and T3 every 1-2 days. If TSH does not trend down or T4/T3 do not improve, increase levothyroxine and/or add liothyronine; high T3: reduce (ATA 2014 Rec 21d)
  • Supportive: treat hypothermia, hypoventilation (ventilate if needed), volume depletion, hypoglycemia and hyponatremia; empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics if sepsis is possible (ATA 2014). Passive rewarming is usual practice; active external rewarming can cause vasodilation and hypotension (Practical). Severe symptomatic hyponatremia: hypertonic saline within the correction limits on card 12 (Practical)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Myxedema coma or impending coma
  • Hypothermia (<95°F/35°C)
  • Respiratory failure or hypoventilation
  • Hemodynamic instability, severe bradycardia (<40)
  • Severe hyponatremia (<120 mEq/L)
  • Altered mental status
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Mentating normally, afebrile
  • Hemodynamically stable, HR >50
  • Tolerating oral levothyroxine
  • Sodium >130 mEq/L and stable
  • Precipitating cause treated
  • Endocrinology follow-up arranged
  • TSH recheck 4-6 weeks after the oral dose is set (ATA 2014)
💎 PEARLS
  • Steroid BEFORE thyroid hormone in crisis: treating hypothyroidism may speed cortisol metabolism, and thyroid hormone has unmasked adrenal insufficiency (ATA 2014)
  • Rewarming: passive rewarming is the usual approach; active external warming can cause peripheral vasodilation and hypotension (Practical)
  • Hyponatremia improves with treatment: reflects impaired free-water excretion (Practical). Do not overcorrect (card 12)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Levothyroxine, 💊 Hydrocortisone, 💊 IV Fluids
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 Free T4/Free T3, 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

33. ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY / CRISIS

Primary (Addison's) • Secondary • Crisis = Emergency

Chronic AI Presentation: Fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia. PRIMARY (Addison's) ALSO has: hyperkalemia, hyperpigmentation (↑ACTH stimulates melanocytes), salt craving. SECONDARY: no hyperkalemia or hyperpigmentation; hyponatremia can still occur (Practical)

Adrenal Crisis (Emergency): Shock (refractory hypotension), abdominal pain/vomiting (mimics acute abdomen), fever, severe dehydration, AMS/confusion. Precipitants: infection, surgery, trauma, missed doses or abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal. Test acutely ill patients with otherwise unexplained volume depletion, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, fever, abdominal pain or hyperpigmentation (Endocrine Society 2016 Rec 1.1)

Glucocorticoid users: with current or recent use of any glucocorticoid, by any route and at any dose, and no testing, consider adrenal crisis when there is hemodynamic instability, vomiting or diarrhea, and treat with parenteral glucocorticoid and fluids (ESE/ES 2024 R 3.2)

Diagnosis:

  • Crisis: treat first. If it causes no delay, draw cortisol and ACTH before hydrocortisone; confirm later with cosyntropin testing, pausing glucocorticoid once the patient is stable (Endocrine Society 2016 Rec 1.3)
  • Cosyntropin stimulation test (preferred): 250 mcg IV; cortisol at 30 or 60 min. Peak <18 mcg/dL (500 nmol/L) indicates adrenal insufficiency; the cutoff is assay dependent (Endocrine Society 2016 Rec 2.1; ESE/ES 2024). Newer assays and LC-MS/MS read lower, so use the lab's cutoff (Practical)
  • Morning cortisol if stimulation testing is not feasible: <5 mcg/dL (140 nmol/L) with ACTH is a preliminary test suggesting adrenal insufficiency (Rec 2.3). No evidence supports a random cortisol to rule out adrenal insufficiency (Endocrine Society 2016)
  • Primary vs secondary: with confirmed cortisol deficiency, ACTH >2 times the upper reference limit is consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency (Rec 2.4); low or inappropriately normal ACTH suggests secondary (Practical). In primary, measure renin and aldosterone (Rec 2.5)
  • Cause of primary: autoimmune in most adults; check 21-hydroxylase antibodies; men with negative antibodies: plasma very-long-chain fatty acids (adrenoleukodystrophy); then adrenal CT for infiltration or metastases (Endocrine Society 2016)

Crisis Treatment (DON'T DELAY):

  • Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (or IM) immediately, then 200 mg/24 h by continuous IV infusion or 50 mg IV/IM every 6 h (Endocrine Society 2016 Rec 4.1; ESE/ES 2024); reduce to 100 mg/day the next day and taper to oral as the patient improves (Endocrine Society 2016)
  • Fluids: 1000 mL isotonic saline (or 5% glucose in isotonic saline) within the first hour, then continuous isotonic saline guided by need (Endocrine Society 2016)
  • Hypoglycemia: IV dextrose, D50 25-50 mL as on card 161 (Practical)
  • If hydrocortisone is unavailable: prednisolone; dexamethasone is the least preferred, only if no other glucocorticoid is available (Endocrine Society 2016 Rec 4.2)
  • Treat precipitant: antibiotics if infection (Practical)
  • Fludrocortisone not needed while hydrocortisone exceeds 50 mg/24 h; start it in primary adrenal insufficiency as the dose falls (Endocrine Society 2016)

Chronic Replacement (After Crisis):

  • Hydrocortisone 15-25 mg/day in 2-3 doses, largest on waking, next in the early afternoon (Endocrine Society 2016 Rec 3.2). Alternative: prednisolone 3-5 mg/day (Rec 3.3); avoid dexamethasone (Rec 3.4). Adjust on clinical response, not hormone levels (Rec 3.5-3.6)
  • Fludrocortisone 50-100 mcg daily for confirmed aldosterone deficiency (primary); no salt restriction (Rec 3.7). Not needed in secondary adrenal insufficiency (Practical); not used in glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency (ESE/ES 2024 R 2.12)
  • Sick-day rules: fever: double (>38°C) or triple (>39°C) the dose until recovery, usually 2-3 days (Endocrine Society 2016). Glucocorticoid-induced AI with minor illness: hydrocortisone 40 mg/day in 3 doses (or prednisone 10 mg/day) for 2-5 days (ESE/ES 2024). Vomiting or unable to take tablets: hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or SC (Endocrine Society 2016)
  • Procedures: minor to moderate surgery: hydrocortisone 25-75 mg/24 h, usually 1-2 days. Major surgery, delivery, trauma or intensive care: 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg/24 h by infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 h, tapering as the patient recovers (Endocrine Society 2016; ESE/ES 2024)

Glucocorticoid-induced AI (ESE/ES 2024):

  • Courses under 3-4 weeks: stop without taper or testing, whatever the dose (R 2.1)
  • Long-term therapy: taper only when the disease is controlled, down to a physiologic dose (prednisone 4-6 mg) (R 2.2). Guide: >40 mg: cut 5-10 mg weekly; 20-40 mg: 5 mg weekly; 10-20 mg: 2.5 mg every 1-4 weeks; 5-10 mg: 1 mg every 1-4 weeks (Table 4). Severe withdrawal symptoms: return to the last tolerated dose and slow the taper (R 2.3)
  • Do not test while on supraphysiologic doses (R 2.4). At a physiologic dose, keep tapering with clinical monitoring or check a morning cortisol: >10 mcg/dL (300 nmol/L) indicates recovery, stop; 5-10 mcg/dL continue and repeat in weeks to months; <5 mcg/dL continue and repeat in a few months (R 2.6-2.7). Dynamic tests are not routine (R 2.8)
  • Also consider it with high-dose or long-term (>1 year) inhaled or topical glucocorticoids, intra-articular injection in the previous 2 months, several formulations at once, or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (R 2.9)
  • Untested current or recent users need stress-dose cover: oral for minor stress; parenteral for moderate to major stress, procedures under general or regional anesthesia, instability, or prolonged vomiting or diarrhea (R 3.1)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Adrenal crisis with refractory hypotension
  • Shock requiring vasopressors
  • Severe altered mental status
  • Severe electrolyte abnormalities (K >6.5, Na <120)
  • Hypoglycemia not responding to dextrose
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable off pressors
  • Tolerating oral hydrocortisone ± fludrocortisone
  • Electrolytes normalized (Na >130, K <5.5)
  • Precipitating cause treated
  • Patient educated on sick-day dosing and on parenteral self- or lay-administration of emergency glucocorticoid (Endocrine Society 2016 Rec 4.4)
  • Steroid emergency card and medical alert identification (Rec 4.5); emergency injectable hydrocortisone prescribed (Practical)
  • Endocrinology follow-up arranged; for glucocorticoid-induced AI, referral after an adrenal crisis or when the HPA axis has not recovered by 1 year on a physiologic dose (ESE/ES 2024 R 2.11)
💎 PEARLS
  • Don't wait to treat crisis: give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, after drawing cortisol and ACTH if that causes no delay; confirm later (Endocrine Society 2016). Use hydrocortisone, not dexamethasone: dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is the least preferred alternative (Endocrine Society 2016)
  • Hyperkalemia + hyponatremia = PRIMARY: Aldosterone deficiency. Secondary AI has normal K (aldosterone intact), though hyponatremia can still occur (Practical)
  • Hyperpigmentation = PRIMARY: ↑ACTH stimulates melanocytes. Look: knuckles, palmar creases, scars, mucous membranes
  • Glucocorticoid-induced AI: HPA suppression is an inevitable effect of chronic glucocorticoid therapy, and at least 1% of the population takes it long term (ESE/ES 2024). Courses under 3-4 weeks need no taper; longer courses taper as above
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Hydrocortisone, 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Dextrose D50/D10
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low Cortisol, 🔬 ACTH, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hyperglycemia, 🔬 Hypoglycemia
