34. HYPERCALCEMIA

"Stones, Bones, Groans, Psychiatric Overtones"

Severity (albumin-adjusted calcium; ES 2023): mild <12 mg/dL, moderate 12-14, severe >14. Use albumin-adjusted or ionized calcium, especially with low albumin; corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL) (Practical). Symptoms track severity and the speed of the rise (ES 2023)

Symptoms: Mild: often asymptomatic, or fatigue, constipation, cognitive change. Moderate to severe: polyuria/polydipsia (nephrogenic DI), constipation, nausea/vomiting, weakness, confusion, lethargy, shortened QT interval. Severe: AMS, coma, arrhythmias (Practical)

Causes (most cases are these 2; Practical):

  • Primary hyperparathyroidism: usually outpatient and mild. Diagnosis: albumin-adjusted calcium high with elevated or inappropriately normal intact PTH on two occasions at least 2 weeks apart; consider familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (urine calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01), thiazides, lithium (5th International Workshop 2022). Parathyroidectomy if symptomatic, or if any of: calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limit; vertebral fracture or T-score ≤−2.5 at any site; eGFR or creatinine clearance <60; nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis; urine calcium >250 mg/day (women) or >300 mg/day (men); age <50 (Workshop 2022)
  • Malignancy: usually inpatient, moderate to severe. PTH suppressed (below the assay range). Mechanisms: PTHrP (humoral, without bone metastases), local osteolysis (including myeloma), calcitriol production (lymphoma), parathyroid carcinoma (ES 2023). Tumor examples: PTHrP in squamous, renal and breast cancer (Practical)
  • Other: Granulomatous disease (sarcoid, TB - ↑calcitriol), meds (thiazides, lithium, vitamin D intoxication), immobilization

Treatment (moderate 12-14, severe >14, or symptomatic):

  • IV fluids first: isotonic saline 1-2 L bolus, then 200-500 mL/h to keep urine output 100-150 mL/h; lowers calcium about 1-1.5 mg/dL over 24 h; tailor to cardiac function and watch for volume overload (ES 2023 Table 1, UGPS 1)
  • Antiresorptive for hypercalcemia of malignancy (IV bisphosphonate or denosumab; ES 2023 Rec 1, strong). ES suggests denosumab over an IV bisphosphonate (Rec 2, conditional); the US denosumab (Xgeva) label limits this use to bisphosphonate-refractory disease
  • Zoledronic acid 3-4 mg IV over 15-30 min (repeat in 7 days if needed, then every 3-4 weeks) or pamidronate 60-90 mg IV over 2-24 h. Onset 48-72 h. Check creatinine clearance first; if <60 mL/min use renal dosing (zoledronic acid over 30-60 min); kidney injury risk especially with GFR <30-35 (ES 2023 Table 1, UGPS 4-5)
  • Denosumab 120 mg SC, repeated at weeks 1, 2 and 4, then monthly (ES 2023 Table 1); label: every 4 weeks with extra doses on days 8 and 15. Onset 3-10 days. Not renally cleared, but GFR <30 raises hypocalcemia risk; consider a lower dose (ES 2023). Correct hypocalcemia first; severe and fatal hypocalcemia has occurred (US label)
  • Calcitonin 4-8 units/kg IM or SC every 6-12 h for 48-72 h: onset 4-6 h, lowers calcium 1-2 mg/dL, tachyphylaxis after 48-72 h. Severe (>14 mg/dL): add calcitonin to the IV bisphosphonate or denosumab (ES 2023 Rec 3)
  • Loop diuretic: not routine; only after volume repletion, when needed to prevent fluid overload in renal insufficiency or heart failure (ES 2023 Table 1)
  • Parathyroid carcinoma: cinacalcet (FDA-approved) or IV bisphosphonate/denosumab; cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily, titrated every 2-4 weeks; surgical consultation (ES 2023 Rec 6-8, UGPS 8)
  • Also: monitor and replete magnesium and phosphate (UGPS 6); check vitamin D to avoid hypocalcemia on antiresorptives (UGPS 3); oral exam before antiresorptives (UGPS 2); oncology consultation (UGPS 7) (ES 2023)
  • Dialysis: severe hypercalcemia with kidney failure or refractory disease (Practical)
  • Avoid thiazides, lithium, vitamin D/calcium supplements (Practical)

Special Cases:

  • Calcitriol-mediated (granulomatous disease, lymphoma): glucocorticoids: hydrocortisone 200-400 mg IV/day for 3-5 days, or prednisone 60 mg/day for 10 days, or 10-20 mg/day for 7 days (ES 2023 Table 1). Lymphoma still severe or symptomatic on glucocorticoids: add IV bisphosphonate or denosumab (ES 2023 Rec 5); treat the malignancy
  • Vitamin D intoxication: Stop vitamin D, steroids, fluids, bisphosphonates
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe hypercalcemia (Ca >14 mg/dL)
  • Altered mental status, obtundation, coma
  • Cardiac arrhythmias (short QT, bradycardia, heart block)
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Refractory to IV fluids and bisphosphonates
  • Need for emergent dialysis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Calcium <12 mg/dL and downtrending
  • Mentally at baseline, tolerating PO
  • Hemodynamically stable, euvolemic
  • Underlying cause addressed (malignancy workup initiated if indicated)
  • Offending medications stopped
  • Appropriate follow-up (oncology, endocrinology) arranged
  • Recheck calcium in 1-2 weeks scheduled
💎 PEARLS
  • PTH tells you the cause: high or inappropriately normal PTH = PTH-mediated (primary hyperparathyroidism; also familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, lithium, thiazides) (Workshop 2022). Suppressed PTH = malignancy, granulomatous disease, vitamin D excess, others (Practical)
  • Outpatient vs inpatient: Outpatient mild hypercalcemia = hyperparathyroidism. Inpatient severe = malignancy (Practical)
  • Calcitonin is a bridge: works in 4-6 h but tachyphylaxis after 48-72 h; limit to 48-72 h (ES 2023)
  • Antiresorptives are the mainstay: IV bisphosphonate onset 48-72 h, denosumab 3-10 days. Check renal function before a bisphosphonate and use renal dosing below 60 mL/min (ES 2023)
  • Loop diuretics are not routine: only after volume repletion, to prevent fluid overload in renal insufficiency or heart failure (ES 2023)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Zoledronic Acid, 💊 Hydrocortisone, 💊 Denosumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hypercalcemia, 🔬 Elevated PTH, 🔬 Low PTH, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 LDH
↑ Back to Table of Contents

35. HYPOMAGNESEMIA

Mg <1.5 • Often With HypoK/HypoCa

Causes: GI losses (diarrhea, malabsorption), renal losses (diuretics - loops/thiazides, PPIs, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin), alcohol, DKA, refeeding syndrome, chronic PPI use

Symptoms: Often asymptomatic until Mg <1. Tremor, muscle fasciculations, weakness, tetany (Trousseau/Chvostek signs), seizures, arrhythmias (torsades de pointes, afib, PVCs), personality changes. Refractory hypokalemia/hypocalcemia (Mg needed for K/Ca homeostasis)

ECG: Prolonged QT, widened QRS, peaked T waves, torsades de pointes

Treatment:

  • Asymptomatic/Mild (Mg >1): Magnesium oxide 400-800mg PO BID-TID (poorly absorbed, causes diarrhea). OR Mag glycinate/citrate better tolerated
  • Moderate (Mg <1) or Symptomatic: Magnesium sulfate 2g IV over 15-30min, repeat q6h until Mg >1.5. Then transition to PO
  • Severe/Life-Threatening (Torsades, seizure, tetany): Magnesium sulfate 2-4g IV over 10-15min, then continuous infusion 1-2g/hr. Monitor DTRs (loss = hypermagnesemia). Cardiac monitor
  • Replete K and Ca simultaneously: Won't normalize until Mg corrected. Check all three, replete together
  • Monitor serum Mg q6-12h during repletion. Goal >1.5-2 mg/dL
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Torsades de pointes or other malignant arrhythmias
  • Seizures
  • Severe tetany or respiratory muscle weakness
  • Mg <1.0 mg/dL with symptoms
  • Refractory arrhythmias despite repletion
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Mg >1.5 mg/dL and stable
  • Potassium and calcium normalized
  • No arrhythmias on telemetry
  • Tolerating oral magnesium supplementation
  • Underlying cause addressed (medication adjusted, PPI stopped)
  • Recheck labs in 1 week arranged
💎 PEARLS
  • Refractory hypokalemia = check Mg: Can't fix K until Mg replete. Mg needed for K channel function
  • Hypocalcemia with Mg deficiency: Mg needed for PTH secretion/action. Replete Mg first, Ca will follow
  • Torsades de pointes: 2g Mg IV over 1-2min (even if Mg normal). First-line treatment
  • Monitor DTRs: Loss of reflexes = hypermagnesemia (>4-5). Stop infusion if DTRs lost
  • PPI-induced hypomagnesemia: Chronic PPI use (months-years) → severe hypomagnesemia. Stop PPI, switch to H2 blocker
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Magnesium
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hypomagnesemia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hypophosphatemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

36. RHABDOMYOLYSIS

CK >1000 • Myoglobinuria • AKI Risk

Causes - "CRAMPS": Crush injury/trauma, Recreational drugs (cocaine, PCP, MDMA, amphetamines), Alcohol/Anesthetics (malignant hyperthermia, NMS), Meds (statins, fibrates, colchicine), Prolonged immobilization/seizures, Strenuous exercise, Heat stroke, Infections (influenza, HIV)

Classic Triad (only 10% have all 3): Myalgias, weakness, dark urine (tea/cola-colored from myoglobinuria)

Presentation: Muscle pain/tenderness/swelling, weakness, dark urine. May have compartment syndrome (tense compartments, pain out of proportion, 5 P's). Severe: AKI, hyperkalemia, arrhythmias

Labs:

  • CK (creatine kinase): >1000 (often >5000, can be >100,000). Peak 24-36hr, normalize in 3-5 days. Trend daily
  • Urine: Dipstick positive for blood (myoglobin cross-reacts) but NO RBCs on microscopy. Urine myoglobin (rarely sent, not needed)
  • BMP: AKI (Cr rising), hyperkalemia (released from muscle - LIFE-THREATENING), hypocalcemia early (Ca deposits in necrotic muscle), hypercalcemia late (resorption), hyperphosphatemia (released from muscle), elevated anion gap (lactate)
  • ABG: Metabolic acidosis
  • Check: LDH, AST/ALT (elevated from muscle, not liver), uric acid (elevated)

Treatment (Aggressive IVF is Key):

  • IV Fluids: NS 200-300 mL/hr (or 1-1.5 L/hr if severe). Goal: UOP >200-300 mL/hr (flush myoglobin before it precipitates in tubules). Continue until CK downtrending <5000 AND Cr improving
  • Monitor: Strict I/Os, UOP hourly, daily CK/BMP/Ca/Phos, cardiac telemetry (hyperK risk)
  • Alkalinize urine (controversial, not routinely recommended): Some add NaHCO3 to IVF (3 amps in 1L D5W at 200 mL/hr) to maintain urine pH >6.5 (prevents myoglobin precipitation). But no proven benefit, risks volume overload/alkalosis
  • Avoid: NSAIDs, nephrotoxins
  • Hyperkalemia: Treat aggressively (insulin/dextrose, calcium, kayexalate, dialysis if severe)
  • Hypocalcemia (early): DO NOT treat unless symptomatic (seizures, tetany, long QT). Repleting Ca can worsen later hypercalcemia
  • Dialysis if: Severe AKI (oliguric, Cr >5-6), refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, volume overload
  • Compartment syndrome: Ortho/surgery consult URGENTLY. Fasciotomy if pressures >30 mmHg
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • CK >100,000 or rapidly rising
  • Severe hyperkalemia (K >6.5) or cardiac arrhythmias
  • AKI with oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) or need for RRT
  • Compartment syndrome (surgical emergency)
  • Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2)
  • Volume overload from aggressive resuscitation
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • CK downtrending <5000 U/L
  • Creatinine stable or improving
  • Potassium normalized
  • Good urine output maintained
  • Underlying cause addressed (medication stopped, dehydration corrected)
  • No compartment syndrome concerns
  • Recheck CK/BMP in 2-3 days arranged
💎 PEARLS
  • IVF, IVF, IVF: Aggressive volume expansion is treatment. Prevents AKI by flushing myoglobin. Goal UOP >200 mL/hr
  • Hyperkalemia kills: Released from necrotic muscle. Check K q6-12h initially. Cardiac monitor. Treat aggressively
  • Don't treat early hypocalcemia: Ca deposits in muscle. Later, gets resorbed → hypercalcemia. Treating early worsens late
  • Dipstick + but no RBCs = myoglobinuria: Myoglobin cross-reacts with hemoglobin on dipstick. Microscopy negative for RBCs
  • Statin-induced rhabdo: Risk factors: Asian, elderly, CKD, drug interactions (gemfibrozil, azoles, macrolides). Check CK before starting if high risk
  • Compartment syndrome: Tense compartment, pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch. Pressures >30 mmHg. SURGICAL EMERGENCY - fasciotomy
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Sodium Bicarbonate, 💊 Furosemide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Urinalysis, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Low Bicarbonate
↑ Back to Table of Contents

38. PLEURAL EFFUSION

Transudate vs Exudate • Light's Criteria
DIAGNOSIS AND MANAGEMENT

Presentation: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough. Exam: Decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus

CXR: Blunting of the costophrenic angle needs at least 175 mL on a PA film; a lateral view shows smaller effusions. Loculated fluid does not layer on decubitus films, and CXR alone misses about 10% of parapneumonic effusions (AATS 2017)

Thoracic Ultrasound: Perform at presentation and again immediately before every pleural procedure (BTS 2023). Image-guided thoracentesis should always be used (BTS 2023, strong by consensus; ATS/STS/STR 2018 for malignant effusion, conditional, very low certainty; AATS 2017 for pleural infection, Class I, LOE B): fewer pneumothoraces and more successful taps

CT: If aspiration is not safe: CT thorax with pleural-phase (venous) contrast, or chest, abdomen and pelvis if malignancy is suspected (BTS 2023). A negative CT does not exclude malignancy (BTS 2023, strong by consensus). Suspected pleural infection: contrast CT chest (AATS 2017, Class IIa, LOE B)

Light's Criteria (Exudate if ≥1 of 3; BTS 2023 Table 1):

  • Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein >0.5
  • Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH >0.6
  • Pleural fluid LDH >2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH

Send serum protein and LDH at the same time as the tap (BTS 2023). Diuretic-treated cardiac or hepatic transudates are often misclassified as exudates (Practical). If the picture is clinically transudative: serum minus pleural albumin >1.2 g/dL favors a transudate (Practical; >1.1 g/dL suggests hepatic hydrothorax, AASLD 2021), and serum NT-proBNP supports heart failure (BTS 2023, conditional)

Transudate (↑Hydrostatic Pressure or ↓Oncotic Pressure):

  • Heart failure (most common): Usually bilateral (BTS 2023). Treat with diuretics. Practical: tap if unilateral or markedly asymmetric, febrile, pleuritic, or not resolving with diuresis
  • Hepatic hydrothorax: Usually right-sided (73%); 9% have no clinical ascites; serum minus pleural albumin >1.1 g/dL is suggestive (AASLD 2021). Sodium restriction and diuretics; thoracentesis without routine platelet or plasma transfusion. Refractory or recurrent: TIPS or liver transplant evaluation. Avoid chest tubes (high morbidity); an IPC may be considered with caution (AASLD 2021)
  • Hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome: Nephrotic: serum albumin <2.5 g/dL with proteinuria >3.5 g/day (Practical)
  • Less common: Mitral stenosis, peritoneal dialysis, constrictive pericarditis, chronic hypothyroidism (BTS 2023 Table 2)

Exudate (Inflammation, Infection, Malignancy):

  • Pneumonia/Parapneumonic: Most common exudate. Look for an effusion in every pneumonia and unexplained sepsis, and when pneumonia fails to respond (AATS 2017, Class I, LOE B). Ultrasound-guided tap if >1 cm on CXR or >2 cm on CT (AATS 2017). Chest tube if pH <7.2 (Class I, LOE B), or LDH >1000 IU/L, glucose <40 mg/dL, or loculation (Class IIa, LOE B) (AATS 2017). Otherwise antibiotics, with regular review and a repeat tap if not improving (BTS 2023). BTS 2023 (non-US) drains at pH ≤7.2 and, at pH 7.2-7.4, considers drainage if LDH >900 IU/L
  • Empyema: Pus, or positive Gram stain or culture (AATS 2017, Class I, LOE B): chest tube plus antibiotics. Thoracentesis alone is not adequate (Class III, LOE C). Image-guided drain for early, minimally septated empyema (Class I, LOE B); small-bore catheter for septated effusions if not a surgical candidate (Class IIa, LOE C); routine flushing (Class I, LOE B); CT to confirm drainage (Class I, LOE C). Incomplete drainage: VATS first-line for stage II empyema (Class IIa, LOE B). Intrapleural tPA + DNase: not routine per AATS 2017 (Class IIa, LOE A); BTS 2023 (non-US) suggests tPA 10 mg + DNase 5 mg twice daily for 3 days for a residual collection after drainage (conditional, by consensus). Details: card 173
  • Malignancy: Lung, breast, lymphoma, ovarian most common (Practical). Often bloody. Send 25-50 mL for cytology (BTS 2023, strong by consensus). Cytology sensitivity is about 60% overall (BTS 2023 Pleural Procedures Statement; 46% pooled in the guideline review), varies by tumour type, and is low in mesothelioma. Negative cytology with ongoing suspicion: image-guided or thoracoscopic biopsy; no blind biopsy (BTS 2023, strong). Management: see Treatment
  • TB: Lymphocytic exudate. Pleural fluid ADA has high sensitivity and specificity (pooled 91% and 88%); in low-prevalence populations use ADA mainly to exclude TB (BTS 2023, conditional). Practical: ADA >40 U/L is the usual cut-off; fluid AFB smear and culture are often negative. Pleural tissue for culture and histology (granulomas) is preferred (BTS 2023, strong by consensus)
  • PE: A common exudate (BTS 2023 Table 2); may be bloody (Practical). When no diagnosis is reached, reconsider PE, TB, lymphoma and heart failure (BTS 2023). CTPA if suspected (card 8)
  • Pancreatitis: Left-sided, elevated pleural fluid amylase (>serum)

Send Pleural Fluid for:

  • Always: Protein and LDH (with serum protein and LDH), cell count and differential, Gram stain and culture. Culture: from the tap itself, not an existing drain; inoculate 5-10 mL into aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles plus a plain sterile container (AATS 2017, Class I, LOE B; BTS 2023, strong by consensus)
  • Suspected infection, non-purulent fluid: pH within 1 hour in a blood gas analyzer; lidocaine and heparin lower it, air in the syringe raises it (AATS 2017; BTS 2023). Glucose if pH is unavailable. Not needed if frank pus. Thresholds: parapneumonic bullet above
  • Suspected malignancy: Cytology, 25-50 mL; more than 50 mL adds no yield (BTS 2023). If a small sample was non-diagnostic, send a larger one
  • Suspected TB: ADA, AFB smear and culture; pleural biopsy for culture and histology
  • Bloody: Hematocrit (pleural Hct >50% of blood Hct supports hemothorax; BTS 2023; see Condition 316)
  • Suspected pancreatitis or esophageal rupture: Amylase
  • Milky: Triglycerides >110 mg/dL = chylothorax; cholesterol >200 mg/dL with low triglycerides = pseudochylothorax (BTS 2023 Table 5; matches card 317)

Treatment:

  • Treat the underlying cause
  • Therapeutic thoracentesis (symptomatic effusion): Ultrasound-guided; drain slowly by syringe or gravity, never by vacuum bottle or wall suction; in general max 1.5 L per attempt; stop for chest tightness, pain, persistent cough, or worsening dyspnea. Routine manometry does not reduce risk (BTS 2023 Pleural Procedures Statement)
  • Bleeding risk: Review anticoagulants and antiplatelets before elective taps; small studies show no excess bleeding with clopidogrel (BTS 2023 Pleural Procedures Statement). Cirrhosis: no routine platelet or plasma transfusion (AASLD 2021)
  • Chest tube: Pleural infection meeting drainage criteria (card 173); hemothorax (card 316). Avoid in hepatic hydrothorax (AASLD 2021)
  • Malignant effusion (ATS/STS/STR 2018; all conditional): Asymptomatic: no therapeutic drainage. Unclear whether dyspnea is from the effusion or whether the lung expands: large-volume thoracentesis first. Expandable lung: IPC or chemical pleurodesis as first-line definitive therapy (IPC: fewer hospital days and re-interventions, more cellulitis). Pleurodesis agent: talc (poudrage or slurry), the most effective agent. Nonexpandable lung, failed pleurodesis, or loculated effusion: IPC. IPC infection: antibiotics, usually without removing the catheter. BTS 2023 concurs
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Empyema with sepsis/septic shock
  • Massive effusion with respiratory failure
  • Re-expansion pulmonary edema after thoracentesis
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Hemothorax requiring surgical intervention
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Dyspnea improved, stable oxygen requirements
  • Underlying cause addressed (CHF optimized, infection treated)
  • If chest tube placed, removed with no reaccumulation on CXR
  • No signs of complicated parapneumonic/empyema
  • Follow-up imaging and appointments arranged
  • Outpatient thoracentesis arranged if needed for symptomatic malignant effusion
💎 PEARLS
  • Light's criteria rule in exudates: Diuretics can push a transudate over the line. If the result does not fit the clinical picture, use the serum-pleural albumin gradient or serum NT-proBNP
  • CHF effusions are bilateral/symmetric: If unilateral or asymmetric, tap it (could be empyema, malignancy, PE)
  • pH <7.2 = drain it: Also drain for pus, positive Gram stain or culture, LDH >1000 IU/L, glucose <40 mg/dL, or loculation (AATS 2017). These effusions are unlikely to resolve with antibiotics alone
  • TB effusion is lymphocytic: ADA is the best fluid test; pleural tissue for culture and histology is preferred (BTS 2023)
  • Max 1.5 L per tap: Re-expansion pulmonary edema is rare (symptomatic in <1%) but can be fatal, usually within the first hour. Stop for chest tightness, cough, or pain; routine manometry does not reduce the risk (BTS 2023 Pleural Procedures Statement)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Albumin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Pleural Fluid Analysis, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated Lipase
↑ Back to Table of Contents

39. PNEUMOTHORAX

Primary • Secondary • Iatrogenic • TENSION = Emergency
DIAGNOSIS AND MANAGEMENT

Types:

  • Primary Spontaneous (PSP): No known lung disease (most still have emphysema-like changes on CT). Typically young, tall, thin men; smoking raises the risk. Treat as SSP if age >50 with a smoking history (BTS 2023)
  • Secondary Spontaneous (SSP): Underlying lung disease: COPD (most common), CF, PCP pneumonia, necrotizing pneumonia, TB, interstitial lung disease (Practical)
  • Iatrogenic: Central line placement (subclavian > IJ), thoracentesis, transbronchial or CT-guided lung biopsy, mechanical ventilation (barotrauma), CPR. Often resolves without intervention (BTS 2023)
  • Traumatic: Blunt or penetrating chest trauma, rib fractures. Managed per WSES-AAST 2025 (see Special Situations)
  • Familial or catamenial: Family history (about 10%): consider Birt-Hogg-Dubé, LAM, tuberous sclerosis, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, and get a CT. Recurrent, usually right-sided PTX within 72 h of menses: catamenial (endometriosis) (BTS 2023)

Presentation: Acute-onset pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea. Exam: Decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus on affected side. Tracheal deviation usually absent in small/simple PTX; large PTX or tension PTX deviates trachea AWAY from the affected side

TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX - EMERGENCY:

  • Pathophys: One-way valve → air enters pleural space but can't escape → ↑pressure collapses lung, shifts mediastinum, compresses contralateral lung + great vessels → ↓venous return → shock
  • Presentation: Severe respiratory distress, hypotension, tachycardia, JVD, tracheal deviation AWAY from affected side, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, cyanosis
  • CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS - DON'T WAIT FOR CXR!
  • Treatment: Decompress immediately; do not wait for imaging (BTS 2023 Pleural Procedures Statement). Bedside ultrasound can confirm it without delay (WSES-AAST 2025). Needle decompression at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line or the 5th ICS midaxillary line, or finger thoracostomy, which works when a needle dislodges or stops working (WSES-AAST 2025). Practical: insert just above the rib; short catheters often fail to reach the pleura, so use the longest large-bore catheter available. Then chest tube, the treatment of choice (WSES-AAST 2025, LoE moderate, GoR strong)

Imaging: CXR: visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it; an upright film is more sensitive. Supine CXR misses many PTX (sensitivity 28-75%); look for the deep sulcus sign. Ultrasound (E-FAST) is more sensitive than CXR in trauma; CT if stable and findings are equivocal (WSES-AAST 2025). Size (Practical: chest wall to lung edge at the hilum; 2 cm or more = large) affects the safety of an intervention, not whether one is needed (BTS 2023)

Spontaneous PTX, Non-Tension (BTS 2023; ERS/EACTS/ESTS 2024): symptoms and stability drive treatment, not size

  • PSP, minimally symptomatic and stable: Conservative care regardless of size (ERS conditional, very low certainty; BTS conditional, by consensus). Observe at least 4 h; discharge only if walking comfortably; CXR in 2-4 weeks (ERS; BTS). Practical: analgesia; oxygen if hypoxemic
  • PSP, symptomatic: Needle aspiration (16-gauge catheter or 8 Fr catheter in the trials) over a chest drain (ERS strong, low certainty: shorter stay, fewer complications). Ambulatory device where expertise and follow-up exist (ERS conditional, low; BTS conditional). Chest drain if aspiration fails or is unsuitable. Early surgery can be offered if preventing recurrence is the priority (ERS conditional, low)
  • SSP: Practical: admit; a chest drain is usual. ERS makes no recommendation for or against conservative care or aspiration in SSP and suggests against 8 Fr ambulatory devices (conditional, very low). Consider chemical pleurodesis to prevent recurrence, even after a first episode with major decompensation (BTS conditional). Thoracic surgical opinion early
  • Drain size and technique: Small-bore (<14F) suits most cases; larger bore for unstable trauma and PTX on mechanical ventilation (BTS 2023 Pleural Procedures Statement). Underwater seal; no recommendation for or against suction (ERS). Do not clamp a bubbling drain. Remove once the lung is re-expanded and the air leak has stopped (BTS)
  • Oxygen: Give for hypoxemia; with high-flow O2 in chronic lung disease, check a blood gas at 30 min for hypercapnia (BTS 2023 Pleural Procedures Statement). Practical: high-flow O2 may speed resorption (low-certainty evidence)
  • Recurrence prevention, surgical opinion (BTS 2023): Second ipsilateral or first contralateral PTX; synchronous bilateral PTX; tension, or SSP with major physiological compromise, at first episode; air leak despite 5-7 days of drainage or failure to re-expand; spontaneous hemothorax; high-risk professions (pilots, divers); pregnancy. VATS access with surgical pleurodesis and/or bullectomy (conditional)

Special Situations:

  • Mechanical ventilation: Chest tube; almost mandatory under positive pressure (WSES-AAST 2025); larger bore (BTS)
  • Traumatic: Chest tube is the treatment of choice (WSES-AAST 2025, LoE moderate, GoR strong): 8.5-16 Fr or 18-24 Fr, inserted laterally at the 4th-6th ICS, anterior or mid axillary line. With hemothorax or hemopneumothorax, size the tube as in Condition 316 (large-bore if unstable; guidelines disagree for stable patients). Small (2 cm or less) PTX in a stable patient: observe at least 24 h (LoE low, GoR moderate). Open PTX: three-sided occlusive dressing, then chest tube. No antibiotic prophylaxis for tubes placed for blunt or spontaneous PTX (WSES-AAST 2025)
  • Bilateral PTX: Higher risk of respiratory compromise; synchronous bilateral spontaneous PTX warrants surgical advice (BTS 2023)
  • Persistent air leak: Surgical opinion (BTS lists 5-7 days of drainage). Not fit for surgery: autologous blood patch (BTS GPP; ERS conditional for SSP, very low) or endobronchial valves (BTS GPP; ERS no recommendation)
  • LAM: Suspect in a young or middle-aged woman with PTX and diffuse thin-walled cysts on CT. Offer ipsilateral pleurodesis after the first PTX rather than waiting for a recurrence (ATS/JRS 2017, conditional, very low confidence); chemical or surgical by shared decision, done by clinicians experienced in LAM. Prior pleurodesis or pleurectomy is not a contraindication to lung transplant (ATS/JRS 2017, conditional, very low)
  • Cystic fibrosis: CF-specific advice differs (CFF 2010, reviewed 2025): no pleurodesis after a first pneumothorax; surgical pleurodesis for a recurrent large pneumothorax; withhold BiPAP while the pneumothorax is present; no flying, lifting >5 lb, or spirometry for 2 weeks after resolution. See Condition 255
  • Pregnancy: Observe if small (<2 cm), not dyspneic, and no fetal distress; otherwise aspiration or chest drain (BTS 2023)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Tension pneumothorax
  • Bilateral pneumothorax
  • Respiratory failure requiring intubation
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Hemopneumothorax
  • SSP with severe underlying lung disease
  • Persistent large air leak
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Symptoms controlled and walking comfortably (ERS: after at least 4 h of observation when managed conservatively)
  • Lung re-expanded, or PTX stable on CXR; drain removed once the air leak has stopped
  • Stable oxygen requirements, minimal dyspnea
  • Return precautions: come back at once if breathlessness worsens (BTS)
  • No flying until radiological resolution, then wait at least 7 days (ERS conditional; BTS). No scuba diving unless a definitive surgical prevention such as pleurectomy has been done (BTS; ERS)
  • Respiratory follow-up; CXR at 2-4 weeks after observation or aspiration (BTS)
  • Smoking cessation: smokers recur more often (ERS conditional)
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Tension PTX is a clinical diagnosis: Respiratory distress, hypotension, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance: decompress now, image later
  • Tracheal deviation: PTX adds volume, so any deviation is AWAY from the affected side, most marked with tension; a small PTX usually causes none. Deviation TOWARD the affected side points to volume loss (e.g., atelectasis)
  • Treat the patient, not the size: Minimally symptomatic, stable PSP can be managed conservatively whatever its size. In the main RCT, conservative care meant fewer procedures, a shorter stay and fewer recurrences at 12 months (ERS 2024)
  • SSP is more dangerous than PSP: Less reserve; usually needs a drain and admission; think about pleurodesis early
  • Aspiration first for symptomatic PSP: Needle aspiration beats a chest drain on length of stay and complications (ERS, strong). Not established for SSP
  • Flying: Wait 7 days after a CXR shows full resolution (BTS; ERS)
  • Recurrence prevention: Surgery after a second ipsilateral or first contralateral PTX, or earlier for high-risk jobs or tension at the first episode (BTS)

40. SYNCOPE

Vasovagal • Cardiac • Orthostatic • Neurologic
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Transient loss of consciousness (LOC) with loss of postural tone, followed by spontaneous complete recovery. Caused by global cerebral hypoperfusion. Duration typically <20 seconds

Classic: Sudden LOC, fall, rapid spontaneous recovery without intervention. Patient recalls events before and after (vs seizure with postictal confusion)

Key Historical Questions:

  • Prodrome: Nausea, diaphoresis, tunnel vision, lightheadedness = vasovagal. No warning = cardiac
  • Position: Standing → orthostatic or vasovagal. Supine → cardiac (very concerning!)
  • Activity: Exertional syncope = cardiac until proven otherwise (HOCM, AS, arrhythmia, PE)
  • Triggers: Pain, emotion, standing, prolonged standing, hot environment = vasovagal. Post-micturition/defecation = situational
  • Recovery: Immediate = syncope. Confusion/lethargy = seizure or stroke
  • Witnesses: Tonic-clonic movements? (can occur in syncope but brief <15sec, vs prolonged in seizure). Tongue biting/incontinence more typical of seizure

Alternate Presentations by Etiology:

  • Vasovagal (Neurocardiogenic): Most common (40-50%). Prodrome of nausea, diaphoresis, visual changes. Triggered by emotional stress, pain, prolonged standing, hot environment. Young patients. Benign
  • Orthostatic Hypotension: Syncope upon standing from sitting/supine. Elderly, autonomic dysfunction, medications (α-blockers, diuretics, vasodilators), volume depletion. BP drop ≥20/10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing
  • Cardiac Arrhythmia: No warning, sudden collapse. Palpitations before/after. High-risk: age >60, exertional, supine, no prodrome, heart disease. Bradyarrhythmias (sick sinus, AV block) or tachyarrhythmias (VT, SVT)
  • Structural Cardiac: Aortic stenosis (exertional syncope, systolic murmur), HOCM (young athletes, exertional, family history sudden death), cardiac tamponade, myxoma, PE (dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain)
  • Neurologic (RARE cause): Vertebrobasilar TIA (diplopia, ataxia, vertigo), subclavian steal, seizure (postictal confusion differentiates from syncope)
  • Situational: Specific triggers - micturition (post-void), defecation, cough, swallow. Vasovagal-mediated
  • Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity: Elderly men, triggered by tight collar, head turning, shaving. Bradycardia/hypotension with carotid massage
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

ALL Patients Must Have:

  • Detailed History: Events before/during/after, position, activity, prodrome, recovery time, witnesses, prior episodes, medications, cardiac history
  • Physical Exam: Complete cardiac exam (murmurs, JVD, edema), neurologic exam (focal deficits?), orthostatic vitals (supine → standing at 1 and 3 min)
  • ECG (MANDATORY for ALL): Look for: prolonged QT (>480ms = high risk for Torsades), Brugada pattern (ST elevation V1-V3), pre-excitation (WPW = short PR, delta wave), epsilon wave (ARVC), pathologic Q waves (old MI), heart block, SVT/VT

Risk Stratification - San Francisco Syncope Rule (HIGH RISK if ANY):

  • History of CHF
  • ECG abnormal (any non-sinus rhythm or new changes)
  • Anemia (Hct <30%)
  • Respiratory - Shortness of breath
  • Triage systolic BP <90 mmHg
  • SFSR is a decision aid, not an admission rule: risk scores are Class 2b and are not the primary determinant of admission, and SFSR performs worse in validation than in derivation. Admit when a serious medical condition relevant to the syncope is identified (Class 1; eg, arrhythmia, structural heart disease, ACS, PE, significant bleeding or anemia). Presumed reflex syncope without a serious condition can be managed as an outpatient (2a) (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Syncope guideline)

Labs (Based on Clinical Suspicion):

  • Basic: CBC (anemia?), BMP (electrolytes - hypokalemia can cause QT prolongation), glucose (hypoglycemia?)
  • If cardiac suspected: Troponin (ACS?), BNP (heart failure?), D-dimer if PE suspected
  • If volume depletion suspected: BUN/Cr ratio, orthostatic vitals
  • Pregnancy test: All women of childbearing age (ectopic pregnancy can present as syncope)

Advanced Testing (If Indicated):

  • Echocardiography: If structural heart disease suspected (murmur, abnormal ECG, exertional syncope, known heart disease). Assess for AS, HOCM, RV strain (PE), tamponade, LV function
  • Telemetry/Holter Monitor: If arrhythmia suspected. Admit for telemetry if high-risk features. Outpatient Holter (24-48hr) or event monitor (30 days) for recurrent syncope
  • Exercise Stress Test: If exertional syncope (evaluate for ischemia, arrhythmias). Contraindicated if severe AS suspected
  • Tilt Table Test: Indications (2a): suspected VVS when the diagnosis is unclear after initial evaluation (most useful if recurrent); suspected delayed OH; suspected psychogenic pseudosyncope; convulsive syncope vs epilepsy. Usually 70° for 30-40 min; nitrate or isoproterenol provocation raises sensitivity but lowers specificity. Positive = reproduction of the patient's own presyncope or syncope with hypotension, with or without bradycardia (neither ACC/AHA/HRS nor ESC uses a fixed BP/HR cutoff); classify as cardioinhibitory, vasodepressor, or mixed. Moderate sensitivity, specificity and reproducibility, with false positives in controls: a positive test shows susceptibility, not proof of cause. Do NOT use to predict or monitor drug response (Class 3: No Benefit) (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS; 2018 ESC)
  • Electrophysiology Study (EP Study): For unexplained syncope with structural heart disease or high suspicion for arrhythmia. Can induce/document VT, assess sinus/AV node function
  • CT Head: Only if focal neurologic deficits, head trauma, persistent altered mental status. Syncope alone does NOT require head CT
  • Carotid Ultrasound: NOT recommended in syncope evaluation without focal neurological findings (Class 3: No Benefit). Syncope reflects global, not unilateral, cerebral hypoperfusion; inpatient series found carotid duplex almost never explains syncope but often finds incidental stenosis. A bruit alone is not an indication to image for syncope. Suspected vertebrobasilar ischemia needs CTA or MRA of the head and neck, not carotid duplex (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS; AAN Choosing Wisely)
  • Carotid Sinus Massage: Indicated (ESC Class I) in patients >40 y with unexplained syncope compatible with a reflex mechanism. Massage the right then left carotid sinus for 5 sec each, supine and upright, with continuous ECG and beat-to-beat BP. Carotid sinus syndrome = reproduction of syncope with asystole >3 sec or AV block (cardioinhibitory), SBP drop ≥50 mmHg (vasodepressor), or both (mixed). Contraindicated with a carotid bruit, or TIA, stroke or MI within 3 months, unless carotid Doppler excludes significant stenosis. Pacing is reasonable for cardioinhibitory or mixed CSS (2a); dual-chamber may be reasonable (2b) (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS; 2018 ESC)
  • CT PE Protocol: If dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, tachycardia, RV strain on ECG

Orthostatic Vitals Technique:

  • Supine × 5 minutes → measure BP/HR
  • Stand immediately → measure at 1 minute and 3 minutes
  • Positive: SBP drop ≥20 mmHg OR DBP drop ≥10 mmHg OR HR increase ≥30 bpm (or HR >120)
  • Symptoms (lightheadedness, presyncope) with standing = clinical orthostasis even if BP criteria not met
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

General Principles:

  • Treatment depends on underlying cause
  • Admit if high-risk features (see San Francisco Syncope Rule, cardiac cause suspected)
  • Discharge if low-risk and clear benign etiology (young, vasovagal, normal ECG, normal exam)

Vasovagal Syncope (Reflex/Neurocardiogenic):

  • Reassurance: Benign condition, excellent prognosis. Explain pathophysiology
  • Trigger Avoidance: Avoid prolonged standing, hot environments, dehydration, emotional stress. Sit/lie down at first prodromal symptom
  • Hydration: 2-3 L fluid/day and 6-9 g salt/day (about 1-2 teaspoons) may be reasonable (2b) if no hypertension, renal disease, HF, or cardiac dysfunction; evidence limited
  • Physical Counterpressure Maneuvers: At first sign of prodrome: leg crossing + tensing, squatting, arm tensing. Can abort episode
  • Tilt Training: Usefulness uncertain (2b); RCTs show no sustained reduction in recurrence
  • Pharmacologic (Refractory cases only):
    • Midodrine (α-agonist; 2a): recurrent VVS with no hypertension, HF, or urinary retention. Dose as for orthostatic hypotension below (daytime only, boxed warning for supine hypertension)
    • Fludrocortisone 0.1-0.2 mg daily (2b): recurrent VVS with inadequate response to salt and fluids, unless contraindicated; monitor potassium
    • β-blockers (2b): only in patients ≥42 years with recurrent VVS; RCTs overall negative
  • Pacemaker: Dual-chamber pacing might be reasonable (2b) in selected patients ≥40 years with recurrent VVS and prolonged spontaneous pauses; tilt-positive pacing benefit came from open-label trials and should be interpreted cautiously (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Syncope guideline)

Orthostatic Hypotension:

  • Identify and Address Causes:
    • Volume depletion → IV fluids, oral hydration
    • Medications → stop/reduce α-blockers, diuretics, vasodilators, antihypertensives, antidepressants
    • Autonomic dysfunction → treat underlying (diabetes, Parkinson's, amyloidosis)
  • Non-Pharmacologic:
    • Rise slowly from supine/sitting (sit at edge of bed × 1 min before standing)
    • Acute water bolus (about 480 mL; peak pressor effect at ~30 min) for temporary relief (Class 1). Fluid 2-3 L/day and salt 6-9 g/day may be reasonable (2b) if no hypertension, renal disease, HF, or cardiac dysfunction
    • Compression garments (2a): at least thigh-high, preferably including the abdomen (shorter garments not proven); put on before rising (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Syncope guideline)
    • Elevate head of bed 10-20 degrees at night (reduces nocturnal diuresis)
    • Avoid large meals (can cause postprandial hypotension)
    • Physical counterpressure maneuvers
  • Pharmacologic:
    • Midodrine (2a, neurogenic OH): 2.5-5 mg TID to start (2.5 mg if renal impairment), titrate to the usual 10 mg TID; dose about every 4 h while upright (on arising, midday, late afternoon), last dose not after 6 PM and at least 4 h before bedtime. BOXED WARNING: marked supine hypertension (can exceed 200 systolic); check supine BP. Contraindicated in severe organic heart disease, acute renal disease, urinary retention, pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, persistent supine hypertension
    • Fludrocortisone 0.1-0.3 mg daily (2a, neurogenic OH): watch for hypokalemia, edema, supine hypertension; use other agents first if supine hypertension is present; adrenal suppression risk above 0.3 mg/day
    • Droxidopa (2a, neurogenic OH from Parkinson disease, pure autonomic failure, MSA): 100 mg TID (arising, midday, late afternoon, at least 3 h before bed), increase by 100 mg TID every 24-48 h to max 600 mg TID. BOXED WARNING: supine hypertension; carbidopa may reduce effect
    • Pyridostigmine 60 mg TID (2b): neurogenic OH refractory to other treatments (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Syncope guideline; FDA labels)

Cardiac Syncope - ADMIT for Telemetry:

  • Arrhythmia Management:
    • Bradycardia (sick sinus, AV block) → Cardiology consult, consider pacemaker
    • Tachyarrhythmia (VT, SVT) → Antiarrhythmics, ablation, ICD evaluation
    • Long QT syndrome → Remove offending drugs, electrolyte repletion (Mg, K), β-blockers, ICD if high risk
    • Brugada, ARVC → EP study, ICD placement
  • Structural Disease:
    • Aortic stenosis → Cardiology/CT surgery referral for valve replacement if severe + symptomatic
    • HOCM → β-blockers, avoid volume depletion/vasodilators. ICD if high risk. Septal reduction if refractory
    • Pulmonary embolism → Anticoagulation, thrombolytics if massive PE
    • Cardiac tamponade → Pericardiocentesis
  • Ischemia: If syncope due to ACS → treat per ACS protocol (aspirin, heparin, cath lab)

Situational Syncope:

  • Micturition syncope → Sit to void, avoid straining, stay hydrated
  • Defecation syncope → Avoid straining (stool softeners), adequate hydration
  • Cough/swallow syncope → Treat underlying cause (GERD, cough), maneuvers to reduce triggering

Neurologic Syncope (Rare):

  • Vertebrobasilar TIA → Neurology consult, antiplatelet therapy, imaging (MRA/CTA neck)
  • Subclavian steal → Vascular surgery referral
  • Seizure (if postictal confusion suggests) → Neurology consult, antiepileptics, EEG
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • ECG is MANDATORY for ALL syncope patients: Single most important test. Can diagnose Brugada, long QT, WPW, ARVC, heart block, old MI. Never discharge syncope patient without ECG
  • Syncope while supine = cardiac until proven otherwise: Vasovagal almost never occurs supine. If patient syncopizes lying down, think arrhythmia and admit for telemetry
  • Exertional syncope = high-risk: Think HOCM (young athletes), AS (elderly), VT, coronary ischemia. These patients need echo, stress test, and cardiology evaluation
  • Red flags for cardiac syncope: Age >60, exertional, supine position, no prodrome, known heart disease, abnormal ECG, family history sudden cardiac death. Admit these patients
  • Vasovagal has a prodrome, cardiac doesn't: If patient describes nausea, diaphoresis, tunnel vision before passing out = vasovagal (low risk). No warning, sudden collapse = cardiac (high risk)
  • Don't confuse syncope with seizure: Syncope = brief LOC (<20 sec), rapid complete recovery, may have brief myoclonic jerks (<15 sec). Seizure = prolonged LOC, tonic-clonic movements, tongue biting, incontinence, postictal confusion/lethargy. But can be tough to distinguish!
  • Head CT rarely useful: Only if focal neurologic findings, head trauma, or persistent altered mental status. Syncope is due to global hypoperfusion, not focal brain lesion. Don't reflexively order head CT
  • San Francisco Syncope Rule is your friend: If none of the 5 criteria (CHF, abnormal ECG, Hct <30%, SOB, SBP <90), patient is low-risk (pooled systematic review data: ≤5% serious outcome) and can likely be discharged with outpatient follow-up if vasovagal etiology clear
  • Orthostatic vitals technique matters: Must be supine × 5 min first, then check at 1 and 3 minutes standing. Immediate standing without adequate supine time can give false positives
  • Young healthy patient with classic vasovagal story needs minimal workup: Prodrome, triggered by standing/heat/emotion, quick recovery, normal ECG = can discharge with reassurance and anticipatory guidance. Don't over-test these patients
  • Medications are a common culprit: α-blockers (BPH meds), diuretics, antihypertensives, TCAs, antipsychotics, PDE5 inhibitors. Always review medication list carefully
  • Carotid massage to diagnose carotid sinus hypersensitivity: Only perform if safe (no carotid bruits, no recent stroke/TIA). Massage one side × 5 seconds. Positive = >3 sec asystole or >50 mmHg BP drop. Never massage both sides simultaneously!
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Syncope with ongoing chest pain suggesting acute MI
  • Hemodynamically unstable (persistent hypotension, shock)
  • Malignant arrhythmia (sustained VT/VF requiring cardioversion)
  • High-grade AV block (Mobitz II, complete heart block) requiring pacing
  • Massive pulmonary embolism with hypotension
  • Cardiac tamponade
  • Aortic dissection
  • Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemorrhagic shock
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Clear benign etiology identified (vasovagal, orthostatic)
  • NO high-risk features (San Francisco Syncope Rule negative)
  • Normal or unchanged ECG
  • Normal vital signs and orthostatics
  • No concerning cardiac exam findings
  • Labs normal (if obtained)
  • No recurrent episodes during observation
  • Able to ambulate safely without recurrence
  • Patient counseled on trigger avoidance (if vasovagal)
  • Close follow-up arranged (PCP within 1 week, Cardiology if needed)
  • Clear return precautions: recurrent syncope, chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea
  • Driving restrictions discussed (varies by state, typically 3-6 months abstinence after cardiac syncope)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

From Syncope Episode: Trauma from fall (head injury, fractures, lacerations), motor vehicle accidents (if driving), sudden cardiac death (if malignant arrhythmia), prolonged cerebral hypoperfusion causing ischemia (rare)

From Underlying Cardiac Cause: Sudden cardiac death (VT/VF, complete heart block), acute MI/ACS, cardiac arrest, stroke from arrhythmia with thrombus formation, progression of structural heart disease (AS, HOCM)

From Recurrent Episodes: Injury from repeated falls, impaired quality of life, anxiety/depression, loss of driving privileges, loss of employment (especially if operate machinery), social isolation

From Treatment: Supine hypertension (midodrine, fludrocortisone - can cause nocturnal HTN), hypokalemia (fludrocortisone), edema (fludrocortisone), bradycardia (β-blockers), pacemaker complications (infection, lead malfunction), ICD shocks (appropriate or inappropriate)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Atropine, 💊 Midazolam

41. PERICARDITIS/PERICARDIAL EFFUSION/CARDIAC TAMPONADE

Inflammatory • Effusion • Tamponade Physiology
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Pericarditis: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain worse with inspiration and lying flat, relieved by sitting forward. Friction rub (scratchy, triphasic sound)

Pericardial Effusion: Often asymptomatic if slow-accumulating. Dyspnea, muffled heart sounds, enlarged cardiac silhouette on CXR

Cardiac Tamponade: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus >10mmHg, tachycardia, dyspnea, shock

Alternate Presentations:

  • Uremic pericarditis: ESRD patients, often painless. May indicate need for urgent dialysis
  • Post-cardiac injury syndrome (Dressler, post-pericardiotomy, post-procedure): Dressler syndrome now occurs in <1% of MIs, typically 1-2 weeks after, mainly with large or late-reperfused infarcts; pericarditis follows about 10% of AF ablations. Diagnosis needs 2 of 5: fever without other cause, pericardial or pleuritic pain, rub, pericardial effusion, pleural effusion with raised CRP. Treat with high-dose aspirin (first choice after MI, Class I) plus colchicine; early post-MI pericarditis: aspirin for 5-7 days with colchicine. RED FLAG: post-MI pericardial effusion >10 mm needs evaluation for subacute free-wall rupture (2025 ESC)
  • Malignant effusion: Gradual dyspnea, weight loss. Lung/breast cancer, lymphoma most common
  • TB pericarditis: Endemic areas, HIV patients. Chronic symptoms, large effusions
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: CBC, CRP/ESR (elevated), troponin (mildly elevated if myopericarditis), BUN/Cr, TSH, ANA if autoimmune suspected

ECG: Classic: widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, evolving through 4 stages (ST elevation → normalization → T inversion → resolution). Often absent; because the pericardium is electrically silent, ST-T changes imply myocardial involvement, so check troponin for myopericarditis (2025 ESC)

Diagnosis (2025 ACC Concise Clinical Guidance): Pericarditic chest pain (sharp, pleuritic, relieved by sitting up or leaning forward; must be present) plus additional findings: friction rub, ECG changes (diffuse ST elevation and/or PR depression), raised CRP/ESR, new or worsening effusion on imaging, or pericardial inflammation on CMR (CT alternative). 0 additional = unlikely, 1 = possible, 2 or more = definite. CMR: Recommended for recurrent or incessant pericarditis; Reasonable for acute pericarditis, especially complicated or indeterminate cases; not recommended for surveillance of acute pericarditis (ACC 2025). ESC 2025: CMR recommended for suspected pericarditis to confirm inflammation (Class I)

Imaging:

  • CXR: Enlarged cardiac silhouette if >250mL effusion ("water bottle heart")
  • Echocardiogram: First-line: TTE to identify effusion and assess for tamponade (ACC 2025 CCG: Recommended). Size at end-diastole: small <1.0 cm, moderate 1.0-1.9 cm, large 2.0-2.5 cm, very large >2.5 cm (ACC 2025). Tamponade physiology: RV diastolic collapse (most specific), RA inversion >1/3 of the cycle, respiratory inflow variation, plethoric IVC (see tamponade card). CT/CMR or TEE if TTE inconclusive (Recommended)
  • CT chest: If imaging for etiology (malignancy, TB, trauma)

Pericardiocentesis: Recommended for cardiac tamponade, and diagnostically when a bacterial, tuberculous, or malignant cause is suspected; NOT recommended for effusion without tamponade; with an inflammatory effusion and no concern for tamponade, give anti-inflammatory therapy first (ACC 2025 CCG). ESC 2025 differs: also Class I for symptomatic moderate-large effusion despite medical therapy. Measure CRP BEFORE the tap (it rises afterward). Send cell count, Gram stain and cultures, cytology, and adenosine deaminase if TB suspected; do NOT apply Light's criteria to pericardial fluid (they misclassify most fluids as exudates) (2025 ESC; 2025 ACC Concise Clinical Guidance)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Acute Pericarditis (no effusion/tamponade):

  • Admit complicated high-risk cases (ACC 2025 CCG): Large effusion and/or tamponade, severe pain refractory to first-line therapy, or symptomatic constrictive pericarditis. Poor-prognosis features: high fever, subacute course, large effusion with tamponade features, failure to respond to NSAIDs, concomitant myocarditis (ACC 2025). ESC 2025 (Class I) specifics: major features fever >38°C, subacute onset, large effusion (>20 mm end-diastolic), tamponade, no response to aspirin/NSAID after at least 1 week; minor features trauma, oral anticoagulation. Without these, treat as an outpatient with early reassessment of response
  • First-line: High-dose aspirin OR an NSAID, PLUS colchicine (ACC 2025 CCG: Recommended; ESC 2025 Class I), with a PPI for gastric protection (ACC 2025: often co-prescribed; ESC 2025 Class I). Ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or indomethacin 25-50 mg TID, weeks (acute) to months (recurrent), tapered weekly once symptoms resolve and CRP normalizes (ACC 2025 Table 6); ESC 2025: ibuprofen for 1-2 weeks, then taper by 200 mg every 1-2 weeks. Colchicine 0.6 mg BID, or 0.6 mg once daily if <70 kg or severe renal/hepatic impairment; 0.3-0.6 mg/day with strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors (eg, clarithromycin); no loading dose; 3 months for a first episode, at least 6 months if recurrent. Colchicine roughly halves recurrence
  • Aspirin instead of an NSAID: 500-1000 mg TID (325-650 mg TID also used), tapered weekly (ACC 2025 Table 6); preferred with ischemic heart disease or another indication for aspirin (ACC 2025). ESC 2025: 750-1000 mg TID for 1-2 weeks, then taper by 250 mg every 1-2 weeks; first choice for post-MI pericarditis, where NSAIDs are avoided (2025 ACC Concise Clinical Guidance; 2025 ESC Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases guideline)
  • Steroids: Restrict to cases refractory to or intolerant of other therapies, usually at low-to-medium dose (ACC 2025: Reasonable); use in a first episode increases recurrence (ACC 2025; ESC 2025 Class III as first-line without a specific indication). Also for autoimmune disease or the non-inflammatory (normal CRP) phenotype (ACC 2025). Prednisone 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day (avoid higher doses), always with colchicine. Continue until symptoms resolve and CRP normalizes, then taper slowly over months; high doses and fast tapers drive relapse. PJP and osteoporosis prophylaxis if >20 mg/day prednisone for 1 month or longer (ACC 2025)
  • Recurrent pericarditis (readmission despite aspirin/NSAID + colchicine): Check CRP; obtain CMR if available to define phenotype. Second line (ACC 2025 CCG): anti-IL-1 agents (Recommended) after failure of first-level therapy and/or steroids, preferred over steroids for the inflammatory phenotype (fever, CRP >10 mg/L, or CMR pericardial inflammation); steroids (Reasonable) for the non-inflammatory or autoimmune phenotype. ESC 2025 differs: adds low-to-medium-dose prednisone and reserves anti-IL-1 for steroid failure with raised CRP (Class I) or CMR inflammation regardless of CRP (IIa). Rilonacept (FDA-approved for recurrent pericarditis): 320 mg SC load (two 160 mg injections), then 160 mg weekly; first dose under healthcare supervision; screen hepatitis B/C, HIV and TB first; requires prior authorization, so arrange with cardiology before discharge rather than bridging with high-dose steroids. Anakinra 1-2 mg/kg/day (max 100 mg) is off-label in the US. Continue colchicine; never stop steroids abruptly in steroid-dependent patients (2025 ACC Concise Clinical Guidance; 2025 ESC; Arcalyst FDA label)
  • Activity restriction: Restrict exercise for at least 1 month after diagnosis or a flare and until clinical remission, keeping heart rate <100 bpm during activity (ACC 2025 CCG: Recommended). ESC 2025 (Class I): applies to athletes and non-athletes, with remission defined by normalized symptoms, CRP, and imaging; a β-blocker should be considered (IIa) if still symptomatic with resting HR >75 despite full anti-inflammatory therapy

Pericardial Effusion (no tamponade):

  • Small/moderate: Treat the cause. Inflammatory effusion without tamponade: anti-inflammatory therapy first (ACC 2025); ESC 2025: empiric anti-inflammatory therapy is futile for chronic effusions without inflammation, and effusion without raised CRP increases the likelihood of cancer (LR 2.9). Asymptomatic moderate or larger effusion: TTE surveillance is reasonable (ACC 2025), about every 6 months (ESC 2025); asymptomatic mild idiopathic effusion needs no routine monitoring (ESC 2025)
  • Large (2.0 cm or more): Admission may be necessary (ACC 2025); ESC 2025: high-risk feature, admit (Class I). Repeat echo with any change in symptoms or signs. Drain for tamponade or a suspected bacterial, tuberculous, or malignant cause (ACC 2025); ESC 2025 also for symptoms despite therapy. Worsening large effusion without systemic inflammation: CT to exclude cancer (2025 ESC)

Cardiac Tamponade (EMERGENCY):

  • Immediate: Drainage is the treatment; do not delay pericardiocentesis in unstable patients. While awaiting drainage, a temporary fluid bolus (about 250-500 mL) can help stabilize, mainly if SBP <100 or hypovolemic; it raised cardiac output in only about half of patients and lowered it in about a third. AVOID diuretics, vasodilators, and positive-pressure ventilation/intubation if possible (can precipitate collapse) (2025 ESC Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases guideline; Sagristà-Sauleda, Circulation 2008)
  • Definitive: Urgent pericardiocentesis for tamponade (ACC 2025: Recommended), guided by echocardiography, fluoroscopy, and/or CT (ACC 2025). Aspirating a small amount can greatly improve the patient (ESC 2025)
  • Approach: In an emergency, subxiphoid or apical (ACC 2025); otherwise where fluid is most accessible with the least risk to vital structures. Leave a drain; remove when output is <30 mL/day (ESC 2025)
  • Refractory: Pericardial window after prior pericardiocentesis for recurrent large effusion or tamponade (ACC 2025: Reasonable). Surgical drainage when percutaneous drainage is not feasible (e.g., loculated) or the effusion is purulent (ESC 2025 I C). Practical: traumatic hemopericardium goes to surgery
  • Post-procedure: Monitor for re-accumulation. Practical: repeat echo in 24-48 h

Specific Etiologies:

  • Uremic: Urgent dialysis. Most resolve after adequate dialysis
  • Malignant: Pericardiocentesis for tamponade (Class I) with extended catheter drainage for 3-6 days to reduce recurrence (Class I); send cytology (Class I). Systemic antineoplastic therapy is the baseline treatment (Class I). Recurrence is common (>50%): pericardial window or balloon pericardiotomy for recurrent effusion; tumour-directed intrapericardial chemotherapy (eg, cisplatin in lung, thiotepa in breast cancer) only with oncology and only if refractory to systemic therapy (IIb). Do NOT use talc or similar sclerosants (less effective than a window, risk of constriction). Care is often palliative; involve oncology early (2025 ESC Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases guideline)
  • Purulent: Urgent pericardiocentesis and/or surgical window for diagnosis (Class I) and surgical drainage for complete evacuation and to prevent constriction (Class I). Start empiric IV antibiotics until cultures return (eg, vancomycin + ceftriaxone; regimen not specified by ESC), then pathogen-directed, for at least 3 weeks and until fever and clinical signs resolve. Loculated effusion: intrapericardial fibrinolysis should be considered (IIa); subxiphoid pericardiotomy with rinsing. Constriction risk is high (20-30%)
  • TB: Diagnostic pericardiocentesis if not confirmed non-invasively (Class I). Standard 6-month regimen (RIPE x 2 months, then rifampin/isoniazid x 4 months) to prevent constriction (Class I). Adjunctive corticosteroids should be considered only if HIV-negative (IIa). Pericardiectomy if not improving or worse after 4-8 weeks of therapy (Class I). Empiric anti-TB treatment only in endemic areas; not recommended in non-endemic areas (Class III) (2025 ESC Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases guideline)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Pericarditis ECG vs STEMI: Pericarditis has diffuse ST elevation (multiple leads) with PR depression, STEMI has localized ST elevation with reciprocal changes. Pericarditis ST is concave ("smiling"), STEMI is convex ("frowning")
  • Pulsus paradoxus: >10mmHg drop in SBP with inspiration. Normal <10mmHg. Also seen in COPD, PE, severe asthma
  • Colchicine is key: Roughly halves recurrence after a first episode: COPE 32% → 11%; ICAP incessant or recurrent pericarditis 38% → 17% at 18 months (NNT 4-5), without excess GI adverse effects. Use in all cases unless contraindicated: with aspirin or an NSAID as first-level therapy, 3 months for acute and 6 months for recurrent pericarditis (ACC 2025 CCG: Recommended; ESC 2025 Class I)
  • Low-pressure tamponade: Can occur with hypovolemia or RV dysfunction. Tamponade physiology without elevated JVP
  • Electrical alternans: Beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude. Classic for large effusion/tamponade but uncommon (10-20%)
  • Avoid steroids if possible: 2-4× increased risk of recurrence. Reserve for refractory cases or contraindication to NSAIDs
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Cardiac tamponade (SBP <90, pulsus paradoxus >20mmHg)
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Large/rapidly accumulating effusion
  • Need for urgent pericardiocentesis
  • Myopericarditis with arrhythmias or reduced EF
  • Purulent pericarditis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Pain controlled on oral NSAIDs
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • No evidence of tamponade on echo
  • CRP trending down
  • If effusion: Small/stable on repeat echo
  • Follow-up arranged (repeat echo in 1 week if effusion present)
  • Activity restrictions counseled
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Cardiac tamponade (most feared), myopericarditis (troponin ↑, EF ↓), arrhythmias (rare)

Chronic: Recurrent pericarditis (15-30%, higher without colchicine), constrictive pericarditis (chronic inflammation → calcification → restricted filling, often post-TB/radiation/cardiac surgery)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Colchicine, 💊 Indomethacin, 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Anakinra
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR

42. INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS

Native Valve • Prosthetic Valve • Duke Criteria
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Fever (90%), new or changing murmur (85%), embolic phenomena, positive blood cultures. Subacute: weeks of constitutional symptoms

Acute Presentation: Rapid valve destruction, heart failure, septic shock. More common with S. aureus

Peripheral Stigmata (classic but rare <10%):

  • Osler nodes: Painful, raised, red nodules on fingers/toes (immunologic)
  • Janeway lesions: Painless, red macules on palms/soles (septic emboli)
  • Splinter hemorrhages: Linear red-brown streaks under nails
  • Roth spots: Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers (rare)

Complications at Presentation:

  • Heart failure: Acute regurgitation from valve destruction (most common cause of death)
  • Embolic stroke: 15-30%, highest risk with mitral valve and S. aureus
  • Mycotic aneurysm: Brain, splenic, coronary arteries
  • Perivalvular abscess: New heart block (AV node near aortic valve)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP (Duke Criteria)

Blood Cultures: 3 sets from separate sites BEFORE antibiotics. Time spacing less critical than previously thought (can obtain all within 1-2hr if clinically unstable)

Imaging:

  • TTE: First-line. Sensitivity 60-70% for vegetations. Excellent for assessment of valve function and complications
  • TEE: Gold standard. Sensitivity 90-95%. REQUIRED if: prosthetic valve, negative TTE with high suspicion, suspected abscess/perforation, S. aureus bacteremia
  • Cardiac CT/MRI: If TEE contraindicated or to evaluate perivalvular extension
  • Brain MRI: If neurologic symptoms (ischemic stroke, hemorrhage, abscess, mycotic aneurysm)

Labs: CBC (anemia of chronic disease), ESR/CRP (elevated), UA (hematuria/proteinuria), RF (positive in subacute), creatinine, LFTs

Duke Criteria (Definite IE = 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor):

  • Major: (1) Positive blood cultures with typical organisms in ≥2 separate cultures, OR persistently positive cultures; (2) Echocardiographic evidence (vegetation, abscess, new dehiscence of prosthetic valve, new valvular regurgitation)
  • Minor: Predisposing condition, fever >38°C, vascular phenomena (emboli, mycotic aneurysm), immunologic phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, RF), microbiologic evidence not meeting major criteria
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Empiric Antibiotics (start after blood cultures × 3):

  • Native valve: Vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q12h + ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h
  • Prosthetic valve: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone + gentamicin 1mg/kg IV q8h (or cefepime instead of ceftriaxone)
  • IVDU: Same as native valve (covers S. aureus, Streptococcus, gram-negatives)

Organism-Specific Therapy:

  • Viridans Streptococcus (most common, ~30%): Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h OR ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h × 4 weeks. Can add gentamicin × 2 weeks for synergy
  • S. aureus (MSSA): Nafcillin/oxacillin 2g IV q4h × 4-6 weeks. Consider adding gentamicin × 3-5 days for synergy
  • S. aureus (MRSA): Vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q12h × 6 weeks. Consider daptomycin 8-10mg/kg if persistent bacteremia
  • Enterococcus: Ampicillin 2g IV q4h + gentamicin 1mg/kg q8h (or ceftriaxone 2g q12h instead of gent) × 4-6 weeks
  • HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella): Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h × 4 weeks
  • Culture-negative (10-15%): Continue empiric therapy. Consider Bartonella, Coxiella, Brucella, fungi in specific epidemiology

Duration: Native valve 4-6 weeks (S. aureus 6 weeks), prosthetic valve 6 weeks minimum. Time from FIRST negative blood culture

Surgical Indications (Cardiothoracic Surgery Consult):

  • Heart failure: From severe acute regurgitation or valve obstruction (Class I indication, emergent)
  • Uncontrolled infection: Perivalvular abscess, persistent bacteremia >5-7 days on appropriate antibiotics, fungal endocarditis
  • Prevention of embolism: Large mobile vegetation (>10mm) with embolic event, especially anterior mitral valve
  • Prosthetic valve: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (<1 year), heart failure, dehiscence, persistent bacteremia
  • Timing: Emergent (heart failure/cardiogenic shock), urgent (uncontrolled infection, abscess), elective (large vegetation, embolic prevention)

Post-Stroke Timing for Surgery: If intracranial hemorrhage, delay surgery if possible. If ischemic stroke without hemorrhage, surgery can proceed but discuss risk/benefit

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • S. aureus bacteremia = TEE: 25% have IE even without murmur. Always get TEE for S. aureus bacteremia unless clear alternative source + no cardiac risk factors
  • Culture first, antibiotics second: Don't delay cultures waiting for fever spike. Get 3 sets ASAP then start empiric therapy (unless stable subacute presentation)
  • Right-sided endocarditis: IVDU, indwelling catheters. Tricuspid valve most common. Septic pulmonary emboli (not stroke). Better prognosis than left-sided
  • New heart block = perivalvular abscess: AV node near aortic valve. High-grade block indicates abscess until proven otherwise. Surgical emergency
  • Anticoagulation controversy: If on warfarin for other indication (prosthetic valve, AFib), continue but avoid starting new anticoagulation (doesn't prevent emboli, may increase hemorrhagic stroke)
  • Mycotic aneurysm: Not fungal! Bacterial infection of arterial wall. Can rupture. Brain MRA if headache or neurologic symptoms
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hemodynamic instability/cardiogenic shock
  • Acute heart failure (pulmonary edema)
  • High-grade heart block (perivalvular abscess)
  • Embolic stroke with decreased level of consciousness
  • Septic shock despite antibiotics
  • Perioperative (cardiac surgery for IE)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Appropriate IV antibiotics for ≥7-14 days (bloodstream clearance documented)
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Blood cultures negative × 2-3 sets
  • No indication for urgent surgery
  • Plan for completion of IV antibiotics (home IV, long-term facility, or outpatient infusion)
  • Follow-up with Infectious Disease and Cardiology arranged
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Cardiac: Heart failure (most common cause of death, 50-60%), perivalvular abscess (10-40% prosthetic, 10-15% native), valve perforation, fistula formation

Neurologic: Ischemic stroke (15-30%), intracerebral hemorrhage (5%), mycotic aneurysm rupture (rare but devastating), brain abscess

Embolic: Spleen (abdominal pain), kidneys (hematuria, infarction), bones (osteomyelitis, vertebral), coronary arteries (MI)

Immunologic: Glomerulonephritis (immune complex deposition), arthritis, splinter hemorrhages

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Nafcillin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine
🧫 ABX COMPANION Cunha Empiric Framework
→ Infective Endocarditis
