43. MYOCARDITIS

Viral • Immune-mediated • Fulminant
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Three classic presentations: chest pain (mimics MI), arrhythmia (palpitations, syncope), or HF/cardiogenic shock (dyspnea, fatigue); some patients are asymptomatic or have vague symptoms. Suspicion rises with a recent viral respiratory or GI illness in a young person, prior myocarditis or autoimmune disease, a family history of cardiomyopathy or unexplained sudden death, or cardiotoxin exposure (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary: chest pain is the presenting symptom in about 75%, and the viral illness is typically 2-4 weeks before (2025 ESC)

Risk Stratification (2024 ACC ECDP stages and Table 3; 2025 ESC secondary):

  • Stage A, at risk: eg, ICI therapy, prior myocarditis, systemic immune-mediated or connective tissue disease, a pathogenic cardiomyopathy gene variant, cocaine or methamphetamine. Stage B: asymptomatic, with CMR features of myocarditis, or elevated hs-troponin plus supportive evidence
  • Stage C, low risk: symptomatic, with all of: normal LVEF, no LGE, hemodynamic and electrical stability
  • Stage C, medium/high risk: any of: reduced LVEF, NSVT or higher-grade ventricular ectopy, significant bradyarrhythmia, LGE on CMR, increased FDG uptake on PET, hemodynamic instability or clinical HF
  • Stage D, advanced: hemodynamic instability needing inotropes, vasopressors, or temporary circulatory support (SCAI SHOCK stage C or higher), or electrical instability needing intervention (high-grade AV block, frequent salvos of multifocal PVCs or NSVT, VT, VF)
  • Fulminant: Cardiogenic shock or rapidly progressive LV dysfunction needing inotropes and/or mechanical support, often with arrhythmias. Worse short- and long-term survival than non-fulminant myocarditis (see pearl)
  • ESC tiers (2025 ESC Table 7, secondary): Low risk: stable or few symptoms, LVEF ≥50% with no or limited LGE (<2 segments); ACC low risk requires no LGE. Intermediate risk: new or progressive dyspnea, non-sustained VT, persistent or relapsing troponin release, new LVEF 41-49% or wall motion abnormality, or LVEF ≥50% with LGE in ≥2 segments. High risk: acute HF or cardiogenic shock, NYHA III-IV refractory to therapy, cardiac arrest or syncope, VF or sustained VT, high-grade AV block, new LVEF <40%, or extensive LGE
  • Disposition: Admit suspected symptomatic myocarditis (2024 ACC ECDP Figure 9; Figure 8 ties Stage C admission to a presentation that is not low risk). Refer to an advanced HF center with a multidisciplinary myocarditis team for any of: hemodynamic instability or rapidly worsening HF, severely reduced LV function, unexplained cardiogenic shock, unexplained sustained ventricular arrhythmia or advanced AV block, features of eosinophilic, giant-cell, or sarcoid myocarditis, extracardiac systemic immune-mediated disease, or a relapsing course with prolonged troponin release (Figure 9). Stage D: ICU admission and advanced HF center referral; transfer anyone needing inotropes (2024 ACC ECDP). Low risk: discharge when stable, with early follow-up. ESC: admit intermediate- and high-risk myocarditis (Class I); a clinic patient with suspected myocarditis and elevated troponin is referred to hospital (2025 ESC Figure 6)

Alternate Presentations:

  • Sudden cardiac death: Ventricular arrhythmias in young, previously healthy patients
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy: Chronic presentation after subclinical acute phase
  • Pericardial involvement: Myopericarditis (chest pain, friction rub, ST elevation + troponin elevation)
  • Post-COVID: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C in children, MIS-A in adults)
  • Vaccine-related: mRNA COVID vaccines: rare, highest after the second dose in young males. VAERS reporting rates per million second doses: 105.9 in males 16-17 and 70.7 in males 12-15 (BNT162b2); 52.4 and 56.3 in men 18-24 (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273). Median onset 2 days after the dose; 82% male; no confirmed myocarditis deaths under age 30 in that series (Oster, JAMA 2022). Good mid-term outcomes without death or transplant in a multicentre follow-up (2025 ESC)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: Initial workup with ECG and echo: CBC with differential (eosinophils), hs-troponin, and in some cases CRP and NT-proBNP/BNP (2024 ACC ECDP Step 1). hs-troponin is usually elevated, but a normal value does not exclude myocarditis; normal values were reported even in fulminant and giant-cell myocarditis with less-sensitive assays (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary: basic labs also include renal function and electrolytes, TSH, and hepatic function (2025 ESC Table 9); routine viral serology is not recommended (Class III), except HIV, hepatitis C, and Lyme when suspected; viral PCR belongs on EMB tissue with paired blood (2025 ESC)

ECG: Obtain in all suspected cases, but sensitivity is only about 47%, and a normal or nonspecific ECG does not rule out myocarditis. Common findings are nonspecific: sinus tachycardia, ST-T changes, low voltage, PR depression. Pathological Q waves, LBBB, QRS ≥120 ms, QT prolongation, high-grade AV block, malignant tachyarrhythmias, fragmented QRS, and T-wave inversion are associated with reduced LV function, LV scar, and poor prognosis; conduction-system involvement raises suspicion for sarcoidosis, giant-cell myocarditis, or Lyme disease (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary: ST elevation is the most common finding (about 58%), often widespread but sometimes infarct-like in a non-coronary distribution; other ST-T changes about 24%; conduction block about 10%; normal in about 15%; changes evolve over hours to days (2025 ESC)

Imaging:

  • Echocardiogram: First-line screen: LV dilatation or reduced EF, regional wall motion abnormalities, increased wall thickness from edema, diastolic dysfunction, pericardial effusion, LV thrombus. Sensitivity is not adequate to rule out myocarditis. Fulminant myocarditis often shows a smaller LV cavity with mildly increased wall thickness; LV global longitudinal strain adds value beyond EF (2024 ACC ECDP)
  • Cardiac MRI: Pivotal diagnostic test once the patient is stable (2024 ACC ECDP Step 3; guideline Class 1, eg 2025 ESC Class I). Updated (2018) Lake Louise criteria: at least one T2-based marker of edema (T2 mapping or T2-weighted signal) plus at least one T1-based marker (native T1, ECV, or LGE; LGE typically mid-wall or subepicardial, mainly lateral and inferior, vs subendocardial in MI). One marker alone can still support the diagnosis in the right clinical setting, with less specificity; pericarditis and LV systolic dysfunction are supportive. Sensitivity >85% in experienced centers (2024 ACC ECDP; Ferreira, JACC 2018). In unstable patients, EMB comes first (2025 ESC Figure 5)
  • Coronary assessment: Exclude obstructive CAD by invasive or CT coronary angiography as clinically appropriate (2024 ACC ECDP Step 1; 2025 ESC Class I when ACS is suspected). Normal coronaries support myocarditis

Endomyocardial Biopsy: Purpose: a definite diagnosis that allows etiology-specific therapy, and exclusion of mimics. Perform (2024 ACC ECDP Figure 6) in Stage D; in Stage C with LV dysfunction, symptomatic HF, arrhythmia (high-degree AV block, frequent multifocal PVCs, VT, or VF), peripheral eosinophilia, or an uncertain diagnosis when CMR cannot be obtained; and in Stage B from ICI therapy. Not indicated: Stage B not from ICI therapy, or low-risk Stage C (normal LVEF, no or minimal LGE, hemodynamic and electrical stability). EMB within 2 days of ICU admission was associated with better survival free of transplant or LVAD at 1 year; transfer patients who may need EMB to an advanced HF center with myocarditis capability. Major complications <1% in experienced centers. Technique: early (within 2-4 weeks of onset), at least 3 samples of 1-2 mm, with histology, immunohistochemistry, and viral PCR on tissue plus peripheral blood (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary (Class I): high-risk myocarditis (acute HF or cardiogenic shock, NYHA III-IV refractory to therapy) or hemodynamic instability, intermediate-risk myocarditis not responding to conventional therapy, and suspected giant-cell myocarditis; in fulminant myocarditis biopsy as soon as possible, even on mechanical support; arrest, sustained VT/VF, high-grade AV block, new LVEF <40%, or extensive LGE alone are case-by-case (Table 7); samples: at least 3 for histology and immunohistology plus 1-2 for viral PCR (2025 ESC)

Etiologies:

  • Viral (most common): Coxsackie B, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, HHV-6, COVID-19, influenza
  • Autoimmune: Giant cell myocarditis, cardiac sarcoidosis, lupus, eosinophilic myocarditis
  • Toxic: Cocaine, alcohol, chemotherapy (anthracyclines), clozapine
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors: Pembrolizumab, nivolumab. High mortality if not recognized early
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Supportive Care (Mainstay):

  • Activity restriction: Stage C/D: no strenuous physical activity or competitive sports for 3-6 months; activities of daily living are fine, and excessive sedentary behavior should be avoided (2024 ACC ECDP sec 4.6, 4.6.3, Figure 8). Return only after symptoms resolve and testing is normal (see pearl). Athletes: no exercise for at least 3-6 months after disease resolution (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, text). ESC secondary (diverges): complete rest during the acute phase, since exercise in active myocarditis has been linked to arrhythmias and sudden death, then sedentary levels until remission (normal symptoms, biomarkers, and imaging), at least 1 month, individualized (2025 ESC sec 6.2.1.1; Rec Table 26, Class I)
  • Heart failure management: Treat HFrEF, HFmrEF, and shock per the HF guideline (2024 ACC ECDP): GDMT and diuretics as on the ADHF card (ARNI, ACE-I, or ARB; evidence-based β-blocker; MRA; SGLT2 inhibitor), started low once stable and held in cardiogenic shock (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA). If LVEF was ≤40% and has improved (HFimpEF), continue GDMT to prevent relapse, even if asymptomatic (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, 1, B-R); ACC notes substantial relapse risk after GDMT withdrawal in recovered nonischemic DCM, with myocarditis-specific data lacking. ESC secondary: continue HF therapy for at least 6 months after complete LV recovery (IIa); in acute myocarditis, especially with troponin elevation, a β-blocker continued for at least 6 months should be considered for symptoms and arrhythmia prevention (IIa) (2025 ESC)
  • Arrhythmia monitoring: Telemetry. Treat ventricular arrhythmias per ACLS, and pace bradyarrhythmias as needed (2024 ACC ECDP). Life-threatening VT/VF: refer to a center with mechanical support and advanced arrhythmia care (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, Class I, C-LD). New VT or second- or third-degree AV block with new HF: think giant-cell myocarditis (see Giant cell). ICD: in giant-cell myocarditis with VF or hemodynamically unstable VT on GDMT, an ICD and/or antiarrhythmic drug may be considered if meaningful survival over 1 year is expected (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, IIb, C-LD); ICD implantation before discharge needs consideration in some patients (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary: ICD decisions are usually deferred 3-6 months after the acute episode; consider an ICD early with heart block or symptomatic VA in giant-cell myocarditis or cardiac sarcoid (2025 ESC)
  • Anticoagulation: Low EF alone is not an indication: no prophylactic anticoagulation in dilated or nonischemic cardiomyopathy without a specific indication (2022 AHA LV thrombus statement; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, 3: No Benefit in chronic HFrEF). Anticoagulate for LV thrombus (at least 3-6 months, stopping if LVEF recovers to >35% and the thrombus has resolved; a DOAC is a reasonable alternative to warfarin), AF, or embolism. Exception: eosinophilic myocarditis, where it can be considered in the acute phase (2025 ESC; 2022 AHA). Practical: standard pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis while on bed rest, as on the ADHF card

Immunosuppression (CONTROVERSIAL):

  • Not routine: Not all myocarditis needs immunosuppression (2024 ACC ECDP Figure 10). Exclude active viral infection with viral PCR on EMB tissue before starting (ACC: advised by expert centers, no broad consensus; 2025 ESC: avoid with active viral infection on EMB or blood PCR). ESC secondary: no immunosuppression in acute myocarditis with preserved LV function (Class III: no outcome benefit)
  • Indicated or considered: General consensus (2024 ACC ECDP Figure 10): eosinophilic, giant-cell, and granulomatous (sarcoid) myocarditis, ICI myocarditis, and myocarditis with other autoimmune conditions; by stage, select Stage B (eg, ICI) and Stage C, and more often Stage D, especially histologically confirmed noninfectious immune-mediated forms. Virus-negative chronic lymphocytic myocarditis: some expert centers treat (TIMIC), no consensus (the ACC writing committee was split). IVIG can be considered in inflammatory, antibody-mediated, or autoimmune disorders. Antivirals are evolving: use only with ID or expert input. Stop a suspected trigger drug (eg, clozapine, ICI) (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary: giant-cell combined therapy (Class I); corticosteroids should be considered in fulminant non-infectious myocarditis (IIa) and may be considered if LVEF stays impaired despite HF therapy (IIb) (2025 ESC)
  • Regimen (if indicated): IV methylprednisolone 7-14 mg/kg/day for 3 days, then oral prednisone starting at 1 mg/kg/day and tapered, with steroid-sparing agents (2024 ACC ECDP Figure 10; benefit in case series). Giant-cell: higher-level immunosuppression, typically adding a calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine or tacrolimus) (ACC). Timing: start once the diagnosis is established, or, in some clinically unstable patients, when highly suspected (2024 ACC ECDP Figure 1 text). ESC secondary: non-severe, prednisone 1 mg/kg/day orally, then taper; second line azathioprine or mycophenolate, cyclosporine, methotrexate (2025 ESC Table 12); in fulminant myocarditis with a suspected non-infectious cause, EMB first, even on mechanical support, then pulse steroids while histology and PCR are pending, stopping or revising if infection is found (2025 ESC sec 6.3.1.2). Co-manage with advanced HF cardiology; add rheumatology or clinical immunology for systemic autoimmune disease (ACC)

Fulminant Myocarditis (ICU Management):

  • Inotropes: In cardiogenic shock, IV inotropes to maintain perfusion and end-organ function (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, 1, B-NR): dobutamine, milrinone, or epinephrine for a low-output state. Deterioration can be rapid: transfer anyone needing inotropes to an advanced HF center (2024 ACC ECDP)
  • Mechanical support: Temporary MCS is reasonable in cardiogenic shock when end-organ function cannot be maintained pharmacologically (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, 2a, B-NR), with management by a multidisciplinary shock team (2a, B-NR); if not rapidly responding to initial measures, triage to a center that can provide temporary MCS (2b, C-LD). Devices: IABP, Impella, or VA-ECMO; myocarditis is often biventricular, so VA-ECMO or other biventricular support is commonly needed; data do not favor one device; Impella LV unloading may aid recovery. No recovery on temporary support: durable LVAD and/or transplant evaluation (2024 ACC ECDP). Life-threatening VT/VF: a center with mechanical support and advanced arrhythmia care (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, Class I, C-LD). ESC secondary: early Shock Team discussion (Class I); temporary MCS should be considered (IIa), IABP first, escalating within 1 h at most if hemodynamics and perfusion do not improve (2025 ESC); ACC instead stresses frequent need for biventricular support
  • Temporary pacing: Second- or third-degree AV block with symptoms or hemodynamic compromise refractory to medical therapy: temporary transvenous pacing is reasonable (2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia, IIa, B-NR); temporary pacing is part of the ACC treatment step (2024 ACC ECDP Figure 1). ESC secondary: high-degree AV block, temporary transvenous pacing as a bridge to recovery (2025 ESC, IIa)
  • AVOID NSAIDs with symptomatic HF or shock: sodium and water retention and worse HF (2024 ACC ECDP; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline, Class 3: Harm in HFrEF). Use acetaminophen for pain. Pericardial-type pain with normal or low-normal EF is different (see pearl)

Specific Etiologies:

  • Giant cell: Suspect with new HF of up to 2 weeks plus new ventricular arrhythmias or second- or third-degree AV block, or no response to usual care within 1-2 weeks (2025 ESC). Refer to an advanced HF center and biopsy (2024 ACC ECDP Figures 6 and 9; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, EMB 2a, B-NR when a specific diagnosis would change therapy; ESC Class I). Immunosuppression: corticosteroids plus a calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine or tacrolimus) (2024 ACC ECDP; ESC combined therapy, Class I), with or without azathioprine or mycophenolate; second line ATG, cyclophosphamide, rituximab (2025 ESC). VF or unstable VT on GDMT: ICD and/or antiarrhythmic drug may be considered if survival over 1 year is expected (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, IIb, C-LD); ESC advises early ICD consideration. Relapse has followed taper as late as 8 years (2025 ESC). Transplant evaluation if refractory: post-transplant survival is comparable, with recurrence in about 8% (2024 ACC ECDP)
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitor: Stop the ICI: hold at any grade (grade 1, troponin only: recheck in 6 h, may resume if normalized or unrelated) and discontinue for grade 2 or higher (ASCO 2021); permanent discontinuation is warranted for grade 2-4 myocarditis (NCCN v1.2026). Immediate cardiology consultation, preferably cardio-oncology, with ICU- or CCU-level monitoring and temporary or permanent pacing as required (NCCN; ASCO; SITC). Start high-dose corticosteroids early, within 24 h (ASCO; 2025 ESC, Class I, with triage within 24 h). Regimen (NCCN v1.2026, the most recent US guideline): IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3-5 days; if responding and stable, prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, tapered slowly over 6-12 weeks guided by clinical response and biomarkers. Other US: SITC 2021, methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3-5 days until troponin normalizes, then a 4-6 week prednisone taper from 1-2 mg/kg; ASCO 2021, prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day oral or IV, escalating to methylprednisolone 1 g/day if no immediate response. ESC secondary: IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg/day (severe: 7-14 mg/kg/day) for 3 days, then an oral prednisone taper (17-20 weeks in the 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guideline). Co-manage with cardio-oncology
  • ICI: escalation and overlap: No improvement within 24-48 h on steroids: add immunosuppression with cardio-oncology. NCCN v1.2026 options: abatacept, alemtuzumab, ATG, IVIG, methotrexate, mycophenolate, plasmapheresis, or infliximab (extreme caution with reduced LVEF); abatacept with ruxolitinib has been used for concomitant myositis and myocarditis. ASCO 2021: methylprednisolone 1 g/day plus mycophenolate, infliximab, or ATG, with abatacept or alemtuzumab if life-threatening (infliximab is contraindicated at doses >5 mg/kg in moderate-severe HF). SITC 2021: no response within 24 h, ATG, mycophenolate, abatacept, or alemtuzumab; caution against infliximab. ESC second-line (IIa): eg, abatacept, mycophenolate, ATG, alemtuzumab. Screen for overlap myositis and myasthenia (CK; proximal, bulbar, and ocular weakness; respiratory function): concurrent respiratory muscle failure worsens survival (2025 ESC), and screening with early ventilation plus abatacept/ruxolitinib was linked to lower fatality in a non-randomized series (Salem, Cancer Discov 2023). With myasthenia overlap, high-dose steroids can worsen respiratory function, but life-threatening cardiac involvement still warrants them; involve neurology (Palaskas, JACC CardioOnc 2024). Telemetry for conduction block. PJP prophylaxis may be considered at prednisone ≥20 mg/day for 4 weeks or more, or >30 mg/day for 3 weeks or more (ASCO 2021)
  • Eosinophilic: Immunosuppression by general consensus; EMB is indicated with peripheral eosinophilia (2024 ACC ECDP). Corticosteroids as for lymphocytic myocarditis, plus treatment of the cause: stop a suspected drug (hypersensitivity) and evaluate for EGPA, hypereosinophilic syndrome, parasites, and cancer. Peripheral eosinophilia is absent in up to 25%. Ventricular thrombi in about 12%: anticoagulation can be considered in the acute phase (2025 ESC)
  • Chagas: Acute or early infection: treat the parasite as soon as possible, with ID: benznidazole 5-7 mg/kg/day in 2 doses for 60 days, or nifurtimox 8-10 mg/kg/day in 3 doses for 60-90 days (2025 ESC Table 12). Established Chagas cardiomyopathy: antiparasitic therapy is not routine (BENEFIT: benznidazole did not reduce cardiac deterioration at 5 years) but can be considered in early, mild forms; treat HF per guidelines; ICD decisions case by case (2025 ESC)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Myocarditis vs MI: Favors myocarditis: younger age, a recent viral prodrome, few CAD risk factors, ST elevation outside a single coronary territory, and normal coronaries on angiography or CT. CMR separates the two: mid-wall or subepicardial LGE vs subendocardial in MI (2025 ESC)
  • Cardiac MRI reading: Mid-wall or subepicardial LGE (vs subendocardial in MI) plus edema. With the 2018 Lake Louise criteria, sensitivity was 88% and specificity 96% in one validation cohort (Luetkens, Radiol Cardiothorac Imaging 2019), so a negative scan does not exclude myocarditis when suspicion is high
  • Fulminant is NOT benign: The old "fulminant paradox" (better long-term outcome if the patient survives) came from 15 clinically diagnosed patients (McCarthy, NEJM 2000) and has been overturned. In 220 biopsy-proven cases with LV dysfunction, cardiac death or transplant was 28.0% vs 1.8% at 60 days and 47.7% vs 10.4% at 7 years, fulminant vs non-fulminant; giant-cell histology did worst (Ammirati, JACC 2019). LVEF often improves sharply in hospital but stays lower long term (Ammirati, Circulation 2017). Early improvement is not reassurance: biopsy early, transfer early (2025 ESC; 2024 ACC ECDP)
  • Return to strenuous exercise is test-guided: ESC calls the older fixed 3-6 month abstention windows arbitrary and now uses a remission-based approach. Before clearance, ACC advises CMR or echo, 24-hour ECG monitoring, and exercise stress testing at the end of the restriction period (2024 ACC ECDP; 2025 ESC)
  • NSAIDs and colchicine depend on the phenotype: The old NSAID ban rested on murine data. Pericardial-type chest pain with normal or low-normal LVEF: NSAID with a PPI plus weight-adjusted colchicine, dosed and interaction-checked as on the Pericarditis card (2024 ACC ECDP; 2025 ESC, IIa each). Colchicine cut recurrence in myopericarditis, 19% vs 44% in a matched cohort (Collini, Heart 2024); NSAIDs showed no harm with preserved EF (Berg, Open Heart 2019; Mirna, JCDD 2022). Symptomatic HF or shock: avoid NSAIDs; acetaminophen for pain. Practical (no guideline statement covers this): in a hemodynamically stable patient with reduced EF and a clear pericarditic component, colchicine alone is reasonable if renal/hepatic function and interactions allow. It is not contraindicated in HF (FDA label) and was neutral in stable HFrEF (Deftereos, JACC HF 2014), but it is unstudied in myocarditis with reduced EF
  • One troponin value is not prognostic; the trend is: Baseline troponin alone does not predict outcome, since many patients with high troponin and an MI-like presentation have preserved biventricular function. Biventricular dysfunction is the main independent predictor of death or transplant. Serial values add information: in fulminant myocarditis a fall in hs-troponin I over 24-48 h was associated with lower in-hospital mortality, and in ICI myocarditis hs-troponin T within 72 h was prognostic. Follow hs-troponin serially in symptomatic myocarditis (2024 ACC ECDP sec 4.5.1, 4.7.2)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Fulminant myocarditis (needs inotropes, vasopressors, or mechanical support)
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Sustained ventricular arrhythmias
  • High-grade AV block
  • Need for inotropes or mechanical support
  • Respiratory failure
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable off inotropes
  • No sustained arrhythmias ≥48hr
  • On appropriate heart failure meds
  • Activity restriction counseled: daily activities are fine and prolonged sedentary behavior should be avoided, but no strenuous or competitive exercise for 3-6 months, until cleared by cardiology after testing (2024 ACC ECDP)
  • Follow-up (2024 ACC ECDP Table 3): symptomatic HFrEF, visit within 1 week of discharge. By 2-4 weeks: office visit and echo (with strain when feasible) for all Stage C/D; add ECG and biomarkers (hs-troponin; natriuretic peptide and CRP if elevated at baseline) for medium/high-risk Stage C or Stage D, with GDMT uptitration at interval visits. At 6 months: echo (low risk) or CMR (medium/high risk or Stage D); CMR at 3 months may be preferable in athletes. ESC secondary: clinical review, ECG, and troponin/CRP within 1 month, at 3-6 months, and at 12 months, with Holter or exercise testing at 3-6 months (2025 ESC Table 15). Offer genetic counseling and testing (2024 ACC ECDP)
  • Wearable defibrillator: may be reasonable in myocarditis at increased SCD risk (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, IIb, B-NR); ACC calls its role uncertain without outcome data (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary: should be considered for 3-6 months after sustained VT/VF in the acute phase (2025 ESC, IIa). Practical: also consider with LVEF ≤35% while awaiting recovery, mirroring the ICD threshold; reassess LVEF and the ICD question at 3-6 months
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Cardiogenic shock (fulminant myocarditis), sustained VT/VF (sudden death risk), complete heart block, acute heart failure

Chronic: Biopsy-proven acute myocarditis resolves in about 50% within the first 2-4 weeks; about 25% develop persistent dysfunction, and 12-25% deteriorate to death or end-stage DCM and transplant (2024 ACC ECDP; ESC gives 10-25%). Long-term risk of death, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia, HF, and recurrence is increased even after acute myocarditis; LGE, especially anteroseptal, predicts adverse outcome. Recurrence after Stage C: about 3-10% per year; young age and a prior episode predicted relapse (2024 ACC ECDP). Ventricular aneurysm

Recovery: Uncomplicated cases with preserved EF usually recover. LVEF recovery ranges from 50% to 94% depending on presentation (2025 ESC). Fulminant cases improve sharply in hospital but more often recover incompletely (LVEF <55% at follow-up in 29% vs 9% non-fulminant; Ammirati, Circulation 2017). Repeat imaging guides therapy duration and ICD decisions

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 IVIG
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Anemia

44. CARDIOGENIC SHOCK

Pump Failure • Mechanical Complications • MCS
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: A cardiac disorder causing clinical and biochemical evidence of sustained tissue hypoperfusion (2025 ACC CS guidance). Usual criteria: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <60 for >30 min, or vasopressors needed to keep SBP ≥90 or MAP ≥60, PLUS hypoperfusion (altered mentation, cold extremities or livedo, urine output <30 mL/h, lactate >2 mmol/L). If measured: cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m² and PCWP >15 mmHg (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Tables 22-23). Hypotension is typical but not required; normotensive hypoperfusion is stage C (2026 SCAI; 2025 ACC)

Classic: Hypotension, cool extremities, altered mental status, oliguria, elevated lactate. Following acute MI, myocarditis, or acute decompensated heart failure

Clinical Signs:

  • Hypoperfusion: Cold, clammy skin, delayed capillary refill (>3 sec), weak pulses, confusion, oliguria (<0.5mL/kg/hr)
  • Congestion: Elevated JVP, pulmonary edema, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema (often "cold and wet")
  • Compensatory: Tachycardia (attempt to maintain cardiac output), tachypnea

SCAI Shock Stages:

  • Stage A (At risk): No signs or symptoms of CS but at meaningful risk (eg, large acute MI or prior infarction, acute or acute-on-chronic HF, selected high-risk cardiac procedures); normal perfusion and lactate
  • Stage B (Beginning): Hemodynamic instability (relative hypotension or tachycardia) WITHOUT hypoperfusion; normal lactate
  • Stage C (Classic): Hypoperfusion requiring drug or device intervention beyond volume; lactate ≥2 mmol/L. Normotensive hypoperfusion counts: hypotension is not required. Invasive hemodynamics strongly recommended
  • Stage D (Deteriorating): Like C but worsening or not improving despite the initial support strategy: lactate rising and/or persistently >2, escalating or added pressors, or added MCS. Reassess by 2-3 h to catch clear worsening and by 4-6 h to judge failure to respond
  • Stage E (Extremis): Actual or impending circulatory collapse with imminent risk of death: typically unconscious, profound hypotension despite maximal support, ongoing CPR, lactate ≥8, pH ≤7.2. Therapies alone (MCS, ECLS) do not set the stage; restage serially. The arrest modifier applies at any stage with cardiac arrest and ongoing CPR (2026 SCAI)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: Lactate (>2 suggests shock), BMP (creatinine rising), LFTs (hepatic hypoperfusion, transaminitis), CBC, troponin, BNP, blood gas (metabolic acidosis)

Imaging:

  • ECG: Assess for acute MI (most common cause), arrhythmia
  • Echocardiogram: URGENT. Assess EF, wall motion, valvular pathology, mechanical complications (VSD, acute MR, free wall rupture), pericardial effusion/tamponade, RV function
  • CXR: Pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly
  • Coronary angiography: Emergently in ACS with shock, STEMI or NSTE-ACS (see ACS with shock)

Hemodynamic Monitoring (PA catheter: may be considered, 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA 2b; strongly recommended at SCAI stage C or worse, 2026 SCAI):

  • Cardiogenic shock profile: CI <2.2 L/min/m², PCWP >15 mmHg, SVR usually high. Cardiac power output (CO × MAP / 451) <0.6 W marks high risk (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Table 23)
  • RV involvement: RAP >15 mmHg, RAP/PCWP ≥0.8, or PA pulsatility index [(PASP − PADP)/RAP] <0.9 in AMI-CS (2025 ACC; the HF guideline uses <1.0); PAPi is most useful when RAP >10 mmHg (2025 ACC)
  • Evidence: No randomized trial supports PA catheters in contemporary CS; registry and claims data associate them with better outcomes, and ESCAPE does not apply to today's CS population (2025 ACC)
  • Helps differentiate: From distributive shock (high CI, low SVR), hypovolemic shock (low PCWP)

Etiologies:

  • Acute MI: The most frequent single cause (2017 AHA): large anterior MI, RV infarction, or mechanical complications (VSR, papillary muscle rupture with acute MR, free wall rupture)
  • Acute-on-chronic HF: Decompensated chronic cardiomyopathy; up to 30% of CS cases (2017 AHA)
  • Mixed shock: CS plus a vasodilatory (eg, sepsis or a post-MI inflammatory state), hypovolemic or hemorrhagic, or obstructive component; about 20% of CS admissions in contemporary cardiac ICUs (2026 SCAI)
  • Acute valvular: Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture, endocarditis), acute severe AR (endocarditis, dissection)
  • Myocarditis: Fulminant, usually viral or autoimmune
  • RV failure: Massive PE, RV infarction
  • Arrhythmia: Sustained VT, bradycardia, uncontrolled AFib with RVR
  • Tako-tsubo (stress cardiomyopathy): Apical ballooning, mimics MI
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

General Principles:

  • Shock team and transfer: Management by a multidisciplinary shock team is reasonable (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, 2a); patients not rapidly responding to initial measures may be triaged to a center that can provide temporary MCS (2b). ACC strongly recommends early contact with the regional Level 1 shock center once CS is confirmed: starting vasoactive therapy, considering MCS, or arrest with tenuous neurologic status should prompt the call, and refractory AMI-CS after revascularization should almost always be transferred. Hospitals without these resources should name an on-site "shock champion" (2025 ACC CS guidance)
  • Treat underlying cause: Emergent revascularization (PCI/CABG) for MI, surgery for mechanical complications, cardioversion for arrhythmia
  • Optimize preload: Careful fluid management (avoid overload if already congested, give fluids if underfilled - esp RV MI)
  • Improve contractility: Inotropes
  • Reduce afterload: Vasodilators (if adequate BP)
  • Mechanical circulatory support: If refractory to medical therapy

Vasoactive Agents (ICU, arterial line):

  • Sequence: Hypotensive CS: start norepinephrine, then add an inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) once pressure is supported. Normotensive CS with high SVR: an inotrope or vasodilator alone may be considered. Use the lowest doses that restore perfusion, for the shortest time (2025 ACC CS guidance; 2017 AHA Table 5). Inotropes are Class 1 to maintain perfusion in CS (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA)
  • Norepinephrine: 0.05-1 mcg/kg/min. Reasonable first choice for most hypotensive CS; fewer arrhythmias than dopamine (2025 ACC Table 2; 2017 AHA)
  • Dobutamine: 2-10 mcg/kg/min (2025 ACC Table 2; label usually 2.5-15, rarely up to 40). Inotrope with vasodilation; can lower BP when given alone. Risk: tachycardia, arrhythmias
  • Milrinone: 0.125-0.5 mcg/kg/min (2025 ACC Table 2); label maintenance 0.375-0.75 after an optional 50 mcg/kg load, which is usually skipped when hypotensive. Inodilator that works despite β-blockade; renally cleared, so use judiciously with worsening renal function (2025 ACC). No outcome difference vs dobutamine (DOREMI). Risk: hypotension, arrhythmias
  • Epinephrine: 0.01-0.5 mcg/kg/min (2025 ACC Table 2). Not a preferred first agent in AMI-CS: vs norepinephrine, more refractory shock (37% vs 7%; trial stopped early), tachycardia, and lactic acidosis (OptimaCC, JACC 2018)
  • Dopamine: 2-20 mcg/kg/min (2025 ACC Table 2). Not preferred: more arrhythmias than norepinephrine, and higher mortality in the CS subgroup of SOAP II (NEJM 2010; 2017 AHA)
  • Vasopressin: 0.01-0.04 U/min (2025 ACC Table 2). Raises SVR with a neutral effect on pulmonary vascular resistance; an option in RV shock (2017 AHA Table 5)

Vasodilators (only if adequate BP, SBP >90):

  • Nitroprusside: Start 0.3-0.5 mcg/kg/min, increase by 0.5 every 5 min (max 10), arterial line, shortest possible duration. Lowers afterload and improves forward flow in normotensive CS with high SVR (2025 ACC CS guidance). Cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity risk at ≥3 mcg/kg/min and/or ≥3 days, higher with renal or hepatic dysfunction (dosing as on the Hypertensive Emergency card; 2025 AHA/ACC HBP Table 26)
  • Nitroglycerin: Mainly venodilation (preload) at low doses, less afterload reduction than nitroprusside. Avoid in RV infarction and with a PDE5 inhibitor in the past 24-48 h (dosing and cautions as on the ADHF card)

Mechanical Circulatory Support (MCS) - Cardiology/CT Surgery Consult:

  • Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP): Diastolic inflation (coronary perfusion), systolic deflation (afterload reduction); modest hemodynamic effect. Routine use in AMI-CS is not recommended (2025 ACS, 3: No Benefit; IABP-SHOCK II showed no 30-day mortality effect). Still reasonable as a bridge to surgery for mechanical complications (2a, see below)
  • Microaxial flow pump (Impella): Unloads the LV into the aorta; needs adequate RV function and oxygenation. Reasonable to reduce death in selected STEMI with severe or refractory CS (2025 ACS, 2a), meaning DanGer Shock-type patients: STEMI-CS under 24 h, SBP <100 or on vasopressors, lactate ≥2.5 mmol/L and/or SvO2 <55%, LVEF <45%, SCAI C-E, not comatose after arrest (GCS ≥8), no overt RV failure, and femoral access suitable for a large-bore device. 180-day mortality fell 12.7% absolute (NNT 8), with more bleeding, limb ischemia, and renal replacement therapy; best timing unclear (2025 ACS). Not studied in large RCTs in HF-related CS (2025 ACC)
  • VA-ECMO: Full cardiopulmonary support, but it raises LV afterload. Routine early use in AMI-CS is not recommended (2025 ACS, 3: No Benefit; ECLS-SHOCK showed no 30-day mortality benefit). Watch for LV distension and unload (eg, LV venting) or adjust support (2025 ACC). Practical: reserve for refractory shock or arrest at an experienced center, as a bridge to recovery, decision, durable VAD, or transplant
  • Surgical VAD: For bridge to transplant or destination therapy in refractory chronic cardiogenic shock

Specific Scenarios:

  • ACS with shock: Emergency revascularization of the culprit vessel by PCI, or CABG when PCI is not feasible or fails, irrespective of time from symptom onset (2025 ACS, Class 1); in STEMI-CS, PCI as soon as possible, ideally within 90 min of first medical contact. Do NOT routinely stent non-culprit arteries during primary PCI (2025 ACS, 3: Harm; CULPRIT-SHOCK: more death or renal replacement therapy at 30 days and 1 year). In SHOCK, emergency revascularization lowered 6-month mortality by an absolute amount similar to DanGer Shock's 12.7% (2025 ACS). Consider MCS if refractory (see above)
  • Mechanical complications post-MI: Surgery (VSR repair, MV repair/replacement, free wall rupture repair). Short-term mechanical support is reasonable for stabilization as a bridge to surgery (2025 ACS, 2a); most reported experience is with IABP, and VA-ECMO outcomes are mixed across registries (2025 ACS)
  • RV MI/shock: Revascularize the culprit (often the RCA). Avoid nitrates and diuretics, which drop preload (nitroglycerin: avoid in suspected RV infarction, 2025 ACS). Give fluid boluses guided by hemodynamics, then norepinephrine or vasopressin (neutral on pulmonary vascular resistance) and inotropes as needed; treat bradycardia and restore AV synchrony (2017 AHA Table 5). Practical: give small boluses with reassessment, and stop when right atrial pressure climbs (above about 15 mmHg, the ACC marker of RV congestion) without a rise in output, because a dilated RV pushes the septum into the LV and cuts LV filling (2026 SCAI; 2025 ACC)
  • Fulminant myocarditis: See the Myocarditis card. Transfer anyone needing inotropes to an advanced HF center; myocarditis is often biventricular, so VA-ECMO or other biventricular support is commonly needed, and data do not favor one device; EMB within 2 days of ICU admission was associated with better survival free of transplant or LVAD; immunosuppression by etiology (2024 ACC ECDP). ESC secondary: IABP first, escalating within 1 h if perfusion does not improve (2025 ESC). Not benign: cardiac death or transplant 28% at 60 days and 48% at 7 years in biopsy-proven cases (Ammirati, JACC 2019)

Avoid in Cardiogenic Shock:

  • β-blockers: Avoid with low output or signs of HF; early use in CS was linked to higher 30-day mortality (TRIUMPH analysis). Reasonable to start once euvolemic and off inotropes and vasopressors for at least 24 h (2017 AHA)
  • ACE-I/ARB/ARNI and MRA: Avoid with hypotension. Can be started once off vasopressors for 24 h, with renal function near baseline and low risk of hyperkalemia or hypotension (2017 AHA); then build GDMT as on the ADHF card
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: Hold during shock: labeling calls for temporary discontinuation in conditions that predispose to ketoacidosis (acute illness, reduced intake, volume depletion) or with reduced intake or fluid losses; resume when clinically stable and eating (FDA labeling, eg empagliflozin)
  • Excessive fluids: If already volume overloaded (worsens pulmonary edema). RV MI needs measured fluid, not unlimited fluid
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • "Time is muscle": In STEMI with shock, each 10-min delay in primary PCI beyond 60 min from first medical contact added 3-4 deaths per 100 (FITT-STEMI, cited in 2025 ACS). Culprit revascularization is the cornerstone; the only other intervention with randomized mortality benefit is a microaxial flow pump in selected STEMI-CS (DanGer Shock)
  • Warm vs Cold, Dry vs Wet: Cold = hypoperfused (needs inotropes ± MCS), Warm = adequate perfusion. Wet = congested (needs diuresis), Dry = needs volume. Most CS is "cold and wet"
  • Lactate trends matter: Elevated and rising lactate = worsening shock, need for escalation. Clearing lactate = improving
  • RV MI is different: Hypotension + clear lungs + raised JVP. Preload-dependent: no nitrates or diuretics; give fluid in measured boluses with reassessment; revascularize the RCA
  • Mechanical complications timing: Usually within the first week after AMI (2025 ACS), and in CS most often within 24 h of admission (2017 AHA). New murmur, recurrent chest pain, or HF or shock out of proportion = echo STAT; manage at a center with cardiac surgery (2025 ACS, Class 1). Surgical mortality is about 40%
  • Mortality remains high: Short-term mortality 30-40%, 1-year mortality approaching or exceeding 50% (2025 ACC); early mortality 40-50% in STEMI-CS (2025 ACS). Early recognition and culprit revascularization improve survival, and shock-team care is associated with better outcomes; routine MCS has not shown benefit apart from a microaxial pump in DanGer-type STEMI-CS
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL cardiogenic shock patients require ICU
  • Need for inotropes/pressors
  • Hypotension (SBP <90mmHg)
  • End-organ hypoperfusion (oliguria, AMS, lactate >2)
  • Mechanical circulatory support
  • Post-cardiac catheterization/surgery
✓ ICU → FLOOR CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable off inotropes ≥24hr
  • SBP >90-100mmHg consistently
  • Adequate end-organ perfusion (normal lactate, UOP, mentation)
  • No mechanical support
  • Underlying cause treated (revascularized, etc)
  • Transitioned to oral heart failure medications
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Death (short-term 30-40%; 2025 ACC), multi-organ failure (renal, hepatic, intestinal ischemia), arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, stroke, and major bleeding (as high as 60% in AMI-CS; 2025 ACC)

MCS-related: Bleeding, vascular injury, infection, hemolysis (ECMO), limb ischemia (IABP, Impella; linked to a 2-fold higher risk of in-hospital death), LV distension/thrombus (VA-ECMO)

Chronic (survivors): Chronic heart failure, need for transplant, durable VAD, recurrent ischemic events, chronic kidney disease

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Dobutamine, 💊 Milrinone, 💊 Vasopressin, 💊 Dopamine, 💊 Aspirin, 💊 UFH
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR

45. SYMPTOMATIC BRADYCARDIA/HEART BLOCK (PACING)

Sinus Bradycardia • AV Block • Pacing Indications
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Lightheadedness, presyncope, syncope, dyspnea, chest pain, fatigue with bradycardia. Threshold: sinus rate <50 bpm (2018 SND definition; NIH uses <60); ACLS 2025: HR typically <50 if bradyarrhythmia. Unstable (ACLS 2025): hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute HF. May be asymptomatic if chronic and compensated

Emergency Presentations:

  • Syncope: Sudden loss of consciousness from inadequate cerebral perfusion
  • Shock/hypotension: Bradycardia-induced low cardiac output
  • Heart failure: Pulmonary edema from inadequate heart rate compensation
  • Ventricular escape rhythms: Wide-complex slow rhythms (unreliable, unstable)

Types of Bradycardia:

  • Sinus bradycardia: Normal P waves, normal PR, slow rate. Can be physiologic (athletes) or pathologic
  • 1° AV block: PR >200ms. Every P conducted. Usually benign; pace only for marked PR prolongation with symptoms clearly attributable to it (IIa)
  • 2° AV block Mobitz I (Wenckebach): Progressive PR prolongation until dropped QRS. Usually AV nodal and benign; pace only if symptoms are clearly attributable to the block (IIa)
  • 2° AV block Mobitz II: Fixed PR with intermittent dropped QRS. High risk of complete heart block. Acquired and not reversible: PPM regardless of symptoms (I)
  • 3° AV block (complete): No AV conduction. Atria and ventricles beat independently. Always pathologic
  • High-grade AV block: ≥2 consecutive P waves not conducted. Unstable, high-risk
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

ECG: Characterize rhythm, measure intervals, identify level of block (AV node vs infranodal)

  • Narrow QRS escape: Block at AV node (more benign, responds to atropine)
  • Wide QRS escape: Infranodal block (His-Purkinje). More unstable, less responsive to atropine, needs pacing

Labs: Electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca), digoxin level if on digoxin, TSH, troponin (if concern for MI), Lyme serology with endemic exposure, pH; target to clinical suspicion (2018 IIa, C-LD)

Imaging: TTE is recommended for new LBBB, Mobitz II, high-grade, or 3° AVB, with or without known structural heart disease (2018 I, B-NR); reasonable for other bradycardia if structural disease is suspected (IIa). Advanced imaging (TEE, CT, cardiac MRI, nuclear) if structural disease (eg, sarcoid, amyloid) is suspected but not confirmed (IIa). Not routinely indicated for asymptomatic sinus bradycardia or 1° AVB without structural disease (III: No Benefit). Also assess for pericardial effusion/tamponade if suspected

Identify Reversible Causes:

  • Medications: β-blockers, CCBs (diltiazem/verapamil), digoxin, antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol). Symptomatic 2° or 3° AVB on chronic stable doses of a medically necessary β-blocker or antiarrhythmic: proceeding to PPM without waiting for washout is reasonable (2018 IIa, B-NR)
  • Ischemia: Inferior MI (RCA → AV node), anterior MI with BBB/complete heart block (LAD → His-Purkinje)
  • Infiltrative (usually NOT reversible): Sarcoid, amyloid, hemochromatosis. Sarcoid with 2° or 3° AVB: pace, with ICD capability if needed, without waiting for reversibility (2018 IIa, B-NR); treating sarcoid usually does not remove the pacing indication
  • Inflammatory: Lyme disease (endemic areas), endocarditis (perivalvular abscess)
  • Metabolic: Hypothyroidism, hyperkalemia, hypoxia
  • Increased vagal tone: Athletes, sleep, vasovagal. Sleep-related bradycardia or conduction disorder: screen for sleep apnea (I, B-NR) and treat documented OSA (CPAP, weight loss) (I, B-NR); it does not by itself warrant PPM (III: Harm)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

ACLS for Unstable Bradycardia:

  • Atropine: 1 mg IV q3-5 min, max 3 mg (ACLS 2025). Reasonable for symptomatic SND or AV block at the AV nodal level (2018 IIa, C-LD). Short-acting: a bridge to infusion or pacing. Unlikely to help His-Purkinje block; use judiciously with a wide-QRS escape. Do NOT use for sinus bradycardia after heart transplant without reinnervation (III: Harm); aminophylline 6 mg/kg IV over 20-30 min or theophylline is reasonable instead (IIa, C-LD)
  • If atropine ineffective (ACLS 2025): Transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion. These are parallel options, not a fixed sequence. Then consider expert consultation and transvenous pacing
  • Transcutaneous pacing (TCP): Bridge until transvenous pacing or PPM, or until the bradycardia resolves (2018 IIb, B-R). Painful, and capture is hard to confirm. Apply pads, set rate 60-80, increase output until capture (usually 50-100mA). Sedate if conscious. Practical: confirm mechanical capture with a pulse or arterial line, not the monitor alone
  • Dopamine: 5-20 mcg/kg/min, titrate to response, taper slowly (ACLS 2025)
  • Epinephrine: 2-10 mcg/min infusion, titrate to response (ACLS 2025)
  • β-agonist caveat: Isoproterenol, dopamine, dobutamine, or epinephrine may be considered when coronary ischemia is unlikely (2018 IIb). They can provoke ventricular arrhythmias and ischemia; isoproterenol can worsen hypotension. Isoproterenol: 20-60 mcg IV bolus, then 10-20 mcg doses, or 1-20 mcg/min infusion (2018 Table 8)
  • Acute inferior MI with 2° or 3° AVB: IV aminophylline 250 mg bolus may be considered (2018 IIb, C-LD; dose from Table 8)

Transvenous Pacing (Temporary):

  • Indications: Persistent hemodynamically unstable SND refractory to medical therapy (2018 IIa, C-LD); symptomatic or hemodynamically significant 2° or 3° AVB refractory to medical therapy (IIa, B-NR); acute MI with medically refractory symptomatic or hemodynamically significant bradycardia (I, B-NR). Do NOT place for SND with minimal or infrequent symptoms and no hemodynamic compromise (III: Harm). In MI, prioritizing reperfusion over temporary pacing for rate support may improve outcomes
  • Approach: Wire to the RV. Internal jugular access, fluoroscopic or echo guidance, and a balloon-tipped catheter have lower complication rates (nonrandomized data); use the most experienced available operator. Set rate 60-80, output 2× threshold
  • Temporary bridge: To permanent pacemaker or until reversible cause resolves. Use for the minimum duration necessary: complications rise after 48 h and include venous thrombosis, dislodgment and loss of capture, perforation, and higher infection risk for a later PPM (reported adverse event rates 14-40%). If block is judged irreversible and PPM implantation is available, go directly to PPM. Prolonged pacing (eg, Lyme, device infection): externalized active-fixation lead (IIa, B-NR)

Permanent Pacemaker Indications (Cardiology Consult):

  • AV block/conduction disease, pace regardless of symptoms (Class I):
    • Acquired Mobitz II, high-grade, or 3° AVB not attributable to a reversible or physiologic cause (I, B-NR)
    • Neuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy type 1, Kearns-Sayre) with 2° or 3° AVB or HV ≥70 ms (I, B-NR); add ICD capability if needed and survival >1 yr expected
    • Syncope with bundle branch block and HV ≥70 ms or infranodal block at EPS (I, C-LD)
    • Alternating bundle branch block (I, C-LD)
  • Symptom-driven (Class I):
    • SND with symptoms directly attributable to bradycardia (I, C-LD). No minimum heart rate or pause duration defines the need; document symptom-rhythm correlation
    • Permanent AF with symptomatic bradycardia (I, C-LD)
    • Symptomatic sinus bradycardia or AVB caused by GDMT that has no alternative and must continue (I)
  • Class IIa: Symptomatic chronotropic incompetence (rate-responsive pacing, C-EO); tachy-brady syndrome with bradycardia symptoms (C-EO); marked 1° AVB or Mobitz I with symptoms clearly attributable to the block (C-LD); infiltrative cardiomyopathy (sarcoid, amyloid) with Mobitz II, high-grade, or 3° AVB (B-NR), with ICD capability if needed. Sarcoid with 2° or 3° AVB: pace without waiting for reversibility (IIa, B-NR)
  • Do NOT pace (Class III: Harm): Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia or pauses from high vagal tone; sleep-related bradycardia or pauses without another indication; symptoms documented in the absence of bradycardia; asymptomatic or symptom-discordant 1° AVB, Mobitz I, or 2:1 block at the AV node; asymptomatic vagally mediated AVB; AVB fully resolved after treatment of a reversible, nonrecurrent cause; asymptomatic isolated conduction disease with 1:1 AV conduction
  • Post-MI: Temporary pacing for medically refractory symptomatic or hemodynamically significant bradycardia (I, B-NR). Observe for a waiting period before deciding on PPM (I, B-NR). PPM indicated for Mobitz II, high-grade AVB, alternating BBB, or 3° AVB (persistent or infranodal) after the waiting period (I, B-NR); 2025 ACS: PPM recommended when high-degree AVB persists >72 h. Do NOT pace: transient AVB that resolves, or new BBB/fascicular block without 2° or 3° AVB (III: Harm)
  • Device selection: SND: atrial-based pacing over single-chamber ventricular (I, B-R); dual-chamber or single-chamber atrial if AV conduction intact (I, B-R); program dual-chamber devices to minimize ventricular pacing (IIa, B-R). AV block: dual-chamber over single-chamber ventricular (I, A); VVI is acceptable if frequent ventricular pacing is not expected or comorbidities limit the benefit (I, A). Permanent or persistent AF with no rhythm-control plan: no atrial lead (III: Harm). Pacemaker syndrome on VVI in sinus rhythm: upgrade to dual-chamber (I, B-R)
  • Physiologic pacing (prevents pacing-induced cardiomyopathy, PICM): Pacing indication, LVEF 36-50%, expected substantial ventricular pacing (≥20-40%): CRT, His bundle, or left bundle branch area pacing is reasonable over RV pacing (2023 HRS 2a; 2018 IIa for >40%). Normal LVEF with substantial pacing: physiologic pacing may be reasonable (2b). LVEF >35% with less than substantial pacing: RV lead, minimize RV pacing (2a). LVEF ≤35% on GDMT with expected pacing >40%: CRT (HF 2022, 2a). Substantial RV pacing that cannot be programmed down: periodic LV function assessment (2023 HRS 1); PICM: upgrade to CRT (1) or conduction system pacing (2a)
  • Shared decision-making: Base device decisions on the evidence plus the patient's goals of care, preferences, and values (I, C-LD); inform patients of benefits, risks, and alternatives before implant, lead revision, or generator change (I, C-LD). Do not implant or replace a pacemaker when comorbidities make meaningful benefit unlikely or goals of care preclude it (III: No Benefit). A patient with capacity, or the legal surrogate, may refuse or request withdrawal of pacing even if pacemaker-dependent; the guideline treats this as palliative end-of-life care, not physician-assisted suicide. Discontinuing pacing is reasonable when the original indication has resolved or is in question, after monitoring with pacing off (IIa, C-LD)

Treating Reversible Causes:

  • Medications: Hold or reduce offending agents (β-blockers, CCBs, digoxin, antiarrhythmics). Symptomatic or hemodynamically significant toxicity (2018, IIa, C-LD; doses from 2018 Table 8): β-blocker or CCB overdose: glucagon 3-10 mg IV, then 3-5 mg/h (transient effect; nausea and vomiting, protect the airway); high-dose insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then 0.5 units/kg/h (follow glucose and potassium); pressor support is often needed. CCB overdose: 10% calcium chloride 1-2 g IV or 10% calcium gluconate 3-6 g IV every 10-20 min, or infusion (gluconate is gentler on peripheral veins). Digoxin toxicity: digoxin Fab, dosed by amount ingested or serum level (one vial binds about 0.5 mg digoxin), given over at least 30 min, may repeat; monitor potassium. Dialysis does not remove digoxin (III: No Benefit)
  • Ischemia: Revascularization. Inferior MI with AV block often temporary (RCA supplies AV node). Anterior MI with high-grade block is more permanent (LAD supplies His bundle)
  • Hypothyroidism: Levothyroxine replacement (bradycardia improves over weeks). Symptomatic 2° or 3° AVB with thyroid abnormality but no clinical myxedema: PPM without further observation may be considered (2018 IIb, C-LD)
  • Lyme carditis: Admit with continuous ECG monitoring if PR >300 ms, other arrhythmias, or myopericarditis (IDSA 2020, strong). Hospitalized: ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily until clinical improvement, then switch to oral (doxycycline 100 mg BID, amoxicillin 500 mg TID, or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg BID) to complete 14-21 days total (weak). Outpatient: oral regimen (weak). Azithromycin is second line, only if the others are contraindicated. Symptomatic bradycardia not managed medically: temporary pacing, NOT a permanent pacemaker (IDSA strong; 2018 I, B-NR). For prolonged temporary pacing, an externalized active-fixation lead is reasonable (2018 IIa, B-NR). Continue ECG monitoring until conduction substantially improves
  • Hyperkalemia: ECG changes: IV calcium first; it stabilizes the membrane but does not lower K (UKKA 2026, 2C; ACEP 2021). Gluconate is preferred (chloride causes necrosis if it extravasates); chloride if hemodynamically unstable or peri-arrest. Repeat ECG in 5 min and repeat calcium if changes persist (ACEP). Shift K: insulin with dextrose (UKKA: 10 units with 25 g glucose, 1B if K ≥6.5; ACEP: 5 units if CKD or insulin-naive), with glucose checks for up to 6 h; nebulized albuterol 10-20 mg as an adjunct (UKKA 1B), never alone (1A). Remove K: SZC (UKKA 1B for severe) or patiromer (1C), only with a functional GI tract. SPS is not recommended acutely (ACEP), and UKKA no longer uses resin binders acutely. Loop diuretic only as an adjunct, if eGFR ≥45 (ACEP). Hemodialysis is the most effective option and the choice in life-threatening hyperkalemia. IV bicarbonate only with metabolic acidosis (UKKA 2C; ACEP). Reassess K every 2-4 h. Details: see Hyperkalemia card
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Mobitz I vs Mobitz II: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) = progressive PR prolongation, block at AV node, usually benign. Mobitz II = sudden dropped beat without PR change, infranodal block, high risk of complete heart block, often needs pacing
  • Atropine can worsen infranodal block: By increasing sinus rate, more beats reach diseased His-Purkinje → paradoxical worsening. Use cautiously if wide-complex escape or known infranodal disease
  • Inferior MI vs Anterior MI: Inferior (RCA occlusion) → AV nodal ischemia → transient block, usually resolves. Anterior (LAD) → septal infarct, His-Purkinje damage → often permanent, needs PPM
  • High-grade AV block ≠ 3° AVB: High-grade = ≥2 consecutive non-conducted P waves but occasional conduction still present. Still dangerous, often progresses to complete
  • PPM after MI timing: The 2018 guideline sets no fixed waiting period; the 2025 ACS guideline recommends PPM when high-degree AVB persists >72 h. Inferior MI block is usually AV nodal and transient. Anterior MI with AV conduction impairment reflects extensive myocardial damage and carries a worse prognosis
  • Lyme carditis can cause ANY degree of AV block: Think Lyme in endemic areas (Northeast US) with new AV block, especially if young, no CAD. Typically AV nodal, often rapidly fluctuating complete heart block; onset averages 21 days after infection and only about 40% recall erythema migrans. IDSA: virtually all recover within 3-7 days; 2018: median resolution 6 days (range to 42). PPM only if block does not resolve
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Unstable vital signs (hypotension, shock)
  • Syncope/presyncope
  • 3° AV block or high-grade 2° AV block
  • Mobitz II 2° AV block
  • Need for temporary pacing (TCP or transvenous)
  • Bradycardia + acute MI
  • Ventricular escape rhythm
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Asymptomatic on telemetry monitoring
  • Reversible cause identified and treated
  • If permanent pacemaker placed: functioning appropriately, no complications
  • Stable heart rate and rhythm ≥24-48hr
  • No syncope/presyncope episodes
  • Device check arranged (if PPM placed)
  • Cardiology follow-up arranged
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Syncope/falls, progression to complete heart block, asystole, ventricular escape rhythms (unstable), cardiogenic shock

Post-PPM: Pneumothorax (CXR post-placement), lead dislodgment, infection (pocket or endocarditis), hematoma, venous thrombosis, pacemaker syndrome (AV dyssynchrony in VVI pacing)

Chronic: Pacemaker-dependent (if complete heart block), need for generator replacement (battery life 5-15 years), lead complications, heart failure (if excessive RV pacing)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Atropine, 💊 Dopamine, 💊 Norepinephrine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 Digoxin Level, 🔬 Elevated Troponin

46. VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA/VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION

Wide Complex Tachycardia • Sudden Cardiac Arrest • ICD
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

VT (Ventricular Tachycardia): Wide-complex (QRS >120ms) tachycardia at rate >100bpm. Can be stable or unstable

  • Stable (Monomorphic VT): Palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, presyncope. Hemodynamically stable, conscious
  • Unstable: Syncope, hypotension (SBP <90), altered mental status, pulmonary edema, shock
  • Pulseless VT: Cardiac arrest. No pulse, unconscious. Treat as VF

VF (Ventricular Fibrillation): Chaotic ventricular activity, no organized QRS complexes. Cardiac arrest. Pulseless, unconscious. Rapidly fatal without defibrillation

Special Types:

  • Polymorphic VT: Varying QRS morphology. Often degenerates to VF. If QT prolonged = Torsades de Pointes
  • Torsades de Pointes: Polymorphic VT with prolonged QT (>500ms). "Twisting of the points". Caused by QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte abnormalities
  • Ischemic VT: Post-MI scar-related reentry. Most common in adults
  • Non-ischemic VT: Dilated cardiomyopathy, sarcoid, ARVD, genetic (Brugada, Long QT)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Immediate (During Event):

  • ECG/Telemetry: Document rhythm. Assess QRS width, morphology, rate, AV dissociation
  • Differentiate VT from SVT with aberrancy: Brugada criteria, AV dissociation (diagnostic of VT), capture/fusion beats, very wide QRS (>140ms), extreme axis deviation
  • Pearl: If wide-complex tachycardia and unsure, assume VT (safer). "When in doubt, it's VT"

Post-Event Workup:

  • Labs: Troponin (MI trigger?), BMP (K, Mg - correct abnormalities), CBC, digoxin level if on digoxin
  • ECG: Baseline rhythm, assess for MI, QT interval, epsilon wave (ARVD), Brugada pattern, pre-excitation
  • Echo: Assess EF, wall motion (scar), structural disease
  • Coronary angiography: If concern for ischemia/MI as trigger
  • Cardiac MRI: Assess for scar, infiltrative disease (sarcoid, ARVD), myocarditis
  • EP study: If recurrent VT, to map and potentially ablate VT circuit

Identify Triggers/Causes:

  • Ischemia/MI: Most common. VT/VF in acute MI mostly occurs within 48 h and reflects acute ischemia; sustained monomorphic VT later after MI is usually scar-related. VT/VF at any time after MI raises 90-day mortality, late (>48 h) more than early (2017)
  • Cardiomyopathy: Low EF (<35%) is strongest predictor of sudden death
  • Electrolytes: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia (prolong QT → Torsades)
  • Medications: QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, macrolides)
  • Genetic: Long QT syndrome, Brugada, ARVD, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (CPVT), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  • Toxic: Cocaine, methamphetamine, digoxin toxicity
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Pulseless VT/VF (Cardiac Arrest - ACLS):

  • Defibrillation: Shock once a shockable rhythm is identified, then resume CPR immediately for 2 min; single shocks, not stacked (2a). Biphasic: manufacturer's recommended energy (eg, initial 120-200 J); if unknown, use the maximum available. Subsequent shocks equivalent; higher energy may be considered (2b). Monophasic: 360 J
  • CPR: 100-120/min, depth at least 2 inches (5 cm), full recoil, minimize interruptions, avoid excessive ventilation, change compressor every 2 min. Waveform capnography: if ETCO2 is low or falling, reassess CPR quality
  • Epinephrine: 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min (2a). Shockable rhythm: give after initial defibrillation attempts fail (2a, B-NR; algorithm: after the 2nd shock). Vasopressin offers no advantage; high-dose epinephrine is not recommended (3: No Benefit)
  • Amiodarone or lidocaine for VF/pVT unresponsive to defibrillation (2b, B-R; algorithm: after the 3rd shock): amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO, then 150 mg; OR lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg. Each improved survival to hospital admission but not to discharge. β-blockers, procainamide, sotalol, bretylium: uncertain benefit (2b). Routine calcium, bicarbonate, or magnesium: not recommended (3: No Benefit); magnesium is for torsades
  • Refractory VF/pVT (after ≥3 shocks): Correct defibrillation technique first (pad contact and position). Vector change and double sequential defibrillation: usefulness not established (2b, B-R). Most VF seen on post-shock rhythm checks is recurrence after a successful shock, not shock failure
  • Treat reversible causes: H's and T's (Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, H⁺ [acidosis], Hypo/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis [pulmonary or coronary])

Unstable VT (With Pulse; hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute HF):

  • Synchronized cardioversion (2025 1, B-NR): Monomorphic VT: 100 J (2025 cardioversion algorithm), or the device's recommended energy; increase energy for subsequent shocks if unsuccessful. Resynchronize after each shock; if synchronization is delayed and the patient is critical, go directly to unsynchronized shocks. Sedate whenever feasible. If refractory: add an antiarrhythmic, treat the underlying cause, get expert consultation
  • If polymorphic VT: Immediate unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy (maximum manufacturer's setting) (2025 1, B-NR); it cannot be synchronized reliably
  • Post-cardioversion (recurrence prevention): Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min (FDA label); repeat 150 mg for breakthrough VT. Treat ischemia and electrolytes

Stable Monomorphic VT (With Pulse, Hemodynamically Stable):

  • Procainamide (preferred; 2017 IIa, A; 2025 2b): 20-50 mg/min IV until the arrhythmia is suppressed, hypotension occurs, QRS widens >50%, or 17 mg/kg is given; maintenance 1-4 mg/min. Avoid if prolonged QT or HF. Monitor QT and BP
  • Amiodarone (2017 IIb, B-R; 2025 2b): 150 mg IV over 10 min, repeat if VT recurs, then 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min × 18 h. Slower onset; can cause hypotension; not more effective than procainamide (2025)
  • Sotalol (IV): 2017 IIb (B-R); 2025 2b, with efficacy similar to procainamide. NOT a simple weight-based bolus — FDA-approved IV sotalol is dosed by CrCl and target oral dose, infused over 1 hour (expedited loading protocol) or 5 hours (substitution-for-oral protocol), with QTc monitoring q15min during infusion. See Drug Reference for exact dosing table; do not administer as a rapid push
  • Adenosine: May be considered for stable, regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin, for treatment or diagnosis (2025 2b, B-NR). Do NOT give if unstable, irregular, or polymorphic (3: Harm). Verapamil or diltiazem: harmful in wide-complex tachycardia (3: Harm)
  • Safety: Do not combine antiarrhythmics (additive proarrhythmia); keep a defibrillator at the bedside
  • If drugs fail or are contraindicated: Synchronized cardioversion (2025 1, B-NR), with sedation when feasible

Torsades de Pointes (Polymorphic VT with Long QT):

  • Sustained or unstable: Immediate unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy (2025 1, B-NR); shock may not prevent recurrence
  • Magnesium sulfate: 1-2 g IV for recurrent torsades with acquired QT prolongation (2017 I, C-LD; 2025 2b); works even when serum Mg is normal and without necessarily shortening QT; repeat doses as needed
  • Correct electrolytes: K to ≥4.0 mmol/L and Mg to normal (2017 I, C-LD)
  • Increase heart rate (bradycardia- or pause-dependent torsades not suppressed by magnesium): Atrial or ventricular pacing, or isoproterenol 1-20 mcg/min titrated to heart rate (2017 I, B-NR; 2018 bradycardia Table 8 dose); 2025 advises expert consultation
  • STOP QT-prolonging agents: Review medication list, discontinue offending drugs; QT-prolonging drugs are potentially harmful in congenital or acquired long QT (2017 III: Harm). Antiarrhythmics can prolong QT further, and acute β-blockade can precipitate torsades by worsening bradycardia (2025)

Polymorphic VT With Normal QT (usually acute ischemia):

  • Sustained: Immediate unsynchronized shock (2025 1, B-NR)
  • Treat ischemia: Emergency angiography and revascularization with STEMI (2017 I, B-NR); IV β-blocker (2017 IIa, B-R)
  • Recurrences: IV lidocaine or amiodarone may be considered (2025 2b, C-LD). Routine magnesium is not recommended when QT is normal (2025 3: No Benefit)

VT/VF Storm (≥3 episodes of sustained VT, VF, or appropriate ICD shocks within 24 h):

  • Amiodarone infusion: 150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min (FDA label). Amiodarone or sotalol suppresses recurrent VA in ischemic heart disease (2017 I, B-R)
  • β-blockers: IV β-blocker for VT/VF storm after recent MI (2017 IIa, B-NR); metoprolol or esmolol
  • Sedation: Sedation or general anesthesia to reduce sympathetic tone (propofol, benzodiazepines); described in 2017 supportive text, no formal recommendation
  • Correct triggers: Ischemia, electrolytes, medications. Revascularization alone does not prevent recurrent sustained monomorphic VT (2017 III: No Benefit)
  • Catheter ablation: Recommended for prior MI with VT storm despite or intolerant of amiodarone (2017 I, B-R) or other antiarrhythmics (I, B-NR); fewer storms and ICD shocks than escalating drugs (VANISH). Urgent EP consultation
  • Refractory to drugs and ablation: Cardiac sympathetic denervation may be reasonable (2017 IIb, C-LD)
  • Avoid: Class IC drugs (flecainide, propafenone) after MI (2017 III: Harm). Do not implant an ICD during incessant VT/VF until it is controlled (2017 III: Harm)

ICD Indications (Cardiology/EP Consult; all require expected meaningful survival >1 yr):

  • Secondary prevention (2017, Class I):
    • Survived SCA from VT/VF, or hemodynamically unstable VT (B-R) or stable sustained VT (B-NR), not due to a reversible cause; applies to ischemic heart disease and NICM
    • Ischemic heart disease with unexplained syncope and inducible sustained monomorphic VT at EP study (B-NR)
    • NICM with syncope presumed due to VA, not meeting primary prevention criteria: ICD or EP study for risk stratification can be beneficial (IIa, B-NR)
  • Primary prevention, ischemic (2017 Class I; 2025 ACS 1, A): At least 40 days post-MI AND at least 90 days post-revascularization, on GDMT: LVEF ≤35% with NYHA II-III (A), or LVEF ≤30% with NYHA I (B-R). NSVT from prior MI with LVEF ≤40% and inducible sustained VT/VF at EP study (B-R)
  • Primary prevention, NICM (2017): LVEF ≤35% with NYHA II-III after at least 3 months of GDMT (I, A); NYHA I (IIb, B-R); lamin A/C mutation with ≥2 risk factors (NSVT, LVEF <45%, nonmissense mutation, male sex) (IIa, B-NR)
  • NYHA IV: ICD reasonable only for outpatients who are transplant or LVAD candidates (IIa, B-NR); not indicated for medication-refractory class IV without transplant, LVAD, or CRT-D candidacy (III: No Benefit)
  • Early after MI: Routine ICD within 40 days of MI does not improve survival (DINAMIT: fewer arrhythmic deaths, offset by more nonarrhythmic deaths). Clinically relevant VA >48 h and within 40 days of MI: ICD is reasonable (2025 ACS 2a, C-EO)
  • Wearable defibrillator (LifeVest): Reasonable when an ICD must be removed (eg, infection) in a patient with prior SCA or sustained VA (2017 IIa, B-NR). May be reasonable for increased SCD risk without current ICD eligibility: awaiting transplant, LVEF ≤35% within 40 days of MI, newly diagnosed NICM, revascularization within 90 days, myocarditis or secondary cardiomyopathy, systemic infection (2017 IIb, B-NR). After MI with LVEF ≤35%, usefulness is uncertain (2025 ACS 2b, B-R; VEST: no reduction in sudden or arrhythmic death at 90 days; all-cause death, a secondary endpoint, was lower)

Treating Underlying Causes:

  • Ischemia: Polymorphic VT or VF with STEMI: emergency angiography and revascularization (2017 I, B-NR). Revascularization alone does not prevent recurrent sustained monomorphic (scar) VT (2017 III: No Benefit). Prophylactic lidocaine or high-dose amiodarone in suspected AMI is potentially harmful (2017 III: Harm)
  • Electrolytes: K ≥4.0 mmol/L and Mg in the normal range (2017 I for torsades with acquired long QT; commonly applied to all VT/VF)
  • Long QT syndrome: β-blocker if QTc >470 ms (2017 I, B-NR); reasonable if asymptomatic with QTc <470 ms (IIa). Propranolol, atenolol, or nadolol; metoprolol appears less effective (2017 text; agent choice as on the Long QT card). High-risk symptomatic patients despite or intolerant of β-blocker: add LQTS type-guided drugs, left cardiac sympathetic denervation, and/or ICD (I, B-NR). QT-prolonging drugs are potentially harmful (III: Harm)
  • Brugada: ICD for spontaneous type 1 pattern with cardiac arrest, sustained VA, or recent syncope presumed arrhythmic (2017 I, B-NR). Quinidine or catheter ablation for recurrent ICD shocks from polymorphic VT, or for symptomatic VA when an ICD is not possible or declined (I, B-NR). Asymptomatic with only drug-induced type 1 pattern: observation (I, B-NR). Treat fever early and aggressively; avoid triggers (some psychotropics and anesthetics, cocaine, excess alcohol; brugadadrugs.org). Sodium channel blockers (procainamide, flecainide) unmask the pattern: use only as a monitored diagnostic challenge (IIa, B-NR)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Wide complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise: Especially with structural heart disease. Treating VT as SVT can be fatal (e.g., adenosine in VT can cause VF). Presume VT if the diagnosis is unclear (2017 I, C-EO). If stable: procainamide (preferred) or synchronized cardioversion
  • AV dissociation proves VT: P waves and QRS complexes independent. Capture beats (narrow QRS when P captures ventricle) and fusion beats also diagnostic
  • ICD timing after MI: VT/VF from acute ischemia (usually <48 h) is a reversible cause and is not by itself an ICD indication; revascularize and reassess LVEF. Clinically relevant VA >48 h and within 40 days: ICD is reasonable (2025 ACS 2a, C-EO); manage first with β-blockers and/or antiarrhythmics. Otherwise reassess for primary prevention at ≥40 days post-MI and ≥90 days post-revascularization
  • Torsades: shock, then magnesium: Shock if sustained; magnesium 1-2 g IV for recurrences, even if serum Mg is normal; correct K and Mg; stop QT-prolonging drugs. If bradycardia- or pause-dependent and magnesium fails, raise the heart rate (pacing or isoproterenol) to shorten QT
  • Adenosine in wide-complex tachycardia only if stable, regular, and monomorphic (2025 2b): Never if unstable, irregular, or polymorphic (3: Harm); it can cause VF in VT and precipitate AF with rapid conduction in WPW
  • ICD is NOT primary treatment: ICD prevents sudden death but doesn't treat VT. Still need optimal medical therapy (β-blockers, ACE-I, etc) and treatment of underlying cause
  • VT storm is an emergency: ≥3 sustained VT/VF episodes or appropriate ICD shocks in 24 h, with severe sympathetic surge. IV β-blocker (IIa after recent MI), sedation, amiodarone, correct triggers, and early EP consultation for catheter ablation (Class I after MI when drugs fail)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Pulseless VT/VF (post-ROSC)
  • Unstable VT (hypotension, AMS, pulmonary edema)
  • VT storm (recurrent episodes)
  • Post-cardioversion/defibrillation
  • Continuous antiarrhythmic infusions
  • Acute MI with ventricular arrhythmias
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Stable rhythm ≥24-48hr on telemetry
  • No recurrent VT/VF
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Underlying cause identified and treated
  • If ICD indicated: device placed or scheduled; wearable defibrillator only when the criteria above apply
  • Optimal medical therapy initiated (β-blockers, etc)
  • Cardiology/EP follow-up arranged
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Sudden cardiac death (if not defibrillated), cardiogenic shock, hypoxic brain injury (post-arrest), recurrent VT/VF (VT storm), ICD shocks (painful, psychological impact)

Post-ICD: Inappropriate shocks (lead malfunction, SVT misdetected), infection (pocket or lead endocarditis), lead dislodgment, pneumothorax, psychological impact of living with ICD

Chronic: Recurrent VT (may need ablation), progression of heart failure, need for transplant, complications of underlying disease (CAD, cardiomyopathy)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Amiodarone, 💊 Magnesium, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Sotalol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hypokalemia, 🔬 Hypomagnesemia, 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
