47. ACUTE LIMB ISCHEMIA

Vascular Emergency • 6 P's • Revascularization
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic 6 P's:

  • Pain: Severe, sudden onset. Often at rest
  • Pallor: White, mottled appearance
  • Pulselessness: Absent distal pulses (femoral, popliteal, DP, PT)
  • Paresthesias: Numbness, tingling. Early sign of nerve ischemia
  • Paralysis: Weakness, inability to move limb. LATE finding, indicates severe ischemia
  • Poikilothermia: Cool to touch compared to contralateral limb

Limb Viability Category (Rutherford/SVS; 2024 PAD Figure 8). ALI = symptoms <14 days. Use a handheld continuous-wave Doppler for arterial AND venous signals; pulse palpation is unreliable:

  • Category I (Viable): Audible arterial and venous signals. Normal motor function, no sensory loss. Not immediately threatened; revascularize urgently with heparin
  • Category IIa (Marginally threatened): Inaudible arterial, audible venous. Motor intact; sensory loss limited to the toes, if present; no muscle weakness. Salvageable if treated urgently
  • Category IIb (Immediately threatened): Inaudible arterial, audible venous. Sensory loss beyond the toes; mild or moderate muscle weakness. Salvageable only with emergency revascularization
  • Category III (Irreversible): Inaudible arterial AND venous. Complete loss of motor function and complete sensory loss. Major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage is inevitable: do NOT revascularize (3: Harm); primary amputation

Etiologies:

  • Embolism: Sudden onset, no prior claudication. Cardiac: AF (left atrial or appendage thrombus), LV thrombus (MI, cardiomyopathy), endocarditis, valvular disease (eg, mitral stenosis), paradoxical embolism through a PFO. Also artery-to-artery and aneurysm-related (eg, popliteal) embolism. Typically lodges at arterial bifurcations
  • Thrombosis (underlying PAD): Progressive onset, history of claudication/PAD. Thrombosis at a stenosis, of a bypass graft, or of a stent. Most ALI from PAD occurs after prior revascularization or amputation, or with ABI ≤0.60
  • Trauma and iatrogenic: Fracture, dislocation, penetrating injury; access-site thrombosis after femoral catheterization
  • Other (2024 PAD Table 20): Aortic or arterial dissection; hypercoagulable states (antiphospholipid syndrome, HIT, cancer-associated); cancer therapy (platinum agents, tyrosine kinase inhibitors); systemic inflammation (vasculitis, sepsis, viral illness including COVID-19); popliteal artery entrapment. With chemotherapy-related or viral prothrombotic ALI, a more deliberate plan before revascularization may be reasonable, on heparin meanwhile (2b, C-LD)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Exam: Vascular exam (pulses, capillary refill, temperature, color), neurologic exam (sensation, motor function), compare to contralateral limb

Handheld Doppler: Arterial and venous signals at the bedside define the viability category (see above). Loss of the arterial signal means a threatened limb; loss of both means a likely nonsalvageable limb

Labs: CBC, BMP (creatinine - may worsen with revascularization/rhabdo), CK (rhabdomyolysis if elevated), lactate, coagulation studies, type & screen

ECG: Assess for AF (cardioembolic source), recent MI. Take a full history and exam for the cause (2024 PAD 1, C-EO); testing for a cardiac source (ECG, rhythm monitoring, echocardiography) can be useful (2a, C-LD). Do not delay treatment for it

Imaging: initial assessment of viability and salvage needs NO imaging (2024 PAD 1, C-LD); do not delay revascularization for it. Imaging is reasonable before revascularization after multiple prior revascularization procedures (2b, C-EO) or in unusual cases such as suspected aortic dissection:

  • CT Angiography (CTA): When imaging is needed: level of occlusion, collaterals, aneurysm or dissection. Fast
  • Conventional angiography: Diagnostic + therapeutic (catheter-directed thrombolysis). Done in angio suite
  • Duplex ultrasound: If concern for DVT, popliteal aneurysm

Echocardiogram: If embolic source suspected (AF, LV thrombus, endocarditis, valvular disease, PFO). In one series of ALI not explained by PAD or aortic disease, a major cardioembolic cause (AF, mitral stenosis, or intracardiac thrombus) was found in 44%

Embolism vs Thrombosis Clues:

  • Embolism: Sudden onset, no prior symptoms, AF, normal contralateral pulses, emboli elsewhere
  • Thrombosis: Progressive symptoms, history of claudication, abnormal contralateral pulses, chronic PAD
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management (All Patients):

  • URGENT Vascular Surgery Consult: Emergency evaluation by a clinician able to assess viability and revascularize (2024 PAD 1, C-EO); if that expertise is not available locally, arrange transfer. Skeletal muscle tolerates about 4-6 h of ischemia: category IIa urgent, IIb emergent
  • IV Heparin: Therapeutic IV unfractionated heparin on diagnosis, regardless of cause or level of occlusion, unless contraindicated (2024 PAD 1, C-EO). Contraindications: active bleeding or high bleeding risk, ALI from aortic dissection or major vascular trauma. Prior HIT: direct thrombin inhibitor. Limits propagation and distal embolization. Do not delay for imaging. Practical: weight-based nomogram (eg, 80 units/kg bolus, 18 units/kg/h) titrated to aPTT or anti-Xa per institutional protocol
  • Analgesia: IV opioids for severe pain
  • IV fluids: Aggressive hydration (prevent contrast-induced nephropathy, prepare for reperfusion injury)
  • Keep limb in dependent position: Improves blood flow. Do NOT elevate
  • Keep warm: Room warm, but avoid direct heat to limb (can increase metabolic demand)
  • Avoid flexing knee: Can worsen ischemia by compressing popliteal artery

Revascularization Strategies (Vascular Surgery):

  • Indication: Salvageable limb (category I, IIa, or IIb): revascularization, endovascular or surgical including catheter-directed thrombolysis, is indicated to prevent amputation (2024 PAD 1, A). Category IIa: urgent; IIb: emergent. Category III (nonsalvageable): do NOT revascularize (3: Harm); primary amputation
  • Choosing the approach: Thrombolysis and surgery give similar limb salvage in 4 RCTs and meta-analyses, with more bleeding after thrombolysis. Choose by acuity, severity, anatomy, patient factors, and local resources, with the vascular team
  • Catheter-directed thrombolysis: Most effective for native artery or bypass graft occlusion of <14 days; little benefit beyond 14 days. Graft occlusion within 14 days of the original operation: weigh against surgical-site bleeding. Treat the unmasked culprit lesion with adjunctive endovascular or surgical revascularization (2a, C-EO). Ultrasound-accelerated thrombolysis shortens lysis time and lytic dose; pharmacomechanical or aspiration thrombectomy is supported by case series
  • Surgical thromboembolectomy: Arterial cutdown with an embolectomy (Fogarty) catheter
  • Bypass surgery: If severe underlying PAD, long-segment occlusion, or failed endovascular approach
  • Hybrid approach: Combination of surgical and endovascular techniques

Reperfusion Injury Prevention:

  • IV fluids: Aggressive hydration to maintain UOP >1mL/kg/hr (prevent myoglobin-induced AKI)
  • Bicarbonate: Consider alkalinizing urine if rhabdomyolysis (keeps myoglobin soluble)
  • Monitor electrolytes: Watch for hyperkalemia (reperfusion releases K from ischemic muscle)
  • Fasciotomy: Monitor for and treat compartment syndrome with fasciotomy after any revascularization, including thrombolysis (2024 PAD 1, C-EO). Prophylactic fasciotomy is reasonable for threatened but salvageable limbs (category IIa or IIb) based on clinical findings (2a, B-NR); early fasciotomy is associated with fewer amputations. Risks: nerve injury, wound complications, infection

Post-Revascularization Care:

  • Monitor for compartment syndrome: Severe pain (out of proportion), pain with passive stretch, tense compartments, paresthesias, rising CK. Lower leg is the most common site. Risk rises with longer and more severe ischemia. SURGICAL EMERGENCY - fasciotomy of all involved compartments
  • Anticoagulation: Cardioembolic source: oral anticoagulation per that indication. AF: long-term; prevents recurrence (2024 PAD). LV thrombus (2022 AHA statement; VKA or DOAC): after acute MI, typically 3 months, then repeat imaging and stop if resolved; remote MI or ischemic cardiomyopathy, at least 3-6 months, then shared decision on indefinite therapy; nonischemic DCM, at least 3-6 months, stop if LVEF improves to >35% with thrombus resolved. Without another indication, full-intensity oral anticoagulation to reduce MACE or limb events is harmful (2024 PAD 3: Harm, A). On full-intensity anticoagulation after revascularization and not at high bleeding risk: adding single antiplatelet therapy is reasonable (2a, C-LD)
  • Antithrombotic after revascularization (PAD): Antiplatelet therapy is recommended (2024 PAD 1, B-R). Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin is recommended to reduce MACE and major limb events (1, A). After endovascular revascularization, DAPT (P2Y12 inhibitor plus low-dose aspirin) is reasonable for at least 1-6 months (2a, C-LD); after a prosthetic bypass graft, DAPT for at least 1 month may be reasonable (2b, B-R)
  • Statin: High-intensity, aiming for ≥50% LDL-C reduction (2024 PAD 1, A). LDL-C goal per the 2026 dyslipidemia guideline: <70 mg/dL, or <55 mg/dL if very high risk (symptomatic PAD counts as a major ASCVD event); add ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 mAb on maximally tolerated statin to reach goal (very high risk: 1, A). Details on the PAD and statin cards
  • Monitor CK, potassium, creatinine: For rhabdomyolysis and AKI

If Irreversible (Class III):

  • Amputation: Primary amputation of nonviable tissue as the index procedure (revascularization is 3: Harm). With prolonged ischemia in a limb being revascularized, concurrent and early amputation can avoid reperfusion morbidity (2a, C-EO). Prevents systemic complications (rhabdomyolysis, sepsis from necrotic tissue)
  • Supportive care: Aggressive hydration, treat hyperkalemia, monitor for systemic toxicity
  • Do NOT revascularize: Reperfusion of necrotic tissue releases toxins (K, myoglobin, lactate) → systemic collapse
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • "Time is limb": Skeletal muscle tolerates about 4-6 h of ischemia; the longer symptoms last, the lower the chance of salvage. Urgency follows category, not a fixed clock: IIa urgent, IIb emergent. New motor weakness marks IIb or worse
  • Heparin first, imaging second: Start heparin on the clinical diagnosis unless contraindicated (think aortic dissection or major trauma first). Don't delay for imaging confirmation
  • Paralysis is bad: Motor deficit indicates advanced ischemia (nerve damage). Urgent revascularization needed. Sensation goes before motor
  • Compartment syndrome after revascularization: Reperfusion causes swelling. High index of suspicion. Pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch. Don't wait for pulselessness or pressure measurement - clinical diagnosis!
  • Blue toe syndrome: Emboli to digital arteries from proximal atherosclerotic plaque. Still palpable pulses. Suggests proximal source (aorta, iliac, popliteal aneurysm)
  • Don't revascularize Class III: Reperfusion of necrotic tissue causes systemic toxicity (hyperkalemia, myoglobin → cardiac arrest, AKI). Amputation is life-saving
  • Check for bilateral involvement: Emboli can lodge in multiple locations. Assess contralateral limb, visceral arteries
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Class IIB/III (threatened or irreversible ischemia)
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Post-revascularization (monitor for reperfusion injury)
  • Rhabdomyolysis (CK >5000, rising creatinine)
  • Severe hyperkalemia
  • Compartment syndrome requiring fasciotomy
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Successful revascularization with palpable pulses
  • No signs of compartment syndrome
  • Stable renal function (no rhabdo-induced AKI)
  • Electrolytes normalized
  • On appropriate anticoagulation/antiplatelet
  • Vascular surgery follow-up arranged
  • If embolic: Cardiology follow-up, address source (AF, LV thrombus)
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Limb loss (amputation 10-30% depending on severity), compartment syndrome (post-reperfusion swelling), rhabdomyolysis → AKI, hyperkalemia → cardiac arrest, sepsis from necrotic tissue, death (15-20% in-hospital mortality)

Post-reperfusion: Compartment syndrome, reperfusion injury (release of toxins → systemic inflammation), AKI (myoglobin), cardiac arrhythmias (hyperkalemia), recurrent thrombosis/embolism

Chronic: Chronic limb ischemia (incomplete revascularization), nerve damage (foot drop from peroneal nerve), chronic pain, graft/stent thrombosis, recurrent events if embolic source not addressed

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 UFH, 💊 tPA, 💊 Aspirin

48. ACUTE EXACERBATION OF INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE (ILD)

Progressive Dyspnea • Ground-Glass Opacities • High Mortality
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Patient with known or newly diagnosed fibrotic ILD (IPF, connective tissue disease-related ILD, fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, others) with worsening dyspnea and hypoxemia over days to weeks and new bilateral ground-glass opacities on CT.

  • Definition (International Working Group 2026, AE of fibrotic ILD): An acute respiratory event with increased respiratory symptoms or signs and radiologic or histologic features of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), with or without organizing pneumonia, in known or newly diagnosed fibrotic ILD. Revises the 2016 AE-IPF definition and extends it to all fibrotic ILDs.
    • Clinical: New or worsening dyspnea, exercise intolerance, and/or worsening oxygenation; onset typically <1 month
    • CT: New and/or worsening bilateral ground-glass opacity, with or without consolidation, superimposed on fibrotic ILD and not solely explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload
    • Histology (rarely available; biopsy is not advised to make the diagnosis): DAD
    • Triggered or idiopathic: Triggered when a cause is found (infection, surgery or procedure, drug, aspiration); idiopathic when none is found after full evaluation. Infection does not exclude AE; it can be the trigger
  • Acute respiratory worsening (ARW, IWG 2026): Umbrella term for any acute worsening in fibrotic ILD. Non-AE causes: pneumonia, pulmonary edema, PE, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, drug- or aspiration-induced pneumonitis, COPD exacerbation. No new GGO on CT excludes AE
  • Not AE: Rapidly progressive ILD (e.g., anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis) as a first presentation, and the gradual worsening of progressive pulmonary fibrosis over months (IWG 2026)
  • Symptoms:
    • Dyspnea and hypoxemia progressing over days to weeks (mean symptom duration about 2 weeks) (IWG 2026)
    • Cough is common but nonspecific (IWG 2026)
    • Fever or productive cough suggests an infectious trigger (IWG 2026)
    • Onset over hours suggests PE, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, or acute infection; chest pain, vomiting, or choking suggests PE, pneumothorax, or aspiration (IWG 2026)
    • Fatigue, malaise
  • Physical Exam:
    • Tachypnea, hypoxemia (often severe), accessory muscle use (IWG 2026)
    • Bibasilar inspiratory crackles (Velcro-like): common but may only reflect the underlying ILD (IWG 2026)
    • Digital clubbing (if chronic ILD present)
    • Cyanosis in severe cases
    • Clues to a non-AE cause: asymmetric breath sounds (pneumothorax, effusion); raised JVP, gallop, edema (heart failure); unilateral leg swelling (VTE) (IWG 2026)
  • Incidence, Risk Factors, and Triggers (IWG 2026):
    • IPF: 4-8 events per 100 patient-years in trials; 1-year risk 8-14% and 3-year risk 20-28% in real-world cohorts. Non-IPF fibrotic ILD: broadly comparable; higher with a UIP pattern
    • Severity: Low FVC or DLCO, higher GAP index, hypoxemia or home oxygen, worse dyspnea; UIP pattern and extent of honeycombing on CT
    • Triggers: Respiratory infection (bacterial; viral, including SARS-CoV-2; fungal, including Pneumocystis); thoracic surgery or surgical lung biopsy; bronchoscopy (BAL, transbronchial biopsy, cryobiopsy); drugs (chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors); aspiration; air pollution
    • Medications: Systemic corticosteroids and other immunomodulators are associated with higher AE risk in IPF
  • Prognosis (IWG 2026, pooled): 30-day mortality 30%, 1-year mortality 56%; worse in IPF than in non-IPF fibrotic ILD; in-hospital mortality up to 80% with ICU admission
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

High-Resolution CT Chest (HRCT):

  • Typical Findings (IWG 2026):
    • New or worsened bilateral ground-glass opacities, with or without consolidation
    • Superimposed on fibrosis (reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing)
    • Usually diffuse; can be multifocal or peripheral, especially early
    • No new GGO excludes AE and points to another cause of worsening
  • Clues to Alternatives (IWG 2026): Lobar consolidation (pneumonia); upper-lobe ground glass (alveolar hemorrhage); perihilar ground glass or effusions (pulmonary edema); centrilobular nodules (aspiration, bronchiolitis). If PE is possible, CTPA (with Doppler ultrasound), with an inspiratory HRCT acquired just before contrast

Laboratory Studies: No test is sensitive and specific for AE; labs look for triggers and alternatives (IWG 2026)

  • ABG: Hypoxemia (PaO2 <60 mmHg), elevated A-a gradient, respiratory alkalosis (early) or acidosis (late)
  • CBC: Leukocytosis or anemia may point to infection or hemorrhage (IWG 2026)
  • Chemistries, troponin, BNP, D-dimer: Screen for renal failure, pulmonary edema, PE (IWG 2026)
  • Procalcitonin: Suggests bacterial infection, but performance is marginal (IWG 2026)
  • LDH and blood neutrophil count: Higher values are associated with worse prognosis (IWG 2026)
  • Autoimmune serologies, including anti-MDA5: When the worsening is the first presentation of ILD (IWG 2026)
  • Inflammatory Markers: CRP, ESR elevated (non-specific)
  • KL-6 (Krebs von den Lungen-6): Higher serum levels are associated with AE risk (IWG 2026); not widely available in the US (Practical)

Microbiologic Studies (cultures, urinary antigens, viral PCR, NAAT: IWG 2026):

  • Blood Cultures: Rule out bacteremia
  • Sputum Culture/Gram Stain: If productive cough
  • Respiratory Viral PCR / NAAT: Influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, other viruses
  • Urine Antigens: Legionella, Pneumococcus
  • Long-term immunosuppression: Test for Pneumocystis jirovecii and mycobacteria (IWG 2026); fungal markers (beta-D-glucan, galactomannan) (Practical)

Bronchoscopy with BAL (Bronchoalveolar Lavage), selective (IWG 2026):

  • When: Mainly in mechanically ventilated patients; consider when immunosuppressed or when infection or alveolar hemorrhage is suspected but not confirmed noninvasively
  • If done: Broad microbiology (bacterial, fungal, viral, mycobacterial, Pneumocystis). A higher BAL neutrophil count is associated with worse prognosis
  • Risk: May worsen hypoxemia; BAL and transbronchial biopsy have been reported to trigger AE

Echocardiogram:

  • Purpose: Assess for cardiogenic pulmonary edema and pulmonary hypertension (IWG 2026)
  • Findings: May show elevated RVSP (pulmonary HTN), RV dysfunction, but preserved LV function

Lung Biopsy:

  • Role: Rarely performed (high mortality risk, little effect on management); only in exceptional cases after multidisciplinary discussion (IWG 2026)
  • Histology (if performed): Diffuse alveolar damage (hyaline membranes in the acute phase, then organizing changes), superimposed on background fibrosis (IWG 2026)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Supportive Care (Foundation of Treatment):

  • Oxygen and Noninvasive Support:
    • Management is supportive: correct hypoxemia, treat triggers, relieve symptoms (IWG 2026)
    • Practical: no AE-specific SpO2 target exists; avoid hyperoxia (e.g., aim for 92-96%); use 88-92% only if at risk of hypercapnia
    • HFNC rather than standard oxygen for de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ATS 2026, strong, moderate certainty); NIV or CPAP is an alternative (conditional, low certainty). The guideline does not address AE of fibrotic ILD specifically, so this applies indirectly
    • In AE of fibrotic ILD, HFNC and NIV may improve oxygenation and symptoms but have not shown a survival benefit; they can be used to avoid intubation or for palliation (IWG 2026)
    • Monitor closely and escalate promptly if noninvasive support fails (ATS 2026)
  • Mechanical Ventilation and ECMO:
    • Very poor prognosis; consider in selected patients, such as a bridge to lung transplant or when meaningful recovery is reasonably possible (IWG 2026)
    • Lung-protective ventilation with low PEEP (IWG 2026). Practical: tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure <30 cm H2O
    • Discuss goals of care BEFORE intubation, guided by the advance care plan, expected trajectory, and transplant candidacy (IWG 2026)

Pharmacologic Treatment:

  • Corticosteroids (unproven; use cautiously, IWG 2026):
    • No RCT. In AE-IPF, observational results range from no benefit to increased mortality, which challenges the previous guideline advice to treat most patients with AE-IPF (IWG 2026)
    • Non-IPF fibrotic ILD: High-dose therapy (>1.0 mg/kg prednisolone-equivalent) has been associated with better short-term survival; a more favorable role than in IPF (IWG 2026)
    • AE-IPF: If used, a short course of high-dose therapy may be preferred (IWG 2026). High-dose regimens in the studies included methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg IV daily for 3 days (IWG 2026, Figure 12)
    • EXAFIP2, the first placebo-controlled RCT of corticosteroids in AE-IPF, is in progress (IWG 2026)
  • Other Immunosuppression (not standard; avoid add-on cyclophosphamide):
    • IV cyclophosphamide: In the EXAFIP RCT (added to high-dose glucocorticoids in AE-IPF), no survival benefit and a trend toward higher mortality: 3-month mortality 45% vs 31% with placebo, p=0.10 (Naccache, Lancet Respir Med 2022; IWG 2026)
    • Cyclosporine, tacrolimus: No survival benefit in cohort and propensity-matched studies (IWG 2026)
    • Combined immunosuppression: No survival advantage, and possibly worse short-term outcomes, in IPF and non-IPF fibrotic ILD (IWG 2026)
    • IVIG and/or plasma exchange: Preliminary case series and small pilot studies only (IWG 2026)
  • Antimicrobials:
    • Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics are commonly given, guided by local recommendations and likely pathogens, including opportunistic ones (IWG 2026). Practical: a CAP regimen as on card 5, e.g., ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg daily (IV or PO)
    • Azithromycin: Small retrospective studies suggest a possible survival benefit (IWG 2026)
    • Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic use has not changed outcomes in AE-IPF (IWG 2026)
    • Antiviral therapy if influenza or COVID-19 is identified (Practical)
    • PJP prophylaxis (Practical: if prednisone >20 mg/day for >1 month is planned): TMP-SMX DS 1 tablet daily (FDA label; half the usual regimen if CrCl 15-30 mL/min, not recommended below 15); if TMP-SMX is not tolerated, atovaquone 1,500 mg once daily with food (FDA label)
  • Antifibrotics (nintedanib, pirfenidone, nerandomilast):
    • Treating the AE: Most studies show no mortality benefit (IWG 2026)
    • Prevention: Nintedanib and pirfenidone may reduce AE risk in IPF. High-dose nerandomilast reduced AE risk in progressive pulmonary fibrosis, but not in IPF (IWG 2026)
    • During the AE: Whether to continue, and when to restart, is not established; optimal timing and duration are unclear (IWG 2026). Practical: decide with the treating pulmonologist

Rescue Therapies (not standard, IWG 2026):

  • Polymyxin B direct hemoperfusion (PMX-DHP): Inconsistent mortality data; not a standard treatment
  • Recombinant thrombomodulin: RCT showed no survival benefit, a trend toward harm, and more bleeding; not a standard treatment
  • ECMO: Very poor prognosis; consider only as a bridge to lung transplant or when meaningful recovery is reasonably possible
  • Lung Transplant: May be performed during an AE in carefully selected patients

Palliative Care:

  • Early Involvement: Given high mortality, involve palliative care early
  • Goals of Care Discussion: Clarify code status, mechanical ventilation wishes, comfort measures
  • Symptom Management: Opioids for dyspnea, anxiolytics for anxiety
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • AE Is Defined by DAD, Not by Exclusion: Infection, surgery, drugs, or aspiration can trigger an AE. Look for triggers and alternatives in parallel; no new bilateral GGO on CT excludes AE (IWG 2026).
  • Not Only IPF: AE occurs across fibrotic ILDs at broadly comparable rates, more often with a UIP pattern. In IPF, the real-world 1-year risk is 8-14% (IWG 2026).
  • Prognosis: Pooled 30-day mortality 30% and 1-year mortality 56%; up to 80% in-hospital mortality with ICU admission. Discuss goals of care early (IWG 2026).
  • Ground-Glass Opacities on Background Fibrosis = Key Imaging Clue: New bilateral GGO superimposed on pre-existing honeycombing/traction bronchiectasis is classic for AE-ILD. Helps distinguish from new-onset ILD.
  • Steroids Are Unproven: Possibly harmful in IPF, more favorable in non-IPF fibrotic ILD. If used in AE-IPF, a short high-dose course may be preferred; the first placebo-controlled RCT (EXAFIP2) is in progress (IWG 2026).
  • No Add-On Cyclophosphamide: In the EXAFIP RCT it gave no survival benefit and a trend toward higher mortality (IWG 2026).
  • BAL Is Selective: Mainly for ventilated or immunosuppressed patients, or when infection or hemorrhage is suspected but unconfirmed by noninvasive tests (IWG 2026).
  • Noninvasive Support: HFNC is first-line for de novo hypoxemic respiratory failure (ATS 2026; indirect for AE). In AE of fibrotic ILD, HFNC and NIV improve oxygenation and comfort but have not improved survival (IWG 2026).
  • Intubation and ECMO: Very poor prognosis; reserve for a bridge to transplant or a reasonable chance of recovery, guided by the patient's advance care plan (IWG 2026).
  • Lung Transplant: Refer eligible patients before an AE occurs (Practical); transplant during an AE is possible only in carefully selected patients (IWG 2026).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Respiratory failure requiring high-flow oxygen or non-invasive ventilation
  • Hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen (SpO2 <88% on >6 L/min nasal cannula)
  • Need for mechanical ventilation
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Rapid clinical deterioration
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Oxygen requirements improved and stable (ideally <4 L/min nasal cannula or back to baseline)
  • Able to ambulate without severe desaturation
  • Trigger addressed (infection treated or excluded)
  • If corticosteroids were given: a written stop date or taper plan
  • Close pulmonology follow-up arranged (within 1-2 weeks)
  • Patient/family educated on poor prognosis, recurrence risk
  • Palliative care involvement arranged if appropriate
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Nintedanib, 💊 Pirfenidone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated A-a Gradient

49. HEMOPTYSIS (MASSIVE)

Life-Threatening Airway • Bronchial Artery Source • Emergent Intervention
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Bleeding from below the glottis in an amount that threatens the airway, gas exchange, or hemodynamics. A medical emergency; death is mainly from asphyxiation, not exsanguination (Practical).

  • Severity:
    • No agreed volume threshold: definitions vary widely across the literature (SCII 2023, non-US)
    • Life-threatening (massive): Any amount causing airway compromise, respiratory failure, or hemodynamic instability (Practical). Example volume cutoffs: >150 mL in 24 hours or 100 mL/hour (SCII 2023, non-US)
    • ACR 2020 uses "massive (life-threatening)" and "nonmassive (non-life-threatening)" without volume cutoffs
    • Focus on clinical impact (airway threat, gas exchange, shock) rather than volume
  • Mechanism of Death: Asphyxiation from blood filling alveoli (hypoxemia), NOT exsanguination. Airway protection is priority.
  • Common Causes (Practical; frequency varies by region):
    • Bronchiectasis (including cystic fibrosis): hypertrophied, tortuous bronchial arteries
    • Tuberculosis: Active or prior TB (cavities, post-TB bronchiectasis); Rasmussen aneurysm is a pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm in a TB cavity
    • Lung cancer: Primary or metastatic tumor eroding into vessels
    • Aspergilloma or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis: Fungus ball in a pre-existing cavity (old TB, sarcoidosis) with friable vessels in the wall
    • Necrotizing pneumonia or lung abscess: Vessel erosion
    • Cryptogenic: No cause found after evaluation
  • Source Vessels (Practical): Usually bronchial or nonbronchial systemic arteries (high pressure, from the aorta and its branches). Pulmonary artery sources are less common but need different treatment
  • Less Common Causes:
    • Pulmonary artery sources: Pseudoaneurysm (Rasmussen, infection, trauma), arteriovenous malformation (hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia), pulmonary artery catheter injury, Behcet disease
    • Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary infarction
    • Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage: Anti-GBM disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lupus; usually anemia, hypoxemia, and diffuse infiltrates rather than massive hemoptysis
    • Bleeding diathesis: Anticoagulants, antiplatelet drugs, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy
  • Iatrogenic Causes: Post-bronchoscopy, transbronchial biopsy, pulmonary artery (Swan-Ganz) catheter placement
  • Presentation:
    • Coughing up frank blood (bright red)
    • Blood-tinged frothy sputum (from alveoli)
    • Sensation of warmth/bubbling in chest preceding cough
    • Dyspnea, tachypnea (airway obstruction from blood)
    • Hypoxemia (SpO2 drop from blood in alveoli)
    • Hemodynamic instability if massive volume loss (rare, late sign)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Assessment (EMERGENT):

  • ABCs: Airway patency (can they talk?), breathing (oxygen saturation), circulation (BP, HR)
  • Distinguish from Hematemesis:
    • Hemoptysis: Cough, frothy/bright red, alkaline pH, mixed with air/sputum
    • Hematemesis: Vomiting, dark/coffee-ground, acidic pH, mixed with food
    • Nasopharyngeal bleed: Usually obvious source, blood drips posteriorly
  • Lateralize Bleeding Side: Ask patient which side they feel bleeding from, listen for unilateral decreased breath sounds or crackles (blood-filled lung)

Laboratory Studies:

  • CBC: Hemoglobin (baseline, check for anemia from blood loss), platelets (thrombocytopenia?)
  • Coagulation Studies: PT/INR, PTT (anticoagulation, coagulopathy)
  • Type & Screen: Prepare for transfusion
  • ABG: Assess oxygenation, ventilation
  • BMP: Renal function (contrast for CT, uremia affects platelets)

Imaging (ACR 2020, massive hemoptysis, initial imaging):

  • Usually appropriate: Chest radiograph; CT chest with IV contrast; CTA chest with IV contrast; bronchial arteriography with embolization. CT without contrast: may be appropriate. CT without and with contrast: usually not appropriate
  • Chest radiograph (portable if unstable): May show infiltrate (blood or the underlying lesion), cavity, or mass, or be normal; can suggest the bleeding side
  • CTA: Maps bronchial, nonbronchial systemic, and pulmonary arteries and localizes the source before embolization. Practical: obtain once the airway is secure and the patient can travel; do not delay airway control or resuscitation
  • Recurrent hemoptysis (ACR 2020): Chest radiograph, CTA, and bronchial arteriography with embolization are usually appropriate

Bronchoscopy (Practical; not rated by ACR):

  • Rigid bronchoscopy, where available: Large-bore suction, clot removal, tamponade, and ventilation through the scope; usually in the OR by interventional pulmonology or thoracic surgery
  • Flexible bronchoscopy: Bedside, ICU, or OR; localizes the site and delivers topical therapy or a bronchial blocker; the small channel clots easily
  • Timing: After the airway is secured; do not delay embolization when CTA has shown a target vessel
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Resuscitation (PRIORITY = AIRWAY):

  • Positioning:
    • Place patient in lateral decubitus position with bleeding side DOWN (protects non-bleeding lung from aspiration of blood)
    • If side unknown, place in Trendelenburg or semi-upright to prevent aspiration
  • Oxygen: High-flow O2 via non-rebreather mask (goal SpO2 >90%)
  • Large-Bore IV Access: Two 18g IVs for resuscitation, blood transfusion
  • IV Fluids: Normal saline or LR bolus if hypotensive
  • Correct Coagulopathy (Practical):
    • Warfarin: Vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC
    • Dabigatran: Idarucizumab
    • Factor Xa inhibitors: Andexanet alfa is no longer available in the US (withdrawn December 2025 after an FDA safety communication on thromboembolic events; AABB 2025). 4-factor PCC is used
    • Platelet transfusion if <50,000/µL
    • FFP if INR >1.5 and bleeding (when PCC is not indicated)
    • Desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 mcg/kg IV for uremic platelet dysfunction

Airway Management (CRITICAL):

  • Indications for Intubation:
    • Massive hemoptysis with airway compromise
    • Respiratory failure (hypoxemia despite high-flow O2)
    • Altered mental status, inability to protect airway
    • Hemodynamic instability
  • Intubation Strategy:
    • Use largest ETT possible (8.0-9.0 mm) to allow suctioning of blood clots
    • Consider awake fiberoptic intubation if time permits (maintain spontaneous ventilation)
    • Prepare for difficult intubation (blood obscures view)
    • Have rigid bronchoscopy available as backup
  • Lung Isolation (Advanced Airway Management):
    • Double-Lumen ETT: Allows selective ventilation of non-bleeding lung, protects non-bleeding lung from blood aspiration
    • Bronchial Blocker: Balloon catheter placed via bronchoscope to occlude bleeding bronchus
    • Selective Mainstem Intubation: Intubate into non-bleeding mainstem bronchus (right for left-sided bleed, vice versa)
    • Requires expertise; consult anesthesia or interventional pulmonology

Pharmacologic Hemostasis (Temporizing Measures):

  • Tranexamic Acid (TXA; off-label for hemoptysis):
    • CHEST 2026 (non-CF bronchiectasis): Suggests TXA for hemoptysis (conditional, very low certainty). In 3 small RCTs of mixed causes, TXA reduced escalation of care (RR 0.17), blood volume, and hospital stay; experts prefer nebulized TXA in a monitored setting
    • Trial regimens: Nebulized TXA 500 mg three times daily (Wand, Chest 2018: resolution within 5 days 96% vs 50% with placebo). Nebulized vs IV TXA, both 500 mg three times daily: cessation at 30 minutes in 40 of 55 vs 28 of 55 (Gopinath, Chest 2023). Nebulized dosing is not standardized (CHEST 2026)
    • Massive hemoptysis: The RCTs studied nonmassive hemoptysis (Wand 2018 excluded >200 mL/24 h and unstable patients). TXA is only an adjunct to airway control and embolization (Practical)
    • IV label (Cyklokapron): Reduce the dose in renal impairment; contraindicated with active intravascular clotting; risk of thromboembolism (weigh with PE or recent thrombosis); IV only, never neuraxial (boxed warning)
  • Topical Therapies via Bronchoscopy (Practical):
    • Cold saline lavage (vasoconstriction)
    • Epinephrine 1:10,000 (1-2 mL aliquots) via bronchoscope
    • Thrombin (topical)
    • Balloon tamponade with bronchial blocker

Definitive Treatment:

  • Bronchial Artery Embolization (BAE), first-line definitive therapy:
    • ACR 2020: Bronchial arteriography with embolization is usually appropriate in massive and in recurrent hemoptysis
    • Outcomes (meta-analysis of observational studies, Karlafti, J Pers Med 2023): Pooled technical success 97%, clinical success 92%, recurrence 21%, mortality 3.5%
    • Procedure: Interventional radiology; selective catheterization of bronchial and nonbronchial systemic arteries; embolization with particles, coils, or glue
    • Complications: Chest discomfort, fever, dysphagia, paresis (Karlafti 2023); spinal cord ischemia and paraplegia if the anterior spinal artery is embolized (CIRSE 2025, non-US)
    • Recurrence is common; repeat embolization or surgery may be needed (Practical)
  • Surgery (Lung Resection):
    • Indications (Practical): Embolization fails or is unavailable; localized disease (resectable tumor, destroyed lobe, aspergilloma); recurrent hemoptysis
    • Procedure: Lobectomy or pneumonectomy
    • Timing: Outcomes are worse when surgery is emergent and better with elective resection at experienced centers (CHEST 2026, in bronchiectasis). Prefer control first, then elective surgery
  • Pulmonary Artery Embolization: For pulmonary artery sources (less common): Rasmussen or other pseudoaneurysm, AVM, catheter injury (Practical)

Supportive Care:

  • Blood Transfusion: PRBC to maintain Hgb >7 g/dL; more as needed with ongoing bleeding (Practical)
  • Antibiotics: If infection suspected (TB, pneumonia, abscess)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Death from Asphyxiation, Not Exsanguination: Massive hemoptysis kills by drowning in blood (hypoxemia from alveoli filling with blood), not from bleeding out. Priority is AIRWAY protection, not just volume resuscitation. Position bleeding side down to protect good lung.
  • Most Bleeding Is from Systemic Arteries: Bronchial and nonbronchial systemic arteries (high pressure) are the usual source, which is why embolization works. Pulmonary artery sources need pulmonary artery embolization or surgery (Practical).
  • Leading Causes: Bronchiectasis (including CF) and active or prior TB, then cancer, aspergilloma, and necrotizing infection; the mix varies by region (Practical).
  • Aspergilloma = Fungus Ball in Cavity: Bleeding comes from friable vessels in the cavity wall. Control it with embolization or resection; antifungal therapy is adjunctive, not hemostatic (Practical).
  • Rigid vs Flexible Bronchoscopy: Rigid scopes give large-bore suction, clot removal, tamponade, and ventilation but need the OR and specialized training; flexible scopes localize and treat but clot quickly (Practical).
  • Embolization Works, but Bleeding Recurs: Pooled clinical success 92% and recurrence 21% (Karlafti 2023). Plan follow-up; repeat embolization or surgery may be needed.
  • Position Patient Bleeding Side Down: Gravity prevents blood from healthy lung filling with blood. If you know right lung is bleeding, place patient in right lateral decubitus. This is critical to prevent asphyxiation of good lung.
  • TB Can Cause Rasmussen Aneurysm: A TB cavity erodes a pulmonary artery branch, forming a pseudoaneurysm that can rupture. Treat with pulmonary artery embolization or surgery, not bronchial artery embolization alone (Practical).
  • Avoid Emergency Surgery When Possible: Outcomes are worse when resection is emergent (CHEST 2026, in bronchiectasis). Stabilize with embolization, then operate electively if needed.
  • TXA Is an Adjunct: Nebulized TXA helps in nonmassive hemoptysis (CHEST 2026: conditional, very low certainty). In massive hemoptysis it does not replace airway control or embolization.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL massive hemoptysis requires ICU admission
  • Respiratory failure or airway compromise
  • Need for mechanical ventilation or advanced airway
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Ongoing bleeding requiring transfusion
  • Post-bronchial artery embolization monitoring
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • No active bleeding for >48 hours (Practical; no validated threshold)
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Hemoglobin stable without transfusion requirement
  • Oxygenating adequately on room air or baseline oxygen
  • Definitive intervention completed (BAE or surgery) OR bleeding clearly self-limited
  • Underlying etiology identified and treated (antibiotics for infection, etc.)
  • Close pulmonology follow-up arranged (within 1-2 weeks)
  • If BAE performed: Interventional radiology follow-up arranged
  • Patient educated on return precautions (recurrent hemoptysis)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 TXA
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR, 🔬 Elevated PTT, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia

50. ACUTE HYPERCAPNIC RESPIRATORY FAILURE

Elevated PaCO2 • Respiratory Acidosis • Alveolar Hypoventilation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Patient with acute or acute-on-chronic elevation in arterial CO2 (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) causing respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35), typically presenting with altered mental status, dyspnea, and/or respiratory distress. Results from alveolar hypoventilation - inadequate minute ventilation to eliminate CO2 produced by metabolism.

  • Pathophysiology: Minute ventilation (VE) = Tidal Volume × Respiratory Rate. If VE inadequate → CO2 retention → respiratory acidosis → CNS depression → further hypoventilation (vicious cycle)
  • Acute vs Chronic Hypercapnia:
    • Acute: pH <7.35, elevated PaCO2, normal HCO3 (kidneys haven't compensated yet)
    • Chronic: pH 7.35-7.40, elevated PaCO2, elevated HCO3 (renal compensation)
    • Acute-on-Chronic: pH <7.35, very elevated PaCO2 (>55-60), elevated HCO3 (baseline compensation insufficient for acute rise)
  • Compensatory Response: Kidneys retain HCO3 to buffer respiratory acidosis; takes 3-5 days. For every 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2, HCO3 rises ~1 mEq/L acutely, ~3.5 mEq/L chronically

Common Etiologies (by Mechanism):

  • Decreased Respiratory Drive (CNS Depression):
    • Opioid overdose (most common iatrogenic cause in hospitalized patients)
    • Sedative/hypnotic overdose (benzodiazepines, barbiturates)
    • CNS lesions (stroke, tumor, trauma)
    • Severe metabolic alkalosis (depresses respiratory drive)
  • Neuromuscular Weakness (Respiratory Muscle Failure):
    • Guillain-Barré syndrome
    • Myasthenia gravis crisis
    • ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis)
    • Muscular dystrophy
    • Phrenic nerve injury
    • Spinal cord injury (C3-C5 affects diaphragm)
    • Critical illness myopathy/polyneuropathy
  • Increased Airway Resistance (Obstructive Lung Disease):
    • COPD exacerbation (most common cause overall)
    • Severe asthma exacerbation
    • Upper airway obstruction (foreign body, tumor, laryngospasm)
  • Restrictive Lung Disease / Chest Wall Disorders:
    • Severe obesity (obesity hypoventilation syndrome)
    • Kyphoscoliosis
    • Flail chest (trauma)
    • Pneumothorax, pleural effusion (large)
  • Increased CO2 Production (Rare Primary Cause, Usually Multifactorial):
    • Malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome
    • Thyroid storm
    • Sepsis, fever
    • Overfeeding (especially carbohydrates in critically ill)

Clinical Manifestations:

  • CNS Effects (Hypercapnia = Cerebral Vasodilation + CNS Depression):
    • Altered mental status: Confusion, lethargy, somnolence
    • CO2 narcosis: Progressive obtundation → stupor → coma (PaCO2 >70-90 mmHg)
    • Headache (from cerebral vasodilation)
    • Tremor, asterixis (flapping tremor), myoclonus
    • Papilledema (if severe, prolonged)
    • Seizures (rare, severe hypercapnia)
  • Respiratory:
    • Dyspnea, tachypnea (early, trying to compensate)
    • Bradypnea, shallow breathing (late, respiratory fatigue or CNS depression)
    • Use of accessory muscles, paradoxical abdominal breathing
  • Cardiovascular:
    • Tachycardia, hypertension (catecholamine surge from hypercapnia/hypoxemia)
    • Arrhythmias (acidosis lowers threshold)
    • Warm, flushed skin (peripheral vasodilation from hypercapnia)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) - GOLD STANDARD:

  • Diagnostic Criteria: PaCO2 >45 mmHg with pH <7.35 (respiratory acidosis)
  • Interpretation:
    • Acute: pH low, PaCO2 high, HCO3 normal (22-26 mEq/L)
    • Chronic: pH near-normal (7.35-7.40), PaCO2 high, HCO3 high (>26 mEq/L, compensated)
    • Acute-on-chronic: pH very low (<7.30), PaCO2 very high (>55-60), HCO3 elevated (baseline compensation insufficient)
  • Assess Oxygenation: PaO2, calculate A-a gradient (elevated in V/Q mismatch, normal in pure hypoventilation)
  • Alveolar Gas Equation: PAO2 = FiO2 × (Patm - PH2O) - PaCO2/0.8. A-a gradient = PAO2 - PaO2. Normal <10-15 mmHg.
  • Expected Compensation: For pure respiratory acidosis, HCO3 increases ~1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2 (acute) or ~3.5 mEq/L (chronic). If HCO3 doesn't fit, suspect mixed disorder.

Venous Blood Gas (VBG):

  • Use: Can estimate arterial pH and PaCO2 (venous pH ~0.03-0.05 lower, venous PCO2 ~5-8 mmHg higher than arterial)
  • Limitation: Cannot assess oxygenation (PvO2 not useful); ABG preferred if available

Identify Underlying Cause:

  • History:
    • COPD/asthma history (exacerbation?)
    • Medications: Opioids, benzodiazepines, sedatives
    • Neuromuscular disease (GBS, MG, ALS)
    • Recent trauma, surgery
    • Symptoms: Cough, fever (pneumonia), chest pain (PTX)
  • Physical Exam:
    • Respiratory: Wheezing (COPD, asthma), decreased breath sounds (PTX, effusion), crackles (pneumonia, pulmonary edema)
    • Neurologic: Weakness (neuromuscular), altered mental status (CNS cause), pupils (pinpoint = opioids)
    • Chest wall: Kyphoscoliosis, obesity, flail segment

Chest X-ray:

  • Findings: Pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion, COPD hyperinflation, pulmonary edema, aspiration

Laboratory Studies:

  • BMP: Assess HCO3 (metabolic compensation), K+ (acidosis causes hyperkalemia), renal function
  • CBC: Leukocytosis (infection), polycythemia (chronic hypercapnia)
  • Toxicology Screen: If overdose suspected (opioids, benzodiazepines, barbiturates)
  • CK: Rhabdomyolysis (if prolonged immobility, seizures)

Additional Testing (Based on Suspected Etiology):

  • Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs): If stable, assess for obstructive or restrictive lung disease (not in acute setting)
  • Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF, also called MIP): Measures inspiratory muscle strength. NIF is a negative number, and weakness moves it toward zero: a NIF weaker than about -20 to -30 cm H2O (for example -15) suggests significant weakness. Follow serial values with vital capacity (Practical)
  • EMG/Nerve Conduction Studies: If neuromuscular disease suspected (GBS, MG)
  • CT Chest: If CXR non-diagnostic and etiology unclear (PE, ILD, bronchiectasis)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

General Principles:

  • Treat Underlying Cause: Bronchodilators for COPD/asthma, antibiotics for pneumonia, naloxone for opioids, etc.
  • Improve Alveolar Ventilation: Increase minute ventilation (non-invasive or invasive ventilation)
  • Avoid Over-Oxygenation in COPD: High FiO2 can worsen hypercapnia (primarily V/Q mismatch, plus Haldane effect and some loss of hypoxic drive)

Oxygen Therapy:

  • Target SpO2 88-92% if at risk of hypercapnia (e.g., COPD, OHS, neuromuscular or chest wall disease; BTS 2017, non-US): aim for 88-92% pending blood gases; adjust to 94-98% (BTS usual target; no single US target, see Condition 154) if PaCO2 is normal, unless prior hypercapnic failure needed NIV or invasive ventilation; recheck gases after 30-60 minutes
    • Excess oxygen raises PaCO2 mainly through worse V/Q matching (release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) and the Haldane effect; loss of hypoxic drive plays a smaller part (Practical)
    • Controlled delivery (Practical): Venturi mask 24-28% or nasal cannula 1-2 L/min, titrated to the target
    • Nebulizers: Air-driven rather than oxygen-driven in COPD exacerbations, to avoid raising PaCO2 (GOLD 2026)
  • Exception (Practical): In life-threatening hypoxemia, give enough oxygen to correct it and prepare ventilatory support; do not withhold oxygen to avoid hypercapnia

Noninvasive Ventilation (NIV, bilevel) - FIRST-LINE for Acute Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure:

  • ATS 2026: NIV by facemask is recommended over standard oxygen for adults with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (strong recommendation, moderate certainty). Pooled vs standard oxygen (42 RCTs, mostly COPD): mortality RR 0.47, intubation RR 0.43. Best delivered in an ICU or intermediate care unit where rapid intubation is available
  • When to Start (GOLD 2026), at least one of:
    • Respiratory acidosis: PaCO2 45 mmHg or higher and arterial pH 7.35 or lower
    • Severe dyspnea with signs of respiratory muscle fatigue or increased work of breathing (accessory muscle use, paradoxical abdominal motion, intercostal retraction)
    • Persistent hypoxemia despite supplemental oxygen
    • COPD exacerbation with hypercapnia but no acidosis: NIV not suggested (ERS/ATS 2017, conditional)
  • Effect in COPD: Success rate 80-85% in RCTs; reduces intubation and mortality (GOLD 2026). There is no lower pH limit below which a trial of NIV is inappropriate, but failure is more likely as pH falls: monitor closely with rapid access to intubation (ERS/ATS 2017)
  • Mechanism: IPAP (inspiratory pressure) augments tidal volume; EPAP (expiratory pressure) prevents alveolar collapse
  • Settings (Practical): Start IPAP 10-12 cm H2O and EPAP 4-5 cm H2O; raise IPAP to improve tidal volume and lower PaCO2. HAPPEN trial (JAMA 2024; 300 patients, China; stopped early): in patients still hypercapnic after 6 hours of low-intensity NIV, titrating IPAP to tidal volume 10-15 mL/kg predicted body weight (vs 6-10) lowered the proportion meeting intubation criteria (4.8% vs 13.7%) but not actual intubation (3.4% vs 3.9%); abdominal distension was more common (37.4% vs 25.5%)
  • High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC): Suggested as an alternative to NIV only with mild acidemia (e.g., pH >7.25) when monitoring and prompt escalation to NIV are available (ATS 2026, conditional, low certainty). About one-third of patients started on HFNC needed escalation to NIV. May be less effective when hypercapnia is not rapidly reversible (OHS, neuromuscular disease). Flows of 30-40 L/min have been suggested, with limited data (ATS 2026)
  • CPAP: No recommendation for or against in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure; trials are old and heterogeneous, and CPAP is rarely used for COPD exacerbation (ATS 2026)
  • Contraindications to NIV (Practical):
    • Inability to protect airway (coma, copious secretions, persistent vomiting)
    • Hemodynamic instability (shock)
    • Facial trauma, burns (mask cannot seal)
    • Recent upper airway or upper GI surgery (relative)
    • Unable to cooperate or tolerate the mask
  • NIV Failure: Patients who will respond usually improve in pH or respiratory rate within the first 1-4 hours (ERS/ATS 2017). If pH or PaCO2 worsens, mental status declines, or there is no improvement: intubate without delay. Morbidity, length of stay, and mortality are higher when invasive ventilation follows failed NIV (GOLD 2026)
  • Stopping NIV: Once the patient tolerates at least 4 hours of unassisted breathing, NIV can be stopped without a weaning period (GOLD 2026)

Invasive Mechanical Ventilation (Intubation):

  • Indications (GOLD 2026):
    • Failure of an NIV trial, or unable to tolerate HFNC and/or NIV
    • Persistent life-threatening hypoxemia despite HFNC or NIV
    • Respiratory or cardiac arrest
    • Diminished consciousness, or agitation not controlled by sedation
    • Massive aspiration or persistent vomiting; persistent inability to clear secretions
    • Severe hemodynamic instability without response to fluids and vasoactive drugs; severe ventricular or supraventricular arrhythmias
  • Goals of Care: In very severe COPD, the decision depends on the likely reversibility of the trigger, the patient's wishes, and ICU availability; an advance directive helps (GOLD 2026)
  • Ventilator Settings for Hypercapnic Failure (Practical):
    • Mode: Assist-control (volume or pressure)
    • Tidal Volume: 6-8 mL/kg predicted body weight
    • Obstructive disease (COPD, asthma): Lower respiratory rate and shorter inspiratory time to lengthen expiration; measure auto-PEEP and plateau pressure; hypotension after intubation may be from hyperinflation
    • FiO2: Start 100%, then wean to SpO2 88-92% in patients at risk of hypercapnia
    • PEEP: 5-8 cm H2O; in obstruction, set with reference to measured auto-PEEP
    • Goal: pH >7.30, NOT a normal PaCO2; aim for the patient's baseline PaCO2 in chronic retainers
  • Avoid Rapid CO2 Correction in Chronic Hypercapnia (Practical):
    • Chronic CO2 retainers have a compensatory high HCO3
    • Rapid PaCO2 drop leaves a post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis (seizures, arrhythmias)
    • Lower PaCO2 gradually toward baseline over 24-48 hours, aiming for pH 7.30-7.35 initially

Etiology-Specific Treatment:

  • COPD Exacerbation (GOLD 2026; see card 6):
    • Bronchodilators: Short-acting beta-agonist with or without a short-acting anticholinergic (albuterol with or without ipratropium). Nebulizer: one dose every hour for 2-3 doses, then every 2-4 hours by response; avoid high SABA doses; air-driven nebulizers
    • Corticosteroids: Prednisone 40 mg (or equivalent) daily for 5 days. Oral is as effective as IV; use IV only if unable to take oral, at an equivalent dose (Practical: methylprednisolone 32 mg = prednisone 40 mg)
    • Antibiotics: Give if on NIV or invasive ventilation, if sputum purulence is increased plus more dyspnea, fever, or more sputum volume, or if a prior exacerbation had a positive sputum culture. Choose by local resistance: amoxicillin-clavulanate, a macrolide, a tetracycline, or in selected patients a quinolone; 5-7 days. Culture sputum or airway samples if ventilated (Pseudomonas, resistant organisms)
    • NIV: First-line for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (see above)
    • Thromboprophylaxis: Hospitalized COPD patients are at increased risk of DVT and PE; give prophylaxis
  • Opioid/Sedative Overdose (FDA labels):
    • Naloxone, opioid overdose: 0.4-2 mg IV; repeat every 2-3 minutes if needed. If no response after 10 mg, question the diagnosis
    • Naloxone, postoperative or other prescribed-opioid depression: 0.1-0.2 mg IV every 2-3 minutes to adequate ventilation. Abrupt reversal can cause withdrawal, hypertension, ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, pulmonary edema, and cardiac arrest
    • Recurrence: Some opioids outlast naloxone; keep monitoring and repeat doses (often at 1-2 hour intervals) or start an infusion
    • Flumazenil: Not routine. Boxed warning for seizures (long-term benzodiazepine use, cyclic antidepressant overdose); do not use when seizures are likely. Not established as a treatment for benzodiazepine-induced hypoventilation. If used for overdose: 0.2 mg IV over 30 seconds, then 0.3 mg, then 0.5 mg every minute to a cumulative 3 mg
    • Support ventilation (NIV or intubation) until the drug wears off
  • Neuromuscular Weakness:
    • GBS: IVIG or plasmapheresis, supportive ventilation
    • Myasthenia gravis: Pyridostigmine, IVIG, plasmapheresis, avoid triggering drugs (aminoglycosides, beta-blockers)
    • Track vital capacity and NIF serially; low threshold for intubation with bulbar weakness, poor cough, or rapid decline; NIV only in selected patients without bulbar dysfunction (Practical; see cards 52 and 53)
  • Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS):
    • Acute: NIV for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (ATS 2026); HFNC may be less effective when hypercapnia is not rapidly reversible
    • Discharge: Suspected OHS with respiratory failure: start NIV before discharge and continue until outpatient sleep study and PAP titration, ideally within 3 months (ATS 2019, conditional)
    • Stable OHS: PAP during sleep; CPAP first-line if severe OSA (AHI >30 events/hour) (ATS 2019, conditional)
    • Weight loss: Sustained loss of 25-30% of body weight is most likely needed to resolve hypoventilation; consider bariatric surgery evaluation (ATS 2019)
    • Diuretics if concurrent right heart failure (cor pulmonale) (Practical)

Adjunctive Therapies:

  • Bronchodilators: If airway obstruction present (albuterol, ipratropium)
  • Diuretics: If volume overload contributing (pulmonary edema, cor pulmonale)
  • Treat Infection: Antibiotics for pneumonia, bronchitis
  • Avoid Respiratory Depressants: Minimize opioids, benzodiazepines, sedatives
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • CO2 Narcosis = CNS Depression from Hypercapnia: Obtundation, stupor, or coma from severe hypercapnia (Practical). Treat with ventilatory support, NOT just oxygen.
  • Don't Over-Oxygenate Patients at Risk of Hypercapnia: Excess oxygen raises PaCO2 mainly through worse V/Q matching and the Haldane effect; loss of hypoxic drive plays a smaller part. Target SpO2 88-92% (BTS 2017, non-US) with controlled delivery, and use air-driven nebulizers in COPD (GOLD 2026).
  • NIV Reduces Intubation and Mortality: Versus standard oxygen in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure: mortality RR 0.47, intubation RR 0.43 (ATS 2026, strong recommendation). Start when pH is 7.35 or lower with PaCO2 45 mmHg or higher (GOLD 2026); do not wait until the patient is moribund.
  • Normalize pH, NOT PaCO2: In chronic CO2 retainers, aim for the patient's baseline PaCO2, not 40 mmHg. Kidneys have compensated with high HCO3, so rapid correction leaves a metabolic alkalosis (Practical).
  • A-a Gradient Differentiates Cause: Normal A-a gradient (<15 mmHg) suggests pure hypoventilation (CNS depression, neuromuscular weakness, obesity). Elevated A-a gradient suggests V/Q mismatch (COPD, pneumonia, PE). Use alveolar gas equation: A-a gradient = PAO2 - PaO2, where PAO2 = FiO2×(760-47) - PaCO2/0.8.
  • Opioids Are a Common Iatrogenic Cause in Hospitalized Patients: Especially in older adults, renal failure (reduced clearance), and OSA. Use the lowest effective dose and non-opioid alternatives; reverse with small naloxone doses (0.1-0.2 mg IV) to avoid abrupt withdrawal (naloxone label).
  • Intubation Doesn't Cure Hypercapnia, It Buys Time: Mechanical ventilation supports the patient while the cause is treated. In irreversible disease (end-stage COPD, ALS), discuss goals of care before intubation; the decision depends on reversibility of the trigger and the patient's wishes (GOLD 2026).
  • Permissive Hypercapnia Is Acceptable If pH Adequate: In severe ARDS or COPD, allowing PaCO2 to rise (50-60 mmHg) to avoid barotrauma (high tidal volumes, plateau pressures) is acceptable as long as pH >7.25-7.30. Kidneys will compensate over 3-5 days.
  • Acute vs Chronic Compensation Takes 3-5 Days: In acute hypercapnia, HCO3 rises ~1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑ PaCO2 (immediate buffering). In chronic hypercapnia, kidneys retain HCO3 → HCO3 rises ~3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑ PaCO2 (takes 3-5 days). Use this to estimate acuity.
  • Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS): BMI >30 kg/m2, sleep-disordered breathing, and awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg at sea level) after other causes are excluded (ATS 2019). About 90% have OSA; unlike OSA alone, OHS has hypercapnia while awake. Admitted with respiratory failure and suspected OHS: discharge on NIV pending a sleep study (ATS 2019).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe respiratory acidosis (pH <7.30) with altered mental status
  • Need for NIV (ICU or intermediate care unit with rapid access to intubation; ATS 2026) or invasive mechanical ventilation
  • Rapidly worsening hypercapnia despite treatment
  • CO2 narcosis (obtundation, coma from severe hypercapnia)
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Respiratory arrest or peri-arrest
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • PaCO2 improved or back to baseline (if chronic CO2 retainer)
  • pH normalized (>7.35) or back to compensated baseline
  • Respiratory rate <24/min, no accessory muscle use
  • SpO2 >88-90% on room air or baseline oxygen requirement
  • Underlying cause treated (COPD exacerbation resolved, infection treated, etc.)
  • Able to ambulate and perform ADLs without significant dyspnea
  • Stable off acute NIV (Practical; no validated duration)
  • Close pulmonology follow-up arranged (within 1-2 weeks; Practical)
  • If COPD: On appropriate home oxygen, inhalers optimized, smoking cessation counseling. Long-term home NIV: do not start during the admission; reassess 2-4 weeks after resolution (ATS 2020, conditional)
  • If suspected OHS: Discharge on NIV until outpatient sleep study and PAP titration, ideally within 3 months (ATS 2019, conditional)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Albuterol, 💊 Ipratropium, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Naloxone, 💊 Flumazenil
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated PaCO2, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Low Bicarbonate

51. TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC ATTACK (TIA)

Stroke Warning • ABCD² Score • Urgent Workup
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Transient episode of neurologic dysfunction from focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia WITHOUT acute infarction. Symptoms resolve within 24hr (most <1hr)

Classic Symptoms (sudden onset, focal):

  • Motor: Unilateral weakness (face, arm, leg). Arm drift, facial droop
  • Sensory: Unilateral numbness, paresthesias
  • Speech: Aphasia (expressive or receptive), dysarthria (slurred speech)
  • Visual: Monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax - retinal TIA), hemianopia, diplopia
  • Ataxia: Unsteady gait, incoordination (posterior circulation)
  • Vertigo: With other posterior circulation symptoms (NOT isolated vertigo)

TIA Mimics (NOT TIA): Seizure with Todd's paralysis, migraine with aura, hypoglycemia, syncope, peripheral vertigo alone, isolated sensory symptoms without other deficits

High-Risk Features:

  • Multiple TIAs in short period (crescendo TIAs)
  • Symptoms >1 hour
  • Carotid stenosis >50%
  • AF or cardioembolic source
  • ABCD² score ≥4
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Urgent Imaging (within 24hr, ideally emergently):

  • Brain MRI with DWI: GOLD STANDARD. Detects acute infarction in 30-50% of "TIAs". DWI-positive = stroke, not TIA
  • CT head (if MRI unavailable): Rule out hemorrhage, large stroke. Less sensitive for acute ischemia
  • CTA or MRA head/neck: Assess for large vessel stenosis/occlusion (carotid, vertebral, intracranial). Identify surgical candidates

Vascular Studies:

  • Carotid Doppler ultrasound: Screen for carotid stenosis. If >50% stenosis, confirm with CTA/MRA
  • Consider CTA chest: If concern for aortic arch atheroma

Cardiac Workup:

  • ECG: Assess for AF (most important modifiable risk factor for cardioembolic stroke)
  • Telemetry: 24hr minimum. Consider prolonged monitoring (30-day event monitor) if no AF found and high suspicion
  • Transthoracic echo (TTE): Assess for cardioembolic source (LV thrombus, valvular disease, reduced EF)
  • TEE: If high suspicion for cardioembolic source and TTE negative. Better visualization of LA appendage (thrombus), PFO, aortic arch atheroma

Labs: CBC, BMP, lipid panel, HbA1c, PT/PTT (if anticoagulation planned), ESR (if vasculitis concern), hypercoagulable workup (if age <50, unprovoked, recurrent)

ABCD² Score (Stroke Risk Stratification):

  • Age ≥60: 1 point
  • BP ≥140/90: 1 point
  • Clinical features: Unilateral weakness (2 points), Speech impairment without weakness (1 point)
  • Duration: ≥60min (2 points), 10-59min (1 point)
  • Diabetes: 1 point
  • Score 0-3: Low risk (1% 2-day stroke risk). Outpatient workup possible if reliable
  • Score 4-5: Moderate risk (4% 2-day stroke risk). Admit for expedited workup
  • Score 6-7: High risk (8% 2-day stroke risk). Admit for urgent workup
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management (Goal: Prevent stroke within 48-90 days):

  • Aspirin: 325mg loading dose immediately (if not already on antiplatelet). Reduces early stroke risk by 80%
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): Aspirin 81mg + clopidogrel 75mg daily × 21 days, then aspirin alone. Reduces stroke risk by 32% compared to aspirin alone (POINT/CHANCE trials). Start within 24hr of symptom onset
  • BP management: Goal <140/90 long-term. Avoid aggressive lowering in acute phase unless hypertensive emergency
  • Statin: High-intensity (atorvastatin 40-80mg or rosuvastatin 20-40mg). Start immediately regardless of LDL. Reduces recurrent stroke

Etiology-Specific Treatment:

  • Atrial fibrillation: Anticoagulation (DOAC preferred: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran). Start within 4-14 days depending on stroke risk. CHA₂DS₂-VASc score guides decision
  • Carotid stenosis 70-99% (symptomatic): Urgent CEA (carotid endarterectomy) within 2 weeks. NNT=6 to prevent stroke. Consider CAS (carotid artery stenting) if high surgical risk
  • Carotid stenosis 50-69%: CEA beneficial (NNT=15). Consider if good surgical candidate
  • Carotid stenosis <50%: Medical management. No benefit from CEA
  • Intracranial stenosis: Aggressive medical management (dual antiplatelet × 90 days, statin, BP control). Stenting NOT superior to medical therapy
  • Cardioembolic (not AF): Antiplatelet vs anticoagulation depending on source. TEE to identify source
  • Cryptogenic (no identified cause): Aspirin. Consider extended cardiac monitoring for paroxysmal AF. PFO closure if large PFO + no other cause (controversial, age <60)

Risk Factor Modification (CRITICAL):

  • BP control: Goal <130/80 (ACC/AHA) or <140/90 (ESH/ESC). ACE-I or ARB preferred
  • Diabetes control: HbA1c <7%
  • Lipids: LDL <70mg/dL (consider <55 if very high risk)
  • Smoking cessation: Doubles stroke risk. Counsel + pharmacotherapy (varenicline, bupropion, NRT)
  • Exercise: 30min moderate activity 5× week
  • Diet: Mediterranean diet, low sodium
  • Weight loss: If overweight/obese

Admission vs Outpatient:

  • Admit: ABCD² ≥4, crescendo TIAs, within 48hr of symptom onset, unreliable for follow-up, unable to complete workup as outpatient
  • Outpatient: ABCD² <3, reliable patient, can complete MRI/vascular imaging/echo within 48hr, no high-risk features
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • TIA = stroke until proven otherwise: 30-50% of "TIAs" have infarction on DWI-MRI. If DWI-positive, it's a stroke, not TIA. Treat aggressively either way
  • Highest stroke risk is within 48hr: 5-10% have stroke within 90 days, half of those within 48hr. TIA is an EMERGENCY. Expedited workup prevents stroke
  • Dual antiplatelet (ASA + clopidogrel) for 21 days: POINT and CHANCE trials showed 32% relative risk reduction. Start within 24hr. Then continue aspirin alone
  • Amaurosis fugax = retinal TIA: Transient monocular blindness ("curtain coming down"). Ipsilateral carotid stenosis or emboli. Same stroke risk as hemispheric TIA
  • NOT all transient neuro symptoms are TIA: Isolated vertigo, isolated diplopia, isolated sensory symptoms = low likelihood. Need focal symptoms (motor/speech/visual field loss)
  • Carotid stenosis timing matters: Symptomatic stenosis 70-99% needs CEA within 2 weeks. Benefit diminishes after that. Asymptomatic stenosis has different indications
  • Extended cardiac monitoring increases AF detection: 30-day monitors detect AF in 10-20% of cryptogenic TIA/stroke. Consider if no cause found
⚠️ ESCALATE/ADMIT IF:
  • ABCD² score ≥4 (moderate-high risk)
  • Crescendo TIAs (multiple in short period)
  • Symptoms occurred within 48hr
  • Carotid stenosis >50% (needs urgent evaluation for CEA)
  • Atrial fibrillation (needs anticoagulation)
  • Unable to complete urgent outpatient workup
  • Unreliable for follow-up
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Imaging complete (MRI/CTA or CT/carotid Doppler)
  • Cardiac evaluation done (ECG, telemetry ≥24hr, echo)
  • Started on appropriate therapy (antiplatelet or anticoagulation + statin)
  • If carotid stenosis >50%: Vascular surgery consult, CEA scheduled
  • Risk factors addressed (BP, lipids, diabetes)
  • Neurology follow-up arranged (within 1-2 weeks)
  • Patient educated on stroke warning signs
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Stroke (5-10% within 90 days, highest risk first 48hr), recurrent TIA (15-20% have another TIA), progression to stroke during evaluation

Procedural: CEA complications (stroke 2-3%, MI, cranial nerve injury, bleeding), CAS complications (stroke, dissection, access site complications)

Chronic: Recurrent stroke/TIA (if risk factors not controlled), bleeding on antiplatelets/anticoagulation, cognitive decline (vascular dementia), disability from eventual stroke if not treated aggressively

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Clopidogrel, 💊 Atorvastatin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperglycemia, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated LDL, 🔬 Elevated D-dimer, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR
↑ Back to Table of Contents

52. GUILLAIN-BARRÉ SYNDROME (GBS)

Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy • Ascending Paralysis • IVIG/Plasmapheresis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad: (1) Progressive symmetric weakness, (2) Areflexia/hyporeflexia, (3) Symptoms progress over days-weeks (peak at 2-4 weeks)

Typical Presentation: Ascending symmetric weakness starting in legs → arms → bulbar → respiratory muscles. Paresthesias in hands/feet (glove-stocking distribution). Preceding illness 1-3 weeks prior (URI, GI infection)

Motor Findings:

  • Weakness: Symmetric, ascending (legs before arms typically). Proximal and distal affected
  • Areflexia: Absent or markedly diminished deep tendon reflexes (hallmark finding)
  • Bulbar involvement: Facial weakness (bilateral), dysphagia, dysarthria (30-50%)
  • Respiratory failure: 20-30% require mechanical ventilation. Progressive weakness of diaphragm/intercostals

Sensory Findings: Paresthesias, numbness (glove-stocking). Pain (back, radicular) in 50%. Sensory exam often normal despite symptoms

Autonomic Dysfunction (60%): Tachycardia, bradycardia, arrhythmias, labile BP (hyper/hypotension), ileus, urinary retention, SIADH

Variants:

  • AIDP (Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy): Most common in US/Europe (90%). Classic ascending paralysis
  • AMAN/AMSAN (Axonal variants): More common in Asia. Axonal damage. Worse prognosis
  • Miller Fisher syndrome: Triad of ataxia, areflexia, ophthalmoplegia. Anti-GQ1b antibodies (90%)
  • Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant: Starts with bulbar/arm weakness

Triggers (preceding infection in 60-70%):

  • Campylobacter jejuni (30%): Most common. Diarrheal illness 1-3 weeks prior
  • Upper respiratory infections: CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma
  • Other: Zika virus, COVID-19, vaccines (rare, <1 per million), surgery, trauma
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis (primarily): Brighton Criteria or Asbury & Cornblath Criteria. Diagnosis based on clinical features + CSF + EMG

Lumbar Puncture (CSF Analysis):

  • Albuminocytologic dissociation (CLASSIC): Elevated protein (>45mg/dL) with normal or mildly elevated WBC (<10 cells/µL)
  • Timing: Protein elevation may not appear until week 2. If early and normal, repeat LP in 1 week if high suspicion
  • WBC >50: Consider alternative diagnosis (infection, malignancy, sarcoid)

Electrodiagnostic Studies (EMG/NCS):

  • Findings: Prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities, conduction block, prolonged/absent F-waves (demyelination)
  • Timing: Abnormalities may not appear until 2 weeks. Early studies may be normal
  • Axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN): Low-amplitude CMAPs with normal velocities

Bedside Respiratory Assessment (CRITICAL):

  • Vital capacity (VC): Measure q4-6hr if progressive. VC <20mL/kg or rapidly declining = high risk for intubation
  • Negative inspiratory force (NIF): <-30cmH₂O = respiratory muscle weakness
  • Single-breath count: Unable to count to 20 in one breath = severe weakness
  • 20/30/40 rule: VC <20mL/kg, NIF >-30cmH₂O, MIP <40cmH₂O = likely need intubation

Labs: CBC, CMP, LFTs (baseline before IVIG), ABG (if respiratory concern), serology for infections (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma), anti-ganglioside antibodies (anti-GM1, anti-GQ1b - supportive but not required)

MRI spine: Consider to rule out mimics (cord compression, transverse myelitis). May show nerve root enhancement in GBS

Mimics to Rule Out: Spinal cord compression, transverse myelitis, myasthenia gravis, botulism, tick paralysis, acute intermittent porphyria, critical illness polyneuropathy, vasculitis, HIV, Lyme, West Nile virus

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immunotherapy (Equally Effective - choose one):

  • IVIG (Intravenous Immunoglobulin): 0.4g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2g/kg). First-line in most centers. Easier to administer than plasmapheresis
  • Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange): 5 exchanges over 7-14 days (200-250mL/kg total). Equally effective as IVIG. Use if IVIG contraindicated (IgA deficiency) or failed
  • NO benefit to combination: IVIG + plasmapheresis NOT better than either alone
  • Timing: Start within 2 weeks of symptom onset for maximum benefit. Still beneficial up to 4 weeks
  • Steroids NOT beneficial: Corticosteroids do not work in GBS. Do NOT use

Respiratory Management (CRITICAL):

  • Monitor closely: Vital capacity, NIF q4-6hr if progressive weakness
  • Indications for intubation: VC <15-20mL/kg, rapidly declining VC, NIF >-30cmH₂O, hypoxia, hypercapnia, inability to clear secretions, bulbar weakness with aspiration
  • Intubation considerations: Avoid succinylcholine (hyperkalemia risk in denervation). Use non-depolarizing paralytics
  • Ventilation strategy: Lung-protective ventilation. Avoid over-sedation (need to assess neuro status)
  • Tracheostomy: Consider if anticipated ventilation >2 weeks (many GBS patients)

Autonomic Management:

  • Cardiac monitoring: Telemetry for all patients. Risk of arrhythmias (brady, tachy, heart block)
  • BP lability: Avoid aggressive treatment of transient hyper/hypotension. Short-acting agents if needed. Fluid boluses for hypotension
  • Avoid: β-blockers (can worsen bradycardia), aggressive BP lowering (can precipitate hypotension)

Supportive Care:

  • DVT prophylaxis: SCDs + heparin/LMWH (high risk due to immobility)
  • GI: Proton pump inhibitor (stress ulcer prophylaxis), bowel regimen (ileus common)
  • Bladder: Foley catheter if urinary retention
  • Pain management: Gabapentin, pregabalin for neuropathic pain. Opioids if needed
  • Physical therapy: Early mobilization when stable. Prevent contractures
  • Nutrition: Consider NG/NJ tube if dysphagia. Assess swallow before PO
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Areflexia is the key finding: Absent reflexes + ascending weakness = GBS until proven otherwise. DTRs are lost early and universally
  • Respiratory failure is the biggest risk: 20-30% need intubation. Monitor VC closely. Don't wait for hypoxia/hypercapnia (late findings). Intubate early if declining
  • CSF protein may be normal early: Classic albuminocytologic dissociation may not appear until week 2. Repeat LP if high suspicion and initially normal
  • IVIG = Plasmapheresis in efficacy: Both equally effective. IVIG easier to give. Combination NOT better. Start within 2 weeks of symptom onset
  • Steroids don't work in GBS: Unlike most autoimmune conditions, corticosteroids are NOT beneficial and should NOT be used
  • Prognosis overall good but slow: 80-85% recover fully, but takes months-year. 5-10% permanent disability. 3-5% mortality (respiratory failure, autonomic dysfunction)
  • Campylobacter-associated GBS has worse prognosis: More likely to be axonal variant (AMAN). Slower recovery, more residual deficits
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL GBS patients need ICU or stepdown with close monitoring
  • VC <20mL/kg or rapidly declining
  • NIF >-30cmH₂O
  • Bulbar weakness (dysphagia, dysarthria)
  • Autonomic instability (arrhythmias, labile BP)
  • Rapid progression (can't walk → respiratory failure in days)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Respiratory status stable (if intubated, successfully extubated)
  • No autonomic instability × 72hr
  • Weakness plateaued or improving
  • Completed course of IVIG or plasmapheresis
  • Able to swallow safely (speech/swallow eval)
  • DVT prophylaxis in place
  • Inpatient rehab arranged (most need extensive PT/OT)
  • Neurology follow-up arranged
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute: Respiratory failure (20-30%, #1 cause of death), autonomic dysfunction (arrhythmias, labile BP, sudden death), aspiration pneumonia, DVT/PE (immobility), ileus, urinary retention, pressure ulcers

Treatment-related: IVIG (aseptic meningitis, hemolysis, thrombosis, renal failure), Plasmapheresis (hypotension, line infection, citrate toxicity, bleeding)

Chronic: Residual weakness (10-15% permanent disability), chronic neuropathic pain (30%), fatigue (persistent in 50%), relapse (3-5%, usually within 2 months - consider CIDP if relapses), CIDP (chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy - GBS-like but chronic/relapsing)

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IVIG, 💊 Albumin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 CSF Analysis, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP
