59. TUBERCULOSIS (ACTIVE DISEASE)

Mycobacterium tuberculosis • Pulmonary + Extrapulmonary • Multi-Drug Regimen • Airborne Isolation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Tuberculosis (TB) Overview: Infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Transmitted via airborne droplets. Can affect lungs (pulmonary TB, 80-85%) or other organs (extrapulmonary TB, 15-20%). Highly contagious. Public health emergency requiring isolation and reporting

Latent TB vs Active TB:

  • Latent TB Infection (LTBI): Infected with M. tuberculosis but no symptoms, not contagious. Positive TST/IGRA, normal CXR. 5-10% lifetime risk of reactivation (higher if immunocompromised)
  • Active TB Disease: Symptomatic, contagious (if pulmonary/laryngeal), abnormal CXR, positive AFB smear/culture. Requires multi-drug treatment

PULMONARY TB (Most Common, 80-85%):

Classic Presentation (Subacute/Chronic):

  • Chronic cough: ≥3 weeks duration. Initially dry, becomes productive. Hallmark symptom
  • Hemoptysis: Blood-tinged sputum (25-50%). Can be massive in cavitary disease
  • Constitutional symptoms ("B symptoms"): Fever (low-grade, evening), night sweats (drenching, change clothes), weight loss (>10% body weight), anorexia, malaise, fatigue
  • Chest pain: Pleuritic (if pleural involvement), dull ache
  • Dyspnea: If extensive disease, pleural effusion, or miliary TB

Physical Exam (Often Unremarkable): May have rales/crackles over involved lung fields, dullness to percussion (consolidation, effusion), amphoric breath sounds (cavity), cachexia (advanced disease). Exam may be entirely normal despite extensive radiographic disease

EXTRAPULMONARY TB (15-20%, Higher in HIV/Immunocompromised):

  • Tuberculous Lymphadenitis (Most Common EPTB): Painless, firm, matted cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes. May suppurate (cold abscess). Slow progression over weeks-months
  • Pleural TB: Exudative pleural effusion. Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea. Effusion often lymphocyte-predominant. Pleural fluid ADA (adenosine deaminase) >40 U/L highly suggestive
  • Tuberculous Meningitis (TB Meningitis): Subacute headache, fever, altered mental status, cranial nerve palsies (especially CN VI), seizures. CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein. HIGH MORTALITY (20-50%) even with treatment
  • Miliary TB (Disseminated): Hematogenous spread to multiple organs. High fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly. CXR: bilateral diffuse miliary (millet seed) nodules (1-3mm). Often in HIV, elderly, immunocompromised
  • Skeletal TB (Pott's Disease): Vertebral osteomyelitis (thoracic/lumbar spine most common). Back pain, paravertebral abscess, cord compression, gibbus deformity. MRI shows vertebral destruction, abscess
  • Genitourinary TB: Dysuria, hematuria, flank pain, sterile pyuria. Can cause ureteral strictures, hydronephrosis, chronic kidney disease
  • Pericardial TB: Pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis (chronic). High mortality
  • Abdominal TB: Peritonitis (ascites, abdominal pain), intestinal involvement (chronic diarrhea, obstruction, perforation). Ascites: high protein, lymphocyte-predominant, ADA >39 U/L

High-Risk Populations:

  • HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200): 10-20x increased risk. More likely disseminated/extrapulmonary TB. TB accelerates HIV progression
  • Immunosuppression: TNF-α inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab - screen before starting), transplant recipients, chronic steroids (≥15mg prednisone daily), chemotherapy
  • Close contact: Household contact with active TB case (20-30% infection rate)
  • Endemic areas: India, China, Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, Eastern Europe
  • Congregate settings: Homeless shelters, prisons, nursing homes
  • Healthcare workers: Exposure to undiagnosed TB patients
  • Other: Diabetes, chronic kidney disease, silicosis, malignancy, malnutrition, alcoholism, IV drug use

Drug-Resistant TB:

  • Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB): Resistant to isoniazid (INH) + rifampin (RIF). 5% of new cases globally. Higher in HIV, prior TB treatment. WHO 2022: preferred regimen is BPaLM (6 months) — see treatment section. Legacy regimens required 18-24 months.
  • Extensively Drug-Resistant TB (XDR-TB): MDR-TB + resistance to fluoroquinolones. Very poor prognosis. BPaLM also applicable (same 6-month regimen). Mortality historically 30-50% with older regimens
  • Risk factors for resistance: Prior TB treatment, non-adherence, endemic areas (Russia, South Africa, India), HIV co-infection, close contact with known drug-resistant case
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) & Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA):

  • Use: Screen for LATENT TB infection. NOT for diagnosis of active TB disease
  • TST (Mantoux test): Intradermal injection. Read at 48-72hr. Induration ≥5mm (HIV, immunocompromised, close contact), ≥10mm (immigrants, healthcare workers, high-risk), ≥15mm (low-risk) considered positive
  • IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold, T-SPOT): Blood test. Measures T-cell response to TB antigens. Not affected by BCG vaccination (unlike TST). Preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals
  • Both can be negative in active TB: Anergy from severe illness, immunosuppression. Don't rule out active TB based on negative TST/IGRA alone

Chest X-Ray (CXR) - Essential:

  • Primary TB (children, recent infection): Hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, middle/lower lobe infiltrates, Ghon complex (calcified granuloma + lymph node)
  • Reactivation TB (adults): Upper lobe infiltrates (apical/posterior segments), cavitary lesions (thin-walled cavities with air-fluid levels), fibronodular opacities, volume loss. Right upper lobe most common
  • Miliary TB: Bilateral diffuse miliary (millet seed) nodules, 1-3mm
  • Pleural effusion: Unilateral, moderate-large. May be only finding
  • Advanced disease: Fibrosis, traction bronchiectasis, destroyed lung

Note: CXR can be normal in early disease or extrapulmonary TB. HIV patients may have atypical or normal CXR despite active pulmonary TB

Sputum Testing (GOLD STANDARD for Pulmonary TB):

  • Collection: 3 separate sputum samples on 3 different days (ideally early morning, deep cough). If unable to produce sputum: induced sputum (nebulized hypertonic saline), bronchoscopy with BAL, gastric aspirate (children)
  • AFB Smear (Acid-Fast Bacilli): Ziehl-Neelsen or Auramine-rhodamine stain. Results in 24hr. Positive = patient is infectious. Sensitivity 50-60% (needs 5,000-10,000 organisms/mL). Negative smear does NOT rule out TB. Semi-quantitative: 1+ to 4+ (higher = more infectious)
  • Mycobacterial Culture (GOLD STANDARD): Solid media (Lowenstein-Jensen) takes 3-8 weeks. Liquid media (MGIT) faster (1-3 weeks). Definitive diagnosis. Allows drug susceptibility testing (DST). ESSENTIAL
  • Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT):
    • Xpert MTB/RIF (GeneXpert): Rapid PCR test (results in 2 hours). Detects M. tuberculosis + rifampin resistance. Sensitivity 80-90% (higher if smear-positive). WHO-recommended. Use on first sputum sample
    • Cepheid Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra: Improved sensitivity (90-95%). Detects lower bacterial loads
  • Histopathology (if tissue available): Caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells. Supportive but not specific (fungi, sarcoid can mimic)

Extrapulmonary TB Diagnosis:

  • Pleural fluid: Lymphocyte-predominant exudate, ADA >40 U/L (90% sensitivity), low glucose, high protein. Pleural biopsy (caseating granulomas, culture) more sensitive than pleural fluid culture
  • CSF (TB meningitis): Lymphocytic pleocytosis (50-500 cells/µL), low glucose (<45mg/dL or <50% serum), high protein (>100mg/dL). AFB smear low sensitivity (10-20%). Culture takes weeks. Large volume (6-10mL) increases yield. Xpert MTB/RIF on CSF (sensitivity 50-60%)
  • Lymph node: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) for AFB smear/culture, or excisional biopsy (caseating granulomas, culture)
  • Urine: 3 early morning urine samples for AFB culture. Xpert MTB/RIF on urine (moderate sensitivity)
  • Biopsy: Any suspected site (bone, peritoneum, pericardium) - send for AFB smear, culture, histopathology

Labs:

  • CBC: Anemia of chronic disease, lymphopenia (miliary TB), monocytosis
  • CMP: Hyponatremia (SIADH in TB meningitis, miliary TB), elevated alkaline phosphatase (hepatic TB, drug toxicity)
  • ESR/CRP: Elevated (nonspecific inflammatory markers)
  • HIV test: Obtain in ALL TB patients. HIV/TB co-infection common
  • Baseline LFTs: Before starting treatment (INH, RIF, PZA are hepatotoxic)

Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST): CRITICAL. Perform on all initial isolates. Guides therapy. Tests susceptibility to INH, RIF, PZA, ethambutol, fluoroquinolones, second-line drugs. Takes 2-4 weeks. Don't wait for results to start treatment. Adjust regimen when results available

Additional Testing:

  • CT chest: If CXR abnormal or high suspicion with normal CXR. Better delineates cavities, lymphadenopathy, complications
  • Bronchoscopy with BAL: If unable to produce sputum, high suspicion with negative sputum, suspected endobronchial TB
  • MRI spine: If Pott's disease suspected (back pain, neurologic deficits)
  • Ophthalmology exam: Check for choroidal tubercles (miliary TB), before starting ethambutol (monitor for optic neuritis)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

ISOLATION (CRITICAL - Airborne Precautions):

  • Airborne isolation room: Negative pressure, ≥6 air changes/hour, HEPA filtration. Private room. Door closed
  • N95 respirators: For all healthcare workers entering room. Fit-tested. Surgical mask for patient when leaving room
  • Duration: Until 3 consecutive negative AFB smears (usually 2-4 weeks of treatment) OR clinically improving + receiving appropriate therapy × 2 weeks. TB meningitis/extrapulmonary TB (non-pulmonary) generally NOT infectious - standard precautions
  • Reporting: TB is REPORTABLE to public health department. Contact investigation for close contacts

STANDARD TREATMENT REGIMEN (Drug-Susceptible TB):

Intensive Phase (First 2 Months) - RIPE:

  • Rifampin (R): 600mg PO daily (or 10mg/kg/day, max 600mg)
  • Isoniazid (I/INH): 300mg PO daily (or 5mg/kg/day, max 300mg) + Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) 25-50mg daily (prevent peripheral neuropathy)
  • Pyrazinamide (P/PZA): 1000-2000mg PO daily (weight-based: 40-55kg = 1000mg, 56-75kg = 1500mg, 76-90kg = 2000mg, >90kg = 2000mg)
  • Ethambutol (E): 800-1600mg PO daily (weight-based: 40-55kg = 800mg, 56-75kg = 1200mg, 76-90kg = 1600mg, >90kg = 1600mg)
  • Duration: 2 months (8 weeks) OR until AFB smear-negative and clinical improvement

Continuation Phase (Next 4-7 Months) - Rifampin + Isoniazid:

  • Rifampin 600mg PO daily + Isoniazid 300mg PO daily (+ pyridoxine 25-50mg daily)
  • Duration:
    • Uncomplicated pulmonary TB (cavitary disease, smear-negative at 2 months): 4 months continuation (total 6 months therapy)
    • Cavitary disease + positive smear at 2 months: 7 months continuation (total 9 months)
    • TB meningitis, miliary TB, bone/joint TB: 10-12 months continuation (total 12 months therapy)

Total Treatment Duration:

  • Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB: 6 months (2 months RIPE, then 4 months RI)
  • Extrapulmonary TB (lymph nodes, pleura): 6 months (same as pulmonary)
  • TB meningitis, miliary TB, bone/spine TB: 9-12 months
  • MDR/RR-TB (preferred): BPaLM 6 months (WHO 2022) — see Drug-Resistant TB section below. Legacy regimens: 18-24 months (if BPaLM unavailable or contraindicated)

Directly Observed Therapy (DOT): STRONGLY RECOMMENDED for all TB patients. Healthcare worker observes patient taking medications (3-5 times/week or daily). Ensures adherence, prevents resistance, improves cure rates. Public health department coordinates DOT

Alternative Dosing (Intermittent Therapy): 3 times weekly dosing (after initial 2 weeks daily therapy) acceptable if DOT ensured. Used in resource-limited settings. Doses higher than daily dosing (consult ID/TB expert for dosing)

Drug-Resistant TB:

  • Rifampin-Resistant (RR-TB): Detected by Xpert MTB/RIF. Treat as MDR-TB until full DST results
  • MDR/RR-TB — Preferred (WHO 2022): BPaLM × 6 months: Bedaquiline 400mg daily × 2 weeks then 200mg 3×/week + Pretomanid 200mg daily + Linezolid 600mg daily + Moxifloxacin 400mg daily. Replaces 18-24 month injectable-based regimens as first-line for most MDR/RR-TB patients with or without fluoroquinolone resistance. CONSULT ID/TB SPECIALIST — requires DST, baseline ECG (QTc monitoring for BDQ), monitoring for linezolid toxicity (peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression). BPaL (without moxifloxacin) preferred if fluoroquinolone resistance confirmed.
  • MDR-TB — Legacy Regimen (if BPaLM unavailable): 18-24 months using fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) + bedaquiline + linezolid + clofazimine + pyrazinamide ± ethambutol (individualized based on DST)
  • XDR-TB: MDR-TB + resistance to fluoroquinolones. BPaLM still applicable (uses bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid + moxifloxacin or BPaL if FQ-resistant). MUST consult TB expert.

HIV Co-Infection (TB-HIV):

  • Start TB treatment immediately: Don't delay for ART initiation
  • When to start ART:
    • CD4 <50: Start ART within 2 weeks of starting TB treatment (balance immune reconstitution vs TB treatment)
    • CD4 >50: Start ART within 8 weeks of TB treatment
    • TB meningitis: DELAY ART until 8 weeks (risk of IRIS with neurologic worsening)
  • Drug interactions: Rifampin induces CYP450 (decreases ART levels). Integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir, raltegravir) or efavirenz preferred. Avoid protease inhibitors with rifampin. Consider rifabutin (less CYP induction) instead of rifampin if needed

TB Meningitis (Special Considerations):

  • Adjunctive corticosteroids: Dexamethasone 0.3-0.4mg/kg/day IV × 4 weeks, then taper over 4 weeks. Reduces mortality and disability. START WITH FIRST DOSE OF TB DRUGS
  • Duration: 9-12 months total treatment
  • Monitor: Repeat lumbar punctures if worsening symptoms (hydrocephalus, increased ICP). Shunt if needed

Monitoring During Treatment:

  • Clinical: Weekly initially, then monthly. Assess adherence, symptoms, side effects
  • Sputum smears: Monthly until 2 consecutive negatives, then at end of treatment
  • LFTs: Baseline, then monthly (or sooner if symptoms of hepatitis). Hold drugs if ALT >3× ULN with symptoms or >5× ULN asymptomatic
  • CMP: Monitor creatinine (ethambutol cleared renally), uric acid (pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia)
  • Visual acuity & color vision: Monthly (ethambutol optic neuritis). Baseline ophthalmology exam
  • CXR: At 2 months, end of treatment, then as needed. Improvement may lag clinical improvement

Treatment Failure: Persistent positive sputum cultures after 4 months of treatment. Suggests drug resistance, non-adherence, malabsorption. Repeat DST. Consult ID/TB specialist. Do NOT add single drug to failing regimen (creates resistance)

Supportive Care:

  • Nutrition: High-calorie, high-protein diet. Many patients malnourished
  • Diabetes control: Rifampin decreases efficacy of oral hypoglycemics. May need insulin
  • Symptom management: Cough suppressants, antipyretics, analgesics PRN
  • Contact investigation: Public health screens close contacts (TST/IGRA, CXR). Treat LTBI if indicated
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • TB is "the great mimicker": Can present as pneumonia, lymphoma, cancer, chronic meningitis, osteomyelitis. High index of suspicion in endemic areas, immunocompromised, chronic symptoms
  • Don't wait for culture to treat: Cultures take weeks. Start treatment based on clinical/radiographic suspicion and positive AFB smear or Xpert. Adjust when DST results available
  • Never add a single drug to a failing regimen: Creates resistance. If treatment failing, add ≥2 new drugs and consult TB specialist
  • Rifampin turns body fluids orange: Warn patients (urine, tears, sweat). Contact lenses permanently stained. Not harmful
  • INH peripheral neuropathy is preventable: Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 25-50mg daily with INH to ALL patients. Essential in diabetics, HIV, pregnant women, alcoholics, malnourished
  • Ethambutol optic neuritis is dose-dependent: Monitor visual acuity and color vision monthly. Mostly reversible if caught early. Higher risk if renal insufficiency (dose-adjust) or >2 months use
  • TB-HIV co-infection is deadly but treatable: Start TB treatment first, then ART (within 2-8 weeks depending on CD4). Watch for IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) - paradoxical worsening when starting ART
  • TB meningitis needs steroids: Dexamethasone reduces mortality and disability. Start with first dose of TB drugs. Delay ART until 8 weeks (risk of IRIS neurologic worsening)
  • Sputum cultures must be done: Only way to confirm diagnosis and perform drug susceptibility testing. Negative smears don't rule out TB (sensitivity only 50-60%). Culture is gold standard
  • Adherence is everything: Non-adherence → treatment failure → drug resistance → MDR-TB/XDR-TB. DOT (directly observed therapy) is highly effective and recommended for ALL patients
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (extensive TB pneumonia, ARDS)
  • TB meningitis with decreased consciousness (GCS <13), increased ICP, neurologic deterioration
  • Hemodynamically unstable (septic shock rare but possible)
  • Massive hemoptysis (>200mL in 24hr)
  • Drug-induced hepatotoxicity (ALT >10× ULN, coagulopathy, encephalopathy)
  • Severe IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) in HIV patients starting ART
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Clinically stable and improving (no fever, improved symptoms)
  • Tolerating PO medications
  • 3 consecutive negative AFB smears (pulmonary TB) OR clinically improving on treatment × 2 weeks
  • Appropriate outpatient TB regimen prescribed (DOT arranged)
  • Public health notified (contact investigation underway)
  • Close follow-up arranged (ID clinic, public health DOT program)
  • Patient counseled on adherence, side effects, infectivity
  • Isolation precautions no longer needed (3 negative smears or appropriate duration on therapy)
  • Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) arranged through public health
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Acute (During Active Disease): Respiratory failure (extensive pneumonia, ARDS), massive hemoptysis (eroded pulmonary artery - requires bronchial artery embolization or surgery), pneumothorax (cavitary disease rupture), empyema (pleural space infection), pericardial tamponade (pericardial TB), spinal cord compression (Pott's disease with epidural abscess), obstructive hydrocephalus (TB meningitis - may need shunt), ARDS (miliary TB, severe pneumonia)

Treatment-Related Complications:

  • Hepatotoxicity (INH, RIF, PZA): Transaminitis (10-20%), symptomatic hepatitis (1-3%). Monitor LFTs monthly. Hold drugs if ALT >5× ULN or >3× ULN with symptoms. Rechallenge drugs sequentially when LFTs normalize. INH most hepatotoxic
  • Peripheral neuropathy (INH): Prevented by pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Higher risk in diabetes, HIV, alcohol, malnutrition
  • Optic neuritis (Ethambutol): Decreased visual acuity, red-green color blindness. Monitor monthly. Usually reversible if caught early. Dose-adjust in renal insufficiency
  • Hyperuricemia/gout (Pyrazinamide): Elevated uric acid. Treat with NSAIDs, colchicine. Allopurinol if recurrent gout (but wait until after PZA phase)
  • Thrombocytopenia (Rifampin): Immune-mediated. Stop rifampin. Can use rifabutin instead
  • Orange discoloration (Rifampin): Body fluids (urine, tears, sweat) turn orange-red. Harmless. Warn patients (contact lenses stained)
  • Drug interactions (Rifampin): CYP450 inducer. Decreases levels of: oral contraceptives (use barrier method), warfarin, anticonvulsants, antiretrovirals, immunosuppressants
  • IRIS (Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome): Paradoxical worsening when starting ART in HIV patients on TB treatment. Inflammatory reaction to dead/dying TB. Can be severe (lymph node enlargement, worsening infiltrates, fever). Manage with NSAIDs or steroids. Don't stop ART or TB drugs

Chronic (Post-Treatment): Chronic pulmonary sequelae (fibrosis, bronchiectasis, destroyed lung, aspergilloma in old cavities - hemoptysis risk), chronic pericarditis (constrictive - may need pericardiectomy), chronic meningitis sequelae (hydrocephalus, seizures, cranial nerve palsies, cognitive impairment), skeletal deformities (gibbus deformity from vertebral collapse), chronic kidney disease (GU TB), relapse (5% after adequate treatment - usually within 1 year, higher if HIV, drug-resistant TB, non-adherence)

Prevention: Treat LTBI (latent TB infection) in high-risk individuals: INH 300mg daily × 9 months OR rifampin 600mg daily × 4 months OR INH-rifapentine weekly × 3 months (3HP). BCG vaccine (limited efficacy in adults, not used in US). Infection control (airborne precautions, N95 respirators). Contact investigation and treatment of close contacts

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Isoniazid, 💊 Rifampin, 💊 Pyrazinamide, 💊 Ethambutol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 QuantiFERON/TB Gold, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Anemia

60. HIV/AIDS COMPLICATIONS

Advanced HIV Disease • CD4 <200 • Opportunistic Infections • Antiretroviral Therapy
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

HIV/AIDS Overview: Advanced HIV disease occurs when CD4 count <200 cells/μL (AIDS-defining) or presence of opportunistic infections. Patients vulnerable to infections, malignancies, and complications related to severe immunosuppression

Common AIDS-Defining Illnesses by CD4 Count:

  • CD4 <500: Herpes zoster (shingles), tuberculosis reactivation, recurrent bacterial pneumonia, oral/vaginal candidiasis
  • CD4 <200: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), candidal esophagitis, CNS toxoplasmosis, disseminated histoplasmosis/coccidioidomycosis, chronic cryptosporidiosis
  • CD4 <50: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis/colitis, Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) disseminated infection, primary CNS lymphoma, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

PNEUMOCYSTIS JIROVECII PNEUMONIA (PCP) - Most Common AIDS-Defining Illness:

  • Presentation: Subacute onset (weeks) of dyspnea, dry cough, fever. Progressive hypoxemia. Typically CD4 <200
  • Physical exam: Tachypnea, hypoxemia (O₂ sat low, often 80s-90s on room air), clear lung sounds or fine crackles. NO consolidation
  • CXR: Diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates ("ground glass"). Can be normal in 10-20%. Pneumothorax can occur
  • Diagnosis: Induced sputum (methenamine silver stain, DFA), bronchoscopy with BAL (gold standard, sensitivity >95%)
  • LDH: Markedly elevated (>500, often >1000). Nonspecific but sensitive

CANDIDAL ESOPHAGITIS:

  • Presentation: Odynophagia (painful swallowing), dysphagia, retrosternal chest pain. Usually oral thrush present (white plaques on tongue/buccal mucosa). CD4 typically <200
  • Diagnosis: Clinical (presence of oral thrush + odynophagia highly specific). Endoscopy if atypical or no response to treatment (shows white plaques in esophagus)

CNS TOXOPLASMOSIS (Toxoplasma encephalitis):

  • Presentation: Altered mental status, focal neurologic deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia, ataxia), seizures, headache, fever. CD4 typically <100
  • MRI brain: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions (80%), typically at gray-white junction, basal ganglia. Mass effect, edema
  • Toxoplasma IgG: Positive in 90% (past exposure). Negative IgG makes toxoplasmosis less likely
  • Diagnosis: Presumptive based on imaging + CD4 <100 + positive Toxoplasma IgG. Empiric treatment trial (if improvement in 7-14 days → confirms diagnosis). Brain biopsy if no response or IgG negative

CMV RETINITIS:

  • Presentation: Painless vision loss, floaters, visual field defects. CD4 <50
  • Fundoscopy: "Pizza pie" or "cottage cheese and ketchup" appearance. Hemorrhagic necrosis along retinal vessels
  • Risk: Retinal detachment, permanent blindness if untreated. OPHTHALMOLOGY EMERGENCY

CMV COLITIS:

  • Presentation: Chronic diarrhea (watery or bloody), abdominal pain, fever, weight loss. CD4 <50
  • Diagnosis: Colonoscopy with biopsy (CMV inclusion bodies, immunostaining)

MYCOBACTERIUM AVIUM COMPLEX (MAC):

  • Presentation: Disseminated disease. High fever, night sweats, weight loss, anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy. Chronic diarrhea (GI involvement). CD4 <50
  • Labs: Pancytopenia, elevated alkaline phosphatase
  • Diagnosis: Blood cultures (mycobacterial blood cultures - takes 2-4 weeks). Positive in 90%

CRYPTOCOCCAL MENINGITIS:

  • Presentation: Subacute headache (weeks), fever, altered mental status, nausea/vomiting. Minimal meningeal signs. CD4 <100
  • CSF: Elevated opening pressure (>25cmH₂O in 75%), lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein. India ink (encapsulated yeast), cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) nearly 100% sensitive
  • Serum CrAg: Also highly sensitive. Positive in disseminated disease
  • Imaging: MRI may be normal or show hydrocephalus, cryptococcomas

IMMUNE RECONSTITUTION INFLAMMATORY SYNDROME (IRIS):

  • Definition: Paradoxical worsening of opportunistic infection after starting ART (antiretroviral therapy). Occurs as CD4 count rises and immune system "awakens"
  • Timing: Typically 2-12 weeks after starting ART
  • Presentation: Fever, worsening symptoms/imaging of prior infection (e.g., TB lymphadenitis enlarges, PCP infiltrates worsen). Can be severe (respiratory failure, neurologic deterioration)
  • Management: Continue ART + continue OI treatment. Corticosteroids if severe (prednisone 0.5-1mg/kg/day)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Essential Labs:

  • CD4 count: Determines risk of opportunistic infections. <200 = AIDS. <50 = highest risk
  • HIV viral load: Assesses disease control, treatment response. Goal <20-50 copies/mL (undetectable)
  • CBC: Anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia common in advanced disease. Pancytopenia (think MAC, disseminated infection)
  • CMP: Renal function (before nephrotoxic drugs), electrolytes, liver enzymes
  • LDH: Elevated in PCP, lymphoma, hemolysis
  • Blood cultures: Bacterial (if fever/sepsis), mycobacterial (if CD4 <50 with fever/night sweats - rule out MAC, TB)

Imaging Based on Presentation:

  • CXR: If respiratory symptoms (PCP, TB, bacterial pneumonia, Kaposi sarcoma)
  • CT chest: If CXR nondiagnostic but high suspicion for PCP or other pulmonary process
  • MRI brain (with contrast): If altered mental status, focal deficits, seizures (toxoplasmosis, lymphoma, PML, cryptococcoma)
  • CT abdomen/pelvis: If abdominal pain, diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly (CMV colitis, MAC, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma)

Specific OI Diagnostics:

  • PCP: ABG (A-a gradient), induced sputum or BAL (methenamine silver stain, DFA, PCR). β-D-glucan elevated
  • Toxoplasmosis: MRI brain, Toxoplasma IgG serology
  • Cryptococcus: Serum CrAg (screening if CD4 <100), lumbar puncture (opening pressure, CSF CrAg, India ink, fungal culture)
  • CMV: Ophthalmology exam (retinitis), colonoscopy with biopsy (colitis), CMV PCR (viremia)
  • MAC: Mycobacterial blood cultures (hold 4-6 weeks)
  • TB: Sputum AFB smear/culture/PCR (Xpert MTB/RIF), mycobacterial blood cultures if disseminated

Lumbar Puncture Indications: Headache, altered mental status, seizures, fever with neurologic symptoms. Check opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain/culture, CrAg, VDRL (syphilis), consider Toxoplasma PCR, JC virus PCR (PML)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY (ART) - Foundation:

  • Start ART in ALL patients: Regardless of CD4 count. Reduces mortality, prevents disease progression, reduces transmission
  • Timing: Start within 2 weeks of OI diagnosis (balance immune recovery vs IRIS risk). EXCEPTION: TB meningitis (delay ART 8 weeks to reduce IRIS-related neurologic complications), cryptococcal meningitis (delay 4-6 weeks after starting antifungals)
  • Regimen: Integrase inhibitor-based (dolutegravir, bictegravir) + 2 NRTIs (tenofovir/emtricitabine). Consult HIV specialist for regimen selection
  • Drug interactions: Many ART drugs interact with rifampin (TB treatment), azoles (fungal treatment). Adjust doses or choose alternative agents

PCP TREATMENT:

  • First-line: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) 15-20mg/kg/day (based on TMP component) IV or PO divided TID-QID × 21 days. Example: 2 DS tablets PO TID
  • Alternative (if sulfa allergy): Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV daily × 21 days (nephrotoxic, pancreatitis, hypoglycemia), OR clindamycin 600mg IV q6h + primaquine 15-30mg PO daily × 21 days (check G6PD first)
  • Adjunctive corticosteroids: Prednisone 40mg PO BID × 5 days, then 40mg daily × 5 days, then 20mg daily × 11 days (total 21 days). INDICATION: PaO₂ <70mmHg on room air OR A-a gradient >35mmHg. START WITHIN 72 HOURS of antibiotics. Reduces mortality and respiratory failure
  • Secondary prophylaxis: After completion, continue TMP-SMX 1 DS tablet PO daily until CD4 >200 × 3 months

CANDIDAL ESOPHAGITIS TREATMENT:

  • First-line: Fluconazole 200-400mg PO/IV daily × 14-21 days
  • Alternative (fluconazole-refractory): Itraconazole 200mg PO daily, posaconazole 400mg PO BID, voriconazole 200mg PO BID, OR micafungin 150mg IV daily, caspofungin 70mg IV load then 50mg daily
  • Response: Symptoms improve in 3-5 days. If no improvement by 7 days → endoscopy (confirm diagnosis, rule out CMV/HSV co-infection)

CNS TOXOPLASMOSIS TREATMENT:

  • First-line (acute therapy × 6 weeks): Pyrimethamine 200mg PO load, then 50-75mg PO daily (weight-based) + sulfadiazine 1-1.5g PO QID + leucovorin (folinic acid) 10-25mg PO daily (prevents bone marrow toxicity)
  • Alternative: Pyrimethamine + leucovorin + clindamycin 600mg IV/PO q6h (if sulfa allergy)
  • Second-line: TMP-SMX 5mg/kg (TMP component) IV q12h
  • Anticonvulsants: If seizures occur. Levetiracetam preferred (fewer drug interactions than phenytoin)
  • Corticosteroids: Dexamethasone if significant mass effect/edema. Use cautiously (can mask treatment failure)
  • Clinical response: 80-90% improve by 7-14 days. Repeat MRI at 2 weeks. If worsening → consider brain biopsy (lymphoma vs other diagnosis)
  • Secondary prophylaxis: After acute treatment, continue pyrimethamine 25-50mg daily + sulfadiazine 2-4g daily (divided) + leucovorin 10-25mg daily until CD4 >200 × 6 months

CRYPTOCOCCAL MENINGITIS TREATMENT:

  • Induction (2 weeks): Amphotericin B lipid complex 3-4mg/kg IV daily + flucytosine 25mg/kg PO QID. Goal: sterilize CSF
  • Consolidation (8 weeks): Fluconazole 400mg PO daily
  • Maintenance (≥1 year): Fluconazole 200mg PO daily until CD4 >200 × 6 months AND undetectable viral load
  • Elevated ICP management (CRITICAL): Daily therapeutic lumbar punctures (remove 20-30mL CSF) to maintain opening pressure <20cmH₂O. Persistent elevated ICP → lumbar drain. Untreated elevated ICP causes blindness, death
  • Monitor: Creatinine (amphotericin nephrotoxic), potassium/magnesium (wasting), CBC (flucytosine bone marrow suppression)

CMV RETINITIS TREATMENT:

  • Induction (2-3 weeks): Ganciclovir 5mg/kg IV q12h OR foscarnet 90mg/kg IV q12h OR valganciclovir 900mg PO BID (if can tolerate PO)
  • Maintenance: Valganciclovir 900mg PO daily OR ganciclovir 5mg/kg IV 5-7×/week until immune recovery (CD4 >100 × 6 months)
  • Ophthalmology: Urgent consultation. Consider intravitreal injections if sight-threatening

CMV COLITIS TREATMENT:

  • Induction: Ganciclovir 5mg/kg IV q12h × 3-6 weeks (until symptoms resolve)
  • Maintenance: Valganciclovir 900mg PO daily until CD4 >100 × 6 months

MAC TREATMENT:

  • Therapy: Clarithromycin 500mg PO BID + ethambutol 15mg/kg PO daily + rifabutin 300mg PO daily (if ART allows). Continue until CD4 >100 × 12 months AND ≥12 months treatment AND asymptomatic
  • Alternative: Azithromycin 500-600mg daily (instead of clarithromycin)

IRIS MANAGEMENT:

  • Continue ART: Do not stop (benefit of immune recovery outweighs IRIS risk in most cases)
  • Continue OI treatment: Ensure adequately treating underlying infection
  • Corticosteroids if severe: Prednisone 0.5-1mg/kg/day × 2 weeks, then taper. Consider if respiratory failure, neurologic deterioration, or life-threatening symptoms
TEACHING PEARLS

💡 Start ART early: Within 2 weeks of OI diagnosis in most cases (except TB meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis). Early ART reduces mortality

💡 PCP prophylaxis indications: CD4 <200, prior PCP, or CD4 <14%. TMP-SMX 1 DS tablet daily or 3×/week. Prevents #1 AIDS-defining illness

💡 Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis: CD4 <100 + positive Toxoplasma IgG. TMP-SMX 1 DS daily (also covers PCP)

💡 MAC prophylaxis: CD4 <50. Azithromycin 1200mg weekly or clarithromycin 500mg BID

💡 Ring-enhancing brain lesions in HIV: #1 = Toxoplasmosis (multiple lesions, CD4 <100). #2 = Primary CNS lymphoma (solitary, CD4 <50, EBV-associated). Empiric toxo treatment trial for 2 weeks; if no response → biopsy

💡 Cryptococcal meningitis ICP crisis: Elevated opening pressure (>25cmH₂O) is the rule, not exception. Daily LPs to drain CSF are MANDATORY. Failure to control ICP → blindness, death despite antifungals

💡 PCP in pregnancy: TMP-SMX contraindicated in 1st trimester (folate antagonist). Use pentamidine. After 1st trimester, TMP-SMX is safe

💡 CMV viremia vs disease: Positive CMV PCR alone is not disease. Need end-organ involvement (retinitis, colitis, esophagitis, pneumonitis). Don't treat viremia alone

💡 Rifampin drug interactions: Rifampin is potent CYP450 inducer. Decreases levels of protease inhibitors, NNRTIs, many other drugs. Use rifabutin (less induction) or integrase inhibitors (less affected) with HIV treatment

💡 Diarrhea in AIDS: Broad differential. Infectious (CMV, MAC, Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium, Isospora, C. diff), medication-related (protease inhibitors), HIV enteropathy. Workup: stool cultures, ova & parasites, CMV PCR, colonoscopy if refractory

💡 PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy): JC virus reactivation. CD4 <50. Progressive focal neurologic deficits, no fever, no enhancement on MRI. White matter lesions. CSF JC virus PCR diagnostic. NO specific treatment. Only ART (immune restoration)

💡 Kaposi sarcoma: HHV-8 associated. Violaceous skin lesions, oral lesions, GI/pulmonary involvement. Can occur at any CD4 but more common <200. Treatment: ART (causes regression in most)

ICU ESCALATION CRITERIA
  • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (severe PCP, ARDS)
  • Septic shock (bacterial sepsis, disseminated infection)
  • Altered mental status with airway compromise (meningitis, encephalitis)
  • Seizures refractory to treatment (toxoplasmosis, CNS infection)
  • Hemodynamic instability (MAC with bacteremia, overwhelming sepsis)
  • Severe electrolyte abnormalities from treatment (amphotericin-induced hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia)
DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Clinical improvement of OI on appropriate therapy
  • Tolerating oral medications (or has outpatient IV access for continued treatment)
  • No longer requiring IV medications that cannot be given outpatient
  • ART started (if treatment-naive) or regimen optimized
  • Prophylaxis medications prescribed for OI prevention
  • Follow-up arranged with HIV specialist
  • Social support/housing stable (critical for medication adherence)
  • Patient educated on warning signs, medication adherence, side effects
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

IRIS (Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome): Paradoxical worsening of OI after starting ART (2-12 weeks). Can be life-threatening. Continue ART, continue OI treatment, add corticosteroids if severe

Medication Toxicities: Amphotericin (nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, infusion reactions), ganciclovir/valganciclovir (bone marrow suppression), TMP-SMX (rash, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction), pentamidine (hypoglycemia, pancreatitis, nephrotoxicity)

ART Side Effects: GI intolerance, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity (tenofovir), neuropsychiatric effects (efavirenz), rash (nevirapine, abacavir - check HLA-B*5701), lipodystrophy, metabolic syndrome

Drug Interactions: ART interacts with many medications (azoles, rifamycins, anticonvulsants, PPIs, statins). Consult pharmacist/HIV specialist for regimen selection

Non-adherence: Complex regimens, side effects, social issues → resistance development. Directly observed therapy, social work support, simplify regimens

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Biktarvy, 💊 Dolutegravir
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 HIV Testing, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated Ferritin, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT

61. OPPORTUNISTIC INFECTIONS IN IMMUNOCOMPROMISED HOST

Non-HIV Immunosuppression • Transplant • Chemotherapy • Biological Agents
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Immunocompromised Host Overview: Patients with impaired immune function due to underlying disease (hematologic malignancy, solid organ/stem cell transplant), medications (chemotherapy, high-dose steroids, biologics), or inherited immunodeficiency. Susceptible to infections by organisms that rarely cause disease in immunocompetent hosts

Types of Immunosuppression:

  • Neutropenia: ANC <500 cells/μL (severe <100). Risk of bacterial/fungal infections. Duration and depth critical
  • Cell-mediated immunity defects: Solid organ transplant, chronic steroids (>20mg prednisone daily × >2 weeks), TNF-α inhibitors, lymphoma. Risk: intracellular pathogens (Listeria, Nocardia, mycobacteria), fungi (Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis), viruses (CMV, VZV)
  • Humoral immunity defects: Multiple myeloma, CLL, splenectomy, complement deficiencies. Risk: encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis)
  • Combined defects: Stem cell transplant, intensive chemotherapy regimens, HIV/AIDS

INVASIVE FUNGAL INFECTIONS (Most Feared Complications):

Invasive Aspergillosis:

  • Risk factors: Prolonged neutropenia, hematologic malignancy (AML, allogeneic stem cell transplant), high-dose steroids, lung transplant
  • Pulmonary aspergillosis (most common): Fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis. CT chest: nodules with surrounding ground-glass opacity ("halo sign" early, "air-crescent sign" late), cavitation
  • Invasive sinusitis: Facial pain, nasal congestion, black necrotic eschars in nasal cavity, cranial nerve palsies (cavernous sinus extension)
  • CNS aspergillosis: Altered mental status, focal deficits, seizures. MRI: ring-enhancing lesions, hemorrhage
  • Diagnosis: Galactomannan (serum/BAL - sensitivity 70-80% in high-risk), β-D-glucan (nonspecific but sensitive), CT-guided biopsy (gold standard - septate hyphae with acute-angle branching)

Invasive Candidiasis:

  • Risk factors: Central lines, TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotics, GI surgery/perforation, neutropenia
  • Candidemia: Fever unresponsive to antibiotics, hemodynamic instability. Blood cultures positive (but can be negative in tissue-invasive disease)
  • Hepatosplenic candidiasis (chronic disseminated): Persistent fever during neutropenia recovery. RUQ pain, elevated alkaline phosphatase. Imaging: "bulls-eye" or target lesions in liver/spleen
  • Candida endophthalmitis: Chorioretinal lesions (white fluffy infiltrates) on fundoscopy. Screen all candidemia patients

Mucormycosis (Zygomycosis):

  • Risk factors: Diabetic ketoacidosis, neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, deferoxamine use, iron overload
  • Rhinocerebral mucormycosis: AGGRESSIVE. Facial/periorbital swelling, facial pain, black necrotic eschars (palate, nasal turbinates), proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, vision loss. Can invade brain (cavernous sinus thrombosis, stroke). HIGH MORTALITY (>50%)
  • Pulmonary mucormycosis: Fever, cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain. CT: nodules, consolidation, cavitation. Angioinvasive → infarction
  • Diagnosis: Tissue biopsy (broad, ribbon-like, non-septate hyphae with right-angle branching). Cultures often negative

Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PCP):

  • Risk factors: Prolonged high-dose steroids (>20mg prednisone × >1 month), hematologic malignancy, solid organ transplant, chemotherapy (especially fludarabine, alemtuzumab), TNF-α inhibitors. NOT just HIV
  • Presentation: Subacute dyspnea, dry cough, fever. Progressive hypoxemia. CXR: bilateral interstitial infiltrates. LDH markedly elevated
  • Diagnosis: Induced sputum, BAL (methenamine silver stain, DFA, PCR). β-D-glucan elevated (80-90% sensitive)

VIRAL INFECTIONS:

CMV (Cytomegalovirus) Disease:

  • Risk factors: Solid organ transplant (especially lung, heart), stem cell transplant, high-dose steroids
  • CMV viremia vs disease: Viremia = PCR positive without symptoms. Disease = end-organ involvement (pneumonitis, colitis, retinitis, hepatitis, encephalitis)
  • CMV pneumonitis: Dyspnea, fever, hypoxemia. CXR/CT: bilateral interstitial infiltrates. BAL: CMV by culture/PCR + cytopathic inclusions. HIGH MORTALITY in stem cell transplant
  • CMV colitis: Diarrhea (bloody), abdominal pain, fever. Colonoscopy: ulcers, biopsy shows inclusions
  • Monitoring: Weekly CMV PCR in high-risk transplant patients (preemptive therapy if viral load rising)

Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) - Disseminated/Severe:

  • Risk: Can disseminate in immunocompromised (visceral involvement: pneumonitis, hepatitis, encephalitis)
  • Presentation: Dermatomal zoster BUT lesions outside dermatome (disseminated), hemorrhagic vesicles, visceral symptoms
  • Treatment: Acyclovir 10mg/kg IV q8h (vs PO for immunocompetent shingles)

BK Virus (Polyomavirus):

  • Risk: Kidney transplant recipients. Can cause BK nephropathy → graft loss
  • Presentation: Rising creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria (mimics rejection)
  • Diagnosis: Urine/plasma BK PCR (high viral load), kidney biopsy (viral inclusions, tubular injury)

BACTERIAL INFECTIONS:

Nocardia:

  • Risk: Solid organ transplant (especially lung), chronic steroids, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
  • Presentation: Pulmonary (most common): cough, fever, nodules/cavitation on imaging. Can disseminate to CNS (brain abscess), skin (subcutaneous abscesses)
  • Diagnosis: Sputum/tissue culture (slow-growing, modified AFB stain positive, Gram-positive branching filaments)

Listeria monocytogenes:

  • Risk: Cell-mediated immunity defects (transplant, steroids, TNF-α inhibitors, elderly)
  • Presentation: Meningitis (headache, fever, altered mental status), bacteremia. CSF: lymphocytic or neutrophilic pleocytosis. Blood cultures often positive

Mycobacteria (TB, NTM):

  • Risk: TNF-α inhibitors (screen with IGRA/TST before starting), solid organ transplant, high-dose steroids
  • Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM): M. avium complex, M. abscessus. Pulmonary disease (nodules, cavitation), disseminated disease (in severe immunosuppression)

PARASITIC INFECTIONS:

Toxoplasma gondii:

  • Risk: Stem cell transplant (especially if donor seropositive/recipient seronegative), heart transplant (reactivation in donor heart)
  • Presentation: Similar to HIV-related toxoplasmosis (CNS lesions, fever, altered mental status)

Strongyloides stercoralis Hyperinfection:

  • Risk: Endemic exposure (tropical/subtropical regions) + immunosuppression (steroids). Parasite can persist for decades in immunocompetent, then hyperinfect
  • Presentation: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, ileus, pulmonary symptoms. Can cause Gram-negative bacteremia (larvae carry gut bacteria). HIGH MORTALITY
  • Diagnosis: Stool ova & parasites (multiple samples), serology. Larvae in sputum/BAL if pulmonary involvement
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

History - CRITICAL for Risk Stratification:

  • Type/duration of immunosuppression: Chemotherapy regimen, transplant type/date, biologic agents (infliximab, rituximab, etc.), steroid dose/duration
  • Neutropenia: ANC, duration (>7 days = high risk)
  • Prophylaxis medications: PCP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX), antifungal (fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole), antiviral (acyclovir, valganciclovir)
  • Exposures: Travel (endemic fungi - Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Blastomyces), pets, construction sites (Aspergillus), undercooked meat (Toxoplasma), gardening/soil (Nocardia)
  • Prior infections: Latent TB, endemic fungi, VZV, CMV serostatus

Laboratory Studies:

  • CBC with differential: ANC (neutropenic fever defined as ANC <500 + fever ≥38.3°C once or ≥38°C × 1hr), anemia, thrombocytopenia
  • CMP: Renal function (before antifungals, antivirals), liver enzymes (hepatic involvement)
  • Blood cultures × 2 sets: Bacterial, fungal (if prolonged fever/neutropenia)
  • Fungal biomarkers: Galactomannan (Aspergillus), β-D-glucan (Candida, Aspergillus, PCP - NOT Mucor), Cryptococcal antigen
  • Viral studies: CMV PCR (quantitative), EBV PCR, BK virus PCR (transplant patients), respiratory viral panel
  • Sputum: Gram stain/culture, AFB smear/culture, fungal culture, PCP stain (if indicated)

Imaging:

  • CT chest (high-resolution): Preferred over CXR. Aspergillus (halo sign, air crescent, nodules), PCP (ground-glass), Mucor (nodules, infarction), Nocardia (cavitary nodules)
  • CT sinus: If facial pain/congestion (Aspergillus, Mucor sinusitis)
  • MRI brain (with contrast): If altered mental status, focal deficits (Toxoplasma, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Listeria, Cryptococcus)
  • CT abdomen/pelvis: If abdominal pain (hepatosplenic candidiasis, CMV colitis, typhlitis)

Invasive Diagnostics (Often Necessary):

  • Bronchoscopy with BAL: PCP, Aspergillus, viral pneumonitis (CMV). Send for bacterial/fungal/viral cultures, PCP stain, Galactomannan, cytology
  • CT-guided biopsy: Lung nodules (Aspergillus, Mucor, Nocardia - definitive diagnosis). Liver/spleen lesions (hepatosplenic candidiasis)
  • Lumbar puncture: Altered mental status. Cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain/culture, cryptococcal antigen, Toxoplasma PCR, VZV/HSV PCR. Opening pressure (Cryptococcus)
  • Endoscopy/colonoscopy: GI symptoms (CMV colitis, esophagitis). Biopsy for CMV inclusions, cultures
  • Skin biopsy: Rash (disseminated fungal infection, Nocardia, cutaneous viruses)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

EMPIRIC THERAPY FOR NEUTROPENIC FEVER (ANC <500 + Fever):

  • Start within 1 hour: Delays increase mortality
  • Regimen: Cefepime 2g IV q8h OR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h OR meropenem 1g IV q8h (if prior ESBL, Pseudomonas, or critically ill)
  • Add vancomycin 15-20mg/kg q8-12h IF: Hemodynamic instability, concern for catheter-related infection, skin/soft tissue infection, MRSA colonization, mucositis
  • Duration: Continue until ANC >500 AND afebrile × 48hr (minimum 7 days even if culture-negative)
  • If persistent fever at 4-7 days: ADD empiric antifungal (voriconazole, caspofungin, or liposomal amphotericin B). Repeat imaging, fungal workup

INVASIVE ASPERGILLOSIS:

  • First-line: Voriconazole 6mg/kg IV q12h × 2 doses (loading), then 4mg/kg IV q12h (maintenance). Switch to PO when stable (200-300mg PO BID)
  • Alternative: Isavuconazole 372mg IV q8h × 6 doses (loading), then 372mg IV daily, OR liposomal amphotericin B 3-5mg/kg IV daily
  • Salvage/combination: Voriconazole + anidulafungin (echinocandin) for severe/refractory disease
  • Duration: Minimum 6-12 weeks. Continue until lesions resolve AND immune reconstitution (ANC recovery, reduced immunosuppression if possible)
  • Monitor: Voriconazole levels (trough 1-5.5 mcg/mL - wide inter-patient variability, hepatotoxicity, visual changes)

MUCORMYCOSIS:

  • Medical: Liposomal amphotericin B 5-10mg/kg IV daily. High-dose required. Alternative: posaconazole 300mg PO BID (loading × 1 day, then 300mg daily) or isavuconazole
  • Surgical debridement: MANDATORY for rhinocerebral, sino-orbital disease. Extensive debridement of necrotic tissue (repeat surgeries often needed). Medical therapy alone = FAILURE
  • Reverse immunosuppression: Reduce steroids, optimize diabetes control, discontinue deferoxamine if applicable
  • Duration: Several months (12+ weeks). Continue until clinical/radiographic resolution
  • Mortality: 40-80% despite aggressive treatment

INVASIVE CANDIDIASIS:

  • Candidemia/invasive candidiasis: Echinocandin (first-line): Micafungin 100mg IV daily, caspofungin 70mg IV load then 50mg daily, OR anidulafungin 200mg IV load then 100mg daily
  • Alternative (if stable, Candida albicans): Fluconazole 800mg IV load, then 400mg IV/PO daily
  • Remove central line: Candidemia requires line removal within 24-48hr (unless no alternative access)
  • Ophthalmology exam: Within 1 week to rule out endophthalmitis (5-10% of candidemia)
  • Duration: 14 days after first negative blood culture AND resolution of symptoms. Longer if endocarditis, osteomyelitis, or abscess (4-6 weeks minimum)

PCP (Non-HIV):

  • Treatment: TMP-SMX 15-20mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV or PO divided TID-QID × 21 days
  • Alternative: Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV daily × 21 days (if sulfa allergy)
  • Adjunctive steroids: Prednisone 40mg BID × 5 days → 40mg daily × 5 days → 20mg daily × 11 days. INDICATION: PaO₂ <70mmHg OR A-a gradient >35mmHg. START within 72 hours of antibiotics
  • Note: PCP in non-HIV often MORE severe presentation, higher mortality than HIV-related PCP

CMV DISEASE:

  • Treatment: Ganciclovir 5mg/kg IV q12h (induction × 2-3 weeks) → valganciclovir 900mg PO daily (maintenance until viremia clears + immune recovery)
  • CMV pneumonitis in stem cell transplant: Ganciclovir + IV immunoglobulin (IVIG 0.5g/kg every other day × 10 doses). HIGH MORTALITY despite treatment
  • Alternative (if renal dysfunction, ganciclovir resistance): Foscarnet 90mg/kg IV q12h
  • Monitoring: Weekly CMV PCR to assess treatment response. Monitor CBC (ganciclovir causes neutropenia)

NOCARDIA:

  • Treatment: TMP-SMX 5-10mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV or PO divided BID-TID. High-dose required
  • Duration: Prolonged. Pulmonary: 6-12 months. CNS: 12 months minimum. Often combined with other agents (imipenem, amikacin, linezolid) for severe/CNS disease
  • Susceptibilities: Check antibiotic sensitivities (resistance patterns vary by species)

LISTERIA MENINGITIS:

  • Treatment: Ampicillin 2g IV q4h + gentamicin 5-7mg/kg IV daily (synergistic) × 21 days minimum
  • Alternative (if penicillin allergy): TMP-SMX 5mg/kg (TMP component) IV q6h
  • Note: Ceftriaxone does NOT cover Listeria. Ampicillin is mandatory

STRONGYLOIDES HYPERINFECTION:

  • Treatment: Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg PO daily × 2 days. Repeat in 2 weeks. For hyperinfection: continue daily until stool/sputum negative × 2 weeks
  • Add albendazole 400mg PO BID (if severe): Not proven but often used in combination
  • Reduce immunosuppression: If possible (critical for cure)
  • Treat Gram-negative bacteremia: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (often concurrent)

REDUCING IMMUNOSUPPRESSION:

  • Balance: Need immune function to clear infection BUT must prevent organ rejection (transplant) or manage underlying disease
  • Steroids: Taper if possible (cannot stop abruptly if chronic use - adrenal insufficiency). Life-threatening infections may require reduction
  • Transplant immunosuppression: Reduce calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), hold antimetabolites (mycophenolate) temporarily. Maintain some immunosuppression to prevent rejection. Consult transplant team
  • Biologic agents: Hold TNF-α inhibitors, rituximab during active infection
TEACHING PEARLS

💡 Neutropenic fever = emergency: Start empiric antibiotics within 1 hour. Cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam. Add vancomycin if unstable or catheter-related infection suspected

💡 Think Aspergillus if: Prolonged neutropenia + pulmonary nodules with halo sign on CT. Start voriconazole immediately while awaiting biopsy. Don't wait for culture (often negative)

💡 Mucor = aggressive surgical debridement + amphotericin: Medical therapy alone fails. Rhinocerebral mucor requires extensive ENT surgery, often multiple procedures

💡 Black necrotic eschar in immunocompromised: Mucormycosis until proven otherwise. Biopsy urgently. Broad, non-septate hyphae

💡 CMV viremia vs disease: Positive PCR alone is NOT disease. Need end-organ involvement (pneumonitis, colitis, retinitis). Preemptive therapy if rising viral load in transplant patients

💡 Listeria not covered by ceftriaxone: Ampicillin is mandatory for Listeria meningitis. Think Listeria in transplant/steroid patient with meningitis

💡 Nocardia mimics TB: Pulmonary nodules, cavitation. Weakly acid-fast positive. Long treatment course (6-12 months). Can disseminate to CNS (brain abscess)

💡 Screen for Strongyloides before immunosuppression: Serology in patients from endemic areas (tropics). Hyperinfection can occur decades after initial exposure when steroids started. Give ivermectin preemptively if positive

💡 β-D-glucan elevated in: Candida, Aspergillus, PCP. NOT Mucor or Cryptococcus. Use to monitor treatment response

💡 PCP in non-HIV: More severe presentation, worse outcomes than HIV-related PCP. Still use TMP-SMX + steroids if hypoxemic

💡 VZV in immunocompromised: Always treat with IV acyclovir 10mg/kg q8h. Can disseminate (visceral organs). Don't use oral therapy

💡 Duration of antifungal therapy: Aspergillosis requires months (minimum 6-12 weeks). Continue until immune recovery AND radiographic improvement. Early discontinuation = relapse

ICU ESCALATION CRITERIA
  • Septic shock requiring vasopressors
  • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (severe PCP, Aspergillus pneumonia)
  • Neutropenic fever with hemodynamic instability
  • CNS infection with altered mental status/airway compromise
  • Mucormycosis requiring urgent surgical debridement + aggressive medical management
  • Refractory hypoxemia despite maximal support
DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Clinical improvement on appropriate antimicrobial therapy
  • ANC recovering if neutropenic (>500 cells/μL)
  • Hemodynamically stable, afebrile × 48-72hr
  • Tolerating oral medications (or has outpatient IV access arranged)
  • Appropriate prophylaxis prescribed (if indicated)
  • Follow-up arranged with oncology/transplant/infectious disease
  • Immunosuppression regimen adjusted (if modifications needed)
  • Patient/family educated on warning signs, when to return
COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Persistent/Recurrent Infections: Inadequate immune recovery (prolonged neutropenia, ongoing immunosuppression), resistance (fungi, bacteria), inadequate source control (abscess, catheter), wrong diagnosis (biopsy needed)

Medication Toxicities: Amphotericin (nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, infusion reactions - rigors, fever), voriconazole (hepatotoxicity, visual changes, drug interactions), ganciclovir (bone marrow suppression), TMP-SMX (hyperkalemia, nephrotoxicity, rash)

Organ Rejection (Transplant Patients): Reducing immunosuppression to treat infection can precipitate rejection. Monitor allograft function closely

Secondary Infections: Broad-spectrum antibiotics → C. difficile. Prolonged antifungals → resistant organisms. Prophylaxis helps but doesn't eliminate risk

Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS): Paradoxical worsening when ANC recovers or immunosuppression reduced. Especially with fungal infections (Aspergillus, Cryptococcus). May require steroids

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 TMP-SMX, 💊 Fluconazole, 💊 Voriconazole, 💊 Ganciclovir, 💊 Azithromycin

62. SIADH (SYNDROME OF INAPPROPRIATE ADH)

Euvolemic Hyponatremia • Dilutional Hyponatremia
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Asymptomatic hyponatremia discovered on routine labs OR neurologic symptoms (confusion, headache, nausea) in euvolemic patient with concentrated urine

Symptoms (Correlate with Na Level and Rate of Drop):

  • Mild (Na 130-135): Often asymptomatic, subtle cognitive changes
  • Moderate (Na 125-129): Headache, nausea, confusion, lethargy
  • Severe (Na <125): Vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, coma
  • Critical (<120 or ACUTE drop): Cerebral edema → seizures, respiratory arrest, brainstem herniation, death

Physical Exam: EUVOLEMIC - no edema, normal skin turgor, moist mucous membranes, normal JVP, no orthostatic vitals

Common Causes:

  • Malignancy (most common): SCLC (most classic), pancreatic/duodenal CA, lymphoma, head/neck cancers
  • Pulmonary: Pneumonia, TB, COPD exacerbation, aspergillosis, positive pressure ventilation
  • CNS: Meningitis, encephalitis, SAH, subdural hematoma, brain tumors, trauma, stroke
  • Medications: SSRIs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, NSAIDs, PPIs, MDMA/ecstasy
  • Post-operative: Physiologic response to surgery (transient)
  • Endocrine: Severe hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency (must exclude first!)
  • Idiopathic: 10-15% of cases
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

SIADH Diagnostic Criteria (Must meet ALL):

  • Hyponatremia: Na <135 mEq/L (usually <130)
  • Plasma hypo-osmolality: Serum osm <275 mOsm/kg
  • Inappropriately concentrated urine: Urine osm >100 mOsm/kg (typically >300-400)
  • Elevated urine sodium: Urine Na >40 mEq/L (on normal salt diet)
  • Clinical euvolemia: No edema, no volume depletion
  • Normal thyroid, adrenal, renal function: TSH, cortisol, Cr normal
  • No diuretic use

Essential Labs:

  • Serum: BMP (Na, K, Cr), serum osmolality, glucose, TSH, cortisol (AM or random)
  • Urine: Urine sodium, urine osmolality, specific gravity
  • Calculate serum osmolality: 2(Na) + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8

Workup for Underlying Cause:

  • Medication review: Stop offending agents if possible
  • CT chest: Screen for SCLC, pneumonia
  • Head CT/MRI: If neurologic symptoms or CNS cause suspected
  • Consider: Lumbar puncture if meningitis/encephalitis suspected, CXR, additional malignancy workup

Key Lab Pattern:

  • ↓ Serum Na + ↓ Serum Osm + ↑ Urine Osm + ↑ Urine Na + Euvolemia = SIADH
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Treatment Depends on Severity and Acuity:

⚡ SEVERE/SYMPTOMATIC (Na <120 OR seizures/coma/respiratory arrest):

  • 3% Hypertonic Saline: 100 mL IV bolus over 10 minutes, can repeat × 2-3 as needed
  • Alternative: 2 mL/kg bolus over 10-20 minutes
  • Goal: Raise Na by 4-6 mEq/L acutely to abort seizures, then STOP acute correction
  • Check Na q2-4h during active correction
  • ⚠️ DO NOT exceed 8-10 mEq/L rise in first 24 hours! Risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS)

MODERATE (Na 125-129, mild symptoms):

  • Fluid restriction: 800-1000 mL/day (primary therapy)
  • Goal: Negative fluid balance of 500-1000 mL/day
  • Consider salt tablets 1-2g TID to increase osmolar load
  • Monitor Na daily initially

CHRONIC/MILD (Na 130-135, asymptomatic):

  • Treat underlying cause first
  • Fluid restriction 1000-1500 mL/day
  • High-salt, high-protein diet
  • Monitor outpatient

Adjunct Pharmacotherapy:

  • Urea: 15-30g PO BID (osmotic diuretic, increases free water excretion) - rarely used in US
  • Demeclocycline: 300-600 mg PO BID (induces nephrogenic DI) - slow onset (3-5 days), risk of photosensitivity, nephrotoxicity
  • Vaptans (V2 receptor antagonists):
    • Tolvaptan (Samsca): 15 mg PO daily (can increase to 30-60 mg). ONLY for euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia
    • Reserved for severe, refractory SIADH
    • Very expensive, requires close monitoring (risk of overly rapid correction)
    • ⚠️ Risk of osmotic demyelination if used incorrectly
    • Contraindicated: Hypovolemic hyponatremia, anuric renal failure, hepatic impairment

⚠️ CRITICAL CORRECTION LIMITS (Prevent Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome):

  • Maximum correction: 8-10 mEq/L in first 24 hours
  • Maximum correction: 18 mEq/L in first 48 hours
  • High-risk groups for ODS: Chronic hyponatremia (>48 hours), alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease, hypokalemia
  • If overcorrect → consider giving D5W to re-lower Na

Treat Underlying Cause:

  • Stop offending medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine)
  • Treat pneumonia, CNS infection
  • Oncology consult for malignancy-related SIADH
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Euvolemia is KEY: If patient has edema (CHF, cirrhosis) or volume depletion → NOT SIADH. Must be euvolemic
  • Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS): Caused by overly rapid Na correction. Presents 2-6 days later with dysarthria, dysphagia, paraplegia, "locked-in" syndrome. Irreversible and devastating
  • "8 in 24" rule: Never raise Na >8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours, especially in chronic hyponatremia
  • SCLC = classic: Ectopic ADH production. SIADH may be first presentation of lung cancer
  • SSRIs underrecognized cause: Especially in elderly patients. Can occur weeks-months after starting
  • Exercise-induced hyponatremia: Endurance athletes (marathons) drinking excessive hypotonic fluids. Treat with fluid restriction, NOT IV saline
  • Don't give NS for SIADH: Makes it WORSE! Kidneys excrete the sodium, keep the water → Na drops further. Exception: severe symptomatic needing 3% hypertonic
  • Fluid restriction is hard: Most patients fail 800mL/day restriction. Compliance is poor
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma, respiratory arrest)
  • Na <120 mEq/L with symptoms
  • Need for 3% hypertonic saline
  • Rapidly dropping Na despite treatment
  • Altered mental status
  • Requiring q2h Na monitoring
  • Suspected or confirmed osmotic demyelination
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Na >125-130 mEq/L and stable/trending up
  • Asymptomatic or mild symptoms only
  • Underlying cause identified and addressed
  • Patient/family educated on fluid restriction
  • Offending medications discontinued
  • Close follow-up arranged (PCP or endocrine)
  • Discharge instructions include fluid restriction goal
  • Na recheck in 2-3 days
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Tolvaptan
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Urine Osmolality, 🔬 Serum Osmolality, 🔬 Urine Sodium/FENa

63. BOWEL OBSTRUCTION (SMALL/LARGE)

Mechanical Intestinal Blockage • Surgical Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Tetrad: Abdominal pain, distension, nausea/vomiting, obstipation (inability to pass stool or flatus)

Small Bowel Obstruction (SBO):

  • Pain: Crampy, colicky, periumbilical, intermittent (initially)
  • Vomiting: Early and prominent, bilious initially → feculent if prolonged
  • Distension: Variable (minimal if proximal obstruction)
  • Bowel sounds: High-pitched, hyperactive "rushes" early → absent if ischemia/perforation
  • Most common causes: Adhesions (about 70%), then malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, hernias (EAST 2012); also radiation enteritis. Check for external hernias on exam (EAST 2012)

Large Bowel Obstruction (LBO):

  • Pain: Lower abdominal, constant, progressive
  • Distension: MARKED, progressive
  • Vomiting: Late finding (if competent ileocecal valve) or absent
  • Bowel sounds: Decreased to absent
  • Most common mechanical causes: Obstructing colon or rectal cancer, diverticular stricture, colonic volvulus; volvulus is 10-15% of LBO in the US (sigmoid 60-75%, cecal 25-40%) (ASCRS 2021). Also consider acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (nonmechanical)

⚠️ RED FLAGS for Complicated/Strangulated Bowel (peritonitis or deterioration with fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, or continuous pain: timely surgical exploration, EAST 2012 Level 1):

  • Fever: Suggests ischemia, perforation, or necrosis
  • Tachycardia, hypotension: Sepsis, hypovolemia from third-spacing
  • Peritoneal signs: Guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness → perforation/necrosis
  • Severe, constant pain: Rather than colicky → ischemia
  • Bloody stool: Suggests mucosal ischemia
  • Leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis: Ischemia, bacterial translocation
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs:

  • CBC, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, lactate: Minimum initial labs (WSES 2018, non-US). Leukocytosis, acidosis, and metabolic derangement may suggest ischemia, but specificity is low (EAST 2012)
  • CMP: Hypokalemia, hypochloremia (from vomiting), elevated BUN/Cr (dehydration), metabolic acidosis (ischemia)
  • Lactate: Part of the initial workup (WSES 2018, non-US); no validated threshold in EAST or WSES
  • Practical: lipase to exclude pancreatitis; type and screen if surgery is likely

Imaging:

  • Abdominal X-ray:
    • Sensitivity for SBO 59-93%, operator-dependent; less sensitive for partial obstruction; still used for availability and serial follow-up (EAST 2012). WSES 2018 (non-US) does not recommend plain films
    • Colonic volvulus: plain films first in stable patients, CT to confirm (ASCRS 2021 rec 2, strong)
    • Practical: dilated small bowel over 3 cm, colon over 6 cm, cecum over 9 cm; free air on upright or left lateral decubitus film
  • CT abdomen/pelvis: Consider in all patients with SBO (EAST 2012 Level 1); multidetector CT with multiplanar reconstruction if available (Level 3)
    • 83-94% accurate for obstruction; identifies level (93%) and cause (80-91%) (EAST 2012)
    • Key findings: transition point with proximal dilation and distal decompression, decompressed colon, contrast failing to pass the transition point (EAST 2012)
    • Ischemia (85-100% sensitive): reduced wall enhancement, wall thickening, mesenteric venous congestion, mesenteric fluid, unusual mesenteric vessel course, ascites. CT signs of ischemia lower the threshold for surgery (EAST 2012 Level 2)
    • Small bowel volvulus: multiple transition points, posterior location, whirl sign (EAST 2012). Colonic volvulus: CT nearly 100% sensitive, over 90% specific (ASCRS 2021)
    • WSES 2018 (non-US): CT with oral water-soluble contrast preferred, with abdominal X-ray at 24 h
  • Alternatives: MRI and ultrasound (EAST 2012 Level 3; logistical limits). Practical: CT enterography if Crohn's suspected; colonoscopy if malignant LBO suspected
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Initial Management (All Patients):

  • NPO and decompression: Nasogastric tube or long intestinal tube (WSES 2018, non-US)
  • Supportive care: Fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolytes, nutritional support, aspiration prevention (WSES 2018, non-US). Practical: isotonic crystalloid titrated to volume status
  • Long tubes: Trilumen long naso-intestinal tubes were more effective than NG tubes in one trial but need endoscopic placement (WSES 2018, non-US, level IIC). A Dobhoff is a feeding tube, not a decompression tube
    • Practical: NG tube is standard initial decompression
  • Correct electrolytes: Practical: replace K and Cl (vomiting causes hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis)
  • Pain control: Opioids do not increase diagnostic error or treatment-decision error in acute abdominal pain (Cochrane 2011, 8 RCTs)
  • Antiemetics: Practical: ondansetron 4-8 mg IV q8h

🚨 URGENT SURGICAL CONSULTATION for:

  • All SBO: admit to a surgical service (EAST 2012 Level 3)
  • Generalized peritonitis or clinical deterioration (fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, continuous pain): timely surgical exploration (EAST 2012 Level 1)
  • CT signs of ischemia: low threshold for surgery (EAST 2012 Level 2)
  • Perforation (free air, peritonitis)
  • Colonic volvulus: urgent sigmoid resection if detorsion fails or colon is nonviable or perforated (ASCRS 2021 rec 4); cecal volvulus: resection (rec 9)
  • Practical: closed-loop obstruction
  • Cecal diameter: in acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, ischemia or perforation in 0%, 7%, and 23% with cecum under 12, 12-14, and over 14 cm (ASCRS 2021)
  • No resolution of SBO by days 3-5 of nonoperative management: water-soluble contrast study or surgery (EAST 2012 Level 3)

Nonoperative Management (SBO):

  • Indications: Partial or complete SBO without peritonitis or clinical deterioration; complete obstruction fails more often (EAST 2012 Level 1)
  • NPO + NG tube + IV fluids
  • Serial abdominal exams and labs (EAST 2012). Practical: every 4-6 h
  • Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin): diagnostic and therapeutic
    • Consider if partial SBO has not resolved by 48 h: improves time to bowel movement and shortens stay (EAST 2012 Level 2); a normal study rules out operative SBO (Level 2)
    • Contrast not in the colon on X-ray 24 h after administration strongly predicts failure (WSES 2018, non-US)
  • Nonoperative success 65-80%; most improve within 2-5 days; ischemia develops in 3-6% of partial SBO (EAST 2012)
  • No resolution by days 3-5: water-soluble contrast study or surgery (EAST 2012 Level 3)

Antibiotics:

  • Uncomplicated SBO: Limited data to support or refute antibiotics (EAST 2012)
  • Ischemia or perforation (intra-abdominal infection): Lower risk: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole, or ertapenem. Higher risk: piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, or cefepime plus metronidazole. Do not use cefoxitin or cefazolin plus metronidazole routinely (SIS 2017)
  • Duration: Ischemic, nonperforated bowel: 24 h or less; after adequate source control: 4 days (SIS 2017)

Special Considerations:

  • Sigmoid volvulus: If stable without peritonitis or perforation, endoscopic detorsion and decompression (ASCRS 2021 rec 3, strong; success 60-95%), then sigmoid colectomy in the same admission (rec 5, strong; recurrence 43-75% without). Endoscopic fixation if surgery is prohibitive (rec 7, weak)
  • Cecal volvulus: No endoscopic reduction (ASCRS 2021 rec 8, strong); segmental resection (rec 9, strong)
  • Malignant LBO: Practical: stent as bridge to surgery, or palliation if metastatic
  • SBO with no prior abdominal surgery: Practical: high suspicion for hernia or mass; low threshold for surgical exploration
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Adhesions = #1 cause of SBO: About 70% (EAST 2012). Nonoperative management is safe without peritonitis or deterioration (EAST 2012 Level 1)
  • Never-operated abdomen: Practical: SBO without prior surgery suggests hernia (check all hernial orifices), malignancy, or Crohn's
  • Vomiting pattern: Early vomiting = proximal obstruction, late/absent vomiting = distal or large bowel obstruction
  • Gastrografin challenge: Contrast in the colon by 24 h predicts resolution (WSES 2018, non-US); also shortens stay (EAST 2012 Level 2)
  • "Rule of 3-6-9": Practical: normal small bowel under 3 cm, colon under 6 cm, cecum under 9 cm. In pseudo-obstruction, perforation risk rises with cecum over 12 cm (ASCRS 2021)
  • Closed-loop obstruction: Practical: both ends obstructed, rapid progression to ischemia (e.g., volvulus, internal hernia)
  • Strangulated bowel: Peritonitis or deterioration (fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia, acidosis, continuous pain) requires timely surgery (EAST 2012 Level 1)
  • LBO without prior surgery: Obstructing cancer is a leading mechanical cause (ASCRS 2021); needs colonoscopy or surgery for diagnosis and treatment
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: septic shock or vasopressor need, peritonitis with hemodynamic instability, severe metabolic acidosis, multiorgan dysfunction, respiratory failure (aspiration, abdominal compartment syndrome), postoperative complications
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Conservative management successful:
  • Resolution of symptoms (pain, nausea, vomiting)
  • Passing flatus and/or stool
  • Tolerating regular diet without N/V
  • Non-distended, soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds
  • No peritoneal signs
  • Post-operative (if surgery):
  • Return of bowel function
  • Tolerating diet, ambulating
  • Adequate pain control on PO meds
  • Surgical follow-up arranged
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Ondansetron, 💊 Morphine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Hypokalemia
