71. OPIOID OVERDOSE/WITHDRAWAL

Opioid Toxicity • Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

OPIOID OVERDOSE - "Classic Triad":

  • CNS depression: Altered mental status, drowsiness, coma (GCS <15)
  • Respiratory depression: Bradypnea (RR <12), shallow breathing, hypoxia, apnea
  • Miosis: Pinpoint pupils (2-3mm) - highly specific but not 100% sensitive

Additional Features:

  • Cardiovascular: Bradycardia, hypotension (usually mild)
  • Decreased bowel sounds
  • Hypothermia
  • Pulmonary edema: Can occur, especially with heroin ("heroin lung")
  • Track marks: May be present in IV drug users

Common Agents:

  • Prescription: Oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, hydromorphone (Dilaudid), fentanyl, methadone, tramadol
  • Illicit: Heroin, illicit fentanyl (50-100× more potent than morphine), carfentanil
  • Special concern: Fentanyl-laced pills ("pressed pills" sold as oxycodone/Xanax) → epidemic of overdose deaths

Exceptions to Miosis:

  • Meperidine (Demerol): Can cause mydriasis
  • Tramadol: Serotonergic properties, may have normal/dilated pupils
  • Severe hypoxia/anoxia: Pupils dilate due to brain injury
  • Co-ingestion with anticholinergics: Dilated pupils

OPIOID WITHDRAWAL - Miserable but NOT Life-Threatening:

  • Timing: Onset 6-12 hours after last short-acting opioid (heroin), 24-48 hours for long-acting (methadone)
  • Peak: 36-72 hours, duration 5-10 days
  • Symptoms ("flu-like"):
    • Early: Anxiety, restlessness, yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, diaphoresis, mydriasis
    • Late: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, myalgias, piloerection ("goose flesh"), tachycardia, HTN, fever
  • Key: Uncomfortable but NOT dangerous (unlike alcohol/benzo withdrawal which CAN be fatal)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

OVERDOSE - Clinical Diagnosis:

  • Don't wait for confirmatory testing - TREAT clinically!
  • Essential: Vitals (RR most important), pulse ox, glucose, ECG
  • ABG/VBG: If severe respiratory depression (assess pCO₂, hypercapnia)
  • Labs: CBC, CMP, lactate, acetaminophen level (co-ingestion common with prescription opioids), salicylate, ethanol
  • Urine drug screen:
    • Often positive but NOT required for treatment
    • Caveats: Fentanyl/methadone often NOT detected on standard screens. Screens typically only detect morphine, codeine, hydromorphone
    • Synthetic opioids require special testing
  • CXR: If hypoxia persists after naloxone (pulmonary edema, aspiration)
  • Head CT: If no response to naloxone, concern for trauma/intracranial pathology

WITHDRAWAL - Clinical Diagnosis + Assessment:

  • COWS (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale): Objective scoring tool
    • Score 5-12 = mild, 13-24 = moderate, 25-36 = moderately severe, >36 = severe
    • Assesses: VS, GI upset, tremor, restlessness, pupil size, anxiety, gooseflesh, etc.
  • Labs usually not needed unless concern for complications
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

OPIOID OVERDOSE:

Immediate Resuscitation:

  • Airway/Breathing:
    • Bag-valve-mask ventilation if apneic/severe respiratory depression
    • Supplemental O₂ to maintain SpO₂ >90%
    • Consider intubation if no response to naloxone or prolonged
  • IV access, monitor

🎯 NALOXONE (Narcan) - Opioid Antagonist:

  • Indications: Respiratory depression (RR <12) OR coma/unresponsive from suspected opioid
  • IV/IM/SC dosing:
    • Start: 0.04-0.4 mg IV, titrate up by 0.4 mg q2-3min until respiratory drive restored
    • Goal: Adequate respiration (RR >12), NOT full reversal/consciousness
    • Maximum: 10 mg (if no response after 10 mg, reconsider diagnosis)
  • Intranasal: 4 mg (1 spray) in each nostril, repeat q2-3min PRN (easier for EMS/lay public)
  • IM/SC: 0.4-2 mg, repeat q2-3min PRN (if no IV access)
  • ⚠️ Suspected illicit fentanyl (pressed pills, fentanyl-laced supply): Start with higher doses — 2 mg IV/IM or 4 mg IN per nostril. Repeat every 2-3 min. Fentanyl's high receptor affinity may require cumulative doses of 10+ mg. Do not stop at standard dose if no response — keep escalating and repeating.
  • Duration: 30-90 minutes (shorter than most opioids!) → re-sedation common
    • Especially with long-acting opioids (methadone, sustained-release formulations, fentanyl)
    • May need continuous naloxone infusion (2/3 of effective bolus dose per hour)
  • Caution: Naloxone precipitates acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients (uncomfortable but not dangerous). Use lowest effective dose

Observation Period:

  • Short-acting opioids (heroin, oxycodone): Observe 4-6 hours after last naloxone dose
  • Long-acting opioids (methadone, fentanyl, sustained-release): Admit for 24 hours monitoring
  • Watch for re-sedation, respiratory depression

Post-Overdose Care:

  • Take-home naloxone kit: ALWAYS prescribe intranasal naloxone at discharge + educate patient/family
  • Harm reduction counseling: Never use alone, avoid mixing with benzodiazepines/alcohol, fentanyl test strips
  • Addiction treatment referral: Offer medication-assisted treatment (MAT) - buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone
  • Social work consult

OPIOID WITHDRAWAL TREATMENT:

Symptom Management (Supportive):

  • Clonidine: 0.1-0.2 mg PO q6h PRN (max 0.8 mg/day)
    • α₂-agonist, reduces sympathetic hyperactivity
    • Helps: Anxiety, agitation, tachycardia, HTN, diaphoresis
    • Monitor BP (can cause hypotension)
  • Ondansetron: 4-8 mg IV/PO q8h PRN for N/V
  • Loperamide: 4 mg PO initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day) for diarrhea
  • NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 600-800 mg PO q8h for myalgias
  • Hydroxyzine or promethazine: 25-50 mg q6h PRN for anxiety/insomnia
  • Avoid benzodiazepines (high abuse potential, unless severe anxiety/insomnia)

Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) - PREFERRED Long-Term:

  • Buprenorphine (Suboxone):
    • Partial μ-opioid agonist - treats withdrawal, reduces cravings, low overdose risk
    • Can initiate in ED once patient in moderate withdrawal (COWS ≥8-12)
    • Start: 2-4 mg SL, repeat 2-4 mg q2-4h PRN (max 8-12 mg day 1)
    • Maintenance: 12-16 mg SL daily
    • Requires X-waiver to prescribe outpatient (or prescribe 3-day bridge to clinic)
  • Methadone:
    • Full μ-opioid agonist - highly effective but requires special clinic
    • Start 10-30 mg PO daily, titrate slowly
    • Cannot prescribe for outpatient addiction treatment (only federally-licensed clinics)
  • Naltrexone (Vivitrol):
    • Opioid antagonist - blocks effects if relapse occurs
    • 50 mg PO daily OR 380 mg IM monthly
    • Must be opioid-free ≥7-10 days before starting (will precipitate withdrawal)

Key Principle: MAT (buprenorphine, methadone) is MORE effective than detox alone. Reduces mortality by 50-70%

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Naloxone goal = restore respiration, NOT consciousness: Overtitrating causes severe withdrawal and patient will leave AMA. Just enough to breathe (RR >12)
  • Fentanyl epidemic: Illicit fentanyl now in everything (fake pills, heroin, cocaine). Much more potent → may need higher/repeated naloxone doses
  • Re-sedation is common: Naloxone wears off faster than most opioids. Long-acting opioids (methadone, fentanyl patch) require prolonged monitoring
  • Withdrawal uncomfortable but NOT deadly: Unlike alcohol/benzo withdrawal. Can't die from opioid withdrawal (though it feels like you might!)
  • Give naloxone kit at discharge: ~50% of OD patients will overdose again within 1 year. Take-home naloxone saves lives
  • Start buprenorphine in the ED: Best time to engage patients in treatment. Can bridge to outpatient clinic with 3-day supply
  • Urine drug screen limitations: Standard screens miss fentanyl, methadone, synthetic opioids. Clinical diagnosis >> lab test
  • Stigma kills: Opioid use disorder is a medical disease, not a moral failure. Use non-judgmental language, offer treatment
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Overdose:
  • Persistent respiratory depression despite naloxone
  • Need for intubation
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Severe co-ingestion (benzos, alcohol)
  • Need for continuous naloxone infusion
  • Withdrawal:
  • Usually does NOT require ICU
  • Exception: Severe co-morbidities, elderly with cardiac disease
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Overdose:
  • Normal mental status and respiratory rate
  • Observed 4-6 hours (short-acting) or 24 hours (long-acting) after last naloxone
  • No re-sedation
  • MUST provide: Take-home naloxone kit + training
  • Harm reduction counseling completed
  • Addiction treatment referral offered/accepted
  • Started on buprenorphine (if appropriate)
  • Withdrawal:
  • Symptoms controlled with outpatient meds
  • Tolerating PO, hydrated
  • Discharge Rx: Clonidine, ondansetron, loperamide
  • MAT arranged (buprenorphine or methadone clinic)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Naloxone
↑ Back to Table of Contents

72. ACUTE APPENDICITIS

RLQ Pain • Periumbilical → RLQ Migration • Surgical Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic History: Periumbilical pain migrating to RLQ over 12-24 hours, anorexia, nausea/vomiting (typically after pain onset)

Physical Exam:

  • McBurney's point tenderness: 1/3 distance from ASIS to umbilicus
  • Rovsing sign: RLQ pain with LLQ palpation
  • Psoas sign: Pain with right hip extension (retrocecal appendix)
  • Obturator sign: Pain with internal rotation of flexed right hip (pelvic appendix)
  • Rebound/guarding: Suggests peritonitis (perforation)

Atypical Presentations:

  • Elderly: Blunted symptoms, often present with perforation
  • Pregnant: Pain may be RUQ/flank (displaced appendix)
  • Retrocecal: Flank pain, less peritoneal signs
  • Pelvic: Suprapubic pain, urinary symptoms
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Practical: Alvarado Score (MANTRELS):

  • Migration of pain to RLQ (1)
  • Anorexia (1)
  • Nausea/vomiting (1)
  • Tenderness in RLQ (2)
  • Rebound pain (1)
  • Elevated temperature >37.3°C (1)
  • Leukocytosis >10,000 (2)
  • Shift to left >75% neutrophils (1)
  • Interpretation (Practical): 0-4 low risk, 5-6 intermediate, 7-10 high risk. WSES 2025 (non-US) suggests the AIR, AAS, or PAS scores to rule out low-risk patients and select intermediate-risk patients for imaging or observation (recs 1, 2, conditional); SAGES 2024 names no score

Labs: Practical: CBC (leukocytosis with left shift), CMP, lipase, UA (rule out UTI; mild pyuria can occur from an inflamed appendix), pregnancy test (all women of childbearing age)

Imaging:

  • Ultrasound: Reasonable first-line study (SAGES 2024, expert opinion); first-line in children and adolescents (WSES 2025 rec 3.2)
  • CT: CT and MRI are the most definitive studies (SAGES 2024). Adults: low-dose CT (under 2-3 mSv) preferred where available; CT over US with obesity or older age; CT remains the standard when the presentation is unclear (WSES 2025 recs 1, 3.1, 3.3, 3.4)
  • MRI: In pregnancy if US is negative or inconclusive and suspicion persists (WSES 2025 rec 4, conditional, moderate)
  • Findings (Practical): Appendix over 6 mm, noncompressible, periappendiceal fat stranding, appendicolith, abscess
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Surgical Consultation: URGENT. Operative management suggested for uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis (SAGES 2024, conditional)

Pre-operative:

  • NPO
  • IV fluids: Resuscitate if dehydrated
  • Uncomplicated: Single preoperative prophylactic dose; no further antibiotics while awaiting surgery within 24 h and none postoperatively (WSES 2025 recs 15.1, 17.1). SIS 2017: no more than 24 h for nonperforated appendicitis (1-A). Practical: cefazolin plus metronidazole, or cefoxitin, as prophylaxis
  • Complicated or perforated: Preoperative prophylaxis plus therapeutic antibiotics while awaiting surgery (WSES 2025 rec 16.1, strong). Empiric agents per SIS 2017: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole, or ertapenem (lower risk); piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem, or cefepime plus metronidazole (higher risk)
  • Postoperative duration, complicated: Short course after source control: 4 days (SIS 2017, 1-A; STOP-IT, cited by SAGES 2024); 2-3 days suggested by WSES 2025 (rec 19.1)
  • Pain control: IV opioids; they do not increase diagnostic or treatment-decision errors in acute abdominal pain (Cochrane 2011)

Operative Approach:

  • Laparoscopic appendectomy: Preferred approach (WSES 2025 rec 9.1); no routine drains (SAGES 2024; WSES 2025)
  • Timing: Immediate (under 12 h) or delayed (over 12 h) both acceptable (SAGES 2024, conditional, very low); within 24 h of admission (WSES 2025 rec 9.1, strong)
  • Periappendiceal abscess: Age under 35: early laparoscopic appendectomy (WSES 2025 rec 13.1). Age 35 or older: initial nonoperative management, then interval appendectomy at 6-12 weeks because of neoplasm risk up to 14.3% (WSES 2025 recs 13.1, 14.1, strong). SAGES 2024 suggests interval appendectomy after nonoperative treatment of complicated appendicitis in adults (pooled neoplasm 14%)

Non-operative Management: SAGES 2024 suggests surgery but accepts antibiotics if the patient accepts recurrence risk; 1-year success 58-75%, lower with an appendicolith. WSES 2025 (non-US) suggests antibiotics as an alternative for uncomplicated appendicitis with monitoring and shared decision-making (rec 5.1, conditional, moderate)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Anorexia: Practical: if the patient is hungry, reconsider the diagnosis
  • Vomiting follows pain: Practical: if vomiting precedes pain, consider gastroenteritis
  • Don't delay imaging: Practical: delayed diagnosis, not CT, leads to perforation
  • Pain medication doesn't mask diagnosis: Opioids do not increase diagnostic error (Cochrane 2011); give analgesia while awaiting imaging
  • Consider in all RLQ pain: Including women with ovarian pathology as differential
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Metronidazole
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Urinalysis
↑ Back to Table of Contents

73. ACUTE CHOLANGITIS

Biliary Infection • Charcot's Triad • Biliary Drainage Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Charcot's Triad (very specific; sensitivity 50-70% in older series, 21-26% in recent multicenter series; not usable as diagnostic criteria, TG18):

  • 1. Fever/chills
  • 2. RUQ pain
  • 3. Jaundice

Practical: Reynolds' Pentad (severe/suppurative cholangitis):

  • Charcot's triad PLUS:
  • 4. Altered mental status
  • 5. Hypotension

Risk Factors: Choledocholithiasis (most common), biliary strictures, malignancy, prior ERCP/biliary stents, parasites (endemic areas)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) Diagnostic Criteria (non-US; no US criteria):

  • A. Systemic inflammation: Fever over 38°C and/or shaking chills, OR labs: WBC under 4 or over 10 (×1,000/μL), CRP 1 mg/dL or more
  • B. Cholestasis: Jaundice (total bilirubin 2 mg/dL or more), OR ALP, GGT, AST, or ALT over 1.5× ULN
  • C. Imaging: Biliary dilation, OR evidence of etiology (stricture, stone, stent)
  • Definite: one item each in A, B, and C | Suspected: one in A plus one in B or C. RUQ or upper abdominal pain and prior biliary disease, procedures, or stents support the diagnosis (TG18)

Labs:

  • CBC (leukocytosis), CMP, LFTs (cholestatic pattern: elevated ALP, GGT, direct bili)
  • Practical: blood cultures before antibiotics
  • Practical: lipase to rule out pancreatitis

Imaging:

  • RUQ ultrasound: First test; highly specific but insensitive: 42% for a dilated CBD and 38% for duct stones (TG18). Practical: CBD over 6 mm (over 8 mm after cholecystectomy) suggests dilation
  • MRI/MRCP: Recommended when US or CT leaves the diagnosis or cause uncertain (TG18, level C)
  • CT: Shows duct dilation and causes of stenosis; stone detection only 25-90% sensitive (TG18)

Severity Grading (TG18, non-US):

  • Grade III (Severe): Dysfunction of any one organ: hypotension needing dopamine 5 μg/kg/min or more or any norepinephrine; disturbed consciousness; PaO2/FiO2 under 300; oliguria or creatinine over 2.0 mg/dL; INR over 1.5; platelets under 100,000
  • Grade II (Moderate): Any TWO of: WBC over 12,000 or under 4,000; fever 39°C or more; age 75 or older; total bilirubin 5 mg/dL or more; albumin under 0.7× LLN
  • Grade I (Mild): Meets neither; if no response to initial supportive care and antibiotics, early biliary drainage (TG18)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Resuscitation:

  • IV fluids, vasopressors if septic shock
  • Correct coagulopathy only for a reason. Chronic cholestasis or malnutrition: vitamin K can lower the INR (AASLD 2021; card 302); Practical: in obstructive jaundice give it parenterally, since oral absorption needs bile (dose: Drug Reference, Vitamin K). Warfarin: no routine FFP or vitamin K; if reversal is needed, PCC over FFP (ACG-CAG 2022; card 15). Cirrhosis: do not correct the INR before procedures (AASLD 2021); if correction is truly needed, low-volume cryoprecipitate or 4-factor PCC rather than FFP (AASLD 2024 ACLF; card 302). Sphincterotomy bleeding in cholangitis occurs mainly with coagulopathy or ongoing anticoagulant use (ASGE 2021)

Antibiotics (start immediately; SIS 2017):

  • Lower risk: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole (1-A), or ertapenem (1-A)
  • Higher risk (sepsis or septic shock, APACHE II 10 or more): piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, or cefepime plus metronidazole (2-A)
  • Higher risk not on piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem: consider ampicillin or vancomycin for enterococci (2-B); enterococcal risk factors include prior hepatobiliary instrumentation and prior broad-spectrum antibiotics. Vancomycin for MRSA or E. faecium (2-B)
  • Duration: 4 days after adequate source control (SIS 2017, 1-A)

Biliary Drainage (CRITICAL; ASGE 2021):

  • ERCP over percutaneous drainage (PTBD) (rec 1, conditional, very low)
  • Timing: ERCP within 48 h (rec 2, conditional, very low); within 48 h, inpatient and 30-day mortality were about halved in database studies. Septic shock not responding to fluids: consider ERCP within 24 h
  • Extent: Sphincterotomy and stone removal with drainage rather than stent alone (rec 3, conditional, low), unless too unstable for more extensive therapy
  • TG18 (non-US): Grade I patients not responding to initial treatment need early drainage
  • If ERCP not feasible: PTBD is acceptable in critically ill patients not suited for ERCP; EUS-guided drainage is not well studied in cholangitis (ASGE 2021)

Cholecystectomy: Practical: if gallstone etiology, during the same admission or soon after once infection is controlled

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Cholangitis is a biliary sepsis: Source control (drainage) is as important as antibiotics
  • Charcot's triad has low sensitivity: 21-26% in recent multicenter series; use TG18 criteria instead (TG18)
  • Ascending infection: Practical: bacteria ascend from the duodenum when bile flow is obstructed
  • CBD stones cause cholangitis, GB stones cause cholecystitis: Different pathophysiology
  • Drainage saves lives: Surgical management carries 10-40% mortality; ERCP decompresses with markedly less morbidity and mortality (ASGE 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Amp-Sulbactam
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Bilirubin, 🔬 Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
🧫 ABX COMPANION Cunha Empiric Framework

74. ACUTE CHOLECYSTITIS

Gallbladder Inflammation • RUQ Pain • Murphy's Sign
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Presentation (Practical):

  • RUQ/epigastric pain lasting >6 hours (differentiates from biliary colic)
  • Fever, nausea, vomiting
  • Often precipitated by fatty meal
  • May radiate to right shoulder/scapula (referred pain)

Physical Exam:

  • Murphy's sign: Inspiratory arrest with RUQ palpation. Sensitivity 20.5%, specificity 87.5% (TG18, non-US); the TG criteria are more accurate than Murphy's sign alone
  • RUQ tenderness, possible palpable GB
  • Guarding (suggests perforation/gangrene)

Calculous vs Acalculous (Practical):

  • Calculous (most cases): Gallstone impacted in cystic duct
  • Acalculous: ICU patients, burns, TPN, sepsis, vasculitis; higher mortality (see card 301)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Tokyo Guidelines 2018 Diagnostic Criteria (non-US; no US criteria):

  • A. Local signs: Murphy's sign, RUQ mass/pain/tenderness
  • B. Systemic signs: Fever, elevated CRP, elevated WBC
  • C. Imaging: Findings characteristic of acute cholecystitis
  • Suspected: one item in A + one in B | Definite: A + B + C. Exclude acute hepatitis, other acute abdominal disease, and chronic cholecystitis (TG18)

Labs:

  • Practical: CBC, CMP, LFTs (marked elevation suggests a CBD stone), lipase. Total bilirubin is needed to grade Grade III risk (TG18 flowchart)

Imaging:

  • RUQ Ultrasound: Preferred first test; sensitivity 81%, specificity 83% (TG18 meta-analysis)
  • Findings: Wall thickening 4 mm or more, gallbladder enlargement (long axis 8 cm or more, short axis 4 cm or more), stones or debris, pericholecystic fluid, linear shadows in pericholecystic fat (TG18)
  • HIDA scan: Higher diagnostic yield than US in every comparative study, but US is preferred for cost and availability (TG18)
  • CT or MRI: If US is nondiagnostic or gangrenous cholecystitis is suspected (TG18); MRI sensitivity 85%, specificity 81%. CT recommended for suspected emphysematous cholecystitis (rec 2, level D)

Severity Grading (TG18, non-US):

  • Grade I (Mild): Meets neither Grade II nor III; healthy patient, mild local inflammation, low-risk cholecystectomy
  • Grade II (Moderate): Any ONE of: WBC over 18,000; palpable tender RUQ mass; symptoms over 72 h; marked local inflammation (gangrenous, emphysematous, pericholecystic or hepatic abscess, biliary peritonitis)
  • Grade III (Severe): Dysfunction of any one organ: hypotension needing dopamine 5 μg/kg/min or more or any norepinephrine; decreased consciousness; PaO2/FiO2 under 300; oliguria or creatinine over 2.0 mg/dL; INR over 1.5; platelets under 100,000
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Initial Management:

  • NPO
  • IV fluids
  • Pain control: Analgesics with fluids, electrolyte correction, and antimicrobials as initial treatment (TG18 flowchart). Practical: NSAIDs (ketorolac) plus opioids as needed
  • Antiemetics

Antibiotics:

  • Agents (SIS 2017): Lower risk: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole, or ertapenem. Higher risk (sepsis, septic shock, APACHE II 10 or more): piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem, or cefepime plus metronidazole
  • Duration: Acute or gangrenous cholecystitis without perforation: 24 h or less after cholecystectomy (SIS 2017, 1-A); perforation with adequate source control: 4 days (1-A)
  • Practical: continue until cholecystectomy or drainage if surgery is delayed

Cholecystectomy:

  • Laparoscopic over open cholecystectomy (TG18 rec 2, level A). Early surgery for patients who can withstand it, regardless of exactly how long since onset (rec 2, level B); TG13's 72 h rule was dropped
  • Grade I: Early Lap-C if CCI 5 or less and ASA-PS 2 or less; otherwise conservative treatment, then delayed surgery (TG18)
  • Grade II: Early Lap-C at an advanced center if CCI 5 or less and ASA-PS 2 or less (consider open or subtotal cholecystectomy as needed); otherwise conservative treatment and gallbladder drainage (TG18)
  • Grade III: Organ support plus antibiotics. Early Lap-C at an advanced center only if organ failure is favorable (cardiovascular or renal, improving), no negative predictors (neurological or respiratory dysfunction, bilirubin 2 mg/dL or more), CCI 3 or less, and ASA-PS 2 or less; otherwise early or urgent drainage, then delayed Lap-C (TG18)
  • Early vs delayed: In a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs, early surgery had similar bile duct injury, shorter total stay, and lower cost (within 72 h) (TG18)

High-Risk/Poor Surgical Candidates:

  • Percutaneous cholecystostomy (gallbladder drainage): For patients who cannot withstand surgery; surgical risk factors CCI 6 or more or ASA-PS 3 or more (Grades I-II) (TG18 Q5, level C)
  • Timing of interval cholecystectomy after drainage: no consensus (TG18 Q4, level C)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Biliary colic vs cholecystitis: Practical: colic resolves within about 6 h; cholecystitis pain persists
  • Murphy's sign: Specific (87.5%) but insensitive (20.5%) (TG18). Practical: sonographic Murphy's sign is helpful
  • Acalculous cholecystitis: Practical: think of it in ICU patients; low threshold to treat (see card 301)
  • Early surgery is safe: Similar bile duct injury to delayed surgery, shorter stay (TG18 meta-analysis)
  • Emphysematous cholecystitis: Gas-forming infection with a high perforation rate and rapid course; diagnose with CT; Grade II (TG18). Practical: classically clostridial, in diabetics
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Amp-Sulbactam, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Metronidazole
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Blood Cultures

75. ENCEPHALITIS

Brain Parenchymal Inflammation • AMS + Fever • HSV Most Common
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad:

  • 1. Fever
  • 2. Altered mental status (confusion, personality change, decreased LOC)
  • 3. Focal neurologic deficits (seizures, aphasia, hemiparesis, movement disorders)

Distinguishing Features (vs Meningitis):

  • Encephalitis = brain parenchyma involvement → altered mentation, seizures, focal deficits
  • Meningitis = meninges → headache, stiff neck, photophobia
  • Often overlap (meningoencephalitis)

Common Etiologies:

  • HSV-1: Most common sporadic cause. Temporal lobe predilection
  • Arboviruses: West Nile, Eastern equine, St. Louis (summer/fall, mosquito exposure)
  • Enteroviruses: Summer/fall epidemics
  • VZV: Immunocompromised, may have rash
  • Autoimmune: Anti-NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2 (consider if young, psychiatric symptoms)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Lumbar Puncture (ESSENTIAL):

  • CSF profile: Lymphocytic pleocytosis (usually 10-500 WBC), normal-mildly elevated protein, normal glucose
  • HSV PCR: Sensitivity 96%, specificity 99%. SEND ON ALL PATIENTS
  • Viral panel PCR: HSV, VZV, enteroviruses, West Nile, others based on exposure
  • RBC in CSF: Suggests hemorrhagic encephalitis (HSV)
  • Cytology, autoimmune panel: If no infectious cause identified

Imaging:

  • MRI Brain with contrast: Study of choice
  • HSV findings: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in temporal lobes (medial > lateral), insular cortex, cingulate gyrus. Often asymmetric
  • CT: May be normal early; temporal lobe hypodensity seen later

EEG: Periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) in temporal region suggests HSV

Additional Labs: CBC, CMP, HIV test, blood cultures, consider paraneoplastic/autoimmune panel if no infectious cause

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Empiric Therapy (START IMMEDIATELY - do not wait for LP/imaging):

  • Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h: Continue until HSV PCR negative. If HSV+, treat 14-21 days
  • Adjust for renal function
  • Ensure adequate hydration (prevent acyclovir crystalluria/AKI)

If Meningitis Also Suspected:

  • Add empiric bacterial meningitis coverage (ceftriaxone + vancomycin ± ampicillin)
  • Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h if bacterial meningitis suspected (give before or with first abx dose)

Seizure Management:

  • Load levetiracetam 20-30 mg/kg IV if seizures occur
  • Continuous EEG monitoring if persistent AMS

Supportive Care:

  • ICU admission for severe cases
  • Manage cerebral edema (elevate HOB, osmotic therapy if needed)
  • DVT prophylaxis (mechanical preferred if seizures)

Autoimmune Encephalitis:

  • If workup negative for infectious causes, consider autoimmune
  • Treatment: High-dose steroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis
  • Screen for underlying malignancy (ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Treat first, diagnose second: Start acyclovir immediately if encephalitis suspected. HSV mortality untreated 70%, treated <20%
  • HSV PCR can be negative early: If high suspicion, repeat LP in 3-7 days. Continue acyclovir pending repeat
  • Temporal lobe = HSV until proven otherwise: Classic MRI finding
  • West Nile: Flaccid paralysis + encephalitis in summer should raise suspicion
  • Don't forget autoimmune: Young patients with psychiatric symptoms, movement disorders, seizures - think anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Acyclovir, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 IVIG
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 CSF Analysis, 🔬 CMV/EBV Viral Loads, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP
↑ Back to Table of Contents

76. INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE (ICH)

Hypertensive Hemorrhage • Acute Stroke • BP Control Critical
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Presentation:

  • Sudden onset focal neurologic deficit (similar to ischemic stroke)
  • Headache (more common than ischemic stroke)
  • Vomiting, decreased LOC (suggests elevated ICP/larger hemorrhage)
  • Seizures (5-15% at onset)

Cannot Distinguish ICH from Ischemic Stroke Clinically: MUST have imaging

Location-Based Deficits:

  • Basal ganglia/putamen (most common): Contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss
  • Thalamus: Sensory > motor, eyes deviate downward ("looking at nose")
  • Cerebellum: Ataxia, vertigo, nystagmus, can deteriorate rapidly
  • Pons: Quadriparesis, pinpoint pupils, "locked-in" syndrome
  • Lobar: Deficits depend on location (frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal)

Common Causes:

  • Hypertension (60-70%): Deep structures (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum)
  • Cerebral amyloid angiopathy: Elderly, lobar hemorrhages, often recurrent
  • Anticoagulation/coagulopathy
  • Vascular malformations: AVM, cavernous malformation (younger patients)
  • Hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic stroke
  • Tumor, cocaine/sympathomimetics
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging:

  • Non-contrast CT head: First-line. Hyperdense (bright) lesion with surrounding edema
  • CT angiography: "Spot sign" (contrast extravasation) predicts hematoma expansion
  • MRI: Better for underlying lesion (tumor, cavernoma, amyloid angiopathy)
  • Conventional angiography: If vascular malformation suspected

ICH Score (Prognosis):

  • GCS 3-4 (2 pts), GCS 5-12 (1 pt), GCS 13-15 (0 pts)
  • ICH volume ≥30 mL (1 pt)
  • Intraventricular extension (1 pt)
  • Infratentorial origin (1 pt)
  • Age ≥80 (1 pt)
  • 30-day mortality: Score 0 = 0%, Score 5 = 100%

Labs: CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, blood type/screen, CMP, troponin, toxicology screen

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Blood Pressure Management (CRITICAL):

  • Target SBP <140 mmHg: Intensive BP lowering within 6 hours is safe and may improve outcomes (INTERACT2, ATACH-2)
  • Agents: Nicardipine or clevidipine infusion (titratable). Labetalol IV bolus alternative
  • Avoid: Precipitous drops (>60 mmHg in 1 hour)
  • Exception: Avoid aggressive lowering if large infarct with hemorrhagic transformation

Anticoagulation Reversal (URGENT):

  • Warfarin: 4-factor PCC (25-50 units/kg) + Vitamin K 10mg IV. Goal INR <1.4
  • Dabigatran: Idarucizumab 5g IV (if available) or 4-factor PCC
  • Factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban): 4-factor PCC 50 units/kg (or fixed 2,000 units, ACC 2020) or aPCC may be considered (AHA/ASA 2022, 2b). Andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025 (AABB 2025)
  • Heparin: Protamine (1mg per 100 units heparin given in last 2-3 hours)
  • Thrombocytopenia: Platelet transfusion if <100,000

ICP Management:

  • Elevate head of bed 30°
  • Osmotic therapy: Mannitol 1g/kg or hypertonic saline 23.4% 30mL
  • Consider EVD if intraventricular hemorrhage with hydrocephalus
  • Avoid hyperthermia (increases ICP and poor outcomes)

Seizure Prophylaxis:

  • Not routinely recommended (AHA guidelines 2022)
  • Treat clinical seizures; consider continuous EEG if decreased LOC out of proportion to imaging

Surgical Consultation:

  • Cerebellar hemorrhage >3cm: Urgent surgical evacuation (can herniate rapidly)
  • Supratentorial: Consider for superficial lobar hemorrhages, especially if deteriorating
  • Minimally invasive surgery: Emerging option (MISTIE III trial)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • You cannot tell ICH from ischemic stroke without CT: Always image before thrombolytics
  • Hematoma expansion is the enemy: 30-40% expand in first 3-6 hours. BP control and reversal critical
  • Cerebellar hemorrhage is surgical emergency: Small posterior fossa, can herniate quickly
  • SBP <140 is a reasonable target — but individualize: INTERACT2 showed modest benefit from lowering to <140; ATACH-2 showed no overall benefit vs <180, and subgroup data suggested harm in patients with very high baseline SBP aggressively reduced to <140 (higher cardiac/renal adverse events). Current AHA/ASA 2022 guideline: SBP <140 "can be effective" (Class IIa, Level B) for mild-moderate ICH presenting with SBP 150–220. For large ICH or SBP >220 at presentation, a more gradual reduction is prudent — don't reflexively push SBP to 130
  • ICH score is self-fulfilling: Don't withdraw care based solely on score
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Nicardipine, 💊 Labetalol, 💊 Mannitol, 💊 TXA, 💊 Vitamin K, 💊 4-Factor PCC, 💊 Idarucizumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated PT/INR, 🔬 Elevated PTT, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Troponin

77. GI PERFORATION

Surgical Emergency • Free Air • Peritonitis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Presentation:

  • Sudden onset severe abdominal pain
  • Peritoneal signs: Rigidity, rebound tenderness, guarding
  • Fever, tachycardia, hypotension (septic shock)
  • Absent bowel sounds

Location-Based Features:

  • Peptic ulcer (gastric/duodenal): Sudden epigastric pain, may radiate to shoulder (diaphragmatic irritation), NSAIDs/H. pylori history
  • Appendiceal: Initially RLQ, then diffuse
  • Colonic (diverticular, tumor, ischemic): LLQ or diffuse, feculent peritonitis (higher mortality)
  • Small bowel: Trauma, ischemia, foreign body, Crohn's disease

Special Populations:

  • Elderly: May have blunted symptoms, minimal peritoneal signs despite perforation
  • Immunocompromised/steroids: Masked inflammatory response
  • Post-procedure: Colonoscopy, ERCP, endoscopy
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging:

  • CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: Most useful when the diagnosis is uncertain; the standard in high-income settings (WSES 2017, non-US)
  • Findings: Pneumoperitoneum (free air), extraluminal contrast, inflammatory changes at perforation site, abscess
  • Upright CXR: Practical: quick bedside screen for free air under the diaphragm; a negative film does not exclude perforation
  • Left lateral decubitus abdominal XR: If upright not possible

Labs:

  • Practical: CBC, CMP, lactate (elevation suggests ischemia or shock)
  • Practical: type and screen
  • Lipase (rule out pancreatitis)
  • Practical: blood cultures (do not delay antibiotics in sepsis or septic shock)

Free Air DDx:

  • True perforation (most common)
  • Recent surgery/procedure
  • Barotrauma (mechanical ventilation)
  • Extension from pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum
  • Benign pneumatosis (less peritoneal signs)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Resuscitation (Parallel with Surgical Consult):

  • NPO
  • Source control: Within 24 h of diagnosis, more urgently with sepsis or septic shock, by the least invasive adequate approach; temporizing approaches if physiologically unstable (SIS 2017, 2-B, 2-C, 1-B, 2-B)
  • Practical: large-bore IV access, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors for refractory hypotension
  • Practical: NG tube for decompression; Foley catheter for urine output

Antibiotics (Start Immediately):

  • Timing: Within 1 h if sepsis or septic shock (SIS 2017, 2-B); as soon as feasible otherwise (2-C)
  • Agents by risk, not by site (SIS 2017): Lower risk: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole, or ertapenem. Higher risk (sepsis, septic shock, APACHE II 10 or more): piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem, or cefepime plus metronidazole. Consider antifungals in critically ill patients with an upper GI source (2-B)
  • Duration (SIS 2017): Gastroduodenal perforation operated within 24 h: 24 h or less (1-C). Traumatic bowel perforation operated within 12 h: 24 h or less (1-A). Adequate source control: 4 days (1-A). No definitive source control: consider 5-7 days, then reassess (2-C)

Surgical Intervention:

  • Surgery is the treatment of choice for perforated peptic ulcer and small bowel perforation (WSES 2017, non-US, 1A and 1B)
  • Peptic ulcer: Simple closure with or without omental patch for small (under 2 cm) perforations (1A); in one study an omental patch added no benefit over simple closure; laparoscopic repair safe for experienced surgeons (1A) (WSES 2017, non-US)
  • Small bowel: Primary repair of small perforations (WSES 2017, non-US, 1B)
  • Colon: Hartmann procedure for diffuse peritonitis in critically ill patients; if stable, primary resection with anastomosis, with or without diverting stoma (1B); laparoscopic lavage is not the treatment of choice for diffuse peritonitis (1A) (WSES 2017, non-US)
  • Post-colonoscopy perforation with diffuse peritonitis: Immediate surgery, primary repair or resection (WSES 2017, non-US, 1B)

Conservative Management (Select Cases):

  • Non-interventional management only where evidence supports a good outcome (SIS 2017, 1-A). Practical: stable patient, contained (walled-off) perforation, no diffuse peritonitis
  • Practical: NPO, IV antibiotics, close monitoring, early surgery if worsening
  • Abscess: Least invasive adequate source control (SIS 2017, 1-B); diverticular abscess over 3 cm in a stable patient: image-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics (ASCRS 2020, 1B; card 103)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Free air = surgery until proven otherwise: Practical: even small amounts are significant
  • Elderly can have perforation without classic peritonitis: Practical: high index of suspicion; stress ulcer perforation can be silent in sedated ICU patients (WSES 2017)
  • Perforated peptic ulcer mortality: Up to 30% (WSES 2017). Practical: feculent (colonic) peritonitis carries higher bacterial load
  • Sepsis plus free air: Antibiotics within 1 h and urgent source control (SIS 2017)
  • Post-colonoscopy perforation: Consider in any recent procedure; diffuse peritonitis needs immediate surgery (WSES 2017, non-US). Practical: presentation can be delayed
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Cefepime
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR

78. SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE (SAH)

Thunderclap Headache • Aneurysm Rupture • Neurosurgical Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Presentation:

  • "Worst headache of my life" - sudden onset, maximal intensity at onset (thunderclap)
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Neck stiffness (meningismus)
  • Photophobia
  • Syncope at onset (25-50%)
  • Seizures

Sentinel Headache: 20-50% report minor "warning leak" headache days-weeks before major rupture

Hunt and Hess Grade:

  • Grade 1: Mild headache, no neurologic deficit
  • Grade 2: Severe headache, stiff neck, no deficit other than cranial nerve palsy
  • Grade 3: Drowsy, confused, mild focal deficit
  • Grade 4: Stupor, hemiparesis
  • Grade 5: Coma, decerebrate posturing

Causes:

  • Aneurysmal (85%): Most common locations - anterior communicating, posterior communicating, MCA bifurcation
  • Non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic (10%): Benign, venous origin
  • Other (5%): AVM, trauma, vasculitis, coagulopathy
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging:

  • Non-contrast CT head: First-line. Sensitivity 95-100% within 6 hours, decreases over time
  • Look for: Hyperdensity in subarachnoid space (basilar cisterns, Sylvian fissures, interhemispheric fissure)
  • CT Angiography: If CT positive, obtain immediately to identify aneurysm (sensitivity 95-100%)

Lumbar Puncture:

  • Indicated if: CT negative but clinical suspicion high
  • Wait 6-12 hours from headache onset (allows RBC lysis → xanthochromia)
  • Positive findings: Elevated RBCs (not clearing from tube 1 to tube 4), xanthochromia (yellow CSF on visual inspection or spectrophotometry)
  • Xanthochromia: Bilirubin from RBC breakdown. Most reliable indicator of true SAH vs traumatic tap

Ottawa SAH Rule (for clinical decision-making):

  • Investigate for SAH if thunderclap headache + any of: Age ≥40, neck pain/stiffness, witnessed LOC, onset with exertion, limited neck flexion
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Initial Stabilization:

  • ABCs: Intubate if decreased LOC (GCS ≤8)
  • BP control: SBP <160 mmHg before aneurysm secured (prevent rebleeding)
  • Pain control: Avoid hypertensive spikes (use short-acting opioids)
  • Seizure prophylaxis: Often given (levetiracetam), though controversial
  • Stool softeners: Avoid Valsalva

Aneurysm Treatment (Within 24-72 hours):

  • Endovascular coiling: Preferred for many aneurysms (less invasive)
  • Surgical clipping: For certain locations/morphologies
  • Goal: Secure aneurysm before rebleeding (highest risk day 0-1)

Prevention of Complications:

  • Vasospasm (peak days 4-14):
    • Nimodipine 60mg PO/NG q4h for 21 days (only proven agent to improve outcomes)
    • Monitor with TCDs or CTA
    • Treat symptomatic vasospasm: Induced hypertension, endovascular intervention
  • Hydrocephalus: External ventricular drain (EVD) if needed
  • Hyponatremia: Common (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting). Monitor sodium closely
  • DVT prophylaxis: Mechanical first, then chemical after aneurysm secured
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • "Worst headache of life" = SAH until proven otherwise: Always investigate
  • CT sensitivity drops over time: ~100% at 6hr, ~50% at 7 days. LP needed if CT negative and high suspicion
  • Nimodipine is neuroprotective, not BP control: Continue even if hypotensive
  • Rebleeding is catastrophic: Mortality 70%. Secure aneurysm early
  • Vasospasm kills in the second week: Monitor closely days 4-14
  • Sentinel headache: Mild headaches preceding SAH are often missed. High index of suspicion
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Nicardipine, 💊 Mannitol, 💊 Labetalol, 💊 Fosphenytoin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated PT/INR, 🔬 Elevated PTT, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 CSF Analysis, 🔬 Elevated Troponin

79. ESOPHAGEAL SPASM

Dysphagia • Chest Pain • Normal Endoscopy • Manometry Diagnosis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Dysphagia and/or non-cardiac chest pain; these symptoms are what make a manometric spastic or hypercontractile pattern clinically relevant (CCv4.0). Motility disorders can cause squeezing retrosternal pain, often with dysphagia, and history often cannot separate esophageal from cardiac pain (AHA/ACC 2021). Practical: triggers include hot or cold liquids and stress.

  • Symptoms:
    • Practical: dysphagia is intermittent, to solids and liquids
    • Chest pain: squeezing retrosternal pain (AHA/ACC 2021); Practical: may radiate to back, jaw, or arms
    • Practical: triggers include hot or cold liquids, rapid eating, emotional stress
    • Practical: episodes last seconds to minutes, occasionally hours
    • Relief with nitroglycerin does not separate esophageal from cardiac pain and should not be used as a diagnostic criterion (AHA/ACC 2021)
  • Types:
    • Distal Esophageal Spasm (DES): premature (spastic) contractions with normal EGJ relaxation (CCv4.0)
    • Hypercontractile Esophagus: excessive peristaltic vigor without mechanical obstruction; jackhammer esophagus is one subgroup (CCv4.0)
    • Type III (spastic) Achalasia: premature contractions with impaired EGJ relaxation and no peristalsis; this is achalasia, treat per the achalasia section below (CCv4.0)
    • Nutcracker esophagus is not a CCv4.0 diagnosis; use the hypercontractile criteria
  • Associated Conditions: Opioid use (associated with type III achalasia; CCv4.0). GERD is the most likely cause of recurring unexplained esophageal chest pain (AHA/ACC 2021)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Evaluation:

  • Rule Out Cardiac First: ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, high-sensitivity troponin preferred (AHA/ACC 2021). In recurrent chest pain without a cardiac or pulmonary cause, evaluation for GI causes is reasonable (AHA/ACC 2021, COR 2a)
  • Upper Endoscopy (before manometry): Mechanical obstruction must be excluded; it precludes a CCv4.0 diagnosis (CCv4.0). When an esophageal cause is suspected, consider upper endoscopy; dysphagia, odynophagia, GI bleeding, unexplained iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, or recurrent vomiting merit early evaluation, usually within 2 weeks; eosinophilic esophagitis is diagnosed by biopsy (AHA/ACC 2021). If achalasia is suspected, endoscopy rules out pseudoachalasia from an obstructing mass; significant short-term weight loss in an older patient raises that concern (ACG 2020)
  • Barium Esophagram: Practical: "corkscrew" or "rosary bead" appearance supports spasm; a normal study does not exclude it. Timed barium esophagram (TBE) is the supportive test when manometry is equivocal for achalasia or outflow obstruction (CCv4.0)

Definitive Testing:

  • High-Resolution Manometry (HRM) Defines the Diagnosis: Chicago Classification v4.0 (CCv4.0, international working group; no US society guideline defines these disorders)
    • Distal Esophageal Spasm: normal median integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) and 20% or more premature contractions; premature = distal latency under 4.5 s with distal contractile integral (DCI) 450 mmHg·s·cm or more (CCv4.0)
    • Hypercontractile Esophagus: normal median IRP and 20% or more hypercontractile supine swallows (DCI over 8,000 mmHg·s·cm); diagnose only when achalasia and DES criteria are not met and mechanical obstruction has been carefully ruled out (CCv4.0)
    • Abnormal median IRP with 20% or more premature contractions: no peristalsis = type III achalasia; with peristalsis = inconclusive (EGJ outflow obstruction with spastic features if EGJOO criteria are met), and clinically relevant EGJOO requires TBE and/or functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) support (CCv4.0)
    • Clinically relevant DES or hypercontractile esophagus requires dysphagia or non-cardiac chest pain plus a conclusive manometric diagnosis; the pattern alone may be clinically irrelevant (CCv4.0)
    • Study off opioids if possible, timing the stop by half-life (CCv4.0)
  • pH Monitoring: If endoscopy is normal and symptoms persist despite a trial of acid suppression, consider esophageal function testing and pH monitoring (AHA/ACC 2021)
  • Labs: Practical: usually normal; TSH if thyroid dysfunction suspected
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

First-Line: Conservative Medical Therapy (no US guideline gives drug doses for DES or hypercontractile esophagus):

  • Approach: Medical therapy before endoscopic or surgical intervention, with caution about treating contractile vigor as the endpoint (CCv4.0, hypercontractile esophagus). In nonachalasia spastic disorders, POEM is considered only after less invasive approaches are exhausted (AGA 2024)
  • Calcium Channel Blockers:
    • Practical: diltiazem 30-60 mg PO before meals, TID-QID
    • Practical: nifedipine (immediate-release) 10-30 mg before meals; ACG 2020 lists nifedipine 10-30 mg sublingual before meals for achalasia
  • Nitrates:
    • Practical: isosorbide dinitrate 5-10 mg SL before meals (ACG 2020 lists 5 mg SL before meals for achalasia)
    • Practical: isosorbide mononitrate 30-60 mg PO daily
    • Never with sildenafil or another PDE5 inhibitor: the combination is contraindicated (FDA label)
  • Side Effects: Short action (30-120 minutes) means multiple daily doses, with headache, hypotension, and pedal edema (ACG 2020, achalasia)
  • PPI Therapy: If a GERD component; Practical: omeprazole 20 mg PO daily, as on card 149

Second-Line Therapy (no guideline source):

  • Tricyclic Antidepressants:
    • Practical: imipramine 25-50 mg PO qHS (pain modulation)
  • Trazodone (serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor; not a TCA):
    • Practical: 100-150 mg PO qHS (pain modulation)
  • Phosphodiesterase-5 Inhibitors: Practical: sildenafil 50 mg PO before meals (limited data). Contraindicated with nitrates in any form, including PRN sublingual nitroglycerin (FDA label)
  • Peppermint Oil: Practical: non-enteric-coated preparation before meals; enteric-coated capsules are designed to release beyond the esophagus

Interventional Therapy (Refractory Spasm):

  • Botulinum Toxin Injection: Practical: injection into the distal esophageal body; relief is temporary
  • Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM):
    • Nonachalasia spastic disorders: comprehensive evaluation with symptom correlation; evidence for POEM is limited, so consider it only case by case after less invasive approaches are exhausted (AGA 2024)
    • Optimal myotomy length is not established; intraprocedural FLIP may help tailor it (AGA 2024)
  • Surgical Myotomy: Practical: rarely used

If HRM Shows Achalasia (Including Type III): Definitive Therapy

  • Types I and II: POEM, laparoscopic Heller myotomy (LHM), and pneumatic dilation (PD) are all effective; choose by shared decision making based on patient and disease characteristics, preference, and local expertise (ACG 2020; AGA 2024). SAGES 2024: POEM conditionally favored over PD; POEM with appropriate PPI use or LHM with fundoplication are both options.
  • Type III: POEM should be considered the preferred treatment (AGA 2024; SAGES 2024). ACG 2020 recommends tailored POEM or LHM over PD (strong).
  • Pneumatic Dilation: Graded 3.0, 3.5, then 4.0 cm balloons; good to excellent relief in 50-93%. Perforation median 1.9% (range 0-16%) in experienced hands, so every PD candidate must also be a surgical candidate (ACG 2020). In men under 45, starting PD at 3.5 cm, LHM, or POEM may be considered first (ACG 2020).
  • Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy: Add a Dor or Toupet fundoplication to control reflux (ACG 2020). Symptom improvement averaged 89% across 39 laparoscopic series (ACG 2020).
  • POEM: Symptom improvement comparable to LHM, with more post-procedure GERD than LHM with fundoplication or PD (ACG 2020). Strongly consider acid suppression after POEM and monitor all patients for GERD (AGA 2024).
  • Botulinum Toxin: First-line for patients unfit for definitive therapy (ACG 2020, strong): 100 units above the squamocolumnar junction; relief falls from 70% at 3 months to about 41% at 12 months (ACG 2020).
  • Medical (Nitrates/CCB): Least effective; only for patients who cannot undergo definitive therapy and have failed botulinum toxin (ACG 2020).

Achalasia Treatment Selection: Subtype guides prognosis and choice: type II has very good outcomes with any therapy; type III needs a longer myotomy (ACG 2020). Practical: refer to a center with motility and POEM expertise.

Lifestyle Modifications:

  • Practical: Avoid triggers: Very hot/cold foods, carbonated beverages, rapid eating
  • Practical: Small, frequent meals
  • Practical: Stress reduction techniques
  • Practical: Avoid late-night eating
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Cardiac Mimicry: Exclude cardiac causes first. About 10-20% of outpatients with chest pain have a GI cause. Relief with nitroglycerin is not diagnostic of ischemia and should not be used as a diagnostic criterion, because esophageal spasm responds comparably (AHA/ACC 2021).
  • Pattern Is Not Disease: DES and hypercontractile patterns are clinically relevant only with dysphagia or non-cardiac chest pain plus a conclusive manometric diagnosis (CCv4.0). CCv4.0 advises caution in treating contractile vigor as an endpoint.
  • GERD Connection: GERD is the most likely cause of recurring unexplained esophageal chest pain. Without alarm symptoms, an empiric acid-suppression trial may be reasonable; if endoscopy is normal and symptoms persist, consider esophageal function testing and pH monitoring (AHA/ACC 2021). Suspected GERD that does not respond to acid suppression should be evaluated for achalasia (ACG 2020, strong).
  • Manometry Timing: Perform HRM after a careful index endoscopy (CCv4.0). The CCv4.0 protocol asks for a 4-hour fast and does not require stopping PPIs; Practical: off-PPI testing applies to reflux monitoring. Requires a motility lab.
  • Natural History: Practical: if dysphagia progresses or weight loss develops, re-evaluate for achalasia or an obstructing lesion.
  • Medications: Opioids are associated with type III achalasia; study off opioids if possible (CCv4.0). Ask about NSAIDs, potassium supplements, iron, and bisphosphonates in suspected esophageal chest pain (AHA/ACC 2021); Practical: these cause pill esophagitis, not spasm.
  • Corkscrew Sign: Practical: classic barium finding, but a normal barium study does not exclude spasm; HRM makes the diagnosis (CCv4.0).
  • POEM Is Not First-Line for Spasm: In nonachalasia spastic disorders, evidence for POEM is limited; consider it case by case only after less invasive approaches are exhausted. In type III achalasia, POEM should be considered the preferred treatment (AGA 2024).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: Severe chest pain unresponsive to medical management
  • Practical: acute coronary syndrome not yet excluded (manage as possible ACS)
  • Practical: Significant dehydration or inability to tolerate oral intake
  • Practical: Hemodynamic instability
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Pain controlled on oral medications
  • Practical: Able to tolerate oral intake without dysphagia
  • Practical: Cardiac causes excluded (negative troponin, normal ECG)
  • Practical: Follow-up arranged with GI/primary care
  • Practical: prescription for a calcium channel blocker or nitrate if used; never a nitrate with a PDE5 inhibitor (FDA label)
  • Practical: Patient educated on trigger avoidance and medication use
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Diltiazem, 💊 Isosorbide
