80. GASTRITIS / GASTRIC EROSIONS

Epigastric Pain • NSAID Use • H. pylori • Endoscopic Diagnosis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Dyspepsia with epigastric pain, nausea, and early satiety. May be asymptomatic or present with upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) if erosive/hemorrhagic.

  • Symptoms:
    • Epigastric pain/burning: Postprandial or fasting
    • Nausea/vomiting: May have coffee-ground emesis
    • Early satiety and bloating
    • Anorexia and weight loss (chronic cases)
    • GI bleeding: Melena, hematemesis (if erosive)
  • Types of Gastritis:
    • Erosive (Acute): NSAIDs, alcohol, stress, bile reflux
    • Non-Erosive (Chronic): H. pylori, autoimmune, eosinophilic
    • Hemorrhagic: Stress-related mucosal disease (SRMD) in ICU
    • Atrophic: Chronic H. pylori or autoimmune (pernicious anemia)
  • Risk Factors:
    • NSAIDs/aspirin
    • H. pylori infection (chronic gastritis develops in all who do not clear the infection; ACG 2024)
    • Alcohol (dose-dependent mucosal injury)
    • Stress: Critical illness, burns, trauma, post-surgical
    • Bile reflux (post-gastrectomy)
    • Autoimmune (pernicious anemia, type 1 DM, thyroiditis)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Labs:

  • CBC: Anemia (acute blood loss or chronic B12 deficiency in atrophic gastritis)
  • BMP: Assess for dehydration, renal function
  • If Bleeding: Type & screen, coagulation studies

H. pylori Testing (ACG 2024):

  • Who to Test and Treat (Table 4): Active or prior peptic ulcer; uninvestigated dyspepsia under age 60 without alarm features (age 45-50 in groups at high gastric cancer risk); functional dyspepsia; long-term NSAID use or starting long-term low-dose aspirin; unexplained iron deficiency anemia; ITP; MALT lymphoma; atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, or dysplasia; autoimmune gastritis; adult household members of a positive patient; first-degree relative with gastric cancer (shared decision)
  • Non-Invasive:
    • Urea breath test or stool antigen: positive result indicates active infection; both also serve as the test of cure
    • Serology: not recommended in low-prevalence populations without high pretest probability (e.g., peptic ulcer); never for test of cure (antibodies persist months to years)
  • Invasive (At time of endoscopy):
    • Rapid urease test: a negative result alone does not prove eradication
    • Histology: add special stains (Giemsa, silver, immunohistochemistry) when chronic active gastritis shows no organisms
    • Susceptibility testing (culture or molecular): whenever the choice of therapy remains unclear after considering prior treatment, antibiotic exposure, and penicillin allergy (Key Concept 6)
  • Testing Notes: Stop PPIs 2 weeks and bismuth and antibiotics 4 weeks before breath, stool, or biopsy testing (false negatives); standard-dose H2RAs and antacids do not affect accuracy

Endoscopy (EGD) - Indications:

  • Urgent: Inpatient upper GI bleeding: endoscopy within 24 h of presentation (ACG 2021 UGIB); see card 15
  • Prompt: Dyspepsia with alarm features (vomiting, GI bleeding, unexplained iron deficiency, weight loss), other indications (dysphagia, refractory heartburn, regurgitation), or risk factors for peptic ulcer (aspirin or NSAID use) or gastric cancer (family history, immigration from a high-incidence region) (ACG 2024); age 60 or older falls outside the ACG test-and-treat range
  • Routine: Practical: persistent symptoms despite PPI therapy

Endoscopic Findings:

  • Erosive Gastritis: Multiple shallow erosions, erythema, friability, may have active bleeding
  • Non-Erosive: Erythema, nodularity (H. pylori), pallor (atrophic)
  • Hemorrhagic: Petechiae, submucosal hemorrhage, overlying clot
  • Biopsy (suspected atrophy): Updated Sydney protocol, 5 biopsies (2 antrum, 2 corpus, 1 incisura); at minimum body and antrum/incisura in separately labeled jars, plus targeted biopsies of any abnormality (AGA 2021 CPU, BPA 4)

Additional Testing (Atrophic Gastritis; AGA 2021 CPU):

  • Vitamin B12 and Iron: Evaluate for deficiency in all atrophic gastritis, especially corpus-predominant (BPA 11)
  • Antiparietal Cell Antibodies: Most sensitive serum marker for autoimmune gastritis; false positives with H. pylori and other autoimmune disease (BPA 5)
  • Anti-Intrinsic Factor Antibodies: High specificity, low sensitivity (under 30% in many studies); positive later in the course (BPA 5)
  • Thyroid: Screen for autoimmune thyroid disease in autoimmune gastritis (BPA 12)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Acute Management:

  • Discontinue Offending Agents: NSAIDs, alcohol, smoking
  • Acid Suppression (Practical; no US guideline on disk addresses erosive gastritis):
    • PPI: Omeprazole 40 mg PO BID or pantoprazole 40 mg IV BID (if NPO or bleeding)
    • Continue 4-8 weeks for erosive gastritis; step down to once daily after the acute phase
    • Bleeding ulcer after endoscopic hemostasis: high-dose PPI, continuous or intermittent, for 3 days (ACG 2021 UGIB, strong)
  • If Active Bleeding (ACG 2021 UGIB; full protocol on card 15):
    • Practical: 2 large-bore IVs, crystalloid resuscitation
    • Transfuse at Hgb under 7 g/dL; 8 g/dL reasonable with pre-existing cardiovascular disease; hypotensive patients may be transfused before Hgb reaches 7
    • Erythromycin infusion before endoscopy; endoscopy within 24 h of presentation
    • Endoscopic therapy for ulcers with active spurting, active oozing, or a nonbleeding visible vessel; epinephrine never alone

H. pylori Eradication (If Positive; ACG 2024; all regimens 14 days):

  • First-Line: Optimized Bismuth Quadruple Therapy (strong, moderate):
    • Standard-dose PPI PO BID, 30-60 minutes before a meal
    • Bismuth subcitrate 120-300 mg or bismuth subsalicylate 300 mg PO QID (no subsalicylate with salicylate allergy)
    • Tetracycline 500 mg PO QID (doxycycline is not a substitute)
    • Metronidazole 500 mg PO TID or QID (1,500-2,000 mg/day)
  • Alternatives (conditional):
    • Rifabutin triple (Talicia): 4 capsules PO TID; each capsule omeprazole 10 mg, amoxicillin 250 mg, rifabutin 12.5 mg
    • PCAB dual: vonoprazan 20 mg PO BID plus amoxicillin 1,000 mg PO TID
    • PCAB triple: vonoprazan 20 mg, clarithromycin 500 mg, amoxicillin 1,000 mg PO BID; reserve clarithromycin regimens for documented susceptibility
    • Concomitant therapy: not suggested over bismuth quadruple
  • Penicillin Allergy: Only optimized bismuth quadruple therapy is suitable; if it is not an option, refer to an allergist to confirm the allergy and consider desensitization
  • Test of Cure (all treated patients): Urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy test at least 4 weeks after therapy, with PPIs stopped 2 weeks before; never serology

Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis (ICU; SCCM/ASHP 2024):

  • Give SUP: Critically ill adults with coagulopathy, shock, or chronic liver disease, including those on enteral feeds; neurocritical care patients (all conditional). The guideline gives no numeric definitions. Mechanical ventilation alone is probably not a risk factor
  • No SUP: Enterally fed and no risk factor (conditional)
  • Agent: PPI or H2RA, enteral or IV, at low dose: pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily or famotidine 20 mg IV BID (low dose: PPI 40 mg/day or less; famotidine 40 mg/day or less)
  • Stop: When the risk factor resolves or critical illness ends, and before transfer out of the ICU; review pre-ICU acid suppression in patients without risk factors

Atrophic Gastritis Follow-Up (AGA 2021 CPU):

  • H. pylori: Test everyone with atrophic gastritis; treat and confirm eradication with a non-serologic test (BPA 6)
  • Surveillance: Advanced atrophic gastritis: consider EGD every 3 years (BPA 7). Autoimmune gastritis: interval unclear, individualize (BPA 8); ESGE (non-US) suggests 3-5 years
  • Autoimmune Gastritis: EGD screening for type 1 gastric NETs; resect small NETs, then EGD every 1-2 years depending on burden (BPA 10). New pernicious anemia without recent endoscopy: EGD with topographic biopsies (BPA 9)
  • B12 Supplementation: Practical: 1000 mcg IM monthly (lifelong) for pernicious anemia
  • PPI: Practical: generally not needed (achlorhydria already present)

Supportive Care:

  • Practical: ondansetron 4-8 mg IV/PO Q8H PRN
  • Practical: sucralfate 1 g PO QID as mucosal protectant if not on PPI
  • Practical: small frequent meals, avoid irritants (spicy, acidic foods, caffeine)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • NSAID and Aspirin Users: Test and treat H. pylori in long-term NSAID users and before long-term low-dose aspirin (ACG 2024). Practical: consider PPI co-therapy when GI risk is high (prior ulcer or bleed, anticoagulant or antiplatelet co-therapy, older age).
  • H. pylori Testing Strategy: Test-and-treat for uninvestigated dyspepsia under age 60 without alarm features; endoscopy for alarm features. Never use serology for test of cure; antibodies persist months to years (ACG 2024).
  • Drugs Before Testing: Stop PPIs 2 weeks and bismuth and antibiotics 4 weeks before breath, stool, or biopsy testing; standard-dose H2RAs and antacids do not interfere (ACG 2024).
  • Avoid Empiric Clarithromycin: Clarithromycin- and levofloxacin-containing regimens should be avoided without demonstrated susceptibility; first-line is optimized bismuth quadruple therapy (ACG 2024 Key Concept 3, rec 1).
  • Gastric Cancer Prevention: H. pylori is causally associated with gastric cancer. Eradication was associated with a 46% lower gastric adenocarcinoma incidence in 2 meta-analyses (mostly Asian data); in US veterans, confirmed eradication vs persistent infection: subhazard ratio 0.24 (ACG 2024). Advanced atrophic gastritis: consider surveillance EGD every 3 years (AGA 2021 CPU).
  • Autoimmune Gastritis Triad: Pernicious anemia (B12 deficiency), achlorhydria (high gastrin), and increased risk of gastric carcinoid tumors (due to hypergastrinemia causing ECL cell hyperplasia).
  • Stress Gastropathy: Coagulopathy, shock, and chronic liver disease raise the absolute risk of clinically important bleeding by 4.8%, 2.6%, and 7.6%; mechanical ventilation alone does not justify SUP. Versus no SUP, PPIs showed no conclusive effect on pneumonia, C. difficile, or mortality; PPIs prevent more bleeding than H2RAs, with uncertain mortality effect in the sickest patients (SCCM/ASHP 2024).
  • Erosions vs. Ulcers: Erosions are superficial breaches that do not cross the muscularis mucosae; ulcers breach it (PathologyOutlines, Weisenberg). Ulcers with active bleeding or a nonbleeding visible vessel need endoscopic therapy (ACG 2021 UGIB; card 15).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: active GI bleeding with hemodynamic instability (SBP under 90, HR over 120)
  • Massive hematemesis or large-volume melena
  • Practical: hemoglobin drop over 3 g/dL despite transfusion
  • Practical: need for more than 4 units PRBC
  • Signs of perforation (peritoneal signs, free air on imaging)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: hemodynamically stable for more than 24 hours
  • Hemoglobin stable without transfusion requirement
  • No evidence of active bleeding (no melena, stable Hgb)
  • Tolerating oral intake
  • Practical: on PPI therapy (omeprazole 40 mg daily or equivalent)
  • H. pylori treatment started if positive; test of cure at least 4 weeks after therapy (ACG 2024)
  • Practical: follow-up EGD arranged if indicated (within 4-8 weeks)
  • Patient educated on NSAID avoidance and PPI adherence
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pantoprazole, 💊 Famotidine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR
↑ Back to Table of Contents

81. HEMORRHOIDS

Bright Red Blood Per Rectum • Anal Pain • Prolapse • Straining
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Painless bright red blood per rectum on toilet paper or coating stool, often with straining or constipation. External hemorrhoids may cause anal pain, especially if thrombosed.

  • Internal Hemorrhoids (Above Dentate Line):
    • Painless bleeding: Bright red, on paper or dripping into toilet
    • Prolapse: May reduce spontaneously or require manual reduction
    • Mucus discharge and pruritus
    • No pain (unless thrombosed or strangulated)
    • Covered by mucosa (insensate above dentate line)
  • External Hemorrhoids (Below Dentate Line):
    • Painful swelling: Especially if thrombosed
    • Skin tags: Residual from previous thrombosis
    • Itching and irritation
    • Acute thrombosis: Severe pain, purple/blue nodule
    • Covered by anoderm (sensate below dentate line)
  • Grades of Internal Hemorrhoids:
    • Grade I: Bleeding only, no prolapse (confined to anal canal)
    • Grade II: Prolapse with straining, spontaneously reduces
    • Grade III: Prolapse with straining, requires manual reduction
    • Grade IV: Irreducible prolapse, risk of strangulation
  • Risk Factors: Constipation and abnormal bowel habits: straining, prolonged sitting, frequent bowel movements (ASCRS 2024). Practical: pregnancy, low-fiber diet, chronic diarrhea
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis (History and Examination):

  • History:
    • Bleeding pattern: Bright red, on paper vs. mixed with stool
    • Pain: Suggests external or thrombosed hemorrhoid
    • Prolapse: Timing (with defecation, constant), reducibility
    • Duration and severity of symptoms
    • Associated symptoms: Weight loss, change in bowel habits (red flags for malignancy)
  • Physical Examination:
    • Inspection: Look for external hemorrhoids, skin tags, thrombosis, prolapse, fissures
    • Digital rectal exam: Assess for masses, tenderness, tone
    • Anoscopy: Visualize internal hemorrhoids, classify grade
    • Note: Internal hemorrhoids typically not palpable on DRE

Additional Evaluation:

  • Labs:
    • CBC: If significant bleeding or symptoms of anemia
    • Iron studies: If chronic bleeding suspected
  • Colonoscopy (ASCRS 2024 rec 2, conditional):
    • Rectal bleeding should not automatically be attributed to hemorrhoids
    • High-risk personal or family history on history and exam
    • No obvious anorectal bleeding source, or associated abdominal pain, distention, or new or progressive constipation
    • Hematochezia persisting after otherwise successful hemorrhoid treatment
    • Due for colorectal cancer screening: counsel accordingly (USPSTF 2021 screening applies to asymptomatic average-risk adults 45-75; bleeding is a symptom)

Differential Diagnosis:

  • Anal fissure (painful, sentinel tag, visible tear)
  • Colorectal cancer or polyp (older age, constitutional symptoms)
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (diarrhea, abdominal pain)
  • Rectal prolapse (circumferential, concentric rings)
  • Abscess/fistula (fever, purulent drainage)
  • Proctitis (tenesmus, mucus, urgency)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Conservative Medical Management (First-Line for Grades I-II):

  • Dietary and Behavioral Modification (ASCRS 2024 rec 3, strong, moderate; first-line):
    • Increase fiber and fluid intake in all patients
    • Fiber vs no fiber (Cochrane, 7 RCTs): persistent symptoms RR 0.47, bleeding RR 0.50; little effect on prolapse, pain, or itching
    • Practical: psyllium or methylcellulose supplement; increase gradually to limit bloating
  • Stool Softener: Practical: docusate 100 mg PO daily to TID (OTC label maximum 300 mg/day)
  • Topical Therapy (ASCRS 2024 rec 4, conditional, low):
    • Hydrocortisone, phenylephrine, pramoxine, witch hazel, local anesthetics: limited data, minimal harm, possible symptom relief
    • Short-term only: prolonged use can cause allergic reactions or sensitization, with no evidence of long-term benefit
    • Late pregnancy: hydrocortisone 1%/pramoxine 1% foam controlled pain, itching, and swelling without adverse fetal effects
    • Practical: lidocaine 5% ointment for pain
  • Sitz Baths: Practical: warm water 15-20 minutes TID and after bowel movements
  • Bowel Habit Modification (ASCRS 2024):
    • Avoid straining and limit time on the toilet
    • Practical: respond promptly to the urge to defecate

Thrombosed External Hemorrhoid (ASCRS 2024 rec 6, conditional, low):

  • Early Excision (select patients):
    • Excision under local anesthesia: faster symptom resolution (3.9 vs 24 days in one series), lower recurrence and reintervention
    • Excision beat thrombectomy (incision and clot evacuation) and topical nitroglycerin for day-4 pain and 1-year recurrence
    • No evidence defines the optimal time window
  • Nonoperative:
    • Diet, stool softeners, oral and topical analgesics, sitz baths; most patients eventually resolve
    • Median 5 days to improvement and 8 days to complete resolution (range 1-45)
    • Practical: may leave a residual skin tag
  • Pain Control (Practical):
    • NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 600 mg PO Q8H or naproxen 500 mg PO BID
    • Acetaminophen: 650-1000 mg PO Q6H
    • Short course narcotics if severe (oxycodone 5 mg PO Q6H PRN ×3-5 days)

Office-Based Procedures (ASCRS 2024 rec 5, strong, moderate):

  • Rubber Band Ligation (most effective office treatment):
    • Indications: symptomatic grade I-II, and select grade III refractory to conservative treatment
    • Band placed proximal to the dentate line
    • Outcomes (single center, 2,635 patients): 86.7% asymptomatic at 8 weeks; 15.5% symptomatic recurrence at 2 years, treated with repeat banding or surgery
    • Complications: pain most common; severe bleeding about 1%, at 10-14 days when the band sloughs; perineal sepsis very rare (see pearls)
    • Anticoagulants or antiplatelets may raise bleeding risk: consider pausing when possible; sclerotherapy is an alternative
    • Practical: stage multiple columns 2-4 weeks apart
  • Sclerotherapy and Infrared Coagulation:
    • Sclerotherapy: bleeding resolved in 69-88% of grade I; an option for patients on anticoagulants
    • Infrared coagulation: bleeding resolved in 78% (grade I), 52% (grade II), and 22% (grade III) in one RCT
    • Both more often need further therapy than banding; banding causes more pain but less bleeding

Surgical Management:

  • Excisional Hemorrhoidectomy (ASCRS 2024 rec 7, strong, high):
    • Indications: external hemorrhoids, or symptomatic combined internal and external hemorrhoids (grades III-IV); failure of, intolerance of, or unsuitability for office procedures
    • Closed technique: less pain, faster healing, and less bleeding than open
    • Complications: postoperative hemorrhage 1-2%; urinary retention 1-15% (limit IV fluids to under 750 mL, adequate analgesia); late stricture and incontinence
    • Practical: recovery 2-4 weeks with significant postoperative pain
  • Doppler-Guided Hemorrhoid Artery Ligation (rec 8, conditional, moderate): Internal hemorrhoids; less pain but more recurrence than excisional hemorrhoidectomy
  • Stapled Hemorrhoidopexy (rec 9, conditional, moderate): Not routinely recommended first-line. Less pain in the first 6 weeks, but more recurrence and reoperation than excision; does not treat external hemorrhoids; unique risks (rectovaginal fistula, staple-line bleeding, stricture, rectal perforation)

Discharge Instructions:

  • Continue fiber and fluid intake (ASCRS 2024)
  • Return if: severe pain, fever, urinary retention, excessive bleeding (after banding, these suggest perineal sepsis)
  • Practical: follow-up in 2-4 weeks to assess response
  • Colonoscopy per the indications above
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Not All BRBPR is Hemorrhoids: Rectal bleeding attributed to hemorrhoids is the most often missed opportunity to diagnose colorectal cancer. Use personal and family history and exam to find high-risk patients; colonoscopy when no obvious anorectal source or with abdominal symptoms (ASCRS 2024).
  • Rectal Varices Are Not Hemorrhoids: Patients with cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension can have rectal varices, which appear to have low bleeding rates; manage on gastric varix principles (AASLD 2024). Practical: consider them when a patient with cirrhosis bleeds per rectum.
  • Thrombosed External Hemorrhoid: Early excision may help select patients (faster resolution, less recurrence); no evidence defines the optimal time window. Most nonoperative cases resolve, median 8 days (ASCRS 2024).
  • Banding Red Flags: Perineal sepsis is very rare but severe: fever, severe anal pain, difficulty urinating, fecal incontinence, nausea or vomiting. Treat with broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent examination under anesthesia. Severe delayed bleeding (about 1%) occurs at 10-14 days as the band sloughs (ASCRS 2024).
  • Fiber is First-Line: Fiber reduced persistent symptoms (RR 0.47) and bleeding (RR 0.50) vs no fiber, with little effect on prolapse, pain, or itching (Cochrane, 7 RCTs, via ASCRS 2024). Practical: increase gradually to limit gas and bloating.
  • Topical Products: Short courses only. Prolonged use of anesthetic, steroid, emollient, and antiseptic preparations can cause allergic reactions or sensitization, with no evidence of long-term benefit (ASCRS 2024).
  • Internal Hemorrhoids Don't Hurt: If patient has significant pain, think external hemorrhoid, thrombosis, fissure, or abscess. Internal hemorrhoids above dentate line lack somatic innervation (unless strangulated/necrotic).
  • Pregnancy: Hydrocortisone 1%/pramoxine 1% foam controlled symptoms in late pregnancy without adverse fetal effects (ASCRS 2024). Practical: conservative care during pregnancy; defer elective procedures until after delivery.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Massive hemorrhoidal bleeding causing hemodynamic instability (rare)
  • Fever, severe anal pain, or urinary difficulty after banding (perineal sepsis): broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent examination under anesthesia (ASCRS 2024)
  • Post-operative hemorrhoidectomy complications requiring ICU monitoring
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Pain controlled on oral analgesics
  • No active bleeding or bleeding controlled
  • Able to tolerate oral intake and pass stool
  • Thrombosed hemorrhoid managed (either conservative or excised)
  • Patient educated on stool softeners, high-fiber diet, sitz baths
  • Follow-up with primary care or colorectal surgery if needed
  • Return precautions given (severe pain, fever, inability to urinate)
↑ Back to Table of Contents

82. INTRA-ABDOMINAL ABSCESS

Fever • Abdominal Pain • Post-Operative • CT Diagnosis • Source Control
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Persistent fever with abdominal pain in patient with recent surgery, perforated viscus, or intra-abdominal infection. May present insidiously with non-specific symptoms.

  • Clinical Features:
    • Fever: Often persistent despite antibiotics
    • Abdominal pain: Localized or diffuse, depending on location
    • Ileus: Nausea, vomiting, decreased bowel sounds, distension
    • Systemic signs: Tachycardia, leukocytosis, sepsis
    • Subacute presentation: Anorexia, weight loss, failure to thrive
  • Common Locations:
    • Subphrenic: Right/left upper quadrant, under diaphragm
    • Perihepatlic: Morrison's pouch, perihepatic space
    • Lesser Sac: Behind stomach, anterior to pancreas
    • Pelvis: Pouch of Douglas (rectouterine/rectovesical)
    • Paracolic Gutters: Right or left lateral
    • Inter-loop: Between bowel loops
    • Retroperitoneal: Perirenal, psoas, paraspinal
  • Etiologies:
    • Post-operative: Anastomotic leak, contamination (most common after colorectal surgery)
    • Perforated viscus: Appendicitis, diverticulitis, PUD, bowel perforation
    • Infected pancreatitis: Pancreatic necrosis (typically >2-3 weeks after onset)
    • Primary peritonitis: Cirrhosis with ascites (SBP)
    • Intra-abdominal sepsis: Cholecystitis, cholangitis
    • Trauma: Penetrating or blunt with hollow viscus injury
    • Crohn's disease: Penetrating disease with abscess formation
  • Risk Factors: Recent abdominal surgery, immunosuppression, diabetes, malignancy, prior abscess, IBD, complicated appendicitis/diverticulitis
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Labs:

  • CBC: Leukocytosis (may be normal in immunosuppressed), left shift, bandemia
  • CMP: Assess for electrolyte abnormalities, renal function, hepatic dysfunction
  • Liver Enzymes: Elevated if hepatobiliary or subphrenic abscess
  • Lactate: Elevated in sepsis, bowel ischemia
  • Blood Cultures: Send before antibiotics (positive in 20-30% of intra-abdominal infections)
  • Inflammatory Markers: ESR and CRP elevated (not specific but trend useful)

Imaging (CT Abdomen/Pelvis with IV Contrast - Gold Standard):

  • Findings Consistent with Abscess:
    • Fluid collection with enhancing wall ("rim enhancement")
    • Gas bubbles within collection (pathognomonic)
    • Mass effect on adjacent structures
    • Surrounding inflammation/fat stranding
  • Sensitivity/Specificity: >95% for abscess detection
  • Planning Drainage: CT guides percutaneous vs. surgical approach

Alternative Imaging:

  • Ultrasound:
    • Useful for hepatic, pelvic abscesses
    • Limited by bowel gas, obesity
    • Advantages: Bedside, no radiation, can guide drainage
  • MRI:
    • If contrast-allergy or pregnancy
    • Excellent for liver, pelvis, retroperitoneum
    • Time-consuming, limited availability

Microbiologic Diagnosis:

  • Abscess Fluid Analysis:
    • Gram stain and culture (aerobic and anaerobic)
    • Cell count and differential
    • Consider fungal cultures if immunosuppressed or persistent fever
  • Common Organisms:
    • Polymicrobial (80%): Enteric gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella) + anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis)
    • Enterococcus (20-30%, controversial pathogenicity)
    • Fungi: Candida (immunosuppressed, prolonged antibiotics, post-op)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Source Control (Most Important):

  • Percutaneous Drainage (Preferred if feasible):
    • CT or ultrasound-guided catheter placement
    • Success rate: 70-90% for simple abscesses
    • Advantages: Less invasive, lower morbidity, can be repeated
    • Criteria: Safe access route, unilocular or few loculations, >3-4 cm size
    • Catheter management: Daily outputs, flush if needed, remove when <10-20 mL/day
  • Surgical Drainage (Indications):
    • No safe percutaneous access
    • Multiloculated or complex collections
    • Failed percutaneous drainage (persistent fever/leukocytosis >72h)
    • Associated with bowel perforation, fistula, or necrotic tissue
    • Phlegmon or organized infection requiring debridement
  • Timing: Urgent drainage for sepsis/septic shock; otherwise within 24 hours of diagnosis

Empiric Antibiotic Therapy:

  • Community-Acquired, Mild-Moderate Severity:
    • Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g IV Q6H or 4.5g IV Q8H
    • Alternative: Ceftriaxone 2g IV Q24H + metronidazole 500 mg IV Q8H
    • Alternative: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV Q12H + metronidazole 500 mg IV Q8H
  • High Severity or Healthcare-Associated:
    • Meropenem 1g IV Q8H
    • Imipenem 500 mg IV Q6H or doripenem 500 mg IV Q8H
    • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6H (extended infusion)
    • Consider: Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV Q8-12H if MRSA risk (penetrating trauma, prior MRSA)
  • Add Antifungal Coverage (if indicated):
    • Indications: Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, immunosuppressed, recurrent abscess, Candida in cultures/operative findings
    • Fluconazole 800 mg IV ×1, then 400 mg IV Q24H
    • If azole-resistant: Echinocandin (micafungin 100 mg IV Q24H or caspofungin 70 mg IV ×1, then 50 mg Q24H)
  • Duration:
    • 4-7 days if adequate source control achieved
    • Extend to 10-14 days if slow clinical response or incomplete drainage
    • Can transition to PO when afebrile ×24h, improving WBC, tolerating PO
  • De-escalation: Narrow based on culture results and clinical improvement

Supportive Care:

  • Resuscitation: IV fluids, vasopressors for septic shock (norepinephrine first-line)
  • NPO/Bowel Rest: If ileus or concern for bowel involvement
  • NG Tube: For decompression if significant ileus or vomiting
  • Nutrition: Enteral if tolerated; TPN if prolonged NPO expected
  • DVT Prophylaxis: Heparin 5000 units SC TID or enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
  • Monitor: Serial exams, vital signs, WBC, drain outputs

Follow-Up Imaging:

  • Repeat CT if persistent fever/leukocytosis >72h despite drainage and antibiotics
  • Confirm resolution if patient slow to improve or had complex abscess
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Source Control is Everything: Antibiotics alone fail in 90% of intra-abdominal abscesses. The KEY to successful treatment is adequate drainage - "pus somewhere, must go somewhere." Persistent fever on antibiotics = inadequate source control until proven otherwise.
  • The 72-Hour Rule: If no clinical improvement (defervescence, decreasing WBC) within 72 hours of drainage + antibiotics, assume inadequate drainage. Get repeat imaging and consider re-intervention or surgical drainage.
  • Post-Op Fever Timing: Intra-abdominal abscesses typically present 5-10 days post-operatively. Earlier fever (days 1-3) is more likely atelectasis, UTI, or wound infection. Later fever (>14 days) consider retained foreign body or anastomotic leak.
  • Pancreatic Abscess Exception: Infected pancreatic necrosis shouldn't be drained in first 2-3 weeks (worsens outcomes). Initial management is antibiotics alone. Delay intervention until necrosis is organized/walled-off (≥4 weeks).
  • Enterococcus Dilemma: Enterococcus in intra-abdominal infections is often a colonizer, not a pathogen. IDSA guidelines don't recommend routine coverage unless immunosuppressed, valvular heart disease, or enterococcus bacteremia. Drain the abscess first.
  • Candida Coverage Controversies: Routine antifungal coverage not recommended for community-acquired infections. Reserve for high-risk patients: upper GI perforation, recurrent infection, immunosuppression, or Candida in perioperative cultures.
  • Drain Not Draining: If percutaneous drain outputs suddenly decrease with persistent fever, assume drain malfunction (kinked, clotted, malpositioned). Flush catheter and obtain repeat imaging. Don't pull drain until abscess resolved and output minimal.
  • Interloop Abscess Challenge: Small abscesses between bowel loops are difficult to drain percutaneously (bowel in the way). Often require surgical approach or prolonged antibiotic therapy with serial imaging to ensure resolution.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Septic shock requiring vasopressor support
  • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
  • Acute renal failure requiring dialysis
  • Multi-organ dysfunction
  • Large abscess with impending perforation or rupture
  • Post-operative complications (anastomotic leak, bleeding)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable without vasopressors for >24 hours
  • Afebrile for >24 hours (or downtrending fever)
  • Improving leukocytosis and inflammatory markers
  • Abscess adequately drained (percutaneous or surgical)
  • Tolerating oral intake
  • Completed initial antibiotics course (typically 4-7 days IV, then transition to PO)
  • Drain output decreasing (if percutaneous drain placed)
  • Imaging shows resolution or improvement of abscess
  • Follow-up arranged with surgery and infectious disease
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Metronidazole
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
↑ Back to Table of Contents

83. MALLORY-WEISS TEAR

Hematemesis After Retching • Non-Variceal Bleeding • Usually Self-Limited
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Hematemesis following forceful or prolonged vomiting/retching episodes. Typically in patients with alcohol use, hyperemesis, or eating disorders.

  • Typical Presentation:
    • Initial non-bloody vomiting: Forceful retching from alcohol, gastroenteritis, hyperemesis
    • Hematemesis: Bright red blood after multiple vomiting episodes
    • Volume: Usually small to moderate (rarely massive)
    • Practical: bleeding is usually self-limited
    • Epigastric/chest discomfort: From retching, not the tear itself
  • Associated Conditions:
    • Alcohol use: binge drinking with vomiting
    • Hyperemesis: Gravidarum, chemotherapy, gastroenteritis
    • Eating disorders: Bulimia with self-induced vomiting
    • Hiatal hernia
    • Severe coughing; NSAIDs (predispose to bleeding)
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Mucosal tear in gastroesophageal junction or distal esophagus
    • Caused by sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure + negative intrathoracic pressure
    • Linear tear, usually single (can be multiple)
    • Location: gastric or esophageal side of the GE junction
  • Mallory-Weiss vs. Boerhaave:
    • Mallory-Weiss: Mucosal tear only, bleeding, no perforation
    • Boerhaave: Full-thickness perforation, pneumomediastinum, sepsis, surgical emergency
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Assessment:

  • History:
    • Recent forceful vomiting/retching (key historical feature)
    • Alcohol consumption
    • NSAID/anticoagulant use
    • Prior GI bleeding, liver disease, coagulopathy
  • Physical Exam:
    • Vital signs: Usually stable (hematemesis typically limited)
    • Volume status: Orthostatics, skin turgor, mucous membranes
    • Abdominal exam: Epigastric tenderness common
    • Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease

Labs:

  • CBC: Baseline hemoglobin/hematocrit, platelets
  • CMP: BUN:Cr ratio over 30 favors an upper GI source (LR 7.5; Srygley, JAMA 2012)
  • Coagulation Studies: PT/INR if anticoagulated or liver disease suspected
  • Type & Screen: Prepare for possible transfusion
  • Lactate: If concerned for shock/hypoperfusion

Risk Stratification (Glasgow-Blatchford Score; ACG 2021):

  • Score 0-1: Very low risk: discharge from the ED with outpatient follow-up rather than admission (conditional)
  • Score 2 or more: Admit or observe
  • Components: Hemoglobin, BUN, systolic BP, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic/cardiac disease

Upper Endoscopy (EGD):

  • Timing (ACG 2021):
    • Within 24 h of presentation for admitted or observed patients, after resuscitation (conditional)
    • High-risk features: ACG 2021 dropped the earlier suggestion of endoscopy within 12 h; resuscitate first
    • Suspected variceal bleeding (cirrhosis): within 12 h (AASLD 2024; see card 299)
  • Endoscopic Findings:
    • Linear mucosal tear at the GE junction
    • A nonbleeding Mallory-Weiss tear is a low-risk finding that should allow discharge with outpatient follow-up (ACG 2021)
    • Stigmata (active spurting or oozing, visible vessel, adherent clot) are described in ulcer terms; ACG 2021 hemostasis recommendations are written for ulcers, with none specific to Mallory-Weiss tears
  • Endoscopic Therapy (ACG 2021, ulcer-derived):
    • Bipolar electrocoagulation, heater probe, or absolute ethanol injection (strong); clips, argon plasma coagulation, or soft monopolar electrocoagulation (conditional); TC-325 powder for active bleeding (conditional)
    • Epinephrine injection only in combination with another modality, never alone (strong)

Imaging (If Boerhaave Suspected):

  • CXR: Practical: look for pneumomediastinum, pleural effusion, subcutaneous emphysema
  • CT Chest with Oral Contrast: Practical: imaging of choice if perforation is suspected (severe chest pain, fever, sepsis); no guideline on disk
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Initial Resuscitation:

  • IV Access and Fluids: Practical: 2 large-bore IVs; crystalloid resuscitation
  • Transfusion (ACG 2021): Transfuse at Hgb under 7 g/dL; 8 g/dL reasonable with pre-existing cardiovascular disease; hypotensive patients may be transfused before Hgb reaches 7
  • Antithrombotics (ACG-CAG 2022, all conditional; details on card 15):
    • Warfarin: no FFP and no vitamin K; if reversal is needed, PCC over FFP
    • Dabigatran: no routine idarucizumab. Rivaroxaban or apixaban: no andexanet alfa. DOACs: no PCC
    • Antiplatelet agents: no platelet transfusion. Cardiac aspirin for secondary prevention: do not hold
    • Practical: platelets if under 50,000 with active bleeding from thrombocytopenia (not for antiplatelet effect)

Medical Management:

  • Proton Pump Inhibitor:
    • Before endoscopy: ACG 2021 could not reach a recommendation for or against PPI
    • High-dose PPI for 3 days (80 mg IV bolus, then 8 mg/h) is for ulcers after endoscopic hemostasis (ACG 2021, strong); no Mallory-Weiss-specific guideline on disk
    • Practical: pantoprazole 40 mg IV or PO BID, then omeprazole 20-40 mg PO daily for 4-8 weeks
  • Antiemetics (Practical):
    • Ondansetron 4-8 mg IV/PO Q8H PRN
    • Prevent further vomiting to allow healing
  • Prokinetic (Practical; if gastroparesis contributing):
    • Metoclopramide 10 mg IV/PO TID (30 min before meals)
  • Avoid: NSAIDs, alcohol (counsel patient)

Endoscopic Intervention (Minority of Cases):

  • Indications for Therapy:
    • Active bleeding at endoscopy (Forrest Ia or Ib)
    • Visible vessel (Forrest IIa)
    • Adherent clot (Forrest IIb) - controversial, consider clot removal
  • No Therapy Needed: Clean-based tear (Forrest III) - most common finding

Supportive Care:

  • NPO Initially: Advance to clear liquids after stabilization, then regular diet as tolerated
  • Monitor: Serial Hgb/Hct, vital signs, stool color (melena)
  • NG Tube: Practical: not routinely needed

Disposition:

  • ICU: Practical: active bleeding, hemodynamic instability, significant comorbidities
  • Floor: Practical: most admitted patients (stable, EGD completed)
  • Discharge: From the ED if Glasgow-Blatchford 0-1; after EGD, a nonbleeding tear should allow discharge with outpatient follow-up (ACG 2021). Practical: stable vital signs and Hgb, tolerating PO

Follow-Up:

  • Practical: GI follow-up in 2-4 weeks
  • Practical: PPI for 4-8 weeks
  • Alcohol cessation counseling
  • Address underlying cause (hyperemesis, bulimia, etc.)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Low-Risk Lesion: A nonbleeding Mallory-Weiss tear is a low-risk endoscopic finding that should allow discharge with outpatient follow-up (ACG 2021). Practical: bleeding usually stops spontaneously; avoid overtreatment.
  • Classic History is Key: The diagnosis is strongly suggested by history of forceful vomiting followed by hematemesis. If history is atypical (no vomiting, chronic bleeding), consider alternative diagnoses (PUD, erosive gastritis, Cameron lesions).
  • High-Risk Features (Practical): Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, active bleeding at endoscopy, cirrhosis, and large tears warrant closer monitoring.
  • PPI Evidence: ACG 2021 makes no recommendation on pre-endoscopic PPI, and its high-dose post-hemostasis regimen applies to ulcers. Practical: PPI for coexisting esophagitis or gastritis.
  • Don't Confuse with Boerhaave: Boerhaave syndrome is full-thickness esophageal rupture (Mackler's triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema), a surgical emergency. Mallory-Weiss is mucosal only.
  • BUN:Cr Ratio Clue: A ratio over 30 favors an upper GI source (LR 7.5; Srygley, JAMA 2012).
  • Therapeutic Endoscopy: Practical: most endoscopies are diagnostic only (clean or healed tear).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Active bleeding with hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation
  • Hemoglobin <7 g/dL with ongoing transfusion requirements
  • Practical: need for more than 4 units PRBC
  • Failed endoscopic hemostasis requiring repeat intervention or surgery
  • Esophageal perforation (rare complication)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: hemodynamically stable for more than 24 hours
  • Hemoglobin stable without transfusion requirement
  • No evidence of rebleeding
  • Tolerating oral intake
  • Practical: on PPI therapy (omeprazole 40 mg daily for 4-8 weeks)
  • Alcohol cessation counseling if applicable
  • Follow-up with GI and primary care arranged
  • Return precautions for recurrent hematemesis, melena, dizziness
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pantoprazole
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated INR
↑ Back to Table of Contents

84. NEUROGENIC SHOCK

Spinal Cord Injury • Bradycardia + Hypotension • Warm Extremities • Loss of Sympathetic Tone
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Hypotension with paradoxical bradycardia and warm, dry skin following acute spinal cord injury above T6. Results from loss of sympathetic tone with unopposed parasympathetic activity.

  • Clinical Triad (Distinguishes from other shock states):
    • Hypotension: SBP <90 mmHg (variable severity)
    • Bradycardia: HR 50-60 bpm (pathognomonic when combined with hypotension)
    • Warm, Dry Skin: Peripheral vasodilation (unlike hypovolemic/cardiogenic shock)
  • Mechanism - Loss of Sympathetic Outflow:
    • Spinal sympathetic pathway disrupted (T1-L2 sympathetic chain)
    • Loss of vasomotor tone → Peripheral vasodilation → Decreased SVR
    • Loss of cardiac sympathetic innervation (T1-T4) → Bradycardia
    • Unopposed vagal tone → Further bradycardia
    • Venous pooling → Decreased preload
  • Spinal Cord Injury Level:
    • Above T6: Classic neurogenic shock (significant sympathetic disruption)
    • Cervical (C3-C5): Most severe, includes diaphragm (respiratory failure)
    • Below T6: Less likely to cause shock (preserved upper sympathetics)
  • Causes of Spinal Cord Injury:
    • Trauma: MVA, falls, sports injuries, penetrating injury
    • Non-traumatic: Epidural abscess, hematoma, tumor, cord infarction
    • Iatrogenic: Epidural anesthesia (rare high block), spinal surgery complication
  • Spinal Shock vs. Neurogenic Shock:
    • Spinal Shock: Neurologic - flaccid paralysis, areflexia (lasts days-weeks)
    • Neurogenic Shock: Hemodynamic - hypotension/bradycardia from sympathetic loss
    • These often coexist but are distinct entities
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis (Key Features):

  • History: Recent trauma or acute neurologic event
  • Vital Signs: Hypotension + Bradycardia (or inappropriately normal HR for degree of hypotension)
  • Neurologic Exam:
    • Flaccid paralysis below level of injury
    • Loss of reflexes (spinal shock)
    • Sensory level
    • Priapism (pathognomonic in males)
    • Poikilothermia (inability to thermoregulate)
  • Skin: Warm, flushed, dry (vasodilated) above injury level; may be cool below injury

Rule Out Other Shock States (Critical):

  • Hypovolemic Shock:
    • Tachycardia, cold/clammy skin, narrow pulse pressure
    • Rule out: Hemorrhage (intra-abdominal, chest, pelvic/long bone fractures)
    • Neurogenic shock does NOT cause tachycardia or cold extremities
  • Cardiogenic Shock: Elevated JVP, pulmonary edema, cold extremities
  • Septic Shock: Fever, tachycardia (usually), warm extremities (early), altered mental status
  • Mixed Shock: Spinal injury patients may have concurrent hemorrhagic shock (polytrauma)

Labs:

  • CBC: Baseline hemoglobin (rule out hemorrhage)
  • CMP: Electrolytes, renal function
  • Lactate: May be elevated but less than hypovolemic/septic shock (if isolated neurogenic)
  • ABG: If respiratory compromise (high cervical injury)
  • Troponin: If concern for concurrent cardiac injury/MI
  • Blood Cultures: If sepsis cannot be excluded

Imaging:

  • CT Spine (Cervical/Thoracic):
    • Identify level and extent of spinal injury
    • Fractures, subluxation, epidural hematoma
    • STAT in trauma patients
  • MRI Spine (If stable):
    • Assess cord edema, contusion, compression
    • Evaluate for ligamentous injury, disc herniation
    • Gold standard for cord pathology
  • Trauma Imaging (Rule out concurrent injuries):
    • FAST exam or CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for hemorrhage
    • Chest X-ray
    • Pelvic X-ray if mechanism warrants

Hemodynamic Monitoring:

  • Arterial Line: Continuous BP monitoring
  • Central Venous Catheter: CVP monitoring, vasopressor infusion
  • Foley Catheter: Urine output monitoring (neurogenic bladder common)
  • Consider PA Catheter or ECHO: If hemodynamics unclear or mixed shock
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

ABCs and Initial Resuscitation:

  • Airway:
    • C-spine precautions: In-line stabilization, avoid hyperextension
    • Intubate if: C5 or above injury (diaphragm paralysis), respiratory distress, GCS ≤8
    • Video laryngoscopy preferred (less neck manipulation)
  • Breathing:
    • High-flow O2 to maintain SpO2 >95%
    • Monitor for respiratory failure (cervical injuries)
    • Mechanical ventilation with lung-protective strategies if intubated
  • Circulation:
    • Large-bore IV access (2 peripheral IVs)
    • Spinal precautions during all procedures

Hemodynamic Goals:

  • MAP Target: 85-90 mmHg (for 7 days post-injury)
    • Maintains spinal cord perfusion pressure
    • Higher MAP associated with improved neurologic outcomes
    • AANS/CNS guidelines recommend MAP 85-90 mmHg ×7 days
  • Heart Rate: 60-100 bpm (treat symptomatic bradycardia)

Fluid Resuscitation:

  • Initial Fluid Bolus:
    • NS or LR 500-1000 mL IV bolus
    • Reassess BP and perfusion
    • Caution: Excessive fluids worsen cord edema and pulmonary edema
  • Goal: Euvolemia (avoid both hypo- and hypervolemia)
  • Monitoring: CVP, urine output, clinical exam

Vasopressors (First-Line After Fluids):

  • Norepinephrine (Preferred):
    • Start: 0.01-0.05 mcg/kg/min (central line preferred)
    • Titrate to MAP 85-90 mmHg
    • Alpha-1 agonist (vasoconstriction) + beta-1 (inotropy/chronotropy)
  • Dopamine (Alternative):
    • Start: 5-10 mcg/kg/min
    • Increases HR and contractility (may help bradycardia)
    • Higher arrhythmia risk than norepinephrine
  • Phenylephrine (Pure Alpha Agonist):
    • If excessive tachycardia with norepinephrine/dopamine
    • May worsen bradycardia (reflex response)
  • Avoid: Excessive fluids as sole therapy (worsens cord edema)

Bradycardia Management:

  • Atropine:
    • 0.5-1 mg IV bolus (can repeat Q3-5min, max 3 mg)
    • For symptomatic bradycardia (HR <50 with hypotension/altered mental status)
    • May have limited effect (denervated heart)
  • Transcutaneous Pacing:
    • If atropine fails or severe/persistent bradycardia
    • Temporary transvenous pacing for refractory cases
  • Dopamine or Epinephrine Infusion: For persistent symptomatic bradycardia

Spinal Cord Injury Specific Management:

  • Spinal Immobilization: C-spine collar until cleared by imaging
  • Neurosurgical Consultation: STAT for surgical evaluation/decompression
  • High-Dose Steroids (Controversial, Generally NOT Recommended):
    • Methylprednisolone was previously used (NASCIS protocols)
    • No longer recommended per AANS/CNS guidelines (no proven benefit, increased complications)
    • May be considered on case-by-case basis by neurosurgery
  • Early Surgical Decompression (If Indicated):
    • Within 24 hours improves outcomes
    • Indications: Compression, unstable fracture, progressive deficit

Supportive Care:

  • DVT Prophylaxis:
    • SCDs initially (within 24h)
    • Enoxaparin 30 mg SC BID (once hemorrhage ruled out, typically after 72h)
    • Spinal cord injury = VERY high DVT risk
  • Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis: PPI (pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily)
  • Foley Catheter: Neurogenic bladder common (monitor urine output, avoid over-distension)
  • Temperature Management: External warming/cooling (poikilothermia common)
  • Early Mobilization/Rehab: Once hemodynamically stable and spine cleared/stabilized

Disposition:

  • ICU Admission: All patients with neurogenic shock
  • Monitoring: Continuous cardiac, arterial line, central access, neuro checks Q1H
  • Duration: Shock typically resolves over days to weeks as sympathetic tone recovers (or doesn't)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Hypotension + Bradycardia = Neurogenic Until Proven Otherwise: This paradoxical combination is pathognomonic for neurogenic shock. All other shock states cause tachycardia (compensatory). If you see "HR 58, BP 85/50" after trauma, think spinal cord injury.
  • Don't Overcorrect the Bradycardia: HR 50-60 bpm is expected in neurogenic shock and does NOT need treatment unless symptomatic (hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain). Treat the MAP, not the number. Excessive atropine can cause tachycardia and worsen myocardial O2 demand.
  • Fluid Caution: Unlike hypovolemic shock, aggressive crystalloid resuscitation WORSENS outcomes in neurogenic shock by causing pulmonary/spinal cord edema. Give modest fluid bolus (1-2L), then start vasopressors early to achieve MAP goals.
  • MAP 85-90 mmHg for 7 Days: Specific guideline for acute SCI to maintain spinal cord perfusion. Higher than usual MAP goal. This is time-limited (7 days), then transition to standard goals (MAP 65+).
  • Rule Out Hemorrhage: Polytrauma patients can have BOTH neurogenic and hemorrhagic shock. Neurogenic shock alone doesn't cause narrow pulse pressure, cold extremities, or profound tachycardia (if present, assume hemorrhage). Get FAST/CT to rule out bleeding.
  • Priapism is Pathognomonic: Sustained erection in male patient with spinal injury is virtually diagnostic of cord injury and neurogenic shock. Results from loss of sympathetic tone with unopposed parasympathetic activity.
  • Methylprednisolone Controversy: Despite NASCIS trials, high-dose steroids are NO LONGER recommended per AANS/CNS guidelines (2013). Increased infection/complications, no proven benefit. Don't give unless neurosurgery specifically requests.
  • Sympathetic Recovery is Variable: Some patients regain sympathetic function over weeks-months. Others have permanent dysfunction (chronic orthostasis, thermoregulation issues, autonomic dysreflexia). Early rehab and education essential.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL patients with neurogenic shock require ICU admission
  • Vasopressor requirement (norepinephrine, phenylephrine)
  • Spinal cord injury (any level)
  • Hemodynamic instability (SBP <90, bradycardia <60 with hypotension)
  • Need for mechanical ventilation (high cervical injury)
  • Ongoing fluid resuscitation requirements
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable without vasopressor support for >48-72 hours
  • MAP consistently >65 mmHg
  • Heart rate normalized or stable (typically 60-80 with injury)
  • Spinal shock resolved (return of reflexes below lesion)
  • No further progression of neurologic deficits
  • Appropriate disposition arranged (acute rehab for spinal cord injury)
  • Urinary catheter management plan in place
  • DVT prophylaxis established (LMWH once spinal hematoma risk assessed)
  • Follow-up with neurosurgery and physical medicine/rehab arranged
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Phenylephrine, 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Methylprednisolone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Leukocytosis

85. RUPTURED ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM

Abdominal/Back Pain • Hypotension • Pulsatile Mass • Surgical Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad: Abdominal/back pain + Hypotension + Pulsatile abdominal mass. Do not wait for all three: NICE NG156 (1.1.7) says to think of rupture with new abdominal and/or back pain, cardiovascular collapse, or loss of consciousness, more so with known AAA, age >60, smoking history, or hypertension. Ruptured AAA is a surgical emergency. Overall mortality is estimated at 80-90%, and most patients never reach the hospital; in those who do, historical mortality after open repair was about 50% (2022 Aortic).

  • Symptoms:
    • Pain: Abdominal, back, or flank pain (sudden or gradually worsening)
    • Radiation: Back, groin, flank, or hip
    • Character: Tearing, ripping, or constant dull ache
    • Pain may be absent: collapse or loss of consciousness alone should raise the question (NICE NG156 1.1.7)
  • Hemodynamic Status:
    • Frank Rupture (Free Intraperitoneal): Profound hypotension/shock, rapid exsanguination
    • Contained Rupture (Retroperitoneal): Relative hemodynamic stability initially, may compensate temporarily
    • Syncope or near-syncope
  • Physical Exam:
    • Pulsatile Abdominal Mass: Supports the diagnosis; suspected AAA on palpation warrants aortic ultrasound (NICE NG156 1.1.6). Practical: absence does not exclude AAA, especially with obesity or hypotension
    • Abdominal distension and peritoneal signs
    • Hypotension or shock
    • Femoral pulses may be diminished or absent
    • Grey Turner sign: Flank ecchymosis (late, rare)
    • Cullen sign: Periumbilical ecchymosis (late, rare)
  • Atypical Presentations:
    • GI bleeding (aortoenteric fistula)
    • Lower extremity ischemia (distal embolization)
    • Isolated back pain mimicking renal colic/MSK pain
    • Syncope without obvious cause
  • Risk Factors for AAA:
    • Age >65 years (especially men)
    • Smoking (strongest modifiable risk factor)
    • Male sex (prevalence about 6 times higher than in women, but AAAs are more likely to rupture in women; NICE NG156)
    • Family history (screening first-degree relatives finds AAA in 10-20%, up to 25% of brothers; 2022 Aortic)
    • Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, CAD, PAD
    • Known AAA (rupture risk rises with maximal diameter; repair is recommended at ≥5.5 cm in men or ≥5.0 cm in women, 2022 Aortic 1, A; in UKSAT, mean diameter at rupture was 6.0 cm in men and 5.0 cm in women)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis in Unstable Patients:

  • High Clinical Suspicion + Hemodynamic Instability:
    • Do NOT delay for imaging if patient unstable
    • Bedside ultrasound if immediately available (see below)
    • Activate vascular surgery and go directly to OR

Bedside Ultrasound (FAST Extended for AAA):

  • Indication: Unstable patient, rapid screening
  • Findings:
    • AAA: aortic diameter >3.0 cm, outer edge to outer edge (2022 Aortic ultrasound criterion; USPSTF 2019 uses ≥3.0 cm)
    • Intraperitoneal free fluid (ruptured)
    • Sensitivity for AAA presence approaches 100%, but obesity and bowel gas limit imaging (2022 Aortic). NICE NG156 (1.1.9): discuss immediately with vascular surgery if ultrasound shows AAA, or if it is unavailable or non-diagnostic and AAA is still suspected
  • Limitation: Can't definitively diagnose rupture or assess proximal/distal extent

CT Angiography (CTA) Abdomen/Pelvis - Gold Standard:

  • Indication: Hemodynamically stable or stabilized patient. Most patients who reach hospital alive are stable enough for CTA, which ESVS 2024 recommends promptly for suspected rupture, including the thoracoabdominal aorta and access vessels (Rec 70, I B)
  • Findings:
    • AAA size and extent (infrarenal vs. suprarenal)
    • Active extravasation or contained rupture
    • Retroperitoneal hematoma
    • Vessel anatomy for surgical/endovascular planning
  • Too Unstable for CT: go directly to the OR for open repair or intraoperative imaging (ESVS 2024). ESVS defines instability as loss or reduced level of consciousness or SBP <80 mmHg, but notes it is relative and CTA is usually both preferable and feasible

Labs (Don't Delay Surgery):

  • Type & Cross: Practical: crossmatch early for massive transfusion; no guideline gives a unit number, so follow the local massive transfusion protocol
  • CBC: Baseline hemoglobin (may be normal acutely due to hemoconcentration)
  • CMP: Renal function (contrast), electrolytes
  • Coagulation Studies: PT/INR, PTT (baseline, anticipate coagulopathy)
  • Lactate: Assess perfusion/shock
  • Troponin: If concern for MI (may delay surgery)

ECG and CXR:

  • Rule out MI/arrhythmia (if time permits and patient stable)
  • Don't delay surgery for these tests if diagnosis clear

Differential Diagnosis (The Great Mimicker):

  • Renal colic (unilateral, colicky, hematuria)
  • Diverticulitis (LLQ pain, fever, CT shows colonic inflammation)
  • Acute MI (chest pain radiating, ECG changes)
  • Perforated viscus (peritonitis, free air)
  • Pancreatitis (epigastric pain, elevated lipase)
  • Mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion, lactate)
  • Musculoskeletal back pain (no vascular symptoms)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Pre-Hospital and ED Resuscitation:

  • IV Access: 2 large-bore peripheral IVs (16g or larger) or intraosseous if unable
  • Permissive Hypotension (Key Concept):
    • Goal: the lowest SBP that maintains mentation, typically 60-90 mmHg (2022 Aortic 2a, C-LD). ESVS 2024 recommends permissive hypotension (I, C) while the patient stays conscious, with a target SBP of 70-90 mmHg; it notes IMPROVE data that 70 mmHg may be too low and that targets derived from young trauma patients may be too low for older patients
    • Maintain perfusion to vital organs WITHOUT increasing bleeding
    • Aim is to decrease the rate of bleeding. No rAAA RCTs; the benefit is extrapolated from trauma hemorrhagic shock data and rAAA case series
    • "Pop the clot" phenomenon
  • Limited Fluid Resuscitation:
    • Practical: give minimal crystalloid in small boluses only to keep the patient mentating (no guideline volume)
    • Avoid large-volume resuscitation before surgical control
    • Immediate surgical intervention is priority, not normalization of BP
  • Blood Products (Once Activated):
    • Massive Transfusion Protocol: resuscitate preferentially with blood products; ESVS 2024 suggests an FFP:RBC ratio close to 1:1 and defers to established massive transfusion principles and local protocols. Practical: 1:1:1 pRBC:FFP:platelets, as in trauma protocols
    • Consider O-negative blood immediately if unstable
    • Tranexamic acid (TXA): not routine. Neither the 2022 ACC/AHA nor the ESVS 2024 guideline addresses it. NICE NG156 (2020) found no rAAA evidence, notes TXA is not routinely used in rAAA, and recommends research; its evidence review adds thrombotic risk and that the trauma time window cannot be applied because rupture time is unknown
  • Cardiac Arrest: No guideline reviewed (2022 ACC/AHA Aortic, ESVS 2024, NICE NG156) advises withholding chest compressions. NG156 (1.3.2, transfer decisions) notes that people with confirmed rupture who have a cardiac arrest and/or persistent loss of consciousness have a negligible chance of surviving repair; where repair is considered inappropriate, it directs to end-of-life care (1.3.3). ESVS 2024 notes that mortality may approach 100% when CPR is needed before repair, yet 5 of 13 such patients survived repair in a Dutch series; these patients should not necessarily be denied intervention, though a restrictive, selective approach is reasonable. Do not select patients for palliation based solely on scoring systems or age (ESVS 2024 Rec 79, III B; NG156 1.4.4-1.4.5). Practical: run ACLS and treat hypovolemia while deciding with vascular surgery, and the patient's known wishes, whether repair is appropriate
  • Abdominal Palpation: Not contraindicated. Palpation appears safe and has not been reported to precipitate rupture, but it cannot exclude AAA, especially if rupture is possible (Lederle and Simel, JAMA Rational Clinical Examination, 1999). Practical: do not let the exam delay bedside ultrasound or the vascular call

Immediate Consultation:

  • Vascular Surgery: STAT consultation (as soon as diagnosis suspected). SVS 2018 suggests a door-to-intervention time under 90 minutes, based on a 30-30-30 minute framework (weak recommendation)
  • Anesthesia: Activate OR, prepare for emergency surgery
  • Blood Bank: Massive transfusion protocol

Definitive Management - Surgical Repair:

  • Open Surgical Repair (OSR):
    • Traditional approach: Midline laparotomy, aortic cross-clamp, graft replacement
    • Advantages: Definitive repair, no anatomic limitations
    • Disadvantages: High physiologic stress, longer recovery
    • Mortality: historically about 50% after open repair of rupture; 34% at 30 days vs 21% with EVAR in a propensity-matched registry (VQI)
  • Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR):
    • Minimally invasive: Femoral access, stent-graft deployment
    • Advantages: Lower physiologic stress; can be done under local anesthesia. RCTs showed no early survival benefit (unstable patients were excluded), but IMPROVE showed better survival from 90 days to 3 years (HR 0.57), and registries show lower 30-day mortality
    • Disadvantages: Requires suitable anatomy, risk of endoleak, not always available emergently
    • Recommended over open repair when anatomy is suitable (2022 Aortic 1, B-R; ESVS 2024 first line, I A). NICE NG156 (1.6.1) is more selective: EVAR benefits most people, especially men over 70 and women of any age, while open repair likely gives a better balance of benefits and harms in men under 70
  • Decision Factors:
    • Hemodynamically stable: CT to assess suitability for EVAR is recommended (2022 Aortic 1, B-R); if a CT already answers the question, do not repeat it. Unstable: rupture protocols use endovascular aortic balloon occlusion under fluoroscopy and immediate transfer to the OR; ESVS 2024 downgraded balloon occlusion for proximal control to may be considered (Rec 74, IIb C)
    • Anatomic suitability (proximal/distal landing zones)
    • Institutional resources/expertise

Intraoperative Management:

  • Anesthesia: Local anesthesia is preferred for EVAR (2022 Aortic 2a, B-NR; ESVS 2024 IIa, B; NICE NG156 1.6.4; lower mortality in the IMPROVE subanalysis). Induction of general anesthesia removes the catecholamine response and can cause circulatory collapse. Practical: if general anesthesia is needed, induce with the surgical team scrubbed and ready for aortic control
  • Permissive Hypotension Until Aortic Control: Avoid BP augmentation until cross-clamp applied
  • Massive Transfusion: continue the massive transfusion protocol (FFP:RBC close to 1:1, ESVS 2024). Practical: whole blood if available
  • Correct Coagulopathy:
    • Maintain temperature >36°C (warming devices)
    • Calcium replacement (citrate from transfusions)
    • Fibrinogen replacement if <150 mg/dL (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate)

Post-Operative Management (ICU):

  • Complications to Monitor:
    • Abdominal Compartment Syndrome: Can follow EVAR or open repair. Post-operative intra-abdominal pressure monitoring is recommended (ESVS 2024 Rec 81, I B); the ESVS algorithm uses serial IAP measurements every 4 hours in all at-risk patients, and NICE NG156 (1.6.5-1.6.6) says to assess if the patient does not improve. Defined as sustained intra-abdominal (bladder) pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (WSACS 2013). Treat ACS with decompressive laparotomy (ESVS 2024 Rec 82, I B; WSACS 2013, 1D). Pooled incidence after EVAR for rupture is about 9% (ESVS 2024)
    • Acute Kidney Injury: Contrast, ischemia, rhabdomyolysis (common, may need CRRT)
    • Colonic Ischemia: Inferior mesenteric artery occlusion (bloody diarrhea, acidosis). If suspected, flexible sigmoidoscopy should be considered to confirm it (ESVS 2024 Rec 84, IIa C)
    • Spinal Cord Ischemia: Paraplegia (spinal artery compromise)
    • Lower Extremity Ischemia: Distal embolization or graft thrombosis
    • ARDS/Multi-Organ Failure: From massive transfusion, shock
  • Supportive Care:
    • Mechanical ventilation (often prolonged)
    • Vasopressor support
    • Renal replacement therapy if needed
    • Nutrition (early enteral if tolerated)
    • VTE prophylaxis: LMWH or UFH post-operatively unless there is ongoing bleeding or significant coagulopathy (ESVS 2024 Rec 78, IIa C); mechanical prophylaxis until the bleeding risk subsides, with pharmacologic prophylaxis usually safe to start within 24-48 h of surgery

Prognosis:

  • Overall mortality: estimated 80-90%, most never reaching the hospital (2022 Aortic)
  • Reaching the hospital: historical open-repair mortality about 50%; as low as 18.5% after repair in one observational series using an endovascular-repair-first protocol (2022 Aortic)
  • Better outcomes: Younger age, contained rupture, EVAR, expedient surgery
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Think AAA in "The Big Three": Any elderly patient with: (1) Abdominal/back pain, (2) Hypotension/syncope, or (3) Known AAA. Have extremely low threshold to image - ruptured AAA kills 80-90% overall, and early diagnosis saves lives.
  • Permissive Hypotension Until Aortic Control: Keep the SBP that maintains mentation, typically 60-90 mmHg, until surgical or balloon control (2022 Aortic 2a, C-LD; ESVS 2024 I, C, with a 70-90 mmHg target). Resuscitating to a "normal" BP before control may increase bleeding. The evidence is extrapolated from trauma and rAAA case series, not rAAA RCTs.
  • Most Patients Can Have CTA; the Truly Unstable Go to the OR: Most patients with rupture who reach hospital alive are stable enough for CTA, which plans EVAR (ESVS 2024 I, B). If the patient is too unstable (reduced consciousness or SBP <80 mmHg), go directly to the OR; a bedside ultrasound showing AAA warrants immediate discussion with vascular surgery (NICE NG156 1.1.9).
  • Ruptured AAA Mimics Renal Colic: Elderly patient with "renal colic" and hematuria may actually have ruptured AAA causing ureteral compression. Always consider AAA in older patients with flank/back pain, especially if hypotensive or no prior stone history.
  • Normal Hemoglobin Doesn't Exclude: Hgb may be normal initially after rupture due to hemoconcentration (blood loss not yet equilibrated). Don't be falsely reassured by "normal labs" in acute setting.
  • EVAR Improving Outcomes: RCTs showed no early survival benefit for EVAR over open repair; IMPROVE showed late survival benefit, and a propensity-matched registry (VQI) showed 30-day mortality of 21% vs 34%. EVAR is recommended over open repair when anatomy is suitable (2022 Aortic 1, B-R).
  • Don't Forget Screening Guidelines: Ultrasound screening is recommended for men ≥65 who have ever smoked (2022 Aortic 1, B-R) and for men or women ≥65 with a first-degree relative with AAA (1, C-LD), and is reasonable for women ≥65 who have ever smoked (2a, C-EO). USPSTF (2019) grades one-time screening B only for men 65-75 who have ever smoked. In a national inpatient sample, 24% of patients with ruptured AAA were <65 (2022 Aortic).
  • Cardiac Arrest in Ruptured AAA: Survival after arrest is poor: NICE NG156 (1.3.2) calls the chance of surviving repair negligible, and ESVS 2024 says mortality may approach 100% but that these patients should not necessarily be denied intervention. No guideline reviewed advises withholding CPR, and age or risk scores alone should not decide palliation (ESVS 2024 III B). Practical: clarify goals of care early in any suspected rupture, so the repair-or-comfort decision is made before arrest.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL patients with ruptured AAA require ICU (surgical ICU preferred)
  • Post-operative management after EVAR or open repair
  • Ongoing transfusion requirements or coagulopathy
  • Vasopressor support
  • Mechanical ventilation
  • Acute kidney injury or dialysis requirement
  • Abdominal compartment syndrome
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable off vasopressors (Practical: no guideline sets a duration)
  • No evidence of ongoing bleeding or rebleeding
  • Stable hemoglobin without transfusion requirement
  • Extubated and breathing comfortably on room air or low-flow O2
  • Adequate renal function (or stable on dialysis with outpatient plan)
  • Tolerating oral intake, bowel function returned
  • Wound healing appropriately without signs of infection
  • Pain controlled on oral medications
  • Follow-up with vascular surgery arranged
  • Surveillance imaging: after EVAR, CT at 1 month, then duplex ultrasound at 12 months and annually if there is no endoleak or sac enlargement (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR); after open repair, CT or MRI within 1 year, then every 5 years (2a, C-LD)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 TXA
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia

86. B12 / FOLATE DEFICIENCY ANEMIA

Macrocytic Anemia • Neurologic Symptoms (B12) • Hypersegmented Neutrophils
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Macrocytic anemia with fatigue, glossitis, and neurologic symptoms (B12 only). Often insidious onset over months to years.

  • General Anemia Symptoms:
    • Fatigue, weakness, dyspnea on exertion
    • Pallor
    • Tachycardia, heart failure (if severe)
    • Symptoms often develop slowly (compensated)
  • Specific to B12/Folate Deficiency:
    • Glossitis: Beefy red, smooth tongue (atrophic papillae)
    • Angular cheilitis: Cracks at corners of mouth
    • Hyperpigmentation: Especially hands, knuckles (melanin deposition)
    • Jaundice: Mild, from ineffective erythropoiesis (hemolysis of megaloblasts in marrow)
  • Neurologic Manifestations (B12 ONLY, NOT Folate):
    • Subacute Combined Degeneration: Demyelination of dorsal/lateral columns
      • Posterior column: Loss of position/vibration sense, sensory ataxia
      • Lateral corticospinal: Weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign
      • Classic: Gait ataxia + paresthesias + weakness
    • Peripheral neuropathy: Stocking-glove distribution, paresthesias
    • Cognitive/Psychiatric: Memory loss, dementia, depression, psychosis
    • Optic neuropathy: Visual changes (rare)
    • CRITICAL: Neuro damage may be irreversible if prolonged deficiency
  • Folate-Specific: Neural tube defects in pregnancy (if deficient periconceptionally)
ETIOLOGIES

Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Deficiency:

  • Pernicious Anemia (Most Common in Developed Countries):
    • Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells
    • Loss of intrinsic factor → Impaired B12 absorption
    • Associated: Autoimmune disorders (thyroiditis, vitiligo, type 1 DM)
    • Antiparietal cell antibodies (85-90%), anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (50-70%, more specific)
    • Atrophic gastritis on endoscopy
  • Dietary Deficiency:
    • Strict vegans (B12 only in animal products)
    • Rare in developed countries (liver stores last 3-5 years)
  • Malabsorption:
    • Gastrectomy or gastric bypass (loss of intrinsic factor production)
    • Terminal ileum disease: Crohn's, resection, bacterial overgrowth
    • Pancreatic insufficiency (need pancreatic proteases to cleave R-protein)
    • Celiac disease
    • Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm)
  • Medications:
    • Metformin (decreases B12 absorption, 10-30% of users)
    • PPIs/H2 blockers (chronic use, impaired cleavage from food)
    • Nitrous oxide (inactivates B12, seen in anesthesia/recreational use)

Folate (Folic Acid) Deficiency:

  • Dietary Deficiency (Most Common Cause):
    • Poor intake: Elderly, alcoholics, poverty
    • Folate depletes rapidly (body stores only 2-3 months)
  • Increased Demand:
    • Pregnancy and lactation
    • Hemolytic anemias (increased RBC turnover: sickle cell, thalassemia)
    • Malignancy, inflammatory states
    • Dialysis (folate removed)
  • Malabsorption:
    • Celiac disease, tropical sprue
    • Small bowel resection
  • Medications:
    • Methotrexate (dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor)
    • Trimethoprim, sulfasalazine, phenytoin
    • Alcohol (impairs absorption and utilization)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Complete Blood Count:

  • Anemia: Hemoglobin variable (may be severe, <7 g/dL)
  • Macrocytosis: MCV >100 fL (often 110-140 fL in severe deficiency)
  • Pancytopenia: May have leukopenia and thrombocytopenia (megaloblastic changes affect all cell lines)

Peripheral Blood Smear (Diagnostic):

  • Macro-ovalocytes: Large, oval RBCs
  • Hypersegmented Neutrophils (Pathognomonic): ≥5 lobes in neutrophil (normal ≤4)
  • Anisocytosis and poikilocytosis: Variable RBC size/shape
  • Howell-Jolly bodies: Nuclear remnants in RBCs

Vitamin Levels:

  • Serum B12:
    • <150 pg/mL: Deficient
    • 150-400 pg/mL: Borderline/low (consider methylmalonic acid if symptomatic)
    • >400 pg/mL: Normal
    • Note: Can be falsely normal in myeloproliferative disorders, liver disease
  • Serum Folate:
    • <3 ng/mL: Deficient
    • Less reliable (reflects recent intake, not tissue stores)
  • RBC Folate:
    • Better reflects tissue stores than serum folate
    • <150 ng/mL: Deficient

Confirmatory Tests (If B12 Borderline or Normal with High Suspicion):

  • Methylmalonic Acid (MMA):
    • Elevated (>0.4 µmol/L) in B12 deficiency (NOT elevated in folate deficiency)
    • Most sensitive test for B12 deficiency
    • Also elevated in renal failure (confounding factor)
  • Homocysteine:
    • Elevated in BOTH B12 and folate deficiency (less specific)
    • Normal: <15 µmol/L
    • Also elevated in renal failure, hypothyroidism

Etiology Workup (Once Deficiency Confirmed):

  • For B12 Deficiency:
    • Anti-Intrinsic Factor Antibodies: Specific for pernicious anemia (50-70% sensitive)
    • Anti-Parietal Cell Antibodies: Less specific (85-90% sensitive, but also in 10% of normal elderly)
    • Gastrin Level: Elevated in pernicious anemia (achlorhydria)
    • EGD: Consider if atrophic gastritis suspected (increased gastric cancer risk)
  • For Folate Deficiency:
    • Dietary history
    • Alcohol use screening
    • Consider celiac antibodies (TTG-IgA) if malabsorption suspected

Additional Labs:

  • Reticulocyte Count: Inappropriately low for degree of anemia (ineffective erythropoiesis)
  • LDH: Elevated (intramedullary hemolysis)
  • Indirect Bilirubin: Mildly elevated (hemolysis)
  • Haptoglobin: Low (hemolysis)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

CRITICAL RULE: Always Treat B12 First (or Simultaneously) Before Folate:

  • Rationale: Giving folate alone to a B12-deficient patient can correct the anemia BUT precipitate/worsen neurologic damage (subacute combined degeneration)
  • Safe Approach: Treat both if unsure, or confirm B12 status before folate monotherapy

Vitamin B12 Replacement:

  • Acute/Severe Deficiency or Neurologic Symptoms:
    • Cyanocobalamin (B12) 1000 mcg IM daily ×1 week
    • Then: 1000 mcg IM weekly ×4 weeks
    • Then: 1000 mcg IM monthly (lifelong if pernicious anemia or malabsorption)
  • Maintenance or Mild Deficiency:
    • Oral Cyanocobalamin 1000-2000 mcg PO daily
    • Effective even in pernicious anemia (1-2% absorbed by mass action, bypasses intrinsic factor)
    • Requires patient adherence
  • Alternative Routes:
    • Sublingual cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily
    • Intranasal cyanocobalamin 500 mcg weekly (expensive, lower adherence)
  • Hydroxocobalamin: Alternative to cyanocobalamin (longer-acting, less commonly used in US)

Folate Replacement:

  • Treatment Dose:
    • Folic Acid 1-5 mg PO daily
    • Duration: Until deficiency corrected and underlying cause addressed (usually 1-4 months)
  • Prophylaxis (High-Risk Groups):
    • Pregnancy: 400-800 mcg daily (prenatal vitamins)
    • Chronic hemolysis: 1 mg daily
    • Dialysis: 1 mg daily
    • Methotrexate: Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue or folic acid 1 mg daily

Monitoring Response:

  • Reticulocytosis: Peaks at 5-7 days (indicates bone marrow response)
  • Hemoglobin: Begins to rise by 1 week, normalizes in 6-8 weeks
  • MCV: Gradually decreases to normal over 2-3 months
  • Neurologic Symptoms: May take weeks to months to improve (may be irreversible if longstanding)
  • Recheck B12/Folate: 4-8 weeks after starting treatment

Supportive Care:

  • Transfusion:
    • If symptomatic (chest pain, dyspnea, CHF exacerbation) or Hgb <7 g/dL
    • Transfuse SLOWLY (1 unit over 3-4 hours) to avoid volume overload
    • Goal: Hgb 7-9 g/dL (NOT full correction acutely)
  • Potassium Supplementation:
    • Monitor K+ closely in first week of treatment
    • Rapid cell production depletes K+ ("refeeding hypokalemia")
    • Supplement if K+ <3.5 mEq/L

Address Underlying Cause:

  • Pernicious anemia: Lifelong B12 replacement
  • Dietary: Nutrition counseling, supplementation
  • Medications: Adjust/discontinue if possible, supplement as needed
  • Malabsorption: Treat underlying condition (celiac, Crohn's), may need parenteral supplementation

Long-Term Follow-Up:

  • Pernicious Anemia: Lifelong replacement, surveillance EGD (increased gastric cancer risk - consider every 3-5 years)
  • Check B12/Folate Levels: Annually if on maintenance therapy
  • Screen for Autoimmune Disorders: If pernicious anemia (thyroid, diabetes, etc.)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Never Give Folate Without B12: Treating folate deficiency alone in a B12-deficient patient can WORSEN or PRECIPITATE irreversible neurologic damage (subacute combined degeneration). Always check B12 or treat both empirically if uncertain.
  • Hypersegmented Neutrophils are Pathognomonic: ≥5% of neutrophils with ≥5 lobes (or any with ≥6 lobes) is diagnostic for megaloblastic anemia. This finding persists even if patient already started replacement, making it useful diagnostically.
  • MMA is the Best Confirmatory Test: Methylmalonic acid is elevated in B12 deficiency but NOT folate deficiency, making it the most specific test. Use it when B12 level is borderline (150-400) but clinical suspicion is high.
  • Metformin and B12: 10-30% of long-term metformin users develop B12 deficiency. Check B12 annually in diabetics on metformin, especially if peripheral neuropathy develops (often attributed to diabetes but may be B12).
  • Oral B12 Works Even in Pernicious Anemia: High-dose oral B12 (1000-2000 mcg daily) is effective even without intrinsic factor because 1-2% is absorbed by passive diffusion. Cost-effective alternative to IM if patient adherent.
  • Nitrous Oxide = Instant B12 Deficiency: N₂O inactivates B12 (oxidizes cobalt atom) within hours. Recreational "whippet" use or prolonged anesthesia exposure can cause acute subacute combined degeneration in previously borderline patients.
  • Neuro Damage May Be Irreversible: If subacute combined degeneration is present >6-12 months before treatment, neurologic recovery is often incomplete. Early recognition and treatment is critical. Anemia may be minimal but neuro symptoms prominent.
  • Pernicious Anemia = Gastric Cancer Risk: Atrophic gastritis and achlorhydria in pernicious anemia increase gastric adenocarcinoma risk 3-6 fold. Consider surveillance EGD every 3-5 years per ACG guidelines.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe neurologic compromise requiring ICU-level monitoring
  • Hemodynamic instability from severe anemia (Hgb <4-5 g/dL)
  • Heart failure or myocardial ischemia from severe anemia
  • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
  • Multi-organ dysfunction from severe deficiency
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Hemoglobin improving or stable (typically >7-8 g/dL for discharge)
  • No active cardiac ischemia or heart failure
  • B12/folate replacement initiated (B12 1000 mcg IM or folate 1 mg PO daily)
  • No evidence of alternative causes requiring hospital-level care
  • Outpatient hematology follow-up arranged if needed
  • Patient educated on lifelong B12 replacement if pernicious anemia
  • Return precautions for worsening neurologic symptoms, severe fatigue
