100. DIABETES INSIPIDUS

Polyuria • Polydipsia • Hypernatremia • Dilute Urine
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Polyuria (>50 mL/kg/24 h, about 3.5 L/day in a 70-kg adult) with inappropriately dilute urine (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 1.17); intense thirst and preference for cold water (Practical); hypernatremia when water intake cannot keep up (Practical). Current names: AVP deficiency (central DI) and AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI) (2022 renaming position statement, via OpenEvidence).

  • Pathophysiology: Central DI results from inadequate ADH (vasopressin) secretion from posterior pituitary due to hypothalamic/pituitary damage. Nephrogenic DI results from renal resistance to ADH at the collecting duct level (aquaporin-2 dysfunction). Both lead to inability to concentrate urine and free water loss.
  • Risk Factors: Neurosurgery (especially transsphenoidal), traumatic brain injury, pituitary/hypothalamic tumors (craniopharyngioma, germinoma), infiltrative diseases (sarcoidosis, histiocytosis X, lymphoma), hypoxic brain injury, medications (lithium, demeclocycline, amphotericin, foscarnet), hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, pregnancy (vasopressinase), genetic (X-linked nephrogenic DI, autosomal AVPR2/AQP2 mutations)
  • Symptoms: Polyuria (large volume, dilute urine), intense thirst and polydipsia, nocturia (3-6 times/night), preference for ice-cold water, irritability, fatigue, confusion (if unable to maintain adequate intake), dehydration signs if fluid intake inadequate
  • Physical Exam: May appear normal if maintaining adequate oral intake. With inadequate intake: tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, altered mental status. Weight loss. Check for visual field defects (pituitary mass), signs of panhypopituitarism
  • Variants/Subtypes: Central DI (ADH deficiency) vs Nephrogenic DI (ADH resistance) vs Primary Polydipsia (psychogenic, compulsive water drinking). After pituitary surgery: transient DI, possible SIADH 7-10 days after surgery (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 3.10), then possible permanent DI; phase timing varies (Practical). Partial DI (some residual ADH function)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Serum Sodium: Often elevated (>145 mEq/L, can be >160 mEq/L); may be normal if patient maintaining adequate intake
  • Serum Osmolality: High (>295 mOsm/kg) when water intake is restricted or inadequate (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 1.17)
  • Urine Osmolality: With serum osmolality >295, normal kidneys concentrate urine to about 600 mOsm/kg (urine/plasma ratio ≥2); a lower ratio indicates DI (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 1.17). Urine osmolality 300-800 is indeterminate (partial forms) (review, via OpenEvidence)
  • Urine Output: Typically >3 L/day, up to 10-20 L/day in severe cases; hourly output >200-300 mL/h (Practical). ES 2016 defines polyuria as >50 mL/kg/24 h, about 3.5 L/day at 70 kg (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 1.17)
  • 24-Hour Urine Volume: Confirms polyuria; simultaneous osmolality measurement
  • Plasma ADH Level: Not recommended; AVP assays are unreliable, and copeptin is used instead (review, via OpenEvidence)
  • Other: BUN, creatinine, glucose (rule out hyperglycemia/DKA), calcium (hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic DI), potassium (hypokalemia causes nephrogenic DI)

Diagnostic Testing:

  • Water Deprivation Test: Plasma osmolality >295 with urine/plasma osmolality ratio <2 during deprivation confirms DI (ES 2016 hypopituitarism Table 3). Diagnostic accuracy about 77%, lower than copeptin testing (NEJM 2018 trial, via OpenEvidence). Protocol: withhold fluids for 8 hours from 8 a.m.; weigh and measure urine volume hourly; plasma and urine osmolality every 2-3 hours; at 4 p.m. give desmopressin 2 mcg IM and allow drinking, then urine osmolality and volume hourly for 4 hours; give desmopressin earlier if plasma osmolality exceeds 305 mOsm/kg; stop if weight loss exceeds 3% (ES 2016 hypopituitarism Table 3). After desmopressin: urine >800 mOsm/kg indicates central DI (AVP deficiency), <300 mOsm/kg nephrogenic DI (AVP resistance) (ES 2016 hypopituitarism Table 3); by percentage, a rise of more than 50% indicates complete AVP deficiency and a smaller rise AVP resistance (review, via OpenEvidence). Partial DI and primary polydipsia concentrate urine partially (300-800 mOsm/kg) and need further testing (ES 2016 hypopituitarism Table 3)
  • Desmopressin Challenge (hypernatremic patient): no guideline or label gives a diagnostic dose; the US label DI dose is 2-4 mcg/day IV or SC. Interpret by the >50% rise above (review, via OpenEvidence); an absolute 600 mOsm/kg cutoff is not supported (via OpenEvidence)
  • Copeptin: baseline >21.4 pmol/L indicates AVP resistance. Hypertonic saline test (target sodium ≥150 mmol/L): copeptin ≤4.9 pmol/L indicates AVP deficiency, accuracy 96.5% vs 76.6% for water deprivation (NEJM 2018). Arginine test at 60 min: ≤3.0 pmol/L AVP deficiency, >5.2 pmol/L primary polydipsia (NEJM 2023). Trials and reviews, no guideline (via OpenEvidence). Hypertonic saline test needs sodium checks every 30 min; avoid in heart failure or seizure disorder (review, via OpenEvidence)

Imaging:

  • MRI Brain with Pituitary Protocol: Essential in central DI. Look for: loss of normal posterior pituitary "bright spot" on T1 (absent in central DI, present in nephrogenic DI and normal), hypothalamic/pituitary masses, infiltrative diseases, evidence of trauma/surgery, ectopic posterior pituitary. Evaluate entire pituitary stalk and hypothalamus
  • CT Head: If MRI contraindicated; less sensitive but can identify masses, hemorrhage, calcifications

Diagnostic Criteria:

  • DI Diagnosis: polyuria (>50 mL/kg/24 h) with serum and urine osmolality measured together; serum >295 mOsm/kg with urine/plasma ratio <2 and a negative urine glucose (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 1.17)
  • Distinguish AVP deficiency vs resistance: desmopressin response (>50% rise = complete AVP deficiency; review, via OpenEvidence) or copeptin (above)
  • Rule Out: Primary polydipsia (low serum osmolality), osmotic diuresis (glucose, urea, mannitol), post-obstructive diuresis
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management:

  • Assess volume status and hemodynamics; establish IV access
  • Strict I&O monitoring (hourly urine output initially, may need Foley catheter)
  • Measure serum sodium, osmolality, urine osmolality STAT
  • Calculate free water deficit: Free water deficit (L) = 0.6 × body weight (kg) × [(current Na/140) - 1]; use 0.5 for women and add ongoing urine losses (review, via OpenEvidence)
  • Allow oral free water intake if patient alert and able to drink (preferred)
  • If hypernatremic with altered mental status or unable to drink: give hypotonic fluids IV (0.45% saline or D5W)
  • CORRECT SODIUM SLOWLY: in hypernatremia present for more than a few hours, lower sodium about 10 mEq/L per day and no faster than 0.5 mEq/L per hour (review, NEJM 2000, via OpenEvidence); no guideline sets this limit

Pharmacologic Treatment (Central DI):

  • Desmopressin (DDAVP) - First Line:
    • IV/SC: 2-4 mcg per day in one or two divided doses (US label)
    • Oral: start 0.05 mg twice daily; usual 0.1-0.8 mg/day in divided doses; range 0.1-1.2 mg/day in two or three doses (US label)
    • Intranasal (10 mcg/spray): 10 mcg once daily, up to 40 mcg/day in one to three doses (US label, via OpenEvidence)
    • Contraindicated: creatinine clearance <50 mL/min, hyponatremia or a history of it (US label). Injection label: boxed hyponatremia warning; contraindicated with loop diuretics, systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids, or illness causing fluid or electrolyte imbalance; serum sodium must be normal before starting (US label). ES 2016 hypopituitarism does not mention this glucocorticoid contraindication (checked in the guideline text)
    • Individualized schedules; educate every patient about the risk of overdosing; at least weekly, allow a phase of polyuria after the dose wears off, to prevent hyponatremia (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 2.15)
    • Sodium: within 1 week and about 1 month after starting, then periodically (US label); more often during inpatient titration (Practical)
  • After pituitary surgery: initial therapy with short-acting subcutaneous aqueous vasopressin (ADH), which is safer because most postoperative DI resolves on its own (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 3.9, weak). US vasopressin labels cover only intravenous use for vasodilatory shock, so this is off-label, and the guideline gives no dose (US label). No prescheduled desmopressin in the first week (risk of hyponatremia when transient DI resolves, and of SIADH 7-10 days after surgery); after discharge, oral or intranasal desmopressin only for significant polyuria; try at least once to stop it in the weeks or months after surgery (ES 2016 hypopituitarism recs 3.10, 3.11, 2.16)

Pharmacologic Treatment (Nephrogenic DI):

  • Desmopressin: ineffective in AVP resistance (US label)
  • Thiazide: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once or twice daily (maximum 50 mg/day) with reduced salt intake; off-label; consensus for congenital AVP resistance (2025 international consensus, non-US, via OpenEvidence). Thiazides reduce lithium clearance (via OpenEvidence)
  • Amiloride for lithium-induced AVP resistance: small trials only, no guideline; US label maximum 20 mg/day, boxed hyperkalemia warning (via OpenEvidence). Monitor lithium level and potassium (Practical)
  • NSAIDs: the 2025 consensus advises stopping COX inhibitors in adults because of nephrotoxicity (via OpenEvidence); not routine
  • Low Sodium Diet: <2 g/day reduces urine output by decreasing solute excretion
  • Treat Underlying Cause: Discontinue lithium if possible, correct hypercalcemia, correct hypokalemia

Fluid Management:

  • Match urine output with free water replacement (PO preferred if possible)
  • If IV fluids needed: D5W or 0.45% saline at rate matched to urine output losses
  • Avoid rapid sodium correction (about 10 mEq/L per day; see above)
  • Check serum sodium q4-6h initially, then q12h once stable (Practical)
  • Known central DI, NPO or impaired thirst: do not omit desmopressin; give it parenterally if oral intake is not allowed, with maintenance isotonic fluids and sodium about every 6 h (review, via OpenEvidence). Adipsic DI: careful desmopressin and fluid titration with frequent weights and sodium checks (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 2.17)
  • Daily weights to assess fluid balance

Endocrinology Consultation:

  • Consult for all cases of confirmed or suspected DI
  • Assess for panhypopituitarism (check TSH, free T4, cortisol, LH, FSH, testosterone/estradiol, IGF-1)
  • Central DI + anterior pituitary dysfunction suggests pituitary/hypothalamic disease
  • Long-term management planning and DDAVP dosing adjustment

Disposition:

  • ICU if: severe hypernatremia (>160 mEq/L), altered mental status, hemodynamic instability, post-neurosurgical patients, unable to maintain oral intake
  • Floor with telemetry: moderate hypernatremia (148-160 mEq/L), new diagnosis requiring DDAVP titration, stable patients transitioning to oral therapy
  • Discharge once: sodium normalized or stable (140-145 mEq/L), adequate oral intake maintained, DDAVP regimen established, endocrine follow-up arranged within 1-2 weeks
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Triphasic Response Post-Neurosurgery: After transsphenoidal surgery, transient DI can be followed by SIADH 7-10 days after surgery (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 3.10) and then by permanent DI. Do not schedule desmopressin in the first week (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 3.10). Phase durations and the permanent-DI rate vary (Practical).
  • Loss of Posterior Pituitary Bright Spot: Normal posterior pituitary appears bright on T1 MRI (ADH-containing vesicles). In central DI, this "bright spot" is absent. In nephrogenic DI, it's present (ADH production intact). (Practical) Also look for ectopic bright spot along pituitary stalk (ectopic neurohypophysis).
  • Central DI + Anterior Pituitary Dysfunction = Think Infiltrative Disease: Isolated central DI can be idiopathic or post-surgical. But if patient also has hypopituitarism (low TSH, ACTH, GH, gonadotropins), think infiltrative process: histiocytosis X (most common in children), sarcoidosis, lymphoma, metastases (especially breast, lung). Requires extensive pituitary imaging and sometimes biopsy.
  • Distinguish from Primary Polydipsia: Both cause polyuria and dilute urine, but primary polydipsia tends toward low-normal serum osmolality and sodium, and DI toward high-normal or high values (Practical); copeptin testing separates them best (NEJM 2018, via OpenEvidence). Water deprivation test: primary polydipsia, like partial DI, concentrates urine only partially (300-800 mOsm/kg), so further testing is needed (ES 2016 hypopituitarism Table 3).
  • Lithium-Induced Nephrogenic DI is Common and Often Irreversible: Lithium enters collecting duct principal cells via ENaC channels, accumulates, and downregulates aquaporin-2. Amiloride (blocks ENaC) is supported only by small trials; see dosing limits above (via OpenEvidence). Stopping lithium may improve but not fully resolve DI if damage is extensive (Practical).
  • Don't Overcorrect Hypernatremia Too Rapidly: Rapid sodium correction in DI can cause cerebral edema (reverse osmotic demyelination). The brain adapts to chronic hypernatremia by accumulating organic osmolytes. Rapid lowering of serum osmolality causes water shift into brain cells. Target about 10 mEq/L per day and no faster than 0.5 mEq/L per hour (review, NEJM 2000, via OpenEvidence); a 2023 cohort associated faster first-day correction with lower mortality, so the limit is debated (via OpenEvidence).
  • Hypovolemic Patients May Not Show Severe Polyuria Initially: If patient is volume-depleted on presentation, reduced GFR may mask the full extent of polyuria. After IV fluid resuscitation, urine output may suddenly increase dramatically to 500-1000 mL/hour as GFR improves and the DI becomes clinically apparent (Practical). Anticipate this and have DDAVP ready.
  • Intranasal DDAVP Can Be Unreliable: Intranasal desmopressin absorption varies with nasal congestion, rhinitis, or upper respiratory infections. If patient not responding to intranasal DDAVP, switch to oral or SC route. Oral doses are much higher than intranasal doses (US label ranges above).
  • Risk of Hyponatremia with DDAVP Overtreatment: DDAVP has a prolonged antidiuretic effect (Practical). Giving too much or too frequently without allowing kidney to excrete free water causes dilutional hyponatremia. Allow a phase of polyuria at least weekly (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 2.15). If Na falls below 135 mEq/L, hold the next dose and allow diuresis (Practical).
  • Nephrogenic DI from Hypercalcemia or Hypokalemia: Hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic DI by impairing collecting duct response to ADH and causing interstitial nephropathy. Hypokalemia downregulates aquaporin-2. Always check and correct calcium and potassium in patients with polyuria. Correcting the electrolyte abnormality often resolves the DI without need for specific DI treatment (Practical).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe hypernatremia (serum sodium >160 mEq/L)
  • Altered mental status, confusion, seizures
  • Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia unresponsive to fluids)
  • Post-neurosurgical patient (especially within 10 days of transsphenoidal surgery)
  • Urine output >500 mL/hour despite treatment (Practical)
  • Unable to maintain adequate oral intake despite thirst
  • Rapid sodium changes requiring frequent monitoring and IV fluid adjustments
  • Suspected panhypopituitarism with adrenal crisis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Serum sodium normalized (138-145 mEq/L) or stable near-normal range
  • Urine output controlled (<3 L/day) on DDAVP regimen
  • Patient able to maintain adequate oral fluid intake (matching urine losses)
  • Patient and family educated on DDAVP administration (timing, dose, route)
  • Patient educated on monitoring for signs of overtreatment (hyponatremia: headache, nausea, confusion)
  • Patient educated on monitoring for signs of undertreatment (recurrent polyuria, thirst)
  • Endocrinology follow-up arranged within 1-2 weeks for DDAVP titration
  • MRI brain completed (if central DI) or scheduled as outpatient
  • If post-neurosurgical: cleared by neurosurgery, aware of triphasic response potential
  • Written instructions including when to call doctor (urine output >4 L/day, severe thirst, confusion, headache)

101. PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA CRISIS

Hypertensive Emergency • Catecholamine Excess • Palpitations • Diaphoresis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Paroxysmal or sustained hypertension with headache, sweating, palpitations, tachycardia or pallor episodes (NCCN 2026). Crisis can follow anesthesia, surgery, tumor manipulation or drugs; avoid drugs that precipitate hormone-mediated crisis (NCCN 2026; examples such as metoclopramide and opioids: Practical)

  • Definitions: pheochromocytoma (PCC) arises from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells; paraganglioma (PGL) from extra-adrenal sympathetic or parasympathetic ganglia. Adrenal PCCs more often secrete metanephrine and PGLs normetanephrine; about 40% of PGLs secrete catecholamines, head and neck PGLs only about 5% (often dopamine) (NCCN 2026)
  • Complications: catecholamine-induced (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, MI, hypertensive emergency, shock, syncope, arrhythmia, aortic dissection, AKI, stroke (NANETS 2021); hyperglycemia (NCCN 2026)
  • Hereditary: up to 40% of adult and 80% of pediatric PCC/PGL, >20 susceptibility genes. Age <45 or multifocal, bilateral or recurrent tumors make a heritable variant more likely, but many carriers present with a solitary tumor and no family history (NCCN 2026)
  • Metastatic potential: all PCC/PGL are potentially malignant, with a lifelong metastatic risk of 5-15%; "benign" and "malignant" are no longer used. SDHB variants carry a 40-60% risk of metastatic disease (NCCN 2026)
  • Who to test (Practical): adrenal mass, known syndrome or family history, resistant or paroxysmal hypertension, hypertension triggered by anesthesia, surgery or drugs
  • Symptoms (Practical): headache, sweating, palpitations; anxiety, sense of impending doom, pallor, tremor, nausea/vomiting, abdominal or chest pain, dyspnea. Episodes last minutes to hours
  • Physical exam (Practical): sustained or paroxysmal hypertension, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension (volume depletion), pallor or flushing, diaphoresis, tremor, fever, hypertensive retinopathy, abdominal mass if large, café-au-lait spots (NF1), thyroid nodules (MEN2)
  • Secretory phenotype: norepinephrine-predominant tumors tend to cause sustained hypertension and epinephrine-predominant tumors paroxysmal hypertension (Practical). Dopamine-secreting tumors are usually asymptomatic; when symptomatic, hypotension is most common (NANETS 2021)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies - Biochemical Testing (Definitive Diagnosis):

  • First test: plasma free metanephrines or 24-h urine fractionated metanephrines (NCCN 2026). Elevation 3 times above the upper limit of normal is diagnostic (NCCN 2026); use the laboratory's reference interval. If that interval is for supine sampling, draw supine after rest (Practical)
  • Interfering drugs (review before testing): acetaminophen, labetalol, sotalol, α-methyldopa, tricyclic antidepressants, buspirone, phenoxybenzamine, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics, cocaine, sulfasalazine, levodopa; the discussion adds serotonin-reuptake inhibitors (NCCN 2026)
  • Catecholamines: urine or plasma catecholamines are no longer routinely recommended, because 15-20% of patients with PCC have normal urine catecholamines; both catecholamines and metanephrines can be falsely positive. Cervical PGL: serum or 24-h urine fractionated catecholamines (dopamine) or methoxytyramine if available (NCCN 2026)
  • Chromogranin A (Practical): nonspecific; falsely elevated with PPIs
  • Supporting labs: hyperglycemia (NCCN 2026); hemoconcentration, leukocytosis, hypercalcemia if MEN2A with hyperparathyroidism (Practical)

Imaging - Tumor Localization:

  • Anatomic: adrenal-protocol CT or MRI if not already done. CT is most helpful for adrenal masses and PGLs; some extra-adrenal PGLs are seen better on MRI. MRI may be preferable for germline carriers to limit radiation (NCCN 2026). MRI in pregnancy; heterogeneous enhancing mass, usually >10 HU on unenhanced CT (Practical)
  • Suspected metastatic or multifocal disease: multiphasic abdomen/pelvis CT or MRI, SSTR-PET/CT or PET/MRI (68Ga-DOTATATE, 64Cu-DOTATATE, 68Ga-DOTATOC), FDG-PET/CT, chest CT, MIBG with SPECT/CT; the preferred functional method remains unclear (NCCN 2026)
  • Functional imaging choice: MIBG is less sensitive than FDG-PET and 68Ga-DOTATATE for metastatic and multifocal disease in VHL and SDH syndromes; obtain MIBG if considering I-131 MIBG therapy (NCCN 2026). SSTR-PET/CT first-line when metastatic disease is suspected; FDG-PET/CT an alternative, especially SDHB-associated or rapidly progressive disease; no routine functional imaging for every primary tumor (NANETS 2021)

Cardiac Evaluation:

  • ECG: Sinus tachycardia, LVH, ST-T wave changes, QT prolongation, rarely MI pattern
  • Echocardiogram: Assess for catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo pattern with apical ballooning), LVH, systolic/diastolic dysfunction, valvular disease. Important for preoperative risk stratification
  • Troponin: May be elevated (myocardial strain, type 2 MI from demand ischemia)

Genetic Testing:

  • Genetic counseling and testing for inherited syndromes in every patient with PCC/PGL (NCCN 2026)
  • Genes: RET (MEN2), NF1, VHL, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2, TMEM127, MAX, FH, MDH2 (NCCN 2026)
  • Carriers: lifelong biochemical and clinical screening, starting at age 6-10 for SDHB and 10-15 for other hereditary PCC/PGL, timed by gene (NCCN 2026)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management (Acute Crisis):

  • ICU, continuous cardiac monitoring and arterial line (Practical)
  • IV access; avoid palpating the abdomen (Practical); avoid drugs that precipitate hormone-mediated crisis (NCCN 2026)
  • ECG, cardiac enzymes, strict I&O
  • BP target: AHA/ACC 2025 lists catecholamine excess (eg, pheochromocytoma) among states that require rapid BP lowering, with no numeric target. Its general hypertensive-emergency path: lower SBP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to <160/100 over the next 2-6 h, then to 130-140 systolic over 24-48 h
  • NEVER give a beta-blocker before alpha blockade and volume expansion: unopposed alpha stimulation can cause hypertensive crisis (NANETS 2021)

Pharmacologic Treatment - Acute Hypertensive Crisis:

  • Agents: nitroprusside, phentolamine or nicardipine (NCCN 2026). For catecholamine excess, AHA/ACC 2025 lists clevidipine, nicardipine or phentolamine (alphabetical, no order of preference). NANETS 2021 also lists IV magnesium sulfate
  • Phentolamine: 5 mg IV bolus; repeat every 10 min as needed to target; maximum cumulative 50 mg/24 h (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • Nicardipine: 5 mg/h IV, increase by 2.5 mg/h every 5 min to a maximum of 15 mg/h (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • Clevidipine: 1-2 mg/h IV, doubling every 90 s until BP nears target, then smaller increases every 5-10 min; maximum 21 mg/h and 72 h (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • Nitroprusside: 0.3-0.5 mcg/kg/min, increase by 0.5 mcg/kg/min every 5 min to a maximum of 10 mcg/kg/min; shortest possible duration; intra-arterial BP monitoring recommended (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • Tachycardia, only after alpha blockade: beta-1-selective or nonselective beta-blocker (NCCN 2026). Esmolol 500-1000 mcg/kg IV over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min, increasing by 50 mcg/kg/min to a maximum of 300 mcg/kg/min (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • Arrhythmias: esmolol or lidocaine (NCCN 2026)
  • Labetalol and other combined alpha/beta blockers: not recommended (NCCN 2026); labetalol should not be initial therapy (NANETS 2021)
  • Volume: aggressive volume repletion with alpha blockade (NCCN 2026); patients are often volume-depleted, give isotonic crystalloid as tolerated (Practical)

Preoperative Medical Preparation (Once Diagnosis Confirmed):

  • Who and how long: alpha blockade for every hormonally secreting PCC/PGL regardless of symptoms, with aggressive volume repletion and a high-salt diet, for 7-14 days or until stable (NCCN 2026). NANETS 2021: alpha blockade 7-14 days before any procedure, including nonsecreting metastatic disease
  • Agent: alpha-1-selective (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin) or nonselective (phenoxybenzamine) (NCCN 2026). No consensus on the agent; a randomized trial of phenoxybenzamine vs doxazosin in 134 patients found no difference in hemodynamic outcomes (NANETS 2021). Doxazosin has a longer half-life and is often more available (NCCN 2026)
  • Starting doses: phenoxybenzamine 10 mg every 12 h, doxazosin 2 mg once daily, or prazosin 1-2 mg once daily, at bedtime; titrate every 2-3 days to the highest tolerated dose and BP goal. Usual doses: phenoxybenzamine 10-20 mg every 8-12 h, doxazosin 2-8 mg every 12-24 h, prazosin 2-5 mg every 8 h, terazosin 4-8 mg every 12-24 h (NANETS 2021). Phenoxybenzamine label: 10 mg twice daily, increased every other day, usually to 20-40 mg 2-3 times daily (US label)
  • Targets: seated BP <130/80, standing SBP >90, heart rate <90 (70-80 long-term if possible), individualized for age and cardiovascular disease; orthostatic hypotension is an adverse effect of alpha-blockers, not the target (NANETS 2021)
  • Beta-blocker: only after alpha blockade and volume expansion, for tachycardia: metoprolol tartrate 25-50 mg every 12 h, atenolol 25-50 mg once or twice daily, or propranolol 20-40 mg every 8-12 h; aim HR <90 (NANETS 2021). Combined alpha/beta blockers not recommended (NCCN 2026)
  • Calcium channel blocker: dihydropyridine CCB if more BP control is needed after alpha blockade; not as monotherapy unless alpha blockade is not tolerated (NCCN 2026). Amlodipine 5-10 mg daily or nifedipine 30-60 mg every 12 h (NANETS 2021)
  • Metyrosine: may be added to alpha blockade to stabilize BP (NCCN 2026); 250-500 mg, titrated up to every 6 h; expensive, not always available, significant adverse effects (NANETS 2021)
  • Salt and fluids: high-sodium diet and increased fluid intake (NANETS 2021)

Definitive Treatment - Surgical Resection:

  • Resection for resectable tumors; minimally invasive approach preferred when safe and feasible (NCCN 2026)
  • Open approach for large or invasive tumors (Practical)
  • Timing: after alpha blockade for 7-14 days or until stable (NCCN 2026)
  • Perioperative: IV phentolamine can be used intraoperatively; hypotension and hypoglycemia can follow resection, so give IV fluids for volume expansion with dextrose (NCCN 2026). Continue the alpha-blocker until the morning of surgery (Practical)
  • Locally unresectable or metastatic disease: observe if asymptomatic or slow-growing, low-volume disease; for secreting tumors continue alpha blockade with a clinical trial, cytoreductive resection, radiotherapy or systemic therapy (NCCN 2026)

Consultations:

  • Endocrinology: Immediate consult for diagnosis confirmation, biochemical testing, preoperative optimization
  • Surgery (Endocrine Surgery): For definitive resection planning
  • Anesthesiology: Early involvement for perioperative planning (high-risk surgery)
  • Cardiology: If cardiomyopathy, severe arrhythmias, or CAD
  • Genetics: For germline mutation testing and family counseling

Disposition:

  • ICU: All patients in hypertensive crisis, catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy, or perioperative period
  • Floor with telemetry: Stable patients undergoing preoperative alpha/beta blockade titration
  • Discharge: after resection and postoperative recovery with stable BP off IV agents (Practical). First postoperative H&P, BP and plasma free or 24-h urine metanephrines 12 weeks to 12 months after resection, earlier if symptomatic (NCCN 2026)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Never Beta-Block Before Alpha-Blockade ("Rule of Alpha First"): a beta-blocker given first leaves alpha stimulation unopposed and can precipitate hypertensive crisis; start beta blockade only after alpha blockade and volume expansion (NANETS 2021). Think: "A before B in the alphabet, alpha before beta in pheo."
  • The Rule of 10s Is Outdated: up to 40% of adult PCC/PGL are hereditary, and all are potentially malignant with a lifelong metastatic risk of 5-15% (NCCN 2026). The classic triad is often incomplete; sustained or resistant hypertension, or hypertension triggered by anesthesia or surgery, should prompt testing (Practical)
  • Test Metanephrines, Not Catecholamines: catecholamine secretion can be intermittent, and 15-20% of patients with PCC have normal urine catecholamines (NCCN 2026). A normal plasma free metanephrine result makes PCC/PGL unlikely (Practical)
  • Up to 40% Are Hereditary: Offer Genetic Testing to All: genetic counseling and testing for every patient (NCCN 2026). Syndromes: MEN2 (RET), VHL, NF1, hereditary PCC/PGL (SDHx, TMEM127, MAX) (NCCN 2026); features such as medullary thyroid cancer (MEN2), hemangioblastoma and renal cell cancer (VHL), and café-au-lait spots (NF1) guide the exam (Practical). Results guide surveillance and family screening
  • Orthostatic Hypotension in a Hypertensive Patient: catecholamine excess can cause orthostatic hypotension (NANETS 2021); hypertension with an orthostatic drop should prompt PCC/PGL testing (Practical)
  • Perioperative Management Is High-Risk: tumor manipulation releases catecholamines (hypertensive crisis, arrhythmias, MI, stroke); after removal, hypotension and hypoglycemia can follow. IV phentolamine intraoperatively; IV fluids with dextrose postoperatively (NCCN 2026). Experienced anesthesia team and arterial line (Practical)
  • Preoperative Targets, Not Orthostasis: titrate alpha blockade to seated BP <130/80, standing SBP >90 and HR <90, with a high-sodium diet and extra fluids; orthostatic hypotension is an adverse effect (NANETS 2021)
  • Labetalol Is Not Initial Therapy: its alpha:beta blocking ratio of 1:5 to 1:9 can cause paradoxical hypertension and crisis (NANETS 2021). Combined alpha/beta blockers are not recommended; use an alpha-blocker first, then a separate beta-blocker if needed (NCCN 2026)
  • Catecholamine-Induced Cardiomyopathy Can Mimic MI: Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy pattern: apical ballooning, ST elevations, troponin elevation, but normal coronary arteries on angiography. Caused by catecholamine myocardial toxicity. Can also see true type 2 MI from demand ischemia. Echo shows wall motion abnormalities that typically resolve after tumor resection. Cardiac MRI can help distinguish from acute MI.
  • Follow-up After Resection: lifelong metastatic risk 5-15%. H&P, BP and metanephrines 12 weeks to 12 months after resection, then annually; consider chest and abdomen/pelvis imaging (NCCN 2026). Annual plasma free or 24-h urine metanephrines for every primary PPGL; consider annual imaging for higher-risk, especially nonsecreting, tumors (NANETS 2021). Germline carriers: gene-specific lifelong screening (NCCN 2026)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hypertensive emergency: BP >180/120 with acute target organ damage (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • Hypertensive crisis requiring IV antihypertensive drip (phentolamine, nicardipine, nitroprusside)
  • Acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, ECG changes, troponin elevation)
  • Catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo, heart failure, pulmonary edema)
  • Cerebrovascular event (stroke, hypertensive encephalopathy, seizures)
  • Tachydysrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia)
  • Perioperative patients (during tumor resection or immediate post-op period)
  • Suspected pheochromocytoma crisis triggered by surgery/anesthesia
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Successful tumor resection completed
  • Postoperative recovery complete (typically 3-5 days)
  • BP controlled (<140/90 mmHg) off IV medications, on oral regimen or no medications
  • No ongoing chest pain, dyspnea, or neurologic symptoms
  • Postoperative H&P, BP and plasma free or 24-h urine metanephrines scheduled 12 weeks to 12 months after resection, earlier if symptomatic (NCCN 2026)
  • Patient educated on symptoms of recurrence (lifelong metastatic risk 5-15%; NCCN 2026)
  • Endocrinology follow-up arranged (Practical)
  • Genetic testing results discussed or scheduled for outpatient
  • Family members referred for screening if hereditary syndrome identified
  • Annual H&P, BP and metanephrines after the first year (NCCN 2026); annual metanephrines for every primary PPGL (NANETS 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Nicardipine, 💊 Nitroprusside, 💊 Esmolol, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Atenolol, 💊 Amlodipine

102. SEVERE ACUTE DIARRHEA / VOLUME DEPLETION

Frequent Watery Stools • Dehydration • Electrolyte Abnormalities • Acute Kidney Injury
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Abrupt onset of ≥3 loose/watery stools per day lasting <14 days, often with nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and signs of volume depletion (tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, decreased urine output, acute kidney injury).

  • Pathophysiology: Infectious (bacterial, viral, parasitic), medication-induced (antibiotics causing C. difficile), inflammatory, osmotic, or secretory mechanisms causing increased intestinal fluid secretion and decreased absorption. Volume depletion results from GI losses exceeding oral intake, with secondary renal hypoperfusion causing prerenal AKI. Electrolyte losses (Na, K, bicarbonate) can cause metabolic acidosis and dysrhythmias.
  • Risk Factors: Recent antibiotic use (C. difficile), recent travel (traveler's diarrhea), immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy, transplant), contaminated food/water, nursing home residence, hospitalization, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes (autonomic neuropathy), laxative abuse, elderly age, chronic kidney disease
  • Symptoms: Loose or watery stools, 3 or more in 24 h above baseline (ACG 2016), abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, fever (infectious), tenesmus, fecal urgency, fecal incontinence, thirst, dizziness, weakness, decreased urine output, confusion (elderly)
  • Physical Exam: Tachycardia, orthostatic vital signs (BP drop >20 mmHg systolic or HR increase >20 bpm on standing), hypotension (if severe), dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, delayed capillary refill, cool extremities, decreased urine output, altered mental status, abdominal tenderness (diffuse or focal), hyperactive bowel sounds, occult blood on rectal exam (inflammatory/invasive diarrhea)
  • Variants/Subtypes: Watery diarrhea (most common: viral, ETEC, cholera) vs Inflammatory/Bloody diarrhea (Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, EHEC, C. difficile, IBD flare). Secretory (persists with fasting: VIPoma, carcinoid) vs Osmotic (stops with fasting: lactose intolerance, sorbitol). Hospital-acquired vs Community-acquired
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Basic Metabolic Panel: Practical: elevated BUN and creatinine, sodium disorders, hypokalemia, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from stool bicarbonate loss
  • Complete Blood Count: Not for determining the cause (IDSA 2017 rec 22); shows hemoconcentration with volume depletion; with STEC, follow Hgb and platelets for HUS (rec 23)
  • Lactate: Practical: elevated with hypoperfusion, sepsis, or mesenteric ischemia
  • Urinalysis and Urine Chemistries: Volume depletion maximally concentrates the urine; high urine osmolality with low urine sodium shows intact tubular function but does not prove benign prerenal azotemia (KDIGO 2012 AKI)
  • Stool Studies (IDSA 2017; ACG 2016):
    • Fever, bloody or mucoid stools, severe cramping or tenderness, or sepsis: test for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile, and STEC (IDSA rec 8)
    • Dysentery, moderate-severe disease, or symptoms over 7 days: stool studies to direct therapy (ACG rec 2)
    • C. difficile: after antimicrobial use or with healthcare-associated diarrhea; one diarrheal specimen (IDSA rec 18)
    • Parasites: travelers with diarrhea lasting 14 days or longer (IDSA rec 13)
    • Immunocompromised: broad testing; AIDS with persistent diarrhea: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora, microsporidia, MAC, CMV (IDSA rec 12)
    • Do not use fecal leukocytes or lactoferrin to establish the cause (IDSA rec 20)
  • Blood Cultures (IDSA rec 9): Signs of septicemia or suspected enteric fever, systemic manifestations, immunocompromise, high-risk conditions such as hemolytic anemia, or febrile illness after travel to an enteric fever-endemic area

Imaging:

  • CT Abdomen/Pelvis with IV Contrast: Practical: severe abdominal pain, peritoneal signs, suspected toxic megacolon, ischemic colitis, perforation, or abscess; findings include colonic wall thickening (C. difficile, CMV colitis), pneumatosis, free air, thumbprinting (ischemic colitis). IDSA 2017 rec 25: consider imaging in older patients with invasive Salmonella or Yersinia and sustained fever or bacteremia despite therapy
  • Abdominal X-ray: suspected toxic megacolon (transverse colon over 6 cm with loss of haustra; AGA inpatient IBD 2026). Practical: obstruction, free air

Endoscopy:

  • Colonoscopy: Consider for clinical colitis or proctitis, persistent unexplained diarrhea in AIDS or certain underlying conditions, or persistent diarrhea with anal intercourse (IDSA rec 24). Not recommended for persistent symptoms (14-30 days) with a negative stool workup (ACG rec 12). Practical: caution in acute severe colitis (perforation risk)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management:

  • Practical: assess hemodynamics (orthostatic vitals, BP, HR)
  • Practical: IV access (two large-bore IVs if severe dehydration or hypotension)
  • Isotonic IV fluid (LR or NS) for severe dehydration, shock, altered mental status, failed ORS, or ileus (IDSA rec 41); Practical: 1-2 L bolus, reassess
  • Continue IV fluid until pulse, perfusion, and mental status normalize, then replace the remaining deficit with ORS (IDSA rec 42)
  • Practical: strict I&O (consider Foley catheter if critically ill)
  • Infection control: gloves, gowns, and hand hygiene, with the product chosen by suspected pathogen (IDSA rec 53)

Fluid and Electrolyte Replacement:

  • Oral Rehydration (first-line for mild-moderate dehydration): Reduced-osmolarity ORS (IDSA rec 39). Balanced ORS for the elderly with severe diarrhea or any traveler with cholera-like watery diarrhea; most adults keep up with water, juices, sports drinks, soups, and saltine crackers (ACG rec 5). Replace ongoing stool losses with ORS (IDSA rec 43)
  • IV Fluid Resuscitation (indications above):
    • Lactated Ringer's or 0.9% saline (IDSA rec 41); Practical: 1-2 L bolus initially
    • Practical: 150-250 mL/h, adjusted to ongoing losses (may need 3-6 L/day)
  • Potassium Replacement (Practical): If K under 3.0 mEq/L: 40-80 mEq PO or 20-40 mEq IV (max 10 mEq/h peripheral, 20 mEq/h central); recheck K every 4-6 h
  • Bicarbonate (Practical): Usually corrects with volume resuscitation; consider sodium bicarbonate if pH under 7.2 or HCO3 under 10
  • Magnesium (Practical): Replace if Mg under 1.5 mg/dL (2-4 g IV over 4 hours)

Antimicrobial Therapy (if indicated):

  • C. difficile Infection (IDSA/SHEA 2021; see card 22):
    • Initial episode, preferred: fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID for 10 days, or BID for 5 days then every other day for 20 days
    • Alternative: vancomycin 125 mg PO QID for 10 days; metronidazole 500 mg PO TID for 10-14 days only for nonsevere CDI when neither is available
    • Nonsevere: WBC 15,000/µL or less and creatinine under 1.5 mg/dL. Fulminant: hypotension or shock, ileus, or megacolon
    • Fulminant only: vancomycin 500 mg PO or NG QID plus metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h; consider rectal vancomycin if ileus
    • Stop the offending antibiotic if possible
  • Empiric Therapy: Not recommended for most acute watery or bloody diarrhea (IDSA recs 30, 36; ACG recs 9-10). Exceptions: fever documented in a medical setting with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea or dysentery presumed Shigella; recent international travel with temperature 38.5°C or higher or sepsis; immunocompromised with severe illness and bloody diarrhea. Agent: ciprofloxacin or azithromycin by local susceptibility and travel history (IDSA rec 31)
  • Traveler's Diarrhea (ACG 2016 Table 4): Azithromycin 1,000 mg once or 500 mg daily for 3 days (preferred for dysentery or fever); levofloxacin 500 mg once or for 3 days; ciprofloxacin 750 mg once or 500 mg for 3 days; rifaximin 200 mg TID for 3 days (not for invasive diarrhea)
  • Campylobacter: Azithromycin first choice; ciprofloxacin alternative (IDSA Table 6). Practical: azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days
  • Shigella: Azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone; TMP-SMX or ampicillin if susceptible; avoid fluoroquinolones if the ciprofloxacin MIC is 0.12 µg/mL or higher, even if reported susceptible (IDSA Table 6). XDR strains (resistant to azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, TMP-SMX, and ampicillin) were about 5% of US infections in 2022: get culture and susceptibilities (CDC HAN 486, 2023)
  • Salmonella (nontyphoidal): Usually not indicated for uncomplicated infection. Treat if at risk for invasive infection (age 3 months or younger, over 50 with suspected atherosclerosis, immunosuppression, valvular or endovascular cardiac disease, significant joint disease): ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, TMP-SMX, or amoxicillin if susceptible; ceftriaxone preferred for invasive disease (IDSA Table 6)
  • Giardia: Tinidazole or nitazoxanide first choice; metronidazole alternative (not FDA approved for giardiasis) (IDSA Table 6). Tinidazole 2 g PO once with food (FDA label)
  • Cryptosporidium: Nitazoxanide (HIV-uninfected, or HIV with effective ART); in HIV, immune reconstitution with ART drives response (IDSA Table 6). Nitazoxanide 500 mg PO every 12 h with food for 3 days (FDA label); the label notes it has not been shown effective for Cryptosporidium diarrhea in HIV-infected or immunodeficient patients
  • STEC (E. coli O157 and Shiga toxin 2 producers): Avoid antibiotics (IDSA rec 35, strong); monitor Hgb, platelets, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and a blood smear for HUS (rec 23)

Symptomatic Management:

  • Antimotility Agents:
    • Loperamide may be given to immunocompetent adults with acute watery diarrhea, once hydrated (IDSA recs 46-47)
    • Avoid with inflammatory diarrhea or diarrhea with fever (toxic megacolon risk) (IDSA rec 47, strong); Practical: avoid with C. difficile or suspected STEC
    • Dose: 4 mg, then 2 mg after each loose stool; ACG text caps self-treatment at 8 mg/day for no more than 48 h; with antibiotics for traveler's diarrhea, up to 16 mg/24 h (ACG 2016 Table 4). Boxed warning: torsades, cardiac arrest, and death above recommended doses (FDA label)
  • Antiemetics: May be considered once hydrated; not a substitute for fluids (IDSA rec 46). Practical: ondansetron 4-8 mg IV/PO q8h PRN. Ondansetron is FDA-labeled only for chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and postoperative nausea; QT prolongation: avoid in congenital long QT, ECG monitoring with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, or other QT-prolonging drugs; severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh 10 or more): no more than 8 mg/day (FDA label)
  • Bismuth Subsalicylate: Controls stool passage in mild-moderate illness (ACG rec 7, strong): 30 mL (525 mg) liquid or 2 tablets (263 mg each) every 30-60 min, maximum 8 doses/24 h; causes black stools and tongue
  • Probiotics: US guidelines differ: ACG 2016 recommends against them for acute diarrhea in adults except postantibiotic-associated illness (strong); IDSA 2017 says they may be offered (weak)

Nutrition:

  • Resume the usual diet during or right after rehydration (IDSA rec 45)
  • Practical: BRAT diet unnecessary; soups, broths, and saltine crackers are fine (ACG 2016)
  • Practical: Avoid dairy temporarily if lactose intolerance suspected
  • Encourage oral fluids with electrolytes

Disposition:

  • Practical: ICU: Septic shock, severe electrolyte disturbances, toxic megacolon, fulminant C. difficile
  • Practical: Floor: Moderate-severe volume depletion requiring IV fluids, unable to tolerate adequate PO intake, elderly with comorbidities, AKI requiring monitoring
  • Practical: Discharge: Mild-moderate diarrhea, tolerating PO, hemodynamically stable, improving symptoms, able to follow-up
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Volume Depletion and AKI: High urine osmolality with low urine sodium in oliguric azotemia shows intact tubular function but does not prove benign prerenal azotemia (KDIGO 2012). Practical: an elevated BUN:Cr ratio that corrects with fluids supports a prerenal cause.
  • Antimotility Agents Are Not Banned: Loperamide may be given to immunocompetent adults with acute watery diarrhea (IDSA, weak) and is a recommended adjunct to antibiotics in traveler's diarrhea (ACG rec 8). Avoid with inflammatory diarrhea or fever (IDSA, strong).
  • STEC and HUS: Avoid antibiotics for E. coli O157 and Shiga toxin 2 producers (IDSA rec 35). Test for Shiga toxin when STEC is suspected (rec 6), and follow Hgb, platelets, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and a blood smear for early HUS (rec 23).
  • ORS First: Reduced-osmolarity ORS is first-line for mild-moderate dehydration in adults (IDSA rec 39); switch from IV to ORS once pulse, perfusion, and mental status normalize (rec 42).
  • Fulminant C. difficile: Defined by hypotension or shock, ileus, or megacolon (IDSA/SHEA 2021); WBC over 15,000 or creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or higher alone is not fulminant. Give vancomycin 500 mg PO or NG QID plus metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h; consider rectal vancomycin if ileus. Practical: early surgical consultation for toxic megacolon or perforation.
  • Hypokalemia (Practical): Common with large stool losses; can cause arrhythmias, weakness, and ileus. K 2.5-3.0: 40-80 mEq PO; under 2.5: 40 mEq IV over 4 hours (central line preferred above 10 mEq/h); recheck every 4-6 h until above 3.5.
  • Lactate (Practical): Elevation may reflect hypoperfusion, sepsis, or metformin accumulation with AKI. Lactate from hypoperfusion should clear with fluids; hold metformin with AKI.
  • Non-Anion Gap Acidosis (Practical): Stool bicarbonate loss causes a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap acidosis that usually corrects with volume repletion; an anion gap acidosis (lactic, keto) points to a more serious process.
  • Immunocompromised Hosts: Use a broad differential with culture, viral studies, and parasite exam; in AIDS with persistent diarrhea add Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora, microsporidia, MAC, and CMV (IDSA rec 12); consider endoscopy (rec 24). CMV colitis: ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h (HHS OI 2025). Practical: MAC, azithromycin plus ethambutol.
  • Consider Ischemic Colitis in Older Adults with Bloody Diarrhea (Practical): Acute bloody diarrhea with abdominal pain, especially with vascular disease, AF, hypotension, or cocaine use; watershed areas (splenic flexure, sigmoid); CT wall thickening or thumbprinting. Gangrene, peritonitis, or shock needs urgent surgery.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: Septic shock (hypotension requiring vasopressors, lactate >4 mmol/L)
  • Practical: Severe dehydration with persistent hypotension despite 3-4 L IV fluids
  • Acute kidney injury with oliguria/anuria requiring urgent dialysis consideration
  • Practical: Life-threatening electrolyte disturbances (K <2.5 or >6.5 mEq/L, severe acidosis pH <7.2)
  • Toxic megacolon: transverse colon over 6 cm with loss of haustra, with systemic toxicity (AGA inpatient IBD 2026; card 181)
  • Fulminant C. difficile: hypotension or shock, ileus, or megacolon (IDSA/SHEA 2021)
  • Altered mental status, seizures from severe electrolyte abnormalities
  • GI bleeding with hemodynamic instability
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Hemodynamically stable (BP >90/60, HR <100, normal orthostatics)
  • Practical: Tolerating adequate oral fluids (>1-1.5 L/day) without vomiting
  • Practical: Diarrhea frequency decreasing or stable (<5 stools/day)
  • Practical: Electrolytes normalized or improving trend (K >3.5, Na 135-145, normal bicarb)
  • Renal function improved or stable (Cr at or near baseline)
  • Afebrile for 24 hours if infectious etiology
  • Appropriate antibiotics prescribed if indicated (C. diff, Shigella, Giardia)
  • Patient educated on hydration, signs of worsening, when to return (severe abdominal pain, bloody stools, fever, dizziness, decreased urine output)
  • Practical: Follow-up arranged with PCP within 3-7 days
  • If C. difficile: Practical: counsel on recurrence risk, soap-and-water hand hygiene, and avoiding unnecessary PPIs

103. DIVERTICULITIS (COMPLICATED)

LLQ Pain • Fever • Leukocytosis • Abscess/Perforation/Fistula
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Acute left lower quadrant (LLQ) abdominal pain with fever and leukocytosis. Complicated diverticulitis involves abscess formation, perforation with peritonitis, fistula (colovesical, colovaginal), or stricture/obstruction.

  • Pathophysiology: Diverticula form where the mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscularis propria at points where the vasa recta penetrate the wall. Complicated diverticulitis means phlegmon, abscess, or perforation, with stricture and fistula as delayed complications (ACG 2026 Table 1); abscess is the most common complication (ACG 2026), occurring in 15-40% of patients presenting with acute sigmoid diverticulitis (ASCRS 2020). Colovesical fistula: pneumaturia, fecaluria
  • Risk Factors: Smoking, heavy alcohol use, obesity, physical inactivity, regular NSAID or aspirin use, diet high in red meat and processed grains (ACG 2026 recs 4-10); immunosuppression. Constipation is no longer presumed to play a role (ACG 2026)
  • Symptoms: Acute LLQ abdominal pain (constant, may radiate to back/groin), fever >38°C, anorexia, nausea, change in bowel habits (diarrhea or constipation), dysuria/frequency if bladder involvement, pneumaturia/fecaluria (colovesical fistula), vaginal passage of stool/flatus (colovaginal fistula)
  • Physical Exam: LLQ tenderness (most sensitive finding), palpable tender mass (phlegmon or abscess), rebound tenderness, guarding, rigidity (if peritonitis), fever, tachycardia, hypotension (if septic), diminished bowel sounds, rectal exam: tenderness, palpable mass if low abscess
  • Variants/Subtypes (modified Hinchey, CT-based; ACG 2026 Table 1): Stage 0, mild clinical diverticulitis (wall thickening, pericolic inflammation); Ia, confined pericolic inflammation or phlegmon; Ib, pericolic or mesocolic abscess; II, pelvic, intra-abdominal, or retroperitoneal abscess; III, generalized purulent peritonitis; IV, generalized fecal peritonitis. Stages 0-I are typically managed nonoperatively; higher stages often need drainage or surgery
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Complete Blood Count: Practical: leukocytosis with left shift; marked leukocytosis raises concern for abscess or perforation
  • C-Reactive Protein: CRP over 150 mg/L discriminated complicated from uncomplicated disease in one retrospective study; evidence is limited and supports no single algorithm (ASCRS 2020)
  • Basic Metabolic Panel: Acute kidney injury (prerenal from sepsis/dehydration), electrolyte abnormalities
  • Liver Function Tests: Usually normal; if elevated, consider liver abscess or biliary pathology
  • Lactate: Practical: elevated with sepsis, hypoperfusion, mesenteric ischemia, or perforation
  • Lipase: To rule out pancreatitis (similar presentation)
  • Urinalysis: May show pyuria, hematuria if colovesical fistula or bladder irritation from adjacent inflammation. True UTI vs sterile pyuria (inflammation without infection)
  • Blood Cultures: Practical: fever, septic appearance, or immunocompromise

Imaging - CT Abdomen/Pelvis with IV Contrast (Gold Standard):

  • Indications: CT is the most appropriate initial imaging for suspected diverticulitis (ASCRS 2020, 1B), especially at first presentation and in severe cases (ACG 2026). Low-dose CT, even without contrast, is about 95% sensitive and specific for acute abdominal complaints including diverticulitis (ASCRS 2020)
  • Classic CT Findings:
    • Colonic wall thickening
    • Pericolic fat stranding (inflammation)
    • Diverticula visible
    • Abscess: loculated fluid collection with enhancing rim (Hinchey Ib/II)
    • Free air (pneumoperitoneum): perforation; diffuse peritonitis needs urgent colectomy, but selected stable patients without diffuse peritonitis can be managed nonoperatively (ASCRS 2020)
    • Extraluminal air/fecalith: microperforation contained by mesentery
    • Bowel obstruction: dilated bowel proximal to inflamed segment (stricture)
    • Colovesical fistula: air in bladder (pneumaturia) without urinary catheter
  • Contraindications: Renal insufficiency (relative; consider non-contrast CT or MRI), contrast allergy (can premedicate or use MRI)

Alternative Imaging:

  • Ultrasound: Alternative when CT is unavailable or contraindicated, including pregnancy (ASCRS 2020, 1C); can miss complicated diverticulitis, so should not be the only imaging if that is suspected; user-dependent and limited in obesity
  • MRI Abdomen/Pelvis: If pregnancy, renal insufficiency, contrast allergy. Excellent for evaluating pelvic abscesses and fistulas
  • Abdominal X-ray: Low sensitivity but can detect free air (upright CXR or left lateral decubitus), bowel obstruction, ileus. Not diagnostic for diverticulitis

Colonoscopy:

  • Not During the Acute Episode: Do not perform within 6-8 weeks of an acute episode (incomplete exam, complications) (ACG 2026)
  • After Recovery: Recommended after complicated diverticulitis (ACG 2026 rec 1, strong; ASCRS 2020, 1C); suggested after uncomplicated diverticulitis with alarm features or if not current with colorectal cancer screening (ACG 2026 rec 2). Malignancy found in 7.9-11% after complicated vs 0.7-1.3% after uncomplicated diverticulitis (ASCRS 2020)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management:

  • Practical: IV access, hemodynamic stabilization (IV fluids if tachycardic, hypotensive)
  • Practical: NPO initially, advance diet as tolerated (clear liquids → low-residue diet)
  • Practical: pain control with IV opioids (morphine 2-4 mg IV q2-4h, hydromorphone 0.5-1 mg IV q3-4h); avoid NSAIDs
  • Practical: Antiemetics: Ondansetron 4-8 mg IV q8h PRN
  • Practical: Strict I&O monitoring

Antibiotic Therapy:

  • Uncomplicated Diverticulitis: Selected patients can be treated without antibiotics (ASCRS 2020, 1A); ACG 2026 suggests against routine antibiotics for low-risk patients (rec 3). Low risk requires all: immunocompetent, outpatient, no complicated disease, hemodynamically stable, no fever, tachycardia, or leukocytosis, not frail, tolerating PO, no recent antibiotics, reliable follow-up (ACG 2026 Table 6)
  • Give Antibiotics: Complicated disease, immunocompromise, frailty, significant comorbidity, systemic signs, vomiting or inability to take PO, markedly elevated CRP, fluid collection or long inflamed segment on imaging, or inadequate outpatient support (ACG 2026 Table 6; ASCRS 2020)
  • Regimens:
    • Oral (ACG 2026 Table 6): Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h, or moxifloxacin 400 mg PO daily; or metronidazole 500 mg PO q8h plus TMP-SMX DS q12h, ciprofloxacin 500 mg q12h, or levofloxacin 500 mg q24h. Usual duration 4-7 days
    • IV, lower-risk complicated (SIS 2017, 1-A):
      • Ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV q24h or cefotaxime 1-2 g IV q6-8h, plus metronidazole 500 mg IV q6-8h
      • Or ertapenem 1 g IV q24h
      • Serious beta-lactam allergy: ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h plus metronidazole, or moxifloxacin 400 mg IV q24h
      • Higher-risk patients (e.g., septic shock): piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375-4.5 g IV q6h, meropenem 1-2 g IV q8h, or cefepime plus metronidazole
    • Duration (SIS 2017): 4 days after adequate source control (1-A); 5-7 days without definitive source control, then reassess for source control if not responding (2-C)
    • Switch to oral agents once GI function returns, to complete a short course, not to extend it (SIS 2017, 1-B)

Abscess Management (ASCRS 2020):

  • Abscess 3 cm or smaller: Antibiotics alone are typically successful; stable patients can often be treated as outpatients
  • Abscess over 3 cm, stable patient: Image-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics (1B)
    • Antibiotics alone fail in up to 34% of larger abscesses; nonoperative care (antibiotics with or without drainage) succeeds in up to 80%
    • Recurrence after drainage 15-25% vs 25-60% after antibiotics alone; abscess size does not predict drainage failure
    • No safe drainage window, or failure of medical treatment and drainage: surgery
    • Practical: IR pigtail drain; remove when output is minimal and the patient has improved

Surgical Management:

  • Urgent Sigmoid Colectomy (ASCRS 2020, 1C):
    • Diffuse (multiquadrant) peritonitis: purulent or feculent (Hinchey III-IV)
    • Failure of nonoperative management, including persistent pain or inability to tolerate enteral nutrition
    • Overwhelming systemic inflammatory response; resuscitate and give antibiotics before operation
    • Selected stable patients with pneumoperitoneum but no diffuse peritonitis may be managed nonoperatively
  • Operative Choices (ASCRS 2020):
    • Restoring continuity (1B): Decide by patient factors, intraoperative factors, and surgeon preference. Primary anastomosis with or without diverting ileostomy vs Hartmann procedure: similar morbidity and mortality in RCTs, with higher stoma-free rates and fewer reversal complications after primary anastomosis with diversion
    • Hartmann procedure: Sigmoid resection, end colostomy, rectal stump; once standard, now one of the options above
    • Laparoscopic lavage: Not recommended for feculent peritonitis (1A); colectomy preferred over lavage for purulent peritonitis (higher secondary intervention rates with lavage) (1A)
  • Elective Colectomy:
    • After successful nonoperative treatment of an abscess: typically consider elective resection (ASCRS 2020, 1B)
    • Fistula, obstruction, or stricture: elective colectomy typically recommended (ASCRS 2020, 1B)
    • After uncomplicated diverticulitis: individualize (ASCRS 2020, 1B); recurrent uncomplicated disease that impairs quality of life: surgical referral (ACG 2026 rec 11)
    • Immunosuppressed after uncomplicated diverticulitis: individualize; elective surgery carries higher major morbidity and wound dehiscence (ASCRS 2020, 1C)
    • Young age alone: not an indication (ASCRS 2020, 1C; ACG 2026)

Consultations:

  • Surgery (General Surgery or Colorectal Surgery): Consult early for all complicated diverticulitis cases. Emergent consult if peritonitis, free air, septic shock
  • Interventional Radiology: CT-guided drainage of abscesses over 3 cm (ASCRS 2020)
  • Gastroenterology: For outpatient colonoscopy 6-8 weeks post-discharge (rule out colon cancer)

Disposition:

  • Practical: ICU: Septic shock, Hinchey III/IV requiring emergent surgery, post-operative from emergent surgery
  • Practical: Floor: Complicated diverticulitis (abscess, unable to tolerate PO, severe pain, immunocompromised), requiring IV antibiotics
  • Practical: Discharge/Outpatient: Mild-moderate diverticulitis, CT-confirmed, able to tolerate PO, hemodynamically stable, reliable for follow-up, adequate oral antibiotic coverage
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • CT Confirms and Grades Diverticulitis: Clinical evaluation alone is inaccurate; CT confirms the diagnosis, excludes alternatives, grades severity, and localizes disease (ACG 2026). CT grade correlates with failure of nonoperative management and later complications (ASCRS 2020).
  • Modified Hinchey Classification (ACG 2026): 0 mild clinical; Ia phlegmon or confined pericolic inflammation; Ib pericolic or mesocolic abscess; II pelvic, intra-abdominal, or retroperitoneal abscess; III purulent peritonitis; IV fecal peritonitis. Abscess over 3 cm in a stable patient: percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics; diffuse peritonitis: urgent colectomy (ASCRS 2020).
  • Colovesical Fistula: Fecaluria, pneumaturia, or pyuria suggest colovesical fistula; stool per vagina suggests colovaginal fistula (ASCRS 2020). Fistula is an indication for elective colectomy (ASCRS 2020, 1B). Practical: CT shows air in the bladder without a catheter.
  • Antibiotics Are Not Routine for Low-Risk Uncomplicated Diverticulitis: AVOD and DIABOLO found no difference in complications, recurrence, or recovery with or without antibiotics in mostly healthy patients with early-stage disease (ASCRS 2020, 1A); ACG 2026 suggests against routine antibiotics for low-risk patients (rec 3). Antibiotics remain appropriate for all other stages and for high-risk patients.
  • Colonoscopy After Recovery, Not During the Episode: Wait 6-8 weeks (ACG 2026). Recommended after complicated diverticulitis (malignancy 7.9-11%); after uncomplicated disease, colonoscopy only for alarm features, atypical course, or if not current with screening (ACG 2026; ASCRS 2020).
  • Immunosuppressed Patients: Lower threshold for admission, antibiotics, and surgical consultation (Practical). Elective colectomy after uncomplicated disease is individualized; elective surgery has higher major morbidity (OR 1.46) and wound dehiscence (OR 2.69) in immunosuppressed patients (ASCRS 2020).
  • Young Age Is Not an Indication for Surgery: Younger patients have more readmissions but a similar risk of emergency surgery (1.8% vs 2.0%) (ASCRS 2020); elective resection based on young age is not recommended (ASCRS 2020, 1C; ACG 2026).
  • Percutaneous Drainage Bridges to Elective Surgery: For stable patients with abscesses over 3 cm, drainage plus antibiotics; nonoperative care succeeds in up to 80% (ASCRS 2020). After a successfully treated abscess, consider elective resection (1B), allowing an operation under better conditions.
  • Diet and Lifestyle After Recovery: Healthy diet high in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes; no need to avoid nuts, corn, seeds, or popcorn; avoid regular NSAIDs unless indicated; stop smoking; moderate alcohol; weight loss; regular activity (ACG 2026 recs 4-10, conditional). Not recommended for recurrence prevention: mesalamine (strong), probiotics, rifaximin (ACG 2026 recs 12-14).
  • Hartmann vs Primary Anastomosis: Hartmann was once standard for emergency surgery. RCTs in Hinchey III-IV show similar morbidity and mortality with primary anastomosis plus diverting ileostomy, higher stoma-free rates (90% vs 57%; 96% vs 65%), and fewer serious reversal complications (ASCRS 2020). The choice depends on patient, intraoperative factors, and surgeon (1B).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: Septic shock (hypotension requiring vasopressors, lactate >4 mmol/L)
  • Diffuse peritonitis (Hinchey III purulent or IV fecal) needing urgent colectomy
  • Hemodynamic instability despite aggressive fluid resuscitation
  • Post-operative from emergent Hartmann procedure or bowel resection
  • Clinical deterioration despite antibiotics and abscess drainage
  • Practical: Severe lactic acidosis (lactate >4 mmol/L), concern for bowel ischemia/necrosis
  • Respiratory failure from sepsis or abdominal compartment syndrome
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Afebrile for >24-48 hours (Temp <38°C without antipyretics)
  • Tolerating regular or low-residue diet without nausea/vomiting
  • Pain adequately controlled on oral analgesics
  • Practical: WBC normalized or trending down (<12k, ideally <10k)
  • Hemodynamically stable (normal vital signs without tachycardia)
  • Able to ambulate independently
  • Antibiotics if indicated; usual oral course 4-7 days (ACG 2026)
  • Practical: Follow-up arranged with PCP or GI within 1-2 weeks
  • Colonoscopy after 6-8 weeks if complicated, alarm features, or not current with screening (ACG 2026)
  • Educated on lifestyle after recovery (healthy diet; avoiding nuts and seeds NOT necessary) (ACG 2026)
  • Red flag symptoms discussed: worsening pain, fever, unable to tolerate PO, vomiting, distension (obstruction)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Amp-Sulbactam, 💊 Pip-Tazo
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
