104. CIRRHOSIS COMPLICATIONS (VARICEAL BLEEDING, HEPATORENAL SYNDROME)

Portal Hypertension • GI Bleeding • Renal Failure • Ascites
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Decompensated cirrhosis presenting with acute variceal hemorrhage (hematemesis, melena, hemodynamic instability) or hepatorenal syndrome (rapidly progressive renal failure with oliguria, resistant ascites, without other cause of renal dysfunction).

  • Pathophysiology: Variceal Bleeding: Portal hypertension; clinically significant portal hypertension is HVPG 10 mm Hg or higher (AASLD 2024). Variceal rupture causes acute variceal hemorrhage, with 6-week mortality still 10-15% (AASLD 2024). Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS-AKI): Extreme splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial blood volume, activating vasoactive systems that constrict the renal vessels and lower renal blood flow and GFR (AGA 2024); by definition there is no structural kidney injury (AASLD 2021). Practical: usually reverses after liver transplant
  • Risk Factors: Decompensated cirrhosis; higher CTP class, larger varices, and variceal red wale marks raise the risk of a first variceal bleed (AASLD 2024). Practical: SBP and other infection, recent binge alcohol, NSAIDs, anticoagulation
  • Symptoms - Variceal Bleeding: Hematemesis (bright red or coffee-ground), melena, hematochezia (if brisk bleeding), dizziness, syncope, dyspnea, chest pain (if severe anemia), altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy from blood in GI tract)
  • Symptoms - Hepatorenal Syndrome: Oliguria, abdominal distension (ascites), confusion (hepatic encephalopathy), nausea, weakness. The old term type 1 HRS has been replaced by HRS-AKI (AASLD 2021)
  • Physical Exam: Stigmata of cirrhosis: jaundice, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, caput medusae. Tense ascites (fluid wave, shifting dullness). Asterixis (hepatic encephalopathy). Hypotension, tachycardia (variceal bleeding). Splenomegaly (portal hypertension)
  • Variants/Subtypes: Bleeding: esophageal varices, gastric varices (cardiofundal GOV2/IGV1), ectopic varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy (AASLD 2024). HRS-AKI (formerly type 1): AKI by ICA criteria meeting HRS criteria; the historical definition was a doubling of creatinine to over 2.5 mg/dL in under 2 weeks (AASLD 2021)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Complete Blood Count: Anemia (acute blood loss or chronic disease), thrombocytopenia (<100k common in cirrhosis from splenic sequestration, bone marrow suppression), leukopenia
  • Comprehensive Metabolic Panel: Elevated BUN (GI bleeding), elevated Cr (HRS), hyponatremia (<130 mEq/L common in advanced cirrhosis), hypoglycemia possible, elevated bilirubin
  • Liver Function Tests: Elevated AST/ALT (usually <300 unless acute hepatitis superimposed), elevated alkaline phosphatase, hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL), hyperbilirubinemia (both direct and indirect)
  • Coagulation Studies: PT/INR is often prolonged in cirrhosis. In variceal bleeding, do not give FFP or platelets to reach INR or platelet targets; FFP may cause harm (AASLD 2024)
  • Lactate: Elevated if hypovolemic shock, hepatic hypoperfusion, or mesenteric ischemia
  • Type & Screen / Crossmatch: Essential for variceal bleeding; anticipate transfusion needs
  • Ammonia Level: Not needed to guide HE treatment (ACG 2026 HE, conditional); a normal level with altered mental status should prompt a search for other causes
  • Blood Cultures: Draw before antibiotics if concern for SBP or bacteremia

HRS-AKI Diagnostic Criteria (AASLD 2021, Table 11):

  • Cirrhosis with ascites
  • AKI by ICA criteria: creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours, or 50% or more known or presumed within the prior 7 days
  • No response after 2 consecutive days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin 1 g/kg/day (cap 100 g/day, AGA 2024)
  • No shock
  • No current or recent nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast)
  • No structural kidney injury: proteinuria over 500 mg/day, microhematuria over 50 RBC/hpf, or abnormal renal ultrasound
  • Older criteria (creatinine over 1.5 mg/dL, urine sodium under 10, FENa under 1%) are not part of this definition

Imaging:

  • Renal Ultrasound: To rule out obstructive uropathy, assess kidney size (normal to slightly enlarged in HRS, small kidneys suggest chronic kidney disease)
  • CT Abdomen/Pelvis: If concern for other cause of renal failure (obstruction, abscess, hepatocellular carcinoma with vascular invasion)
  • Doppler Ultrasound of Liver: Assess portal vein patency (portal vein thrombosis can worsen portal hypertension, precipitate bleeding)

Endoscopy - URGENT Upper Endoscopy (EGD):

  • Perform within 12 hours of presentation for suspected variceal bleeding
  • Diagnostic: confirms variceal source, grades varices (small vs large)
  • Therapeutic: band ligation (preferred over sclerotherapy), bleeding control
  • If not variceal: peptic ulcer, gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tear, portal hypertensive gastropathy

Paracentesis (if ascites present):

  • Rule out SBP (fluid PMN >250/µL)
  • Send ascitic fluid for: cell count with differential, culture (blood culture bottles at bedside), albumin, total protein, Gram stain
  • Calculate serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG): Serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin. SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or higher indicates portal hypertension with about 97% accuracy (AASLD 2021)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

VARICEAL BLEEDING MANAGEMENT:

Immediate Resuscitation:

  • Practical: IV access: Two large-bore IVs (18-gauge or larger)
  • Practical: Hemodynamic monitoring: continuous telemetry, frequent vitals q15min initially
  • Transfusion: Target hemoglobin ~7 g/dL unless comorbidities require more (AASLD 2024)
  • FFP and Platelets: Not given to reach INR or platelet targets (AASLD 2024)
  • Practical: avoid over-resuscitation with fluids

Pharmacologic Therapy for Variceal Bleeding:

  • Vasoactive Therapy - start as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected, before endoscopy (AASLD 2024; AGA 2024):
    • Octreotide, the vasoactive drug of choice (AGA 2024): 50 mcg IV bolus, then 25-50 mcg/h infusion (AASLD 2024 Table 5)
    • Duration: 2-5 days after endoscopic hemostasis (AASLD 2024; AGA 2024)
  • Antibiotics (start with vasoactive therapy, as soon as possible; AASLD 2024):
    • Tailor to local resistance and allergies; most commonly ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 h for up to 5 days
    • Stop once bleeding is controlled if there is no active infection
  • Proton Pump Inhibitor: Stop once variceal bleeding is confirmed as the source, unless another indication exists (AASLD 2024)

Endoscopic Therapy - URGENT (within 12 hours):

  • Esophageal Variceal Band Ligation (EVL): Perform when esophageal variceal bleeding is confirmed, within 12 h of presentation; repeat every 2-4 weeks until obliteration, then endoscopy at 6 months and every 12 months (AASLD 2024)
  • Practical: Sclerotherapy: Inject sclerosant into varices. Alternative if banding not feasible. Higher complication rate than banding
  • If Bleeding Not Controlled with Above Measures: Consider rescue therapies below

Rescue Therapies (if endoscopic therapy fails):

  • Balloon Tamponade or Covered Esophageal Stent:
    • Bridge to TIPS for uncontrolled bleeding (AASLD 2024)
    • Practical: high complication risk (perforation, aspiration, pressure necrosis); limit inflation to 24 h; protect the airway first
  • TIPS (AASLD 2024):
    • Preemptive TIPS within 72 h (ideally within 24 h) of the first endoscopy: CTP class B score over 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or CTP class C score 10-13, absent absolute contraindications; transfer if TIPS is not available locally
    • Salvage TIPS for uncontrolled bleeding; rescue TIPS for rebleeding despite vasoactive therapy and EVL
    • Practical: complications include hepatic encephalopathy, shunt dysfunction, and liver failure; contraindications include severe HE and heart failure

HEPATORENAL SYNDROME MANAGEMENT:

Diagnostic Confirmation: Apply the HRS-AKI criteria above (AASLD 2021 Table 11). Start treatment early: higher creatinine predicts lower response, and creatinine over 5 mg/dL rarely responds (AGA 2024)

Pharmacologic Treatment (HRS-Specific):

  • Terlipressin plus Albumin: preferred (AASLD 2021; AGA 2024):
    • FDA approved (2022) for HRS with rapid reduction in kidney function; peripheral IV, no ICU required (Terlivaz label; AGA 2024)
    • Dose (label): 0.85 mg IV over 2 min every 6 h on days 1-3. Day 4: if creatinine fell 30% or more, continue; if less than 30%, may increase to 1.7 mg every 6 h; if at or above baseline, stop. Continue until 24 h after two creatinine values of 1.5 mg/dL or less at least 2 h apart, maximum 14 days
    • Albumin: 1 g/kg (max 100 g) on day 1, then 20-40 g/day, as most patients in the terlipressin trials received (AGA 2024; median 50 g/day in CONFIRM, Terlivaz label, rev 06/2026); AASLD 2021 gives 40-50 g/day. Reassess need daily by volume status (AGA 2024)
    • Boxed warning: serious or fatal respiratory failure. Check SpO2 first; do not start if SpO2 is under 90%; monitor continuously; avoid with volume overload or ACLF grade 3. Contraindicated with ongoing coronary, peripheral, or mesenteric ischemia (label)
    • Benefit unlikely with creatinine over 5 mg/dL; may not outweigh risk with MELD 35 or higher when listed for transplant (label; AGA 2024). Verified HRS reversal in CONFIRM: 29% vs 16% with placebo (label)
  • Norepinephrine plus Albumin (if terlipressin unavailable; ICU):
    • Start 0.5 mg/h; increase by 0.5 mg/h every 4 h to a maximum of 3 mg/h, aiming for a MAP rise of at least 10 mm Hg or urine output over 200 mL/4 h (AASLD 2021)
    • Fewer data; the largest RCT favored terlipressin (AGA 2024)
  • Midodrine plus Octreotide plus Albumin (only if neither is available):
    • Midodrine 5-15 mg PO every 8 h plus octreotide 100-200 mcg SC every 8 h or 50 mcg/h IV (AASLD 2021)
    • Low efficacy; unclear benefit over placebo (AASLD 2021; AGA 2024)
  • Response and Duration: Response is creatinine under 1.5 mg/dL or within 0.3 mg/dL of baseline, over a maximum of 14 days; may stop if creatinine stays at or above pretreatment after 4 days at maximum tolerated doses; retreat recurrence (AASLD 2021)

Supportive Care for HRS:

  • Stop all diuretics (worsens renal perfusion)
  • Avoid nephrotoxins: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast
  • Maintain euvolemia: avoid aggressive diuresis and over-resuscitation
  • Treat precipitating factors: SBP (if present), GI bleeding, infections
  • Paracentesis: Large-volume paracentesis (>5 L) requires albumin 6-8 g per liter removed

Definitive Treatment (HRS):

  • Liver Transplantation: Consider urgent transplant evaluation for all patients with cirrhosis and AKI (AASLD 2021). Practical: HRS usually resolves after transplant; creatinine raises MELD priority
  • Renal Replacement Therapy: Practical: bridge to transplant; CRRT if hemodynamically unstable

Consultations:

  • Gastroenterology/Hepatology: URGENT for variceal bleeding (endoscopy), HRS management, transplant evaluation
  • Interventional Radiology: For TIPS if refractory variceal bleeding
  • Nephrology: For HRS management, dialysis consideration
  • Transplant Surgery: For liver transplant evaluation (expedite if HRS Type 1)

Disposition:

  • Practical: ICU for active variceal bleeding, hemodynamic instability, HRS-AKI on norepinephrine, post-TIPS, balloon tamponade, grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy
  • Practical: floor with telemetry for controlled bleeding after endoscopy, HRS-AKI on terlipressin (peripheral IV, no ICU required per AGA 2024), grade 1-2 HE
  • Practical: discharge when stable after variceal bleeding (stable Hgb, no rebleeding for 48-72 h) with secondary prophylaxis started: NSBB plus EVL (AASLD 2024)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Restrictive Transfusion: Target Hgb ~7 g/dL unless comorbidities require more; do not give FFP or platelets to reach INR or platelet targets (AASLD 2024).
  • Start Vasoactive Therapy and Antibiotics Before Endoscopy: As soon as variceal bleeding is suspected (AASLD 2024; AGA 2024). Octreotide 50 mcg bolus, then 25-50 mcg/h for 2-5 days; ceftriaxone 1 g/24 h for up to 5 days, stopped once bleeding is controlled without active infection (AASLD 2024).
  • Band Ligation: EVL when esophageal variceal bleeding is confirmed (AASLD 2024). Practical: sclerotherapy only if banding is not feasible.
  • Preemptive TIPS: CTP B over 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or CTP C 10-13: TIPS within 72 h (ideally 24 h) of the first endoscopy, absent absolute contraindications; transfer if unavailable (AASLD 2024). Calculate CTP at presentation.
  • HRS-AKI Is a Diagnosis of Exclusion: Requires cirrhosis with ascites, AKI by ICA criteria, no response to 2 days of albumin and diuretic withdrawal, no shock, no nephrotoxins, and no structural kidney injury (AASLD 2021). Vasoconstrictors are for HRS-AKI only, not other AKI in cirrhosis (AGA 2024). Consider urgent transplant evaluation in all patients with cirrhosis and AKI (AASLD 2021).
  • Vasoconstrictor plus Albumin: Terlipressin is preferred (AASLD 2021; AGA 2024); norepinephrine if unavailable (ICU); midodrine plus octreotide has low efficacy. Failure to respond to albumin is part of the definition. Response: creatinine under 1.5 mg/dL or within 0.3 mg/dL of baseline, maximum 14 days (AASLD 2021).
  • Stop Diuretics in HRS - They Worsen Renal Perfusion: Common mistake: continuing spironolactone, furosemide in HRS patient with refractory ascites. Diuretics cause volume depletion, worsen renal hypoperfusion, accelerate renal failure. In HRS, hold ALL diuretics. Treat ascites with large-volume paracentesis + albumin (6-8 g per liter removed if more than 5 L; AASLD 2021). Accept some ascites - prioritize kidney function over comfort. Restart diuretics only if HRS resolves.
  • Large-Volume Paracentesis Requires Albumin: Give 6-8 g of albumin per liter removed when more than 5 L are removed, to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction; risk may rise above 8 L in one session (AASLD 2021; AGA 2024). Example: 8 L removed, 48-64 g albumin.
  • Beta-Blockers for Variceal Prophylaxis: Carvedilol is the preferred NSBB: 6.25 mg once daily at bedtime for 2-3 days, then 12.5 mg/day (one dose or 6.25 mg twice daily) if tolerated; maintenance 6.25-12.5 mg/day; no heart-rate goal (AASLD 2024, statement 2 and Table 3). Propranolol 20-40 mg BID or nadolol 20-40 mg at bedtime, titrated every 2-3 days to HR 55-60 with SBP 90 or higher (AASLD 2024 Table 3). After AVH without TIPS, start NSBB when vasoactive therapy stops, plus EVL (AASLD 2024). Reduce or stop if SBP stays under 90.
  • SAAG and SBP: SAAG 1.1 g/dL or higher suggests portal hypertension with about 97% accuracy (AASLD 2021). Ascitic PMN over 250/mm3: start IV antibiotics; community-acquired SBP, third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime 2 g IV q12h); nosocomial, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, or sepsis, broad-spectrum therapy (AASLD 2021).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: Active variceal hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability (SBP <90, HR >120)
  • Massive GI bleeding (Hgb <7 despite transfusion, ongoing hematemesis)
  • Requires balloon tamponade (Minnesota/Sengstaken-Blakemore tube)
  • Refractory bleeding despite endoscopic therapy (needs TIPS)
  • HRS-AKI requiring norepinephrine
  • Hepatic encephalopathy grade 3-4 (stupor, coma)
  • Acute liver failure or acute-on-chronic liver failure
  • Septic shock from SBP or bacteremia
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Variceal bleeding controlled, no rebleeding for 48-72 hours
  • Hemoglobin stable (>7 g/dL) without ongoing transfusion requirements
  • Practical: Hemodynamically stable (SBP >90, HR <100)
  • Tolerating PO diet without nausea/vomiting
  • On NSBB for secondary prophylaxis plus EVL: carvedilol preferred (6.25-12.5 mg/day), or propranolol or nadolol titrated to HR 55-60 with SBP 90 or higher (AASLD 2024)
  • EVL repeated every 2-4 weeks until obliteration (AASLD 2024)
  • Patient educated on avoiding NSAIDs, alcohol, hepatotoxic drugs
  • Practical: Hepatology follow-up within 1-2 weeks
  • If HRS: NOT a discharge diagnosis - requires ongoing treatment, transplant evaluation, or hospice discussion
  • Antibiotics completed (ceftriaxone up to 5 days) or stopped once bleeding is controlled without infection (AASLD 2024)
↑ Back to Table of Contents

105. ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC LIVER FAILURE (ACLF)

Acute Decompensation • Organ Failure • High Short-Term Mortality • Precipitating Event
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Advanced chronic liver disease (F3 fibrosis or cirrhosis) with liver failure (bilirubin 5 mg/dL or more and INR 1.5 or more) plus extrahepatic organ dysfunction or failure, often after a precipitant such as infection, alcohol, drug injury, a viral flare, GI bleeding, or surgery (2026 global consensus). 28-day mortality is 30% to 50% across definitions (AASLD 2024 ACLF).

  • Pathophysiology: Acute deterioration in advanced chronic liver disease, with liver failure as the core and extrahepatic organ dysfunction or failure driving severity; type A arises without prior decompensation, type B after prior decompensation (2026 global consensus). Bacterial infection is the most frequent precipitant; others are alcohol, HBV reactivation or superinfection, drug-induced liver injury, GI bleeding, and major surgery or procedures; often no trigger is found (2026 global consensus).
  • Risk Factors: Alcohol-related liver disease is the leading cause of ACLF worldwide (2026 global consensus). For infection-triggered ACLF: younger men, alcohol-associated cirrhosis, high MELD, invasive procedures and lines; multidrug-resistant organisms raise the risk of ACLF and death (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Symptoms: Jaundice (rapid onset or worsening), abdominal pain/distension (ascites, peritonitis), confusion/altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy grade 2-4), dyspnea (hepatopulmonary syndrome, pleural effusions, pulmonary edema), oliguria (HRS), hematemesis/melena (variceal bleeding), fever (infection)
  • Physical Exam: Jaundice, altered mental status (confusion, asterixis, obtundation, coma), signs of cirrhosis (spider angiomata, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, caput medusae), tense ascites, hypotension (circulatory failure, septic shock), tachypnea, hypoxia, decreased breath sounds (pleural effusions), bleeding (coagulopathy)
  • Grades (2026 global consensus, AASLD, EASL, APASL, ALEH, SOLDA): Grade 1: liver failure plus one extrahepatic organ dysfunction (circulatory or respiratory dysfunction counts only in a monitored or ICU setting). Grade 2: liver failure plus one extrahepatic organ failure. Grade 3: liver failure plus 2 or more extrahepatic organ failures. Mortality rises with grade. The consensus builds on, and does not replace, the EASL-CLIF, NACSELD, and APASL definitions used in scores and studies.
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Complete Blood Count: Leukocytosis (infection), leukopenia (sepsis, bone marrow suppression), thrombocytopenia (<50k), anemia
  • Comprehensive Metabolic Panel: Bilirubin 5 mg/dL or more (with INR 1.5 or more) defines liver failure (2026 global consensus); creatinine for KDIGO AKI staging. Practical: hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, AST/ALT pattern for the precipitant
  • Coagulation Studies: INR 1.5 or more is part of the liver failure definition (2026 global consensus); INR should not be used to gauge bleeding risk (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Lactate: Elevated (>4 mmol/L) in septic shock, hepatic hypoperfusion
  • Ammonia: Routine testing in altered mental status is not recommended (AASLD 2024 ACLF); a low or normal level makes HE unlikely and should prompt a search for other causes (AASLD 2024 ACLF; 2026 global consensus)
  • Arterial Blood Gas: Metabolic acidosis (sepsis, lactic acidosis), respiratory alkalosis (hepatopulmonary syndrome), hypoxemia
  • Blood Cultures: Before antibiotics, as part of the full infection workup (AASLD 2024 ACLF)

Organ Dysfunction and Failure (2026 global consensus, Table 2):

  • Liver Failure (required): Bilirubin 5 mg/dL or more AND INR 1.5 or more
  • Kidney: Dysfunction = KDIGO AKI stage 1; failure = AKI stage 2-3 or new RRT
  • Brain: Dysfunction = West Haven grade 2 HE; failure = grade 3-4 HE or mechanical ventilation for HE
  • Circulatory: Dysfunction = MAP under 65 mmHg (monitored setting only); failure = vasopressor use, not counting vasoconstrictors given only for HRS-AKI
  • Respiratory: Dysfunction = PaO2/FiO2 over 225 to 300, or SpO2/FiO2 over 244 to 333 (monitored setting only); failure = mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, PaO2/FiO2 225 or less, or SpO2/FiO2 244 or less
  • Prognosis: Use ACLF-specific scores (CLIF-C ACLF, NACSELD, AARC) rather than MELD or Child-Pugh in critically ill patients, recalculated serially (AASLD 2024 ACLF; 2026 global consensus)

Infectious Workup (CRITICAL - infection most common precipitant):

  • Paracentesis (if ascites): Cell count, culture, Gram stain. SBP: PMN >250/µL. Send 10 mL into blood culture bottles at bedside
  • Chest X-ray: Pneumonia, pleural effusions
  • Urinalysis and Urine Culture: UTI common
  • Blood Cultures: X 2 sets from separate sites
  • Other: Sputum culture if pneumonia, stool studies if diarrhea. Repeat the infection workup with any change in status: new or worse ascites, HE, AKI, or organ failure (AASLD 2024 ACLF)

Imaging:

  • Chest X-ray: Pneumonia, pleural effusions, pulmonary edema, ARDS
  • CT Abdomen/Pelvis: Assess for intra-abdominal abscess, portal vein thrombosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, bowel perforation
  • Liver Ultrasound with Doppler: Assess portal vein patency (thrombosis), hepatic vein patency (Budd-Chiari), hepatic masses

Additional Testing:

  • Viral Hepatitis Panel: Test immediately for hepatotropic viruses: HAV, HBV (HBsAg, HBV DNA for reactivation), HCV (RNA), HDV, HEV; test non-hepatotropic viruses (CMV, EBV, HSV, others) by clinical context (2026 global consensus)
  • Acetaminophen Level: If concern for overdose (intentional or unintentional)
  • Alcohol Level: If intoxication suspected
  • Toxicology Screen: For other hepatotoxins
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management:

  • Practical: ICU or high-dependency unit for grade 2-3 or any organ failure needing support. Circulatory and respiratory dysfunction can only be graded in a monitored setting (2026 global consensus)
  • West Haven grade 3-4 HE or GCS under 12 (aspiration risk): ICU where possible; GCS under 9 should prompt consideration of intubation (2026 global consensus). Intubation is individualized: inability to protect the airway, massive upper GI bleeding, respiratory distress (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Early assessment of volume status, perfusion, and cardiac function, including bedside echocardiography (AASLD 2024 ACLF; 2026 global consensus)
  • Practical: IV access, arterial line, central line if needed; strict intake and output
  • Minimize Foley catheters and PPIs to prevent infection (AASLD 2024 ACLF)

Identify and Treat Precipitating Factor:

  • Bacterial Infection (most common precipitant, 48% in AASLD 2024 ACLF):
    • Full workup, then empiric antibiotics early, with the first dose in the ED; choose by site, severity, community vs health care or nosocomial acquisition, and local resistance; de-escalate once cultures return (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
    • SBP, community-acquired: third-generation cephalosporin, e.g., cefotaxime 2 g IV q12h. Nosocomial or MDRO risk: piperacillin-tazobactam (add vancomycin if MRSA history, daptomycin if VRE); meropenem if known MDR gram-negative organisms or recent piperacillin-tazobactam (AASLD 2021)
    • SBP: add albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 (AASLD 2021). Albumin is not recommended for infections other than SBP (ACG 2022 ACLF)
    • Repeat paracentesis at 48 h; a PMN fall under 25% means failure: broaden coverage and rule out secondary peritonitis (AASLD 2021)
    • ICU ACLF without improvement after 48 h: broaden for MDR organisms and consider antifungal coverage (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis:
    • Severe AH (MELD over 20): prednisolone 40 mg PO daily for 28 days (IV methylprednisolone 32 mg daily if unable to take PO), with IV N-acetylcysteine as an adjuvant; no pentoxifylline (ACG 2024 ALD)
    • ACLF grade 3: no corticosteroids; 2 organ failures: case-by-case (response about 40%) (2026 global consensus)
    • Lille score at day 4 or day 7: stop steroids if over 0.45 (ACG 2024 ALD)
    • Thiamine to help prevent Wernicke encephalopathy (ACG 2024 ALD); Practical: thiamine 100 mg IV daily, folate, multivitamin; addiction medicine consult
  • Drug-Induced Liver Injury (Including Acetaminophen):
    • Stop the offending agent immediately; refer early for transplant evaluation if disease progresses (2026 global consensus)
    • Acetaminophen: IV N-acetylcysteine 300 mg/kg total, e.g., the label three-bag regimen of 150 mg/kg over 1 h, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h (FDA label). Do not stop at 21 h by default: continue at 6.25 mg/kg/h or more until acetaminophen is under 10 mcg/mL, INR under 2.0, AST/ALT normal or falling 25-50% from peak, and the patient is clinically well (US/Canada acetaminophen consensus 2023)
  • Viral Hepatitis:
    • Start antivirals as soon as possible, preferably within 24 h of confirmation; do not delay transplant to achieve viral suppression (2026 global consensus)
    • HBV: entecavir 1 mg PO daily (the labeled dose for decompensated liver disease) or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg PO daily, adjusted for renal function (FDA labels; AASLD/IDSA 2025). Tenofovir alafenamide label: not recommended in Child-Pugh B or C
    • HCV: pangenotypic DAAs, avoiding protease inhibitor regimens in decompensated cirrhosis and ACLF; give before or after transplant depending on severity (2026 global consensus)
    • HEV: ribavirin may be considered; HSV: acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h (HHS OI 2025, as on card 155); CMV: ganciclovir (2026 global consensus)
  • Variceal Bleeding: Vasoactive therapy, antibiotics, band ligation, preemptive or rescue TIPS (see Card 104, Cirrhosis Complications)

Organ Support:

  • Hepatic Encephalopathy:
    • Lactulose by mouth or NG, or as an enema for grade 3-4 HE (300 mL lactulose in 700 mL water), titrated to mental status while watching for dehydration and hypernatremia; polyethylene glycol if ileus risk (AASLD 2024 ACLF). Practical: 30-45 mL every 2-4 h until bowel movements, then 2-3 soft stools daily
    • Rifaximin: role as an add-on in ACLF is unclear (AASLD 2024 ACLF); not routinely added to broad-spectrum antibiotics for overt HE in critically ill ACLF (2026 global consensus)
    • Avoid benzodiazepines and minimize opioids; if intubated, use short-acting sedation (propofol, dexmedetomidine) (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
    • Treat precipitants (infection, GI bleeding, electrolytes, AKI, constipation, sedatives) and look for non-HE causes, especially with a first episode or no response (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Kidney (AKI and HRS-AKI):
    • Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins, treat precipitants (especially infection), then albumin 1 g/kg/day (maximum 100 g/day) for 48 h (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
    • HRS-AKI stage 2 or higher: vasoconstrictor plus albumin 20-40 g/day. Terlipressin if no ACLF grade 3 (EASL-CLIF) and no major cardiopulmonary or vascular disease; norepinephrine is the alternative and may be preferred with shock (AASLD 2024 ACLF). Terlipressin dosing and stop rules: see Card 104
    • RRT is individualized: recommended for HRS-AKI that fails pharmacotherapy in patients listed or being considered for transplant; continuous RRT if hemodynamically unstable (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Circulatory Support:
    • Fluids: balanced crystalloids (e.g., lactated Ringer's); albumin for its established indications (large-volume paracentesis, SBP, HRS-AKI), not routine resuscitation, since trials showed more pulmonary edema and fluid overload, especially with 20% albumin (AASLD 2024 ACLF; 2026 global consensus). Guide volume with hemodynamic monitoring and echocardiography. With any paracentesis in ACLF, give albumin 6-8 g per liter removed, regardless of volume (AGA 2024; card 16)
    • Norepinephrine first-line (0.01-0.5 mcg/kg/min); MAP target 65 mmHg with ongoing perfusion assessment; vasopressin as second-line when norepinephrine doses rise (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
    • Refractory shock on high-dose vasopressors: hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h or 200 mg/day infusion for 7 days or until ICU discharge (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Respiratory Support:
    • Treat hydrothorax or tense ascites with thoracentesis or paracentesis; evaluate for hepatopulmonary syndrome (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
    • High-flow nasal cannula for hypoxemic respiratory failure with close monitoring; do not delay intubation (AASLD 2024 ACLF; 2026 global consensus)
    • Acute lung injury on the ventilator: tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure under 30 cm H2O; low PEEP (under 10 cm H2O) if PaO2/FiO2 200-300, higher PEEP may be needed if under 200 (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Coagulopathy:
    • INR should not be used to gauge bleeding risk; viscoelastic tests better capture hemostasis but are not yet clinically validated (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
    • No transfusion for abnormal coagulation tests without bleeding or a planned procedure (ACG 2022 ACLF); paracentesis and thoracentesis need no routine preprocedure coagulation testing (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
    • When correction is needed, low-volume cryoprecipitate or 4-factor PCC is preferred over high-volume FFP (AASLD 2024 ACLF)

Nutrition (AASLD 2024 ACLF):

  • Involve the nutrition support team early; assess nutrition risk (e.g., NUTRIC) at ICU admission
  • Enteral over parenteral, started after resuscitation; hold enteral feeding if norepinephrine is over 0.15 mcg/kg/min or equivalent
  • Calories: start at 12-25 kcal/kg; protein 1.2-2.0 g/kg ideal body weight/day; no protein restriction
  • Standard formulas: branched-chain amino acid formulas show no benefit in ICU ACLF
  • Monitor for refeeding syndrome; glucose target 140-180 mg/dL

Liver Transplant Evaluation (Expedited):

  • Severe ACLF warrants expedited multidisciplinary assessment and rapid access to transplant (2026 global consensus)
  • MELD may underestimate the risk of death in severe ACLF (2026 global consensus)
  • Offer transplant only if expected 1-year survival is over 75-80% (2026 global consensus). Stabilization or improvement of organ failure, especially in the first 72 h to 1 week, favors candidacy (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Likely barriers: lactate over 9 mmol/L, severe respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 under 150), rising vasopressor needs, uncontrolled sepsis (AASLD 2024 ACLF); persistent deterioration with 3 or more organ failures (2026 global consensus). Active alcohol use and untreated infection may be prohibitive but reversible (AASLD 2024 ACLF); a minimum abstinence period should not be required before listing (2026 global consensus)

Consultations:

  • Hepatology: Immediate consult for all ACLF, co-manage with ICU
  • Transplant Surgery: Urgent evaluation for Grade 2-3 ACLF
  • Nephrology: For HRS management, CRRT
  • Critical Care: ICU admission, multiorgan support
  • Palliative Care: Consider for every patient with ACLF or cirrhosis in the ICU to define prognosis and goals of care; transplant evaluation or listing does not preclude it (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Infectious Disease: If multidrug-resistant organisms, fungal infection, or unusual infections

Disposition:

  • Practical: ICU or high-dependency unit for organ failure needing support, grade 3-4 HE, shock, or respiratory failure
  • Do not deny ICU admission on initial presentation alone; use a time-limited trial with reassessment at days 3-7 (2026 global consensus)
  • Futility signals: CLIF-C ACLF over 64 or AARC over 10 despite maximal therapy (2026 global consensus); CLIF-C ACLF over 70 at admission or day 3 carried about 90% 90-day mortality (AASLD 2024 ACLF). Not a transplant candidate: palliative care or hospice
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • ACLF Is Not Simple Decompensation: ACLF requires liver failure (bilirubin 5 mg/dL or more and INR 1.5 or more) plus extrahepatic organ dysfunction or failure (2026 global consensus). 28-day mortality is 30-50% across definitions (AASLD 2024 ACLF) and rises with grade. Grade early, treat the precipitant, and start transplant and goals-of-care discussions early.
  • Infection Is the Most Common Precipitant (48%): Fever is often absent; new or worse decompensation (confusion, hyponatremia, AKI) may be the only sign (AASLD 2024 ACLF). Do the full workup (paracentesis, blood and urine cultures, chest x-ray) and give the first antibiotic dose in the ED, because each hour of delay raises mortality (AASLD 2024 ACLF). SBP: albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 (AASLD 2021).
  • ACLF Can Occur Without Established Cirrhosis: Advanced chronic liver disease (F3 fibrosis or more) qualifies, shown by biopsy, known disease, elastography, or clinical and imaging signs. Elastography alone cannot separate ACLF from acute liver failure, because acute injury raises liver stiffness (2026 global consensus).
  • Do Not Restrict Protein: Protein restriction is not recommended; give 1.2-2.0 g/kg ideal body weight/day (AASLD 2024 ACLF). Treat HE with lactulose and precipitant control, not protein restriction.
  • Albumin Has Specific Indications, Not Routine Resuscitation: Use albumin for SBP (AASLD 2021), large-volume paracentesis, and AKI or HRS-AKI (AASLD 2024 ACLF). For shock, start with balanced crystalloids: routine albumin resuscitation is not supported, and trials found more pulmonary edema and fluid overload, especially with 20% albumin (2026 global consensus). Albumin is not recommended for infections other than SBP (ACG 2022 ACLF).
  • Grade on Admission and Regrade: Grade 1: liver failure plus one extrahepatic organ dysfunction; grade 2: plus one organ failure; grade 3: plus 2 or more organ failures (2026 global consensus). Serial ACLF-specific scores (CLIF-C ACLF, NACSELD, AARC) predict outcome better than MELD or a single baseline value (AASLD 2024 ACLF; 2026 global consensus).
  • Do Not Correct INR Without Bleeding or a Procedure: INR does not measure bleeding risk in cirrhosis (AASLD 2024 ACLF). Skip routine coagulation testing before paracentesis or thoracentesis. When correction is truly needed, prefer low-volume cryoprecipitate or 4-factor PCC over FFP (AASLD 2024 ACLF).
  • Corticosteroids in Severe Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis: MELD over 20 (Maddrey 32 or more is the historical threshold): prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days plus IV N-acetylcysteine; stop if the Lille score is over 0.45 at day 4 or 7 (ACG 2024 ALD). No steroids in ACLF grade 3; case-by-case with 2 organ failures; steroids raise invasive fungal infection risk, so stop promptly in non-responders (2026 global consensus).
  • Transplant: Early, Expedited, Selective: The window is narrow, so assess severe ACLF early; offer transplant only if expected 1-year survival is over 75-80% (2026 global consensus). Stabilization or improvement of organ failure favors success; severe respiratory failure, rising vasopressors, lactate over 9 mmol/L, or uncontrolled sepsis are likely barriers (AASLD 2024 ACLF).
  • N-Acetylcysteine Indications: Acetaminophen toxicity, continued until stopping criteria are met (US/Canada acetaminophen consensus 2023); adjuvant to corticosteroids in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (ACG 2024 ALD); early non-acetaminophen acute liver failure and selected severe drug injury (2026 global consensus, Table 4). AASLD 2024 ACLF and ACG 2022 ACLF make no recommendation for NAC in other ACLF.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: any extrahepatic organ failure needing support (vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, RRT)
  • West Haven grade 3-4 HE or GCS under 12 (2026 global consensus)
  • Respiratory failure: mechanical ventilation, PaO2/FiO2 225 or less, or SpO2/FiO2 244 or less (2026 global consensus)
  • Circulatory failure: vasopressor requirement (2026 global consensus)
  • Kidney failure: KDIGO AKI stage 2-3 or RRT (2026 global consensus)
  • Practical: active bleeding with hemodynamic instability
  • Practical: septic shock or lactate over 4 mmol/L
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: ACLF is NOT a discharge diagnosis - most patients either improve (downgrade to compensated cirrhosis) or deteriorate (transplant or death)
  • Practical: If patient improves from ACLF to compensated cirrhosis: precipitant treated, organ failures resolved, stable for 48-72 hours off organ support
  • Practical: Close hepatology follow-up within 1 week
  • Practical: Transplant evaluation completed or scheduled
  • Practical: Abstinence from alcohol if relevant
  • Practical: Medications optimized: diuretics, beta-blockers, lactulose/rifaximin if history of encephalopathy
  • Practical: Patient/family educated on red flags: jaundice, confusion, abdominal pain, fever, bleeding, dyspnea

106. ISCHEMIC BOWEL / MESENTERIC ISCHEMIA

Severe Abdominal Pain • Pain Out of Proportion • Lactic Acidosis • Bowel Necrosis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Acute onset of severe, diffuse abdominal pain that is "out of proportion to physical exam findings" (severe pain with minimal tenderness), often with bloody diarrhea, lactic acidosis, and rapid clinical deterioration. Most common in elderly with atrial fibrillation or atherosclerotic disease.

  • Pathophysiology: Acute interruption of intestinal blood flow, progressing to infarction if not reversed. Arterial occlusion causes about two thirds of AMI, roughly half embolic and half thrombotic, with a shift toward thrombotic occlusion in recent series; in one prospective study the split was arterial 55%, venous 18%, and non-occlusive (NOMI) 13%, with in-hospital mortality 49% (ESVS 2025, non-US). Embolic sources: AF, valvular disease, MI, mural thrombus. NOMI: low-flow states (shock, low cardiac output, dialysis) with mesenteric vasoconstriction. Venous: hypercoagulable states, intra-abdominal inflammation, cirrhosis.
  • Risk Factors: Arterial: Atrial fibrillation (most important), recent MI, valvular heart disease (endocarditis), aortic atherosclerosis, prior embolism, hypotension, vasopressor use, cocaine. Venous: Hypercoagulable states (Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, malignancy, OCP use, pregnancy), portal hypertension, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, intra-abdominal infection/abscess
  • Symptoms: Sudden severe abdominal pain with few exam findings (disproportionate pain), bowel emptying (vomiting, diarrhea), and an embolic source such as AF form the classic triad of embolic SMA occlusion; pain may ease for a while before peritonitis develops (ESVS 2025, non-US). Disproportionate pain should also raise suspicion of mesenteric vein thrombosis (ACG 2020). Practical: distension and bloody stool are late
  • Practical: Physical Exam: Early (hours 0-6): Minimal abdominal tenderness despite severe pain (hallmark), normal or hypoactive bowel sounds, tachycardia, no peritoneal signs. Late (hours 6-24): Peritoneal signs develop (rebound, guarding, rigidity), absent bowel sounds (ileus), abdominal distension, hemodynamic instability (shock), bloody rectal exam (late finding). Classically described as "pain out of proportion" - patient writhing in agony but abdomen soft on exam (early).
  • Variants/Subtypes: Acute mesenteric ischemia (discussed here) vs Chronic mesenteric ischemia ("intestinal angina" - postprandial pain, weight loss, food fear, chronic). Colonic ischemia (separate entity, see pearl)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Lactate: A single lactate should not be used to confirm or rule out AMI or NOMI; high lactate reflects systemic hypoperfusion and risk of death rather than bowel ischemia itself (ESVS 2025, non-US). A normal lactate does not exclude AMI: if suspected, get CTA
  • Complete Blood Count: Leukocytosis (>15k common, >20k suggests necrosis), hemoconcentration, later: leukopenia (sepsis)
  • Basic Metabolic Panel: Metabolic acidosis (elevated anion gap from lactic acidosis), elevated BUN/Cr (prerenal from hypovolemia), hyperkalemia (cell death)
  • Liver Function Tests: Elevated AST/ALT (hepatic hypoperfusion), elevated alkaline phosphatase, elevated LDH (nonspecific)
  • Amylase/Lipase: Can be mildly elevated (nonspecific); helps rule out pancreatitis
  • D-dimer: Not to be used alone to exclude AMI; it rises with almost any acute abdominal process, and the 2017 ESVS advice to use it as a rule-out test was withdrawn (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • Arterial Blood Gas: Metabolic acidosis (pH <7.35, low HCO3), elevated lactate, base deficit
  • Coagulation Studies: PT/INR and PTT before anticoagulation. Mesenteric vein thrombosis without cirrhosis and no obvious cause: thrombophilia workup including JAK2 for myeloproliferative neoplasm (ACG 2020); also look for intra-abdominal malignancy or inflammation, CMV or SARS-CoV-2 infection, and chronic liver disease (ESVS 2025, non-US)

Imaging: CT Angiography (CTA) Abdomen/Pelvis (Initial Test of Choice):

  • CTA with IV contrast is usually appropriate as the initial imaging for suspected AMI (ACR 2018)
  • Urgent CTA with arterial and venous phases and 1 mm slices or thinner, regardless of renal function; state the suspicion of AMI on the request (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • Findings - Arterial occlusion: SMA filling defect/occlusion, lack of contrast enhancement of bowel wall, pneumatosis intestinalis (air in bowel wall - ominous), portal venous gas (late sign, poor prognosis), free air (perforation)
  • Findings - Venous thrombosis: SMV or portal vein thrombus, bowel wall thickening, mesenteric edema/stranding, ascites
  • Findings - NOMI: In a patient in shock, lack of bowel enhancement, small bowel thickening, pneumatosis, or portal venous gas without significant SMA stenosis suggests NOMI (ESVS 2025, non-US)

Alternative Imaging:

  • Abdominal X-ray: May be appropriate (ACR 2018) but cannot exclude AMI; late findings: pneumatosis, portal venous gas, free air, ileus, thumbprinting
  • Duplex Ultrasound: May be appropriate for suspected AMI (ACR 2018); first-line for suspected chronic mesenteric ischemia (ESVS 2025, non-US); operator-dependent and limited by bowel gas
  • Catheter Angiography: Now mainly therapeutic: aspiration embolectomy, thrombolysis, angioplasty and stenting, vasodilator infusion for NOMI (ACR 2022)

Diagnostic Laparotomy/Laparoscopy:

  • Practical: If high clinical suspicion (severe pain, lactate elevated, peritonitis) but imaging non-diagnostic or unavailable, proceed to exploratory laparotomy
  • Practical: "Don't let the sun set on mesenteric ischemia" - early surgery improves survival
  • Practical: Directly visualize bowel: necrotic bowel (black, gangrenous), lack of peristalsis, lack of pulsations in mesenteric vessels
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management (TIME IS BOWEL - Urgent Action Required):

  • Practical: NPO, nasogastric decompression, two large-bore IVs
  • Practical: crystalloid resuscitation guided by perfusion, MAP 65 mmHg or more; limit vasoconstrictors when possible
  • Systemic anticoagulation (UFH) once AMI is diagnosed, unless contraindicated: usually appropriate in embolic, thrombotic, and non-occlusive AMI (ACR 2022)
  • Antibiotics for all AMI (ESVS 2025, non-US); within 1 hour if sepsis or septic shock (SIS 2017)
  • Urgent vascular surgery, interventional radiology, and general surgery; treat at a center with 24/7 open and endovascular revascularization (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • Urgent CTA regardless of renal function (ESVS 2025, non-US). Practical: peritonitis with instability goes straight to the OR

Antibiotics (Recommended in AMI; ESVS 2025, non-US):

  • Bowel ischemia is a risk factor for treatment failure in intra-abdominal infection (SIS 2017, Table 4)
  • Higher-risk regimens: piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375-4.5 g IV q6h or meropenem 1-2 g IV q8h; lower-risk: ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV q24h plus metronidazole 1 g IV, then 500 mg q6-8h (SIS 2017, Table 11)
  • Duration: 24 h for resected ischemic, non-perforated bowel; no more than 4 days after adequate source control (SIS 2017)

Anticoagulation:

  • Arterial (Embolic or Thrombotic) and NOMI: Systemic anticoagulation is usually appropriate (ACR 2022). Practical: UFH 80 units/kg IV bolus (max 5000), then 18 units/kg/h, aPTT 60-80 s; resume after surgery when safe
  • Mesenteric Vein Thrombosis:
    • Anticoagulate all acute symptomatic MVT without contraindication (ACG 2020, strong), starting soon after diagnosis with UFH or LMWH; UFH can be reversed with protamine if laparotomy is needed (ESVS 2025, non-US). Practical: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h
    • Duration: at least 6 months if the cause is reversible and there is no thrombophilia; indefinite with thrombophilia (ACG 2020) or if idiopathic or with a permanent risk factor (ESVS 2025, non-US)
    • Maintenance: LMWH or warfarin (ACG 2020); DOACs may be considered (ESVS 2025, non-US). ACG 2020 notes limited DOAC experience and possible poor absorption with intestinal edema
    • Worsening on anticoagulation: endovascular thrombolysis or thrombectomy may be considered (ESVS 2025, non-US); ACR 2022 also rates transhepatic pharmacomechanical thrombolysis usually appropriate

Specific Treatments by Etiology:

  • Arterial Embolism or Thrombosis, No Peritonitis:
    • Endovascular first: aspiration embolectomy or transcatheter thrombolysis for embolus; angioplasty and stenting for atherosclerotic occlusion (ACR 2022, usually appropriate); endovascular should be considered first-line (ESVS 2025, non-US)
    • Open embolectomy, endarterectomy, or bypass may be appropriate (ACR 2022); retrograde open SMA stenting if percutaneous stenting is not possible (ESVS 2025, non-US)
    • Practical: laparotomy afterward if bowel viability is in doubt
  • Peritonitis or Bowel Infarction: Surgical revascularization with laparotomy (ACR 2022, usually appropriate); revascularize before resecting bowel (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • NOMI:
    • Treat the low-flow state. Practical: limit vasoconstrictors
    • Angiography with intra-arterial vasodilator plus systemic anticoagulation (ACR 2022, usually appropriate); e.g., papaverine 80 mg bolus into the SMA, then 30-60 mg/h for 24-72 h, watching for systemic hypotension (ESVS 2025, non-US)
    • Abdominal compartment syndrome: urgent decompression laparotomy (ESVS 2025, non-US); resect necrotic bowel
    • Mortality about 70% (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • Venous Thrombosis: Anticoagulation (ACG 2020; ACR 2022). Practical: surgery for peritonitis or necrosis, with anticoagulation continued

Surgical Principles:

  • Revascularization before bowel resection (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • Practical: after revascularization, reassess viability (color, peristalsis, pulsations); quantitative indocyanine green imaging may help (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • Resect clearly necrotic bowel (black, no pulses, no peristalsis)
  • Resection without primary anastomosis and a planned second-look laparotomy (ESVS 2025, non-US); temporary abdominal closure when a second look is planned for mesenteric ischemia (SIS 2017)
  • Practical: If extensive necrosis (>50% of small bowel): discuss prognosis with family, consider short bowel syndrome implications

Postoperative Care:

  • Practical: ICU monitoring; serial lactate as a marker of systemic perfusion
  • Antibiotics: no more than 4 days after adequate source control (SIS 2017)
  • Anticoagulation (arterial and venous cases)
  • Nutrition: delay enteral feeding with overt bowel ischemia and start parenteral nutrition within 3-7 days; watch for refeeding syndrome (ESVS 2025, non-US)
  • Scheduled "second look" laparotomy if planned (24-48 hours after initial surgery)

Consultations:

  • Practical: Vascular Surgery: URGENT consult within 1 hour for arterial occlusion (embolectomy, bypass)
  • General Surgery: URGENT consult for bowel resection, exploratory laparotomy
  • Interventional Radiology: Aspiration embolectomy, thrombolysis, angioplasty and stenting, vasodilator infusion for NOMI (ACR 2022)
  • Critical Care: ICU admission for hemodynamic support

Disposition:

  • Practical: ICU: ALL patients with mesenteric ischemia require ICU care (pre-op and post-op)
  • Operating Room: EMERGENTLY if peritonitis, bowel necrosis, or arterial occlusion
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Disproportionate Pain Is the Clue, Not Proof: Severe pain with few exam findings, bowel emptying, and an embolic source (often AF) is the classic triad of embolic SMA occlusion; pain may ease before peritonitis, which marks irreversible ischemia. Suspect acute SMA embolism in every patient with AF and acute abdominal pain (ESVS 2025, non-US), and get CTA.
  • Time Is Bowel: Do not wait on labs or observe: urgent CTA, anticoagulation, antibiotics, and revascularization at a center with 24/7 open and endovascular capability (ESVS 2025, non-US; ACR 2022). Practical: peritonitis with instability goes to the OR.
  • Atrial Fibrillation and Embolism: AF was present in about one third (32%) of patients with AMI; about a third of AMI is embolic, and thrombotic occlusion is becoming more common (ESVS 2025, non-US). Practical: anticoagulation for AF also protects the mesenteric circulation.
  • Lactate and D-dimer Cannot Rule AMI In or Out: A single lactate or D-dimer should not be used to confirm or exclude AMI or NOMI. Lactate reflects systemic hypoperfusion and death risk, not bowel ischemia itself; D-dimer rises with almost any acute abdomen (ESVS 2025, non-US). Clinical suspicion drives urgent CTA.
  • CTA Is the Test: Arterial and venous phases with thin slices, done urgently regardless of renal function (ESVS 2025, non-US); usually appropriate initial imaging (ACR 2018). CTA has replaced catheter angiography for diagnosis; angiography is now for treatment (ACR 2022).
  • NOMI Has the Worst Prognosis: About 13-15% of AMI, in low-flow states; mortality about 70% (ESVS 2025, non-US). Treat the low-flow state, give intra-arterial vasodilators with systemic anticoagulation (ACR 2022), decompress abdominal compartment syndrome, and resect necrotic bowel (ESVS 2025, non-US).
  • Mesenteric Vein Thrombosis Is Usually Medical: Anticoagulate all acute symptomatic MVT without contraindication (ACG 2020, strong); endovascular thrombolysis if worsening on anticoagulation (ESVS 2025, non-US); Practical: surgery for peritonitis or necrosis. Duration: at least 6 months if reversible, indefinite with thrombophilia; check JAK2 and a thrombophilia panel when no cause is obvious (ACG 2020).
  • Second-Look Laparotomy: After revascularization and resection, leaving bowel in discontinuity with a planned second look should be considered (ESVS 2025, non-US), with temporary abdominal closure (SIS 2017). Practical: borderline bowel declares itself over 24-48 h, which limits over-resection.
  • Colon Ischemia Is a Different Disease: Sudden mild cramping pain, urge to defecate, and bloody stool within 24 h; CT with IV and oral contrast first; colonoscopy within 48 h with minimal insufflation, avoided with peritonitis or gangrene (ACG 2015). Most cases resolve without specific therapy; antibiotics only for moderate or severe disease (ACG 2015). Isolated right colon ischemia, severe pain without bleeding, or AF may herald AMI: get multiphasic CTA (ACG 2015).
  • Pneumatosis and Portal Venous Gas: Signs of advanced ischemia: in colon ischemia they predict transmural infarction (ACG 2015); in a patient in shock without SMA stenosis they suggest NOMI (ESVS 2025, non-US). Practical: usually means emergency surgery.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: any suspected or confirmed acute mesenteric ischemia
  • Practical: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam
  • Practical: any clinical suspicion of AMI, whatever the lactate
  • Practical: Peritoneal signs (rebound, guarding, rigidity)
  • Practical: Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia, shock)
  • Practical: Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, lactate >4 mmol/L)
  • Practical: Post-operative from bowel resection/revascularization
  • Surgical emergency: in-hospital mortality about 49% (ESVS 2025, non-US)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: discharge after revascularization or other definitive treatment and recovery; mesenteric vein thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation (ACG 2020)
  • Post-operative patients discharge when:
    • Bowel function returned (passing flatus/stool, tolerating PO diet)
    • No signs of infection (afebrile, WBC normalizing)
    • Adequate pain control on oral analgesics
    • Lactate normalized
    • Anticoagulation established if indicated; for MVT, LMWH or warfarin (ACG 2020), DOAC may be considered (ESVS 2025, non-US)
    • Cardiology follow-up for AF if relevant (rate/rhythm control, long-term anticoagulation)
    • Vascular surgery follow-up within 1-2 weeks
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 UFH, 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Meropenem
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 LDH

107. CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE COMPLICATIONS

Hyperkalemia • Volume Overload • Metabolic Acidosis • Uremia • Dialysis Urgency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Patient with known CKD (GFR <60 mL/min/1.73m²) presenting with acute decompensation: severe hyperkalemia, volume overload with pulmonary edema, worsening uremia, metabolic acidosis, or acute-on-chronic renal failure requiring urgent dialysis consideration.

  • Pathophysiology: Progressive nephron loss leads to inability to maintain fluid/electrolyte homeostasis, acid-base balance, and toxin excretion. Acute decompensation triggered by: medication non-compliance (missed dialysis, dietary indiscretion), infection, volume overload, NSAIDs/nephrotoxins, obstruction, hypotension. Key complications: (1) Hyperkalemia (K >6.0 mEq/L, cardiac arrest risk), (2) Volume overload (pulmonary edema, hypertensive urgency), (3) Metabolic acidosis (HCO3 <15 mEq/L), (4) Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding), (5) Mineral-bone disease (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism)
  • Risk Factors: CKD Stage 4-5 (GFR <30 mL/min), diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ESRD on dialysis (missed sessions), medication non-adherence, dietary indiscretion (high K, high Na, high fluid), ACE-I/ARB use, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, contrast exposure, infections (UTI, sepsis), obstructive uropathy
  • Symptoms: Dyspnea (pulmonary edema), chest pain (pericarditis, ACS), muscle weakness (hyperkalemia), nausea/vomiting (uremia), confusion/altered mental status (uremic encephalopathy), pruritus (uremia), decreased urine output (oliguria/anuria), palpitations (arrhythmias from hyperkalemia)
  • Physical Exam: Hypertension (often severe, >180/110), rales/crackles (pulmonary edema), elevated JVP, peripheral edema (2-4+), pericardial friction rub (uremic pericarditis), altered mental status, asterixis, uremic frost (white crystalline deposits on skin - rare), pallor (anemia), excoriation marks (pruritus)
  • Variants/Subtypes: CKD Stage 3a (GFR 45-59, usually stable) vs Stage 3b (GFR 30-44) vs Stage 4 (GFR 15-29, pre-dialysis) vs Stage 5 (GFR <15, ESRD requiring RRT). Acute-on-chronic kidney injury (rapid GFR decline superimposed on CKD). Dialysis-dependent ESRD (missed dialysis sessions = acute decompensation)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Basic Metabolic Panel: Elevated BUN/Cr (baseline Cr varies; acute rise >0.3 mg/dL concerning), hyperkalemia (K >5.5 mEq/L concerning, >6.5 mEq/L emergency), metabolic acidosis (HCO3 <22 mEq/L in CKD, <15 mEq/L severe), hyperphosphatemia (PO4 >5.5 mg/dL), hyponatremia or hypernatremia, elevated anion gap (uremic acidosis)
  • Complete Blood Count: Normocytic anemia (low Hgb typical 8-10 g/dL in CKD from low EPO), thrombocytopenia if uremia severe
  • Calcium/Magnesium: Hypocalcemia (ionized Ca <1.0 mmol/L), hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
  • Arterial Blood Gas: Metabolic acidosis (pH <7.35, low HCO3, elevated anion gap), assess for respiratory compensation
  • ECG (CRITICAL for hyperkalemia): Peaked T waves (K 5.5-6.5), loss of P waves (K 6.5-7.0), widened QRS (K >7.0), sine wave pattern (K >8.0, pre-cardiac arrest), bradycardia, AV blocks, ventricular arrhythmias
  • Urinalysis: Assess for infection (pyuria, bacteria), obstruction, new proteinuria/hematuria
  • Other: PTH (elevated in CKD-MBD), albumin, troponin (if chest pain), BNP (if dyspnea/volume overload)

Imaging:

  • Chest X-ray: Pulmonary edema (perihilar infiltrates, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions), cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion (uremic pericarditis)
  • Renal Ultrasound: Assess kidney size (small echogenic kidneys = chronic disease), hydronephrosis (obstruction), renal artery stenosis (Doppler). Helps differentiate acute vs chronic kidney disease
  • Echocardiogram: If pericardial effusion suspected (pericardial friction rub, muffled heart sounds), assess LV function, valvular disease

Assessment of Acute vs Chronic Kidney Injury:

  • Acute-on-chronic: Rapid rise in Cr (>0.3 mg/dL in 48 hours or >1.5x baseline in 7 days)
  • Chronic: Small kidneys (<9 cm), anemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, elevated PTH
  • Review prior Cr values (establish baseline renal function)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management (Priority-Based):

  • 1. Hyperkalemia (MOST URGENT - cardiac arrest risk): See detailed protocol below
  • 2. Volume Overload/Pulmonary Edema: Oxygen, diuresis, consider dialysis
  • 3. Severe Metabolic Acidosis (pH <7.2): Sodium bicarbonate, consider dialysis
  • 4. Uremic Complications: Urgent dialysis if pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding

HYPERKALEMIA MANAGEMENT (K >6.0 mEq/L or ECG changes):

  • Step 1 - Cardiac Membrane Stabilization (if ECG changes present):
    • Calcium gluconate 10% 1-2 grams (10-20 mL) IV over 2-5 minutes
    • Or Calcium chloride 10% 0.5-1 gram (5-10 mL) IV over 2-5 minutes (via central line preferred)
    • Onset: 1-3 minutes, Duration: 30-60 minutes
    • Does NOT lower K, just stabilizes cardiac membranes
    • Repeat dose if ECG changes persist after 5 minutes
  • Step 2 - Shift Potassium Intracellularly:
    • Insulin + Glucose: Regular insulin 10 units IV + D50 50 mL (25 grams dextrose) IV push. Onset: 15-30 minutes, Duration: 4-6 hours, Lowers K by 0.5-1.2 mEq/L. Check glucose q1h (risk of hypoglycemia). If glucose >250 mg/dL, give insulin without dextrose
    • Albuterol Nebulized: 10-20 mg nebulized over 10 minutes (4-8 times standard dose). Onset: 30 minutes, Duration: 2 hours, Lowers K by 0.5-1.0 mEq/L. Synergistic with insulin
    • Sodium Bicarbonate (if acidotic): 150 mEq (3 amps, 50 mEq each) in 1 L D5W over 2-4 hours. Only effective if metabolic acidosis present (pH <7.2, HCO3 <15). Lowers K by 0.5 mEq/L
  • Step 3 - Remove Potassium from Body:
    • Diuretics (if residual kidney function): Furosemide 40-80 mg IV push (increase to 160-200 mg if CKD Stage 4-5). Promotes renal K excretion
    • Patiromer (Veltassa): 8.4 g PO daily, increase to 25.2 g daily. Onset: 4-7 hours. GI K binder. For non-emergent or chronic management
    • Sodium Zirconium Cyclosilicate (Lokelma): 10 g PO TID x 48 hours, then 10 g PO daily. Onset: 1 hour. Faster than patiromer
    • Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate) - AVOID if possible: 15-30 g PO/PR. Onset: 2-4 hours. Risk of bowel necrosis (especially with sorbitol). Use only if other binders unavailable
    • Hemodialysis: MOST EFFECTIVE. Removes 50-75 mEq K per session. Indicated if K >6.5 mEq/L with ECG changes, K >7.0 mEq/L, refractory to medical management, or anuric ESRD patient
  • Monitoring: Continuous telemetry, repeat K q2h until <5.5 mEq/L, repeat ECG after interventions

VOLUME OVERLOAD / PULMONARY EDEMA MANAGEMENT:

  • Oxygen: Supplemental O2 to maintain SpO2 >92%
  • Positioning: Upright position (reduces preload)
  • Diuretics (if residual kidney function, GFR >15 mL/min):
    • Furosemide 80-200 mg IV push (higher doses in CKD)
    • If inadequate response: Furosemide continuous infusion 10-40 mg/hr
    • Add thiazide diuretic for synergy: Metolazone 5-10 mg PO 30 minutes before furosemide
  • Nitroglycerin (if hypertensive): 0.4 mg SL q5min x 3, or IV infusion 10-200 mcg/min
  • Ultrafiltration/Dialysis: If minimal urine output (<400 mL/day), refractory pulmonary edema, or GFR <15 mL/min. Can remove 2-4 L fluid per session

METABOLIC ACIDOSIS MANAGEMENT:

  • Sodium Bicarbonate (if pH <7.2 or HCO3 <15 mEq/L):
    • Acute: 1-2 amps (50-100 mEq) IV push, can repeat
    • Infusion: 150 mEq (3 amps) in 1 L D5W at 100-150 mL/hr
    • Goal: pH >7.2, HCO3 >15-18 mEq/L (avoid over-correction)
    • Caution: worsens volume overload, hypernatremia
  • Dialysis: Most effective for severe acidosis in ESRD

URGENT DIALYSIS INDICATIONS ("AEIOU"):

  • A - Acidosis (refractory metabolic acidosis, pH <7.2)
  • E - Electrolytes (severe hyperkalemia K >6.5 mEq/L with ECG changes, refractory to medical therapy)
  • I - Intoxication (dialyzable toxins: methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates)
  • O - Overload (volume overload, pulmonary edema refractory to diuretics)
  • U - Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding diathesis)

Nephrology Consultation:

  • STAT consult for urgent dialysis consideration
  • All CKD Stage 4-5 admissions for ongoing management
  • Acute-on-chronic kidney injury
  • Dialysis catheter placement (if no AV fistula/graft available)

Chronic CKD Management (Once Stabilized):

  • Anemia: ESA (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin) if Hgb <10 g/dL, goal Hgb 10-11.5 g/dL. Iron supplementation (IV iron preferred in CKD)
  • Mineral-Bone Disease: Phosphate binders (calcium acetate, sevelamer), vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, paricalcitol), calcimimetics (cinacalcet) if elevated PTH
  • Dietary: Low potassium (<2-3 g/day), low phosphorus (<800-1000 mg/day), fluid restriction (1-1.5 L/day if oliguric), sodium restriction (<2 g/day)
  • Medications to Avoid: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast (if possible), metformin (hold if GFR <30), digoxin (reduce dose), renally-cleared drugs (adjust for GFR)

Disposition:

  • ICU: Severe hyperkalemia (K >7.0, ECG changes), pulmonary edema requiring BiPAP/intubation, hemodynamic instability, urgent dialysis needed, uremic pericarditis with tamponade
  • Floor with Telemetry: Moderate hyperkalemia (K 6.0-7.0), volume overload managed with diuretics, acute-on-chronic kidney injury
  • Discharge: Hyperkalemia resolved (K <5.5 mEq/L), euvolemic, stable renal function, follow-up arranged with nephrology
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • ECG Changes Predict Cardiac Arrest Risk Better Than Absolute K Level: Hyperkalemia is dangerous because of cardiac arrhythmias, not the number itself. K 6.5 mEq/L with peaked T waves is more dangerous than K 7.5 mEq/L with normal ECG. ECG progression: Peaked T waves (K 5.5-6.5) → Loss of P waves + widened QRS (K 6.5-7.5) → Sine wave pattern (K >8.0, pre-arrest). ANY ECG change from hyperkalemia = give calcium gluconate immediately to stabilize cardiac membrane, then shift K intracellularly (insulin+glucose, albuterol), then remove K (dialysis). Don't wait for "critical" K level.
  • Calcium Gluconate Does NOT Lower Potassium - It Stabilizes Cardiac Membranes: Common misconception: calcium lowers K. FALSE. Calcium antagonizes K's effect on cardiac myocyte membranes, preventing arrhythmias, but K level unchanged. Think of it as buying time (30-60 minutes) while you actually lower K with insulin/glucose, albuterol, dialysis. Give calcium if ANY ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS), don't wait for sine wave. Can repeat calcium q5min if ECG changes persist. Calcium gluconate 1-2 g IV over 2-5 minutes (10-20 mL of 10% solution).
  • Insulin+Glucose+Albuterol is the Fastest Way to Lower K Acutely (Besides Dialysis): Insulin drives K into cells via Na-K-ATPase. Give regular insulin 10 units IV + D50 50 mL (if glucose <250 mg/dL). Lowers K by 0.5-1.2 mEq/L in 15-30 minutes, lasts 4-6 hours. Add albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized (4-8x standard dose) - synergistic, lowers K by another 0.5-1.0 mEq/L. Combined, can lower K by 1-2 mEq/L. Pitfall: insulin without glucose causes hypoglycemia (check glucose q1h x 4 hours). If glucose >250 mg/dL, give insulin alone without dextrose.
  • Hemodialysis is Most Effective K Removal - Lower Threshold in CKD Stage 4-5: Dialysis removes 50-75 mEq K per 4-hour session, lowering K by 2-3 mEq/L. Most definitive treatment. Indications: K >6.5 mEq/L with ECG changes, K >7.0 mEq/L regardless of ECG, refractory to medical therapy, or anuric ESRD patient (can't excrete K renally). Don't delay dialysis hoping medical management will work in CKD Stage 5 patient with K 7.0 - just dialyze. Medical management is temporizing; dialysis is definitive in these patients.
  • "AEIOU" Mnemonic for Urgent Dialysis Indications: A = Acidosis (pH <7.2 refractory), E = Electrolytes (severe hyperkalemia K >6.5 with ECG changes), I = Intoxication (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates - dialyzable toxins), O = Overload (volume overload, pulmonary edema refractory to diuretics), U = Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding). If any AEIOU criterion met, consult nephrology STAT for urgent dialysis. Don't delay with prolonged medical management attempts.
  • Kayexalate (Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate) is Obsolete and Dangerous: Old-school K binder with minimal efficacy (only lowers K by 0.5-1.0 mEq/L after 4-6 hours) and serious risk of bowel necrosis (especially with sorbitol). FDA black box warning. Newer K binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) are safer and faster. Use Lokelma (10 g PO, onset 1 hour) or Veltassa (8.4 g PO, onset 4-7 hours) instead. Reserve Kayexalate only if newer binders unavailable. Never give Kayexalate with sorbitol. For acute severe hyperkalemia, use insulin/glucose/albuterol/dialysis - not Kayexalate.
  • CKD Patients Need Much Higher Furosemide Doses for Diuresis: Loop diuretics work at thick ascending limb of loop of Henle. In CKD, reduced drug delivery to site of action (low GFR) + structural changes in nephrons = resistance to diuretics. Standard furosemide dose (20-40 mg IV) is inadequate. CKD Stage 3: 80 mg IV; Stage 4: 120-160 mg IV; Stage 5: 160-200 mg IV bolus. If inadequate diuresis, use continuous furosemide infusion 10-40 mg/hr or add metolazone 5-10 mg PO (thiazide + loop = synergistic diuresis). Alternatively, dialyze for volume removal (ultrafiltration).
  • Target Hgb 10-11.5 g/dL in CKD Anemia - Higher Targets Increase Mortality: CKD causes anemia (low erythropoietin production). Treat with ESAs (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin) + IV iron. But targeting higher Hgb (>13 g/dL) with aggressive ESA dosing increases stroke, MI, thrombosis, mortality (TREAT trial). Current guidelines: start ESA if Hgb <10 g/dL, target 10-11.5 g/dL. Never transfuse to Hgb >12 g/dL. Iron supplementation essential: check ferritin, TSAT; give IV iron if ferritin <500 ng/mL or TSAT <30% (oral iron poorly absorbed in CKD).
  • Secondary Hyperparathyroidism in CKD Requires Triple Therapy: CKD causes hyperphosphatemia (kidneys can't excrete PO4) → binds Ca → hypocalcemia → elevated PTH → bone disease. Management: (1) Phosphate binders with meals (calcium acetate, sevelamer, lanthanum) to reduce PO4 absorption, goal PO4 <5.5 mg/dL; (2) Vitamin D analogs (calcitriol 0.25-0.5 mcg daily or paricalcitol) to suppress PTH; (3) Calcimimetics (cinacalcet 30-180 mg daily) if PTH remains >300 pg/mL despite above. Goal PTH 150-300 pg/mL in CKD Stage 5. Uncontrolled secondary hyperparathyroidism causes renal osteodystrophy (bone pain, fractures) and vascular calcification.
  • Avoid Metformin if GFR <30 mL/min - Risk of Lactic Acidosis: Metformin is renally excreted. Accumulation in renal failure causes lactic acidosis (type B, non-hypoxic). Mortality 30-50% if metformin-associated lactic acidosis develops. FDA guidelines: Hold metformin if GFR <30 mL/min. If patient on metformin presents with AKI + lactic acidosis (lactate >5-10 mmol/L, pH <7.35, anion gap acidosis), assume metformin-induced until proven otherwise. Treatment: hemodialysis (removes metformin + lactate). Similarly, avoid contrast in CKD (risk of contrast-induced nephropathy); if unavoidable, IV fluids before/after, hold metformin 48 hours pre/post-contrast.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe hyperkalemia (K >7.0 mEq/L) or any hyperkalemia with ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, sine wave)
  • Refractory hyperkalemia despite medical management (requires urgent dialysis)
  • Pulmonary edema with respiratory failure (requiring BiPAP, intubation)
  • Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1) refractory to bicarbonate
  • Uremic pericarditis with hemodynamic compromise or cardiac tamponade
  • Altered mental status from uremic encephalopathy
  • Hypertensive emergency (BP >220/120 with end-organ damage)
  • Dialysis catheter placement needed emergently but no existing access
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Potassium normalized (<5.5 mEq/L) and stable for 24 hours
  • Volume status optimized (euvolemic, no dyspnea at rest, SpO2 >92% on room air)
  • Renal function stable or improved (Cr at or near baseline for patient)
  • Metabolic acidosis corrected (HCO3 >18-20 mEq/L) or chronic compensated
  • Blood pressure controlled (<160/100 mmHg on oral regimen)
  • If new dialysis: first outpatient dialysis session scheduled within 48 hours, dialysis catheter functional
  • Patient educated on low-potassium diet, fluid restriction, medication adherence
  • Nephrology follow-up arranged within 1-2 weeks (sooner if dialysis-dependent)
  • Medications reconciled (nephrotoxins stopped, doses adjusted for GFR)
  • Patient/family understand signs of hyperkalemia, fluid overload, when to seek emergency care
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Calcium Gluconate, 💊 Sodium Bicarbonate, 💊 Sevelamer, 💊 Erythropoietin, 💊 IV Iron, 💊 Dapagliflozin, 💊 Empagliflozin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Low eGFR, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hypocalcemia, 🔬 Low Bicarbonate, 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Low Vitamin D, 🔬 Elevated INR
