108. UREMIC SYNDROME

End-Stage Renal Failure • Uremic Pericarditis • Encephalopathy • Bleeding • Dialysis Required
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Patient with ESRD (GFR <15 mL/min) or acute severe kidney injury presenting with systemic manifestations of uremic toxin accumulation: nausea/vomiting, altered mental status, pericarditis, bleeding, pruritus, asterixis - indicating urgent need for renal replacement therapy.

  • Pathophysiology: Accumulation of uremic toxins (urea, creatinine, guanidine compounds, middle molecules, protein-bound solutes) when kidneys fail to excrete metabolic waste. Affects multiple organ systems. Key manifestations: (1) Uremic pericarditis (fibrinous pericarditis, risk of tamponade), (2) Uremic encephalopathy (confusion, seizures, coma), (3) Platelet dysfunction (prolonged bleeding time despite normal platelet count), (4) Neuropathy (peripheral neuropathy, restless legs), (5) Pruritus, (6) GI symptoms (nausea, anorexia, uremic fetor - ammonia breath smell)
  • Risk Factors: ESRD (any cause: diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, glomerulonephritis), missed dialysis sessions, acute kidney injury (AKI with BUN >100 mg/dL, Cr >8-10 mg/dL), delayed initiation of dialysis, malnutrition, elderly age
  • Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia (early), metallic taste, uremic fetor (ammonia or "fishy" breath smell), confusion/lethargy (uremic encephalopathy), seizures, chest pain (pericarditis), dyspnea, pruritus (intense, generalized itching), fatigue, weakness, restless legs syndrome, hiccups (persistent, from diaphragmatic irritation)
  • Physical Exam: Altered mental status (confusion, somnolence), asterixis (flapping tremor, similar to hepatic encephalopathy), pericardial friction rub (pathognomonic for uremic pericarditis), tachycardia, hypotension (if tamponade), pallor (anemia), uremic frost (white crystalline urea deposits on skin - very rare, extreme uremia), excoriations from scratching (pruritus), peripheral edema, peripheral neuropathy (decreased reflexes, sensory loss)
  • Variants/Subtypes: Uremic pericarditis vs Uremic encephalopathy vs Uremic bleeding diathesis. Acute uremia (AKI with rapid toxin accumulation) vs Chronic uremia (ESRD with gradual onset)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Basic Metabolic Panel: Markedly elevated BUN (typically >80-100 mg/dL, can be >150-200 mg/dL), markedly elevated Cr (>8-10 mg/dL), hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, elevated anion gap
  • BUN/Cr Ratio: Usually >20:1 in uremia (indicates poor renal function with urea accumulation)
  • Complete Blood Count: Normocytic anemia (Hgb 6-10 g/dL), normal or elevated WBC, platelet count usually normal (dysfunction is qualitative, not quantitative)
  • Coagulation Studies: PT/INR normal, PTT normal, but bleeding time prolonged (platelet dysfunction from uremic toxins)
  • Arterial Blood Gas: Metabolic acidosis (pH <7.35, HCO3 <18 mEq/L)
  • Other: Elevated phosphate, low calcium, elevated PTH, hypoalbuminemia

ECG:

  • Pericarditis: Diffuse ST elevations (concave upward), PR depression (highly specific for pericarditis)
  • Hyperkalemia: Peaked T waves, widened QRS, loss of P waves (see CKD complications)
  • Low voltage (if pericardial effusion)

Imaging:

  • Echocardiogram (if pericarditis suspected): Pericardial effusion (can be small to large), fibrinous strands, assess for tamponade physiology (RV collapse, exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral inflow), assess LV function
  • Chest X-ray: Cardiomegaly (if effusion), pulmonary edema (if volume overload)

Diagnostic Criteria for Uremic Pericarditis:

  • Clinical: Chest pain, pericardial friction rub, dyspnea
  • ECG: Diffuse ST elevations, PR depression
  • Echo: Pericardial effusion
  • Context: ESRD or severe AKI (BUN >60-80 mg/dL)
  • Uremic pericarditis is "dialysis-requiring" pericarditis - absolute indication for urgent dialysis
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management:

  • Assess hemodynamic stability (BP, HR, oxygen saturation)
  • IV access, continuous telemetry
  • NPO initially (nausea, vomiting common)
  • Antiemetics: Ondansetron 4-8 mg IV q8h PRN
  • URGENT Nephrology Consult for dialysis consideration

URGENT DIALYSIS - Primary Treatment for Uremic Syndrome:

  • Indications (Absolute for Uremia):
    • Uremic pericarditis (MOST IMPORTANT - prevents cardiac tamponade)
    • Uremic encephalopathy (confusion, seizures, coma)
    • Uremic bleeding (platelet dysfunction causing GI bleeding, epistaxis)
    • Intractable nausea/vomiting despite antiemetics
    • BUN >100 mg/dL with symptoms
    • Also: AEIOU criteria (see CKD complications - acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload)
  • Modality: Hemodialysis preferred for urgent indications (faster clearance than peritoneal dialysis)
  • Access: Temporary dialysis catheter (internal jugular or femoral vein) if no AV fistula/graft. Place urgently
  • Frequency: Initially daily or every other day until uremia resolves, then 3x/week (standard ESRD schedule)
  • Response: Symptoms typically improve within 24-48 hours of initiating dialysis. Pericarditis resolves over 1-2 weeks

Specific Management by Complication:

  • Uremic Pericarditis:
    • Dialysis is PRIMARY treatment (resolves pericarditis in 85-90% of cases)
    • NSAIDs and Colchicine are CONTRAINDICATED (worsen renal function, ineffective for uremic pericarditis)
    • Heparin-free dialysis (avoid anticoagulation during dialysis if pericardial effusion, bleeding risk)
    • If large effusion (>2 cm on echo) or tamponade: Pericardiocentesis or pericardial window
    • Monitor with serial echos q2-3 days until effusion resolves
  • Uremic Encephalopathy:
    • Dialysis is treatment (clears uremic toxins)
    • Avoid sedatives (benzodiazepines worsen encephalopathy)
    • Seizures: Levetiracetam 500-1000 mg IV (renally cleared but safer than phenytoin in uremia)
    • Airway protection if altered mental status (GCS <8)
  • Uremic Bleeding (Platelet Dysfunction):
    • Dialysis improves platelet function (but takes days)
    • For acute bleeding:
      • DDAVP (Desmopressin): 0.3 mcg/kg IV over 30 minutes. Increases vWF release, improves platelet adhesion. Onset 1-2 hours, duration 4-8 hours. Can repeat q12-24h
      • Cryoprecipitate: 10 units IV. Contains vWF, Factor VIII. Onset 1 hour, duration 12-24 hours. More effective than DDAVP
      • Conjugated Estrogens: 0.6 mg/kg IV daily x 5 days. Improves platelet function, but onset 6-12 hours, used for refractory bleeding
      • Platelet Transfusion: Generally NOT effective (transfused platelets also become dysfunctional in uremic environment)
    • Correct anemia: Transfuse PRBCs if Hgb <7 g/dL (improves platelet function by increasing RBC-platelet interactions)
  • Pruritus:
    • Dialysis (most effective)
    • Topical: Moisturizing creams, capsaicin cream
    • Oral: Gabapentin 100-300 mg post-dialysis, Pregabalin 25-75 mg post-dialysis (both renally cleared, dose after dialysis)
    • UVB phototherapy if refractory
  • Nausea/Vomiting:
    • Ondansetron 4-8 mg IV q8h
    • Metoclopramide 5-10 mg IV q6h (use cautiously, risk of extrapyramidal symptoms in uremia)
    • Dialysis improves nausea within 24-48 hours

Supportive Care:

  • Nutrition: Protein restriction (0.8-1.0 g/kg/day pre-dialysis, 1.2 g/kg/day on dialysis), low potassium, low phosphorus
  • Phosphate binders with meals (prevent hyperphosphatemia)
  • Treat anemia: ESAs, IV iron
  • Avoid nephrotoxins: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast

Consultations:

  • Nephrology: URGENT - for dialysis initiation, access placement, ongoing management
  • Cardiology: If uremic pericarditis with large effusion or tamponade (may need pericardiocentesis)
  • Vascular Surgery: For AV fistula creation (long-term dialysis access)

Disposition:

  • ICU: Uremic pericarditis with tamponade, severe uremic encephalopathy (GCS <12, seizures), active bleeding from uremia, hemodynamic instability
  • Floor with Telemetry: Uremia requiring dialysis initiation, uremic encephalopathy (mild confusion), stable pericardial effusion
  • Discharge: Only after dialysis initiated, symptoms improved, effusion (if present) stable/resolving, outpatient dialysis arranged (3x/week)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Uremic Pericarditis is an ABSOLUTE Indication for Urgent Dialysis: Unlike viral or idiopathic pericarditis (treated with NSAIDs/colchicine), uremic pericarditis ONLY responds to dialysis. NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated (worsen renal function, ineffective). Uremic pericarditis = fibrinous "bread-and-butter" pericarditis from direct toxic effect of uremic toxins on pericardium. Friction rub is pathognomonic. Can progress to large effusion and tamponade. Dialysis resolves pericarditis in 85-90% of cases over 1-2 weeks. If large effusion or tamponade: consider pericardiocentesis, but still need dialysis as primary treatment.
  • BUN >100 mg/dL is Not Diagnostic of Uremia - Symptoms Define Uremia: Uremic syndrome is clinical diagnosis: presence of uremic symptoms (nausea, encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding, pruritus) in setting of kidney failure. BUN >80-100 mg/dL typically correlates with symptoms, but some patients tolerate BUN >150 mg/dL without symptoms (chronic uremia, gradual rise). Conversely, acute rise to BUN 60-80 mg/dL can cause symptoms (acute uremia). Diagnosis uremia based on symptoms + elevated BUN/Cr, not BUN number alone. Dialysis indicated if symptomatic uremia regardless of exact BUN level.
  • Uremic Frost is Pathognomonic but Extremely Rare: White crystalline deposits on skin from evaporation of sweat with high urea content (urea crystallizes on skin surface). Looks like white powder, typically on face, neck. Only occurs with extreme uremia (BUN >200 mg/dL). Historical curiosity - almost never seen in modern medicine because dialysis initiated before BUN reaches such levels. If you see uremic frost, patient has been severely neglected (missed dialysis x weeks-months). Immediately initiate dialysis.
  • Asterixis is Not Specific to Hepatic Encephalopathy - Also Seen in Uremic Encephalopathy: Asterixis = "flapping tremor," best elicited by having patient extend arms/wrists with fingers spread (like "stop" sign), observe for irregular lapses in wrist extension. Results from disruption of diencephalic-brain stem pathways controlling postural tone. Seen in any metabolic encephalopathy: hepatic, uremic, hypercapnia, drug toxicity. Not specific but helpful clinical sign. In uremic encephalopathy, asterixis indicates moderate-severe uremia - need urgent dialysis.
  • Uremic Platelet Dysfunction Causes Prolonged Bleeding Time Despite Normal Platelet Count and PT/INR/PTT: Uremia causes qualitative platelet defect (impaired adhesion/aggregation from uremic toxins interfering with vWF-platelet binding), not quantitative defect. CBC shows normal platelet count. PT/INR/PTT normal (coagulation cascade intact). But bleeding time prolonged (>10 minutes, normal <10 min). Clinically: mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, GI bleeding, menorrhagia), easy bruising. Treatment: dialysis (most effective, but takes days), DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV (rapid onset 1-2 hr, short duration 4-8 hr), cryoprecipitate (10 units IV, more effective than DDAVP).
  • DDAVP vs Cryoprecipitate for Uremic Bleeding: Both improve uremic platelet dysfunction by increasing vWF (platelet adhesion). DDAVP (desmopressin) stimulates endogenous vWF release from endothelial cells - easier to give, onset 1-2 hours, duration 4-8 hours, can repeat q12-24h. Cryoprecipitate provides exogenous vWF + Factor VIII - more effective than DDAVP, onset 1 hour, duration 12-24 hours, but requires blood product. Use DDAVP first-line for mild bleeding; cryoprecipitate for severe/refractory bleeding. Platelet transfusion NOT effective (transfused platelets become dysfunctional in uremic environment).
  • NSAIDs are Absolutely Contraindicated in Uremic Pericarditis: Common error: treating chest pain from uremic pericarditis with NSAIDs (ibuprofen, indomethacin) like viral pericarditis. BAD. NSAIDs worsen renal function (inhibit prostaglandin-mediated renal blood flow), cause further AKI, and are ineffective for uremic pericarditis (doesn't respond to anti-inflammatory drugs). Similarly, colchicine ineffective. Uremic pericarditis is NOT an inflammatory process - it's direct toxic effect of uremic toxins on pericardium. Only treatment: DIALYSIS (clears toxins, resolves pericarditis). Pain control: use opioids (fentanyl, hydromorphone) or acetaminophen, not NSAIDs.
  • Heparin-Free Dialysis is Required if Pericardial Effusion or Bleeding Risk: Standard hemodialysis uses heparin anticoagulation (prevents clotting in dialysis circuit). But if patient has uremic pericarditis with pericardial effusion or active bleeding, heparin worsens bleeding/hemorrhagic pericardial effusion. Use "heparin-free" or "minimal heparin" dialysis: saline flushes of circuit, regional citrate anticoagulation, or frequent circuit changes. Discuss with nephrology before first dialysis session if pericardial effusion on echo. Hemorrhagic pericardial effusion can progress to tamponade.
  • Dialysis Disequilibrium Syndrome is Risk with First Dialysis in Severe Uremia: Rapid reduction in BUN during aggressive first dialysis (BUN drops from 150 to 50 mg/dL in 4 hours) creates osmotic gradient - brain slower to equilibrate than serum, causing cerebral edema. Symptoms during or after dialysis: headache, nausea, confusion, seizures, coma. More common when BUN >150-175 mg/dL, rapid/aggressive dialysis, first dialysis session. Prevention: "gentle" first dialysis (2 hours instead of 4, lower blood flow rate, limit BUN reduction to <40% per session), use higher dialysate sodium. If symptoms develop: slow/stop dialysis, mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg IV, supportive care.
  • Uremic Fetor is Pathognomonic for Uremia: Characteristic ammonia or "fishy" smell to breath. Caused by breakdown of urea in saliva by bacterial urease → ammonia. Described as "urinous" odor. Can smell from across room in severe cases. Highly specific for uremia (BUN >80-100 mg/dL). Also associated with metallic taste, decreased appetite. Resolves with dialysis. If you smell uremic fetor, patient needs dialysis ASAP.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Cardiac tamponade from uremic pericarditis (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg)
  • Large pericardial effusion (>2 cm on echo) with hemodynamic compromise
  • Severe uremic encephalopathy (GCS <12, stupor, coma)
  • Seizures from uremic encephalopathy
  • Active life-threatening bleeding (GI bleed, intracranial hemorrhage) from uremic platelet dysfunction
  • Severe hyperkalemia (K >7.0 mEq/L) or ECG changes from hyperkalemia
  • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
  • Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Dialysis initiated with at least 2-3 sessions completed
  • BUN trending down (goal <80 mg/dL, though may not fully normalize if ESRD)
  • Uremic symptoms resolved: no nausea/vomiting, mental status at baseline, no chest pain
  • If pericardial effusion: stable or decreasing in size, no tamponade physiology
  • Hemodynamically stable (normal BP, HR)
  • Tolerating PO intake without nausea
  • Outpatient dialysis center arranged (3x/week schedule)
  • Dialysis access functional (tunneled catheter or AV fistula/graft)
  • Nephrology follow-up within 1 week
  • Patient/family educated on dialysis schedule, dietary restrictions, medication compliance
  • If uremic pericarditis: cardiology follow-up arranged for repeat echo in 2-4 weeks

109. HYPOCALCEMIA

Tetany • Paresthesias • QT Prolongation • Seizures • Trousseau/Chvostek Signs
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Acute onset of perioral paresthesias, finger/toe tingling, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm (tetany), with positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, QT prolongation on ECG, with low albumin-adjusted or ionized calcium (Practical). Emergency: cardiac, respiratory or significant neurologic symptoms, or albumin-adjusted calcium <7.0 mg/dL (2nd International Workshop 2022); IV calcium at any calcium level for QTc >450 ms (men) or >470 ms (women), laryngospasm, bronchospasm, seizures or tetany, and possibly for albumin-corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL (International Best Practice 2025)

  • Pathophysiology: Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability (calcium normally stabilizes neuronal membranes). Low ionized calcium → spontaneous neuronal depolarization → tetany, paresthesias, seizures. Also impairs cardiac conduction (prolonged QT, torsades risk). Causes: (1) Hypoparathyroidism (post-thyroidectomy, autoimmune, genetic), (2) Vitamin D deficiency, (3) Hypomagnesemia (Mg required for PTH secretion and action), (4) CKD (hyperphosphatemia binds Ca), (5) Acute pancreatitis (fat saponification), (6) Tumor lysis syndrome, (7) Massive transfusion (citrate binds Ca), (8) Drugs (bisphosphonates, denosumab, cinacalcet, foscarnet). Denosumab (Prolia): FDA boxed warning (January 2024) for severe hypocalcemia in advanced CKD, particularly dialysis (FDA)
  • Risk Factors: Post-thyroidectomy/parathyroidectomy surgery, CKD, vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption (Crohn's, celiac), chronic PPI use (impairs Ca absorption), alcoholism (low Mg), loop diuretics (renal Ca wasting), chemotherapy (tumor lysis), critical illness, sepsis, acute pancreatitis
  • Symptoms: Perioral paresthesias (numbness/tingling around mouth), acral paresthesias (fingers, toes), muscle cramps (calves, feet), carpopedal spasm (hand/foot spasms with flexion), laryngospasm (life-threatening - stridor, difficulty breathing), tetany, seizures (generalized tonic-clonic), confusion, irritability, anxiety, palpitations (arrhythmias)
  • Physical Exam: Chvostek Sign: Tap facial nerve anterior to ear → ipsilateral facial muscle twitching (can be positive with normal calcium; Practical). Trousseau Sign: Inflate BP cuff above systolic BP for 3 minutes → carpopedal spasm (hand contracts into flexion with thumb adduction, "obstetrician's hand"; more specific than Chvostek; Practical). Hyperreflexia, prolonged QT on ECG, papilledema (if chronic, increased ICP), cataracts (chronic hypocalcemia), basal ganglia calcifications (chronic), dry skin/brittle nails
  • Variants/Subtypes: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, laryngospasm - EMERGENCY) vs Chronic asymptomatic hypocalcemia (gradually compensated). Hypocalcemia with high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism from vit D deficiency, CKD) vs low PTH (hypoparathyroidism)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Serum Calcium (Total and Ionized):
    • Total Calcium: Below the laboratory reference range; adjust for albumin (Practical)
    • Corrected Calcium: Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 - albumin). Accounts for protein-bound Ca; an estimate only (Practical; same formula as card 34)
    • Ionized Calcium: Preferred when albumin is abnormal or the patient is critically ill; normal range per laboratory, often 1.15-1.35 mmol/L (Practical). Ionized or albumin-adjusted calcium is acceptable for diagnosing hypoparathyroidism (2nd International Workshop 2022). Measures metabolically active (free) calcium, unaffected by albumin. Order ionized Ca if any doubt
  • Phosphate: Elevated in CKD, hypoparathyroidism, tumor lysis. Low in vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption
  • Magnesium: Check ALWAYS in hypocalcemia. Hypomagnesemia (<1.5 mg/dL) impairs PTH secretion and Ca reabsorption. Cannot correct hypocalcemia without correcting hypomagnesemia first
  • Parathyroid Hormone (PTH):
    • PTH Low/Inappropriately Normal: Hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical, autoimmune, genetic), hypomagnesemia
    • Hypoparathyroidism diagnosis: low ionized or albumin-adjusted calcium with undetectable, low or inappropriately normal intact PTH on two occasions at least 2 weeks apart; postsurgical hypoparathyroidism is permanent if it persists >12 months. After total thyroidectomy, PTH >10 pg/mL at 12-24 h makes permanent hypoparathyroidism unlikely (2nd International Workshop 2022)
    • PTH Elevated: Appropriate response to hypocalcemia - indicates secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, CKD, malabsorption
  • 25-Hydroxyvitamin D: Assess vitamin D status. Deficiency <20 ng/mL (Practical). In hypoparathyroidism, keep 25(OH)D in the normal range (2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • 1,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D (Calcitriol): Active form. Low in CKD (kidneys can't activate vit D)
  • Albumin: For corrected calcium calculation
  • BUN/Creatinine: CKD common cause of hypocalcemia
  • Alkaline Phosphatase: Elevated in vitamin D deficiency (bone disease)
  • Lipase: If acute pancreatitis suspected

ECG (CRITICAL):

  • Prolonged QTc: >450 ms (men) or >470 ms (women) warrants IV calcium at any calcium level (International Best Practice 2025). Most important finding; torsades risk is highest above 500 ms (Practical)
  • T wave changes (flattening, inversion)
  • Bradycardia
  • Heart block (rare, severe hypocalcemia)
  • Compare to prior ECGs, calculate QTc (QT corrected for heart rate)

Imaging (if indicated):

  • Head CT (non-contrast): If chronic hypocalcemia, seizures, movement disorder. May show basal ganglia calcifications (Fahr's syndrome), cerebral calcifications
  • Neck Ultrasound/Sestamibi Scan: If hypoparathyroidism, assess for parathyroid glands (absent after surgery vs auto immune destruction)

Diagnostic Algorithm:

  • Step 1: Confirm hypocalcemia (ionized or albumin-adjusted calcium below the reference range; 2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • Step 2: Check Mg (if low, correct Mg first)
  • Step 3: Check PTH
    • If PTH low/normal → Hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical, autoimmune)
    • If PTH elevated → Check 25-OH vit D (low = vit D deficiency), check PO4 (high = CKD), check renal function
  • Step 4: Consider other causes (pancreatitis, tumor lysis, drugs)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

ACUTE SYMPTOMATIC HYPOCALCEMIA - EMERGENCY (IV calcium indications):

  • Cardiac, respiratory or significant neurologic symptoms, or albumin-adjusted calcium <7.0 mg/dL (2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • At any calcium level: QTc >450 ms (men) or >470 ms (women), laryngospasm, bronchospasm, seizures or tetany; also if unable to take oral calcium or with a seizure history. Albumin-corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL (1.9 mmol/L) may also need IV calcium; no universally accepted threshold exists (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Step 1 - IV Calcium (Immediate Treatment):
    • Calcium Gluconate 10%: 1-2 g (90-180 mg elemental calcium) IV over 10-20 minutes with cardiac monitoring (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025), through a secure large-bore IV (International Best Practice 2025). Dilute to 10-50 mg/mL in D5W or NS; do not exceed 200 mg/minute; may repeat every 6 hours (US label)
    • Calcium gluconate is preferred: less soft tissue necrosis than calcium chloride if extravasation occurs. 1 g calcium gluconate = 90 mg elemental calcium; 1 g calcium chloride = 272 mg (International Best Practice 2025)
    • Or Calcium Chloride 10%: 0.5-1 gram (5-10 mL) IV over 10 minutes via CENTRAL line only (scleroses peripheral veins, tissue necrosis if extravasation) (Practical)
    • Onset: 5-10 minutes, Duration: 2-4 hours (Practical)
  • Step 2 - Continuous IV Calcium Infusion (usually follows the bolus):
    • 10 ampules of calcium gluconate (900 mg elemental calcium) in 1 L D5W or NS, titrated to serum calcium: start at 50 mL/h (2nd International Workshop 2022) or 100 mL/h (International Best Practice 2025). Elemental calcium 15 mg/kg over 4-6 h raises serum calcium about 0.5-0.75 mmol/L (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025). Do not add bicarbonate or phosphate to the bag (International Best Practice 2025; US label). Label: start 5.4-21.5 mg/kg/h of calcium gluconate (about 0.5-2 mg/kg/h elemental), diluted to 5.8-10 mg/mL (US label)
    • Start oral calcium and calcitriol 0.25-0.5 mcg twice daily at the same time (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025); continue the infusion until symptoms are controlled and oral therapy is effective
    • Serum calcium every 1-4 h during continuous infusion, every 4-6 h with intermittent doses; renal impairment: start at the lowest dose and check every 4 h (US label). International Best Practice 2025: every 6 h, then daily until stable, preferably ionized calcium if available. Goal: just below the normal range (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025)
    • Infuse via central line if possible (avoid phlebitis) (Practical)
  • Step 3 - Correct Hypomagnesemia (CRITICAL):
    • If Mg <1.5 mg/dL: Magnesium sulfate 1-2 grams IV over 15-60 minutes, then 1-2 grams IV q6h until Mg >2.0 mg/dL
    • Or Magnesium sulfate 4-6 grams in 1000 mL NS at 100-150 mL/hr
    • CANNOT correct hypocalcemia without correcting hypomagnesemia first (Mg required for PTH secretion)
  • Airway Protection (if Laryngospasm):
    • Laryngospasm = vocal cord spasm, stridor, respiratory distress. LIFE-THREATENING
    • Immediate IV calcium gluconate as in Step 1; even when a rapid bolus is required, no faster than 200 mg/minute in adults (1 g over at least 5 minutes) with ECG monitoring (US label)
    • Bag-mask ventilation with 100% O2
    • If refractory: intubation (succinylcholine for paralysis), ICU
  • Seizure Management:
    • IV calcium (corrects underlying cause)
    • If ongoing seizure despite Ca: Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV
    • Avoid phenytoin (can worsen hypocalcemia, decreases Ca absorption)

CHRONIC/ASYMPTOMATIC HYPOCALCEMIA (none of the IV calcium indications above):

  • Oral Calcium Supplementation:
    • Elemental calcium PO in divided doses with meals, titrated to symptoms and serum calcium; no guideline in the library sets a dose outside hypoparathyroidism (Practical). Hypoparathyroidism doses: see below
    • Calcium citrate preferred with PPI use (2nd International Workshop 2022) or achlorhydria (Practical)
  • Vitamin D Supplementation (if deficient):
    • Ergocalciferol (Vitamin D2) 50,000 units PO weekly x 8 weeks (if 25-OH vit D <20 ng/mL) (Practical)
    • Or Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) 1000-2000 units PO daily (maintenance) (Practical)
    • In CKD: Calcitriol (active vit D) 0.25-0.5 mcg PO daily (kidneys can't activate vit D) (Practical)
  • Correct Hypomagnesemia: Magnesium oxide 400 mg PO BID or Magnesium chloride 500 mg PO BID (Practical); aim for normal magnesium (2nd International Workshop 2022)

HYPOPARATHYROIDISM-SPECIFIC TREATMENT:

  • First line: conventional therapy, calcium plus an active vitamin D analog (2nd International Workshop 2022, Rec 6.1, weak)
  • Target: serum calcium in the lower half of the normal range or just below it; avoid hypercalciuria; keep magnesium normal and 25(OH)D in the normal range (2nd International Workshop 2022, 6.2-6.7)
  • Doses: calcium with meals and calcitriol 0.25-3 mcg/day in divided doses (2nd International Workshop 2022, Table 4). After total thyroidectomy with PTH <10 pg/mL: 2-3 g elemental calcium daily plus calcitriol 0.5-1.5 mcg/day; 70-80% recover within a month (2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • Hypercalciuria: thiazide (25-100 mg/day) with a low-sodium diet, monitoring BP, magnesium, potassium and renal function; not with adrenal insufficiency or in pregnancy (2nd International Workshop 2022, 6.8, 7.5, Table 4)
  • PTH replacement if inadequately controlled (symptomatic hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, renal insufficiency, hypercalciuria, or poor quality of life), or if calcium >2 g/day or active vitamin D >2 mcg/day is needed (2nd International Workshop 2022, 6.9-6.10)
  • Palopegteriparatide (Yorvipath): indicated for hypoparathyroidism in adults; not studied for acute post-surgical hypoparathyroidism. Before the first dose: 25(OH)D normal and albumin-corrected calcium ≥7.8 mg/dL. Start 18 mcg SC once daily; adjust by 3 mcg, no more often than every 7 days (increase) or every 3 days (decrease); range 6-30 mcg once daily (US label)
  • Teriparatide (PTH 1-34, approved for osteoporosis) is an off-label alternative if Yorvipath is unavailable (Practical)

Monitoring:

  • Cardiac monitoring during IV calcium bolus and infusion (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025; US label); continuous telemetry if QTc prolonged or symptomatic (Practical)
  • Serum calcium every 1-4 h during continuous IV calcium, every 4-6 h with intermittent doses, every 4 h in renal impairment (US label); every 6 h, then daily until stable, preferably ionized calcium (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Serum Mg q4-6h until >2.0 mg/dL (Practical)
  • ECG q4-8h to monitor QTc (Practical)
  • Oral therapy: check calcium within several days of any significant dose change (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025). Stable hypoparathyroidism: calcium, albumin, phosphorus, magnesium and creatinine/eGFR every 3-12 months by stability (International Best Practice 2025; every 6-12 months in the 2nd International Workshop 2022). Weekly checks for the first month after discharge (Practical)
  • 24-hour urine calcium and creatinine in hypoparathyroidism to detect hypercalciuria, every 6-24 months (International Best Practice 2025)

Cautions:

  • Digoxin or other cardiac glycosides: avoid IV calcium gluconate; if needed, give it slowly in small amounts with close ECG monitoring. Hypercalcemia increases digoxin toxicity, and digoxin may be ineffective during hypocalcemia (US label)
  • Do NOT give IV calcium in same line as bicarbonate or phosphate (precipitates) (US label; International Best Practice 2025)
  • Ceftriaxone: never at the same time through the same line or a Y-site; sequential use with a thorough line flush is allowed in adults (US label)
  • Calcium infusion via peripheral IV can cause phlebitis (use central line if prolonged infusion) (Practical); calcinosis cutis can occur with or without extravasation: stop IV calcium at that site (US label)
  • Calcium chloride MUST go via central line (tissue necrosis if extravasation) (Practical)
  • Rapid IV calcium causes hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias and cardiac arrest: bolus over 10-20 minutes (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025), never faster than 200 mg/minute (US label)
  • Thiazides lower urine calcium and are used for hypercalciuria in hypoparathyroidism; monitor for hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hyponatremia; avoid with adrenal insufficiency and in pregnancy (2nd International Workshop 2022)

Consultations:

  • Endocrinology: All cases of hypoparathyroidism, refractory hypocalcemia, complex cases
  • Nephrology: If CKD-related hypocalcemia

Disposition (Practical; no guideline gives these QTc or ionized calcium cut points):

  • ICU: Symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, laryngospasm), QTc >500 ms, requires continuous IV calcium infusion, hemodynamic instability
  • Floor with Telemetry: Mild symptoms, ionized Ca 0.8-1.0 mmol/L, QTc 480-500 ms, able to take PO, requiring IV calcium boluses (not continuous infusion)
  • Discharge: Asymptomatic, ionized Ca >1.0 mmol/L on oral regimen, Mg corrected, QTc <480 ms, follow-up arranged with endocrinology/PCP within 1 week
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Always Check Ionized Calcium - It's the Metabolically Active Form: Total calcium includes protein-bound and ionized (free) calcium. Only ionized Ca is metabolically active. Hypoalbuminemia (common in hospitalized patients) causes low total Ca but normal ionized Ca - patient is NOT hypocalcemic. Corrected calcium formula estimates ionized Ca but is imperfect. Measure ionized calcium directly when albumin is abnormal, the patient is critically ill, or total calcium is borderline (Practical). Hypoparathyroidism can be diagnosed on ionized or albumin-adjusted calcium (2nd International Workshop 2022).
  • Cannot Correct Hypocalcemia Without Correcting Hypomagnesemia First: Magnesium is required for PTH secretion from parathyroid glands AND for PTH action on target tissues (bone, kidney). If Mg low, PTH secretion impaired → hypocalcemia worsens. Also, low Mg directly impairs renal calcium reabsorption. Clinically: patient with hypocalcemia gets IV calcium, Ca normalizes transiently, then drops again hours later - check Mg. If Mg <1.5 mg/dL, replete magnesium as in Step 3 and recheck (Practical); keep magnesium normal (2nd International Workshop 2022). Only after Mg corrected will calcium stay normal. Hypomagnesemia common in alcoholics, diuretic use, diarrhea, PPI use.
  • Trousseau Sign is More Specific Than Chvostek Sign for Hypocalcemia: Chvostek sign (tap facial nerve → facial twitching) can be positive in people with normal calcium (Practical). Trousseau sign (inflate BP cuff above systolic BP x 3 minutes → carpopedal spasm/"obstetrician's hand") is more specific (Practical). If Trousseau positive, hypocalcemia highly likely. Mechanism: ischemia from BP cuff + hypocalcemia → increased neuromuscular excitability → tetany. Trousseau takes 3 minutes to elicit (be patient), Chvostek is instant. Do Trousseau if suspecting hypocalcemia.
  • Rapid IV Calcium Causes Bradycardia and Cardiac Arrest - Always Give It SLOWLY: Bolus over 10-20 minutes with cardiac monitoring (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025). Even when a rapid bolus is required (laryngospasm, seizures, torsades), calcium gluconate must not exceed 200 mg/minute in adults, about 5 minutes per gram, with ECG monitoring; rapid injection can cause vasodilation, hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, syncope and cardiac arrest (US label). If heart rate drops, slow or stop the infusion (Practical). On digoxin: avoid IV calcium if possible; if needed, give it slowly in small amounts with close ECG monitoring (US label).
  • Calcium Chloride vs Calcium Gluconate - Know the Difference: Calcium gluconate 10%: 1 g = 90-93 mg elemental calcium (10 mL vial) (International Best Practice 2025; US label); preferred because extravasation causes less soft tissue necrosis than calcium chloride (International Best Practice 2025). Give it through a secure IV line; calcinosis cutis can occur even without extravasation (US label). Calcium chloride 10%: 1 g = 272 mg elemental calcium, about 3x more per gram (International Best Practice 2025); give it via a central line and never push it peripherally (Practical).
  • Prolonged QT from Hypocalcemia Increases Torsades Risk - Monitor ECG Closely: Hypocalcemia prolongs phase 2 of cardiac action potential (plateau phase) → prolonged QT interval (QTc >500 ms = high risk, Practical). Torsades de pointes can occur. Check ECG on all hypocalcemia patients. Calculate QTc (QT corrected for HR). If QTc >500 ms: continuous telemetry, IV calcium immediately, avoid other QT-prolonging drugs (antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, ondansetron). Monitor QTc after calcium repletion - should shorten as Ca normalizes. Hypocalcemia is correctable cause of torsades (unlike congenital long QT syndrome).
  • Post-Thyroidectomy Hypocalcemia: Inadvertent parathyroid injury or removal during thyroidectomy causes hypoparathyroidism; symptoms typically appear 24-72 hours after surgery (Practical). Check PTH 12-24 h after total thyroidectomy: >10 pg/mL makes permanent hypoparathyroidism unlikely. If PTH <10 pg/mL, start 2-3 g elemental calcium daily plus calcitriol 0.5-1.5 mcg/day; 70-80% recover within a month, and hypoparathyroidism persisting >12 months is permanent (2nd International Workshop 2022).
  • Vitamin D Deficiency Causes Hypocalcemia With High PTH (Practical): Vitamin D deficiency (25-OH vit D <20 ng/mL). Causes: inadequate sun exposure, dark skin (melanin blocks UVB), obesity (vit D sequestered in fat), malabsorption, CKD, elderly. Low vit D → decreased intestinal Ca absorption → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH elevated trying to compensate). Labs: low Ca, low vit D, elevated PTH, low/normal PO4. Treatment: Ergocalciferol 50,000 units weekly x 8 weeks, then maintenance 1000-2000 units daily. Plus oral calcium. Check 25-OH vit D in hypocalcemia.
  • Tumor Lysis Syndrome Causes Hypocalcemia via Hyperphosphatemia: Rapid tumor cell lysis (chemotherapy for hematologic malignancies) → massive release of intracellular contents → hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia. Mechanism of hypocalcemia: High phosphate binds calcium → calcium-phosphate precipitates in tissues → hypocalcemia worsens. Also, high phosphate suppresses 1,25-vit D production. Labs: low Ca, very high PO4 (>6-8 mg/dL), high K, high uric acid, elevated LDH. Treatment: aggressive IV fluids, allopurinol/rasburicase (prevent uric acid nephropathy), correct electrolytes, dialysis if severe. Do NOT give calcium if PO4 very high (>6.5 mg/dL) - worsens tissue calcium-phosphate deposition, unless life-threatening hypocalcemia.
  • Hungry Bone Syndrome After Parathyroidectomy for Hyperparathyroidism: Patient with chronic primary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH, high Ca, bone resorption for years) undergoes parathyroidectomy → PTH suddenly drops → bone aggressively takes up calcium to remineralize ("hungry bones") → severe hypocalcemia. More likely if pre-op Ca >12 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase (bone turnover), or vitamin D deficiency. Postoperative days 1-7: Ca can drop to 6-7 mg/dL, requires large doses of IV then oral calcium with calcitriol, titrated to serum calcium, for weeks to months; no guideline in the library gives doses (Practical). Monitor Ca closely post-parathyroidectomy.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Laryngospasm (stridor, respiratory distress) - airway emergency
  • Seizures from hypocalcemia
  • Tetany refractory to IV calcium boluses (requires continuous calcium infusion)
  • QTc >500 ms (high risk of torsades de pointes) (Practical)
  • Hemodynamically significant arrhythmias (bradycardia, torsades)
  • Ionized calcium <0.8 mmol/L with symptoms
  • Requiring continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium infusion
  • Heart block from severe hypocalcemia
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Calcium stable on the oral regimen (practical floor: ionized >1.0 mmol/L or albumin-corrected >8.0 mg/dL); in hypoparathyroidism, lower half of the normal range or just below (2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • Asymptomatic (no paresthesias, tetany, muscle cramps)
  • Tolerating oral calcium and vitamin D supplementation
  • Magnesium normal (2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • QTc normalized (<480 ms, Practical)
  • No seizures or arrhythmias
  • Patient educated on oral calcium regimen (timing, dosing, take with food)
  • Follow-up arranged with endocrinology (if hypoparathyroidism) or PCP within 1 week
  • Recheck Ca, Mg, and PTH scheduled for 1 week
  • If post-thyroidectomy: surgical team aware, monitoring calcium closely
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Calcium Gluconate/Chloride, 💊 Magnesium, 💊 Denosumab, 💊 Teriparatide

110. HYPERMAGNESEMIA / HYPOMAGNESEMIA

Muscle Weakness • Arrhythmias • Tetany • Deep Tendon Reflex Changes
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

HYPOMAGNESEMIA (Mg <1.5 mg/dL): Muscle cramps, tremor, tetany, cardiac arrhythmias (especially torsades de pointes), concurrent hypocalcemia/hypokalemia that's refractory to replacement, seizures, and hyperreflexia.

HYPERMAGNESEMIA (Mg >2.5 mg/dL): Muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, lethargy, bradycardia, hypotension, respiratory depression (Mg >5-6 mg/dL), cardiac arrest (Mg >12-15 mg/dL).

  • Pathophysiology: Hypomagnesemia: Impairs PTH secretion → hypocalcemia. Increases renal potassium wasting → hypokalemia. Destabilizes cardiac membranes → arrhythmias (prolonged QT, torsades). Causes: GI losses (diarrhea, malabsorption, PPI use), renal losses (diuretics, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin), alcoholism (most common), DKA, hungry bone syndrome. Hypermagnesemia: Excess Mg antagonizes calcium channels → neuromuscular blockade, cardiac conduction delays. Usually iatrogenic (Mg infusions, laxatives/antacids in CKD) or renal failure (inability to excrete Mg). Severe hypermagnesemia (>12-15 mg/dL) causes cardiac arrest (asystole)
  • Risk Factors - HYPOMAGNESEMIA: Chronic diarrhea, Crohn's disease, celiac disease, chronic PPI use (decreases Mg absorption), alcoholism (decreased intake + increased losses), loop/thiazide diuretics, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, foscarnet, DKA (osmotic diuresis), post-parathyroidectomy (hungry bone syndrome)
  • Risk Factors - HYPERMAGNESEMIA: CKD/ESRD (GFR <30 mL/min), excessive Mg administration (IV Mg for eclampsia/tocolysis, Mg-containing laxatives, antacids), rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis syndrome, Addison's disease
  • Symptoms - HYPOMAGNESEMIA: Muscle cramps (calves, feet), fasciculations, tremor, tetany, paresthesias, weakness, palpitations, nausea, seizures (if severe), personality changes
  • Symptoms - HYPERMAGNESEMIA: Nausea, vomiting (Mg 3-5 mg/dL), flushing, warmth (vasodilation), muscle weakness, lethargy, confusion (Mg 5-7 mg/dL), respiratory depression (Mg >7-10 mg/dL), coma (Mg >10-12 mg/dL)
  • Physical Exam - HYPOMAGNESEMIA: Hyperreflexia, positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs (if concurrent hypocalcemia), tachycardia, arrhythmias
  • Physical Exam - HYPERMAGNESEMIA: Hyporeflexia (DTRs lost at Mg 4-6 mg/dL), bradycardia (Mg >5 mg/dL), hypotension, respiratory depression (decreased respiratory rate, shallow breathing at Mg >7 mg/dL), cardiac arrest (Mg >12-15 mg/dL)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Serum Magnesium: Normal 1.5-2.5 mg/dL (1.25-2.1 mEq/L or 0.6-1.0 mmol/L)
    • Hypomagnesemia: <1.5 mg/dL. Severe <1.0 mg/dL
    • Hypermagnesemia: >2.5 mg/dL. Moderate 2.5-5 mg/dL, Severe >5 mg/dL, Critical >7-10 mg/dL
  • Calcium (total and ionized): Check always with Mg abnormalities. Hypomagnesemia causes hypocalcemia (impaired PTH secretion). Mg and Ca often abnormal together
  • Potassium: Hypomagnesemia causes hypokalemia (renal K wasting). Check and correct
  • Phosphate: May be low in malnutrition/alcoholism (same causes as hypomagnesemia)
  • Basic Metabolic Panel: BUN/Cr (assess renal function - hypermagnesemia common in CKD)
  • ECG:
    • Hypomagnesemia: Prolonged QT interval (risk of torsades de pointes), T wave flattening, U waves, atrial/ventricular arrhythmias
    • Hypermagnesemia: Prolonged PR interval (Mg >5 mg/dL), widened QRS (Mg >7 mg/dL), heart block, bradycardia, asystole (Mg >12-15 mg/dL)
  • 24-Hour Urine Magnesium (if hypomagnesemia etiology unclear): Distinguish renal vs GI losses
    • Urine Mg >24 mg/24hr (or fractional excretion >2%) with hypomagnesemia = Renal wasting (diuretics, drugs)
    • Urine Mg <12 mg/24hr = Appropriate renal conservation, GI losses (diarrhea, malabsorption)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

HYPOMAGNESEMIA TREATMENT:

Severe Symptomatic Hypomagnesemia (Mg <1.0 mg/dL, Seizures, Arrhythmias):

  • IV Magnesium Sulfate:
    • Loading dose: 2-4 grams (16-32 mEq) IV over 15-60 minutes (slower if not life-threatening)
    • Maintenance: 1-2 grams IV q6h or continuous infusion 1-2 grams/hr until Mg >1.5 mg/dL
    • Alternative: 6 grams (48 mEq) in 1000 mL NS at 100-150 mL/hr over 6-8 hours
    • Monitor: DTRs q2h (if lost, stop infusion - hypermagnesemia), Mg q6-12h
  • Torsades de Pointes from Hypomagnesemia: Magnesium sulfate 2 grams IV push over 2-5 minutes, can repeat x1. Then continuous infusion

Mild-Moderate Hypomagnesemia (Mg 1.0-1.5 mg/dL, Symptomatic):

  • Oral Magnesium (if able to tolerate PO):
    • Magnesium oxide 400-800 mg PO BID-TID (poorly absorbed, causes diarrhea)
    • Or Magnesium chloride 500 mg PO BID (better absorbed)
    • Or Magnesium gluconate 500 mg PO TID
    • Or Magnesium citrate 300 mg PO BID (good absorption)
    • Total elemental Mg 300-600 mg/day divided doses
  • IV Magnesium (if NPO or severe GI losses): 1-2 grams IV q6-12h

Concurrent Electrolyte Correction (CRITICAL):

  • Hypocalcemia: Correct Mg FIRST before giving calcium (hypocalcemia won't correct without Mg)
  • Hypokalemia: Correct Mg FIRST (hypokalemia won't correct without Mg, renal K wasting continues). Then give potassium
  • Check Ca, K, Mg together; replace Mg first, then Ca/K

HYPERMAGNESEMIA TREATMENT:

Immediate Management:

  • STOP all Mg sources (IV Mg, laxatives, antacids)
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring
  • IV access, assess airway/breathing

Severe Life-Threatening Hypermagnesemia (Mg >7-10 mg/dL, Respiratory Depression, Cardiac Toxicity):

  • Calcium Gluconate (Immediate Antagonist):
    • Calcium gluconate 10% 1-2 grams (10-20 mL) IV over 5-10 minutes
    • Directly antagonizes Mg effects on neuromuscular junction and cardiac conduction
    • Does NOT lower Mg level, just reverses toxicity temporarily (30-60 minutes)
    • Can repeat q1h as needed while arranging definitive treatment
  • HEMODIALYSIS (Definitive Treatment):
    • MOST EFFECTIVE for severe hypermagnesemia
    • Rapidly removes Mg (can lower Mg by 50% in 3-4 hours)
    • Indications: Mg >7-10 mg/dL with symptoms, Mg >4-5 mg/dL in anuric patient, respiratory depression, cardiac toxicity
    • URGENT Nephrology consult
  • Supportive Care:
    • Respiratory support: Supplemental O2, BiPAP, intubation if respiratory failure (Mg >10 mg/dL)
    • Cardiac support: Atropine for bradycardia, pacing if high-grade AV block, pressors if hypotensive

Moderate Hypermagnesemia (Mg 2.5-5 mg/dL, Asymptomatic or Mild Symptoms):

  • IV Fluids + Diuresis (if normal renal function):
    • Normal saline 1-2 L bolus, then 150-250 mL/hr
    • PLUS Furosemide 40-80 mg IV q6-8h (promotes renal Mg excretion)
    • Monitor Mg q4-6h, goal Mg <2.5 mg/dL
    • Replace calcium/potassium losses from diuresis
  • If Renal Failure: Dialysis required (kidneys can't excrete Mg)

Monitoring:

  • Hypomagnesemia: Recheck Mg q6-12h during repletion. Check DTRs q2h during IV Mg infusion (loss of DTRs = stop infusion, hypermagnesemia developing). Check concurrent Ca, K levels
  • Hypermagnesemia: Continuous telemetry if Mg >5 mg/dL. Recheck Mg q2-4h. Monitor respiratory rate, DTRs, level of consciousness. ECG q4-6h to assess conduction

Disposition:

  • ICU: Severe hypomagnesemia with torsades, seizures; Severe hypermagnesemia (Mg >5-7 mg/dL) with respiratory depression, cardiac toxicity, requiring dialysis
  • Floor with Telemetry: Symptomatic hypomagnesemia requiring IV Mg, moderate hypermagnesemia (Mg 4-5 mg/dL)
  • Discharge: Asymptomatic or mild symptoms, Mg normalized, able to take oral Mg (if hypomagnesemia), underlying cause addressed
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Hypomagnesemia is Extremely Common but Often Missed (10-20% of Hospitalized Patients): Rarely checked unless specifically ordered. Causes refractory hypocalcemia, refractory hypokalemia. If patient has hypocalcemia or hypokalemia that won't correct despite aggressive replacement, CHECK MAGNESIUM. Hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion (hypocalcemia) and increases renal K wasting (hypokalemia). Cannot correct Ca or K without correcting Mg first. Clinical pearl: If giving IV calcium or potassium and levels won't stay up, think hypomagnesemia.
  • Loss of Deep Tendon Reflexes Indicates Mg >5-6 mg/dL - Stop Magnesium Immediately: DTRs are best clinical monitor for Mg toxicity. As Mg rises: Normal reflexes (Mg <4) → Hyporeflexia (Mg 4-5) → Loss of DTRs (Mg 5-6) → Respiratory depression (Mg 7-10) → Cardiac arrest (Mg >12-15). When giving IV Mg infusion, check patellar reflex (knee jerk) q2h. If reflex lost, STOP Mg infusion immediately (hypermagnesemia developing). DTRs lost BEFORE respiratory depression, so provides early warning. Bedside clinical sign that prevents iatrogenic hypermagnesemia during Mg repletion for eclampsia/pre-eclampsia.
  • Calcium is Immediate Antidote for Severe Hypermagnesemia: Calcium directly antagonizes Mg effects on neuromuscular junction and cardiac conduction. Give calcium gluconate 1-2 grams IV over 5-10 minutes if Mg >7 mg/dL with respiratory depression, bradycardia, heart block. Effect is immediate (within minutes) but temporary (30-60 minutes). Buys time while arranging dialysis (definitive treatment). Can repeat calcium q1h as needed. Mechanism: Calcium and Mg compete for same channels; calcium reverses Mg-induced neuromuscular blockade and cardiac conduction delays.
  • Chronic PPI Use is a Common Cause of Hypomagnesemia: PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole) decrease intestinal Mg absorption (mechanism unclear, possibly involving TRPM6/7 channels). FDA warning in 2011 - chronic PPI use (>1 year) causes hypomagnesemia in 5-10% of users. Presents as muscle cramps, arrhythmias, concurrent hypocalcemia. If patient on chronic PPI with unexplained hypomagnesemia, try stopping PPI (switch to H2 blocker like famotidine) or increase oral Mg supplementation. Check Mg levels in all patients on chronic PPI who present with arrhythmias or tetany.
  • Loop Diuretics Cause Magnesium Wasting - Thiazides Spare Magnesium: Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) inhibit Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in thick ascending limb → increased Mg excretion → hypomagnesemia (also causes hypokalemia, hypocalcemia). Chronic loop diuretic use in CHF patients commonly causes hypomagnesemia. Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) have less effect on Mg (primarily cause hypokalemia, hypercalcemia). If patient on chronic loops with hypomagnesemia, consider switching to thiazide or add Mg supplementation. Also consider K-sparing diuretic (spironolactone, amiloride) which reduces K wasting.
  • Torsades de Pointes from Hypomagnesemia - Give Magnesium Immediately Even if QT Not Prolonged: Hypomagnesemia prolongs QT interval (like hypocalcemia, hypokalemia) → torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT with "twisting" QRS). If patient with hypomagnesemia develops torsades: Give magnesium sulfate 2 grams IV push over 2-5 minutes, can repeat x1, then continuous infusion 1-2 grams/hr. Magnesium is treatment of choice for torsades even if Mg level normal (stabilizes cardiac membranes). Magnesium shortens QT interval, suppresses early afterdepolarizations that trigger torsades. Also defibrillate if hemodynamically unstable.
  • Alcoholism is Most Common Cause of Hypomagnesemia: Chronic alcoholism causes hypomagnesemia via: (1) Decreased intake (poor nutrition), (2) Increased GI losses (diarrhea, vomiting), (3) Increased renal losses (alcohol directly increases urinary Mg excretion, secondary hyperaldosteronism), (4) Impaired intestinal Mg absorption. Alcoholics presenting with DTs, seizures, arrhythmias often have hypomagnesemia + hypocalcemia + hypokalemia + hypophosphatemia (refeeding syndrome if malnourished). Check and repletes all four electrolytes. Magnesium repletion may reduce alcohol withdrawal symptoms, seizure risk. Give thiamine (prevent Wernicke's), folate, multivitamin as well.
  • Aminoglycosides and Cisplatin Cause Renal Magnesium Wasting: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin) and cisplatin chemotherapy damage renal tubules → urinary Mg wasting persists for weeks-months after drug stopped. Up to 50% of cisplatin patients develop hypomagnesemia. If patient on aminoglycosides/cisplatin develops muscle cramps, arrhythmias, check Mg (and Ca, K). May need aggressive oral Mg supplementation 400-800 mg/day. Hypomagnesemia can persist for months after cisplatin, requiring long-term supplementation. Also, amphotericin B, foscarnet, pentamidine cause renal Mg wasting.
  • Hypermagnesemia Almost Always Iatrogenic or Renal Failure: Healthy kidneys excrete excess Mg efficiently, so hypermagnesemia rare unless: (1) Excessive administration (IV Mg for eclampsia/tocolysis, Mg-containing laxatives/antacids in elderly), (2) CKD/ESRD (GFR <30, can't excrete Mg), (3) Rhabdomyolysis/tumor lysis (cellular release), (4) Addison's disease (rare). Most common scenario: Elderly patient with CKD taking Mg-containing laxatives (Milk of Magnesia) or antacids daily → progressive hypermagnesemia over weeks. Always ask about laxative/antacid use in hypermagnesemia. Stop Mg sources, dialyze if severe.
  • Pregnant Women with Eclampsia Receiving IV Magnesium Need Close Monitoring: Magnesium sulfate is first-line for eclampsia seizure prophylaxis and treatment. Loading dose 4-6 grams IV over 15-20 minutes, then maintenance 1-2 grams/hr. Therapeutic range 4-6 mg/dL (prevents seizures). Risk of hypermagnesemia toxicity: Loss of DTRs (5-6 mg/dL), respiratory depression (7-10 mg/dL), cardiac arrest (>12-15 mg/dL). Monitor: DTRs q2h (if lost, stop Mg), respiratory rate q1h (if <12/min, stop Mg), Mg level q4-6h. Antidote: Calcium gluconate 1 gram IV push. Toxicity more common if renal insufficiency (pre-eclampsia can cause AKI). Mg infusion requires ICU/L&D with close monitoring.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hypomagnesemia: Torsades de pointes, refractory ventricular arrhythmias, seizures
  • Hypermagnesemia: Mg >7-10 mg/dL, respiratory depression/failure (RR <10, hypoxia), cardiac toxicity (bradycardia <40, heart block, hypotension), loss of deep tendon reflexes (Mg >5-6 mg/dL), altered mental status/coma, requiring urgent dialysis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Magnesium normalized (1.5-2.5 mg/dL) and stable
  • Concurrent electrolyte abnormalities corrected (Ca, K normalized)
  • Asymptomatic (no arrhythmias, tetany, muscle weakness)
  • If hypomagnesemia: on oral Mg supplementation, underlying cause addressed (stop PPI if possible, diuretic adjusted)
  • If hypermagnesemia: Mg sources stopped (laxatives, antacids discontinued)
  • Normal ECG (QT normalized if hypomagnesemia, conduction normalized if hypermagnesemia)
  • Deep tendon reflexes normal
  • Follow-up arranged to recheck Mg in 1 week

111. HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA / HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA

Muscle Weakness • Rhabdomyolysis • Hemolysis • Cardiac Dysfunction • Tissue Calcification
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA (PO4 <2.5 mg/dL): Progressive muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure, hemolytic anemia, altered mental status, typically developing over hours-days with severe depletion (PO4 <1.0 mg/dL).

HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA (PO4 >4.5 mg/dL): Often asymptomatic acutely, but causes secondary hypocalcemia (PO4 binds Ca), metastatic calcification (soft tissue, vascular), and long-term complications (CKD-mineral bone disease).

  • Pathophysiology: Hypophosphatemia: Phosphate essential for ATP production. Severe depletion (PO4 <1.0 mg/dL) causes cellular energy crisis → muscle dysfunction (weakness, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure from diaphragm weakness), RBC dysfunction (hemolysis, decreased 2,3-DPG → left-shifted O2 curve), WBC/platelet dysfunction. Causes: Refeeding syndrome (most dangerous), DKA treatment (insulin shifts PO4 into cells), alcoholism, chronic diarrhea, vitamin D deficiency, antacids. Hyperphosphatemia: Excess PO4 binds calcium → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism → bone disease. Also causes metastatic calcification (calcium-phosphate precipitates in vessels, soft tissue, organs). Causes: CKD (most common - kidneys can't excrete PO4), tumor lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis (cellular release)
  • Risk Factors - HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA: Refeeding syndrome (malnourished patient restarted nutrition), DKA (insulin treatment shifts PO4 intracellularly), chronic alcoholism, vitamin D deficiency, chronic antacid use (aluminum/magnesium antacids bind PO4), chronic diarrhea, burns, sepsis, respiratory alkalosis (shifts PO4 into cells)
  • Risk Factors - HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA: CKD Stage 4-5 (GFR <30 mL/min), ESRD on dialysis, tumor lysis syndrome (chemotherapy for hematologic malignancies), rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hypoparathyroidism, excessive vitamin D supplementation, phosphate-containing enemas/laxatives
  • Symptoms - HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA: Mild (PO4 2.0-2.5 mg/dL): Asymptomatic. Moderate (PO4 1.0-2.0 mg/dL): Muscle weakness, myalgias. Severe (PO4 <1.0 mg/dL): Progressive generalized weakness, rhabdomyolysis (myoglobinuria, elevated CK), respiratory failure (diaphragm weakness), confusion, seizures, coma, hemolytic anemia, ileus
  • Symptoms - HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA: Usually asymptomatic acutely. Symptoms of hypocalcemia if PO4 very high (tetany, paresthesias). Chronic: pruritus, bone pain (CKD-MBD), soft tissue calcification (vascular calcification increases CV mortality)
  • Physical Exam - HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA: Muscle weakness (proximal > distal, difficulty standing from chair), hyporeflexia, confusion/delirium, tachypnea (compensating for weakness), rhabdomyolysis (muscle tenderness, dark urine)
  • Physical Exam - HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA: Usually normal. If severe hypocalcemia: Chvostek/Trousseau signs, tetany. Chronic: soft tissue calcifications (palpable), band keratopathy (corneal calcium deposits), calciphylaxis (painful skin lesions, ulcers - rare, in ESRD)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Serum Phosphate: Normal 2.5-4.5 mg/dL
    • Hypophosphatemia: <2.5 mg/dL. Mild 2.0-2.5, Moderate 1.0-2.0, Severe <1.0 mg/dL
    • Hyperphosphatemia: >4.5 mg/dL. Moderate 4.5-6.0, Severe >6.0 mg/dL
  • Calcium (total and ionized): Hyperphosphatemia causes hypocalcemia (PO4 binds Ca). Check together. If hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia: DO NOT give calcium if PO4 >6.5 mg/dL (worsens tissue calcium-phosphate deposition)
  • Magnesium: Hypomagnesemia often coexists with hypophosphatemia (same causes: alcoholism, malnutrition, refeeding)
  • Potassium: Check with phosphate disorders (often abnormal together in DKA, refeeding, tumor lysis)
  • BUN/Creatinine: CKD most common cause of hyperphosphatemia. AKI can cause both hyper- and hypophosphatemia
  • Creatine Kinase (CK): Elevated if rhabdomyolysis (from severe hypophosphatemia or cause of hyperphosphatemia)
  • PTH: Elevated in secondary hyperparathyroidism (response to hyperphosphatemia in CKD). Low in hypoparathyroidism (causes hyperphosphatemia)
  • 25-Hydroxyvitamin D: Deficiency causes hypophosphatemia (decreased intestinal PO4 absorption)
  • LDH, Uric Acid, Potassium: If tumor lysis syndrome suspected (elevated in TLS)
  • Urinalysis: Myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis from severe hypophosphatemia)
  • 24-Hour Urine Phosphate (if etiology unclear): Assess renal PO4 handling
    • FePO4 (Fractional Excretion of Phosphate) = (Urine PO4 × Serum Cr) / (Serum PO4 × Urine Cr) × 100
    • FePO4 >5% with hypophosphatemia = Renal phosphate wasting
    • FePO4 <5% = Appropriate renal conservation, extrarenal losses

Additional Testing Based on Suspected Etiology:

  • Hypophosphatemia: Glucose (DKA), ABG (respiratory alkalosis), nutritional history (refeeding risk), alcohol use history
  • Hyperphosphatemia: Renal function, tumor lysis labs (LDH, uric acid, K, Ca), recent chemotherapy history
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA TREATMENT:

Severe Symptomatic Hypophosphatemia (PO4 <1.0 mg/dL, Weakness, Rhabdomyolysis, Respiratory Failure):

  • IV Sodium Phosphate or Potassium Phosphate:
    • Dose: 0.08-0.16 mmol/kg (typically 15-30 mmol) IV over 6 hours
    • Sodium phosphate preferred if hyperkalemia; potassium phosphate if hypokalemia
    • Max rate: 7 mmol/hr (faster causes hypocalcemia, hypotension)
    • Can repeat dose q6-12h based on recheck PO4 levels
    • Monitor PO4 q6-8h during repletion
    • CAUTION: IV phosphate can cause severe hypocalcemia, hypotension, tissue calcification if given too rapidly. Always give slowly
  • Monitoring:
    • Check calcium (ionized Ca) before and during IV phosphate (risk of hypocalcemia)
    • Check magnesium, potassium (replace concurrently)
    • Monitor respiratory status (if ventilated from diaphragm weakness, may wean after PO4 corrected)
    • Monitor CK if rhabdomyolysis (should trend down as PO4 corrects)

Moderate Hypophosphatemia (PO4 1.0-2.0 mg/dL, Mild Symptoms or High-Risk Patients):

  • Oral Phosphate (Preferred if GI Tract Functional):
    • Sodium/potassium phosphate (Neutra-Phos, K-Phos) 500 mg (16 mmol) PO TID-QID
    • Or Sodium phosphate/potassium phosphate packets: 1-2 packets PO TID
    • Total daily dose: 50-80 mmol/day divided
    • Side effect: Diarrhea (dose-limiting). Start lower dose, titrate up
  • IV Phosphate (if NPO or severe GI dysfunction): 15-30 mmol IV over 6 hours, repeat as needed

Mild Asymptomatic Hypophosphatemia (PO4 2.0-2.5 mg/dL):

  • Dietary Supplementation: High-phosphate foods (dairy, meats, nuts, legumes, whole grains)
  • Oral Phosphate: 500 mg PO BID-TID if dietary insufficient
  • Address underlying cause (stop antacids, treat vitamin D deficiency, optimize nutrition)

REFEEDING SYNDROME PREVENTION (HIGH-RISK PATIENTS):

  • Risk Factors: Chronic malnutrition, alcoholism, anorexia nervosa, prolonged fasting, marasmus, chronic illness
  • Prevention Strategy:
    • Check baseline PO4, K, Mg, glucose before refeeding
    • Start nutrition slowly: 20-25 kcal/kg/day (50% of estimated needs), increase gradually over 4-7 days
    • Supplement thiamine 200-300 mg IV daily x 3 days (prevent Wernicke's), then 100 mg PO daily
    • Prophylactic supplementation: Phosphate 500 mg PO TID, Potassium 40 mEq PO BID, Magnesium 400 mg PO BID
    • Monitor electrolytes daily x 7 days (PO4, K, Mg, Ca)
    • If PO4 drops <2.0 mg/dL: slow/stop nutrition, give IV phosphate

HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA TREATMENT:

Immediate Management:

  • Identify and treat underlying cause (CKD, tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis)
  • Stop phosphate sources (phosphate-containing laxatives/enemas, vitamin D supplements)
  • Check calcium (expect hypocalcemia). If symptomatic hypocalcemia: hold IV calcium if PO4 >6.5 mg/dL (worsens tissue calcification)

Acute Severe Hyperphosphatemia (PO4 >6-7 mg/dL or Tumor Lysis Syndrome):

  • IV Fluids: NS 150-250 mL/hr (promote renal PO4 excretion, dilute serum PO4)
  • Dialysis: If severe (PO4 >10 mg/dL), symptomatic hypocalcemia, renal failure, tumor lysis syndrome. Hemodialysis removes PO4 rapidly
  • Phosphate Binders (limited role acutely): Sevelamer 800 mg PO TID with meals, or Calcium acetate 667 mg PO TID with meals. Effect delayed (binds dietary PO4 in gut)

Chronic Hyperphosphatemia (CKD Patients):

  • Dietary Phosphate Restriction: <800-1000 mg/day (avoid dairy, processed foods, cola, nuts)
  • Phosphate Binders (First-Line):
    • Sevelamer (Renagel, Renvela): 800-1600 mg PO TID with meals. Non-calcium-based, doesn't worsen vascular calcification
    • Calcium Acetate (PhosLo): 667-1334 mg PO TID with meals. Cheaper, but risk of hypercalcemia, vascular calcification
    • Lanthanum Carbonate: 500-1000 mg PO TID with meals. Alternative if sevelamer not tolerated
    • Aluminum Hydroxide: 300-600 mg PO TID with meals. Effective but risk of aluminum toxicity (encephalopathy, bone disease). Use short-term only (<4 weeks)
    • Take with meals (binds dietary PO4)
  • Dialysis: 3x/week HD removes PO4, maintains PO4 4.5-5.5 mg/dL
  • Goal: PO4 3.5-5.5 mg/dL in CKD (KDIGO guidelines)

Monitoring:

  • Hypophosphatemia: Recheck PO4 q6-12h during IV repletion, daily once on oral. Monitor concurrent Ca, Mg, K
  • Hyperphosphatemia: Recheck PO4 q12-24h acutely, then weekly-monthly in chronic CKD. Monitor calcium, PTH, vitamin D

Disposition:

  • ICU: Severe hypophosphatemia (PO4 <1.0 mg/dL) with respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis; Severe hyperphosphatemia (PO4 >10 mg/dL) with symptomatic hypocalcemia, tumor lysis requiring dialysis
  • Floor: Moderate hypophosphatemia requiring IV repletion, moderate hyperphosphatemia (PO4 5-7 mg/dL) in CKD
  • Discharge: Phosphate corrected or stable on oral regimen, asymptomatic, follow-up arranged
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Refeeding Syndrome is a Lethal Complication of Restarting Nutrition in Malnourished Patients: Chronic starvation depletes total body PO4, K, Mg (though serum levels may be normal). When nutrition restarted, insulin surges → glucose + PO4/K/Mg shift intracellularly → severe hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia within 24-72 hours. Can cause respiratory failure (diaphragm weakness), cardiac arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, death. High risk: anorexia nervosa, chronic alcoholism, marasmus, prolonged fasting, very low BMI (<16 kg/m²). Prevention: Start nutrition slowly (20-25 kcal/kg/day), thiamine 200-300 mg IV, prophylactic PO4/K/Mg supplementation, monitor electrolytes daily x 7 days.
  • Severe Hypophosphatemia (PO4 <1.0 mg/dL) Causes Respiratory Failure from Diaphragm Weakness: Phosphate essential for ATP. Severe depletion causes cellular energy crisis, diaphragm muscle dysfunction → respiratory failure. Patient may be intubated for "unknown reason," difficult to wean. Check PO4 in all intubated patients, especially if malnourished, alcoholic, or refeeding. Correcting PO4 (IV phosphate 15-30 mmol over 6 hours) improves respiratory muscle strength, enables weaning within 24-48 hours. Classic scenario: alcoholic patient intubated, PO4 0.8 mg/dL, after IV PO4 repletion successfully extubated next day.
  • IV Phosphate Can Cause Severe Hypocalcemia and Hypotension - Always Give Slowly: IV phosphate must be given over 6 hours minimum (max rate 7 mmol/hr). Rapid infusion causes: (1) Acute hypocalcemia (PO4 binds Ca → calcium-phosphate precipitates), can cause tetany, cardiac arrhythmias, (2) Hypotension, (3) Tissue calcification (especially in kidneys, blood vessels). Before giving IV PO4: check calcium (have calcium gluconate available), give slowly, monitor calcium q6h during infusion. If hypocalcemia develops: slow/stop PO4 infusion, give calcium. Never push IV phosphate as bolus.
  • Hemolytic Anemia from Severe Hypophosphatemia is Rare but Specific: Phosphate needed for RBC 2,3-DPG production and ATP. Severe hypophosphatemia (PO4 <1.0 mg/dL) causes: (1) Hemolytic anemia (RBC membrane instability), (2) Left-shifted oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve (decreased 2,3-DPG → poor tissue oxygen delivery despite normal SpO2). Labs: low Hgb, elevated LDH, elevated indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, schistocytes on smear (microangiopathic hemolysis). Correct PO4 → hemolysis resolves. Also causes WBC/platelet dysfunction (increased infection risk, bleeding).
  • CKD Patients with Hyperphosphatemia Have Increased Cardiovascular Mortality from Vascular Calcification: Chronic hyperphosphatemia (PO4 >5.5 mg/dL) in CKD causes calcium-phosphate precipitation in blood vessels, heart valves, soft tissues. Vascular calcification → coronary artery disease, MI, heart failure, stroke. Calcium-phosphate product (Ca × PO4) >55 mg²/dL² increases calcification risk exponentially. Goal in CKD: PO4 3.5-5.5 mg/dL, Ca 8.5-10.5 mg/dL, Ca × PO4 <55 mg²/dL². Treatment: phosphate binders (sevelamer preferred - doesn't add calcium), dietary PO4 restriction (<1000 mg/day), dialysis. Avoid excessive calcium-based binders (worsen vascular calcification).
  • Tumor Lysis Syndrome Causes Hyperphosphatemia + Hypocalcemia + Hyperkalemia + Hyperuricemia: Rapid tumor cell lysis (chemotherapy for hematologic malignancies) → massive release of intracellular contents. Classic labs within 24-72 hours of chemotherapy: High PO4 (>6-8 mg/dL), low Ca (PO4 binds Ca), high K (>6 mEq/L), high uric acid (>10 mg/dL), high LDH, AKI (uric acid crystals, calcium-phosphate precipitates in kidneys). Prevention: aggressive IV fluids 3 L/day, allopurinol or rasburicase (prevent uric acid nephropathy), monitor electrolytes q6-8h. Treatment: IV fluids, correct electrolytes, dialysis if severe (PO4 >10 mg/dL, K >6.5 mEq/L, AKI). Do NOT give calcium unless life-threatening hypocalcemia (worsens kidney injury).
  • Phosphate Binders MUST Be Taken With Meals to Work: Phosphate binders (sevelamer, calcium acetate, lanthanum) work by binding dietary phosphate in GI tract, preventing absorption. If taken between meals, no dietary PO4 present → ineffective. Always instruct patients: take phosphate binder WITH first bite of meal. Common error: patient takes binders morning/evening regardless of meals → PO4 remains high → doctor increases dose unnecessarily. Proper timing crucial. Also, sevelamer can bind other medications - separate dosing by 2 hours.
  • Respiratory Alkalosis Causes Intracellular Phosphate Shift → Hypophosphatemia: Acute respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation from pain, anxiety, sepsis, early ventilator settings) increases pH → stimulates glycolysis → increases intracellular PO4 consumption → PO4 shifts into cells → serum PO4 drops. Can see PO4 drop from 3.5 to 1.5 mg/dL within hours of intubation/hyperventilation. Usually asymptomatic (PO4 rarely drops <1.0 mg/dL). Resolves when respiratory alkalosis corrected. Don't aggressively replace PO4 unless severe (<1.0 mg/dL) or patient at risk (already malnourished, alcoholic). Fix the ventilator settings (decrease minute ventilation, allow pCO2 to normalize).
  • DKA Treatment Causes Hypophosphatemia - Monitor and Replace Carefully: DKA causes total body PO4 depletion (osmotic diuresis), but initial serum PO4 normal/high (cellular release from acidosis, insulin deficiency). When insulin given → glucose + PO4 shift intracellularly → serum PO4 drops precipitously within 4-6 hours of treatment. PO4 can drop to <1.0 mg/dL. Risk of respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias. Management: Check PO4 before insulin, then q4-6h during DKA treatment. If PO4 <1.0 mg/dL: give IV phosphate 15-30 mmol over 6 hours. If PO4 1.0-2.0 mg/dL: give oral phosphate or add potassium phosphate to IV fluids (instead of potassium chloride). Don't wait for PO4 to drop critically before replacing.
  • Aluminum-Based Phosphate Binders Cause Aluminum Toxicity - Avoid Long-Term Use: Aluminum hydroxide (Amphojel, AlternaGel) is very effective phosphate binder (binds more PO4 per mg than sevelamer). But aluminum accumulates in body, especially in CKD (kidneys can't excrete aluminum). Chronic use (>4 weeks) causes: (1) Aluminum-induced bone disease (osteomalacia, fractures), (2) Aluminum-induced encephalopathy (dementia, seizures, death), (3) Microcytic anemia (aluminum inhibits heme synthesis). Current recommendation: Use aluminum binders short-term only (<4 weeks) for severe acute hyperphosphatemia. Long-term: use sevelamer, calcium acetate, or lanthanum. If aluminum binders needed chronically, monitor serum aluminum levels (goal <20 mcg/L).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Hypophosphatemia: PO4 <1.0 mg/dL, respiratory failure from diaphragm weakness, rhabdomyolysis (CK >10,000), hemolytic anemia, altered mental status, seizures
  • Hyperphosphatemia: PO4 >10 mg/dL, tumor lysis syndrome with AKI, symptomatic hypocalcemia with PO4 >6.5 mg/dL, requiring urgent dialysis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Phosphate normalized (2.5-4.5 mg/dL) or stable in acceptable range for patient (CKD patients may tolerate PO4 4-5.5 mg/dL)
  • Asymptomatic (no weakness, rhabdomyolysis resolved, respiratory function normal)
  • Concurrent electrolyte abnormalities corrected (Ca, Mg, K normalized)
  • If hypophosphatemia: on oral phosphate or high-phosphate diet, underlying cause addressed
  • If hyperphosphatemia (CKD): on phosphate binders, dietary restriction counseled
  • If refeeding syndrome: nutrition plan established, thiamine supplemented
  • Follow-up arranged (nephrology if CKD, PCP within 1 week)
  • Recheck PO4, Ca, Mg scheduled for 1 week
