112. METABOLIC ALKALOSIS

Elevated pH • High Bicarbonate • Hypokalemia • Hypochloremia • Volume Depletion
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Arterial blood gas showing elevated pH (>7.45), elevated HCO3 (>28 mEq/L), typically with hypokalemia, hypochloremia, and either volume depletion (vomiting, diuretics) or volume expansion (mineralocorticoid excess). Often presents with muscle weakness, cramps, arrhythmias, confusion.

  • Pathophysiology: Metabolic alkalosis results from net gain of bicarbonate or net loss of acid (H+). Requires two components: (1) Generation: Event that initiates alkalosis (vomiting, diuretics, alkali administration), (2) Maintenance: Factors preventing kidney from excreting excess HCO3 (volume depletion, hypokalemia, hypochloremia). Kidneys normally excrete HCO3 rapidly, so sustained alkalosis indicates maintenance factor present. Classification: Saline-responsive (urine Cl <20 mEq/L - volume depleted) vs Saline-resistant (urine Cl >20 mEq/L - mineralocorticoid excess, severe K depletion)
  • Risk Factors: Vomiting/NG suction (most common), loop/thiazide diuretics, primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's syndrome, licorice ingestion, massive blood transfusion (citrate converted to HCO3), alkali administration (sodium bicarbonate, citrate in TPN), milk-alkali syndrome, hypercalcemia, Bartter/Gitelman syndrome
  • Symptoms: Often asymptomatic if mild (pH 7.45-7.50). Moderate-severe (pH >7.50): confusion, lethargy, muscle weakness/cramps, paresthesias (perioral, fingers), nausea, polyuria, palpitations (arrhythmias from hypokalemia), tetany (rare, if concurrent hypocalcemia)
  • Physical Exam: Signs of volume depletion (vomiting, diuretics): orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor. Signs of volume expansion (mineralocorticoid excess): hypertension, edema. Neuromuscular: hyporeflexia, muscle weakness, Chvostek/Trousseau signs if severe alkalosis (alkalosis shifts ionized Ca down). Arrhythmias if severe hypokalemia
  • Variants/Subtypes: Saline-Responsive (Chloride-Responsive): Vomiting, NG suction, diuretics, post-hypercapnia. Urine Cl <20 mEq/L. Respond to saline + KCl. Saline-Resistant (Chloride-Resistant): Hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's, severe hypokalemia. Urine Cl >20 mEq/L. Do NOT respond to saline alone.
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) - Diagnostic:

  • pH: Elevated >7.45 (7.45-7.55 mild-moderate, >7.55 severe)
  • HCO3: Elevated >28 mEq/L (can be >40-45 mEq/L in severe cases)
  • pCO2: Elevated (respiratory compensation). Expected pCO2 = 0.7 × HCO3 + 20 (±5). For every 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3, expect pCO2 to rise 0.7 mmHg
  • Compensation: Respiratory compensation is LIMITED (pCO2 rarely >55 mmHg even with severe metabolic alkalosis - respiratory drive prevents further hypoventilation). If pCO2 >55 mmHg, consider mixed disorder (metabolic alkalosis + respiratory acidosis)

Serum Electrolytes:

  • Hypokalemia: Almost always present (K <3.5 mEq/L, often <3.0 mEq/L). Alkalosis shifts K+ intracellularly. H+ and K+ inversely related
  • Hypochloremia: Cl <95 mEq/L (loss of HCl from vomiting, or Cl loss with diuretics). Chloride deficiency maintains alkalosis
  • Hyponatremia or Normal Sodium: Na can be low (diuretics), normal, or elevated (mineralocorticoid excess)
  • Elevated Bicarbonate: HCO3 >28 mEq/L (same as ABG)

Urine Chloride (MOST IMPORTANT TEST to Classify Etiology):

  • Urine Cl <20 mEq/L: Saline-responsive (chloride-responsive) metabolic alkalosis
    • Causes: Vomiting, NG suction, remote diuretic use (>24 hours ago), post-hypercapnia, villous adenoma
    • Interpretation: Kidneys appropriately retaining chloride (volume depleted state)
    • Treatment: Normal saline + KCl
  • Urine Cl >20 mEq/L: Saline-resistant (chloride-resistant) metabolic alkalosis
    • Causes: Active diuretic use, primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's syndrome, severe hypokalemia (K <2.0 mEq/L), Bartter/Gitelman syndrome, licorice ingestion
    • Interpretation: Kidneys inappropriately wasting chloride despite alkalosis
    • Treatment: Treat underlying cause (stop diuretic, correct severe hypokalemia, treat hyperaldosteronism)

Additional Testing Based on Classification:

  • If Saline-Responsive (Urine Cl <20): Clinical history usually sufficient (vomiting, NG suction, diuretics)
  • If Saline-Resistant (Urine Cl >20):
    • Check blood pressure: Hypertensive (think primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's, renovascular hypertension) vs Normotensive (think severe K depletion, Bartter/Gitelman syndrome, licorice, diuretic abuse)
    • Plasma Renin and Aldosterone: If hypertensive + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis
      • Low renin + High aldosterone = Primary hyperaldosteronism (adrenal adenoma, bilateral adrenal hyperplasia)
      • High renin + High aldosterone = Secondary hyperaldosteronism (renovascular hypertension, renin-secreting tumor)
      • Low renin + Low aldosterone = Exogenous mineralocorticoid (licorice, Cushing's, exogenous steroids)
    • 24-Hour Urine Cortisol or Dexamethasone Suppression Test: If concern for Cushing's syndrome
    • Abdominal CT/MRI: If primary hyperaldosteronism confirmed (look for adrenal adenoma)

ECG:

  • Hypokalemia findings: U waves, T wave flattening, prolonged QT, PVCs, atrial/ventricular arrhythmias
  • Alkalosis itself can prolong QT interval
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

General Principles:

  • Metabolic alkalosis is rarely life-threatening (unlike severe acidosis)
  • Focus on treating underlying cause and correcting maintenance factors
  • Most cases respond to fluid + electrolyte repletion (saline-responsive)
  • Do NOT attempt to directly lower pH (dangerous) - correct underlying disorder

SALINE-RESPONSIVE METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (Urine Cl <20 mEq/L) - MOST COMMON:

  • Step 1 - Volume Repletion with Normal Saline:
    • 0.9% Normal Saline 1-2 L bolus, then 100-200 mL/hr
    • Provides chloride (repletes chloride deficit) + volume (improves renal HCO3 excretion)
    • Monitor: Assess volume status clinically, goal orthostatic vitals resolved, good urine output
  • Step 2 - Potassium Chloride Repletion (CRITICAL):
    • Most patients have profound K depletion (K <3.0 mEq/L, often <2.5 mEq/L)
    • KCl 40-80 mEq IV in first liter of NS (if K <3.0 mEq/L)
    • Then continue KCl 20-40 mEq in each liter NS until K >3.5 mEq/L
    • Or KCl 40-80 mEq PO q6-8h if able to tolerate PO
    • Goal: K >3.5 mEq/L (often need 200-400 mEq total replacement)
    • Cannot correct alkalosis without correcting hypokalemia (low K maintains alkalosis via renal mechanisms)
  • Step 3 - Treat Underlying Cause:
    • Vomiting: Antiemetics (ondansetron 4-8 mg IV q8h), treat underlying GI pathology
    • NG suction: Reduce suction rate if possible, or give IV HCl (see below) if must continue suction
    • Diuretics: Stop diuretic if possible, or switch to K-sparing diuretic (spironolactone)
  • Monitoring:
    • ABG q6-12h to assess pH, HCO3, pCO2
    • BMP q6-12h to monitor K, Cl, HCO3
    • Continuous telemetry if K <2.5 mEq/L or arrhythmias present
    • Goal: pH <7.45, HCO3 <28 mEq/L, K >3.5 mEq/L, Cl >95 mEq/L
  • Expected Response: With adequate saline + KCl, alkalosis corrects within 24-48 hours

SALINE-RESISTANT METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (Urine Cl >20 mEq/L):

  • Active Diuretic Use: Stop diuretic if possible. If must continue (CHF, cirrhosis), switch to acetazolamide (promotes HCO3 excretion) or add K-sparing diuretic (spironolactone 25-50 mg PO daily)
  • Severe Hypokalemia (K <2.0 mEq/L):
    • Aggressive KCl repletion: 40-80 mEq IV q4-6h until K >2.5 mEq/L (requires central line for higher rates)
    • Alkalosis persists until K >2.5 mEq/L (severe K depletion maintains alkalosis independent of volume status)
  • Primary Hyperaldosteronism:
    • Spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) 50-100 mg PO BID, or Eplerenone 50-100 mg PO daily
    • Blocks aldosterone effect → reduces K wasting, improves metabolic alkalosis
    • Definitive: Surgical adrenalectomy if unilateral adenoma (cures 50-60%)
  • Cushing's Syndrome: Treat underlying cause (pituitary adenoma, adrenal tumor, ectopic ACTH). May need ketoconazole or metyrapone to lower cortisol acutely
  • Bartter/Gitelman Syndrome: Chronic K supplementation, NSAIDs (reduce renal prostaglandin-mediated K wasting), K-sparing diuretics

SEVERE LIFE-THREATENING METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (pH >7.55-7.60):

  • Indications for Aggressive Treatment: pH >7.55-7.60, seizures, severe arrhythmias, hemodynamic instability
  • Acetazolamide (Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor) - Promotes Bicarbonate Excretion:
    • Dose: 250-500 mg IV q6-12h
    • Mechanism: Inhibits proximal tubule HCO3 reabsorption → increases renal HCO3 excretion → lowers pH
    • Onset: 4-6 hours
    • Caution: Worsens hypokalemia (check K q4-6h, replace aggressively). Contraindicated if severe hypokalemia (K <2.5 mEq/L) - correct K first
  • Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) Infusion - MOST RAPID but HIGH RISK:
    • 0.1-0.2 N HCl infusion via CENTRAL LINE ONLY (scleroses peripheral veins)
    • Dose: Calculate HCl needed = 0.5 × body weight (kg) × (HCO3 current - HCO3 goal). Infuse half this amount over 8-12 hours
    • Mechanism: Directly titrates HCO3 with H+
    • Complications: Tissue necrosis if extravasation, hemolysis, acidemia overshoot. Requires ICU, central line, close monitoring
    • Rarely used (reserved for life-threatening alkalosis refractory to other measures)
  • Hemodialysis with Low-Bicarbonate Dialysate:
    • If renal failure prevents renal HCO3 excretion
    • Dialysate with low HCO3 (e.g., 20 mEq/L instead of standard 35-40 mEq/L) removes HCO3
    • Consult nephrology

Supportive Care:

  • Supplemental oxygen if hypoxemic (alkalosis shifts O2-Hgb curve left, impairs O2 release)
  • Correct concurrent hypomagnesemia (impairs K correction)
  • Treat arrhythmias (usually improve as K and pH normalize)

Disposition:

  • ICU: Severe alkalosis (pH >7.55), severe hypokalemia (K <2.5 mEq/L) with arrhythmias, requiring HCl infusion or acetazolamide, altered mental status, seizures
  • Floor with Telemetry: Moderate alkalosis (pH 7.45-7.55), hypokalemia (K 2.5-3.5 mEq/L), requiring IV KCl repletion
  • Discharge: Alkalosis corrected or mild (pH <7.45, HCO3 <30 mEq/L), K >3.5 mEq/L, underlying cause addressed, able to maintain oral K supplementation if needed
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Urine Chloride is THE Key Test to Classify Metabolic Alkalosis Etiology: Not urine sodium, not urine pH - URINE CHLORIDE. Distinguishes saline-responsive (<20 mEq/L) from saline-resistant (>20 mEq/L). Saline-responsive (95% of cases): vomiting, NG suction, diuretics (>24 hours ago), post-hypercapnia. Treat with NS + KCl. Saline-resistant: active diuretics, primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's, severe hypokalemia. Treat underlying cause. Always send spot urine chloride in metabolic alkalosis before starting treatment - guides entire management.
  • Metabolic Alkalosis Requires Both Generation and Maintenance - Kidneys Normally Excrete HCO3 Rapidly: Healthy kidneys can excrete enormous amounts of HCO3 (thousands of mEq/day). So transient alkalosis (one-time vomiting, alkali load) self-corrects rapidly. Sustained metabolic alkalosis requires maintenance factor preventing renal HCO3 excretion: (1) Volume depletion (activates RAAS → increases proximal HCO3 reabsorption), (2) Chloride depletion (impairs distal HCO3 secretion), (3) Hypokalemia (increases renal H+ secretion, generates new HCO3). Treatment must address maintenance factor, not just generation. Example: Patient vomiting x 1 day gets 1 L NS → alkalosis resolves. Patient vomiting x 5 days needs NS + KCl for days to correct.
  • Cannot Correct Metabolic Alkalosis Without Correcting Hypokalemia: Hypokalemia maintains alkalosis via renal mechanisms: (1) Low serum K → K shifts out of cells → H+ shifts into cells → intracellular acidosis → kidney excretes H+ (generates HCO3, worsens alkalosis), (2) Hypokalemia increases proximal tubule H+ secretion (generates HCO3), (3) Aldosterone effect enhanced when K low. Clinically: giving NS without KCl in vomiting patient → pH stays elevated, K stays low. Must give both NS and KCl. Typical requirement: 200-400 mEq KCl total to correct alkalosis + hypokalemia. Check K q6-8h during repletion.
  • Contraction Alkalosis from Diuretics is Due to Chloride Depletion, Not Just Volume Loss: Loop and thiazide diuretics cause metabolic alkalosis via: (1) Volume depletion (activates RAAS, increases HCO3 reabsorption), (2) Chloride depletion (kidneys cannot excrete HCO3 without Cl−), (3) Hypokalemia (see above). The chloride depletion is key - giving dextrose in water (volume without Cl) won't correct alkalosis. Must give saline (provides Cl−) + KCl. Urine Cl <20 mEq/L if diuretic stopped >24 hours ago (becomes saline-responsive). Urine Cl >20 mEq/L if actively taking diuretic (saline-resistant - stop diuretic).
  • Post-Hypercapnic Alkalosis Occurs After Rapid Correction of Chronic Respiratory Acidosis: Patient with chronic CO2 retention (COPD, obesity hypoventilation) has compensatory metabolic alkalosis (kidneys retain HCO3 to buffer chronic acidosis, HCO3 may be 35-45 mEq/L). If pCO2 corrected rapidly (intubation, BiPAP, treating exacerbation) → pCO2 normalizes but HCO3 still elevated → metabolic alkalosis (pH can be >7.50). Takes days for kidneys to excrete excess HCO3. Treatment: Saline + KCl (saline-responsive, urine Cl <20 mEq/L). Acetazolamide can speed correction. Don't over-ventilate COPD patients - causes post-hypercapnic alkalosis and difficult weaning.
  • Severe Metabolic Alkalosis (pH >7.55) is Dangerous - Causes Arrhythmias, Seizures, Decreased Coronary Blood Flow: Alkalosis shifts K+ and Ca2+ intracellularly (ionized Ca drops) → arrhythmias (prolonged QT, VT, atrial fib), neuromuscular excitability (tetany, seizures). Alkalosis also causes cerebral vasoconstriction (decreased cerebral blood flow → confusion, seizures), coronary vasoconstriction (angina in CAD patients), impaired oxygen delivery (left-shift O2-Hgb curve). pH >7.60 is medical emergency. Unlike metabolic acidosis (can tolerate pH 7.10-7.20), severe alkalosis poorly tolerated. If pH >7.55-7.60: consider acetazolamide or HCl infusion.
  • Acetazolamide Promotes Bicarbonate Excretion but Worsens Hypokalemia: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in proximal tubule → blocks HCO3 reabsorption → increased renal HCO3 excretion (bicarbonaturia) → lowers pH. Dose 250-500 mg IV q6-12h. Onset 4-6 hours, effective for pH >7.50. BUT acetazolamide also increases distal Na delivery → K wasting → worsens hypokalemia. Must check K q4-6h, give aggressive KCl (40-80 mEq q4-6h) while on acetazolamide. Do NOT use if K <2.5 mEq/L (correct K first, then use acetazolamide if still needed). Side effects: paresthesias, metabolic acidosis (if overdone).
  • Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome) Classic Triad: Hypertension + Hypokalemia + Metabolic Alkalosis: Excess aldosterone → renal K wasting + Na retention → hypokalemia (K 2.5-3.5 mEq/L) + hypertension + metabolic alkalosis (HCO3 30-40 mEq/L). Urine Cl >20 mEq/L (saline-resistant). Screening: plasma aldosterone/renin ratio. If ratio >20-30 and aldosterone >15 ng/dL → primary hyperaldosteronism. Confirm with saline suppression test or captopril test. Imaging: adrenal CT/MRI (look for adenoma). Treatment: spironolactone 50-100 mg BID (blocks aldosterone), or surgical adrenalectomy if unilateral adenoma. Classic scenario: 40-year-old with hypertension, K 2.8 mEq/L, HCO3 35 mEq/L, resistant to treatment.
  • Milk-Alkali Syndrome: Triad of Hypercalcemia + Metabolic Alkalosis + Acute Kidney Injury: From excessive calcium and alkali ingestion (calcium carbonate antacids, calcium supplements, calcium-fortified foods). Hypercalcemia → nephrogenic DI, volume depletion, AKI. Calcium carbonate → alkali load → metabolic alkalosis. Classic patient: woman taking calcium carbonate 3000-5000 mg/day for osteoporosis prevention + vitamin D, presents with confusion, nausea, Ca 12-14 mg/dL, HCO3 32-38 mEq/L, Cr 2.5-4.0 mg/dL. Treatment: stop calcium/vitamin D, IV saline, calcitonin if Ca >14 mg/dL. Third most common cause of hypercalcemia (after primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy).
  • Never Give Bicarbonate to "Correct" Metabolic Alkalosis - You'll Make It Worse: Common error: seeing "metabolic" and thinking "give opposite" (like giving bicarb for metabolic acidosis). NO. Giving bicarbonate in metabolic alkalosis adds more HCO3, worsens alkalosis, can cause pH >7.60 (life-threatening). Treatment is NOT to "neutralize" pH but to remove maintenance factors (give saline + KCl for volume/Cl/K repletion, stop diuretics, treat hyperaldosteronism). Only exception: if patient has MIXED disorder (metabolic alkalosis + severe metabolic acidosis from different cause, pH near normal, very sick) - but this is rare and complex.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe metabolic alkalosis (pH >7.55-7.60)
  • Severe hypokalemia (K <2.5 mEq/L) with cardiac arrhythmias (PVCs, VT, atrial fibrillation)
  • Altered mental status, confusion, seizures from alkalosis
  • Requiring hydrochloric acid (HCl) infusion
  • Respiratory depression from compensatory hypoventilation (pCO2 >55 mmHg, hypoxemia)
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Requiring central line for rapid KCl infusion (>20 mEq/hr)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • pH normalized (<7.45) or near-normal (7.42-7.45)
  • Bicarbonate normalized (<28 mEq/L) or near-normal (26-28 mEq/L)
  • Potassium corrected (>3.5 mEq/L, ideally >4.0 mEq/L)
  • Chloride normalized (>95 mEq/L)
  • Volume status optimized (euvolemic, normal orthostatics)
  • Asymptomatic (no muscle weakness, cramps, palpitations, confusion)
  • Underlying cause addressed (vomiting controlled, diuretic stopped/adjusted)
  • If ongoing risk (e.g., continued diuretics for CHF): on oral KCl supplementation 20-40 mEq PO BID
  • Follow-up arranged with PCP within 1 week
  • Recheck BMP (K, Cl, HCO3) scheduled for 1 week

113. SICKLE CELL CRISIS (VASO-OCCLUSIVE, ACUTE CHEST SYNDROME)

Severe Pain • Acute Chest Syndrome • Stroke Risk • Exchange Transfusion
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Patient with known sickle cell disease presenting with severe, excruciating bone/joint pain (vaso-occlusive crisis), or fever, chest pain, hypoxia, and new infiltrate on chest X-ray (acute chest syndrome - leading cause of death in SCD).

  • Pathophysiology: Hemoglobin S (HbS) polymerizes under hypoxic/acidotic conditions, causing RBC sickling. Sickled cells occlude microvasculature leading to tissue ischemia, infarction, and severe pain (vaso-occlusive crisis - VOC). Acute chest syndrome (ACS) results from pulmonary vaso-occlusion, fat embolism from bone marrow infarction, and/or infection, creating a cycle of hypoxia → more sickling → worsening pulmonary compromise. Can progress to ARDS, multiorgan failure, death. Other crises: aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19), splenic sequestration (massive splenomegaly, hypovolemic shock), hemolytic crisis
  • Risk Factors: Sickle cell disease (HbSS most severe, HbSC moderate, HbS-beta-thal variable), triggers: dehydration, infection (pneumonia, osteomyelitis, UTI), hypoxia, acidosis, cold exposure, extreme exertion, pregnancy, alcohol, noncompliance with hydroxyurea. VOC triggered by weather changes, physical stress, emotional stress. ACS often precipitated by VOC, post-operative state, fat embolism
  • Symptoms - Vaso-Occlusive Crisis: Severe, deep, aching bone pain (most common: long bones, back, chest, abdomen), pain intensity 8-10/10, often described as "worst pain imaginable," lasts hours to days. Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children. Abdominal pain (mesenteric ischemia, splenic infarction). Priapism (urologic emergency). Headache, altered mental status (stroke)
  • Symptoms - Acute Chest Syndrome: Fever (>38.5°C), chest pain (pleuritic), dyspnea, cough, hypoxia (O2 sat <90%), rapid respiratory decompensation. Often develops 24-72 hours after VOC or post-operatively. Progressive infiltrates on CXR
  • Physical Exam: Tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, fever. Severe pain with minimal external findings (hallmark of VOC). Tenderness over affected bones/joints. ACS: decreased breath sounds, rales/crackles, dullness to percussion, respiratory distress. Jaundice, scleral icterus (chronic hemolysis). Splenomegaly (children; adults have autoinfarction). Stroke: focal neurologic deficits, altered mental status
  • Variants/Subtypes: VOC (most common crisis, 90%), Acute Chest Syndrome (ACS - second most common, leading cause of death), Splenic Sequestration (massive splenomegaly, hypovolemia, shock), Aplastic Crisis (parvovirus B19, profound anemia with reticulocytopenia), Hemolytic Crisis (accelerated hemolysis beyond baseline), Stroke (ischemic from large vessel occlusion or hemorrhagic), Multiorgan Failure Syndrome (MOFS - liver, kidney, lung failure)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Complete Blood Count: Baseline anemia (Hgb 6-9 g/dL in HbSS is typical; acute drop suggests sequestration or aplastic crisis). Elevated WBC (15,000-25,000/µL common in VOC from demargination, not infection). Low platelets (<150,000/µL) concerning for sequestration or sepsis. Reticulocyte count: elevated (5-15%) at baseline; LOW in aplastic crisis (<1%)
  • Hemolysis Labs: Elevated LDH (often 400-1000 U/L), elevated indirect bilirubin (2-5 mg/dL at baseline, higher in hemolytic crisis), low haptoglobin (<25 mg/dL or undetectable), elevated AST
  • Peripheral Smear: Sickled RBCs (elongated, crescent-shaped), target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), nucleated RBCs, polychromasia
  • Type and Screen: ALWAYS in preparation for transfusion. Extended phenotype matching (Rh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd antigens) to reduce alloimmunization
  • Basic Metabolic Panel: Assess renal function (Cr often mildly elevated at baseline), electrolytes, anion gap (lactic acidosis from tissue ischemia)
  • Hepatic Panel: Elevated transaminases (hepatic sequestration, ischemia), elevated bilirubin (hemolysis)
  • Arterial Blood Gas: If hypoxia or respiratory distress. Assess oxygenation, acidosis (pH <7.35 worsens sickling)
  • Lactate: Elevated in severe vaso-occlusion, tissue ischemia, multiorgan failure
  • Blood Cultures: If fever (>38.5°C) or ACS. Encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Salmonella) due to functional asplenia

Imaging:

  • Chest X-ray: MANDATORY if fever, chest pain, dyspnea, hypoxia. ACS: new infiltrate (can be subtle initially, progresses over 24-48 hours), pleural effusion, consolidation. May be normal early in ACS
  • CT Chest (if CXR equivocal or severe): Better characterize infiltrates, assess for pulmonary embolism (increased risk in SCD)
  • MRI/MRA Brain (if stroke symptoms): Acute ischemic stroke (MCA territory most common), hemorrhagic stroke, chronic silent infarcts. STAT imaging for any focal neurologic deficit
  • Ultrasound Abdomen: If RUQ pain or elevated LFTs. Assess for cholelithiasis (pigment stones from chronic hemolysis), hepatic sequestration, splenic infarction/sequestration
  • X-rays of Painful Areas: Rule out osteomyelitis (difficult to distinguish from bone infarction; Salmonella osteomyelitis classic), pathologic fracture, avascular necrosis (femoral head, humeral head)

Special Considerations:

  • Hemoglobin Electrophoresis: If new diagnosis or unknown SCD type. HbSS (Hb 6-9 g/dL, 85-95% HbS), HbSC (Hb 10-12 g/dL, HbS + HbC), HbS-beta-thal (variable based on beta-zero vs beta-plus)
  • Parvovirus B19 PCR/IgM: If aplastic crisis suspected (Hgb drop, low/absent reticulocytes)
  • Transcranial Doppler (TCD) Ultrasound: Screen for stroke risk in children (velocities >200 cm/s = high risk). Not acute test
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management - Vaso-Occlusive Crisis:

  • IV access, continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitoring
  • AGGRESSIVE HYDRATION: NS or D5½NS at 1.5-2× maintenance (150-200 mL/hr initially). Target urine output 1-2 mL/kg/hr. Avoid overhydration (can precipitate ACS)
  • OXYGEN THERAPY: Maintain O2 sat >95% (hypoxia worsens sickling). Supplemental O2 via nasal cannula or face mask as needed. Do NOT over-oxygenate (suppresses erythropoiesis)
  • PAIN CONTROL (PRIORITY): Treat pain aggressively and immediately (delays worsen crisis):
    • Morphine 0.1-0.15 mg/kg IV q2-4h (preferred) or hydromorphone 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV q2-4h
    • PCA pump if available (better pain control, reduces ED visits)
    • Adjunct: Ketorolac 15-30 mg IV q6h (if normal renal function, limit 5 days)
    • AVOID MEPERIDINE (neurotoxic metabolite normeperidine causes seizures)
    • Reassess pain q1-2h, uptitrate opioids as needed
  • Correct acidosis (worsens sickling): Treat underlying cause, consider NaHCO3 if pH <7.25
  • Antibiotics if fever: Ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV q24h (covers encapsulated organisms)

Management - Acute Chest Syndrome (MEDICAL EMERGENCY):

  • Supplemental Oxygen: Maintain O2 sat >95%. Escalate to high-flow nasal cannula, BiPAP, or mechanical ventilation as needed
  • BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS (START IMMEDIATELY):
    • Ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV q24h PLUS Azithromycin 500 mg IV/PO daily (covers atypical pathogens: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia)
    • OR: Ceftriaxone + Levofloxacin 750 mg IV daily
  • AGGRESSIVE HYDRATION: But AVOID overhydration (worsens pulmonary edema)
  • INCENTIVE SPIROMETRY: 10 breaths q2h while awake (prevents atelectasis, reduces ACS risk in VOC patients)
  • SIMPLE TRANSFUSION (if Hgb <8 g/dL): 1-2 units PRBCs to increase O2 carrying capacity. Target Hgb 9-10 g/dL (DO NOT exceed Hgb 10 g/dL - increases viscosity, worsens vaso-occlusion)
  • EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION (if severe ACS): Indications: rapidly progressive infiltrates, O2 sat <90% despite O2, severe hypoxia/respiratory distress, neurologic symptoms, multiorgan involvement. Goal: reduce HbS% to <30%, increase HbA to >70%. Hematology consult STAT for exchange transfusion
  • Bronchodilators: Albuterol/ipratropium nebulizers if bronchospasm
  • Pain control: Continue opioids as in VOC

Transfusion Therapy:

  • Simple Transfusion: For symptomatic anemia (Hgb <6 g/dL or drop of 2+ g/dL from baseline), acute chest syndrome with Hgb <8 g/dL, pre-operative preparation, stroke prevention. Transfuse 1-2 units PRBCs to target Hgb 9-10 g/dL (NEVER >10 g/dL)
  • Exchange Transfusion (Urgent Hematology Consult): Severe ACS, acute stroke, multiorgan failure syndrome, severe priapism (>4 hours). Can be manual (phlebotomy + transfusion) or automated (apheresis). Goal: HbS <30%
  • Use EXTENDED PHENOTYPE-MATCHED blood (Rh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd) to reduce alloimmunization (30-50% of SCD patients develop antibodies)

Specific Crisis Management:

  • Stroke: STAT MRI/MRA, neurology consult, exchange transfusion (reduce HbS <30%). Treat as acute ischemic stroke (consider tPA if no contraindication, discuss with hematology). Chronic transfusion therapy to prevent recurrence
  • Priapism: Hydration, opioid analgesia, ice packs. If >4 hours: urology consult for aspiration/irrigation. Exchange transfusion if refractory
  • Splenic Sequestration: Acute splenomegaly, Hgb drop >2 g/dL, hypovolemia. IV fluids, emergent simple transfusion (1-2 units), monitor closely (can autoresolve and cause hyperviscosity). Splenectomy for recurrent episodes
  • Aplastic Crisis: Parvovirus B19 infection. Hgb <5-6 g/dL, reticulocytopenia (<1%). Simple transfusion to target Hgb 7-8 g/dL. Self-limited (bone marrow recovery in 7-10 days)

Chronic Disease-Modifying Therapy (Long-term):

  • Hydroxyurea: Increases HbF (fetal hemoglobin), reduces sickling frequency by 50%, reduces VOC, ACS, mortality. Dose 15-35 mg/kg/day PO. All patients with SCD should be on hydroxyurea unless contraindicated
  • L-Glutamine (Endari): Reduces oxidative stress. 5-15 g PO BID. Adjunct to hydroxyurea
  • Voxelotor (Oxbryta) — ⛔ WITHDRAWN September 25, 2024: Pfizer voluntarily withdrew all lots from all worldwide markets. FDA issued alert to STOP PRESCRIBING. Post-marketing data showed imbalance in vaso-occlusive crises and fatal events; overall benefit no longer outweighs risk. Do NOT prescribe. Patients previously on voxelotor should be transitioned to alternative therapy.
  • Crizanlizumab (Adakveo): P-selectin inhibitor. 5 mg/kg IV q4 weeks. ⚠️ Clinical uncertainty: Phase 3 STAND trial (2023) failed to confirm benefit over placebo (VOC rate 2.49 vs 2.30, non-significant). EU and UK revoked marketing authorization in 2023–2024. Remains US FDA-approved (original accelerated approval 2019 based on Phase 2 data), but confirmatory evidence is negative. Consult hematology before initiating; benefit-risk should be discussed with patient.
  • Chronic transfusion therapy: For recurrent stroke, recurrent ACS
  • Gene Therapy (Potentially Curative — Hematology Referral Required): FDA approved December 2023: Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel, CRISPR-based) and Lyfgenia (lovotibeglogene autotemcel, lentiviral). Both for patients ≥12 years with recurrent VOC. Single-treatment, potentially curative approach. Highly specialized centers only; not a point-of-care decision.

Hematology Consultation:

  • MANDATORY for all ACS, stroke, severe VOC requiring exchange transfusion, multiorgan failure, first SCD crisis presentation
  • Consider for refractory pain, transfusion needs, management optimization

Disposition:

  • ICU: Acute chest syndrome, respiratory failure (O2 sat <90%, requiring >4L O2), severe hypoxia, stroke, multiorgan failure, exchange transfusion needed, hemodynamic instability
  • Floor: VOC requiring IV opioids, mild ACS (stable O2 sat), fever/infection requiring IV antibiotics
  • Discharge: Pain well-controlled on PO opioids, normal O2 sat, tolerating PO intake, reliable follow-up
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Acute Chest Syndrome is the Leading Cause of Death in SCD: ACS causes 25% of SCD deaths and develops in 50% of SCD patients during their lifetime. Often precipitated by VOC, post-operative state, or infection. Diagnosis: fever + chest pain + new infiltrate on CXR + hypoxia. KEY: Can present initially as simple VOC, then develop ACS 24-72 hours later. Early recognition and aggressive treatment (antibiotics, O2, transfusion/exchange) are critical. Fat embolism from bone marrow infarction during VOC is a major contributor.
  • Do NOT Transfuse to Hemoglobin >10 g/dL: Increasing Hgb above 10 g/dL increases blood viscosity and worsens vaso-occlusion (hyperviscosity syndrome). Target Hgb is 9-10 g/dL maximum with simple transfusion. This is counterintuitive but critical - more is NOT better in SCD. For severe complications requiring exchange transfusion, goal is to REPLACE HbS with HbA (reduce HbS% to <30%), not just increase total hemoglobin.
  • Pain Crisis Delays Worsen Outcomes: Delayed or inadequate pain control leads to prolonged hospital stays, increased complications, and higher readmission rates. VOC pain is SEVERE (8-10/10) and requires aggressive opioid therapy immediately. Use morphine or hydromorphone IV q2-4h or PCA pump. Do NOT use meperidine (Demerol) - the metabolite normeperidine accumulates and causes seizures, especially in SCD patients with renal dysfunction. Reassess pain frequently and uptitrate aggressively.
  • Incentive Spirometry Prevents ACS: Patients with VOC (especially chest/rib pain) have shallow breathing from pain, leading to atelectasis and hypoventilation. This hypoxia triggers more sickling and can precipitate ACS. Incentive spirometry 10 breaths q2h while awake has been shown to reduce ACS incidence by 50% in hospitalized VOC patients. It's simple, low-cost, and highly effective - make it a standing order.
  • Functional Asplenia Increases Infection Risk: By age 5, most SCD patients have autoinfarction of the spleen (repeated splenic infarcts lead to fibrosis). This creates functional asplenia, increasing risk of sepsis from encapsulated organisms: S. pneumoniae (most common), H. influenzae, Salmonella (especially osteomyelitis). Fever >38.5°C requires immediate blood cultures and empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone). Patients should receive pneumococcal, H. influenzae, and meningococcal vaccines, plus penicillin VK prophylaxis (250 mg PO BID) lifelong.
  • Exchange Transfusion vs Simple Transfusion: Simple transfusion increases Hgb by adding RBCs (for symptomatic anemia, Hgb <6-8 g/dL). Exchange transfusion REPLACES patient's HbS-containing RBCs with donor HbA-containing RBCs (goal: HbS% <30%, HbA% >70%). Indications for exchange: severe ACS, acute stroke, multiorgan failure, severe priapism. Exchange is preferred over simple transfusion in emergencies because it improves oxygen delivery AND reduces sickling without increasing viscosity. Requires hematology consult for apheresis or manual exchange.
  • Hydroxyurea is Disease-Modifying: Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels, which inhibits HbS polymerization. Clinical benefits: 50% reduction in VOC frequency, 50% reduction in ACS episodes, reduced mortality, reduced transfusion needs. ALL patients with SCD (including HbSC and HbS-beta-thal) should be offered hydroxyurea starting in infancy. Dose 15-35 mg/kg/day, titrated to maintain WBC 4000-8000/µL and ANC >2000/µL. Common misconception: hydroxyurea is NOT chemotherapy; it's a safe, well-tolerated, disease-modifying therapy.
  • Avoid Over-Hydration in ACS: While aggressive hydration is critical for VOC (1.5-2× maintenance), in ACS be cautious about overhydration which can worsen pulmonary edema and respiratory status. In ACS, maintain euvolemia with careful fluid balance monitoring. If patient is developing ACS from VOC, reduce IV fluids to maintenance rate and focus on oxygen therapy, antibiotics, and transfusion. Monitor intake/output closely and daily weights.
  • Stroke Risk and Prevention: 10% of children with SCD have a stroke by age 20. Transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasound screens for stroke risk by measuring cerebral blood flow velocities. TCD >200 cm/s = high risk (10% annual stroke rate if untreated). Prevention: chronic transfusion therapy to maintain HbS <30% reduces stroke risk by 90%. Acute stroke treatment: exchange transfusion STAT to reduce HbS <30%, then chronic transfusion therapy or hematopoietic stem cell transplant (curative).
  • Salmonella Osteomyelitis is Classic in SCD: SCD patients have 100× increased risk of Salmonella osteomyelitis (vs S. aureus in general population). Mechanism: gut translocation of Salmonella during sickling episodes affecting mesenteric vessels, then hematogenous spread to infarcted bone. Presentation: fever, localized bone pain, difficulty distinguishing from bone infarction (both cause pain, elevated WBC, elevated ESR). Diagnosis requires MRI with contrast (shows abscess, periosteal reaction) and bone biopsy/culture. Treatment: prolonged antibiotics (ceftriaxone or fluoroquinolone × 4-6 weeks).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Acute chest syndrome (fever, chest pain, new infiltrate, hypoxia)
  • Hypoxia: O2 saturation <90% on room air or requiring >4L O2 via nasal cannula
  • Acute stroke or altered mental status (focal neurologic deficits, confusion, decreased consciousness)
  • Severe respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure
  • Multiorgan failure (acute kidney injury with Cr >2× baseline, liver failure with INR >2, encephalopathy)
  • Exchange transfusion required (ACS, stroke, multiorgan failure)
  • Hemodynamic instability (hypotension SBP <90, tachycardia HR >120 unresponsive to fluids)
  • Rapidly progressive infiltrates on chest X-ray
  • Splenic sequestration with hypovolemic shock
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Pain controlled on oral opioids (pain score ≤4/10)
  • Oxygen saturation ≥95% on room air
  • Afebrile for ≥24 hours (if ACS or infection)
  • Tolerating oral intake and adequate hydration (drinking 2-3 L/day)
  • Chest X-ray stable or improving (if ACS)
  • No signs of ACS, stroke, or other complications
  • Hemoglobin stable (no further drop from admission)
  • Patient/family educated on hydration, pain management, when to return
  • Hematology follow-up arranged within 1-2 weeks
  • Home medications reconciled (hydroxyurea, folic acid, opioids as needed)
  • Prescription for oral opioids (hydrocodone/oxycodone) with clear instructions and limits
  • Incentive spirometry instructions if recent VOC/ACS

114. HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA

Elevated LDH • Low Haptoglobin • Reticulocytosis • Jaundice • Schistocytes
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Acute onset of jaundice, dark urine (hemoglobinuria), and anemia with laboratory evidence of hemolysis: elevated LDH (>400 U/L), elevated indirect bilirubin (>2 mg/dL), low/undetectable haptoglobin (<25 mg/dL), and reticulocytosis (>2-3%).

  • Pathophysiology: Hemolysis is premature RBC destruction (normal RBC lifespan 120 days). Can be INTRAVASCULAR (RBCs destroyed within vessels: PNH, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia like TTP/HUS/DIC, cold agglutinin disease, transfusion reactions) or EXTRAVASCULAR (RBCs destroyed by macrophages in spleen/liver: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency). Intravascular releases free hemoglobin into plasma (hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, low haptoglobin). Extravascular produces indirect hyperbilirubinemia, jaundice, splenomegaly. Bone marrow compensates with increased RBC production (reticulocytosis) unless bone marrow failure coexists.
  • Risk Factors - Immune: Autoimmune diseases (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis), lymphoproliferative disorders (CLL, lymphoma), medications (penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides, methyldopa, quinine), infections (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV, HIV), malignancies, transfusion reactions (ABO incompatibility)
  • Risk Factors - Non-Immune: G6PD deficiency (triggered by infections, fava beans, sulfa drugs, antimalarials), hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), mechanical heart valves, thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS), DIC, HELLP syndrome (pregnancy), burns, snake venom
  • Symptoms: Fatigue, weakness, dyspnea on exertion (anemia). Jaundice (extravascular hemolysis). Dark urine, tea-colored or cola-colored (hemoglobinuria in intravascular hemolysis). Abdominal pain (splenic infarction, cholelithiasis). Back pain, chest pain (intravascular hemolysis). Fever (AIHA, TTP). Pallor. Symptoms of underlying disorder (thrombosis in PNH, neurologic symptoms in TTP)
  • Physical Exam: Jaundice (scleral icterus), pallor, tachycardia, flow murmur. Splenomegaly (extravascular hemolysis, especially AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis). Hepatomegaly (if severe hemolysis). Petechiae/purpura (if thrombocytopenia coexists as in TTP, DIC). Lymphadenopathy (lymphoma, CLL). Dark urine on inspection (hemoglobinuria). Signs of underlying disease (SLE rash, prosthetic valve click)
  • Variants/Subtypes:
    • Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA): Warm (IgG, treated with steroids) vs Cold (IgM, cold agglutinins, treat with rituximab, avoid cold). Coombs-positive
    • Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA): TTP (fever, neurologic symptoms, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis), HUS (diarrhea, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis), DIC, HELLP, malignant hypertension, prosthetic valve hemolysis. Schistocytes on smear
    • G6PD Deficiency: X-linked, episodic hemolysis after oxidative stress. Bite cells, Heinz bodies on smear
    • Hereditary Spherocytosis: Autosomal dominant, chronic hemolysis, splenomegaly, cholelithiasis. Spherocytes on smear, positive osmotic fragility test
    • Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH): Acquired stem cell disorder, intravascular hemolysis (worse at night/morning), thrombosis, pancytopenia. Flow cytometry shows CD55/CD59 deficiency
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Laboratory Studies - Confirm Hemolysis:

  • Complete Blood Count: Anemia (Hgb often <10 g/dL in acute hemolysis, can be <6-7 g/dL in severe cases). MCV may be elevated if reticulocytosis (reticulocytes are larger than mature RBCs). Thrombocytopenia (concerning for TTP, DIC, HELLP)
  • Reticulocyte Count: ELEVATED (>2-3%, absolute count >100,000/µL) indicating bone marrow response. If LOW reticulocytes with hemolysis, think aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19), bone marrow infiltration, or nutritional deficiency
  • Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH): MARKEDLY ELEVATED (often >400-1000 U/L, can be >1500 U/L). Released from lysed RBCs. Most sensitive marker of hemolysis
  • Haptoglobin: LOW or UNDETECTABLE (<25 mg/dL). Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin; depleted in intravascular hemolysis. Can be falsely normal in inflammation (acute phase reactant). Absent in 1-2% of population (genetic ahaptoglobinemia)
  • Indirect (Unconjugated) Bilirubin: ELEVATED (>1.2 mg/dL, often 2-5 mg/dL) from heme breakdown. Predominantly indirect hyperbilirubinemia (direct <0.3 mg/dL)
  • Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT, Coombs Test): POSITIVE in autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). Detects antibodies or complement on RBC surface. Warm AIHA: IgG positive. Cold agglutinin disease: C3d positive. Negative DAT rules out autoimmune cause

Peripheral Blood Smear (CRITICAL for Diagnosis):

  • Schistocytes (Fragmented RBCs): Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, prosthetic valve). Helmet cells, triangular cells. If schistocytes present, URGENT evaluation for TTP
  • Spherocytes: Warm AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis. Small, round RBCs without central pallor
  • Bite Cells, Blister Cells, Heinz Bodies: G6PD deficiency (after oxidative stress). Heinz bodies require supravital stain (crystal violet)
  • Agglutination: Cold agglutinin disease (IgM antibodies cause RBC clumping at room temperature)
  • Sickle Cells: Sickle cell disease
  • Target Cells: Liver disease, thalassemia, hemoglobinopathies
  • Polychromasia: Reticulocytes (bluish-gray tinge on Wright-Giemsa stain)

Specialized Testing to Determine Etiology:

  • Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT/Coombs): Positive = immune-mediated (AIHA, drug-induced). IgG positive = warm AIHA. C3 positive = cold agglutinin disease
  • Cold Agglutinin Titer: If DAT positive for C3. Titer >1:64 diagnostic of cold agglutinin disease
  • G6PD Level: If bite cells/Heinz bodies or hemolysis after oxidative stress (infection, fava beans, medications). NOTE: may be falsely normal during acute hemolysis (reticulocytes have normal G6PD); recheck 3 months after acute episode
  • Osmotic Fragility Test: If spherocytes and family history. Positive in hereditary spherocytosis
  • Flow Cytometry for CD55/CD59: If intravascular hemolysis (hemoglobinuria) + thrombosis + cytopenias. Diagnostic for PNH
  • Hemoglobin Electrophoresis: If sickle cells or family history. Diagnose sickle cell disease, thalassemia
  • ADAMTS13 Activity: If schistocytes + thrombocytopenia + neurologic symptoms. <10% diagnostic of TTP. SEND BEFORE PLASMAPHERESIS
  • Coagulation Studies (PT, PTT, Fibrinogen, D-dimer): If schistocytes or concern for DIC. DIC: prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen (<200 mg/dL), elevated D-dimer (>500 ng/mL)
  • Free Hemoglobin (Plasma): Elevated in intravascular hemolysis (>25 mg/dL). Plasma appears pink or red
  • Urinalysis: Hemoglobinuria (positive blood without RBCs on microscopy). Indicates intravascular hemolysis. Also check for hemosiderinuria (chronic intravascular hemolysis)

Additional Testing Based on Clinical Suspicion:

  • Mycoplasma IgM, EBV serologies, HIV test (infection-triggered AIHA)
  • ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement levels (SLE-associated AIHA)
  • Peripheral lymphocyte flow cytometry (CLL, lymphoma)
  • Medication review (drug-induced hemolysis: penicillins, cephalosporins, methyldopa, quinine, sulfonamides)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management:

  • Assess hemodynamic stability: BP, HR, orthostatics, signs of shock
  • Supplemental oxygen if symptomatic anemia or hypoxia
  • Type and screen, crossmatch (extended phenotyping if warm AIHA or history of alloantibodies)
  • IV access, continuous monitoring if severe anemia (Hgb <7 g/dL)
  • Identify and treat underlying cause (stop offending medication, treat infection, manage TTP/DIC)
  • Folic acid 1 mg PO daily (increased demand from RBC turnover)

Transfusion Therapy:

  • Indications: Symptomatic anemia (dyspnea, chest pain, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability), Hgb <7 g/dL, or rapid Hgb drop
  • Challenges in AIHA: Crossmatching difficult due to antibodies. All units may be "incompatible" but can still transfuse least incompatible units if life-threatening
  • Transfuse PRBCs slowly: 1 unit over 2-4 hours with close monitoring. Risk of hemolysis of transfused cells, transfusion reactions
  • Goal: Hgb 7-8 g/dL (avoid overtransfusion which suppresses reticulocyte response)
  • Washed RBCs: Consider if recurrent severe transfusion reactions

Treatment - Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (IgG, DAT positive):

  • First Line - Corticosteroids: Prednisone 1 mg/kg PO daily (60-80 mg daily) or methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV daily. Response in 7-14 days (reticulocyte count drops, Hgb stabilizes/rises). Taper slowly over 3-6 months once Hgb >10 g/dL
  • Second Line (if refractory or relapsing): Rituximab 375 mg/m² IV weekly × 4 weeks (anti-CD20 antibody depletes B cells). Response rate 80-90%, slower onset (4-8 weeks)
  • Third Line: Splenectomy (removes site of RBC destruction), immunosuppressants (azathioprine 1-2 mg/kg/day, mycophenolate 1000 mg BID, cyclophosphamide)
  • Refractory Severe: IVIG 1 g/kg IV daily × 2 days (temporary response, days to weeks), plasmapheresis (limited efficacy in warm AIHA)

Treatment - Cold Agglutinin Disease (IgM, C3 positive DAT):

  • Avoid Cold Exposure: Keep patient warm (blankets, warm IV fluids, warm room). Cold triggers IgM binding and complement activation
  • Corticosteroids: Generally INEFFECTIVE (unlike warm AIHA)
  • First Line: Rituximab 375 mg/m² IV weekly × 4 weeks. Response rate 50-60%
  • Second Line: Rituximab + bendamustine or rituximab + fludarabine
  • Supportive: Transfuse through blood warmer if needed
  • Treat underlying disorder: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (azithromycin), lymphoproliferative disease

Treatment - Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (TTP/HUS/DIC):

  • TTP (Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura): MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) IMMEDIATELY, before confirmatory ADAMTS13 results. Delay increases mortality. Plasma exchange daily until platelets >150,000/µL and LDH normalizing. Adjunct: rituximab, caplacizumab (anti-vWF antibody)
  • HUS (Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome): Supportive care (hydration, avoid antibiotics in Shiga toxin HUS), dialysis if needed. Eculizumab for atypical HUS (complement-mediated)
  • DIC: Treat underlying cause (sepsis, malignancy). Transfuse platelets if bleeding, FFP/cryoprecipitate if coagulopathy and bleeding
  • DO NOT TRANSFUSE PLATELETS in TTP (unless life-threatening bleeding) - may worsen thrombosis

Treatment - G6PD Deficiency:

  • STOP offending agent: sulfa drugs, antimalarials (primaquine, dapsone), fava beans, naphthalene (mothballs), rasburicase
  • Supportive care: hydration, transfuse if severe anemia
  • Self-limited: hemolysis resolves once oxidative stress removed
  • Patient education: avoid triggers lifelong

Treatment - Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH):

  • Eculizumab (Soliris): Monoclonal antibody inhibiting complement C5. 600 mg IV weekly × 4 weeks, then 900 mg q2 weeks. Reduces hemolysis, thrombosis risk. MUST vaccinate against N. meningitidis before starting
  • Alternative: Ravulizumab (longer-acting C5 inhibitor), pegcetacoplan (C3 inhibitor)
  • Anticoagulation: For history of thrombosis (warfarin INR 2-3)
  • Transfuse for symptomatic anemia, treat iron deficiency
  • Allogeneic stem cell transplant: Curative for young patients with severe disease

Treatment - Drug-Induced Hemolytic Anemia:

  • STOP offending medication immediately
  • Hemolysis typically resolves within days to weeks after drug discontinuation
  • Supportive care, transfuse if severe
  • Corticosteroids if severe (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day)

Hematology Consultation:

  • MANDATORY for all cases of hemolytic anemia
  • URGENT consultation for TTP, severe AIHA, PNH, refractory hemolysis

Disposition:

  • ICU: Severe anemia (Hgb <5-6 g/dL), hemodynamic instability, TTP requiring plasmapheresis, acute kidney injury, transfusion-dependent, rapid hemolysis
  • Floor: Moderate anemia (Hgb 6-8 g/dL) requiring transfusion or IV steroids, new diagnosis requiring workup
  • Discharge: Mild hemolysis (Hgb >8-9 g/dL), chronic compensated hemolysis, hemolysis controlled on oral medications, close hematology follow-up arranged
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Haptoglobin is the Most Specific Marker for Intravascular Hemolysis: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin released from lysed RBCs. Low/undetectable haptoglobin (<25 mg/dL) is highly specific for hemolysis, particularly intravascular hemolysis. However, haptoglobin is an acute phase reactant - can be falsely elevated (normal) in inflammatory states even with hemolysis. Also, 1-2% of the population has genetic ahaptoglobinemia (congenitally absent haptoglobin). In these cases, rely on other markers: elevated LDH, indirect bilirubin, hemoglobinemia/hemoglobinuria.
  • Peripheral Smear is the Key to Diagnosis: The smear reveals the MECHANISM of hemolysis. Schistocytes = microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, prosthetic valve) - think mechanical destruction. Spherocytes = AIHA or hereditary spherocytosis - think membrane loss. Bite cells/Heinz bodies = G6PD deficiency - think oxidative damage. Sickle cells = sickle cell disease. Agglutination at room temperature = cold agglutinin disease. Always review the smear yourself or request hematopathology review - it guides the entire workup and treatment.
  • TTP is a "Do Not Miss" Emergency Requiring Immediate Plasmapheresis: Classic pentad: thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes), neurologic changes, renal failure, fever - but only 40% have full pentad. If you see thrombocytopenia + schistocytes + any neurologic change (confusion, headache, focal deficit), treat as TTP immediately. Send ADAMTS13 level (<10% confirms TTP) but START PLASMAPHERESIS BEFORE results return. Mortality is 90% without treatment, 10-20% with treatment. Every hour of delay increases mortality.
  • Warm AIHA Responds to Steroids, Cold Agglutinin Disease Does NOT: Warm AIHA (IgG antibodies, DAT IgG-positive) responds well to corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) with 70-85% response rate. Cold agglutinin disease (IgM antibodies, DAT C3-positive) does NOT respond to steroids. Instead, treat cold agglutinin disease with avoidance of cold, rituximab, and keeping the patient warm (heated blankets, warm IV fluids, warm room). Do NOT waste time with steroids in cold agglutinin disease.
  • G6PD Testing Can Be Falsely Normal During Acute Hemolysis: G6PD deficiency is X-linked; older RBCs have lower G6PD activity. During acute hemolytic crisis, the oldest (most deficient) cells are destroyed, and young reticulocytes (which have NORMAL G6PD levels) predominate. Testing during crisis may show falsely normal G6PD. If clinical suspicion is high (acute hemolysis after oxidative trigger in African or Mediterranean male), presume G6PD deficiency and recheck G6PD level 3 months after acute event when RBC population normalizes.
  • Don't Overtransfuse in Hemolytic Anemia: In hemolytic anemia, the bone marrow is actively producing RBCs (reticulocytosis). Overtransfusion (targeting Hgb >10 g/dL) suppresses erythropoietin and shuts down this compensatory response, making the patient transfusion-dependent. Additionally, in AIHA, transfused RBCs may also be destroyed by autoantibodies. Transfuse only for symptoms or critical anemia (Hgb <7 g/dL), target Hgb 7-8 g/dL, and allow the body's own reticulocyte response to recover the Hgb over time with definitive treatment.
  • PNH Triad: Hemolysis + Thrombosis + Cytopenias: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is an acquired clonal stem cell disorder causing deficiency of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins (CD55, CD59). Clinical triad: (1) intravascular hemolysis (worst at night/morning from nocturnal acidosis activating complement), (2) thrombosis in unusual sites (hepatic vein = Budd-Chiari, portal vein, cerebral venous sinus), (3) pancytopenia. Diagnose with flow cytometry showing absent CD55/CD59. Treat with eculizumab (complement inhibitor), which dramatically reduces hemolysis and thrombosis risk.
  • Crossmatching Blood is Difficult in AIHA: In warm AIHA, autoantibodies react with ALL donor RBCs, making crossmatch appear incompatible for every unit. Blood bank will provide "least incompatible" units. Transfuse these units if patient is symptomatic or critically anemic - they will be hemolyzed by autoantibodies but provide temporary oxygen-carrying capacity until definitive treatment (steroids, rituximab) takes effect. Communicate clearly with blood bank about diagnosis. Consider extended phenotype matching to avoid alloimmunization.
  • Drug-Induced Hemolytic Anemia Mechanisms Vary: Drugs cause hemolysis via three mechanisms: (1) Hapten mechanism - drug binds RBC, antibody forms against drug-RBC complex (penicillins, cephalosporins), (2) Immune complex mechanism - drug-antibody complexes activate complement (quinine, rifampin), (3) Autoantibody induction - drug induces true autoantibody formation (methyldopa, levodopa, fludarabine). All require DAT (Coombs) positive. Treatment: STOP THE DRUG. Hemolysis resolves in days to weeks. Corticosteroids may help if severe.
  • Splenectomy is Effective in Refractory Warm AIHA and Hereditary Spherocytosis: The spleen is the primary site of RBC destruction in warm AIHA and hereditary spherocytosis (extravascular hemolysis). Splenectomy has a 70-80% response rate in refractory warm AIHA (after failing steroids and rituximab) and is curative in hereditary spherocytosis. However, splenectomy increases lifelong risk of infection from encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis) and venous thromboembolism. Vaccinate 2 weeks before splenectomy (pneumococcal, H. influenzae, meningococcal) and give lifelong penicillin VK prophylaxis (250-500 mg PO BID).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe anemia with hemoglobin <5-6 g/dL
  • Hemodynamic instability (hypotension SBP <90, tachycardia HR >120, shock)
  • Symptomatic anemia with chest pain, dyspnea, altered mental status, syncope
  • Suspected TTP (schistocytes + thrombocytopenia + neurologic changes) - requires urgent plasmapheresis
  • Acute kidney injury with oliguria or rising creatinine (>2 mg/dL or 2× baseline)
  • Rapid hemolysis with Hgb dropping >2 g/dL per day despite treatment
  • Transfusion-dependent hemolysis requiring multiple units PRBCs
  • Severe hemoglobinuria with acute kidney injury (intravascular hemolysis)
  • DIC with active bleeding and coagulopathy
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemoglobin stable and >8-9 g/dL (or stable at patient's baseline for chronic hemolysis)
  • No symptoms of anemia (no dyspnea, chest pain, or significant fatigue at rest)
  • Hemodynamically stable (normal BP, HR <100, no orthostatic hypotension)
  • Hemolysis controlled or improving (LDH trending down, haptoglobin stabilizing)
  • Underlying cause identified or under investigation with outpatient plan
  • Appropriate therapy initiated (steroids for AIHA, eculizumab for PNH, offending drug stopped)
  • No evidence of TTP, DIC, or other life-threatening complications
  • Patient educated on medication compliance (steroids, immunosuppressants), avoidance of triggers (cold exposure, specific drugs)
  • Hematology follow-up arranged within 1-2 weeks
  • Folic acid 1 mg daily prescribed
  • Clear instructions on when to return: worsening fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, jaundice, dark urine, bleeding

115. ONCOLOGIC EMERGENCIES

SVC Syndrome • Spinal Cord Compression • Hypercalcemia of Malignancy • Tumor Lysis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Cancer patient presenting with life-threatening complication requiring urgent intervention: superior vena cava syndrome (facial edema, dilated chest veins), malignant spinal cord compression (back pain, weakness, bowel/bladder dysfunction), hypercalcemia of malignancy (confusion, polyuria), or tumor lysis syndrome (hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury).

  • Pathophysiology:
    • Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome: Obstruction of SVC by external compression (lung cancer, lymphoma, mediastinal mass, thrombus). Impaired venous drainage from head, neck, upper extremities causes facial/upper body edema, venous distension. Can progress to cerebral edema, respiratory compromise, death if untreated
    • Malignant Spinal Cord Compression (MSCC): Tumor invasion into epidural space (vertebral body metastases collapse onto cord, or direct invasion through intervertebral foramina). Compresses spinal cord causing ischemia and permanent neurologic damage. Irreversible paraplegia if not treated within 24-48 hours. Most common: thoracic spine (70%), then lumbar (20%), cervical (10%)
    • Hypercalcemia of Malignancy: (1) PTHrP-mediated (squamous cell lung cancer, RCC, breast, bladder - 80% of cases) - tumor secretes PTHrP mimicking PTH, increasing bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption, OR (2) Osteolytic bone metastases (breast, multiple myeloma, lymphoma - 20% of cases) - direct bone destruction releases calcium. Causes polyuria, dehydration, worsening hypercalcemia (vicious cycle), confusion, coma
    • Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS): Massive tumor cell death (spontaneous or treatment-induced chemo/radiation) releases intracellular contents: potassium, phosphate, uric acid, nucleic acids. Causes hyperkalemia (cardiac arrhythmias), hyperphosphatemia → hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures), hyperuricemia → uric acid nephropathy (AKI), acute kidney injury from crystal deposition
  • Risk Factors: Lung cancer (SVC syndrome, MSCC, hypercalcemia), breast cancer (bone mets, MSCC, hypercalcemia), prostate cancer (bone mets, MSCC), multiple myeloma (hypercalcemia, MSCC), renal cell carcinoma (hypercalcemia), lymphoma (SVC syndrome, TLS), leukemia (TLS), cancers with high proliferation rates (Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukemias - highest TLS risk)
  • Symptoms by Emergency Type:
    • SVC Syndrome: Facial swelling (worse in morning, improves when upright), neck swelling, upper extremity edema, dyspnea, cough, dysphagia, hoarseness, headache (worse when bending forward/lying down), visual changes, chest pain
    • MSCC: Back pain (90% - progressive, severe, localized, worse at night or with Valsalva), lower extremity weakness (85%), sensory changes (paresthesias, numbness), bowel/bladder dysfunction (urinary retention, incontinence, constipation), gait difficulty
    • Hypercalcemia: "Stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones" - polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, confusion, lethargy, weakness, bone pain
    • TLS: Often asymptomatic initially, then nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, muscle cramps/tetany (hypocalcemia), cardiac arrhythmias (hyperkalemia), decreased urine output, seizures
  • Physical Exam:
    • SVC Syndrome: Facial edema (especially periorbital), plethora, cyanosis, distended neck veins, dilated chest wall veins (collaterals), upper extremity edema (non-pitting), Pemberton sign (raising arms above head causes facial plethora/cyanosis), stridor if severe tracheal compression
    • MSCC: Focal tenderness to percussion over spinous processes, decreased strength (upper motor neuron pattern: spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing Babinski), sensory level, decreased rectal tone, saddle anesthesia
    • Hypercalcemia: Altered mental status, dry mucous membranes (dehydration), decreased skin turgor, bradycardia, shortened QT interval on ECG
    • TLS: Usually normal exam early, then lethargy, decreased urine output, muscle twitching/tetany (hypocalcemia), cardiac arrhythmias
  • Variants/Subtypes: Acute vs subacute presentation (SVC syndrome can present over days to weeks; MSCC can be acute/subacute). Complete vs incomplete cord compression. Symptomatic vs asymptomatic hypercalcemia (treatment based on symptoms AND calcium level). Laboratory TLS (abnormal labs only) vs Clinical TLS (labs + organ dysfunction)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Studies:

  • Basic Metabolic Panel: Hypercalcemia (>11 mg/dL moderate, >14 mg/dL severe), hyperkalemia (K >5.5 mEq/L in TLS), elevated Cr (AKI from hypercalcemia or TLS), hyperphosphatemia (PO4 >4.5 mg/dL in TLS)
  • Ionized Calcium: More accurate than total calcium. Ionized Ca >1.35 mmol/L (5.4 mg/dL) diagnostic of hypercalcemia. Correct total calcium for albumin: Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 - albumin)
  • Complete Blood Count: Anemia, leukocytosis or leukopenia (underlying malignancy), thrombocytopenia
  • PTH Level: Suppressed (<20 pg/mL) in hypercalcemia of malignancy (negative feedback from high calcium). Normal/elevated PTH suggests primary hyperparathyroidism
  • PTHrP Level: Elevated in PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia (squamous cell cancers, RCC). Helps differentiate mechanism
  • Uric Acid: Elevated (>8 mg/dL) in TLS from purine metabolism of lysed tumor cells
  • LDH: Markedly elevated in TLS (tumor lysis releases LDH). Also elevated in lymphoma/leukemia at baseline
  • Phosphate: Elevated in TLS (>4.5 mg/dL, can be >10 mg/dL). Low in hypercalcemia (PTHrP increases renal phosphate wasting)
  • ECG: Shortened QT interval (hypercalcemia), peaked T waves/widened QRS (hyperkalemia in TLS), prolonged QT (hypocalcemia in TLS)

Imaging:

  • SVC Syndrome:
    • CT Chest with IV Contrast (URGENT): Visualize SVC obstruction, identify cause (mass vs thrombus), assess collateral circulation, evaluate tracheal compression. Preferred initial test
    • Chest X-ray: May show widened mediastinum, right hilar mass, pleural effusion. Less sensitive than CT but can be done immediately
    • Venography or Doppler Ultrasound: If concern for SVC thrombus (for intervention planning)
  • Malignant Spinal Cord Compression:
    • MRI Spine with Gadolinium (STAT WITHIN 1 HOUR): Gold standard. Visualize entire spine (tumor can be at multiple levels). Shows epidural mass, cord compression, vertebral body involvement. If MRI unavailable or contraindicated, CT myelography is alternative
    • Plain X-rays Spine: Show vertebral body destruction (lytic or blastic lesions), compression fracture. Do NOT rule out cord compression - 10% of MSCC have normal X-rays. Cannot delay definitive imaging
  • Hypercalcemia/TLS:
    • Renal Ultrasound: Assess for hydronephrosis (can worsen kidney function), nephrocalcinosis
    • Skeletal Survey or PET-CT: Identify bone metastases (for hypercalcemia from osteolytic lesions)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

SUPERIOR VENA CAVA SYNDROME:

  • Immediate Stabilization:
    • Elevate head of bed 30-45 degrees (improve venous drainage)
    • Supplemental oxygen as needed
    • AVOID IV access in upper extremities (impaired venous drainage). Use lower extremity or central line if needed
    • Diuretics: Furosemide 20-40 mg IV (reduce edema, but use cautiously to avoid dehydration)
  • Corticosteroids (if lymphoma or chemosensitive tumor): Dexamethasone 10 mg IV, then 4 mg IV q6h. Rapidly reduces tumor burden and edema. Do NOT give if diagnosis uncertain (obscures histology)
  • Radiation Therapy (Definitive Treatment for Most Cases): Consult radiation oncology URGENTLY. Fractionated radiation (2-4 Gy per day × 10-20 fractions) to mediastinal mass. Improvement in 70-90% of patients within 3-7 days. Preferred for non-small cell lung cancer, small cell lung cancer
  • Chemotherapy: For chemosensitive tumors (lymphoma, small cell lung cancer, germ cell tumors). Consult oncology. Can result in rapid tumor shrinkage
  • Endovascular Stenting: For severe symptoms or lack of response to radiation/chemo. Interventional radiology places expandable metallic stent in SVC. Immediate symptom relief in 90% of cases. Consider if: severe symptoms (stridor, respiratory distress, cerebral edema), previously radiated mediastinum, SVC thrombus
  • Anticoagulation: If SVC thrombus identified. Heparin or LMWH. Thrombolysis for acute severe thrombosis

MALIGNANT SPINAL CORD COMPRESSION (TRUE EMERGENCY - HOURS MATTER):

  • High-Dose Corticosteroids (START IMMEDIATELY, do not wait for MRI):
    • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV STAT, then 4-6 mg IV q6h. Reduces vasogenic edema, stabilizes/improves neurologic function in 75% if given early. Continue until definitive treatment
    • PPI prophylaxis (pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily) for GI protection with high-dose steroids
  • URGENT Radiation Oncology Consult (within 2 hours): Emergent radiation therapy (EBRT) is the definitive treatment for most patients. 30 Gy in 10 fractions over 2 weeks typical. Start within 24 hours of diagnosis. Effective in 70-80% for pain relief and neurologic stabilization
  • URGENT Neurosurgery Consult (within 2 hours): Surgical decompression (laminectomy) indications: (1) Neurologic deterioration despite radiation, (2) Spinal instability or pathologic fracture, (3) Unknown primary cancer (need tissue diagnosis), (4) Previously radiated area (cannot re-radiate), (5) Radioresistant tumor (RCC, melanoma, sarcoma). Surgery followed by radiation improves outcomes vs radiation alone in selected patients
  • Medical Oncology Consult: For concurrent chemotherapy if chemosensitive tumor (lymphoma, myeloma, prostate cancer)
  • Bowel/Bladder Management: Foley catheter if urinary retention. Bowel regimen to prevent constipation. Physical therapy/rehab consultation

HYPERCALCEMIA OF MALIGNANCY:

  • AGGRESSIVE IV HYDRATION (First-Line):
    • Normal saline 200-300 mL/hr initially (goal 3-4 L over first 24 hours). Enhances renal calcium excretion
    • Monitor for volume overload (especially in elderly, heart failure patients). Titrate based on urine output, clinical exam
    • Replace electrolytes: Hypomagnesemia (Mg <1.5 mg/dL) and hypokalemia common with saline diuresis
    • Goal urine output 100-150 mL/hr. This ALONE lowers calcium by 1-3 mg/dL over 24-48 hours
  • Bisphosphonates (Definitive Treatment):
    • Zoledronic Acid (Zometa) 4 mg IV over 15-30 minutes: Preferred. Inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Calcium normalizes in 4-7 days, effect lasts 2-4 weeks. Dose-adjust for renal impairment (use 3.5 mg if CrCl 50-60, 3.3 mg if CrCl 40-49, 3 mg if CrCl 30-39, avoid if CrCl <30)
    • Pamidronate (Aredia) 60-90 mg IV over 2-4 hours: Alternative if zoledronic acid unavailable. Less potent. Normalizes calcium in 7-10 days
    • Precautions: Can cause acute kidney injury (ensure adequate hydration first). Risk of osteonecrosis of jaw (rare, with prolonged use). Hold if CrCl <30 mL/min
  • Calcitonin (Rapid Onset but Short Duration):
    • Calcitonin 4 units/kg SC or IM q12h. Lowers calcium within 4-6 hours (vs 4-7 days for bisphosphonates). Effect modest (decrease calcium 1-2 mg/dL) and short-lived (tachyphylaxis after 48 hours)
    • Use as BRIDGE therapy while waiting for bisphosphonates to work, especially if severe symptomatic hypercalcemia (Ca >14 mg/dL with altered mental status)
  • Denosumab (if refractory to bisphosphonates): Denosumab 120 mg SC weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly. Fully humanized monoclonal antibody against RANKL (inhibits osteoclast activation). More potent than bisphosphonates. Use if CrCl <30 or bisphosphonate failure
  • Loop Diuretics (Controversial, USE CAUTIOUSLY): Furosemide 20-40 mg IV q6-12h ONLY AFTER adequate hydration (euvolemic/hypervolemic). Increases renal calcium excretion. AVOID if hypovolemic (worsens dehydration and hypercalcemia). Modern guidelines de-emphasize routine use
  • Hemodialysis (Severe Refractory Hypercalcemia): If Ca >18 mg/dL with severe symptoms, AKI, or heart failure precluding aggressive hydration. Rapidly lowers calcium. Calcium-free dialysate
  • Treat Underlying Malignancy: Oncology consult for chemotherapy/targeted therapy (definitive long-term treatment)

TUMOR LYSIS SYNDROME:

  • Prevention (High-Risk Patients Before Chemo):
    • Aggressive IV hydration: NS or D5½NS at 2-3 L/m²/day (goal urine output >100 mL/m²/hr or 2-3 mL/kg/hr)
    • Allopurinol 300-600 mg PO daily (or 200-400 mg/m² IV if unable to take PO): Xanthine oxidase inhibitor, prevents uric acid formation from purine breakdown. Start 24-48 hours before chemotherapy
    • Rasburicase (Elitek) 0.2 mg/kg IV daily × 1-7 days (HIGH RISK ONLY): Recombinant urate oxidase, converts uric acid to allantoin (10× more soluble, easily excreted). Rapidly lowers uric acid within 4 hours. Indications: baseline uric acid >8 mg/dL, high tumor burden (Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukemias), baseline CrCl <60. Contraindications: G6PD deficiency (causes severe hemolysis), pregnancy
    • Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides)
    • Monitor labs q6-8h during first 24-72 hours of chemotherapy: BMP, phosphate, uric acid, calcium, LDH
  • Treatment of Established TLS:
    • Aggressive IV Hydration: NS at 200-300 mL/hr (3-4 L/day). Goal urine output >100 mL/hr. Promotes excretion of uric acid, phosphate, potassium
    • Rasburicase (if not already given): 0.2 mg/kg IV × 1 dose. Rapidly corrects hyperuricemia
    • Allopurinol: 300-600 mg PO daily. Prevents NEW uric acid formation (does not lower existing levels - that's rasburicase)
    • Manage Hyperkalemia: K >6.0 mEq/L or ECG changes:
      • Calcium gluconate 1-2 g (10-20 mL of 10% solution) IV over 2-3 min (cardiac membrane stabilization)
      • Insulin 10 units IV + Dextrose 50% 25 g (1 amp D50) IV (shifts K intracellularly)
      • Albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized (shifts K intracellularly)
      • Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) 30 g PO or 50 g PR (GI K excretion, slow onset)
      • Hemodialysis if refractory or K >7.0 mEq/L
    • Manage Hyperphosphatemia: Phosphate binders: Sevelamer 800-1600 mg PO TID with meals, or calcium acetate 667 mg (169 mg elemental Ca) 2-3 tabs PO TID with meals. AVOID aluminum-based binders (neurotoxicity)
    • Manage Hypocalcemia: Usually asymptomatic (from calcium-phosphate binding). Treat only if symptomatic (tetany, seizures, QTc >500 ms): Calcium gluconate 1-2 g IV over 10 min, then infusion. Avoid aggressive calcium repletion if phosphate >5 mg/dL (risk of metastatic calcification)
    • Hemodialysis (if refractory): Indications: K >7 mEq/L despite treatment, severe AKI (Cr >5 mg/dL or oliguria), fluid overload, symptomatic hypocalcemia with high phosphate. Removes potassium, phosphate, uric acid rapidly

Oncology Consultation:

  • MANDATORY for all oncologic emergencies
  • URGENT consultation for SVC syndrome, MSCC, severe hypercalcemia, TLS

Disposition:

  • ICU: MSCC, severe SVC syndrome (respiratory distress, stridor, altered mental status), severe hypercalcemia (Ca >15 mg/dL or altered mental status), clinical TLS with AKI/hyperkalemia, need for emergent intervention (surgery, stenting, dialysis)
  • Floor: SVC syndrome (mild-moderate symptoms), hypercalcemia (Ca 12-14 mg/dL without severe symptoms), laboratory TLS without organ dysfunction
  • Discharge: Hypercalcemia resolved/controlled, close oncology follow-up for definitive treatment of underlying cancer
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Malignant Spinal Cord Compression is a "Hours Not Days" Emergency: Neurologic function at presentation predicts outcome. If patient is ambulatory at diagnosis, 80-90% remain ambulatory after treatment. If already paraplegic, only 10% regain ambulation. EVERY HOUR COUNTS. Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV IMMEDIATELY (even before MRI), get MRI within 1 hour, consult radiation oncology and neurosurgery within 2 hours. Do NOT delay for "routine" MRI scheduling - this is a STAT test. Back pain + new weakness = MSCC until proven otherwise.
  • SVC Syndrome is NOT Always an Emergency Requiring Immediate Biopsy: Classic teaching says "never biopsy before diagnosis" is WRONG. Most SVC syndrome cases develop gradually over days to weeks and are NOT immediately life-threatening. The vast majority of patients can safely undergo tissue diagnosis (biopsy, bronchoscopy) before definitive treatment. Tissue diagnosis is CRITICAL because treatment differs: lymphoma gets chemotherapy, NSCLC gets radiation, SCLC gets chemo+radiation. Only give empiric steroids/radiation for TRUE emergencies: stridor, respiratory failure, severe cerebral edema. Otherwise, GET TISSUE FIRST.
  • Hypercalcemia of Malignancy Has TWO Distinct Mechanisms Requiring Different Long-term Management: (1) PTHrP-mediated (80%): squamous cell lung, RCC, breast - tumor secretes PTHrP which is NOT detected on standard PTH assay (need specific PTHrP test). Treat with bisphosphonates + treat tumor. (2) Osteolytic metastases (20%): breast, myeloma - direct bone destruction. PTH suppressed in BOTH. Distinguish by PTHrP level, bone scan, or clinical context. Long-term: monthly bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid 4 mg IV) or denosumab 120 mg SC prevent recurrent hypercalcemia and reduce skeletal-related events.
  • Calcitonin Works Fast but Doesn't Last - Use as Bridge Therapy Only: Calcitonin lowers calcium within 4-6 hours (fastest acting agent) but effect is modest (1-2 mg/dL decrease) and short-lived (tachyphylaxis after 48 hours). Bisphosphonates take 4-7 days to work but last weeks. Strategy: Use calcitonin for severe symptomatic hypercalcemia (Ca >14 mg/dL with confusion) as a bridge while waiting for bisphosphonates to kick in. Give BOTH together initially. After 48-72 hours, calcitonin becomes ineffective so discontinue.
  • Tumor Lysis Syndrome Prevention is Better Than Treatment: High-risk patients (high tumor burden Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukemias with WBC >50,000/µL, bulky lymphoma) should receive TLS prophylaxis BEFORE starting chemotherapy: aggressive hydration (3-4 L/day), allopurinol 300-600 mg daily, rasburicase for highest risk. Monitor labs q6-8h during first 48-72 hours after starting chemo. Once TLS develops with AKI, treatment is difficult and requires hemodialysis. Prevention saves kidneys.
  • Rasburicase is Contraindicated in G6PD Deficiency (Causes Severe Hemolysis): Rasburicase converts uric acid to hydrogen peroxide, which causes oxidative stress. In G6PD-deficient patients, this triggers massive hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, and can be fatal. ALWAYS check G6PD level before giving rasburicase. If G6PD deficient, use allopurinol + aggressive hydration only. African Americans, Mediterranean descent, Asians have higher G6PD deficiency prevalence.
  • Do NOT Aggressively Treat Hypocalcemia in Tumor Lysis Syndrome if Phosphate is Elevated: In TLS, calcium is LOW because it binds to phosphate (calcium-phosphate product). If you give IV calcium when phosphate is >5 mg/dL, you create metastatic calcification (calcium-phosphate crystals deposit in kidneys, heart, lungs, soft tissues), worsening organ damage. Only treat hypocalcemia if SYMPTOMATIC (tetany, seizures, QTc >500 ms) AND cautiously (small doses calcium gluconate 1 g IV slowly). Focus on lowering phosphate with binders and dialysis.
  • Loop Diuretics for Hypercalcemia Have Fallen Out of Favor: Old teaching: give aggressive saline PLUS furosemide to enhance calciuresis. Modern evidence shows loop diuretics provide minimal additional calcium lowering, increase risk of dehydration (which worsens hypercalcemia), cause electrolyte abnormalities, and may impair renal function. Current approach: aggressive saline hydration FIRST, then bisphosphonates. Only use furosemide if patient develops volume overload from aggressive fluids (CHF, renal failure). Do NOT use furosemide routinely.
  • Radiation Therapy is the Primary Treatment for MOST Malignant Spinal Cord Compression: Surgery is beneficial in SELECT patients: unknown primary (need tissue), spinal instability/fracture, radioresistant tumor (RCC, melanoma, sarcoma), previously irradiated spine, rapid neurologic decline despite radiation. For the majority of patients with known cancer and intact spine, EMERGENT radiation therapy (within 24 hours) is the standard. Exception: the landmark Patchell study showed surgical decompression FOLLOWED by radiation was superior to radiation alone in patients who were ambulatory, had good performance status, and had single-level compression from solid tumor metastases. Discuss with neurosurgery AND radiation oncology.
  • Denosumab is More Potent Than Bisphosphonates but Has Unique Toxicities: Denosumab (monoclonal antibody against RANKL) is superior to zoledronic acid for preventing skeletal-related events and treating hypercalcemia of malignancy. Advantages: can use in renal failure (unlike bisphosphonates), no renal toxicity, more potent. Disadvantages: (1) Rebound hypercalcemia when stopped (must transition to bisphosphonates if stopping), (2) Severe hypocalcemia if baseline low calcium or vitamin D deficiency (give calcium/vitamin D supplementation), (3) Increased osteonecrosis of jaw risk with long-term use. Dose: 120 mg SC weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Malignant spinal cord compression (ANY degree of weakness or bowel/bladder dysfunction) - neurosurgical emergency
  • Severe SVC syndrome with respiratory distress, stridor, or altered mental status
  • Severe hypercalcemia (ionized Ca >1.75 mmol/L or total Ca >15 mg/dL) with altered mental status
  • Clinical tumor lysis syndrome with acute kidney injury (Cr >2 mg/dL or oliguria)
  • Hyperkalemia >7.0 mEq/L or ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS)
  • Need for emergent hemodialysis (refractory hyperkalemia, severe AKI, fluid overload)
  • Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia)
  • Respiratory failure requiring intubation
  • Seizures (from hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia, or CNS involvement)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • No acute life-threatening emergency (no MSCC, severe SVC syndrome, severe hypercalcemia/TLS)
  • Hypercalcemia corrected or controlled (calcium <11.5 mg/dL, asymptomatic)
  • Tumor lysis syndrome resolved (electrolytes normalized, renal function stable)
  • SVC syndrome mild and stable (minimal symptoms, no respiratory compromise)
  • Definitive treatment plan in place (radiation therapy scheduled, chemotherapy regimen determined)
  • Close oncology follow-up arranged (within 1-7 days depending on urgency)
  • Adequate hydration maintained (able to drink 2-3 L/day)
  • No need for ongoing IV medications or interventions
  • Patient/family educated on warning signs to return (worsening weakness, confusion, respiratory distress, severe nausea/vomiting)
  • Pain controlled on oral medications
