119. ARDS (ACUTE RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME)

Global Definition 2024 • P/F or SpO2/FiO2 Ratio • Lung-Protective Ventilation • Prone Positioning
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure within 1 week of a predisposing risk factor (pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, transfusion, shock), with bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusions, atelectasis, or nodules.

Key Features (Global Definition 2024):

  • Timing: Within 1 week of the predisposing risk factor or of new or worsening respiratory symptoms
  • Hypoxemia: P/F ≤300 or SpO2/FiO2 ≤315 (if SpO2 ≤97%); intubated on PEEP ≥5 cm H2O, or not intubated on HFNC ≥30 L/min or NIV/CPAP ≥5 cm H2O
  • Bilateral opacities: On CXR or CT, or bilateral B lines and/or consolidations on ultrasound by a trained operator
  • Edema not primarily cardiogenic: ARDS can coexist with heart failure or fluid overload if a predisposing risk factor is present (echo helps)

Common Etiologies:

  • Pulmonary (Direct): Pneumonia (most common), aspiration, pulmonary contusion, inhalation injury, drowning
  • Extrapulmonary (Indirect): Sepsis (most common), pancreatitis, trauma, massive transfusion (TRALI), burns, drug overdose
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Global Definition of ARDS (2024; extends Berlin 2012) - All Required:

  • Risk factor and timing: Acute predisposing risk factor (pneumonia, nonpulmonary infection, trauma, transfusion, aspiration, shock); onset or worsening within 1 week of the risk factor or of new or worsening respiratory symptoms
  • Imaging: Bilateral opacities on CXR or CT, or bilateral B lines and/or consolidations on ultrasound (trained operator), not fully explained by effusions, atelectasis, or nodules/masses
  • Origin of edema: Not exclusively or primarily cardiogenic edema or fluid overload; ARDS can still be diagnosed when these coexist if a predisposing risk factor is present
  • Oxygenation:
    • Intubated: P/F ≤300 or SpO2/FiO2 ≤315 (if SpO2 ≤97%) on PEEP ≥5 cm H2O; graded mild, moderate, severe (below)
    • Not intubated: P/F ≤300 or SpO2/FiO2 ≤315 (if SpO2 ≤97%) on HFNC ≥30 L/min or NIV/CPAP with ≥5 cm H2O end-expiratory pressure
    • Resource-limited settings: SpO2/FiO2 ≤315 (if SpO2 ≤97%); no PEEP or minimum oxygen flow required
  • Measuring: At rest, at least 30 minutes after changes in position, FiO2, or flow (Global Definition). Pulse oximetry is less accurate in shock, with darker skin, or with SpO2 below 90%; ABG is preferred when available (SSC 2026)

Labs: ABG (P/F ratio calculation), CBC, CMP, lactate, procalcitonin, blood cultures, BNP/NT-proBNP (rule out cardiogenic)

Imaging: CXR (bilateral infiltrates), CT chest if diagnostic uncertainty, Echo (rule out cardiogenic pulmonary edema, assess RV function)

Additional: BAL if pneumonia suspected, respiratory viral panel, consider bronchoscopy

SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION (Intubated, PEEP ≥5; SpO2/FiO2 only if SpO2 ≤97%)
  • Mild ARDS: P/F >200 to ≤300 mmHg or SpO2/FiO2 >235 to ≤315 (Berlin 2012 cohort mortality 27%)
  • Moderate ARDS: P/F >100 to ≤200 mmHg or SpO2/FiO2 >148 to ≤235 (mortality 32%)
  • Severe ARDS: P/F ≤100 mmHg or SpO2/FiO2 ≤148 (mortality 45%)

P/F Ratio Calculation: PaO2 (from ABG) ÷ FiO2 (as decimal). Example: PaO2 80 on 60% FiO2 = 80/0.6 = 133 (moderate ARDS)

MANAGEMENT

Before Intubation (ATS 2026, acute hypoxemic respiratory failure):

  • HFNC: Recommended over standard oxygen (strong, moderate certainty). NIV or CPAP by facemask or helmet: suggested (conditional, low certainty). No recommendation between HFNC and NIV
  • Monitor closely and intubate promptly if gas exchange or work of breathing does not improve; persistent high inspiratory effort may injure the lung

Lung-Protective Ventilation (ATS 2024; ARDSNet protocol):

  • Low Tidal Volume: 6 mL/kg PREDICTED body weight (PBW), range 4-8 mL/kg, with plateau pressure <30 cm H2O (ATS 2024, strong; SSC 2026)
  • PBW Calculation: Male: 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches - 60); Female: 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches - 60)
  • Plateau Pressure: Measure with an inspiratory hold; if above 30 cm H2O, lower tidal volume toward 4 mL/kg (ARDSNet protocol)
  • PEEP:
    • Moderate-severe ARDS (P/F ≤200): Higher PEEP without recruitment maneuvers (ATS 2024, conditional, low to moderate certainty); SSC 2026 also suggests higher PEEP
    • Methods used in trials: Higher PEEP/FiO2 table, PEEP raised to the maximal safe plateau pressure, or titration to best compliance; monitor mechanics and blood pressure after each change
    • Mild ARDS: No recommendation; higher PEEP showed no benefit and a possible trend toward harm (ATS 2024)
  • Recruitment Maneuvers: Do NOT use prolonged maneuvers (PEEP >35 cm H2O for >60 seconds): strong recommendation against, higher mortality (ATS 2024). SSC 2026 also recommends against an incremental PEEP titration strategy
  • Driving Pressure (Plateau - PEEP): The ventilator variable most strongly associated with survival in an individual-patient analysis of 3,562 patients from 9 RCTs (Amato, NEJM 2015; observational). No trial-tested target; keeping it below about 15 cm H2O is Practical
  • Permissive Hypercapnia (Practical): Accept a lower pH and higher PaCO2 to keep tidal volume and plateau pressure protective; the ARDSNet protocol pH goal is 7.30-7.45

Oxygenation Goals (ARDSNet protocol):

  • SpO2: 88-95% (avoid hyperoxia)
  • PaO2: 55-80 mmHg

Adjunctive Therapies:

  • Prone Positioning: Severe ARDS: prone for more than 12 hours/day (ATS 2024, strong). PROSEVA enrolled P/F <150 on FiO2 ≥0.6 and PEEP ≥5, with sessions of at least 16 consecutive hours: 28-day mortality 16.0% vs 32.8%. SSC 2026 suggests prone >12 hours/day for sepsis with moderate-severe ARDS
  • Neuromuscular Blockade: Early (within 48 hours) severe ARDS (P/F ≤100): suggested (ATS 2024, conditional, low certainty). Mortality benefit was seen against deep sedation, not against light sedation (ROSE). Limit to 48 hours when possible; cisatracurium was used in the largest trials; bolus or infusion (ATS 2024). SSC 2026 suggests intermittent boluses over continuous infusion in sepsis-associated moderate-severe ARDS
  • Corticosteroids: Suggested for ARDS (ATS 2024, conditional, moderate certainty; mortality RR 0.84). Optimal regimen unknown. One trial regimen: dexamethasone 20 mg IV daily on days 1-5, then 10 mg daily on days 6-10, stopped at extubation (DEXA-ARDS: P/F ≤200 on PEEP ≥10; 60-day mortality 21% vs 36%). Severe CAP, COVID-19, or PJP with HIV: use those established regimens. Starting more than 2 weeks after ARDS onset may cause harm. Monitor glucose (serious hyperglycemia RR 1.11) and infection, especially if immunocompromised
  • Conservative Fluid Management: After shock resolves, target CVP <4 or PAOP <8 mmHg (FACTT: more ventilator-free days, 14.6 vs 12.1; no difference in 60-day mortality)

Refractory Hypoxemia:

  • First: Confirm low tidal volume, higher PEEP, prone positioning, and neuromuscular blockade are in place before escalating (ATS 2024)
  • Inhaled Pulmonary Vasodilators: Inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation transiently but does not reduce mortality and increases renal impairment (Cochrane 2016). Inhaled epoprostenol: oxygenation rescue only (Practical)
  • VV-ECMO: Suggested in selected severe ARDS (ATS 2024, conditional, low certainty; pooled mortality RR 0.76). Candidates: reversible cause, P/F <80 or pH <7.25 with PaCO2 ≥60 despite optimal care, and early (<7 days of ventilation). Futility risks: irreversible cause, ventilation >7 days, immunosuppression, multiorgan failure, older age, bleeding or contraindication to anticoagulation, life expectancy <1 year, CNS hemorrhage. Discuss early with an ECMO center and transfer when feasible
  • High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation: Recommended against routine use in moderate or severe ARDS (ATS 2024, strong, high certainty)
TREAT UNDERLYING CAUSE
  • Sepsis: Early antibiotics, source control
  • Pneumonia: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, consider fungal/viral coverage
  • Aspiration: Antibiotics only if clear infection (not routine for aspiration pneumonitis)
  • Pancreatitis: Supportive care, NPO, IV fluids
  • TRALI: Supportive care, avoid implicated donor
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • PREDICTED Body Weight is Critical: ALWAYS use predicted (ideal) body weight for tidal volume calculation, NOT actual weight. Obese patients don't have bigger lungs. Using actual weight in obesity leads to dangerous over-ventilation and VILI.
  • Driving Pressure Tracks Lung Stress: Driving pressure (Plateau - PEEP) was the ventilator variable most strongly linked to survival in an individual-patient analysis of 3,562 patients; lower tidal volume or higher PEEP helped only when driving pressure fell (Amato, NEJM 2015; observational). Example: Pplat 28 with PEEP 16 gives a driving pressure of 12.
  • Prone Early and Prone Long: Don't wait until the patient is moribund. PROSEVA proned early (P/F <150 on FiO2 ≥0.6) for at least 16 consecutive hours per session and cut 28-day mortality from 32.8% to 16.0%. ATS 2024 strongly recommends prone positioning for more than 12 hours/day in severe ARDS.
  • Conservative Fluids AFTER Resuscitation: FACTT's conservative strategy gave more ventilator-free days without changing 60-day mortality, and it applies after shock resolves. Don't withhold fluids from a hypotensive septic patient to "keep lungs dry."
  • ARDS is a Syndrome, Not a Disease: Always search for and treat the underlying cause. ARDS from pneumonia needs antibiotics; ARDS from pancreatitis needs supportive care. The ventilator strategy is the same, but disease-specific treatment differs.
  • Higher PEEP Only in Moderate-Severe ARDS: Older single trials (ALVEOLI, LOV, ExPress) showed no mortality difference, but pooled analyses favor higher PEEP without recruitment maneuvers in moderate-severe ARDS (network meta-analysis RR 0.77), with possible harm in mild ARDS and higher mortality with prolonged recruitment maneuvers (ATS 2024).
  • Don't Anchor on the CXR: Bilateral infiltrates can look identical in ARDS and cardiogenic pulmonary edema; use BNP, echo, and clinical context. The two can coexist: ARDS can be diagnosed with heart failure or fluid overload present if a predisposing risk factor exists (Global Definition 2024).
  • Steroids Early, Not Late: ATS 2024 suggests corticosteroids for ARDS, but starting more than 2 weeks after onset may cause harm. Many trials stopped them at extubation.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • All ARDS patients require ICU care
  • Need for invasive mechanical ventilation
  • Refractory hypoxemia despite high-flow nasal cannula or NIV
  • P/F ratio <200 (moderate-severe ARDS)
  • Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors
  • Need for prone positioning
  • Consideration for ECMO
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Liberated from mechanical ventilation for >48 hours
  • Stable on room air or low-flow O2 (≤4L NC) with SpO2 >92%
  • Oxygenation stable at rest and with exertion on room air or low-flow O2 (Practical)
  • Underlying cause treated and resolving
  • No ongoing need for ICU-level monitoring
  • Pulmonary rehab referral if prolonged ventilation
  • Follow-up arranged (pulmonary clinic in 2-4 weeks)
  • Patient educated on gradual recovery timeline (weeks to months)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Propofol, 💊 Midazolam, 💊 Fentanyl, 💊 Rocuronium, 💊 Succinylcholine, 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Dexamethasone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated A-a Gradient, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

120. ACUTE PULMONARY EDEMA / FLASH PULMONARY EDEMA

Cardiogenic vs Non-Cardiogenic • BiPAP • Diuresis • Afterload Reduction
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Acute onset severe dyspnea, orthopnea, pink frothy sputum, diffuse crackles/rales, hypoxemia. Often with hypertension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and anxiety ("air hunger").

Flash Pulmonary Edema: Rapid onset (minutes to hours), often with severe hypertension, may occur without significant fluid overload. Common in renal artery stenosis, acute MR, acute MI, and hypertensive crisis.

Key Features:

  • Symptoms: Severe dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, cough with pink frothy sputum
  • Signs: Tachypnea, hypoxemia, diffuse crackles, JVD, S3 gallop, lower extremity edema (may be absent in flash)
  • Vital Signs: Hypertension common (may be hypotensive if cardiogenic shock), tachycardia, low SpO2

Differentiate from ARDS:

  • Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema: Natriuretic peptides above the rule-in thresholds below, echo evidence of LV dysfunction or valve disease, cardiac history. Practical: rapid response to diuretics or vasodilators supports it
  • ARDS/Non-cardiogenic: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure from lung inflammation with a risk factor (e.g., sepsis, pneumonia); edema not exclusively or primarily attributable to cardiogenic edema or fluid overload, though ARDS can be diagnosed alongside them when an ARDS risk factor is present. The 2023 global definition has no PCWP criterion (Matthay, AJRCCM 2024)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Immediate: SpO2, ECG (ischemia, arrhythmia), CXR (cardiomegaly, cephalization, Kerley B lines, effusions, bat-wing infiltrates)

Labs: BNP/NT-proBNP (elevated in cardiogenic), troponin (rule out ACS), BMP (renal function, electrolytes), CBC, ABG if severe

Imaging: CXR portable, bedside echo (LV function, valve pathology, pericardial effusion), lung ultrasound (B-lines)

Consider: CT chest if uncertain etiology, cardiac catheterization if ACS suspected

BNP Interpretation:

  • BNP <100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL: Heart failure unlikely (NT-proBNP <300: 98% NPV in ICON)
  • BNP >400 pg/mL, or NT-proBNP >450 (age <50), >900 (50-75), or >1800 pg/mL (>75): Heart failure likely (ICON, Eur Heart J 2006; validated in ICON-RELOADED, JACC 2018; same as the ADHF card)
  • Gray zone values: Use clinical context
MANAGEMENT

Immediate Interventions (First 30 Minutes):

  • Position: Sit patient upright (reduces preload)
  • Oxygen: Only for hypoxemia: SpO2 <90% or PaO2 <60 mmHg (ESC 2026 I C). Indiscriminate O2 in non-hypoxemic patients may be harmful (ESC 2026)
  • BiPAP/CPAP: Start NIV as soon as possible for respiratory distress (RR >25, SpO2 <90%) to relieve distress and avoid intubation (ESC 2026 IIa B2). CPAP or bilevel both acceptable, no evidence favoring one (ERS/ATS 2017, strong rec; pooled mortality RR 0.80, intubation RR 0.60); that recommendation excludes ACS and cardiogenic shock. Caution in hypotension or low preload reserve (e.g., RV failure): NIV lowers venous return, cardiac output, and BP (ESC 2026). Practical: bilevel if hypercapnic; typical start BiPAP 10/5, titrate to 15/10
  • IV Access: Establish immediately for medications

Medical Therapy:

  • Nitroglycerin (key therapy when SBP is high, especially flash/SCAPE): Without systemic hypotension, IV nitroglycerin may be considered as an adjunct to diuretics for dyspnea relief (AHA 2022 2b B-NR); ESC 2026 also allows it as initial therapy when SBP >110 mmHg (IIb C); lowered intubation risk in a meta-analysis but no effect on death or length of stay; monitor BP closely, vasodilator hypotension is harmful (ESC 2026). Dosing (same as the ADHF card): start 10-20 mcg/min (label: 5 mcg/min with non-PVC tubing), increase by 5-10 mcg/min every 3-5 min to symptom/BP response; usual max ~200 mcg/min. Practical: SL 400 mcg q5min can bridge until IV access. Contraindicated with a PDE5 inhibitor or riociguat. High-dose NTG with elevated BP (SCAPE): consider as a safe and effective option (ACEP 2022 Level C, consensus; Ann Emerg Med 2022;80:e31-e59, doi:10.1016/j.annemergmed.2022.05.027); ESC 2026 does not address dose. ACEP: infusions up to 400 mcg/min have been called standard dosing; some consider ≥200 mcg/min high dose; 2,000 mcg IV boluses q3-5 min have been described. Regimens studied in SCAPE: ≥100 mcg/min infusion, or 600-1000 mcg IV bolus then 100 mcg/min. Evidence: one small open-label RCT (26 vs 26) showed faster symptom resolution (Siddiqua, Emerg Med J 2024, doi:10.1136/emermed-2023-213285); a 2026 meta-analysis (3 comparative studies, 534 patients) found faster BP and symptom improvement but no reduction in intubation (RR 0.91) or ICU admission (RR 0.92) and more hypotension (RR 1.41; 95% CI 1.02-1.94) (Jandali, Am J Emerg Med 2026;110:453-465, doi:10.1016/j.ajem.2026.09.014). If used: arterial line and continuous BP monitoring (Practical)
  • Furosemide (when volume overloaded): Prompt IV loop diuretic for significant fluid overload (AHA 2022 Class 1 B-NR; ESC 2026 I A). Doses (AHA 2022 gives none; from ESC 2026 Fig 15): diuretic-naive 40 mg IV; on a home loop diuretic, IV dose 2× the daily oral dose; higher starting dose in CKD. Adequate response: spot urine Na ≥70 mmol/L at 2 h or urine output ≥100 mL/h over the first 6 h; if not, double the dose (ESC 2026). APO from fluid redistribution without total-body overload usually does not need high diuretic doses but may need vasodilators (ESC 2026 7.3.3)
  • Morphine/opiates: NOT routine (ESC 2026 III C). Limit to carefully selected patients with severe anxiety or distress refractory to other treatment, or severe/intractable pain; risk of respiratory failure (ESC 2026). Practical: if used, 2-4 mg IV

Hypertensive Pulmonary Edema:

  • Setting: BP >180/120 with pulmonary edema is a hypertensive emergency: ICU admission for continuous BP and target organ monitoring and parenteral therapy (2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline 1, B-NR)
  • Goal: Lower SBP by no more than 25% in the first hour; if stable, to <160/100 over the next 2-6 h, then cautiously to 130-140 over 24-48 h (2025 AHA/ACC BP 1, C-LD). In acute HF with severe hypertension, small trials showed less dyspnea when SBP fell about 15% (20-40 mmHg) within 30 min without added harm
  • Preferred agents (2025 AHA/ACC BP Table 27): Clevidipine, nitroglycerin, or nitroprusside. Clevidipine: 1-2 mg/h, doubling every 90 s until near target, then smaller increases every 5-10 min (max 21 mg/h, max 72 h); contraindicated with soy or egg allergy or defective lipid metabolism. Nitroprusside: 0.3-0.5 mcg/kg/min, increase by 0.5 every 5 min (max 10), shortest possible duration, arterial line (Table 26). FDA boxed warning: precipitous hypotension (continuous BP monitoring) and lethal dose-related cyanide toxicity; avoid with a PDE5 inhibitor or riociguat. Nitroglycerin dosing: see Medical Therapy above. Nicardipine is not among the Table 27 agents for pulmonary edema
  • Avoid: Beta blockers (contraindicated in acute pulmonary edema, 2025 AHA/ACC BP Table 27). Practical: avoid aggressive diuresis before afterload reduction when there is no volume overload

Hypotensive Pulmonary Edema (Cardiogenic Shock):

  • Vasopressors: Norepinephrine preferred in cardiogenic shock to raise BP and organ perfusion (ESC 2026 IIb C); dopamine caused more arrhythmias than norepinephrine in an RCT of shock (ESC 2026)
  • Inotropes: In cardiogenic shock, IV inotropic support should be used to maintain systemic perfusion and end-organ function (AHA 2022 Class 1 B-NR). ESC 2026 is more restrictive: SBP <90 with hypoperfusion not responding to standard treatment, including a fluid challenge (IIb C), not routine (arrhythmia and ischemia risk). Milrinone and dobutamine performed alike in an RCT; on a beta-blocker, milrinone (or levosimendan where available) may be preferred over dobutamine (ESC 2026)
  • Mechanical support: Temporary MCS is reasonable when end-organ function cannot be maintained pharmacologically, with management by a multidisciplinary shock team (AHA 2022 2a B-NR each); if not rapidly responding, consider triage to an MCS-capable center (2b C-LD). ESC 2026 detail: Shock Team for any MCS candidate (I C); STEMI shock with LV dysfunction and no risk of hypoxic brain injury: microaxial flow pump (Impella) should be considered (IIa B1); unselected AMI shock: temporary MCS not recommended, risk of harm (III B1); unselected cardiogenic shock: IABP not recommended (III B1); MI mechanical complication: MCS as a bridge (IIa C)
  • Avoid: Aggressive diuresis without hemodynamic support

Refractory Cases:

  • Ultrafiltration: Role uncertain; may be considered in selected patients with insufficient response to diuretic escalation (ESC 2026)
  • Intubation: For persistent or progressive respiratory failure despite O2 or NIV (ESC 2026 I C): cardiac or respiratory arrest; worsening mental status; PaO2 <60, PaCO2 >50, and pH <7.35 despite NIV, or NIV intolerance; persistent hemodynamic instability; need for airway protection
  • Urgent cardiology/cardiac surgery: If acute valvular pathology (acute MR, acute AI)
IDENTIFY AND TREAT PRECIPITANTS
  • ACS: Troponin, ECG → cardiology/cath lab
  • Arrhythmia: Rate control for AF with RVR, cardioversion if unstable
  • Hypertensive crisis: Aggressive BP control
  • Acute valvular disease: Urgent echo, surgical evaluation
  • Medication non-adherence: Restart home medications
  • Dietary indiscretion: Sodium/fluid restriction education
  • Renal artery stenosis: Consider if flash pulmonary edema with minimal fluid overload
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • NIV Unloads the Heart: Positive intrathoracic pressure lowers venous return (preload) and LV transmural pressure (afterload), so many patients improve on CPAP/BiPAP before any diuretic works. Don't skip it. The same physiology can drop cardiac output and BP: use caution in hypotension or preload-dependent states such as RV failure (ESC 2026).
  • Flash Pulmonary Edema ≠ Fluid Overload: Flash pulmonary edema is often due to acute afterload increase (hypertensive crisis) or acute valvular pathology, NOT total body volume overload. These patients may have normal weight and no peripheral edema. Treat with vasodilators, not just diuretics.
  • Renal Artery Stenosis Pearl: Bilateral RAS is a classic cause of "flash pulmonary edema" - acute, severe pulmonary edema that resolves quickly but recurs. Suspect in patients with resistant hypertension, acute rise in creatinine with ACE-I, or minimal peripheral edema during episodes.
  • Morphine is Out: Traditional teaching was "LMNOP" (Lasix, Morphine, Nitrates, Oxygen, Position). Routine opiates are now not recommended because of risk of harm (ESC 2026 III C). Its basis, the MIMO RCT (open-label, stopped early, 111 patients with ACPE plus dyspnea and anxiety): no difference in in-hospital mortality, morphine 17.9% vs midazolam 12.7% (p=0.60), but more serious adverse events with morphine, 42.9% vs 18.2% (p=0.007) (Dominguez-Rodriguez, Eur J Heart Fail 2022;24:1953-62, doi:10.1002/ejhf.2602). Reserve for refractory severe anxiety/distress or intractable pain.
  • Wet and Warm vs. Wet and Cold: "Wet and warm" (congested but adequate perfusion) - diurese aggressively. "Wet and cold" (congested AND hypoperfused) - need inotropes/vasopressors before aggressive diuresis or patient will crash.
  • The BNP Gray Zone: BNP 100-400 is the "gray zone." Use clinical context: obese patients have lower BNP, renal failure causes higher BNP, AF causes higher BNP. Trend from baseline is often more useful than absolute value.
  • Don't Forget the Echo: Bedside echo in the ED/ICU can rapidly differentiate cardiogenic (reduced EF, elevated E/e', valve pathology) from non-cardiogenic (normal LV function) pulmonary edema. This guides therapy immediately.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Requiring intubation or failing BiPAP
  • Hypotension (SBP <90) or cardiogenic shock
  • Need for IV vasoactive medications (pressors, inotropes, nitroprusside)
  • Acute coronary syndrome as precipitant
  • New/worsening acute valvular pathology
  • Refractory hypoxemia despite BiPAP
  • Hemodynamic instability or arrhythmias
  • Need for mechanical circulatory support
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Symptoms resolved or returned to baseline
  • Off supplemental O2 or at baseline O2 requirement
  • Stable on oral diuretics with adequate urine output
  • Weight stable or decreasing (not gaining)
  • No IV vasoactive medications for >24 hours
  • Precipitant identified and addressed
  • Transitioned to oral heart failure medications
  • Clinical evidence of congestion resolved before discharge (AHA 2022 Class 1 B-NR); ESC 2026 adds a structured pre-discharge check: exam, natriuretic peptide, kidney function and electrolytes, imaging (I C)
  • Follow-up generally within 7 days of discharge (AHA 2022 2a B-NR); rapid initiation and uptitration of foundational HF therapy with frequent visits over the first 6 weeks (ESC 2026 I B2)
  • Patient educated on daily weights, sodium restriction, medication adherence
  • Clear return precautions given
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Nitroglycerin, 💊 Morphine, 💊 Norepinephrine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

121. VIRAL HEPATITIS (ACUTE)

HAV • HBV • HCV • Acute Liver Failure Risk • Serologic Diagnosis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Prodrome of fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nausea, RUQ discomfort, followed by jaundice, dark urine (bilirubinuria), pale stools. May have low-grade fever. Many cases are anicteric (subclinical).

By Virus Type:

  • Hepatitis A (HAV): Fecal-oral: person-to-person contact or contaminated food or water. Risk groups: travel to endemic countries, MSM, drug use (injection or not), homelessness. Incubation average 28 days (range 15-50). Jaundice in more than 70% of older children and adults; 70% of infections under age 6 are asymptomatic. No chronic infection, but 10-15% of symptomatic patients have prolonged or relapsing illness for up to 6 months (ACIP 2020). Practical: peak ALT often >1000
  • Hepatitis B (HBV): Blood or body fluid exposure (sexual, perinatal, needlestick, injection drug use). Incubation average 90 days (range 60-150) to jaundice. Symptomatic in 30-50% of older children and adults. Chronic infection in 80-90% of those infected in infancy, 30% infected before age 6, and less than 1% to 12% infected as older children or adults (ACIP 2018)
  • Hepatitis C (HCV): Parenteral blood exposure, mostly injection drug use; also needlestick, and condomless receptive anal sex, mainly among MSM. Usually asymptomatic; jaundice in less than 25%. Spontaneous clearance in 20-50%; the rest become chronic (AASLD/IDSA)
  • Hepatitis D (HDV): Only with HBV (requires HBsAg). Acute HBV-HDV coinfection progresses to ALF in up to 20%, and HDV superinfection in 5%, with up to 80% mortality without transplant (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Hepatitis E (HEV): Fecal-oral; genotype 1 in endemic areas. Underrecognized in Western countries: in US and German studies, up to one fifth to one half of ALF attributed to drug injury was HEV (ACG 2023 ALF). Usually self-limited. In pregnancy, genotype 1 (especially third trimester) can progress to liver failure and death (CDC Yellow Book 2024), with mortality as high as 25% (ACG 2023 ALF). Genotype 3 can become chronic in immunosuppressed patients, especially solid organ transplant recipients (CDC Yellow Book 2024)

Severity Spectrum:

  • Mild: Practical: elevated transaminases, no jaundice, preserved synthetic function
  • Moderate: Practical: jaundice and symptoms, but normal INR and mental status
  • Acute Liver Failure: Encephalopathy (any grade) plus coagulopathy (INR 1.5 or higher), illness under 26 weeks, no preexisting liver disease (ACG 2023)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Labs: AST/ALT, total/direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, GGT, albumin, INR/PT, CBC. Practical: AST/ALT often >10× ULN in acute viral hepatitis

Viral Serologies:

  • Hepatitis A: IgM anti-HAV for acute infection; test only symptomatic patients with suspected HAV, to limit false positives. Total anti-HAV positive with IgM negative means immunity from past infection or vaccination (ACIP 2020)
  • Hepatitis B: HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc (IgM for acute, total for any exposure), HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA
  • Hepatitis C: Suspected acute HCV: test both HCV antibody and HCV RNA (AASLD/IDSA, I, C). Antibody may be negative for the first 6 weeks after exposure. Acute infection: RNA positive with antibody negative, or new seroconversion after a prior negative antibody (AASLD/IDSA)
  • Hepatitis D: Anti-HDV (only if HBsAg positive)
  • Hepatitis E: IgM anti-HEV; HEV RNA in serum or stool confirms. Immunosuppressed: repeated positive HEV RNA suggests chronic HEV whatever the antibody result (CDC Yellow Book 2024). Test with endemic exposure, pregnancy, immunosuppression, or ALF labeled drug-induced (ACG 2023 ALF)

HBV Serology Interpretation:

  • Acute HBV: HBsAg+, total and IgM anti-HBc+, anti-HBs-, HBV DNA+. HBsAg alone early in infection, or transiently up to 18 days after vaccination
  • Acute Resolving (Window): HBsAg-, IgM anti-HBc+, anti-HBs + or -
  • Chronic HBV: HBsAg+ for more than 6 months, total anti-HBc+, IgM anti-HBc-, anti-HBs-
  • Recovered (Immune): HBsAg-, anti-HBc+, anti-HBs+
  • Vaccinated: Anti-HBs+ only (immune if 10 mIU/mL or more after a complete series)
  • Isolated anti-HBc (IgM-): False positive, past infection with waned anti-HBs, or low-level chronic infection; HBV DNA detectable in less than 10% (ACIP 2018)

Additional Studies: Exclude other or coexisting causes (other hepatitis viruses, HDV if HBsAg positive, autoimmune hepatitis) and test for HIV (AASLD/IDSA). Practical: RUQ ultrasound to rule out biliary obstruction; consider Wilson disease and drug-induced injury

MANAGEMENT

General Supportive Care (All Types):

  • Hydration: Practical: IV fluids if poor oral intake or vomiting
  • Antiemetics: Practical: ondansetron for nausea
  • Avoid hepatotoxins: No alcohol; avoid acetaminophen in acute HCV (AASLD/IDSA). Practical: limit acetaminophen in other types and review all medications
  • Avoid sedatives: Practical: risk of encephalopathy if liver function declining
  • Isolation (HAV): Standard precautions, plus contact precautions if incontinent (ACIP 2020). Practical: same approach for HEV

Hepatitis A:

  • Supportive care; no proven antiviral. HAV ALF: early transplant, when needed, has good outcomes (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis for unvaccinated contacts, as soon as possible and within 2 weeks of exposure (ACIP 2020):
    • Healthy, 12 months to 40 years: 1 dose of single-antigen HepA vaccine
    • Over 40 years: HepA vaccine; add IG 0.1 mL/kg IM based on provider risk assessment
    • Immunocompromised or chronic liver disease (12 months or older): HepA vaccine plus IG 0.1 mL/kg, at separate sites
    • Under 12 months or vaccine contraindicated: IG 0.1 mL/kg only
    • Second vaccine dose at 6 months for long-term immunity (not needed for PEP). Twinrix is not used for PEP. Efficacy beyond 2 weeks is not established
  • ALF is rare (less than 1%) but was more frequent in the outbreaks since 2016; risk is higher with older age and chronic liver disease (ACIP 2020)

Hepatitis B (Acute):

  • About 95% of acute infections in immunocompetent adults resolve; supportive care (ACIP 2018)
  • Antiviral therapy only if: acute liver failure, or a protracted, severe course: total bilirubin >3 mg/dL (direct >1.5), INR >1.5, encephalopathy, or ascites (AASLD 2018)
  • Preferred antivirals: Entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), until HBsAg clearance is confirmed, or indefinitely after liver transplant; peginterferon is contraindicated (AASLD 2018). Doses: entecavir 0.5 mg PO daily, 1 mg for decompensated liver disease; TDF 300 mg PO daily; TAF 25 mg PO daily, not recommended in Child-Pugh B or C; adjust entecavir and TDF for renal function (FDA labels)
  • HBV ALF: Antiviral benefit in primary acute infection is uncertain; for ALF from HBV reactivation, start entecavir- or tenofovir-based therapy (ACG 2023, Rec 8, strong). Up to 75% of patients with HBV ALF need transplant or die (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months means chronic infection (ACIP 2018): manage per chronic HBV guidance
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (nonoccupational): Unvaccinated, HBsAg-positive source: HBIG plus HepB vaccine series, preferably within 24 h (effective window likely no more than 7 days after percutaneous or 14 days after sexual exposure). Unvaccinated, unknown source: vaccine series alone. Documented complete series without post-vaccination testing: 1 vaccine dose if source HBsAg-positive, nothing if source unknown (ACIP 2018)

Hepatitis C (Acute):

  • Spontaneous clearance in 20-50%, mostly within 6 months; one undetectable RNA does not prove clearance (AASLD/IDSA)
  • Treat at diagnosis once HCV RNA is quantifiable, without waiting for spontaneous clearance (AASLD/IDSA, I, B), with the same regimens as for chronic HCV (IIa, C); shortened courses (eg, 6 weeks) are not recommended (AASLD/IDSA 2023 update)
  • Monitor ALT, AST, and bilirubin (INR if bilirubin rising) every 2-4 weeks; avoid alcohol and acetaminophen; refer to addiction medicine if related to substance use. INR >1.5 or any sign of ALF: refer to a liver transplant center immediately (AASLD/IDSA)
  • Antiviral post-exposure prophylaxis is not recommended (AASLD/IDSA, III, C)

Acute Liver Failure Management:

  • Hepatology consultation as soon as ALF is identified and early contact with a transplant center; transfer early if at risk of poor outcome (ACG 2023)
  • ICU for grade 2 or higher encephalopathy; intubate for grade 3-4. Monitor and correct glucose, fluids, and electrolytes; assess early for infection, since signs are often absent. INR does not reflect bleeding risk (ACG 2023)
  • IV N-acetylcysteine is suggested in non-acetaminophen ALF (ACG 2023, Rec 7); the US trial benefit was in early coma grade (I-II)
  • Prognosis: King's College Criteria or MELD; meeting KCC or MELD >25 means high risk of poor outcome (ACG 2023, Rec 10)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • The "Hepatitis A Doesn't Kill" Myth: ALF is rare (less than 1%), but severity rises with age, adults over 40 are more often hospitalized, and chronic liver disease (including HBV and HCV) raises the risk of fulminant hepatitis. Vaccinate everyone with chronic liver disease (ACIP 2020)
  • IgM Anti-HBc is the Key to Acute HBV: In acute resolving infection (the window), HBsAg can be negative before anti-HBs appears, while IgM anti-HBc is positive (ACIP 2018). In HBV ALF, HBsAg and HBV DNA may be undetectable at presentation (ACG 2023 ALF). Don't miss acute HBV because you only checked HBsAg.
  • Acute HCV Needs an RNA Test: HCV antibody may be negative for the first 6 weeks after exposure, and seroconversion may be delayed or absent with immunosuppression (eg, HIV with CD4 <200). Diagnose by RNA positive with antibody negative, or documented seroconversion. RNA can be transiently negative: repeat it if suspicion is high (AASLD/IDSA)
  • Practical: AST/ALT >10,000 is Usually Ischemic, Not Viral: While viral hepatitis causes very high transaminases, levels >10,000 U/L are more suggestive of ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) or acetaminophen toxicity. Viral hepatitis typically peaks in the 1,000-3,000 range.
  • Always Check INR, Not Just Transaminases: In acute HCV, INR >1.5 or any sign of ALF means immediate referral to a transplant center (AASLD/IDSA); ALF is INR 1.5 or higher with encephalopathy (ACG 2023). Practical: ALT 50 with INR 3.0 is sicker than ALT 5000 with INR 1.0; transaminases reflect hepatocyte injury, not function
  • HBV Reactivation is a Real and Preventable Problem: Test HBsAg and anti-HBc before any immunosuppressive, cytotoxic, or immunomodulatory therapy. HBsAg-positive: start entecavir, TDF, or TAF before (or at the latest with) therapy and continue at least 6 months after it ends (12 months after anti-CD20). HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive: monitor ALT, HBV DNA, and HBsAg and treat on demand, except prophylaxis with anti-CD20 therapy (eg, rituximab) or stem cell transplant (AASLD 2018). ALF from reactivation: start antivirals (ACG 2023, strong)
  • Hepatitis E in Pregnancy is an Emergency: Mortality as high as 25% (ACG 2023 ALF), from genotype 1, especially in the third trimester (CDC Yellow Book 2024); DIC is a distinctive feature of HEV ALF in pregnancy. Pregnancy-related ALF: multidisciplinary care and prompt delivery (ACG 2023). Pregnant patient with acute hepatitis and endemic exposure: test for HEV; Practical: involve OB and hepatology immediately
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • INR >1.5 or any encephalopathy: contact a liver transplant center (AASLD/IDSA; ACG 2023)
  • Grade 2 or higher encephalopathy: ICU; grade 3-4: intubate for airway protection (ACG 2023)
  • Practical: Hypoglycemia (liver unable to maintain glucose)
  • Practical: Acute kidney injury (hepatorenal physiology)
  • Practical: Hemodynamic instability
  • Practical: Need for frequent monitoring (q1-2h labs)
  • Liver transplant evaluation: transfer early if at risk of poor outcome (ACG 2023)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Tolerating oral intake without significant nausea/vomiting
  • Practical: INR ≤1.5 and stable or improving
  • Practical: Bilirubin stable or downtrending (peak may take 1-2 weeks)
  • Practical: No hepatic encephalopathy
  • Practical: Transaminases downtrending (don't need to be normal)
  • Practical: Hepatology/GI follow-up arranged within 1-2 weeks
  • Practical: Patient educated on alcohol avoidance, hepatotoxic medication avoidance
  • Close contacts offered post-exposure prophylaxis: HAV within 2 weeks of exposure (ACIP 2020); HBV by exposure and vaccination status (ACIP 2018)
  • Practical: Return precautions: confusion, worsening jaundice, bleeding
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sofosbuvir-Velpatasvir, 💊 Glecaprevir-Pibrentasvir, 💊 N-Acetylcysteine, 💊 Ondansetron
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hepatitis Panel, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Bilirubin, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Low Albumin
↑ Back to Table of Contents

122. ISCHEMIC HEPATITIS (SHOCK LIVER)

Hypoperfusion Injury • Massive Transaminase Elevation • Rapid Resolution
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Marked aminotransferase rise (AST often >10,000 U/L) after reduced hepatic blood flow or oxygen delivery: heart failure, cardiogenic or septic shock, cardiac arrest, severe hypoxemia, trauma, or major surgery (ACG 2023 ALF). Also called hypoxic hepatitis. A documented hypotensive episode is not always found (ACG 2023 ALF); it is absent in up to half of cases (Waseem 2016)

Diagnostic Criteria:

  • Setting: Cardiac, circulatory, or respiratory failure (Waseem 2016)
  • Marked aminotransferase rise: 20 times ULN is the usual cutoff; some studies use 2.5-10 times (Waseem 2016)
  • Exclusion of other causes, especially viral or drug-induced hepatitis; supported by a rapid fall once perfusion is restored (Waseem 2016)

Common Causes:

  • Cardiac (39-70%): Acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, acute MI, arrhythmias with hypotension (Waseem 2016)
  • Sepsis (about 23%): Septic shock (Waseem 2016)
  • Respiratory (about 15%): Severe hypoxemia, respiratory failure. Cardiac, septic, and respiratory causes together account for over 90% (Waseem 2016)
  • Hypovolemic: Trauma, major surgery (ACG 2023 ALF). Practical: hemorrhagic shock, severe dehydration
  • Obstructive: Practical: massive PE, cardiac tamponade

Key Differentiator: The time course: aminotransferases peak early and fall quickly once perfusion is restored (AHA 2017) (Waseem 2016). Hemodynamic instability is often, but not always, documented; suspect ischemic injury in heart failure with hepatic congestion even without recorded hypotension (Waseem 2016)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Pattern:

  • AST/ALT: Massive elevation; >10,000 U/L is generally seen only with shock liver or drug or toxin injury (ACG 2017)
  • AST > ALT: Generally AST-predominant (ACG 2017, Table 4)
  • LDH: Markedly elevated; an ALT/LDH ratio <1.5 favors ischemic injury (AHA 2017). Viral hepatitis has lower LDH peaks (Waseem 2016)
  • Bilirubin: Often normal at first, then rises with the INR while aminotransferases improve (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • INR/PT: Prothrombin time often rises (AHA 2017); INR 1.5 or higher with encephalopathy means acute liver failure (ACG 2023)
  • Practical: Lactate: Often elevated due to underlying shock

Timeline:

  • Peak: AST, ALT, bilirubin, LDH, and PT peak at 24-72 hours (AHA 2017); some series report the aminotransferase peak within 24 hours (Waseem 2016)
  • Bilirubin: Rises while aminotransferases fall (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Resolution: Aminotransferases fall to about half of peak 24-72 hours after the peak (Waseem 2016) and return to baseline within 5-10 days (AHA 2017) to 2 weeks (Waseem 2016) once perfusion is restored

Exclude Other Causes:

  • Acetaminophen toxicity: Level and history; ALT or AST >15 times ULN or >10,000 calls for assessing acetaminophen toxicity and ischemic hepatopathy (ACG 2017, Rec 18)
  • Viral hepatitis: HAV IgM, HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, HCV RNA (ACG 2017, Rec 17)
  • Budd-Chiari syndrome: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction causes severe intrahepatic ischemia (ACG 2023 ALF); ultrasound with Doppler
  • Biliary obstruction: Practical: RUQ ultrasound
  • Autoimmune hepatitis: ANA, ASMA, globulin or IgG level, particularly with other autoimmune conditions (ACG 2017, Rec 8)

Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler (ACG 2023 ALF workup) to exclude Budd-Chiari syndrome and biliary obstruction; a dilated IVC and hepatic veins from passive congestion support hypoxic hepatitis (Waseem 2016)

MANAGEMENT

Primary Goal: Restore Hepatic Perfusion

  • Treat underlying cause: The only established treatment (Waseem 2016); care is supportive, aimed at restoring hemodynamic stability (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Optimize cardiac output: Treat heart failure and arrhythmias; dobutamine has been proposed for low cardiac index, based on small studies (Waseem 2016)
  • Restore blood pressure: Vasopressors as needed to maintain MAP (ACG 2023 ALF). Septic shock: initial MAP target 65 mm Hg (SSC 2026, strong), 60-65 mm Hg if 65 or older (SSC 2026, conditional). Cardiogenic shock: no validated MAP target; 65 mm Hg is extrapolated from other populations (AHA 2017)
  • Practical: Correct hypoxemia: Oxygen, mechanical ventilation if needed
  • Practical: Volume resuscitation: If hypovolemic (caution if cardiogenic shock)

Supportive Care:

  • Practical: Avoid hepatotoxins: Hold unnecessary medications, avoid acetaminophen
  • Monitor for complications: Hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, hyperammonemia (Waseem 2016); INR and mental status. Practical: glucose every 4-6 h
  • Practical: Nutrition: Enteral nutrition when stable, avoid excessive protein restriction unless encephalopathy
  • No proven liver-directed therapy: Evidence for antioxidants including N-acetylcysteine is lacking (Waseem 2016); NAC case reports and an ALFSG series are not yet confirmed (ACG 2023 ALF). If the injury progresses to acute liver failure (INR 1.5 or higher with encephalopathy), IV NAC is suggested for non-acetaminophen ALF (ACG 2023, Rec 7). Liver transplant is not usually indicated (ACG 2023 ALF)

Monitoring:

  • Daily LFTs initially; expect a fall to about half of peak within 24-72 hours (Waseem 2016)
  • Practical: Monitor INR, glucose, mental status for hepatic dysfunction
  • Practical: If transaminases NOT falling as expected, reconsider diagnosis

Prognosis:

  • In-hospital mortality is above 50%, usually from the underlying condition rather than the liver injury (Waseem 2016); prognosis is dictated by the underlying condition (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Rapid clinical improvement with restored hemodynamics is usual (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Aminotransferases return to baseline within 5-10 days (AHA 2017) to 2 weeks (Waseem 2016); persistent elevation suggests ongoing injury or another diagnosis
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • The "Shock Liver" Misnomer: Up to half of cases have no documented hypotension or shock (Waseem 2016) (ACG 2023 ALF). Passive congestion from right heart failure strongly predisposes: congestion plus any acute fall in hepatic blood flow (Waseem 2016). Practical: look for JVD, hepatomegaly, and elevated CVP
  • LDH is Your Friend: A marked LDH rise with an ALT/LDH ratio <1.5 favors ischemic injury (AHA 2017); viral hepatitis has lower LDH peaks (Waseem 2016). Practical: hemolysis and muscle injury also raise LDH
  • The 50% Rule: Aminotransferases fall to about half of peak within 24-72 hours (Waseem 2016). Practical: if they do not, reconsider the diagnosis or look for ongoing hypoperfusion; viral hepatitis has a more prolonged course
  • Don't Chase the Transaminases: Trend and synthetic function matter more than the peak. Acute hepatitis with an elevated prothrombin time or encephalopathy needs immediate referral to a liver specialist (ACG 2017, Rec 19). Practical: ALT 15,000 with INR 1.1 and clinical improvement usually does well; ALT 500 with INR 4.0 may need transplant evaluation
  • Congestive Hepatopathy vs. Ischemic Hepatitis: Right-sided heart failure causes chronic to subacute liver test abnormalities from venous congestion, distinct from the acute ischemic spike (AHA 2017). Congestion predisposes to superimposed ischemic hepatitis with any acute fall in hepatic blood flow (Waseem 2016). Practical: congestive pattern is mild aminotransferase elevation with raised bilirubin
  • The Bilirubin Lag: Bilirubin is often normal at first and rises with the INR while aminotransferases improve (ACG 2023 ALF). Practical: expected, and not by itself a sign of treatment failure
  • Centrilobular (Zone 3) Necrosis: The histologic hallmark is necrosis around the central veins (Waseem 2016). Practical: these hepatocytes sit at the low-oxygen end of the sinusoid, so they fail first; AST predominance fits (ACG 2017, Table 4)
  • Cardiac Arrest Pearl: Hypoxic hepatitis develops in a median 16% (range 7-25%) of cardiac arrest survivors and is associated with higher all-cause mortality (OR 3.49) and poor neurologic outcome (OR 2.73) (meta-analysis, Gao 2024). Practical: treat it as a marker of severity, not a reassuring finding
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: ICU when the underlying shock, arrest, or respiratory failure requires it; hypoxic hepatitis can occur without documented shock (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Practical: Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors
  • Practical: Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
  • Elevated PT/INR or encephalopathy: immediate referral to a liver specialist (ACG 2017, Rec 19); grade 2 or higher encephalopathy: ICU (ACG 2023)
  • Practical: Hypoglycemia requiring dextrose infusion
  • Practical: Underlying cardiac arrest or cardiogenic shock
  • Practical: Multi-organ failure
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Underlying cause treated and hemodynamically stable
  • Practical: Transaminases clearly downtrending (usually >50% from peak)
  • Practical: INR normal or stable/improving
  • Practical: No hepatic encephalopathy
  • Practical: Glucose stable without IV dextrose
  • Practical: Off vasopressors and mechanical ventilation
  • Practical: Able to tolerate oral medications and nutrition
  • Practical: Follow-up arranged (may need cardiology, hepatology depending on underlying cause)
  • Practical: Patient and family understand diagnosis and expected recovery
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Dobutamine, 💊 IV Fluids
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 LDH, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated Lactate

123. AORTIC DISSECTION

Stanford Type A • Type B • Hypertensive Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Abrupt onset of severe chest or back (sometimes abdominal) pain, maximal at the start, sometimes radiating. Patients more often describe it as "sharp" or "stabbing" than the textbook "tearing" or "ripping" (2022 Aortic). Practical: pain may migrate as the dissection propagates.

Stanford Classification:

  • Type A: Involves ascending aorta (regardless of origin) – SURGICAL EMERGENCY
  • Type B: Does not involve the ascending aorta; medical management if uncomplicated. Dissections with the entry tear in the arch and a spared ascending aorta are termed non-A non-B (EACTS/ESVS 2019, cited in 2022 Aortic)
  • Chronicity (SVS/STS 2020): Hyperacute <24 h, acute 1-14 d, subacute 15-90 d, chronic >90 d (2022 Aortic Table 3)

Associated Findings:

  • Pulse deficits: Pulse deficit or SBP differential between limbs (ADD-RS high-risk exam feature; no threshold is given); measure BP in both arms and both legs (2022 Aortic)
  • Neurologic: Stroke (carotid involvement), syncope, altered mental status, paraplegia (spinal artery involvement)
  • Cardiac: Aortic regurgitation murmur (diastolic, Type A), tamponade, MI (coronary ostia involvement)
  • Abdominal: Mesenteric ischemia, renal failure

Risk Factors: Hypertension (most common; over 70% of acute type B, ESVS 2026), connective tissue disease (e.g., Marfan), family history of aortic disease, bicuspid aortic valve, Turner syndrome, known thoracic aortic aneurysm, recent aortic manipulation (2022 Aortic Table 24); stimulant use (cocaine, amphetamines), pregnancy, intense physical exertion (ESVS 2026)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Risk Stratification:

  • ADD-RS (0-3, one point per category): High-risk conditions (Marfan or other connective tissue disease, family history of aortic disease, known aortic valve disease, recent aortic manipulation, known thoracic aortic aneurysm); high-risk pain (abrupt, severe, or ripping/tearing chest, back, or abdominal pain); high-risk exam (pulse deficit or SBP differential, focal neurologic deficit with pain, new aortic regurgitation murmur with pain, hypotension or shock). 0 low, 1 moderate, 2-3 high risk (2022 Aortic Table 24)

Imaging (Confirm Diagnosis):

  • CT Angiography (CTA): Recommended for initial diagnostic imaging given its availability, accuracy, speed, and anatomic detail (2022 Aortic 1, C-LD). Shows intimal flap, true and false lumens, extent of dissection, branch vessel involvement
  • TEE or MRI: Reasonable alternatives for initial imaging (2022 Aortic 2a, C-LD). Practical: TEE can be done at the bedside in unstable patients
  • CXR: Neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose AAS (2022 Aortic). Suggestive signs: mediastinal widening, abnormal aortic knob contour, calcium sign (>5 mm), double density, rightward tracheal or NG tube deviation; most useful when new compared with prior films (Table 23)

Laboratory:

  • D-dimer: With ADD-RS ≤1 and a highly sensitive D-dimer <500 ng/mL, acute nontraumatic dissection can be excluded without advanced imaging (ACEP 2025 clinical policy, Level B; failure rate 0.3% in the 1,850-patient ADvISED cohort). Use only in patients suspected of dissection who would otherwise be imaged, not all comers. 2022 ACC/AHA: a low risk score plus D-dimer <500 ng/mL may be a useful strategy to exclude AAS. No biomarker is diagnostic (2022 Aortic), and an elevated D-dimer is non-specific
  • Troponin: May be elevated if coronary involvement – but elevated troponin does NOT rule out dissection
  • CBC, BMP, coags, type and screen: Baseline for potential surgery

ECG: Often normal or non-specific. May show LVH, ischemic changes if coronary involvement. STEMI + dissection = catastrophic combination.

MANAGEMENT

Immediate Goals:

  • Setting: Prompt anti-impulse therapy with an arterial line in an ICU is recommended as initial treatment to decrease aortic wall stress (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR)
  • Pain control: Recommended as needed to help hemodynamic management (2022 Aortic 1, C-EO). Practical: IV opioids (morphine 2-4 mg IV or fentanyl 25-50 mcg IV)
  • Target HR 60-80 bpm (2022 Aortic 1, C-LD). ESVS 2026 targets HR <60 bpm in acute type B dissection (I C), adjustable to maintain organ perfusion
  • Target SBP <120 mmHg or the lowest BP that maintains adequate end-organ perfusion (2022 Aortic 1, C-LD; ESVS 2026 I C). The 2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline (Table 27) advises reaching SBP ≤120 mmHg within 20 min; ESVS notes that rapid BP lowering is associated with renal, cardiac, and cerebral ischemia and that no RCTs support these targets; reassess the target if renal hypoperfusion develops
  • BETA-BLOCKER FIRST: IV beta blocker unless contraindicated (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR); add an IV vasodilator only if BP stays uncontrolled after beta blockade (1, C-LD)

Anti-Impulse Therapy (HR Control FIRST):

  • Esmolol: 500-1000 mcg/kg over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min; repeat the bolus and increase by 50 mcg/kg/min as needed (max 300 mcg/kg/min). Short-acting and titratable. Contraindicated with concurrent beta blocker therapy, bradycardia, or decompensated HF (2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline Table 26; esmolol or labetalol preferred for dissection, Table 27)
  • Labetalol: 0.3-1 mg/kg (max 20 mg) slow IV every 10 min, OR infusion 0.4-1 mg/kg/h up to 3 mg/kg/h; max cumulative 300 mg/24 h. Avoid in reactive airway or obstructive pulmonary disease, HF, second- or third-degree heart block, or bradycardia (2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline Table 26)
  • If beta blocker contraindicated or not tolerated: IV non-dihydropyridine CCB is reasonable for HR control (2022 Aortic 2a, B-NR): diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 min, then infusion 5-15 mg/hr (FDA label, as on the AF card)

Blood Pressure Control (After HR Controlled):

  • Nicardipine: Initial 5 mg/hr, increase by 2.5 mg/hr every 5 min (max 15 mg/hr); contraindicated in advanced aortic stenosis (2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline Table 26)
  • Nitroprusside: ONLY after adequate beta blockade. Initial 0.3-0.5 mcg/kg/min, increase by 0.5 mcg/kg/min every 5 min (max 10 mcg/kg/min), shortest possible duration, arterial line recommended; cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity risk at ≥3 mcg/kg/min and/or ≥3 days (2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline Table 26)

Type A Dissection – SURGICAL EMERGENCY:

  • Emergency surgical consultation and immediate surgical intervention for suspected or confirmed type A (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR)
  • Untreated, early mortality is 1-2% per hour after symptom onset, higher with tamponade, myocardial ischemia, stroke, or malperfusion (2022 Aortic)
  • Stable enough for transfer: transfer from a low- to a high-volume aortic center is reasonable (2a, B-NR)
  • Malperfusion (renal, mesenteric, or limb): proceed to immediate repair of the ascending aorta (1, B-NR); with clinically significant mesenteric malperfusion, immediate ascending repair or mesenteric revascularization first are both reasonable (2a, C-LD)
  • Nonhemorrhagic stroke: surgery is reasonable over medical therapy (2a, B-NR)

Type B Dissection – Usually Medical Management:

  • Uncomplicated: Medical therapy is the initial strategy (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR; ESVS 2026 I C): anti-impulse therapy with ICU or high-dependency monitoring. ESVS 2026 suggests serial cross-sectional imaging at 48 h, 1 week, and 1 and 3 months (Rec 38, IIa C)
  • Complicated (2022 Aortic Table 27): Rupture (free or contained, including hemothorax or enlarging periaortic or mediastinal hematoma); branch occlusion or malperfusion; proximal or distal extension (including retrograde type A); aortic enlargement in the acute phase; intractable pain; uncontrolled hypertension. Intervention is recommended (1, C-LD); for rupture with suitable anatomy, endovascular stent grafting over open repair (1, C-EO); for other complications, endovascular over open is reasonable (2a, C-LD). ESVS 2026: immediate TEVAR to cover the primary entry tear for rupture or malperfusion (Rec 40, I C); open repair in selected patients unsuitable for endovascular repair (Rec 45, IIa C)
  • Uncomplicated with high-risk features: Endovascular management may be considered (2022 Aortic 2b, B-R). High-risk features (Table 28): maximal aortic diameter >40 mm, false lumen >20-22 mm, entry tear >10 mm or on the lesser curvature, diameter increase >5 mm between studies, bloody pleural effusion, imaging-only malperfusion, refractory hypertension on >3 drug classes at maximal doses, refractory pain >12 h, readmission. ESVS 2026: routine TEVAR is not indicated outside clinical trials (Rec 37, IIIa B); TEVAR may be considered with early expansion or initial diameter >4.0 cm, preferably in the subacute phase (Rec 39, IIb C)

Intramural Hematoma (IMH) and Penetrating Aortic Ulcer (PAU):

  • Both are acute aortic syndromes; the acute medical management recommendations above apply to all AAS (2022 Aortic)
  • IMH: Complicated (malperfusion, periaortic hematoma, pericardial effusion with tamponade, persistent or recurrent pain, rupture): urgent repair (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR). Uncomplicated type A: prompt open repair (1, B-NR); expectant medical management may be considered in selected patients at high operative risk without high-risk imaging features (2b, C-LD). Uncomplicated type B: medical therapy first (1, B-NR); intervention may be reasonable with high-risk imaging features (2b, C-LD; Table 30)
  • PAU: With rupture, or in the ascending aorta with IMH: urgent repair (1, B-NR); arch or descending aorta with IMH: urgent repair is reasonable (2a, C-LD). Isolated PAU with persistent pain that correlates with imaging: repair (1, B-NR). ESVS 2026: uncomplicated PAU or IMH of the descending thoracic aorta, conservative management with serial imaging (Rec 47, I C); complicated, TEVAR should be considered (Rec 48, IIa C)

AVOID: Fibrinolytics: suspected aortic dissection is an absolute contraindication, even with STEMI (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline Table 14). Vasodilators before beta blockade (2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline Table 27; 2022 Aortic 1, C-LD). Practical: hold anticoagulant and antiplatelet loading until dissection is excluded in suspected cases; neither the 2022 ACC/AHA nor the ESVS 2026 guideline addresses anticoagulation in acute dissection

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • The STEMI-Dissection Trap: Type A dissection can cause STEMI by occluding coronary ostia. Giving thrombolytics without considering dissection can be fatal. If ANY features suggest dissection, get CTA BEFORE heparin/cath.
  • Beta-Blocker BEFORE Vasodilator: Vasodilators cause reflex tachycardia, which increases aortic shear stress and can propagate dissection. Control heart rate first (60-80 bpm per 2022 ACC/AHA; <60 bpm per ESVS 2026 for type B).
  • Pain Onset: Dissection pain is abrupt and maximal at the start, more often described as sharp or stabbing than tearing (2022 Aortic). Practical: ACS pain more often builds over minutes.
  • Normal CXR Does NOT Rule Out Dissection: Chest x-ray is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude AAS (2022 Aortic). If clinical suspicion is high, proceed to CTA.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU / OR IF:
  • ALL Type A dissections – immediate surgical consult
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Signs of tamponade or rupture
  • End-organ malperfusion
  • Refractory hypertension or pain
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA (Type B Only)
  • Uncomplicated Type B with stable imaging
  • Pain controlled on oral medications
  • Oral regimen in place: long-term beta blocker unless contraindicated, adding ACEi or ARB as needed for BP (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR); long-term BP target <130/80 mmHg for chronic type B (ESVS 2026 Rec 49, I C)
  • Surveillance CT or MRI at 1, 6, and 12 months, then annually if stable, whether treated medically or with repair (2022 Aortic 1, B-NR); elective repair if chronic residual dissection reaches a total diameter ≥5.5 cm (1, B-NR)
  • First-degree relatives: screening aortic imaging is recommended, even without a known family history or pathogenic variant (2022 Aortic 1, C-LD)
  • Reliable follow-up with vascular or cardiothoracic surgery
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Esmolol, 💊 Labetalol, 💊 Nicardipine, 💊 Nitroprusside
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR
↑ Back to Table of Contents

124. CARDIAC TAMPONADE

Beck's Triad • Pulsus Paradoxus • Pericardiocentesis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Beck's Triad (classic in acute surgical tamponade; may be absent with slowly accumulating medical effusions, 2025 ESC):

  • Hypotension: Due to decreased cardiac output
  • Jugular Venous Distension (JVD): Due to impaired venous return
  • Muffled Heart Sounds: Fluid dampens sound transmission

Pulsus Paradoxus: Inspiratory fall in systolic BP of at least 10 mmHg, from exaggerated ventricular interdependence (2025 ESC). Acute tamponade usually brings tachycardia and SBP <90; BP is only slightly reduced in subacute or chronic tamponade

Other Signs: Dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, cool extremities, anxiety

Acute vs. Chronic:

  • Acute (hemopericardium: trauma, myocardial or aortic rupture): 200-300 mL can cause tamponade (2025 ESC)
  • Slowly accumulating (e.g., malignancy, uremia): May reach 1-2 L before tamponade; a small further increase can then precipitate it (2025 ESC)

Common Etiologies: Malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma), uremia, infection (viral, TB), post-cardiac surgery, post-MI, autoimmune, trauma, aortic dissection (Type A), idiopathic

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Echocardiography (Test of Choice):

  • Pericardial effusion: Anechoic space surrounding heart
  • Echo is essential; correlate with symptoms, heart rate, and BP (ACC 2025 CCG; TTE to identify effusion and assess tamponade: Recommended):
  • RV diastolic collapse: The most specific finding (ACC 2025). ESC 2025 Table 17: sensitivity 48-100%, specificity 72-100%
  • RA collapse: Inversion lasting more than one-third of the cardiac cycle (ACC 2025). ESC 2025: collapse >0.34 of the cycle, sensitivity >90%, specificity 100%
  • Respiratory variation: Transmitral E >30%, transtricuspid E >60% (ACC 2025). ESC 2025: mitral >25-30%, tricuspid >40-60%
  • IVC plethora: IVC >2.1 cm with minimal or no respiratory variation: a sensitive screen that does not confirm tamponade (ACC 2025). ESC 2025: sensitivity 97%, specificity 40%
  • Swinging heart in a large effusion

ECG: Sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, electrical alternans (2025 ESC); alternans is uncommon (see pericarditis card)

CXR: "Water bottle" heart – may be normal in acute tamponade

Cross-link: 🔬 BMP Reference

MANAGEMENT

Hemodynamically UNSTABLE:

  • PERICARDIOCENTESIS: Recommended for cardiac tamponade (ACC 2025 CCG), performed urgently with echo guidance; admit (ACC 2025: admission may be necessary for large effusion and/or tamponade; ESC 2025: admit all tamponade). Practical: in shock, drain without delay. Without shock, the ESC 2025 triage score (Figure 12: aetiology, presentation, imaging) favors immediate drainage at >6 points from at least two categories
  • Volume: Temporary fluid can help stabilize while awaiting drainage (2025 ESC). A 250-500 mL bolus, mainly if SBP <100 or hypovolemic, raised cardiac output in only about half of patients and lowered it in about a third (Sagristà-Sauleda, Circulation 2008; as on the pericarditis card)
  • AVOID: Diuretics and positive-pressure mechanical ventilation (2025 ESC). Practical: avoid vasodilators

Pericardiocentesis:

  • Guidance: Echocardiography, fluoroscopy, and/or CT (ACC 2025; ESC 2025 I C); surgical drainage if percutaneous drainage is not feasible or the effusion is purulent (ESC 2025 I C). CT/CMR for routine assessment of tamponade: not recommended (ACC 2025)
  • Approach: In an emergency, subxiphoid or apical (ACC 2025); otherwise where fluid is most accessible with the least risk to vital structures (ACC 2025). 16-20 gauge needle (ESC 2025)
  • Volume and drain: Aspirating a small amount can greatly improve the patient; avoid draining a large volume at once (usually <500 mL) to prevent pericardial decompression syndrome; leave a drain and remove it when output is <30 mL/day (2025 ESC)

Specific Etiologies:

  • Malignancy: Extended catheter drainage 3-6 days and cytology (ESC 2025 I). Pericardial window after prior pericardiocentesis for recurrent large effusion or tamponade: Reasonable (ACC 2025); ESC 2025 also lists balloon pericardiotomy (see pericarditis card)
  • Uremic: Practical: intensify dialysis (2025 ESC lists uremia as a cause but gives no specific therapy)
  • Aortic dissection (Type A): Emergency surgical consultation and evaluation and immediate surgical intervention for suspected or confirmed type A (2022 ACC/AHA Aortic 1, B-NR; ESC 2024 Aortic I B); go straight to the OR. Pericardiocentesis is not the definitive treatment. Exception (no US recommendation): impending or actual cardiac arrest from tamponade: emergency pericardial puncture as a temporary life-saving measure before transfer to the OR (ESC 2024 Aortic text and Figure 33, no class; basis: controlled drainage series, Hayashi Circulation 2012, doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.111.082685; Cruz Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care 2015, doi:10.1177/2048872614549737). Practical: remove only enough to restore perfusion, not to empty the pericardium
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Tamponade is CLINICAL, Not Radiographic: Echo is essential, but the diagnosis rests on correlating it with symptoms, heart rate, and BP (ACC 2025; ESC 2025). Hemodynamic impact depends on the speed of accumulation, not the volume: large slow effusions can be tolerated; small rapid ones cannot (ACC 2025).
  • Pulsus Paradoxus: An inspiratory SBP fall of at least 10 mmHg is abnormal (2025 ESC) and scores 2 points in the ESC triage score.
  • Don't Rely on Beck's Triad: Classic triad is often incomplete. Trust pulsus paradoxus and echo findings.
  • Type A Dissection with Tamponade = Operating Room: Surgery is the treatment (2022 ACC/AHA Aortic 1, B-NR; ESC 2024 Aortic I B). Only a peri-arrest patient gets a bridge pericardial puncture before the OR (ESC 2024 Aortic; no US recommendation). Practical: full drainage can raise aortic pressure and worsen bleeding, so remove just enough to restore perfusion.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU / CATH LAB IF:
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Any clinical tamponade: admit for therapy and monitoring (ESC 2025; ACC 2025: admission may be necessary for large effusion and/or tamponade)
  • Echo evidence of chamber collapse
  • Need for emergent pericardiocentesis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Tamponade drained, no reaccumulation
  • Underlying cause identified and being treated
  • Stable vital signs
  • Follow-up arranged
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Norepinephrine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR
↑ Back to Table of Contents

125. LOWER GI BLEED

Diverticular • Angiodysplasia • Risk Stratification
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz. Usually presents with hematochezia.

Key Point: In a study of patients with hematochezia and high-risk features who had EGD first, 15% had an upper source. Hematochezia with hemodynamic instability may mean UGIB: do an upper endoscopy if suspicion is high (ACG 2023)

Common Etiologies:

  • Diverticular bleeding: Most common cause; frequency varies widely by study (64% in one cohort, counting presumed cases) (ACG 2023). Practical: painless
  • Angioectasias: Usually occult loss with iron deficiency, sometimes overt bleeding; older age and anticoagulants raise the risk of active bleeding (ACG 2023). Practical: associated with CKD and aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome)
  • Hemorrhoids: Practical: bright red blood on toilet paper or in the bowl
  • Colitis: Ischemic, inflammatory, infectious, or radiation-related (ACG 2023). Practical: bloody diarrhea with pain
  • Neoplasm: Colorectal polyps and cancer (ACG 2023)
  • Postpolypectomy: Endoscopic therapy if active bleeding or stigmata at the site; 43% needed no hemostatic therapy in one study (ACG 2023). Practical: often 1-2 weeks after the procedure
  • Other: Rectal, stercoral, or NSAID ulcers, radiation proctopathy, Dieulafoy lesion, colorectal varices (ACG 2023)

Distinguishing LGIB from UGIB:

  • BUN/Cr ratio >30: Likelihood ratio 7.5 for an upper source; clots in the stool make UGIB unlikely (LR 0.05) (ACG 2023)
  • Melena: Raises the likelihood of an upper source (ACG 2023)
  • Hemodynamic instability + hematochezia: May indicate UGIB; upper endoscopy if suspicion is high. Nasogastric aspirate is insensitive and not recommended routinely (ACG 2023)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory: Assess severity, likely location, and cause at presentation while resuscitating (ACG 2023). Practical: CBC (trend q6-8h), BMP (BUN/Cr ratio), coags, type and screen/crossmatch, lactate if concern for ischemia

Risk Stratification, Oakland Score: A score ≤8 predicted a 95% probability of safe discharge; use it to identify low-risk patients for early discharge and outpatient evaluation, as a supplement to clinical judgment (ACG 2023, Rec 1, conditional)

Colonoscopy:

  • Who: Most hospitalized patients (ACG 2023, Rec 6a, strong); may be skipped if bleeding has stopped and a high-quality colonoscopy within 12 months showed only diverticulosis (Rec 6b)
  • Timing: Nonemergent inpatient colonoscopy; urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours does not improve rebleeding or mortality (ACG 2023, Rec 9, strong)
  • Bowel prep: 4-6 L PEG historically; split-dose or low-volume preps can be considered. No unprepared exam or flexible sigmoidoscopy alone unless the source is anorectal or distal (ACG 2023)
  • Therapy: Treat active bleeding or stigmata whatever the cause (ACG 2023); diverticular stigmata: through-the-scope clips, band ligation, or coagulation (Rec 10, strong)

Imaging and Further Testing:

  • Upper endoscopy: If an upper source is suspected (ACG 2023)
  • CT angiography: First test for ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia; low yield once bleeding has subsided (ACG 2023, Rec 7). Positive CTA: prompt referral to IR for angiography and possible embolization (Rec 8, strong); angiography within 90 minutes was 9 times more likely to show extravasation (ACG 2023)
  • Tagged RBC scan: Rapidly diminishing role; only if CTA is unavailable or contraindicated (ACG 2023)
  • Rebleeding: Repeat colonoscopy depending on stability (ACG 2023). Practical: detection thresholds about 0.3-0.5 mL/min for CTA, 0.1 mL/min for RBC scan, 0.5-1 mL/min for angiography

Cross-link: 🔬 CBC Reference, 📚 Upper GI Bleed

MANAGEMENT

Initial Resuscitation:

  • Practical: IV access: Two large-bore IVs (18G or larger)
  • Fluids: IV fluid resuscitation to optimize blood pressure and heart rate before endoscopy if unstable or actively bleeding (ACG 2023). Practical: MAP >65
  • Blood transfusion: Restrictive threshold, Hgb 7 g/dL, if hemodynamically stable (ACG 2023, Rec 2; AABB 2023); 8 g/dL with preexisting cardiovascular disease (AABB 2023) and can be considered in acute coronary syndrome (ACG 2023)
  • Warfarin: Most patients do not need reversal; reverse for life-threatening bleeding with INR well above range, using 4-factor PCC rather than FFP (ACG 2023, Rec 3). Endoscopic hemostasis is safe with INR 2.5 or less (ACG 2023)
  • DOACs: Reverse only for life-threatening bleeding that does not respond to resuscitation and stopping the drug; idarucizumab for dabigatran taken within 24 h (ACG 2023, Rec 4). ACG 2023 also names andexanet alfa, which was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025 after an FDA safety communication (AABB 2025). ACG-CAG 2022 suggests against routine PCC, idarucizumab, or andexanet in DOAC-associated GI bleeding
  • Platelets: Keep above 30,000 in severe bleeding, above 50,000 if endoscopic procedures are needed; no routine platelets for patients on antiplatelets (ACG 2023)
  • Antiplatelets: Continue aspirin for secondary prevention if possible; hold nonaspirin antiplatelets initially in severe bleeding; multidisciplinary decision if a coronary stent was placed within 1 year (ACG 2023)

Endoscopic Therapy: For active bleeding or stigmata: through-the-scope or over-the-scope clips, band ligation, contact or noncontact thermal therapy (eg, APC), dilute epinephrine injection, topical agents (ACG 2023)

Interventional Radiology: Angiography with possible embolization, promptly after a positive CTA (ACG 2023, Rec 8)

Surgery: Limited role, only after endoscopic or radiologic therapy fails (0.2% of cases in a UK audit; 20% major complications in one series). Localize the source first for a limited resection: nonlocalized hemicolectomy has more rebleeding (ACG 2023)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Hematochezia ≠ LGIB: 15% of patients with hematochezia and high-risk features had an upper source (ACG 2023). Consider UGIB in unstable patients.
  • Most LGIB Settles Without Intervention: Conservative management is initially enough for most patients (ACR 2021); nearly 80% of patients with a negative CTA had no further bleeding or intervention (ACG 2023)
  • Practical: Hemoglobin Lag: Initial Hgb may be normal – equilibration takes 8-24 hours.
  • Practical: Heyde Syndrome: Aortic stenosis + angiodysplasia + acquired vWF deficiency.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: Hemodynamic instability
  • Practical: Massive transfusion requirement
  • Practical: Active ongoing hemorrhage
  • Practical: Need for emergent intervention
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Bleeding stopped, stable hemoglobin
  • Practical: Colonoscopy completed or follow-up arranged
  • Practical: Tolerating oral intake
  • Practical: GI follow-up arranged
  • After diverticular bleeding: stop nonaspirin NSAIDs (Rec 11a, strong); stop aspirin used for primary prevention (11b); continue aspirin for established cardiovascular disease (11c); reassess P2Y12 inhibitors with a multidisciplinary team (11d, strong) (ACG 2023)
  • Resume anticoagulation once bleeding stops; it lowers thromboembolism and mortality (ACG 2023, Rec 12, strong)
📖 Drug Reference: Tranexamic acid is NOT recommended in LGIB (ACG 2023, Rec 5, strong): in a trial of over 12,000 patients with GI bleeding (HALT-IT), it did not reduce death from bleeding or overall mortality, and venous thromboembolism and seizures were more frequent
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Blood Cultures

126. TTP/HUS (THROMBOTIC MICROANGIOPATHY)

PLASMIC Score • Plasmapheresis • DO NOT Transfuse Platelets
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic "Pentad" (Full Pentad in <10%):

  • Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA): Schistocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin
  • Thrombocytopenia: Usually severe (median ~15,000)
  • Neurologic symptoms: Headache, confusion, seizures, focal deficits
  • Renal dysfunction: Mild in TTP, severe in HUS
  • Fever: Non-specific

TTP vs. HUS:

  • TTP: ADAMTS13 activity <10%. More neurologic, milder renal
  • STEC-HUS: Shiga toxin E. coli (O157:H7). Bloody diarrhea prodrome, severe renal
  • Atypical HUS: Complement dysregulation. Severe renal, no diarrhea
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Essential Labs:

  • CBC with smear: Thrombocytopenia + schistocytes (>1%)
  • Hemolysis labs: LDH (markedly elevated), haptoglobin (undetectable), indirect bilirubin, reticulocytes
  • Direct Coombs: NEGATIVE (rules out AIHA)
  • Coags: PT, PTT, fibrinogen – typically NORMAL (vs. DIC)

ADAMTS13 Activity: SEND BEFORE PLASMA. Activity <10% confirms TTP. Don't wait for results to treat.

PLASMIC Score (Predicts ADAMTS13 <10%):

  • Platelet <30k (+1)
  • Lysis (hemolysis markers) (+1)
  • Active cancer absent (+1)
  • Stem cell/organ transplant absent (+1)
  • MCV <90 (+1)
  • INR <1.5 (+1)
  • Creatinine <2.0 (+1)
  • Score ≥6 = High risk (~72% ADAMTS13 <10%)

Cross-link: 🔬 CBC Reference, 🔬 LDH Reference

MANAGEMENT
⚠️ CRITICAL: DO NOT TRANSFUSE PLATELETS

Platelet transfusion can precipitate thrombosis and worsen disease. Only if life-threatening bleeding.

Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (TPE):

  • START IMMEDIATELY: Don't wait for ADAMTS13. Mortality >90% untreated vs. <20% with TPE.
  • Regimen: Daily 1-1.5 plasma volumes until platelets >150k × 2 days
  • If TPE not available: Give FFP 30 mL/kg as bridge

Corticosteroids: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day OR methylprednisolone 1g IV daily × 3 days

Rituximab: For refractory/relapsed TTP. 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 weeks

Caplacizumab: Anti-vWF nanobody. 11 mg IV before first TPE, then 11 mg SQ daily

STEC-HUS: Supportive care only. AVOID antibiotics (may worsen). NO TPE.

Atypical HUS: Eculizumab (C5 inhibitor) – treatment of choice. Vaccinate for meningococcus.

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Don't Wait for Pentad: MAHA + thrombocytopenia alone is enough to suspect TTP and start treatment.
  • Coags are NORMAL: Unlike DIC, PT/PTT/fibrinogen are normal in TTP.
  • Send ADAMTS13 BEFORE Plasma: Plasma contains ADAMTS13 and falsely elevates levels.
  • NO PLATELETS: Can trigger catastrophic thrombosis. Exception: life-threatening bleeding.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • All suspected TTP – hematologic emergency
  • Severe neurologic manifestations
  • Severe thrombocytopenia (<10k)
  • Need for emergent TPE
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Platelets >150k × 2 consecutive days
  • LDH normalizing
  • No neurologic symptoms
  • TPE course completed
  • Hematology follow-up arranged
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 ADAMTS13, 🔬 Direct Coombs (DAT), 🔬 LDH, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Peripheral Smear
