127. HEPARIN-INDUCED THROMBOCYTOPENIA (HIT)

4T Score • Argatroban/Bivalirudin • Warfarin Bridging
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia from antibodies against PF4-heparin complexes. Causes THROMBOSIS, not bleeding.

Timing:

  • Typical HIT: Platelet drop 5-10 days after heparin exposure
  • Rapid-onset HIT: Within 24 hours if heparin in past 100 days

Key Features:

  • Thrombocytopenia: ~50% drop from baseline (nadir usually 20,000-150,000)
  • Thrombosis: 50% of untreated HIT develop thrombosis (DVT, PE, limb ischemia, stroke)
  • Skin necrosis: At injection sites

Risk Factors: UFH > LMWH (10× higher risk), surgical > medical patients, duration >4 days

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

4T Score:

Feature 2 Points 1 Point 0 Points
Thrombocytopenia>50% fall or nadir 20-100k30-50% fall or nadir 10-19k<30% fall or nadir <10k
TimingDays 5-10 or ≤1 day if recent heparinDays 5-10 unclear≤4 days without recent heparin
ThrombosisNew thrombosis or skin necrosisProgressive/suspected thrombosisNone
Other causesNone evidentPossible other causeDefinite other cause

Score: 0-3 = Low (<5%); 4-5 = Intermediate (10-30%); 6-8 = High (40-80%)

Laboratory:

  • Anti-PF4/heparin ELISA: High sensitivity (~99%), lower specificity
  • Serotonin release assay (SRA): Gold standard, high specificity (~99%)
MANAGEMENT

Immediate Actions:

  • STOP ALL HEPARIN: UFH, LMWH, heparin flushes, heparin-coated catheters
  • Start alternative anticoagulation: Even without thrombosis
  • Duplex legs: Screen for occult DVT

Alternative Anticoagulation:

  • Argatroban: 2 mcg/kg/min IV (no bolus), adjust to aPTT 1.5-3× baseline. Hepatically cleared.
  • Bivalirudin: 0.15-0.2 mg/kg/hr IV. Renally cleared.
  • Fondaparinux: Weight-based SC daily: <50 kg = 5 mg, 50–100 kg = 7.5 mg, >100 kg = 10 mg. No cross-reactivity with HIT antibodies.
  • DOACs: Can use in stable patients.

Warfarin Bridging (CRITICAL):

  • DO NOT start warfarin until platelets >150,000: Can cause venous limb gangrene
  • Start low dose (5 mg daily) when platelets recovered
  • Overlap ≥5 days with alternative anticoagulant until INR therapeutic × 2 days
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • HIT Causes Thrombosis: Despite low platelets, HIT is hypercoagulable. Treat with anticoagulation.
  • 4T Score is Essential: Low score (<4) essentially rules out HIT.
  • Timing is Everything: Classic HIT = days 5-10. Day 2 drop without recent heparin is NOT HIT.
  • Warfarin Danger: Never start warfarin while platelets are low – causes limb gangrene.
  • Argatroban Elevates INR: Target INR >4 before stopping argatroban when bridging.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Acute arterial thrombosis
  • Massive PE
  • Venous limb gangrene
  • Need for emergent surgery
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Platelets >150,000 and stable
  • On oral anticoagulation
  • No new thrombosis
  • Patient educated to avoid heparin
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Argatroban, 💊 Fondaparinux
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 HIT Workup
↑ Back to Table of Contents

128. WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY

Thiamine Deficiency • Give Thiamine BEFORE Glucose • Korsakoff Syndrome
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad (Present in Only ~30%):

  • Encephalopathy: Confusion, disorientation, apathy (most common, >80%)
  • Oculomotor dysfunction: Nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, ophthalmoplegia
  • Gait ataxia: Wide-based, unsteady; may be unable to walk

High-Risk Populations:

  • Alcohol use disorder: Most common
  • Malnutrition: Anorexia, starvation, refeeding syndrome
  • Hyperemesis gravidarum
  • Bariatric surgery
  • Prolonged TPN without thiamine
  • Dialysis

Korsakoff Syndrome: Untreated Wernicke → irreversible anterograde amnesia, confabulation. ~80% of untreated cases progress.

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

WERNICKE IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS: Do NOT wait for labs or imaging to treat.

Laboratory (Supportive):

  • Thiamine level: Can confirm deficiency but takes days
  • Magnesium: Often low; required for thiamine utilization

MRI Brain: T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray. Sensitivity ~50% – normal MRI does NOT rule out.

MANAGEMENT
⚠️ CRITICAL: THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE

Glucose consumes thiamine in glycolysis. Giving glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke. ALWAYS give thiamine before or with glucose.

Thiamine Dosing (TREATMENT):

  • High-dose IV: 500 mg IV TID × 2-3 days
  • Then: 250 mg IV daily × 3-5 days
  • Then: 100 mg PO TID until no longer at risk

Why IV and High-Dose? Oral absorption limited (~5 mg/day max). Brain stores depleted – need aggressive repletion.

Prophylaxis (At-Risk Without Symptoms): 100-200 mg IV daily while NPO

Magnesium Repletion: Cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes. Target Mg >2.0 mg/dL.

Expected Response:

  • Oculomotor findings: Hours to days
  • Ataxia: Days to weeks; may not fully resolve
  • Encephalopathy: Days to weeks; may not fully resolve
  • Korsakoff amnesia: Usually irreversible

Cross-link: 🔬 Magnesium Reference, 📚 Alcohol Withdrawal

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Clinical Diagnosis: Don't wait for labs. If you suspect it, treat it.
  • Triad is a Myth: Only ~30% present with classic triad. Suspect in ANY confused patient with risk factors.
  • THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE: Boards-relevant and clinically critical.
  • Low-Dose is Inadequate: "Banana bag" (100 mg) insufficient for established Wernicke. Use 500 mg IV TID.
  • Korsakoff is Irreversible: Early aggressive treatment prevents progression.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe encephalopathy (coma)
  • Concurrent severe alcohol withdrawal
  • Respiratory compromise
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Mental status improved
  • Gait stable
  • Tolerating oral thiamine
  • Magnesium repleted
  • Alcohol cessation resources provided
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Thiamine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hypomagnesemia
↑ Back to Table of Contents

129. NEPHROTIC SYNDROME

>3.5g Proteinuria • Thrombosis Risk • Infection Risk
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Diagnostic Criteria:

  • Proteinuria >3.5 g/day (or UPCR >3.5)
  • Hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL)
  • Peripheral edema
  • Hyperlipidemia

Primary Causes:

  • Minimal Change: Most common in children; responds to steroids
  • FSGS: Most common primary cause in adults; often steroid-resistant
  • Membranous Nephropathy: Most common in older adults; high thrombosis risk; associated with malignancy

Secondary Causes: Diabetes (most common overall), SLE, amyloidosis, hepatitis B/C, HIV, malignancy, drugs (NSAIDs)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Confirm Diagnosis: 24-hour urine protein or spot UPCR, serum albumin, lipid panel

Workup for Etiology:

  • HbA1c, fundoscopic exam (diabetes)
  • ANA, anti-dsDNA, C3/C4 (SLE)
  • Hepatitis B/C, HIV serologies
  • Anti-PLA2R antibody (primary membranous)
  • SPEP/UPEP, free light chains (amyloidosis)
  • Age-appropriate cancer screening

Renal Biopsy: Definitive diagnosis in most cases; not required if clear diabetic nephropathy

Cross-link: 🔬 Albumin Reference

MANAGEMENT

Supportive Care (All Patients):

  • Sodium restriction: <2 g/day
  • Loop diuretics: Furosemide 40-80 mg daily; may need high doses
  • ACE-I or ARB: Reduces proteinuria; use even if BP normal
  • Statin: For hyperlipidemia

Thrombosis Prevention:

  • High risk – loss of antithrombin III, protein S
  • VTE risk highest with membranous and albumin <2.5
  • Consider prophylactic anticoagulation in high-risk patients
  • Renal vein thrombosis: Classic complication – flank pain, hematuria

Infection Risk: Loss of immunoglobulins → increased infection risk. Ensure pneumococcal vaccination.

Disease-Specific:

  • Minimal change: High-dose prednisone
  • FSGS: Steroids; if resistant, calcineurin inhibitors or rituximab
  • Membranous: Rituximab or cyclophosphamide + steroids if high-risk
  • Diabetic: Glycemic control, ACE-I/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Nephrotic vs. Nephritic: Nephrotic = heavy proteinuria, low albumin, edema. Nephritic = hematuria, RBC casts, HTN.
  • Thrombosis is a Big Deal: VTE risk 10-40% in membranous. Consider DVT/PE in symptomatic patients.
  • Membranous + Cancer: In adults >50, consider occult malignancy workup.
  • SGLT2 Inhibitors: Standard of care for proteinuric CKD regardless of diabetes (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Massive PE
  • Severe AKI requiring dialysis
  • Severe pulmonary edema
  • Sepsis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Edema controlled with oral diuretics
  • Renal function stable
  • On ACE-I/ARB
  • Nephrology follow-up arranged
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Enoxaparin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR, 🔬 Elevated LDL, 🔬 Elevated Triglycerides

130. ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA / PNEUMONITIS

Chemical Pneumonitis vs. Infection • Anaerobic Coverage Only for Abscess or Empyema
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Pneumonitis vs. Pneumonia:

FeatureAspiration PneumonitisAspiration Pneumonia
PathophysiologyChemical inflammation from gastric acidBacterial infection
OnsetHours after witnessed aspirationDays (often no witnessed event)
CourseImproves 24-48 hrsProgressive without antibiotics
AntibioticsUsually NOT indicatedYes

Risk Factors: Decreased consciousness, dysphagia, impaired gag reflex, NG tube, GERD, poor dentition

Location: Dependent lung segments: superior or posterior basal segments of a lower lobe, or the posterior segment of an upper lobe. Imaging cannot distinguish pneumonitis from pneumonia (Merck Manual 2026)

MANAGEMENT

Aspiration Pneumonitis:

  • Supportive care: Supplemental oxygen and, if needed, mechanical ventilation (Merck Manual 2026)
  • Many resolve within 24-48 hours with supportive care alone, without antibiotics (2019 ATS/IDSA)
  • Antibiotics: Not routine after witnessed aspiration. Observe and start them if the course suggests bacterial superinfection, which develops in about a quarter of patients; empiric antibiotics started early can be stopped if the patient improves rapidly (Merck Manual 2026). Practical: reassess at about 48 hours; many clinicians treat early when illness is severe or gastric contents are likely colonized (small bowel obstruction, acid suppression)
  • Corticosteroids: Not routinely recommended; benefit not established (Merck Manual 2026)

Aspiration Pneumonia (treat as CAP; see card 5):

  • Community-onset, nonsevere inpatient (2019 ATS/IDSA): β-lactam (ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily or ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5-3 g IV q6h) PLUS azithromycin 500 mg daily, OR levofloxacin 750 mg daily alone. Both ampicillin-sulbactam and levofloxacin need renal dose adjustment (FDA labels). Practical: switch to PO when able
  • Severe CAP, or MRSA or Pseudomonas risk: Use the card 5 regimens
  • Hospital-onset aspiration (including tube-fed or ventilated patients): Treat as HAP or VAP (card 131)
  • Anaerobic coverage: Do not add routinely; add only if lung abscess or empyema is suspected (2019 ATS/IDSA, conditional, very low quality). In 3,999 inpatients with aspiration pneumonia, extended anaerobic coverage did not lower in-hospital mortality and was linked to more C. difficile colitis (Bai, Chest 2024; observational)
  • Abscess or empyema suspected: A β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor such as ampicillin-sulbactam covers anaerobes (2019 ATS/IDSA). Drainage, agent, and duration: cards 173 (empyema) and 174 (lung abscess)
  • Duration: At least 5 days and until clinically stable (2019 ATS/IDSA). ATS 2025: less than 5 days (minimum 3) for nonsevere CAP once stable (conditional); 5 or more days for severe CAP. Details on card 5

Prevention (Practical): Swallowing evaluation when dysphagia is suspected, oral hygiene, head of bed elevation 30-45°, minimal sedation. Thickened liquids have little firm supporting evidence (Merck Manual 2026)

Cross-link: 🦠 ID Guide: Respiratory Infections

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Pneumonitis ≠ Pneumonia: Pneumonitis is chemical injury, not infection; many resolve within 24-48 hours without antibiotics (2019 ATS/IDSA).
  • 48-Hour Rule (Practical): After witnessed aspiration, observe for about 48 hours. If worsening or not improving → start antibiotics.
  • Anaerobic Coverage Overprescribed: Add it only for lung abscess or empyema (2019 ATS/IDSA). Extended anaerobic coverage was linked to more C. difficile colitis without lower mortality (Bai, Chest 2024).
  • Procalcitonin Does Not Decide: Start antibiotics for clinically suspected, radiographically confirmed pneumonia regardless of the initial procalcitonin level (2019 ATS/IDSA, strong recommendation).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe hypoxemia
  • Respiratory failure
  • Septic shock
  • ARDS
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Oxygenation adequate
  • Afebrile
  • Tolerating oral intake safely
  • Aspiration precautions in place
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Amp-Sulbactam, 💊 Azithromycin, 💊 Levofloxacin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin

131. HOSPITAL-ACQUIRED / VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED PNEUMONIA (HAP/VAP)

MDR Risk Factors • Empiric Coverage • De-escalation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definitions:

  • HAP: Pneumonia ≥48 hours after admission
  • VAP: Pneumonia >48 hours after intubation

Common Pathogens: Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli, Acinetobacter, MRSA, S. pneumoniae

MDR Risk Factors:

  • IV antibiotics in prior 90 days
  • Hospitalization ≥5 days
  • Septic shock at time of VAP
  • ARDS before VAP
  • Renal replacement therapy
  • Prior MRSA/Pseudomonas infection
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical: New infiltrate + ≥2 of: fever, leukocytosis/leukopenia, purulent secretions, declining oxygenation

Cultures: Sputum/ETA, blood cultures, consider BAL if not responding

MRSA Nasal PCR: High NPV (~95%). If negative, can discontinue MRSA coverage.

Cross-link: 🦠 ID Guide: Respiratory Infections

MANAGEMENT

NO MDR Risk Factors:

  • Single anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam: Pip-tazo 4.5g q6h, Cefepime 2g q8h, OR Meropenem 1g q8h

WITH MDR Risk Factors:

  • Two anti-pseudomonal agents: Beta-lactam + fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside
  • PLUS MRSA coverage if risk factors: Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h OR Linezolid 600mg q12h

De-escalation (at 48-72h):

  • Review cultures and narrow coverage
  • If MRSA nasal PCR negative → stop vancomycin
  • If Pseudomonas not isolated → narrow to single agent

Duration: 7 days for most HAP/VAP. Longer for Pseudomonas, MRSA bacteremia, abscess, empyema.

VAP Prevention Bundle: HOB elevation, daily sedation vacation, DVT/PUD prophylaxis, oral care with chlorhexidine

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • MDR Risk Assessment is Key: Not everyone needs double Pseudomonas coverage + vancomycin.
  • De-escalate Early: 48-72h culture review is critical. Narrow when possible.
  • MRSA Nasal PCR: Use it to stop unnecessary vancomycin.
  • 7 Days is Usually Enough: Longer courses = more resistance, more C. diff.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Most HAP/VAP patients already in ICU
  • Septic shock
  • Severe hypoxemia
  • Need for mechanical ventilation
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Afebrile >48 hours
  • Stable oxygenation
  • WBC normalizing
  • Able to take oral medications
  • Plan to complete antibiotic course
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Cefepime, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Linezolid, 💊 Ciprofloxacin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Blood Cultures
↑ Back to Table of Contents

132. CRITICAL AORTIC STENOSIS

Vmax ≥4 m/s or Mean Gradient ≥40 mmHg • Syncope/Angina/HF • AVR Indications
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Symptom Triad:

  • Angina: Increased myocardial O2 demand and reduced coronary perfusion pressure
  • Syncope: Exertional; fixed cardiac output cannot meet demand
  • Heart Failure: LV decompensation
  • Natural history without AVR: Median survival about 5 years after angina, 3 years after syncope, and under 2 years after HF (Ross and Braunwald, Circulation 1968). Exertional dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance is now the most common first symptom (2020 ACC/AHA)

Physical Exam:

  • Murmur: Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at RUSB, radiates to carotids
  • Parvus et tardus: Weak and delayed carotid upstroke (classic but insensitive)
  • Paradoxical S2 split: Prolonged LV ejection delays A2
  • S4 gallop: Stiff, hypertrophied LV
  • Narrow pulse pressure: Reduced stroke volume

Severity Classification:

  • Severe high-gradient AS (Stage C1/D1): Vmax ≥4 m/s or mean gradient ≥40 mmHg; AVA typically ≤1.0 cm² (indexed ≤0.6 cm²/m²) but not required (2020 ACC/AHA Table 13)
  • Very severe AS: Vmax ≥5 m/s or mean gradient ≥60 mmHg (Table 13). "Critical AS" is not a guideline stage; an indexed AVA ≤0.6 cm²/m² is the severe threshold

Etiologies: Calcific/degenerative (most common in elderly), bicuspid aortic valve (younger patients), rheumatic (rare in developed countries)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Echocardiography (Diagnostic Standard):

  • Valve area by continuity equation
  • Mean and peak gradients
  • Peak aortic jet velocity
  • LV function (EF)
  • LV wall thickness (concentric hypertrophy typical)

Low-Flow, Low-Gradient AS:

  • Stage D2 (LVEF <50%): AVA ≤1.0 cm² with Vmax <4 m/s or mean gradient <40 mmHg; may be true severe or pseudo-severe AS. Low-dose dobutamine stress testing is reasonable (2020 ACC/AHA 2a, B-NR); severe if Vmax >4 m/s with AVA ≤1.0 cm² at any point (maximum dobutamine 20 mcg/kg/min)
  • Stage D3 (normal LVEF): Same valve criteria with a small LV and low stroke volume; optimize BP control before measuring severity (1, B-NR)
  • Both D2 and D3: Outflow tract to aortic velocity ratio and CT aortic valve calcium score are reasonable to define severity (2a, B-NR)
  • Exercise testing: Do NOT perform in symptomatic severe AS (3: Harm, B-NR)

Other Studies:

  • ECG: LVH with strain pattern, LAE, conduction abnormalities
  • CXR: Cardiomegaly, calcified aortic valve, pulmonary congestion if decompensated
  • Cardiac cath: Pre-operative coronary assessment; direct gradient measurement if echo inconclusive
  • CT calcium scoring: Reasonable in low-flow, low-gradient AS (see above)

Cross-link: 🔬 BNP Reference

MANAGEMENT

Medical Management (Temporizing Only):

  • No medical therapy prevents progression – definitive treatment is valve replacement. Statins do not slow hemodynamic progression (2020 ACC/AHA 3: No Benefit, A) but are indicated for atherosclerosis prevention by standard risk (1, A)
  • Hypertension: Treat per GDMT, starting at a low dose and titrating gradually with monitoring (2020 ACC/AHA 1, B-NR). Practical: nitrates and other rapid vasodilators can cause profound hypotension in severe AS; the 2020 guideline makes no recommendation on vasodilators in acute decompensation
  • Diuretics: Practical: cautious use for pulmonary congestion; avoid over-diuresis (preload dependent)
  • Negative inotropes: Practical: use beta blockers cautiously and avoid them when decompensated
  • Rhythm: Practical: maintain sinus rhythm; loss of atrial contraction is poorly tolerated with a stiff, hypertrophied LV

Indications for Intervention (2020 ACC/AHA Guidelines):

  • Class I: Symptomatic severe high-gradient AS (D1: exertional dyspnea, HF, angina, syncope, or presyncope) (1, A); asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF <50% (C2) (1, B-NR); severe AS with other cardiac surgery (1, B-NR); symptomatic low-flow, low-gradient AS with reduced LVEF (D2) (1, B-NR) or normal LVEF (D3) if AS is the most likely cause (1, B-NR)
  • Class IIa (asymptomatic, low surgical risk): Abnormal exercise test (reduced tolerance or SBP fall ≥10 mmHg) (2a, B-NR); very severe AS, Vmax ≥5 m/s (2a, B-R); BNP >3 times normal (2a, B-NR); progression ≥0.3 m/s per year (2a, B-NR)
  • Class IIb: LVEF falling to <60% on at least 3 serial studies (2b, B-NR); moderate AS with other cardiac surgery (2b, C-EO)

Intervention Options:

  • Bioprosthetic AVR choice (2020 ACC/AHA): Age <65 or life expectancy >20 years: SAVR (1, A). Age 65-80 without anatomic contraindication: SAVR or transfemoral TAVI after shared decision-making (1, A). Age >80 or life expectancy <10 years: transfemoral TAVI in preference to SAVR (1, A). High or prohibitive surgical risk: TAVI if predicted post-TAVI survival >12 months with acceptable quality of life (1, A). Asymptomatic with a Class IIa indication: SAVR in preference to TAVI (1, B-NR)
  • Palliative care: If predicted survival after TAVI or SAVR is <12 months or minimal quality-of-life gain is expected, after shared decision-making (1, C-EO)
  • Balloon aortic valvuloplasty: May be considered as a bridge to SAVR or TAVI in critically ill patients (2b, C-EO). Practical: not definitive therapy

Acute Decompensation Management:

  • ICU admission; urgent cardiology and cardiac surgery (heart team) consultation
  • Practical: gentle diuresis avoiding hypotension; an inotrope (e.g., dobutamine) for low output; avoid rapid vasodilators unless used with invasive hemodynamic monitoring
  • Definitive: urgent AVR per the choice criteria above; balloon aortic valvuloplasty may be considered as a bridge in critically ill patients (2020 ACC/AHA 2b, C-EO)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Symptoms = Intervention: AVR is indicated for symptomatic severe AS (2020 ACC/AHA 1, A); without it, median survival is about 5, 3, and under 2 years after angina, syncope, and HF (Ross and Braunwald, 1968).
  • Vasodilators With Care: Practical: rapid-acting vasodilators such as nitrates can cause severe hypotension because the fixed obstruction limits any rise in cardiac output. Chronic hypertension should still be treated, starting low and titrating (2020 ACC/AHA 1, B-NR); after TAVI, an ACE inhibitor or ARB may be considered (2b, B-NR).
  • The Murmur May Soften: As AS progresses and LV fails, the murmur may become softer (less flow across valve). Don't be fooled – soft murmur ≠ mild AS in a failing ventricle.
  • Heyde Syndrome: AS + GI bleeding from angiodysplasia + acquired von Willebrand syndrome. Acquired type 2A von Willebrand syndrome is common in severe AS, tracks with severity (loss of the largest vWF multimers under high shear), and improves after valve replacement unless there is patient-prosthesis mismatch (Vincentelli, NEJM 2003).
  • TAVI vs SAVR: Chosen by age, life expectancy, anatomy, and shared decision-making with the heart team, not by surgical risk alone (2020 ACC/AHA; see above).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Cardiogenic shock
  • Acute pulmonary edema
  • Syncope with hemodynamic instability
  • New arrhythmias (especially AF with RVR)
  • Need for inotropic support
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Euvolemic on oral diuretics
  • Intervention plan established (SAVR/TAVR scheduled)
  • Cardiology follow-up arranged
  • Patient educated on activity restrictions and symptoms
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Norepinephrine

133. ACUTE MITRAL REGURGITATION

Papillary Muscle Rupture • Chordae Tendineae • Surgical Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Key Distinction from Chronic MR: In acute MR, the LA is non-compliant (no time to dilate) → acute elevation of LA pressure → flash pulmonary edema. Chronic MR allows LA dilation, delaying symptoms.

Symptoms:

  • Acute, severe dyspnea
  • Flash pulmonary edema
  • Hypotension, cardiogenic shock
  • May have chest pain if ischemic etiology

Physical Exam:

  • Murmur may be SOFT or ABSENT: The murmur may be short and unimpressive, as may the color jet on TTE, because the falling LV-LA pressure gradient confines MR to early systole (2020 ACC/AHA)
  • S3 gallop: Volume overload
  • Rales: Pulmonary edema
  • Hypotension: Reduced forward cardiac output

Etiologies:

  • Papillary muscle rupture: After STEMI, usually with an inferior infarction (2020 ACC/AHA); mechanical complications typically present within the first week with disproportionate HF, cardiogenic shock, or a new murmur (2025 ACC/AHA ACS). Practical: the posteromedial papillary muscle is most often involved
  • Chordae tendineae rupture: Myxomatous degeneration (MVP), endocarditis, trauma
  • Infective endocarditis: Valve perforation, vegetation interference
  • Prosthetic valve dysfunction: Dehiscence, stuck leaflet
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Echocardiography (Urgent):

  • TTE: Initial imaging of choice: LV and RV function, pulmonary artery pressure, and mechanism of MR (2020 ACC/AHA); the jet may look deceptively small. Papillary muscle rupture shows an eccentric or broad jet of severe MR and a mobile mass prolapsing into the LA (2025 ACC/AHA ACS Figure 9)
  • TEE: Especially helpful after MI with sudden instability, a hyperdynamic LV on TTE, and no other cause: detects papillary muscle or chordal rupture, vegetations, and annular abscess (2020 ACC/AHA)
  • Findings: Hyperdynamic LV (volume overload), dilated LA (if any chronicity), pulmonary hypertension, flail leaflet

Other Studies:

  • CXR: Pulmonary edema. Practical: may be asymmetric with an eccentric jet
  • ECG: May show ischemia if post-MI; AF common
  • BNP: Practical: elevated; supports HF but does not identify the cause
  • Coronary angiography: If ischemic etiology suspected and patient stable enough

Cross-link: 📚 Acute Coronary Syndrome, 📚 Infective Endocarditis

MANAGEMENT

Medical Stabilization (Bridge to Surgery):

  • Afterload reduction: A titratable vasodilator infusion (nitroprusside or nicardipine) lowers aortic impedance, decreasing MR and increasing forward output; its use is often limited by hypotension (2020 ACC/AHA). Nitroprusside dosing and FDA boxed warning: see the Hypertensive Emergency card
  • Inotropes: Practical: dobutamine if hypotensive
  • Diuretics: Practical: for pulmonary edema
  • IABP / MCS: IABP can help in acute severe MR: it lowers systolic aortic pressure (less regurgitation, more forward flow) and raises diastolic and mean aortic pressure; a percutaneous assist device may stabilize before the procedure (2020 ACC/AHA). After MI, short-term MCS is reasonable as a bridge to surgery (2025 ACC/AHA ACS 2a, B-NR)
  • Avoid: Practical: pure vasoconstrictors (raise afterload and worsen MR)

Definitive Treatment = SURGERY:

  • Prompt mitral valve surgery, preferably repair, is lifesaving in symptomatic acute severe primary MR; most patients need surgery, and complete papillary muscle rupture is poorly tolerated (2020 ACC/AHA)
  • Post-MI papillary rupture: Manage in a facility with cardiac surgical expertise (2025 ACC/AHA ACS 1, C-EO). Medical therapy alone carries a high risk of early death. Surgical mortality is highest with cardiogenic shock and early emergency surgery; lower mortality after delayed (>7 days) surgery partly reflects patient selection, and MCS has increased delayed approaches. Percutaneous repair is an evolving option when surgical risk is prohibitive (2025 ACS)

Specific Etiologies:

  • Post-MI: Emergent surgery ± CABG
  • Endocarditis: Valve dysfunction causing HF: early surgery during the initial hospitalization, before completing antibiotics (2020 ACC/AHA 1, B-NR), with timing decided by the Heart Valve Team (1, B-NR)
  • Prosthetic valve: Re-operation or transcatheter intervention depending on mechanism
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Murmur May Be Soft: Unlike chronic MR, acute severe MR may have a soft or short murmur due to rapid pressure equilibration. Don't rely on murmur intensity to assess severity.
  • Post-MI Timing: Mechanical complications usually present within the first week after MI, often as sudden deterioration with disproportionate HF or shock (2025 ACC/AHA ACS).
  • Posteromedial > Anterolateral: Practical: the posteromedial papillary muscle (single blood supply from the PDA) ruptures more often than the anterolateral (dual supply).
  • IABP as a Bridge: IABP lowers systolic aortic pressure and raises diastolic pressure, reducing regurgitation and supporting perfusion (2020 ACC/AHA); after MI, short-term MCS is reasonable as a bridge to surgery (2025 ACS 2a, B-NR).
  • Surgery is the Treatment: Medical therapy is temporizing only. Mortality without surgery is extremely high.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU/OR IF:
  • All acute severe MR – surgical emergency
  • Cardiogenic shock
  • Flash pulmonary edema
  • Need for IABP or mechanical support
✓ POST-OP CONSIDERATIONS
  • ICU monitoring post-operatively
  • Anticoagulation if mechanical valve
  • Endocarditis prophylaxis education
  • Cardiac rehab referral
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Nitroglycerin, 💊 Norepinephrine

134. SUPRAVENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA (SVT)

AVNRT • AVRT • Adenosine • Cardioversion
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: SVT: rate >100 bpm at rest with a mechanism involving tissue at or above the His bundle (AF excluded). PSVT, the focus of this card, is a regular rapid tachycardia of abrupt onset and termination, usually AVNRT or AVRT, less often AT (2015 SVT Table 3). QRS usually narrow (<120 ms).

Types of SVT:

  • AVNRT: Reentry within the AV node region. Most common SVT; >60% of cases in women; rate often 180-200 bpm (range 110 to >250). Typical form: P wave at the end of the QRS (pseudo-R' in V1, pseudo-S in inferior leads) (2015 SVT)
  • AVRT: Accessory pathway (eg, WPW). Orthodromic (antegrade via AV node) = narrow complex; P wave usually in the early ST-T segment. Relatively more common in adolescents; accessory-pathway tachycardia becomes less frequent with age (2015 SVT)
  • Atrial tachycardia: Focal or reentrant atrial source; P wave morphology differs from sinus. Focal AT is about 3-17% of patients referred for SVT ablation; relative proportion higher in older patients (2015 SVT)

Symptoms:

  • Palpitations (sudden onset, sudden offset)
  • Lightheadedness, presyncope
  • Chest discomfort, dyspnea
  • Polyuria, particularly with AVNRT (higher right atrial pressure and atrial natriuretic peptide) (2015 SVT)
  • Rarely syncope or hemodynamic collapse

Triggers: Caffeine, alcohol, stress, decongestants, hyperthyroidism, electrolyte abnormalities

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

ECG During Tachycardia:

  • Narrow QRS (<120 ms). If QRS >120 ms, distinguish VT from SVT with aberrancy, pre-existing bundle-branch block, or pre-excitation (2015 SVT); wide-complex management on card 46
  • Regular R-R intervals
  • Rate typically ≥150/min for a tachyarrhythmia (2025 ALS Figure 6); AVNRT often 180-200 bpm (2015 SVT)
  • P wave location helps identify mechanism

Baseline ECG (After Conversion):

  • Look for delta wave (WPW) – short PR, slurred QRS upstroke
  • Pre-excitation syndromes have risk of rapid AF with accessory pathway conduction

Labs (Practical):

  • Electrolytes (K, Mg)
  • TSH
  • Troponin if chest pain or hemodynamic compromise

Cross-link: 🔬 Electrolytes Reference, 🩺 Atrial Fibrillation

MANAGEMENT

Hemodynamically UNSTABLE (hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute HF):

  • Synchronized cardioversion (Class 1): 100 J initial for narrow-complex tachycardia; sedate whenever feasible; increase energy if refractory (2025 AHA ALS Figures 6 and 7; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline)
  • If regular and narrow: Consider adenosine; cardiovert when vagal maneuvers or adenosine are ineffective or not feasible (2025 ALS Figure 6; 2015 SVT)
  • Confirm the tachycardia is the cause: Instability may come from another diagnosis (eg, sepsis with sinus tachycardia). Immediate cardioversion is generally not needed if HR ≤150/min (2025 ALS)

Hemodynamically STABLE – Step-wise Approach:

Step 1: Vagal Maneuvers (Class 1, B-R; perform supine)

  • Modified Valsalva (preferred): 15 s strain at 40 mm Hg, semi-recumbent (REVERT used a manometer; blowing into a 10 mL syringe to move the plunger is a substitute, but syringe pressure varies by brand), then immediately lie flat with legs passively raised to 45° for 15 s. Terminated 43% vs 17% for standard Valsalva in REVERT; up to 50% with modified techniques vs 20-30% standard (2025 ALS)
  • Standard Valsalva: Bear down against a closed glottis for 10-30 s, at least 30-40 mm Hg (2015 SVT)
  • Carotid sinus massage: Steady unilateral pressure for 5-10 s after confirming no bruit; can precipitate stroke with carotid atherosclerosis (2015 SVT; 2025 ALS). Contraindicated with a carotid bruit, or TIA, stroke, or MI within 3 months, unless carotid Doppler excludes significant stenosis (2017 ACC/AHA/HRS syncope guideline text, as on the Syncope card). Practical: with known carotid disease, use a modified Valsalva or adenosine instead
  • Diving reflex: Ice-cold wet towel to the face (2015 SVT). Never press on the eyeballs (dangerous, abandoned)

Step 2: Adenosine (Class 1, B-R)

  • First dose: 6 mg rapid IV push over 1-2 s, as proximal as possible, followed by rapid NS flush (2015 SVT Table 6; 2025 ALS Figure 6). Practical: 20 mL flush with arm elevation
  • Second dose: 12 mg if no result within 1-2 min
  • Third dose: 12 mg may be repeated once (2015 SVT Table 6)
  • Reduced dose: Central line or heart transplant recipient: profound effect; 1 mg IV may be adequate (2025 ALS)
  • Warn patient: Transient chest discomfort, flushing, sense of "impending doom" – resolves in seconds
  • Contraindications/precautions: Asthma (can cause severe bronchospasm; contraindicated per 2025 ALS); AV block greater than first degree or sinus node dysfunction without a pacemaker; concomitant verapamil or digoxin; pre-excitation (may precipitate AF with rapid conduction, so have cardioversion available); pre-excited AF or any irregular or polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia (3: Harm) (2015 SVT Table 6 and AVRT section; 2025 ALS)

Step 3: If Adenosine Fails

  • Before IV CCB or beta-blocker: Confirm the rhythm is not VT or pre-excited AF (risk of collapse or VF). Avoid diltiazem/verapamil with suspected systolic HF. Avoid both classes with hypotension, decompensated HF, or AV block greater than first degree without a pacemaker; beta-blockers with caution in reactive airway disease. Either CCB may be infused slowly (up to 20 min) to lessen hypotension (2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline and Table 6; 2025 AHA ALS)
  • Diltiazem (IIa, B-R): 0.25 mg/kg actual body weight IV over 2 min (about 20 mg); if inadequate after 15 min, 0.35 mg/kg over 2 min (about 25 mg); then infusion 5-15 mg/hr (2015 SVT Table 6; FDA label)
  • Verapamil (IIa, B-R): 5-10 mg (0.075-0.15 mg/kg) IV over 2 min; if no response, 10 mg (0.15 mg/kg) 30 min after the first dose (2015 SVT Table 6)
  • Beta-blockers (IIa, C-LD): Metoprolol tartrate 2.5-5 mg IV over 2 min, may repeat every 10 min, up to 3 doses; or esmolol 500 mcg/kg IV over 1 min, then 50-300 mcg/kg/min with a repeat bolus before each increase (2015 SVT Table 6)
  • Known pre-excitation (WPW), regular orthodromic AVRT: IV diltiazem, verapamil, or beta-blockers are IIa only if the resting sinus-rhythm ECG shows no pre-excitation. With resting pre-excitation they are IIb, only after other therapies fail, with cardioversion available (AVRT may convert to AF with rapid accessory-pathway conduction) (2015 SVT AVRT recs)

Step 4: Cardioversion

  • If drugs are ineffective or contraindicated (Class 1, B-NR), or the patient decompensates
  • Synchronized cardioversion 100 J after adequate sedation (2015 SVT; 2025 ALS Figure 7)

Pregnancy (2015 SVT pregnancy recs, all C-LD):

  • Vagal maneuvers (I), then adenosine (I) at the same 6/12/12 mg dosing; its short half-life makes fetal exposure unlikely
  • Synchronized cardioversion (I) if unstable and drugs are ineffective or contraindicated: reported safe at all stages, same energy as nonpregnant, pads directed away from the uterus, fetal monitoring if time allows and after
  • If adenosine is ineffective or contraindicated: IV metoprolol or propranolol (IIa); IV verapamil (IIb; more maternal hypotension than adenosine); IV procainamide (IIb); IV amiodarone (IIb) only for potentially life-threatening SVT when others fail (fetal adverse effects)

Long-Term Management:

  • EP study with option of ablation (I, B-NR): First-line and potentially curative. Acute success 96-97% for AVNRT and 93% for AVRT; recurrence 5% and 8% (2015 SVT Table 8)
  • Prevention of recurrence (I, B-R): Oral beta-blocker, diltiazem, or verapamil if no pre-excitation on the resting ECG and ablation is not chosen (2015 SVT)
  • Pill-in-the-pocket (IIb, C-LD): Single oral dose of a beta-blocker, diltiazem, or verapamil for infrequent, well-tolerated AVNRT episodes; seek care if it fails (2015 SVT)
  • Teach vagal maneuvers (I, C-LD): Valsalva performed supine, to abort future episodes (2015 SVT)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Modified Valsalva Works Better: Strain, then immediately supine with passive leg raise: 43% vs 17% conversion in the REVERT RCT; up to 50% vs 20-30% across studies (2025 ALS)
  • Adenosine Technique Matters: Rapid bolus as proximal as possible with an immediate saline flush. Its very short half-life means slow or distal administration may be ineffective (2015 SVT Table 6; 2025 ALS)
  • WPW Danger (pre-excited AF: irregular, wide QRS with varying morphology): IV digoxin, IV amiodarone, IV or oral beta-blockers, diltiazem, and verapamil are potentially harmful (3: Harm, C-LD); adenosine is 3: Harm in irregular or polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia (2025 ALS). These can accelerate accessory-pathway conduction and cause VF. Unstable: synchronized cardioversion (I, B-NR). Stable: ibutilide or IV procainamide (I, C-LD) (2015 SVT AVRT recs). Ibutilide 1 mg IV over 10 min (0.01 mg/kg if <60 kg), may repeat once if not terminated within 10 min; contraindicated if QTc >440 ms; ECG monitoring at least 4 h (2015 SVT Table 6). Procainamide 20-50 mg/min IV until the arrhythmia is suppressed, hypotension occurs, QRS widens >50%, or 17 mg/kg is given; maintenance 1-4 mg/min; avoid if prolonged QT or HF (2025 ALS Figure 6)
  • Record the Strip: Record a continuous ECG during adenosine. Transient AV block can unmask atrial flutter or AT, and the strip distinguishes failure to terminate from termination with immediate reinitiation (2015 SVT)
  • Ablation is Curative: For recurrent SVT, refer to EP. Slow-pathway ablation for AVNRT succeeds in >95% with <1% risk of AV block; accessory-pathway ablation succeeds in about 93-95% with about 3% major complications (2015 SVT)
⚠️ ESCALATE IF:
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Refractory to adenosine and IV CCB or beta-blocker
  • Wide-complex tachycardia (may be VT)
  • Pre-excited AF (WPW with AF)
  • Associated ischemia or heart failure
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Converted to sinus rhythm
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • No ongoing symptoms
  • Taught vagal maneuvers; preventive beta-blocker, diltiazem, or verapamil if recurrent and no pre-excitation (2015 SVT)
  • EP/Cardiology follow-up for ablation discussion
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Adenosine, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Diltiazem

136. PULMONARY HYPERTENSION CRISIS

RV Failure • Avoid Systemic Hypotension • Pulmonary Vasodilators
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Acute RV failure in setting of pulmonary hypertension, often triggered by an acute event. Life-threatening emergency.

Symptoms:

  • Severe dyspnea, worsening exercise intolerance
  • Syncope or presyncope
  • Chest pain (RV ischemia)
  • Altered mental status (low cardiac output)

Signs:

  • Hypotension, tachycardia
  • Elevated JVP, RV heave
  • Loud P2, TR murmur
  • Peripheral edema, hepatomegaly
  • Cool extremities (low output)

Common Triggers:

  • Infection/sepsis
  • Arrhythmia (especially AF)
  • PE (acute-on-chronic)
  • Non-compliance with PH therapy
  • Anesthesia/surgery
  • Pregnancy (high mortality in PH)
  • Volume overload
  • Hypoxemia
MANAGEMENT

Goals:

  • Three tenets: Optimize preload, reduce RV afterload, augment contractility; also rate and rhythm control, oxygenation, and ventilation (HFSA 2026)
  • Maintain aortic pressure: Protects right coronary perfusion and prevents RV ischemia. MAP 70-75 mmHg suggested, without comparative studies (7th WSPH 2024; HFSA 2026); ESC/ERS 2022: keep mean BP above 60 mmHg
  • Relieve congestion: Most patients need a negative fluid balance to reduce RV preload and improve RV geometry (ESC/ERS 2022); loop diuretics are the mainstay (HFSA 2026; 7th WSPH). Balance decongestion against perfusion (see Diuresis)
  • Support cardiac output: Inotrope for low output (see below)
  • Reduce RV afterload: Correct hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis, which worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction (HFSA 2026); pulmonary vasodilators as below
  • Treat the precipitating trigger

Immediate Interventions:

  • Oxygen: Keep SaO2 above 90%; high-flow oxygen if needed (7th WSPH)
  • Avoid intubation if possible: Invasive ventilation carries a high risk of further hemodynamic deterioration and death (ESC/ERS 2022); noninvasive ventilation is preferred when feasible (HFSA 2026); avoid hypercapnia and hyperinflation (7th WSPH)
  • If intubation is unavoidable (HFSA 2026): Awake intubation is preferred over rapid sequence intubation when feasible; ketamine has been linked to more cardiovascular derangement, while etomidate has less direct myocardial depression; low tidal volume and no high PEEP. Practical: most experienced operator, vasopressor running before induction
  • Monitoring: Arterial line; internal jugular central line for CVP and ScvO2 in severe cases; echocardiography; BNP or NT-proBNP, troponin, lactate, renal and liver tests. PA catheter if PH is a new diagnosis or hemodynamics are complex (7th WSPH)

Hemodynamic Support:

  • Dobutamine: First-line inotrope for low cardiac output with preserved BP (7th WSPH); often used first when acutely unstable (HFSA 2026). Start 2.5 mcg/kg/min and uptitrate; do not exceed 5-7.5 mcg/kg/min (higher doses lower SVR without raising output, cause tachycardia, and increase myocardial O2 demand) (7th WSPH)
  • Norepinephrine or vasopressin: Drugs of choice for hypotension; low-dose norepinephrine and vasopressin are preferred (7th WSPH; HFSA 2026). Vasopressin adds pulmonary vasodilatory and natriuretic effects with less tachyarrhythmia
  • Milrinone: Inodilator with stronger pulmonary vasodilation, useful in PH-related RV failure or after recent beta-blocker; typical 0.25-0.5 mcg/kg/min, adjusted for renal function (accumulates in kidney impairment) (HFSA 2026). Lowers SVR and often needs a vasopressor; use with caution in PH (7th WSPH)
  • Epinephrine: Not preferred (tachycardia, lactic acidosis); 7th WSPH says do not use it; HFSA 2026: may be required in refractory cases with severely reduced cardiac output
  • Avoid systemic vasodilators (Practical): They drop systemic BP more than PVR and worsen RV ischemia

Pulmonary Vasodilators:

  • Role: A mainstay for selected patients with acute RV failure; inhaled agents are more pulmonary-selective; IV agents carry more systemic adverse effects such as hypotension and V/Q mismatch (HFSA 2026)
  • Inhaled nitric oxide: Lowers PVR; doses of 10-40 ppm studied, with no greater PVR reduction above 10 ppm; wean to avoid rebound (HFSA 2026). With dobutamine it may help some patients as a bridge, though clinical evidence is limited (7th WSPH). Off-label in adults (US label: neonates, 20 ppm)
  • Inhaled epoprostenol: Reasonable alternative to iNO where iNO is unavailable or cost-prohibitive; needs a specialized delivery system (HFSA 2026)
  • IV epoprostenol: HFSA 2026: generally preferred for severe RV failure in PAH (potent, rapid onset, titratable); adverse effects include hypotension. 7th WSPH: PAH-specific therapy is not an emergency drug before hemodynamic stability. Practical: start only with PH expertise and vasopressor support
  • Newly diagnosed PAH with low cardiac output: Combination therapy including IV or SC prostacyclin should be considered, with a PH center (ESC/ERS 2022; 7th WSPH); HFSA 2026: prostacyclin-containing combinations are particularly effective when RV failure is the first presentation of PAH
  • Continue home PH medications: Never interrupt IV or SC prostacyclin. The US epoprostenol label warns of rebound PH with abrupt withdrawal or interruptions; the UK label calls the rebound potentially fatal. Continue ERA and PDE5i unless hypotension forces a hold (Practical)

Diuresis:

  • IV loop diuretics are the cornerstone (7th WSPH): If already on oral diuretics, continuous IV infusion starting above the home dose; otherwise a bolus, then adjust to response
  • Balance decongestion against perfusion (HFSA 2026): Overdiuresis can cause hypotension and renal dysfunction, especially in low-output RV failure; consider invasive hemodynamics if volume status is unclear, renal function worsens, or hemodynamics are unstable. IV fluid only in rare cases such as RV infarction with relative volume depletion
  • Inadequate response: add a thiazide, with inotropic or vasopressor support if needed (7th WSPH; HFSA 2026)
  • Ultrafiltration or renal replacement therapy: For persistent congestion (HFSA 2026); 7th WSPH: only selected patients without severe instability, continuous hemodiafiltration preferred; bridging candidates with severe cardiorenal syndrome: ECLS instead

Treat Underlying Trigger (7th WSPH Table 1):

  • Supraventricular arrhythmia: 7th WSPH: avoid beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers; consider digoxin for rate and amiodarone for medical cardioversion; electrical cardioversion or ablation by type and tolerance. HFSA 2026: rate-control drugs may work at first but carry negative inotropy and hypotension; cardioversion success is variable; digoxin evidence is limited
  • Infection: Early empirical treatment after cultures; remove the central line if it is infected (IV epoprostenol)
  • Pulmonary embolism: Therapeutic anticoagulation
  • Anemia: Transfusion
  • Also hypoxemia, surgery or anesthesia, and nonadherence (education)

Refractory Cases:

  • VA-ECMO: Peripheral VA-ECMO, ideally in an awake patient, as a bridge to transplant or recovery in selected patients; with high PVR, prefer configurations that bypass the RV and pulmonary circulation (7th WSPH). ESC/ERS 2022: mechanical support may be an option (IIa); transfer if unavailable on site. Other temporary MCS (Impella RP, ProtekDuo, surgical RVAD) are chosen by etiology, isolated vs biventricular support, and hemodynamic status (HFSA 2026)
  • Atrial septostomy: NOT in the acute crisis; 7th WSPH recommends against urgent atrial septostomy (excess morbidity and mortality). Palliative option or bridge to lung transplant in end-stage PH; not an option with RAP >20 mmHg, significant hypoxia, or PVR index >55 U/m2 (HFSA 2026)
  • Early transplant evaluation; palliative care when rescue therapy is not an option (7th WSPH)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Keep Aortic Pressure Up: RV coronary perfusion depends on aortic pressure; systemic hypotension → RV ischemia → worse RV failure. Normal BP does not exclude severe RV failure, because reflex vasoconstriction can hold BP up (7th WSPH).
  • Never Stop Home Prostacyclin: Interrupting IV or SC prostacyclin causes rebound PH (US label); the UK label calls it potentially fatal. Keep the infusion running in crisis.
  • Avoid Intubation if Possible: High risk of hemodynamic collapse and death in advanced RV failure (ESC/ERS 2022). If required: awake intubation when feasible, low tidal volume, no high PEEP (HFSA 2026); vasopressor running before induction (Practical).
  • Diurese, Do Not Fill: Most patients in decompensated PH are volume overloaded; a negative fluid balance improves RV geometry and function (ESC/ERS 2022).
  • Inhaled Vasodilators First: iNO or inhaled epoprostenol lower PVR with little systemic effect (HFSA 2026); outcome evidence is limited (7th WSPH). IV prostacyclin is potent but drops systemic BP.
  • The Death Spiral: RV dilation → TR worsens → RV CO drops → systemic hypotension → RV ischemia → RV fails further. Must break this cycle early.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • All PH crisis – ICU mandatory
  • Hypotension, shock
  • Need for vasopressors or inotropes
  • Respiratory failure
  • Syncope
✓ STABILIZATION GOALS
  • MAP 70-75 mmHg (7th WSPH; HFSA 2026; ESC/ERS 2022: above 60)
  • SpO2 >90%
  • Resolving end-organ dysfunction
  • Weaning vasopressors
  • PH specialist consultation
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sildenafil, 💊 Milrinone, 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Dobutamine, 💊 Vasopressin, 💊 Furosemide

139. HYPERVISCOSITY SYNDROME

Waldenstrom's • Multiple Myeloma • Plasmapheresis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Increased blood viscosity causing impaired microvascular flow. Classic triad: bleeding, neurologic symptoms, visual disturbances.

Classic Triad:

  • Bleeding: Mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gingival), GI bleeding, menorrhagia. Paraprotein interferes with platelet function and coagulation factors.
  • Neurologic: Headache, confusion, altered mental status, ataxia, vertigo, hearing loss, stroke-like symptoms
  • Visual: Blurred vision, diplopia, vision loss. Fundoscopy shows "sausage-link" or "boxcar" retinal veins, retinal hemorrhages, papilledema.

Other Manifestations:

  • Dyspnea, hypoxia (pulmonary infiltrates)
  • Heart failure (increased cardiac workload)
  • Cryoglobulinemia (if cryoglobulins present)

Common Causes:

  • Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (IgM): Most common cause. IgM is large pentamer – small increases cause large viscosity changes.
  • Multiple myeloma (IgA, IgG3): Less common than WM. IgA tends to polymerize.
  • Polycythemia vera / Leukostasis: Cellular hyperviscosity (WBC >100k or Hct >60%)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Serum Viscosity:

  • Normal: 1.4-1.8 centipoise (relative to water)
  • Symptoms typically occur at >4 cp (but varies by individual)
  • Some patients symptomatic at lower levels; others asymptomatic at higher levels

Laboratory:

  • SPEP/UPEP: M-spike
  • Immunofixation: Identifies paraprotein type (IgM, IgA, IgG)
  • Quantitative immunoglobulins: Elevated monoclonal Ig
  • CBC: Anemia common (dilutional, marrow infiltration)
  • Coagulation studies: May be abnormal (paraprotein interference)

Fundoscopic Exam: Essential – look for retinal vein engorgement, hemorrhages, papilledema

Cross-link: 🔬 SPEP Reference

MANAGEMENT

Emergent Treatment – Plasmapheresis:

  • Removes circulating paraprotein – rapidly reduces viscosity
  • Single session can reduce IgM by 30-50%
  • Usually 1-2 exchanges initially, then as needed
  • Bridge to definitive chemotherapy

Supportive Measures:

  • IV hydration: Improves rheology
  • AVOID transfusion of PRBC: Will worsen viscosity. If anemia severe and transfusion necessary, do after plasmapheresis.
  • Treat bleeding: Supportive; may need platelet transfusion

Definitive Treatment – Chemotherapy:

  • Waldenstrom: Rituximab-based regimens (but rituximab can cause IgM flare – sometimes defer until after plasmapheresis), BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib)
  • Multiple myeloma: Bortezomib-based regimens, IMiDs

Rituximab Flare: Rituximab can cause transient increase in IgM (tumor lysis or cytokine release). In hyperviscosity, may need plasmapheresis before rituximab.

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • IgM is the Worst Offender: IgM is a pentamer (large) – small increases cause disproportionate viscosity increase. Waldenstrom's is more likely to cause hyperviscosity than myeloma at same paraprotein level.
  • Check the Eyes: Fundoscopic exam is essential. "Sausage-link" retinal veins are classic. Visual changes may be the presenting symptom.
  • Don't Transfuse RBCs: This will worsen viscosity. If patient needs blood, do plasmapheresis first.
  • Plasmapheresis is Temporary: Reduces paraprotein but doesn't treat underlying disease. Chemotherapy is definitive treatment.
  • Symptoms Don't Correlate Perfectly with Viscosity: Some patients are symptomatic at viscosity 3, others asymptomatic at 6. Treat symptoms, not just numbers.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Altered mental status, obtundation
  • Stroke-like symptoms
  • Severe bleeding
  • Respiratory failure
  • Urgent plasmapheresis needed
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Symptoms resolved
  • Viscosity improved
  • Chemotherapy plan established
  • Hematology/Oncology follow-up
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 SPEP/UPEP/Free Light Chains, 🔬 LDH, 🔬 Hyponatremia

143. ACETAMINOPHEN OVERDOSE

Rumack-Matthew Nomogram • N-Acetylcysteine • Acute Liver Failure
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Stages of Toxicity:

  • Stage 1 (0-24h): Often asymptomatic or nonspecific (nausea, vomiting, malaise). Labs normal.
  • Stage 2 (24-72h): RUQ pain, elevated AST/ALT. Stage 1 symptoms may resolve.
  • Stage 3 (72-96h): Peak hepatotoxicity. Markedly elevated transaminases, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, possible renal failure.
  • Stage 4 (4d-2wk): Recovery (if survived) or death from fulminant hepatic failure.

Key Point: Patients may appear well initially. Don't be reassured by lack of early symptoms.

Toxic Dose:

  • >150 mg/kg (or >7.5-10g in adults) acute ingestion – potential for hepatotoxicity
  • Chronic ingestion: lower thresholds, nomogram doesn't apply
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Serum Acetaminophen Level:

  • Draw at 4 hours post-ingestion (or immediately if >4h since ingestion)
  • Plot on Rumack-Matthew Nomogram

Rumack-Matthew Nomogram:

  • Treatment line starts at 150 mcg/mL at 4h post-ingestion
  • Level above the line → treat with NAC
  • Only valid for single acute ingestion with known time

Other Labs:

  • AST/ALT (may be normal initially)
  • INR, bilirubin
  • BMP (creatinine – renal failure can occur)
  • Serum salicylate (common co-ingestant)

Cross-link: 🔬 LFT Reference

MANAGEMENT

Decontamination:

  • Activated charcoal: If <4h from ingestion and patient alert. 1 g/kg (max 50g).

N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) – The Antidote:

  • Indication: Level above treatment line, unknown ingestion time with detectable level and transaminitis, massive ingestion, late presentation with hepatotoxicity
  • Most effective if started within 8 hours – but give even if late if hepatotoxicity present

IV NAC Protocol (21-hour):

  • Loading: 150 mg/kg in 200mL D5W over 1 hour
  • Second dose: 50 mg/kg in 500mL D5W over 4 hours
  • Third dose: 100 mg/kg in 1000mL D5W over 16 hours
  • If ongoing hepatotoxicity, continue third dose rate until INR <2, AST/ALT declining, and no encephalopathy

Oral NAC Protocol (72-hour):

  • Loading: 140 mg/kg PO × 1
  • Maintenance: 70 mg/kg PO q4h × 17 doses

Anaphylactoid Reactions to IV NAC:

  • Common (10-20%) – flushing, urticaria, bronchospasm
  • Usually rate-related – slow or pause infusion, give antihistamines
  • True anaphylaxis rare – can usually rechallenge at slower rate

Liver Transplant Criteria (King's College Criteria):

  • pH <7.3 after resuscitation, OR
  • All three: INR >6.5, Cr >3.4, Grade 3-4 encephalopathy
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • 8-Hour Window: NAC is nearly 100% effective if started within 8 hours. Efficacy decreases after that but still give it.
  • Patients Look Well Initially: Stage 1 is asymptomatic. Don't discharge early based on how patient "looks."
  • Nomogram Only for Acute Single Ingestion: Chronic supratherapeutic ingestion, staggered dosing, or unknown time → nomogram doesn't apply. Use clinical judgment, lower threshold to treat.
  • AST >1000: This should make you think of APAP toxicity (or ischemic/viral hepatitis). Not typical of other drug reactions.
  • Anaphylactoid ≠ Stop NAC: Slow the rate, give antihistamines, usually can resume. Don't withhold life-saving antidote.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Elevated INR or transaminases
  • Encephalopathy
  • Massive ingestion (>500 mg/kg)
  • Concerning trajectory
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Level below treatment line at 4h+ post-ingestion
  • Normal AST/ALT, INR
  • Psychiatry clearance if intentional
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 N-Acetylcysteine, 💊 Activated Charcoal
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Acetaminophen Level, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated Lactate

144. SALICYLATE TOXICITY

Mixed Acid-Base • Alkalinization • Dialysis Indications
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Early (Mild): Tinnitus, nausea, vomiting, tachypnea (respiratory alkalosis from direct CNS stimulation)

Moderate: Hyperthermia, diaphoresis, altered mental status, mixed acid-base disorder

Severe: Seizures, coma, cerebral edema, pulmonary edema, cardiovascular collapse, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy

Classic Acid-Base Pattern:

  • Early: Respiratory alkalosis (CNS stimulation of respiratory center)
  • Later: Anion gap metabolic acidosis (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation, lactate, ketones)
  • Mixed: Often see combined respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis

Toxic Dose: >150 mg/kg acute ingestion (single dose >6.5g in adults)

MANAGEMENT

Decontamination:

  • Activated charcoal: Effective even several hours post-ingestion (enteric-coated formulations, bezoar formation)
  • May repeat charcoal doses for significant ingestions

Urinary Alkalinization:

  • Goal: Urine pH 7.5-8.0. Traps ionized salicylate in urine, enhances elimination.
  • Method: Sodium bicarbonate 150 mEq in 1L D5W at 1.5-2× maintenance
  • Monitor: Urine pH, serum K (alkalinization causes hypokalemia – must replace K to achieve urinary alkalinization)

Hemodialysis Indications:

  • Salicylate level >100 mg/dL (acute) or >80 mg/dL (chronic)
  • Severe altered mental status or coma
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Seizures
  • Renal failure (can't alkalinize)
  • Clinical deterioration despite treatment

DO NOT INTUBATE without Good Reason:

  • Patients with salicylate toxicity have massive compensatory hyperventilation
  • If intubated, must match their minute ventilation – otherwise pH drops rapidly, salicylate enters CNS, death
  • If intubation required, use high RR and tidal volume

Cross-link: 🩺 Acid-Base Framework

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • The Intubation Trap: Salicylate-toxic patients hyperventilate massively to compensate. If you intubate and normalize their CO2, pH crashes, salicylate enters brain, they die. Avoid intubation if possible; if required, match their high minute ventilation.
  • Alkalemia is Protective: At alkaline pH, salicylate is ionized and can't cross blood-brain barrier. Acidemia allows uncharged salicylate into CNS → cerebral toxicity.
  • Chronic Toxicity is More Dangerous: Chronic salicylate toxicity presents at lower levels with worse symptoms. Older patients on chronic aspirin are at high risk.
  • Check K Before Alkalinizing: Hypokalemia prevents urinary alkalinization. Must replace K aggressively.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Level >50 mg/dL
  • Altered mental status
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Need for dialysis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Declining salicylate levels
  • Resolved symptoms
  • Normal pH
  • Psychiatry clearance if intentional
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sodium Bicarbonate, 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Activated Charcoal
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Salicylate Level, 🔬 Anion Gap, 🔬 Low PaCO2, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Hyperkalemia
