145. TOXIC ALCOHOL INGESTION

Methanol • Ethylene Glycol • Osmol Gap • Fomepizole
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

General Features: Inebriation without ethanol smell, anion gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmol gap

Methanol:

  • Sources: Windshield washer fluid, wood alcohol, moonshine
  • Toxic metabolite: Formic acid
  • Features: Visual disturbances (blurred vision, "snowfield" vision, blindness), headache, abdominal pain
  • Classically causes basal ganglia hemorrhage

Ethylene Glycol:

  • Sources: Antifreeze (sweet-tasting)
  • Toxic metabolites: Glycolic acid, oxalic acid
  • Features: Renal failure (calcium oxalate crystal deposition), hypocalcemia
  • Calcium oxalate crystals on urinalysis (envelope-shaped)

Isopropanol:

  • Sources: Rubbing alcohol
  • Metabolite: Acetone (ketosis without acidosis)
  • Features: CNS depression, GI irritation, NO anion gap acidosis
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Osmol Gap:

  • Calculated Osm = 2[Na] + [Glucose]/18 + [BUN]/2.8 + [EtOH]/4.6
  • Osmol gap = Measured Osm – Calculated Osm
  • Normal <10. Elevated in toxic alcohol ingestion (before metabolism)

Anion Gap:

  • Elevated AG indicates toxic metabolites present
  • Early: High osmol gap, low/normal AG (parent compound present)
  • Late: Low osmol gap, high AG (metabolized to acids)

Specific Levels: Methanol and ethylene glycol levels (send but don't wait for results to treat)

Cross-link: 🔬 Electrolytes Reference

MANAGEMENT

Fomepizole (Antidote):

  • Inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase – prevents formation of toxic metabolites
  • Dosing: 15 mg/kg IV load, then 10 mg/kg IV q12h × 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg q12h
  • Continue until level <20 mg/dL and patient asymptomatic with normal pH

Ethanol (Alternative if Fomepizole Unavailable):

  • Same mechanism (competitive ADH inhibition)
  • Target serum ethanol 100-150 mg/dL
  • More difficult to titrate, more side effects

Hemodialysis Indications:

  • Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.25)
  • Visual disturbances (methanol)
  • Renal failure (ethylene glycol)
  • Level >50 mg/dL
  • Clinical deterioration

Adjunctive Therapy:

  • Methanol: Folic acid 50 mg IV q4h (enhances formate metabolism)
  • Ethylene glycol: Pyridoxine 100 mg IV q6h, Thiamine 100 mg IV q6h (enhance metabolism to nontoxic metabolites)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Osmol vs. Anion Gap Timing: Early = high osmol gap (parent compound). Late = high anion gap (metabolites). Both gaps may not be elevated simultaneously.
  • Visual Symptoms = Methanol: Formic acid is toxic to the optic nerve. Any visual symptoms → think methanol.
  • Renal Failure + Crystals = Ethylene Glycol: Calcium oxalate crystals in urine are classic but not always present.
  • Fomepizole is First-Line: Easier to use than ethanol, fewer side effects. Give empirically if high suspicion – don't wait for specific levels.
  • Isopropanol is Different: Causes ketosis (acetone) but NOT acidosis. Osmol gap without anion gap.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • All significant toxic alcohol ingestions
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Need for dialysis
  • Visual changes or AKI
✓ TREATMENT ENDPOINTS
  • Level <20 mg/dL
  • Normal pH
  • Resolved symptoms
  • Improving renal function (EG)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Fomepizole, 💊 Sodium Bicarbonate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Toxic Alcohol Panel, 🔬 Osmolar Gap, 🔬 Anion Gap, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

146. OPIOID OVERDOSE

Naloxone • Respiratory Depression • Harm Reduction
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad:

  • Miosis: Pinpoint pupils
  • CNS depression: Decreased LOC, coma
  • Respiratory depression: Decreased RR, hypoxia, apnea

Other Features: Hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, decreased bowel sounds, track marks

Complications:

  • Aspiration pneumonia
  • Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema
  • Rhabdomyolysis (from prolonged immobility)
  • Compartment syndrome
MANAGEMENT

Immediate:

  • Airway: Open airway, provide ventilation if needed
  • Naloxone: See below

Naloxone (Narcan):

  • Initial dose: 0.04-0.4 mg IV/IM/SC/IN. Start low if opioid-dependent (avoid precipitating severe withdrawal).
  • Goal: Restore adequate spontaneous respiration – NOT full alertness
  • Repeat: q2-3 min until adequate respiration (can give up to 10-15 mg total for synthetic opioids)
  • Half-life: 30-90 min – shorter than most opioids. Watch for recurrent sedation.

Special Considerations:

  • Fentanyl and analogues: May require higher naloxone doses (2-10+ mg)
  • Long-acting opioids (methadone): May need naloxone infusion (2/3 of reversal dose per hour)
  • Precipitated withdrawal: Severe but not life-threatening. Supportive care.

Observation Period:

  • Short-acting opioid (heroin): 4-6 hours post-naloxone
  • Long-acting/sustained-release: 12-24 hours (consider admission)

Harm Reduction at Discharge:

  • Prescribe naloxone kit (Narcan nasal spray)
  • Offer MAT (medication-assisted treatment): buprenorphine, methadone
  • Connect to addiction medicine resources
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Titrate to Respiration, Not Alertness: Goal is adequate breathing, not fully awake patient. Over-reversal causes severe withdrawal.
  • Fentanyl Needs More Naloxone: Synthetic opioids are highly potent. May need 10× typical naloxone dose.
  • Watch for Re-sedation: Naloxone wears off before most opioids. Observe 4-6h minimum; longer for long-acting opioids.
  • Prescribe Naloxone at Discharge: This saves lives. Ensure patient and family have take-home naloxone.
  • Offer Treatment: Every overdose is an opportunity to offer MAT. ED-initiated buprenorphine improves outcomes.
⚠️ ADMIT IF:
  • Long-acting opioid ingestion
  • Recurrent sedation
  • Needed naloxone infusion
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Concern for co-ingestion
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Alert and oriented
  • Adequate respiration off naloxone ≥4h
  • Ambulating safely
  • Naloxone kit prescribed
  • Harm reduction resources provided
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Naloxone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

147. VASCULITIS EMERGENCIES

DAH • Rapidly Progressive GN • Pulse Steroids + Cyclophosphamide
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Life-Threatening Manifestations:

  • Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage (DAH): Hemoptysis (may be absent), dyspnea, hypoxia, diffuse infiltrates, dropping hemoglobin. BAL shows progressively bloodier returns.
  • Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN): AKI over days-weeks, hematuria, RBC casts, proteinuria
  • Pulmonary-Renal Syndrome: DAH + RPGN = classic for ANCA vasculitis or anti-GBM disease

Vasculitides Causing Emergencies:

  • GPA (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis): cANCA/PR3+. Upper airway, lung, kidney involvement.
  • MPA (Microscopic Polyangiitis): pANCA/MPO+. Lung and kidney predominant.
  • Anti-GBM Disease (Goodpasture): Anti-GBM antibodies. Classic pulmonary-renal syndrome.
  • EGPA (Eosinophilic GPA): Asthma, eosinophilia, vasculitis.
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Serologies:

  • ANCA: cANCA/PR3 (GPA), pANCA/MPO (MPA)
  • Anti-GBM antibodies: Goodpasture syndrome
  • ANA, complement: Evaluate for SLE

Urinalysis: RBC casts = glomerulonephritis

Bronchoscopy with BAL: Confirms DAH (serial aliquots increasingly bloody, hemosiderin-laden macrophages)

Renal Biopsy: Pauci-immune crescentic GN (ANCA vasculitis), linear IgG staining (anti-GBM)

Cross-link: 🔬 Autoimmune Labs Reference, 📚 Glomerulonephritis

MANAGEMENT

Pulse Steroids (First-Line):

  • Methylprednisolone: 500-1000 mg IV daily × 3 days
  • Then prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 80mg) with taper

Cyclophosphamide or Rituximab:

  • Cyclophosphamide: 15 mg/kg IV q2weeks × 3, then q3weeks OR 2 mg/kg/day PO
  • Rituximab: 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 OR 1g × 2 doses 2 weeks apart. Now considered first-line for many patients (RAVE trial).

Plasmapheresis:

  • Anti-GBM disease: Clearly beneficial — removes circulating anti-GBM antibodies. Indicated for all confirmed anti-GBM disease.
  • ANCA vasculitis: PEXIVAS trial (NEJM 2020, n=704, largest RCT in AAV) showed plasma exchange did not reduce the composite endpoint of death or end-stage kidney disease vs no plasma exchange — including in the dialysis-dependent subgroup. Routine PLEX is NOT recommended for ANCA vasculitis. May be considered on a case-by-case basis for catastrophic DAH or in concert with anti-GBM co-positivity (≈30% of ANCA patients).
  • PEXIVAS steroid finding: Reduced-dose glucocorticoids were non-inferior to standard dose with significantly fewer serious infections — consider reduced-dose regimen when initiating steroid induction.

Supportive Care:

  • Respiratory support (may need intubation for DAH)
  • Renal replacement therapy if needed
  • PJP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) with immunosuppression
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Pulmonary-Renal Syndrome: DAH + RPGN = think ANCA vasculitis or anti-GBM disease. Requires aggressive immunosuppression.
  • Anti-GBM Needs Plasmapheresis — ANCA Does Not: PEXIVAS (NEJM 2020) showed PLEX provides no mortality or ESKD benefit in ANCA vasculitis, including dialysis-dependent disease. Anti-GBM disease is the clear plasmapheresis indication — removes pathogenic antibodies.
  • Don't Wait for Biopsy: In life-threatening vasculitis, start treatment empirically based on clinical picture and serologies. Biopsy can confirm but shouldn't delay therapy.
  • Rituximab is an Option: RAVE trial showed rituximab non-inferior to cyclophosphamide. Often preferred in younger patients (fertility) and relapsing disease.
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
  • Respiratory failure
  • Dialysis-dependent AKI
  • Need for plasmapheresis
✓ TREATMENT GOALS
  • Stabilize respiratory status
  • Preserve/recover renal function
  • Induce remission with immunosuppression
  • Transition to maintenance therapy
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Cyclophosphamide, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 ANCA, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 Anemia
↑ Back to Table of Contents

148. SCLERODERMA RENAL CRISIS

ACE Inhibitors • Malignant Hypertension • MAHA
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Life-threatening complication of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) characterized by acute renal failure and severe hypertension.

Classic Presentation:

  • Severe hypertension: Often >150/90, may be malignant (>180/120 with end-organ damage)
  • Rapidly progressive AKI: Over days
  • MAHA: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin)
  • Thrombocytopenia: May mimic TTP/HUS

Associated Features:

  • Hypertensive encephalopathy (headache, confusion, seizures)
  • Flash pulmonary edema
  • Cardiac involvement (pericardial effusion, arrhythmias)

Risk Factors:

  • Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (especially early, rapidly progressive skin disease)
  • Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies (strongest association)
  • High-dose corticosteroids (may precipitate SRC)
  • First 5 years of disease
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory:

  • BMP (elevated creatinine, hyperkalemia)
  • CBC with smear (MAHA – schistocytes, thrombocytopenia)
  • LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin (hemolysis)
  • Urinalysis (proteinuria, possible hematuria)
  • Coagulation studies (usually normal, unlike DIC)

Differentiate from TTP:

  • SRC has severe hypertension (TTP usually doesn't)
  • SRC occurs in scleroderma patients
  • ADAMTS13 normal in SRC

Renal Biopsy: Not usually required for diagnosis. Shows thrombotic microangiopathy, "onion-skin" arterial lesions.

Cross-link: 🔬 BMP Reference, 📚 TTP/HUS

MANAGEMENT
⚠️ ACE INHIBITORS ARE LIFE-SAVING

ACE inhibitors are the cornerstone of treatment. Start immediately and titrate aggressively. Do NOT withhold due to elevated creatinine.

ACE Inhibitor Therapy:

  • Captopril: Preferred due to short half-life and rapid titration. Start 6.25-12.5 mg PO q8h, titrate up rapidly (can increase every few hours).
  • Goal: Normalize BP within 72 hours. May need very high doses (up to 450 mg/day).
  • Continue even if dialysis required: Renal recovery can occur weeks-months later if ACE-I continued.

If ACE-I Insufficient for BP Control:

  • Add IV calcium channel blocker (nicardipine) or nitroprusside
  • ARBs can be added but not first-line
  • Avoid beta-blockers (can worsen Raynaud's and peripheral vasoconstriction)

Dialysis:

  • Required in ~50% of patients acutely
  • Continue ACE-I even on dialysis – 30-50% may recover renal function over months

Avoid or Use Cautiously:

  • Corticosteroids: May precipitate SRC. If needed for other scleroderma manifestations, use lowest effective dose.
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • ACE-I is THE Treatment: Before ACE inhibitors, SRC was uniformly fatal. Now ~80% survive. Do not withhold ACE-I due to creatinine – it saves lives.
  • Steroids Can Precipitate SRC: High-dose corticosteroids are a risk factor. Use with extreme caution in scleroderma, especially early diffuse disease.
  • Continue ACE-I on Dialysis: Unlike typical AKI where ACE-I might be held, in SRC continue treatment. Renal recovery possible even after months of dialysis.
  • Normotensive SRC Exists: 10% of SRC patients have normal or only mildly elevated BP. Consider diagnosis in scleroderma patient with unexplained AKI + MAHA.
  • MAHA + Severe HTN + Scleroderma = SRC: This triad is essentially diagnostic. Don't confuse with TTP (no hypertension in TTP).
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Malignant hypertension
  • Hypertensive encephalopathy
  • Flash pulmonary edema
  • Need for IV antihypertensives
  • Severe hyperkalemia
✓ TREATMENT GOALS
  • BP normalization within 72h
  • Maximum-tolerated ACE-I dose
  • Dialysis as needed
  • Monitor for renal recovery (may take months)
  • Rheumatology follow-up
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lisinopril
↑ Back to Table of Contents

149. GERD / ESOPHAGITIS

Erosive • Non-Erosive • Eosinophilic • Pill-Induced
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Typical GERD Symptoms: Heartburn and regurgitation are the classic symptoms (ACG 2022). Practical: worse after meals or lying down; triggers vary by patient (large or fatty meals, alcohol, caffeine, chocolate)

Atypical/Extraesophageal: Chronic cough, hoarseness/laryngitis, asthma, chest pain. Evaluate for non-GERD causes first (strong). Without heartburn or regurgitation: reflux testing before starting a PPI (strong). With typical symptoms as well: consider twice-daily PPI for 8-12 weeks before more testing (conditional). Chest pain: exclude heart disease, then test objectively for GERD (ACG 2022). Practical: dental erosions, globus

Alarm Features (Need EGD): Dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, vomiting, or anemia: endoscopy as soon as feasible; also multiple risk factors for Barrett esophagus (ACG 2022). Practical: odynophagia, new symptoms after age 60, family history of esophageal or gastric cancer

Types of Esophagitis:

  • Erosive (GERD): Mucosal breaks on EGD, graded by the Los Angeles (LA) classification A-D. LA grade C is virtually always diagnostic and Barrett esophagus is specific for GERD; grade A alone is not sufficient (ACG 2022). Practical: A = breaks no longer than 5 mm; D = breaks involving at least 75% of the circumference
  • Non-Erosive Reflux Disease (NERD): Symptoms with a normal EGD; when the diagnosis is unclear, reflux monitoring off therapy establishes it (ACG 2022). Practical: the majority of patients with reflux symptoms
  • Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE): Symptoms of esophageal dysfunction plus at least 15 eos/hpf after excluding other causes (ACG 2025, Rec 1); at least 6 biopsies from at least 2 levels (Rec 3); biopsy at the time of a food impaction (ACG 2025). Practical: young men with atopy, solid-food dysphagia; rings, furrows, strictures on EGD
  • Pill Esophagitis: Practical: NSAIDs, doxycycline, bisphosphonates, KCl, iron; sharp odynophagia, discrete ulcer at the aortic arch level
  • Infectious: Candida: white plaques; an empiric antifungal trial before endoscopy is appropriate (IDSA 2016). CMV: distal esophageal ulcers with inclusion bodies on biopsy; PCR or culture alone is not enough (HHS OI 2025). HSV: Practical: punched-out ulcers
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis: Heartburn and regurgitation without alarm symptoms: 8-week empiric PPI trial, once daily before a meal (strong). If symptoms respond, try to stop the PPI (conditional); response alone does not prove GERD. No response, or symptoms return off PPI: endoscopy, ideally 2-4 weeks off PPI (strong) (ACG 2022)

EGD Indications: Alarm symptoms or multiple Barrett risk factors (strong); typical symptoms that fail an 8-week PPI trial or return after stopping (strong). Not used to diagnose GERD-related asthma, chronic cough, or laryngopharyngeal reflux (ACG 2022). Practical: Barrett surveillance, before fundoplication

pH/Impedance Testing: Off therapy (PPI stopped for 7 days) when the diagnosis is unclear and EGD is not diagnostic, and before antireflux surgery; not needed with LA grade C/D or long-segment Barrett. Impedance-pH on twice-daily PPI for proven GERD not responding to twice-daily PPI (ACG 2022)

Esophageal Manometry: High-resolution manometry before antireflux surgery or endoscopic therapy, to rule out achalasia and absent contractility (strong); not a diagnostic test for GERD (ACG 2022). Practical: dysphagia with a negative EGD

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Lifestyle Modifications:

  • Weight loss if overweight or obese (ACG 2022, strong)
  • Elevate the head of the bed (or use a wedge) for nighttime symptoms (conditional). Practical: 6-8 inch blocks, not pillows
  • Avoid meals within 2-3 hours of bedtime (conditional)
  • Avoid individual trigger foods (conditional). Practical: fatty foods, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, mint, citrus, tomatoes
  • Avoid tobacco/smoking (conditional)
  • Practical: Avoid tight-fitting clothes

Pharmacotherapy:

  • PPI (First-Line): PPI over H2RA for healing and for maintaining healing of erosive esophagitis (ACG 2022, strong); take 30-60 min before a meal (strong); 8-week course. Practical: omeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg, or esomeprazole 20-40 mg once daily
  • Refractory: Optimize the PPI first: timing, adherence, twice-daily dosing, or one switch to another PPI (more than one switch is not supported). Then reflux testing. No routine add-on drugs; no prokinetic without gastroparesis; no baclofen without objective GERD (ACG 2022)
  • H2 Blockers: Less effective than PPI for erosive esophagitis. An as-needed bedtime H2RA may help nocturnal symptoms despite PPI; tolerance develops within about a month (ACG 2022). Practical: famotidine 20 mg BID
  • Antacids/Alginates: On-demand symptom relief only (ACG 2022). Practical: calcium carbonate; alginate (Gaviscon) forms a raft
  • Maintenance: No erosive esophagitis or Barrett and symptoms resolved: try to stop the PPI. If maintenance is needed, use the lowest effective dose. LA grade C/D: indefinite PPI or antireflux surgery (strong). NERD: on-demand or intermittent PPI (conditional) (ACG 2022)

PPI Long-Term Safety: PPIs are the most effective medical treatment for GERD. Studies linking long-term use to infections, pneumonia, fractures, CKD, vitamin and mineral deficiencies, heart attack, stroke, dementia, and death are flawed and not definitive; high-quality studies show no significant increase in any of these except intestinal infections (ACG 2022). Practical: use the lowest effective dose and stop when there is no indication

Surgical: Antireflux surgery by an experienced surgeon for objectively proven GERD; most benefit with LA grade C/D, large hiatal hernia, or persistent troublesome symptoms (strong). Magnetic sphincter augmentation for regurgitation failing medical therapy (strong); Roux-en-Y gastric bypass for eligible obese patients (conditional); transoral incisionless fundoplication if no severe esophagitis or hernia >2 cm (conditional). Manometry first (strong). No procedure without objective evidence of reflux (ACG 2022)

Specific Esophagitis Treatment:

  • Eosinophilic: First-line options: PPI (adults: double the reflux dose, eg, omeprazole 20 mg BID), swallowed topical steroid (budesonide 2-4 mg/day or fluticasone 1,760 mcg/day, divided), or empiric elimination diet. Dupilumab (300 mg SC weekly if 40 kg or more) for age 12 or older not responding to PPI. Dilation for strictures with medical therapy; continue effective therapy. PPI response no longer excludes EoE (ACG 2025)
  • Pill: Practical: stop the offending drug or use a liquid form; take pills with a full glass of water and stay upright 30 min
  • Candida: Systemic therapy always: fluconazole 200-400 mg (3-6 mg/kg) PO daily for 14-21 days; if unable to take oral, fluconazole 400 mg IV daily or an echinocandin; fluconazole-refractory: itraconazole solution or voriconazole (IDSA 2016, strong)
  • HSV: Severe disease or immunocompromised: acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h, then oral (valacyclovir 1 g BID or acyclovir 400 mg TID) once lesions regress, until healed (HHS OI 2025, severe mucocutaneous HSV in HIV). Practical: oral therapy if mild and able to swallow
  • CMV: Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h, switch to valganciclovir 900 mg PO q12h when tolerated (valganciclovir from the start if mild), for 21-42 days or until symptoms resolve; adjust both for renal function (HHS OI 2025)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: Upper GI bleeding with hemodynamic instability
  • Practical: Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave's - post-vomiting chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema)
  • Practical: Complete esophageal obstruction/food impaction with respiratory compromise
  • Practical: Severe infectious esophagitis with sepsis
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Tolerating oral intake
  • Practical: Pain controlled
  • Practical: No signs of bleeding or perforation
  • Practical: On appropriate PPI regimen
  • Practical: EGD performed or scheduled if alarm features
  • Practical: Lifestyle modifications reviewed
  • Practical: GI follow-up if needed
💎 PEARLS
  • Chest pain workup: Exclude heart disease first, then test objectively for GERD (endoscopy and/or reflux monitoring) rather than assuming it (ACG 2022)
  • PPI timing matters: Take 30-60 min before a meal, not at bedtime (ACG 2022, strong). Practical: PPIs block actively secreting pumps, which a meal stimulates
  • NERD: A normal EGD does not exclude GERD; reflux monitoring off therapy settles it when unclear, and on-demand PPI is reasonable for NERD (ACG 2022)
  • Food impaction: think EoE. Take biopsies at the time of the impaction once the bolus is cleared; EoE is often missed when they are not taken (ACG 2025)
  • Practical: Doxycycline esophagitis: Always take with full glass of water, stay upright. Mid-esophagus (aortic arch level)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pantoprazole, 💊 Famotidine, 💊 Fluconazole, 💊 Acyclovir, 💊 Ganciclovir

150. BARRETT'S ESOPHAGUS

Intestinal Metaplasia • Dysplasia • Cancer Surveillance
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells) in the tubular esophagus, with columnar mucosa extending at least 1 cm above the gastroesophageal junction (ACG 2022, Recs 1-2). Associated with chronic GERD; the only known precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma (ACG 2022)

Risk Factors: Chronic reflux symptoms (weekly for 5 or more years), male sex, age >50, White race, smoking, central obesity, family history of BE or esophageal adenocarcinoma (ACG 2022). Practical: hiatal hernia

Presentation: Found in 5%-12% of patients with chronic GERD symptoms (ACG 2022). Practical: usually found on EGD done for reflux; symptoms do not track disease (metaplastic epithelium may be less acid-sensitive)

Cancer Risk: Without dysplasia, annual progression to adenocarcinoma is low and depends on length: 0.06% for segments <3 cm vs 0.31% for ≥3 cm (meta-analysis cited in ACG 2022). About 0.7% per year with low-grade dysplasia (ACG 2022). An AGA 2026 update puts nondysplastic risk at about 0.1%-0.3% per year

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

EGD Findings: Salmon-colored mucosa extending above GE junction (replacing normal pale squamous mucosa). Described by length: short-segment (<3cm) vs long-segment (≥3cm). Prague classification: C (circumferential) and M (maximum extent)

Histology (Required for Diagnosis): Intestinal metaplasia in the tubular esophagus (ACG 2022, Rec 1). Do not routinely biopsy a normal Z line, or a Z line displaced less than 1 cm without visible lesions (Rec 2)

Biopsy Protocol: Screening EGD with possible BE: at least 8 biopsies, Seattle protocol for segments longer than 4 cm (Rec 3). Surveillance: high-definition white light plus chromoendoscopy (ACG 2022, Rec 8, strong; AGA 2025, Rec 3) and a structured protocol (Rec 9, strong): visible lesions first, then 4-quadrant biopsies at intervals of 2 cm or less; every 1 cm with any history of dysplasia (AGA 2025; ACG 2022)

Dysplasia Classification:

  • No dysplasia (NDBE): Lowest risk; rate depends on segment length (see Cancer Risk)
  • Indefinite for dysplasia: Confirm with an expert GI pathologist, intensify antireflux therapy, repeat EGD within 6 months; pooled annual incidence of HGD or cancer 1.5 per 100 person-years (ACG 2022)
  • Low-grade dysplasia (LGD): Dysplasia of any grade must be confirmed by a second pathologist with GI expertise (ACG 2022, Rec 4, strong). About 0.7% annual progression to cancer (ACG 2022)
  • High-grade dysplasia (HGD): Endoscopic eradication therapy recommended (ACG 2022, Rec 17, strong). Practical: may harbor occult cancer

Screening Recommendations: One screening EGD for chronic GERD symptoms plus 3 or more additional risk factors: male sex, age >50, White race, smoking, obesity, family history of BE or esophageal adenocarcinoma in a first-degree relative (Rec 5, conditional). A swallowable nonendoscopic capsule device with a biomarker is an acceptable alternative (Rec 6). No repeat screening after a negative EGD (Rec 7) (ACG 2022)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

All Barrett's Patients:

  • At least once-daily PPI to reduce neoplastic progression (ACG 2022, Rec 14; AGA 2025, Rec 7; both conditional); PPI rather than antireflux surgery for this purpose (AGA 2025, Rec 8; ACG 2022, Rec 16). Higher doses only if needed for symptoms; no recommendation on aspirin (ACG 2022, Rec 15)
  • Practical: Lifestyle modifications (weight loss, smoking cessation)
  • Surveillance EGD at intervals set by dysplasia grade and segment length (ACG 2022)

Surveillance Intervals:

  • No dysplasia: EGD every 3 years, extended to every 5 years for segments <3 cm (ACG 2022, Rec 11, strong; AGA 2025, Rec 1 and Figure 1). Columnar-lined segment <1 cm with intestinal metaplasia and no neoplasia: no surveillance (AGA 2025, Rec 2). Stop at any age if the patient could not undergo endoscopic therapy, surgery, or cancer treatment; life expectancy under 5 years with multiple conditions also supports stopping (AGA 2026 clinical practice update)
  • Indefinite for dysplasia: Repeat EGD by an expert endoscopist on twice-daily PPI within 2-6 months, with Seattle biopsies and resection of any visible lesion, to exclude prevalent HGD or cancer (AGA 2025; ACG 2022, Table 5). If IND is confirmed: no endoscopic eradication; EGD in 1 year, then annually until the grade changes (AGA 2025)
  • Low-grade dysplasia: Confirmed by a second expert pathologist (ACG 2022, Rec 4) and a repeat EGD by an expert endoscopist on maximal acid suppression within 2-6 months; referral finds a visible lesion needing resection in up to 27% and upgrades LGD to HGD in up to 26% (AGA 2025). Endoscopic eradication therapy suggested (ACG 2022, Rec 18, conditional) by shared decision; if surveillance is chosen, EGD every 6 months for 1 year, then annually (AGA 2025; ACG 2022)
  • High-grade dysplasia or intramucosal cancer: Endoscopic eradication therapy rather than esophagectomy (Rec 17, strong), resecting any visible lesion first (Rec 19), at a high-volume center (Rec 20) (ACG 2022)

Endoscopic Eradication Therapy:

  • Endoscopic resection (EMR): For visible lesions, before ablation; removes tissue for staging (ACG 2022, Rec 19)
  • Radiofrequency ablation (RFA): Preferred ablative technique (ACG 2022). Practical: multiple sessions usually needed
  • Cryotherapy: An alternative when RFA fails (ACG 2022, key concept)
  • Continue PPI. Surveillance after complete eradication of intestinal metaplasia (Rec 21, strong): prior LGD: 1 year, 3 years, then every 2 years; prior HGD or intramucosal cancer: 3, 6, and 12 months, then annually (ACG 2022, Table 7)

Surgery (Esophagectomy): Endoscopic eradication is recommended over esophagectomy for HGD and intramucosal cancer (ACG 2022, Rec 17, strong). Practical: esophagectomy for invasive cancer or failed endoscopic therapy; high morbidity (leak, stricture)

⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: Post-procedure perforation or bleeding
  • Practical: Esophageal cancer with obstruction or bleeding
  • Practical: Post-esophagectomy complications (anastomotic leak, respiratory failure)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: Tolerating diet after EGD/ablation
  • Practical: No signs of perforation or bleeding
  • On at least once-daily PPI (ACG 2022)
  • Practical: Surveillance interval established
  • Practical: GI follow-up scheduled
  • Practical: Pathology results reviewed and plan communicated
💎 PEARLS
  • Barrett's doesn't reverse with PPI: At least daily PPI is suggested; observational data suggest less neoplastic progression, but certainty is very low (ACG 2022). Practical: metaplasia persists
  • Long-segment = higher risk: Annual cancer progression 0.31% for ≥3 cm vs 0.06% for <3 cm, which sets the 3- vs 5-year interval (ACG 2022)
  • Practical: Symptoms may improve: Metaplastic epithelium is less acid-sensitive. Fewer symptoms ≠ less disease
  • Expert pathology confirmation: Dysplasia of any grade must be confirmed by a second pathologist with GI expertise before treatment decisions (ACG 2022, Rec 4, strong)
  • Endoscopic therapy is standard: Eradication therapy rather than esophagectomy for HGD and intramucosal cancer (Rec 17, strong); suggested for confirmed LGD (Rec 18) (ACG 2022)
  • Surveillance continues after ablation: Recurrence can occur; surveillance after complete eradication is recommended (Rec 21, strong), and stopping it is not recommended unless overall health dictates (ACG 2022)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pantoprazole

152. COSTOCHONDRITIS / CHEST WALL PAIN

Tietze Syndrome • Musculoskeletal Chest Pain
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Costochondritis: Inflammation of costochondral junctions (where ribs meet cartilage). Sharp, localized chest pain. Reproducible with palpation. Worse with movement, deep breathing, coughing. No swelling. Most common at ribs 2-5. Often bilateral

Tietze Syndrome: Similar to costochondritis BUT with visible swelling at costochondral junction. Usually single site, ribs 2-3. Younger patients. Less common

Risk Factors/Triggers: Recent upper respiratory infection (repetitive coughing), physical strain, repetitive activities, trauma, recent exercise, fibromyalgia, inflammatory arthritis

Key Features:

  • Reproducible tenderness on palpation (most important finding)
  • Sharp or pressure-like pain
  • Worse with movement, twisting, deep breathing
  • May radiate to arm or back
  • Duration: weeks to months (often chronic/recurrent)

Differential Diagnosis (Must Exclude):

  • Cardiac: ACS, pericarditis, aortic dissection
  • Pulmonary: PE, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pleuritis
  • GI: GERD, esophageal spasm, PUD
  • Other MSK: Rib fracture, muscle strain, herpes zoster (pre-rash), xiphodynia, slipping rib syndrome
  • Malignancy: Metastatic disease to ribs/sternum
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis: Costochondritis is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Key: reproducible tenderness on palpation + no concerning features

When to Test:

  • ECG: If ANY cardiac concern (risk factors, exertional, associated symptoms). Low threshold
  • Troponin: If ACS concern
  • CXR: If pulmonary symptoms, trauma, concern for pneumothorax
  • D-dimer/CTPA: If PE concern (Wells score, risk factors)
  • CT chest/MRI: If concern for malignancy, persistent unexplained pain
  • Labs (ESR, CRP): If inflammatory arthritis suspected or Tietze syndrome

Red Flags Requiring Further Workup:

  • Exertional chest pain
  • Associated dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea
  • Cardiac risk factors (DM, HTN, smoking, family history, hyperlipidemia)
  • Age >40 with new chest pain
  • Abnormal vital signs
  • Radiation to jaw/arm
  • Recent immobilization/surgery (PE risk)
  • Fever, weight loss (malignancy, infection)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

First-Line (Conservative):

  • NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 400-800mg TID or Naproxen 500mg BID × 1-2 weeks. Most effective
  • Topical NSAIDs: Diclofenac gel to affected area TID-QID. Fewer systemic side effects
  • Heat/Ice: Local application for comfort
  • Rest: Avoid aggravating activities, repetitive movements
  • Acetaminophen: If NSAIDs contraindicated

Second-Line (Refractory):

  • Local corticosteroid injection: Triamcinolone 20-40mg + lidocaine into costochondral junction. Consider if failed NSAIDs × 2-4 weeks
  • Physical therapy: Stretching exercises, posture correction
  • Intercostal nerve block: For severe refractory cases

Patient Education:

  • Benign condition, not dangerous
  • May take weeks to months to resolve
  • Can be recurrent
  • Activity modification during flares
  • Return precautions: exertional pain, dyspnea, radiation, new symptoms
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Not applicable - costochondritis does not require ICU
  • If patient has costochondritis AND develops cardiac symptoms, treat as ACS until proven otherwise
  • Misdiagnosis concern: Always reconsider if patient deteriorates or develops new symptoms
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Cardiac causes confidently excluded
  • Reproducible tenderness on exam
  • No red flag symptoms
  • Pain controlled with oral medications
  • Clear return precautions provided
  • PCP follow-up if symptoms persist >2-4 weeks
💎 PEARLS
  • Reproducible = reassuring: Pain reproduced by palpation strongly suggests MSK cause. BUT can coexist with cardiac disease - still need to exclude
  • Costochondritis is diagnosis of exclusion: Rule out life-threatening causes first, especially in patients with risk factors
  • Tietze has swelling: Visible/palpable swelling at costochondral junction. Costochondritis = tenderness without swelling
  • Can mimic ACS: Chest pain, radiation to arm, worse with exertion (if using arms). Low threshold to evaluate cardiac
  • Duration weeks-months: Set expectations. Not a quick fix. Recurrence common
  • NSAIDs work: First-line, most effective. Try for at least 1-2 weeks before declaring failure
↑ Back to Table of Contents

153. UROSEPSIS

Sepsis from Urinary Source • UTI with SIRS/Organ Dysfunction
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Sepsis (life-threatening organ dysfunction from dysregulated host response) caused by urinary tract infection. 20-30% of all sepsis cases. Second most common source after pneumonia

Risk Factors:

  • Urinary obstruction (kidney stones, BPH, stricture, tumor) - MOST IMPORTANT
  • Indwelling urinary catheter
  • Recent urologic procedure/instrumentation
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Immunosuppression
  • Neurogenic bladder
  • Pregnancy
  • Elderly, nursing home residents
  • Anatomic abnormalities

Presentation:

  • Urinary symptoms: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, flank pain (pyelonephritis), CVA tenderness, hematuria. May be absent in elderly/catheterized
  • Sepsis features: Fever (or hypothermia), tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status
  • Severe sepsis/Septic shock: Hypotension (SBP <90 or MAP <65) refractory to fluids, lactate >2 mmol/L, organ dysfunction (AKI, coagulopathy, altered mental status)

Common Organisms:

  • E. coli: Most common (50-80%)
  • Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter: Other gram-negatives
  • Pseudomonas: Healthcare-associated, catheter-related
  • Enterococcus: Especially with instrumentation
  • Candida: Immunocompromised, prolonged antibiotics, catheters
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory:

  • Urinalysis: Pyuria (WBC), bacteriuria, nitrites (gram-negatives), leukocyte esterase. May be absent early
  • Urine culture: BEFORE antibiotics (but don't delay antibiotics). >10⁵ CFU/mL significant (lower threshold with catheter or symptoms)
  • Blood cultures: × 2 sets before antibiotics. Positive in 20-40% of pyelonephritis, higher in urosepsis
  • CBC: Leukocytosis (or leukopenia = worse prognosis), left shift, thrombocytopenia (DIC)
  • BMP: AKI (Cr elevation), electrolyte abnormalities
  • Lactate: >2 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion. Prognostic. Trend to assess response
  • Procalcitonin: Elevated in bacterial sepsis. Can guide antibiotic duration
  • Coagulation: PT/INR, fibrinogen, D-dimer if DIC concern

Imaging:

  • CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast: First-line if obstruction suspected. Identifies hydronephrosis, stones, abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis
  • Renal ultrasound: If CT contraindicated (contrast allergy, AKI). Good for hydronephrosis, less sensitive for stones/abscess
  • Urgent imaging indications: Not responding to antibiotics 48-72hr, concern for obstruction, abscess, emphysematous infection
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Hour-1 Bundle (Sepsis):

  • Measure lactate - remeasure if initial >2
  • Blood cultures before antibiotics
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
  • IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate ≥4
  • Vasopressors if hypotensive despite fluids (target MAP ≥65)

Empiric Antibiotics (Start Broad, Narrow Based on Culture):

  • Community-acquired, no risk factors: Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily OR Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h or levofloxacin 750mg IV daily) - check local resistance patterns
  • Healthcare-associated or resistant organism risk: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h OR Cefepime 2g IV q8h OR Meropenem 1g IV q8h (if ESBL concern)
  • Pseudomonas risk (catheter, recent hospitalization, structural abnormality): Antipseudomonal coverage - pip-tazo, cefepime, or meropenem
  • MRSA risk (rare in UTI): Add vancomycin
  • Enterococcus concern: Ampicillin 2g IV q4h (if susceptible) or vancomycin

Source Control (CRITICAL):

  • Obstruction: Urgent decompression within 24 hours. Options: percutaneous nephrostomy (IR) or ureteral stent (urology). Antibiotics alone will fail
  • Abscess: Drainage (percutaneous or surgical) if >3-5 cm or not responding to antibiotics
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis: Life-threatening. Drainage ± nephrectomy. High mortality
  • Infected catheter: Replace or remove if possible

Duration:

  • Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 7-14 days (can be as short as 5-7 days with fluoroquinolones if responding)
  • Complicated UTI/urosepsis: 10-14 days
  • Abscess, prostatitis: 4-6 weeks
  • Procalcitonin-guided discontinuation if available
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Septic shock (hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation requiring vasopressors)
  • Lactate >4 mmol/L or rising despite treatment
  • Respiratory failure requiring intubation
  • Multi-organ dysfunction (AKI + coagulopathy + encephalopathy)
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis or necrotizing infection
  • Failure to respond to initial resuscitation
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Afebrile >24-48 hours
  • Hemodynamically stable off vasopressors
  • Lactate normalized
  • WBC normalizing
  • Tolerating oral antibiotics and fluids
  • Source control achieved (obstruction relieved, abscess drained)
  • Creatinine at baseline or improving
  • Culture sensitivities back, on appropriate narrow-spectrum oral antibiotic
  • Urology follow-up if structural abnormality or stones
  • Duration of antibiotics clearly documented
💎 PEARLS
  • Obstruction = emergency: Infected, obstructed kidney is urologic emergency. Antibiotics won't penetrate. Needs drainage within 24hr
  • E. coli is king: Causes 50-80% of UTI/urosepsis. But consider Pseudomonas, ESBL if healthcare-associated
  • Catheter = think Pseudomonas and Enterococcus: Broader coverage needed. Remove/replace catheter
  • CT if not improving at 48-72hr: Look for abscess, obstruction, emphysematous pyelonephritis
  • Emphysematous = high mortality: Gas in renal parenchyma on CT. Usually diabetics. Aggressive drainage, may need nephrectomy
  • Procalcitonin guides duration: Can shorten antibiotic course safely. Trend to assess response
  • Better prognosis than other sepsis: Urosepsis generally has lower mortality than pneumonia-related sepsis (with appropriate source control)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Norepinephrine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Urinalysis, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate

154. ACUTE RESPIRATORY FAILURE

Type 1 (Hypoxic) • Type 2 (Hypercapnic) • Mixed • Oxygen Delivery • Ventilation
CLASSIFICATION

Definition: Failure of the respiratory system to oxygenate (Type 1), to ventilate (Type 2), or both (Mixed). The thresholds below are conventional (Practical)

Type 1: Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure

  • Definition: PaO2 <60 mmHg (roughly SpO2 <90%) on room air. On supplemental oxygen, follow severity with the P/F (or SpO2/FiO2) ratio; a low P/F alone does not define ARDS (see ABG Interpretation)
  • Mechanism: V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion impairment, low inspired O2 (e.g., altitude)
  • PaCO2: Normal or low (hyperventilation)
  • A-a Gradient: Elevated for age: the problem is at the alveolar-capillary interface
  • Common Causes: Pneumonia, ARDS, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, PE, ILD, atelectasis

Type 2: Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure

  • Definition: PaCO2 >45 mmHg with respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35)
  • Mechanism: Alveolar hypoventilation (inadequate minute ventilation)
  • PaO2: May be low from hypoventilation; corrects readily with supplemental O2
  • A-a Gradient: Normal in pure hypoventilation (drive, neuromuscular, chest wall); elevated when lung disease coexists, as in COPD
  • Common Causes: COPD exacerbation, opioid overdose, neuromuscular disease (GBS, MG), obesity hypoventilation, severe asthma
  • → See Condition 50: Acute Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure for detailed management

Mixed (Type 1 + Type 2):

  • Definition: Both hypoxemia AND hypercapnia
  • Mechanism: Severe parenchymal disease with respiratory muscle fatigue
  • Common Causes: Severe COPD with pneumonia, late-stage ARDS, cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema, severe asthma with fatigue
  • Practical: Rising PaCO2 in a hypoxemic patient suggests a tiring respiratory pump; watch closely for fatigue and arrest
RAPID ASSESSMENT

ABCs + Vital Signs:

  • Airway: Patent? Secretions? Stridor? Can patient speak in full sentences?
  • Breathing: RR (>30 = severe), accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, SpO2
  • Circulation: HR, BP (hypotension = shock, may need intubation for resuscitation)
  • Disability: Mental status (confusion, agitation, somnolence = ominous)

Immediate Red Flags (Consider Immediate Intubation; Practical):

  • Apnea or agonal breathing
  • Severe altered mental status / inability to protect airway
  • Refractory hypoxemia (SpO2 <88% despite high-flow O2)
  • Hemodynamic instability / cardiac arrest
  • Severe respiratory acidosis (pH <7.20) with declining mental status
  • Respiratory muscle fatigue (paradoxical breathing, declining RR with worsening status)
  • pH cutoffs on this card are graded, not competing: <7.30 needs ICU-level care; <7.25 with declining mental status is an intubation trigger; <7.20 with declining mental status calls for immediate intubation

ABG Interpretation:

  • P/F Ratio (PaO2 ÷ FiO2): Normal is about 400-500 at sea level (Practical). A low P/F means ARDS only when the full ARDS definition is met:
    • Global Definition of ARDS 2024: Acute risk factor within 1 week; bilateral opacities on CXR, CT, or ultrasound; edema not primarily cardiogenic; P/F ≤300 or SpO2/FiO2 ≤315 (if SpO2 ≤97%)
    • Required support: Not intubated, on HFNC ≥30 L/min or NIV/CPAP ≥5 cm H2O; intubated, on PEEP ≥5 cm H2O
    • Severity (intubated): Mild P/F >200 to ≤300; moderate >100 to ≤200; severe ≤100 (see Condition 119: ARDS)
  • A-a Gradient: PAO2 - PaO2, where PAO2 = (FiO2 × 713) - (PaCO2 ÷ 0.8); 713 assumes sea level (Practical)
    • Expected normal rises with age: about (Age ÷ 4) + 4 mmHg; a flat cutoff of 15 overcalls abnormality in older adults (Practical)
    • Elevated = V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion defect (parenchymal disease)
    • Normal = pure hypoventilation (CNS, neuromuscular, chest wall)
  • Acute vs Chronic Respiratory Acidosis (Practical):
    • Acute: ↑ HCO3 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑ PaCO2
    • Chronic: ↑ HCO3 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑ PaCO2
OXYGEN DELIVERY LADDER

Escalate based on response. Don't delay escalation if patient deteriorating.

SpO2 Targets: No single US guideline sets a target for all patients. SSC 2026 (sepsis with hypoxemic respiratory failure): conservative or liberal targets are both acceptable; panelists target SpO2 about 90-96%. BTS 2017 (non-US): 94-98% for most acutely ill patients. At risk of hypercapnia (COPD, OHS, neuromuscular disease): 88-92% (BTS 2017, non-US; see Condition 50). Device FiO2 values below are approximate (Practical).

1. Nasal Cannula (NC):

  • Flow: 1-6 L/min → ~24-44% FiO2 (variable, depends on patient's minute ventilation)
  • Use: Mild hypoxemia, stable patients
  • Limitation: FiO2 unreliable, max ~44% even at 6L

2. Simple Face Mask:

  • Flow: 6-10 L/min → ~35-55% FiO2
  • Use: Moderate hypoxemia, short-term (procedures, transport)
  • Limitation: Must run ≥5 L/min to avoid CO2 rebreathing

3. Venturi Mask:

  • Flow: Set to specific FiO2 (24%, 28%, 31%, 35%, 40%, 50%)
  • Use: COPD and other chronic CO2 retainers who need precise, controlled FiO2; start at 24-28% (Practical; see Condition 50)
  • Advantage: Reliable FiO2 regardless of patient's breathing pattern

4. Non-Rebreather Mask (NRB):

  • Flow: 10-15 L/min → ~60-90% FiO2
  • Use: Severe hypoxemia, CO poisoning, trauma
  • Limitation: Max FiO2 ~90% (not truly 100%), uncomfortable for prolonged use

5. High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC):

  • Flow: 20-60 L/min, FiO2 21-100%, heated and humidified
  • Mechanism (Practical): Matches inspiratory flow (more reliable FiO2), modest PEEP effect (about 2-5 cm H2O with the mouth closed), dead-space washout, less work of breathing
  • Hypoxemic failure: Recommended over standard oxygen for de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ATS 2026, strong, moderate certainty); no recommendation between HFNC and NIV. SSC 2026 (sepsis): HFNC suggested over conventional oxygen when P/F <200 or SpO2/FiO2 <235, and as initial therapy over NIV (conditional)
  • Hypercapnic failure: An alternative to NIV only with mild acidemia (e.g., pH >7.25) when monitoring and prompt escalation are available (ATS 2026, conditional; see Condition 50)
  • After extubation: See NIPPV below (ATS 2026)
  • Starting Settings (Practical): Flow 40-60 L/min; titrate FiO2 to the SpO2 target
  • Evidence: FLORALI (NEJM 2015; non-hypercapnic, P/F ≤300): intubation by day 28 was 38% with HFNC, 47% with standard oxygen, 50% with NIV (P=0.18, not significant); 90-day mortality, a secondary outcome, was lower with HFNC
  • ROX Index = (SpO2/FiO2) ÷ RR (Roca, AJRCCM 2019; pneumonia): ≥4.88 at 2, 6, or 12 h = lower risk of intubation; <2.85 at 2 h, <3.47 at 6 h, or <3.85 at 12 h = high risk of HFNC failure
  • Advantages over NIPPV (Practical): Better tolerated, allows eating and speaking, less claustrophobia
  • When to escalate: Rising FiO2 needs, RR >30 with high work of breathing, worsening gas exchange, or ROX below the time-specific high-risk cutoff (Practical). Monitor closely and do not delay intubation (ATS 2026)

6. Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV):

  • CPAP: Single pressure throughout the cycle (e.g., 5-10 cm H2O)
    • Uses: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema (CPAP or bilevel NIV recommended; ERS/ATS 2017, strong, moderate certainty); de novo hypoxemic failure (CPAP by facemask or helmet suggested over standard oxygen; ATS 2026, conditional, low certainty); OSA
  • BiPAP (bilevel NIV): IPAP (inspiratory) + EPAP (expiratory) adds pressure support
    • Uses: Hypercapnic failure with acidosis (NIV by facemask recommended; ATS 2026, strong, moderate certainty; see Condition 50); cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ERS/ATS 2017); de novo hypoxemic failure (facemask or helmet suggested; ATS 2026, conditional, low certainty)
    • Starting settings (Practical): IPAP 10-12, EPAP 4-5 cm H2O; FiO2 to the SpO2 target
    • Titrate (Practical): Raise IPAP to improve ventilation (lower PaCO2); raise EPAP to improve oxygenation
  • After extubation (ATS 2026, conditional, moderate certainty): HFNC or NIV suggested over standard oxygen after ICU extubation; NIV suggested over standard oxygen or HFNC at high risk of extubation failure (e.g., age ≥65, obesity, hypercapnia, prolonged ventilation, severe illness). Do not use NIV to treat established postextubation failure (ERS/ATS 2017, conditional, low certainty)
  • Contraindications (Practical): Cannot protect the airway or clear secretions (judge function, not a GCS cutoff), respiratory or cardiac arrest, hemodynamic instability, facial trauma, recent upper GI or upper airway surgery, vomiting, uncooperative patient
  • Failure Signs (Practical): Worsening pH/PaCO2, declining mental status, or persistent hypoxemia or distress despite optimized settings: intubate without delay. Reassess within 1-2 hours of starting

7. Intubation / Mechanical Ventilation:

  • See "Intubation Indications" and "Initial Vent Settings" below
INTUBATION

Indications (SOAP ME mnemonic; Practical):

  • Secretions: unable to clear, aspiration risk
  • Oxygenation failure: refractory hypoxemia despite maximal noninvasive support
  • Airway protection: e.g., GCS ≤8, loss of gag or cough, inability to protect from aspiration
  • Patient trajectory: worsening despite treatment, impending arrest
  • Mechanical ventilation needed: severe acidosis, fatigue, anticipated prolonged failure
  • Expected course: OR, procedures, transport of an unstable patient

Clinical Triggers (Practical):

  • Respiratory rate >35-40/min with distress
  • SpO2 <88% on maximal non-invasive O2
  • PaO2 <60 mmHg on FiO2 >0.6
  • PaCO2 >50 with pH <7.25 and declining mental status
  • Signs of fatigue: paradoxical breathing, decreasing RR with worsening mental status
  • "Intubate the trajectory, not the number": if rapidly worsening, don't wait

Pre-Intubation Checklist:

  • Prepare (Practical): Suction, BVM, ETT (7.0-8.0), bougie, laryngoscope. A video laryngoscope raised first-attempt success over direct laryngoscopy in ED and ICU patients (DEVICE, NEJM 2023: 85.1% vs 70.8%)
  • Preoxygenate: HFNC or NIV by facemask recommended over standard oxygen (ATS 2026, strong, moderate certainty), with no preference between them; about 3 minutes, with apneic oxygenation during the attempt (Practical). SCCM 2023: NIPPV if P/F <150; HFNO when laryngoscopy is expected to be difficult (conditional, low certainty). PREOXI (NEJM 2024): NIV preoxygenation lowered peri-intubation hypoxemia vs an oxygen mask (9.1% vs 18.5%)
  • Position: Head and torso inclined (semi-Fowler) (SCCM 2023, conditional, very low certainty); ramp if obese (Practical)
  • Hypotension plan (Practical): Have a vasopressor ready (e.g., push-dose phenylephrine or epinephrine). SCCM 2023 found insufficient evidence to favor peri-intubation vasopressors or IV fluids
  • RSI Medications (SCCM 2023): Give a sedative-hypnotic induction agent with a neuromuscular blocker (NMBA: strong recommendation); no difference between etomidate and other induction agents (conditional, moderate certainty); rocuronium or succinylcholine if no contraindication (conditional, low certainty); no corticosteroids after etomidate (conditional, low certainty). RSI trial (NEJM 2025; 2,365 US patients): ketamine did not lower 28-day in-hospital mortality vs etomidate (28.1% vs 29.1%) and caused more cardiovascular collapse (22.1% vs 17.0%)
  • Plan B: Supraglottic airway (LMA), surgical airway equipment available

Initial Ventilator Settings (Post-Intubation):

  • Mode (Practical): Volume assist-control (AC/VC) or pressure assist-control (AC/PC)
  • Tidal Volume: 6-8 mL/kg predicted body weight (PBW) (Practical); ARDS: 4-8 mL/kg PBW, start at 6, with plateau pressure <30 cm H2O (ATS 2024, strong)
    • PBW (kg): Males = 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches - 60); Females = 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches - 60)
  • Respiratory Rate (Practical): 14-20/min, adjusted for pH/PaCO2
  • FiO2: Start 100%, then wean to the SpO2 target (no single US target): about 90-96% in sepsis (SSC 2026 panel practice), 94-98% for most acutely ill patients (BTS 2017, non-US), 88-95% in ARDS (ARDSNet; see Condition 119), 88-92% if at risk of hypercapnia
  • PEEP: Start 5 cm H2O (Practical); moderate-severe ARDS: higher PEEP without recruitment maneuvers (ATS 2024, conditional; see Condition 119)
  • Plateau Pressure: Keep <30 cm H2O (ATS 2024)

Post-Intubation:

  • Confirm placement: waveform end-tidal CO2, bilateral breath sounds, CXR for depth (Practical)
  • Secure tube, note depth at teeth (typically 21-23 cm) (Practical)
  • Analgesia and sedation (PADIS 2018; 2025 update): Treat pain before sedation; target light sedation (often defined as RASS -2 to +1) rather than deep (conditional); propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines (conditional); dexmedetomidine over propofol when light sedation or less delirium is the priority (2025, conditional, moderate certainty). Benzodiazepine infusions are not first-line
  • ABG in 30-60 min, adjust vent settings (Practical)
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis (SCCM/ASHP 2024): Only with risk factors (coagulopathy, shock, chronic liver disease); mechanical ventilation alone is not an established risk factor; not for enterally fed low-risk patients (conditional). SSC 2026: PPI suggested in sepsis with GI bleeding risk factors
  • Other: OG/NG tube; pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis unless contraindicated (SSC 2026 for sepsis, strong); head of bed 30-45° (SHEA/IDSA/APIC 2022 VAP prevention, essential practice)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Immediate (Bedside):

  • ABG: Defines type (hypoxic vs hypercapnic vs mixed), severity, acid-base status
  • CXR (portable): Infiltrates (pneumonia, ARDS, edema), effusion, pneumothorax, cardiomegaly
  • ECG: Ischemia, arrhythmia, RV strain (PE)
  • Bedside Echo (POCUS): LV function, RV dilation (PE), pericardial effusion, IVC for volume status

Laboratory:

  • CBC: Anemia (reduced O2 carrying capacity), leukocytosis (infection)
  • BMP: Metabolic derangements, renal function
  • BNP/NT-proBNP: In hospitalized patients, BNP ≥100 or NT-proBNP ≥300 pg/mL supports heart failure (Universal Definition of HF 2021, HFSA/HFA/JHFS)
  • Troponin: ACS, PE with RV strain, demand ischemia
  • Lactate: Tissue hypoxia, shock
  • Procalcitonin: Does not decide whether to start antibiotics: treat clinically suspected, radiographically confirmed CAP regardless of the level (2019 ATS/IDSA, strong; see Condition 5)
  • D-dimer: If PE suspected (use Wells score first)

Advanced Imaging:

  • CT Chest: Characterize infiltrates, ILD, malignancy
  • CTPA (CT pulmonary angiography): If PE suspected (see Condition 8: PE)
  • Formal Echo: Detailed cardiac assessment if cardiogenic cause suspected

Etiology-Based Workup:

Clinical Picture Consider Key Tests
Fever + productive cough + infiltrate Pneumonia Chest imaging; blood and sputum cultures and urinary antigens if severe CAP or MRSA/Pseudomonas risk (2019 ATS/IDSA; see Condition 5)
Orthopnea + JVD + crackles + edema CHF / Pulmonary Edema BNP, TTE, CXR (cephalization, Kerley B lines)
Pleuritic CP + hypoxia out of proportion to CXR PE D-dimer, CTPA, RV strain on echo/ECG
Bilateral opacities + risk factor within 1 week + P/F ≤300 or SpO2/FiO2 ≤315 on PEEP/CPAP ≥5 or HFNC ≥30 L/min ARDS Global Definition 2024 (extends Berlin); echo to assess for a cardiac cause
COPD history + wheezing + ↑ PaCO2 COPD Exacerbation ABG, CXR, sputum if purulent
Wheezing + air trapping, known asthma Asthma Exacerbation Peak flow, ABG if severe
Pinpoint pupils + ↓RR + ↑ PaCO2 Opioid Overdose Tox screen, response to naloxone
Ascending weakness + ↓ NIF GBS / Neuromuscular NIF, VC, LP, EMG/NCS
Absent breath sounds + tracheal deviation Tension Pneumothorax Clinical diagnosis → needle decompression before CXR
TREATMENT BY ETIOLOGY (QUICK REFERENCE)

All patients: Supplemental O2 to the SpO2 target (no single US target: about 90-96% in sepsis, SSC 2026 panel practice; 94-98%, BTS 2017, non-US; 88-92% if at risk of hypercapnia), treat underlying cause, monitor closely for deterioration

  • Pneumonia: Antibiotics (CAP vs HAP/VAP coverage), supportive care → CAP, HAP/VAP
  • CHF / Pulmonary Edema: Diuresis (furosemide), CPAP or bilevel NIV (ERS/ATS 2017), nitrates if hypertensive, reduce afterload → Heart Failure
  • PE: Anticoagulation; systemic thrombolysis by AHA/ACC category: reasonable in E1-E2, may be considered in D1-D2, harmful in A1-C2 (2026 AHA/ACC PE) → PE
  • ARDS: Lung-protective ventilation (6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat <30), prone >12 h/day if severe (ATS 2024), conservative fluids once shock resolves (FACTT) → ARDS
  • COPD Exacerbation: Bronchodilators, steroids, NIV for hypercapnic failure, antibiotics when GOLD 2027 criteria are met (purulent sputum plus another cardinal symptom, a prior positive sputum culture, or ventilation) → COPD, Hypercapnic Failure
  • Asthma: Bronchodilators, steroids, IV magnesium if severe and not responding to initial treatment (GINA 2026) → Asthma
  • Opioid Overdose: Naloxone, support ventilation → Opioid Overdose
  • Pneumothorax: Needle decompression (tension) or chest tube → Pneumothorax
  • Neuromuscular: IVIG/PLEX (GBS, MG crisis), intubation often needed → GBS, MG Crisis
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF (Practical; local criteria vary):
  • Need for HFNC, NIPPV, or mechanical ventilation
  • P/F ratio <200 (moderate-severe hypoxemia)
  • Respiratory acidosis with pH <7.30
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Altered mental status from respiratory failure
  • High likelihood of deterioration / need for close monitoring
  • Requiring FiO2 >50% to maintain adequate SpO2
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA (Practical)
  • SpO2 >92% on ≤2L NC (or baseline O2 requirement)
  • Respiratory rate <24, no accessory muscle use
  • Underlying cause treated or controlled
  • ABG normalized or at baseline (chronic CO2 retainers)
  • Off NIPPV/HFNC for >24 hours
  • Able to ambulate without significant desaturation
  • Home O2 arranged if needed
  • Pulmonary/cardiology follow-up as appropriate
  • Clear return precautions (worsening dyspnea, chest pain, fever)
💎 PEARLS
  • Intubate the trajectory (Practical): If patient is rapidly deteriorating, don't wait for a specific number. A patient who "looks bad" and is getting worse needs the tube before they arrest.
  • HFNC is not just "fancy nasal cannula": It delivers reliable FiO2, a modest PEEP effect, dead-space washout, and less work of breathing (Practical). Recommended over standard oxygen for de novo hypoxemic failure (ATS 2026, strong); in FLORALI it did not significantly reduce intubation, though 90-day mortality was lower.
  • ROX index predicts HFNC failure: (SpO2/FiO2) ÷ RR. ROX ≥4.88 (at 2, 6, or 12h) = low risk of intubation. High-risk cutoffs are time-specific: <2.85 at 2h, <3.47 at 6h, <3.85 at 12h: escalate early if below these thresholds (Roca, AJRCCM 2019).
  • BiPAP for CO2; CPAP or BiPAP for cardiogenic edema: BiPAP provides pressure support to augment ventilation (lowers CO2). CPAP reduces preload/afterload (treats pulmonary edema); bilevel NIV works too (ERS/ATS 2017). Both provide PEEP.
  • Normal A-a gradient = hypoventilation: If A-a gradient is normal, the lungs are not the main problem: the issue is inadequate respiratory drive (opioids, CNS) or pump failure (neuromuscular). Support ventilation, and give naloxone if opioid toxicity is suspected (see Opioid Overdose).
  • SpO2 88-92% for chronic CO2 retainers: High O2 in COPD can worsen hypercapnia, mainly through worse V/Q matching and the Haldane effect; loss of hypoxic drive plays a smaller part (Practical). Target lower SpO2, use Venturi mask for precise FiO2.
  • 6 mL/kg PBW saves lives in ARDS: Lung-protective ventilation reduces mortality (ATS 2024, strong). Use predicted body weight (from height and sex, not actual weight), keep plateau pressure <30.
  • Post-intubation hypotension is common: Loss of catecholamine surge, positive pressure reduces venous return, sedation causes vasodilation. Have a vasopressor ready (Practical).
  • Don't forget the simple stuff (Practical): Before intubating, make sure you've tried positioning (upright), suctioning secretions, treating bronchospasm, and draining large effusions.
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Albuterol, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Naloxone, 💊 Etomidate, 💊 Ketamine, 💊 Rocuronium, 💊 Succinylcholine, 💊 Propofol, 💊 Dexmedetomidine

155. ACUTE LIVER FAILURE

Fulminant Hepatic Failure • Coagulopathy • Encephalopathy • Transplant Evaluation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) plus any degree of encephalopathy, with illness under 26 weeks, in a patient without preexisting liver disease or cirrhosis (ACG 2023). Subtypes by interval from jaundice to encephalopathy (O'Grady 1993): hyperacute (<7 days: highest cerebral edema risk, lowest risk of death), acute (7-21 days), subacute (>21 days to <26 weeks: lowest cerebral edema risk, highest risk of death) (ACG 2023, Table 4)

Etiologies:

  • Acetaminophen (46% of US ALF; Reuben 2016): Unintentional repeated overdose was more common than suicidal ingestion in the US registry (Reuben 2016). Evaluation thresholds: single ingestion over 10 g or 200 mg/kg; repeated ingestion of 6 g/day or 150 mg/kg/day over 24-48 h, or 4 g/day or 100 mg/kg/day beyond 48 h, whichever is less (US/Canada consensus 2023). Fasting or alcohol add risk even at recommended doses (ACG 2023)
  • Idiosyncratic drug-induced (11%; Reuben 2016): Antimicrobials most often (antituberculosis drugs, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, terbinafine, azole antifungals), then herbal and dietary supplements, which rose from 2.9% to 24.1% of drug-induced ALF over 25 years; check LiverTox (ACG 2023)
  • Viral hepatitis (about 12% of US ALF): HBV 7% (acute or reactivation; HDV coinfection or superinfection raises risk), HAV 3%, HEV 2% (in pregnancy, mortality as high as 25%, ACG 2023; 56% for HEV ALF in pregnancy in Indian studies, AGA 2017); HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV, and adenovirus rarely, mostly in immunocompromised patients. HCV is not an established cause (ACG 2023)
  • Autoimmune hepatitis (7%; Reuben 2016): De novo or a flare of chronic AIH; ANA, anti-smooth muscle (F-actin), IgG. Up to 60% of ALF called indeterminate may be AIH (ACG 2023)
  • Ischemic (6%; Reuben 2016): Shock liver with heart failure, sepsis, trauma, or major surgery; AST often >10,000 IU/L; documented hypotension is not always found (ACG 2023)
  • Budd-Chiari syndrome (under 1%; Reuben 2016): Abdominal pain and ascites, AST > ALT in the 1000s; look for a hypercoagulable state (ACG 2023)
  • Wilson disease (about 3% of ALF; AASLD 2022): Usually ages 5-35, female 2:1 or more; Coombs-negative hemolysis, modest AST/ALT (typically under 2000) with AST > ALT, alkaline phosphatase often under 40 IU/L, rapid renal failure; Kayser-Fleischer rings absent in half (ACG 2023; AASLD 2022)
  • Pregnancy-related: HELLP and acute fatty liver of pregnancy, third trimester or postpartum; half of ALF in pregnancy has non-pregnancy causes, mostly acetaminophen (ACG 2023)
  • Amatoxin mushrooms: Gastroenteritis 6-12 h after ingestion, a quiet phase at 24-36 h, then liver and multiorgan failure at 4-7 days; ask every ALF patient about mushroom ingestion (ACG 2023)
  • Malignant infiltration (1.4% of US registry cases): Lymphoma or leukemia, breast, colon; hepatomegaly with raised alkaline phosphatase; diagnosis usually needs liver or marrow biopsy; 85% die within 3 weeks (ACG 2023)
  • Indeterminate (12% at enrollment; Reuben 2016): On expert re-review only 5.5% stayed indeterminate; acetaminophen and AIH were the causes most often found (ACG 2023)

Clinical Features:

  • Jaundice: Rapidly progressive
  • Coagulopathy: INR ≥1.5, but the INR does not reflect bleeding risk (rebalanced hemostasis); clinically significant bleeding is uncommon and causes about 5% of deaths (ACG 2023)
  • Hepatic Encephalopathy: Confusion → somnolence → coma (Grade I-IV)
  • Cerebral Edema: Highest risk in hyperacute ALF; intracranial hypertension is less frequent than before but still carries high mortality (ACG 2023). Neurologic causes fell from 19.0% to 7.6% of ALF deaths between 1998-2005 and 2006-2013 (Reuben 2016). Practical: Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations) is a late sign
  • Hypoglycemia: From depleted glycogen, impaired gluconeogenesis, and insulin resistance; worsens encephalopathy and is linked to higher mortality (ACG 2023)
  • Infections: Bacterial infections are common and fungi cause up to 32%; fever and leukocytosis are absent in up to 30% of infected patients (ACG 2023)
  • Multi-organ failure: AKI in up to 70% (30% need RRT); hyperdynamic, sepsis-like circulation; ARDS is rare in ALF, unlike ACLF (ACG 2023)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Confirm ALF:

  • INR ≥1.5 + any grade of encephalopathy + illness under 26 weeks (ACG 2023)
  • No preexisting cirrhosis (distinguishes ALF from ACLF, which is managed and listed differently), except Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, and Budd-Chiari syndrome, which can present as ALF on underlying fibrosis or cirrhosis (ACG 2023)

Etiology Workup:

  • General: CBC, CMP, Mg, phosphate, LDH, CK, PT/INR, fibrinogen, ABG with arterial lactate, blood and urine cultures, ABO type and screen; transplant candidates also HIV, QuantiFERON, cryptococcal antigen, treponemal antibody, echocardiogram (ACG 2023, Table 8)
  • Acetaminophen level + Rumack-Matthew nomogram only for ingestion within a 24-h period with known timing, not repeated ingestion over more than 24 h (US/Canada consensus 2023). The level may be undetectable at presentation; treat on suspicion (ACG 2023)
  • Viral: HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, HBV DNA, HCV RNA, HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV PCR (ACG 2023, Table 8); HBsAg and HBV DNA can be undetectable in HBV ALF (ACG 2023). HEV IgM and RNA with endemic exposure, pregnancy, immunosuppression, or ALF attributed to a drug (ACG 2023; CDC Yellow Book 2024)
  • Autoimmune: ANA, anti-smooth muscle (F-actin), IgG, IgM, IgA (ACG 2023, Table 8)
  • Wilson: Alkaline phosphatase to total bilirubin ratio <4 plus AST:ALT >2.2 strongly suggests Wilson ALF in adults. Ceruloplasmin predicts poorly in ALF; serum copper (usually >200 mcg/dL) and urine copper are high but slow to result; slit lamp for KF rings (absent in half). Do not wait for results to refer (AASLD 2022)
  • Serum beta-hCG in all females (ACG 2023, Table 8)
  • Toxicology: Serum acetaminophen and salicylate, urine drug screen; urine ethyl glucuronide or serum PEth if alcohol use is suspected (ACG 2023)
  • Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler (Budd-Chiari, vascular patency), CT head if encephalopathic, ECG, chest x-ray; in transplant candidates, contrast-enhanced imaging if renal function allows (ACG 2023, Table 8)
  • Liver biopsy (transjugular preferred) only to exclude infiltrative disease or malignancy, support AIH, or find a transplant contraindication (ACG 2023)

Severity/Prognosis:

  • King's College Criteria (non-acetaminophen): INR >6.5 (PT >100 s), OR any 3 of: age <10 or >40; etiology indeterminate (non-A, non-B), halothane, or idiosyncratic drug reaction; jaundice to encephalopathy >7 days; INR >3.5 (PT >50 s); bilirubin >300 µmol/L (17.5 mg/dL); any encephalopathy grade (O'Grady 1989, Table 4; INR equivalents ACG 2023, Table 11). Sensitivity 68%, specificity 82% (ACG 2023)
  • King's College Criteria (acetaminophen): Arterial pH <7.3 at any encephalopathy grade (after resuscitation, ACG 2023), OR all of: INR >6.5 (PT >100 s), creatinine >3.4 mg/dL (300 µmol/L), and grade 3-4 encephalopathy (O'Grady 1989, Table 4). Sensitivity 65%, specificity 93%; adding lactate >3 mmol/L raises sensitivity to 91% (ACG 2023, Table 11)
  • MELD: Prognostic, not for listing: MELD >25 or meeting KCC means high risk of poor outcome (ACG 2023, Rec 10); pooled sensitivity 74% vs 59% for KCC, specificity 67% vs 79%. ALF transplant candidates are listed as Status 1A (ACG 2023)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate:

  • Level of care: Grade 1 encephalopathy: contact a transplant center, start transfer, baseline CT head. Grade 2 or higher: ICU with hourly neuro checks. Grade 3-4: intubate (ACG 2023, Table 7)
  • Refer every ALF patient to a transplant center for urgent evaluation (AASLD/AST 2025, strong), ideally within hours of presentation and before full ALF criteria are met; substance use or infection should not stop referral (AASLD/AST 2025). Hepatology consult as soon as ALF is identified; patients deteriorate quickly and acetaminophen ALF can progress fastest (ACG 2023)
  • IV N-acetylcysteine: Acetaminophen: start as soon as toxicity is suspected, at any time after ingestion (ACG 2023, Rec 6, strong): 150 mg/kg over 1 h, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h, weight capped at 100 kg. Do not stop at 21 h by default: continue at 6.25 mg/kg/h or more until acetaminophen <10 mcg/mL, INR <2.0, AST/ALT normal or falling 25-50% from peak, and clinically well (US/Canada consensus 2023; AASLD 2023 DILI); in ALF, the endpoint ACG reports as most used is INR <1.5 (ACG 2023). Non-acetaminophen ALF: IV NAC suggested in adults (ACG 2023, Rec 7; AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 40, not in children; the older AGA 2017 guideline limited it to clinical trials); the US trial used the same first two steps, then 6.25 mg/kg/h to 72 h total (Lee 2009)

Supportive Care:

  • Coagulopathy: Do not correct routinely; plasma, platelets, or cryoprecipitate only for active bleeding or before a high-risk procedure such as ICP monitor placement (ACG 2023, Rec 2). Before procedures, judge bleeding risk by viscoelastic testing rather than INR, platelets, and fibrinogen (SCCM 2020, strong). Red cell transfusion threshold hemoglobin 7 g/dL (SCCM 2020)
  • Hypotension: Fluids first, preferably albumin, especially if serum albumin is low; no hydroxyethyl starch (SCCM 2020). Norepinephrine first-line (ACG 2023, Rec 4; SCCM 2020; both strong); add low-dose vasopressin if still hypotensive (ACG 2023, Rec 5; SCCM 2020). MAP 65 mmHg with assessment of perfusion (SCCM 2020); with raised ICP, keep cerebral perfusion pressure 60-80 mmHg (ACG 2023). Arterial line in shock; stress-dose steroids if shock persists despite fluids and vasopressors (SCCM 2020)
  • Glucose and electrolytes: Target glucose 110-180 mg/dL (SCCM 2020, strong); treat hypoglycemia with continuous dextrose 10% (ACG 2023 aims for 150-180). Avoid hypotonic fluids (hyponatremia worsens cerebral edema); check Mg and phosphate every 8-12 h (ACG 2023). Practical: bedside glucose every 1-2 h
  • Raised ICP: Hypertonic saline if at risk of intracranial hypertension (ammonia >150 µmol/L, high-grade encephalopathy, or multiorgan failure), raising Na gradually to 145-155 mmol/L (SCCM 2023; the older AGA 2017 guideline suggested against empiric ICP-lowering treatment), no faster than 6-8 mmol/L per 24 h and below 160 (ACG 2023). Hyperosmolar therapy, hyperventilation, and CRRT are first-line for raised ICP (ACG 2023). Mannitol 0.25 g/kg IV over 30 min, may repeat every 6-8 h; contraindicated in anuria (FDA label). Invasive ICP monitoring not suggested (SCCM 2023); ACG 2023 limits it to selected patients at expert centers. No induced hypothermia below 34°C (SCCM 2023). Practical: head of bed 30°, minimal stimulation
  • Encephalopathy and ammonia: CRRT is first-line for hyperammonemia, started early with grade 2 or higher encephalopathy even without usual RRT indications (ACG 2023, Rec 1; SCCM 2023); plasma exchange where available for ammonia >150 µmol/L (SCCM 2023). Insufficient evidence for lactulose or rifaximin in ALF (ACG 2023; SCCM 2023); lactulose can distend bowel before transplant and is stopped at grade 3-4 (ACG 2023). Sedation: avoid opioids and benzodiazepines; consider propofol (ACG 2023, Table 7)
  • Infection: No routine prophylactic antimicrobials; prophylaxis did not lower bloodstream infection or 21-day mortality (ACG 2023, Rec 3). Surveillance blood, urine, and sputum cultures; empiric antibacterial and antifungal therapy if the patient deteriorates; procalcitonin is unreliable (ACG 2023). Antibiotics within 1 h of septic shock (SCCM 2023)
  • Renal failure: Start RRT early in ALF with AKI, or for electrolyte or metabolic derangement or volume overload (SCCM 2020; ACG 2023); CRRT rather than intermittent HD (ACG 2023). Practical: avoid nephrotoxins
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis: Coagulopathy and shock are risk factors; low-dose PPI or H2RA (pantoprazole 40 mg or famotidine 40 mg daily or less), stopped when the risk factor resolves (SCCM/ASHP 2024)
  • Nutrition: Enteral rather than parenteral (SCCM 2020), started if oral intake is not expected within 5-7 days (ACG 2023). Protein: SCCM 2020 advises against restriction (1.2-2.0 g/kg/day); ACG 2023 suggests 1.0-1.5 g/kg/day, delayed 24-48 h and restarted at 1.0 g/kg if ammonia is over 150 µmol/L

Etiology-Specific:

  • Acetaminophen: NAC as above; if the level would return more than 8 h after ingestion, start NAC before it is back (US/Canada consensus 2023). Single-dose activated charcoal 1 g/kg (maximum 50 g) if ingestion was within 4 h and the airway is safe (AASLD 2023 DILI; ACG 2023 gives 1-2 g/kg)
  • Idiosyncratic DILI: Stop the drug and transfer early; spontaneous survival in drug-induced ALF is only about 25% (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 36). IV NAC as above (ACG 2023; AASLD statement 40). Corticosteroids only for severe hypersensitivity, DRESS, or autoimmune features: prednisone 40-60 mg daily, or methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for checkpoint-inhibitor injury with ALT over 5 times ULN (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 41, Table 9; ACG 2023)
  • Amatoxin mushroom: Call poison control. IV silibinin as soon as possible (not FDA approved); IV penicillin G only if silibinin is unavailable (ACG 2023, Rec 9); IV NAC; gastric lavage within 1 h and activated charcoal early; IV fluids for urine output 100-200 mL/h. Escudie criteria can trigger transplant evaluation before encephalopathy (ACG 2023)
  • Autoimmune: IV corticosteroids for acute severe AIH; once it has progressed to ALF, steroid benefit is uncertain, and early transplant evaluation should not wait for a steroid response (ACG 2023)
  • HSV or VZV: Empiric IV acyclovir without waiting for PCR when features suggest it; skin lesions are often absent; foscarnet if acyclovir-resistant (ACG 2023). Dose 10 mg/kg IV every 8 h (HHS OI 2025, visceral or disseminated HSV), by ideal body weight if obese, each dose over 1 h with hydration; CrCl 25-50: every 12 h, 10-25: every 24 h, under 10: half dose every 24 h (FDA label)
  • CMV: IV ganciclovir (ACG 2023), 5 mg/kg every 12 h, adjusted for renal function (HHS OI 2025)
  • HBV: Reactivation ALF: entecavir or tenofovir (ACG 2023, Rec 8, strong; no data for TAF). Acute HBV with ALF: antiviral therapy also indicated (AASLD 2018). Entecavir 0.5 mg daily (1 mg labeled for decompensated liver disease) or TDF 300 mg daily, adjusted for renal function (FDA labels)
  • HAV or HEV: Supportive; no proven antiviral; transplant if failing (ACG 2023)
  • Wilson disease: Immediate transplant referral; recovery with medical therapy alone is rare (AASLD 2022, statement 28). Plasma exchange, albumin dialysis, or continuous hemofiltration only temporize; chelators are ineffective in acute decompensation (ACG 2023)
  • Budd-Chiari: IV heparin first unless contraindicated; TIPS if anticoagulation fails; angioplasty for membranous webs; transplant if no response (ACG 2023). In acute liver failure, transplant may be the first step, with TIPS or DIPS considered while waiting, since it may improve liver function and avoid transplant (AASLD 2021; card 325)
  • HELLP or AFLP: Prompt delivery with multidisciplinary care; transplant evaluation if no improvement after delivery (ACG 2023)
  • Ischemic: Restore perfusion and treat the cause; transplant usually not needed (ACG 2023)

Transplant:

  • Liver transplant for ALF not recovering with medical therapy; post-transplant survival about 80% at 1 year and 75% at 5 years (ACG 2023)
  • Listed as Status 1A (highest priority) (ACG 2023)
  • Contraindications: brain death is the only absolute one; multiorgan dysfunction, sepsis, ARDS, pancreatitis, and cancer are relative, judged by the multidisciplinary transplant team (ACG 2023). Substance use or systemic infection may delay or prevent listing but should not prevent referral (AASLD/AST 2025)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Grade 2 or higher encephalopathy: ICU (ACG 2023)
  • Grade 3-4 encephalopathy: intubate for airway protection (ACG 2023)
  • Any ALF: urgent transplant-center referral (AASLD/AST 2025); encephalopathy in acute liver injury, KCC met, or MELD >25 should trigger transfer (ACG 2023)
  • Practical: hypotension needing vasopressors, need for CRRT, hypoglycemia needing continuous dextrose, or signs of raised ICP
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Many recover without transplant: 21-day transplant-free survival was 56% in 2006-2013 (US ALFSG; Reuben 2016)
  • Practical: discharge once INR is normalizing, encephalopathy has resolved, and synthetic function is stable
  • Etiology identified and treated
  • Close hepatology follow-up
  • Acetaminophen: Psychiatric evaluation if intentional OD
💎 PEARLS
  • NAC beyond acetaminophen: In non-acetaminophen ALF, IV NAC raised transplant-free survival only with grade I-II encephalopathy (52% vs 30%; no benefit in grade III-IV), so start it early (Lee 2009; ACG 2023, Rec 7)
  • Don't correct the INR: It is a prognostic marker, not a gauge of bleeding risk; plasma and platelets only for active bleeding or a high-risk procedure (ACG 2023)
  • Transfer early: Patients deteriorate rapidly. Transfer to transplant center before too unstable to move
  • Acetaminophen ALF has the best prognosis: 21-day transplant-free survival 70% vs 34.5% for other causes (US ALFSG 1998-2013; Reuben 2016)
  • Hyperacute: best survival, highest brain risk: Highest cerebral edema risk but the best outcome without transplant; typical of acetaminophen, HAV, HEV, and ischemia (ACG 2023, Table 4)
  • Wilson ALF = immediate transplant referral: Mortality 80-99% without transplant; Coombs-negative hemolysis with ALP:bilirubin <4 and AST:ALT >2.2 are the clues (AASLD 2022)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 N-Acetylcysteine, 💊 Lactulose, 💊 Rifaximin, 💊 Albumin, 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Mannitol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated Ammonia, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Hypoglycemia
