156. ALCOHOLIC HEPATITIS

Acute Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis • Maddrey Score • Lille Model • Steroids
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Clinical syndrome of recent onset or worsening jaundice with heavy alcohol use; the histologic correlate is alcohol-associated steatohepatitis (AASLD 2019). NIAAA criteria for probable AH: jaundice within 60 days of heavy alcohol use (more than 50 g/day) for at least 6 months (ACG 2024, Table 5)

Clinical Features:

  • Jaundice: Recent onset or worsening; bilirubin >3 mg/dL is a diagnostic criterion (ACG 2024, Table 5 and Figure 3)
  • Constitutional: Malaise, fever, anorexia (ACG 2024, Figure 3). SIRS (2 or more of: temperature >38 or <36 °C, HR >90, RR >20 or PaCO2 <32 mmHg, WBC >12 × 10^9/L) can occur without infection and carries nearly 3-fold mortality (ACG 2024)
  • Hepatomegaly, abdominal pain (AASLD 2019, Table 6)
  • Malnutrition and sarcopenia: Severe malnutrition is common in severe AH and predicts worse short-term survival (ACG 2024)
  • Portal hypertension: Ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding (ACG 2024, Figure 3); can appear even with minimal prior liver disease (ACG 2024)
  • Stigmata of chronic liver disease: Spider angiomata, palmar erythema, gynecomastia (AASLD 2019, Table 6)
  • Alcohol withdrawal signs if drinking stopped recently (ACG 2024)

Lab Pattern:

  • AST 50-400 U/L with AST:ALT >1.5 (NIAAA criteria; ACG 2024, Table 5). AST above 400 falls outside the criteria: look for another cause (ACG 2024, Figure 3)
  • Bilirubin >3 mg/dL; bilirubin and PT/INR are inputs to MDF, MELD, and Lille (AASLD 2019, Table 7)
  • Elevated INR
  • Leukocytosis: WBC >12 × 10^9/L is a SIRS criterion and can occur without infection (ACG 2024); infection is present at admission in 12%-26% (AASLD 2019)
  • Low albumin (a Lille score input; AASLD 2019, Table 7)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis (NIAAA probable AH; biopsy not required without confounding factors, ACG 2024, key concept 19):

  • Heavy alcohol use (more than 50 g/day) for at least 6 months, with jaundice onset within 60 days of heavy use
  • Bilirubin >3 mg/dL
  • AST 50-400 U/L, AST:ALT >1.5
  • No other cause of acute hepatitis (ACG 2024, Table 5)
  • Possible AH (unclear alcohol history, jaundice for more than 3 months, or another liver disease suspected): transjugular liver biopsy (ACG 2024, Figure 3)

Exclude Other Causes (ACG 2024, Figure 3):

  • Imaging for HCC and biliary obstruction; Doppler ultrasound for acute portal vein thrombosis and Budd-Chiari syndrome (AASLD 2019 also prefers ultrasound with Doppler)
  • Viral: IgM anti-HAV, anti-HBc, HBsAg, HEV, HCV antibody and HCV RNA
  • Autoimmune: ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody (high titers), IgG, antimitochondrial antibody
  • Drug-induced liver injury: medications, supplements, pharmacy records; LiverTox
  • Ischemic hepatitis: hypotension, septic shock, massive bleeding, recent cocaine use
  • Practical: ceruloplasmin in younger patients (Wilson disease)

Screen for Infection Before Steroids:

  • Cultures (blood, urine, and ascitic fluid by diagnostic paracentesis if ascites) and chest radiograph at presentation (AASLD 2019)
  • Infection present: start antibiotics immediately (AASLD 2019); corticosteroids can be started once infection is controlled (ACG 2024)
  • No universal prophylactic antibiotics in severe AH (ACG 2024, Rec 15, strong)

Severity Scoring:

  • MELD (original MELD): >20 = severe AH (about 20% 90-day mortality); ≤20 = moderate AH (ACG 2024, key concepts 20 and 23). MELD-Na performs similarly (ACG 2024)
  • Maddrey discriminant function (MDF): 4.6 × (patient PT - control PT, seconds) + total bilirubin (mg/dL) (Carithers 1989)
    • MDF ≥32 = severe; 30-day mortality approximately 20%-50% (ACG 2024). AASLD 2019 uses MDF ≥32 for steroid decisions
    • MDF <32 = mild to moderate
  • Lille score: Day 4 or day 7 of corticosteroids (ACG 2024, key concept 27); inputs: age, albumin, creatinine, PT, and the change in bilirubin (AASLD 2019, Table 7; calculator at lillemodel.com)
    • Lille ≤0.45 = responder: continue corticosteroids to 28 days (ACG 2024, Figure 3)
    • Lille >0.45 = nonresponder: stop corticosteroids (ACG 2024, Figure 3). Partial response (0.46-0.56) is an uncertain zone (AASLD 2019, Table 8)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

All Patients:

  • Abstinence: The single most important factor for survival (AASLD 2019); sustained abstinence is associated with long-term survival after AH (ACG 2024, key concept 22). Start AUD treatment in hospital (see below)
  • Nutrition: 35 kcal/kg/day with 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day protein (ACG 2024, key concept 24). Oral nutritional supplements if intake is inadequate, enteral nutrition if still inadequate (ACG 2024, Rec 16, strong). Intake <21.5 kcal/kg/day is associated with higher mortality; feeding tubes can be placed with varices that are not bleeding and not recently banded (ACG 2024)
  • Micronutrients: Thiamine, vitamin B12, and zinc deficiencies are common and should be supplemented (ACG 2024, key concept 25); consider therapeutic zinc in moderate and severe AH (AASLD 2019). Thiamine to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy: typically 100 mg IV/IM daily for 3-5 days, IV/IM preferred with poor nutrition or malabsorption, oral also acceptable; thiamine and glucose in any order (ASAM 2020, V.7). Practical: folate and a multivitamin
  • Alcohol withdrawal: CIWA-Ar (ACG 2024, key concept 12), symptom-triggered. Benzodiazepines with caution and careful monitoring: they can precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy (ACG 2024, Rec 13, strong). Short- or intermediate-acting agents (lorazepam, oxazepam) are safer with poor liver function; oral route preferred; moderate or severe withdrawal is typically monitored in an ICU (ACG 2024)
  • Kidneys: Avoid IV contrast, aminoglycosides, and NSAIDs; use diuretics cautiously; treat AKI early with IV albumin and vasoconstrictors (AASLD 2019)
  • Cirrhosis complications (ascites, encephalopathy, varices): manage as for other causes of cirrhosis (ACG 2024, key concept 17)

Severe AH (MELD >20; MDF ≥32 is the historical threshold):

  • Corticosteroids (ACG 2024, Rec 17, strong): prednisolone 40 mg PO daily × 28 days; prednisone 40 mg daily is an alternative (prednisolone is more studied and generally used); methylprednisolone 32 mg IV daily if unable to take PO. No evidence favors rapid vs slow taper after 4 weeks (ACG 2024)
    • Benefit is concentrated at MELD 21-39, limited at 40-50, and absent above 50 (ACG 2024 text; key concept 26 gives 25-39). ACG Figure 3 routes MELD >50 to early LT, palliative care, or trials
    • Contraindications: active infection including untreated HBV, uncontrolled diabetes, GI bleeding, severe renal failure; corticosteroids can be started once these are controlled (ACG 2024). GI bleeding is not an absolute contraindication: prednisolone was started a mean of 5 days after bleeding with no survival difference (AASLD 2019)
  • Add IV N-acetylcysteine to corticosteroids (ACG 2024, Rec 20, strong). Trial regimen: day 1, 150 mg/kg in 250 mL D5W over 30 min, then 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL over 16 h; days 2-5, 100 mg/kg/day in 1000 mL D5W. 1-month mortality 8% vs 24% (P = 0.006); 6-month 27% vs 38% (P = 0.07) (Nguyen-Khac, NEJM 2011)
  • Lille at day 4 or 7 (ACG 2024, key concept 27):
    • Lille ≤0.45: continue corticosteroids to 28 days
    • Lille >0.45: stop corticosteroids; early LT evaluation, palliative care if multiorgan failure, or clinical trials (ACG 2024, Figure 3)
  • Not recommended: pentoxifylline (ACG 2024, Rec 18, strong against); universal prophylactic antibiotics (Rec 15, strong against). G-CSF and microbiome therapies: insufficient data (Rec 19)

Moderate AH (MELD ≤20): No proven drug therapy; outpatient hepatology care and clinical trials (ACG 2024, Figure 3); focus on AUD treatment (AASLD 2019)

Alcohol Use Disorder Treatment (start in hospital):

  • Integrated multidisciplinary care with behavioral and/or drug therapy (ACG 2024, Rec 14, strong); brief motivational interventions (Rec 8, strong)
  • Baclofen (Rec 9, strong, compensated ALD): 5 mg TID, increase every 3-5 days as tolerated to a maximum of 15 mg TID; used safely in AH (ACG 2024). Can impair mentation; patients with hepatic encephalopathy were excluded from the cirrhosis RCT (AASLD 2019)
  • Acamprosate 666 mg TID or naltrexone 50 mg/day PO (AASLD 2019, Table 4) (Rec 10, conditional, compensated ALD). Acamprosate: no hepatic metabolism; adjust dose if CrCl 30-50, avoid if <30. Naltrexone: avoid in decompensated cirrhosis or liver failure. No data for either in AH (ACG 2024)
  • Gabapentin or topiramate: conditional option (Rec 11). Disulfiram: not recommended at any stage of ALD (Rec 12)

Transplant Evaluation:

  • Severe AH: consider referral for liver transplantation (ACG 2024)
  • Early LT for highly selected patients unresponsive to medical therapy, per regional and institutional protocols (ACG 2024, Rec 21, conditional). Selection should not rest solely on a fixed sobriety interval; psychosocial evaluation by a social worker and an addiction specialist (key concept 29)
  • Outcomes: first prospective series (n = 26), 2-year survival 72% vs 24% in patients not eligible for LT; US ACCELERATE-AH (n = 147), 3-year survival 84% (ACG 2024); sustained alcohol use 10% at 1 year and 17% at 3 years (AASLD 2019)
  • Nonresponders with 4 or more organ failures who are not early LT candidates: palliative care (ACG 2024, key concept 28)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Moderate or severe alcohol withdrawal (ACG 2024: typically monitored in an ICU)
  • SIRS or multiorgan failure: multidisciplinary care with hepatology, critical care, infectious disease, and nephrology (AASLD 2019)
  • Practical: grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy, active GI bleeding, septic shock, AKI needing vasoconstrictors or dialysis, respiratory failure
  • MDF >90 or MELD >30: very severe disease; search carefully for occult infection and other steroid contraindications (AASLD 2019). The older MDF >54 harm signal was not confirmed; the top MDF quartile (≥68) responded to steroids like lower quartiles (AASLD 2019)
  • Severe AH, especially Lille >0.45 nonresponse: contact a transplant center (ACG 2024; Figure 3)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • AUD treatment arranged in an integrated care model (ACG 2024, Rec 14) and relapse-prevention medication considered (Recs 9-12)
  • On corticosteroids: complete 28 days total; no evidence favors rapid vs slow taper afterward (ACG 2024)
  • MELD ≤20: outpatient hepatology care (ACG 2024, Figure 3)
  • Practical: bilirubin downtrending, INR improving or stable, encephalopathy resolved or at baseline, tolerating oral nutrition, no active infection, glucose monitoring on corticosteroids, hepatology follow-up within 1-2 weeks
💎 PEARLS
  • MELD >20 is the ACG steroid threshold: more accurate than MDF, uses INR instead of PT, and includes creatinine (ACG 2024, Rec 17)
  • AST above 400 or AST:ALT 1.5 or less: outside NIAAA criteria; look for ischemia, drug injury, viral hepatitis, or biliary obstruction (ACG 2024, Table 5 and Figure 3)
  • Lille at day 4 is as accurate as day 7 (ACG 2024); stop steroids if >0.45
  • Treat infection, then start steroids: Lille response predicts survival despite infection (AASLD 2019); no universal prophylactic antibiotics (ACG 2024, Rec 15)
  • Add IV NAC to steroids (ACG 2024, Rec 20, strong)
  • Pentoxifylline: recommended against (ACG 2024, Rec 18, strong); no survival benefit in STOPAH
  • Abstinence drives long-term survival (ACG 2024, key concept 22): start AUD treatment before discharge; baclofen has the most data in advanced ALD (ACG 2024)
  • Early LT: selection should not rest solely on sobriety duration (ACG 2024, key concept 29)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone (no prednisolone entry yet), 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 N-Acetylcysteine (NAC), 💊 Lorazepam, 💊 Acamprosate, 💊 Naltrexone, 💊 Thiamine, 💊 Folic Acid
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Bilirubin, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated Ammonia, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia

157. ISCHEMIC COLITIS

Colonic Ischemia • Watershed Areas • Thumbprinting • Supportive Care
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Colon ischemia (CI): colonic blood flow falls below the level needed to maintain cellular function; injury may be reversible (colopathy, colitis) or irreversible (gangrene, fulminant colitis, stricture, chronic ischemic colitis). CI causes 9%-24% of hospitalizations for acute lower GI bleeding; incidence rises with age, especially after 49, and 57%-76% of patients are women (ACG 2015)

Classic Presentation (ACG 2015, Rec 1, strong):

  • Sudden, cramping, mild abdominal pain (typically left lower quadrant)
  • Urgent desire to defecate
  • Bright red or maroon blood or bloody diarrhea within 24 hours
  • Fewer than one-third of patients follow this classic sequence; hematochezia favors CI that is not isolated to the right colon (Rec 2) (ACG 2015)
  • Isolated right colon ischemia (IRCI): pain without rectal bleeding is common (bleeding in only 25%-46%); consider it with severe pain in dialysis, sepsis, or hypotension (ACG 2015)

Risk Factors (ACG 2015, summary statements and Tables 2-3):

  • Older age (incidence rises especially after 49) and female sex
  • Cardiovascular disease and diabetes; atrial fibrillation, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, COPD; chronic kidney disease increases mortality
  • Hypotension or shock
  • IBS and constipation
  • Surgery that sacrifices the IMA (e.g., aortic aneurysm repair)
  • Drugs: best supported are constipation-inducing drugs (including opioids), immunomodulators (anti-TNF agents, interferons), and illicit drugs (cocaine, amphetamines); others include diuretics, digoxin, female hormones, alosetron, decongestants, ergots, and vasopressors
  • Thrombophilia: evaluate in young patients and in recurrent CI
  • Long-distance running (at least a dozen reported cases, ages 26-42)

Watershed Areas (ACG 2015):

  • Splenic flexure (Griffith's point): limited arcades between the middle colic (SMA) and left colic (IMA) branches
  • Sigmoid colon (Sudeck's point): last sigmoid branch of the IMA; predisposes the rectosigmoid
  • Rectum uncommonly affected: rich dual blood supply from splanchnic and systemic arteries
  • CI is segmental; classic segment-to-cause patterns are unconfirmed, but IRCI presents differently and does worse than other distributions
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs (ACG 2015, Table 5):

  • Blood: CBC, comprehensive electrolyte panel, albumin, lactate, LDH, CK, amylase
  • Stool: culture, ova and parasites, C. difficile toxin; test for E. coli O157:H7 in all patients with bloody diarrhea
  • Severity markers: low hemoglobin, low albumin, metabolic acidosis; Table 6 thresholds BUN >20 mg/dL, Hgb <12 g/dL, LDH >350 U/L, Na <136, WBC >15 × 10^9/L

Imaging:

  • CT abdomen/pelvis with IV and oral contrast first (ACG 2015, Rec 1, strong)
    • Bowel wall thickening, edema, thumbprinting suggest CI (Rec 2); thickening and fat stranding are nonspecific (also diverticulitis, infection, IBD)
    • Pneumatosis or portomesenteric venous gas predicts transmural infarction (Rec 4)
    • Practical: free air = perforation
  • Multiphasic CT angiography: suspected IRCI, or whenever acute mesenteric ischemia cannot be excluded (Rec 3, strong). If CI may herald AMI (IRCI, severe pain without bleeding, atrial fibrillation) and CTA is negative, consider conventional angiography (Rec 5, conditional)

Colonoscopy (ACG 2015):

  • Within 48 hours of presentation to confirm the diagnosis (Rec 1, strong)
  • Minimal insufflation (Rec 2, conditional); CO2 whenever available
  • Severe CI: CT for distribution, then limited colonoscopy, stopping at the distal-most extent of disease (Rec 3)
  • Biopsy except when gangrene is present (Rec 4)
  • Do not perform with peritonitis or irreversible ischemia (gangrene, pneumatosis) (Rec 5). Practical: defer if hemodynamically unstable
  • Findings: erythema (84%), edema (70%), friability (43%), superficial ulcers including the single-stripe sign (57%), deep ulcers (22%), blue-black nodules suggesting gangrene (5.5%)

Severity Classification (ACG 2015, Table 6 and Figure 1; not validated):

  • Mild: typical symptoms, segmental colitis not isolated to the right colon, none of the moderate factors: observation and supportive care
  • Moderate: up to 3 of: male sex, SBP <90, HR >100, abdominal pain without rectal bleeding, BUN >20 mg/dL, Hgb <12 g/dL, LDH >350 U/L, Na <136, WBC >15 × 10^9/L, mucosal ulceration on colonoscopy: correct cardiovascular abnormalities (volume), broad-spectrum antibiotics, surgical consultation
  • Severe: more than 3 moderate factors, or peritoneal signs, pneumatosis or portal venous gas, gangrene on colonoscopy, or pancolonic or isolated right colon involvement: ICU, emergent surgical consultation, volume, broad-spectrum antibiotics
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Supportive Care (Majority of Cases):

  • Most CI resolves spontaneously without specific therapy (ACG 2015, Rec 1, strong)
  • Bowel rest, IV fluids, correction of precipitating conditions including implicated drugs (Table 3); parenteral nutrition if a protracted course is expected (ACG 2015)
  • Correct cardiovascular abnormalities (Table 6); cardiology consultation if a cardiac embolic source is suspected (ACG 2015)
  • Antibiotics for moderate or severe CI (Rec 3, strong, very low evidence): an anti-anaerobic agent plus a fluoroquinolone, an aminoglycoside, or a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., metronidazole plus ceftriaxone). Continue at least 72 h, then reassess: if improved, consider a 7-day course; if not, consider infectious disease consultation (ACG 2015)
  • No glucocorticoids unless CI complicates vasculitis (ACG 2015)
  • Practical: serial abdominal examinations
  • VTE prophylaxis: heparin prophylaxis was part of medical management in the reviewed series (ACG 2015)

Surgery (ACG 2015, Rec 2 and Table 9):

  • Consider surgery: hypotension, tachycardia, and abdominal pain without rectal bleeding; IRCI; pancolonic CI; gangrene (Rec 2, strong). Surgical consultation for moderate disease, emergent for severe (Table 6)
  • Acute indications: peritoneal signs, massive bleeding, universal fulminant colitis with or without toxic megacolon, portal venous gas or pneumatosis, deteriorating clinical condition
  • Subacute: segmental CI not responding within 2-3 weeks or protein-losing colopathy; apparent healing with recurrent sepsis
  • Chronic: symptomatic stricture or symptomatic segmental ischemic colitis
  • Untreated necrotic bowel: mortality approaches 100%

Prognosis (ACG 2015):

  • Pooled biopsy-proven series (n = 1,049): 80.3% managed medically (mortality 6.2%); 19.6% surgery (mortality 39.3%)
  • Mortality 4%-12% in large series; worse with IRCI, pancolonic CI, and chronic kidney disease
  • Recurrence about 3% at 1 year and 10% at 5-6 years (one series)
  • Surgical mortality risk: use the Ischemic Colitis Mortality Risk (ICMR) factors
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe CI (ACG 2015, Table 6: ICU and emergent surgical consultation): more than 3 moderate factors, peritoneal signs, pneumatosis or portal venous gas, gangrene, pancolonic or isolated right colon involvement
  • Hemodynamic instability (surgery indicated with peritonitis or instability; ACG 2015)
  • IRCI: multiphasic CTA to exclude acute mesenteric ischemia (Rec 3)
  • Practical: septic shock, need for emergent surgery
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: pain resolved, tolerating diet, bowel function returning, afebrile with WBC improving, lactate normal if previously elevated
  • Implicated drugs stopped or reviewed (ACG 2015, Table 3)
  • Antibiotics: about 7 days total if improved at 72 h (ACG 2015)
  • Thrombophilia evaluation if young or recurrent CI; evaluate for a cardiac embolic source if suspected (ACG 2015)
  • Segmental colitis persisting beyond 2-3 weeks, or recurrent sepsis after apparent healing: surgical referral (ACG 2015, Table 9)
  • Practical: GI follow-up; repeat colonoscopy if the first exam was incomplete or symptoms persist (ACG 2015 gives no follow-up colonoscopy recommendation)
💎 PEARLS
  • Pain, urgency, then bloody stool within 24 h is typical (ACG 2015, Rec 1), but fewer than one-third follow the classic sequence
  • IRCI is different: often pain without bleeding, higher mortality, and may herald acute mesenteric ischemia: get multiphasic CTA (ACG 2015, Rec 3)
  • Rectum is uncommonly involved (dual blood supply; ACG 2015). Practical: rectal involvement should prompt consideration of IBD or infection
  • CT findings are nonspecific: wall thickening and fat stranding also occur with diverticulitis, infectious colitis, and IBD (ACG 2015)
  • Test bloody diarrhea for E. coli O157:H7 and C. difficile (ACG 2015)
  • Most cases resolve without specific therapy (Rec 1); surgery for the Table 9 indications
  • No steroids unless CI complicates vasculitis (ACG 2015)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Ciprofloxacin

158. CHOLEDOCHOLITHIASIS

Common Bile Duct Stone • Obstructive Jaundice • ERCP • MRCP
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Stone(s) in the common bile duct (CBD), most often migrated from the gallbladder; present in 10%-20% of patients with symptomatic gallstones. Can cause biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or pancreatitis; choledocholithiasis is the leading cause of acute pancreatitis (ASGE 2019)

Presentation Spectrum:

  • Asymptomatic: Found incidentally on imaging
  • Biliary pain: RUQ or epigastric pain
  • Obstructive jaundice: Painless or painful jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus
  • Acute cholangitis: a high-risk criterion: proceed to ERCP (ASGE 2019). See Cholangitis
  • Gallstone pancreatitis: See Pancreatitis

Lab Pattern:

  • Total bilirubin >4 mg/dL with a dilated CBD: high-risk criterion (ASGE 2019)
  • Abnormal liver biochemical tests: intermediate-risk criterion (ASGE 2019)
  • Practical: direct bilirubin predominates; ALP and GGT rise; transaminases can transiently exceed 1000 with acute obstruction
  • If cholangitis: Leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers
  • If pancreatitis: Elevated lipase
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Risk Stratification (ASGE 2019, Table 15; awaiting prospective validation):

  • High risk (any): CBD stone on US or cross-sectional imaging; clinical ascending cholangitis; total bilirubin >4 mg/dL AND dilated CBD (>6 mm with gallbladder in situ, >8 mm after cholecystectomy)
    • → Proceed to ERCP
  • Intermediate risk (any): Abnormal liver biochemical tests, age >55, or dilated CBD on imaging
    • → EUS or MRCP (Rec 1, conditional, low), or laparoscopic intraoperative cholangiography (IOC) or intraoperative US
  • Low risk: No predictors
    • → Cholecystectomy (if indicated for symptomatic gallstones) with or without IOC or intraoperative US
  • Gallstone pancreatitis is no longer a risk criterion (ASGE 2019)

Imaging (ASGE 2019):

  • RUQ ultrasound: First test; shows gallstones and CBD dilation; often misses CBD stones because the distal duct is obscured
  • MRCP: No sedation or radiation; pooled sensitivity 87%, specificity 92%; can miss small stones (about 6 mm); claustrophobia and pacemakers may preclude it
  • EUS: Pooled sensitivity 97%, specificity 90%; needs sedation and is operator dependent; perforation risk 0.02%-0.07%; GI bypass may preclude it. EUS before ERCP reduces ERCP use and adverse events without more missed stones
  • Intermediate risk: EUS or MRCP, chosen by patient preference, local expertise, and availability (Rec 1, conditional, low)
  • ERCP: Therapeutic; avoid purely diagnostic ERCP. Adverse events 6%-15%, severe (death or stay over 10 days) 1%-2%
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Definitive Treatment (ASGE 2019):

  • ERCP with Sphincterotomy and Stone Extraction (high risk or confirmed stone):
    • Large stones: sphincterotomy plus large balloon dilation rather than sphincterotomy alone (Rec 3, conditional, moderate); clearance 96.9% vs 90.7% in RCTs
    • Large and difficult stones: cholangioscopy-guided laser or electrohydraulic lithotripsy, or conventional therapy with papillary dilation (Rec 4, conditional, very low); pooled clearance 92% with either
    • Incomplete clearance: plastic or covered metal stent with planned exchange or removal (Rec 9); clearance 65%-93% at scheduled removal 2-6 months later. Permanent stents without exchange: 38% recurrent cholangitis; only with very short life expectancy
  • Cholecystectomy after ERCP: Leaving the gallbladder after sphincterotomy raised recurrent biliary pain, jaundice or cholangitis, and mortality (Cochrane, 5 RCTs); recurrent events 39.3% with sphincterotomy alone vs 18.0% with cholecystectomy (cohort, n = 11,808). Mild gallstone pancreatitis: same admission (see below). Practical: same admission when feasible otherwise

Alternative Approaches (ASGE 2019, Rec 7):

  • Timing with cholecystectomy: Preoperative or postoperative ERCP, or laparoscopic bile duct exploration, depending on local surgical and endoscopic expertise
  • Laparoscopic cholecystectomy with bile duct exploration (single step): Clearance and adverse events comparable to ERCP before cholecystectomy, with shorter hospital stay
  • Choledochotomy: Success comparable to postoperative ERCP (98% vs 96%); bile leak 14.6%; caution with inflamed ducts or ducts under 7 mm
  • Percutaneous transhepatic drainage: Acceptable in critically ill patients not suited for ERCP (ASGE 2021). Practical: also when ERCP fails or altered anatomy prevents it
  • Mirizzi syndrome: Cholangioscopic therapy may replace surgery where expertise exists, but the gallbladder must still be removed (Rec 8)

If Cholangitis Present (see Cholangitis):

  • ERCP within 48 h (ASGE 2021, rec 2, conditional); septic shock not responding to fluids: consider within 24 h. With gallstone pancreatitis: ERCP within 24 h (ACG 2024, KC 13)
  • Antibiotics immediately (SIS 2017): ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole, or ertapenem (lower risk); piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem, meropenem, or cefepime plus metronidazole (higher risk); 4 days after adequate source control
  • Practical: volume resuscitation, vasopressors if needed

If Gallstone Pancreatitis Present (see Pancreatitis):

  • No cholangitis or biliary obstruction: no urgent ERCP (ASGE 2019, Rec 2, strong, against ERCP within 48 h; ACG 2024, rec 5, medical therapy over ERCP within 72 h)
  • Cholangitis: ERCP within 24 h (ACG 2024, KC 13). Persistent biliary obstruction or choledocholithiasis is excluded from the ASGE recommendation against early ERCP; ACG reserves urgent ERCP for cholangitis or progressive cholestasis
  • Suspected CBD stone without cholangitis or jaundice: MRCP or EUS first (ACG 2024, KC 14)
  • Mild gallstone pancreatitis: same-admission cholecystectomy (ASGE 2019; ACG 2024, KC 21): biliary events 5% vs 17% with interval surgery (PONCHO trial)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Cholangitis with septic shock: urgent drainage (see Cholangitis)
  • Gallstone pancreatitis with organ failure (ACG 2024; see Pancreatitis)
  • Practical: post-ERCP perforation, severe post-ERCP pancreatitis, or bleeding; multiorgan dysfunction
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • CBD cleared, or stent in place with planned exchange or removal (ASGE 2019, Rec 9)
  • Cholecystectomy done or scheduled; mild gallstone pancreatitis: before discharge (ASGE 2019; ACG 2024)
  • Practical: liver tests improving, tolerating diet, pain controlled, afebrile with WBC normalizing
  • GI follow-up for stent exchange or removal (2-6 months in reported series; ASGE 2019)
💎 PEARLS
  • Transaminase spike: Practical: ALT/AST can exceed 1000 briefly with acute CBD obstruction, then fall quickly; do not assume viral hepatitis
  • Dilated duct thresholds: >6 mm with gallbladder in situ, >8 mm after cholecystectomy (ASGE 2019)
  • Avoid diagnostic ERCP: adverse events 6%-15%; use EUS or MRCP for intermediate risk (ASGE 2019)
  • Remove the gallbladder: sphincterotomy alone does not prevent recurrent biliary events (39.3% vs 18.0%) (ASGE 2019)
  • Gallstone pancreatitis: urgent ERCP only with cholangitis or persistent obstruction; otherwise supportive care (ASGE 2019; ACG 2024)
  • Large stones: sphincterotomy plus large balloon dilation (ASGE 2019, Rec 3)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Ceftriaxone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Bilirubin, 🔬 Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Lipase

159. GASTROPARESIS

Delayed Gastric Emptying • Diabetic Gastroparesis • Prokinetics • Gastric Stimulation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Measurable delay in gastric emptying with upper GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating, upper abdominal pain) in the absence of mechanical obstruction (AGA 2025; ACG 2022). Prevalence 21.5-24.2 per 100,000, disproportionately women (AGA 2025)

Etiologies:

  • Idiopathic and diabetic: the two main types; both current US guidelines address these (AGA 2025; ACG 2022)
  • Medications: opioids (including tramadol and tapentadol) and GLP-1 receptor agonists delay emptying (AGA 2025; ACG 2022). Practical: anticholinergics, dopamine agonists
  • Connective tissue disease (e.g., scleroderma) (AGA 2025)
  • Practical: post-surgical vagal injury (fundoplication, bariatric surgery, esophagectomy); neurologic disease (Parkinson's, MS); amyloidosis

Cardinal Symptoms:

  • Nausea, vomiting, early satiety, postprandial fullness (AGA 2025; ACG 2022)
  • Bloating, upper abdominal pain: when pain predominates, look hard for alternative or coexisting causes (AGA 2025, Rec 1)
  • Overlap with functional dyspepsia is substantial; functional dyspepsia has normal emptying on a 4-hour test (AGA 2025; ACG 2022)
  • Practical: vomiting of food eaten hours earlier; weight loss

Complications:

  • Practical: malnutrition and weight loss, bezoar, aspiration, electrolyte abnormalities from vomiting
  • Erratic glucose control: insulin may act before food leaves the stomach; insulin dose or timing may need adjustment (metoclopramide injection label)
  • Higher mortality, mainly in diabetes-related gastroparesis (AGA 2025)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Step 1: Exclude Mechanical Obstruction:

  • Upper endoscopy or imaging to exclude mechanical obstruction (ACG 2022); rule out alternative or coexisting causes, especially when pain predominates (AGA 2025)
  • Retained food at EGD is not diagnostic of gastroparesis (positive predictive value 55% for delayed emptying) (ACG 2022)

Step 2: Confirm Delayed Gastric Emptying:

  • 4-hour gastric emptying study, not a 2-hour or shorter study (AGA 2025, Rec 1, conditional, low): a 2-hour study had pooled sensitivity 57% and specificity 94% against the 4-hour result
    • Measure retention directly at 4 hours, not extrapolated; the 4-hour threshold applies to scintigraphy and breath testing (AGA 2025)
    • Delayed: more than 10% retention at 4 hours with the standard low-fat egg-white (Eggbeaters) meal (ACG 2022)
    • Test without confounders: hyperglycemia and drugs that alter emptying (opioids, GLP-1 receptor agonists, prokinetics) (AGA 2025). Stop opioids, cannabinoids, prokinetics, antiemetics, and neuromodulators 48 h before the test (ACG 2022, customary practice)
  • 13C-spirulina breath test: reliable alternative (ACG 2022, rec 5, conditional, low)
  • Wireless motility capsule: may be an alternative (ACG 2022, rec 4, conditional, low); radiopaque markers not suggested (rec 3)

Additional Workup:

  • Review medications and stop those that delay emptying (AGA 2025)
  • Practical: HbA1c in diabetes; TSH; ANA and Scl-70 if scleroderma is suspected
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Acute Flare / Hospitalized Patient:

  • Practical: NPO initially, then small-volume liquids; IV fluids and electrolyte repletion; NG decompression for severe distension or refractory vomiting
  • Glycemic control in diabetes (ACG 2022, rec 1, conditional, low; AGA 2025): acute hyperglycemia delays gastric emptying (ACG 2022)
  • Antiemetics as needed: 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron), H1 antagonists (promethazine), D2 antagonists (prochlorperazine); they relieve symptoms but do not speed emptying (AGA 2025; ACG 2022, rec 11). Practical: ondansetron 4-8 mg IV every 6-8 h
  • Metoclopramide IV or IM if unable to take oral: 10 mg IV given slowly over 1-2 minutes, for up to 10 days, then oral; CrCl below 40 mL/min: start at about half the dose (metoclopramide injection label; no IV frequency stated)
  • Stop drugs that delay emptying: opioids (do not treat gastroparesis pain with opioids, including tramadol and tapentadol; ACG 2022) and GLP-1 receptor agonists (AGA 2025)

Diet and Nutrition:

  • Small-particle diet (ACG 2022, rec 6, conditional, low); low-fat, low-residue diet before or with drug therapy (AGA 2025 panel practice)
  • Practical: small frequent meals; liquids and purees; avoid carbonated drinks; walk after meals
  • Oral intake inadequate: enteral feeding by jejunostomy; parenteral nutrition rarely (ACG 2022)

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Metoclopramide (AGA 2025, Rec 2, conditional, low; the only FDA-approved drug for gastroparesis): 10 mg PO 4 times daily, 30 min before meals and at bedtime, max 40 mg/day. Elderly: start 5 mg 4 times daily, titrate to 10 mg. CrCl below 60, Child-Pugh B or C, CYP2D6 poor metabolizers or strong CYP2D6 inhibitors: 5 mg 4 times daily (max 20 mg); avoid with bupropion, fluoxetine, paroxetine; ESRD 5 mg twice daily (max 10 mg) (Reglan label, 2/2026). AGA practice: start 5 mg before meals, up to 10 mg; intranasal 15 mg before meals and at bedtime. Boxed warning, tardive dyskinesia: avoid more than 12 weeks total; if longer use is unavoidable, monitor for TD. Contraindicated with prior TD, GI bleeding, obstruction or perforation, pheochromocytoma, epilepsy; avoid with antipsychotics, Parkinson's disease, depression. Reassess at 4-8 weeks (AGA 2025)
  • Erythromycin (AGA 2025, Rec 3, conditional, very low): 40-150 mg PO 30 min before meals (ethylsuccinate suspension allows low doses). Tachyphylaxis: drug holidays (e.g., 3 weeks on, 1 week off). Watch QT prolongation, CYP3A interactions, resistance
  • Domperidone: not first line (AGA 2025, Rec 4, conditional, very low). Not FDA approved; requires an expanded-access IND, and the US supplier is exiting. Baseline potassium, magnesium, and ECG (QTc). An option after metoclopramide neurologic effects or with movement disorders
  • Prucalopride: not first line (AGA 2025, Rec 5, conditional, very low); reasonable with coexisting chronic idiopathic constipation; idiopathic gastroparesis responds more than diabetic
  • Not first line: aprepitant (Rec 6), nortriptyline (Rec 7.1), buspirone (Rec 7.2); cannabidiol only in trials (Rec 8) (AGA 2025). Central neuromodulators not recommended (ACG 2022, rec 12, strong); haloperidol and ghrelin agonists not supported (recs 13-14)

Refractory to Medical Therapy:

  • Pyloric botulinum toxin: not routinely (AGA 2025, Rec 9); not recommended (ACG 2022, rec 19, strong)
  • G-POEM: not routinely (AGA 2025, Rec 10, conditional, low); for select patients: 4-hour study with at least moderate delay (20% retention at 4 h, Eggbeaters meal), 6-12 months of moderate symptoms, failed prokinetics and antiemetics. ACG 2022 suggested pyloromyotomy over no treatment (rec 20)
  • Surgical pyloromyotomy or pyloroplasty: no recommendation, knowledge gap (AGA 2025, Rec 11)
  • Gastric electrical stimulation: not routinely (AGA 2025, Rec 12, conditional, very low); aims at nausea and vomiting, not pain; humanitarian use device (ACG 2022, rec 15)
  • Nutrition: jejunostomy feeding; venting gastrostomy second line; parenteral nutrition rarely (ACG 2022)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Practical: aspiration pneumonia with respiratory failure
  • Practical: severe electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypochloremia)
  • Practical: DKA in diabetic gastroparesis
  • Practical: hemodynamic instability from dehydration
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Practical: tolerating oral liquids or soft diet; nausea and vomiting controlled; electrolytes normal; glucose control optimized
  • Drugs that delay emptying stopped or replaced (AGA 2025)
  • Metoclopramide counseling: tardive dyskinesia, total course of 12 weeks or less unless benefit clearly outweighs risk (label); reassess at 4-8 weeks (AGA 2025)
  • Diet instruction: small-particle, low-fat, low-residue (ACG 2022; AGA 2025)
  • Practical: GI follow-up; 4-hour gastric emptying study if not yet done
💎 PEARLS
  • Use a 4-hour test: a 2-hour study misses about 4 in 10 cases that are delayed at 4 hours (sensitivity 57%) (AGA 2025, Rec 1)
  • Exclude obstruction first; retained food at EGD is not diagnostic (ACG 2022)
  • Confounders: hyperglycemia, opioids, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and prokinetics distort the emptying study (AGA 2025)
  • Metoclopramide: boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia; reduce the dose for age, renal or hepatic impairment, and CYP2D6 status (Reglan label, 2/2026)
  • Erythromycin: low doses with drug holidays for tachyphylaxis; check QT and CYP3A interactions (AGA 2025)
  • No opioids for gastroparesis pain, including tramadol and tapentadol (ACG 2022)
  • Botulinum toxin, G-POEM, GES: not routine; select refractory patients only (AGA 2025, Recs 9, 10, 12)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Metoclopramide, 💊 Ondansetron, 💊 Prochlorperazine, 💊 Promethazine

160. SEROTONIN SYNDROME

Drug-Induced Hyperserotonergic State • Clonus • Cyproheptadine • Hunter Criteria
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Potentially life-threatening drug-induced condition caused by excessive serotonergic activity in the CNS, typically from drug interactions or overdose. Onset usually within 24 hours of drug initiation, dose change, or adding another serotonergic agent

Classic Triad:

  • Mental Status Changes: Agitation, anxiety, confusion, hypomania, hallucinations
  • Autonomic Instability: Hyperthermia, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, diarrhea
  • Neuromuscular Abnormalities: Clonus (spontaneous, inducible, or ocular), hyperreflexia, tremor, rigidity, ataxia

Key Clinical Features:

  • Clonus: Most important diagnostic finding. Look for ankle clonus, patellar clonus, or ocular clonus (slow horizontal eye movements)
  • Hyperreflexia: More pronounced in lower extremities
  • Hyperthermia: May be severe (>41°C/106°F in severe cases)
  • Onset: Usually within 6-24 hours of causative agent; 60% within 6 hours

Causative Agents (Drug Classes):

  • SSRIs: Fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram
  • SNRIs: Venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine
  • MAOIs: Phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline (highest risk combinations)
  • TCAs: Amitriptyline, nortriptyline, clomipramine
  • Opioids: Tramadol, meperidine, fentanyl, methadone (serotonin reuptake inhibition)
  • Triptans: Sumatriptan and other migraine medications
  • Antibiotics: Linezolid (weak MAOI), tedizolid
  • Antiemetics: Ondansetron, metoclopramide
  • Illicit Drugs: MDMA (ecstasy), cocaine, amphetamines
  • Supplements: St. John's wort, tryptophan
  • Other: Methylene blue (MAOI), dextromethorphan, lithium

High-Risk Combinations:

  • MAOI + ANY serotonergic agent = highest risk (potentially fatal)
  • SSRI + tramadol or meperidine
  • SSRI + linezolid or methylene blue
  • Multiple serotonergic agents at high doses
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Hunter Criteria (Most Accurate — Sensitivity 84%, Specificity 97%):

  • Must have taken a serotonergic agent AND one of the following:
  • 1. Spontaneous clonus
  • 2. Inducible clonus + agitation OR diaphoresis
  • 3. Ocular clonus + agitation OR diaphoresis
  • 4. Tremor + hyperreflexia
  • 5. Hypertonia + temperature >38°C + ocular clonus OR inducible clonus

Laboratory (Supportive, Not Diagnostic):

  • CBC: Leukocytosis common
  • BMP: Electrolyte abnormalities, AKI if severe
  • CK: Elevated if rhabdomyolysis (from muscle rigidity, agitation)
  • LFTs: Transaminitis in severe cases
  • Coagulation: DIC in severe cases
  • Lactate: Elevated in severe cases
  • No specific diagnostic test — diagnosis is clinical

Differential Diagnosis:

Condition Key Differentiating Features
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) Lead-pipe rigidity (not clonus), bradyreflexia, develops over days (not hours), caused by dopamine antagonists
Malignant Hyperthermia Exposure to inhaled anesthetics or succinylcholine, OR setting
Anticholinergic Toxicity Dry skin (not diaphoretic), urinary retention, decreased bowel sounds, mydriasis
Sympathomimetic Toxicity Similar features but no clonus, often with significant hypertension
Meningitis/Encephalitis Nuchal rigidity, focal neurologic findings, CSF abnormalities

Key distinguishing feature of serotonin syndrome: CLONUS and hyperreflexia (vs rigidity and bradyreflexia in NMS)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Management:

  • Stop ALL serotonergic agents — most important step
  • Supportive care: IV fluids, continuous monitoring
  • Benzodiazepines: First-line for agitation, muscle rigidity, seizure prevention
    • Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV or diazepam 5-10 mg IV, repeat as needed
    • Controls agitation and reduces muscle hyperactivity

Hyperthermia Management:

  • External cooling: Ice packs, cooling blankets, evaporative cooling
  • Avoid antipyretics: Acetaminophen/NSAIDs ineffective (not prostaglandin-mediated fever)
  • If temp >41°C: Consider intubation and paralysis with non-depolarizing agent (stops muscle hyperactivity generating heat)

Cyproheptadine (Serotonin Antagonist):

  • Mechanism: 5-HT2A receptor antagonist
  • Dose: 12 mg initial dose, then 2 mg q2h until improvement
  • Maintenance: 8 mg q6h once stabilized
  • Max: 32 mg/day
  • Route: PO only (can crush and give via NG if intubated)
  • Side effects: Sedation (often beneficial), anticholinergic effects
  • Note: Evidence is anecdotal but widely recommended

Severe Cases (ICU):

  • Intubation for airway protection or severe hyperthermia
  • Paralysis (non-depolarizing NMB) for refractory hyperthermia
  • Avoid succinylcholine (risk of hyperkalemia with rhabdomyolysis)
  • Aggressive IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis
  • Pressors if needed (avoid serotonergic agents like dopamine; use norepinephrine or phenylephrine)

What to Avoid:

  • Physical restraints: Increase muscle rigidity → worsen rhabdomyolysis and hyperthermia
  • Antipyretics: Ineffective
  • Succinylcholine: Hyperkalemia risk
  • Dopamine: Theoretical serotonergic activity
  • Bromocriptine/dantrolene: These are for NMS, not serotonin syndrome
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Temperature >40°C (104°F)
  • Severe muscle rigidity
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Altered mental status (GCS <13)
  • Seizures
  • Rhabdomyolysis with AKI
  • DIC or multi-organ dysfunction
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Symptoms resolved (typically within 24-72 hours after stopping agent)
  • Afebrile
  • Mental status at baseline
  • No clonus or hyperreflexia
  • CK normalizing (if elevated)
  • Clear plan for psychiatric medication management
  • Offending agent(s) documented and patient educated
  • Psychiatry or PCP follow-up arranged for medication reconciliation
💎 PEARLS
  • Clonus is the key: The most distinguishing feature from NMS. If you see clonus + serotonergic drug exposure = serotonin syndrome until proven otherwise
  • NMS is slow, SS is fast: NMS develops over days with gradual rigidity. Serotonin syndrome develops within hours with hyperreflexia/clonus
  • Stop the drug and most cases resolve: 70% resolve within 24 hours of stopping the offending agent. Supportive care is often sufficient
  • Cyproheptadine only works orally: No IV formulation. Crush and give via NG if patient intubated
  • Linezolid is a sneaky cause: Weak MAOI activity. Avoid with SSRIs/SNRIs if possible. Also methylene blue (used in methemoglobinemia, sentinel lymph node mapping)
  • Tramadol is a common culprit: Often overlooked as a serotonergic agent. Avoid with SSRIs/MAOIs
  • MAOI washout periods matter: MAOIs require 2-week washout before starting serotonergic agents. Fluoxetine requires 5-week washout before MAOI (long half-life)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lorazepam
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

161. HYPOGLYCEMIA

Glucose <70 mg/dL • Whipple's Triad • Insulin vs Sulfonylurea • Insulinoma
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition in diabetes (ADA SOC 2026): Level 1: glucose <70 and ≥54 mg/dL. Level 2: <54 mg/dL, the threshold at which neuroglycopenic symptoms begin; act immediately. Level 3: a severe event with altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance, at any glucose. In hospital any value <70 is treated and prompts a review of the plan (Rec 16.13)

Without diabetes (Endocrine Society 2009): Evaluate only when Whipple's triad is documented: (1) symptoms, signs, or both consistent with hypoglycemia, (2) a low plasma glucose, (3) resolution when the glucose is raised. Diagnostic criteria use plasma glucose <55 mg/dL, measured by a precise lab method, not a meter

Autonomic (Adrenergic) Symptoms:

  • Tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias
  • Adrenergic responses begin near 70 mg/dL in people without diabetes (ADA SOC 2026); in healthy people symptoms appear at a mean glucose of about 55 mg/dL (Endocrine Society 2009)
  • Thresholds shift lower after recurrent hypoglycemia (impaired awareness) (Endocrine Society 2009); beta-blockers can blunt symptoms (Practical)

Neuroglycopenic Symptoms:

  • Confusion, difficulty concentrating, behavioral changes, slurred speech
  • Visual disturbances, weakness, fatigue, dizziness
  • Seizures, loss of consciousness, coma (severe)
  • Begin at about 54 mg/dL (ADA SOC 2026, level 2)

Etiologies in Hospitalized Patients:

  • Insulin excess (most common): Too much insulin for intake, missed meal, insulin stacking. Drugs, often with critical illness including renal failure, are the most common cause of hypoglycemia in hospitals (Endocrine Society 2009)
  • Sulfonylureas: Glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride; many have active metabolites, and duration of action is often longer than the half-life (Klein-Schwartz 2016); risk rises in kidney failure (Practical)
  • Reduced oral intake: NPO status without adjusting insulin, anorexia, N/V
  • Renal failure: Reduced insulin clearance, reduced gluconeogenesis
  • Hepatic failure: Impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
  • Sepsis: Increased glucose utilization, hepatic dysfunction
  • Adrenal insufficiency: Cortisol is counter-regulatory hormone
  • Alcohol: Inhibits gluconeogenesis

Etiologies in Non-Diabetics (Rare):

  • Insulinoma: Fasting hypoglycemia, elevated insulin/C-peptide, negative sulfonylurea screen
  • Factitious hypoglycemia: Exogenous insulin (high insulin, LOW C-peptide) or sulfonylurea ingestion
  • Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia: IGF-2 producing tumors (mesenchymal tumors)
  • Autoimmune: Anti-insulin antibodies, insulin receptor antibodies
  • Post-gastric bypass: Reactive/postprandial hypoglycemia
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Immediate:

  • Glucose: treat on a point-of-care value. Without diabetes, confirm with a lab plasma glucose; a low value in a well patient may be pseudohypoglycemia (delayed sample processing, especially with erythrocytosis, leukocytosis or thrombocytosis) (Endocrine Society 2009)
  • No diabetes and cause unclear: during the episode draw plasma glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate and an oral hypoglycemic agent screen (sulfonylureas and glinides), then correct with glucagon 1 mg IV and record the glucose response; also send insulin antibodies (Endocrine Society 2009). Never delay treatment of severe hypoglycemia to draw samples (Practical)

Interpretation (drawn during hypoglycemia, glucose <55 mg/dL; Endocrine Society 2009):

Diagnosis Insulin C-peptide Proinsulin β-OHB Glucose rise after glucagon Oral agent screen
Insulinoma (also NIPHS, post-gastric bypass) ↑ ↑ ↑ Low ≥25 Negative
Sulfonylurea or glinide ↑ ↑ ↑ Low ≥25 Positive
Exogenous insulin ↑↑ ↓ ↓ Low ≥25 Negative
Insulin autoimmune (insulin antibodies positive) ↑↑ ↑↑* ↑↑* Low ≥25 Negative
IGF-mediated (non-islet cell tumor) ↓ ↓ ↓ Low ≥25 Negative
Not insulin- or IGF-mediated ↓ ↓ ↓ High <25 Negative

Cutoffs: insulin ≥3 µU/mL, C-peptide ≥0.6 ng/mL (0.2 nmol/L) and proinsulin ≥5 pmol/L document endogenous hyperinsulinism; β-hydroxybutyrate ≤2.7 mmol/L and a glucose rise ≥25 mg/dL after 1 mg IV glucagon indicate insulin (or IGF) mediation. *Free C-peptide and proinsulin are low in insulin autoimmune hypoglycemia (Endocrine Society 2009)

Additional Workup (if etiology unclear):

  • Cortisol: a low value during spontaneous hypoglycemia is not sufficient evidence of adrenal insufficiency, because recurrent hypoglycemia lowers the glucose threshold for cortisol release (Endocrine Society 2009); confirm with a cosyntropin stimulation test (Practical)
  • LFTs, renal function
  • Prolonged supervised fast (up to 72 h) for suspected fasting hypoglycemia: continue until Whipple's triad, or plasma glucose <55 mg/dL if the triad was documented before, unless a progressive rise in β-hydroxybutyrate signals a negative fast; measure glucose by a precise lab method (Endocrine Society 2009)
  • Postprandial symptoms: mixed-meal test over 5 h; never an oral glucose tolerance test (Endocrine Society 2009)
  • Localize only after biochemical diagnosis: CT detects 70-80% and MRI about 85% of insulinomas, and negative imaging does not exclude one; endoscopic ultrasound is more sensitive (Endocrine Society 2009)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Treatment:

  • Conscious, able to swallow: 15 g of glucose (preferred) or another glucose-containing carbohydrate; avoid high-fat or high-protein foods for initial treatment. Recheck every 15 min and repeat until glucose is stable above 70 (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 6.15; sec. 16). On acarbose: pure glucose only (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Altered, unable to swallow or NPO:
    • D50: 25-50 mL (12.5-25 g glucose) IV push, can repeat (Practical); drug overdose: 50-100 mL (25-50 g) (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
    • D10: 100-250 mL if no D50 or prefer slower correction (Practical)
    • Glucagon if no IV access: 1 mg IM/SC (Klein-Schwartz 2016). Ready-to-use forms (nasal, prefilled injection) are preferred over kits that need reconstitution (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 6.16; Endocrine Society 2023 Rec 10, outpatients). Not useful with glycogen depletion, as in alcohol use or liver failure, and not routine in sulfonylurea toxicity because it also releases insulin (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Once alert and corrected: give a meal or complex carbohydrates to prevent recurrence (Klein-Schwartz 2016)

Sulfonylurea-Induced Hypoglycemia (CRITICAL):

  • Prolonged, recurrent hypoglycemia expected: many sulfonylureas have active metabolites and act longer than their half-lives; hypoglycemia may recur and persist for up to 8 days (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Manage in hospital: all intentional overdoses, unintentional ingestion by a person without diabetes, and anyone symptomatic or with persistent hypoglycemia (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Octreotide (off-label) is the main treatment after the first IV dextrose bolus: start after the first hypoglycemic episode rather than waiting for recurrence. Adults: 50-100 mcg SC (preferred) every 6-12 h, or 50 mcg IV then 25 mcg/h; give for 12 h initially (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Dextrose: titrated 5-20% infusion for persistent hypoglycemia; excess dextrose drives insulin release and rebound hypoglycemia. No prophylactic IV dextrose; feed alert patients (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Activated charcoal within 2 h of an immediate-release sulfonylurea overdose; can be considered later for extended-release products (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Monitoring: glucose hourly at first, then every 2-6 h; potassium, magnesium and phosphate (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Observation: at least 12 h after IV dextrose and octreotide stop; the period varies with drug, formulation and dose; never discharge late at night (Klein-Schwartz 2016)

Prevention in Hospitalized Diabetics:

  • NPO or poor intake: hold prandial insulin and use basal or basal plus correction (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.8b; card 233); type 1 diabetes always needs basal insulin (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Reduce insulin in AKI: kidney failure is an important risk factor, possibly from decreased insulin clearance (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Watch the triggers: sudden steroid dose reduction, emesis, insulin mistimed to meals, reduced IV dextrose rate, interrupted enteral or parenteral feeding, prolonged procedures, missed glucose checks (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Avoid correction-only insulin without basal insulin (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.10)
  • Hospital-wide, nurse-initiated protocol for glucose <70, embedded in insulin orders; review the plan after any value <70 (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.12-16.13)
  • EHR-based glycemic surveillance for inpatients at risk (Endocrine Society 2023 Rec 6); start CGM in select high-risk inpatients and continue personal CGM (Rec 4-5)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Refractory hypoglycemia requiring continuous dextrose infusion
  • Seizures or prolonged altered mental status
  • Sulfonylurea overdose (intentional)
  • Recurrent hypoglycemia despite treatment
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Overdose or sulfonylurea toxicity: at least 12 h without recurrence after IV dextrose and octreotide stop; not late at night (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Cause identified and addressed; a level 2 or 3 event prompts review of the plan, deintensifying or switching drugs if appropriate (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 6.19)
  • Glucagon prescribed for anyone on insulin or at high risk, ready-to-use form preferred (Rec 6.16)
  • Structured education on prevention and treatment (Rec 6.18)
  • Follow-up arranged
💎 PEARLS
  • Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs: it can persist up to 8 days after overdose. Never discharge after a single correction; observe at least 12 h after dextrose and octreotide stop (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Octreotide early for sulfonylurea toxicity: start after the first IV dextrose bolus, not only for refractory cases; 50-100 mcg SC every 6-12 h (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
  • Draw labs before correcting when there is no diabetes and the cause is unclear: insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate and oral-agent screen, then glucagon 1 mg IV (Endocrine Society 2009). Do not delay treating severe hypoglycemia (Practical)
  • High insulin with low C-peptide = exogenous insulin: endogenous insulin is secreted with C-peptide (Klein-Schwartz 2016). Low C-peptide alone also fits IGF-mediated and non-insulin causes (Endocrine Society 2009)
  • Impaired hypoglycemia awareness: level 2 hypoglycemia without symptoms suggests it; screen at least yearly (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 6.11). The first sign may be neuroglycopenic (confusion, seizure)
  • Glucagon needs hepatic glycogen: it is not useful with glycogen depletion and it releases insulin, so it is not routine in sulfonylurea toxicity; use IV dextrose (Klein-Schwartz 2016)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Dextrose D50/D10, 💊 Glucagon, 💊 Regular Insulin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hypoglycemia, 🔬 Low Cortisol, 🔬 ACTH

162. NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME (NMS)

Antipsychotic-Induced • Lead-Pipe Rigidity • Hyperthermia • Bromocriptine/Dantrolene
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, antiemetics) characterized by hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability. Mortality 5-20% even with treatment

Classic Tetrad:

  • Hyperthermia: Often >40°C (104°F), can exceed 41°C
  • Muscle Rigidity: "Lead-pipe" rigidity (constant resistance throughout ROM), NOT clonus
  • Altered Mental Status: Confusion, agitation, stupor, coma
  • Autonomic Instability: Tachycardia, labile BP (hyper- or hypotension), diaphoresis, tachypnea

Time Course:

  • Onset typically within 2 weeks of starting/increasing antipsychotic (90% within 10 days)
  • Can occur after years of stable therapy (rare)
  • Develops over 24-72 hours (slower than serotonin syndrome)
  • Duration: Days to weeks even after stopping offending agent

Causative Agents:

  • Typical Antipsychotics (Higher Risk): Haloperidol, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine
  • Atypical Antipsychotics: Risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, clozapine (all can cause)
  • Antiemetics: Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine
  • Dopamine Withdrawal: Abrupt discontinuation of levodopa/dopamine agonists in Parkinson's

Risk Factors:

  • High-potency typical antipsychotics
  • Rapid dose escalation, IM administration
  • Dehydration, agitation, exhaustion
  • Prior NMS episode (17-30% recurrence risk)
  • Organic brain disease
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis — No Specific Test:

  • Recent dopamine antagonist exposure + classic tetrad
  • Rule out other causes (infection, other drug toxicity)

Laboratory Findings (Supportive):

  • CK: Markedly elevated (often >1000, can be >100,000) — from rigidity-induced rhabdomyolysis
  • WBC: Leukocytosis (10-40k) — not infection
  • LFTs: Often elevated
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Myoglobinuria
  • Electrolytes: Hypocalcemia, hyper/hyponatremia
  • Iron: Low serum iron (acute phase reactant — sensitive early marker)

Differential Diagnosis (NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome):

Feature NMS Serotonin Syndrome
Causative Agent Dopamine antagonists Serotonergic drugs
Onset Days (24-72 hrs) Hours (<24 hrs)
Muscle Findings Lead-pipe rigidity Clonus, hyperreflexia
Reflexes Normal or decreased Hyperreflexia
Pupils Normal Mydriasis
Bowel Sounds Decreased/absent Hyperactive
Resolution Days to weeks 24-72 hours
Treatment Bromocriptine, dantrolene Cyproheptadine
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate:

  • STOP offending agent — most important step
  • ICU admission
  • Supportive care: IV fluids, cooling, monitoring

Cooling:

  • External cooling (ice packs, cooling blankets, evaporative)
  • Antipyretics NOT effective (not prostaglandin-mediated)
  • Target temperature <38.5°C

Specific Pharmacotherapy:

  • Bromocriptine (Dopamine Agonist):
    • 2.5 mg PO/NG q8h, increase to 5 mg q8h as needed
    • Max 40 mg/day
    • Continue until symptoms resolve, then taper over 10 days
  • Dantrolene (Muscle Relaxant):
    • 1-2.5 mg/kg IV q6h (max 10 mg/kg/day)
    • Reduces rigidity and heat production
    • Monitor for hepatotoxicity
  • Benzodiazepines: For agitation (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV q4-6h PRN)
  • Amantadine: 100 mg PO BID — alternative dopaminergic agent

Supportive Measures:

  • Aggressive IV fluids (prevent AKI from rhabdomyolysis)
  • DVT prophylaxis
  • Intubation if needed for airway protection or severe rigidity
  • Avoid succinylcholine (hyperkalemia risk from rhabdo)
  • ECT may be considered for refractory cases

Duration:

  • Symptoms resolve over 7-14 days with treatment
  • Longer with depot antipsychotics (weeks)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • ALL NMS patients require ICU
  • Hyperthermia >40°C
  • Severe rigidity
  • Rhabdomyolysis (CK >10,000)
  • Respiratory compromise
  • Hemodynamic instability
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Afebrile for >48 hours
  • Rigidity resolved
  • Mental status at baseline
  • CK downtrending/normalized
  • Renal function stable
  • Psychiatric plan for alternative antipsychotic (if needed)
  • May cautiously rechallenge with low-potency agent after 2+ weeks if psychiatrically necessary
💎 PEARLS
  • Lead-pipe rigidity, NOT clonus: Key distinction from serotonin syndrome. NMS = rigid. SS = hyperreflexic/clonus
  • NMS is slow, SS is fast: NMS develops over days. SS develops within hours
  • CK is massively elevated: Often >1000, frequently >10,000. Rhabdomyolysis is the rule, not the exception
  • Low iron is early marker: Serum iron drops before CK rises. Useful for early diagnosis
  • Metoclopramide can cause NMS: Often forgotten. It's a dopamine antagonist
  • Parkinson's patients at risk from dopamine withdrawal: Abruptly stopping levodopa can trigger NMS-like syndrome
  • 17-30% recurrence: If antipsychotic needed in future, wait 2+ weeks, use low-potency atypical, start very low dose
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lorazepam
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Leukocytosis

163. OSTEOMYELITIS

Vertebral • Diabetic Foot • Hematogenous • MRI Gold Standard
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Infection of bone, classified by mechanism (hematogenous vs contiguous vs direct inoculation), duration (acute <2 weeks vs chronic), and location

Vertebral Osteomyelitis:

  • Presentation: Back pain (>90%), fever (50%), neurologic deficits (30% — epidural abscess)
  • Risk factors: IVDU, endocarditis, recent bacteremia, spinal procedures, immunosuppression
  • Location: Lumbar > thoracic > cervical
  • Organisms: S. aureus (50%), Strep species, gram-negatives (UTI source), TB (Pott's disease)
  • Complications: Epidural abscess (urgent), psoas abscess, spinal instability, cord compression

Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis:

  • Presentation: Non-healing ulcer, probe-to-bone positive, may lack systemic signs (neuropathy masks pain)
  • Organisms: Polymicrobial — S. aureus, streptococci, enterococci, Pseudomonas, anaerobes
  • Key question: Can probe touch bone through ulcer? → ~85% predictive of osteomyelitis

Contiguous/Post-Traumatic:

  • Open fractures, surgical site infections, hardware infections
  • Often polymicrobial including skin flora and gram-negatives

Hematogenous (Children > Adults):

  • Metaphysis of long bones in children
  • Vertebrae in adults
  • Usually monomicrobial (S. aureus dominant)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs:

  • ESR and CRP: Elevated in >90%. CRP normalizes faster (good for monitoring treatment)
  • WBC: May be normal in chronic osteomyelitis
  • Blood cultures: Positive in 50% of vertebral, less in other types. GET BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS
  • Procalcitonin: May help distinguish soft tissue vs bone infection

Imaging:

  • Plain X-ray: First-line but insensitive early (changes take 10-14 days). Shows periosteal elevation, lytic lesions, sequestra
  • MRI with Contrast: GOLD STANDARD
    • Sensitivity 90-100%, Specificity 80-90%
    • Shows bone marrow edema, soft tissue involvement, abscesses
    • Essential for vertebral osteo (epidural abscess?)
  • CT: Good for cortical bone detail, sequestrum, surgical planning
  • Nuclear Medicine: Triple-phase bone scan if MRI contraindicated. WBC scan more specific but less sensitive

Bone Biopsy/Culture (CRITICAL):

  • Obtain BEFORE antibiotics if possible
  • CT-guided biopsy: For vertebral osteomyelitis — 75% yield if not on antibiotics
  • Surgical debridement specimens: Best yield
  • Diabetic foot: Bone biopsy through non-infected tissue (not through ulcer base)
  • Send for: Aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, mycobacterial cultures + histopathology
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Empiric Antibiotics (While Awaiting Culture):

  • Vertebral: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone (or ciprofloxacin if gram-neg suspected)
  • Diabetic Foot: Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam (or vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole)
  • Hardware-associated: Vancomycin + cefepime (cover Pseudomonas)

Duration:

  • Vertebral osteomyelitis: 6 weeks total. Early IV-to-oral switch after initial stabilization (typically 1-2 weeks IV) is evidence-based and preferred — OVIVA trial (NEJM 2019, n=1054) demonstrated oral antibiotics non-inferior to prolonged IV for complex bone/joint infections, with ~10% IV catheter complication rate in the IV arm. Choose an oral agent with high bioavailability (fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX, linezolid, clindamycin, rifampin) based on organism and susceptibilities. Consult ID for step-down selection.
  • Diabetic foot:
    • Soft tissue only: 1-2 weeks
    • Osteomyelitis with residual infected bone: 4-6 weeks
    • Osteomyelitis with amputation/complete resection: 2-5 days post-op
  • Chronic osteomyelitis: Often requires surgical debridement + 4-6 weeks antibiotics

Surgical Indications:

  • Vertebral: Epidural abscess with neuro deficits (emergent), spinal instability, failure of medical therapy
  • Diabetic foot: Extensive necrosis, abscess, failure of antibiotics, exposed bone. Amputation if limb-threatening
  • Hardware-associated: Often requires hardware removal for cure

Monitoring:

  • CRP weekly — should decline by 2 weeks
  • ESR slower to normalize (follows over months)
  • Repeat imaging if not improving clinically
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Epidural abscess with neurologic compromise (SURGICAL EMERGENCY)
  • Sepsis or septic shock
  • Spinal cord compression
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Culture data available, on appropriate antibiotics
  • CRP downtrending
  • Afebrile, pain controlled
  • PICC line placed (if IV antibiotics continuing)
  • Outpatient IV antibiotic plan established
  • ID and/or orthopedic surgery follow-up
  • No surgical emergency
💎 PEARLS
  • GET CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS: Bone biopsy yield drops significantly after antibiotics started. Hold antibiotics for biopsy if patient stable
  • Probe-to-bone = osteomyelitis: If metal probe reaches bone through diabetic foot ulcer, PPV ~85% for osteomyelitis
  • MRI is essential for vertebral: Must rule out epidural abscess. Clinical exam cannot reliably exclude it
  • Staph aureus dominates: ~50% of all osteomyelitis. Get blood cultures — positive in half of hematogenous cases
  • Epidural abscess = emergency: Progressive neuro deficits need emergent surgical decompression. Don't wait
  • X-ray changes take 2 weeks: Normal X-ray doesn't rule out early osteomyelitis. MRI is far more sensitive
  • IVDU + back pain = vertebral osteo: Until proven otherwise. Get MRI, blood cultures, echocardiogram
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Nafcillin, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 TMP-SMX
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Blood Cultures

→ Osteomyelitis

164. SEPTIC ARTHRITIS

Joint Emergency • Arthrocentesis • Synovial WBC >50,000 • Urgent Drainage
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Bacterial infection of a joint — orthopedic emergency requiring urgent diagnosis and drainage to prevent permanent joint destruction

Classic Presentation:

  • Monoarticular (90%) — knee most common (50%), then hip, ankle, wrist, shoulder
  • Acute onset joint pain, swelling, warmth, erythema
  • Severely limited ROM — patient guards joint
  • Fever (50-75%)
  • Unable to bear weight (if lower extremity)

Risk Factors:

  • Pre-existing joint disease (RA, OA, gout)
  • Prosthetic joint
  • Recent joint surgery or injection
  • Skin infection, bacteremia
  • IVDU
  • Immunosuppression (DM, steroids, biologics)
  • Age >80

Organisms:

  • S. aureus: Most common overall (40-50%), including MRSA
  • Streptococci: Group A, B, pneumococcus
  • N. gonorrhoeae: Young sexually active adults — often migratory polyarthralgia → monoarthritis, rash, tenosynovitis
  • Gram-negatives: Elderly, immunocompromised, IVDU
  • Prosthetic joints: Coagulase-negative staph, Propionibacterium, S. aureus
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

ARTHROCENTESIS — MANDATORY:

  • Do not delay for imaging — clinical diagnosis + tap
  • Send: Cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, crystal analysis

Synovial Fluid Interpretation:

Finding Normal Non-inflammatory Inflammatory Septic
WBC/mm³ <200 200-2,000 2,000-50,000 >50,000
PMN % <25% <25% 50-70% >90%

Key Points:

  • WBC >50,000 with >90% PMNs = septic until proven otherwise
  • WBC >100,000 = almost always septic
  • Gram stain: Positive in only 50-75% (low sensitivity)
  • Culture: Positive in 80-90% (gold standard)
  • Crystals don't rule out infection: Gout and septic arthritis can coexist!

Additional Workup:

  • Blood cultures: Positive in 50%
  • CBC, CRP, ESR: Usually elevated but non-specific
  • X-ray: Usually normal early. Shows soft tissue swelling. Late: joint space narrowing, erosions
  • MRI: If suspect adjacent osteomyelitis, or deep joint (hip, SI joint)
  • Gonococcal: NAAT from urethra, cervix, pharynx, rectum + blood/synovial culture
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Empiric Antibiotics (Start Immediately After Arthrocentesis):

  • Standard: Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h (cover MRSA)
  • Add gram-negative coverage if: Immunocompromised, IVDU, elderly, recent surgery
    • Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily OR cefepime 2g IV q8h
  • Suspected gonococcal: Ceftriaxone 1g IV q24h monotherapy (2021 CDC STI Guidelines — azithromycin dropped due to rising resistance). Add doxycycline 100mg PO BID × 7 days only if chlamydia co-infection has not been excluded

DRAINAGE — ESSENTIAL:

  • Joint destruction occurs within days without adequate drainage
  • Options:
    • Serial arthrocentesis: Daily needle drainage until effusion resolves (often adequate for accessible joints)
    • Arthroscopic lavage: If fails serial taps, large joint, loculations
    • Open arthrotomy: Hip (difficult to aspirate), shoulder, failed arthroscopy
  • HIP = SURGICAL EMERGENCY: Difficult to drain percutaneously, high risk of AVN. Early surgical drainage recommended

Duration of Antibiotics:

  • Native joint: 2-4 weeks (2 weeks often adequate for uncomplicated)
  • Gonococcal: 7-14 days (often responds rapidly)
  • Prosthetic joint: 6 weeks + often requires hardware removal or exchange
  • Adjacent osteomyelitis: 6 weeks
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Sepsis or septic shock
  • Hip septic arthritis (surgical emergency)
  • Polyarticular septic arthritis (suggests bacteremia/endocarditis)
  • Rapid joint destruction
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Joint adequately drained (no reaccumulation)
  • Improving pain, ROM, swelling
  • Afebrile
  • CRP downtrending
  • Culture results available, on appropriate antibiotics
  • PICC line if continuing IV antibiotics
  • PT/OT arranged for rehabilitation
  • Orthopedic/ID follow-up
💎 PEARLS
  • Tap before antibiotics, but don't delay antibiotics for tap: If significant delay, start antibiotics. Joint damage is worse than slightly lower culture yield
  • WBC >50k, >90% PMNs = septic: This is the threshold. Don't wait for culture
  • Crystals ≠ not infected: Gout and septic arthritis coexist in 1.5% of gout flares. If high suspicion, treat for both
  • Hip = urgent surgery: Hard to drain, high AVN risk. Don't attempt serial aspiration — call ortho early
  • Gonococcal is different: Young, healthy, sexually active. Often polyarticular then localizes. Skin lesions, tenosynovitis. Responds well to antibiotics
  • Prosthetic joint infection needs ID + ortho: Often requires hardware removal. Long-term antibiotics. Complex management
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Nafcillin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Synovial Fluid Analysis, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated CRP

165. SPINAL EPIDURAL ABSCESS

Neurologic Emergency • Classic Triad • MRI Whole Spine • Urgent Decompression
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Pyogenic infection in the epidural space — neurologic emergency requiring urgent diagnosis and often surgical decompression to prevent permanent paralysis

Classic Triad (Present in Only 10-15%):

  • Fever
  • Back pain
  • Neurologic deficit

Clinical Stages (Progressive Over Days):

  1. Stage 1: Back pain (often severe, localized), fever
  2. Stage 2: Radicular pain (nerve root irritation)
  3. Stage 3: Motor weakness, sensory deficits, bowel/bladder dysfunction
  4. Stage 4: Paralysis (often irreversible if >24-48 hours)

Risk Factors:

  • IVDU (most common in many series)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Spinal procedures (epidural injection, surgery)
  • Bacteremia from any source
  • Immunosuppression
  • Chronic renal failure
  • Alcohol use disorder
  • Adjacent vertebral osteomyelitis

Location:

  • Posterior epidural space (most common)
  • Thoracolumbar > lumbar > cervical
  • May span multiple vertebral levels

Organisms:

  • S. aureus: 60-70% (including MRSA)
  • Streptococci, gram-negatives (10-15% each)
  • Coagulase-negative staph (post-procedure)
  • TB (Pott's disease with epidural extension)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

MRI WITH GADOLINIUM — GOLD STANDARD:

  • Image ENTIRE spine — can be multifocal
  • Sensitivity >90%
  • Shows epidural collection, cord compression, vertebral osteomyelitis, paraspinal abscess
  • Do NOT delay for MRI if clinical picture clear — emergent surgical consultation

CT Myelogram:

  • If MRI contraindicated (pacemaker, severe claustrophobia)
  • Less sensitive than MRI

Labs:

  • WBC: Elevated in 60-80%
  • ESR: Elevated in >95% (often >50)
  • CRP: Elevated in >90%
  • Blood cultures: Positive in 60% — GET BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS

Image-Guided Aspiration/Biopsy:

  • If blood cultures negative and diagnosis uncertain
  • Don't delay treatment for culture
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Emergent Surgical Consultation:

  • ANY neurologic deficit = emergent surgical decompression
  • Goal: Decompression within 24 hours (ideally <12 hours) of motor deficit
  • Recovery correlates with pre-op neurologic status and time to surgery

Surgical Indications (Absolute):

  • Neurologic deficit (weakness, bowel/bladder dysfunction)
  • Spinal instability
  • Failure of medical therapy
  • Large abscess with significant cord compression

Medical Management Alone (Select Cases):

  • No neurologic deficit
  • High surgical risk
  • Extensive multilevel disease
  • CLOSE monitoring: Neuro checks q4h, serial imaging, low threshold for surgery

Empiric Antibiotics:

  • Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h (cover MRSA)
  • PLUS Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h or Cefepime 2g IV q8h (cover gram-negatives)
  • Adjust based on cultures

Duration:

  • Epidural abscess alone: 4-6 weeks
  • With vertebral osteomyelitis: 6-8 weeks
  • Transition to oral therapy possible with appropriate agents and good source control
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Any neurologic deficit (surgical emergency)
  • Sepsis or septic shock
  • Respiratory compromise (cervical involvement)
  • Post-operative monitoring
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Neurologically stable or improving
  • Post-surgical wound healing
  • Afebrile
  • CRP downtrending
  • On appropriate IV antibiotics (PICC line)
  • Rehab placement if neurologic deficits
  • ID and neurosurgery/orthopedic follow-up
💎 PEARLS
  • Back pain + fever + IVDU = epidural abscess until proven otherwise: Get emergent MRI
  • Classic triad present in only 10-15%: Back pain is most consistent symptom. Don't wait for neuro deficits
  • Time is paralysis: Pre-op neurologic status predicts outcome. Surgery within 24 hours of motor deficit is critical
  • Image the WHOLE spine: Can have multiple non-contiguous abscesses
  • ESR almost always elevated: ESR >20 has 98% sensitivity. Normal ESR + CRP makes diagnosis very unlikely
  • Don't LP if you suspect epidural abscess: Risk of meningitis from seeding. MRI first
  • Medical management requires close monitoring: Neuro checks q4h. Any decline = emergent surgery
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Meropenem
↑ Back to Table of Contents

166. CATHETER-RELATED BLOODSTREAM INFECTION (CLABSI)

Central Line Infection • Line Removal • Differential Time to Positivity
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Bacteremia/fungemia in a patient with central venous catheter (CVC) where the catheter is the attributable source. One of the most common healthcare-associated infections

Clinical Features:

  • Fever, chills, rigors
  • Hypotension, sepsis
  • May have no localizing signs
  • Exit site findings (may or may not be present): Erythema, purulence, tenderness
  • Tunnel infection: Erythema/tenderness along subcutaneous tract (tunneled catheters)

Risk Factors:

  • Duration of catheterization (risk increases after day 5-7)
  • Femoral > internal jugular > subclavian site
  • TPN administration
  • Multiple lumens
  • Frequent manipulation
  • Neutropenia, immunosuppression
  • Poor insertion/maintenance technique

Common Organisms:

  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci: Most common (30-40%), often low virulence
  • S. aureus: 15-20%, high virulence, metastatic complications
  • Enterococci: 10-15%
  • Gram-negatives: 15-20% (Klebsiella, E. coli, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter)
  • Candida: 5-10%, especially TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotics
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Blood Cultures:

  • Paired cultures: One from catheter, one from peripheral vein (BEFORE antibiotics)
  • Differential time to positivity (DTTP): Catheter culture positive ≥2 hours before peripheral = catheter source (sensitivity 85%, specificity 90%)
  • If no peripheral access: Draw from two different lumens

Catheter Tip Culture (If Removed):

  • Roll-plate method (Maki technique)
  • ≥15 CFU = colonization/infection
  • Same organism in tip and blood = confirmed CLABSI

Definitions:

  • Definite CLABSI: Same organism from catheter tip (≥15 CFU) and peripheral blood
  • Probable CLABSI: Bacteremia with CVC, defervescence after removal, no other source
  • DTTP-defined: Catheter blood positive ≥2 hours before peripheral

Additional Workup Based on Organism:

  • S. aureus bacteremia: Echocardiogram (TEE preferred), consider ophthalmology exam, repeat cultures until negative
  • Candida: Ophthalmology exam (endophthalmitis), echocardiogram
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Catheter Removal — Definite Indications:

  • S. aureus — ALWAYS remove (high complication rate)
  • Candida — ALWAYS remove
  • Pseudomonas — usually remove
  • Tunnel infection or port pocket infection
  • Septic shock
  • Suppurative thrombophlebitis
  • Persistent bacteremia (>72 hours on appropriate antibiotics)
  • Metastatic infection (endocarditis, osteomyelitis)

Catheter Salvage (May Attempt in Select Cases):

  • Coagulase-negative staph (low virulence)
  • No tunnel/pocket infection
  • Limited vascular access
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • Use antibiotic lock therapy + systemic antibiotics
  • If persistent bacteremia >72 hours, REMOVE

Empiric Antibiotics:

  • Vancomycin (cover MRSA, CoNS)
  • ADD gram-negative coverage if: Septic, immunocompromised, femoral catheter, known colonization
    • Cefepime 2g IV q8h OR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h
  • ADD antifungal if: TPN, prolonged antibiotics, Candida colonization, immunocompromised
    • Micafungin 100mg IV daily or fluconazole 400mg IV daily

Duration (From First Negative Culture):

  • Coagulase-negative staph: 5-7 days (if catheter removed and uncomplicated)
  • S. aureus: Minimum 4 weeks (2 weeks only if TEE negative, no hardware, rapid clearance, catheter removed)
  • Gram-negatives: 7-14 days
  • Candida: 14 days after first negative culture
  • Complicated (endocarditis, septic thrombosis): 4-6 weeks
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Septic shock
  • S. aureus bacteremia with hemodynamic instability
  • Suppurative thrombophlebitis
  • Endocarditis with acute decompensation
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Catheter removed (or salvaged with documented clearance)
  • Blood cultures negative
  • Afebrile
  • Hemodynamically stable
  • If S. aureus/Candida: Echo completed, no endocarditis
  • PICC line for ongoing antibiotics if needed
  • ID follow-up for duration guidance
💎 PEARLS
  • S. aureus = remove the line: No exceptions. High rate of endocarditis and metastatic infection with retained catheter
  • Candida = remove the line: Fungal biofilms don't respond to antifungals. Also get ophthalmology consult
  • Coag-neg staph = can consider salvage: Low virulence, may try antibiotic lock. But if persistent >72h, remove
  • S. aureus needs echo: TEE preferred. 25% of S. aureus bacteremia has endocarditis. Changes duration dramatically
  • Repeat cultures until negative: For S. aureus and Candida. Persistent positivity = look for metastatic focus
  • DTTP helps when can't remove: Catheter culture positive ≥2 hours before peripheral confirms catheter source
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Daptomycin, 💊 Cefepime, 💊 Meropenem
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated Lactate
