181. TOXIC MEGACOLON

Acute Colonic Dilation • IBD Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Acute nonobstructive colonic dilation with systemic toxicity: transverse colon over 6 cm with loss of haustra (AGA inpatient IBD 2026), or total or segmental dilation of 5.5 cm or more, usually with a thin colon wall (ASCRS UC 2021). Occurs in fewer than 5% of acute severe colitis (ACG UC 2025) and is an indication for urgent surgery (ACG UC 2025 KC 54)

Diagnostic Criteria (Jalan, 1969): colonic dilation on imaging PLUS at least 3 of the first 4 PLUS 1 or more of the last line. Source: Jalan 1969 as stated in Liggett and Alam 2024 (peer-reviewed review); no US society guideline sets diagnostic criteria

  • Fever over 38.6°C (101.5°F)
  • Heart rate over 120 bpm
  • WBC over 10,500/μL
  • Anemia
  • PLUS 1 or more of: dehydration, altered mental status, electrolyte abnormality, hypotension

Clinical Features:

  • Abdominal distension, tenderness, tympany, ileus (absent bowel sounds); examine for rebound and guarding (ACG UC 2025)
  • Fever, tachycardia, hypotension (Jalan criteria above)
  • Signs of perforation or peritonitis may be masked by ongoing immunosuppressive therapy (ASCRS UC 2021)
  • Practical: stool frequency may fall as the colon dilates; do not read this as improvement

Causes:

  • IBD: ulcerative colitis is the most common cause (Liggett and Alam 2024); also ileocolonic Crohn disease (Autenrieth 2012)
  • C. difficile: next most common (Liggett and Alam 2024); megacolon makes CDI fulminant (IDSA/SHEA 2017; ACG CDI 2021 KC 3)
  • Other infections: CMV, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter; E. coli O157 with HUS (Autenrieth 2012)
  • Ischemic colitis (rare) (Liggett and Alam 2024)

Precipitants:

  • Infection (C. difficile, CMV), antimotility agents, electrolyte derangements (AGA inpatient IBD 2026). Practical: e.g., hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia
  • Opioids and anticholinergic drugs may precipitate colonic dilation and toxicity (ACG UC 2025)
  • Antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide) are contraindicated in untreated CDI, fulminant CDI, and severe colonic IBD (AGA CDI 2026; ACG CDI 2021)
  • Full colonoscopy in severe colitis (Liggett and Alam 2024)
  • Practical: abrupt steroid withdrawal
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging:

  • Suspected toxic megacolon: timely abdominal film and/or CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast, and discussion with colorectal surgery (AGA inpatient IBD 2026)
  • Plain film: transverse colon over 5.5 cm predicts a worse outcome; also loss of haustra, mucosal islands; 3 or more dilated small bowel loops predict nonresponse to medical therapy (ACG UC 2025)
  • CT abdomen/pelvis: for suspected perforation or extraluminal complication (ACG UC 2025); low threshold in fulminant CDI to assess colitis and rule out megacolon or perforation (ACG CDI 2021). Toxic megacolon on CT: dilation, segmental wall thinning, abnormal haustra (Liggett and Alam 2024)
  • Practical: no barium enema

Laboratory:

  • CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel (AGA inpatient IBD 2026 checklist). CRP at baseline and daily (ACG UC 2025 KC 50, Figure 3; AGA inpatient IBD 2026). WBC and creatinine grade CDI severity (ACG CDI 2021 KC 2). Albumin: low albumin predicts poor outcome in CDI (ACG CDI 2021); in acute severe UC, albumin below 2.5 g/dL: consider infliximab dose intensification (ACG UC 2025 KC 57)
  • C. difficile testing in every patient (ACG UC 2025 rec 46, strong), with a multistep toxin-based algorithm (AGA CDI in IBD 2026 BPA 2; ACG CDI 2021 rec 3). With ileus, a rectal swab PCR is reasonable (ACG CDI 2021). Stool culture or GI pathogen panel (AGA inpatient IBD 2026)
  • CMV: diagnose on sigmoidoscopy biopsies (ACG UC 2025 KC 48)
  • Practical: magnesium, lactate; blood cultures if febrile

Endoscopy:

  • Avoid full colonoscopy: risk of perforation and of toxic megacolon (Liggett and Alam 2024)
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy with minimal insufflation by an experienced endoscopist, within 72 h and preferably 24 h in acute severe UC, to grade severity and biopsy for CMV (ACG UC 2025 KC 48; Liggett and Alam 2024)
  • IBD with CDI and no improvement 48-72 h after CDI treatment starts: endoscopy for IBD activity and CMV (AGA CDI in IBD 2026 BPA 8)

Surgical Consultation: At diagnosis; suspected toxicity warrants surgical consultation (ACG UC 2025 KC 52), and toxic megacolon is an indication for urgent surgery (ACG UC 2025 KC 54; ASCRS UC 2021 Rec 2). Multidisciplinary team: GI, surgery, ID, critical care (AGA CDI 2026 BPA 10; ASCRS UC 2021 Rec 1; AGA inpatient IBD 2026 BPA 6; AGA CDI in IBD 2026). Not responding in a community hospital: consider transfer to a high-volume IBD center (AGA inpatient IBD 2026)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

General Supportive Measures:

  • IV hydration, electrolyte repletion, treatment of acute anemia (AGA inpatient IBD 2026 BPA 2); volume resuscitation in fulminant CDI (ACG CDI 2021 rec 9). Practical: replace K and Mg
  • STOP opioids, anticholinergics, antidiarrheals, NSAIDs (ACG UC 2025 KC 51; AGA CDI 2026; Liggett and Alam 2024); avoid opioids for pain if possible (AGA inpatient IBD 2026)
  • VTE prophylaxis: pharmacologic for all hospitalized acute colitis, safe even with active UC bleeding (ACG UC 2025 rec 47, strong, low); SC LMWH or fondaparinux unless absolutely contraindicated (AGA inpatient IBD 2026 BPA 5). Practical: e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
  • Nutrition: bowel rest adds no benefit in acute severe UC (ASCRS UC 2021); no TPN for bowel rest (ACG UC 2025 rec 49). Practical: NPO with megacolon, ileus, or impending surgery
  • Practical: NG decompression for ileus or vomiting; position changes (rolling) to help decompress the colon

Medical Therapy (IBD-related):

  • IV corticosteroids: methylprednisolone 60 mg/day total or hydrocortisone 100 mg 3-4 times daily; no benefit above 60 mg (ACG UC 2025 rec 50; AGA inpatient IBD 2026 BPA 7). Do not withhold steroids for pending CDI tests when a flare is likely; if results will be delayed, start CDI therapy at the same time, after the stool sample is sent (AGA CDI in IBD 2026). Continue IBD therapy while CDI is treated (ACG UC 2025 Figure 3; AGA CDI in IBD 2026 BPA 7; ACG CDI 2021 KC 5); in fulminant CDI, consider a temporary hold of nonessential immunosuppressants until CDI improves (AGA CDI in IBD 2026, Table 1)
  • Antibiotics: not routine in acute severe UC (ACG UC 2025 rec 48, strong, low); restrict to suspected extraluminal complications or systemic signs of toxicity (ACG UC 2025), which toxic megacolon has by definition (ASCRS UC 2021). Practical: piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g IV q6h, or cefepime 2 g IV q8h plus metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
  • Rescue therapy is for acute severe UC without adequate response to IV steroids by day 3: infliximab 5 mg/kg, consider 10 mg/kg if albumin is under 2.5 g/dL, or IV cyclosporine 2 mg/kg/day (ACG UC 2025 rec 51, KC 57). Established toxic megacolon is an indication for urgent surgery, not for continued medical therapy (ACG UC 2025 KC 54; ASCRS UC 2021 Rec 2)

Medical Therapy (fulminant C. diff):

  • Stop the inciting antibiotic as soon as possible (IDSA/SHEA 2017)
  • Vancomycin 500 mg PO or by NG tube every 6 hours (IDSA/SHEA 2017, strong, moderate; ACG CDI 2021 rec 9; AGA CDI 2026 BPA 10). High dose for at least the first 48 h (AGA) to 72 h (ACG); after clinical response, usually 3-5 days, step down to vancomycin 125 mg every 6 hours alone. Treat at least 10 days; AGA favors 14 (AGA CDI 2026; ACG CDI 2021)
  • PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours, particularly with ileus (IDSA/SHEA 2017, strong, moderate; AGA CDI 2026 BPA 10; ACG CDI 2021 rec 9, conditional)
  • Ileus: ADD rectal vancomycin 500 mg in about 100 mL normal saline every 6 hours as a retention enema, in addition to oral or NG vancomycin (IDSA/SHEA 2017, weak, low; ACG CDI 2021 rec 10; AGA CDI 2026 BPA 10; AGA CDI in IBD 2026 Supplementary Table 3)
  • No fidaxomicin for fulminant CDI: no supporting data (IDSA/SHEA 2021; ACG CDI 2021)
  • FMT: consider multi-dose FMT by lower endoscopy (AGA CDI 2026 BPA 11); ACG suggests it for severe or fulminant CDI refractory to antibiotics, especially poor surgical candidates (ACG CDI 2021 rec 11, strong, low). Not with perforation or obstruction (AGA CDI 2026). Rebyota and Vowst are not studied or approved for severe or fulminant CDI (AGA CDI 2026 BPA 11)
  • Not improved or worse after 48 h of aggressive therapy: consider FMT or colectomy (AGA CDI 2026); ACG: reassess at 48-72 h (ACG CDI 2021)
  • Avoid empiric antibiotics not directed at CDI; treat coinfections with ID input (AGA CDI 2026)

Indications for URGENT Surgery (Colectomy):

  • Toxic megacolon, perforation, massive or refractory hemorrhage, refractoriness to medical therapy (ACG UC 2025 KC 54; ASCRS UC 2021 Rec 2)
  • Fulminant CDI not improving on maximal therapy, especially with toxic megacolon, ischemia, or perforation (ACG CDI 2021; AGA CDI 2026); timely colectomy can be lifesaving in toxic megacolon (AGA CDI in IBD 2026)
  • Persistent colonic distention predicts poor response to further medical therapy; prolonged nonoperative care risks perforation (ASCRS UC 2021)
  • Delayed surgery worsens outcomes (ACG UC 2025); mortality rises as the interval from perforation to surgery lengthens (ASCRS UC 2021)
  • Practical: rising WBC, fever, new peritoneal signs

Surgical Procedure: UC: subtotal or total abdominal colectomy with end ileostomy; avoid proctectomy and avoid ileal pouch-anal anastomosis at the urgent operation (ASCRS UC 2021 Rec 2; ACG UC 2025; Liggett and Alam 2024). Fulminant CDI: subtotal colectomy with rectal preservation (IDSA/SHEA 2017, strong, moderate) or diverting loop ileostomy with colonic lavage and antegrade vancomycin flushes (IDSA/SHEA 2017, weak, low; ACG CDI 2021 KC 4). Prior infliximab or cyclosporine does not increase postoperative complications; do not defer surgery for it (ACG UC 2025 KC 55)

Monitoring:

  • Daily: vital signs, abdominal exam, stool frequency, rectal bleeding, CRP (ACG UC 2025 KC 50, Figure 3)
  • Daily abdominal films until dilation decreases or surgery is planned (Liggett and Alam 2024)
  • Practical: abdominal exams every 4-6 h; WBC, electrolytes, lactate every 12-24 h
💎 PEARLS
  • Toxic megacolon is a surgical emergency: urgent colectomy, not prolonged medical therapy (ACG UC 2025 KC 54; ASCRS UC 2021 Rec 2)
  • Immunosuppression masks perforation: peritoneal signs may be absent (ASCRS UC 2021)
  • Test every patient for C. difficile, including known IBD (ACG UC 2025 rec 46)
  • Pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis, even with bloody stools (ACG UC 2025 rec 47 and text)
  • Stop opioids, anticholinergics, antidiarrheals, NSAIDs (ACG UC 2025 KC 51; ACG CDI 2021)
  • Fulminant CDI: vancomycin 500 mg every 6 hours PO or NG plus IV metronidazole; add rectal vancomycin for ileus; no fidaxomicin (IDSA/SHEA 2017, 2021; AGA CDI 2026 BPA 10)
  • Practical: falling stool frequency can mean worsening dilation, not improvement
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Hydrocortisone, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Cefepime, 💊 KCl, 💊 Magnesium
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Hypokalemia

182. POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA

PMR • Giant Cell Arteritis Association
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Presentation: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain/stiffness in patient >50 years. Morning stiffness lasting >45 minutes. Difficulty with ADLs (combing hair, rising from chair)

Key Features:

  • Age: Almost always >50 years (peak 70-80)
  • Symmetric proximal pain: Shoulders (most common), neck, hips, thighs
  • Morning stiffness: Prolonged (>45 min), improves with activity
  • Sudden onset: Patients can often pinpoint when symptoms started
  • Constitutional symptoms: Fatigue, malaise, low-grade fever, weight loss (30-50%)
  • NO true muscle weakness: Weakness is from pain, not myopathy. Normal CK

Physical Exam:

  • Limited active ROM of shoulders and hips (passive ROM preserved)
  • Tenderness over shoulder and hip girdles
  • No synovitis of small joints (unlike RA)
  • Normal muscle strength on formal testing

Association with Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA):

  • 10-30% of PMR patients have GCA
  • 40-60% of GCA patients have PMR symptoms
  • RED FLAGS for GCA: New headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormality

Differential Diagnosis:

  • Late-onset RA: More small joint involvement, RF/CCP positive
  • Inflammatory myopathy: True weakness, elevated CK
  • Hypothyroidism: Check TSH
  • Malignancy: Consider if atypical features or not responding to steroids
  • Infection: Endocarditis, TB can mimic
  • Fibromyalgia: Tender points, normal inflammatory markers
  • RS3PE: Pitting edema of hands, good prognosis
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Laboratory Findings:

  • ESR: Elevated (often >40-50, frequently >100). Normal ESR makes diagnosis unlikely
  • CRP: Elevated. May be more sensitive than ESR
  • CBC: Normocytic anemia (anemia of chronic disease), thrombocytosis
  • CK: NORMAL (distinguishes from myositis)
  • RF, Anti-CCP: Negative (distinguishes from RA)
  • ANA: Negative
  • Liver enzymes: Mild elevation (especially Alk phos) in some patients

Imaging:

  • Ultrasound: Biceps tenosynovitis, subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis, hip synovitis. Can support diagnosis
  • MRI: Shows bursitis and synovitis. Not routinely needed
  • PET-CT: Shows FDG uptake in shoulders, hips, spinous processes. Research tool, not standard

Evaluate for GCA (if any concerning features):

  • Temporal artery biopsy
  • Temporal artery ultrasound ("halo sign")

2012 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria:

  • Age ≥50 years
  • Bilateral shoulder aching
  • Abnormal ESR (>40) or CRP
  • Plus scoring system including morning stiffness, hip involvement, absence of RF/CCP, absence of peripheral joint involvement

Response to Steroids: DRAMATIC improvement within 24-72 hours of prednisone is virtually diagnostic. If no response, reconsider diagnosis

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Initial Treatment - Prednisone:

  • Starting dose: Prednisone 12.5-25 mg daily (lower doses than GCA)
  • Response: Dramatic improvement expected within 24-72 hours
  • If no response in 1 week: Consider higher dose (up to 30mg) or alternative diagnosis

Tapering Schedule (Gradual - total duration 1-2 years):

  • Initial taper: After 2-4 weeks of symptom control, reduce by 2.5mg every 2-4 weeks until 10mg
  • Below 10mg: Reduce by 1mg every 4-8 weeks
  • Maintenance: Most patients need 5-10 mg for many months
  • Monitor: ESR/CRP with each taper. Symptoms should stay controlled

Relapse Management:

  • Relapse common (30-50%) especially during taper below 10mg
  • Increase to last effective dose, then taper more slowly
  • Consider steroid-sparing agent if multiple relapses

Steroid-Sparing Agents:

  • Methotrexate: 7.5-15mg weekly. May allow lower steroid dose and faster taper. Mixed evidence
  • Sarilumab (Kevzara) — FDA-Approved for PMR (February 2023): 200 mg SC q2 weeks. IL-6 receptor antagonist. First and only biologic FDA-approved specifically for PMR. SAPHYR trial (NEJM 2023): 28% sustained remission vs 10% placebo, with 52-week steroid taper vs 14-week taper. Indicated for inadequate response to corticosteroids or inability to taper. Monitor for neutropenia, infection, lipid elevations.
  • Tocilizumab: IL-6 receptor antagonist. Off-label for PMR (not FDA-approved for PMR, though FDA-approved for GCA). Supportive evidence from randomized trials (JAMA 2022 trial showed lower prednisone requirements). Alternative to sarilumab.

Monitoring and Prevention of Steroid Complications:

  • Bone protection: Calcium 1000-1200mg + Vitamin D 800-1000 IU daily. DEXA scan. Consider bisphosphonate
  • PPI if GI risk factors
  • Monitor glucose, blood pressure
  • Pneumococcal and influenza vaccination
  • Consider PJP prophylaxis if high-dose steroids prolonged (controversial in PMR)

If GCA Suspected:

  • START high-dose steroids immediately (prednisone 40-60mg or 1mg/kg) - don't wait for biopsy
  • Add aspirin 81mg daily
  • Urgent temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound
CLINICAL PEARLS
  • Dramatic steroid response: If patient doesn't feel significantly better within 1-3 days of prednisone, reconsider the diagnosis
  • Always think about GCA: Ask about headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms at every visit. PMR can evolve to GCA
  • Normal CK: Elevated CK means it's not PMR. Consider myositis
  • Age matters: PMR essentially doesn't occur before age 50. If <50, wrong diagnosis
  • Slow taper below 10mg: This is where relapses happen. Go slowly (1mg every 4-8 weeks)
  • Flares during taper: Common. Increase dose, control symptoms, then try slower taper
  • Can't get off steroids: If can't taper below 5mg after 2 years, consider alternative diagnosis or steroid-sparing agent
  • Screen for malignancy: Age-appropriate cancer screening. PMR can be paraneoplastic
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Tocilizumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 ANA

183. MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER

SIG E CAPS Criteria • SSRIs First-Line • Screen for Bipolar
DIAGNOSIS (DSM-5)

Criteria: ≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks (must include #1 or #2)

SIG E CAPS Mnemonic:

  • Sleep disturbance (insomnia or hypersomnia)
  • Interest loss (anhedonia) — REQUIRED
  • Guilt or worthlessness
  • Energy loss / fatigue
  • Concentration problems
  • Appetite changes (increased or decreased)
  • Psychomotor agitation or retardation
  • Suicidal ideation

Plus: Depressed mood — REQUIRED (one of the two)

Screening Tools:

  • PHQ-2: Depressed mood + anhedonia. Score ≥3 = positive → do PHQ-9
  • PHQ-9: 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 mod-severe, ≥20 severe

Rule Out: Hypothyroidism, anemia, B12 deficiency, medications (β-blockers, steroids), substance use, BIPOLAR (screen before starting antidepressant!)

TREATMENT

Mild: Psychotherapy (CBT) OR medication (patient preference)

Moderate-Severe: Medication + psychotherapy

First-Line Medications (SSRIs):

  • Sertraline 50mg daily — Good safety, fewer drug interactions
  • Escitalopram 10mg daily — Well tolerated
  • Fluoxetine 20mg daily — Long half-life, activating

Alternatives:

  • SNRIs: Venlafaxine, duloxetine (also for neuropathic pain)
  • Bupropion: No sexual side effects; good for fatigue; avoid in seizures/eating disorders
  • Mirtazapine: Sedating, weight gain; good for insomnia, poor appetite

Timeline: 2-4 weeks for initial response; 6-8 weeks for full effect. Continue 6-9 months after remission (lifelong if recurrent)

💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Always screen for bipolar before starting antidepressant: "Have you ever had a period of unusually elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts?" Antidepressants can trigger mania
  • Black box warning <25 years: Monitor closely for suicidal ideation in first weeks
  • Sexual dysfunction common with SSRIs: Switch to bupropion or mirtazapine, or add bupropion
  • QTc prolongation: Citalopram max 40mg (20mg if elderly or hepatic impairment)
SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT

SAD PERSONS Risk Factors: Sex (male), Age (elderly/young), Depression, Previous attempt (strongest), Ethanol/drugs, Rational thinking loss, Social support lacking, Organized plan, No spouse, Sickness

Ask Directly: Ideation (passive vs active), plan, intent, access to means, protective factors

High Risk: Plan + intent + means → Psychiatric hospitalization

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sertraline, 💊 Gabapentin/Pregabalin, 💊 Mirtazapine, 💊 Trazodone

184. ANXIETY DISORDERS (GAD / PANIC)

SSRIs/SNRIs First-Line • CBT Effective • Avoid Long-Term Benzos
GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER (GAD)

Criteria: Excessive worry about multiple events, more days than not for ≥6 months, difficult to control

Plus ≥3 of: Restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance

Treatment:

  • First-line: SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline) or SNRIs (venlafaxine XR, duloxetine)
  • CBT: Equally effective as medication; combination often best
  • Buspirone: Non-sedating, no dependence; takes 2-4 weeks; good adjunct
  • Avoid long-term benzodiazepines: Dependence, falls in elderly, cognitive impairment
PANIC DISORDER

Panic Attack (≥4 symptoms, peak within minutes):

  • Palpitations, sweating, trembling, SOB, choking sensation
  • Chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/hot flashes
  • Paresthesias, derealization, fear of losing control, fear of dying

Panic Disorder: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + ≥1 month of concern about attacks OR maladaptive behavior

Treatment:

  • First-line: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or SNRIs
  • CBT with exposure therapy: Highly effective
  • Acute attacks: Benzodiazepine PRN (lorazepam 0.5-1mg) — limit use

Rule Out: Hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, cardiac arrhythmia, PE, stimulant use

PTSD

Criteria: Exposure to trauma + symptoms >1 month from each category:

  • Intrusion: Flashbacks, nightmares, distressing memories
  • Avoidance: Avoiding reminders
  • Negative cognition/mood: Detachment, anhedonia, negative beliefs
  • Arousal: Hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, sleep disturbance

Treatment: Trauma-focused therapy (PE, CPT, EMDR); SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine FDA-approved); Nightmares: image rehearsal therapy is recommended; prazosin may be used, downgraded after a large negative VA trial (AASM 2018). Avoid benzodiazepines (may worsen outcomes)

💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Beta-blockers only for performance anxiety: Not effective for GAD or panic disorder
  • Benzodiazepines are NOT first-line: Use short-term only; risk of dependence, falls, cognitive impairment
  • SSRIs take 2-4 weeks: Warn patients; may initially worsen anxiety briefly
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lorazepam, 💊 Sertraline, 💊 Metoprolol
↑ Back to Table of Contents

185. BIPOLAR DISORDER

DIG FAST Criteria • Mood Stabilizers • NO Antidepressant Monotherapy
DIAGNOSIS

Bipolar I: ≥1 manic episode (may have depressive episodes)

Bipolar II: ≥1 hypomanic episode + ≥1 major depressive episode (no full mania)

Manic Episode — DIG FAST (≥3 symptoms, ≥1 week or any duration if hospitalized):

  • Distractibility
  • Indiscretion / impulsivity (risky behavior, spending sprees)
  • Grandiosity
  • Flight of ideas / racing thoughts
  • Activity/Agitation increased
  • Sleep decreased (feels rested with little sleep)
  • Talkativeness (pressured speech)

Hypomania vs Mania:

  • Hypomania: ≥4 days, no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalization
  • Mania: ≥7 days, marked impairment, may have psychosis, often hospitalized
TREATMENT

Acute Mania:

  • Mood stabilizers: Lithium, valproate
  • Atypical antipsychotics: Quetiapine, aripiprazole, olanzapine, risperidone
  • Benzodiazepines: Adjunct for agitation/insomnia

Bipolar Depression:

  • Quetiapine (monotherapy) — FDA-approved
  • Lurasidone (monotherapy or with mood stabilizer)
  • Lamotrigine (maintenance, depression prevention)
  • Olanzapine-fluoxetine combination (OFC)
⚠️ NEVER USE ANTIDEPRESSANT MONOTHERAPY

Can trigger mania or rapid cycling. If antidepressant needed, must use WITH mood stabilizer.

Lithium Monitoring:

  • Therapeutic range: 0.6-1.2 mEq/L
  • Baseline: TSH, Cr, Ca, ECG, pregnancy test
  • Monitoring: Lithium level, TSH, Cr every 6 months
  • Toxicity: Tremor → ataxia → confusion → seizures
  • Drug interactions: NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, thiazides INCREASE lithium levels
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Screen for mania before starting any antidepressant: "Have you ever had periods of elevated mood, decreased sleep, racing thoughts, impulsive behavior?"
  • Valproate is teratogenic: Neural tube defects — avoid in pregnancy
  • Lithium narrow therapeutic window: Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi can precipitate toxicity
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lithium, 💊 Valproic Acid, 💊 Quetiapine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

186. CHRONIC URTICARIA

≥6 Weeks Duration • 2nd-Generation Antihistamines First-Line • Omalizumab, Dupilumab, or Remibrutinib for Refractory
CLASSIFICATION & WORKUP

Definition: Wheals (hives): sharply circumscribed, itchy swellings that usually resolve within 30 min to 24 h; angioedema can occur with or without wheals (International 2026)

Classification:

  • Acute: <6 weeks (JTF 2014)
  • Chronic spontaneous (CSU): 6 weeks or more, no definite eliciting factor; episodes may recur after months or years of remission
  • Chronic inducible (CIndU): definite trigger (eg, cold, pressure, cholinergic, solar, dermographism); diagnose with provocation testing (International 2026)

Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria:

  • Not typically allergic: skin or in vitro IgE testing for inhalants or foods and extensive laboratory testing are not recommended (JTF 2014)
  • Thyroid autoantibodies are common, but routine testing is not recommended (JTF 2014); IgG anti-TPO and total IgE in specialist care (International 2026)
  • Urticarial vasculitis can have lesions lasting under 24 h, so a short history does not exclude it; confirm by biopsy showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis (JTF 2014)

Limited Workup: CBC with differential, ESR and/or CRP, liver enzymes, TSH (JTF 2014); further tests only as history and examination indicate. Track activity and control with UAS7 and the Urticaria Control Test (International 2026)

TREATMENT

Goal: Complete symptom control (International 2026). Stop drugs suspected of worsening CSU, eg, NSAIDs (International 2026)

Stepwise Approach:

  1. Step 1: Standard-dose second-generation H1 antihistamine, taken regularly (eg, cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) (JTF 2014; International 2026, strong)
  2. Step 2: Up-dose the same second-generation antihistamine up to 4-fold (International 2026, strong; off-label); not above 4-fold, and do not combine different H1 antihistamines (International 2026). Adding an H2 antagonist or a leukotriene receptor antagonist is a JTF 2014 option; the International 2026 guideline makes no recommendation for them
  3. Step 3, add-on if still uncontrolled on high-dose antihistamine:
  • Omalizumab (Xolair): 150 or 300 mg SC every 4 weeks, not dependent on IgE or weight; 12 yr and older. BOXED WARNING: anaphylaxis; start in a healthcare setting (label). International 2026: strong recommendation
  • Dupilumab (Dupixent): adults 600 mg SC, then 300 mg every 2 weeks; approved from age 2 (label). International 2026: weak recommendation
  • Remibrutinib (Rhapsido, oral BTK inhibitor): 25 mg PO twice daily; adults; also approved for symptomatic dermographism. Bleeding risk (mucocutaneous bleeding 9%), more with antithrombotics; hold 3-7 days before and after surgery; avoid live vaccines (label). International 2026: weak recommendation

Step 4: Cyclosporine 3-5 mg/kg/day, off-label, if unresponsive to licensed treatments (International 2026, weak; JTF 2014 step 4)

Corticosteroids: No long-term or depot use; a short rescue course for an acute exacerbation, up to 10 days (International 2026); JTF 2014: 1-3 weeks when needed to gain control

Pregnancy and Lactation: Same algorithm with caution after risk-benefit assessment; do not use drugs contraindicated in pregnancy (International 2026)

Avoid:

  • First-generation antihistamines: Sedation, anticholinergic effects, interactions with alcohol and other drugs (International 2026). JTF 2014 lists hydroxyzine or doxepin as step 3 options; the International 2026 algorithm does not include them
  • Long-term corticosteroids (International 2026)
  • NSAIDs if suspected of worsening CSU (International 2026)
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Up-dose before adding: second-generation antihistamine up to 4-fold, then add omalizumab, dupilumab, or remibrutinib (International 2026)
  • Omalizumab in CSU: 150 or 300 mg every 4 weeks regardless of IgE or weight; anaphylaxis boxed warning (label)
  • Remibrutinib: oral; watch for bleeding, especially with antithrombotics; hold around surgery (label)
  • Urticarial vasculitis: lesions can last under 24 h; biopsy confirms (JTF 2014)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Montelukast, 💊 Famotidine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

187. HEREDITARY ANGIOEDEMA (HAE)

C1-INH Deficiency • Low C4 • Epinephrine/Antihistamines INEFFECTIVE
DIAGNOSIS

Types (US HAEA 2020):

  • HAE-C1INH type I (about 85%): Low C1-INH antigen and function (JTF 2013)
  • HAE-C1INH type II (about 15%): Normal or high C1-INH antigen, low function; clinically indistinguishable from type I (JTF 2013)
  • HAE with normal C1-INH (HAE-nl-C1INH): Normal C4 and C1-INH; subtypes by mutation in F12 (factor XII), PLG (plasminogen), ANGPT1, KNG1 (kininogen), or unknown (HAE-U) (US HAEA 2020). Some kindreds need high estrogen levels to manifest (JTF 2013)

Clinical Features:

  • Recurrent angioedema WITHOUT urticaria (US HAEA 2020)
  • Face, lips, neck, extremities, genitalia, GI tract (abdominal attacks in 70%-90%, can mimic an acute surgical abdomen), oral cavity, larynx (WAO 2025)
  • Laryngeal edema can be fatal (asphyxiation)
  • Swelling worsens over about 24 h, then subsides over 48-72 h; first attack before age 10 in about half (WAO 2025)
  • Family history in most patients (JTF 2013)

Diagnosis (US HAEA 2020 Table II): Test C4, C1-INH antigen, and C1-INH function

  • HAE-C1INH: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria and no causative drug, plus C1-INH antigen or function <50% of normal, plus low C4 (at baseline or during an attack)
  • C1q, not C3, separates acquired C1-INH deficiency: C1q low in 80% of acquired deficiency, rarely low in HAE; check it with onset after age 40 or with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease (US HAEA 2020). C3 is normal in HAE and low-normal in acquired deficiency (JTF 2013 Table E1)
  • HAE-nl-C1INH: Normal or near-normal C4 and C1-INH, plus a causative mutation, or a family history plus no response to high-dose antihistamine (cetirizine 40 mg/day or equivalent) for at least 1 month (US HAEA 2020)
  • Screen all first-degree relatives (US HAEA 2020)

Triggers: Trauma, especially dental and surgical procedures, and stress (US HAEA 2020); estrogens (oral contraceptives, hormone replacement): use only with caution (US HAEA 2020); avoid ACE inhibitors (JTF 2013)

TREATMENT
⚠️ EPINEPHRINE, ANTIHISTAMINES, STEROIDS DO NOT WORK

HAE is bradykinin-mediated, NOT histamine-mediated. Standard anaphylaxis treatment is INEFFECTIVE.

Acute Attack: Treat every attack as early as possible, whatever its site or severity (US HAEA 2020). Upper airway swelling: on-demand therapy at once and emergency care (WAO 2025). First-line (WAO 2025): IV C1-INH, icatibant, or sebetralstat

  • Plasma-derived C1-INH (Berinert): 20 IU/kg IV; do not give less than 20 IU/kg; adults and children (label)
  • Recombinant C1-INH (Ruconest): 50 IU/kg IV if <84 kg, 4200 IU if 84 kg or more; may repeat once, no more than 2 doses in 24 h; adolescents and adults. Contraindicated with allergy to rabbits or rabbit-derived products. Effectiveness not established for laryngeal attacks (label)
  • Icatibant (Firazyr): 30 mg SC; repeat at intervals of at least 6 h if needed, no more than 3 doses in 24 h; adults 18 yr and older; self-administered (label)
  • Sebetralstat (Ekterly): 600 mg PO at the earliest recognition of an attack; a second 600 mg at least 3 h later if needed; max 1200 mg in 24 h; 12 yr and older. 300 mg per dose with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors or moderate hepatic impairment; avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, strong or moderate CYP3A4 inducers, or severe hepatic impairment (label; FDA 2025)
  • Ecallantide (Kalbitor): 30 mg SC as three 10-mg injections; may repeat once within 24 h; 12 yr and older. BOXED WARNING: anaphylaxis (3% with SC use); give only by a healthcare professional able to manage anaphylaxis (label); observe at least 60 min (ED consensus 2014)
  • Response: Relief should begin within 30-120 min; a second dose is generally not warranted unless the attack worsens (US HAEA 2020); about 10% of attacks need one (ED consensus 2014)
  • Plasma, third-line: Only if no targeted drug is available; solvent detergent-treated plasma preferred over FFP (WAO 2025). FFP can worsen attacks precipitously (US HAEA 2020)
  • Not for attacks: Tranexamic acid, danazol (WAO 2025)

Long-Term Prophylaxis: Decide individually, not by rigid criteria (US HAEA 2020); reassess at every visit; on-demand therapy stays available (WAO 2025). First-line: IV C1-INH, SC C1-INH, or lanadelumab (US HAEA 2020); SC pdC1-INH, lanadelumab, berotralstat, garadacimab, or donidalorsen, with IV pdC1-INH second-line (WAO 2025)

  • SC pdC1-INH (Haegarda): 60 IU/kg SC twice weekly (every 3-4 days); 6 yr and older (label)
  • Lanadelumab (Takhzyro, anti-kallikrein antibody): 300 mg SC every 2 weeks (12 yr and older); every 4 weeks may be considered in some patients (label)
  • Berotralstat (Orladeyo, oral kallikrein inhibitor): 150 mg PO once daily with food (12 yr and older); not for acute attacks; no extra or higher doses (QTc prolongation); avoid P-gp inducers (label)
  • Garadacimab (Andembry, anti-FXIIa antibody): 400 mg SC loading dose, then 200 mg SC monthly; 12 yr and older (label; FDA 2025)
  • Donidalorsen (Dawnzera, prekallikrein antisense): 80 mg SC every 4 weeks, or every 8 weeks may be considered; 12 yr and older (label; FDA 2025)
  • IV pdC1-INH (Cinryze): 1000 IU IV every 3-4 days (12 yr and older); up to 2000 IU, not over 80 IU/kg, by response (label)
  • Second-line (WAO 2025): Danazol, now limited to 200 mg/day, with CBC, chemistry, lipids, and urinalysis every 6 months and a yearly liver ultrasound; tranexamic acid 30-50 mg/kg in 2-3 doses per day (adults up to 3 g/day), less effective
  • Pregnancy and breast-feeding: C1-INH for on-demand and prophylactic use (US HAEA 2020)

Short-Term Prophylaxis before dental work, upper airway procedures, surgery with intubation, or other invasive procedures (WAO 2025); consider before stressful life events (US HAEA 2020):

  • First-line: IV pdC1-INH 20 IU/kg 1-12 h before (US HAEA 2020); less than 6 h before (WAO 2025); 1000-2000 U, or 20 U/kg in children (JTF 2013). rhC1-INH 50 IU/kg has also been used, with less data (US HAEA 2020)
  • Second-line, only if IV C1-INH is unavailable (WAO 2025): danazol 400-600 mg/day from 5-7 days before to 2-5 days after (US HAEA 2020); or FFP (400 mL; WAO 2025) when there is no time for androgens (US HAEA 2020)
  • Not for short-term prophylaxis: Icatibant and ecallantide (short half-life; US HAEA 2020); tranexamic acid (WAO 2025)
  • Always: On-demand therapy readily available; attacks can occur despite prophylaxis (WAO 2025); watch for delayed swelling after the procedure (US HAEA 2020)
  • Vaginal delivery: No routine prophylaxis unless attacks are frequent; deliver in hospital with on-demand therapy available; monitor at least 72 h (attacks up to 48 h postpartum) (WAO 2025)
HAE vs ACE INHIBITOR ANGIOEDEMA
  • Both bradykinin-mediated
  • Both present WITHOUT urticaria
  • ACEi: Highest risk in the first 30 days, but risk persists beyond 1 year of use (ED consensus 2014) and for at least 6 weeks after stopping (JTF 2013)
  • ACEi: Substantially higher risk in African American patients (JTF 2013)
  • ACEi: Stop the ACE inhibitor. There is a modest risk of recurrence on switching to an ARB, but most patients can use ARBs safely (JTF 2013)
HAE vs ALLERGIC ANGIOEDEMA
  • HAE: NO urticaria; C4 low
  • Allergic: Often WITH urticaria; responds to epinephrine
  • HAE: Family history common
  • HAE: Recurrent without clear trigger
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Any upper airway swelling: on-demand therapy at once and emergency care (WAO 2025)
  • Signs of upper airway involvement: consider intubation, cricothyroidotomy, or tracheotomy promptly (WAO 2025); elective intubation if respiratory distress is not improving after treatment (US HAEA 2020)
  • Attack still worsening after a second on-demand dose (Practical)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Swelling improving after on-demand therapy; airway stable (Practical)
  • On-demand medication for at least 2 attacks; patient or caregiver trained to self-administer (WAO 2025)
  • Written management plan; HAE expert consultation; symptom and treatment diary (US HAEA 2020)
  • First-degree relatives referred for screening (US HAEA 2020)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 TXA

188. ALLERGIC RHINITIS

Intranasal Steroids Preferred Monotherapy • No 1st-Generation Antihistamines • Montelukast Not First-Line (Boxed Warning) • Immunotherapy by Shared Decision
DIAGNOSIS & CLASSIFICATION

Symptoms: Nasal congestion, rhinorrhea (clear), sneezing, nasal pruritus, postnasal drip, ocular symptoms (itching, tearing)

Physical Exam: Allergic shiners (dark circles), allergic salute (transverse nasal crease), pale/boggy turbinates; these support the diagnosis, but no finding is pathognomonic for allergic vs non-allergic vs infectious rhinitis (JTF 2020)

Red Flags (suggest another diagnosis): Epistaxis, unilateral rhinorrhea, unilateral nasal blockage, severe headache, or anosmia; investigate for CSF rhinorrhea, sinonasal tumor, or chronic rhinosinusitis (AAO-HNS 2015)

Workup:

  • Confirm AR with aeroallergen skin prick testing or serum specific IgE when the history fits (JTF 2020, strong). AAO-HNS 2015 targets testing to non-response to empiric treatment, an uncertain diagnosis, or when the specific allergen is needed to target therapy
  • No food skin prick or food IgE testing in the routine AR evaluation (JTF 2020, strong)
  • Review all current medications for drug-induced rhinitis (JTF 2020, strong)
  • No routine sinonasal imaging (AAO-HNS 2015)

Classification:

  • Seasonal: Pollens (trees spring, grasses summer, weeds fall); the same aeroallergen can be seasonal or perennial in different climatic regions (JTF 2020)
  • Perennial: Dust mites, mold, animal dander, cockroach
  • Episodic: Exposure not normally in the patient's environment, eg, visiting a home with pets (AAO-HNS 2015)
  • Intermittent: <4 days/week or <4 consecutive weeks/year (JTF 2020)
  • Persistent: >4 days/week and >4 consecutive weeks/year (JTF 2020); the cutoffs are strict, so symptoms 3 days/week year-round count as intermittent
  • Severity: Mild vs moderate-severe guides treatment; a 0-10 visual analogue scale score of 5 or more has been used for moderate-severe, and a validated instrument is suggested to grade severity and track control (JTF 2020)
TREATMENT

First-Line (adult doses from FDA labels):

  • Intranasal corticosteroid (INCS): preferred monotherapy for persistent AR (JTF 2020, strong); use over montelukast for initial treatment of moderate-severe seasonal AR, age 15+ (JTF 2020, strong)
    • Fluticasone propionate 50 mcg/spray: 2 sprays each nostril once daily for week 1, then 1-2 sprays each nostril once daily (age 12+)
    • Mometasone 50 mcg/spray: 2 sprays each nostril once daily (age 12+)
    • Onset starts 3-5 to 36 h after the first dose; continuous use is more effective than intermittent use (AAO-HNS 2015)
  • Intranasal antihistamine (INAH; azelastine, olopatadine): initial option for seasonal AR (JTF 2020, strong) and first-line for episodic AR (JTF 2020); faster onset than INCS or oral antihistamines, and better than oral antihistamines for congestion (JTF 2020). Azelastine (Astepro Allergy): 2 sprays each nostril once daily, or 1-2 sprays each nostril every 12 h; max 4 sprays per nostril per 24 h (age 12+)
  • Second-generation oral antihistamine for sneezing and itching (AAO-HNS 2015, strong): cetirizine 10 mg once daily (drowsiness may occur), loratadine 10 mg once daily, or fexofenadine 180 mg once daily with water (not with fruit juice or aluminum/magnesium antacids). Kidney disease (all three), liver disease (cetirizine, loratadine), or age 65+ (cetirizine, fexofenadine): labels defer the dose to a clinician
  • Moderate-severe seasonal AR, age 12+: INCS + INAH as initial therapy (JTF 2020, conditional), and for treatment-resistant moderate-severe seasonal or perennial AR (JTF 2020, conditional); more effective, with faster onset, than either component (JTF 2020). Azelastine-fluticasone (Dymista): 1 spray each nostril twice daily (age 6+)

Symptom-Specific Add-Ons (JTF 2020):

  • Rhinorrhea: intranasal ipratropium 0.03% for perennial AR or non-allergic rhinitis when rhinorrhea is the main symptom, or added to INCS for persistent rhinorrhea; no significant effect on congestion or sneezing
  • Congestion: intranasal decongestant short-term and intermittently; up to 5 days when severe mucosal edema impairs delivery of other sprays; added to INCS (or INCS + INAH) for persistent congestion, up to 4 weeks. Pseudoephedrine may be added to an oral antihistamine, when tolerated
  • Episodic AR: intranasal cromolyn just before the allergen exposure

Not First-Line:

  • Montelukast: FDA boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events (agitation, aggression, depression, sleep disturbances, suicidal thoughts and behavior, including suicide). For AR, reserve for inadequate response or intolerance to alternative therapies; stop it and contact a clinician if neuropsychiatric symptoms occur. 10 mg once daily, age 15+ (label). JTF 2020 suggests against it for initial AR treatment; with an oral antihistamine, it is an option (conditional) for seasonal AR not controlled on an oral antihistamine when the patient prefers not to use nasal sprays
  • Oral antihistamine + INCS as initial therapy in preference to INCS alone: not recommended (JTF 2020, strong for seasonal AR, age 12+)

Allergen Avoidance: For identified allergens that match symptoms, avoidance or environmental controls (pet removal, air filtration, bed covers, acaricides) are an option (AAO-HNS 2015). In an RCT, mite-impermeable bed covers lowered mattress mite levels without improving symptoms (AAO-HNS 2015)

Allergen Immunotherapy (SCIT or SLIT):

  • Offer by shared decision-making for moderate-severe AR not controlled with avoidance and/or medication, when the patient chooses it (eg, to avoid long-term medication), or to prevent or reduce comorbid conditions such as asthma (JTF 2020, conditional)
  • SLIT tablets: Grastek and Oralair (grass), Ragwitek (short ragweed), Odactra (house dust mite); for AR confirmed by skin or in vitro IgE testing; ages 5-65. Boxed warning: life-threatening allergic reactions; first dose in the office with at least 30 minutes of observation; prescribe epinephrine; do not give with severe, unstable, or uncontrolled asthma (labels)

Avoid / Caution:

  • First-generation antihistamines (eg, diphenhydramine): Sedation, anticholinergic effects; JTF 2020 recommends against them (strong)
  • Intranasal decongestant as continuous monotherapy: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion), which may develop within 3 days of use or not after 6 weeks of daily use (JTF 2020)
  • Oral decongestants in higher-risk patients: Use with caution in older adults, children under 4, and anyone with cardiac arrhythmia, angina, cerebrovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, bladder outlet obstruction, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism, or Tourette syndrome (JTF 2020)
  • Montelukast for non-allergic rhinitis (JTF 2020)

Pregnancy (JTF 2020): Nasal saline is a good first-line option. INCS: budesonide has Swedish registry safety data (old FDA category B), and newer data support mometasone and fluticasone; triamcinolone is the exception (higher rate of congenital respiratory defects in one cohort; chance finding not excluded). Cetirizine and loratadine have reassuring safety data. Avoid oral decongestants in the first trimester (strong); first-trimester oxymetazoline has been associated with gastroschisis and pyloric stenosis. Immunotherapy: generally do not start; it can be continued

💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • INCS are the most effective monotherapy: INAH act faster, and INCS vs INAH comparisons conflict (JTF 2020)
  • Immunotherapy: A meta-analysis confirmed a short-term reduction in the risk of developing asthma in AR; evidence that it prevents new sensitizations is doubtful. Decide on continuation after the initial 3-5 years (JTF 2020)
  • Non-allergic rhinitis (eg, vasomotor: temperature change, irritants, spicy foods, alcohol): INAH (strong) or INCS (conditional) as first-line monotherapy; ipratropium when rhinorrhea dominates; not montelukast (JTF 2020)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Montelukast, 💊 Ipratropium, 💊 Epinephrine

189. FOOD ALLERGY

IgE-Mediated = Epinephrine • Big 9 Allergens • Oral Immunotherapy Emerging
TYPES & DIAGNOSIS

IgE-Mediated (Type I): Minutes to 2 hours; urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis, vomiting

Non-IgE-Mediated: Hours to days; enterocolitis (FPIES), eosinophilic esophagitis

Food Intolerance (Non-Immune): Lactose intolerance — GI symptoms only, not allergic

"Big 9" Allergens: Peanut, tree nuts, milk, egg, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, sesame

Diagnosis:

  • History is most important: Timing, symptoms, reproducibility
  • Skin prick testing: High NPV; positive doesn't confirm clinical allergy
  • Specific IgE: Same limitations
  • Oral food challenge: Gold standard (supervised)
MANAGEMENT

All Patients with IgE-Mediated Food Allergy:

  • Strict avoidance of allergen
  • Epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) — carry at all times
  • Education on label reading
  • Anaphylaxis action plan
  • Medic-Alert bracelet

Oral Immunotherapy (OIT):

  • FDA-approved for peanut (Palforzia) in children/adolescents
  • Reduces risk of severe reaction to accidental exposure
  • Does NOT cure allergy; must continue avoidance
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis: Anaphylaxis occurs when exercise follows specific food (wheat, shellfish). Either alone doesn't cause symptoms
  • Oral allergy syndrome: Pollen-food cross-reactivity; oral tingling with raw fruits/vegetables; usually not systemic
  • Most children outgrow milk, egg, soy, wheat allergy: Peanut, tree nut, fish, shellfish usually lifelong
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Epinephrine, 💊 Diphenhydramine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

190. GERIATRIC SYNDROMES (FALLS / BEERS / ELDER ABUSE)

Multifactorial Falls Assessment • Beers Criteria • Mandatory Reporting
FALL PREVENTION

Annual Screening: "Have you fallen in the past year? Do you feel unsteady? Do you worry about falling?" — Yes to any → Full assessment

Assessment:

  • Timed Up and Go (TUG): Rise, walk 3m, return, sit. ≥12 seconds = increased risk
  • Orthostatic vitals
  • Vision screening
  • Medication review (see Beers Criteria)
  • Footwear assessment
  • Home safety evaluation

Evidence-Based Interventions:

  • Exercise (balance + strength): Most effective (Tai Chi, PT)
  • Vitamin D 800-1000 IU daily if deficient
  • Medication reduction: Stop fall-risk medications
  • Home modifications: Remove rugs, improve lighting, grab bars
BEERS CRITERIA — MEDICATIONS TO AVOID

High-Risk Medications in Elderly:

ClassExamplesConcern
First-gen antihistaminesDiphenhydramine, hydroxyzineAnticholinergic; confusion, falls
BenzodiazepinesAllFalls, fractures, cognitive impairment
Non-benzo hypnoticsZolpidem, eszopicloneFalls, minimal benefit
Muscle relaxantsCyclobenzaprine, methocarbamolAnticholinergic; poorly tolerated
Long-acting sulfonylureasGlyburideProlonged hypoglycemia
NSAIDs (chronic)AllGI bleed, AKI, CV events
PPIs (>8 weeks)All without indicationC. diff, fractures, hypomagnesemia
AnticholinergicsOxybutynin, TCAsConfusion, falls, constipation

Deprescribing Approach: Review all medications → Identify PIMs → Assess ongoing indication → Prioritize by harm → Taper appropriately → Monitor

ELDER ABUSE

Types: Physical, emotional, sexual, financial, neglect, self-neglect

Red Flags:

  • Unexplained injuries or injuries in various stages of healing
  • Delay in seeking care
  • Inconsistent history
  • Poor hygiene, malnutrition, dehydration
  • Fearful behavior around caregiver
  • Caregiver speaks for patient, won't leave room
⚠️ MANDATORY REPORTING

Most states require reporting suspected elder abuse to Adult Protective Services (APS). Document carefully. Report even if not certain.

📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Melatonin, 💊 Quetiapine, 💊 Haloperidol, 💊 Thiamine

191. PREVENTIVE CARE & CANCER SCREENING

USPSTF Grades • Age-Appropriate Screening • Know When to Stop
USPSTF GRADING
  • Grade A: High certainty of substantial benefit → RECOMMEND
  • Grade B: Moderate-high certainty of moderate benefit → RECOMMEND
  • Grade C: Small benefit → OFFER SELECTIVELY (shared decision-making)
  • Grade D: No benefit or harms outweigh → DO NOT OFFER
  • Grade I: Insufficient evidence
CANCER SCREENING (USPSTF A/B)
CancerPopulationMethodInterval
ColorectalAge 45-75Colonoscopy OR FIT OR FIT-DNA10y / 1y / 1-3y
BreastWomen 40-74MammographyEvery 2 years
CervicalWomen 21-65Pap ± HPVEvery 3-5 years
Lung50-80, ≥20 pack-years, current/quit <15yLow-dose CTAnnual

When to STOP Screening:

  • Life expectancy <10 years
  • Age >75 for CRC (individualize 76-85; stop >85)
  • Age >65 for cervical if adequate prior screening
OTHER SCREENINGS

Recommended:

  • AAA: Men 65-75 who ever smoked — ONE TIME ultrasound
  • Hepatitis C: All adults 18-79 at least once
  • Hepatitis B: All adults at least once
  • HIV: All adults 15-65 at least once
  • Diabetes: Adults 35-70 with overweight/obesity
  • Depression: All adults (PHQ-2)
  • Osteoporosis (DEXA): Women ≥65

Grade D (Do NOT Screen):

  • Ovarian cancer (CA-125, ultrasound)
  • Routine PSA (shared decision 55-69)
  • Thyroid cancer (palpation, ultrasound)
  • Carotid stenosis in asymptomatic
  • Routine ECG in asymptomatic low-risk
  • Aspirin for primary prevention age ≥60
IMMUNIZATIONS (ADULTS)
  • Influenza: Annual, all adults (high-dose for ≥65)
  • COVID-19: Updated vaccine annually
  • Tdap: Once, then Td every 10 years
  • Pneumococcal: PCV20 OR PCV15→PPSV23 for all ≥65
  • Shingles (RZV): 2 doses, age ≥50
  • Hepatitis B: 3-dose series if not immune
  • RSV: Single dose, age ≥60 (shared decision)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Atorvastatin, 💊 Metformin, 💊 Lisinopril

192. MEDICAL ETHICS & CAPACITY ASSESSMENT

Four Principles • Decision-Specific Capacity • Advance Directives
FOUR PRINCIPLES OF MEDICAL ETHICS
  • Autonomy: Respect patient's right to make decisions (informed consent, right to refuse)
  • Beneficence: Act in patient's best interest
  • Non-maleficence: Do no harm
  • Justice: Fair distribution of resources
INFORMED CONSENT

Elements:

  1. Disclosure: Nature of procedure, risks, benefits, alternatives
  2. Understanding: Patient comprehends information
  3. Voluntariness: Decision made without coercion
  4. Competence: Patient has capacity to decide
  5. Consent: Patient agrees to proceed

Exceptions: Emergency (imminent threat, no surrogate), waiver, therapeutic privilege (rare), incapacity (surrogate consents)

CAPACITY ASSESSMENT

Capacity vs Competence:

  • Capacity: Clinical determination by physician; decision-specific
  • Competence: Legal determination by court; global

Four Elements of Capacity:

  1. Understanding: Can state the medical problem and proposed treatment
  2. Appreciation: Acknowledges how this applies to their situation
  3. Reasoning: Can weigh risks/benefits and consider alternatives
  4. Choice: Can clearly communicate a decision
⚠️ KEY PRINCIPLES
  • Capacity is decision-specific — patient may have capacity for some decisions but not others
  • Capacity can fluctuate (delirium, time of day)
  • Disagreement with physician ≠ lack of capacity
  • Patient WITH capacity can refuse any treatment, even life-saving
ADVANCE DIRECTIVES

Types:

  • Living Will: Written preferences for specific situations (terminal illness, PVS)
  • Healthcare Proxy/Durable POA: Designates decision-maker if patient loses capacity
  • POLST/MOLST: Physician orders for life-sustaining treatment — actionable medical orders

DNR/DNI:

  • DNR = No CPR; DNI = No intubation
  • DNR/DNI does NOT mean "do not treat"
  • Address before surgery — may suspend during procedure with consent

Surrogate Hierarchy (if no proxy): Spouse → Adult children → Parents → Siblings → Other family

Decision Standards:

  • Substituted judgment: What would patient want? (preferred)
  • Best interest: If patient's wishes unknown
💎 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Withholding = Withdrawing treatment: Ethically and legally equivalent
  • Palliative care ≠ Hospice: Palliative can be concurrent with curative treatment
  • Break confidentiality when: Imminent harm to identifiable third party, mandatory reporting (abuse, certain diseases), court order

193. POLYCYSTIC OVARY SYNDROME (PCOS)

2023 International Criteria (Rotterdam-Based) • Insulin Resistance • Metabolic Syndrome
DIAGNOSIS: 2023 INTERNATIONAL CRITERIA (2 of 3 in adults)
  1. Ovulatory dysfunction: irregular cycles from 3 years after menarche: <21 or >35 days, or <8 cycles a year; any single cycle >90 days after the first year (International PCOS 2023)
  2. Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism: hirsutism (acne or hair loss alone are weak predictors); total and free testosterone (free androgen index), by LC-MS/MS; androstenedione and DHEAS only if testosterone is not elevated (International PCOS 2023)
  3. Polycystic ovarian morphology: follicle number per ovary ≥20 in at least one ovary; with older equipment or transabdominal scan, ovarian volume ≥10 mL or follicles per section ≥10; or serum AMH instead of ultrasound in adults (not both; never as a single test) (International PCOS 2023)

Simplifications (International PCOS 2023): irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism is enough; no ultrasound or AMH needed. Adolescents need both hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction; ultrasound and AMH are not recommended

Rule Out: TSH, prolactin, 17-OH progesterone (non-classic CAH), FSH; Cushing's syndrome and adrenal tumors if clinically indicated (International PCOS 2023). Markedly high androgens or rapid onset or progression of symptoms: consider an androgen-secreting tumor (International PCOS 2023)

Labs: lipid profile at diagnosis; glycemic status by 75 g OGTT, or fasting glucose or HbA1c if OGTT cannot be done (International PCOS 2023). Insulin assays are not recommended in routine care (International PCOS 2023). LH:FSH ratio is not a diagnostic criterion (Practical)

TREATMENT

Lifestyle (all patients): healthy eating and physical activity; weight management (prevent gain, modest loss); benefits occur even without weight loss (International PCOS 2023)

Menstrual Irregularity/Hyperandrogenism:

  • Combined OCPs: for hirsutism and/or irregular cycles in adults; low-dose ethinylestradiol (<30 mcg) works as well as higher doses for hirsutism; apply general-population prescribing rules, considering weight and cardiovascular risk (International PCOS 2023)
  • Spironolactone (anti-androgen): for hirsutism after at least 6 months of COCP and/or cosmetic therapy with a suboptimal response, or when COCP is contraindicated or poorly tolerated; 25-100 mg/day; effective contraception required (risk of undervirilization of a male fetus) (International PCOS 2023)
  • Metformin: should be considered alone in adults with BMI ≥25 for metabolic outcomes; may be used over COCP for metabolic indications, and for cycles if COCP is not an option. Increase by 500 mg every 1-2 weeks; maximum 2.5 g/day in adults; check B12 if at risk (International PCOS 2023)

Infertility: letrozole is first-line for ovulation induction in anovulatory women with no other infertility factors; clomiphene, alone or with metformin, is an alternative; exclude pregnancy first (International PCOS 2023)

Screen for (International PCOS 2023): cardiovascular risk (lipids at diagnosis, blood pressure yearly); diabetes (OGTT preferred); OSA symptoms; depression and anxiety in all patients. Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer: higher risk but low absolute risk, so no routine screening; if the endometrium is excessively thick, consider biopsy and a withdrawal bleed

💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism = PCOS (after excluding other causes); no ultrasound or AMH needed (International PCOS 2023)
  • Letrozole > clomiphene for ovulation induction (better ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates) (International PCOS 2023)
  • Endometrial protection: long-standing untreated amenorrhea raises hyperplasia and cancer risk; prevent with cycle regulation or regular progestogen (International PCOS 2023)
  • OGTT is the most accurate glycemic test in PCOS, regardless of BMI (International PCOS 2023)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Metformin, 💊 Spironolactone
↑ Back to Table of Contents

194. INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS

EBV • Heterophile Antibody • Avoid Contact Sports
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Classic Triad: Fever, pharyngitis (exudative), lymphadenopathy (posterior cervical)

Other Features: Fatigue (can be prolonged), splenomegaly (50%), hepatomegaly, palatal petechiae, periorbital edema

Labs:

  • Atypical lymphocytosis (>10% atypical lymphocytes)
  • Heterophile antibody (Monospot): 85% sensitive by week 2; may be negative early or in children
  • EBV-specific antibodies: VCA IgM (acute), VCA IgG (past), EBNA (appears later = past infection)
  • Mild transaminitis common

Differential: CMV (heterophile-negative mono), HIV acute infection, strep pharyngitis, toxoplasmosis

MANAGEMENT

Supportive: Rest, hydration, acetaminophen/NSAIDs for pain/fever

Avoid:

  • Contact sports for 3-4 weeks (splenic rupture risk) — some recommend until spleen normalizes
  • Amoxicillin/ampicillin: Causes diffuse maculopapular rash (not true allergy — do NOT label as penicillin allergic)

Steroids: Only if airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Ampicillin rash ≠ penicillin allergy: EBV-specific phenomenon; don't mislabel
  • Heterophile-negative mono: Think CMV, HIV, or early EBV (check EBV-specific serology)
  • Splenic rupture: Rare but life-threatening; avoid contact sports × 3-4 weeks minimum
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Acyclovir
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Rapid Strep/Monospot, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 LDH

195. ADULT-ONSET STILL'S DISEASE (AOSD)

Quotidian Fever • Salmon-Colored Rash • Ferritin >10,000
CLINICAL FEATURES — YAMAGUCHI CRITERIA

Major Criteria:

  • Quotidian fever ≥39°C for ≥1 week: Daily spikes, returns to normal
  • Arthralgia/arthritis ≥2 weeks
  • Typical rash: Salmon-colored, evanescent, maculopapular; appears with fever
  • Leukocytosis ≥10,000 with ≥80% granulocytes

Minor Criteria: Sore throat, lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly, liver dysfunction, negative ANA and RF

Diagnosis: ≥5 criteria (≥2 major) + exclusion of infection, malignancy, other rheumatic diseases

LABS & TREATMENT

Characteristic Labs:

  • Ferritin markedly elevated (often >10,000 ng/mL) — highly suggestive
  • Glycosylated ferritin <20% (more specific)
  • Elevated ESR/CRP, leukocytosis, anemia of chronic disease, elevated LFTs
  • ANA and RF typically NEGATIVE

Treatment:

  • NSAIDs: Mild disease
  • Corticosteroids: Moderate-severe (prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg)
  • IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab): Highly effective, often first-line steroid-sparing
  • IL-6 inhibitors (tocilizumab): Alternative
  • Methotrexate for chronic arthritis

Complications: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) — medical emergency

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Ferritin >10,000: Think Still's disease (or MAS, HLH)
  • Quotidian fever + salmon rash + negative ANA/RF + sky-high ferritin = AOSD
  • IL-1 inhibitors highly effective: Anakinra often dramatic response
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Methotrexate, 💊 Anakinra, 💊 Tocilizumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Ferritin, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT
↑ Back to Table of Contents

196. BEHÇET'S DISEASE

Oral + Genital Ulcers • Uveitis • Pathergy • Silk Road Disease
CLINICAL FEATURES

Required: Recurrent oral ulcers (≥3 episodes/year) — painful aphthous ulcers

Plus ≥2 of:

  • Genital ulcers: Painful, scarring (scrotal/vulvar)
  • Eye involvement: Anterior/posterior uveitis, retinal vasculitis — can cause blindness
  • Skin lesions: Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustular lesions
  • Positive pathergy test: Papule/pustule at site of needle prick (24-48h)

Other Features: CNS (neuro-Behçet's — meningoencephalitis, sinus thrombosis), vascular (arterial aneurysms, DVT), GI (ileocecal ulcers like Crohn's), arthritis

Demographics: "Silk Road" — Turkey, Middle East, East Asia; young adults; HLA-B51 associated

TREATMENT

Mucocutaneous: Topical steroids, colchicine, apremilast

Ocular (sight-threatening): High-dose steroids + azathioprine or anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab)

Vascular/Neurologic: High-dose steroids + immunosuppression (azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, anti-TNF)

Venous thrombosis: Anticoagulation controversial; immunosuppression may be more important

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Oral + genital ulcers + uveitis = Behçet's until proven otherwise
  • Pathergy test: Pustule at needle stick site — fairly specific but not sensitive
  • Leading cause of blindness in Behçet's: Posterior uveitis — requires aggressive treatment
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Colchicine, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Azathioprine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Leukocytosis
↑ Back to Table of Contents

197. RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS

Symmetric Polyarthritis • RF/Anti-CCP • Early DMARD Therapy
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Classic Presentation: Symmetric polyarthritis affecting small joints — MCP, PIP, wrists, MTP. Morning stiffness >1 hour (inflammatory)

Joints Spared: DIP joints (think OA, psoriatic), thoracolumbar spine

Deformities (Late): Ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb

Extra-Articular: Rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces), interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, Felty syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), scleritis, vasculitis

Labs:

  • RF: 70-80% sensitive; not specific (also in Sjögren's, HCV, elderly)
  • Anti-CCP: More specific (~95%); predicts erosive disease
  • Elevated ESR/CRP, anemia of chronic disease

Imaging: X-ray — periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, erosions (marginal). MRI/US more sensitive early

TREATMENT — TREAT TO TARGET

Principle: Early aggressive treatment prevents joint damage. Target = remission or low disease activity

First-Line:

  • Methotrexate: Anchor drug; 15-25mg weekly + folic acid
  • Monitor: CBC, LFTs, creatinine; avoid alcohol; teratogenic

If Inadequate Response:

  • Add biologic DMARD: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept), IL-6 inhibitors (tocilizumab), T-cell costimulation blocker (abatacept), B-cell depletion (rituximab)
  • JAK inhibitors: Tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib. ⚠️ FDA Black Box Warning (2023, based on ORAL Surveillance trial): Increased risk of serious cardiovascular events (MACE), malignancy (including lymphoma), thrombosis, and death vs TNF inhibitors — particularly in patients ≥50 years with ≥1 cardiovascular risk factor. Reserve for patients with inadequate response to TNF inhibitors or when TNF inhibitors are contraindicated. Counsel patients on risks before initiating.

Adjuncts: NSAIDs (symptom control only), low-dose prednisone (bridge, ≤3 months)

Screening Before Biologics: TB (quantiferon/PPD), hepatitis B/C, assess infection risk

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Anti-CCP + RF = high specificity and predicts erosive disease
  • Methotrexate is first-line — start early to prevent joint destruction
  • Screen for latent TB before starting biologics (especially TNF inhibitors)
  • C-spine instability: Atlantoaxial subluxation — assess before intubation/surgery
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Methotrexate, 💊 Hydroxychloroquine, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Adalimumab, 💊 Rituximab, 💊 Tocilizumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Rheumatoid Factor, 🔬 Anti-CCP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Low Albumin
↑ Back to Table of Contents

198. SPONDYLOARTHROPATHIES

HLA-B27 • Axial Involvement • Enthesitis • RF-Negative
OVERVIEW

Common Features: Inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis, enthesitis (tendon/ligament insertions), dactylitis ("sausage digit"), uveitis, HLA-B27 association, RF-negative

Types:

  • Ankylosing Spondylitis: Axial predominant; young men; bamboo spine
  • Psoriatic Arthritis: Skin psoriasis + arthritis (DIP involvement, dactylitis, pencil-in-cup)
  • Reactive Arthritis: Post-infectious (Chlamydia, enteric); "can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree"
  • Enteropathic Arthritis: Associated with IBD
ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS

Inflammatory Back Pain (≥4 of 5): Age onset <40, insidious, improves with exercise, no improvement with rest, night pain

Imaging: Sacroiliitis on X-ray (bilateral, symmetric) or MRI (bone marrow edema). Late: bamboo spine, squaring of vertebrae

Extra-Articular: Acute anterior uveitis (30%), aortitis/AR, apical pulmonary fibrosis, IgA nephropathy

Treatment: NSAIDs (first-line — continuous), physical therapy. If inadequate: TNF inhibitors or IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab). Methotrexate NOT effective for axial disease

PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS

Patterns: DIP arthritis (classic), asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis (RA-like), spondylitis, arthritis mutilans

Clues: Nail pitting/onycholysis, dactylitis, enthesitis, skin psoriasis (may be hidden — scalp, umbilicus, gluteal cleft)

X-ray: Pencil-in-cup deformity, periostitis, DIP erosions

Treatment: NSAIDs, DMARDs (methotrexate for peripheral), TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, IL-12/23 inhibitors (ustekinumab)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Inflammatory back pain + young male + HLA-B27 = ankylosing spondylitis
  • DIP involvement: Psoriatic arthritis or OA (NOT RA)
  • TNF inhibitors first-line biologic for axial spondyloarthropathy
  • Methotrexate doesn't work for axial disease — only peripheral arthritis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Indomethacin, 💊 Adalimumab, 💊 Methotrexate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Rheumatoid Factor

199. OSTEOARTHRITIS

Degenerative • DIP/PIP/Knee/Hip • Osteophytes • Non-Inflammatory
CLINICAL FEATURES

Presentation: Joint pain worse with use, better with rest. Stiffness <30 minutes (vs >1 hour in RA)

Joints Affected: DIP (Heberden's nodes), PIP (Bouchard's nodes), first CMC, knees, hips, cervical/lumbar spine. MCP spared (think RA)

Exam: Bony enlargement, crepitus, reduced ROM, no warmth/erythema (non-inflammatory)

X-ray Findings: Joint space narrowing (asymmetric), osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts

Labs: Normal ESR/CRP, RF negative, synovial fluid non-inflammatory (WBC <2000)

TREATMENT

Non-Pharmacologic (First-Line): Weight loss, exercise (strengthening, aerobic), physical therapy, assistive devices

Pharmacologic:

  • Topical NSAIDs: First-line for knee OA
  • Acetaminophen: Modest benefit; safer than oral NSAIDs
  • Oral NSAIDs: Effective but GI/CV/renal risks; use lowest dose, shortest duration
  • Intra-articular steroids: Short-term relief; limit frequency
  • Duloxetine: Adjunct for chronic OA pain

NOT Recommended: Glucosamine/chondroitin (no proven benefit), hyaluronic acid injections (mixed evidence), opioids

Surgery: Joint replacement for severe, refractory disease

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • DIP + PIP involvement = OA; MCP + PIP = RA
  • Topical NSAIDs first-line for knee OA (better safety profile)
  • Inflammatory OA of hands: Erosive OA — DIP/PIP erosions, more pain; can mimic inflammatory arthritis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Acetaminophen, 💊 Ketorolac, 💊 Indomethacin
↑ Back to Table of Contents

200. LUPUS NEPHRITIS

ISN/RPS Classification • Class III/IV Most Severe • Biopsy Required
CLASSIFICATION (ISN/RPS)
ClassDescriptionTreatment
IMinimal mesangialSupportive
IIMesangial proliferativeSupportive ± low-dose steroids
IIIFocal proliferative (<50% glomeruli)Immunosuppression
IVDiffuse proliferative (>50% glomeruli) — MOST COMMON, MOST SEVEREAggressive immunosuppression
VMembranousImmunosuppression if nephrotic
VISclerosing (>90% sclerosed)Supportive; consider transplant
DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

When to Suspect: SLE patient with proteinuria (>500mg/day), hematuria, RBC casts, rising creatinine

Labs: Low C3/C4 (consumed), positive anti-dsDNA (correlates with activity), elevated anti-dsDNA titers

Biopsy: Required to determine class and guide treatment

Treatment (Class III/IV):

  • Induction: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) + glucocorticoids (preferred) OR cyclophosphamide + glucocorticoids
  • Maintenance: MMF or azathioprine + low-dose steroids
  • Add voclosporin or belimumab for enhanced response

Adjuncts: Hydroxychloroquine (ALL SLE patients), ACEi/ARB for proteinuria, BP control

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Class IV = diffuse proliferative = worst prognosis without treatment
  • All SLE patients should be on hydroxychloroquine (reduces flares, mortality)
  • Anti-dsDNA and complement levels correlate with disease activity
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Mycophenolate, 💊 Cyclophosphamide, 💊 Hydroxychloroquine, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 Hematuria, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Anti-dsDNA, 🔬 Complement C3/C4, 🔬 ANCA, 🔬 Urinalysis

201. DRUG-INDUCED LUPUS

Anti-Histone Antibodies • Resolves with Drug Cessation • Renal/CNS Rare
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Common Culprits (HIGH RISK):

  • Hydralazine (most common)
  • Procainamide (highest incidence with chronic use)
  • Isoniazid
  • Minocycline, TNF inhibitors, methyldopa, quinidine

Clinical Features: Arthralgia/arthritis, myalgia, serositis (pleuritis, pericarditis), fever, rash. Typically milder than SLE

Usually ABSENT: Renal disease, CNS involvement, severe cytopenias (major distinguishing feature from SLE)

Labs:

  • ANA positive (usually homogeneous pattern)
  • Anti-histone antibodies positive (~95%) — most specific
  • Anti-dsDNA typically NEGATIVE (unlike SLE)
  • Complement levels usually NORMAL
MANAGEMENT

Primary Treatment: Discontinue offending drug — symptoms resolve within weeks to months

Symptomatic: NSAIDs for arthralgia/myalgia; short-course steroids if severe

Serologies: ANA may remain positive for months after drug cessation

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Anti-histone antibodies + drug exposure + no renal/CNS = drug-induced lupus
  • Hydralazine #1 cause; procainamide highest incidence with prolonged use
  • Resolves with drug discontinuation — don't need long-term immunosuppression
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Hydroxychloroquine, 💊 Prednisone
↑ Back to Table of Contents

202. SYSTEMIC SCLEROSIS (SCLERODERMA)

Limited (CREST) vs Diffuse • Anti-Scl-70 vs Anti-Centromere • Renal Crisis
CLASSIFICATION
FeatureLimited (CREST)Diffuse
Skin involvementDistal to elbows/knees, faceProximal (trunk, upper arms/thighs)
Raynaud'sYears before skin changesWithin 1 year of skin changes
AntibodyAnti-centromereAnti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I)
Organ involvementPulmonary HTN (late), less ILDILD, renal crisis, cardiac
PrognosisBetter (except PAH)Worse

CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias

CLINICAL FEATURES & MANAGEMENT

Skin: Tight, thickened skin; "salt and pepper" pigmentation; digital ulcers

GI: Esophageal dysmotility (GERD, dysphagia), gastroparesis, small bowel dysmotility (bacterial overgrowth), watermelon stomach (GAVE)

Pulmonary: ILD (ground-glass → fibrosis on HRCT), pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)

Treatments by Manifestation:

  • Raynaud's: CCBs (nifedipine), avoid cold
  • GI: PPI, prokinetics, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth
  • ILD: Mycophenolate, nintedanib, tocilizumab
  • PAH: PDE5 inhibitors, endothelin receptor antagonists, prostacyclins
  • Renal crisis: See below
⚠️ SCLERODERMA RENAL CRISIS
  • Presentation: Acute HTN, AKI, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
  • Risk factors: Diffuse disease, early disease, high-dose steroids, anti-RNA polymerase III
  • Treatment: ACE INHIBITORS (captopril) — even if creatinine rising
  • Do NOT use steroids — can precipitate crisis
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Anti-centromere = limited/CREST; Anti-Scl-70 = diffuse
  • ACE inhibitors for scleroderma renal crisis — continue even if Cr rises
  • High-dose steroids can precipitate renal crisis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sildenafil, 💊 Mycophenolate, 💊 Lisinopril
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anti-Smith/RNP/SSA/SSB, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Proteinuria

203. INFLAMMATORY MYOPATHIES

Dermatomyositis vs Polymyositis • Proximal Weakness • CK Elevated
CLASSIFICATION & FEATURES
FeatureDermatomyositisPolymyositisInclusion Body Myositis
WeaknessProximal, symmetricProximal, symmetricAsymmetric, distal (finger flexors, quads)
Skin findingsHeliotrope rash, Gottron's papulesNoneNone
CKElevated (10-50×)Elevated (10-50×)Normal or mildly elevated
Malignancy riskHIGH (screen)ModerateLow
Treatment responseGoodGoodPoor

Dermatomyositis Skin Findings:

  • Heliotrope rash: Violaceous eyelid discoloration
  • Gottron's papules: Erythematous papules over MCP, PIP, DIP
  • V-sign: Rash on anterior chest/neck
  • Shawl sign: Rash on upper back/shoulders
  • Mechanic's hands: Cracked, fissured skin on fingers
DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Diagnosis:

  • CK elevated (can be very high)
  • EMG: Myopathic pattern (short, small polyphasic potentials)
  • MRI: Muscle edema
  • Muscle biopsy: Gold standard (perifascicular atrophy in DM, endomysial inflammation in PM)
  • Myositis-specific antibodies: Anti-Jo-1 (antisynthetase syndrome — ILD, arthritis, Raynaud's, mechanic's hands)

Treatment:

  • High-dose glucocorticoids (prednisone 1mg/kg) first-line
  • Steroid-sparing: Methotrexate, azathioprine, IVIG
  • Rituximab for refractory cases

Malignancy Screening (Dermatomyositis): Age-appropriate cancer screening + CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; ovarian cancer screen in women

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Heliotrope + Gottron's = dermatomyositis — screen for malignancy
  • Anti-Jo-1: Antisynthetase syndrome — ILD + arthritis + mechanic's hands
  • Inclusion body myositis: Older men, asymmetric, distal weakness, poor treatment response
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Methotrexate, 💊 Azathioprine, 💊 IVIG, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated CK/CK-MB, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Anemia

204. SJÖGREN'S SYNDROME

Sicca Symptoms • Anti-SSA/SSB • Lymphoma Risk
CLINICAL FEATURES

Sicca Symptoms:

  • Dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca): Gritty sensation, burning
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia): Difficulty swallowing dry foods, dental caries

Extraglandular: Arthralgia/arthritis, Raynaud's, interstitial nephritis (RTA type 1), peripheral neuropathy, ILD, parotid enlargement

Primary vs Secondary: Secondary occurs with other autoimmune diseases (RA, SLE, scleroderma)

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Labs:

  • Anti-SSA (Ro): 70% — also seen in SLE; associated with neonatal lupus, congenital heart block
  • Anti-SSB (La): 40% — more specific for Sjögren's
  • RF positive (common), ANA positive

Tests: Schirmer test (tear production), salivary gland biopsy (focal lymphocytic infiltration — most specific)

Treatment:

  • Dry eyes: Artificial tears, cyclosporine drops (Restasis), punctal plugs
  • Dry mouth: Saliva substitutes, pilocarpine, cevimeline (muscarinic agonists), good dental care
  • Systemic: Hydroxychloroquine (fatigue, arthralgia), immunosuppression for severe organ involvement
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Anti-SSA in pregnancy: Risk of neonatal lupus and congenital heart block — monitor fetal heart
  • Lymphoma risk increased (especially MALT, marginal zone) — monitor for parotid enlargement, lymphadenopathy
  • Type 1 RTA: Distal RTA with hypokalemia — think Sjögren's
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Hydroxychloroquine, 💊 Prednisone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anti-Smith/RNP/SSA/SSB, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Rheumatoid Factor

205. MIXED CONNECTIVE TISSUE DISEASE (MCTD)

Overlap Syndrome • High-Titer Anti-U1 RNP • Raynaud's Universal
CLINICAL FEATURES

Definition: Overlap of features from SLE, scleroderma, and polymyositis with high-titer anti-U1 RNP antibodies

Common Features:

  • Raynaud's phenomenon: Nearly universal
  • Swollen "sausage" fingers
  • Arthritis/arthralgia
  • Myositis
  • Esophageal dysmotility
  • Pulmonary HTN (leading cause of death)

Usually Spared: Severe renal disease, CNS involvement (unlike SLE)

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Labs:

  • High-titer anti-U1 RNP (required for diagnosis)
  • ANA positive (speckled pattern)
  • RF may be positive

Treatment: Treat specific manifestations — NSAIDs/hydroxychloroquine for arthritis, steroids for myositis/serositis, CCBs for Raynaud's, PAH-specific therapy

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • High-titer anti-U1 RNP + Raynaud's + overlap features = MCTD
  • Pulmonary HTN is major cause of morbidity/mortality
  • May evolve into a single defined CTD over time
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Hydroxychloroquine, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Mycophenolate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anti-Smith/RNP/SSA/SSB, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP
