206. ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME (APS)

Thrombosis + Pregnancy Loss • Lupus Anticoagulant • Lifelong Anticoagulation
CLINICAL CRITERIA (SYDNEY)

Clinical (≥1 required):

  • Vascular thrombosis: Arterial, venous, or small vessel (DVT, PE, stroke, MI)
  • Pregnancy morbidity: ≥1 unexplained fetal death ≥10 weeks, ≥1 premature birth <34 weeks due to preeclampsia/placental insufficiency, ≥3 consecutive spontaneous abortions <10 weeks

Laboratory (≥1 required, positive on 2 occasions ≥12 weeks apart):

  • Lupus anticoagulant (LA): Most specific; prolongs PTT but is prothrombotic
  • Anticardiolipin antibodies (IgG or IgM, medium-high titer)
  • Anti-β2 glycoprotein I antibodies (IgG or IgM)
TREATMENT

Thrombosis:

  • First venous thrombosis: Warfarin (INR 2-3) — lifelong if unprovoked
  • Arterial thrombosis: Warfarin (INR 2-3) ± aspirin
  • Recurrent thrombosis on warfarin: Higher INR (3-4) or add aspirin or LMWH
  • DOACs: NOT recommended (inferior to warfarin in APS, especially triple-positive)

Pregnancy: LMWH + low-dose aspirin

Primary Prevention (asymptomatic antibodies): Low-dose aspirin if high-risk (triple positive)

⚠️ CATASTROPHIC APS (CAPS)

Multi-organ thrombosis over days-weeks. High mortality. Treat with anticoagulation + steroids + plasma exchange or IVIG.

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Prolonged PTT + thrombosis = think lupus anticoagulant (PTT doesn't correct with mixing study)
  • Warfarin preferred over DOACs in APS (especially triple-positive)
  • False-positive VDRL/RPR can occur with antiphospholipid antibodies
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 UFH, 💊 Warfarin, 💊 Hydroxychloroquine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated PT/INR, 🔬 Elevated PTT, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Elevated D-dimer
↑ Back to Table of Contents

207. SARCOIDOSIS

Non-Caseating Granulomas • Bilateral Hilar LAD • Multi-Organ
CLINICAL FEATURES

Demographics: African Americans, Northern Europeans, women; age 25-45

Pulmonary (>90%): Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), ILD, cough, dyspnea

Staging: Stage 0 = normal CXR; I = BHL only; II = BHL + parenchymal; III = parenchymal only; IV = fibrosis

Extrapulmonary:

  • Skin: Erythema nodosum (good prognosis), lupus pernio (violaceous facial plaques — poor prognosis)
  • Eyes: Uveitis (anterior most common) — screen all patients
  • Cardiac: Heart block, cardiomyopathy, sudden death
  • Neuro: CN VII palsy (most common), meningitis, hypothalamic involvement
  • Renal: Hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria (granulomas produce 1,25-vitamin D), nephrolithiasis
  • Liver/spleen: Hepatomegaly, elevated ALP

Löfgren Syndrome: BHL + erythema nodosum + ankle arthritis + fever — excellent prognosis

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Labs: ACE level (non-specific, not for diagnosis), hypercalcemia, elevated ALP

Diagnosis: Biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas + compatible clinical/radiographic findings + exclusion of other causes (TB, fungal)

Treatment:

  • Observation: Stage I often resolves spontaneously
  • Corticosteroids: First-line for symptomatic pulmonary, cardiac, neuro, ocular, hypercalcemia
  • Steroid-sparing: Methotrexate, azathioprine; anti-TNF for refractory
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Bilateral hilar LAD on CXR in young adult = think sarcoidosis
  • Löfgren syndrome: Erythema nodosum + BHL + arthritis = excellent prognosis, often resolves
  • Hypercalcemia: Granulomas convert 25-OH to 1,25-OH vitamin D
  • Lupus pernio = poor prognosis; erythema nodosum = good prognosis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Methotrexate, 💊 Azathioprine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hypercalcemia, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 LDH, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT
↑ Back to Table of Contents

208. IgG4-RELATED DISEASE

Tumefactive Lesions • Elevated Serum IgG4 • Autoimmune Pancreatitis
CLINICAL FEATURES

Overview: Fibroinflammatory condition with tumefactive (mass-forming) lesions; can mimic malignancy

Organ Involvement:

  • Pancreas: Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis (diffuse pancreatic enlargement "sausage pancreas")
  • Biliary: Sclerosing cholangitis (mimics cholangiocarcinoma)
  • Salivary/lacrimal glands: Mikulicz disease (bilateral gland enlargement)
  • Retroperitoneum: Retroperitoneal fibrosis
  • Kidney: Tubulointerstitial nephritis
  • Aorta: Periaortitis
  • Thyroid: Riedel's thyroiditis
DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Labs: Elevated serum IgG4 (>135 mg/dL) — not required for diagnosis; can be normal in 30%

Histology: Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with IgG4+ plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis

Treatment:

  • Glucocorticoids: First-line — typically dramatic response
  • Rituximab: Steroid-sparing, relapsed/refractory
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Painless jaundice + "sausage pancreas" = autoimmune pancreatitis (IgG4-related)
  • Can mimic pancreatic cancer — check IgG4, consider biopsy before Whipple
  • Responds dramatically to steroids — diagnostic and therapeutic
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Low Albumin

209. AMYLOIDOSIS

AL vs AA vs ATTR • Congo Red Birefringence • Multi-Organ
TYPES
TypePrecursor ProteinAssociated ConditionsKey Features
AL (Primary)Immunoglobulin light chainsMultiple myeloma, plasma cell dyscrasiasHeart, kidney, nerve, liver, tongue
AA (Secondary)Serum amyloid AChronic inflammation (RA, IBD, chronic infections)Kidney (nephrotic), liver, spleen
ATTR (hereditary)Transthyretin (mutant)Familial (Val30Met common)Neuropathy, cardiomyopathy
ATTR (wild-type)Transthyretin (wild-type)Elderly menCardiomyopathy, carpal tunnel
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Clues to AL Amyloidosis:

  • Nephrotic syndrome (most common renal manifestation)
  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy with low-voltage ECG and "sparkling" myocardium on echo
  • Macroglossia (pathognomonic)
  • Periorbital purpura ("raccoon eyes")
  • Peripheral/autonomic neuropathy
  • Hepatomegaly with elevated ALP
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome (bilateral)

Diagnosis:

  • Tissue biopsy: Fat pad aspirate, bone marrow, or affected organ
  • Congo red stain: Apple-green birefringence under polarized light
  • Mass spectrometry: Identify amyloid type
  • Workup for AL: SPEP/UPEP, serum free light chains, bone marrow biopsy
TREATMENT

AL Amyloidosis: Treat underlying plasma cell dyscrasia — daratumumab + CyBorD, autologous stem cell transplant if eligible

AA Amyloidosis: Treat underlying inflammatory condition

ATTR: Tafamidis (TTR stabilizer) for cardiomyopathy; liver transplant (hereditary); patisiran/inotersen (gene silencers)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Nephrotic syndrome + cardiomyopathy + neuropathy = think AL amyloidosis
  • Macroglossia is pathognomonic for AL amyloidosis
  • Low-voltage ECG + thick walls on echo = infiltrative cardiomyopathy (amyloid)
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 SPEP/UPEP/Free Light Chains, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated INR

210. OSTEOPOROSIS

T-Score ≤-2.5 • FRAX Risk • Bisphosphonates First-Line
DIAGNOSIS & SCREENING

DXA Screening (USPSTF 2025): women ≥65; postmenopausal women <65 at increased risk by clinical risk assessment. Men: evidence insufficient (I statement). Not for secondary osteoporosis or chronic glucocorticoid use

Definitions (WHO T-score at lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip; Practical):

  • Normal: T-score ≥-1.0
  • Low bone mass (osteopenia): T-score between -1.0 and -2.5
  • Osteoporosis: T-score ≤-2.5

Who to Treat (US thresholds, ES 2019): hip or vertebral fracture; T-score ≤-2.5 at femoral neck, total hip, or lumbar spine; or T-score -1.0 to -2.5 with US-adapted FRAX 10-year risk ≥20% major osteoporotic or ≥3% hip. Treat especially after a recent fracture

Risk Categories (ES 2019): high = prior spine or hip fracture, T-score ≤-2.5 at hip or spine, or FRAX hip ≥3% or major ≥20%; very high = multiple spine fractures plus T-score ≤-2.5 at hip or spine

Secondary Causes (Practical): vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism (card 336), hyperthyroidism, Cushing's (card 215), celiac disease, chronic glucocorticoids, hypogonadism

TREATMENT

Non-Pharmacologic: weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention (Practical). Calcium and vitamin D as an adjunct to osteoporosis drugs (ES 2019): total calcium 1000-1200 mg/day, preferably dietary, with supplements kept <1000 mg/day (renal stones) (ES 2019); vitamin D 800-1000 IU/day (Practical)

First-Line (ES 2019):

  • Bisphosphonates: alendronate 70 mg weekly, risedronate 35 mg weekly, zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly, ibandronate 150 mg monthly (ibandronate is not recommended for hip or nonvertebral fracture reduction)
  • Kidney function: only with eGFR >35 mL/min (alendronate, zoledronic acid) or >30 (risedronate, ibandronate); infuse zoledronic acid over at least 15 minutes in a well-hydrated patient
  • Oral: take fasting with plain water and stay upright 30 minutes (Practical)
  • Side effects: upper GI (oral); acute-phase reaction after the first zoledronic acid infusion in about 1 in 4 (1-7 days; acetaminophen or ibuprofen reduces it); osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures are extremely rare
  • After hip fracture: zoledronic acid reduced clinical fractures 35% and mortality 28% in one trial; the mortality reduction was not shown in other trials

Alternatives:

  • Denosumab: 60 mg SC every 6 months, alternative initial therapy. Do not delay or stop it without a follow-on antiresorptive (usually a bisphosphonate): rebound bone turnover, rapid BMD loss, more fractures; no drug holiday. Usable at eGFR ≤35, but hypocalcemia risk is higher with eGFR <30 or dialysis: check calcium within 14 days in predisposed patients (ES 2019). FDA boxed warning (January 2024) for severe hypocalcemia in advanced CKD, particularly dialysis (FDA)
  • Teriparatide or abaloparatide: very high risk (e.g., severe or multiple vertebral fractures), up to 2 years, then an antiresorptive to keep the gains (ES 2019). Teriparatide: longer than 2 years only if fracture risk remains or returns to high (US label)
  • Romosozumab: very high risk (T-score <-2.5 with fractures, or multiple vertebral fractures): 210 mg SC monthly for 12 months, then an antiresorptive. Boxed warning for serious cardiovascular events; not for women at high cardiovascular or stroke risk, including prior MI or stroke (ES 2020 update)

Bisphosphonate Holiday (ES 2019): reassess fracture risk after 3-5 years (3 years for yearly zoledronic acid). High risk: continue. Low to moderate risk: consider a holiday of up to 5 years, reassessing every 2-4 years and restarting earlier with a significant BMD decline or a new fracture. Monitor BMD by DXA every 1-3 years on treatment

💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Bisphosphonates first-line; FRAX thresholds apply to T-scores between -1.0 and -2.5 (ES 2019)
  • Denosumab: never stop or delay without a follow-on antiresorptive (rebound bone loss, fractures) (ES 2019)
  • After hip fracture: start treatment; zoledronic acid lowered later fractures and, in one trial, mortality (ES 2019)
  • Kidney function: no bisphosphonate below eGFR 30-35; denosumab in advanced CKD needs calcium monitoring (ES 2019; FDA)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Alendronate, 💊 Zoledronic Acid, 💊 Denosumab, 💊 Teriparatide, 💊 Romosozumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low Vitamin D, 🔬 Hypercalcemia, 🔬 Elevated PTH, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

211. PAGET'S DISEASE OF BONE

Elevated ALP • Normal Ca/Phos • Bisphosphonates
CLINICAL FEATURES

Pathophysiology (Practical): increased osteoclast then osteoblast activity; disorganized bone remodeling

Common Sites (ES 2014): pelvis, vertebrae, skull, femur, tibia

Presentation:

  • Often asymptomatic (incidental elevated ALP); bone pain occurs in only a minority (ES 2014)
  • Bone pain, usually mild to moderate and deep (ES 2014)
  • Skeletal deformity: enlarged or misshapen bone, bowing of femur or tibia (ES 2014)
  • Hearing loss (skull involvement) (Practical)

Complications: fractures through pagetic bone, osteoarthritis of adjacent joints, spinal stenosis or cord compression, heart failure with extensive disease, hypercalcemia when immobilized (also look for coexisting primary hyperparathyroidism) (ES 2014; International 2019). Osteosarcoma or other sarcoma in <1% (about 0.3%), usually with multiple bones involved (ES 2014; International 2019)

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Labs:

  • Serum total ALP with liver function tests (International 2019); with liver or biliary disease, use P1NP or another specific bone marker (ES 2014). ALP can be normal in monostotic disease (ES 2014)
  • Calcium and phosphorus usually normal (Practical); hypercalcemia suggests immobilization or coexisting primary hyperparathyroidism (ES 2014)
  • 25(OH)D before bisphosphonate treatment (ES 2014)

Imaging: plain X-rays of the abdomen, skull and facial bones, and tibias (lytic and sclerotic areas, cortical thickening, bone expansion); radionuclide bone scan to define extent (ES 2014; International 2019). CT or MRI not recommended for diagnosis (International 2019)

Who to Treat (the guidelines disagree):

  • ES 2014: bisphosphonate for most patients with active disease at risk of future complications; before elective surgery on pagetic bone; with hearing loss or heart failure; aim bone turnover below the midpoint of the reference range
  • International 2019 (endorsed by ASBMR): treat bone pain; symptom-directed treatment over a treat-to-target strategy normalizing ALP; insufficient evidence that bisphosphonates prevent fractures, osteoarthritis progression, hearing loss, deformity, or perioperative blood loss
  • Paraplegia from spinal Paget's: immediate IV bisphosphonate plus neurosurgical consultation (ES 2014)

Treatment:

  • Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV once over 15 minutes: first choice (ES 2014); most likely to relieve pain (International 2019). Retreatment seldom needed within 5 years. Do not give if GFR <35 mL/min (ES 2014)
  • Before infusion: replete vitamin D (symptomatic hypocalcemia with 25(OH)D <25 nmol/L) (ES 2014)
  • Oral: alendronate 40 mg daily for 6 months or risedronate 30 mg daily for 2 months (ES 2014)
  • Zoledronic acid: acute-phase reaction; uveitis in about 1% (ES 2014)
  • Follow-up: biochemical markers detect relapse better than symptoms; P1NP <40 mcg/L or ALP <80 IU/L 6 months after zoledronic acid predicts >90% chance of no relapse (ES 2014)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Raised ALP with normal calcium and phosphorus suggests Paget's; confirm on X-ray and check liver tests (ES 2014; International 2019)
  • New or worse pain at a pagetic site: think fracture or sarcoma (Practical; sarcoma <1%, ES 2014)
  • Zoledronic acid single dose: retreatment seldom needed within 5 years; follow ALP or P1NP for relapse (ES 2014)
  • Before zoledronic acid: GFR ≥35 mL/min and vitamin D replete (ES 2014)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Zoledronic Acid, 💊 Alendronate
↑ Back to Table of Contents

212. OSTEONECROSIS (AVASCULAR NECROSIS)

Hip Most Common • Steroids/Alcohol • MRI Most Sensitive
ETIOLOGY & CLINICAL FEATURES

Risk Factors:

  • Corticosteroids (most common non-traumatic cause)
  • Alcohol abuse
  • Sickle cell disease
  • Hip fracture/dislocation (traumatic)
  • SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Radiation, Gaucher disease, decompression sickness (Caisson disease)

Common Sites: Femoral head (hip) most common, humeral head, femoral condyles, talus

Presentation: Gradual onset of joint pain, worse with weight-bearing; may be bilateral

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Imaging:

  • X-ray: May be normal early; later shows crescent sign, subchondral collapse, sclerosis
  • MRI: Most sensitive for early detection — "double-line sign" (pathognomonic)

Treatment:

  • Early (pre-collapse): Protected weight-bearing, bisphosphonates (limited evidence), core decompression
  • Late (collapse): Total joint arthroplasty
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Hip pain + steroid use = think AVN (MRI if X-ray negative)
  • MRI most sensitive — order if high suspicion and normal X-ray
  • Screen contralateral hip — often bilateral
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Alendronate, 💊 Zoledronic Acid
↑ Back to Table of Contents

213. FIBROMYALGIA

Widespread Pain • Normal Labs • Central Sensitization
DIAGNOSIS

Criteria (2010/2016):

  • Widespread pain index (WPI) + symptom severity scale (SSS)
  • Symptoms present ≥3 months
  • No other disorder that would explain symptoms

Clinical Features:

  • Widespread pain: Both sides, above and below waist
  • Fatigue
  • Non-restorative sleep
  • Cognitive symptoms ("fibro fog")
  • Associated: Headache, IBS, interstitial cystitis, depression, anxiety

Labs: All normal — CBC, CMP, TSH, ESR/CRP. Order only to rule out other conditions

TREATMENT

Non-Pharmacologic (Cornerstone):

  • Exercise: Aerobic + strength training — most effective intervention
  • Sleep hygiene
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy

Pharmacologic:

  • Duloxetine (SNRI): FDA-approved; also helps depression
  • Milnacipran (SNRI): FDA-approved
  • Pregabalin: FDA-approved; helps pain and sleep
  • Amitriptyline (low-dose): Helps pain and sleep
  • Avoid: Opioids (ineffective, harmful), NSAIDs (limited benefit)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Normal labs + widespread pain + fatigue + sleep problems = fibromyalgia
  • Exercise is most effective treatment
  • Avoid opioids — not effective and may worsen outcomes
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Gabapentin/Pregabalin, 💊 Sertraline
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 ANA

214. CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME

Surgical Emergency • Saddle Anesthesia • Urinary Retention
CLINICAL FEATURES

Etiology: Large central disc herniation (most common), tumor, abscess, hematoma, trauma

Red Flag Symptoms:

  • Saddle anesthesia: Numbness in perineum/perianal area
  • Urinary retention (most common) or incontinence
  • Fecal incontinence
  • Bilateral leg weakness/numbness
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Low back pain with bilateral sciatica

Exam: Decreased anal tone, absent bulbocavernosus reflex, post-void residual >100-200mL

CES-INCOMPLETE vs CES-COMPLETE
Feature CES-Incomplete (CES-I) CES-Complete (CES-R)
Bladder Altered sensation but some control retained Painless urinary retention (overflow incontinence)
Urgency More urgent — higher recovery potential Still urgent — window closing
Prognosis Better — intervene ASAP Worse — especially if delayed >24–48h

Distinction matters: CES-I has the most to gain from surgery — don't wait for retention to "complete" before acting.

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT
⚠️ SURGICAL EMERGENCY — TIME = NERVES

Permanent bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction result from delayed decompression. MRI + neurosurgery consult immediately upon clinical suspicion.

Step 1 — Bladder Scan: Post-void residual (PVR) >200 mL supports diagnosis. Bladder catheterize for retention AND to protect the bladder during workup

Step 2 — Imaging: MRI lumbar spine (emergent, no contrast required initially) — identifies disc herniation, tumor, abscess, or hematoma. CT myelogram if MRI contraindicated

Step 3 — Consult: Neurosurgery stat. Most cases require posterior laminectomy + discectomy

Timing:

  • <24 hours: Best evidence for neurologic recovery — target for CES-I especially
  • 24–48 hours: Still beneficial; widely cited threshold in guidelines
  • >48 hours: Diminishing returns; permanent deficits increasingly likely

Steroids: No high-quality evidence supports routine steroid use in CES; may be used peri-operatively at neurosurgeon discretion

Do NOT: Perform lumbar puncture if CES is suspected — pressure change can worsen cord/root compression

CONUS MEDULLARIS vs CAUDA EQUINA
Feature Conus Medullaris (L1–L2) Cauda Equina (Below L2)
Reflexes Mixed UMN + LMN (bulbocavernosus may be preserved) LMN only — absent reflexes, flaccidity
Pain Back pain bilateral, symmetric, less radicular Severe radicular (sciatica), asymmetric
Bladder/Bowel Spastic (UMN) or flaccid (LMN) — mixed Flaccid, atonic — painless retention
Recovery Generally poor (upper sacral cord) Better potential — peripheral nerves can regenerate
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Back pain + saddle anesthesia + urinary retention = cauda equina until proven otherwise — don't wait for the full triad; any two warrant MRI
  • PVR is your fastest bedside test — a painless, distended bladder with PVR >200 mL in a back pain patient means CES until MRI says otherwise
  • LP is contraindicated if CES is suspected — don't decompress one end and potentially worsen the other
  • CES-I has the most to gain from surgery — don't wait for complete retention to confirm the diagnosis; act when incomplete
  • MRI without contrast is sufficient for initial diagnosis — contrast adds time; if disc herniation is the concern, plain MRI is enough
  • Sexual dysfunction is often ignored but is a core symptom — ask specifically in young patients with back pain and urinary changes
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Dexamethasone
↑ Back to Table of Contents

215. CUSHING SYNDROME

Hypercortisolism • ACTH-Dependent vs Independent • Dexamethasone Suppression
CLINICAL FEATURES

Classic Features:

  • More discriminating features: reddish purple striae, facial plethora, proximal muscle weakness, bruising without obvious trauma, unexplained osteoporosis (ES 2008)
  • Central obesity with thin extremities; moon facies, buffalo hump, supraclavicular fat pads; thin skin (Practical)
  • Features common in the general population: obesity, depression, diabetes, hypertension, menstrual irregularity (ES 2008); also hypokalemia, hirsutism, cognitive changes (Practical)
  • Who to test: unusual features for age (e.g., osteoporosis, hypertension); multiple and progressive features; children with falling height percentile and rising weight; adrenal incidentaloma compatible with adenoma. Take a drug history to exclude exogenous glucocorticoids first (ES 2008 recs 3.1-3.2)

Etiology:

  • Exogenous glucocorticoids: most common cause overall (ES 2008)
  • ACTH-dependent (about 80%, Practical): pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease, the most common endogenous cause; Pituitary Society 2021); ectopic ACTH (lung cancer, neuroendocrine tumors)
  • ACTH-independent (about 20%, Practical): adrenal adenoma, adrenal carcinoma, bilateral adrenal disease (ES 2015)
DIAGNOSIS

Step 1: Confirm Hypercortisolism (ES 2008; Pituitary Society 2021):

  • Start with one of: 24-hour urine free cortisol (2-3 collections); late-night salivary cortisol (2-3 samples, at usual bedtime; not for night-shift workers); 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (8 am cortisol >1.8 mcg/dL [50 nmol/L] = abnormal) (ES 2008 rec 3.4; Pituitary Society 2021)
  • After one abnormal test, perform another recommended test; two concordantly abnormal tests: proceed to find the cause; two concordantly normal tests: stop, unless cyclic disease is suspected (ES 2008 recs 3.9-3.9.4)
  • Suspected adrenal tumor: start with the DST (Pituitary Society 2021); DST may be unreliable with oral estrogen, and a dexamethasone level helps if a false positive is suspected (Pituitary Society 2021). Pregnancy: UFC, not DST (ES 2008 4.1); antiepileptics that speed dexamethasone clearance: avoid DST (ES 2008 4.2); severe renal failure: DST rather than UFC (ES 2008 4.3)
  • Not for diagnosis: random cortisol or ACTH, imaging, or the 8-mg DST (ES 2008 3.5); IPSS (Pituitary Society 2021)
  • Pseudo-Cushing (psychiatric disorders, alcohol use disorder, PCOS, obesity): mild abnormalities, UFC almost always within 3 times normal; review history and repeat testing, often over 3-6 months (Pituitary Society 2021)

Step 2: Determine ACTH Dependence:

  • ACTH suppressed (e.g., <5 pg/mL; cutoff Practical): ACTH-independent → Adrenal imaging (CT)
  • ACTH normal/elevated: ACTH-dependent → Pituitary MRI (3T preferred where available; about one-third of MRIs are negative in Cushing disease) (Pituitary Society 2021)

Step 3: Localize ACTH-Dependent Disease (Pituitary Society 2021):

  • CRH or desmopressin stimulation: a rise in ACTH and cortisol usually indicates Cushing disease; no single test is definitive, and results are discordant in up to one-third. The high-dose (8 mg) DST has low overall accuracy
  • Inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS): gold standard to exclude ectopic ACTH, in a specialized center, while the patient is hypercortisolemic; a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient <2 before or <3 after stimulation suggests ectopic ACTH; not reliable for lateralization
  • Pituitary lesion ≥10 mm with dynamic tests consistent with Cushing disease: IPSS not needed; lesion <6 mm: IPSS; 6-9 mm: most experts recommend IPSS
  • Suspected ectopic ACTH (e.g., a man with very high UFC and/or profound hypokalemia): neck-to-pelvis thin-slice CT; Ga-68 DOTATATE PET localizes about 65% of ectopic tumors
TREATMENT

First line, resect the source (ES 2015 rec 3.1): Cushing disease: transsphenoidal surgery by an experienced pituitary surgeon (ES 2015 3.1c), ideally at a pituitary tumor center of excellence (Pituitary Society 2021); remission (postoperative cortisol <2 mcg/dL) in about 80% with microadenomas and 60% with macroadenomas (Pituitary Society 2021). Benign unilateral adrenal disease: unilateral adrenalectomy by an experienced adrenal surgeon (ES 2015 3.1a). Ectopic ACTH: localize and resect, with node dissection as appropriate (ES 2015 3.1b)

After Surgery: glucocorticoid replacement and adrenal insufficiency education when hypocortisolemic, until HPA axis testing is normal (ES 2015 5.1-5.2); after transsphenoidal surgery, sodium several times over days 5-14 and free T4 and prolactin within 1-2 weeks (ES 2015 3.1ci-cii); VTE risk assessment and perioperative prophylaxis (ES 2015 2.4-2.5, weak). Recurrence 5-35%, half after 5 years: lifelong monitoring, with yearly late-night salivary cortisol after HPA axis recovery (Pituitary Society 2021)

Medical Therapy (individualized; Pituitary Society 2021):

  • Steroidogenesis inhibitors (usually first): osilodrostat (US label: endogenous hypercortisolemia in Cushing syndrome when surgery is not an option or not curative; start 2 mg twice daily, maximum 30 mg twice daily; correct potassium and magnesium and obtain a baseline ECG first); levoketoconazole (US label: same indication; boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and QT prolongation); ketoconazole and metyrapone (approved for Cushing disease in Europe, not the US; ketoconazole needs regular LFTs) (Pituitary Society 2021). Osilodrostat and metyrapone act within hours, ketoconazole within days (Pituitary Society 2021)
  • Mifepristone (glucocorticoid receptor antagonist): US label limited to hyperglycemia from endogenous Cushing syndrome with type 2 diabetes or glucose intolerance after failed or unsuitable surgery; boxed warning: termination of pregnancy. Cortisol cannot be used to monitor it, it often worsens hypokalemia, and it should be used only by experienced clinicians (Pituitary Society 2021)
  • Pituitary-directed: pasireotide (high rate of hyperglycemia) or cabergoline (less effective, slower; avoid with bipolar or impulse control disorder) (Pituitary Society 2021)
  • Severe or refractory: combinations; IV etomidate if hospitalized and unable to take oral drugs; bilateral adrenalectomy (Pituitary Society 2021; ES 2015 6.1a)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Reddish purple striae, plethora, proximal weakness, easy bruising, unexplained osteoporosis discriminate Cushing syndrome better than obesity, hypertension, or diabetes (ES 2008)
  • Exogenous glucocorticoids are the most common cause: take a drug history before testing (ES 2008 3.1)
  • Ectopic ACTH: often severe, rapid onset, prominent hypokalemia (Practical); a man with very high UFC and/or profound hypokalemia warrants CT for an ectopic source (Pituitary Society 2021)
  • Pseudo-Cushing (depression, alcohol use disorder, obesity, PCOS) gives mildly abnormal tests; repeat testing before treating (Pituitary Society 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Hydrocortisone, 💊 Etomidate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Cortisol, 🔬 ACTH, 🔬 Hyperglycemia, 🔬 Elevated LDL
↑ Back to Table of Contents

216. PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM (CONN SYNDROME)

HTN + Hypokalemia • ARR Screening • Adrenal Adenoma vs Hyperplasia
CLINICAL FEATURES & SCREENING

Who to Screen (ES 2025 rec 1, conditional): all adults with hypertension, with aldosterone and plasma renin (activity or concentration). Hypokalemia is present in only 9-37%; most patients are normokalemic (ES 2025)

Higher Pretest Probability:

  • Resistant hypertension or hypertension + hypokalemia (spontaneous or diuretic-induced) (ES 2025)
  • After a negative screen, rescreen for unexplained worsening or resistant hypertension, new hypokalemia, or atrial fibrillation without structural heart disease or hyperthyroidism (ES 2025)
  • Hypertension with adrenal incidentaloma, sleep apnea, or family history of early-onset hypertension or stroke; metabolic alkalosis; weakness or cramps with marked hypokalemia (Practical)

Screening, Aldosterone and Renin (ES 2025):

  • Morning, seated, without dietary sodium restriction in the prior few days; measure potassium at the same time (low potassium can falsely lower aldosterone), drawn without fist clenching and at least 5 seconds after tourniquet release
  • Positive screen: suppressed renin (PRA ≤1 ng/mL/h or DRC ≤8.2 mU/L) with aldosterone ≥10 ng/dL by immunoassay (≥7.5 ng/dL by LC-MS/MS), and ARR >20 (aldosterone ng/dL to PRA ng/mL/h) or >70 (pmol/L to mU/L) by immunoassay. Use local laboratory cut points where available
  • Medications: screening can start without withdrawal. Negative screen with hypokalemia or moderate to high pretest probability: correct potassium and repeat, ideally after stopping MRAs, ENaC inhibitors, and other diuretics for 4 weeks and ACE inhibitors and ARBs for 2 weeks if safe. Positive screen on beta blockers, clonidine, or methyldopa (which lower renin): repeat after 2 weeks off if safe; on beta blockers, aldosterone above 15 ng/dL (immunoassay) still makes PA likely
  • Agents to use during withdrawal: hydralazine (with a negative chronotrope such as verapamil SR), alpha-1 blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs (Table 6)
CONFIRMATORY TESTING & SUBTYPE

Aldosterone Suppression Testing (ES 2025 rec 4, conditional): mainly when the probability of lateralizing PA is intermediate and the patient would have surgery. Not needed with overt PA (resistant hypertension or hypokalemia, with PRA <0.2 ng/mL/h or DRC <2 mU/L and aldosterone >20 ng/dL by immunoassay), when MRA therapy will be given without surgery, or in familial hyperaldosteronism

  • Oral sodium: 4-5 g sodium per day for 3-4 days; 24-h urine aldosterone <10 mcg/24 h, with urine sodium ideally >200 mEq, makes PA unlikely (Table 8 prints the unit as "mcg/nmol/24 hours")
  • Saline suppression: 2 L normal saline over 4 hours, seated; aldosterone <7.8 ng/dL by immunoassay (<5.8 ng/dL by LC-MS/MS) makes PA unlikely. Do not perform with uncontrolled blood pressure, heart failure, or advanced CKD
  • Captopril challenge: 50 mg; 2-h aldosterone <10 ng/dL by immunoassay with suppressed renin makes PA unlikely
  • Normalize potassium first; thresholds are probabilistic, and false negatives occur

Subtype Differentiation (ES 2025):

  • Adrenal CT plus adrenal vein sampling (AVS) in surgical candidates who want surgery, to separate lateralizing from bilateral disease (rec 6, conditional)
  • AVS may be unnecessary when a unilateral adenoma is very likely: age <35 years, marked PA with hypokalemia, and a >1.0-cm unilateral adenoma on CT
  • Mild PA is usually bilateral and may go straight to medical therapy, as may poor surgical candidates (rec 5)
  • PA with an adrenal adenoma: 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test; cortisol >1.8 mcg/dL suggests autonomous cortisol secretion (rec 8; card 215)
TREATMENT

Lateralizing PA, Surgical Candidate: total unilateral adrenalectomy, usually laparoscopic (ES 2025 rec 5). With cortisol co-secretion, check early-morning cortisol after surgery and prepare for possible glucocorticoid insufficiency (ES 2025). Hypokalemia resolves in nearly all; hypertension cure depends on its duration and severity (Practical)

Bilateral PA, Unknown Lateralization, or No Surgery: lifelong MRA (ES 2025 recs 2 and 5)

  • Spironolactone preferred over other MRAs for cost and availability (rec 9, conditional); eplerenone has fewer androgen and progesterone effects. MRAs preferred over amiloride or triamterene (rec 10) (ES 2025)
  • Start spironolactone 12.5-25 mg/day or eplerenone 25 mg once or twice daily; severe PA or profound hypokalemia: spironolactone 50 mg/day or eplerenone 50 mg twice daily. Most patients need spironolactone 50-100 mg/day to raise renin (ES 2025 Fig. 3)
  • Check electrolytes, renal function, and renin 2-3 months after starting and after each dose change; adjust every 8-12 weeks (spironolactone by 25-50 mg). If blood pressure is uncontrolled and renin is still suppressed, increase the MRA (rec 7) (ES 2025)
  • Hyperkalemia: monitor closely in frail patients and with ACE inhibitors or ARBs (ES 2025 Fig. 3) and with CKD (Practical)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Most patients are normokalemic (hypokalemia in only 9-37%): screen all adults with hypertension (ES 2025)
  • Suppressed renin is the hallmark; aldosterone may be only modestly elevated (ES 2025)
  • Screen without stopping drugs first; repeat after targeted withdrawal only when the result could be falsely negative or positive (ES 2025)
  • AVS before adrenalectomy in most surgical candidates (ES 2025)
  • Treatment lowers cardiovascular risk: adrenalectomy or an adequate MRA dose ameliorates the excess cardiovascular risk of PA (ES 2025)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Spironolactone, 💊 Eplerenone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hypokalemia, 🔬 ACTH
↑ Back to Table of Contents

217. PROLACTINOMA

Most Common Pituitary Adenoma • Cabergoline First-Line; Expert Surgery an Option if Non-Invasive
CLINICAL FEATURES

Hyperprolactinemia Effects:

  • Women: Amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, decreased libido
  • Men: Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia, infertility (often present late with large tumors)
  • Both: Osteoporosis (hypogonadism)

Mass Effects (macroadenoma >10mm):

  • Headache
  • Visual field defects: Bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm compression)
  • Hypopituitarism (compression of normal pituitary)
DIAGNOSIS

Labs: Serum prolactin

  • A single level above ULN, drawn without excessive venipuncture stress, confirms hyperprolactinemia (ES 2011); repeat if <5x ULN, with cannulated sampling if stress is suspected (venipuncture stress can raise prolactin two- to fourfold) (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Adenoma size and prolactin generally correlate; a mismatch should prompt a search for other causes (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • >250 ng/mL usually means prolactinoma; >500 ng/mL is diagnostic of a macroprolactinoma. Risperidone, metoclopramide and phenothiazines can exceed 200 ng/mL without an adenoma (ES 2011)
  • Hook effect: large or giant adenoma with normal or only mildly raised prolactin: ask the lab to re-measure after 1:100 dilution before calling it nonfunctioning (Pituitary Society 2023; ES 2011)
  • Moderate elevation (<200 ng/mL) with discordant clinical or imaging findings: check macroprolactin (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Inconsistent symptoms and values: consider biotin or heterophile antibody assay interference (Pituitary Society 2023)

Rule Out Other Causes of Hyperprolactinemia:

  • Medications: antipsychotics are the most common drug cause; also metoclopramide, antidepressants, opiates, verapamil. Drug-induced levels are usually 25-100 ng/mL (ES 2011; Pituitary Society 2023)
  • On an antipsychotic: prolactin >10x ULN is uncommon and should raise suspicion of prolactinoma; dose reduction or a switch to aripiprazole, with the psychiatrist, separates drug effect from prolactinoma in most patients (Pituitary Society 2023). Other drugs: stop for 3 days or substitute, then remeasure; if the drug cannot be stopped and onset did not coincide with starting it, get an MRI (ES 2011)
  • Pregnancy (Pituitary Society 2023; check β-hCG, Practical)
  • Primary hypothyroidism (check TSH; TRH stimulates prolactin; reverses with thyroid hormone), renal insufficiency, liver failure (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Stalk effect: nonfunctioning adenoma or other sellar mass compressing the stalk; prolactin up to about 6x ULN (Pituitary Society 2023). In 226 nonfunctioning macroadenomas, prolactin >94 ng/mL separated prolactinomas from nonfunctioning adenomas (ES 2011)

Imaging: Pituitary MRI with dynamic gadolinium contrast; use gadolinium with caution in CKD (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis) (Pituitary Society 2023)

TREATMENT

Choosing First-Line Treatment:

  • Cabergoline is the preferred dopamine agonist (higher efficacy, long half-life, better tolerated) and is primary medical therapy (Pituitary Society 2023; ES 2011)
  • Microprolactinoma or well-encased macroprolactinoma (Knosp 0-1): surgery by an expert pituitary neurosurgeon is a first-line option to discuss alongside cabergoline before starting treatment (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Invasive (Knosp ≥2) or giant prolactinoma: cabergoline (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Response: cabergoline normalized prolactin in 92% with microprolactinoma or idiopathic hyperprolactinemia and 77% with macroadenoma in one retrospective series (ES 2011)

Dosing:

  • Cabergoline: 0.25 mg PO twice weekly; increase by 0.25 mg twice weekly at intervals of no less than 4 weeks; maximum 1 mg twice weekly (US label). Doses used in practice range 0.5-3.5 mg/week (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Bromocriptine: 1.25-2.5 mg PO once daily, increased as tolerated to 2.5-10 mg once daily for prolactin-secreting adenomas (US label)
  • Before starting either drug (the sources differ): US label: evaluate for valvular heart disease including an echocardiogram; contraindicated with valvulopathy, pericardial or pleural, pulmonary or retroperitoneal fibrosis, or uncontrolled hypertension; cabergoline: repeat echo every 6-12 months. Pituitary Society 2023: baseline echo when long-term >2 mg/week is expected; repeat every 2-3 years above 2 mg/week, after 5-6 years at ≤2 mg/week
  • Adverse effects: nausea, dizziness, fatigue (bedtime or with-food dosing and slow titration may help); impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive buying), more often in men: ask, then reduce the dose or stop (Pituitary Society 2023; US label)

Surgery (Pituitary Society 2023): first-line option as above; rapidly progressive vision loss from mass effect or apoplexy; intolerance or resistance to dopamine agonists. Giant tumors: only for apoplexy, CSF leak, or growth despite optimal treatment

Red Flags on a Dopamine Agonist (Pituitary Society 2023):

  • CSF rhinorrhea as an invasive macroprolactinoma shrinks: test nasal fluid for β2-transferrin or β-trace protein; if confirmed, surgical repair
  • Apoplexy from extensive tumor shrinkage, with visual change: surgery probably warranted

Pregnancy:

  • Stop the dopamine agonist as soon as pregnancy is confirmed; with a large macroprolactinoma, continuing it is an option (Pituitary Society 2023), especially if invasive or abutting the chiasm with no prior surgery or radiation (ES 2011)
  • Drug choice (the sources differ): ES 2011 recommends bromocriptine for symptomatic tumor growth in pregnancy; Pituitary Society 2023 notes most centers now prefer cabergoline as safety data accumulate (weak)
  • Macroprolactinoma: risk of growth and apoplexy; review monthly with visual fields every 3 months. Microprolactinoma: clinical review every 3 months (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Severe headache or visual change: formal visual fields, then MRI without gadolinium. Do not use prolactin levels to judge tumor growth (Pituitary Society 2023; ES 2011)
  • Tumor growth: restart the dopamine agonist; if no response, surgery, or delivery if far enough along (Pituitary Society 2023)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Cabergoline is first-line medical therapy; for microprolactinomas and Knosp 0-1 macroprolactinomas, expert surgery is a first-line option to discuss (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Big tumor, modest prolactin: ask for a 1:100 dilution (hook effect) before calling it a stalk effect (Pituitary Society 2023; ES 2011)
  • Prolactin >250 ng/mL usually means prolactinoma, but risperidone and metoclopramide can exceed 200 (ES 2011); on an antipsychotic, >10x ULN suggests prolactinoma (Pituitary Society 2023)
  • Clear nasal drip or sudden visual loss after starting a dopamine agonist: CSF leak (surgical repair) or apoplexy (surgery probably warranted) (Pituitary Society 2023)
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Prolactin, 🔬 FSH/LH/Testosterone/Estradiol

218. ACROMEGALY

GH Excess • IGF-1 Screening • Transsphenoidal Surgery
CLINICAL FEATURES

Gradual Onset (diagnosis often delayed 5-10 years or more) (Acromegaly Consensus 2024):

  • Acral enlargement: Hands (rings don't fit), feet (shoe size increases)
  • Facial changes: Frontal bossing, prognathism (jaw protrusion), coarsened features, macroglossia
  • Skin: Thickened, oily, hyperhidrosis, skin tags
  • Soft tissue: Carpal tunnel syndrome, deepening voice

Systemic Complications:

  • Cardiovascular: hypertension (about 40%), cardiomyopathy and heart failure, arrhythmias, valve regurgitation (Acromegaly Consensus 2026; ES 2014). Cardiovascular disease remains an important cause of death, but age-related cancers are now the leading cause (Acromegaly Consensus 2026)
  • Metabolic: impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes (15-38%), dyslipidemia (ES 2014)
  • Respiratory: sleep apnea in about 69% of active disease, mainly obstructive; persists in up to 40% after control (ES 2014)
  • Rheumatologic: Arthropathy, osteoarthritis (ES 2014)
  • Neoplastic: colon polyps more common; colonoscopy at diagnosis, then per general screening guidelines (ES 2014; Acromegaly Consensus 2026)

Local Mass Effects: Headache, visual field defects, hypopituitarism

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Screening: IGF-1 level (reflects integrated GH secretion; age-adjusted reference range) (ES 2014; Acromegaly Consensus 2024). Do not rely on random GH (ES 2014)

  • IGF-1 >1.3x ULN for age with typical clinical features confirms the diagnosis (Acromegaly Consensus 2024)
  • IGF-1 can be falsely high, normal or low with liver or renal failure, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, severe infection, and poorly controlled diabetes; oral estrogen lowers it; pregnancy and late adolescence raise it (ES 2014)

Confirmation (equivocal IGF-1; the sources differ): 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)

  • ES 2014: with elevated or equivocal IGF-1, failure of GH to suppress to <1 ng/mL (mcg/L) after documented hyperglycemia confirms the diagnosis
  • Acromegaly Consensus 2024: reserve OGTT for results that baseline hormones do not clarify; GH at 30, 60, 90 and 120 min; BMI-based nadir cutoffs can be considered: 0.4 ng/mL if BMI <25, 0.2 ng/mL if BMI ≥25 (assay dependent). Stop oral estrogen 4 weeks before; interpret GH with caution in uncontrolled diabetes

Imaging: Pituitary MRI (CT if MRI is contraindicated); formal visual fields if the tumor abuts the optic chiasm (ES 2014)

Treatment:

  • First-line: transsphenoidal surgery by an experienced pituitary surgeon in most patients (ES 2014); indicated with visual loss and chiasmal compression (Acromegaly Consensus 2025). Initial remission >85% for microadenomas and 40-50% for macroadenomas; cavernous sinus invasion makes resection unlikely (ES 2014)
  • Perioperative (inpatient): difficult airway (fiberoptic intubation may be needed); sleep apnea can delay extubation. With severe pharyngeal thickening and sleep apnea, or high-output heart failure, a preoperative SRL is suggested to reduce surgical risk. After surgery: sodium and water imbalance, CSF leak, hypopituitarism (ES 2014)
  • Medical therapy: persistent disease after surgery; or primary therapy if surgery cannot cure, extensive cavernous sinus invasion without chiasmal compression, or poor surgical candidate (ES 2014)
    • Somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs), first-line medical (Acromegaly Consensus 2025): octreotide LAR 20 mg IM (gluteal) every 4 weeks for 3 months, after 2 weeks of SC octreotide 50 mcg three times daily; dialysis or cirrhosis: 10 mg. Lanreotide 90 mg deep SC every 4 weeks for 3 months; CrCl <60 mL/min: 60 mg. Then adjust to IGF-1 (US label). Check fasting glucose and HbA1c on SRLs, especially pasireotide (Acromegaly Consensus 2025)
    • Pegvisomant (GH receptor antagonist; acts peripherally, not on the adenoma; GH levels are uninformative on it) (Acromegaly Consensus 2025): 40 mg SC loading dose, then 10 mg SC daily; adjust by 5 mg every 4-6 weeks to IGF-1; maximum 30 mg daily (US label). A first-line medical option with severely impaired glucose metabolism (Acromegaly Consensus 2025). In diabetes, glucose may fall: reduce antidiabetic drugs (US label)
    • Pegvisomant liver tests before starting and during titration (the sources differ on when to stop): US label, stop if ≥5x ULN or ≥3x ULN with any bilirubin rise; Acromegaly Consensus 2025, stop if >5x ULN; ES 2014, consider stopping if >3x ULN
    • Cabergoline: first-line medical only if IGF-1 <2.0-2.5x ULN or a mixed GH-prolactin adenoma; may be added to an SRL regardless of prolactin (Acromegaly Consensus 2025). Not a US-labeled indication; label valve precautions apply (US label; see card 217)
  • Radiation: residual tumor after surgery when medical therapy is unavailable, unsuccessful, or not tolerated; stereotactic preferred (ES 2014)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • IGF-1 first: >1.3x ULN with typical features confirms; OGTT when results are equivocal (Acromegaly Consensus 2024; ES 2014)
  • Surgery first-line in most patients (ES 2014). Prolactinoma differs: cabergoline is first-line medical therapy, with expert surgery an option for non-invasive tumors (card 217)
  • Before pituitary surgery: plan for a difficult airway and sleep apnea (ES 2014)
  • At diagnosis: colonoscopy (ES 2014; Acromegaly Consensus 2026), echocardiogram and polysomnography (Acromegaly Consensus 2026)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Octreotide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 IGF-1, 🔬 Hyperglycemia, 🔬 Elevated HbA1c

219. MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA (MEN) SYNDROMES

Autosomal Dominant • Screen Family Members • Prophylactic Thyroidectomy in MEN2
CLASSIFICATION
SyndromeGeneComponents and estimated penetrance (MEN1 international 2025, Table 1)
MEN1
("3 P's")		 MEN1 (menin)
Tumor suppressor		 Parathyroid adenoma (90%)
Pancreas: duodenopancreatic NETs (30-80%): gastrinoma (40%), insulinoma (10%), nonfunctioning (20-80%)
Pituitary adenoma (about 35 to >50%): prolactinoma most common (about 45-80%)
Also: adrenal tumors (about 40%), bronchopulmonary NET (5-30%), thymic NET (<10%), angiofibromas, collagenomas, lipomas
MEN2A
("2 M's + P")		 RET proto-oncogene (missense, e.g., codon 634) Medullary thyroid carcinoma (90%)
Pheochromocytoma (50%)
Parathyroid adenoma (20-30%)
MEN2B
(also called MEN3)		 RET M918T (>95%) Medullary thyroid carcinoma (>90%); highest-risk RET variant (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
Pheochromocytoma (40-50%)
Marfanoid habitus, mucosal neuromas, medullated corneal nerve fibers, megacolon (40-50%)
No hyperparathyroidism; screen for it in MEN2A only (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
KEY MANAGEMENT POINTS

MEN1 (MEN1 international 2025):

  • Who to test for MEN1 mutations: two or more MEN1 tumors; first-degree relatives of a carrier or patient; primary hyperparathyroidism before age 30 or multigland disease; gastrinoma or multiple pancreatic NETs at any age; thymic NET at any age (Table 4)
  • Screening in carriers (Table 3): serum calcium yearly in adults (PTH no longer included); fasting gastrin yearly in adults; prolactin and IGF-1 (start around age 10; yearly in adults); pancreas/abdomen MRI every 2-3 years from age 10-15; pituitary MRI every 3-5 years from age 15 (may stop at 75 if normal); chest CT every 3-5 years from age 20-25; insulinoma by asking about hypoglycemic symptoms (routine glucose and insulin screening dropped)
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism: parathyroidectomy if symptomatic, target-organ involvement, or calcium consistently >1 mg/dL above the upper reference limit; index operation: subtotal (3 to 3½ gland) parathyroidectomy with transcervical thymectomy by an experienced surgeon (MEN1 international 2025). NCCN NET 2026 also lists total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation, with or without cryopreservation
  • Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison, card 245): fasting gastrin, ideally off PPI for >1 week, but continue the PPI if symptoms are overt or complications are a risk (NCCN NET 2026); endoscopy for symptoms or persistently high fasting gastrin (MEN1 international 2025)
  • Pituitary adenoma: manage as for sporadic tumors (MEN1 international 2025); prolactinoma: card 217

MEN2 (NCCN Thyroid 2026; NCCN NET 2026):

  • Germline RET testing in every patient with MTC (exons 10, 11, 13-16); a germline variant prompts genetic counseling and testing of family members (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
  • Prophylactic total thyroidectomy by RET risk (NCCN Thyroid 2026): highest risk, M918T (MEN2B): in the first year of life. High risk, codon 634 or A883F: before age 5, timed by calcitonin. Moderate risk (other variants): may be delayed if annual calcitonin is normal, annual ultrasound is unremarkable, there is no family history of aggressive MTC, and the family agrees. V804M (lifetime MTC risk about 4%): long-term surveillance may be reasonable. Refer young children to an experienced pediatric thyroid team
  • Neck dissection: guided by ultrasound and preoperative calcitonin; prophylactic dissection may not be needed if calcitonin is <40 (this footnote prints ng/mL; the guideline's other calcitonin thresholds are in pg/mL) (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
  • Always exclude pheochromocytoma before thyroid surgery or any anesthetic or invasive procedure: plasma free or 24-h urine fractionated metanephrines; elevations 3 times the upper limit of normal are diagnostic. If both tumors are present, remove the pheochromocytoma first; synchronous bilateral tumors: bilateral adrenalectomy (NCCN NET 2026; card 101)
  • Screening: pheochromocytoma (MEN2A and MEN2B) and hyperparathyroidism (MEN2A) yearly; less often for codons 768, 790, 804, 891 (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
  • Hyperparathyroidism in MEN2A at operation: single adenoma, excise; multigland disease, autotransplant or leave the equivalent of one normal gland; consider cryopreservation (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
  • MTC: calcitonin, CEA, and neck ultrasound (NCCN NET 2026); calcitonin and CEA again 2-3 months after surgery (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • MEN1 = 3 P's: Parathyroid, Pituitary, Pancreas (duodenopancreatic NETs)
  • MEN2A = MTC + pheo + parathyroid; MEN2B (MEN3) = MTC + pheo + mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus, without hyperparathyroidism (MEN1 international 2025, Table 1)
  • Always rule out pheochromocytoma before thyroid surgery in MEN2, and remove it first if present (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Prophylactic thyroidectomy timing follows the RET variant: M918T in the first year; codon 634 or A883F before age 5; others may be deferred with normal calcitonin and ultrasound (NCCN Thyroid 2026)
  • MEN1 screening changed in 2025: yearly calcium without PTH; no routine glucose/insulin or chromogranin screening; MRI preferred for the pancreas (MEN1 international 2025)

220. PRIMARY BILIARY CHOLANGITIS (PBC)

Anti-Mitochondrial Antibody • Cholestatic LFTs • Ursodiol
CLINICAL FEATURES

Demographics: Mainly women aged 40-70, with a narrowing female-to-male ratio (AGA/AASLD 2026). Associated: Sjögren syndrome, scleroderma (including CREST), Raynaud, thyroid disease (AASLD 2018)

Presentation:

  • Most are asymptomatic at diagnosis (found by elevated ALP) (AASLD 2018)
  • Fatigue: most common symptom, 50-78% (AASLD 2018)
  • Pruritus: 20-70% in early series, less common now; worse in the evening; may wane in very advanced disease (AASLD 2018)
  • Exam: usually normal early; hepatomegaly, excoriations, xanthelasma, xanthoma; jaundice is a late finding (AASLD 2018)

Complications: Cirrhosis; portal hypertension, which can occur before cirrhosis (nodular regenerative hyperplasia); osteoporosis; hyperlipidemia; fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency, uncommon unless jaundiced; slightly increased HCC risk (AASLD 2018). Surveillance: variceal screening at diagnosis if cirrhosis is suspected; HCC surveillance every 6 months for men and for cirrhosis; bone density every 2 years (AASLD 2018)

DIAGNOSIS

Labs:

  • Cholestatic pattern: elevated ALP, mild aminotransferase elevation, raised immunoglobulins (mainly IgM) (AASLD 2018). Practical: GGT elevated
  • AMA: present in 95% and highly disease-specific; absent or low titer in 5-10% (AASLD 2018)
  • AMA negative: test anti-sp100 and anti-gp210 before biopsy. Specificity over 95% but sensitivity about 20%, so a negative result does not exclude PBC (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 1, conditional, very low)
  • Imaging of the liver and biliary tree in every patient with cholestasis; MR cholangiography if the diagnosis is uncertain, to exclude PSC or other biliary disease (AASLD 2018)
  • Liver stiffness (VCTE): 10 kPa or more marks higher risk of adverse outcomes (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 3, conditional, moderate)

Diagnosis (2 of 3) (AASLD 2018):

  1. Cholestatic biochemistry (elevated ALP)
  2. AMA, or another PBC-specific autoantibody (sp100 or gp210) if AMA is negative
  3. Histology: nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis with destruction of interlobular bile ducts

Biopsy is not needed with elevated ALP plus AMA, sp100, or gp210 (AASLD 2018; AGA/AASLD 2026). Consider biopsy if ALT is over 5 times ULN, for concomitant autoimmune hepatitis or other liver disease (AASLD 2018)

TREATMENT

First-Line:

  • Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA, ursodiol) 13-15 mg/kg/day, offered to every patient at diagnosis (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 2, strong, moderate); 2-4 divided doses with food (Urso label); once daily is acceptable (AASLD 2018). Improves liver tests, delays histologic progression, improves transplant-free survival (AGA/AASLD 2026)
  • Do not raise the dose above 15 mg/kg/day for symptoms or persistent ALP elevation; continue UDCA even if ALP stays high (AGA/AASLD 2026)
  • With bile acid sequestrants: give UDCA at least 1 h before or 4 h after (AASLD 2018)
  • Assess response at 6-12 months; at 6 months if high risk (liver stiffness 10 kPa or more, age under 62). Inadequate response: ALP not below 1.5-1.67 times ULN, or bilirubin not normal, at 12 months (AGA/AASLD 2026)

Inadequate Response to or Intolerance of UDCA:

  • PPAR agonist added to UDCA, or alone if UDCA is not tolerated (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 4, conditional, low): elafibranor 80 mg once daily (Iqirvo label) or seladelpar 10 mg once daily (Livdelzi label). Accelerated approval on ALP reduction; survival and decompensation benefit not shown (labels)
  • Not in pregnancy, breastfeeding, or decompensated cirrhosis (AGA/AASLD 2026); labels: not recommended in decompensated cirrhosis. Labs quarterly in year 1 (AGA/AASLD 2026, expert opinion). Elafibranor: screen for myopathy (consider CPK), fracture risk, fetal harm (confirm not pregnant; avoid ethinyl estradiol contraceptives), drug-induced liver injury (Iqirvo label). Seladelpar: fracture risk, liver tests (Livdelzi label). Separate both from bile acid sequestrants by 4 h (labels)
  • Fibrates (fenofibrate): off-label second-line option; bezafibrate is not available in the US (AGA/AASLD 2026)
  • Obeticholic acid (Ocaliva): withdrawn from the US market November 14, 2025, after an FDA request announced September 11, 2025 (Intercept). FDA had reported serious liver injury, including transplant and death, in patients without cirrhosis (FDA Drug Safety Communication, December 12, 2024). Practical: patients previously on it: hepatology to plan the switch

Symptom Management:

  • Pruritus: if UDCA response is also inadequate, start by adding a PPAR agonist (AGA/AASLD 2026 Figure 1). Linerixibat (Lynavoy) 40 mg twice daily, 30 min before food, for moderate to severe cholestatic pruritus; trial 2-12 weeks (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 5, conditional, low; Lynavoy label). Avoid in decompensated cirrhosis; diarrhea is common; check fat-soluble vitamins and INR at baseline and periodically (label)
  • Older options (not compared with linerixibat; AGA/AASLD 2026): anion-exchange resin (cholestyramine) first; refractory: rifampin (rifampicin) 150-300 mg twice daily, naltrexone titrated to 50 mg daily, sertraline 75-100 mg daily (AASLD 2018). Separate resins by 4 h from linerixibat, elafibranor, and seladelpar (labels)
  • Fatigue: look for other causes (hypothyroidism, depression, anemia, sleep disorders) (AASLD 2018)
  • Bone: calcium 1,000-1,500 mg and vitamin D 1,000 IU daily; alendronate 70 mg weekly or another bisphosphonate if osteoporotic; avoid oral bisphosphonates with acid reflux or known varices (AASLD 2018)
  • Fat-soluble vitamins: deficiency is uncommon; measure if jaundiced; replace with water-soluble oral preparations; subcutaneous vitamin K if INR is prolonged and responds to a vitamin K trial (AASLD 2018)
  • Sicca: artificial tears and saliva substitutes; pilocarpine or cevimeline if refractory (AASLD 2018)

Liver Transplant: Refer for decompensated cirrhosis, MELD over 14, bilirubin over 6 mg/dL, or Mayo risk score over 7.8; severe intractable pruritus is an exceptional indication; fatigue is not an indication (AASLD 2018). After transplant: UDCA prophylaxis against recurrence (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 6, conditional, very low)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • AMA is present in 95% and highly disease-specific; with elevated ALP, biopsy is usually unnecessary (AASLD 2018)
  • Woman aged 40-70 with elevated ALP: think PBC (AGA/AASLD 2026)
  • UDCA at diagnosis, 13-15 mg/kg/day; continue it even if ALP stays elevated (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 2)
  • AMA negative: check sp100 and gp210 before biopsy (AGA/AASLD 2026 Rec 1)
  • Obeticholic acid is off the US market (November 14, 2025); second line is a PPAR agonist (AGA/AASLD 2026; Intercept)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ursodiol, 💊 Rifampin, 💊 Naltrexone, 💊 Sertraline, 💊 Alendronate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase, 🔬 Elevated GGT, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Low Albumin

221. NAFLD / NASH / MASLD

Metabolic Syndrome Association • FIB-4 Staging • Weight Loss Primary Treatment
DEFINITIONS & SPECTRUM

Nomenclature (multisociety, 2023):

  • Steatotic liver disease (SLD): umbrella term for hepatic steatosis of any cause (Nomenclature 2023)
  • MASLD (replaces NAFLD): steatosis plus at least 1 of 5 cardiometabolic risk factors, with no other cause. MASH replaces NASH (Nomenclature 2023)
  • Cardiometabolic risk factors (any 1): BMI 25 kg/m² or more (23 or more in Asian people) or waist over 94 cm (men) or 80 cm (women); fasting glucose 100 mg/dL or more, 2-hour glucose 140 mg/dL or more, HbA1c 5.7% or more, or type 2 diabetes or its treatment; BP 130/85 or more or antihypertensive treatment; triglycerides 150 mg/dL or more or lipid-lowering treatment; HDL 40 mg/dL or less (men) or 50 mg/dL or less (women) or lipid-lowering treatment (AASLD MASLD decision tree)
  • Alcohol: MASLD is below the MetALD range. MetALD: 140-350 g/week (women) or 210-420 g/week (men), about 20-50 or 30-60 g/day. ALD: regularly over 50 g/day (women) or 60 g/day (men) (Nomenclature 2023; AASLD MASLD decision tree). ADA 2026 instead uses more than 21 (men) or 14 (women) standard drinks per week over the prior 2 years to exclude MASLD
  • Cryptogenic SLD: steatosis with no cardiometabolic risk factor and no other cause; may be possible MASLD, so reassess periodically. MASLD can coexist with other liver diseases (for example viral or autoimmune hepatitis) (Nomenclature 2023)

Spectrum:

  • Steatosis alone (formerly NAFL): macrovesicular fat in 5% or more of hepatocytes, with or without mild inflammation (AASLD 2023)
  • Steatohepatitis (MASH): steatosis plus inflammation and hepatocyte injury (ballooning), with or without fibrosis. At-risk MASH: MASH with fibrosis stage 2 or higher, at increased risk of cirrhosis and liver complications (AASLD 2023)
  • Fibrosis stage is the best predictor of long-term outcome (AASLD 2023): F0 none, F1 mild, F2 moderate (significant), F3 severe (advanced), F4 cirrhosis (ADA 2026)
  • Cirrhosis: needs HCC surveillance, varices screening, and monitoring for decompensation (AASLD 2023). Steatosis may disappear as fibrosis advances, so its absence does not exclude MASLD (Nomenclature 2023; AASLD NIT 2024)

Risk Factors: Obesity; type 2 diabetes (the most impactful risk factor for MASLD, fibrosis progression, and HCC); prediabetes; PCOS; family history of cirrhosis; more than mild alcohol use (AASLD 2023); hypertension and dyslipidemia (Nomenclature 2023). Cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death in MASH (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update)

DIAGNOSIS

When to Suspect: Steatosis on imaging, or obesity with metabolic risk factors (AASLD 2023). Normal aminotransferases do not exclude MASH with significant fibrosis (AASLD 2023); elevated ALT is over 33 U/L (men) or over 25 U/L (women) (AASLD MASLD decision tree). Standard ultrasound has low sensitivity for steatosis; controlled attenuation parameter (CAP, 275 dB/m or more) or MRI proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) detects and quantifies it (AASLD 2023; AASLD NIT 2024)

Initial Evaluation (AASLD 2023): Quantify alcohol (amount, pattern, duration) and reassess regularly; use AUDIT-C plus phosphatidylethanol (PEth) before MASH drug therapy (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update). Labs: hepatic panel, CBC with platelets, fasting glucose and HbA1c, fasting lipids, creatinine and urine albumin or protein to creatinine ratio, hepatitis C if not previously screened. If liver chemistries are elevated: autoimmune serologies, transferrin saturation, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1 antitrypsin phenotype or genotype. Review medications; consider less common causes (Wilson disease, celiac disease, lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, hypobetalipoproteinemia) in the right setting. Screen for type 2 diabetes and sleep apnea

Fibrosis Risk Stratification:

  • Who: everyone with steatosis or suspected MASLD (AASLD 2023); adults with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, even with normal liver enzymes (ADA 2026 4.22a, B). General population screening is not advised (AASLD 2023)
  • Step 1, FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets): under 1.3 low risk of advanced fibrosis; repeat every 1-2 years with prediabetes, diabetes, or 2 or more metabolic risk factors (AASLD 2023). 1.3 or more: second test. Over 2.67: high risk of advanced fibrosis; refer without further testing (ADA 2026). FIB-4 rules out well but has low positive predictive value in low-prevalence settings (AASLD NIT 2024); not validated under age 35; with diabetes and age 65 or older, use 1.9-2.0 instead of 1.3 (ADA 2026)
  • Step 2 if FIB-4 is 1.3 or more: liver stiffness by vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE, FibroScan) or MR elastography (MRE), or the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test (AASLD 2023; AASLD NIT 2024; ADA 2026 4.23, B)
  • VCTE (kPa): under 8, advanced fibrosis unlikely; repeat in 2 or more years (ADA 2026). AASLD NIT 2024: only under 5 confidently excludes significant fibrosis, and under 8 with FIB-4 1.3 or more is uncertain and needs further assessment; 8-11 at least significant fibrosis; 12 or more advanced fibrosis; 15 or more cirrhosis. MRE (kPa): 3.1-3.5, 3.6 or more, and 4.7 or more for the same steps (AASLD NIT 2024). ELF: 9.8 or more, high risk of advanced fibrosis (ADA 2026)
  • MRE is the most accurate noninvasive test; prefer it with BMI over 35, when VCTE conflicts with the clinical picture, or when VCTE fails (VCTE is less reliable with BMI over 40, severe steatosis, narrow rib spaces) (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update)
  • NAFLD fibrosis score (cut points -1.455 and 0.676) is an alternative to FIB-4 for advanced fibrosis (AASLD NIT 2024); ADA 2026 advises against adding a second blood panel after FIB-4
  • Refer to hepatology: suspected advanced fibrosis or discordant tests (AASLD 2023; ADA 2026 4.24, B). Screen for varices if VCTE is 20 kPa or more with platelets under 150,000, or 25 kPa or more at any platelet count (AASLD NIT 2024)
  • Do not use blood tests or elastography alone to judge fibrosis progression or regression (AASLD NIT 2024)

Liver Biopsy: Not needed to diagnose MASLD (Nomenclature 2023) or to start MASH drug therapy (AASLD 2024 resmetirom update; AASLD 2025 semaglutide update). Consider it for diagnostic uncertainty, discordant or indeterminate noninvasive tests, possible competing diagnoses (autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, iron overload), or liver tests elevated over 6 months. If noninvasive tests, imaging, or clinical findings show cirrhosis, manage as cirrhosis without biopsy (AASLD 2023)

TREATMENT

Lifestyle (Cornerstone, With or Without Drugs):

  • Weight loss: at least 5% reduces steatosis, 7-10% targets inflammation, at least 10% to reverse fibrosis (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update). Lean MASLD: weight loss may not be appropriate, but diet and exercise may help (AASLD 2023)
  • Diet: caloric deficit if overweight or obese; limit carbohydrates and saturated fat, favor fiber and unsaturated fat (for example Mediterranean diet) (AASLD 2023)
  • Exercise: increase activity as much as possible; benefits occur independent of weight loss (AASLD 2023)
  • Alcohol: assess regularly; abstain completely with fibrosis stage 2 or higher (AASLD 2023)
  • Coffee: 3 or more cups daily (caffeinated or not) is associated with less advanced liver disease (AASLD 2023)
  • Bariatric (metabolic) surgery: consider if surgical criteria are met; resolves MASH in most patients without cirrhosis (AASLD 2023). Use with caution in compensated cirrhosis; not recommended in decompensated cirrhosis unless combined with liver transplant (AASLD 2023; ADA 2026 4.32b, B)

Drug Therapy for Noncirrhotic MASH With F2-F3 Fibrosis: Two FDA-approved drugs, both under accelerated approval: resmetirom and semaglutide (Rezdiffra label; Wegovy label). Select by noninvasive tests; a biopsy showing F2-F3 also qualifies but is not routinely needed. Recommended: VCTE 8-15 kPa, MRE 3.1-4.4 kPa, or ELF 9.2-10.5 (9.2-10.4 in the resmetirom update). May be used (specialist decision): VCTE 15-20 kPa, MRE 4.4-5 kPa, ELF 10.5-11.3, or other noninvasive data consistent with F2-F3; at 15-20 kPa, first exclude cirrhosis with a second test or with cross-sectional imaging showing no nodular liver or portal hypertension. Not recommended: cirrhosis (VCTE over 20 kPa, MRE over 5 kPa, ELF over 11.3, or portal hypertension) or other active liver disease. Resmetirom plus semaglutide has not been studied (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update, Figure 1 and text; AASLD 2024 resmetirom update, Figure 1)

  • Resmetirom (Rezdiffra), oral thyroid hormone receptor-beta agonist, FDA 2024:
    • Dose: 80 mg once daily under 100 kg; 100 mg once daily at 100 kg or more (Rezdiffra label)
    • Interactions: moderate CYP2C8 inhibitor (clopidogrel): 60 mg under 100 kg, 80 mg at 100 kg or more; strong CYP2C8 inhibitor (gemfibrozil): not recommended. Statin limits: rosuvastatin or simvastatin 20 mg daily; atorvastatin or pravastatin 40 mg daily (Rezdiffra label)
    • Avoid: decompensated cirrhosis, Child-Pugh B or C (Rezdiffra label). Not recommended with cirrhosis, other active liver disease, alcohol over 20 g/day (women) or 30 g/day (men), or active thyroid disease; check thyroid function before starting (AASLD 2024 resmetirom update)
    • Monitor: safety labs at 3, 6, and 12 months. Stop for hepatotoxicity: ALT or AST over 5 times ULN or ALP over 2 times ULN (or baseline if abnormal) on 2 occasions, or bilirubin over 2.5 mg/dL or INR over 1.5 with elevated liver enzymes (AASLD 2024 resmetirom update). Adverse effects: diarrhea, nausea; gallstones and cholecystitis (Rezdiffra label)
    • Response at 12 months: continue if VCTE falls 25% or more, MRE falls 20% or more, or ALT normalizes or improves significantly; consider stopping if fibrosis tests worsen or ALT rises consistently; otherwise individualize (AASLD 2024 resmetirom update)
  • Semaglutide (Wegovy), weekly subcutaneous GLP-1 receptor agonist, FDA August 15, 2025:
    • Dose: 0.25 mg weekly for 4 weeks, then increase every 4 weeks (0.5, 1, 1.7 mg) to 2.4 mg weekly; if 2.4 mg is not tolerated, use 1.7 mg and consider re-escalation (Wegovy label)
    • Do not use: personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2 (boxed warning); with another GLP-1 receptor agonist; severe gastroparesis (Wegovy label). Do not start with a history of pancreatitis or with active suicidal ideation (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update). Pregnancy: not recommended (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update, Figure 1); the label allows use in pregnancy only if benefit justifies fetal risk and advises stopping at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy unless benefit outweighs risk (Wegovy label)
    • Monitor: GI effects (slow titration, smaller lower-fat meals, hydration); kidney function with vomiting or diarrhea; gallbladder disease; diabetic retinopathy; hypoglycemia with insulin or sulfonylureas; lean mass (resistance exercise, protein 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day); liver tests only as clinically indicated (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update; Wegovy label)
    • Response at 72 weeks (repeat the same test used for eligibility): continue if VCTE falls 30% or more, MRE 20% or more, MRI-PDFF 30% or more, ALT 17 U/L or 20% or more, or ELF 0.5 or more. Re-evaluate if improvement is below these thresholds without progression to cirrhosis (re-optimize lifestyle, consider other therapy, with or without stopping). Stop if tests show worsening or progression to cirrhosis (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update, Figure 2). Worsening ALT also suggests nonresponse (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update)
    • Compensated cirrhosis already on semaglutide for another approved indication: monitor carefully (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update)
  • Pioglitazone 30-45 mg orally daily: improves MASH histology; consider with type 2 diabetes (AASLD 2023; ADA 2026 4.27a, B). Adverse effects: dose-related weight gain, osteoporosis in postmenopausal women, possible worsening of heart failure with cardiac dysfunction, debated bladder cancer risk (AASLD 2023)
  • Vitamin E (RRR-alpha-tocopherol) 800 IU daily: consider in selected patients without diabetes (AASLD 2023); not effective as monotherapy in type 2 diabetes in a small trial (ADA 2026). Discuss bleeding and possible hemorrhagic stroke risk, and conflicting prostate cancer data (AASLD 2023)
  • Tirzepatide (dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist): potential MASH benefit; an option for obesity or glucose control in type 2 diabetes with MASLD (ADA 2026 4.26 and 4.27a, B); not FDA approved for MASH (ADA 2026)
  • Not treatments for MASH (no meaningful histologic benefit): metformin, ursodeoxycholic acid, DPP-4 inhibitors, statins, silymarin; use them only for their own indications (AASLD 2023)

Comorbidities: Statins are safe and recommended for cardiovascular risk reduction across MASLD, including compensated cirrhosis; use with caution and close monitoring in decompensated cirrhosis (AASLD 2023; ADA 2026 4.31b, B). Hypertriglyceridemia: lifestyle, omega-3 fatty acids, icosapent ethyl, or fibrates (AASLD 2023); no gemfibrozil with resmetirom (Rezdiffra label). Type 2 diabetes with MASH or high fibrosis risk: GLP-1 receptor agonist preferred; pioglitazone or tirzepatide can be considered; other glucose-lowering drugs may continue but lack MASH benefit (ADA 2026 4.27a and 4.30a)

Cirrhosis: HCC surveillance with ultrasound plus AFP every 6 months; contrast MRI or multiphase CT if ultrasound visualization is limited, as is common with obesity; no routine HCC surveillance for advanced fibrosis without cirrhosis (AASLD HCC 2023). Varices screening and monitoring for decompensation (AASLD 2023)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • FIB-4 under 1.3 makes advanced fibrosis unlikely; 1.3 or more needs elastography or ELF; FIB-4 is not a stand-alone rule-in test (AASLD 2023; AASLD NIT 2024)
  • Normal ALT does not exclude MASH with significant fibrosis (AASLD 2023)
  • At least 10% weight loss is needed to reverse fibrosis (AASLD 2025 semaglutide update)
  • Two FDA-approved MASH drugs for noncirrhotic F2-F3: resmetirom and semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly (Rezdiffra label; Wegovy label)
  • Statins are safe in MASLD, including compensated cirrhosis (AASLD 2023). On resmetirom: rosuvastatin or simvastatin up to 20 mg, atorvastatin or pravastatin up to 40 mg (Rezdiffra label)
  • Cirrhosis: ultrasound plus AFP every 6 months for HCC (AASLD HCC 2023)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Semaglutide, 💊 Metformin, 💊 Atorvastatin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated GGT, 🔬 Elevated HbA1c, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated Triglycerides

222. CHRONIC CORONARY DISEASE

Stable Angina • GDMT • Secondary Prevention (revascularization: card 224)
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Stable Angina: Chest discomfort provoked by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Describe chest pain as cardiac, possibly cardiac, or noncardiac rather than "atypical" (1, C-LD) (2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline)

Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) Classification (Campeau, Circulation 1976;54:522):

  • Class I: Ordinary activity (walking, climbing stairs) does not cause angina; angina only with strenuous, rapid, or prolonged exertion
  • Class II: Slight limitation; angina walking >2 blocks or >1 flight stairs
  • Class III: Marked limitation; angina walking 1-2 blocks or 1 flight
  • Class IV: Angina at rest or minimal activity

Pretest Probability: Estimate obstructive CAD likelihood from age, sex, and symptoms before testing (2021 chest pain guideline Figure 11; contemporary models, eg, CAD Consortium, outperform Diamond-Forrester); test selection on card 223

GUIDELINE-DIRECTED MEDICAL THERAPY (GDMT)

Anti-Anginal Therapy:

  • Initial (1, B-R): A beta-blocker, CCB, or long-acting nitrate, chosen by comorbidity (eg, beta-blocker with LV dysfunction). Beta-blockers are traditionally used first, but the evidence for that priority is not strong (2023 AHA/ACC CCD guideline)
  • Still symptomatic (1, B-R): Add a second agent from a different class. Non-DHP CCB (verapamil, diltiazem): avoid with significant LV dysfunction; caution with a beta-blocker (bradycardia, LV dysfunction) (2023 CCD)
  • Long-acting nitrates: Need a daily nitrate-free interval to prevent tolerance (see pearl)
  • Ranolazine (1, B-R): If still symptomatic on a beta-blocker, CCB, or long-acting nitrate (late Na+ current inhibition). 500 mg BID, up to 1000 mg BID; max 500 mg BID with diltiazem, verapamil, or other moderate CYP3A inhibitors; contraindicated with strong CYP3A inhibitors, CYP3A inducers, or cirrhosis (2023 CCD; FDA label)
  • Sublingual nitroglycerin or spray (1, B-NR): For immediate relief, or before activity that triggers angina (2023 CCD)
  • Vasospastic angina: CCB first line (eg, verapamil); add a long-acting nitrate second (2023 CCD Table 17)
  • Do not: Add ivabradine to standard antianginal therapy with normal LV function (3: Harm, B-R); combine PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates (3: Harm, B-NR; severe hypotension) (2023 CCD)

Risk-Reducing Therapy:

  • Aspirin 81 mg daily (75-100 mg) (1, A) if no indication for oral anticoagulation; clopidogrel 75 mg daily if aspirin-intolerant (dose per FDA label). Without recent ACS or a PCI indication, adding clopidogrel to aspirin does not reduce MACE (3: No Benefit, A); avoid chronic NSAIDs (3: Harm, B-R) (2023 CCD)
  • High-intensity statin (1, A) (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) for a ≥50% LDL-C reduction (2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline; 2023 CCD)
  • ACEi, or ARB if ACEi-intolerant (1, A) if hypertension, diabetes, LVEF ≤40%, or CKD; may be considered without these (2b, B-R) (2023 CCD)
  • BP target <130/80 (1, B-R); ACEi, ARB, or beta-blocker first-line for compelling indications (eg, recent MI, angina) (2023 CCD; the 2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline defers CCD to it)
  • LDL-C goals (2026 dyslipidemia guideline): Very high risk: LDL-C <55 and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL (1, A); add ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 mAb on maximally tolerated statin to reach goal (1, A). Not very high risk: LDL-C <70 and non-HDL-C <100 mg/dL (1, A); <55 is reasonable (2a, B-R). Very high risk = multiple major ASCVD events (ACS within 12 months, prior MI, ischemic stroke, symptomatic PAD), or 1 major event plus multiple high-risk conditions (age >65, coronary revascularization, smoking, diabetes, HF, hypertension, LDL-C >100 despite statin plus ezetimibe). Most patients with clinical ASCVD qualify
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Beta-blockers in CCD: Recommended with LVEF ≤40%, with or without prior MI (1, A); with LVEF <50%, use metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, or bisoprolol titrated to target (1, A). If started for prior MI without LVEF ≤50%, angina, arrhythmia, or uncontrolled hypertension, it may be reasonable to reassess after 1 year (2b, B-NR). Without prior MI or LVEF ≤50% and no other indication: no MACE benefit (3: No Benefit, B-NR) (2023 CCD)
  • Ranolazine: Antianginal only; no reduction in CV death or MI in MERLIN-TIMI 36 (JAMA 2007;297:1775). Dose-related QT prolongation (FDA label)
  • Nitrate tolerance: A nitrate-free interval of 10-12 h daily is sufficient (FDA nitroglycerin patch labeling: patch on 12-14 h, off 10-12 h); time it when angina is least likely, usually overnight
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Atorvastatin, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Nitroglycerin, 💊 Ranolazine, 💊 Isosorbide

223. STRESS TESTING SELECTION

Exercise vs Pharmacologic • Echo vs Nuclear • Appropriate Use
MODALITY SELECTION

Test Selection by Risk (2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline):

  • Stable chest pain, low risk: A pretest probability model identifies patients in whom testing can be deferred (1, B-NR); if testing, CAC (2a, B-R) or exercise ECG with an interpretable ECG (2a, B-NR)
  • Stable chest pain, intermediate-high risk, no known CAD: CCTA (1, A) or stress imaging with echo, PET/SPECT MPI, or CMR (1, B-R); PET preferred over SPECT if available (2a, B-R); exercise ECG if the ECG is interpretable and the patient can reach ≥5 METs (2a, B-R)
  • Acute chest pain, intermediate risk, no known CAD, after negative or inconclusive ACS evaluation: CCTA (1, A), or exercise ECG, stress echo, PET/SPECT MPI, or stress CMR (1, B-NR)

Exercise vs Pharmacologic:

  • Exercise preferred when the patient can safely reach ≥5 METs; it also measures functional capacity. Failure to complete Bruce stage 1 (<5 METs) or to achieve 85% of age-predicted fitness level signals higher CAD event risk; these are test results, not selection criteria (2021 chest pain guideline)
  • Pharmacologic if: Unable to achieve ≥5 METs or unsafe to exercise (2021 Table 5). With LBBB or ventricular pacing, use pharmacologic rather than exercise stress for perfusion imaging (see pearl)

Pharmacologic Agents:

  • Regadenoson/Adenosine/Dipyridamole (vasodilators; nuclear MPI, stress CMR): Avoid with significant arrhythmia (VT, 2nd/3rd-degree AV block, or sinus bradycardia <45 bpm), SBP <90, known or suspected bronchoconstrictive or bronchospastic disease, recent dipyridamole, methylxanthines (caffeine, aminophylline) within 12 h, severe hypertension (≥200/110), or high-risk unstable angina/ACS/AMI <2 d (2021 chest pain guideline Table 5). Regadenoson label contraindications: 2nd/3rd-degree AV block or sinus node dysfunction unless a functioning pacemaker is present
  • Dobutamine (stress echo): Avoid with AV block, uncontrolled AF, serious ventricular arrhythmia or high risk from QT prolongation, critical AS, hemodynamically significant LVOT obstruction, severe hypertension (≥200/110), uncontrolled HF, acute PE, myopericarditis, or aortic dissection, or ACS/AMI <2 d. Atropine augmentation is avoided in narrow-angle glaucoma, myasthenia gravis, obstructive uropathy, or obstructive GI disorders (2021 Table 5)
ModalityImagingBest ForAvoid If
