Exercise EchoEchoCan exercise, uninterpretable ECGLimited acoustic windows; unable to reach target HR
Exercise NuclearSPECT/PETCan exercise, uninterpretable ECG, need quantificationHigh-risk unstable angina or ACS/AMI <2 d; screen for pregnancy (ionizing radiation)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • LBBB or paced rhythm: Exercise perfusion imaging produces false septal defects; use pharmacologic stress. In 383 patients with LBBB, false-positive septal defects occurred in 46% with exercise vs 10% with pharmacologic stress, and adenosine and dobutamine were similarly specific (Vaduganathan, JACC 1996;28:543)
  • Before vasodilator stress: No caffeine, aminophylline, or theophylline for at least 12 h; withhold dipyridamole at least 2 days when possible (Lexiscan FDA label; 2021 Table 5)
  • Aminophylline 50-250 mg by slow IV injection (50-100 mg over 30-60 s) attenuates severe or persistent regadenoson reactions; methylxanthines are not recommended for a regadenoson-associated seizure (Lexiscan FDA label)
  • Duke Treadmill Score (Bruce protocol): Exercise minutes - (5 × max ST deviation, mm) - (4 × angina index: 0 none, 1 non-limiting, 2 test-limiting). Low risk ≥+5, moderate -10 to +4, high ≤-11 (Mark, NEJM 1991;325:849)
  • Pregnancy: Screen by history or testing before nuclear imaging or CCTA (ionizing radiation), per local imaging policy (2021 Table 5 footnote)

224. PCI vs CABG INDICATIONS

SYNTAX Score • Left Main • Multivessel Disease
REVASCULARIZATION INDICATIONS

Indications for Revascularization:

  • Symptoms (1, A): Lifestyle-limiting angina despite GDMT with significant stenoses amenable to revascularization (2023 AHA/ACC CCD guideline)
  • Survival, CABG over medical therapy (1, B-R): Significant left main disease, or multivessel disease with LVEF ≤35% (2023 CCD; the 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI revascularization guideline states LVEF <35%)
  • Survival, left main PCI (2a, B-NR): Selected patients in whom PCI can provide revascularization equivalent to CABG (2023 CCD)
  • Survival, CABG (2a, B-NR): Selected multivessel CAD with LVEF 35-50%, including a LIMA to LAD graft (2021)
  • Uncertain survival benefit (2b, B-R): 3-vessel CAD with normal EF (CABG may be reasonable; PCI uncertain); proximal LAD stenosis with normal EF (2021)
  • No survival benefit: 1- or 2-vessel CAD without proximal LAD and normal EF (3: No Benefit, B-R); stenoses not significant (<70% non-left main or FFR >0.80) should not be revascularized solely to improve survival (3: Harm, B-NR) (2021)
  • Events (2a, B-R): Multivessel CAD suitable for CABG or PCI: revascularization is reasonable to lower spontaneous MI, urgent revascularization, or cardiac death (2023 CCD)
  • Physiology (1, A): FFR or iFR before PCI of angiographically intermediate stenoses without prior ischemia testing (2023 CCD). Significant stenosis: ≥70% non-left main, ≥50% left main (2021)

SYNTAX Score (2b, B-NR): Anatomic complexity score; may be useful to guide revascularization in multivessel CAD (2021)

  • <33: No difference in all-cause mortality between CABG and PCI (2021 supportive text)
  • ≥33 (high complexity): Lower all-cause mortality with CABG; CABG over PCI is reasonable for multivessel complex or diffuse CAD, eg, SYNTAX >33 (2a, B-R) (2021; 2023 CCD)
PCI vs CABG COMPARISON
FeatureFavors PCIFavors CABG
Left mainSelected patients in whom PCI gives equivalent revascularization (2a, B-NR)Left main with high-complexity CAD (1, B-R)
MultivesselLower complexity (SYNTAX <33: no mortality difference)Complex or diffuse CAD, eg, SYNTAX >33 (2a, B-R)
DiabetesLeft main with low- or intermediate-complexity CAD, eg, SYNTAX ≤33 (2b, B-R); poor surgical candidate with multivessel CAD (2a, B-NR)Multivessel CAD involving the LAD in a CABG candidate: CABG with LIMA to LAD (1, A)
Surgical riskPoor surgical candidate (2a, B-NR); the guideline sets no STS cut-pointAcceptable surgical risk; calculate the STS score (1, B-NR)
PracticalLimited life expectancy; patient preference after shared decision-makingLong life expectancy; complete revascularization not achievable with PCI

CABG Over PCI to Improve Survival (2023 CCD; 2021):

  • Left main disease with high-complexity CAD (1, B-R)
  • Multivessel complex or diffuse CAD, eg, SYNTAX >33 (2a, B-R)
  • Diabetes with multivessel CAD involving the LAD: CABG with LIMA to LAD reduces mortality and repeat revascularization (1, A)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Diabetes with multivessel CAD: CABG with LIMA to LAD is preferred over PCI to reduce mortality and repeat revascularization (1, A); FREEDOM (1900 patients with diabetes and multivessel disease, left main excluded) is the largest supporting trial (2021)
  • LIMA to LAD: An internal mammary artery, preferably the left, should be used to bypass the LAD to improve survival and reduce recurrent ischemia (1, B-NR); radial artery preferred over saphenous vein for the second most important non-LAD target (1, B-R) (2021)
  • Heart Team and shared decisions: Heart Team for complex 3-vessel disease or an unclear strategy (1, B-NR) (2023 CCD); patient-centered decisions with adequate information on benefits, risks, and alternatives (1, C-LD) (2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Clopidogrel, 💊 Ticagrelor, 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Atorvastatin

225. ICD / CRT DEVICE THERAPY

Primary vs Secondary Prevention • CRT Indications • EF Criteria
ICD INDICATIONS

Secondary Prevention (survived SCD):

  • Ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy (1): Survived SCA due to VT/VF or hemodynamically unstable VT (B-R), or stable sustained VT (B-NR), not due to a reversible cause, if meaningful survival >1 year is expected (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline)
  • Syncope: Ischemic heart disease with unexplained syncope and inducible sustained monomorphic VT at EP study (1, B-NR); NICM with syncope presumed due to VA and no primary prevention indication: ICD or EP study (2a, B-NR) (2017)

Primary Prevention:

  • Ischemic (1, A): ≥40 days post-MI and ≥90 days post-revascularization, with LVEF ≤30% and NYHA I-III, LVEF 31-35% and NYHA II-III, or LVEF ≤40% with inducible VT (2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline Table 17; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline)
  • Nonischemic (1, A): LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II-III despite at least 3 months of GDMT (2022 HF; 2017 rec and text). NYHA I with LVEF ≤35%: may be considered (2b, B-R) (2017). Genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with high-risk features and LVEF ≤45%: reasonable (2a, B-NR) (2022 HF)
  • All primary prevention: Requires expected meaningful survival >1 year. ICD/CRT-D not indicated when comorbidities or frailty limit survival with good functional capacity to <1 year (3: No Benefit, C-LD) (2022 HF); no ICD in medication-refractory NYHA IV without transplant, LVAD, or CRT-D candidacy (3: No Benefit, C-EO) (2017)
  • Specific conditions: Disease-specific criteria, eg, Brugada with spontaneous type 1 pattern plus cardiac arrest, sustained VA, or recent arrhythmic syncope (1, B-NR) (2017). See cards 226 (HCM), 339 (LQTS), and 340 (Brugada)

Wait periods:

  • 40 days post-MI: earlier patients were excluded from MADIT-II and SCD-HeFT, and DINAMIT and IRIS showed no survival benefit from early ICD (2017 text); exception: ICD is reasonable for clinically relevant VA >48 h and within 40 days post-MI (2a, C-EO) (2025 ACS)
  • 90 days post-revascularization; LVEF is often reassessed about 3 months after revascularization (2017)
  • At least 3 months of GDMT for NICM before a primary prevention ICD (2017 text)
CRT INDICATIONS

CRT, Class 1 (B-R), all criteria required:

  • LVEF ≤35% AND sinus rhythm AND LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms AND NYHA II, III, or ambulatory IV on GDMT (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline)

CRT, Class 2a (LVEF ≤35% on GDMT unless stated):

  • Sinus rhythm, non-LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA II to ambulatory IV (B-R)
  • Sinus rhythm, LBBB, QRS 120-149 ms, NYHA II to ambulatory IV (B-NR)
  • AF: if ventricular pacing is required or CRT criteria are otherwise met, and AV nodal ablation or rate control will allow near 100% biventricular pacing (B-NR)
  • New or replacement device with anticipated >40% ventricular pacing (B-NR)
  • High-degree or complete heart block with LVEF 36-50% (B-R)

CRT, Class 2b and 3 (2022 HF):

  • 2b (B-NR): sinus rhythm, non-LBBB, QRS 120-149 ms, NYHA III or ambulatory IV; or LVEF ≤30%, ischemic, sinus rhythm, LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA I
  • 3: No Benefit: QRS <120 ms (B-R); NYHA I-II with non-LBBB and QRS <150 ms (B-NR)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms benefits most from CRT; CRT is not recommended for QRS <120 ms, or for NYHA I-II with non-LBBB and QRS <150 ms (2022 HF)
  • Wait 40 days post-MI: Early ICD showed no survival benefit in DINAMIT (NEJM 2004;351:2481) and IRIS (NEJM 2009;361:1427) (2017 VA). In DINAMIT, fewer arrhythmic deaths were offset by more nonarrhythmic deaths (2025 ACS)
  • NICM and DANISH: The US guideline keeps NICM primary prevention ICD at 1 (A). DANISH showed no reduction in total mortality but did reduce SCD, and 58% of each arm had CRT, possibly blunting ICD benefit (2022 HF text)
  • EF may recover: Optimize GDMT, then reassess before implant. A wearable cardioverter-defibrillator early after MI with LVEF ≤35% is of uncertain usefulness (2b, B-R; VEST missed its primary endpoint) (2025 ACS). It may be reasonable in other higher-risk waits, eg, new NICM, revascularization within 90 days, myocarditis, or awaiting transplant (2b, B-NR), and is reasonable after ICD removal for infection with prior SCA or sustained VA (2a, B-NR) (2017)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Amiodarone, 💊 Metoprolol
↑ Back to Table of Contents

226. HYPERTROPHIC CARDIOMYOPATHY

Asymmetric Septal Hypertrophy • LVOT Obstruction • SCD Risk
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Definition: Maximal end-diastolic LV wall thickness ≥15 mm anywhere in the LV by echo or CMR, without another cause of hypertrophy; 13-14 mm can be diagnostic in family members of a patient with HCM or with a positive genetic test (2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline)

Symptoms: Dyspnea, angina, syncope (exertional), palpitations. Often asymptomatic

Physical Exam:

  • Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur (often from SAM with LVOTO), prominent apical impulse, abnormal carotid pulse, S4; examine with maneuvers such as Valsalva, squat-to-stand, passive leg raise, or walking (2024 text)
  • Practical, murmur increases with: Valsalva, standing (decreased preload)
  • Practical, murmur decreases with: Squatting, handgrip (increased afterload/preload)
  • Practical: bifid carotid pulse ("spike and dome"); murmur loudest at the LLSB

Echo: TTE at initial evaluation (1, B-NR) and every 1-2 years if stable. Obstruction is present if peak LVOT gradient ≥30 mm Hg; ≥50 mm Hg at rest or with provocation is the threshold for advanced therapy. If resting gradient <50, TTE with provocative maneuvers (1, B-NR); if symptomatic without ≥50, exercise TTE (1, B-NR). Dobutamine is not advised to provoke LVOTO (2024)

TREATMENT

Symptomatic Obstructive HCM (2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline):

  • First (1, B-NR): Nonvasodilating beta-blocker titrated to effect or maximally tolerated dose
  • Beta-blocker ineffective or not tolerated (1): Substitute verapamil (B-NR) or diltiazem (C-LD)
  • Persistent symptoms (1, B-R), co-equal options: Cardiac myosin inhibitor (adults only); disopyramide with an AV nodal blocking agent; or septal reduction therapy at an experienced HCM center
  • Septal reduction: For symptoms despite GDMT (1, B-NR); myectomy if other cardiac disease needs surgery (1, B-NR); alcohol septal ablation if surgery is contraindicated or too high risk (1, C-LD); not for asymptomatic patients with normal exercise capacity (3: Harm, C-LD)
  • Myosin inhibitors (FDA labels): Mavacamten (Camzyos) and aficamten (Myqorzo, approved December 2025) carry a boxed warning for heart failure from systolic dysfunction, are REMS-restricted, and need echo before and during treatment; initiation is not recommended if LVEF <55%. Mavacamten: start 5 mg daily (2.5-15 mg); interrupt if LVEF <50% or HF symptoms; contraindicated with strong CYP2C19 inhibitors or moderate-to-strong CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 inducers (April 2025 label)

Acute and Inpatient:

  • Hypotension unresponsive to fluids (1, C-LD): IV phenylephrine or another vasoconstrictor without inotropic activity, alone or with a beta-blocker
  • Verapamil is potentially harmful (3: Harm, C-LD) with severe dyspnea at rest, hypotension, or very high resting gradients (eg, >100 mm Hg), and in children <6 weeks
  • Volume overload with high filling pressures despite GDMT: A cautious low-dose oral diuretic may be considered (2b, C-EO)

Atrial Fibrillation (2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline sec 8.4):

  • Anticoagulation, independent of CHA2DS2-VASc: Clinical AF (1, B-NR), or device- or monitor-detected subclinical AF lasting >24 h in an episode (1, C-LD): DOAC first-line, VKA second-line. Subclinical AF >5 min but <24 h: anticoagulation can be beneficial, weighing episode duration, total burden, risk factors, and bleeding risk (2a, C-LD)
  • Rate control (1, C-LD): Beta-blocker, verapamil, or diltiazem, chosen by patient preference and comorbidities
  • Rhythm control: Poorly tolerated AF: cardioversion or antiarrhythmic drugs (2a, B-NR). Symptomatic AF when drugs are ineffective, contraindicated, or not preferred: catheter ablation (2a, B-NR). Myectomy planned: concomitant surgical AF ablation (2a, B-NR)

AVOID or Stop:

  • Pure vasodilators (ACEi, ARBs, dihydropyridine CCBs) and digoxin: stopping them may be reasonable because they can worsen dynamic obstruction (2b, C-EO)
  • Positive inotropes, pure vasodilators, and high-dose diuretics are relatively contraindicated in symptomatic obstructive HCM (2024 text). Practical: nitrates act as vasodilators
SCD RISK STRATIFICATION

ICD (2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline):

  • Secondary prevention (1, B-NR): Prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT
  • Primary prevention, adults with ≥1 major risk factor (2a, B-NR): SCD attributed to HCM in ≥1 first-degree or close relative ≤50 y; massive LVH ≥30 mm in any segment (≥28 mm at clinician discretion); ≥1 recent syncope judged arrhythmic (not vasovagal or from LVOTO); LV apical aneurysm with transmural scar or LGE; LVEF <50%
  • No major risk factor or decision uncertain (2b, B-NR): ICD may be considered with extensive LGE (≥15% of LV mass) or NSVT on ambulatory monitoring (≥3 beats at ≥120 bpm; more weight to frequent, long, or fast runs)
  • Do not (3: Harm, B-NR): ICD without risk factors, or solely to permit competitive athletics
  • Risk assessment (1, B-NR): At initial evaluation and every 1-2 years (personal and family history, echo, ambulatory ECG); CMR if not otherwise high risk or the ICD decision is uncertain (1, B-NR)
  • 5-year risk calculators (2a, B-NR): Useful for shared decision-making once ≥1 major risk factor is present, but no prespecified risk estimate should be the sole arbiter; calculators omit apical aneurysm, LGE, and LVEF <50% (2024)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Murmur dynamics (Practical): Only HCM and MVP murmurs increase with Valsalva/standing
  • Family screening: 3-generation family history (1, B-NR); genetic testing of the patient to enable cascade testing (1, B-NR); TTE in first-degree relatives at initial screening and periodically (1, B-NR) (2024)
  • Myosin inhibitors reduce LVOT gradients; LVEF monitoring is mandatory (see Treatment)
  • Exercise and sports (2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline): Universal restriction from vigorous activity or competitive sports is not indicated for most patients (3: No Benefit, B-NR). Mild- to moderate-intensity recreational exercise is beneficial (1, B-R). Vigorous recreational activity is reasonable after an annual expert evaluation and shared decision-making (2a, B-NR); competitive sports may be considered after the same annual expert review (2b, B-NR). Genotype-positive, phenotype-negative: competitive sports of any intensity is reasonable (2a, B-NR). ICD solely to permit competitive sports should not be placed (3: Harm, C-EO)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Amiodarone

227. DILATED & RESTRICTIVE CARDIOMYOPATHY

DCM Causes • RCM vs Constrictive • Infiltrative Diseases
DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY (DCM)

Definition: LV dilation with global or regional systolic dysfunction not explained by abnormal loading (hypertension, valve disease) or CAD; no EF cutoff (2023 ESC cardiomyopathy)

Exclude ischemic cardiomyopathy first: Evaluation for ischemic heart disease (CT or invasive coronary angiography, or stress imaging) can be useful (2a, B-NR) (2022 HF)

Nonischemic causes to seek (2022 HF Table 5):

  • Familial/Genetic: TTN, LMNA, MYH7. Variants found in 25-40% of DCM with a family history and 10-30% without. 3-generation family history (1, B-NR); genetic counseling and testing in select nonischemic cardiomyopathy (2a, B-NR); screen first-degree relatives of selected patients (1, B-NR) (2022 HF)
  • Toxic: Alcohol, cocaine, methamphetamine, chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab) and other cardiotoxic drugs
  • Myocarditis: Infectious (viral, Chagas, HIV), toxin or medication, immune, hypersensitivity
  • Rhythm-related: Tachycardia-mediated, frequent PVCs, RV pacing
  • Endocrine/metabolic: Thyroid, acromegaly, pheochromocytoma, diabetes, obesity
  • Rheumatologic/autoimmune
  • Infiltrative: Sarcoid, hemochromatosis, amyloid (see RCM below)
  • Peripartum cardiomyopathy
  • Stress cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo): Transient; not DCM (see card 303)

Workup: TTE (1, C-LD); CMR can be useful (2a, B-NR); endomyocardial biopsy only when a specific diagnosis that would change therapy is suspected (2a, B-NR), never routine (3: Harm, C-LD) (2022 HF)

Treatment: HFrEF GDMT per card 2. ICD per card 225: nonischemic, LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II-III after at least 3 months of GDMT (1, A); genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (eg, LMNA) with high-risk features and LVEF ≤45% (2a, B-NR) (2022 HF). Treat the underlying cause

RESTRICTIVE CARDIOMYOPATHY (RCM)

Definition: Impaired ventricular filling due to stiff, non-compliant ventricles; usually preserved EF

Causes:

  • Amyloidosis (AL, or ATTR wild-type or variant)
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Radiation
  • Storage diseases: Fabry, glycogen storage
  • Fibrosis: Scleroderma, endomyocardial fibrosis

Echo: Biatrial enlargement, normal/small ventricles, preserved EF, diastolic dysfunction. Amyloid: increased wall thickness, grade ≥2 diastolic dysfunction, abnormal longitudinal strain with apical sparing (2023 ACC amyloidosis ECDP); "sparkling" myocardium is Practical

Cardiac Amyloidosis (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline; 2023 ACC ECDP; 2025 ACC Concise Clinical Guidance for ATTR-CM):

  • Suspect: LV wall ≥14 mm with fatigue, dyspnea, or edema, especially with QRS voltage discordant with wall thickness (low voltage in only 25-40% of ATTR-CM), or with AS, HFpEF, conduction disease, AF, carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, or autonomic/sensory neuropathy. ATTR is found in about 15% of degenerative AS and of HFpEF. With low suspicion, NT-proBNP <180 pg/mL and hs-TnT <14 ng/L can exclude ATTR-CM (2025 CCG)
  • Step 1 (1, B-NR): Screen for monoclonal light chains: serum and urine immunofixation plus serum free light chains (together about 99% sensitive for AL). Use the κ/λ ratio, not absolute levels; CKD raises the ratio, while a low ratio (excess λ) needs workup (2025 CCG)
  • Step 2 (1, B-NR): If no monoclonal protein, bone scintigraphy (99mTc-PYP; DPD or HDP are alternatives) with SPECT at 2-3 h. Grade 2-3 uptake with a negative screen confirms ATTR-CM without biopsy (PPV 100%). PYP can be positive in AL. Any abnormal monoclonal screen: tissue biopsy with amyloid typing by mass spectrometry; a negative fat pad biopsy excludes neither AL nor ATTR, and cardiac biopsy may be needed (2025 CCG)
  • Step 3 (1, B-NR): TTR gene sequencing once ATTR is diagnosed (variant vs wild-type)
  • AL amyloidosis: Prompt hematology-oncology referral
  • ATTR therapy: Tafamidis for NYHA I-III (1, B-R; 61 mg or tafamidis meglumine 80 mg daily); acoramidis 712 mg twice daily (FDA November 2024); vutrisiran 25 mg SC every 3 months plus vitamin A supplement (FDA March 2025). No head-to-head data: choose by cost, access, and route; vutrisiran preferred for ATTRv with polyneuropathy; routine stabilizer plus silencer combination not recommended. No prior HF hospitalization, no loop diuretic, or wall <12 mm should not preclude therapy. Benefit not shown in advanced disease (NYHA IV, NT-proBNP ≥8,500 pg/mL, eGFR <15, or 6MWD <100-150 m; CCG Figure 3): transplant evaluation or palliative care. Caution: tafamidis with rosuvastatin >20 mg or atorvastatin >40 mg (rhabdomyolysis) (2025 CCG)
  • AF: Anticoagulation is reasonable regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc (2a, C-LD). Rate control: low-dose beta-blocker (2025 CCG); digoxin may be used with close monitoring (2023 ECDP). Rhythm control: amiodarone is generally well tolerated (2023 ECDP)
  • HF therapy (2025 CCG Table 3): Preload dependent and afterload intolerant. Loop diuretics: titrate cautiously (hypotension, AKI); torsemide, bumetanide, or added metolazone for resistance. MRA (spironolactone) and SGLT2i: options to relieve congestion, well tolerated. Beta-blocker: low dose (eg, bisoprolol ≤2.5 mg/day) only if EF ≤40% or for AF rate control; reduce or stop if not tolerated. ACEi/ARB: no observed benefit, frequent hypotension and discontinuation; ARNI may be cautiously attempted
RCM vs Constrictive Pericarditis
FeatureRCMConstrictive
Septal bounce / ventricular septal shiftAbsentPresent
Respirophasic inflow variationMinimalMitral E >25%, tricuspid E >40%
Medial e' (tissue Doppler)ReducedPreserved, >8 cm/s
Hepatic vein expiratory diastolic reversal ratioLow≥0.8 (ACC 2025; Mayo/ESC >0.78)
Pericardium (CT/CMR)NormalUsually thickened, often calcified; normal thickness does not exclude
BNPElevated, often markedlyLower in idiopathic CP; may not differ from RCM after cardiac surgery or radiation
Kussmaul signCan occurCan occur (not discriminating)

ACC 2025 Pericarditis CCG: TTE noninvasive hemodynamic assessment first (Recommended); CMR to identify pericardial inflammation (Recommended); invasive catheterization when noninvasive testing is nondiagnostic or equivocal (Recommended). ACC echo algorithm (Figure 12): medial e' >8 cm/s favors CP, 6-8 cm/s mixed, <6 cm/s RCM. Mayo criteria (ESC 2025): septal bounce or shift plus medial e' >8 cm/s or hepatic vein reversal ratio >0.78 = sens 87%, spec 91% for CP; ESC multimodality imaging for all suspected CP (I, C), catheterization if imaging inconclusive (IIa, C). See card 228. BNP: meta-analysis of 7 small studies (n=204), pooled AUC 0.81, risk of bias high or unclear, no validated cutoff; interpret with caution in CKD (Diaz-Arocutipa, Clin Cardiol 2022). In post-surgical or post-radiation CP, BNP did not differ significantly from RCM, and tissue Doppler e' outperformed BNP (AUC 0.97 vs 0.76) (Sengupta, Am J Cardiol 2008). Practical: Kussmaul sign is reported in both conditions.

Key Diagnostic Clues
  • Amyloid: QRS voltage discordant with wall thickness, apical-sparing strain, diffuse LGE with increased ECV, persistent low-level troponin (2023 ECDP)
  • Sarcoid: Heart block, VT, patchy LGE on CMR
  • Hemochromatosis/iron overload: Reduced myocardial T2* on CMR (<20 ms indicates cardiac iron; all patients with ventricular dysfunction had T2* <20 ms) (Anderson, Eur Heart J 2001;22:2171, cited by the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline)
  • Fabry: LVH, angiokeratomas, α-galactosidase deficiency
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Carvedilol, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Spironolactone, 💊 Sacubitril-Valsartan, 💊 Amiodarone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated CRP

228. CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS

Post-Cardiac Surgery • Ventricular Interdependence • Pericardiectomy
ETIOLOGY & CLINICAL FEATURES

Causes (developed countries, ESC 2025):

  • Idiopathic/viral (42-49%)
  • Post-cardiac surgery (11-37%)
  • Radiation therapy, mostly for breast cancer or Hodgkin lymphoma (9-31%)
  • Connective tissue disease (3-7%)
  • Post-infectious: Purulent or TB (3-6%); TB is a major cause in developing countries
  • Miscellaneous (<10%), including malignancy
  • Risk of progression after acute pericarditis: Bacterial/purulent 20-30%; immune-mediated or neoplastic 2-5%; viral/idiopathic <1%

Presentation: Right HF (dyspnea, fatigue, edema, ascites, hepatomegaly) with preserved biventricular function (ESC 2025)

Physical Exam (ACC 2025 Table 12):

  • Elevated JVP with prominent x and y descents
  • Kussmaul sign: JVP rises with inspiration; also occurs in RCM, so not discriminating
  • Pericardial knock: Early diastolic sound
  • Ascites, peripheral edema
DIAGNOSIS

Approach: TTE noninvasive hemodynamic assessment first (ACC 2025 CCG: Recommended); CMR for supportive evidence when TTE is inconclusive (Reasonable) and to identify pericardial inflammation (Recommended); CT for calcification and pre-pericardiectomy planning (Reasonable); invasive catheterization when noninvasive testing is nondiagnostic or equivocal (Recommended). No single imaging finding is diagnostic (ACC 2025). ESC 2025: multimodality imaging for all suspected CP (I, C); catheterization if imaging inconclusive (IIa, C)

Echo:

  • Septal bounce or respirophasic ventricular septal shift
  • Medial e' >8 cm/s (preserved or increased); annulus reversus (medial e' > lateral e')
  • Hepatic vein expiratory end-diastolic reversal/forward velocity ratio ≥0.8 (ACC 2025; the Mayo/ESC cutoff is >0.78)
  • ACC 2025 echo algorithm (Figure 12): Mitral E/A >0.8 with a dilated IVC, then respirophasic septal motion; medial e' >8 cm/s favors CP, 6-8 cm/s mixed, <6 cm/s RCM; supported by annulus reversus and hepatic vein ratio ≥0.8. Step 1 plus step 2: sensitivity 80%, specificity 96%. Mayo criteria (ESC 2025): septal bounce or shift plus medial e' >8 cm/s or hepatic vein ratio >0.78 = sensitivity 87%, specificity 91%
  • Respirophasic E-wave variation: Mitral >25%, tricuspid >40%
  • Dilated IVC with <50% collapse

CT/CMR: CT for pericardial calcification and surgical planning (Reasonable, ACC 2025); calcification visible on chest x-ray in about one-third. CMR for pericardial thickening (>3 mm on T1-weighted images, ACC 2025), septal shift on free-breathing cine, and pericardial LGE/edema; CMR to identify pericardial inflammation is Recommended (ACC 2025). Up to 20% of CP has normal pericardial thickness (ESC 2025)

Cath: Equalization of RV and LV diastolic pressures with dip-and-plateau ("square root") waveforms, respirophasic ventricular interdependence, intrathoracic-intracardiac dissociation (ACC 2025 Table 12)

BNP: Lower than in RCM in idiopathic CP; may not differ from RCM after cardiac surgery or radiation; not diagnostic alone (see card 227)

TREATMENT

Inflammatory (transient) CP: Hemodynamically stable with new or transient constriction and pericardial inflammation (CRP elevation or pericardial LGE/edema on CMR): anti-inflammatory therapy first (ACC 2025: Recommended; ESC 2025 I, C) for 3-6 months before referral for pericardiectomy; resolves in >50%. Regimen per card 41

Supportive: Diuretics for congestion (Reasonable, ACC 2025). In advanced cases medical therapy only controls symptoms; do not delay surgery (ESC 2025)

Definitive: Radical (complete) pericardiectomy on cardiopulmonary bypass for noninflammatory CP or inflammatory CP failing anti-inflammatory therapy (ACC 2025: Recommended; ESC 2025 I, C after 3-6 months), at an experienced high-volume center. Partial anterior and/or diaphragmatic pericardiectomy: Not recommended (ACC 2025). Tricuspid repair if severe TR (I, C). Earliest surgery (within 6 months of symptom onset) has the lowest operative mortality (ESC 2025)

Surgical risk: Operative mortality historically 6-10%, <1.5% for idiopathic CP; caution with radiation-induced disease, reduced EF, or advanced renal disease (ESC 2025)

TB: Standard 6-month antituberculosis therapy to prevent constriction (I, C); pericardiectomy if not improving or worsening after 4-8 weeks of therapy (I, C); adjunctive corticosteroids should be considered if HIV-negative (IIa, C) (ESC 2025)

Effusive-constrictive: Right atrial pressure fails to fall by 50% or to <10 mm Hg after pericardiocentesis. Pericardiocentesis, then anti-inflammatory therapy; visceral pericardiectomy for persistent cases (ESC 2025 Table 18)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Right HF with preserved EF after cardiac surgery, radiation, or prior pericarditis: think constriction
  • Septal bounce or shift with preserved medial e' favors CP; e' is reduced in RCM (ACC 2025 Table 12)
  • Low BNP favors CP over RCM in idiopathic CP, but not reliably after surgery or radiation
  • Normal pericardial thickness does not exclude CP (up to 20%)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Colchicine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Troponin, 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR

229. BRADYARRHYTHMIAS & PACING

Sick Sinus Syndrome • AV Blocks • Pacemaker Indications
ACUTE SYMPTOMATIC BRADYCARDIA (ALS 2025; 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS)

Treat if: HR typically <50/min with hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute HF

  • First: Identify and treat reversible causes (1, C-EO): ischemia/MI, drugs (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin, antiarrhythmics, lithium), hyperkalemia, hypoxia, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, Lyme disease
  • Atropine: 1 mg IV, repeat every 3-5 min, max 3 mg (2a, B-NR). Acts at the sinus and AV node; unlikely to help, and occasionally worsens, infranodal (His-Purkinje) block. Do not use after heart transplant without reinnervation (3: Harm, C-LD)
  • If atropine fails (2b, C-LD): Transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min infusion, as a bridge to transvenous pacing
  • Temporary transvenous pacing: Persistent unstable bradycardia refractory to medical therapy (2a, C-LD). Not for minimal or infrequent symptoms without hemodynamic compromise (3: Harm, C-LD)
  • Toxin-specific (each 2a, C-LD): CCB overdose: 10% calcium chloride 1-2 g or 10% calcium gluconate 3-6 g IV every 10-20 min. Beta-blocker or CCB overdose: glucagon 3-10 mg IV then 3-5 mg/h; high-dose insulin 1 unit/kg IV then 0.5 units/kg/h (monitor glucose and K). Digoxin toxicity: digoxin Fab; dialysis does not remove digoxin (3: No Benefit, C-LD)
  • Inferior MI with 2nd- or 3rd-degree AV block: Aminophylline 250 mg IV bolus may be considered (2b, C-LD)

Atropine, transcutaneous pacing, infusions, and transvenous pacing: ALS 2025 recommendations 1-4 and Figure 8 (doses). Toxin-specific, aminophylline, transplant, and 3: Harm items: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline recommendations and acute medical therapy table.

SICK SINUS SYNDROME

Definition: SA node dysfunction. Sinus rate <50/min and/or pause >3 s are components of the definition, but treatment depends on symptoms that correlate with the rhythm (2018)

Manifestations:

  • Sinus bradycardia
  • Sinus pauses/arrest
  • Sinoatrial exit block
  • Tachy-brady syndrome: Alternating tachycardia (usually AFib) and bradycardia
  • Chronotropic incompetence (inadequate HR response to exercise)

Treatment: Permanent pacing when symptoms are directly attributable to SND (1, C-LD). Tachy-brady syndrome: pacing is reasonable for bradycardia symptoms and allows rate-control drugs (2a, C-EO); if bradycardia is limited to pauses after AF terminates, ablating the atrial arrhythmia may avoid pacing (2018). Unstable: see acute section above

AV BLOCKS
TypeECG Finding (2018 definitions)Permanent Pacing (2018)
First-degreePR >200 ms with 1:1 conductionNot if asymptomatic or symptoms not temporally related (3: Harm, C-LD). Marked PR prolongation with clearly attributable symptoms: reasonable (2a, C-LD)
Second-degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach)Progressive PR prolongation before a single nonconducted P wave; grouped beatingUsually AV nodal. Not if asymptomatic or symptoms not temporally related (3: Harm, C-LD); reasonable if symptoms clearly attributable (2a, C-LD)
2:1 AV blockEvery other P wave conducts; level cannot be judged from the PR aloneNot if believed AV nodal and asymptomatic or symptoms not temporally related (3: Harm, C-LD)
Second-degree Mobitz IIConstant PR before and after a single nonconducted P waveRecommended regardless of symptoms if not due to a reversible or physiologic cause (1, B-NR)
High-grade (advanced)≥2 consecutive nonconducted P waves with some AV conduction
Third-degree (complete)No AV conduction; P waves and QRS independent

Reversible or transient causes: Drugs (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs, digoxin, antiarrhythmics), hyperkalemia, Lyme carditis, acute MI, cardiac surgery or TAVR, hypothyroidism, vagally mediated block

  • Lyme carditis or drug toxicity: Medical therapy and supportive care, including temporary transvenous pacing if needed, before deciding on permanent pacing (1, B-NR)
  • Block persists despite treating the cause: Permanent pacing (1, C-LD). Complete resolution of a nonrecurrent cause: no pacing (3: Harm, C-LD)
  • On chronic stable doses of a medically necessary antiarrhythmic or beta-blocker: Reasonable to pace without waiting for washout (2a, B-NR); therapeutic doses rarely cause new AV block
  • Cardiac sarcoidosis with 2nd- or 3rd-degree block: Permanent pacing (with ICD if indicated) without waiting for reversibility (2a, B-NR)

Acute MI (2018): Temporary pacing for medically refractory symptomatic bradycardia (1, B-NR). Wait before deciding on permanent pacing (1, B-NR); pace after the waiting period for persistent Mobitz II, high-grade, alternating bundle branch, or third-degree (persistent or infranodal) block (1, B-NR). No permanent pacing for transient AV block that resolves, or for new bundle branch or fascicular block without 2nd- or 3rd-degree block (3: Harm, B-NR). Atropine for sinus bradycardia or AV nodal block (2a, B-NR)

After TAVR (2018, Section 8.1.2.4): New AV block with symptoms or hemodynamic instability that does not resolve: permanent pacing before discharge (1, B-NR). High-degree AV block persists beyond 48 h in 2-20%; implant timing in reports ranged from 2 days to several weeks (median about 3 days). New persistent bundle branch block: careful surveillance for bradycardia (2a, B-NR); with new LBBB, 29% have their first high-degree AV block after discharge, and no monitoring method or protocol has proven superior. New persistent LBBB: PPM may be considered (2b, B-NR); new LBBB occurs in about 10% and resolves in about half by 6-12 months

PACEMAKER INDICATIONS & MODES

Class 1 indications (2018):

  • SND with symptoms directly attributable to it (C-LD)
  • Acquired Mobitz II, high-grade, or third-degree AV block not due to a reversible or physiologic cause, regardless of symptoms (B-NR)
  • Symptomatic bradycardia (SND or AV block) caused by necessary GDMT with no alternative (C-EO for SND, C-LD for AV block)
  • Permanent AF with symptomatic bradycardia (C-LD)
  • Symptomatic AV block from a reversible cause that persists despite treatment (C-LD)
  • Syncope with bundle branch block and HV ≥70 ms or infranodal block at EPS (C-LD)
  • Alternating bundle branch block (C-LD)
  • Neuromuscular disease (eg, myotonic dystrophy type 1, Kearns-Sayre) with 2nd- or 3rd-degree AV block or HV ≥70 ms, regardless of symptoms; add ICD capability if needed (B-NR)

Class 2a (2018): Tachy-brady syndrome with bradycardia symptoms (C-EO); symptomatic chronotropic incompetence, with rate-responsive programming (C-EO); infiltrative cardiomyopathy (sarcoid, amyloid) with Mobitz II or higher block, with ICD capability if needed (B-NR); lamin A/C variant with PR >240 ms and LBBB (B-NR)

Not indicated (2018): Asymptomatic SND, or symptoms documented without bradycardia; asymptomatic bradycardia from physiologic vagal tone; sleep-related bradycardia or pauses (each 3: Harm, C-LD). Asymptomatic isolated conduction disease with 1:1 conduction (3: Harm, B-NR). Nocturnal bradycardia: screen for sleep apnea (1, B-NR). A rate or pause cutoff alone is not an indication; symptom-rhythm correlation drives the decision

AV junction ablation for AF rate control: Requires a pacemaker (see card 3)

Pacemaker Mode Codes: I = chamber paced, II = chamber sensed, III = response to sensing, IV = R for rate modulation (eg, DDDR, VVIR for chronotropic incompetence)

  • DDD(R): Dual chamber; recommended over single-chamber ventricular pacing in SND and AV block (1, A)
  • AAI(R): Atrial only; SND with intact AV conduction (dual-chamber or atrial pacing, 1, B-R). With a dual-chamber device and intact conduction, program to minimize ventricular pacing (2a, B-R)
  • VVI(R): Single-chamber ventricular; acceptable when frequent pacing is not expected or comorbidities limit benefit (1, A for AV block; 2a, C-EO for SND). In permanent or persistent AF without a rhythm-control plan, do not place an atrial lead (3: Harm, C-LD)
  • Physiologic pacing: LVEF 36-50% with expected ventricular pacing >40%: CRT, His bundle, or left bundle branch area pacing over RV pacing is reasonable to prevent pacing-induced cardiomyopathy (2a; B-R in 2018; 2023 HRS: CRT B-R, His/LBBAP B-NR). Expected pacing <40%: RV pacing is reasonable (2a, B-R)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Mobitz II, high-grade, or complete heart block not due to a reversible cause: Pace regardless of symptoms (1, B-NR)
  • Inferior MI: AV block is often AV nodal and reversible. Anterior MI with AV block carries a worse prognosis (2018)
  • Atropine helps sinus and AV nodal block, not infranodal block (2018)
  • Lyme carditis: AV block is almost always reversible; check Lyme serology in a young patient with AV block in an endemic area; antibiotics and temporary pacing if needed before deciding on permanent pacing (1, B-NR)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Atropine, 💊 Dopamine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

230. SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH PREVENTION

Channelopathies • Inherited Arrhythmias • Risk Stratification
CHANNELOPATHIES

Long QT Syndrome (LQTS) (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA):

  • Diagnosis (ESC 2022): QTc ≥480 ms on repeated 12-lead ECGs, or LQTS diagnostic score >3 (I, C); or a pathogenic variant regardless of QTc (I, C). QTc 460-479 ms with arrhythmic syncope and no secondary cause: consider LQTS (IIa, C). Genetic counseling and testing for clinically diagnosed LQTS (1, B-NR; ESC I, C); a negative test does not exclude LQTS. Ambulatory ECG, ECG lying then immediately standing, or exercise testing for suspected LQTS (2a, B-NR)
  • LQT1: Beta-blockers reduce events >95%. Practical: exercise trigger, classically swimming
  • LQT2: Beta-blockers reduce events >75%. Young women with QTc >500 ms are at increased risk, especially in the 9 months postpartum; fever can prolong QT, so treat it. Practical: emotional or auditory trigger
  • LQT3: Beta-blockers reduce events >60% in women; limited data in men. Mexiletine, ranolazine, or flecainide shorten QTc; mexiletine is indicated with a prolonged QTc (ESC 2022 I, C). Practical: rest or sleep trigger
  • Beta-blocker: Recommended if resting QTc >470 ms (1, B-NR); reasonable if asymptomatic with QTc <470 ms (2a, B-NR). Propranolol, atenolol, or nadolol; metoprolol appears less effective. ESC 2022 prefers nonselective agents (nadolol or propranolol) (I, B)
  • Escalation: High-risk symptomatic patients in whom beta-blockers fail or are not tolerated: additional genotype-guided drugs, left cardiac sympathetic denervation, and/or ICD (1, B-NR). Recurrent appropriate ICD shocks on maximal beta-blocker: add drugs or denervation (1, B-NR). Asymptomatic with QTc >500 ms on a beta-blocker: may consider the same options (2b, B-NR). High risk: QTc >500 ms, LQT2 or LQT3, women with LQT2, age <40, symptom onset <10 years, recurrent syncope
  • QT-prolonging drugs: Potentially harmful (3: Harm, B-NR)

Brugada Syndrome:

  • Type 1 pattern: Coved ST elevation with negative T waves in V1 or V2, placed in the 2nd, 3rd, or 4th intercostal space, spontaneous or induced by a sodium channel blocker. Suspected Brugada without a spontaneous type 1 pattern: sodium channel blocker challenge (2a, B-NR). Mostly young men
  • Genetics: Variant found in about 20-30%, mostly SCN5A. Genetic counseling and testing may be useful for cascade screening (2b, C-EO)
  • ICD: Spontaneous type 1 with cardiac arrest, sustained VA, or recent syncope presumed arrhythmic (1, B-NR). Asymptomatic with only a drug-induced type 1 pattern: observation (1, B-NR). Asymptomatic spontaneous type 1: EP study may be considered (2b, B-NR)
  • Quinidine or catheter ablation: Recurrent ICD shocks for polymorphic VT, or symptomatic VA when an ICD is declined or not possible (1, B-NR)
  • Triggers: Treat fever early and aggressively; avoid some psychotropics and anesthetics, cocaine, and excess alcohol (brugadadrugs.org)

CPVT (Catecholaminergic Polymorphic VT):

  • Exertion- or stress-related bidirectional or polymorphic VT; SCA or SCD in 3-13%
  • Normal resting ECG and structurally normal heart
  • Beta-blocker: Recommended at maximally tolerated dose (1, B-NR); some experts prefer nadolol
  • Recurrent sustained VT or syncope on a beta-blocker: Add flecainide, left cardiac sympathetic denervation, and/or ICD (1, B-NR). Inappropriate ICD shocks occur in 20-30%
  • Genetic counseling and testing with clinical VT or exertional syncope (2a, B-NR)
OTHER SCD RISK CONDITIONS

ARVC (Arrhythmogenic RV Cardiomyopathy):

  • Fibrofatty replacement of the myocardium, RV predominant; the LV may be involved (ESC 2023)
  • ECG: T-wave inversion in V1-V3 (Practical: classic criterion). Epsilon waves are often overdiagnosed and add little to the diagnosis; use with caution (ESC 2023)
  • Ventricular arrhythmia of RV origin (LBBB-morphology VT)
  • CMR for diagnosis and risk stratification with VA or ECG abnormalities (1, B-NR)
  • ICD: Resuscitated SCA, sustained VT, or RVEF or LVEF ≤35% (1, B-NR); syncope presumed due to VA (2a, B-NR)
  • Beta-blocker with VA (1, B-NR); avoid intensive exercise (1, B-NR)
  • Family: Screen selected first-degree relatives, with genetic counseling and testing if the proband has a disease-causing variant (1, B-NR); genetic testing in patients can be useful (2a, B-NR)

Commotio Cordis: VF from blunt chest trauma during vulnerable repolarization phase

WPW with Pre-excited AF: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia. IV digoxin, IV amiodarone, beta-blockers, diltiazem, and verapamil are potentially harmful (3: Harm, C-LD), as is adenosine (3: Harm). Unstable: synchronized cardioversion (I, B-NR). Stable: ibutilide or IV procainamide (I, C-LD). Doses on card 134

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • LQTS with syncope despite beta-blockers: Escalate with genotype-guided drugs, left cardiac sympathetic denervation, and/or ICD (1, B-NR); ICD after cardiac arrest (ESC 2022 I, B)
  • Brugada type 1 pattern can appear with fever or after a sodium channel blocker; cocaine and excess alcohol are triggers
  • Epsilon wave suggests ARVC but is often overdiagnosed; rely on imaging and the full criteria (ESC 2023)
  • Pre-excited AF: No AV nodal blockers, adenosine, or IV amiodarone
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Atenolol, 💊 Flecainide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hypokalemia, 🔬 Hypomagnesemia, 🔬 Hypocalcemia

231. PERIPHERAL ARTERY DISEASE

ABI • Claudication • Critical Limb Ischemia
DIAGNOSIS

Clinical subsets (2024 ACC/AHA PAD):

  • Claudication: Exertional leg pain, aching, cramping, or fatigue relieved by rest (within 10 min)
  • Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI): >2 weeks of ischemic rest pain, nonhealing wounds or ulcers, or gangrene from objectively proven arterial occlusive disease (replaces "critical limb ischemia")
  • Acute limb ischemia (ALI): Hypoperfusion of ≤2 weeks; see ALI section below

Resting ABI (1, B-NR) when history or exam suggests PAD:

  • ≤0.90: Abnormal (PAD)
  • 0.91-0.99: Borderline
  • 1.00-1.40: Normal
  • >1.40: Noncompressible; obtain toe pressure/toe-brachial index (TBI) with waveforms (1, B-NR); TBI ≤0.70 is abnormal

Additional Testing: Exercise treadmill ABI if symptomatic with a normal or borderline resting ABI (1, B-NR). Suspected CLTI: toe pressure/TBI, TcPO2, or skin perfusion pressure (2a, B-NR); the ABI can be 0.90-1.40 in about a quarter of CLTI. Duplex ultrasound, CTA, MRA, or angiography only when revascularization is being considered (1, B-NR); CTA, MRA, or angiography solely for anatomy when revascularization is not planned is harmful (3: Harm, B-NR). ABI screening is reasonable if at increased risk (2a, B-NR), not otherwise (3: No Benefit, B-NR)

TREATMENT

All PAD Patients:

  • Smoking cessation: Advise at every visit and offer varenicline, bupropion, and/or nicotine replacement with counseling (1, A)
  • Antithrombotic (2024 ACC/AHA PAD): Symptomatic PAD: single antiplatelet therapy (1, A), clopidogrel 75 mg daily (1, B-R) or aspirin 75-325 mg daily (1, C-LD), with no stated preference. Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin reduces MACE and major adverse limb events (1, A) at the cost of more major bleeding (COMPASS excluded high bleeding risk, prior hemorrhagic or lacunar stroke, severe kidney disease, and need for DAPT or anticoagulation). After endovascular or surgical revascularization: antiplatelet therapy (1, B-R); rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin (1, A); DAPT for 1-6 months after endovascular revascularization is reasonable (2a, C-LD). Asymptomatic PAD: single antiplatelet therapy is reasonable (2a, C-EO). Full-dose anticoagulation without another indication (eg, AF): harmful (3: Harm, A)
  • Lipids: High-intensity statin for a ≥50% LDL-C reduction (1, A). LDL-C goal per the 2026 dyslipidemia guideline: <70 mg/dL, or <55 mg/dL if very high risk (symptomatic PAD counts as a major ASCVD event); add ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 inhibitor to reach goal (see card 222)
  • Hypertension: Treat (1, A) to <130/80 (1, B-R); ACEi or ARB (1, B-R)
  • Type 2 diabetes: GLP-1 RA (liraglutide, semaglutide) or SGLT2i (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) to reduce MACE (1, A)
  • Exercise: Supervised exercise therapy (1, A) or a structured community-based program (1, A), offered as initial treatment for functionally limiting claudication (1, B-R). Supervised: at least 3 sessions/week of 30-45 min walking for at least 12 weeks

Claudication:

  • Cilostazol improves symptoms and walking distance (1, A): 100 mg twice daily, at least 30 min before or 2 h after breakfast and dinner; 50 mg twice daily with strong or moderate CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 inhibitors; stop if no improvement after 3 months (FDA label). Contraindicated in heart failure of any severity (boxed warning; 3: Harm, C-LD)
  • Pentoxifylline and chelation: not recommended (3: No Benefit, B-R)
  • Revascularization: Functionally limiting claudication with an inadequate response to GDMT including structured exercise (2a, B-R); not if the response is adequate (3: No Benefit, C-EO)

Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia:

  • Multispecialty team care (1, B-NR); evaluate revascularization options before amputation (1, C-EO)
  • Revascularization (surgical, endovascular, or hybrid) when feasible to minimize tissue loss, heal wounds, relieve pain, and preserve a functional limb (1, B-R)
  • Foot infection: Prompt antibiotics, debridement, and surgery as needed (1, B-NR); wound care after revascularization (1, C-LD); pressure offloading for diabetic foot ulcers (1, A)
  • Primary amputation when life over limb prevails or the limb is driving instability (ischemia, metabolic derangement, advanced infection) (1, C-EO); level chosen by the team (1, B-NR)
ACUTE LIMB ISCHEMIA (ALI)

Definition: Hypoperfusion of ≤2 weeks: pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesias, and/or paralysis. A vascular emergency. Causes: embolism (AF, LV thrombus, valve or aortic disease), thrombosis of a native artery, graft, or stent, trauma, peripheral aneurysm

Rutherford class: I viable (no sensory or motor loss; audible arterial and venous Doppler). IIa marginally threatened (sensory loss limited to toes, no motor loss). IIb immediately threatened (sensory loss beyond toes, mild-moderate weakness). III irreversible (anesthetic, paralyzed, no arterial or venous Doppler signal)

  • Emergency evaluation by a clinician experienced in judging limb viability (1, C-EO); bedside exam with handheld Doppler is usually enough, without imaging (1, C-LD). Transfer if local expertise is unavailable
  • Unfractionated heparin on diagnosis, regardless of cause or level, unless contraindicated (1, C-EO)
  • Salvageable limb: Revascularization (endovascular, surgical, or catheter-directed thrombolysis) to prevent amputation (1, A). Nonsalvageable limb: do not revascularize nonviable tissue (3: Harm, C-EO)
  • After revascularization: Monitor for and treat compartment syndrome with fasciotomy (1, C-EO); prophylactic fasciotomy is reasonable for class IIa or IIb (2a, B-NR)
  • Find the cause by history and exam (1, C-EO) and testing for a cardiovascular embolic source (2a, C-LD), without delaying revascularization
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • ABI ≤0.90 = PAD; >1.40 = noncompressible, so get a toe-brachial index
  • Cilostazol is contraindicated in heart failure of any severity (boxed warning)
  • Supervised exercise therapy is an initial treatment for functionally limiting claudication (1, B-R)
  • Symptomatic PAD: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin (1, A) if bleeding risk allows
  • ALI: Heparin at diagnosis and emergency vascular evaluation; do not wait for imaging
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Clopidogrel, 💊 Atorvastatin, 💊 Rivaroxaban, 💊 Unfractionated Heparin

232. STATIN THERAPY GUIDELINES

ASCVD Risk • Primary vs Secondary Prevention • LDL Goals
WHO GETS A STATIN (2026 ACC/AHA DYSLIPIDEMIA)

Risk estimation: Ages 30-79 without ASCVD and LDL-C 70-189 mg/dL: PREVENT-ASCVD equations for 10-y risk, low <3%, borderline 3 to <5%, intermediate 5 to <10%, high ≥10% (1, B-NR). Benefit-risk discussion and health behaviors for all (1, A)

  • Clinical ASCVD (ACS, prior MI, angina, coronary or other arterial revascularization, stroke, TIA, PAD including aortic aneurysm): High-intensity statin. Very high risk: LDL-C <55 and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL (1, A); otherwise <70 and <100 (1, A). Risk definition on card 222
  • LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL: Exclude secondary causes (1, B-NR); maximally tolerated statin (1, B-R). Add ezetimibe, a PCSK9 mAb, and/or bempedoic acid to reach LDL-C <100 without other risk (1, B-NR), <70 with HeFH, added risk factors, or coronary calcium (1, B-R), or <55 with clinical ASCVD (1, B-R)
  • Diabetes, ages 40-75, no ASCVD: Moderate-intensity statin with LDL-C goal <100 and non-HDL-C <130 (1, A); high-intensity with goal <70 if multiple risk factors (2a, B-R)
  • Primary prevention by PREVENT risk: High (≥10%): high-intensity statin (1, A), goal <70 reasonable (2a, B-R). Intermediate (5 to <10%): at least moderate-intensity (1, A), goal <100 reasonable (2a, B-NR). Borderline (3 to <5%): moderate-intensity if treating (2a, A). Low (<3%), ages 30-59: health behaviors (1, A); moderate-intensity reasonable if LDL-C 160-189 or 30-y risk ≥10% (2a, C-LD)

Statin Intensity (2026 Table 6):

IntensityLDL ReductionDrugs
High≥50%Atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg
Moderate30-49%Atorvastatin 10-20 mg, rosuvastatin 5-10 mg; also simvastatin 20-40 mg, pravastatin 40-80 mg, lovastatin 40-80 mg, pitavastatin 1-4 mg, fluvastatin XL 80 mg or 40 mg twice daily
Low<30%Simvastatin 10 mg, pravastatin 10-20 mg, lovastatin 20 mg, fluvastatin 20-40 mg
ADD-ON (NONSTATIN) THERAPY (2026)

When: On maximally tolerated statin and not at LDL-C/non-HDL-C goal (goals above; card 222). Ezetimibe is no longer required before a PCSK9 mAb; choose by the LDL-C lowering needed and patient preference. Very high risk: ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 mAb (1, A); bempedoic acid is reasonable (2a, B-R)

  • Ezetimibe 10 mg daily: Lowers LDL-C about 18% alone, about 25% added to a statin
  • PCSK9 mAb (evolocumab, alirocumab): Lowers LDL-C 45-64%; reduces ASCVD events in very high-risk patients on a statin
  • Bempedoic acid: Lowers LDL-C 21-24% alone in statin intolerance, 17-18% more with a statin
  • Inclisiran (siRNA): Lowers LDL-C 48-52%; outcome trials pending. Second-line PCSK9 inhibitor for those unable to tolerate or obtain evolocumab or alirocumab, or who prefer less frequent dosing (2a, B-R)
SAFETY AND SPECIAL SITUATIONS (2026)
  • Pregnancy: Without high ASCVD risk, stop the statin 1-2 months before trying to conceive or when pregnancy is found (1, C-LD). With FH or clinical ASCVD, continuing may be reasonable after discussion (2b, C-LD), preferring a hydrophilic statin such as pravastatin. Bile acid sequestrants are reasonable in pregnancy or lactation (2a, C-EO)
  • Muscle symptoms: Look for secondary causes; check CK and strength if severe (1, C-LD). Explain the risk of stopping (1, B-R). With clinical ASCVD, use a lower statin dose plus bempedoic acid, ezetimibe, or a PCSK9 mAb (1, B-R). Coenzyme Q10: not recommended (3: No Benefit, B-R)
  • Monitoring: Routine CK without severe muscle symptoms (3: No Benefit, A) and routine liver tests without symptoms of hepatotoxicity (3: No Benefit, B-NR) are not useful
  • Liver disease: Statins are reasonable in chronic stable liver disease, including MASLD (2a, B-R)
  • New-onset diabetes on a statin: Continue the statin (1, A)
  • Drug interactions: Review concomitant cardiovascular drugs for interactions before starting (1, B-NR)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Clinical ASCVD: High-intensity statin plus add-on therapy to reach goal (LDL-C <55 mg/dL if very high risk)
  • Ezetimibe is no longer required before a PCSK9 mAb (2026)
  • MASLD or chronic stable liver disease is not a reason to withhold a statin (2a, B-R)
  • Statin muscle symptoms: Exclude secondary causes, check CK if severe, and lower the dose or add a nonstatin rather than stop (1, B-R)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Atorvastatin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated LDL, 🔬 Low HDL, 🔬 Elevated Triglycerides, 🔬 Elevated Lipoprotein(a), 🔬 Elevated HbA1c, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

233. INPATIENT INSULIN MANAGEMENT

Basal-Bolus • Correction-Only Pitfalls • Transition to Outpatient
GLYCEMIC TARGETS

Start or Intensify: persistent glucose ≥180 mg/dL, confirmed twice within 24 h (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.4; ICU: SCCM 2024)

ICU: IV insulin infusion (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.8a; SCCM 2024) run by a protocol with explicit, preferably computerized decision support; check glucose at least hourly while unstable (SCCM 2024). Goal 140-180 mg/dL for most (Rec 16.5a). SCCM 2024 suggests against 80-139 and accepts 140-200, including after cardiac surgery and in neuro-ICU; 110-140 only where hypoglycemia is documented to be negligible (SCCM) or for selected patients such as cardiac surgery (ADA)

Non-ICU: 100-180 mg/dL if achievable without significant hypoglycemia (Rec 16.5b; Endocrine Society 2022). Fasting glucose <100 predicts hypoglycemia within 24 h: adjust basal insulin

Less Stringent (up to 250): terminal illness with short life expectancy, advanced kidney failure or dialysis, high hypoglycemia risk, labile glucose (ADA SOC 2026)

Hypoglycemia (<70): level 1 54-69; level 2 <54; level 3 needs assistance. Treat with 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate if able to swallow, otherwise IV glucose or glucagon; recheck every 15 min until >70. Review the regimen after any value <70 (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.12-16.13)

BASAL-BOLUS INSULIN PROTOCOL

Total Daily Dose (TDD):

  • Usual start: 0.3-0.6 units/kg/day (ADA SOC 2026). Lower end for high hypoglycemia risk (age ≥65, BMI ≤27, CKD stage 3 or worse, liver failure, among others; Endocrine Society 2022); higher end for insulin resistance (Practical)
  • On home insulin: about 80% of the home TDD (ADA SOC 2026); basal-heavy regimens (basal ≥0.6-1.0 units/kg/day) may need a 10-20% basal reduction (Endocrine Society 2022)
  • From an IV infusion: about 60% of the TDD extrapolated from the last 6-8 h (ADA SOC 2026)

Distribution (ADA SOC 2026):

  • 50% Basal: Glargine or degludec once daily (or NPH twice daily). Detemir (Levemir) was discontinued in the US in 2024
  • 50% Nutritional: Divided among meals (rapid-acting: lispro, aspart, glulisine)
  • Premixed insulins (70/30, 75/25, 50/50) are not routinely recommended in hospital (more hypoglycemia)

Correction Scale: Added to meal-time insulin for hyperglycemia; scale proportional to TDD (low <40, medium 40-80, high >80 units/day), usually starting at 140-150 mg/dL (ADA SOC 2026)

  • Correction factor = 1800 / TDD for rapid-acting analogs (how much 1 unit drops BG) (Practical)
  • Typically 1 unit per 50 mg/dL above target on a low scale (Practical)

NPO or Poor Intake: basal insulin or basal plus correction (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.8b); hold prandial insulin. Before surgery: long-acting analogs to 75-80% of the dose, NPH to one-half; reduction may be inappropriate in some people with T1D (ADA SOC 2026)

AVOID SLIDING SCALE ONLY
⚠️ SLIDING SCALE MONOTHERAPY IS REACTIVE, NOT PROACTIVE

Treats hyperglycemia after it occurs; causes glucose variability; delays appropriate management. Correction-only insulin is discouraged for most patients (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.10). Endocrine Society 2022: no prior diabetes, start with correction insulin and add scheduled insulin if ≥2 glucose values ≥180 in 24 h; diet- or noninsulin-treated diabetes, correction or scheduled insulin (scheduled if admission glucose ≥180 is confirmed); insulin-treated diabetes, continue the scheduled regimen adjusted for intake and illness.

TRANSITION TO OUTPATIENT
  • IV to SC: give SC basal insulin 2 h before stopping the infusion (ADA SOC 2026; for DKA see DKA)
  • Structured discharge plan tailored to the patient (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.18) with inpatient diabetes education (Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 4.1); communicate the plan to outpatient clinicians
  • Resume home regimen if A1c at goal; adjust if not (Practical; ADA SOC 2026 describes an algorithm using admission A1C, prior medications and inpatient insulin use)
  • Metformin and iodinated contrast (US label): stop at or before the procedure if eGFR 30-60, liver disease, alcoholism, heart failure, or intra-arterial contrast; recheck eGFR 48 h later and restart if renal function is stable. Hold metformin and other oral agents on the day of surgery (ADA SOC 2026)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Correction-only insulin is discouraged for most (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.10); see the exceptions above
  • Continue basal insulin when NPO (Rec 16.8b); the reduction depends on the insulin and may be inappropriate in T1D
  • Noninsulin agents: insulin is preferred. DPP-4i with correction insulin is an option for mild hyperglycemia in T2D (A1C <7.5%, glucose <180; Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 7.2). SGLT2i may be started or continued for heart failure without contraindications (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.11) but avoided in severe illness, ketosis, prolonged fasting and surgery. Hold GLP-1 RAs in acutely ill patients (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Devices: continue a personal CGM with POC confirmation for dosing (Rec 16.6) and insulin pumps or automated insulin delivery when appropriate, under an institutional protocol (Rec 16.7). If a pump is stopped: give the 24-h basal from the pump profile as glargine; if unknown, 0.2-0.4 units/kg/day (Endocrine Society 2022)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Regular Insulin, 💊 Insulin Glargine, 💊 Insulin Lispro, 💊 Dextrose D50/D10, 💊 Glucagon, 💊 Metformin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperglycemia, 🔬 Hypoglycemia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia

CONCENTRATED INSULINS
  • U-500 Regular (Humulin R U-500): 5× concentrated; only for patients needing >200 units/day (US label). Similar onset but a delayed, blunted, prolonged peak and longer duration than U-100 regular, so it acts like NPH plus regular and is given 2-3 times daily (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Glargine U-300 (Toujeo): 3× concentrated; longer duration than U-100 glargine but modestly lower effect per unit (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Degludec U-200 (Tresiba), lispro U-200 (Humalog), lispro-aabc U-200 (Lyumjev): 2× concentrated; pharmacokinetics similar to their U-100 versions (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Icodec U-700 (Awiqli): once weekly; serious hypoglycemia has followed mix-ups with other insulins, wrong dose selection and dosing-frequency errors (US label)

Caution: High risk of dosing errors. Except U-500, concentrated insulins come only in prefilled pens to limit errors (ADA SOC 2026). Never draw up from a pen with a syringe (US labels: U-500, degludec, icodec). The current U-500 label (rev. 7/2026) lists only the KwikPen; if a vial is used, prescribe U-500 syringes (ADA SOC 2026) and write the dose in units (U-500 label). Never give concentrated insulins IV (US labels).

Hospital: Data on U-300, U-200 and U-500 in hospital are limited; inpatient needs of U-500 users may fall by up to 75% from home doses, so hypoglycemia and dosing errors are a particular concern (ADA SOC 2026)

PREMIXED INSULINS
  • Human 70/30 (Humulin 70/30, Novolin 70/30): 70% NPH + 30% regular
  • Aspart Mix 70/30 (NovoLog Mix 70/30): 70% aspart protamine + 30% aspart; a different product with the same ratio, so write the full product name (NovoLog Mix label)
  • Lispro Mix 75/25 and 50/50 (Humalog Mix): lispro protamine + lispro
  • Given BID (before breakfast and dinner)
  • Fixed ratio: basal and prandial parts cannot be adjusted separately (NovoLog Mix label); human insulins (NPH, human premix) carry more hypoglycemia than analogs (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Hospital: premixed insulins are not routinely recommended (more hypoglycemia) (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Subcutaneous only; never IV (NovoLog Mix label)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • IV insulin: regular is the usual drip (Practical), but U-100 rapid-acting analogs (lispro, aspart including Fiasp, glulisine, Lyumjev U-100) are also labeled for IV use under medical supervision with glucose and potassium monitoring. Never IV: concentrated insulins (U-200, U-300, U-500, U-700), glargine, degludec, or premixes (US labels)
  • NPH peaks about 4-6 hr after a dose (ADA SOC 2026): a bedtime dose peaks overnight, and nocturnal hypoglycemia is more common with NPH than with long-acting analogs (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Basal analogs have flatter, steadier profiles than NPH: U-100 glargine reduces level 2 and nocturnal hypoglycemia vs NPH; U-300 glargine and degludec lower nocturnal hypoglycemia further vs U-100 glargine (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Degludec: half-life about 25 hr; adults may inject it once daily at any time of day (Tresiba label). Icodec, once weekly, now has the longest action
  • Switching basal insulin: often unit for unit, but reduce 10-20% when switching from NPH or U-300 glargine to another insulin, or when hypoglycemia risk is high (ADA SOC 2026)
  • CKD: hypoglycemia risk and duration of insulin action rise as kidney function falls (ADA SOC 2026); renal or hepatic impairment may need a lower dose (Lantus label)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Insulin Glargine, 💊 Insulin Lispro, 💊 Regular Insulin
↑ Back to Table of Contents

235. EUGLYCEMIC DKA

SGLT2 Inhibitor-Associated • Normal Glucose DKA • Delayed Recognition
DEFINITION & PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Definition: DKA with plasma glucose <200 mg/dL; about 10% of DKA. SGLT2 inhibitors account for most cases (2024 consensus)

Mechanism with SGLT2i (Practical):

  • Glycosuria lowers blood glucose
  • Decreased insulin secretion (lower glucose stimulus)
  • Increased glucagon → lipolysis → ketogenesis
  • Volume depletion from osmotic diuresis

Causes (2024 consensus): SGLT2 inhibitors, reduced food intake, pregnancy, alcohol use, liver failure, insulin given before presentation

Triggers on SGLT2i: insulin dose reduction or omission, prolonged fasting, acute illness (2024 consensus Table 4); surgery (ADA SOC 2026). In T2D also very-low-carbohydrate diets, dehydration, excess alcohol and autoimmunity (ADA SOC 2026 sec. 6). In T1D, DKA risk on SGLT2i is 5-17 times that of nonusers (ADA SOC 2026 sec. 6)

Pregnancy: euglycemic DKA may occur; hyperemesis can cause mixed acid-base disturbances; needs immediate senior medical and obstetric care (2024 consensus Table 4)

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Diagnostic Criteria (2024 consensus; same as DKA):

  • Known diabetes (at any glucose) or glucose ≥200 mg/dL
  • β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L, or urine ketone strip 2+ or greater (urine tests can understate early ketosis)
  • pH <7.3 and/or HCO3 <18 mmol/L
  • Glucose may be normal or only mildly elevated

Treatment (2024 consensus: manage as general DKA):

  • Stop SGLT2 inhibitor on admission
  • IV fluids as for DKA (often more volume depleted than apparent)
  • Dextrose from the start: 5% or 10% dextrose with the 0.9% saline when insulin starts; keep glucose 150-200
  • IV insulin per the DKA protocol; the 2024 consensus gives no separate insulin regimen for euglycemic DKA
  • Potassium per the DKA protocol (hold insulin if K <3.5)
  • Resolution: β-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH ≥7.3 or HCO3 ≥18

Key Difference: dextrose is needed from the start because glucose is already low; continue insulin until the ketoacidosis resolves, not until glucose normalizes

After DKA: SGLT2 inhibitors are not recommended in T1D; in T2D, restarting after DKA is not routinely recommended (2024 consensus)

PREVENTION
  • Hold SGLT2i 3 days before scheduled surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin); restart only after ketoacidosis risk factors have resolved (ADA SOC 2026, citing FDA advice)
  • Nonelective surgery on an SGLT2i: monitor for DKA after surgery, including euglycemic DKA (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Hold during acute illness, fasting, or reduced oral intake ("sick day rules"; 2024 consensus)
  • Educate patients on symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue) and on recognition and prevention at discharge (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.17)
  • Check ketones if symptomatic even with normal glucose
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Normal glucose doesn't rule out DKA: in known diabetes, check blood β-hydroxybutyrate and a venous gas at any glucose
  • SGLT2i-associated DKA occurs in T2D as well as T1D; the risk is much higher in T1D
  • Hold SGLT2i before scheduled surgery: 3 days (4 for ertugliflozin)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Regular Insulin, 💊 KCl
↑ Back to Table of Contents

236. DIABETIC MICROVASCULAR COMPLICATIONS

Retinopathy • Nephropathy • Neuropathy
DIABETIC RETINOPATHY

Screening (ADA 2026 unless noted):

  • Type 1 (adults): first dilated, comprehensive eye exam 5 years after onset
  • Type 2: at diagnosis
  • Then: no retinopathy on one or more yearly exams and glycemia at goal: every 1-2 years may be considered; any retinopathy: at least yearly; progressing or sight-threatening: more often, by an ophthalmologist
  • AAO 2025 differs: with no retinopathy, exams stay yearly (type 1 from 5 years after onset, type 2 from diagnosis), with no every-1-2-years option; abnormal findings may need more frequent exams (AAO 2025)
  • Pregnancy (preexisting diabetes): before pregnancy and in the first trimester; may need every trimester and for 1 year postpartum depending on severity. AAO 2025: soon after conception and early in the first trimester, then every 3-12 months (no retinopathy to moderate NPDR) or every 1-3 months (severe NPDR or worse); gestational diabetes alone needs no eye exam (AAO 2025)
  • Retinal photography with remote reading, or FDA-approved AI algorithms, is acceptable screening

Classification:

  • Non-proliferative (NPDR): Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates (Practical)
  • Proliferative (PDR): Neovascularization; sight-threatening (Practical)
  • Diabetic macular edema: Can occur at any stage (Practical)
  • Prompt ophthalmology referral: any macular edema, moderate or worse NPDR, or any PDR (ADA 2026)

Treatment (ADA 2026): glycemic, blood pressure and lipid control; panretinal laser for high-risk PDR (and some severe NPDR); anti-VEGF injections are an alternative for PDR and first-line for center-involved macular edema with vision loss. Check retinopathy status when intensifying glucose lowering (e.g., GLP-1 RAs): rapid A1C reduction can cause initial worsening. Retinopathy is not a contraindication to aspirin

DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY

Screening (ADA 2026): UACR and eGFR at least yearly (type 1 for ≥5 years; all type 2); with CKD, 1-4 times a year by stage. Albuminuria requires 2 of 3 abnormal UACRs within 3-6 months; exercise, infection, fever, heart failure, marked hyperglycemia or marked hypertension can raise UACR

  • Normal to mildly increased: UACR <30 mg/g
  • Moderately increased: 30-299 mg/g
  • Severely increased: ≥300 mg/g

Treatment (ADA 2026):

  • ACEi or ARB with hypertension: recommended for UACR 30-299; strongly for UACR ≥300 and/or eGFR <60; titrate to the maximum tolerated dose. Not for primary prevention when blood pressure, UACR and eGFR are normal; without hypertension, kidney benefit at UACR 30-299 is unproven
  • On ACEi, ARB or MRA: check eGFR and potassium at start and periodically; a creatinine rise up to 30% is not AKI: continue RAS blockade if there is no volume depletion
  • SGLT2 inhibitor: start if eGFR ≥20; can continue until kidney failure
  • GLP-1 RA with proven kidney benefit: recommended in type 2 diabetes with CKD
  • Finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA): recommended with albuminuria if eGFR ≥25; check potassium 1 month after starting. Can be started together with an SGLT2 inhibitor (UACR ≥100, eGFR 30-90, on ACEi or ARB)
  • Blood pressure goal: <130/80 if safely attainable; systolic <120 encouraged
  • Nephrology referral: eGFR <30, rapidly rising albuminuria or falling eGFR, or uncertain cause
DIABETIC NEUROPATHY

Types:

  • Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN): "stocking-glove"; small-fiber pain, burning and tingling; large-fiber numbness, imbalance and loss of protective sensation (ADA 2026)
  • Autonomic: resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, constipation or diarrhea, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, sweating changes. Before diagnosing gastroparesis, exclude drugs (GLP-1-based therapies, opioids) and obstruction (ADA 2026)
  • Mononeuropathies: CN III palsy, carpal tunnel (Practical)
  • Diabetic amyotrophy (lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy): painful proximal leg weakness (Practical)

Screening (ADA 2026): from diagnosis of type 2 and 5 years after type 1, at least yearly: temperature or pinprick plus 128-Hz vibration; 10-g monofilament yearly for ulcer risk; ask about autonomic symptoms. Comprehensive foot exam at least yearly; inspect the feet at every visit if sensory loss or prior ulcer or amputation

Painful Neuropathy Treatment (ADA 2026):

  • Initial: gabapentinoids (pregabalin, gabapentin), SNRIs (duloxetine), tricyclics (amitriptyline), or sodium channel blockers; combinations can add relief
  • Avoid opioids, including tramadol and tapentadol, except in rare circumstances
  • Topical: capsaicin if oral drugs are contraindicated or not preferred; lidocaine patches have limited data (no more than 12 h in 24 h)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Refer promptly: any macular edema, moderate or worse NPDR, or any PDR (ADA 2026)
  • Creatinine up to 30% higher on ACEi or ARB is not AKI; continue if there is no volume depletion (ADA 2026)
  • SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1 RA and finerenone each slow CKD progression; finerenone can start together with an SGLT2 inhibitor (ADA 2026)
  • No opioids (tramadol, tapentadol) for diabetic neuropathic pain (ADA 2026)
  • CN III palsy: pupil sparing favors a microvascular (diabetic) cause; pupil involvement suggests aneurysm and needs urgent imaging (Practical)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Atorvastatin, 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Metformin, 💊 Empagliflozin, 💊 Semaglutide, 💊 Finerenone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated HbA1c, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Elevated LDL, 🔬 Low HDL, 🔬 Elevated Triglycerides

237. SUBCLINICAL HYPOTHYROIDISM

Elevated TSH • Normal T4 • When to Treat
DEFINITION & CAUSES

Definition (AACE/ATA 2012): TSH above the reference range with a normal free T4 (most 4.5-10 mIU/L). Applies only when thyroid function has been stable for weeks or more, the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is normal, and there is no recent or ongoing severe illness

Confirm Before Treating: repeat TSH and free T4 unless TSH >10 mIU/L or pregnant (Practical); with infertility or planning pregnancy, recheck in 4-6 weeks (ATA 2026)

Causes:

  • Chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis: the most common cause in iodine-sufficient areas (AACE/ATA 2012)
  • Recovery from nonthyroidal illness: TSH can rise above normal, generally below 20 mIU/L (AACE/ATA 2012; card 241)
  • Untreated adrenal insufficiency: TSH may be elevated and normalize with glucocorticoids; defer the diagnosis until glucocorticoids are started (AACE/ATA 2012; card 33)
  • Medications: lithium, amiodarone, interferon-alpha, tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib (AACE/ATA 2012); immune checkpoint inhibitors (Practical)
  • Prior radioactive iodine, thyroid surgery, or external beam neck radiation (AACE/ATA 2012)
  • Iodine excess (e.g., kelp) or deficiency (AACE/ATA 2012)
WHEN TO TREAT

Nonpregnant Adults (AACE/ATA 2012):

  • TSH >10 mIU/L: consider levothyroxine (higher risk of heart failure and cardiovascular mortality)
  • TSH above the reference range to 10 mIU/L: individualize; consider treatment particularly with symptoms of hypothyroidism, positive TPO antibodies, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or risk factors for these
  • TPO antibodies: measure when evaluating subclinical hypothyroidism; positive antibodies raise progression to overt hypothyroidism (4.3% vs 2.6% per year) but may or may not change the decision to treat
  • Older adults: mild TSH elevation may be normal aging (12% of people >80 years without thyroid antibodies have TSH >4.5); a lower ischemic heart disease rate with treatment at ages 40-70 was not seen >70 years in one database study
  • Hospitalized: measure TSH only if thyroid dysfunction is suspected; recheck an elevated value after recovery (Practical; card 241)

Pregnancy (ATA 2026):

  • TSH >10 mIU/L: treat with levothyroxine
  • Mild subclinical hypothyroidism found in the first trimester: levothyroxine may be considered
  • Mild subclinical hypothyroidism found after the first trimester: do not offer levothyroxine; recheck TSH in 4-6 weeks
  • TPO antibody status no longer guides the decision; euthyroid TPO positivity is not an indication
  • ACOG (2020) does not recommend treating subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy (via OpenEvidence)

Infertility or Planning Pregnancy (ATA 2026): TSH >10 mIU/L: treat. Otherwise confirm in 4-6 weeks; if persistent, low-dose levothyroxine (25-75 mcg/day) may be started, targeting TSH 0.5-2.5 mU/L

Follow-up if Not Treating: recheck TSH periodically (e.g., every 6-12 months) and with new symptoms (Practical)

TREATMENT

Levothyroxine Dosing:

  • Subclinical hypothyroidism: 25-75 mcg daily, by the degree of TSH elevation (AACE/ATA 2012)
  • Known coronary heart disease: start 12.5-25 mcg/day (AACE/ATA 2012)
  • Combined adrenal insufficiency: glucocorticoids before levothyroxine (AACE/ATA 2012; card 33)
  • Take 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime (3 or more hours after the evening meal) (ATA 2014)
  • Separate from calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate (4 hours is traditional but untested); PPIs and bile acid sequestrants also reduce absorption (ATA 2014)

Monitoring: TSH 4-6 weeks after any dose change (ATA 2014). Nonpregnant: target the laboratory reference range; no evidence supports a specific value within it (AACE/ATA 2012). Pregnant or planning pregnancy: TSH below 2.5 mU/L may be targeted (ATA 2026). Avoid overtreatment: TSH <0.1 mIU/L raises atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis risk, especially in older people and postmenopausal women (ATA 2014)

💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • TSH >10 = consider treating; TSH above the reference range to 10 = individualize (AACE/ATA 2012)
  • Not during acute illness: recovery-phase TSH can exceed the reference range (usually <20); untreated adrenal insufficiency also raises TSH (AACE/ATA 2012)
  • Older adults: mild TSH elevation may be normal aging (AACE/ATA 2012); overtreatment (TSH <0.1) raises atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis risk (ATA 2014)
  • Pregnancy: treat TSH >10; consider treatment only for mild elevation found in the first trimester (ATA 2026)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Levothyroxine
