238. THYROID NODULES

FNA Criteria • TI-RADS • Bethesda System
INITIAL EVALUATION

First Steps (ATA 2015): TSH, and neck ultrasound with a cervical lymph node survey, for every known or suspected nodule

  • Low TSH: radionuclide scan (preferably I-123). A hyperfunctioning ("hot") nodule rarely harbors malignancy: no FNA; evaluate the overt or subclinical hyperthyroidism (ATA 2015; card 31)
  • Normal or high TSH: no radionuclide scan as the first imaging; the ultrasound pattern decides FNA (ATA 2015)
  • Routine serum thyroglobulin is not recommended; no recommendation for or against routine calcitonin (ATA 2015)

Incidental Nodule on CT, MRI, or PET (ATA 2015): dedicated thyroid and neck ultrasound. Focal FDG-PET uptake in a nodule raises cancer risk: FNA if ≥1 cm. Diffuse uptake with ultrasound and clinical evidence of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis needs no further imaging or FNA

Red Flags (ATA 2015): rapid nodule growth, hoarseness or vocal cord paralysis, cervical lymphadenopathy, fixation to surrounding tissue. Progressive dysphagia, respiratory compromise or stridor, or hemoptysis suggests locally invasive disease: contrast CT of the neck. Risk history: childhood head and neck or total-body radiation; family history of thyroid cancer or a syndrome (MEN 2, FAP, Cowden)

Suspicious US Features (ATA 2015): highest specificity (median >90%): microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape

  • Hypoechoic
  • Irregular margins (infiltrative, microlobulated)
  • Taller than wide
  • Microcalcifications
  • Rim calcifications with a small extrusive soft-tissue component
  • Extrathyroidal extension
  • Abnormal cervical lymph nodes (US-guided FNA of suspicious nodes)
FNA INDICATIONS (ATA 2015; ACR TI-RADS 2017)
ATA 2015 US PatternMalignancy RiskFNA Threshold
High suspicion: solid hypoechoic nodule (or solid hypoechoic component) with irregular margins, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape, rim calcifications with extrusive soft tissue, or ETE>70-90%≥1 cm
Intermediate suspicion: hypoechoic solid nodule, smooth margins, none of the above10-20%≥1 cm
Low suspicion: isoechoic or hyperechoic solid nodule, or partially cystic with eccentric solid areas, none of the above5-10%≥1.5 cm
Very low suspicion: spongiform, or partially cystic without any of the above<3%Consider at ≥2 cm, or observe
Benign: purely cystic (no solid component)<1%No FNA (aspirate only for symptoms or cosmesis)

ACR TI-RADS (common on US reports; ACR TI-RADS 2017): TR1 (0 points) and TR2 (2 points): no FNA. TR3 (3 points): FNA if ≥2.5 cm, follow if ≥1.5 cm. TR4 (4-6 points): FNA if ≥1.5 cm, follow if ≥1 cm. TR5 (≥7 points): FNA if ≥1 cm, follow if ≥0.5 cm

Nodules ≤1 cm: FNA not routinely recommended with low-risk features (ATA 2025); biopsy sonographically suspicious lymph nodes (ATA 2015)

BETHESDA SYSTEM 2023 (FNA RESULTS)
CategoryMalignancy Risk, mean (range) (NCCN Thyroid 2026)Management (ATA 2015 unless noted)
I. NondiagnosticNot in library sources (see note)Repeat FNA with US guidance (on-site cytology if available); repeatedly nondiagnostic without a high-suspicion pattern: close observation or surgical excision
II. BenignAbout 4% or lessNo immediate further testing or treatment. Follow-up US by pattern: high suspicion, US and FNA within 12 months; low to intermediate, US at 12-24 months; very low, ≥24 months if repeated. Second benign FNA: stop surveillance for malignancy
III. Atypia of undetermined significance (AUS)22% (13-30%)Repeat FNA or molecular testing; if not done or inconclusive, surveillance or diagnostic surgery
IV. Follicular neoplasm (includes oncocytic)30% (23-34%)Diagnostic surgical excision is the standard; molecular testing may be used first
V. Suspicious for malignancy74% (67-83%)Surgery as for malignant cytology
VI. Malignant97% (97-100%)Surgery generally recommended. Extent (ATA 2025): ≤2 cm without gross ETE, cN0M0: lobectomy; >2-4 cm low risk: lobectomy may be preferred, or total thyroidectomy; >4 cm, gross ETE, or nodal or distant metastases: total thyroidectomy. cT1aN0M0 papillary cancer: active surveillance or US-guided ablation may be offered

Risks include NIFTP (Bethesda 2023, as quoted in NCCN Thyroid 2026); without NIFTP, III-VI are 16%, 23%, 65%, 94%. Category I risk: the 2023 Bethesda paper is not in the library

💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Hot nodule on scan: hyperfunctioning nodules rarely harbor malignancy; no FNA (ATA 2015)
  • Microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape: the most specific US features for thyroid cancer, mostly papillary (ATA 2015)
  • Bethesda III/IV = indeterminate: molecular testing can refine risk before surgery; counsel on its limits and use a CLIA/CAP-certified lab (ATA 2015). If molecular risk is about that of benign cytology (about 4% or less), consider surveillance (NCCN Thyroid 2026). Afirma and ThyroSeq are examples (Practical)
  • A reassuring FNA does not override worrisome clinical or radiographic findings (NCCN Thyroid 2026)

239. THYROIDITIS

Subacute • Silent • Postpartum • Hashimoto's
TYPES OF THYROIDITIS
TypeCausePainRAIUClinical Course
Subacute (de Quervain)Presumed sequel of a viral URI (ATA 2016)YES: moderate to severe, tender thyroid (ATA 2016)LOW (ATA 2016)Thyrotoxic phase in about 50%, lasting 3-6 weeks; hypothyroid phase in about 30%, up to 6 months; euthyroid within 12 months in most; 5-15% persistent hypothyroidism; recurrence 1-4% (ATA 2016)
Silent/PainlessAutoimmune (TPOAb positive in about 50%); also with lithium, interferon-alpha, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ATA 2016)No; ESR and CRP not elevated (ATA 2016)LOW (ATA 2016)Thyrotoxic phase in 5-20%, lasting 3-4 months; hypothyroid phase up to 6 months; 10-20% persistent hypothyroidism; recurrence 5-10% (ATA 2016)
PostpartumAutoimmune, within 12 months of delivery or pregnancy loss (ATA 2026)NoLOW; contraindicated while lactating unless breastfeeding is interrupted (ATA 2026)Thyrotoxicosis 1-6 months postpartum, hypothyroidism 4-8 months, recovery over 2-3 more months (ATA 2026); only 25% have all three phases (ATA 2016)
Hashimoto'sAutoimmune (TPO Ab)NoVariableProgressive hypothyroidism (Practical; card 32)
Drug-inducedAmiodarone (type 1 iodine-induced or type 2 destructive), lithium, interferon-alpha, interleukin-2, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ATA 2016); immune checkpoint inhibitors (ASCO 2021)Usually no (Practical)VariableDepends on drug and type (ATA 2016 Table 16). Checkpoint inhibitor thyroiditis usually resolves in weeks, most often to primary hypothyroidism (ASCO 2021)
Acute (suppurative)Bacterial: hematogenous or via a pyriform sinus fistula (ATA 2016)Yes (Practical)Not used; ultrasound or CT is diagnostic (ATA 2016)Usually euthyroid; antibiotics and drainage (ATA 2016 Rec 119)
SUBACUTE THYROIDITIS (de Quervain)

Presentation: moderate to severe thyroid pain, often radiating to the ears, jaw, or throat, which may spread from one side to the other over weeks; prodrome of malaise, low-grade fever, pharyngitis symptoms, fatigue; firm, tender, slightly enlarged gland (ATA 2016)

Labs and imaging: TSH suppressed in the thyrotoxic phase, free T4 often elevated relative to T3; ESR or CRP elevated (ESR often >50: Practical); mild anemia and leukocytosis common; low-titer thyroid antibodies in up to 25%; low RAIU; ultrasound shows diffuse heterogeneity, focal hypoechoic areas, and decreased or normal Doppler flow (ATA 2016)

Treatment (ATA 2016 Rec 117, strong, low-quality evidence):

  • Mild: beta-blocker as needed for thyrotoxic symptoms plus an NSAID first line; median time to pain resolution with NSAIDs 5 weeks (range 1-20)
  • No response to full-dose NSAIDs over several days, or moderate to severe pain and/or thyrotoxic symptoms: prednisone 40 mg daily for 1-2 weeks, then taper over 2-4 weeks or longer by response. Pain resolves faster than with NSAIDs (mean 8 vs 35 days) but can recur during the taper. A lower start (prednisolone 15 mg, taper by 5 mg every 2 weeks) was also effective; 20% needed more than 8 weeks
  • Hypothyroid phase: levothyroxine may be used, then withdrawn after 3-6 months with thyroid function testing to confirm recovery
  • No antithyroid drugs: no role in destructive thyroiditis, where hormone production is not increased (ATA 2016; ATA 2026)
POSTPARTUM THYROIDITIS

Definition and timing: autoimmune thyroid dysfunction within 12 months after delivery or pregnancy loss; thyrotoxicosis usually 1-6 months postpartum, hypothyroidism usually 4-8 months, then recovery over 2-3 more months (ATA 2026). Only 25% have all three phases; 43% have hypothyroidism alone and 32% thyrotoxicosis alone (ATA 2016)

Risk Factors: TPOAb positivity in the first trimester (risk 33-50%), history of postpartum thyroiditis (70% recurrence), personal history of autoimmune disease, family history of autoimmune thyroid disease (ATA 2026); type 1 diabetes is one such autoimmune disease (Practical)

Postpartum Graves disease vs thyroiditis: thyroiditis starts 1-6 months postpartum, is milder and shorter (thyrotoxic phase 0-3 months), TRAb negative, total T3 (ng/dL) to total T4 (mcg/dL) ratio usually <20; Graves starts 3-12 months postpartum, TRAb positive in most, ratio usually >20 (ATA 2026). Scintigraphy while lactating: pump and discard milk for 3-4 days after I-123 or 36 hours after Tc-99m (ATA 2026)

Management (ATA 2026):

  • Thyrotoxic phase: lowest effective dose of a beta-blocker for symptoms, usually for a few weeks; propranolol or metoprolol if lactating (strong, high-quality evidence). No antithyroid drugs
  • Hypothyroid phase: levothyroxine may be considered if symptomatic, breastfeeding, or pregnancy is planned within 6 months (conditional, low-quality evidence); consider a taper or stop trial after 1 year postpartum if no pregnancy is planned soon. If untreated, recheck thyroid function every 4-8 weeks until euthyroid or persistently hypothyroid, with adequate contraception until thyroid function normalizes
  • Long term: 10-50% of women whose hypothyroid phase resolves later develop permanent hypothyroidism; after normalization, check thyroid function at 1 year or with hypothyroid symptoms (good practice statement)
  • Not recommended: levothyroxine in TPOAb-positive pregnant women to prevent postpartum thyroiditis; routine selenium
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Painful thyroid + elevated ESR + low RAIU = subacute thyroiditis (ATA 2016); early acute suppurative thyroiditis can be mistaken for it, and early imaging may be nonspecific (ATA 2016)
  • Low RAIU distinguishes destructive thyroiditis from Graves disease (high RAIU); TRAb, the T3:T4 ratio, and Doppler flow also help (ATA 2016; ATA 2026)
  • Steroids relieve subacute thyroiditis pain faster than NSAIDs (mean 8 vs 35 days), but pain can recur during the taper (ATA 2016)
  • Checkpoint inhibitor thyroiditis: beta-blocker for symptoms; thyroid function every 2-3 weeks after diagnosis to catch the usual transition to hypothyroidism; low TSH with low free T4 suggests central hypothyroidism (hypophysitis) (ASCO 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Levothyroxine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low TSH, 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 Free T4/Free T3, 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP

240. STEROID-INDUCED HYPERGLYCEMIA

Glucocorticoid Hyperglycemia • Basal-Plus Protocol • Inpatient Management
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY & PATTERN

Mechanism: Glucocorticoids → ↑ hepatic gluconeogenesis + ↑ glycogenolysis + insulin resistance → predominantly postprandial hyperglycemia with relatively preserved fasting glucose (unlike classic T2DM)

Pattern by Steroid Type:

GlucocorticoidTiming of Peak EffectDuration (Practical)Implication
Prednisone/prednisolone (once daily AM)Peak plasma level 4-6 h; glucose normal or mildly high fasting, rising in the afternoon and peaking in the evening (ADA SOC 2026, CGM data)12-16 hrPM glucose spikes most prominent, more so in T2D; NPH with the steroid dose is the usual match
DexamethasoneProlonged, less pronounced peak24-36 hrMore uniform hyperglycemia; fasting affected too; long-acting basal insulin may be needed (ADA SOC 2026)
Methylprednisolone (divided BID-TID)Throughout dayVariableMore consistent elevation; basal-bolus preferred
Hydrocortisone (stress dosing)Around-the-clock8–12 hrContinuous hyperglycemia when used q6-8h
DIAGNOSIS & MONITORING

Who to Monitor: All patients receiving systemic glucocorticoids (not inhaled/topical at standard doses). Up to 10-15% of inpatients receive them and 56-86% of those develop hyperglycemia, with or without diabetes (ADA SOC 2026). Higher risk (Practical): prior diabetes/prediabetes, obesity, family history, high steroid dose (≥20 mg/day prednisone equivalent)

Screening:

  • Check BG at time of steroid administration + 4-6 hours later for first 1-2 days in high-risk patients (Practical)
  • Hyperglycemia is BG >140 mg/dL; start or intensify treatment for persistent BG ≥180 confirmed twice in 24 h (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.4). No prior diabetes: correction insulin first, then scheduled insulin if ≥2 values ≥180 in 24 h (Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 10.1)
  • Pre-existing diabetes: monitor AC/HS (before meals and bedtime) plus targeted PM checks

HbA1c: Order on all patients with steroid-induced hyperglycemia to help separate new steroid-related hyperglycemia from unrecognized pre-existing T2DM; anemia, hemoglobinopathies, CKD, alcohol, drugs and large glucose swings affect HbA1c (Endocrine Society 2022)

TREATMENT PROTOCOLS

Target BG: 100-180 mg/dL non-ICU (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.5b); 140-180 ICU (Rec 16.5a); avoid hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL)

Once-Daily AM Prednisone, NPH-Based Protocol (ADA SOC 2026; Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 2.1: NPH-based or basal-bolus):

  • NPH insulin given with morning prednisone: NPH peaks about 4-6 h after injection, matching intermediate-acting steroids (ADA SOC 2026)
  • NPH can be added to a basal-bolus regimen or to oral agents, depending on the diabetes type and prior treatment (ADA SOC 2026; Endocrine Society 2022)
  • Starting dose (Practical): 0.1 units/kg of NPH if prednisone 20-40 mg/day; 0.2 units/kg if 40-60 mg/day; 0.3+ units/kg if >60 mg/day
  • Titrate NPH by 10-20% every 1-2 days based on afternoon/evening BG readings (Practical); adjust daily to glucose and planned steroid changes (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Add rapid-acting insulin at meals if significant mealtime excursions (>180 mg/dL consistently post-meal)
  • Twice-daily intermediate-acting steroids: divided NPH doses timed to each steroid dose (Endocrine Society 2022)
  • Once-daily AM prednisone: avoid a bedtime NPH dose; the steroid effect wanes overnight and nocturnal hypoglycemia follows (Practical)

Basal-Bolus Protocol (for divided-dose steroids, dexamethasone, high-dose, or complex patients):

  • Calculate TDD: usual start 0.3-0.6 units/kg/day (ADA SOC 2026); lower end for steroid-naive, renal impairment, elderly
  • Start 50% as basal (glargine once daily) and 50% as bolus (lispro/aspart divided among meals); with higher steroid doses, prandial and correction insulin often need to rise 40-60% or more (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Add correction scale for breakthrough hyperglycemia
  • Dexamethasone or multidose/continuous steroids: long-acting basal insulin may be required for fasting glucose (ADA SOC 2026); glargine twice daily is a practice option (Practical)

Mild/Outpatient-Manageable (BG 140–200, low steroid dose):

  • Short courses (<7 days), no prior diabetes: correction insulin with dietary modification, adding scheduled insulin if BG stays ≥180 (Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 10.1)
  • Insulin is preferred in hospital; home oral agents may be continued in selected patients (ADA SOC 2026). Metformin: may continue outpatient if renal function adequate and no contrast planned (Practical)
  • Sulfonylureas: avoid inpatient (unpredictable; hypoglycemia as steroids are tapered) (Practical)

Steroid Taper, Insulin Dose Adjustment:

  • Every regimen needs safeguards against hypoglycemia when steroids are tapered or stopped abruptly (Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 2.1)
  • Reduce insulin proportionally with steroid taper (roughly 20-30% reduction per steroid dose step) (Practical)
  • Monitor closely during taper: hypoglycemia is common if insulin is not adjusted
  • If steroids stopped abruptly: may need to stop NPH entirely; continue basal at 50% if patient has underlying diabetes (Practical)
  • Arrange endocrinology or primary care follow-up for outpatient BG monitoring post-discharge
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • NPH + AM prednisone is the usual match for once-daily steroid regimens: NPH peaks about 4-6 h after the dose, with prednisone's afternoon hyperglycemia (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Fasting glucose is often normal in steroid-induced hyperglycemia; don't be falsely reassured by a normal AM fasting BG; check PM readings (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Steroid-induced hyperglycemia is common (56-86% of treated inpatients, ADA SOC 2026) and is linked to infection, poor wound healing, longer stay and mortality (Practical)
  • Dexamethasone (used for CINV, brain edema, COVID) causes marked, prolonged hyperglycemia (about 25 mg prednisone per 4 mg dexamethasone; Practical); always check BG
  • New hyperglycemia on steroids in a non-diabetic → check HbA1c; if elevated, undiagnosed prediabetes or T2DM is likely; arrange outpatient diabetes follow-up
⚠️ ESCALATE / WATCH FOR:
  • BG persistently >300 despite insulin → consider DKA/HHS workup
  • Hypoglycemia during steroid taper (insulin not reduced proportionally)
  • Hyperosmolar state in elderly on high-dose dexamethasone
  • Steroid + TPN → very high hyperglycemia risk; needs aggressive monitoring
✓ DISCHARGE PLANNING
  • If on NPH inpatient → may transition to glargine outpatient for once-daily convenience
  • Provide patient education on BG monitoring at home during steroid taper, as part of a structured discharge plan (Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 4.1; ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.18)
  • Arrange outpatient follow-up within 1–2 weeks if new hyperglycemia discovered
  • Document steroid-induced hyperglycemia separately from "diabetes" if truly new
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Regular Insulin, 💊 Insulin Glargine, 💊 Insulin Lispro

241. SICK EUTHYROID SYNDROME (NON-THYROIDAL ILLNESS)

TSH Interpretation in Critical Illness • Low T3 Syndrome • Do Not Treat
DEFINITION & PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Definition: Alterations in thyroid hormone levels that occur in the setting of non-thyroidal illness without underlying intrinsic thyroid dysfunction. Also called non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS) or euthyroid sick syndrome.

Pathophysiology:

  • In critical illness T3 falls first, followed by TSH and/or T4, and then free T4 in some sicker patients (ATA 2014): low total and free T3 is the earliest change
  • Increased type 3 deiodinase, which converts T4 to inactive reverse T3 and clears T3, is implicated in the syndrome (ATA 2014); reduced T4-to-T3 conversion also contributes (Practical)
  • In severe illness, falling binding proteins add to the low T4 (Practical)
  • TSH is often low-normal or low during acute illness and may rise transiently during recovery, mimicking hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism respectively (Practical)
  • Whether low T3 is tissue hypothyroidism or an adaptation to illness is unclear (ATA 2014); thyroid hormone treatment has not shown benefit (ATA 2014 recs 22a-22c)
THYROID FUNCTION PATTERNS IN ILLNESS
PatternTSHFree T4T3Most Likely Diagnosis
Low T3 (mild/early illness)Normal or ↓Normal↓↓Nonthyroidal illness, the earliest change (ATA 2014); do not treat (ATA 2014)
Low T3 + Low T4 (severe illness)Normal or ↓↓↓↓Severe nonthyroidal illness; do not treat (ATA 2014); tracks illness severity and mortality (Practical)
TSH suppressed + high free T4↓↓ (<0.1)↑↑ or normalHyperthyroidism likely; exclude biotin and heparin artifacts (ATA 2016). Low TSH with normal free T4: nonthyroidal illness, drug effects, exogenous thyroid hormone, or pituitary disease (ATA 2016)
TSH elevated (recovery phase)↑ (usually <20, Practical)NormalNormalRecovery-phase TSH rise, not hypothyroidism by itself; recheck after recovery (Practical). In known hypothyroidism, a TSH rise while illness is worsening usually means deficiency (ATA 2014)
TSH markedly elevated (>20) + low free T4↑↑ (>20)↓↓Primary hypothyroidism (or myxedema coma) likely; treat (card 32). Cutoff is Practical; no society sets one for acute illness (via OpenEvidence)
Low free T4, TSH low or normal, out of proportion to illness↓ or normal↓↓Consider central hypothyroidism; consider adrenal insufficiency before levothyroxine (ATA 2014 rec 20d; card 243)

Drug and Assay Effects on Thyroid Function Tests:

DrugEffect on TSHEffect on T3/T4Notes
Dopamine, dobutamine↓ (ATA 2014)Not statedCan lead to under-replacement of primary hypothyroidism if dosing follows TSH (ATA 2014)
High-dose glucocorticoids↓ (Practical)↓ T3 (Practical)Practical
AmiodaroneVariable (Practical)↑ T4, ↓ T3, ↑ reverse T3 in clinically euthyroid patients (US label)Inhibits T4-to-T3 conversion; can cause hypothyroidism (up to 10%) or hyperthyroidism (about 2%) (US label). Thyrotoxicosis: type 1 iodine-induced or type 2 destructive thyroiditis (ATA 2016)
HeparinNormal (Practical)Spuriously ↑ free T4In vitro lipoprotein lipase activation releases free fatty acids that displace T4 from binding proteins (ATA 2016)
Biotin (high-dose)Spuriously ↓ (immunometric assays)Spuriously ↑ free T4 (competitive assays)Mimics hyperthyroidism; with high T4 and suppressed TSH, stop biotin and repeat at least 2 days later (ATA 2016)
CLINICAL APPROACH: WHEN TO TREAT

DO NOT treat nonthyroidal illness with thyroid hormone: ATA recommends against levothyroxine in critically ill hospitalized patients with the syndrome (strong; moderate-quality evidence); the few RCTs showed no significant benefit and raised safety concerns. ATA also recommends against liothyronine (weak; no benefit shown, low doses not linked to harm) and against routine liothyronine in heart failure with low T3 (weak) (ATA 2014 recs 22a-22c).

Known hypothyroidism: continue levothyroxine during critical illness; a TSH rise while the illness is worsening usually means deficiency, so start or increase levothyroxine until TSH normalizes (ATA 2014). Not critically ill with an elevated TSH: consider adjusting the dose (ATA 2014 rec 20a). If enteral levothyroxine is not possible, the IV dose is about 75% of the enteral dose (ATA 2014 rec 20c).

When to suspect TRUE thyroid dysfunction in the ICU/inpatient:

  • TSH >20 mIU/L + low free T4 → primary hypothyroidism likely; treat (card 32). Cutoff is Practical (via OpenEvidence)
  • Clinical features of myxedema coma (bradycardia, hypothermia, hypoventilation, profound altered mental status) despite only moderately abnormal TFTs → treat empirically (card 32) (Practical)
  • TSH <0.01 + elevated free T4/T3 + clinical thyrotoxicosis (weight loss, AFib, tremor, tachycardia out of proportion) → treat (card 31) (Practical)
  • Low free T4 with low or normal TSH not explained by illness severity → consider central hypothyroidism; before levothyroxine, rule out adrenal insufficiency or give empiric glucocorticoids (ATA 2014 rec 20d; card 243)
  • History of thyroid disease or thyroidectomy → prior baseline TFTs invaluable; lower threshold to treat (Practical)

Practical Approach to Abnormal TFTs in Hospitalized Patient (Practical unless cited):

  1. Review medications: dopamine, dobutamine (ATA 2014); glucocorticoids; amiodarone (US label); heparin and biotin (assay artifacts, ATA 2016)
  2. Judge severity of illness: the sicker the patient, the more likely the abnormality is nonthyroidal illness
  3. TSH mildly abnormal (0.1-20) and no clinical thyroid syndrome: repeat TFTs 4-6 weeks after recovery, as an outpatient
  4. TSH >20 or <0.01 with clinical suspicion: pursue workup; involve endocrinology
  5. TSH elevated during recovery (common): recheck in 4-6 weeks as an outpatient; usually normalizes
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • "Low T3 = sick patient, not sick thyroid": low T3 is the earliest change in critical illness, and thyroid hormone is not recommended (ATA 2014)
  • Low T3 + low T4 tracks illness severity and mortality (Practical); prognostic only, still not treated (ATA 2014)
  • Recovery-phase TSH rise (usually below 20) is often misread as hypothyroidism and leads to unneeded levothyroxine; recheck TFTs after recovery (Practical). Exception: in known hypothyroidism, a TSH rise while illness is worsening usually means deficiency (ATA 2014)
  • Dopamine and dobutamine lower TSH (ATA 2014), as do high-dose glucocorticoids (Practical): a suppressed TSH in a vasopressor-dependent patient does not diagnose hyperthyroidism
  • Amiodarone raises T4, lowers T3, and raises reverse T3 in euthyroid patients, and can cause hypothyroidism (up to 10%) or hyperthyroidism (about 2%) (US label); see Drug Reference
  • Biotin: high doses give spuriously low TSH and high free T4, mimicking hyperthyroidism; stop biotin and repeat at least 2 days later (ATA 2016)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Levothyroxine, 💊 Amiodarone, 💊 Dopamine, 💊 Dobutamine, 💊 Heparin

242. PERIOPERATIVE GLUCOSE MANAGEMENT

Surgical Hyperglycemia • Insulin Drip Protocols • Transition to Subcutaneous
WHY IT MATTERS

Impact of Perioperative Hyperglycemia: Up to 20% of people having major general surgery have diabetes, and 23-60% have prediabetes or undiagnosed diabetes. Perioperative hyperglycemia is a risk factor for surgical site infection and other complications; the threshold for harm lies somewhere between 100 and 180 mg/dL in most studies (ADA SOC 2026). Basal-bolus coverage after noncardiac general surgery gives better glucose and fewer complications than correction-only insulin (ADA SOC 2026).

Target Glucose Ranges:

SettingTargetNotes
Before, during and after surgery (non-ICU)100-180 mg/dLADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.15; goals may differ by surgery, hypoglycemia risk and therapy. Stricter goals are not advised (no benefit, more hypoglycemia)
ICU, including cardiac surgery140-180 mg/dL (ADA); 140-200 accepted (SCCM 2024)NICE-SUGAR: 80-110 vs 140-180 gave higher mortality (27.5% vs 25%) and 10- to 15-fold more hypoglycemia (ADA SOC 2026). SCCM 2024 manages cardiac surgery like other ICU patients; 110-140 only where hypoglycemia is documented to be negligible
NPO or on insulin infusionMonitoringGlucose at least every 2-4 h while NPO (ADA SOC 2026); at least hourly on an insulin infusion while unstable (SCCM 2024). CGM should not be used alone during surgery (ADA SOC 2026)
Hypoglycemia<70 mg/dLTreat at once; review the regimen after any value <70 (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.13)
PREOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT

Day Before Surgery:

  • A1C: check if not done within 3 months (ACC/AHA 2024, 2a). Preoperative goal <8% (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.14); 14-day CGM GMI <8% or time in range >50% may substitute. Do not postpone surgery on A1C alone (ADA SOC 2026; ACC/AHA 2024: no evidence that deferral improves outcomes)
  • Basal insulin: long-acting analogs to 75-80% of the dose; NPH to one-half; a 25% reduction of the evening-before dose met goals with less hypoglycemia. Individualize: reduction may be inappropriate in some people with T1D (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Discontinue bolus/mealtime insulin while NPO
  • Metformin: ADA SOC 2026 holds it (and other oral agents) on the day of surgery; ACC/AHA 2024 calls continuing it perioperatively reasonable (2a). Iodinated contrast: follow the US label (see Inpatient Insulin)
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: stop canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin ≥3 days and ertugliflozin ≥4 days before scheduled surgery (ACC/AHA 2024; ADA SOC 2026) to reduce perioperative ketoacidosis; after nonelective surgery, monitor for DKA including euglycemic DKA
  • GLP-1 RA or GIP/GLP-1 RA: personalized plan (ADA SOC 2026; multisociety 2024). Continue in patients at low risk of delayed gastric emptying. Higher risk: dose escalation, higher dose, weekly dosing, GI symptoms, gastroparesis or other dysmotility. For them, a 24-h liquid diet before surgery, gastric ultrasound, or full-stomach precautions. If the drug is held: day of surgery for daily agents, 1 week for weekly agents (multisociety 2024), knowing 1 week may not clear gastric contents (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Sulfonylureas: hold day of surgery (hypoglycemia risk while NPO); other oral agents also held on the day of surgery (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Avoid carbohydrate-containing oral fluids before surgery in people with diabetes (Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 8.1)

Morning of Surgery (NPO):

  • Check BG on arrival to preop; target 100-180 (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.15)
  • BG >180: correction insulin (regular insulin 0.05-0.1 units/kg SC or initiate IV insulin drip) (Practical)
  • BG >250: consider delaying elective surgery; workup for DKA/HHS if symptomatic (Practical)
  • BG <100: give D5W IV infusion at 75-100 mL/hr until OR (Practical)
  • Insulin pump: may continue during surgery under institutional policy; if not, start an insulin infusion or basal plus correction before surgery (ADA SOC 2026)
INTRAOPERATIVE & POSTOPERATIVE PROTOCOLS

Intraoperative Insulin Infusion (for major surgery, cardiac, prolonged procedures):

  • Initiate IV regular insulin infusion for BG persistently ≥180 in major surgery or the ICU (SCCM 2024)
  • Use the institution's validated protocol with explicit, preferably computerized decision support (SCCM 2024)
  • Standard concentration: Regular insulin 1 unit/mL in NS (100 units in 100 mL NS) (Practical)
  • Starting rate if no protocol is available (Practical): BG 180-240 → 1-2 units/hr; BG 241-300 → 2-3 units/hr; BG >300 → 3-4 units/hr
  • Check BG at least hourly while on infusion and unstable (SCCM 2024); titrate by 0.5-1 unit/hr increments (Practical)
  • Run concurrent D5W or D10W IV at 75-100 mL/hr to prevent hypoglycemia (especially for NPO patients) (Practical)

Postoperative, Subcutaneous Insulin (when eating):

  • Transition from IV insulin to subcutaneous when patient tolerating oral intake reliably
  • Give SC basal insulin 2 h before stopping the infusion to prevent a hyperglycemia gap (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Calculate SC TDD from IV needs: about 60% of the TDD extrapolated from the last 6-8 h of the infusion (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Distribute as 50% basal (glargine) + 50% nutritional (lispro/aspart at meals) (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Known diabetes on insulin: about 80% of the home insulin dose (ADA SOC 2026)

Postoperative, NPO or Minimal PO (clear liquids only):

  • Basal insulin or basal plus correction (ADA SOC 2026 Rec 16.8b); hold prandial insulin; basal reduction depends on the insulin (see Day Before Surgery)
  • Correction insulin every 4-6 h for hyperglycemia (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Provide IV dextrose if at hypoglycemia risk (D5W or D10W at maintenance rate) (Practical)

Special Situations:

SituationManagement
Cardiac surgery (CABG/valve)IV insulin drip for BG ≥180 intraoperatively and in the ICU; ICU goal as in the table above (ADA 140-180; SCCM accepts 140-200 and does not treat cardiac surgery differently); transition to SC when hemodynamically stable and eating
Post-op corticosteroids (dexamethasone for PONV, spine, brain surgery)Anticipate steroid-induced hyperglycemia; NPH-based or basal-bolus insulin (Endocrine Society 2022 Rec 2.1). NPH with intermediate-acting steroids; long-acting basal for dexamethasone or multidose steroids (ADA SOC 2026). See Steroid-Induced Hyperglycemia protocol
TPN post-operativelyAdd regular insulin to the TPN bag, especially if >20 units of correction insulin were needed in 24 h: start 1 unit per 10 g of dextrose and adjust daily; SC correction insulin as needed (ADA SOC 2026)
Enteral tube feeds (continuous)Do not cover the feeds with basal insulin alone (hypoglycemia risk). Basal plus nutritional insulin, about 1 unit per 10-15 g carbohydrate, as rapid-acting every 4 h, regular every 6 h, or NPH every 8-12 h, plus correction. If feeds are interrupted, give IV dextrose for the duration of active insulin (ADA SOC 2026)
New hyperglycemia, non-diabeticCheck HbA1c; stress hyperglycemia common; if resolves with discharge and HbA1c normal → arrange outpatient BG monitoring and primary care follow-up
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • NICE-SUGAR trial (NEJM 2009): Tight glycemic control (80-110 mg/dL) in ICU → increased mortality vs 140-180 target, with 10- to 15-fold more hypoglycemia (ADA SOC 2026).
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: stop ≥3 days pre-op (ertugliflozin ≥4); euglycemic DKA can present post-op with normal BG but anion gap acidosis and positive ketones. See Euglycemic DKA
  • GLP-1 RAs: personalized plan, not an automatic 1-week hold; one week off a weekly agent may not clear gastric contents (ADA SOC 2026), and many low-risk patients can continue (multisociety 2024)
  • Give SC basal insulin 2 h before stopping the IV drip; stopping the drip without SC coverage causes a hyperglycemia gap (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Hypoglycemia is more dangerous than hyperglycemia in the OR and ICU; run concurrent dextrose when using IV insulin infusion in NPO patients (Practical)
⚠️ HIGH-RISK SCENARIOS:
  • Post-op BG >250 → check ketones/anion gap (euglycemic DKA if SGLT2i use)
  • Cardiac surgery patient: BG >180 in ICU → IV insulin drip
  • New BG >300 in non-diabetic post-op → DKA/HHS workup
  • Insulin drip + NPO without dextrose → hypoglycemia risk
✓ MEDICATION HOLD SUMMARY
  • Hold day of surgery: Bolus insulin, sulfonylureas, TZDs, DPP-4 inhibitors and other oral agents (ADA SOC 2026)
  • Metformin: held day of surgery (ADA SOC 2026) or continued (ACC/AHA 2024, 2a)
  • Hold ≥3 days pre-op: SGLT2 inhibitors (≥4 days for ertugliflozin)
  • GLP-1 RAs: personalized; if held, day of surgery (daily) or 1 week (weekly)
  • Reduce and continue: Basal insulin (analogs 75-80%, NPH one-half)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Regular Insulin, 💊 Insulin Glargine, 💊 Dextrose D50/D10, 💊 Metformin, 💊 Glucagon

243. PITUITARY APOPLEXY

Hemorrhage / Infarction of Pituitary • Neuro-Endocrine Emergency • Surgical vs Medical
DEFINITION & PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Definition: Sudden hemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary gland, usually within a pre-existing pituitary adenoma and evolving over hours or days (UK 2011, non-US); the adenoma is often previously undiagnosed (Practical). Rapid expansion in the sella turcica compresses the optic chiasm, cavernous sinus, and adjacent cranial nerves. Subclinical hemorrhagic infarction (about 25%), found on imaging or histology, is not apoplexy (UK 2011, non-US).

Precipitating Factors (UK 2011, non-US):

  • Systemic hypertension (26%), the most common
  • Major surgery, especially coronary artery bypass (blood pressure swings on bypass, anticoagulation)
  • Dynamic pituitary testing (GnRH, TRH, CRH)
  • Anticoagulation, coagulopathy
  • Starting or stopping a dopamine agonist
  • Estrogen therapy, radiation therapy, pregnancy, head trauma
  • Sheehan syndrome is a separate entity: postpartum necrosis of a non-adenomatous, hyperplastic gland (via OpenEvidence); see pearls
  • Often no identifiable precipitant (Practical)
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Key Features (frequencies, UK 2011, non-US):

  • Sudden severe headache: the earliest and most common symptom (up to 100%); usually retro-orbital, can be bifrontal or diffuse, often with nausea and vomiting (UK 2011, non-US). Can mimic SAH (Practical)
  • Visual disturbance: reduced acuity and field defects, especially bitemporal hemianopia, in about 75% (optic chiasm compression) (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Ocular palsy: about 70% (cavernous sinus compression); CN III is affected in about 50% of those with palsies (UK 2011, non-US). CN III palsy: ptosis, dilated pupil, down-and-out eye (Practical)

Additional Features:

  • Blood or necrotic tissue in the subarachnoid space can cause meningism, fever, photophobia, and altered consciousness (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Altered mental status from mass effect or acute hypocortisolism (Practical)
  • Acute adrenal insufficiency (most critical): in about two-thirds of patients and the major source of mortality (UK 2011, non-US); hypotension, nausea, hyponatremia (up to 40%, from SIADH or hypocortisolism) (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Fever (if hemorrhage causing meningeal irritation)
DIAGNOSIS

Imaging (emergent):

  • MRI pituitary: urgent in all suspected cases to confirm the diagnosis; MRI and MR angiography also help exclude an aneurysm (UK 2011, non-US). Signal depends on the age of the blood: T1 hyperintensity marks subacute blood, while hyperacute and acute blood is often iso- to hypointense on T1 (via OpenEvidence)
  • Dedicated pituitary CT: if MRI is contraindicated or not possible (UK 2011, non-US). CT was diagnostic in only 21-28% of cases, though it showed a sellar mass in up to 80% (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Do not delay steroid treatment for imaging when the patient is unstable (Practical)

Eyes: visual acuity, fields to confrontation, and eye movements at the bedside; formal perimetry (Humphrey or Goldmann) once stable, preferably within 24 h (UK 2011, non-US)

Labs (urgent, drawn before hydrocortisone if this causes no delay):

  • Random cortisol, prolactin, free T4, TSH, IGF-1, GH, LH, FSH, testosterone (men) or estradiol (women), electrolytes, renal and liver function, full blood count, clotting screen (UK 2011, non-US); ACTH may be added (Practical)
  • Test all patients for acute pituitary insufficiency (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 3.23)
  • Do not let a random cortisol value delay hydrocortisone in an unstable patient (Practical). Stable patients without criteria for empiric steroids: consider steroids if 9 am cortisol is <550 nmol/L (about 20 mcg/dL) (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Low prolactin at presentation: highest intrasellar pressure and least likely recovery of pituitary function after decompression (UK 2011, non-US)
  • LP: only if MRI/CT is not diagnostic and SAH must be excluded; RBCs or xanthochromia may come from the apoplexy itself (Practical)
TREATMENT

1. Immediate: Adrenal Crisis Treatment (DO NOT DELAY):

  • Empiric hydrocortisone if hemodynamic instability, altered consciousness, reduced visual acuity, or severe visual field defects, after drawing baseline labs (UK 2011, non-US). Continue glucocorticoids until a laboratory diagnosis is established and pituitary function is shown to be normal (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 3.24)
  • Apoplexy regimen: hydrocortisone 100-200 mg IV bolus, then 2-4 mg/h by continuous IV infusion or 50-100 mg IM every 6 h (UK 2011, non-US); ES 2016 hypopituitarism text gives the same doses. Intermittent IV injections are less favoured (UK 2011, non-US)
  • General adrenal crisis regimen: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM, then 200 mg/24 h by continuous IV infusion, or 50 mg IV every 6 h if an infusion is not feasible (ESE/ES 2024; card 33). The infusion rates differ (2-4 mg/h vs about 8 mg/h); neither source gives every-8-hour dosing
  • Fluids and electrolytes: careful assessment and supportive measures for hemodynamic stability (UK 2011, non-US); isotonic saline as for adrenal crisis (card 33)
  • Anticoagulated or coagulopathic: reverse according to the agent (card 116) (Practical)

2. Neurosurgical vs Conservative Management (decided by a multidisciplinary team: neurosurgery, endocrinology, ophthalmology; stabilize medically first, with steroids if needed) (UK 2011, non-US):

ApproachIndicationsKey Points
Surgery (transsphenoidal)Severely reduced visual acuity; severe and persistent or deteriorating visual field defects; deteriorating level of consciousness (UK 2011, non-US). Apoplexy with visual disturbance (ES 2011 pituitary incidentaloma). Hydrocephalus: external ventricular drain (UK 2011, non-US)Preferably within 7 days of symptom onset; an experienced pituitary surgeon rather than the on-call team unless immediate intervention is needed (UK 2011, non-US)
Conservative (medical) managementNo neuro-ophthalmic signs, or mild and stable signs (UK 2011, non-US). Ocular palsy without loss of acuity or fields is not by itself an indication for immediate surgery (UK 2011, non-US)Acuity and fields daily until clearly improving; neurological checks hourly while acutely unwell, then every 4-6 h; renal function and electrolytes daily; new or worsening visual or neurological deficit: urgent imaging and consider surgery. Ocular palsies typically resolve within days or weeks (UK 2011, non-US)

Pituitary Apoplexy Score (UK 2011, non-US; designed to monitor conservatively managed patients and audit outcomes; no treatment threshold given): consciousness: GCS 15 = 0, GCS 8-14 = 2, GCS <8 = 4; visual acuity: normal = 0, reduced in one eye = 1, both = 2; visual fields: normal = 0, defect in one eye = 1, both = 2; ocular paresis: absent = 0, one side = 1, both = 2

3. Hormone Replacement (panhypopituitarism workup):

  • Cortisol (most urgent): stress dosing as above, then taper quickly to maintenance once recovered: hydrocortisone 20-30 mg/day orally, usually in three doses (UK 2011, non-US), vs 15-20 mg/day in one to three doses, largest on waking (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 2.1). Reassess ACTH reserve 2-3 months after the episode resolves (UK 2011, non-US); lifelong if the ACTH axis does not recover (Practical)
  • After surgery: no cortisol deficiency before surgery: 9 am cortisol on days 2 and 3, omitting the previous evening dose if on hydrocortisone; proven deficiency: continue hydrocortisone and reassess at 4-8 weeks. Free T4 and TSH on day 3 or 4; replace if deficient (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Thyroid: start levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism only with the adrenal axis covered. ES suggests evaluating for adrenal insufficiency first, or empiric glucocorticoids until evaluated (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 2.20, weak); the US label is stricter: glucocorticoids first, and uncorrected adrenal insufficiency is a contraindication (US label, via OpenEvidence). About 1.6 mcg/kg/day, titrated to free T4 in the mid to upper half of the reference range, not to TSH (ES 2016 hypopituitarism recs 2.6, 2.8)
  • Testosterone/estrogen: Assess after acute phase; replace if gonadotropin deficiency confirmed and no contraindications
  • GH: Assess and replace in outpatient setting (not acute priority)
  • Diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency): transient DI after surgery in up to 16% of apoplexy patients; after surgery, hourly fluid balance, and if DI is suspected check electrolytes and plasma and urine osmolality at once (UK 2011, non-US). Diagnostic criteria and desmopressin: card 100
  • Follow-up: endocrine review at 4-8 weeks with full pituitary testing and formal eye assessment, then annual pituitary function testing; MRI at 3-6 months, then annually for 5 years, then every 2 years (UK 2011, non-US). Monitor pituitary axes after surgery or conservative care, because hypopituitarism may develop over time (ES 2016 hypopituitarism rec 3.25)

4. Consultations: Neurosurgery (urgent), ophthalmology (visual fields), endocrinology; transfer to a neurosurgical/endocrine unit with high-dependency care once medically stable (UK 2011, non-US)

💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Acute severe headache, with or without visual or eye-movement signs: consider pituitary apoplexy (UK 2011, non-US); do not anchor solely on SAH (Practical)
  • Acute adrenal insufficiency is the most immediately life-threatening complication; in an unstable patient give hydrocortisone after drawing baseline labs (UK 2011, non-US), without waiting for imaging (Practical)
  • Glucocorticoids before thyroid hormone: the US levothyroxine label requires glucocorticoid replacement before starting treatment (US label, via OpenEvidence)
  • Ocular palsy alone is not an indication for immediate surgery; CN III, IV, and VI palsies typically resolve within days or weeks with conservative management (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary infarction after hemorrhagic shock) is distinct from adenoma apoplexy: the gland is non-adenomatous and hyperplastic (via OpenEvidence); failure to lactate, amenorrhea, fatigue after delivery (Practical)
  • Prolactin: an elevated level does not exclude apoplexy (Practical). Stalk compression by a nonfunctioning mass raises prolactin; in 226 nonfunctioning macroadenomas, prolactin >94 mcg/L separated prolactinomas from nonfunctioning adenomas (ES 2011 hyperprolactinemia)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU / NEUROSURGERY IF:
  • Progressive visual loss or complete visual field defect
  • Hemodynamic instability from adrenal crisis
  • Deteriorating consciousness / GCS decline
  • Severe hyponatremia (<125 mEq/L)
  • Large hemorrhage with midline shift or suprasellar extension
✓ MONITORING PRIORITIES
  • Visual acuity and fields daily until clearly improving (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Neurological checks hourly while acutely unwell, then every 4-6 h when stable (UK 2011, non-US)
  • Renal function and electrolytes daily (UK 2011, non-US); more often for hyponatremia (Practical)
  • After surgery: hourly fluid balance; labs at least daily (UK 2011, non-US)
  • New or worsening visual or neurological deficit: urgent MRI and neurosurgical review; no routine early repeat MRI is set, and the first scheduled MRI is at 3-6 months (UK 2011, non-US)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Hydrocortisone, 💊 Levothyroxine
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low Cortisol, 🔬 ACTH, 🔬 Prolactin, 🔬 IGF-1

244. MALE HYPOGONADISM

Primary vs Secondary • Testosterone Replacement • Monitoring
CLASSIFICATION
TypeLocationLH/FSHCauses
Primary (Hypergonadotropic)Testicular failureHIGHKlinefelter (XXY), orchitis, trauma, radiation, chemotherapy
Secondary (Hypogonadotropic)Pituitary/hypothalamicLOW/NormalPituitary tumor, hyperprolactinemia, Kallmann syndrome, opioids, obesity
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Symptoms: Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, decreased muscle mass, increased body fat, mood changes, decreased bone density

Diagnosis: symptoms and/or signs plus consistently low testosterone (ES 2018; AUA 2018); no routine screening of the general population (ES 2018)

  • Two early-morning total testosterone levels on separate days (fasting, accurate assay, ES 2018; same laboratory and method preferred, AUA 2018)
  • Cutoff (the sources differ): AUA 2018, <300 ng/dL; ES 2018, harmonized lower limit 264 ng/dL (9.2 nmol/L) for CDC-certified assays
  • Do not test during or while recovering from acute illness, or during short-term opioid use (ES 2018). Opioids, glucocorticoids, obesity and systemic illness cause functional, potentially reversible hypogonadism (ES 2018)
  • Free testosterone (equilibrium dialysis or an accurate formula; not direct analog immunoassay) if total T is near the lower limit or SHBG is altered (ES 2018)
  • LH (and FSH) to separate primary from secondary (ES 2018; AUA 2018)
  • Low or low-normal LH: prolactin (AUA 2018; ES 2018), iron saturation (ES 2018); pituitary MRI if total testosterone <150 ng/dL regardless of prolactin (AUA 2018), or in selected cases (ES 2018)
  • Primary of unknown cause, especially testicular volume <6 mL: karyotype for Klinefelter syndrome (ES 2018)
TREATMENT

Who to Treat: symptomatic hypogonadism; not routinely all men ≥65 with low testosterone (individualize); not to improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetes (ES 2018). Counsel all on lifestyle (AUA 2018); functional causes may reverse with treatment of the cause (ES 2018)

Testosterone Replacement Options (typical starting doses) (ES 2018):

  • IM injection: testosterone cypionate or enanthate 150-200 mg every 2 weeks or 75-100 mg weekly; levels peak then fall by the end of the interval
  • Topical gel: 1% gel 50-100 mg, 1.62% gel 20.25-81 mg, or 2% gel 40-70 mg daily. Boxed warning: virilization in children after secondary exposure; children should avoid unwashed or unclothed application sites (US label); discuss transference (AUA 2018)
  • Transdermal patch: 2-4 mg daily; skin irritation common
  • Nasal gel: 11 mg two or three times daily
  • SC pellets: 600-1200 mg implanted; levels sustained 3-6 months
  • Target: mid-normal range (ES 2018); middle tertile, 450-600 ng/dL (AUA 2018)

Do Not Start:

  • Planning fertility in the near term or trying to conceive (testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis) (ES 2018; AUA 2018)
  • Breast or prostate cancer; palpable prostate nodule or induration; PSA >4 ng/mL, or >3 ng/mL with high prostate cancer risk, without urologic evaluation (ES 2018). AUA 2018: measure PSA before starting in all men over 40
  • Hematocrit (the sources differ): ES 2018, baseline >48% (>50% at high altitude) is a relative contraindication; AUA 2018, baseline >50%, consider withholding until the cause is investigated
  • Untreated severe sleep apnea; severe lower urinary tract symptoms (ES 2018)
  • Uncontrolled heart failure; thrombophilia; recent MI or stroke (ES 2018: within the last 6 months; AUA 2018: wait 3-6 months after a cardiovascular event)

Label status (FDA): February 2025: cardiovascular-risk language removed from the boxed warning after TRAVERSE; blood pressure warnings added. June 2026: FDA requested further changes (remove the age-related hypogonadism limitation; contraindicate only in metastatic prostate cancer). Check the current product label

Monitoring:

  • Testosterone 3-6 months after starting (ES 2018; AUA 2018 times the first check by formulation), then every 6-12 months (AUA 2018); injections: check midway between doses and adjust if >600 or <350 ng/dL (ES 2018)
  • Hematocrit: baseline, 3-6 months, then yearly (ES 2018). On therapy ≥54%: ES 2018, stop until it falls to a safe level, evaluate for hypoxia and sleep apnea, restart at a lower dose; AUA 2018, intervene (dose reduction or temporary discontinuation)
  • Prostate (men 55-69, or 40-69 at high risk, who choose monitoring): PSA and DRE at baseline and 3-12 months; urology referral for a confirmed PSA rise >1.4 ng/mL in 12 months, confirmed PSA >4.0, or an abnormal DRE (ES 2018)
  • BMD after 1-2 years in men with osteoporosis (ES 2018). Stopping: consider at 3-6 months if levels normalize without symptom improvement (AUA 2018)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Two early-morning testosterone levels, never during acute illness or short-term opioid use (ES 2018; AUA 2018)
  • Testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis: do not start if conception is planned. Fertility options (the sources differ): ES 2018, gonadotropins restore fertility in secondary (not primary) hypogonadism and clomiphene is empiric and unproven; AUA 2018, aromatase inhibitors, hCG, SERMs or a combination may be used
  • Hematocrit ≥54% on therapy: stop or reduce the dose and look for hypoxia or sleep apnea (ES 2018; AUA 2018)
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 FSH/LH/Testosterone/Estradiol

245. ZOLLINGER-ELLISON SYNDROME

Gastrinoma • Refractory PUD • MEN1 Association
CLINICAL FEATURES

Presentation:

  • Severe and refractory gastroduodenal ulcers or dyspepsia, usually with diarrhea (NCCN 2026)
  • Suspect with peptic ulcers that are multiple, recurrent, refractory, in atypical locations, or without H. pylori or NSAID use; severe GERD; diarrhea that responds to PPI (ENETS 2023, non-US)
  • Early PPI use blunts symptoms; only a minority now have multiple ulcers (ENETS 2023, non-US)
  • Diarrhea and steatorrhea can occur (Thakker 2012); duodenal acid can destroy pancreatic enzymes and cause exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (AGA 2023 EPI); increased luminal acidity inhibits lipase and fat digestion (Merck 2025)

Location and Behavior: Duodenum 60-70%, pancreas 20-30%, lymph nodes about 10-20%, mostly within the gastrinoma triangle; nodal metastases in about 80% even when under 5 mm (ENETS 2023, non-US). Malignant in 60-90% (NANETS 2020; Metz 2017). MEN1 in about 20% (Thakker 2012) to 20-30% (ENETS 2023, non-US); about 70% of MEN1 gastrinomas are duodenal (NCCN 2026)

DIAGNOSIS

Fasting Serum Gastrin (First Test): If normal on repeat testing, ZES is essentially excluded (over 97%) (Metz 2017). Most high gastrin levels come from achlorhydria or PPI or antacid use, not gastrinoma (NCCN 2026). Diagnostic: gastrin over 10 times ULN (generally over 1000 pg/mL) with gastric pH 2 or less, off PPI (Metz 2017; ENETS 2023, non-US); only about 32% of ZES patients meet both (Metz 2017)

Secretin Stimulation Test (gastrin under 10 times ULN with gastric pH 2 or less; Metz 2017): fast at least 12 hours; human secretin 0.4 mcg/kg IV over 1 minute; gastrin twice at baseline, then at 1, 2, 5, 10, and 30 minutes. Positive: rise of more than 110 pg/mL over baseline on any sample (ChiRhoStim label), or 120 pg/mL or more (sensitivity 94%, specificity 100%; Metz 2017). Stop H2 blockers at least 2 days before; for PPIs, follow each PPI label (ChiRhoStim label). False positives with H2 blockers or PPIs (ChiRhoStim label) and with achlorhydria (Metz 2017). Alternative: basal acid output over 15 mEq/h, or over 5 after acid-reducing surgery (Metz 2017). ENETS 2023, non-US: secretin testing and basal acid output have disappeared from clinical practice

Confirm Acid Hypersecretion (Gastric pH 2 or Less) Safely: Gastrin is ideally checked fasting and off PPI for more than 1 week, but continue a PPI or H2 blocker if symptoms are overt or complications are a risk; input from a gastroenterologist familiar with ZES is encouraged (NCCN 2026). Stopping a PPI can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforation (ENETS 2023, non-US). Supervised approach: endoscopy first; heal any active ulcer on PPI before holding it; check gastric pH and fasting gastrin at that endoscopy; prominent gastric folds are seen in over 90% of ZES. Then hold PPI doses, or (likely safer) switch to an H2 blocker and hold it 12-30 hours before gastric pH and gastrin, under close supervision; the patient must report acid-peptic symptoms at once, because massive GI bleeding can occur quickly (Metz 2017)

Localization: Multiphasic CT or MRI of the abdomen, with or without pelvis, for all; as appropriate, somatostatin receptor (SSTR) PET/CT or PET/MRI (Ga-68 DOTATATE, Cu-64 DOTATATE, or Ga-68 DOTATOC), chest CT, and EUS with or without biopsy after multidisciplinary discussion (NCCN 2026). SSTR-PET should replace In-111 pentetreotide scanning (Octreoscan); EUS detects multifocal disease in MEN1 (NANETS 2020)

Screen Every ZES Patient for MEN1: Genetic counseling and testing for every gastrinoma (NCCN 2026). Screen at diagnosis and again over time, because hyperparathyroidism does not always come before ZES (Metz 2017): calcium and PTH (Thakker 2012). In MEN1, ZES does not appear to develop without hyperparathyroidism, and restoring normal calcium improves ZES in as many as 20% (Thakker 2012). If MEN1: calcium and albumin yearly; prolactin, IGF-1, and pituitary MRI every 3-5 years, plus the rest of MEN1 surveillance (NCCN 2026)

TREATMENT
  • Acid control first, with high-dose PPI (NCCN 2026); almost all gastrinomas can be controlled this way (ENETS 2023, non-US). Pantoprazole 40 mg orally twice daily, adjusted to need; doses up to 240 mg/day have been given. IV 80 mg every 12 hours, or every 8 hours if a higher dose is needed (Protonix labels). ENETS 2023, non-US: omeprazole 60 mg/day or equivalent; MEN1 may need 80-120 mg/day. Long term: monitor B12, magnesium, and fracture risk (ENETS 2023, non-US); B12 deficiency and low magnesium are label warnings (Protonix labels)
  • Sporadic, localized: resect (NCCN 2026; NANETS 2020) with systematic lymphadenectomy (ENETS 2023, non-US). Node resection raises biochemical cure and improves survival; biochemical cure is about 60% right after surgery and 30-40% at 5 years (NANETS 2020). Continue PPI at least 3-6 months after curative resection (ENETS 2023, non-US)
  • Not seen on imaging: observation, or exploratory surgery with duodenotomy, intraoperative ultrasound, local resection, and periduodenal node dissection; no pancreatoduodenectomy without tumor localization (NCCN 2026). Refer to a center with gastrinoma expertise; explore only there, and not routinely (NANETS 2020)
  • MEN1: PPI for most (Thakker 2012); surgery most reasonable with nodal metastases, poorly controlled symptoms, or pancreatic-NET-dominant disease (NANETS 2020); consider surgery for symptoms refractory to medical therapy, tumor over 2 cm, or relatively rapid growth over 6-12 months (NCCN 2026). Treat hyperparathyroidism; normal calcium can lessen ZES (Thakker 2012; ENETS 2023)
  • Somatostatin analogs for symptom or tumor control: octreotide LAR 20-30 mg IM or lanreotide 120 mg SC every 4 weeks; octreotide 100-250 mcg SC three times daily for breakthrough symptoms (NCCN 2026). Lanreotide is for deep SC injection only; FDA approved for unresectable, well- or moderately differentiated, locally advanced or metastatic GEP-NETs to improve progression-free survival; monitor for gallstones and glucose changes (Somatuline label)
  • Metastatic: resect metastases and primary if possible and clinically indicated; octreotide LAR or lanreotide; other systemic or locoregional therapy for progression (NCCN 2026)
  • After resection: exam, multiphasic CT or MRI, and biochemical markers as clinically indicated at 12 weeks to 12 months, then every 6-12 months up to 10 years (NCCN 2026); measure gastrin at each follow-up (ENETS 2023, non-US)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Gastrin over 10 times ULN plus gastric pH 2 or less, off PPI, establishes ZES (Metz 2017)
  • Never stop a PPI abruptly to test: keep a PPI or H2 blocker if symptomatic or at risk (NCCN 2026); withdrawal can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforation (ENETS 2023); use a supervised protocol (Metz 2017)
  • Genetic testing for MEN1 in every gastrinoma (NCCN 2026)
  • SSTR-PET, not Octreoscan, for localization (NANETS 2020)
  • Most gastrinomas are duodenal; 60-90% are malignant (ENETS 2023; NANETS 2020)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pantoprazole, 💊 Octreotide

246. SMALL INTESTINAL BACTERIAL OVERGROWTH (SIBO)

Malabsorption • Breath Testing • Rifaximin
RISK FACTORS & PRESENTATION

Risk Factors (consider SIBO whenever there is small-bowel stasis; AGA 2020):

  • Anatomic or postsurgical: blind loops, Roux-en-Y, Billroth II gastrectomy, ileocecal valve resection, small bowel diverticulosis, fistulas (AGA 2020 Table 1; ACG 2020); strictures (Crohn disease, radiation, surgery) are listed by AGA 2020, but ACG 2020 finds no solid validation
  • Motility: scleroderma, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, gastroparesis, intestinal pseudo-obstruction, amyloidosis, hypothyroidism; opioids and other motility-slowing drugs (ACG 2020 Table 4; AGA 2020 Table 1)
  • Low gastric acid: autoimmune gastritis, gastrectomy; PPI use is associated with up to 3-fold risk in a meta-analysis, but the link is debated (ACG 2020)
  • Immune: IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency, HIV (ACG 2020 Table 4)
  • Other: older age, chronic pancreatitis, celiac disease, Crohn disease, cirrhosis, end-stage renal disease (ACG 2020; AGA 2020 Table 1)

Symptoms: Bloating is the most common symptom (ACG 2020), but diarrhea has the strongest association with SIBO (AGA 2020). Also gas, flatulence, distension, abdominal pain, nausea; no symptom is specific (ACG 2020). Steatorrhea and weight loss mainly in severe cases or with blind loops or other structural causes (ACG 2020; AGA 2020)

Deficiencies: Uncommon; usually with blind loops or other structural causes (ACG 2020; AGA 2020). Low B12 (bacteria consume it) with normal or high folate (bacteria make it); fat-soluble vitamin deficiency from bile acid deconjugation (AGA 2020); iron and vitamin D deficiency in severe cases (ACG 2020). Vitamin K can rise, so warfarin dose may need adjustment (AGA 2020). Fecal calprotectin is not useful to detect SIBO (AGA 2020)

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Diagnosis:

  • Whom to test (conditional, very low evidence): symptoms with IBS, a suspected motility disorder, or previous luminal abdominal surgery; methane testing for symptoms with constipation; do not test asymptomatic patients on PPIs (ACG 2020)
  • Breath test: 75 g glucose or 10 g lactulose. Positive: hydrogen rise of 20 ppm or more above baseline within 90 minutes. Methane 10 ppm or more at any point indicates intestinal methanogen overgrowth (IMO), not SIBO (ACG 2020, using the North American Consensus)
  • Breath test preparation: no antibiotics for 4 weeks; no promotility agents or laxatives for at least 1 week; avoid fermentable foods the day before; fast 8-12 hours; no smoking and minimal exertion during the test (ACG 2020)
  • Breath test limits: against aspirate culture, lactulose sensitivity 31-68% and specificity 44-100%; glucose sensitivity 20-93% and specificity 30-86%; lactulose gives false positives with rapid transit; glucose can miss distal SIBO (ACG 2020)
  • Small bowel aspirate culture: 103 CFU/mL or more (ACG 2020; over 103 coliforms/mL, AGA 2020); often considered the gold standard but invasive; agrees with breath testing in about 65% (ACG 2020)

Treatment:

  • Antibiotics for symptomatic SIBO (conditional, low evidence); try to confirm SIBO objectively before treating (ACG 2020)
  • Rifaximin: 550 mg PO three times daily (ACG 2020 Table 5) or 800-1200 mg/day in divided doses (AGA 2020 Table 2); about 70% eradication in a meta-analysis (ACG 2020; AGA 2020). In the US, SIBO is not a recognized indication for rifaximin, and insurance may not cover it (AGA 2020)
  • Duration: a single 7-10 day course improves symptoms in 46-90% (AGA 2020); rifaximin trials used 5-28 days (ACG 2020)
  • Alternatives (ACG 2020 Table 5 doses): amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg BID; ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID; doxycycline 100 mg daily to BID; metronidazole 250 mg TID; neomycin 500 mg BID; tetracycline 250 mg QID; TMP-SMX 160/800 mg BID. AGA 2020 Table 2 lists some different doses (for example amoxicillin-clavulanate 500/125 mg TID, ciprofloxacin 250 mg BID); cover aerobic and anaerobic enteric bacteria (AGA 2020)
  • Methane (IMO) with constipation: rifaximin plus neomycin; in a retrospective review, rifaximin 400 mg TID plus neomycin 500 mg BID for 10 days cleared methane in 87% (ACG 2020; AGA 2020)
  • Recurrence: 12.6% at 3 months, 27.5% at 6 months, 43.7% at 9 months (ACG 2020); more likely with older age, appendectomy, or chronic PPI use. Options: repeat courses (for example the first 5-10 days of each month) or continuous rotating antibiotics; weigh diarrhea, C. difficile, intolerance, and cost (AGA 2020). Retreatment rests on anecdotal evidence and expert opinion (ACG 2020)
  • Retesting: not needed if symptoms respond (AGA 2020)
  • Treat the underlying cause and correct nutritional deficiencies (AGA 2020); prevention avoids repeated antibiotic courses (ACG 2020)
  • Not supported: probiotics (inconsistent data; may cause SIBO and D-lactic acidosis) and fecal microbiota transplant; low-FODMAP diet data are extrapolated from IBS (ACG 2020)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Low B12 with normal or high folate: bacteria consume B12 and make folate (AGA 2020)
  • Rifaximin: about 70% eradication in a meta-analysis of 32 trials, adverse reactions 4.6% (ACG 2020); SIBO is not a recognized indication in the US (AGA 2020)
  • Breath-test symptomatic patients after luminal surgery or with motility disorders such as scleroderma (ACG 2020)
  • Methane 10 ppm or more is IMO, linked to constipation; treat with rifaximin plus neomycin (ACG 2020)
  • Do not breath-test asymptomatic patients on PPIs (ACG 2020)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Rifaximin, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Amoxicillin-Clavulanate, 💊 Doxycycline, 💊 TMP-SMX

247. MALABSORPTION SYNDROMES

Fat vs Carbohydrate • Workup • Etiology-Specific Treatment
CLINICAL FEATURES

General Symptoms: Chronic diarrhea (the most common symptom; Merck 2025), weight loss, abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence (ACG 2023 celiac; AGA 2023 EPI). Test for celiac disease when malabsorption is suspected (ACG 2023 celiac). Can be subtle: iron deficiency may be the only sign of mild malabsorption (Merck 2025)

Fat Malabsorption (Steatorrhea): Foul-smelling, pale, bulky, greasy stools (Merck 2025); visible steatorrhea usually needs moderate dietary fat, and foul-smelling or floating stools alone are nonspecific (AGA 2023 EPI). Vitamin A, D, E, and K deficiencies are the most common deficiencies in EPI (AGA 2023 EPI)

Carbohydrate Malabsorption: Abdominal distention, excess flatus, and watery diarrhea 30-90 minutes after carbohydrate intake suggest disaccharidase deficiency, usually lactase (Merck 2025); osmotic diarrhea from loss of brush-border disaccharidases; lactose intolerance is one of the most common food intolerances (Montoro 2021, non-US review)

Specific Deficiencies:

  • Iron: absorbed mainly in the duodenum (Montoro 2021); unexplained iron deficiency is a reason to test for celiac disease (ACG 2023 celiac)
  • Folate: low with proximal small bowel mucosal disease (Merck 2025); low B12 with high folate suggests SIBO (Merck 2025; AGA 2020 SIBO)
  • B12: pernicious anemia, chronic pancreatitis, SIBO, terminal ileal disease, or extensive distal ileal or gastric resection (Merck 2025), such as more than 30 cm of terminal ileum (Montoro 2021); anemia and neurologic effects (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • Vitamin D and calcium: severe vitamin D deficiency causes hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and osteomalacia (Montoro 2021); in EPI, baseline DXA repeated every 1-2 years (AGA 2023 EPI); metabolic bone disease or premature osteoporosis is a reason to test for celiac disease (ACG 2023 celiac)
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
PhaseCausesKey Features
Luminal (maldigestion)Pancreatic insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic or ampullary tumor, pancreatic resection); bile salt loss (terminal ileal disease or resection over 100 cm, cholestasis); SIBO (Montoro 2021); gastrinoma: acid inhibits lipase (Merck 2025) and destroys pancreatic enzymes (AGA 2023 EPI)Steatorrhea; low fecal elastase in EPI (AGA 2023 EPI)
Mucosal (absorption)Celiac disease (most common), tropical sprue, Whipple disease, Crohn disease, radiation enteritis, lactase deficiency, amyloidosis (Montoro 2021; Merck 2025); other villous atrophy: common variable immunodeficiency, autoimmune enteropathy, eosinophilic enteritis (ACG 2023 celiac)Villous atrophy on biopsy; celiac serology (ACG 2023 celiac); Whipple: PAS-positive small bowel biopsy (Montoro 2021)
Post-mucosal (lymphatic)Intestinal lymphangiectasia, primary or secondary (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, constrictive pericarditis, radiation); abetalipoproteinemia (Montoro 2021); lacteals blocked by lymphoma or tuberculosis (Merck 2025)Protein-losing enteropathy: low albumin, low immunoglobulins, lymphopenia; edema, chylous ascites or pleural effusion (Montoro 2021)

Phases of malabsorption: Montoro 2021, non-US review

WORKUP
  • Celiac serology: tTG-IgA on a gluten-containing diet, with total IgA if not previously tested; if IgA deficient, use IgG-based tests (DGP and/or tTG IgG) (ACG 2023 celiac)
  • Duodenal biopsy: if tTG-IgA is positive, or with high pretest probability even if serology is negative; 1-2 biopsies from the bulb and at least 4 from the distal duodenum (ACG 2023 celiac)
  • Fecal elastase (first test for EPI): on semi-solid or solid stool; under 100 μg/g is good evidence of EPI, 100-200 μg/g is indeterminate; valid on enzyme therapy; watery stool can falsely lower it; insensitive to mild EPI (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • Fecal fat: rarely needed (AGA 2023 EPI). Quantitative: known-fat diet for 5 days with stool collected over the last 3 days; steatorrhea is more than 7% of ingested fat (AGA 2023 EPI); over 7 g/day on at least 100 g fat/day is abnormal; the gold standard, but available routinely in only a few centers (Merck 2025). Sudan stain is a nonquantitative screen (Merck 2025) and is nonspecific for EPI (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • D-xylose test (rarely used; small bowel biopsy has replaced it): absorbed without pancreatic enzymes; normal with moderate to severe steatorrhea indicates pancreatic insufficiency; abnormal needs small bowel biopsy; SIBO can make it abnormal; falsely low with renal disease, portal hypertension, ascites, or delayed gastric emptying (Merck 2025)
  • Blood tests: if no cause is apparent, CBC with indices, ferritin, B12, folate, calcium, albumin, cholesterol, prothrombin time (Merck 2025); in EPI, vitamins A, D, E, K, B12, folate, magnesium, selenium, zinc, and iron studies (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • Other tests: SIBO breath testing (ACG 2020 SIBO); lactose hydrogen breath test only to confirm lactase deficiency; bile acid malabsorption: trial of a bile acid binder such as cholestyramine, because SeHCAT is not available in the US (Merck 2025)
  • Imaging: CT or MR enterography can show diverticula, fistulas, blind loops, strictures, and mucosal disease; video capsule endoscopy reaches the distal small bowel (Merck 2025). CT, MRI, and EUS evaluate the pancreas but cannot diagnose EPI (AGA 2023 EPI). Suspected Crohn disease: MR enterography preferred under age 35 or for serial exams; patency testing before capsule if obstructive symptoms (ACG 2025 Crohn)
  • Do not use an enzyme trial to diagnose EPI; response is unreliable (AGA 2023 EPI)
TREATMENT
  • Treat the cause: strict gluten-free diet for celiac disease, with a dietitian visit after diagnosis (ACG 2023 celiac); antibiotics for symptomatic SIBO (ACG 2020 SIBO)
  • EPI: pancreatic enzyme replacement (PERT) is required (AGA 2023 EPI). Dose by lipase: at least 40,000 USP units with each meal (40,000-50,000 to start), half with snacks, taken during the meal; adjust for meal size and fat; more than 120,000 units per meal is seldom needed (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • PERT products: all porcine and equally effective at equal lipase doses; the non-enteric-coated tablet (Viokace) needs a PPI or H2 blocker; do not use over-the-counter enzymes; rare fibrosing colonopathy, porcine allergy, hyperuricosuria (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • Nutrition: supplement and monitor fat-soluble vitamins; low-to-moderate fat diet with frequent smaller meals; avoid very-low-fat diets (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • Response: less steatorrhea and GI symptoms, gain in weight and muscle, better fat-soluble vitamin levels (AGA 2023 EPI)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Fecal elastase under 100 μg/g on formed stool is good evidence of EPI; 100-200 is indeterminate; watery stool can falsely lower it (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • Start PERT at 40,000 or more USP lipase units per meal, half with snacks, taken during the meal (AGA 2023 EPI)
  • D-xylose normal with moderate to severe steatorrhea = pancreatic insufficiency; abnormal = mucosal disease, confirm by biopsy; rarely used now (Merck 2025)
  • Check total IgA with tTG-IgA; if IgA deficient, use IgG-based celiac serology (ACG 2023 celiac)
  • Low B12 with high folate suggests SIBO (Merck 2025; AGA 2020 SIBO)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Folic Acid, 💊 Vitamin B12, 💊 IV Iron

248. MICROSCOPIC COLITIS

Collagenous vs Lymphocytic • Normal Colonoscopy • Budesonide
CLINICAL FEATURES

Presentation:

  • Chronic watery, nonbloody diarrhea; urgency in 55%, nocturnal stools in about 35%, fecal incontinence in about 26% (UEG 2021, non-US)
  • Mostly age 60 or older, with a female predominance in collagenous colitis (AGA 2016); up to 25% of collagenous colitis patients are under 45 (UEG 2021)
  • Risk factors: female sex, current or former smoking (UEG 2021)
  • Associated autoimmune disorders (AGA 2016); celiac disease in 3.3% vs 0.4% of controls (UEG 2021)

Drug Associations: NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs (AGA 2016); association does not prove causation (UEG 2021)

DIAGNOSIS

Colonoscopy: Normal or almost normal; nonspecific findings in 38.8% (UEG 2021)

Biopsies Make the Diagnosis: colonoscopy with biopsies of multiple segments (AGA 2016), at least right and left colon; rectal biopsies alone are not enough (UEG 2021). If only flexible sigmoidoscopy, biopsy the descending colon as well as the rectosigmoid (AGA 2016)

  • Collagenous colitis: subepithelial collagen band 10 μm or more, plus lamina propria inflammation (UEG 2021)
  • Lymphocytic colitis: 20 or more intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 surface epithelial cells, plus lamina propria inflammation, collagen band under 10 μm (UEG 2021)
  • Incomplete forms: band over 5 but under 10 μm, or over 10 but under 20 intraepithelial lymphocytes (UEG 2021)

Other Tests: Screen for celiac disease (UEG 2021). Fecal calprotectin is not useful to exclude or monitor (UEG 2021). Bile acid diarrhea testing only if budesonide fails (UEG 2021). No histologic monitoring (UEG 2021; AGA 2016); no special colorectal cancer surveillance (UEG 2021)

TREATMENT

Step 1: Stop suspected drugs (NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, or any drug started before the diarrhea) (AGA 2016; UEG 2021); smoking is a risk factor (UEG 2021)

Mild: Loperamide, by expert opinion (UEG 2021)

First-line Induction: Budesonide 9 mg orally once daily (strong recommendation, over no treatment and over mesalamine; AGA 2016); clinical response about 81% at 6-8 weeks in collagenous colitis (UEG 2021). Can stop after 8 weeks; about one-third stay symptom-free (AGA 2016). No follow-up colonoscopy needed for response (AGA 2016)

Maintenance (only after relapse off induction): budesonide 6 mg daily for 6 months, or 3 mg alternating with 6 mg daily for 12 months; taper to the lowest effective dose; consider stopping after 6-12 months; consider osteoporosis screening and prevention (AGA 2016). Needing more than 6 mg/day to stay in remission: consider immunomodulators or biologics (UEG 2021)

If Budesonide Is Not Feasible: AGA 2016 suggests mesalamine, bismuth salicylate, or prednisolone (all conditional); UEG 2021 (non-US) recommends against mesalamine, bismuth, and systemic steroids other than budesonide

Not Recommended: cholestyramine plus mesalamine, Boswellia serrata, probiotics (AGA 2016); antibiotics, methotrexate (UEG 2021)

Refractory: check for celiac disease and bile acid diarrhea (AGA 2016; UEG 2021); bile acid binder if bile acid diarrhea (UEG 2021); thiopurines, anti-TNF agents, or vedolizumab in selected budesonide failures (UEG 2021); limited case-series evidence for azathioprine and anti-TNF (AGA 2016); surgery as a last option (UEG 2021)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Chronic watery diarrhea with a normal-looking colon: biopsy right and left colon (UEG 2021; AGA 2016)
  • Budesonide 9 mg daily is first-line; low systemic bioavailability, but long-term use may cause bone loss (AGA 2016)
  • Maintenance only after relapse, at the lowest effective dose (AGA 2016)
  • Screen for celiac disease (UEG 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Loperamide
