249. HEREDITARY CRC SYNDROMES

Lynch Syndrome • FAP • Screening Protocols
LYNCH SYNDROME (HNPCC)

Genetics: Autosomal dominant; germline variant in a mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) or EPCAM (ACG 2015)

Features:

  • CRC risk and age depend on the gene: average age at CRC 44 y for MLH1 and MSH2, 42-69 y for MSH6, 61-66 y for PMS2; cumulative CRC risk to age 80 is 46-61% (MLH1), 33-52% (MSH2), 10-44% (MSH6), 8.7-20% (PMS2) (NCCN 2026)
  • Right-sided predominance; few adenomas (usually under 10) that progress fast, with polyp-to-cancer dwell time about 35 months (ACG 2015)
  • Metachronous CRC: up to 43% lifetime risk after segmental resection in MLH1 and MSH2 carriers (NCCN 2026)
  • Over 90% of Lynch tumors are MSI-high and/or lack at least one MMR protein on immunohistochemistry (NCCN 2026)

Extra-Colonic Cancers: Endometrial (second most common cancer in Lynch; ACG 2015), ovarian, gastric, small bowel, urothelial (renal pelvis, ureter, bladder), pancreas, biliary tract, brain (usually glioblastoma), and skin: sebaceous adenomas, sebaceous carcinomas, or keratoacanthomas (Muir-Torre syndrome) (NCCN 2026). NCCN advises against the Turcot eponym (Lynch or FAP with brain tumors) as imprecise (NCCN 2026)

Amsterdam II Criteria (3-2-1 rule): At least 3 relatives with a Lynch-associated cancer (colorectal, endometrium, small bowel, ureter, or renal pelvis), with all of: one a first-degree relative of the other two; at least 2 successive generations affected; at least 1 diagnosed before 50; FAP excluded in the CRC cases; tumors verified by pathologic examination (ICG-HNPCC 1999, non-US; ACG 2015 Table 4 says verified whenever possible). Clinical criteria have limited sensitivity; prediction models outperform them (ACG 2015)

Who to Test: Universal Lynch assessment for every colorectal, endometrial, or gastric cancer. Germline multigene panel for CRC under 50 y, CRC 50 y or older (category 2B), endometrial cancer at any age, and any MMR-deficient tumor; tumor MSI or MMR immunohistochemistry if panel testing is not feasible, and may still be needed for treatment selection (NCCN 2026). Also test: known familial Lynch variant; a first-degree relative with CRC, endometrial, or gastric cancer under 50 y; PREMM5 risk 5% or more (NCCN 2026). If no germline variant is found but the family meets Amsterdam II criteria, follow the family as if they have Lynch (NCCN 2026)

Colonoscopy (gene-specific): MLH1, MSH2 (including EPCAM deletions involving MSH2): start at 20-25 y, or 2-5 y before the earliest CRC in a relative if diagnosed before 25 y; repeat every 1-2 y. MSH6, PMS2: start at 30-35 y; repeat every 1-3 y (NCCN 2026)

Other Prevention: Consider daily aspirin to lower CRC risk; decision and dose individualized (NCCN 2026). Upper endoscopy (consider extended duodenal exam) from 30-40 y, every 2-4 y, for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, with gastric biopsies at the first exam for H. pylori and treatment if found (NCCN 2026). Hysterectomy is a risk-reducing option: with BSO from 40 y (MLH1, MSH2); with salpingectomy from 40 y and oophorectomy at 45-50 y (MSH6); with BSO from 50 y or menopause (PMS2). Endometrial biopsy every 1-2 y from 30-35 y can be considered (NCCN 2026)

CRC in Lynch: Segmental or extended colectomy by age and gene; metachronous risk is higher after segmental resection; consider segmental colectomy for PMS2. Rectal cancer: test for MMR deficiency before deciding; immune checkpoint blockade may replace surgery (NCCN 2026)

FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)

Genetics: Autosomal dominant; germline APC variant; family history may be negative (de novo in up to 25%, ACG 2026; 30%, NCCN 2026)

Features:

  • 100 or more cumulative colorectal adenomas (NCCN 2026), progressing to hundreds or thousands without intervention (NCCN 2026)
  • CRC risk approaches 100% without colectomy; median age at CRC 39 y (NCCN 2026); 87% by age 45 and 93% by 50 in the St Mark's series (ACG 2015)
  • Adenomas start in early adolescence (NCCN 2026); mean age at polyp onset 15.9 y, range 8-34 (ACG 2015)

Extra-Colonic: Duodenal and ampullary adenomas and cancer: duodenal cancer is the second leading cancer cause of death (21%, after CRC 42%) (ACG 2026). Also gastric fundic gland polyps and adenomas, desmoid tumors, thyroid cancer (cribriform-morular variant of papillary), hepatoblastoma, CNS tumors (predominantly medulloblastoma), CHRPE, osteomas, dental abnormalities, epidermoid cysts (ACG 2026). Gardner syndrome: FAP with osteomas, soft tissue tumors, desmoids, and dental abnormalities (ACG 2026)

Attenuated FAP: APC variant with 10 to under 100 cumulative adenomas (average 30), often right-sided; CRC later than classical FAP (mean age over 50 y); upper GI and thyroid risks similar to classical FAP (NCCN 2026). Baseline colonoscopy by 18-20 y, then every 1-3 y (ACG 2026)

Surveillance: Colonoscopy (preferred; sigmoidoscopy can miss right-sided polyps; NCCN 2026): baseline by 10-15 y, then every 1-3 y by polyp number, size, and histology (ACG 2026); NCCN advises every 12 months from 10-15 y (NCCN 2026). Upper endoscopy with complete view of the ampulla from 20-25 y, interval by severity of gastric or duodenal polyposis (ACG 2026; NCCN 2026). Baseline thyroid ultrasound by 18 y (ACG 2026)

Treatment: Colectomy is the cornerstone of CRC risk reduction; choice and timing are individualized by CRC risk, rectal involvement, symptoms, desmoid risk, and functional outcome (ACG 2026). Under 18 y without severe polyposis, family history of early cancer, or severe genotype, timing can be individualized with annual colonoscopy until surgery (NCCN 2026). Over 20 rectal adenomas: total proctocolectomy with IPAA suggested; 20 or fewer: total colectomy with IRA suggested. Chemoprevention does not replace colectomy. After surgery: annual endoscopy of the pouch or rectum (ACG 2026)

OTHER SYNDROMES
  • Peutz-Jeghers: STK11; diagnosed by 2 or more PJ polyps, PJ polyps or typical mucocutaneous pigmentation plus a family history, or PJ polyps plus pigmentation (NCCN 2026). Lifetime cancer risk: colorectal 39%, gastric 29%, small bowel 13%, breast up to 54%, pancreas 11-36%, ovary 21% (mostly sex cord tumors) (USMSTF 2022). EGD, colonoscopy, and small bowel capsule or MR enterography from 8-10 y; if no polyps, resume at 18 y; repeat every 2-3 y. Remove small bowel polyps 10 mm or larger, or symptomatic (USMSTF 2022; NCCN 2026 says over 10 mm). Pancreas MRCP or EUS yearly from 35 y (USMSTF 2022)
  • Juvenile Polyposis: 5 or more juvenile polyps of the colon or rectum, any juvenile polyps elsewhere in the GI tract, or any number plus a family history of JPS (first-degree relative, USMSTF 2022; close relative, NCCN 2026); SMAD4 or BMPR1A found in about 50% (NCCN 2026) to 60% (USMSTF 2022). Colon and stomach cancer risk 39-68%, mostly with SMAD4; gastric cancer at least 30% with SMAD4 gastric polyposis, not reported with BMPR1A (USMSTF 2022). SMAD4: evaluate for HHT at diagnosis, including brain and lung AVMs (USMSTF 2022), from the first 6 months of life if familial (NCCN 2026). Colonoscopy and EGD from 12-15 y, every 1-3 y by polyp burden (USMSTF 2022)
  • MUTYH-associated: Biallelic MUTYH (autosomal recessive); usually 10-100 adenomas (ACG 2026), uncommonly 100 or more; serrated polyps may occur; median CRC age over 50 y; duodenal cancer 5% (NCCN 2026). Colonoscopy from 18-20 y every 1-3 y; upper endoscopy from 30-35 y (ACG 2026)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Lynch = MSI-high, right-sided, endometrial cancer (NCCN 2026; ACG 2015)
  • FAP = 100 or more adenomas, CRC near-certain without colectomy, surgery timed individually (NCCN 2026; ACG 2026)
  • Every CRC gets Lynch assessment: germline panel (under 50 y; 50 y or older, category 2B) or tumor MSI/IHC (NCCN 2026)

250. PRIMARY SCLEROSING CHOLANGITIS (PSC)

IBD Association • Beading on MRCP • Cholangiocarcinoma Risk
CLINICAL FEATURES

Demographics: Peak onset 25-45 y (median age at diagnosis 36-39 y) but any age; men about two-thirds, with less male predominance without IBD; at least 70-80% have IBD, about two-thirds of it UC (AASLD 2022)

Presentation:

  • Often found by persistently abnormal liver tests without symptoms (ACG 2015); nearly half of adults have symptoms at diagnosis, and 22% more develop them within 5 y (AASLD 2022)
  • Fatigue (most common), pruritus, abdominal pain, fever (AASLD 2022; ACG 2015); sudden pruritus suggests biliary obstruction; right upper quadrant pain is not prominent (ACG 2015)
  • Bacterial cholangitis (fever, pain); jaundice, ascites, and confusion are late (ACG 2015)
DIAGNOSIS

Labs:

  • Cholestatic pattern: ALP predominant, GGT elevated, aminotransferases modestly elevated; bilirubin and albumin often normal at diagnosis (ACG 2015)
  • IgG4 in every patient to exclude IgG4-sclerosing cholangitis (AASLD 2022; ACG 2015); elevated in about 10%, who may respond to corticosteroids (ACG 2015)
  • ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibodies, and ANCA can be found; AMA, the PBC marker, is not found, and testing helps exclude PBC (ACG 2015)

Imaging:

  • MRI/MRCP (first-line): intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic strictures alternating with normal or slightly dilated segments (AASLD 2022), a "beaded" appearance (ACG 2015)
  • ERCP: avoid for diagnosis (AASLD 2022); used for strictures, cholangitis, and tissue sampling (AASLD 2022)
  • Normal high-quality MRI/MRCP but PSC still suspected: consider liver biopsy for small-duct PSC (AASLD 2022)

Biopsy: Not needed with typical MRI/MRCP findings, except for suspected AIH overlap or small-duct PSC (AASLD 2022). Concentric "onion skin" periductal fibrosis is infrequent and also seen in other obstructive cholangiopathies (AASLD 2022)

COMPLICATIONS & TREATMENT

Complications:

  • Cholangiocarcinoma: cumulative risk 6% at 10 y, 14% at 20 y, and 20% at 30 y of PSC; 160-400 times the general population. Suspect with rapid worsening of symptoms, cholestasis, or weight loss. Annual MRI/MRCP with or without CA 19-9 for CCA and gallbladder cancer (not under 18 y or in small-duct PSC); CA 19-9 alone does not diagnose CCA (AASLD 2022)
  • Strictures: dominant stricture (on ERCP, 1.5 mm or less in the common bile duct or 1 mm or less in a hepatic duct) develops in up to 45%. Relevant stricture: any common bile duct or hepatic duct stricture with obstructive cholestasis or cholangitis. ERCP with brushings for cytology and FISH; antibiotic prophylaxis for ERCP; balloon dilation with or without a stent, plastic stents removed within 4 weeks (AASLD 2022)
  • Bacterial cholangitis: antibiotics, considering MRCP to rule out relevant strictures; ERCP if the response to antibiotics is inadequate (AASLD 2022)
  • Cirrhosis and portal hypertension: screen for varices if liver stiffness over 20 kPa or platelets 150,000 or less; HCC surveillance if cirrhotic (AASLD 2022)
  • Gallbladder polyps over 8 mm: consider cholecystectomy; 8 mm or less: ultrasound every 6 months (AASLD 2022)
  • Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and bone loss: nutrition and vitamin levels at diagnosis and yearly; bone density at diagnosis and every 2-3 y (AASLD 2022)
  • Colorectal cancer (PSC-IBD): high-definition surveillance colonoscopy with biopsies from age 15, every 1-2 y, continuing after transplant (AASLD 2022); dysplasia and cancer risk about 4-5 times IBD without PSC (ACG 2015). No known IBD: ileocolonoscopy with biopsies at diagnosis, then about every 5 y or with symptoms (AASLD 2022)

Treatment:

  • No approved drug; none proven to halt progression; consider clinical trials (AASLD 2022)
  • UDCA: if ALP or GGT stays elevated (observe 6 months first), 13-23 mg/kg/day can be considered; continue only if ALP falls meaningfully or symptoms improve by 12 months. Avoid 28 mg/kg/day or more: high dose raised serious adverse events and, in PSC with UC, colorectal neoplasia (AASLD 2022); doses over 28 mg/kg/day should not be used (strong recommendation, ACG 2015)
  • Pruritus: bile acid sequestrant first, after heat avoidance, emollients, and antihistamines; refractory: sertraline 100 mg daily, naltrexone titrated to 50-100 mg daily, or rifampin 150-300 mg twice daily (AASLD 2022)
  • Oral vancomycin: insufficient evidence to recommend (AASLD 2022)
  • Liver transplant: for complications of end-stage liver disease, recurrent cholangitis, intractable pruritus, or early-stage hepatobiliary cancer; PSC recurs in 20-30% after transplant (AASLD 2022)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • PSC + IBD: surveillance colonoscopy every 1-2 y from age 15, and after transplant (AASLD 2022)
  • MRI/MRCP makes the diagnosis; check IgG4 in everyone; AMA is not found in PSC (AASLD 2022; ACG 2015)
  • No drug slows progression; transplant for end-stage disease, recurrent cholangitis, or early cancer; PSC recurs in 20-30% (AASLD 2022)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ursodiol, 💊 Sertraline, 💊 Naltrexone, 💊 Rifampin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Alkaline Phosphatase, 🔬 Elevated GGT, 🔬 Elevated INR

251. WILSON DISEASE

Copper Overload • Kayser-Fleischer Rings • Ceruloplasmin
CLINICAL FEATURES

Age: Any age; age alone should not exclude Wilson. Children mostly present with liver disease; adults with liver disease with or without neuropsychiatric disease (AASLD 2022)

Hepatic: From asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation or fatty liver to acute hepatitis, an autoimmune hepatitis-like picture, cirrhosis, or acute liver failure (AASLD 2022)

Acute Liver Failure (about 3% of ALF): Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, coagulopathy unresponsive to parenteral vitamin K, aminotransferases typically under 2000 IU/L with AST above ALT, encephalopathy, renal dysfunction. ALP to total bilirubin ratio under 4 plus AST to ALT ratio over 2.2 was 100% sensitive and specific in one adult cohort (less reliable in children). Serum copper usually over 200 μg/dL; ceruloplasmin predicts poorly here (AASLD 2022)

Neurologic: Dysarthria, tremor and other involuntary movements, rigid dystonia, drooling and dysphagia, seizures. Psychiatric: depression, bipolar disorder, personality change, psychosis (AASLD 2022)

Ophthalmologic: Kayser-Fleischer rings: copper in Descemet membrane, by slit-lamp or optical tomography; almost always present in neurologic Wilson at presentation, but in only 44-62% with mainly hepatic disease, usually absent in children with liver disease, and absent in 50% of ALF (AASLD 2022)

Other: Recurrent Coombs-negative hemolysis; renal (Fanconi syndrome, proximal renal tubular acidosis, nephrolithiasis); premature osteoporosis and arthritis; cardiomyopathy and dysrhythmias; pancreatitis; hypoparathyroidism; infertility and repeated miscarriages (AASLD 2022)

DIAGNOSIS

Workup: Liver tests, CBC, INR, serum ceruloplasmin (and serum copper in some), basal 24-h urine copper, slit-lamp exam, neurologic exam, ATP7B testing (AASLD 2022)

  • Serum ceruloplasmin: below normal (usually about 20 mg/dL) is consistent with Wilson and diagnostic with KF rings; under 5 mg/dL is more suggestive; a normal level does not exclude Wilson, and ceruloplasmin alone cannot make the diagnosis. In one genetically confirmed cohort, under 20 mg/dL had a positive predictive value of 48.3%, and 14 mg/dL was 100% sensitive and specific in the validation group (AASLD 2022)
  • Basal 24-h urine copper: typically over 100 μg/24 h in symptomatic patients; over 40 μg/24 h may indicate Wilson in asymptomatic people or children (AASLD 2022)
  • Hepatic copper (liver biopsy): over 250 μg/g dry weight in most patients; under 50 μg/g almost always excludes Wilson if untreated; biopsy also stages disease (AASLD 2022)
  • Serum copper: usually low, in proportion to ceruloplasmin; normal or high with liver injury and greatly elevated in ALF. Non-ceruloplasmin-bound (free) copper is over 25 μg/dL in most untreated patients but was never validated as a diagnostic test and rises in liver failure of any cause (AASLD 2022)
  • Leipzig score: a sum of 4 or more makes Wilson highly likely (AASLD 2022)

Genetic Testing: ATP7B (autosomal recessive); confirms the diagnosis when biochemical tests are not definitive and screens first-degree relatives (AASLD 2022)

Imaging: Brain MRI if neurologic findings: signal changes in basal ganglia, thalami, pons, and white matter, and atrophy (AASLD 2022)

TREATMENT
  • Lifelong therapy for everyone diagnosed (AASLD 2022)
  • Symptomatic: chelator, D-penicillamine or trientine; trientine may be better tolerated (AASLD 2022)
  • D-penicillamine: start 250-500 mg/day, raise by 250 mg every 4-7 days to about 1000-1500 mg/day (15-20 mg/kg/day, maximum 2000 mg/day) in 2-4 divided doses; maintenance 10-15 mg/kg/day (about 750-1000 mg/day) in two doses; add pyridoxine 25-50 mg daily. Severe adverse effects force discontinuation in about 30% (AASLD 2022)
  • Trientine: about 15-20 mg/kg/day (maximum 2000 mg/day) in 2-3 divided doses, ramped up over 2-3 weeks; maintenance 10-15 mg/kg/day (AASLD 2022)
  • Neurologic worsening early in chelation: reported in 10-50% with D-penicillamine (AASLD 2022)
  • Zinc: induces metallothionein and blocks intestinal copper absorption; 150 mg/day elemental zinc in three divided doses for adults, at least twice daily; for asymptomatic patients or maintenance (AASLD 2022)
  • Maintenance after generally more than 1 year with good response: lower-dose chelator or full-dose zinc (AASLD 2022)
  • Diet: keep copper near the RDA (under 0.9 mg/day), especially the first year; avoid nuts, chocolate, most shellfish, soy products, mushrooms, organ meats, and most nondairy milk alternatives (AASLD 2022)
  • Severe liver disease: chelator plus zinc, spaced 4-5 h apart, with liver transplant evaluation at the same time (AASLD 2022)
  • Liver transplant: immediate referral for ALF; prompt consideration for advanced liver disease failing medical therapy; no Wilson treatment needed after transplant; neurologic Wilson is a controversial indication (AASLD 2022)
  • Screen all first-degree relatives (AASLD 2022)
  • Monitoring: liver tests, INR, CBC, and urinalysis at least twice yearly; 24-h urine copper yearly. Pregnancy: continue treatment; reduce chelator dose by about 25-50%; zinc dose unchanged (AASLD 2022)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Unexplained liver disease + neurologic or psychiatric disorder: exclude Wilson, at any age (AASLD 2022)
  • Low ceruloplasmin + Kayser-Fleischer rings = diagnostic (AASLD 2022)
  • ALF + Coombs-negative hemolysis = Wilson until proven otherwise: ALP to bilirubin under 4, AST to ALT over 2.2; refer for transplant immediately (AASLD 2022)

252. HEREDITARY HEMOCHROMATOSIS

Iron Overload • HFE Gene • Phlebotomy
CLINICAL FEATURES

Presentation: No cardinal symptoms; suspicion depends on awareness. Men present earlier, most often in the fourth to fifth decades; women usually after menopause, because menstruation, pregnancy, and lactation offset iron absorption (ACG 2019)

Manifestations:

  • Liver (most commonly affected): asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation, nonspecific RUQ pain, or end-stage liver disease; hepatomegaly, fibrosis, cirrhosis (lifetime incidence approaches 10% in untreated men). Cirrhosis risk rises with ferritin over 1000 ng/mL at diagnosis and with alcohol over 60 g/day (9-fold). With cirrhosis, HCC causes as much as 45% of deaths; ferritin over 2000 ng/mL marks particularly high risk (ACG 2019)
  • Heart: restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias (sick sinus syndrome, atrial fibrillation), heart failure; uncommon in type 1 HH, but cardiomyopathy is the second leading cause of death (ACG 2019)
  • Endocrine: diabetes (about 13-23%); hypogonadism (most common nondiabetic endocrine disorder); hypopituitarism; hypothyroidism; osteoporosis in up to 25% (ACG 2019)
  • Joints: arthropathy mainly of the second and third MCP joints, with hook-shaped osteophytes of the metacarpal heads; arthralgia, chondrocalcinosis (ACG 2019)
  • Skin: bronze or slate-gray hyperpigmentation, possibly an earlier sign (ACG 2019)
  • Infection: iron overload favors Listeria, Yersinia, E. coli, and Vibrio vulnificus (ACG 2019)

Demographics: Northern European descent; prevalence 1 in 300 non-Hispanic whites in the US (ACG 2019)

DIAGNOSIS

Initial Testing:

  • Transferrin saturation (TS) over 45%: preferred initial test, fasting not required; identifies 97.9-100% of C282Y homozygotes, though some younger, early-stage patients are under 45% (ACG 2019)
  • Serum ferritin: under 1000 ng/mL at diagnosis marks low risk of advanced fibrosis. In C282Y homozygotes, ferritin over 1000 ng/mL plus elevated aminotransferases and low platelets predicts cirrhosis in over 80%. Normal ferritin (under 200 ng/mL in premenopausal women, under 300 ng/mL in men and postmenopausal women) with TS under 45% has a 97% negative predictive value for iron overload (ACG 2019)
  • Ferritin is nonspecific: also high in alcohol-related liver disease, hepatitis C, NAFLD, and malignancy. High ferritin with normal TS points toward non-HFE iron overload (ACG 2019)
  • Secondary iron overload (Table 3): iron-loading anemias (thalassemia, sickle cell), RBC transfusions, parenteral iron, long-term hemodialysis, chronic liver disease (hepatitis B or C, alcohol-related, NAFLD, porphyria cutanea tarda), chronic inflammatory states (ACG 2019)

Confirmatory:

  • HFE testing when TS and ferritin are both elevated (Figure 4): C282Y homozygote (type 1A) or C282Y/H63D compound heterozygote (type 1B; clinically significant iron overload in only 0.5-2%, usually with cofactors such as alcohol or hepatitis C) (ACG 2019)
  • H63D or S65C without C282Y: counsel that they are not at increased risk of iron overload. No further genetic testing if negative for C282Y and H63D; non-HFE sequencing may be considered in atypical cases such as a younger patient with endocrine or cardiac involvement (ACG 2019)
  • Penetrance is incomplete: biochemical penetrance about 75% in male and 50% in female C282Y homozygotes (ACG 2019)
  • MRI (T2*, no contrast): measures liver iron in non-C282Y homozygotes with suspected HH; use biopsy instead if fibrosis staging or another liver disease also needs evaluation (ACG 2019)
  • Liver biopsy: mainly to stage fibrosis in C282Y homozygotes with ferritin over 1000 ng/mL. Not indicated with ferritin under 1000 ng/mL unless there is a concurrent cirrhosis risk factor or clinical features of advanced fibrosis. Can be considered before phlebotomy in C282Y homozygotes with elevated liver enzymes to rule out other liver disease (ACG 2019)
TREATMENT
  • Phlebotomy (first-line) for C282Y homozygotes and C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes (strong recommendation, ACG 2019). In compound heterozygotes, evaluate and treat cofactors (NAFLD, diabetes, excess alcohol) before iron removal (ACG 2019)
  • Induction: about 500 mL weekly (1000 mL if tolerated; smaller volumes or longer intervals if not); keep hemoglobin above 11 g/dL; check ferritin monthly until 50-100 ng/mL (ACG 2019)
  • Maintenance: ferritin near 50 ng/mL, usually 3-4 phlebotomies a year. HH does not medically bar blood donation, but there is no universal policy and many blood banks do not accept it (ACG 2019)
  • Likely to improve: abnormal liver tests, heart dysfunction, fatigue, skin pigmentation (slowly); fibrosis can regress, mainly when mild to moderate. Likely not to improve: diabetes, arthralgias, hypogonadism (ACG 2019)
  • Chelation: not first-line (strong recommendation, ACG 2019; hepatic and renal toxicity). Use when phlebotomy is not tolerated, fails, or could harm, as in severe anemia or heart failure (strong recommendation, ACG 2019). Deferasirox 5-15 mg/kg/day lowered ferritin over 48 weeks in a trial; aminotransferase and creatinine elevations were more common at 15 mg/kg/day (ACG 2019). Erythrocytapheresis is an alternative to phlebotomy (ACG 2019)
  • Avoid: iron and vitamin C supplements; dietary iron restriction is not needed. Alcohol and smoking worsen iron overload. PPIs are not recommended as primary treatment (ACG 2019)
  • Screen first-degree relatives (strong recommendation, ACG 2019). For a proband's children, test the other parent; if normal, the child is an obligate heterozygote and needs no further testing (ACG 2019)
  • HCC surveillance: cirrhosis only: ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months, continuing after iron depletion; not routine with fibrosis stage 3 or less (ACG 2019)
  • Liver transplant: consider for decompensated cirrhosis or HCC (strong recommendation, ACG 2019)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • TS over 45% is the preferred first test; elevated TS with elevated ferritin leads to HFE testing (ACG 2019)
  • Ferritin under 1000 ng/mL at diagnosis = low risk of advanced fibrosis; over 1000 ng/mL in a C282Y homozygote = consider biopsy for staging (ACG 2019)
  • Diabetes, arthralgias, and hypogonadism likely will not improve with phlebotomy: the goal is to treat before end-organ damage (ACG 2019)
↑ Back to Table of Contents

253. EOSINOPHILIC ESOPHAGITIS (EoE)

Dysphagia • Food Impaction • Ringed Esophagus
CLINICAL FEATURES

Atopy: immediate-type food allergy, asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis; at least 60-80% have a concomitant allergic condition, and more atopic conditions mean higher likelihood. A family history of EoE also raises suspicion (ACG 2025)

Symptoms:

  • Adolescents and adults: dysphagia and food impaction most common; heartburn and chest pain possible; meal-triggered chest pain; prompt regurgitation of swallowed food (ACG 2025)
  • Infants and young children: poor growth, failure to thrive, feeding intolerance, failure to progress to solids, prolonged eating, food refusal. School-aged children: abdominal pain, vomiting, regurgitation, heartburn (ACG 2025)
  • Ask about IMPACT behaviors, which mask dysphagia: Imbibe fluids, Modify foods, Prolong meal times, Avoid hard textures, Chew excessively, Turn away tablets/pills (ACG 2025, Table 4)
DIAGNOSIS

Criteria (all 3): symptoms of esophageal dysfunction; at least 15 eos/hpf on esophageal biopsy; evaluation for non-EoE causes of esophageal eosinophilia (strong recommendation, ACG 2025). A PPI trial is no longer required for diagnosis (ACG 2025)

EGD:

  • Perform off treatment when possible (no dietary restriction, no PPI, no intranasal or inhaled steroids), which can mask EoE (ACG 2025)
  • Score findings with EREFS: edema, fixed rings, white exudates, linear furrows, strictures. Also narrow caliber, crepe-paper mucosa, and a firm "tug" or "pull" sign on biopsy (ACG 2025)
  • Biopsies: at least 6 from at least 2 levels (proximal/mid and distal), targeting visible findings (strong recommendation, ACG 2025). Biopsy at food impaction endoscopy once the bolus is cleared (ACG 2025)
  • Endoscopy misses esophageal narrowing (sensitivity 14.7% vs a structured esophagram protocol); in children with dysphagia, an esophagram is suggested to evaluate fibrostenotic disease (ACG 2025)

Differential of esophageal eosinophilia: GERD, pill esophagitis, drug hypersensitivity reactions, non-EoE eosinophilic GI diseases, hypereosinophilic syndrome, Crohn disease, achalasia, infections, connective tissue or autoimmune diseases (ACG 2025, Figure 1)

TREATMENT

Initial options (ACG does not rank these against each other; comparative effectiveness is listed as a knowledge gap, ACG 2025, Table 8):

  • PPI (conditional recommendation): adults, double the reflux dose, such as omeprazole 20 mg twice daily or 40 mg daily, or another PPI equivalent; children 2 mg/kg/day (or 1 mg/kg twice daily). Histologic response about 50% in meta-analysis (ACG 2025)
  • Swallowed topical steroids (strong recommendation; fluticasone or budesonide, conditional): adults, budesonide 2-4 mg/day or fluticasone 1760 mcg/day, divided; children, budesonide 1-2 mg/day or fluticasone 110-880 mcg/day by age and size. Fluticasone doses assume a multidose inhaler, swallowed not inhaled (ACG 2025). Budesonide oral suspension (Eohilia): 2 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, age 11 years or older; not shown safe and effective beyond 12 weeks (FDA label, Eohilia, rev 02/2024). Take after meals or at bedtime, then nothing by mouth for 30-60 minutes (ACG 2025). Main side effect: oral or esophageal candidiasis (ACG 2025)
  • Empiric elimination diet (conditional recommendation): dairy only (1FED, 35-45%), dairy and wheat (2FED, 40-45%), plus egg and soy (4FED, 40-50%), plus nuts and seafood (6FED, 40-70%). Less restrictive diets may be tried first. Elemental formula over 90% if adherent, reserved for infants and severe refractory disease. Do not use allergy testing to choose foods. Involve a dietitian; reintroduce foods one at a time with endoscopy and biopsy after each (ACG 2025)

Dupilumab: suggested for PPI nonresponders age 12 years or older (conditional) and ages 1-11 years (conditional); ACG advises it as step-up therapy for difficult-to-treat EoE, or when multiple atopic conditions also qualify (ACG 2025). FDA-approved for EoE in patients 1 year or older weighing at least 15 kg: 15 to under 30 kg, 200 mg every 2 weeks; 30 to under 40 kg, 300 mg every 2 weeks; 40 kg or more, 300 mg weekly (FDA label, Dupixent, rev 02/2026)

Not recommended: omalizumab, cromolyn, montelukast (conditional recommendations against, ACG 2025)

Dilation: adjunct to medical therapy for strictures causing dysphagia (conditional recommendation); always pair with anti-inflammatory treatment, because dilation does not treat inflammation. Start low and go slow; mucosal disruption ("dilation effect") is the expected endpoint; goal diameter in adults and adolescents typically 16 mm or more. Perforation under 0.5%, hospitalization under 1%, symptom improvement 95% (ACG 2025)

Maintenance and monitoring: continue effective diet or drug therapy, since disease almost always recurs when treatment stops (strong recommendation); use the lowest effective dose. Judge response by symptoms plus endoscopy and histology, not symptoms alone (strong recommendation); histologic response threshold under 15 eos/hpf may be used (ACG 2025)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Dysphagia or food impaction, especially with atopy: biopsy at EGD (at least 6, 2 levels), including at food impaction endoscopy (ACG 2025)
  • Diagnosis: symptoms + at least 15 eos/hpf + other causes excluded; no PPI trial needed (ACG 2025)
  • Topical steroids are swallowed, not inhaled; nothing by mouth for 30-60 minutes after (ACG 2025)
  • Dilation fixes the stricture, not the inflammation: always pair it with anti-inflammatory therapy (ACG 2025)

254. IDIOPATHIC PULMONARY FIBROSIS (IPF)

UIP Pattern • Progressive Fibrosis • Antifibrotics
CLINICAL FEATURES

Clinical Suspicion (2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT): Unexplained bilateral pulmonary fibrosis on chest imaging, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, and age >60 years; rarely ages 40-60, especially with features of familial pulmonary fibrosis. Male predominance and smoking history are common (Practical)

Symptoms: Progressive dyspnea, dry cough (months to years)

Exam: Bibasilar inspiratory "Velcro" crackles; clubbing in a minority (Practical)

PFTs: Restrictive pattern (↓FVC, ↓TLC), ↓DLCO (often early and disproportionate)

DIAGNOSIS

HRCT Patterns (2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT):

  • UIP: Subpleural and basal predominant, often heterogeneous; honeycombing with or without traction bronchiectasis/bronchiolectasis; usually with reticulation, possibly mild GGO
  • Probable UIP: Same distribution; reticular pattern with peripheral traction bronchiectasis/bronchiolectasis, without honeycombing
  • Indeterminate for UIP: Fibrosis that does not meet UIP or probable UIP criteria and does not suggest an alternative diagnosis
  • Suggests an alternative diagnosis: Cysts; mosaic attenuation or three-density sign (consider HP); predominant GGO; profuse centrilobular micronodules; upper or mid-lung or peribronchovascular predominance with subpleural sparing; pleural plaques (asbestosis); dilated esophagus (CTD)

Diagnosis: Exclude known causes, then decide at multidisciplinary discussion (MDD). In the appropriate clinical context, a UIP or probable UIP pattern on HRCT establishes IPF without histology (2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT)

Lung Biopsy: Considered at MDD when HRCT is indeterminate or suggests another diagnosis. Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy is an acceptable alternative to surgical lung biopsy in experienced centers (2022, conditional, very low quality evidence)

Rule Out: CTD-ILD, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug-induced, asbestosis

TREATMENT

Antifibrotic Therapy (slows FVC decline; not curative):

  • Nintedanib: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor; diarrhea common
  • Pirfenidone: GI side effects, photosensitivity
  • Nerandomilast: Preferential PDE4B inhibitor; FDA approved for IPF (October 2025) and for progressive pulmonary fibrosis (December 2025); diarrhea is the most common adverse reaction
  • In the hospital (Practical): Continue the home antifibrotic unless there is a specific reason to hold it. During an acute exacerbation, see Condition 48

Supportive: Supplemental O2, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination; palliative care for cough, dyspnea, and anxiety (2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT, consensus)

Respiratory Failure: Invasive ventilation is not recommended for most patients with respiratory failure from IPF (2022, consensus); consider it only in selected patients, such as a bridge to transplant (IWG 2026; see Condition 48). Discuss goals of care early

Lung Transplant: The only treatment that replaces the fibrotic lungs; refer at diagnosis if mortality risk is increased (2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT)

AVOID: Chronic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants for IPF. Prednisone + azathioprine + N-acetylcysteine increased death (8 vs 1) and hospitalization (23 vs 7) vs placebo (PANTHER-IPF, NEJM 2012), and these drugs are associated with a higher risk of acute exacerbation (IWG 2026). Corticosteroids in acute exacerbation are a separate, unproven question (see Condition 48)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • UIP on HRCT is not IPF until known causes are excluded (CTD, HP, drugs, asbestos), ideally at multidisciplinary discussion (2022)
  • Chronic steroids do not help IPF (unlike some other ILDs); in acute exacerbation they are unproven (Condition 48)
  • Early transplant referral: refer at diagnosis if mortality risk is increased (2022)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Nintedanib, 💊 Pirfenidone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated A-a Gradient, 🔬 LDH
↑ Back to Table of Contents

255. CYSTIC FIBROSIS

CFTR Mutation • Bronchiectasis • CFTR Modulators
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY & CLINICAL FEATURES

Genetics: Autosomal recessive; CFTR gene variants (F508del most common)

Pulmonary:

  • Thick secretions, bronchiectasis, recurrent infections
  • Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (most significant), S. aureus (including MRSA), Burkholderia cepacia complex, NTM
  • Progressive decline → respiratory failure

GI:

  • Pancreatic insufficiency (most patients): steatorrhea, malnutrition
  • Meconium ileus (neonates); distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS; adults)
  • CF-related diabetes (CFRD)
  • Hepatobiliary disease

Other: Male infertility (absent vas deferens), sinus disease, osteoporosis

DIAGNOSIS
  • Who to test: Positive newborn screen (immunoreactive trypsinogen), clinical features consistent with CF, or a positive family history (CFF 2017)
  • Sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L: CF can be diagnosed (CFF 2017)
  • Sweat chloride 30-59 mmol/L (intermediate) on two separate occasions: May have CF; consider extended CFTR gene analysis and/or CFTR functional analysis (CFF 2017)
  • Sweat chloride <30 mmol/L: CF unlikely; may still be considered if evolving clinical criteria and/or CFTR genotyping support it (CFF 2017)
  • CFTR genetics: Two CF-causing variants (CFTR2) are consistent with CF, but a sweat chloride test is still needed to confirm; not finding two CF-causing variants does not exclude CF (CFF 2017)
TREATMENT

CFTR Modulators (Disease-Modifying): Eligibility is by CFTR variant per FDA label; about 95% of US people with CF are now eligible (Vertex press release, April 2026)

  • Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta): Age 2 years and older with at least one CFTR variant that is responsive by clinical and/or in vitro data or that results in CFTR protein production (label 03/2026). Age 12 and older: 2 tablets of elexacaftor 100 mg/tezacaftor 50 mg/ivacaftor 75 mg in the morning and 1 tablet of ivacaftor 150 mg in the evening, with fat-containing food
  • Vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (Alyftrek): Once daily; FDA approved December 2024; age 6 years and older with at least one F508del or another responsive variant (label 03/2026), extended in April 2026 to variants that result in CFTR protein production (Vertex). Age 12 and older: 2 tablets of vanzacaftor 10 mg/tezacaftor 50 mg/deutivacaftor 125 mg once daily
  • Ivacaftor (Kalydeco) alone: First approved in 2012 for the G551D gating variant; CFF 2018 also supports it for other gating variants
  • Boxed warning (Trikafta and Alyftrek): drug-induced liver injury and liver failure. LFTs (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) before starting, monthly for the first 6 months, every 3 months for the next 12 months, then at least annually. Interrupt for ALT or AST >5x ULN, ALT or AST >3x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN, or symptoms of liver injury. Child-Pugh B: not recommended; Child-Pugh C: do not use (labels)
  • CYP3A inhibitors (labels, age 12 and older): Strong (ketoconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole, clarithromycin) or moderate (fluconazole, erythromycin) inhibitors need a dose reduction. Trikafta: moderate = 2 elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor tablets one morning, then ivacaftor 150 mg the next morning, alternating; strong = 2 elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor tablets in the morning twice a week; no evening ivacaftor dose with either. Alyftrek: 1 tablet every other day (moderate) or once a week (strong)
  • CYP3A inducers: Strong inducers (rifampin, rifabutin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort) are not recommended with Trikafta; strong or moderate inducers are not recommended with Alyftrek. Avoid grapefruit (Trikafta label)
  • In the hospital (Practical): Continue the home modulator unless one of the above applies; confirm interaction dosing with the CF center pharmacist

Chronic Therapies (CFF 2013, age 6 and older; reviewed 2025): Continue them during an admission (CFF 2009, B)

  • Airway clearance: chest physiotherapy, oscillating devices
  • Dornase alfa (Pulmozyme): DNase; reduces mucus viscosity. Recommended (A for moderate to severe disease; B for mild)
  • Hypertonic saline (nebulized 7%): Recommended at any severity (B)
  • Chronic Pseudomonas: Inhaled tobramycin or inhaled aztreonam (A for moderate to severe disease; B for mild); azithromycin (B; also recommended without chronic Pseudomonas, C)
  • Inhaled corticosteroids: Recommended against without asthma or ABPA (D)
  • New Pseudomonas isolate: Eradicate with inhaled tobramycin 300 mg twice daily for 28 days (CFF 2014, A)

Pulmonary Exacerbation (CFF 2009, reviewed 2021):

  • Antibiotics: Choose by the most recent respiratory cultures and susceptibilities, e.g., Pseudomonas, MRSA, Burkholderia cepacia complex (Practical). Give IV antibiotics in the hospital; CFF recommends against a nonhospital setting unless resources comparable to the hospital are assured (I)
  • Aminoglycosides: Once-daily dosing is preferable to three-times-daily dosing (C). Antibiotic doses in CF are often higher than in other patients; use the CF center or pharmacy dosing protocol and drug levels (Practical)
  • Airway clearance: Increase it (B); continue chronic therapies (B). Continuing inhaled antibiotics during IV therapy: insufficient evidence (I)
  • Insufficient evidence (I): one antipseudomonal agent vs combination, continuous beta-lactam infusion, routine corticosteroids. Routine synergy testing: recommended against (D)
  • Duration: No optimal duration established (CFF 2009, I). STOP2 (adults; AJRCCM 2021): in early responders at 7-10 days, 10 days of IV antibiotics was noninferior to 14 for FEV1; in slower responders, 21 days was not superior to 14

Infection Control (CFF 2014; reviewed 2024, update in progress): Contact precautions (gown and gloves) for all people with CF regardless of culture results; single-patient room when admitted; the patient wears a surgical mask in healthcare settings; at least 6 feet (2 m) from other people with CF. Airborne precautions for NTM: insufficient evidence

Nutrition: Pancreatic enzyme replacement (continue with meals in the hospital, Practical), fat-soluble vitamins, high-calorie diet

Advanced Disease and Lung Transplant (CFF 2019, adults; reviewed 2021):

  • Discuss transplant with everyone whose FEV1 is <50% predicted
  • Refer no later than: FEV1 <50% and rapidly declining (>20% relative decline in 12 months); FEV1 <40% with markers of shortened survival (6-minute walk <400 m, hypoxemia, hypercarbia, pulmonary hypertension); or FEV1 <30%
  • Hospital triggers: Any exacerbation needing positive pressure ventilation, regardless of FEV1. With FEV1 <40%: massive hemoptysis (>240 mL) needing ICU admission or bronchial artery embolization, pneumothorax, >2 exacerbations a year needing IV antibiotics, or BMI <18

Palliative Care (CFF 2021): CF teams deliver primary palliative care from diagnosis onward, including goals-of-care and advance care planning discussions; consult specialty palliative care for needs beyond the team's expertise and when a person is considering or declines transplant

CF Center: Involve the patient's CF center early in an admission (Practical); CF center teams coordinate care between inpatient and outpatient settings (CFF 2024)

COMPLICATIONS TO MONITOR

Hemoptysis (CFF 2010, reviewed 2025): Scant <5 mL; mild to moderate 5-240 mL; massive >240 mL

  • Scant: May not need admission; continue airway clearance and aerosols; contact the CF team for a first-ever episode
  • Mild or more: Treat with antibiotics; stop NSAIDs
  • Massive: Always admit; stop all airway clearance and hypertonic saline; withhold BiPAP. If clinically unstable, bronchial artery embolization (BAE), without bronchoscopy first. Lung resection only as a final option. Airway management: Condition 49
  • Tranexamic acid: No CFF recommendation; CFF notes trials are needed (see Condition 49)

Pneumothorax (CFF 2010, reviewed 2025): CF-specific advice; differs from general secondary pneumothorax advice in Condition 39

  • Small and clinically stable: May be closely observed
  • Large: Always admit and place a chest tube. Small with clinical instability: chest tube
  • Pleurodesis: Not after a first pneumothorax; for a recurrent large pneumothorax, surgical pleurodesis is preferred
  • While present: Withhold BiPAP; no positive expiratory pressure (PEP) or intrapulmonary percussive ventilation airway clearance; continue aerosols
  • After resolution: No flying, lifting >5 lb, or spirometry for 2 weeks
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L = CF when testing follows a positive newborn screen, consistent clinical features, or family history; 30-59 = intermediate; <30 = unlikely (CFF 2017)
  • Modulators are transformative, not curative: median predicted survival is 61 years for people with CF born 2019-2023 in the US (CFF 2024)
  • Every admitted person with CF: contact precautions, single room, surgical mask, and at least 6 feet from other people with CF (CFF 2014)
  • Transplant referral triggers in the hospital: any exacerbation needing positive pressure ventilation; with FEV1 <40%, massive hemoptysis needing ICU or BAE, or pneumothorax (CFF 2019)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Trikafta, 💊 Tobramycin, 💊 Azithromycin, 💊 Albuterol
↑ Back to Table of Contents

256. ALPHA-1 ANTITRYPSIN DEFICIENCY

Early COPD • Panacinar Emphysema • Augmentation Therapy
CLINICAL FEATURES

When to Suspect:

  • COPD/emphysema at young age (<45)
  • COPD in a nonsmoker or minimal smoker
  • Basilar-predominant emphysema (panacinar)
  • Family history of emphysema or liver disease
  • Unexplained liver disease, unexplained bronchiectasis, necrotizing panniculitis, or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
  • The classic picture is not required: patients diagnosed later often have typical apical centrilobular emphysema (GOLD 2026)

Pulmonary: Early-onset COPD; accelerated by smoking

Hepatic: Cirrhosis (misfolded AAT polymers accumulate in hepatocytes); HCC risk

DIAGNOSIS

Who to Test (A1F 2016): All adults with COPD regardless of age or ethnicity (strong; GOLD 2026 also recommends testing everyone with COPD); unexplained chronic liver disease, necrotizing panniculitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, or unexplained bronchiectasis (strong). Offer genetic counseling and testing to parents, siblings, children, and extended family of an identified case (weak)

  • Test method: Genotyping for at least the S and Z alleles; confirm with Pi typing, AAT level, and/or expanded genotyping or gene sequencing (A1F 2016). If level and genotype disagree, consider rare or null variants
  • Serum AAT level: Changes with inflammation and pregnancy, so a level alone cannot identify at-risk individuals (A1F 2016); a level drawn during acute illness may be falsely reassuring (Practical). Severe deficiency: <11 μmol/L (<57 mg/dL) (CTS 2025, non-US); a level <20% of normal is highly suggestive of homozygous deficiency (GOLD 2026)
  • Genotypes: PI*ZZ is the most common severe genotype; more than 95% of severely deficient individuals are ZZ or SZ (A1F 2016)
  • PI*MZ: Intermediate level; higher COPD risk in smokers but not in never-smokers; not a candidate for augmentation (GOLD 2026; A1F 2016)
TREATMENT
  • Smoking cessation: Most important intervention; make every effort to prevent tobacco smoke exposure and help smokers quit (A1F 2016, strong)
  • Standard COPD treatment: Manage as usual COPD; no data show a different response to bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, rehabilitation, oxygen, or vaccines (A1F 2016). Exacerbations: Condition 6
  • Lung volume reduction surgery: Not recommended (A1F 2016, weak)
  • Lung transplant: For advanced disease; survival after transplant is similar to COPD without AATD (A1F 2016)
  • Liver disease: Managed as usual; the AATD diagnosis does not change management, and augmentation does not treat it (A1F 2016). See Condition 16
  • Liver transplant: For end-stage liver disease; the donor liver makes normal AAT, so augmentation is not needed afterward (A1F 2016)

AAT Augmentation Therapy (IV alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor from pooled human plasma; Prolastin-C, Zemaira, Aralast NP, Glassia):

  • Dose: 60 mg/kg IV once weekly (FDA label). Higher weekly doses and trough level monitoring are not recommended (A1F 2016)
  • Recommended (A1F 2016): FEV1 30-65% predicted (strong); FEV1 <30% (weak); FEV1 >65%: discuss uncertain benefit and cost individually; necrotizing panniculitis (strong)
  • Not recommended (A1F 2016): PI*MZ; continued smoking; emphysema or bronchiectasis without airflow obstruction; liver disease; after liver transplant
  • Other guidelines: GOLD 2026: never- or ex-smokers with FEV1 35-60% predicted are most suitable (Evidence B); reserve therapy for continued, rapid progression after quitting smoking. CTS 2025 (non-US): nonsmokers or ex-smokers with emphysema and FEV1 <80%, a deficiency genotype, and a level <11 μmol/L
  • Evidence: Slows loss of lung density on CT in trials (A1F 2016); benefit on exacerbations and emphysema progression not conclusively shown in RCTs (label); an observational cohort, mostly FEV1 <30%, showed improved survival (A1F 2016)
  • Contraindications (label): IgA deficiency with antibodies against IgA (risk of severe hypersensitivity); prior anaphylaxis or severe systemic reaction to alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor
  • In the hospital (Practical): Chronic therapy only; not a treatment for an acute exacerbation
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Test every adult with COPD once, regardless of age or ethnicity, preferably by genotype because levels change with inflammation (A1F 2016; GOLD 2026)
  • Basilar panacinar emphysema in a young nonsmoker = think AATD, but later diagnoses often have apical centrilobular emphysema (GOLD 2026)
  • PI*ZZ = severe deficiency; PI*MZ = intermediate level, higher COPD risk only with smoking, no augmentation
  • Augmentation = 60 mg/kg IV weekly; contraindicated in IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies (label)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Tiotropium, 💊 Albuterol

257. BRONCHIECTASIS

Chronic Productive Cough • Airway Clearance • NTM
ETIOLOGY

Post-Infectious: Childhood pneumonia, TB, NTM, pertussis

Immune: CVID, IgA deficiency, HIV

Genetic: Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, AAT deficiency

Aspiration/Obstruction: Foreign body, tumor, ABPA

Autoimmune: RA, Sjögren's, IBD

Chronic Airway Disease: COPD, asthma (CHEST 2026)

Idiopathic: With postinfective, the most common attribution; the idiopathic share varies widely with how thorough the workup is (CHEST 2026)

CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Symptoms: Chronic productive cough (purulent sputum), hemoptysis, recurrent infections, dyspnea

Exam: Crackles, wheezing, clubbing

HRCT: Confirms the diagnosis (CHEST 2026). Bronchial dilation (internal diameter > adjacent pulmonary artery = "signet ring sign"), lack of tapering, bronchial wall thickening

Workup for Etiology (ERS 2025, non-US; CHEST 2026 also calls for a detailed workup):

  • All patients: CBC with eosinophils, serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM), serum protein electrophoresis; total IgE plus Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG (ABPA); sputum for NTM smear and culture (at least 3 samples or BAL if NTM is suspected)
  • CF and PCD testing if onset in childhood or suggestive features. CF (sweat chloride, CFTR genetics): upper-lobe predominance, chronic rhinosinusitis, male infertility, pancreatitis, Pseudomonas or S. aureus infection; criteria in Condition 255. PCD: situs inversus, neonatal respiratory distress, middle or lower lobe predominance
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin: A1F 2016 (US) recommends testing all unexplained bronchiectasis (strong); ERS 2025 tests only with suggestive features such as basal emphysema or severe airflow obstruction. See Condition 256
  • Autoimmune serologies (ANA, RF, ANCA, ENA, anti-CCP) if systemic or autoimmune features
TREATMENT

Exacerbation (CHEST 2026): Acute worsening of cough, sputum volume or purulence, dyspnea, or a combination, that prompts a change in therapy

  • Sputum culture before antibiotics when possible (CHEST 2026; ERS 2025)
  • Antibiotic choice: Based on prior sputum cultures, particularly known Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa; broad-spectrum empiric therapy if there are no prior results (CHEST 2026, conditional, very low certainty)
  • Agents by prior isolate (BTS 2019, non-US; table uses UK doses, so dose by US label): S. pneumoniae or beta-lactamase-negative H. influenzae: amoxicillin. Beta-lactamase-positive H. influenzae or M. catarrhalis: amoxicillin-clavulanate. MSSA: flucloxacillin (UK agent); alternatives clarithromycin, doxycycline, or amoxicillin-clavulanate. MRSA: oral doxycycline (BTS also lists rifampicin and trimethoprim), linezolid third line; IV vancomycin (monitor levels) or linezolid. Coliforms: oral ciprofloxacin; IV ceftriaxone. P. aeruginosa: oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily (750 mg twice daily if more severe); IV ceftazidime, piperacillin-tazobactam, aztreonam, or meropenem, alone or combined with gentamicin or tobramycin (caution with aminoglycosides). Doxycycline is the second-line oral for most organisms
  • Route: Neither oral nor IV is inherently superior; choose by severity, oral tolerance, prior response, microbiology, and need for hospitalization. Expect improvement by 7 days; if not, consider resistant organisms and switch, e.g., to an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone for Pseudomonas, or to IV therapy if deteriorating (CHEST 2026). BTS 2019: consider IV if particularly unwell, resistant organisms, or failure of oral therapy (most often P. aeruginosa)
  • Duration: ≥10 or <10 days, depending on clinical response (CHEST 2026, conditional, very low certainty). ERS 2025 and BTS 2019 (non-US): 14 days is standard, especially if severe, and always with Pseudomonas (BTS); shorter if mild disease, more susceptible pathogens, or rapid recovery
  • Severe exacerbation features (ERS 2025): Tachypnea, acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory failure, falling oxygen saturation, hypercapnia, hemoptysis, new cyanosis or cor pulmonale, hemodynamic instability, impaired cognition
  • Airway clearance: Continue it, adapting frequency, intensity, and technique during the exacerbation (ERS 2025; CHEST 2026)

Preventing Exacerbations (frequent exacerbations, ≥2 a year; CHEST 2026):

  • Long-term macrolide (conditional, moderate certainty): azithromycin 250 mg daily or three times weekly, or 500 mg three times weekly (ERS 2025 dosing). Screen for NTM first; contraindicated if NTM is cultured. Baseline ECG if at high risk; audiometry if hearing is already impaired (CHEST 2026)
  • Long-term inhaled antibiotics for ≥3 months (conditional, low certainty); ERS 2025 recommends them strongly with chronic Pseudomonas. Bronchospasm in about 10% with tobramycin (CHEST 2026); many clinicians give a supervised test dose (ERS 2025)
  • Brensocatib (Brinsupri) (conditional, moderate certainty): 10 mg or 25 mg orally once daily, age 12 and older (FDA label 03/2026). Monitor for new rashes or skin conditions; regular dental checkups (gingival and periodontal reactions); avoid live attenuated vaccines (label)
  • Not recommended: Long-term atorvastatin (CHEST 2026); long-term inhaled corticosteroids without coexisting COPD or asthma (ERS 2025, non-US)

Airway Clearance (CHEST 2026, all conditional): Breathing techniques (expiration with an open glottis in the lateral position, or active cycle of breathing), oscillatory positive expiratory pressure, or high-frequency chest wall oscillation; nebulized hypertonic saline (isotonic saline is an acceptable alternative). Not dornase alfa (rhDNase): in idiopathic bronchiectasis it increased exacerbations and FEV1 decline; it is for CF only

First Pseudomonas Isolate: No recommendation for or against eradication (CHEST 2026, insufficient evidence); ERS 2025 (non-US) suggests offering eradication

Pulmonary Rehabilitation: For breathlessness or impaired exercise capacity (ERS 2025, strong, non-US)

Bronchodilators: If coexisting airflow obstruction

Hemoptysis: Tranexamic acid suggested (CHEST 2026, conditional, very low certainty); experts prefer the nebulized route in a monitored setting. BTS 2019 (non-US): 10 mL or less in 24 h, oral antibiotic; major hemoptysis, IV antibiotics based on known microbiology, consider TXA, and bronchial artery embolization first line if significant bleeding persists. Massive hemoptysis: Condition 49

Surgery: Consider resection for localized disease (1 or 2 contiguous lobes) with refractory symptoms despite optimized medical management, in appropriate candidates, by an experienced surgeon at a high-volume center (CHEST 2026, conditional, very low certainty); outcomes are worse when surgery is emergent or disease is diffuse

Lung Transplant Referral (BTS 2019, non-US, grade D): Consider at age 65 or younger with FEV1 <30% and significant clinical instability, or rapid progressive deterioration despite optimal management. Refer earlier with poor lung function plus massive hemoptysis, severe secondary pulmonary hypertension, ICU admission, or respiratory failure (particularly needing NIV)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Screen for NTM before chronic azithromycin; do not use it if NTM is cultured (macrolide resistance) (CHEST 2026)
  • Exacerbation: culture first, choose antibiotics by prior cultures, set duration by clinical response (CHEST 2026)
  • Dornase alfa is for CF only: in non-CF bronchiectasis it increased exacerbations (CHEST 2026)
  • Test immunoglobulins and ABPA serologies in everyone; CF testing if suggestive features, even in adults (ERS 2025)
  • Signet ring sign on CT = bronchiectasis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Azithromycin, 💊 Tobramycin, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Albuterol, 💊 TXA

258. HYPERSENSITIVITY PNEUMONITIS

Antigen Exposure • Nonfibrotic vs Fibrotic • Ground Glass + Mosaic
ETIOLOGY & CLASSIFICATION

Common Antigens:

  • Bird fancier's lung: Avian proteins (pigeons, parakeets)
  • Farmer's lung: Thermophilic actinomycetes (moldy hay)
  • Hot tub lung: Mycobacterium avium complex; histology differs from classic HP (ATS 2020), and a positive mycobacterial sputum culture may be the first clue (CHEST 2021), so send mycobacterial cultures. It often resolves with avoidance, with or without corticosteroids, without antimycobacterial drugs (S2k 2025, non-US)
  • Humidifier/AC lung: Bacteria, fungi in water reservoirs
  • No antigen is identified in up to 60% of patients despite a thorough history (ATS 2020)

Classification (ATS 2020; CHEST 2021): Nonfibrotic vs fibrotic HP, by fibrosis on HRCT (reticulation or ground glass with traction bronchiectasis or bronchiolectasis, honeycombing, or lobar volume loss). Fibrosis, not symptom duration, carries the prognosis; the older acute/subacute/chronic scheme is inferior (CHEST 2021)

Acute Presentation: Flu-like illness, cough, and dyspnea hours after a heavy exposure, improving with avoidance (Practical)

DIAGNOSIS

Exposure History (CHEST 2021): Type, extent, and timing of exposures relative to symptoms; an unrevealing history does not exclude HP. Suspected occupational exposure: involve occupational medicine and an environmental hygienist

Serum Antigen-Specific IgG: ATS 2020 suggests it to help identify exposures; do not rely on it alone to confirm or exclude HP (CHEST 2021). A positive result shows exposure, not disease (Practical)

HRCT (ATS 2020; CHEST 2021):

  • Nonfibrotic: Ground-glass opacities, profuse ill-defined centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation with air trapping, three-density pattern
  • Fibrotic: Fibrosis distributed randomly, mid-lung predominant, or relatively sparing the lower zones, with small-airway signs; a basal subpleural UIP-like pattern also occurs and can be indistinguishable from IPF (ATS 2020)
  • Integrate with clinical findings; do not use CT alone for a definite diagnosis (CHEST 2021)

BAL: Lymphocytosis supports HP; ATS 2020 recommends BAL lymphocyte analysis in nonfibrotic and suggests it in fibrotic HP. CHEST 2021: not needed routinely with a compelling exposure and a typical HRCT; lymphocytosis is inconsistent in fibrotic HP; a high count (e.g., ≥40%) may help exclude IPF. S2k 2025 (non-US) diagnostic criteria use lymphocytes >30%

Biopsy: Cryobiopsy or surgical lung biopsy when other data do not give a confident diagnosis (ATS 2020; CHEST 2021). Typical: bronchiolocentric cellular and/or fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, poorly formed non-necrotizing granulomas

Diagnosis: Multidisciplinary discussion when confidence is not high. Not suggested: inhalation challenge or lymphocyte proliferation testing (CHEST 2021)

TREATMENT

Evidence Base: No US guideline addresses HP treatment; the German S2k 2025 guideline (non-US) is the first HP guideline with treatment recommendations. Each point is labeled by its source

  • Antigen avoidance: Most important; identify and remove the inciting antigen and recheck exposure at every visit (CHEST 2021). Clear improvement is seen mainly in nonfibrotic HP; disease may progress despite apparent remediation (CHEST 2021)
  • Corticosteroids, acute or nonfibrotic HP (S2k 2025, non-US): For moderate to severe symptoms and functional impairment, in addition to avoidance; they speed recovery but do not replace avoidance. Typical start: prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg or 40 mg/day (prednisone is equivalent, Practical), tapered over about 2-3 months, then stopped
  • Corticosteroids, chronic fibrotic HP (S2k 2025, non-US): Only with an inflammatory component (centrilobular nodules or ground glass, BAL lymphocytosis, inflammatory histology). Maximum initial dose 0.5 mg/kg; reassess at 4-6 weeks; if responding, taper over 2-3 months to <10 mg/day and continue at least 6 months. Purely fibrotic HP is unlikely to respond and may do worse (S2k 2025; CHEST 2021 also finds response uncommon in fibrotic HP)
  • Steroid-sparing agents: Azathioprine or mycophenolate in steroid responders (S2k 2025; retrospective data only). With prolonged steroids consider PJP prophylaxis, glucose monitoring, and bone protection (Practical)
  • Antifibrotics: Only when fibrotic HP meets progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) criteria: ≥2 of worsening symptoms, physiologic progression (absolute FVC decline >5% or DLCO decline >10% predicted within 1 year), and radiologic progression, within the past year with no alternative explanation (2022 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT). Nintedanib 150 mg orally twice daily with food (FDA label: chronic fibrosing ILDs with a progressive phenotype); 2022 guideline: conditional, for PPF after standard management fails. Nerandomilast is also FDA approved for PPF (December 2025; Condition 254). S2k 2025 (non-US): nintedanib for progressive fibrotic HP; pirfenidone (off-label) if nintedanib fails or is not tolerated; anti-inflammatory plus antifibrotic combination is an option
  • Lung transplant: Evaluate early in progressive fibrotic HP (S2k 2025, non-US); post-transplant survival was better than in IPF (HR 0.25)
  • In the hospital: Remove the patient from the exposure (Practical). Acute exacerbation of fibrotic HP: Condition 48
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Detailed exposure history is key: birds, hot tubs, moldy environments; an unrevealing history does not exclude HP (CHEST 2021)
  • Classify by fibrosis on HRCT, not by symptom duration (CHEST 2021)
  • Fibrotic HP can mimic IPF: mid-lung or lower-zone-sparing fibrosis with air trapping suggests HP, but a basal UIP-like pattern does not exclude it (ATS 2020)
  • BAL lymphocytosis supports HP but is not needed with a compelling exposure and a typical CT (CHEST 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Mycophenolate, 💊 Nintedanib

259. PULMONARY NODULE EVALUATION

Fleischner Criteria • Solid vs Ground-Glass • Malignancy Risk
DEFINITIONS

Pulmonary Nodule: <3 cm; if >3 cm = mass (higher malignancy risk)

Types (Fleischner 2017):

  • Solid: Completely obscures lung parenchyma
  • Pure ground glass (nonsolid): Does not obscure lung parenchyma; often indolent, so follow-up is longer than for solid nodules
  • Part-solid: Ground glass with a solid component; a persistent part-solid nodule with a solid component ≥6 mm is highly suspicious
  • Subsolid covers both pure ground-glass and part-solid nodules

Scope of Fleischner 2017: Incidental nodules in adults ≥35 years. Not for lung cancer screening CT (use ACR Lung-RADS), known primary cancer, or immunocompromised patients; manage those by the clinical situation

RISK STRATIFICATION

Risk Category (Fleischner 2017, using ACCP categories): Low risk = estimated cancer risk <5%; high risk = 5% or more

Higher Malignancy Risk:

  • Older age, heavy smoking, asbestos, uranium, or radon exposure, family history of lung cancer
  • Larger size; irregular or spiculated margins; upper lobe location
  • Emphysema or pulmonary fibrosis on CT
  • Part-solid nodule with a solid component ≥6 mm, or a growing solid component
  • Growth on serial imaging
  • Known cancer: Fleischner does not apply (risk of metastasis)

Lower Malignancy Risk:

  • Smooth margins
  • Benign calcification (central, laminated, popcorn) or internal fat (hamartoma): no follow-up
  • Solid nodule stable for 2 years; subsolid nodules need up to 5 years
  • Perifissural or juxtapleural nodule with lymph node morphology (triangular or lentiform, septal extension to the pleura): no follow-up even if >6 mm
  • Many nodules (5 or more) often reflect prior granulomatous infection; multiple <6 mm pure ground-glass nodules are usually benign
FLEISCHNER SOCIETY GUIDELINES (2017): INCIDENTAL NODULES, ADULTS ≥35

Solid Nodules (size = average of long and short axes):

NodulesRisk<6 mm6-8 mm>8 mm
SingleLowNo routine follow-upCT at 6-12 months, then consider CT at 18-24 monthsConsider CT at 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling
SingleHighOptional CT at 12 monthsCT at 6-12 months, then CT at 18-24 monthsConsider CT at 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling
MultipleLowNo routine follow-upCT at 3-6 months, then consider CT at 18-24 monthsCT at 3-6 months, then consider CT at 18-24 months
MultipleHighOptional CT at 12 monthsCT at 3-6 months, then CT at 18-24 monthsCT at 3-6 months, then CT at 18-24 months

Subsolid Nodules:

Nodule<6 mm≥6 mm
Single pure ground glassNo routine follow-up (suspicious: consider CT at 2 and 4 years)CT at 6-12 months to confirm persistence, then every 2 years until 5 years; if a solid component or growth develops, consider resection
Single part-solidNo routine follow-upCT at 3-6 months to confirm persistence; if unchanged and solid component <6 mm, annual CT for 5 years. Solid component ≥6 mm: highly suspicious; solid component >8 mm, growing solid component, or suspicious morphology: PET/CT, biopsy, or resection
MultipleCT at 3-6 months; if stable, consider CT at 2 and 4 yearsCT at 3-6 months, then manage by the most suspicious nodule

Multiple nodules: Manage by the most suspicious nodule

EVALUATION OPTIONS
  • Serial CT: Intervals as above; low-dose, noncontrast technique for surveillance (ACCP 2013)
  • PET-CT: Solid nodule >8 mm with low to moderate pretest probability (5-65%); not to characterize a nodule with high probability (>65%) (ACCP 2013). Pooled sensitivity about 95% and specificity about 82% in a 2008 meta-analysis, 72-94% sensitivity in later studies; false positives with infection or inflammation, false negatives with less metabolically active tumors. Subsolid nodules are not reliably characterized; do not use PET for part-solid nodules with a solid component ≤8 mm (ACCP 2013)
  • Nonsurgical biopsy (CT-guided or navigational bronchoscopy): when probability is low to moderate (about 10-60%) (ACCP 2013)
  • Surgical diagnosis and resection: When probability is high (>65%) (ACCP 2013) or biopsy is positive
  • In the hospital (Practical): An incidental nodule on an inpatient CT needs a documented follow-up plan in the discharge summary and a named clinician responsible for it
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • <6 mm solid nodule in a low-risk adult ≥35 = no routine follow-up (Fleischner 2017)
  • Persistent part-solid nodule with a solid component ≥6 mm = highly suspicious (Fleischner 2017)
  • 2-year stability suggests benign for solid nodules; subsolid nodules need up to 5 years (Fleischner 2017)
  • Fleischner does not apply to screening CT (Lung-RADS), known cancer, or immunocompromised patients

260. THALASSEMIAS

Alpha vs Beta • Microcytic Anemia • Iron Overload
OVERVIEW

Definition: Inherited disorders of reduced globin chain synthesis (α or β chains)

Result: Microcytic anemia with ineffective erythropoiesis; hemolysis in severe forms

BETA-THALASSEMIA
TypeGenotypeClinical
Minor (trait)β/β⁺ or β/β⁰Mild microcytic anemia; usually asymptomatic
Intermediaβ⁺/β⁺ or β⁺/β⁰Moderate anemia; occasional transfusions
Major (Cooley's)β⁰/β⁰Severe transfusion-dependent anemia; presents in infancy

Labs: Microcytic anemia, target cells, elevated HbA2 (>3.5%) on electrophoresis

Complications (Major): Iron overload (transfusions + increased absorption), extramedullary hematopoiesis, bone deformities, growth retardation

ALPHA-THALASSEMIA
Genes DeletedNameClinical
1 (αα/α-)Silent carrierNormal
2 (α-/α- or αα/--)TraitMild microcytic anemia
3 (α-/--)HbH diseaseModerate hemolytic anemia; HbH (β4) on electrophoresis
4 (--/--)Hb Bart's hydrops fetalisFatal in utero

Note: α-thalassemia trait has NORMAL hemoglobin electrophoresis (need genetic testing)

TREATMENT
  • Trait: No treatment; avoid unnecessary iron supplementation
  • Transfusion-dependent: Regular transfusions to maintain Hb 9-10
  • Iron chelation: Deferasirox (oral daily), deferoxamine (SC/IV), deferiprone
  • Splenectomy: If hypersplenism increasing transfusion needs
  • Curative: Allogeneic stem cell transplant; gene therapy (new)
  • Luspatercept: For transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (reduces transfusion burden)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • β-thal trait: elevated HbA2; α-thal trait: normal electrophoresis
  • Don't give iron for thalassemia trait (already iron-loaded)
  • Mentzer index <13 (MCV/RBC) suggests thalassemia over iron deficiency
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Iron, 💊 Folic Acid, 💊 Hydroxyurea

261. MYELOPROLIFERATIVE NEOPLASMS

PV • ET • MF • JAK2 Mutation
OVERVIEW
DiseasePrimary FindingJAK2 V617FOther Mutations
Polycythemia Vera (PV)Elevated RBC mass95%JAK2 exon 12
Essential Thrombocythemia (ET)Elevated platelets50-60%CALR, MPL
Primary Myelofibrosis (MF)Bone marrow fibrosis50-60%CALR, MPL
POLYCYTHEMIA VERA

Diagnosis: Hb >16.5 (M) or >16 (F), OR Hct >49%/48% + JAK2 mutation + low EPO

Symptoms: Hyperviscosity (headache, visual changes, dizziness), aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, splenomegaly, thrombosis (including unusual sites — Budd-Chiari, portal vein)

Treatment:

  • Phlebotomy: Goal Hct <45%
  • Aspirin 81mg (all patients unless contraindicated)
  • Cytoreduction if high-risk: Hydroxyurea first-line; ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) if refractory
ESSENTIAL THROMBOCYTHEMIA

Diagnosis: Platelets ≥450K, bone marrow biopsy (megakaryocyte proliferation), JAK2/CALR/MPL mutation, exclusion of other causes

Complications: Thrombosis AND bleeding (acquired vWD if platelets very high)

Treatment:

  • Low-risk: Aspirin alone (or observation if CALR+ low-risk)
  • High-risk: Hydroxyurea + aspirin; anagrelide alternative
PRIMARY MYELOFIBROSIS

Features: Bone marrow fibrosis, cytopenias, massive splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, leukoerythroblastic smear (teardrop cells, nucleated RBCs)

Treatment:

  • Ruxolitinib: First-line for symptomatic splenomegaly/symptoms
  • Allogeneic SCT: Only curative option (for eligible high-risk patients)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • PV: Hct goal <45% reduces thrombosis
  • Aquagenic pruritus classic for PV
  • Teardrop cells + nucleated RBCs = myelofibrosis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Hydroxyurea, 💊 Ruxolitinib, 💊 Aspirin

262. CHRONIC MYELOID LEUKEMIA

BCR-ABL • Philadelphia Chromosome • Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors
CLINICAL FEATURES

Presentation: Often asymptomatic (incidental leukocytosis); fatigue, weight loss, early satiety, splenomegaly

Labs:

  • Marked leukocytosis (often 50-200K) with left shift
  • Basophilia and eosinophilia
  • Low LAP (leukocyte alkaline phosphatase) score
  • Anemia, thrombocytosis (or thrombocytopenia in advanced phase)
DIAGNOSIS

Philadelphia Chromosome: t(9;22) — BCR-ABL1 fusion gene

Testing:

  • Bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetics
  • FISH for BCR-ABL
  • PCR for BCR-ABL (quantitative — used for monitoring)
PHASES & TREATMENT
PhaseFeatures
Chronic<10% blasts; most present here
Accelerated10-19% blasts, other criteria
Blast crisis≥20% blasts; like acute leukemia

Treatment:

  • Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs): First-line for all patients
    • Imatinib: First-generation; well-tolerated
    • Dasatinib, Nilotinib, Bosutinib: Second-generation; more potent
    • Ponatinib: For T315I mutation (resistant to others)
  • Monitoring: Quantitative BCR-ABL PCR every 3 months; goal is major molecular response (MMR)
  • TKI discontinuation: Possible in select patients with deep molecular response
  • Allogeneic SCT: Reserved for TKI failure or blast crisis
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • BCR-ABL = Philadelphia chromosome = CML
  • TKIs transformed CML — near-normal life expectancy in chronic phase
  • T315I mutation = resistance; use ponatinib
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Imatinib
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 Peripheral Smear

263. CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA

CD5+ B-cells • Smudge Cells • Watch and Wait
CLINICAL FEATURES

Demographics: Median age 70; most common adult leukemia in Western countries

Presentation: Often asymptomatic (incidental lymphocytosis); lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, B symptoms

Labs:

  • Lymphocytosis (≥5000/μL clonal B-lymphocytes)
  • Smudge cells on peripheral smear
  • Flow cytometry: CD5+, CD19+, CD20 (dim), CD23+

Complications: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, ITP, infections (hypogammaglobulinemia), Richter transformation (to DLBCL)

STAGING & PROGNOSIS
Rai StageFeaturesRisk
0Lymphocytosis onlyLow
I+ LymphadenopathyIntermediate
II+ HepatosplenomegalyIntermediate
III+ Anemia (Hb <11)High
IV+ Thrombocytopenia (<100K)High

Poor Prognostic Markers: del(17p), TP53 mutation, unmutated IGHV, del(11q)

TREATMENT

Early Stage (Rai 0-II) Asymptomatic: Watch and wait — treatment doesn't improve survival

Indications to Treat: Progressive cytopenias, massive/symptomatic splenomegaly/lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, AIHA/ITP refractory to steroids

First-Line Options:

  • BTK inhibitors: Ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib — can be used regardless of del(17p)
  • BCL-2 inhibitor: Venetoclax (+ obinutuzumab for fixed duration)
  • Chemoimmunotherapy (FCR, BR) less commonly used now
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Smudge cells + CD5+ B-cells = CLL
  • Watch and wait for early-stage asymptomatic
  • del(17p)/TP53 = poor prognosis; BTK inhibitors preferred
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ibrutinib, 💊 Venetoclax, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Leukopenia/Neutropenia, 🔬 Peripheral Smear, 🔬 Anemia

264. MULTIPLE MYELOMA

CRAB Criteria • M-Protein • Bone Disease
CLINICAL FEATURES — CRAB
  • C — Calcium elevation (hypercalcemia)
  • R — Renal insufficiency (light chain cast nephropathy)
  • A — Anemia (normocytic)
  • B — Bone disease (lytic lesions, pathologic fractures, bone pain)

Other: Recurrent infections, hyperviscosity (rare), amyloidosis

DIAGNOSIS

Diagnostic Criteria (≥10% clonal plasma cells + end-organ damage OR biomarker):

  • Bone marrow clonal plasma cells ≥10%
  • PLUS: CRAB criteria OR biomarkers (sFLC ratio ≥100, bone marrow plasma cells ≥60%, >1 focal lesion on MRI)

Workup:

  • SPEP/UPEP with immunofixation: M-protein (monoclonal spike)
  • Serum free light chains
  • Bone marrow biopsy
  • Skeletal survey or whole-body low-dose CT (lytic lesions)
  • β2-microglobulin, LDH (prognosis)
TREATMENT

Transplant-Eligible:

  • Induction: VRd (bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone) ± daratumumab
  • Autologous stem cell transplant
  • Maintenance: Lenalidomide

Transplant-Ineligible: VRd or DRd (daratumumab, lenalidomide, dex) until progression

Supportive:

  • Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) or denosumab for bone disease
  • Avoid NSAIDs (nephrotoxic)
  • VTE prophylaxis with IMiDs
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Lytic lesions (not blastic) — bone scan often negative
  • Rouleaux formation on smear
  • MGUS → smoldering → myeloma progression spectrum
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Dexamethasone, 💊 Zoledronic Acid
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 SPEP/UPEP/Free Light Chains, 🔬 Hypercalcemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 LDH, 🔬 Proteinuria

265. VON WILLEBRAND DISEASE

Most Common Inherited Bleeding Disorder • DDAVP
TYPES
TypeDefectInheritanceSeverity
Type 1Partial quantitative deficiencyADMild-moderate (75%)
Type 2Qualitative defect (multiple subtypes)ADModerate
Type 3Complete deficiencyARSevere (rare)
CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

Bleeding Pattern: Mucocutaneous — epistaxis, easy bruising, menorrhagia, GI bleeding, prolonged bleeding after surgery/dental procedures

Labs:

  • Prolonged PTT (vWF carries factor VIII)
  • Normal PT, platelets
  • Prolonged bleeding time (or abnormal PFA-100)

Specific Tests:

  • vWF antigen (vWF:Ag)
  • vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor — vWF:RCo)
  • Factor VIII level
  • vWF multimer analysis (for Type 2 subtypes)
TREATMENT

Type 1:

  • DDAVP (desmopressin): First-line; releases vWF from endothelial stores
  • Test with DDAVP trial before planned procedures

Type 2 & 3 (or DDAVP-unresponsive):

  • vWF-containing factor concentrates (Humate-P)

Adjuncts:

  • Tranexamic acid: For mucosal bleeding, menorrhagia
  • Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Prolonged PTT + mucosal bleeding + normal platelets = vWD
  • DDAVP for Type 1; contraindicated in Type 2B (worsens thrombocytopenia)
  • Most common inherited bleeding disorder
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 DDAVP, 💊 TXA

266. HEMOPHILIA

Factor VIII (A) vs IX (B) • Hemarthrosis • Factor Replacement
CLASSIFICATION
TypeDeficiencyInheritanceFrequency
Hemophilia AFactor VIIIX-linked recessive80-85%
Hemophilia BFactor IXX-linked recessive15-20%

Severity:

  • Severe: <1% factor activity — spontaneous bleeding
  • Moderate: 1-5% — bleeding with minor trauma
  • Mild: 5-40% — bleeding with surgery/major trauma
CLINICAL FEATURES

Bleeding Pattern: Deep tissue/joint bleeding (unlike vWD)

  • Hemarthrosis (knees, elbows, ankles) — hallmark; leads to arthropathy
  • Muscle hematomas (including iliopsoas)
  • Intracranial hemorrhage
  • Prolonged bleeding after circumcision, dental work, surgery

Labs:

  • Prolonged PTT
  • Normal PT, platelets, bleeding time
  • Mixing study corrects (factor deficiency, not inhibitor)
TREATMENT

Factor Replacement:

  • On-demand: For acute bleeding
  • Prophylaxis: Regular infusions to prevent bleeding (severe patients)
  • Recombinant factors preferred over plasma-derived
  • Extended half-life products available

Hemophilia A with Inhibitors:

  • Emicizumab: Bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII function; prophylaxis
  • Bypassing agents: rFVIIa, FEIBA

DDAVP: May work for mild Hemophilia A (releases vWF-bound FVIII)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Hemarthrosis = hemophilia; mucosal = vWD
  • Prolonged PTT that corrects with mixing = factor deficiency
  • Emicizumab revolutionized care for severe Hemophilia A
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 DDAVP, 💊 TXA
