267. MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS

Demyelinating • McDonald Criteria • Disease-Modifying Therapy
CLINICAL FEATURES

Demographics: Young adults (20-40), female predominance

Classic Presentations:

  • Optic neuritis: Unilateral vision loss, pain with eye movement, afferent pupillary defect
  • Transverse myelitis: Sensory level, weakness, bowel/bladder dysfunction
  • Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO): Impaired adduction, nystagmus in abducting eye
  • Lhermitte sign: Electric shock down spine with neck flexion
  • Cerebellar symptoms, trigeminal neuralgia

Patterns:

  • Relapsing-remitting (RRMS): 85% at onset; discrete attacks with recovery
  • Secondary progressive (SPMS): Gradual progression after RRMS
  • Primary progressive (PPMS): Progressive from onset (15%)
DIAGNOSIS — McDONALD CRITERIA (2017)

Requires: Dissemination in space (DIS) AND time (DIT)

  • DIS: ≥1 T2 lesion in ≥2 typical locations (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord)
  • DIT: Simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions OR new T2/enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI OR CSF oligoclonal bands

CSF: Oligoclonal bands (>90%), elevated IgG index

MRI: T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions, "Dawson's fingers" (periventricular)

TREATMENT

Acute Relapse: High-dose IV methylprednisolone (1g daily × 3-5 days)

Disease-Modifying Therapy (DMT):

  • High-efficacy: Natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, alemtuzumab
  • Moderate-efficacy: Dimethyl fumarate, fingolimod, teriflunomide
  • Injectable: Interferons, glatiramer (less commonly used now)

PPMS: Ocrelizumab (only FDA-approved DMT)

Symptomatic: Fatigue (modafinil), spasticity (baclofen), bladder dysfunction

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • INO in young adult = MS until proven otherwise
  • Oligoclonal bands can satisfy DIT
  • Natalizumab risk: PML (check JC virus antibody)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Ocrelizumab, 💊 Natalizumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 CSF Analysis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 ANA
↑ Back to Table of Contents

268. PARKINSON DISEASE

TRAP • Dopaminergic Therapy • Motor Fluctuations
CLINICAL FEATURES — TRAP
  • T — Tremor: Resting, "pill-rolling," 4-6 Hz; improves with action
  • R — Rigidity: Cogwheel (with tremor) or lead-pipe
  • A — Akinesia/Bradykinesia: Slowness of movement; masked facies, micrographia
  • P — Postural instability: Later feature; falls

Asymmetric onset is typical

Non-Motor: Anosmia (early), constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression, cognitive impairment. REM sleep behavior disorder in PD (AASM 2023, all conditional): clonazepam, immediate-release melatonin, or transdermal rivastigmine; not deep brain stimulation; if drug-induced, stop the drug

TREATMENT

Dopaminergic Therapy:

  • Carbidopa-levodopa: Most effective; start when symptoms affect function
  • Dopamine agonists: Pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine — can use early; risk of impulse control disorders
  • MAO-B inhibitors: Selegiline, rasagiline — mild benefit; can be initial monotherapy
  • COMT inhibitors: Entacapone — extends levodopa effect

Motor Complications (after years of levodopa):

  • "Wearing off": End-of-dose deterioration — add COMT inhibitor, increase frequency
  • Dyskinesias: Peak-dose involuntary movements — reduce levodopa dose, add amantadine
  • "On-off" phenomenon: Unpredictable fluctuations

Advanced: Deep brain stimulation (subthalamic nucleus)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Asymmetric resting tremor + bradykinesia = PD
  • Dopamine agonists: Impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality)
  • Drug-induced parkinsonism: Antipsychotics, metoclopramide — symmetric, no tremor
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Levodopa, 💊 Pramipexole, 💊 Ropinirole, 💊 Rasagiline
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated TSH
↑ Back to Table of Contents

269. ESSENTIAL TREMOR

Action Tremor • Alcohol-Responsive • Beta-Blockers
CLINICAL FEATURES

Characteristics:

  • Action/postural tremor (opposite of PD resting tremor)
  • Bilateral and symmetric (vs asymmetric in PD)
  • Affects hands, head ("no-no" or "yes-yes"), voice
  • Frequency 4-12 Hz
  • Improves with alcohol
  • Family history often positive (autosomal dominant)

No other neurologic findings (vs PD which has bradykinesia, rigidity)

TREATMENT

First-Line:

  • Propranolol: 20-80mg BID (or long-acting)
  • Primidone: Start low (25mg), titrate slowly (sedation)

Second-Line: Topiramate, gabapentin, benzodiazepines

Refractory: Deep brain stimulation (VIM thalamus), focused ultrasound thalamotomy

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Action tremor + improves with alcohol = essential tremor
  • Resting tremor + bradykinesia = Parkinson
  • Propranolol or primidone first-line
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Phenobarbital
↑ Back to Table of Contents

270. AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS (ALS)

UMN + LMN Signs • Bulbar Symptoms • Riluzole
CLINICAL FEATURES

Combined Upper AND Lower Motor Neuron Signs:

  • UMN: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign
  • LMN: Weakness, atrophy, fasciculations

Preserved: Sensation, cognition (mostly), eye movements, bowel/bladder (early)

Onset Patterns:

  • Limb-onset (70%): Asymmetric weakness, often hand
  • Bulbar-onset (25%): Dysarthria, dysphagia — worse prognosis

Progression: Relentless; respiratory failure is usual cause of death

DIAGNOSIS

Clinical Diagnosis: UMN + LMN signs in multiple regions, progressive course

El Escorial Criteria: Definite, probable, possible ALS based on regions involved

EMG: Widespread denervation (fibrillations, positive sharp waves, fasciculations) in multiple regions

Rule Out: Cervical myelopathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, Kennedy disease

TREATMENT
  • Riluzole: Glutamate antagonist; prolongs survival by ~3 months
  • Edaravone: Free radical scavenger; may slow functional decline
  • Multidisciplinary care: Pulmonology, nutrition, PT/OT, speech therapy
  • Non-invasive ventilation: Prolongs survival, improves quality of life
  • PEG tube: When dysphagia compromises nutrition

Prognosis: Median survival 3-5 years; bulbar-onset worse

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • UMN + LMN signs without sensory loss = ALS
  • Fasciculations + atrophy + hyperreflexia in same limb = classic
  • Riluzole is disease-modifying but effect is modest
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Riluzole
↑ Back to Table of Contents

271. NORMAL PRESSURE HYDROCEPHALUS

Wet • Wobbly • Wacky • LP Trial
CLINICAL FEATURES — TRIAD
  • Gait disturbance: Magnetic/apraxic gait ("feet stuck to floor"), wide-based, shuffling — earliest and most responsive to treatment
  • Urinary incontinence: Urge incontinence; later frank incontinence
  • Dementia: Subcortical pattern; psychomotor slowing, executive dysfunction

Mnemonic: "Wet, Wobbly, Wacky" (or "Wacky, Wobbly, Wet" — in order of appearance)

DIAGNOSIS

Imaging:

  • CT/MRI: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal enlargement
  • Evans index >0.3 (ratio of frontal horns to maximum brain width)
  • Periventricular white matter changes

Lumbar Puncture: Normal opening pressure (hence "normal pressure")

LP Trial (High-Volume Tap):

  • Remove 30-50 mL CSF
  • Assess gait before and after (video)
  • Improvement predicts response to shunting

Extended Lumbar Drainage: 3-day trial if LP inconclusive

TREATMENT
  • VP (ventriculoperitoneal) shunt: Definitive treatment
  • Gait improves most; dementia may improve less
  • Risks: Infection, subdural hematoma, shunt malfunction
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Gait responds best to shunting; dementia may not improve
  • LP trial predicts surgical response
  • Ventriculomegaly + triad + improvement with LP = NPH
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Acetazolamide
↑ Back to Table of Contents

272. HEADACHE SYNDROMES

Migraine • Tension • Cluster • Trigeminal Neuralgia
COMPARISON
FeatureMigraineTensionCluster
LocationUnilateral (often)Bilateral, band-likeUnilateral, periorbital
QualityPulsating/throbbingPressing/tighteningExcruciating, stabbing
Duration4-72 hours30 min - 7 days15-180 minutes
AssociatedN/V, photophobia, phonophobia, auraNone typicallyLacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis, restlessness
BehaviorSeeks quiet dark roomContinues activityPacing, agitated
CLUSTER HEADACHE

Features: "Suicide headache" — severe; occurs in clusters (weeks-months) then remission; often nocturnal; male predominance

Autonomic Features: Ipsilateral lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis, miosis

Abortive: High-flow O2 (100%, 12-15 L/min) — first-line; sumatriptan SC/nasal

Preventive: Verapamil (first-line), lithium, galcanezumab

TRIGEMINAL NEURALGIA

Features: Brief (seconds) electric shock-like pain in V2/V3 distribution; triggered by touch, chewing, talking

Treatment:

  • Carbamazepine: First-line
  • Oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, baclofen
  • Surgery: Microvascular decompression if refractory (often vascular loop compressing nerve)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Cluster: High-flow O2 and sumatriptan abortive; verapamil preventive
  • Trigeminal neuralgia: Carbamazepine first-line
  • Young woman + visual aura + migraine + OCP = increased stroke risk
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sumatriptan, 💊 Ketorolac, 💊 Prochlorperazine, 💊 Valproic Acid, 💊 Metoprolol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyponatremia, 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 CSF Analysis

273. PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY

Length-Dependent • Workup • Treatable Causes
CLASSIFICATION

By Pattern:

  • Length-dependent (distal symmetric): Stocking-glove; most common
  • Mononeuropathy: Single nerve (carpal tunnel, peroneal palsy)
  • Mononeuritis multiplex: Multiple individual nerves (vasculitis, diabetes)
  • Polyradiculopathy: Multiple nerve roots

By Fiber Type:

  • Large fiber: Vibration, proprioception, reflexes lost first
  • Small fiber: Pain, temperature; burning/stinging pain
COMMON CAUSES
  • Diabetes — most common in US
  • Alcohol
  • B12 deficiency — can cause combined sensory + UMN signs
  • Chemotherapy — platinum, taxanes, vinca alkaloids
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Hereditary — Charcot-Marie-Tooth
  • Inflammatory — GBS, CIDP
  • Paraproteinemia — MGUS, myeloma, amyloid
WORKUP

Initial Labs:

  • Fasting glucose / HbA1c
  • B12 (with MMA if borderline)
  • TSH
  • CBC, CMP
  • SPEP/UPEP with immunofixation

If Initial Negative: ANA, HIV, hepatitis B/C, Lyme, heavy metals, genetic testing

EMG/NCS: Confirms neuropathy; distinguishes axonal vs demyelinating; important for CIDP

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Diabetes + alcohol account for majority
  • B12 deficiency can cause neuropathy + myelopathy
  • Demyelinating pattern on EMG: Think GBS, CIDP, or hereditary
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Gabapentin/Pregabalin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Vitamin B12, 🔬 Folate, 🔬 Elevated HbA1c, 🔬 HIV Testing, 🔬 Elevated TSH
↑ Back to Table of Contents

274. DEMENTIA SYNDROMES

Alzheimer's • Vascular • Lewy Body • FTD
COMPARISON
TypeKey FeaturesPathology
Alzheimer'sMemory loss earliest; gradual declineAmyloid plaques, tau tangles
VascularStepwise decline; focal signs; CV risk factorsInfarcts, white matter disease
Lewy BodyVisual hallucinations, parkinsonism, fluctuations, REM sleep disorderα-synuclein inclusions
FrontotemporalEarly personality/behavior change OR language dysfunction; younger onsetTau or TDP-43
Parkinson dementiaPD for ≥1 year before dementiaα-synuclein
WORKUP

Rule Out Reversible Causes:

  • B12 deficiency
  • Thyroid disease (TSH)
  • Depression ("pseudodementia")
  • NPH
  • Medication effect
  • Neurosyphilis, HIV (if risk factors)

Imaging: MRI (atrophy pattern, vascular changes, masses)

Biomarkers: CSF Aβ42/tau, amyloid PET (for Alzheimer's confirmation)

TREATMENT

Alzheimer's:

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors: Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine — modest benefit
  • Memantine: NMDA antagonist — moderate-severe AD
  • Lecanemab, donanemab: Anti-amyloid monoclonals — early AD

Lewy Body:

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors helpful
  • AVOID antipsychotics — severe sensitivity; use quetiapine if necessary

FTD: No proven disease-modifying therapy; SSRIs for behavioral symptoms

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + fluctuations = Lewy Body
  • Antipsychotics contraindicated in Lewy Body
  • Behavioral variant FTD: Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy — often misdiagnosed as psychiatric

275. VERTIGO

Central vs Peripheral • BPPV • HINTS Exam
CENTRAL VS PERIPHERAL
FeaturePeripheralCentral
OnsetSuddenGradual or sudden
NystagmusHorizontal/torsional; inhibited by fixationAny direction; not inhibited by fixation
Hearing lossMay be presentUsually absent
Neurologic signsAbsentPresent (diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia)
SeverityOften more severe vertigoMay be less severe
HINTS EXAM (for Acute Vestibular Syndrome)
  • Head Impulse: Abnormal (corrective saccade) = peripheral; Normal = central (BAD)
  • Nystagmus: Direction-changing = central
  • Test of Skew: Vertical skew deviation = central

Central Pattern (any one): Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew → MRI/stroke workup

COMMON PERIPHERAL CAUSES

BPPV:

  • Brief episodes (<1 min) triggered by position change
  • Dix-Hallpike positive (torsional upbeat nystagmus with latency)
  • Treatment: Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning)

Vestibular Neuritis:

  • Acute prolonged vertigo (days); often post-viral
  • No hearing loss (vs labyrinthitis)
  • Treatment: Supportive; vestibular rehabilitation; short-term meclizine

Meniere's Disease:

  • Episodic vertigo (20 min - hours) + hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness
  • Treatment: Low-sodium diet, diuretics
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • HINTS beats MRI for detecting stroke in acute vestibular syndrome
  • Normal head impulse test is concerning — suggests central cause
  • BPPV: Posterior canal most common; Epley maneuver curative
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Diazepam, 💊 Prochlorperazine, 💊 Methylprednisolone
↑ Back to Table of Contents

276. ANCA VASCULITIS

GPA • MPA • EGPA • Pulmonary-Renal Syndrome
CLASSIFICATION
DiseaseANCAKey Features
GPA (Wegener's)PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA)Upper airway (sinusitis, saddle nose), lung nodules/hemorrhage, glomerulonephritis
MPAMPO-ANCA (p-ANCA)Glomerulonephritis (pauci-immune), pulmonary hemorrhage; NO upper airway
EGPA (Churg-Strauss)MPO-ANCA (50%)Asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy, cardiac involvement
GPA (GRANULOMATOSIS WITH POLYANGIITIS)

Classic Triad:

  • Upper airway: Chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, saddle nose deformity, subglottic stenosis
  • Lungs: Nodules (may cavitate), infiltrates, hemorrhage
  • Kidneys: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (pauci-immune crescentic)
DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Labs: PR3-ANCA or MPO-ANCA; elevated ESR/CRP; urinalysis (RBC casts)

Induction (Severe):

  • Rituximab OR cyclophosphamide + glucocorticoids
  • Plasmapheresis: For severe renal disease or pulmonary hemorrhage

Maintenance: Rituximab or azathioprine

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Pulmonary-renal syndrome: Think ANCA vasculitis or anti-GBM
  • PR3-ANCA = GPA; MPO-ANCA = MPA or EGPA
  • Saddle nose deformity is classic for GPA
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Cyclophosphamide, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 ANCA, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 Hematuria
↑ Back to Table of Contents

277. POLYARTERITIS NODOSA

Medium-Vessel Vasculitis • HBV Association • Microaneurysms
CLINICAL FEATURES

Key Features:

  • Constitutional: Fever, weight loss, malaise
  • Neurologic: Mononeuritis multiplex (foot drop, wrist drop)
  • Renal: Hypertension, renal infarcts (NOT glomerulonephritis)
  • GI: Mesenteric ischemia, bowel perforation
  • Skin: Livedo reticularis, subcutaneous nodules

SPARES lungs (unlike ANCA vasculitis)

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Association: Hepatitis B (10-30%)

ANCA: Negative

Angiography: Microaneurysms and stenoses

Treatment: Glucocorticoids ± cyclophosphamide; treat HBV if present

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Medium vessel + mononeuritis multiplex + spares lungs = PAN
  • Always check Hepatitis B
  • Microaneurysms on angiography
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Cyclophosphamide, 💊 Rituximab
↑ Back to Table of Contents

278. REACTIVE ARTHRITIS

Post-Infectious • HLA-B27 • Can't See, Can't Pee, Can't Climb a Tree
CLINICAL FEATURES

Classic Triad: Arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis

Triggering Infections: Chlamydia (GU); Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia (GI)

Arthritis: Asymmetric oligoarthritis, lower extremity; 1-4 weeks post-infection

Other: Enthesitis, dactylitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis

TREATMENT
  • NSAIDs: First-line
  • Treat active Chlamydia if present
  • DMARDs: Sulfasalazine, MTX for chronic
  • TNF inhibitors: If DMARD failure
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Asymmetric oligoarthritis + recent GU/GI infection = reactive arthritis
  • HLA-B27 associated
  • Keratoderma blennorrhagicum looks like pustular psoriasis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Indomethacin, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Methotrexate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated ESR, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Synovial Fluid Analysis, 🔬 Urinalysis

279. RAYNAUD PHENOMENON

Primary vs Secondary • Tricolor Change • CCB Treatment
PRIMARY VS SECONDARY

Tricolor Change: White → Blue → Red

FeaturePrimarySecondary
Age onset15-30>30
Tissue damageNoneUlcers, gangrene
ANANegativeOften positive
Nailfold capillariesNormalAbnormal

Secondary Causes: Scleroderma (most common), SLE, MCTD

TREATMENT
  • All: Avoid cold, smoking cessation
  • First-line: Dihydropyridine CCBs (nifedipine, amlodipine)
  • Severe: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors, prostacyclin
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Digital ulcers = secondary; think scleroderma
  • Abnormal nailfold capillaries predict CTD
  • CCBs are first-line
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Amlodipine, 💊 Sildenafil

280. CRYOGLOBULINEMIA

HCV Association • Palpable Purpura • MPGN
CLINICAL FEATURES

Meltzer's Triad: Palpable purpura + arthralgias + weakness

HCV causes 90% of mixed cryoglobulinemia

Other: MPGN, peripheral neuropathy, Raynaud

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Labs: Cryoglobulins (transport at 37°C), low C4, positive RF, HCV RNA

Treatment: Treat HCV (DAAs); rituximab for severe disease

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • HCV causes 90% of mixed cryoglobulinemia
  • Low C4 + positive RF + purpura = cryoglobulinemia
  • Treat HCV first
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Rituximab

281. INVASIVE CANDIDIASIS

Candidemia • Echinocandins • Line Removal
RISK FACTORS & PRESENTATION

Risk Factors: Central lines, TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotics, immunosuppression, GI surgery, ICU stay

Presentation: Fever unresponsive to antibiotics, sepsis

Metastatic Complications: Endophthalmitis (fundoscopic exam required), endocarditis, osteomyelitis, hepatosplenic candidiasis

DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Diagnosis: Blood cultures (often low sensitivity); β-D-glucan (sensitive but not specific)

Treatment:

  • Echinocandin first-line: Caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin
  • Fluconazole: Step-down if susceptible and clinically stable
  • Remove all central lines
  • Dilated fundoscopic exam within first week
  • Duration: 14 days from first negative blood culture

Repeat blood cultures daily until negative

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Echinocandin first-line; remove all lines
  • Fundoscopic exam required to rule out endophthalmitis
  • 14 days from first negative culture
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Micafungin, 💊 Caspofungin, 💊 Anidulafungin, 💊 Fluconazole
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Beta-D-Glucan, 🔬 Blood Cultures, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Procalcitonin, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT
🧫 ABX COMPANION Cunha Empiric Framework
→ Invasive Candida / Sepsis

282. PNEUMOCYSTIS PNEUMONIA (PCP)

HIV/AIDS • TMP-SMX • Adjunctive Steroids
RISK FACTORS & PRESENTATION

At Risk: HIV with CD4 <200; solid organ transplant; high-dose steroids; hematologic malignancy

Presentation:

  • Subacute progressive dyspnea (weeks)
  • Dry cough, fever
  • Hypoxemia, especially with exertion
  • HIV patients: Indolent; Non-HIV: More acute/severe
DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Imaging: Bilateral diffuse ground-glass infiltrates; pneumatoceles; can be normal early

Labs: Elevated LDH (nonspecific), β-D-glucan

Diagnosis: Induced sputum or BAL for PCR or DFA staining

Treatment:

  • TMP-SMX: 15-20 mg/kg/day TMP divided q6-8h × 21 days
  • Alternatives: Pentamidine IV, atovaquone, dapsone + TMP, clindamycin + primaquine
  • Adjunctive steroids if PaO2 <70 or A-a gradient ≥35: Prednisone 40mg BID × 5d, then taper
PROPHYLAXIS
  • HIV: CD4 <200 or CD4 <14% or history of OI
  • TMP-SMX DS daily (or 3×/week); alternatives: dapsone, atovaquone, pentamidine inhaled
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • TMP-SMX + steroids if hypoxic
  • Elevated LDH + bilateral GGO in immunocompromised = PCP
  • 21 days treatment
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 TMP-SMX, 💊 Prednisone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated A-a Gradient, 🔬 LDH, 🔬 Beta-D-Glucan, 🔬 Leukocytosis
🧫 ABX COMPANION Cunha Empiric Framework
→ PCP (Pneumocystis)

283. INVASIVE ASPERGILLOSIS

Neutropenia • Halo Sign • Voriconazole
RISK FACTORS & PRESENTATION

At Risk: Prolonged neutropenia, HSCT, solid organ transplant, high-dose steroids, CGD

Pulmonary: Fever unresponsive to antibiotics, cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain

Other Sites: Sinuses, CNS, disseminated

DIAGNOSIS

CT Findings:

  • Halo sign: Ground-glass surrounding nodule (early)
  • Air-crescent sign: Cavitation (later, with neutrophil recovery)

Biomarkers: Galactomannan (serum, BAL), β-D-glucan

Definitive: Culture/histopath from tissue (septate hyphae, acute angle branching)

TREATMENT
  • Voriconazole: First-line
  • Alternatives: Isavuconazole, liposomal amphotericin B
  • Duration: Minimum 6-12 weeks; until resolution + immune recovery
  • Reduce immunosuppression if possible
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Halo sign on CT in neutropenic patient = aspergillosis
  • Voriconazole first-line; check drug levels
  • Galactomannan useful for diagnosis and monitoring
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Voriconazole, 💊 Isavuconazole, 💊 Posaconazole, 💊 Liposomal AmB, 💊 Caspofungin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Galactomannan, 🔬 Beta-D-Glucan, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Low PaO2

284. CRYPTOCOCCAL MENINGITIS

HIV/AIDS • India Ink • Amphotericin + Flucytosine
CLINICAL FEATURES

At Risk: HIV with CD4 <100, solid organ transplant, prolonged steroids

Presentation: Subacute meningitis — headache, fever, altered mental status; may lack meningismus

Elevated Intracranial Pressure: Common; requires serial LPs or drain

DIAGNOSIS
  • CSF cryptococcal antigen: Highly sensitive/specific
  • Serum cryptococcal antigen: Often positive
  • India ink: Encapsulated yeast (less sensitive)
  • CSF: Elevated opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, elevated protein
TREATMENT

HIV-associated (Induction):

  • Liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine × 2 weeks
  • Followed by fluconazole consolidation (8 weeks) then maintenance

ICP Management: Serial therapeutic LPs (remove 20-30 mL) or lumbar drain; goal OP <20 cm H2O

ART: Delay 4-6 weeks to avoid IRIS

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Cryptococcal antigen is key diagnostic test
  • Elevated ICP management critical — serial LPs
  • Delay ART 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS risk
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Liposomal AmB, 💊 Fluconazole
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 CSF Analysis, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Beta-D-Glucan, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

285. ENDEMIC MYCOSES

Histoplasmosis • Blastomycosis • Coccidioidomycosis
GEOGRAPHIC DISTRIBUTION
FungusRegionExposure
HistoplasmaOhio/Mississippi River valleysBird/bat droppings, caves
BlastomycesGreat Lakes, Ohio/Mississippi valleysDecaying wood, soil
CoccidioidesSouthwest US (Arizona, California)Desert soil (dust storms)
CLINICAL FEATURES

Histoplasmosis:

  • Usually self-limited; can cause chronic pulmonary (mimics TB), disseminated in immunocompromised
  • Mediastinal lymphadenopathy, fibrosing mediastinitis (rare)

Blastomycosis:

  • Pulmonary, skin (verrucous lesions), bone, prostate
  • Less likely to resolve spontaneously — usually treat

Coccidioidomycosis (Valley Fever):

  • 60% asymptomatic; can cause pneumonia, erythema nodosum, disseminated (meningitis, bone)
  • Risk of dissemination: Filipinos, African Americans, immunocompromised, pregnancy
DIAGNOSIS & TREATMENT

Diagnosis: Urine/serum antigen (Histo, Blasto), serology, culture, histopathology

Treatment:

  • Mild-moderate: Itraconazole
  • Severe/disseminated: Amphotericin B → itraconazole
  • Cocci meningitis: Lifelong fluconazole
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Know the geography: Histo=Midwest caves; Cocci=Southwest desert; Blasto=Great Lakes
  • Cocci meningitis requires lifelong fluconazole
  • Always treat blastomycosis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Voriconazole, 💊 Fluconazole, 💊 Liposomal AmB
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Beta-D-Glucan, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 LDH

286. STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME / TEN

Drug Reaction • Mucosal Involvement • Burn Unit Care
DEFINITION & CAUSES

Spectrum, by % BSA of epidermal detachment (BAD 2016, non-US):

  • SJS: <10% BSA, with widespread purpuric macules or flat atypical targets
  • SJS-TEN overlap: 10-30% BSA
  • TEN: >30% BSA
  • Mortality: SJS <10%, TEN 30%, overall about 22% (BAD 2016); US reports 15%-49% (SDH 2020). Systemic sepsis is the most frequent cause of death (BAD 2016)

Causes: A culprit drug is found in about 85% of cases; infection is a rare trigger (Mycoplasma-induced SJS is reported) (BAD 2016). Latency after starting the drug: as early as 4 days and out to 8 weeks (JTF 2022); 5-28 days is most likely, shorter after a previous reaction to the same drug (BAD 2016)

Most Common Drugs (BAD 2016 Table 2, non-US):

  • Allopurinol
  • Anticonvulsants: Carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, phenytoin
  • Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and other sulfur antibiotics; sulfasalazine
  • Oxicam NSAIDs (eg, piroxicam, meloxicam)
  • Nevirapine
CLINICAL FEATURES

Prodrome: Fever, malaise, upper respiratory tract symptoms (BAD 2016)

Skin: Painful rash, initially on the face and chest; purpuric macules or flat atypical targets expand and coalesce, reaching a maximum 5-7 days after onset, then flaccid bullae as necrotic epidermis separates. Nikolsky sign positive (not specific: also positive in pemphigus) (BAD 2016)

Mucosal Involvement: 97% overall: oral 93%, ocular 78%, genital 63% (BAD 2016). Respiratory epithelial necrolysis can cause bronchial obstruction; GI necrolysis causes profuse diarrhea; AKI may occur in the early phase (BAD 2016)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Extent (BAD 2016): Record erythema and epidermal detachment separately on a body map (Lund and Browder chart). Detachment includes detached plus detachable (Nikolsky-positive) epidermis; this figure, not the erythema, carries the prognosis

Labs and Imaging: CBC, ESR, CRP, BMP with magnesium, phosphate, bicarbonate and glucose, LFTs, coagulation studies, Mycoplasma serology, chest X-ray (BAD 2016); ABG at baseline (SDH 2020)

Skin Biopsy (BAD 2016): Lesional skin next to a blister for histology, plus periblister lesional skin sent unfixed for direct immunofluorescence to exclude an immunobullous disorder; swabs of lesional skin for bacteriology; photographs

Differential (BAD 2016): Erythema multiforme major (mucosal erosions too, but typical or raised atypical targets), pemphigus, pemphigoid, other immunobullous disorders

Drug Timeline (BAD 2016): Record every medicine taken in the previous 2 months, including OTC and complementary therapies, with dates; ALDEN algorithm helps define drug causality

SCORTEN (within the first 24 h of admission; BAD 2016, non-US), 1 point each: age >40; malignancy; HR >120; detachment >10% BSA at admission; serum urea >10 mmol/L (BUN >28 mg/dL); glucose >14 mmol/L (>252 mg/dL); bicarbonate <20 mmol/L. Predicted mortality: 0 = 1%, 1 = 4%, 2 = 12%, 3 = 32%, 4 = 62%, 5 = 85%, 6 = 95%, 7 = 99%

MANAGEMENT

Immediately: Stop every potential culprit drug; early withdrawal decreases the risk of death. Continue the patient's other regular medicines (BAD 2016)

Setting (SDH 2020): Medical or burn ICU, staff trained in SJS/TEN; dermatologists directly involved in a multidisciplinary team; private room with temperature and humidity control, at least 1:1 nursing. BAD 2016 (non-US): >10% BSA detachment, admit without delay to a burn center or an ICU experienced with SJS/TEN

Supportive Care (SDH 2020):

  • Skin: Leave detached and detachable epidermis in place as a biological dressing; no debridement of necrotic skin; petrolatum on the entire epidermis; non-adherent dressings on denuded skin, silver-impregnated primary dressings preferred; limit dressing changes; air-fluidized bed
  • Eyes: Ophthalmology exam at the initial assessment, then at least every 24 h; preservative-free artificial tears every 1-2 h for any ocular inflammation; topical corticosteroid drop (eg, prednisolone acetate 1%) for any ocular inflammation; amniotic membrane transplantation ideally within 5 days of onset
  • Mouth: Daily exam; petrolatum to the lips every 2 h; viscous lidocaine 2% rinse for pain; antiseptic rinse twice daily; low threshold for HSV PCR; bacterial and fungal cultures if infection is suspected
  • Urogenital: Exam at the initial assessment and daily, ideally by gynecology, urology, or urogynecology; intravaginal device as early as possible with visible disease to prevent adhesions and stenosis; urinary catheter recommended (pain, obstruction, fluid balance)
  • Pain: Score every 4 h; acetaminophen, then oral tramadol, then morphine or fentanyl (enteral, PCA, or infusion) for moderate to severe pain; avoid NSAIDs (renal and gastric injury)
  • Infection: No prophylactic antibiotics; treat proven or suspected infection, tailored to cultures and the local antibiogram; confusion, hypotension, falling urine output, or falling SpO2 may signal systemic infection
  • Fluids: Peripheral lines through uninjured skin, changed every 48 h if possible; titrate to urine output 0.5-1 mL/kg/h; electrolytes and fluid balance daily
  • Nutrition: 30-35 kcal/kg; nasogastric feeding if unable to eat, unless the nasopharyngeal mucosa is involved; careful glucose monitoring. No pharmacologic stress-ulcer prophylaxis on enteral nutrition; PPI only for high bleeding risk (respiratory failure, coagulopathy, liver disease, renal replacement therapy, 3 or more comorbidities)
  • Airway: Chest X-ray and ABG at baseline. Consider intubation and early tracheostomy with oral involvement plus any one of: initial BSA ≥70%; BSA progression >15% from hospital day 1 to day 3; neurologic diagnosis preventing airway protection; airway involvement on direct laryngoscopy. ARDS-type ventilation
  • VTE: LMWH if immobile; graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression if bleeding or at high risk of major bleeding

Systemic Immunomodulation: No US guideline recommendation (SDH 2020 covers supportive care only). BAD 2016 (non-US): no conclusive evidence that any intervention beats supportive care; if used, under a specialist skin-failure team in a clinical study or case registry. Cochrane 2022: very low certainty evidence for corticosteroids, IVIG, and cyclosporine; etanercept may reduce mortality compared with corticosteroids (low certainty). Decide with dermatology

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Mucosal erosions do not separate SJS/TEN from erythema multiforme major: lesion type does (EMM: typical or raised atypical targets; SJS/TEN: purpuric macules or flat atypical targets) (BAD 2016)
  • Stop the drug immediately: early withdrawal decreases the risk of death (BAD 2016)
  • HLA-B*5801 + allopurinol: test before starting allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian descent (eg, Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) and African American patients (ACR 2020 gout guideline, conditional); universal testing in other groups is conditionally recommended against
  • HLA-B*1502 + carbamazepine: FDA BOXED WARNING. Screen patients with ancestry in at-risk populations (broad areas of Asia) before starting; do not treat if positive unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. Limited evidence links HLA-B*1502 to SJS/TEN in patients of Chinese ancestry taking other antiepileptics associated with SJS/TEN, including phenytoin. HLA-A*3101 (European, Korean, Japanese ancestry) carries a moderate association with hypersensitivity reactions including SJS/TEN, maculopapular eruption, and DRESS (carbamazepine label)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU / BURN CENTER IF:
  • SJS/TEN diagnosed: care in a medical or burn ICU is recommended (SDH 2020)
  • Detachment >10% BSA (BAD 2016)
  • Hypoxemia, dyspnea, or tachypnea: fiberoptic bronchoscopy for bronchial involvement (SDH 2020)
  • Airway criteria under MANAGEMENT; confusion, hypotension, or falling urine output (SDH 2020)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Re-epithelialization progressing, oral intake adequate, pain controlled on oral agents (Practical)
  • Written list of the culprit drug(s) and related drugs that may cross-react given to the patient; allergy documented; MedicAlert bracelet naming the culprit (BAD 2016)
  • No drug challenge with the culprit: SJS/TEN is a contraindication to drug challenge (JTF 2022 Table IV)
  • Report to FDA MedWatch (Practical; BAD 2016 calls for national pharmacovigilance reporting)
  • Dermatology clinic within a few weeks; ophthalmology within a few weeks if the eyes were involved (BAD 2016)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Morphine, 💊 Fentanyl

287. DRESS SYNDROME

Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms
CLINICAL FEATURES

Timing: Usually 2-6 weeks after starting the drug, at minimum 2-3 weeks (JTF 2022); 2-8 weeks, but hours to days on re-exposure (Spanish 2020, non-US). Incidence 2-5 per million per year (Delphi 2024, international)

Features (Delphi 2024):

  • Rash: Infiltrated maculopapular exanthema with facial edema
  • Fever, lymphadenopathy
  • Blood: Eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes
  • Organs: Liver and kidney most often; also lungs, heart, nervous system. Cardiac involvement can occur without signs or symptoms in the acute phase
  • Herpesvirus reactivation (HHV-6, EBV, CMV): common, but not required for the diagnosis
  • Relapse: About 10%-15% of patients
COMMON CAUSES

Most Frequently Reported (Spanish 2020, non-US): Anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, minocycline, vancomycin. Other frequent culprits (Spanish 2020 Table 2):

  • Anticonvulsants: Carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, phenytoin, phenobarbital
  • Allopurinol
  • Antimicrobials: Dapsone, TMP-SMX, minocycline, vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, rifampin, nevirapine, abacavir
  • Sulfasalazine

HLA Associations (JTF 2022 Table X): HLA-B*5801 (allopurinol, SJS/TEN and DRESS); HLA-A*3101 (carbamazepine, DRESS and maculopapular eruption); HLA-B*1301 (dapsone); HLA-A*3201 (vancomycin). HLA-B*1502 does not predict carbamazepine DRESS (carbamazepine label)

DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY

RegiSCAR Score (recommended for diagnosis; Spanish 2020 Table 8):

  • Fever ≥38.5 °C core (>38 °C axillary): absent -1
  • Lymph nodes >1 cm at 2 or more sites: +1
  • Eosinophils 700-1499/µL (10%-19.9% if leukopenic): +1; ≥1500/µL (≥20%): +2
  • Atypical lymphocytes: +1
  • Skin (-2 to +2): rash >50% BSA +1; rash suggesting DRESS (2 or more of facial edema, purpura, infiltration, desquamation) yes +1, no -1; biopsy not suggesting DRESS -1
  • Organ involvement (liver, kidney, lung, muscle or heart, pancreas, other): +1 each, maximum +2
  • Resolution in 15 days or less: -1
  • At least 3 tests for other causes done, all negative (hepatitis A/B/C serology, blood culture, ANA, Chlamydia/Mycoplasma): +1
  • Total: <2 excluded, 2-3 possible, 4-5 probable, >5 definite

Workup, All Patients (Delphi 2024): CBC with differential and platelets; creatinine, urea, eGFR, urine sediment; liver function tests; ECG; serum PCR for HHV-6, EBV, CMV

If Organ Damage Suspected or Severe (Delphi 2024): Heart: troponin T, BNP or NT-proBNP, echo. Coagulation (PT, factor V). Lesional skin biopsy. Lung: chest imaging. Pancreatic enzymes. CNS: brain imaging, lumbar puncture. Hepatitis A, B, C serology if the liver is involved; hepatitis B and C before systemic therapy

Severity (Delphi 2024 Figure 3; ULN = upper limit of normal):

  • Mild (all of): Hb >10 g/dL, neutrophils >1500/µL, platelets >100,000/µL; creatinine <1.5 × ULN; liver enzymes <4 × ULN and/or ALP <3 × ULN
  • Moderate (any of): Hb 7-10 g/dL, neutrophils 500-1500/µL, platelets 50,000-100,000/µL; creatinine >1.5 × ULN; liver enzymes 4-15 × ULN and/or ALP 3-5 × ULN
  • Severe (any of): Hb <7 g/dL, neutrophils <500/µL, or platelets <50,000/µL; pancytopenia; hemophagocytosis; rapidly progressive or major eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis; major kidney failure or rapidly progressive oligo-anuria; liver enzymes >15 × ULN and/or ALP ≥5 × ULN and/or factor V <50%; involvement of any other organ; multiorgan failure
TREATMENT

Immediately: Stop the suspected drug(s) and cross-reacting drugs (Delphi 2024; Spanish 2020). Avoid empiric NSAIDs and empiric antibiotics, especially amoxicillin, in the acute phase. Admit all but the mildest cases; clinical and lab review every 48 h (Spanish 2020)

Corticosteroids by Severity (Delphi 2024): Start in all patients with confirmed DRESS

  • Mild: Very high potency topical steroid (eg, clobetasol 0.05% 2-3 times daily; Spanish 2020); taper over 6 weeks to 3 months
  • Moderate: Very high potency topical steroid, or a systemic glucocorticoid; taper over 6 weeks to 3 months
  • Severe: Systemic glucocorticoid in all; taper over 3 to 6 months

Oral Prednisone Starting Dose (Spanish 2020, non-US; the Delphi set no dose): Kidney (AKI stage 2 or higher): 0.8-1 mg/kg/day for 2-3 weeks. Liver (DILI stage 2-3, or stage 1 not improving 1 week after drug withdrawal): 40-60 mg/day for 3-5 days, then 20 mg/day. Lung or other organ: 0.5-2 mg/kg/day until clinical improvement and normal labs. Relapse on taper: return to the previous dose and taper more slowly

Steroid-Refractory (Delphi 2024): Cyclosporine, anti-IL-5 or anti-IL-5R antibody, or IVIG can be considered (small case series only); IVIG alone without corticosteroids has caused toxic effects. Decide with dermatology

High CMV Viral Load (Delphi 2024): Ganciclovir or valganciclovir can be considered

Supportive (Spanish 2020): Fluids and electrolytes, nutrition, VTE prophylaxis if needed, antipyretics, H1-antihistamines, emollients; organ specialist for moderate or severe organ involvement

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Weeks, not days: usually 2-6 weeks after the drug (JTF 2022). A drug started within 6 months and stopped less than 14 days before onset is a suggestive chronology (Spanish 2020)
  • Score it: RegiSCAR 4-5 probable, >5 definite (Spanish 2020)
  • ECG in every patient: cardiac involvement can be clinically silent (Delphi 2024)
  • Slow steroid taper: DRESS relapses in about 10%-15% (Delphi 2024)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Severe DRESS (Delphi 2024 criteria above): consider ICU admission; organ specialist (Spanish 2020)
  • Hemophagocytosis, major cytopenias, rapidly progressive oligo-anuria, liver enzymes >15 × ULN or factor V <50% (Delphi 2024)
  • Suspected myocarditis: troponin T, BNP, echo (Delphi 2024); arrhythmia or heart failure (Practical)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Organ function improving; written steroid taper (Practical)
  • Culprit and cross-reacting drugs documented as allergies (Practical)
  • No drug challenge with the culprit: DRESS is a contraindication to drug challenge (JTF 2022 Table IV)
  • Follow-up from the first month after discharge, regularly for 6 months: labs per initial organ involvement, autoantibodies and thyroid function in convalescence, steroid adverse effects, psychological support (Delphi 2024)
  • Patch or delayed intradermal testing only after at least 6 months from the reaction and/or 1 month off systemic steroids (JTF 2022)
  • Report to FDA MedWatch (Practical)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 IV Fluids

288. PRIMARY IMMUNODEFICIENCIES

CVID • IgA Deficiency • When to Suspect
WHEN TO SUSPECT AND WORKUP

Investigate for an inborn error of immunity (IEI) with recurrent, severe, or rare infections, autoinflammation, autoimmunity, severe atopy, atypical malignancy, bone marrow failure, or combinations of these (JTF 2025 IEI, Rec 1.1). In adults with antibody deficiency, look for recurrent sinopulmonary infections, autoimmune cytopenias, bronchiectasis, lymphoid hyperplasia, or chronic GI disease (JTF 2025 IEI)

Workup for Suspected Antibody Deficiency (Rec 4.1):

  • Serum IgG, IgA, IgM
  • Antigen-specific antibody responses: protein (tetanus, Hib) and polysaccharide (pneumococcal) titers before and 4 weeks after vaccination, same laboratory
  • Lymphocyte phenotyping: CD19 B cells, CD3, CD4, CD8 T cells, NK cells; class-switched memory B cells
  • Exclude secondary causes: corticosteroids, B-cell-depleting drugs, malignancy (in adults, also MGUS), protein loss (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy: check albumin, proteinuria, stool alpha-1-antitrypsin)
  • Detailed family history; integrated clinical, immunologic, and genetic evaluation; clinical immunology referral (Rec 1.2, 1.3, 1.5)
COMMON VARIABLE IMMUNODEFICIENCY (CVID)

Diagnosis (JTF 2025 IEI, Rec 4.3): Low IgG plus low IgA and/or low IgM, plus impaired antibody response to infection or immunization, after other causes of hypogammaglobulinemia are excluded. Possibly the most frequently encountered symptomatic IEI (about 1:30,000); about 30% have an identifiable genetic cause

Features (JTF 2025 IEI):

  • Recurrent sinopulmonary infections (S pneumoniae, non-typeable H influenzae; Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma, including joints); GI infections (Giardia, norovirus) can be refractory
  • Autoimmunity, most often cytopenias
  • Chronic GI disease (gastritis, enteritis); liver: nodular regenerative hyperplasia
  • Chronic lung disease (asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis); granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease (GLILD)
  • Lymphoproliferation (nodes, spleen) and malignancy
  • Hypogammaglobulinemia with thymoma: Good syndrome

Immunoglobulin Replacement (IgRT; JTF 2025 IEI, Rec 8.1-8.7):

  • Start 400-600 mg/kg per month: IV every 3-4 weeks, or SC in divided weekly or biweekly doses; adjust for response and weight change over 5% (Rec 8.2). Label ranges for primary immunodeficiency: Privigen 200-800 mg/kg IV, Gammagard Liquid 300-600 mg/kg IV, every 3-4 weeks; Hizentra weekly SC dose = prior IV dose in grams × 1.37 ÷ weeks between IV doses
  • Target trough IgG above 800 mg/dL (Rec 8.4); monitor IgG, CBC with differential, chemistry panel (Rec 8.3)
  • Continuous, lifelong therapy (Rec 8.5); route by patient tolerance and preference (Rec 8.7)
  • BOXED WARNING: thrombosis (all products); renal dysfunction and acute renal failure (IV products). In patients at risk, use the minimum dose and infusion rate practicable and hydrate first (label)

Infections: Targeted antimicrobial prophylaxis for increased susceptibility (Rec 9.1); prompt diagnostic testing and longer antimicrobial courses than for immunocompetent patients (Rec 9.4)

IgA DEFICIENCY

Diagnosis (JTF 2025 IEI, Rec 4.4): Age over 4 years, serum IgA below the limit of detection, normal IgG and IgM. The most common IEI: about 1:500 in White populations, 1:3000 to 1:18,000 in Asian populations

Course: Often asymptomatic; a subset have frequent infections (27%), atopy (23%), or autoimmunity (14%); antibiotic prophylaxis might reduce infections; may evolve into CVID (JTF 2025 IEI)

Celiac Testing: IgA deficiency gives false-negative IgA-based celiac antibody tests (JTF 2025 IEI)

IgA-Containing Products: Anaphylaxis to IVIG is reported with anti-IgA IgE antibodies, but most IgA-deficient patients receive IVIG without difficulty; low IgA with low IgG is not a contraindication to IgRT (Rec 8.6)

💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • CVID needs proof of poor antibody function: low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, impaired vaccine or infection response, and secondary causes excluded (Rec 4.3)
  • Low IgG in an adult: rule out secondary causes first: steroids, B-cell-depleting drugs, malignancy, MGUS, protein loss (JTF 2025 IEI)
  • IgA deficiency: the most common IEI; usually asymptomatic; makes IgA-based celiac tests falsely negative
  • IgRT for CVID: 400-600 mg/kg/month, trough IgG above 800 mg/dL, lifelong; low IgA is not a contraindication (Rec 8.2, 8.4, 8.5, 8.6)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IVIG

289. EATING DISORDERS

Anorexia Nervosa • Bulimia • Refeeding Syndrome
ANOREXIA NERVOSA

DSM-5 Criteria:

  • Restriction of intake leading to significantly low body weight
  • Intense fear of gaining weight
  • Distorted body image

Medical Complications:

  • Cardiac: Bradycardia, hypotension, QTc prolongation, arrhythmias
  • Metabolic: Hypothermia, hypoglycemia
  • Endocrine: Amenorrhea, low T3, elevated cortisol
  • Bone: Osteoporosis
  • GI: Constipation, gastroparesis
  • Heme: Pancytopenia
BULIMIA NERVOSA

Features: Binge eating + compensatory behaviors (purging, laxatives, exercise); normal or elevated weight

Medical Complications:

  • Electrolytes: Hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
  • Dental: Enamel erosion
  • Parotid hypertrophy
  • Russell's sign: Calluses on knuckles
  • Esophageal: Mallory-Weiss tears, rarely Boerhaave
REFEEDING SYNDROME

Risk: Severely malnourished patients (BMI <16, minimal intake >10 days)

Pathophysiology: Insulin surge with refeeding → intracellular shift of phosphorus, potassium, magnesium

Complications: Hypophosphatemia (most important), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia → arrhythmias, respiratory failure, cardiac failure

Prevention:

  • Start low, go slow with calories
  • Replace thiamine before feeding
  • Monitor and replace electrolytes
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis = purging
  • Refeeding syndrome: Hypophosphatemia is key; give thiamine first
  • Anorexia has highest mortality of psychiatric disorders
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Olanzapine, 💊 Sertraline
↑ Back to Table of Contents

290. SLEEP DISORDERS

Insomnia • OSA • Narcolepsy • Restless Legs
INSOMNIA

Chronic Insomnia: ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months

Treatment (AASM):

  • CBT-I: First-line; multicomponent CBT-I is a strong recommendation (AASM 2021). Sleep hygiene alone is suggested against as a single treatment
  • Medication (AASM 2017, all conditional): Mainly when CBT-I is unavailable or incompletely effective, or as a temporary adjunct. Sleep onset: zaleplon, triazolam, ramelteon. Sleep maintenance: doxepin, suvorexant. Both: zolpidem, eszopiclone, temazepam. Lemborexant and daridorexant were FDA approved after 2017
  • Suggested against for insomnia (AASM 2017): Trazodone, diphenhydramine, melatonin, tiagabine, tryptophan, valerian
  • Combination (AASM 2026, conditional): CBT-I plus medication over medication alone; not CBT-I plus medication over CBT-I alone
  • Orexin antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant, daridorexant): Contraindicated in narcolepsy (labels)
  • Older adults, including inpatients: Avoid benzodiazepines, Z-drugs (eszopiclone, zaleplon, zolpidem), and first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine: delirium, falls, fractures (Beers 2023, strong)
  • Circadian rhythm disorders (AASM 2015; weak unless stated): Strategically timed melatonin for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder and for non-24-hour disorder in blind adults; evening light for advanced phase. Older adults with dementia and an irregular sleep-wake rhythm: light therapy suggested; sleep-promoting medications recommended against (strong); melatonin suggested against
OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA

Symptoms: Snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime somnolence, morning headaches

Diagnosis: Polysomnography or home sleep test; obstructive events ≥5/hour with typical symptoms, or ≥15/hour even without symptoms (ICSD-3, as stated in AASM 2017)

Treatment:

  • PAP (CPAP or APAP): First-line; recommended with excessive sleepiness, suggested with impaired sleep-related quality of life or hypertension (AASM 2019)
  • Oral appliances: For PAP intolerance or preference for another therapy (AASM 2015)
  • Positional therapy: Secondary therapy for supine-predominant OSA; dietary weight loss combined with a primary treatment (AASM 2006)
  • Full evaluation and management, including inpatient care and newer therapies: Condition 335
NARCOLEPSY

Type 1: Daily sleepiness from loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons; typical cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone with emotion) or low CSF orexin

Type 2: Daily sleepiness without typical cataplexy; CSF orexin normal

Other Features: Sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations

Diagnosis (ICSD-3-TR, per AASM 2024): Type 1: daily sleepiness plus one of: CSF orexin <110 pg/mL; typical cataplexy with a nocturnal sleep-onset REM period (SOREMP; REM within 15 min of sleep onset on PSG); or typical cataplexy with MSLT mean sleep latency ≤8 min and ≥2 SOREMPs. Type 2: MSLT mean sleep latency ≤8 min and ≥2 SOREMPs without typical cataplexy

Treatment (AASM 2021, adults): Strong: modafinil, pitolisant, sodium oxybate, solriamfetol. Conditional: armodafinil, dextroamphetamine, methylphenidate

Oxybates (Xyrem, Xywav, Lumryz): Boxed warning for CNS depression (respiratory depression, obtundation) and abuse and misuse; dispensed only through a REMS (labels)

In the hospital (Practical): Continue home wake-promoting therapy when possible; use caution combining oxybate with opioids or sedatives; do not give orexin antagonist hypnotics

RESTLESS LEGS SYNDROME

Features: Urge to move legs, worse at rest/evening, relieved by movement

Associations: Iron deficiency, pregnancy, end-stage renal disease. Worsened by alcohol, caffeine, antihistaminergic, serotonergic, and antidopaminergic drugs and untreated OSA (AASM 2024)

Treatment (AASM 2024):

  • First step: Address exacerbating factors. Common inpatient offenders: diphenhydramine and other sedating antihistamines, antidopaminergic antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) and antipsychotics, serotonergic antidepressants (Practical examples)
  • Iron studies (ferritin and transferrin saturation, ideally in the morning without iron for 24 hours): oral or IV iron if ferritin ≤75 ng/mL or TSAT <20%; IV iron only if ferritin 75-100 ng/mL (consensus). IV ferric carboxymaltose: strong; IV low molecular weight iron dextran, IV ferumoxytol, oral ferrous sulfate: conditional
  • Ferric carboxymaltose: FDA boxed warning (September 2026) for symptomatic hypophosphatemia (weakness, fatigue, confusion, arrhythmias; osteomalacia and fractures if chronic). Correct low phosphate before dosing; check phosphate in patients at risk and before any repeat course within 3 months; consider stopping permanently for severe symptomatic or persistent hypophosphatemia (FDA)
  • First-line drugs (strong): Gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, pregabalin
  • Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine): suggested against standard use because of augmentation (drug-induced worsening of RLS symptoms with long-term use); may be used when short-term relief is valued over long-term risk; levodopa: suggested against; cabergoline: recommended against
  • Other options (conditional): Extended-release oxycodone and other opioids, dipyridamole, bilateral high-frequency peroneal nerve stimulation
  • ESRD (conditional): Gabapentin; IV iron sucrose if ferritin <200 ng/mL and TSAT <20%; vitamin C
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia (AASM 2021, strong)
  • Cataplexy = narcolepsy type 1; orexin antagonist hypnotics are contraindicated in narcolepsy
  • RLS: check ferritin and TSAT; iron if ferritin ≤75 ng/mL or TSAT <20% (AASM 2024)
  • RLS first-line = gabapentinoids; dopamine agonists cause augmentation (AASM 2024)
  • No benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or diphenhydramine for sleep in older adults (Beers 2023)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Melatonin, 💊 Trazodone, 💊 Gabapentin/Pregabalin, 💊 IV Iron

291. GLOMERULAR DISEASES

IgA Nephropathy • FSGS • Minimal Change • Membranous
NEPHRITIC VS NEPHROTIC
FeatureNephriticNephrotic
Proteinuria<3.5 g/day≥3.5 g/day
HematuriaPresent (RBC casts)Minimal
EdemaMildSevere (anasarca)
OtherHTN, oliguria, AKIHyperlipidemia, lipiduria
KEY GLOMERULAR DISEASES

IgA Nephropathy:

  • Most common GN worldwide
  • Episodic gross hematuria with URI ("synpharyngitic")
  • Biopsy: Mesangial IgA deposits
  • Treatment: ACEi/ARB; steroids if progressive

Minimal Change Disease:

  • Most common nephrotic syndrome in children
  • Biopsy: Normal LM, podocyte effacement on EM
  • Treatment: Highly steroid-responsive

FSGS:

  • Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults (especially African Americans)
  • Primary vs secondary (HIV, heroin, obesity, reflux)
  • Treatment: Steroids (less responsive); SGLT2i

Membranous Nephropathy:

  • Most common nephrotic in white adults
  • Primary: Anti-PLA2R antibodies (70%)
  • Secondary: Malignancy, hepatitis B, lupus, drugs (NSAIDs, gold)
  • High thrombosis risk (renal vein thrombosis)
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • IgA nephropathy: Hematuria with URI (synpharyngitic)
  • Minimal change: Kids, steroid-responsive
  • Anti-PLA2R positive = primary membranous
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Mycophenolate, 💊 Cyclophosphamide, 💊 Rituximab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 ANCA, 🔬 Complement C3/C4, 🔬 Direct Coombs (DAT)

292. ANTI-GBM DISEASE / GOODPASTURE

Pulmonary-Renal Syndrome • Linear IF • Plasmapheresis
CLINICAL FEATURES

Anti-GBM Disease: Antibodies against type IV collagen in glomerular/alveolar basement membrane

Goodpasture Syndrome: Anti-GBM disease with both lung and kidney involvement

Pulmonary: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage — hemoptysis, dyspnea, infiltrates

Renal: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis — hematuria, AKI

Associations: Smoking (exposes pulmonary basement membrane), hydrocarbons

DIAGNOSIS
  • Anti-GBM antibodies (serum)
  • Kidney biopsy: Linear IgG staining on immunofluorescence (pathognomonic)
  • Crescentic GN on light microscopy

Note: ~30% are also ANCA-positive (double-positive)

TREATMENT
  • Plasmapheresis: To remove anti-GBM antibodies (daily × 14 days or until antibodies clear)
  • Cyclophosphamide + high-dose corticosteroids
  • Prognosis depends on creatinine at presentation
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Linear IF staining = anti-GBM (granular = immune complex)
  • Plasmapheresis essential
  • Pulmonary-renal syndrome DDx: Anti-GBM, ANCA vasculitis, SLE
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Cyclophosphamide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 ANCA, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 Hematuria, 🔬 Low PaO2

294. PERIOPERATIVE EVALUATION

RCRI • Cardiac Risk • Medication Management
CARDIAC RISK ASSESSMENT

Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) — 1 point each:

  • High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, suprainguinal vascular)
  • History of ischemic heart disease
  • History of heart failure
  • History of cerebrovascular disease
  • Diabetes requiring insulin
  • Creatinine >2.0

Risk: 0 points = 0.4%; 1 = 0.9%; 2 = 6.6%; ≥3 = 11%

STEPWISE APPROACH (ACC/AHA 2014)
  1. Emergency surgery? → Proceed; perioperative surveillance only
  2. Active cardiac condition? (ACS/unstable angina, decompensated HF, severe symptomatic AS, significant arrhythmia) → Evaluate and treat before elective surgery
  3. Low-risk surgery? (superficial, endoscopy, cataract, breast) → Proceed without cardiac testing
  4. Functional capacity ≥4 METs without symptoms? → Proceed without further testing
  5. <4 METs or unknown + RCRI ≥1? → Consider pharmacologic stress testing only if results will change management

Functional Capacity (METs) Examples:

METs Activity Risk Implication
1–2Eating, dressing, walking slowly indoorsVery poor — consider preop testing
4Climb 1 flight of stairs, walk on level at 4 mphThreshold — acceptable for most surgery
5–6Heavy housework, golf, dancingGood
≥10Strenuous sports (swimming, singles tennis)Excellent — proceed without testing

Preoperative Testing Indications:

  • ECG: Known CAD, significant arrhythmia, structural heart disease, or age >40 with intermediate/high risk surgery
  • Echo: Dyspnea of unknown cause or worsening HF or valvular symptoms
  • CBC/BMP: Major surgery; age >65
  • No routine preop testing in asymptomatic patients undergoing low-risk procedures
MEDICATION MANAGEMENT
Drug Perioperative Management Key Evidence/Notes
Beta-blockers Continue if on chronically. Do NOT start new high-dose day of or day before surgery POISE trial: new high-dose metoprolol ↓ MI but ↑ stroke and death from bradycardia/hypotension. If initiating, start ≥1 week preop at low dose
Statins Continue perioperatively Abrupt discontinuation associated with rebound inflammation and periop MI
ACEi/ARBs Hold morning of surgery; restart 24–48h postop Causes refractory intraoperative hypotension that is vasopressin-responsive; not just a fluid problem
Aspirin Continue if recent DES (<1 year) or BMS (<1 month); otherwise hold 7–10 days for major/neuraxial surgery POISE-2 trial: aspirin didn't reduce periop MI but did increase major bleeding
P2Y12 inhibitors Clopidogrel: hold 5 days | Ticagrelor: hold 5 days | Prasugrel: hold 7 days. Continue if recent stent (within 12 months for DES) Stent thrombosis risk highest in first 30 days; delay elective surgery if possible
Warfarin Hold 5 days preop (INR ≤1.5 for most procedures). Bridge with LMWH if high thrombotic risk High-risk for bridging: mechanical mitral valve, recent VTE (<3 months), AF with stroke/TIA, CHADS₂ ≥5
DOACs Hold 1–2 days for low-bleed-risk; 2–3 days for high-bleed-risk. 3–5 days if CrCl <50 (for dabigatran) No routine bridging — DOACs have short half-life; bridging increases bleeding without reducing thrombosis
SGLT2i Hold 3–4 days preop — risk of euglycemic DKA perioperatively Euglycemic DKA can occur with normal glucose; ketones will be elevated. High risk with fasting/stress
GLP-1 agonists Hold weekly dose 1 week preop; hold daily dose day of surgery — risk of aspiration from delayed gastric emptying ASA/ASGE advisory (2023): full stomach despite adequate fasting; consider point-of-care gastric ultrasound
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • 4 METs = climb one flight of stairs without symptoms — the clinical threshold for "adequate" functional capacity
  • POISE trap: Starting high-dose metoprolol ≤1 day before surgery ↑ stroke and death despite ↓ MI — if you must start beta-blockers, do it ≥1 week preop at low dose
  • ACEi/ARB-induced hypotension is often vasopressin-resistant to pressors — hold the morning dose
  • No routine bridging for DOACs — BRIDGE trial showed bridging warfarin with LMWH increased bleeding without reducing thromboembolism in AF patients
  • SGLT2i = euglycemic DKA risk — hold 3–4 days preop; check ketones if patient develops unexplained acidosis perioperatively despite normal glucose
  • GLP-1 agonist and full stomach — delayed gastric emptying despite NPO; hold weekly dose 1 week before surgery
  • Stress testing only if results change management — if the patient needs the surgery regardless (or if you'd manage the same way), the test adds risk without benefit
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Atorvastatin, 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Insulin Glargine

295. VTE PROPHYLAXIS

Padua Score • Caprini Score • Medical vs Surgical
MEDICAL PATIENTS — PADUA SCORE

High Risk (≥4 points): Pharmacologic prophylaxis indicated

FactorPoints
Active cancer3
Previous VTE3
Reduced mobility3
Thrombophilia3
Recent trauma/surgery2
Age ≥701
Heart failure or respiratory failure1
Acute MI or stroke1
Acute infection or rheumatic disorder1
Obesity (BMI ≥30)1
Hormonal therapy1
PROPHYLAXIS OPTIONS

Pharmacologic — First-Line:

Agent Dose Notes
Enoxaparin (LMWH) 40mg SC daily (CrCl ≥30); 30mg SC daily (CrCl 15–29) First-line for medical/surgical patients; avoid if CrCl <15 (use UFH)
UFH 5000 units SC q8h (or q12h for lower risk) Preferred in severe renal failure (not renally cleared); monitor platelet count (HIT risk)
Fondaparinux 2.5mg SC daily HIT history; avoid if CrCl <30 (renally cleared); no reversal agent (except rFVIIa off-label)
Rivaroxaban 10mg PO daily (orthopedic only) FDA-approved for hip/knee arthroplasty and acutely ill medical patients (MAGELLAN); start 6–10h postop

Mechanical Prophylaxis: Sequential compression devices (SCDs) / intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC)

  • Use when pharmacologic is contraindicated (active bleeding, recent CNS surgery, severe thrombocytopenia PLT <50)
  • Combine with pharmacologic in highest-risk patients (major trauma, malignancy, orthopedic surgery)
  • Must be applied correctly and consistently — patient non-adherence is the major failure mode

Contraindications to Pharmacologic Prophylaxis:

  • Active bleeding (especially CNS) — switch to mechanical only
  • Platelets <50K (or <80K if recent neurosurgery)
  • Recent intracranial, spinal, or ophthalmic surgery (<24–48h depending on procedure)
  • Inherited bleeding disorders (hemophilia) — hematology guidance needed
BLEEDING RISK ASSESSMENT (IMPROVE Score)

For medical inpatients, assess both VTE risk (Padua) AND bleeding risk (IMPROVE) before initiating pharmacologic prophylaxis:

Bleeding Risk Factor Points
Active peptic ulcer4.5
Prior bleeding (≤3 months)4
PLT <50K4
Age ≥853.5
Hepatic failure (INR >1.5)2.5
Renal failure (GFR <30)2.5
ICU or CCU admission2.5
Score ≥7 = high bleeding risk → use mechanical prophylaxis; withhold pharmacologic until risk decreases
EXTENDED PROPHYLAXIS & SPECIAL POPULATIONS
Population Duration Preferred Agent
Hip arthroplasty 35 days LMWH, rivaroxaban, or aspirin
Knee arthroplasty 10–14 days minimum; extend to 35 days in high-risk LMWH, rivaroxaban, or aspirin
Abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery 28 days post-discharge LMWH (enoxaparin preferred)
Medically ill — acutely ill Duration of hospital stay; consider extended (6–14 days) if high Padua + high mobility at discharge LMWH in hospital; rivaroxaban or betrixaban for extended (APEX trial)
ICU patients Throughout ICU stay unless contraindicated UFH q8h or LMWH; add SCDs
Morbid obesity (BMI >40) Standard inpatient duration; higher doses needed Enoxaparin 40mg SC q12h (not 40mg daily — underdoses); anti-Xa monitoring in very obese
Pregnancy Throughout pregnancy if high-risk; postpartum 6 weeks if VTE history LMWH only — DOACs contraindicated; warfarin teratogenic in 1st trimester
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Padua ≥4 = pharmacologic prophylaxis; also assess bleeding risk (IMPROVE) — high bleeding risk = mechanical only until safer
  • Obese patients need higher LMWH doses — enoxaparin 40mg daily underdoses BMI >40; use 40mg q12h or weight-based dosing (0.5 mg/kg q12h) with anti-Xa monitoring
  • Extended prophylaxis for orthopedic and cancer surgery — hip replacement needs 35 days; many hospitals still stop at discharge (an error)
  • Mechanical + pharmacologic for highest risk — additive benefit in trauma, major cancer surgery, ICU patients
  • SCDs must be worn — non-adherence is the most common failure; document compliance daily
  • No bridging needed for most DOACs — short half-life; hold preop, restart 24–48h postop once hemostasis confirmed
  • Fondaparinux for HIT — does not bind PF4-heparin complexes; does not cause HIT and can be used in HIT patients needing prophylaxis
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 UFH, 💊 Fondaparinux, 💊 Apixaban

296. OBESITY MANAGEMENT

GLP-1 Agonists • Bariatric Surgery Criteria • Pharmacotherapy
CLASSIFICATION & INDICATIONS

BMI Classification (ADA 2026):

  • Overweight: 25-29.9
  • Class I obesity: 30-34.9
  • Class II obesity: 35-39.9
  • Class III obesity: ≥40
  • South, Southeast or East Asian adults: overweight 23-24.9; obesity ≥25 (ACP 2026)

Pharmacotherapy: ACP 2026: BMI ≥30, or BMI 27-29.9 with type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, OSA or cardiovascular disease (evidence inadequate below 27). ADA Obesity 2026: offer obesity medication as part of initial treatment to adults with or at high risk of obesity-related disease; the older label criteria (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with a comorbidity) are no longer in several labels

Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS/IFSO 2022): recommended for BMI ≥35 regardless of comorbidity; consider for BMI 30-34.9 with metabolic disease; Asian populations: offer at BMI ≥27.5. Type 2 diabetes: consider at BMI ≥30 (≥27.5 in Asian American individuals) (ADA 2026). The 1991 NIH thresholds (≥40, or ≥35 with comorbidity) are superseded (ASMBS/IFSO 2022)

PHARMACOTHERAPY
DrugMechanismNotes
Semaglutide (Wegovy)GLP-1 RA; SC weeklyFirst-line; reduced all-cause mortality and MACE (ACP 2026). Placebo-subtracted weight loss 11.9%. 0.25 mg weekly, stepped up every 4 weeks to 2.4 mg from week 17. Contraindicated: personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2; severe GI disease (ADA Obesity 2026). Boxed warning: thyroid C-cell tumors (ACP 2026)
Tirzepatide (Zepbound)GIP/GLP-1 RA; SC weeklyFirst-line (ACP 2026). Placebo-subtracted weight loss 16.2%. 2.5 mg weekly, up 2.5 mg every 4 weeks to 15 mg. Same contraindications and boxed warning; significant interaction with oral contraceptives (ADA Obesity 2026; ACP 2026)
Phentermine-topiramateSympathomimetic + anticonvulsantSecond-line (ACP 2026). 8.8%. Teratogenic: effective contraception, REMS (ADA Obesity 2026); monthly pregnancy tests (ACP 2026). Contraindicated: CVD, uncontrolled hypertension, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism (ADA Obesity 2026)
LiraglutideGLP-1 RA; SC dailyThird-line (ACP 2026). 4.5%. 0.6 mg daily, up weekly to 3.0 mg (ADA Obesity 2026). Boxed warning: thyroid C-cell tumors (ACP 2026)
Naltrexone-bupropionOpioid antagonist + NDRIFourth-line (ACP 2026); warning: suicidal ideation (ACP 2026). 4.8%. Contraindicated: uncontrolled hypertension, seizure disorders, glaucoma, anorexia or bulimia, substance use disorder, chronic opioid use (ADA Obesity 2026)
OrlistatLipase inhibitorNot evaluated by ACP 2026. 3.1%. GI effects; contraindicated with malabsorption or cholestasis (ADA Obesity 2026)

Use (ADA Obesity 2026): with type 2 diabetes, prefer a GLP-1 RA or GIP/GLP-1 RA; continue after reaching goals (stopping often brings weight regain); not in pregnancy, when trying to conceive, or during lactation. Weight-loss figures: placebo-subtracted meta-analysis means (ADA Obesity 2026)

TOS/OMA/OAC 2026 (GRADE): strong recommendation (moderate certainty) for semaglutide, tirzepatide and naltrexone-bupropion, for setmelanotide in monogenic obesity (LEPR, POMC, PCSK1, BBS), and for continuing obesity medication during weight maintenance; conditional (low certainty) for phentermine-topiramate, liraglutide, orlistat, and phentermine for 3 months or more (labeled for short-term use). This differs from ACP 2026, which ranks naltrexone-bupropion fourth-line.

Choose by comorbidity (ADA Obesity 2026): ASCVD: a GLP-1 RA with demonstrated benefit (or GIP/GLP-1 RA); HFpEF, MASH with moderate or advanced fibrosis, moderate-to-severe OSA: prioritize agents with demonstrated benefit in that condition. TOS/OMA/OAC 2026 suggests (conditional, low certainty) a GLP-1 RA or GIP/GLP-1 RA in OSA, HFpEF (off-label) and MASH; a GLP-1 RA in osteoarthritis; and semaglutide after myocardial infarction, stroke or symptomatic peripheral vascular disease

Perioperative GLP-1 RA (Multisociety 2024; inpatient): continue in most patients. Higher aspiration risk: escalation phase, higher dose, weekly dosing, GI symptoms, other dysmotility; consider a liquid diet for at least 24 h before. If held: day of surgery for daily drugs, 1 week before for weekly drugs. Reassess symptoms on the day; if retained gastric contents are suspected, weigh rapid sequence intubation against cancellation

BARIATRIC SURGERY

Types:

  • Sleeve gastrectomy: about 80% of the stomach removed, leaving a long, thin sleeve (ADA 2026)
  • Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: small gastric pouch joined to the distal small intestine, bypassing duodenum and jejunum (ADA 2026)
  • Together these are about 90% of operations worldwide (ASMBS/IFSO 2022); metabolic surgery averages >20% weight loss and often leads to diabetes remission (ADA 2026)

Long-term (ADA 2026): lifelong medical and behavioral support with routine micronutrient, nutritional and metabolic monitoring; risks include vitamin and mineral deficiencies, anemia, osteoporosis, dumping syndrome and severe hypoglycemia

Post-bariatric hypoglycemia (ADA 2026; inpatient): typically >1 year after surgery, 1-3 h after a high-carbohydrate meal (dumping, by contrast, starts early and improves); exclude other causes; nutrition therapy with an experienced dietitian, medication as needed; CGM improves safety

💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Semaglutide or tirzepatide first-line (ACP 2026); preferred with type 2 diabetes (ADA Obesity 2026)
  • Surgery at BMI ≥35 regardless of comorbidity; consider at 30-34.9 with metabolic disease (ASMBS/IFSO 2022)
  • GLP-1 RA before a procedure: usually continue; liquid diet for 24 h if aspiration risk is high (Multisociety 2024)
  • Hypoglycemia 1-3 h after meals, >1 year after bariatric surgery: post-bariatric hypoglycemia (ADA 2026)
  • Lifelong micronutrient monitoring after metabolic surgery (ADA 2026)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Semaglutide, 💊 Metformin

298. ALCOHOL & OPIOID USE DISORDERS

MOUD • Naltrexone • Buprenorphine
ALCOHOL USE DISORDER

Pharmacotherapy for AUD:

  • Naltrexone: Opioid antagonist; reduces craving and heavy drinking; PO daily or IM monthly (Vivitrol); contraindicated if on opioids
  • Acamprosate: GABA/glutamate modulator; reduces craving; renally cleared (avoid in CKD); safe in liver disease
  • Disulfiram: Causes aversive reaction with alcohol (flushing, nausea); requires high motivation/supervision

Gabapentin: May help with craving and anxiety; useful if comorbid sleep or anxiety issues

OPIOID USE DISORDER — MOUD

Medications for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD):

MedicationMechanismKey Points
BuprenorphinePartial μ agonistOffice-based; wait for withdrawal before starting (COWS ≥8-12); ceiling effect (safer)
MethadoneFull μ agonistOTP (clinic) only for OUD; daily observed dosing initially; QTc prolongation risk
Naltrexone (XR)μ antagonistMust be opioid-free 7-10 days; monthly IM; prevents relapse but doesn't treat withdrawal

Buprenorphine Induction: Patient must be in withdrawal (COWS score); start low, titrate to effect; can start in ED/hospital

HARM REDUCTION
  • Naloxone prescribing: All patients at risk for overdose
  • Syringe exchange programs
  • Fentanyl test strips
💎 BOARD PEARLS
  • Buprenorphine: Wait for withdrawal (COWS ≥8) to avoid precipitated withdrawal
  • Naltrexone for AUD or OUD: Cannot be on opioids
  • MOUD is gold standard for OUD — reduces mortality

299. VARICEAL BLEEDING

Life-Threatening GI Hemorrhage in Portal Hypertension
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Hematemesis (bright red blood or coffee grounds), melena, signs of hypovolemic shock

Associated Findings: Stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider angiomata, ascites, splenomegaly, caput medusae)

Risk Stratification:

  • Bleeding risk rises with portal pressure (HVPG), liver disease severity (CTP class or MELD score), and varix size and red wale signs (AASLD 2024)
  • Mortality: 6-week mortality still 10-15%; most deaths occur in CTP class C, and patients in CTP class A rarely die of variceal bleeding (AASLD 2024)
  • Rebleeding: up to 60% at 1 year without prophylaxis; highest risk in the first 6 weeks (AASLD 2024)
  • Assume a variceal source: GI bleeding in known or suspected advanced liver disease is managed as portal hypertensive bleeding until endoscopy confirms the source (AASLD 2024)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: Practical: CBC, CMP, liver tests, PT/INR, type and crossmatch, lactate

Risk Scores:

  • CTP score at presentation: decides preemptive TIPS (CTP class B score over 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or CTP class C score 10-13) (AASLD 2024)
  • MELD: mortality is high with MELD over 19 even with intervention, though early TIPS still has lower mortality than standard therapy; assess transplant candidacy promptly (AASLD 2024)

Endoscopy: within 12 hours of presentation (AASLD 2024). Intubate first if mentation is altered or aspiration risk is high; extubate as soon as safely possible. IV erythromycin 125-250 mg 30-120 minutes before endoscopy improves visualization and therapy (AASLD 2024)

Imaging: once stable, contrast CT or MRI, or Doppler ultrasound, for portal vein thrombosis and liver cancer; contrast cross-sectional imaging for bleeding gastric or ectopic varices to define collaterals and venous thrombosis (AASLD 2024)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Resuscitation: manage in an ICU or similar unit; secure IV access and assess the airway (AASLD 2024)

  • Practical: 2 large-bore IVs; avoid over-resuscitation with fluids
  • Restrictive transfusion: target hemoglobin ~7 g/dL unless comorbidities require more (AASLD 2024)
  • No FFP or platelets to reach INR or platelet targets: no benefit, and FFP may harm; INR does not predict hemostasis; liberal transfusion of plasma and other blood products worsens survival and portal pressure; avoid routine cryoprecipitate (AASLD 2024)

2. Vasoactive Drug and Antibiotics (start as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected, before endoscopy; AASLD 2024; AGA 2024):

  • Octreotide (vasoactive drug of choice, AGA 2024): 50 mcg IV bolus, then 25-50 mcg/h (AASLD 2024 Table 5). Continue 2-5 days if portal hypertensive bleeding is confirmed; stop when NSBB starts, no later than day 5 (AASLD 2024). Vasopressin is no longer advised (AGA 2024). Terlipressin is not approved for this indication in North America (AASLD 2024 Table 5)
  • Antibiotics: IV, tailored to local resistance and allergies; most often ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 h until stable for discharge or 5 days, whichever is shorter; stop once bleeding is controlled if there is no active infection (AASLD 2024)
  • PPI: stop once variceal bleeding is confirmed as the source, unless another indication exists (AASLD 2024)

3. Endoscopic Therapy:

  • Esophageal varices, and GOV1 varices treated the same way: band ligation (EVL) when variceal bleeding is confirmed (AASLD 2024)
  • Cardiofundal gastric (GOV2, IGV1) or ectopic varices: endoscopic cyanoacrylate injection, TIPS, or retrograde transvenous obliteration are all first-line options; retrograde obliteration is preferred when TIPS is contraindicated. After cyanoacrylate, add NSBB and repeat treatment every 2-4 weeks until obliteration (AASLD 2024)
  • EVL is repeated every 2-4 weeks until obliteration, then endoscopy at 6 months and every 12 months (AASLD 2024)

4. Uncontrolled Bleeding and TIPS:

  • Bridge to TIPS: intubate, then balloon tamponade (limited to 24 hours) or a covered esophageal stent (up to 1 week; similar efficacy and better safety than tamponade; not FDA approved in the US) (AASLD 2024)
  • Salvage TIPS for uncontrolled bleeding; rescue TIPS for rebleeding despite vasoactive therapy and EVL (AASLD 2024)
  • Preemptive TIPS: CTP class B score over 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or CTP class C score 10-13: TIPS within 72 hours (ideally within 24 hours) of the first endoscopy, absent absolute contraindications; transfer if TIPS is not available locally. Improves bleeding control and survival in most but not all studies (AASLD 2024)

5. After Bleeding Is Controlled:

  • Start enteral feeding; variceal bands do not prevent placing a feeding tube (AASLD 2024)
  • No preemptive TIPS: NSBB starting when vasoactive therapy stops, plus EVL; begin within 7 days of admission. NSBB plus EVL lowers rebleeding versus EVL alone and improves survival in CTP class B and C (AASLD 2024)
  • NSBB (propranolol, nadolol, or carvedilol; AASLD 2024 Table 3): propranolol 20-40 mg twice daily (maximum 320 mg/day, 160 mg/day with ascites) or nadolol 20-40 mg at bedtime (maximum 160 mg/day, 80 mg/day with ascites), titrated every 2-3 days to HR 55-60 with SBP 90 or higher; carvedilol 6.25 mg once daily at bedtime for 2-3 days, then 12.5 mg/day (one dose or 6.25 mg twice daily) if tolerated, maximum 12.5 mg/day, no HR goal, SBP 90 or higher (AASLD 2024 statement 2 and text). Carvedilol lowers HVPG more but causes more hypotension. Reduce or stop NSBB if SBP stays under 90 mm Hg (AASLD 2024)
  • After preemptive TIPS: no further prophylaxis needed. TIPS for secondary prophylaxis can be considered with another TIPS indication such as refractory ascites, and is recommended for rebleeding despite adequate prophylaxis (AASLD 2024)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Restrictive transfusion: hemoglobin ~7 g/dL; no FFP or platelets to INR or platelet targets (AASLD 2024)
  • Vasoactive drug and antibiotics before endoscopy: octreotide 50 mcg bolus, then 25-50 mcg/h; ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 h for up to 5 days (AASLD 2024)
  • EGD within 12 hours; EVL for esophageal varices (AASLD 2024)
  • Calculate CTP at presentation: CTP B over 7 with active bleeding, or CTP C 10-13, means preemptive TIPS within 72 hours, ideally 24 (AASLD 2024)
  • Tamponade or stent is only a bridge to TIPS; tamponade is limited to 24 hours (AASLD 2024)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Octreotide, 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Pantoprazole, 💊 Carvedilol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Blood Cultures
