300. OGILVIE SYNDROME (Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction)

Massive Colonic Dilation Without Mechanical Obstruction
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Presentation: abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, altered bowel function; dilation of the ascending and transverse colon without mechanical obstruction on imaging (ASCRS 2021)

Who: older, hospitalized, or institutionalized patients with comorbid conditions, infection, or recovery from surgery or trauma (ASCRS 2021). Incidence about 100 per 100,000 inpatient admissions per year (ASGE 2020)

Risk Factors:

  • Critical illness, recent surgery, metabolic imbalance, nonoperative trauma (ASGE 2020)
  • Conditions that predispose or prolong it: electrolyte abnormalities, narcotics, anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin or benztropine, infection (ASCRS 2021)

Warning Signs: increasing pain, fever, abdominal tenderness, or leukocytosis suggest ischemia or perforation: urgent surgical evaluation (ASCRS 2021). Ischemia or perforation occurs in 3-10%, more often with cecal diameter over 12 cm and/or dilation over 6 days (ASCRS 2021); spontaneous perforation risk 3-25%, with up to 50% mortality if it occurs (ASGE 2020)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging: mechanical obstruction must be excluded (ASGE 2020; ASCRS 2021)

  • Abdominal X-ray: usually sufficient for diagnosis, but cannot always distinguish mechanical from functional obstruction (ASGE 2020)
  • CT or water-soluble contrast enema reliably distinguishes ACPO from mechanical large-bowel obstruction (ASCRS 2021); CT shows colonic dilation, possibly with a transition zone, and no mechanical cause (ASGE 2020)
  • Endoscopy is not used for diagnosis, given perforation risk, unless distal obstruction is strongly suspected (ASCRS 2021)

Labs: basic metabolic panel for electrolyte derangements and acute kidney injury (ASCRS 2021). Practical: CBC, magnesium, lactate if ischemia is a concern

Cecal Diameter: ischemia or perforation in 0%, 7%, and 23% with cecal diameters under 12 cm, 12-14 cm, and over 14 cm in a pooled review of 400 patients; the rate of change on serial films may matter more than any cutoff (ASCRS 2021)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Supportive Care (first line): for ACPO without fever, leukocytosis, abdominal tenderness, free air, or cecal diameter over 12 cm (ASCRS 2021); ASGE allows up to 72 hours before escalating (ASGE 2020)

  • Correct electrolytes; fluid resuscitation; stop or minimize narcotics and anticholinergics; treat infection (ASCRS 2021)
  • Bowel rest (NPO), nasogastric and/or rectal tube decompression, ambulation, alternating knee-chest or prone positioning (ASCRS 2021)
  • Avoid oral osmotic and stimulant laxatives: they can worsen dilation and add gas (ASCRS 2021)
  • Serial exams and daily abdominal X-rays. Resolves without escalation in 70-90% (ASCRS 2021); success 77-96% (ASGE 2020)

2. Neostigmine (not FDA approved for ACPO, ASCRS 2021):

  • When: failed supportive care (up to 72 hours), not a candidate for it, or at risk for perforation, with no contraindication (ASGE 2020); strong recommendation when supportive care fails (ASCRS 2021)
  • Dose: 2 mg IV over 3-5 minutes (ASGE 2020); bolus doses of 2-2.5 mg (ASCRS 2021). Median response 4 minutes in the Ponec trial (ASCRS 2021)
  • Monitoring: continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring; atropine immediately available for bradycardia; glycopyrrolate may prevent hypersalivation and bronchospasm (ASGE 2020)
  • Contraindications: intestinal or urinary obstruction, hypersensitivity. Relative: bradycardia, asthma, renal insufficiency, peptic ulcer disease, recent MI, acidosis (ASGE 2020). Exclude perforation and mechanical obstruction first (ASCRS 2021)
  • Response: 85-94% in 3 placebo-controlled trials; 89.2% vs 14.8% with placebo in meta-analysis (ASGE 2020). A second dose works in 40-100% of nonresponders or partial responders (ASGE 2020; ASCRS 2021)
  • Refractory to bolus: subcutaneous neostigmine or continuous IV infusion (0.4-0.8 mg/h studied in critical illness-related colonic ileus) (ASGE 2020). After success, daily low-dose polyethylene glycol may reduce recurrence (ASGE 2020)
  • Adverse effects: abdominal pain 50-73%, sialorrhea 23-38%, vomiting 10-20%, bradycardia 5-9% (ASCRS 2021)

3. Colonoscopic Decompression:

  • When: neostigmine contraindicated or ineffective (strong recommendation, ASCRS 2021); ASGE also suggests it as an alternative after failed supportive care, with a decompression tube (ASGE 2020). Retrospective studies favored it over neostigmine first-line, but evidence is too limited for a definitive recommendation (ASGE 2020)
  • Technique: experienced endoscopist; unprepped colon; water infusion with minimal or no CO2 insufflation instead of air; non-narcotic sedation; reach at least the distal transverse colon, then suction extensively. Abdominal X-ray within several hours beforehand to exclude perforation (ASGE 2020)
  • Outcomes: initial success 61-95%, sustained 70-90%, perforation 1-3% (ASCRS 2021); perforation about 2% with 1% mortality, and recurrence about 40%, especially without a decompression tube (ASGE 2020)
  • Decompression tube: ASCRS supports leaving one (ASCRS 2021); ASGE notes no randomized trial and conflicting cohort data (ASGE 2020). Polyethylene glycol after endoscopy can lower recurrence (ASGE 2020)

4. Surgery:

  • Indications: ischemia, perforation, or ACPO refractory to drug and endoscopic therapy (strong recommendation, ASCRS 2021); ASGE adds peritonitis, clinical deterioration, or cecal diameter over 12 cm (ASGE 2020)
  • Refractory dilation occurs in about 10%. Before surgery, percutaneous endoscopic cecostomy may be considered if there is no perforation or ischemia (ASCRS 2021)
  • Options: most commonly stoma with or without resection (ASCRS 2021); surgical or percutaneous cecostomy, or subtotal colectomy. Mortality up to 44% with ischemic or perforated bowel (ASGE 2020)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Exclude mechanical obstruction first: CT or water-soluble contrast enema (ASCRS 2021)
  • Supportive care first if no fever, leukocytosis, tenderness, free air, or cecal diameter over 12 cm; no oral osmotic or stimulant laxatives (ASCRS 2021)
  • Neostigmine 2 mg IV over 3-5 minutes with cardiac monitoring and atropine at the bedside (ASGE 2020)
  • Cecal diameter over 12 cm and dilation over 6 days raise ischemia and perforation risk; trend serial films (ASCRS 2021)
  • Fever, rising pain, tenderness, or leukocytosis: urgent surgical evaluation (ASCRS 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Atropine

301. ACALCULOUS CHOLECYSTITIS

Gallbladder Inflammation Without Stones • ICU-Associated
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: cholecystitis without stones; 5-10% of cholecystectomies done for acute cholecystitis (Merck 2025)

Presentation: symptoms like calculous cholecystitis, but hard to recognize because patients are severely ill; abdominal distension or unexplained fever may be the only clue. Monitor at-risk patients (critically ill, fasting, immunocompromised) for these signs (Merck 2025)

Risk Factors:

  • Major surgery or critical illness (burns, sepsis, shock, trauma) (Merck 2025)
  • Prolonged fasting or parenteral nutrition, which cause bile stasis (Merck 2025)
  • Immune deficiency or HIV infection; vasculitis (SLE, polyarteritis nodosa); diabetes; atherosclerosis (Merck 2025)
  • Young children: after a febrile illness without an identified organism (Merck 2025)

Pathophysiology: inflammatory mediators released by ischemia, infection, or bile stasis; sometimes an organism is found (Salmonella, or cytomegalovirus in immunodeficient patients). Untreated, it can progress rapidly to gangrene and perforation, with sepsis, shock, and peritonitis (Merck 2025)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs: Practical: CBC, liver tests, lipase; blood cultures if septic

Imaging:

  • Ultrasound first for suspected biliary disease (ACR 2022). Suggests acalculous cholecystitis: no stones plus sonographic Murphy sign, or a thickened wall with pericholecystic fluid. A distended gallbladder, sludge, and a thickened wall without pericholecystic fluid can come from critical illness alone (Merck 2025). Ultrasound is of limited use in critically ill patients, in whom gallbladder abnormalities are common without cholecystitis (ACR 2022)
  • Negative or equivocal ultrasound: cholescintigraphy (HIDA) is usually appropriate and remains the imaging examination of choice. It is very sensitive, but direct gallbladder inflammation can give false negatives, and specificity may be limited in critically ill patients, whose gallbladder may not fill despite cholecystokinin. CT, MRI/MRCP, or image-guided cholecystostomy may be appropriate (ACR 2022)
  • CT: nonspecific gallbladder findings are common in critically ill patients, but a completely normal gallbladder on CT makes a surgical finding unlikely. Use IV contrast: wall enhancement and adjacent liver hyperemia, an early finding, are not seen without it (ACR 2022). Contrast CT or MRI for suspected gangrene; CT for emphysematous cholecystitis (TG18, non-US)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Antibiotics (SIS 2017):

  • Lower risk: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole, or ertapenem (SIS 2017)
  • Higher risk (sepsis, septic shock, APACHE II 10 or more): piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem, or cefepime plus metronidazole (SIS 2017)
  • Healthcare-associated (hospitalized 48 hours or more in the prior 90 days, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, postoperative, or known resistant colonization): start with the higher-risk regimens and add coverage for Enterococcus, MRSA, resistant gram-negative bacilli, or Candida based on each patient's risk (SIS 2017, 2-B)
  • Duration: 24 hours or less after cholecystectomy for acute or gangrenous cholecystitis without perforation (1-A); 4 days after adequate source control (1-A); no more than 5-7 days if definitive source control is not performed (SIS 2017)

2. Source Control:

  • Cholecystectomy: studies show benefit from surgery in the first 24-48 hours in acalculous cholecystitis; cholecystectomy for calculous or acalculous disease is recommended within 7 days of admission and 10 days of symptom onset (Merck 2025)
  • Percutaneous cholecystostomy: the alternative for very high surgical risk, including acalculous cholecystitis and ICU patients with burns, trauma, or respiratory failure (Merck 2025). It can be both diagnostic and therapeutic, is usually considered safe in hospitalized patients, and is used more often as treatment than for diagnosis (ACR 2022)

3. Supportive Care: hydration and analgesics (Merck 2025). Practical: NPO, optimize hemodynamics, reassess often for gangrene or perforation

Complications: gangrene and perforation, leading to sepsis, shock, and peritonitis (Merck 2025); emphysematous cholecystitis (TG18, non-US)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Think of it: unexplained fever or abdominal distension in a critically ill, fasting, or immunocompromised patient (Merck 2025)
  • No stones does not exclude cholecystitis, and ultrasound findings are nonspecific in the critically ill (Merck 2025; ACR 2022)
  • Negative or equivocal ultrasound: HIDA is the imaging examination of choice (ACR 2022)
  • Very high surgical risk: percutaneous cholecystostomy is both diagnostic and therapeutic (ACR 2022; Merck 2025)
  • Untreated, it progresses rapidly to gangrene and perforation: do not delay source control (Merck 2025)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Ceftriaxone, 💊 Cefepime, 💊 Ertapenem, 💊 Vancomycin

302. COAGULOPATHY OF LIVER DISEASE

Rebalanced Hemostasis • Complex Bleeding/Thrombosis Risk
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Key Concept: simultaneous changes in procoagulant and anticoagulant pathways produce complex, rebalanced hemostasis that PT, aPTT, and platelet count do not capture; hypercoagulable and hypocoagulable features can coexist and cause thrombosis or bleeding (AASLD 2021)

Changes Promoting Bleeding: low factors II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, and XIII; thrombocytopenia and platelet function defects; anemia; elevated tPA not balanced by PAI-1; low α2-antiplasmin and TAFI (AASLD 2021, Table 1)

Changes Promoting Clotting: low protein C, protein S, and antithrombin; elevated factor VIII and von Willebrand factor; low ADAMTS13; low plasminogen (AASLD 2021, Table 1)

Thrombocytopenia: less thrombopoietin synthesis, splenic sequestration, faster platelet turnover, and less megakaryocyte production (AASLD 2021)

Fibrinolysis: net effect controversial: decompensation appears to favor hyperfibrinolysis, but ACLF or sepsis can severely inhibit fibrinolysis (AASLD 2021, Table 1)

Clinical Implication: neither elevated PT/INR nor thrombocytopenia reliably predicts bleeding, and patients remain at risk of DVT, PE, splanchnic vein thrombosis, and stroke (AGA 2021)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Pre-procedure Testing: in stable cirrhosis undergoing common GI procedures (paracentesis, thoracentesis, variceal banding, colonic polypectomy, ERCP, liver biopsy), AGA suggests against extensive testing, including repeated PT/INR or platelet counts (conditional; AGA 2021). Do not use the INR to gauge procedural bleeding risk unless the patient takes a vitamin K antagonist (AASLD 2021)

Viscoelastic Testing (TEG/ROTEM):

  • Better reflects overall hemostasis but is not clinically validated (AASLD 2021); no recommendation for or against it before common procedures in stable cirrhosis (AGA 2021)
  • Critically ill ALF or ACLF: suggested over INR, platelets, and fibrinogen (conditional), and recommended before procedures (strong, moderate quality) (SCCM 2020)
  • TEG-guided transfusion reduced blood product use in randomized trials of cirrhosis or ACLF with variceal or nonvariceal bleeding, with no difference in bleeding control, rebleeding, or mortality (AASLD 2024 ACLF)

Other Labs: fibrinogen under 100 mg/dL is linked to bleeding, mostly in critical illness (AASLD 2021). D-dimer and other activation markers are cleared by the liver, so high levels may reflect reduced clearance rather than ongoing coagulation or fibrinolysis. Factor V helps separate vitamin K deficiency from impaired synthesis (AASLD 2021)

MANAGEMENT

General Principles:

  • Do not correct the INR before procedures: measures to lower the INR are not recommended in patients not taking vitamin K antagonists, and pre-procedure FFP carries risks with no proven benefit (AASLD 2021)
  • No routine FFP or platelets before common GI procedures in stable cirrhosis (conditional; AGA 2021). Both low- and high-risk procedures can reasonably be done without prophylactically raising the platelet count; individualize for severe thrombocytopenia (AASLD 2021)
  • FFP can cause transfusion-related lung injury and raises portal pressure in proportion to volume, with minimal effect on thrombin generation (AASLD 2021). Blood products also risk circulatory overload, infection, alloimmunization, and transfusion reactions (AGA 2019)
  • Vitamin K: no measurable effect on the INR except in advanced malnutrition or chronic cholestasis (AASLD 2021)
  • Before elective high-risk procedures, correct modifiable risks: antithrombotic drugs, AKI, infection (AASLD 2021)

For Active Bleeding or High-Risk Procedures:

  • Variceal bleeding: no FFP or platelets to reach INR or platelet targets (AASLD 2024 portal hypertension; see card 299)
  • Thresholds that may optimize clot formation with active bleeding or high-risk procedures: hematocrit 25% or more, platelets over 50,000, fibrinogen over 120 mg/dL; INR correction thresholds are not supported by evidence (AGA 2019)
  • Fibrinogen: cryoprecipitate and fibrinogen concentrate are low-volume and raise fibrinogen effectively; correcting to over 100 mg/dL before high-risk procedures could be considered, but benefit is unproven (AASLD 2021)
  • When correction is needed: low-volume cryoprecipitate or 4-factor PCC are preferred over high-volume FFP (AASLD 2024 ACLF). PCC dosing is partly INR-based, which is problematic in cirrhosis, and published experience is limited (AGA 2019)
  • Antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid, aminocaproic acid): may be considered for persistent mucosal oozing or puncture-site bleeding; may worsen existing thrombi (AGA 2019). Not recommended to prevent procedural bleeding; in HALT-IT, high-dose tranexamic acid did not reduce death or bleeding in GI bleeding, and VTE was more frequent in patients with cirrhosis (AASLD 2021)
  • Desmopressin: lacks a sound evidence base because von Willebrand factor is already high; may help with concomitant renal failure (AGA 2019)

Procedures:

  • Low bleeding risk (major bleeding expected under 1.5%): paracentesis, thoracentesis, central venous catheter or PICC placement and removal, diagnostic EGD and routine variceal banding, colonoscopy with biopsy, ERCP without sphincterotomy (AASLD 2021, Table 3)
  • High bleeding risk: liver biopsy, cholecystostomy or percutaneous biliary drain, TIPS, polypectomy, PEG placement, ERCP with sphincterotomy, EUS with FNA (AASLD 2021, Table 3)
  • No data-driven INR or platelet cutoff reliably predicts procedural bleeding; AASLD advises no routine pre-procedure correction of any parameter. Other societies set high-risk thresholds: SIR 2019 platelets over 30,000, INR under 2.5 (corrected with vitamin K, not FFP), fibrinogen over 100; AGA 2019 platelets over 50,000, fibrinogen over 120 (AASLD 2021, Table 4)
  • Bleeding after paracentesis (0-3.3%) and thoracentesis (2%) is low, so no routine pre-procedure coagulation assessment. Liver biopsy bleeding is higher with platelets 50 x 10^9/L or less; transjugular biopsy is relatively safe even with low platelets or a high INR (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • TPO receptor agonists: avatrombopag and lusutrombopag are FDA-approved for thrombocytopenia in chronic liver disease before a scheduled procedure, given as a 2- to 8-day course (AASLD 2021); AGA suggests against routine use (conditional; AGA 2021)

Thrombosis:

  • VTE prophylaxis: hospitalized patients with cirrhosis who meet standard criteria should get standard pharmacologic prophylaxis (conditional; AGA 2021)
  • Therapeutic anticoagulation: non-portal-hypertensive bleeding rates appear similar to the general population; with ACLF and platelets under 50 x 10^9/L, decide case by case (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Portal vein thrombosis: no routine screening, except patients listed for transplant (AGA 2021). Anticoagulate recent PVT that is over 50% occlusive or involves the main portal or mesenteric veins, and urgently with intestinal ischemia; VKA, LMWH, or DOAC are reasonable, with DOACs considered for CTP A and B (AGA 2025); rivaroxaban label: avoid in Child-Pugh B or C or any liver disease with coagulopathy (Xarelto label 5.5, 8.7; card 325)
  • Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulate when indicated (conditional; AGA 2021)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • The INR misleads: do not use it to gauge bleeding risk or to trigger FFP in cirrhosis (AASLD 2021; AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Patients with cirrhosis clot too: give standard VTE prophylaxis when indicated (AGA 2021)
  • No routine FFP or platelets before common procedures; paracentesis and thoracentesis are low risk (AGA 2021; AASLD 2021)
  • If correction is needed, use low-volume cryoprecipitate or 4-factor PCC rather than FFP (AASLD 2024 ACLF)
  • Viscoelastic testing reduces transfusions but is not validated to predict bleeding (AASLD 2021; AASLD 2024 ACLF)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Vitamin K, 💊 4-Factor PCC, 💊 DDAVP, 💊 TXA, 💊 Enoxaparin

303. TAKOTSUBO CARDIOMYOPATHY

Stress-Induced Cardiomyopathy • "Broken Heart Syndrome"
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Post-menopausal woman with acute chest pain and dyspnea following intense emotional or physical stress

Symptoms: Chest pain, dyspnea, or syncope; indistinguishable from AMI at first glance (InterTAK 2018 Part I)

Inpatients: Often atypical: tachycardia, hypotension, heart failure, new biomarker rise, or new ECG changes. In-hospital TTS is more often male and carries higher in-hospital mortality than out-of-hospital TTS (Part I)

Triggers (emotional, physical, or combined; not obligatory):

  • Emotional: Death of loved one, divorce, job loss, argument
  • Physical: Surgery, sepsis, respiratory failure
  • Neurologic: SAH, stroke/TIA, seizure
  • Pheochromocytoma: Counted as a trigger under InterTAK, not an exclusion
  • No identifiable trigger: About one-third of patients

Demographics: About 90% women; mean age 67-70; about 80% older than 50 (Part I)

Important: Can occur in men and younger patients; do not exclude based on demographics. Men present more often after a physical trigger; male sex and physical trigger independently predict in-hospital mortality (Part II)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Diagnostic Algorithm (InterTAK 2018 Part II, Figure 1; expert consensus, no COR):

  • ST elevation: Urgent coronary angiography with LV ventriculography to exclude AMI
  • No ST elevation: Consider the InterTAK Diagnostic Score (below)
  • Score ≤70 (low/intermediate probability): Coronary angiography with LV ventriculography
  • Score >70 (high probability): Consider TTE first. No circumferential ballooning: angiography. Stable with circumferential ballooning: CCTA to exclude CAD. Unstable: TTE (assess LVOTO) plus angiography to rule out AMI
  • Confirmation: Normal coronaries (or CAD that does not explain the whole RWMA), typical pattern, no myocarditis red flags: TTS most likely; confirm with follow-up echo showing recovery

InterTAK Diagnostic Score:

CriterionPoints
Female sex25
Emotional stress24
Physical stress13
No ST depression (except aVR)12
Psychiatric disorder11
Neurologic disorder9
QTc prolongation6

Not derived in pheochromocytoma-induced TTS (atypical patterns more frequent)

ECG: Abnormal in most. InterTAK Registry: ST elevation 44%, T-wave inversion 41%, ST depression 8%; QTc prolongation common. Rare cases have no ECG changes

Biomarkers: Admission troponin similar to ACS, but peak substantially lower; extent of wall motion abnormality greatly exceeds biomarker release. CK only slightly elevated. BNP/NT-proBNP markedly elevated, peak about 24-48 h. High admission troponin predicts worse in-hospital outcome (Part II)

Echocardiogram:

  • Classic "apical ballooning": Apical and mid-ventricular akinesis with hyperdynamic base
  • Variants: Mid-ventricular, basal (reverse takotsubo), focal
  • Wall motion abnormality usually extends beyond a single coronary distribution (rare focal exceptions)
  • Check: LVOTO, significant MR, RV involvement (RV involved in about one-third; predicts worse outcome)

Coronary Angiography: Culprit lesions do not explain the whole wall motion abnormality. Concomitant CAD (10-29%) does not exclude TTS

Cardiac MRI: Recommended to exclude infectious myocarditis and confirm TTS (Part I). Perform when myocarditis red flags present: viral symptoms, elevated ESR/CRP, pericardial effusion (Part II)

InterTAK Diagnostic Criteria (2018):

  • Transient LV dysfunction (hypokinesia, akinesia, or dyskinesia): apical ballooning or midventricular, basal, or focal; RV involvement possible; usually beyond a single epicardial territory
  • Emotional, physical, or combined trigger may precede, but is not obligatory
  • Neurologic disorders (SAH, stroke/TIA, seizure) and pheochromocytoma may be triggers
  • New ECG abnormalities (ST elevation, ST depression, T-wave inversion, QTc prolongation); rare cases without
  • Troponin and CK moderately elevated in most; significant BNP elevation common
  • Significant CAD is not a contradiction
  • No evidence of infectious myocarditis (CMR recommended)
  • Postmenopausal women predominantly affected
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Evidence Base: No RCTs. InterTAK 2018 Part II management is expert consensus (evidence level C); algorithm in Figure 7

Initial (until ACS excluded):

  • Treat as ACS per guideline (aspirin, heparin); transfer to a center with imaging and a cath lab
  • Continuous ECG monitoring: QT prolongation can trigger torsades de pointes; AV block can occur
  • Use QT-prolonging drugs cautiously in the acute phase

Management by Hemodynamic Profile (Figure 7):

ProfileSettingConsiderAvoid
Mild, no HFTelemetry at least 48 hACEi or ARB; beta-blockerInotropes
HF / pulmonary edemaIntermediate careACEi or ARB; beta-blocker; diuretic and nitroglycerin only if no LVOTOInotropes
Shock with LVOTOICUIV fluid (if no HF); short-acting beta-blocker; ImpellaDiuretics, nitroglycerin, IABP, inotropes
Shock, primary pump failureICULevosimendan (if available); Impella; VA-ECMOInotropes

Inotropes to Avoid: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dobutamine, milrinone, isoproterenol. 20% mortality reported with catecholamines (possible selection bias). If catecholamines are used, repeat Doppler to detect an evolving LVOT gradient

Shock Workup: Assess promptly for LVOTO (about 20% of TTS; especially apical ballooning): LV pullback pressure at catheterization or continuous-wave Doppler

Practical (not addressed in InterTAK): LVOTO with hypotension despite fluids: pure vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine), extrapolated from obstructive HCM (2024 AHA/ACC HCM, COR 1, LOE C-LD)

Beta-Blockers:

  • Reasonable until LVEF recovers (no trial data); may improve LVOTO
  • Contraindicated in acute severe HF with low LVEF, hypotension, or bradycardia
  • Use cautiously with bradycardia or QTc >500 ms (pause-dependent torsades)

ACEi/ARB: May facilitate LV recovery

Arrhythmias:

  • Consider beta-blocker; temporary transvenous pacing for hemodynamically significant bradycardia or AV block
  • Wearable defibrillator (life vest) could be considered for excessive QT prolongation or life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia
  • ICD of uncertain value (LV dysfunction and ECG changes reverse); Figure 7 advises avoiding permanent devices

LV Thrombus / Embolism:

  • Thrombus or embolism present: heparin, then VKA or DOAC until first follow-up
  • Consider anticoagulation if LVEF ≤30% and/or large apical dysfunction; post-discharge anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy individualized

After Discharge:

  • ACEi or ARB for 3 months or until wall motion recovers; associated with improved 1-year survival and fewer recurrences (observational)
  • Beta-blockers: no survival benefit and no recurrence prevention; one-third of recurrences occurred on beta-blockade
  • Aspirin and statin if concomitant CAD
  • Depression/anxiety common: combined psycho-cardiac rehabilitation

In-Hospital Complications (Part II, Figure 4):

ComplicationPrevalence
Acute heart failure12-45%
Mitral regurgitation14-25%
LVOTO10-25%
Cardiogenic shock6-20%
Atrial fibrillation5-15%
LV thrombus2-8%
Cardiac arrest4-6%
AV blockAbout 5%

Also: torsades de pointes (QTc prolongation), VT/VF, ventricular septal defect, free wall rupture

Prognosis: Not benign: morbidity and mortality comparable to ACS. InterTAK Registry: death 5.6% and MACCE 9.9% per patient-year. Recurrence 1.8% per patient-year. Wall motion abnormality may persist for a prolonged period (Part I)

Predictors of Adverse In-Hospital Outcome: Physical trigger, male sex, high admission troponin, age ≥75, low LVEF, reversible moderate-severe MR, RV involvement

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Troponin-wall motion mismatch: Admission troponin is similar to ACS, but the peak is lower and the wall motion abnormality far exceeds the biomarker rise
  • ST depression favors ACS: Present in under 10% of TTS vs over 30% of ACS
  • Goes to cath lab: ST elevation means urgent angiography; TTS is often diagnosed when no culprit lesion explains the wall motion abnormality. Concomitant CAD does not exclude TTS
  • Avoid inotropes: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dobutamine, milrinone, isoproterenol; 20% mortality reported with catecholamines
  • Check for LVOTO in shock: Hyperkinetic base plus SAM causes LVOTO and MR. Give IV fluid (if no HF) and a short-acting beta-blocker; avoid nitroglycerin, diuretics, and IABP
  • LV thrombus: Anticoagulate if thrombus or embolism; consider if LVEF ≤30% and/or large apical dysfunction
  • After discharge, ACEi/ARB rather than beta-blocker: ACEi/ARB is associated with better 1-year survival and fewer recurrences; beta-blockers show neither (observational)
  • Not benign: Mortality comparable to ACS (death 5.6% per patient-year)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Losartan, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Unfractionated Heparin, 💊 Apixaban, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Phenylephrine

304. MITRAL STENOSIS

Rheumatic Heart Disease • LA Pressure Overload
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, palpitations (atrial fibrillation), hemoptysis

Demographics: Rheumatic MS about 80% women. Endemic regions: presents in teens to age 30 with pliable leaflets. Low-prevalence regions: presents at 50-70, decades after rheumatic fever, with calcified fibrotic leaflets and comorbidities (2020 ACC/AHA VHD)

Precipitants of Decompensation: Symptoms can worsen without MS progression: new or rapid AF (loss of atrial kick plus shortened diastolic filling), pregnancy, fever, anemia, hyperthyroidism, perioperative hemodynamic shifts (2020)

Physical Exam:

  • Low-pitched diastolic rumble: Best heard at apex with bell in left lateral decubitus
  • Opening snap: Higher pitch, follows S2 (closer to S2 = more severe stenosis)
  • Loud S1: Due to abrupt closure of stenotic valve
  • Signs of RV failure: Late finding (JVD, edema, ascites)

Etiology:

  • Rheumatic: Most MS worldwide; commissural fusion with diastolic doming
  • Nonrheumatic calcific (MAC): Annular calcification extending into leaflet bases, no commissural fusion; increasingly common in the elderly in high-income countries; 5-year survival <50%
  • Other nonrheumatic: Post-radiation; after mitral repair with a small annuloplasty ring
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

ECG: Left atrial enlargement (P mitrale), atrial fibrillation (common), RVH (late)

CXR: Left atrial enlargement (straightening of left heart border), pulmonary congestion, Kerley B lines

TTE (COR 1, LOE B-NR): Establish diagnosis, quantify severity, assess other valve lesions, and define morphology for commissurotomy suitability. Report mean gradient with heart rate (tachycardia overestimates severity)

Stages of MS (2020 ACC/AHA Table 16):

StageMVAPressure half-timeConsequencesSymptoms
B: Progressive>1.5 cm²<150 msMild-moderate LA enlargement; normal PASP at restNone
C: Asymptomatic severe≤1.5 cm²≥150 msSevere LA enlargement; PASP >50 mmHgNone
D: Symptomatic severe≤1.5 cm²≥150 msSevere LA enlargement; PASP >50 mmHgDecreased exercise tolerance, exertional dyspnea

Mean Gradient: Usually >5-10 mmHg in severe MS at normal heart rate, but NOT a severity criterion (varies with heart rate and flow)

TEE (COR 1, LOE C-LD): Before PMBC, to exclude LA/LAA thrombus and grade MR. MR more than mild is a contraindication to PMBC

Exercise Testing (COR 1, LOE C-LD): Symptoms discordant with resting echo: exercise Doppler or invasive hemodynamics (mean gradient and PA pressure response)

Cardiac Catheterization: When TTE/TEE is nondiagnostic or discordant with symptoms; measures LA (wedge), LV, and PA pressures at rest and exercise

Valve Morphology (Wilkins score):

  • Leaflet mobility, thickening, calcification, subvalvular thickening (each 1-4 points)
  • Score ≤8 with pliable, noncalcified leaflets: favorable for PMBC. Commissural calcification also predicts poorer results
  • Score >8 predicts a suboptimal result but is not absolute: 42% still had an optimal outcome; PMBC remains an option in severely symptomatic patients at high surgical risk (see Intervention)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Anticoagulation:

  • VKA (warfarin) indicated (COR 1, LOE C-LD): Rheumatic MS with AF, prior embolic event, or LA thrombus. Target INR 2.5 (2.0-3.0)
  • No DOACs: AF with moderate-severe rheumatic MS is excluded from the DOAC-over-warfarin recommendation (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF). ESC/EACTS 2025: DOACs not recommended with AF and rheumatic MS, MVA ≤2.0 cm² (Class III, Level B; INVICTUS, rivaroxaban vs VKA)
  • Sinus rhythm with LA enlargement or spontaneous contrast only: Anticoagulation controversial; no 2020 recommendation (ESC 2025 text: consider with dense spontaneous contrast or LA >50 mm / LA volume >60 mL/m²)

Rate Control and Symptoms:

  • AF with rapid ventricular response (COR 2a, LOE C-LD): Rate control; slower rate lengthens diastolic filling and lowers LA pressure
  • Sinus rhythm with symptomatic resting or exertional sinus tachycardia (COR 2a, LOE A): Beta-blocker, nondihydropyridine CCB, or ivabradine. Avoid routine rate slowing without tachycardia (chronotropic incompetence, especially in older patients)
  • Diuretics: For volume overload and pulmonary congestion
  • Rhythm control: Harder in rheumatic MS (atrial fibrosis); cardioversion unlikely to succeed with untreated severe MS, consider after successful intervention (ESC 2025). Pre-cardioversion anticoagulation per AF card (at least 3 weeks therapeutic or TEE-guided)

Indications for Intervention (2020 ACC/AHA; PMBC at a Comprehensive Valve Center):

COR / LOEPatientIntervention
1 / ASymptomatic (NYHA II-IV) severe MS (MVA ≤1.5, Stage D), favorable morphology, MR <2+, no LA thrombusPMBC
1 / B-NRNYHA III-IV severe MS AND not a PMBC candidate, failed PMBC, needs other cardiac surgery, or no PMBC accessMitral surgery (repair, commissurotomy, or replacement)
2a / B-NRAsymptomatic severe MS (Stage C), favorable morphology, MR <2+, no LA thrombus, PASP >50 mmHgPMBC
2b / C-LDAsymptomatic severe MS, favorable morphology, new-onset AFPMBC
2b / C-LDSymptomatic, MVA >1.5, exercise PCWP >25 mmHg or mean gradient >15 mmHgPMBC
2b / B-NRNYHA III-IV severe MS, suboptimal anatomy, not a surgical candidate or high surgical riskPMBC
2b / C-LDCalcific (MAC) MS, NYHA III-IV, MVA ≤1.5Intervention only after discussing high procedural risk

Intervention Options:

  • PMBC (balloon commissurotomy): First-line with favorable morphology, MR <2+, no LA thrombus (TEE first). Experienced operators with surgical backup. 70-80% free of recurrent symptoms at 10 years
  • Surgery: Commissurotomy (closed or open) preferred when anatomy is favorable. Valve replacement for severe thickening and subvalvular fibrosis, or when no other option exists with severe limiting symptoms. Add tricuspid repair if moderate-severe TR. Delay surgery until NYHA III-IV (slow progression)

Pregnancy (2020 ACC/AHA):

  • Before pregnancy (COR 2a, LOE C-LD): Asymptomatic severe rheumatic MS with favorable morphology: PMBC before conception
  • During pregnancy: Beta-blocker for heart rate control (COR 2a, LOE C-LD); diuretic if volume overloaded (COR 2a, LOE C-LD); ACEi/ARB contraindicated (COR 3: Harm, LOE B-NR)
  • PMBC during pregnancy (COR 2a, LOE B-NR): Severe MS with NYHA III-IV symptoms despite medical therapy and favorable morphology, at a Comprehensive Valve Center
  • Surgery during pregnancy: Not without severe HF refractory to medical therapy (COR 3: Harm, LOE C-LD)

Acute Decompensation (rapid AF): Anticoagulation plus rate control with AV-nodal blocking agents; diuretics for congestion; cardioversion if rate cannot be controlled with medications (2020 text)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Tachycardia is the enemy: Faster HR shortens diastolic filling and raises LA pressure. Rate-control AF with RVR or symptomatic sinus tachycardia, but do not slow a normal heart rate routinely (chronotropic incompetence)
  • Severity is valve area, not gradient: Severe = MVA ≤1.5 cm². Always read the mean gradient with the heart rate
  • Opening snap timing: Shorter S2-OS interval = more severe stenosis (higher LA pressure opens valve earlier)
  • Wilkins score ≤8, no commissural calcium: Favorable for PMBC (balloon splits fused commissures). TEE first to exclude LA thrombus and more than mild MR
  • Warfarin, not DOAC: Rheumatic valve disease carries >5%/year embolic risk with AF. INVICTUS: rivaroxaban inferior to VKA; DOACs not recommended in moderate-severe rheumatic MS
  • Think rheumatic in the young; think calcific (MAC) in the elderly: Calcific MS has no commissural fusion, so no role for PMBC or surgical commissurotomy; intervene only for severely limiting symptoms
  • Pregnancy unmasks MS: Higher heart rate and volume. Beta-blocker and diuretic first; PMBC if NYHA III-IV despite therapy; no ACEi/ARB
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Warfarin, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Diltiazem, 💊 Ivabradine, 💊 Furosemide
↑ Back to Table of Contents

305. AORTIC REGURGITATION

Acute vs Chronic • Wide Pulse Pressure
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Chronic AR: May be asymptomatic for years → exertional dyspnea, fatigue, palpitations, angina

Acute AR: Sudden LV volume overload: severe pulmonary congestion and low forward output (pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock). EMERGENCY: urgent diagnosis and rapid intervention are lifesaving (2020 ACC/AHA VHD)

Physical Exam (Chronic Severe AR):

  • Wide pulse pressure: High systolic, low diastolic (e.g., 170/50)
  • Diastolic decrescendo murmur: Left sternal border, sitting up, leaning forward
  • Austin Flint murmur: Low-pitched diastolic rumble at apex (AR jet hitting anterior MV leaflet)
  • Eponymous signs: Corrigan's (water-hammer) pulse, de Musset's (head bobbing), Quincke's (nail bed pulsations), Traube's (pistol shot femorals)

Acute AR: May NOT have classic findings: no wide pulse pressure (LV hasn't dilated), soft murmur, tachycardia

Etiology (2020):

  • Chronic, high-income countries: Bicuspid aortic valve; primary disease of the aortic sinuses or ascending aorta (e.g., Marfan)
  • Chronic, low- to middle-income countries: Rheumatic heart disease
  • Calcific valve disease: AR usually accompanies AS and is mild to moderate, not severe
  • Acute: Infective endocarditis (most often), aortic dissection, iatrogenic (transcatheter procedure), blunt chest trauma
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

ECG: LVH (chronic), may be normal in acute

CXR: Cardiomegaly (chronic), pulmonary edema (acute)

TTE (COR 1, LOE B-NR): Cause and severity of AR, LV size and systolic function, prognosis, and timing of intervention. Also indicated in bicuspid valve or known aortic dilation (COR 1, LOE B-NR)

TEE, CMR, or Catheterization (COR 1, LOE B-NR): Moderate or severe AR with suboptimal TTE or clinical-TTE discrepancy (CMR quantifies regurgitant volume/fraction, LV volumes, aorta)

Severe Chronic AR (2020 Table 15): Jet width ≥65% of LVOT; vena contracta >0.6 cm; holodiastolic flow reversal in the proximal abdominal aorta; regurgitant volume ≥60 mL/beat; regurgitant fraction ≥50%; ERO ≥0.3 cm²; angiographic grade 3-4. Diagnosis of chronic severe AR also requires evidence of LV dilation

Moderate AR: Jet width 25-64% of LVOT; vena contracta 0.3-0.6 cm; regurgitant volume 30-59 mL/beat; regurgitant fraction 30-49%; ERO 0.10-0.29 cm²

Stages of Chronic AR:

StageAR SeverityLVSymptoms
B: ProgressiveMild to moderateNormal LVEF; normal volume or mild dilationNone
C1: Asymptomatic severeSevereLVEF >55% and LVESD <50 mmNone (exercise test reasonable to confirm)
C2: Asymptomatic severeSevereLVEF ≤55%, or LVESD >50 mm, or LVESD index >25 mm/m²None
D: Symptomatic severeSevereAny LVEF; moderate to severe dilationExertional dyspnea, angina, or HF

Acute AR (TTE or TEE):

  • Short deceleration time on the AR jet and early mitral valve closure: markers of markedly elevated LV end-diastolic pressure
  • AR pressure half-time <300 ms: rapid aortic-LV diastolic pressure equilibration
  • Holodiastolic flow reversal in the arch: quick semiquantitative estimate of regurgitant fraction
  • Assess etiology: endocarditis, dissection, aortic root

If Aortic Dissection Suspected: CT angiography first (highly accurate, widely available). TEE if CT unavailable and intraoperatively. TTE sensitivity for type A dissection is only 60-80% (TEE 98-100%)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Acute Severe AR (Emergency; 2020 text):

  • Surgery is definitive: Do not delay surgery, especially with hypotension, pulmonary edema, or low flow. Afterload reduction may allow only temporary stabilization
  • IABP contraindicated: Diastolic inflation worsens regurgitation
  • Beta-blockers: Standard in aortic dissection; for other causes use very cautiously if at all (block compensatory tachycardia, can precipitate marked hypotension)
  • Practical (agents not specified in 2020): IV nitroprusside for afterload reduction; inotrope (e.g., dobutamine) if hypotensive, as a bridge to surgery
  • Endocarditis: Surgical timing per endocarditis card

Chronic AR: Indications for Aortic Valve Surgery (2020 ACC/AHA):

COR / LOEIndication
1 / B-NRSymptomatic severe AR (Stage D), regardless of LV systolic function
1 / B-NRAsymptomatic severe AR with LVEF ≤55% (Stage C2), no other cause of LV dysfunction
1 / C-EOSevere AR (Stage C or D) undergoing cardiac surgery for other indications
2a / B-NRAsymptomatic severe AR, LVEF >55%, LVESD >50 mm or LVESD index >25 mm/m² (Stage C2)
2a / C-EOModerate AR (Stage B) undergoing cardiac or aortic surgery for other indications
2b / B-NRAsymptomatic severe AR, LVEF >55% (Stage C1), low surgical risk, with progressive LVEF decline to 55-60% on at least 3 serial studies or LVEDD >65 mm
3: Harm / B-NRTAVI for isolated severe AR in patients with SAVR indications who are surgical candidates

ESC/EACTS 2025 differs: LVESD >50 mm, LVESD index >25 mm/m², or LVEF ≤50% is Class I (B); LVESD index >22 mm/m², LVESV index >45 mL/m², or LVEF ≤55% with low surgical risk is Class IIb (B). TAVI may be considered for symptomatic severe AR ineligible for surgery with suitable anatomy (Class IIb, B)

Procedure: Most patients need valve replacement (mechanical or bioprosthetic). Valve-sparing root replacement in selected patients undergoing aortic root or ascending aorta surgery. TAVI rarely feasible (annular dilation, little calcium; migration and paravalvular leak)

Medical Therapy (Chronic):

  • Hypertension (SBP >140) in Stage B or C (COR 1, LOE B-NR): Treat. ACEi or ARB preferred (no heart rate effect). Beta-blockers can paradoxically raise systolic pressure (slower heart rate increases stroke volume)
  • Severe AR with symptoms or LV dysfunction (C2/D) and prohibitive surgical risk (COR 1, LOE B-NR): GDMT with ACEi, ARB, and/or sacubitril/valsartan
  • No evidence that vasodilators reduce AR or alter its course without hypertension; medical therapy is not a substitute for surgery in candidates

Surveillance Echo (2020 Table 4): Mild every 3-5 years; moderate every 1-2 years; severe asymptomatic every 6-12 months, more often if the LV is dilating. Apparent significant fall in LVEF or LV enlargement: repeat in 3-6 months

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Acute AR is an emergency: Acute LV volume overload causes severe pulmonary congestion and low forward output. Do not delay surgery for medical stabilization
  • No IABP in AR: Balloon inflation in diastole worsens regurgitation; contraindicated in acute severe AR
  • Beta-blocker exception: Avoid in acute AR because they block compensatory tachycardia, EXCEPT in aortic dissection, where they are standard
  • Wide pulse pressure: Classic for chronic AR. Absent in acute AR (LV hasn't dilated yet)
  • Austin Flint ≠ MS: AR jet causes functional mitral stenosis physiology without actual stenosis
  • Early MV closure on echo: Marker of markedly elevated LV end-diastolic pressure in acute severe AR
  • LVEF ≤55% is the Class 1 trigger: In asymptomatic severe AR, LVEF ≤55% is a Class 1 indication for surgery; LVESD >50 mm with LVEF >55% is 2a (ESC 2025: Class I)
  • Check the aorta: Bicuspid valve and aortic root or ascending aorta disease are the leading US causes; aortopathy occurs in 20-40% of bicuspid valves. TAVI is not for surgical candidates with isolated AR
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sodium Nitroprusside, 💊 Dobutamine, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Lisinopril, 💊 Losartan, 💊 Sacubitril/Valsartan

306. PROSTHETIC VALVE DYSFUNCTION

Mechanical & Bioprosthetic Valve Complications
VALVE TYPES AND ANTITHROMBOTIC THERAPY

Mechanical Valves: Durable; lifelong VKA anticoagulation required (COR 1, LOE A)

Bioprosthetic Valves (surgical or TAVI): About 30% of surgical aortic bioprostheses show dysfunction by 10 years; clinically important structural deterioration rises markedly after 10 years. Accelerated (<5 years) with age <60, smoking, diabetes, CKD, initial mean gradient ≥15 mmHg, and valve type (2020 ACC/AHA VHD)

Antithrombotic Therapy (2020 ACC/AHA):

ValveRegimenCOR / LOE
Mechanical AVR (bileaflet or current single tilting disk), no risk factorsVKA, INR 2.5 (2.0-3.0)1 / B-NR
Mechanical AVR with AF, prior thromboembolism, LV dysfunction, hypercoagulable state, or older-generation valve (ball-in-cage)VKA, INR 3.0 (2.5-3.5)1 / B-NR
Mechanical MVRVKA, INR 3.0 (2.5-3.5)1 / B-NR
On-X AVR, no risk factors, starting ≥3 months after surgeryVKA, INR 1.5-2.0, plus aspirin 75-100 mg2b / B-R
Mechanical valve with antiplatelet indication, low bleeding riskAdd aspirin 75-100 mg to VKA2b / B-R
Surgical bioprosthesis (aortic or mitral), no other anticoagulant indicationAspirin 75-100 mg daily2a / B-NR
Surgical bioprosthesis, low bleeding riskVKA, INR 2.5, for at least 3 and up to 6 months2a / B-NR
TAVI, no other anticoagulant indicationAspirin 75-100 mg daily2a / B-R
TAVI, low bleeding riskAspirin plus clopidogrel 75 mg for 3-6 months, or VKA INR 2.5 for at least 3 months2b / B-NR

Use a single INR target; the acceptable range is 0.5 above and below it

DOACs and Mechanical Valves: CONTRAINDICATED: Dabigatran (COR 3: Harm, LOE B-R; RE-ALIGN). Anti-Xa agents not recommended (COR 3: Harm, LOE C-EO). PROACT Xa (Wang, NEJM Evid 2023, doi 10.1056/EVIDoa2300067): apixaban vs warfarin in On-X AVR stopped early for excess thromboembolism with apixaban. ESC/EACTS 2025: DOACs and/or DAPT not recommended in mechanical valves (Class III, Level A)

After TAVI: Rivaroxaban 10 mg plus aspirin without another anticoagulant indication is contraindicated (COR 3: Harm, LOE B-R)

CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS

Prosthetic Valve Obstruction:

  • Mechanical valve thrombosis: Subacute to acute, often with inadequate VKA; rapid-onset dyspnea or acute pulmonary edema; stenotic murmur, muffled closing clicks. Annual rate 0.1-5.7%; highest in the first 3 months and in mitral or tricuspid position
  • Pannus: Chronic tissue ingrowth; more gradual onset; recurrent "thrombosis" may be pannus
  • Bioprosthetic valve thrombosis: Most common in the first 3 months, but seen years later; more common after TAVI than surgical valves; often found as a rising gradient on routine echo
  • Patient-prosthesis mismatch: High gradient with a normally functioning valve too small for the patient; distinguish from stenosis by comparison with the early postoperative baseline echo

Prosthetic Valve Regurgitation:

  • Paravalvular leak: Suture line disruption (technical, suture failure, annular disruption, endocarditis); severe mitral annular calcification predisposes to late leak
  • Transvalvular: Mechanical: pannus, thrombus, or vegetation blocking closure. Bioprosthetic (usual type): leaflet calcification, perforation, or flail; can progress rapidly
  • Presentation: New or unexplained HF, hemolysis with or without anemia, change in valve sounds or new murmur
  • New late paravalvular leak: Exclude endocarditis (needs antibiotics before surgery; contraindicates transcatheter closure)

Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis (PVE):

  • Suspect with fever, new regurgitation or paravalvular leak, embolism, or new conduction block
  • TAVI endocarditis: About two-thirds within 1 year of implant; enterococci, S. aureus, and coagulase-negative staphylococci prevalent (2026 AHA IE statement)
  • Diagnosis and regimens: see endocarditis card (2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria)

Structural Valve Deterioration (Bioprosthetic):

  • Leaflet thickening, calcification, or tear; stent creep. Progressive stenosis and/or regurgitation
  • Risk factors for accelerated deterioration: see Valve Types above
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Baseline TTE (COR 1, LOE B-NR): After every surgical or transcatheter valve (within about 3 months); the reference for all later comparisons

Repeat TTE (COR 1, LOE C-EO): Any change in symptoms or signs suggesting valve dysfunction; compare with baseline. Check the recent INR trend

Additional Imaging (COR 1, LOE C-LD): TEE, gated cardiac CT, or fluoroscopy when dysfunction is suspected, even if TTE is unrevealing

Suspected Mechanical Valve Thrombosis (COR 1, LOE B-NR): Urgent TTE, TEE, fluoroscopy, and/or multidetector CT

  • Obstruction: Mean gradient up >50% from baseline (or >10 mmHg across an aortic prosthesis), after excluding high-output states
  • Leaflet motion: Fluoroscopy or cine-CT (COR 1, LOE C-EO); TEE especially for mitral prostheses
  • Thrombus vs pannus: TEE or CT

Bioprosthetic Stenosis or Suspected Thrombosis (COR 2a, LOE C-LD): 3D TEE or 4D CT to detect leaflet thrombosis

Prosthetic Regurgitation (COR 1, LOE B-NR): TTE plus TEE to define cause, severity, and transvalvular vs paravalvular location. TEE is essential for prosthetic mitral valves (acoustic shadowing on TTE)

Surveillance: Surgical bioprosthesis: TTE at 5 and 10 years, then annually (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). TAVI: TTE annually (COR 2a, LOE C-LD)

Labs: INR, hemolysis labs (LDH, haptoglobin, reticulocyte count, peripheral smear), blood cultures

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Mechanical Valve Thrombosis, Symptomatic Obstruction (left-sided; COR 1, LOE B-NR): Urgent slow-infusion, low-dose fibrinolysis OR emergency surgery, decided by the Heart Valve Team

Favors SurgeryFavors Fibrinolysis
Surgical expertise available; low surgical riskNo surgical expertise; high surgical risk
Contraindication to fibrinolysisNo contraindication
Recurrent valve thrombosisFirst episode
NYHA IVNYHA I-III
Large clot (>0.8 cm²); LA thrombusSmall clot (≤0.8 cm²); no LA thrombus
CAD needing revascularization; other valve diseaseNo or mild CAD; no other valve disease
Possible pannusThrombus visualized

Outcomes (2020 Table 23 and text): surgery 30-day mortality 10-15% (<5% if NYHA I-II); echo-guided slow, low-dose fibrinolysis >90% hemodynamic success, embolism <2%, major bleeding <2%. ESC/EACTS 2025: Heart Team chooses repeat replacement vs low-dose slow-infusion fibrinolysis (Class I, B); fibrinolysis favored with high surgical risk or a right-sided prosthesis. Fibrinolytic dosing per institutional protocol

Non-obstructive Mechanical Valve Thrombus (ESC 2025): Restore therapeutic anticoagulation (bridge to target INR, correct the cause); increase VKA intensity or add low-dose aspirin (Class IIa). Surgery should be considered for a large (>10 mm) thrombus with embolism or persisting despite optimal anticoagulation (Class IIa, C)

Bioprosthetic Valve Thrombosis (COR 2a, LOE B-NR): Hemodynamically stable, no contraindication: VKA first (ESC 2025: VKA before reintervention, Class I, B). Risk of recurrence and early deterioration: close follow-up

Prosthetic Valve Stenosis:

  • Symptomatic severe stenosis (COR 1, LOE B-NR): Repeat surgery unless surgical risk is high or prohibitive
  • Bioprosthetic aortic stenosis, high or prohibitive risk (COR 2a, LOE B-NR): Transcatheter valve-in-valve at a Comprehensive Valve Center

Prosthetic Valve Regurgitation:

  • Intractable hemolysis or HF from transvalvular or paravalvular leak (COR 1, LOE B-NR): Surgery unless surgical risk is high or prohibitive
  • Asymptomatic severe prosthetic regurgitation, low operative risk (COR 2a, LOE B-NR): Surgery reasonable
  • Paravalvular leak with intractable hemolysis or NYHA III-IV, high or prohibitive surgical risk, suitable anatomy (COR 2a, LOE B-NR): Percutaneous leak closure at a Comprehensive Valve Center
  • Bioprosthetic regurgitation with severe HF, high or prohibitive risk (COR 2a, LOE B-NR): Valve-in-valve at a Comprehensive Valve Center
  • Hemolytic anemia, not severe: Folic acid, iron, or periodic transfusion; intervene for symptomatic intractable anemia

Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis:

  • Antibiotics: At least 6 weeks for prosthetic valves; organism-specific regimens on the endocarditis card (2026 AHA IE statement)
  • Staphylococcal PVE: Consensus that gentamicin risk outweighs benefit; no consensus on rifampin, decide with the endocarditis team (2026 AHA)
  • Early surgery (initial hospitalization; COR 1, LOE B-NR): HF from valve dysfunction; left-sided S. aureus, fungal, or highly resistant organism; heart block, annular or aortic abscess, or destructive lesion; persistent bacteremia or fever >5 days on appropriate therapy. Timing set by the Heart Valve Team (COR 1, LOE B-NR)
  • Relapsing PVE after a full course, no other source (COR 1, LOE C-LD): Surgery
  • Recurrent emboli with persistent vegetations despite therapy (COR 2a, LOE B-NR): Early surgery reasonable

Anticoagulation Emergencies and Procedures (mechanical valves):

  • Uncontrollable bleeding needing immediate reversal (COR 2a, LOE C-LD): 4-factor PCC; add IV vitamin K if VKA will not be resumed for 7 days (COR 2a, LOE C-LD)
  • Emergency surgery or invasive procedure on VKA (COR 2a, LOE C-LD): 4-factor PCC
  • INR >5, not bleeding (COR 2b, LOE C-LD): Hold VKA; benefit of oral vitamin K uncertain
  • Minor procedures (dental, cataract) (COR 1, LOE C-EO): Continue VKA at therapeutic INR
  • Bileaflet mechanical AVR, no risk factors (COR 1, LOE C-LD): Interrupt VKA without bridging
  • Mechanical AVR with a risk factor, older-generation AVR, or mechanical MVR (COR 2a, LOE C-LD): Bridging UFH or LMWH while INR is subtherapeutic, individualized
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Muffled clicks = obstruction: Mechanical valve clicks should be crisp. Muffled closing clicks plus a stenotic murmur: suspect thrombosis and image urgently
  • Check the INR trend: Mechanical valve thrombosis is often associated with inadequate VKA anticoagulation
  • Never a DOAC with a mechanical valve: Dabigatran (RE-ALIGN) and apixaban (PROACT Xa, On-X) both caused excess thromboembolism. Warfarin only
  • Bleeding on VKA with a mechanical valve: 4-factor PCC (onset 5-15 minutes) rather than plasma (onset 1-4 hours); IV vitamin K only if VKA will not be restarted for 7 days
  • TEE for prosthetic mitral valves: Acoustic shadowing makes TTE inadequate for mitral prosthetic regurgitation and paravalvular leak
  • Hemolysis suggests paravalvular leak: Unexplained anemia with high LDH and reticulocytes. A new late leak means rule out endocarditis
  • Bioprosthetic durability: About 30% of surgical aortic bioprostheses are dysfunctional by 10 years; earlier with age <60, smoking, diabetes, CKD
  • PVE is dangerous: In a VA cohort, 56% of staphylococcal PVE patients died or relapsed within 1 year; fungal PVE mortality >50% (2026 AHA). Early Heart Valve Team review
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Warfarin, 💊 Unfractionated Heparin, 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Aspirin, 💊 Clopidogrel, 💊 tPA, 💊 4-Factor PCC, 💊 Vitamin K, 💊 Vancomycin

307. PRES (Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome)

Hypertensive Emergency Neurologic Complication
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Tetrad: Headache, altered mental status, seizures, visual disturbances

Visual Symptoms: Cortical blindness, visual field deficits, blurred vision (posterior circulation involvement)

Seizures: Occur in 60-75% of cases; may be presenting symptom

Risk Factors/Triggers:

  • Hypertension: Hypertensive emergency most common; but 20-30% have normal BP!
  • Preeclampsia/Eclampsia: Leading cause in pregnancy
  • Immunosuppressants: Cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus
  • Chemotherapy: Cisplatin, bevacizumab, tyrosine kinase inhibitors
  • Renal disease: Uremia, dialysis
  • Autoimmune: SLE, thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS)
  • Sepsis, organ transplantation

Pathophysiology: Endothelial dysfunction → failure of cerebral autoregulation → vasogenic edema (predominantly posterior circulation)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

MRI Brain (Diagnostic Standard):

  • Classic: Bilateral symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in parietal-occipital white matter
  • Other locations: Frontal, temporal, brainstem, cerebellum (not limited to posterior)
  • DWI: Usually normal or shows facilitated diffusion (vasogenic, not cytotoxic edema)
  • Important: Restricted diffusion = infarction = irreversible damage

CT Head: May show hypodensities but less sensitive than MRI

Labs: BMP, LFTs, CBC, UA, drug levels (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), uric acid (preeclampsia)

Differential: CVA/stroke, venous sinus thrombosis, encephalitis, metabolic encephalopathy

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Blood Pressure Control:

  • Goal: Reduce MAP by 20-25% over first few hours
  • IV agents: Nicardipine, labetalol, clevidipine
  • Eclampsia: Magnesium sulfate + hydralazine or labetalol + delivery
  • Avoid: Precipitous BP drops (can cause watershed infarcts)

2. Seizure Management:

  • Benzodiazepines for acute seizures
  • Levetiracetam, phenytoin, or lacosamide for seizure prophylaxis
  • AEDs often not needed long-term once PRES resolves

3. Remove/Treat Underlying Cause:

  • Discontinue or reduce offending immunosuppressant
  • Deliver fetus in eclampsia
  • Treat underlying infection, autoimmune condition

4. Supportive Care:

  • ICU monitoring for severe cases
  • Manage increased ICP if present

Prognosis: Generally reversible with treatment within days to weeks; MRI normalizes. Permanent deficits if cytotoxic edema/infarction develops

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Not always posterior: Can involve frontal lobes, brainstem — "PRES" is a misnomer
  • Not always hypertensive: 20-30% have normal BP at presentation
  • DWI is key: Restricted diffusion = cytotoxic edema = worse prognosis (infarct, not reversible)
  • Think immunosuppressants: Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) are common culprits
  • Eclampsia is PRES: Classic PRES trigger — treat with magnesium + delivery
  • Can recur: Especially if underlying condition not addressed
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Nicardipine, 💊 Labetalol, 💊 Magnesium
↑ Back to Table of Contents

308. OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME (ODS)

Central Pontine Myelinolysis (CPM) • Sodium Correction Injury
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Timeline: Symptoms develop 2-6 days AFTER overly rapid sodium correction

Biphasic Course:

  • Phase 1: Initial improvement as hyponatremia corrects
  • Phase 2 (day 2-6): Neurologic deterioration — dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis

Central Pontine Myelinolysis:

  • Spastic quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy (dysarthria, dysphagia)
  • "Locked-in syndrome": Severe cases — awake but unable to move except eye movements

Extrapontine Myelinolysis (EPM): Movement disorders, ataxia, cognitive changes (basal ganglia, thalamus involvement)

High-Risk Patients:

  • Chronic alcoholism, malnutrition
  • Liver transplantation
  • Hypokalemia (concurrent)
  • Severely hyponatremic (<105 mEq/L) or chronic hyponatremia (>48h)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

MRI Brain (Diagnostic Standard):

  • Classic "trident" or "bat wing": T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in central pons, sparing periphery
  • EPM: Symmetric lesions in basal ganglia, thalami, cerebral white matter
  • Timing: MRI may be NORMAL in first 2 weeks; repeat if clinical suspicion high
  • DWI may show early changes before T2/FLAIR

Review Sodium Correction: Calculate rate of sodium rise — was it too fast?

Safe Correction Rate: ≤10 mEq/L in first 24h, ≤18 mEq/L in first 48h (some recommend ≤8 mEq/L in high-risk patients)

PREVENTION & TREATMENT

PREVENTION IS KEY:

  • Monitor sodium frequently during correction (q2-4h)
  • Goal: Raise sodium ≤10 mEq/L in 24 hours, ≤8 mEq/L in high-risk patients
  • If overcorrecting: D5W infusion ± DDAVP to re-lower sodium

Rescue Therapy (If Overcorrection Detected):

  • D5W: 3 mL/kg/hr to lower sodium back
  • DDAVP: 2-4 mcg IV/SQ to prevent free water excretion
  • Target: Re-lower sodium to stay within safe correction limits

Treatment of Established ODS:

  • No proven specific treatment
  • Supportive care, rehabilitation
  • Plasmapheresis: Anecdotal reports, not proven
  • Steroids: Sometimes used, no clear evidence

Prognosis:

  • Previously considered uniformly fatal
  • Now: Many patients improve over weeks to months with supportive care
  • Full recovery possible in some; others have permanent deficits
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Prevention, prevention, prevention: ODS is almost entirely iatrogenic. Monitor sodium closely during correction
  • 10 in 24, 18 in 48: Safe sodium correction limits. Use 8 in 24 for high-risk patients
  • Biphasic course is classic: Initial improvement then deterioration days later
  • MRI may be negative early: Changes may not appear for 2 weeks. Repeat MRI if suspicious
  • DDAVP rescue: If correcting too fast, give DDAVP + D5W to re-lower sodium
  • Not always fatal: With supportive care, many patients have meaningful recovery
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids
↑ Back to Table of Contents

309. IIH (Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension)

Pseudotumor Cerebri • Elevated ICP Without Mass
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Patient: Obese woman of childbearing age with headache and papilledema

Headache: Daily, generalized or retro-orbital, worse with Valsalva, may wake from sleep, positional component

Visual Symptoms:

  • Transient visual obscurations: Brief (seconds) episodes of vision loss, often with position changes
  • Diplopia: CN VI palsy (false localizing sign from elevated ICP)
  • Permanent vision loss: Can occur without treatment — optic nerve damage

Other Symptoms: Pulsatile tinnitus (whooshing in ears), neck/back pain, nausea

Papilledema: Bilateral in >95% — MUST examine fundi

Risk Factors:

  • Obesity: 90%+ of patients; weight gain often precedes symptoms
  • Female sex, reproductive age
  • Medications: Vitamin A, tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline), growth hormone, lithium
DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (Modified Dandy)

Required:

  • Signs/symptoms of elevated ICP (headache, papilledema, CN VI palsy)
  • Elevated opening pressure on LP: >250 mm H₂O (lateral decubitus)
  • Normal CSF composition
  • No other cause identified (normal neuroimaging, no mass, no venous thrombosis)

MRI Brain + MRV:

  • Rule out mass, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis
  • IIH findings: Empty sella, flattened posterior globes, optic nerve sheath distension, transverse sinus stenosis

Lumbar Puncture:

  • Opening pressure >250 mm H₂O (some use >200 with symptoms)
  • Normal CSF protein, glucose, cell count
  • Diagnostic AND therapeutic (temporary symptom relief)

Visual Assessment: Formal visual field testing (Humphrey), OCT — baseline and serial monitoring

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Weight Loss:

  • Most effective long-term treatment
  • 5-10% weight loss often produces significant improvement
  • Consider bariatric surgery referral for severe cases

2. Acetazolamide (First-Line Medical Therapy):

  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — decreases CSF production
  • Dose: Start 500 mg BID, titrate to 1-2 g/day (max 4 g/day)
  • Side effects: Paresthesias, dysgeusia, metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis

3. Topiramate (Alternative):

  • Weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor + promotes weight loss
  • May be preferred if weight loss desired

4. Stop Offending Medications: Vitamin A, tetracyclines, growth hormone

5. Surgical Options (Vision-Threatening or Refractory):

  • Optic nerve sheath fenestration: Directly protects optic nerve
  • CSF shunting: Ventriculoperitoneal or lumboperitoneal shunt
  • Venous sinus stenting: If significant transverse sinus stenosis

Monitoring: Serial visual field testing and OCT — vision loss can be permanent!

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Check the fundi: Papilledema is the key finding — don't miss it!
  • Vision loss is real: Despite "benign" ICP elevation, permanent optic nerve damage occurs. Monitor closely
  • Transient visual obscurations: Classic symptom — brief blackouts of vision with position change
  • Weight loss works: Even 5-10% weight loss can resolve symptoms
  • Rule out venous thrombosis: MRV is essential — cerebral venous thrombosis mimics IIH
  • LP is diagnostic AND therapeutic: Provides immediate (temporary) relief
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Acetazolamide, 💊 Furosemide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 CSF Analysis, 🔬 Elevated TSH, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

310. MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE (MOH)

Rebound Headache • Analgesic Overuse
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Chronic daily headache (≥15 days/month) in patient with pre-existing headache disorder who overuses acute medications

Pattern: Worsening headache frequency → increased medication use → more headaches (vicious cycle)

Morning headache: Often present upon waking (medication wearing off)

Medication Thresholds for Overuse:

  • Simple analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs): ≥15 days/month
  • Triptans: ≥10 days/month
  • Opioids: ≥10 days/month
  • Combination analgesics (butalbital-containing): ≥10 days/month
  • Ergots: ≥10 days/month

Risk Factors:

  • Pre-existing migraine or tension-type headache
  • History of anxiety, depression
  • Escalating use of acute medications
DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (ICHD-3)

Criteria:

  • Headache present ≥15 days/month
  • Pre-existing headache disorder
  • Regular overuse of acute headache medication for >3 months
  • Headache not better accounted for by another diagnosis

Highest Risk Medications:

  • Opioids: Highest risk of MOH, hardest to withdraw
  • Butalbital combinations: Very high risk
  • Triptans: Moderate risk (but may be easier to withdraw)
  • NSAIDs/Acetaminophen: Lower risk but still occurs
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Education:

  • Explain the cycle of medication overuse and rebound
  • Set expectations: Initial worsening (1-2 weeks) before improvement
  • Most patients improve within 2 months of withdrawal

2. Withdrawal Approaches:

  • Abrupt withdrawal: Preferred for most (triptans, NSAIDs, acetaminophen)
  • Gradual taper: Required for opioids, butalbital (withdrawal symptoms)
  • Inpatient detox: Consider for severe cases, opioid dependence, failed outpatient attempts

3. Bridge Therapy (During Withdrawal):

  • NSAIDs (scheduled): Naproxen 500 mg BID for 1-2 weeks (if not overusing NSAIDs)
  • Steroids: Prednisone 60-80 mg × 2-5 days taper (limited evidence)
  • Anti-emetics: PRN for nausea
  • DHE infusion: Consider for inpatient protocol

4. Start Preventive Therapy:

  • Begin during or shortly after withdrawal
  • Options: Topiramate, amitriptyline, propranolol, CGRP monoclonal antibodies
  • CGRP antagonists may be effective even before withdrawal complete

5. Limit Future Acute Medication Use:

  • Restrict acute medications to ≤2 days/week
  • Keep headache diary
  • Avoid butalbital and opioids for primary headaches
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Ask about medication use: Many patients don't recognize overuse as the problem
  • Opioids are worst: Highest risk of MOH, hardest to withdraw, least effective for headache
  • Warn about worsening: First 1-2 weeks after withdrawal are usually worse before better
  • ≤2 days/week rule: After recovery, acute medications should be used ≤2 days/week to prevent recurrence
  • Preventive therapy is key: Must address underlying headache disorder, not just stop the overused medication
  • CGRP antibodies help: Newer agents (erenumab, fremanezumab) effective for MOH prevention
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Ketorolac, 💊 Prednisone

311. HLH (Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis)

Cytokine Storm Syndrome • Life-Threatening Hyperinflammation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic: Persistent fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, multi-organ dysfunction

Systemic Inflammation: Often mimics sepsis or severe infection with rapid deterioration

Key Features:

  • Fever: Prolonged, high-grade, unresponsive to antibiotics
  • Hepatosplenomegaly: Present in >90%
  • Cytopenias: ≥2 cell lines affected (anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia)
  • CNS involvement: Altered mental status, seizures (30-50%)
  • Coagulopathy: DIC-like picture, hypofibrinogenemia

Triggers (Secondary HLH in Adults):

  • Infections: EBV (most common), CMV, HIV, other viruses; bacterial, fungal
  • Malignancy: Lymphoma (especially T-cell, NK-cell), leukemia
  • Autoimmune: SLE, Adult-onset Still's disease, sJIA → "MAS" (macrophage activation syndrome)
  • Medications: Immunosuppressants, checkpoint inhibitors
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

HLH-2004 Criteria (≥5 of 8):

  • Fever ≥38.5°C
  • Splenomegaly
  • Cytopenias (≥2 lines): Hgb <9, Plt <100K, ANC <1K
  • Hypertriglyceridemia ≥265 mg/dL OR hypofibrinogenemia <150 mg/dL
  • Hemophagocytosis in bone marrow, spleen, or lymph nodes
  • Low/absent NK-cell activity
  • Ferritin ≥500 ng/mL (often >10,000 — very elevated ferritin is clue!)
  • Elevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) ≥2,400 U/mL

H-Score Calculator: Clinical scoring system; score >169 = 93% probability of HLH

Key Labs:

  • Ferritin: Often >10,000 (very high = think HLH); ferritin >500 is criterion
  • Triglycerides: Elevated
  • Fibrinogen: Low (unusual in other inflammatory states)
  • LDH: Very elevated
  • Soluble IL-2 receptor: Markedly elevated
  • D-dimer: Elevated

Bone Marrow Biopsy: May show hemophagocytosis, but absence doesn't rule out HLH

Workup for Trigger: EBV/CMV viral loads, HIV, CT for lymphoma, PET scan, autoimmune serologies

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Urgency: HLH is rapidly fatal without treatment — mortality >50% untreated. Do not wait for all criteria

1. Treat Underlying Trigger:

  • Treat infection (antivirals for EBV/CMV)
  • Chemotherapy for malignancy-associated HLH
  • Discontinue offending medications

2. Immunosuppression (HLH-94/2004 Protocol):

  • Dexamethasone: 10 mg/m² (potent CNS penetration)
  • Etoposide: 150 mg/m² twice weekly initially
  • Cyclosporine A: Added at week 9 or earlier
  • Intrathecal methotrexate + hydrocortisone: If CNS involvement

3. Alternative/Newer Therapies:

  • Anakinra: IL-1 receptor antagonist — especially for MAS/autoimmune HLH
  • Ruxolitinib: JAK inhibitor — increasing use for refractory HLH
  • Emapalumab: Anti-interferon-gamma — FDA approved for primary HLH

4. Supportive Care:

  • ICU monitoring
  • Transfusion support, coagulopathy management
  • IVIG sometimes used (especially if infection-triggered)

5. Consider Allogeneic HSCT: For primary/familial HLH or refractory cases

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Sky-high ferritin: Ferritin >10,000 is highly specific for HLH. Think HLH when ferritin very elevated
  • Low fibrinogen paradox: Inflammatory state with LOW fibrinogen is unusual — suggests HLH or DIC
  • Don't wait for hemophagocytosis: Bone marrow hemophagocytosis absent in 20-30% — treat based on clinical picture
  • Find the trigger: EBV and lymphoma are common in adults — PET scan, viral PCRs
  • HLH vs sepsis: Both cause cytopenias, organ failure; HLH has very high ferritin, low fibrinogen, splenomegaly
  • Rapid treatment: HLH is a medical emergency — mortality is high without immunosuppression
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Dexamethasone, 💊 Mycophenolate
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Ferritin, 🔬 Thrombocytopenia, 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 LDH, 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated PT/INR

312. IRON DEFICIENCY ANEMIA

Most Common Anemia Worldwide • GI Evaluation Required
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Symptoms: Fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, headache, dizziness

Specific to Iron Deficiency:

  • Pica: Craving non-food items (ice — pagophagia, dirt, starch)
  • Restless legs syndrome
  • Koilonychia: Spoon-shaped nails (late finding)
  • Angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • Plummer-Vinson syndrome: Esophageal web + IDA + dysphagia (rare)

Causes by Population:

  • Premenopausal women: Menstrual blood loss (most common)
  • Men and postmenopausal women: GI blood loss until proven otherwise
  • Dietary: Vegans, restrictive diets (less common in adults)
  • Malabsorption: Celiac disease, gastric bypass, H. pylori, PPI use
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

CBC: Microcytic (low MCV), hypochromic anemia; elevated RDW

Iron Studies:

  • Serum iron: Low
  • Ferritin: Low (<30 ng/mL diagnostic; <15 very specific)
  • TIBC: Elevated (>400 mcg/dL)
  • Transferrin saturation: Low (<20%)

Ferritin Interpretation:

  • Ferritin <15: Diagnostic for IDA
  • Ferritin 15-30: Probable IDA
  • Ferritin >100: IDA unlikely (but can occur with inflammation)
  • Note: Ferritin is acute phase reactant — can be "normal" in IDA + inflammation

Peripheral Smear: Microcytic, hypochromic RBCs, pencil cells, target cells

Reticulocyte Count: Inappropriately low for degree of anemia (inadequate response)

GI EVALUATION (Men and Postmenopausal Women):

  • Colonoscopy: Evaluate for colon cancer, polyps, angiodysplasia
  • EGD: Evaluate for gastric/esophageal pathology, H. pylori
  • Celiac serologies: TTG-IgA (malabsorption)
  • Consider capsule endoscopy: If upper and lower endoscopy negative (small bowel evaluation)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Oral Iron (First-Line for Mild-Moderate):

  • Ferrous sulfate: 325 mg (65 mg elemental iron) daily to TID
  • Every-other-day dosing: May improve absorption and tolerability
  • Take on empty stomach with vitamin C (enhances absorption)
  • Avoid: Antacids, PPIs, calcium, tea, coffee (inhibit absorption)
  • Duration: Continue 3-6 months after Hgb normalizes to replete stores

2. IV Iron (Indications):

  • Oral iron intolerance or non-adherence
  • Malabsorption (celiac, gastric bypass, IBD)
  • Ongoing blood loss exceeding oral replacement
  • CKD on dialysis or ESA therapy
  • Need for rapid repletion (severe symptomatic anemia, preoperative)

IV Iron Formulations:

  • Iron sucrose: 200-300 mg per infusion, well tolerated
  • Ferric carboxymaltose (Injectafer): 750 mg × 2 doses (can give full repletion in 2 visits). FDA boxed warning (September 2026) for symptomatic hypophosphatemia (weakness, fatigue, confusion, arrhythmias; osteomalacia and fractures if chronic). Correct low phosphate before dosing; check phosphate in patients at risk and before any repeat course within 3 months; consider stopping permanently for severe symptomatic or persistent hypophosphatemia (FDA)
  • Ferric derisomaltose (Monoferric): Single 1000 mg dose possible
  • Iron dextran: Test dose required, higher anaphylaxis risk

3. Treat Underlying Cause:

  • Treat H. pylori if positive
  • Gluten-free diet for celiac disease
  • Manage menorrhagia (hormonal therapy, GYN evaluation)
  • Surgical intervention for GI malignancy

Response Monitoring:

  • Reticulocyte count rises in 3-5 days
  • Hemoglobin rises 1-2 g/dL per month
  • Recheck ferritin at 3 months (goal >100 for adequate stores)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • IDA in men = GI workup: Colon cancer until proven otherwise. Don't just give iron without investigating
  • Ferritin <30: Diagnostic for IDA in non-inflammatory states
  • Every-other-day dosing: Better absorbed than daily (hepcidin physiology)
  • Pica (especially ice craving): Highly specific for iron deficiency
  • Think celiac: Unexplained IDA, especially with diarrhea or family history — check TTG-IgA
  • IV iron is underused: Safe, effective, and faster than oral. Use it when indicated
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Iron, 💊 Folic Acid
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Anemia, 🔬 Low MCV, 🔬 Low Ferritin, 🔬 Low Transferrin Saturation, 🔬 Elevated TIBC

313. PARANEOPLASTIC SYNDROMES

Remote Effects of Malignancy • Not Direct Tumor Invasion
OVERVIEW

Definition: Symptoms caused by tumor-secreted substances or immune cross-reactivity, NOT direct tumor invasion or metastasis

Importance: May be presenting symptom of occult malignancy; can precede cancer diagnosis by months to years

Categories: Endocrine, neurologic, hematologic, dermatologic, rheumatologic

ENDOCRINE PARANEOPLASTIC SYNDROMES

SIADH (Hyponatremia):

  • Cancer: Small cell lung cancer (most common), head/neck cancers
  • Mechanism: Ectopic ADH production
  • Treatment: Fluid restriction, treat underlying cancer

Hypercalcemia of Malignancy:

  • PTHrP: Squamous cell carcinomas (lung, head/neck, renal)
  • 1,25-vitamin D: Lymphoma
  • Osteolytic metastases: Breast cancer, myeloma
  • Treatment: IV fluids, bisphosphonates, denosumab, calcitonin

Cushing Syndrome (Ectopic ACTH):

  • Cancer: Small cell lung cancer, carcinoid tumors, medullary thyroid
  • Features: Hypokalemia, hypertension, hyperglycemia (often without classic cushingoid features due to rapid onset)

Hypoglycemia (Non-islet Cell Tumor):

  • Cancer: Large mesenchymal tumors, hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Mechanism: IGF-2 secretion
NEUROLOGIC PARANEOPLASTIC SYNDROMES

Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS):

  • Cancer: Small cell lung cancer (60%)
  • Antibody: Anti-VGCC (voltage-gated calcium channel)
  • Features: Proximal weakness that IMPROVES with exercise, autonomic dysfunction, hyporeflexia
  • Diagnosis: EMG shows incremental response, anti-VGCC antibodies

Paraneoplastic Cerebellar Degeneration:

  • Cancer: Ovarian, breast, SCLC, Hodgkin lymphoma
  • Antibodies: Anti-Yo (ovarian/breast), Anti-Hu (SCLC)
  • Features: Rapidly progressive ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus

Limbic Encephalitis:

  • Cancer: SCLC, testicular (seminoma), thymoma
  • Antibodies: Anti-Hu, Anti-NMDAR, Anti-LGI1
  • Features: Memory loss, seizures, psychiatric symptoms

Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis:

  • Cancer: Ovarian teratoma (young women)
  • Features: Psychiatric symptoms → seizures → movement disorders → autonomic instability
  • Treatment: Tumor removal, immunotherapy (IVIG, steroids, rituximab)
OTHER PARANEOPLASTIC SYNDROMES

Dermatologic:

  • Acanthosis nigricans (malignant): GI adenocarcinomas (especially gastric)
  • Dermatomyositis: Various solid tumors (ovarian, lung, GI, breast)
  • Sweet syndrome: AML, MDS
  • Erythema gyratum repens: Lung, breast, GI cancers
  • Leser-Trélat sign: Explosive seborrheic keratoses — GI malignancy

Hematologic:

  • Polycythemia: Renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma (EPO production)
  • Thrombocytosis: Many solid tumors
  • Trousseau syndrome: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis — pancreatic, lung cancer

Rheumatologic:

  • Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy: Lung cancer — digital clubbing, periostitis
  • Polymyalgia-like syndrome: Various malignancies
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Think cancer: Unexplained hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, or neurologic syndrome → search for malignancy
  • SCLC is the "paraneoplastic cancer": Associated with SIADH, Cushing, LEMS, many neurologic syndromes
  • LEMS vs Myasthenia: LEMS improves with exercise, MG worsens. Check for SCLC in LEMS
  • Dermatomyositis: Cancer screening essential — CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, age-appropriate screening, consider PET
  • Anti-NMDAR encephalitis: Young woman with psychiatric symptoms → check for ovarian teratoma
  • Treatment is cancer treatment: Paraneoplastic syndromes often improve with treatment of underlying malignancy
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 IVIG
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 LDH, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Anemia
