315. CARCINOID SYNDROME

Neuroendocrine Tumor Hormone Excess • Serotonin-Mediated
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: episodic flushing and diarrhea from serotonin, histamine, or tachykinins reaching the systemic circulation, most often from small intestine or appendix NETs; occurs in about 8-28% of NETs (NCCN NET 2026)

Classic Triad: Flushing, diarrhea, wheezing (but full triad uncommon; Practical)

Symptoms:

  • Flushing: Episodic, dry (vs sweating), face/neck, triggered by alcohol, stress, tyramine-rich foods (Practical)
  • Diarrhea: Secretory, watery, can be severe (Practical). Rule out other causes first: pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (including from long-term SSA use), bile acid diarrhea after ileocecectomy or cholecystectomy, short bowel, mesenteric ischemia (ASCO 2025 1.1; NCCN NET 2026)
  • Bronchospasm: Wheezing, dyspnea (Practical)
  • Carcinoid heart disease (50-66% of patients with carcinoid syndrome): tricuspid regurgitation and/or pulmonary stenosis (NCCN NET 2026)

Key Point: intestinal NET products are destroyed by liver enzymes in the portal circulation, so the syndrome usually requires liver metastases or, rarely, retroperitoneal disease (NCCN NET 2026)

  • Bronchial/ovarian NETs: can cause the syndrome without liver metastases (drain directly to the systemic circulation) (Practical)

Carcinoid Crisis:

  • Life-threatening massive release of vasoactive substances, often triggered by tumor manipulation or anesthesia; typically hypotension, diarrhea, and blood pressure fluctuation (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Also with other invasive procedures such as TAE or TACE (ASCO 2025); flushing, bronchospasm, and arrhythmias may occur (Practical)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Biochemical Testing:

  • 24-hour urine or plasma 5-HIAA: serotonin metabolite; routine evaluation in carcinoid syndrome (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Chromogranin A: not specific; PPIs, other drugs, some medical conditions, and certain foods cause false elevations (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Serum serotonin: Less commonly used (Practical)

Avoid for 48 hours before and during 5-HIAA testing: avocados, bananas, cantaloupe, eggplant, pineapples, plums, tomatoes, hickory nuts/pecans, plantains, kiwi, dates, grapefruit, honeydew, walnuts. Medications that can raise 5-HIAA: acetaminophen, ephedrine, diazepam, nicotine, glyceryl guaiacolate (guaifenesin, in some cough medicines), phenobarbital (NCCN NET 2026)

Localization:

  • Multiphase CT or MRI with contrast: primary tumor and liver metastases (NCCN NET 2026)
  • SSTR-PET/CT or PET/MRI (Ga-68 DOTATATE, Cu-64 DOTATATE, Ga-68 DOTATOC): recommended over In-111 octreotide scintigraphy (Octreoscan) by the 2018 Appropriate Use Criteria (NCCN NET 2026)

Cardiac Evaluation:

  • Baseline echocardiogram in carcinoid syndrome, assessing the valves (especially tricuspid and pulmonary) and right heart size and function (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Repeat without carcinoid heart disease: every 1-3 years or as indicated (NCCN NET 2026); every 1-2 years, with a change in clinical status, or with a rising BNP (ASCO 2025 4.2). With established disease: at least yearly (NCCN NET 2026; ASCO 2025 4.7)
  • BNP is higher in carcinoid heart disease; check at baseline and follow-up when symptoms suggest it (ASCO 2025)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Somatostatin Analogs (First-Line for Symptoms; ASCO 2025 1.2, strong):

  • Octreotide LAR 20-30 mg IM every 4 weeks, or lanreotide 120 mg SC every 4 weeks; dose and frequency may be increased, and higher doses have been shown to be safe (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Octreotide LAR reaches therapeutic levels 10-14 days after injection; overlap short-acting SC octreotide early (NCCN NET 2026; ASCO 2025). Breakthrough symptoms from poor absorption of IM octreotide LAR (body habitus): SC lanreotide may work better (ASCO 2025)
  • Breakthrough symptoms: octreotide 100-250 mcg SC every 8 hours as needed (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Also antiproliferative (PROMID, CLARINET) (NANETS 2017)
  • Resectable liver metastases: discuss surgery first or with SSAs (ASCO 2025 1.3)

2. Carcinoid Crisis (sources disagree on prophylaxis):

  • Treatment: vasopressors (e.g., vasopressin or phenylephrine) for hypotension, antihypertensives for hypertension, beta blockers for tachycardia, with octreotide as an adjunct (ASCO 2025 3.1, strong). Octreotide must not delay vasopressors and fluids; vasopressors can be used for severe or prolonged hypotension (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Prophylaxis: ASCO 2025: an SSA may be recommended before surgery or invasive procedures, especially with functional symptoms (conditional, very low-quality evidence). NCCN NET 2026: prophylactic octreotide is likely ineffective and its routine use has been questioned, although it can be used. Procedures only in centers with experienced anesthesiologists (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Dosing if used (expert statement, not a guideline): IV octreotide 50-100 mcg/h starting 12 h before surgery, continued during and after; for crisis, 100-200 mcg IV bolus and up to 200 mcg/h (JACC 2017 expert statement, via OpenEvidence)
  • Morphine and succinylcholine are traditionally avoided (Practical)

3. Managing Refractory Symptoms (ASCO 2025; NCCN NET 2026):

  • Rule out non-carcinoid diarrhea first: pancreatic enzymes for exocrine insufficiency; bile acid binders (e.g., cholestyramine) for bile acid diarrhea (ASCO 2025; NCCN NET 2026)
  • SSA escalation: octreotide LAR 30 mg every 3 or 2 weeks, or 40-60 mg every 4 weeks; lanreotide 120 mg every 2-3 weeks; or add short-acting SC octreotide (ASCO 2025 2.1, conditional). Symptoms late in each cycle: dose every 3 weeks (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Telotristat ethyl 250 mg orally three times daily with food, added to the SSA (continue the SSA), for diarrhea not controlled by an SSA; give short-acting octreotide at least 30 minutes after telotristat; stop if severe constipation develops (US label; ASCO 2025 2.3, conditional). Benefit may take several weeks (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Loperamide or diphenoxylate (ASCO 2025 2.2); ondansetron for refractory diarrhea (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Liver-directed therapy (hepatic resection, TAE, TACE, bland embolization) for uncontrolled syndrome (ASCO 2025 2.5, strong); whole-liver radioembolization: radioembolization-induced chronic hepatic toxicity in 10-20% of patients surviving >2 years (ASCO 2025 2.6)
  • PRRT for persistent refractory symptoms after the options above; continue SSAs after PRRT (ASCO 2025 2.7, conditional)
  • Everolimus is not a preferred option for symptom control (ASCO 2025 2.4; NCCN NET 2026)

4. Tumor-Directed Therapy (NCCN NET 2026):

  • Surgery: Resection of primary and/or metastases when feasible (Practical; resectable liver metastases: ASCO 2025 1.3)
  • PRRT: lutetium Lu 177 dotatate for SSTR-positive tumors progressing on an SSA (category 1 for progressive midgut tumors)
  • GI tract NETs: everolimus; cabozantinib after everolimus or Lu 177 dotatate; above-label SSA doses. Sunitinib is for pancreatic NETs only
  • Liver-directed: TAE, TACE, radioembolization, thermal ablation for limited lesions (ASCO 2025)

5. Carcinoid Heart Disease (ASCO 2025 4.3-4.8):

  • Cardiology referral at the first sign of valve involvement; multidisciplinary care at a NET center
  • Right heart failure: loop and/or thiazide diuretics, aldosterone antagonist, cautious fluid and salt restriction (may reduce cardiac output)
  • Valve surgery for severe regurgitation with symptoms or RV dysfunction; bioprosthetic valves preferred; close a PFO at surgery
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Liver mets = syndrome: intestinal NET products are cleared in the portal circulation, so the syndrome usually needs liver metastases (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Flushing is dry: Unlike pheochromocytoma (sweating), carcinoid flushing is typically dry (Practical)
  • Right heart involvement: tricuspid regurgitation and/or pulmonary stenosis in 50-66% of patients with carcinoid syndrome (NCCN NET 2026)
  • Crisis is treated with fluids and vasopressors; octreotide is an adjunct, and prophylaxis is debated (ASCO 2025; NCCN NET 2026)
  • 5-HIAA (24-h urine or plasma): avoid the listed foods and drugs for 48 h (NCCN NET 2026)
  • PRRT: lutetium Lu 177 dotatate improved PFS in NETTER-1, but the final analysis showed no significant overall survival improvement (NCCN NET 2026)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Octreotide, 💊 Loperamide, 💊 Ondansetron, 💊 Vasopressin, 💊 Phenylephrine

316. HEMOTHORAX

Blood in Pleural Space • Trauma vs Spontaneous
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Symptoms: Chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypotension (if massive)

Physical Exam: Decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, tracheal deviation (massive)

Size and Initial Management (trauma; WSES-AAST 2025):

  • Small (<300 mL), stable: May be observed, with a repeat CXR for up to 24 h (LoE low, GoR moderate)
  • ≥500 mL, stable: Drain, ideally within 72 h (LoE low, GoR moderate). For 300-500 mL there is no guideline threshold; EAST 2020 made no recommendation for or against routine drainage of hemothorax under 500 mL
  • Unstable: Drain with a large-bore tube regardless of size (LoE low, GoR moderate)
  • Massive: Rapid loss of more than 1500 mL into the chest; early recognition, decompression, and blood replacement

Etiology:

  • Traumatic (most common): Blunt or penetrating chest trauma, rib fractures
  • Iatrogenic: Central line placement, thoracentesis, chest tube, cardiac surgery
  • Spontaneous:
    • Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOACs)
    • Malignancy (primary or metastatic)
    • Pulmonary embolism with infarction
    • Aortic dissection/rupture
    • Arteriovenous malformation
    • Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

CXR: Detects large hemothorax (WSES-AAST 2025); supine films miss small collections. Blunting of the costophrenic angle needs roughly 200-300 mL upright (Practical)

Ultrasound (E-FAST): More sensitive and faster than CXR for traumatic hemothorax (97.5% vs 92.5%; 1.3 vs 14.2 min) (WSES-AAST 2025)

CT Chest (stable patients): Best test for intrathoracic bleeding, residual hemothorax, and empyema; fluid blood 30-45 HU, clot 45-70 HU (WSES-AAST 2025)

Pleural Fluid Analysis:

  • Hematocrit: Pleural fluid Hct >50% of blood Hct supports hemothorax (BTS 2023)
  • Bloody effusion with lower Hct: malignancy, PE, parapneumonic (Practical)

Labs: CBC (trending Hgb), coagulation studies, type & screen

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Resuscitation:

  • Large-bore IV access, crystalloid resuscitation
  • Blood transfusion as needed
  • Correct coagulopathy; reverse anticoagulants per Condition 116
  • Traumatic hemorrhage: Massive transfusion protocol and TXA (WSES-AAST 2025); TXA within 3 h of injury, dose in the drug guide

2. Chest Tube (WSES-AAST 2025 unless stated):

  • Treatment of choice when drainage is needed (LoE moderate, GoR strong)
  • Size, unstable or massive: Large-bore. WSES-AAST: 28-40 Fr, no difference above 32 Fr. BTS 2023: 28 Fr balances flow and blockage; larger than 32 Fr unlikely to be needed
  • Size, stable: Guidelines disagree. EAST 2020 conditionally recommends a 14 Fr pigtail (very low-quality evidence); WSES-AAST 2025 advises 28-40 Fr because smaller tubes can leave residual hemothorax
  • Site: Lateral, 4th-6th intercostal space, anterior or mid-axillary line. Avoid a posterior approach, where the intercostal neurovascular bundle is less protected (BTS 2023, pleural procedures)
  • Suction: No difference vs no suction in uncomplicated traumatic hemothorax; low-pressure suction may shorten tube duration and stay
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: Not for blunt trauma; penetrating injury may benefit; indicated when draining retained hemothorax and for operative management
  • Stable patient with prior thoracic surgery or chronic lung disease: image-guided catheter drainage to avoid adhesions

3. Surgery and Retained Hemothorax:

  • Operate (WSES-AAST 2025, GoR strong): Hemodynamic instability from thoracic bleeding, or chest tube output >1500 mL in 24 h or >200 mL/h for 3 consecutive hours, with no other bleeding source. Output alone can mislead; monitor closely. Classic teaching also operates for >1500 mL on insertion (Practical)
  • Stable, persistent bleeding: Consider endovascular control (WSES-AAST 2025)
  • Retained hemothorax: VATS rather than intrapleural thrombolytics (EAST 2020, conditional), performed early, within 4 days (EAST 2020). In trauma, thrombolytics are linked to slower resolution, higher cost, and more complications (WSES-AAST 2025)
  • Spontaneous hemopneumothorax: Surgical opinion (BTS 2023)

4. Complications:

  • Retained hemothorax: Leads to empyema, fibrothorax; residual blood >300 mL raises empyema risk, so aim for complete evacuation (WSES-AAST 2025)
  • Empyema: Drainage, antibiotics, decortication if needed; see Condition 173
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Operate: Instability, >1500 mL in 24 h, or >200 mL/h for 3 h (WSES-AAST 2025)
  • Tube size: Large-bore if unstable; for stable patients EAST 2020 favors a 14 Fr pigtail and WSES-AAST 2025 favors 28-40 Fr
  • Retained hemothorax: Early VATS (within 4 days) over thrombolytics (EAST 2020)
  • Check pleural Hct: >50% of blood Hct supports hemothorax (BTS 2023)
  • Spontaneous hemothorax: Think anticoagulation, malignancy, aortic pathology
  • Complete evacuation: Residual blood >300 mL raises empyema risk (WSES-AAST 2025)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 TXA
↑ Back to Table of Contents

317. CHYLOTHORAX

Lymphatic Fluid in Pleural Space • Thoracic Duct Injury
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Symptoms: Progressive dyspnea, chest discomfort (typically non-painful)

Course: May accumulate rapidly; significant nutritional and immune consequences

Etiology:

  • Traumatic/Surgical (up to half):
    • Thoracic surgery, especially posterior mediastinum (esophagectomy), lung resection, cardiac surgery
    • Central line placement (especially left subclavian)
    • Blunt/penetrating trauma
  • Non-traumatic:
    • Malignancy: most common non-traumatic cause (Agrawal 2024); lymphoma or metastatic carcinoma (BTS 2023)
    • Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) and other lymphatic disorders
    • Sarcoidosis, tuberculosis
    • Superior vena cava or other central venous obstruction
    • Cirrhosis; chylous ascites crossing the diaphragm
    • Congenital lymphatic abnormalities; idiopathic (about 10%, BTS 2023)

Complications:

  • Malnutrition (loss of proteins, fats, vitamins)
  • Immunodeficiency (loss of T lymphocytes, immunoglobulins)
  • Electrolyte abnormalities
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Pleural Fluid Appearance: Milky, white, or turbid (if patient fasting, may be less milky)

Pleural Fluid Analysis (BTS 2023 unless stated):

  • Triglycerides >110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L): Chylothorax; cholesterol low, no cholesterol crystals, chylomicrons usually present
  • Triglycerides <50 mg/dL: Chylothorax unlikely; 50-110 mg/dL: check lipoprotein electrophoresis for chylomicrons (Practical)
  • Chylomicrons present: Confirms chylothorax (Practical)

Other Fluid Features:

  • Usually lymphocytic: BTS 2023 lists chylothorax among lymphocytic effusions (classic >80% lymphocytes, Practical)
  • Usually exudative by Light's criteria; pH >7.4, glucose similar to serum (Practical)

Imaging (ACR 2024 treatment planning):

  • Lymphangiography (conventional or MR): Usually appropriate before treatment in traumatic and nontraumatic chylothorax; conventional lymphangiography is both diagnostic and therapeutic
  • CT chest (identify mass, lymphadenopathy, duct injury), chest radiograph, MRI, lymphoscintigraphy: may be appropriate
  • Ultrasound: usually not appropriate for treatment planning; non-contrast chest CT: usually not appropriate in nontraumatic chylothorax

DDx for Milky Effusion:

  • Chylothorax: High triglycerides, chylomicrons present
  • Pseudochylothorax: Cholesterol >200 mg/dL (5.18 mmol/L), cholesterol crystals often present, triglycerides low, no chylomicrons; chronic effusions (TB, RA) (BTS 2023)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Initial Management (Agrawal 2024 consensus unless stated):

  • Output: High >500 mL/day, low <500 mL/day; persistent if longer than 2 weeks
  • Diet: High-protein, low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs bypass the lymphatics and are absorbed through the portal vein). Implement in all traumatic and consider in all non-traumatic chylothorax. Medical therapy and diet are usually appropriate initial therapy (ACR 2026)
  • Prolonged restricted diet: Supplement fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids (2-4% of daily calories); deficiencies can appear after 5 days
  • TPN with strict NPO: Consider in high-volume traumatic chylothorax refractory to medical management and definitive interventions
  • Drainage: Hospitalized, recurrent, symptomatic: chest tube, small-bore (14 Fr or smaller). Outpatient low-volume: symptom-guided thoracentesis; indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) in selected patients
  • Drugs: Not routinely used. Octreotide (off-label; the consensus gives no dose) may be considered when chylothorax is refractory to diet and chest tube drainage and definitive intervention is not feasible or has failed. Midodrine, etilefrine, orlistat: case reports and small series only

2. Definitive Intervention (Agrawal 2024; ACR 2026):

  • Post-operative, high-volume: Thoracic duct ligation (TDL) first-line; thoracic duct embolization (TDE) is an alternative case by case. Early re-operation (within 5 days) for high-volume leaks may reduce complications
  • After blunt or penetrating trauma, or persistent low-volume post-operative leak: TDL or TDE by local expertise; TDE if not a surgical candidate or TDL fails
  • Non-traumatic: Definitive treatment when high-volume output continues beyond about 7 days, or low output persists beyond 2 weeks with little expected response to disease-directed therapy. First-line: diagnostic lymphangiogram plus TDE; refer early to an expert center
  • ACR 2026, refractory to medical therapy: TDE and pleurodesis usually appropriate; surgery may be appropriate. Pleurodesis is usually not appropriate as initial therapy
  • Pleurodesis with TDL: Not routine; consider if the leak site is not found at surgery. Talc slurry case by case when not an operative candidate and lymphatic intervention is not feasible
  • Refractory high-volume, symptom control: Pleuroperitoneal or pleurovenous shunt, or IPC. IPC as interim control for low-volume non-traumatic chylothorax expected to respond to disease-directed therapy

3. Treat Underlying Cause:

  • Lymphoma or other malignancy: Disease-directed therapy, with symptom-guided drainage while a response is expected (Agrawal 2024)
  • Spontaneous chylothorax with central venous obstruction: Central vein recanalization or thrombectomy, TDE, or abdominal lymphatic embolization may be appropriate (ACR 2026); anticoagulation for thrombosis (Practical)
  • With chylous ascites: TIPS or portal vein recanalization may be appropriate; TDE and pleurodesis usually not appropriate (ACR 2026)

Nutritional Support:

  • Nutrition consultation for all patients (Agrawal 2024)
  • Monitor albumin, prealbumin, lymphocyte count; replace immunoglobulins if significantly depleted (Practical)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Triglycerides >110 mg/dL: Chylothorax (BTS 2023); check lipids on any milky effusion
  • Post-surgical: Consider chylothorax after esophagectomy, cardiac surgery, or central line placement
  • Malignancy: Most common non-traumatic cause (Agrawal 2024)
  • Diet first: High-protein, low-fat diet with MCTs; octreotide is not routine (Agrawal 2024)
  • Nutritional emergency: Losing chyle = losing protein, fat, lymphocytes. Support aggressively
  • Escalate: Persistent or high-volume leaks need definitive TDL or TDE; lymphangiography plans and can treat (Agrawal 2024; ACR 2024)
  • Pseudochylothorax: High cholesterol and cholesterol crystals, not triglycerides (BTS 2023)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Octreotide
↑ Back to Table of Contents

318. RENAL VEIN THROMBOSIS

Nephrotic Syndrome Complication • Hypercoagulable State
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Acute RVT: Flank pain, hematuria, acute kidney injury, nausea/vomiting

Chronic RVT: Often asymptomatic; may present with pulmonary embolism or progressive renal dysfunction

Risk Factors:

  • Nephrotic syndrome (most common in adults): Especially membranous nephropathy (highest risk)
  • Malignancy (renal cell carcinoma with IVC extension)
  • Trauma, surgery
  • Severe dehydration (neonates)
  • Hypercoagulable states (factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome)
  • Oral contraceptives, pregnancy

Nephrotic Syndrome & Thrombosis:

  • Loss of antithrombin III in urine
  • Increased hepatic synthesis of procoagulant factors
  • Membranous nephropathy has highest thrombosis risk (25-35%)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs:

  • Urinalysis: Hematuria, proteinuria
  • BMP: Acute rise in creatinine (especially bilateral RVT)
  • LDH: Elevated in acute thrombosis
  • D-dimer: Elevated (non-specific)

Imaging:

  • CT venography: Test of choice; filling defect in renal vein, enlarged kidney
  • Doppler ultrasound: Absent or reversed diastolic flow; less sensitive than CT
  • MR venography: Alternative if CT contrast contraindicated

Evaluate for Underlying Cause:

  • 24-hour urine protein if not already known
  • Hypercoagulability workup (if not nephrotic)
  • Consider renal malignancy (CT with contrast)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Anticoagulation (Mainstay of Treatment):

  • Acute: Heparin (UFH or LMWH) initially
  • Transition: Warfarin (target INR 2-3) or DOAC
  • Duration: Minimum 6 months; longer if underlying risk persists (e.g., ongoing nephrotic syndrome)

Thrombolysis/Thrombectomy (Rare Indications):

  • Acute bilateral RVT with severe AKI
  • Extension into IVC
  • Failure of anticoagulation

Treat Underlying Condition:

  • Immunosuppression for nephrotic syndrome (steroids, CNI, rituximab depending on etiology)
  • Surgical resection for renal cell carcinoma

Prophylaxis in Nephrotic Syndrome:

  • Consider prophylactic anticoagulation in membranous nephropathy with albumin <2.5 g/dL
  • Risk-benefit analysis required (bleeding vs thrombosis risk)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Membranous = highest risk: Up to 35% develop VTE. Consider prophylactic anticoagulation if albumin <2.5
  • Often asymptomatic: Many cases discovered incidentally or when PE occurs
  • Think RVT: Nephrotic syndrome + flank pain or unexplained AKI worsening
  • Bilateral = AKI: Unilateral usually compensated; bilateral causes acute kidney injury
  • Anticoagulation duration: Continue as long as nephrotic state persists
  • Antithrombin III loss: Heparin may be less effective in severe nephrotic syndrome (AT-III depleted)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Warfarin, 💊 Apixaban
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Proteinuria, 🔬 Elevated D-dimer, 🔬 Low Antithrombin III
↑ Back to Table of Contents

319. ATHEROEMBOLIC RENAL DISEASE

Cholesterol Crystal Embolization • Post-Procedural AKI
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Scenario: Elderly patient with atherosclerosis develops AKI days to weeks after arterial catheterization, vascular surgery, or anticoagulation initiation

Renal Manifestations:

  • Subacute AKI: Progressive over weeks (contrast nephropathy improves; atheroemboli worsen)
  • May be acute or chronic/stuttering course
  • Proteinuria (usually subnephrotic)
  • Hypertension (new or worsening)

Extra-Renal Manifestations:

  • Skin: Livedo reticularis, blue toe syndrome, digital gangrene, ulceration
  • GI: Abdominal pain, GI bleeding, pancreatitis
  • CNS: Stroke, TIA, confusion (if cerebral emboli)
  • Retinal: Hollenhorst plaques (cholesterol crystals in retinal arteries)

Triggers:

  • Arterial catheterization (cardiac cath, angiography)
  • Vascular surgery
  • Anticoagulation initiation (destabilizes plaque)
  • Thrombolytic therapy
  • Spontaneous (rare)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Labs:

  • Eosinophilia: Present in 60-80% (key clue!)
  • Eosinophiluria: May be present
  • Hypocomplementemia: Low C3, C4 (transient)
  • Elevated ESR/CRP
  • Progressive rise in creatinine over days to weeks

Tissue Diagnosis (Gold Standard):

  • Skin biopsy: If livedo or skin lesions present (least invasive)
  • Renal biopsy: Needle-shaped cholesterol clefts in arterioles (pathognomonic)
  • Biopsy shows empty clefts (cholesterol dissolved during processing)

Clinical Diagnosis Often Made Without Biopsy:

  • Typical clinical setting (recent procedure)
  • Characteristic skin findings
  • Eosinophilia + progressive AKI

Differentiate from Contrast Nephropathy:

  • Contrast: Peaks 2-3 days, improves by 7-10 days
  • Atheroemboli: Progressive worsening over weeks, systemic signs
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

No Specific Treatment — Supportive Care:

  • Supportive renal care; dialysis if needed
  • Blood pressure control
  • Wound care for skin lesions

Controversial Interventions:

  • Statins: May stabilize plaque, possibly beneficial
  • Anticoagulation: Controversial — may trigger more emboli, but needed if other indication (AF, mechanical valve)
  • Steroids: Anecdotal benefit, not proven

Prevention:

  • Minimize arterial manipulation in high-risk patients
  • Radial (vs femoral) access when possible
  • Statin therapy before procedures

Prognosis:

  • Poor: 1-year mortality 60-80% in older series
  • ~30-40% require dialysis
  • Spontaneous improvement can occur in some cases
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Blue toes, livedo, eosinophilia: Classic triad after arterial procedure = atheroemboli
  • Timing distinguishes: Contrast nephropathy improves by day 7-10; atheroemboli worsen progressively
  • Eosinophilia is key: Present in 60-80%; helps differentiate from other causes of AKI
  • Hollenhorst plaques: Fundoscopy may show cholesterol crystals in retinal arteries
  • Anticoagulation paradox: Can actually trigger atheroemboli by destabilizing plaque
  • Poor prognosis: Significant mortality — prevention is key
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Atorvastatin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated CRP, 🔬 Hematuria
↑ Back to Table of Contents

320. CATATONIA

Psychomotor Syndrome • Medical Emergency
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Core Features (DSM-5 — ≥3 required):

  • Stupor: No psychomotor activity, not relating to environment
  • Catalepsy: Passive induction and maintenance of postures
  • Waxy flexibility: Slight resistance to positioning by examiner
  • Mutism: No or minimal verbal response
  • Negativism: Opposition or no response to instructions
  • Posturing: Spontaneous maintenance of posture against gravity
  • Mannerisms: Odd, circumstantial caricature of normal actions
  • Stereotypy: Repetitive, non-goal-directed movements
  • Agitation: Not influenced by external stimuli
  • Grimacing
  • Echolalia: Mimicking another's speech
  • Echopraxia: Mimicking another's movements

Subtypes:

  • Retarded (hypokinetic): Stupor, mutism, immobility — most common
  • Excited (hyperkinetic): Agitation, stereotypies, impulsivity — can be dangerous
  • Malignant catatonia: Fever, autonomic instability, rigidity — medical emergency

Underlying Causes:

  • Psychiatric: Mood disorders (most common), schizophrenia, autism
  • Medical: Encephalitis (anti-NMDAR), seizures, metabolic (hepatic, uremic), drugs/toxins
  • Medication-induced: Neuroleptics (NMS overlap), withdrawal (benzodiazepines)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS):

  • Screening: 14 items (presence/absence)
  • Score ≥2 = likely catatonia
  • Full scale rates severity (23 items)

Lorazepam Challenge Test:

  • Procedure: Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV
  • Positive response: Marked improvement within 5-10 minutes
  • Diagnostic and therapeutic: Response supports catatonia diagnosis

Medical Workup (Rule Out Organic Causes):

  • CBC, CMP, LFTs, TFTs, ammonia
  • Urine drug screen
  • Lumbar puncture (encephalitis, anti-NMDAR)
  • MRI brain, EEG (nonconvulsive status epilepticus)
  • CPK (elevated in malignant catatonia)

Differentiate Catatonia vs NMS:

  • Both have rigidity, fever, autonomic instability
  • NMS: Recent neuroleptic exposure, lead-pipe rigidity
  • Catatonia: May have waxy flexibility, responds to benzodiazepines
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Benzodiazepines (First-Line):

  • Lorazepam: 1-2 mg IV/IM/PO q4-8h, titrate up to 8-24 mg/day
  • Response often rapid (within hours)
  • ~70% respond to benzodiazepines
  • Continue for days to weeks, then taper slowly

2. ECT (Electroconvulsive Therapy):

  • Indications: Benzodiazepine-resistant, malignant catatonia, severe/life-threatening
  • Highly effective (>80% response)
  • Bilateral electrode placement, daily treatments initially
  • Often needed urgently — don't delay if not responding to benzos

3. Supportive Care:

  • DVT prophylaxis (immobility risk)
  • Nutrition: NG tube or TPN if prolonged mutism/refusal
  • Monitor for aspiration, pressure ulcers
  • Hydration, temperature management

4. Stop Offending Agents:

  • Discontinue antipsychotics if NMS suspected
  • Hold neuroleptics until catatonia resolves

5. Treat Underlying Cause:

  • Immunotherapy for anti-NMDAR encephalitis
  • Mood stabilizers/antidepressants once catatonia resolves
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Lorazepam challenge: Rapid improvement with 1-2 mg IV lorazepam is diagnostic AND therapeutic
  • Mood disorders > schizophrenia: Catatonia is more often from depression/bipolar than schizophrenia
  • Avoid antipsychotics initially: Can worsen catatonia or precipitate NMS
  • Malignant catatonia = emergency: Fever + rigidity + autonomic instability → needs urgent ECT if not responding to benzos
  • Don't miss anti-NMDAR: Young woman with psychiatric symptoms → check for ovarian teratoma, send antibodies
  • ECT works: Highly effective, even in treatment-resistant cases. Don't delay if benzos fail
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Lorazepam, 💊 Diazepam
↑ Back to Table of Contents

321. MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA

Anesthetic Emergency • Hypermetabolic Crisis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Setting: Occurs during or shortly after general anesthesia with triggering agents

Triggering Agents:

  • Volatile anesthetics: Sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, halothane
  • Succinylcholine: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker

Safe Agents: Propofol, opioids, benzodiazepines, nitrous oxide, non-depolarizing NMBs

Clinical Features (in Order of Appearance):

  • Early:
    • Masseter muscle rigidity (especially after succinylcholine) — may be first sign
    • Unexplained tachycardia
    • Rising ETCO₂ (earliest and most sensitive sign)
    • Tachypnea (in spontaneously breathing patients)
  • Progressive:
    • Hyperthermia (may rise 1-2°C every 5 minutes)
    • Generalized muscle rigidity
    • Mottled skin, diaphoresis
  • Late:
    • Rhabdomyolysis (massively elevated CPK)
    • Hyperkalemia → arrhythmias
    • DIC, myoglobinuria, renal failure
    • Cardiac arrest

Genetics: Autosomal dominant; RYR1 gene mutations (ryanodine receptor) most common

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Diagnosis (During Crisis): Recognize pattern — rising ETCO₂, tachycardia, rigidity, hyperthermia in OR setting

Labs (During Crisis):

  • ABG: Respiratory AND metabolic acidosis, hypercarbia
  • Potassium: Hyperkalemia (life-threatening)
  • CPK: Massively elevated (>10,000 to >100,000)
  • Myoglobin: Elevated (myoglobinuria → AKI)
  • Lactate: Elevated
  • Coagulation studies: May show DIC

Definitive Diagnosis (Post-Crisis Susceptibility Testing):

  • Caffeine-halothane contracture test (CHCT): Gold standard; muscle biopsy required
  • Genetic testing: RYR1 mutation testing; if positive, confirms susceptibility
  • Test patient AND family members
TREATMENT PROTOCOL (EMERGENCY)

1. STOP TRIGGERING AGENTS IMMEDIATELY:

  • Discontinue volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine
  • Hyperventilate with 100% O₂ at high flows (≥10 L/min)
  • Do NOT delay surgery termination if possible

2. DANTROLENE (CRITICAL — GIVE IMMEDIATELY):

  • Dose: 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus
  • Repeat every 5 minutes until symptoms resolve (up to 10 mg/kg or more)
  • Continue 1 mg/kg q4-6h for 24-48 hours (recrudescence risk)
  • Dantrolene is the specific antidote — mechanism: blocks calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum

3. Treat Hyperkalemia:

  • Calcium chloride or gluconate (cardiac stabilization)
  • Insulin + glucose
  • Sodium bicarbonate
  • Avoid calcium channel blockers (interaction with dantrolene → cardiovascular collapse)

4. Active Cooling:

  • Cold IV saline
  • Ice packs to axillae, groin
  • Cooling blankets
  • Target: <38.5°C

5. Treat Arrhythmias:

  • Standard ACLS protocols
  • Avoid calcium channel blockers

6. Prevent Renal Failure:

  • Aggressive IV fluids
  • Maintain UOP >2 mL/kg/hr (force diuresis)
  • Consider mannitol or sodium bicarbonate for myoglobinuria

7. Monitor: ICU admission, serial CPK, K, renal function, coags

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Rising ETCO₂ is earliest sign: Unexplained hypercarbia during anesthesia = think MH
  • Dantrolene saves lives: Mortality dropped from 80% to <5% with dantrolene. Give early, give enough
  • Avoid CCBs: Calcium channel blockers + dantrolene = cardiovascular collapse
  • Fever may be late: Don't wait for fever — other signs appear first
  • Masseter rigidity: Especially after succinylcholine, may be early warning sign
  • Family screening: Autosomal dominant — test and warn family members
  • MH hotline: 1-800-644-9737 (MHAUS) — 24/7 expert consultation
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids
↑ Back to Table of Contents

322. HEPATORENAL SYNDROME

Functional Renal Failure in Cirrhosis • HRS-AKI
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: HRS-AKI is a type of AKI unique to cirrhosis, occurring without hypovolemia or significant kidney histology abnormalities (AASLD 2021). Splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial blood volume, activating vasoactive systems that constrict the renal vessels (AGA 2024)

HRS-AKI (replaces type 1 HRS):

  • AKI by ICA criteria that meets HRS criteria (below). Treatment trials used the historical type 1 definition: creatinine doubling to over 2.5 mg/dL in under 2 weeks (AASLD 2021)
  • AKI in cirrhosis carries 30-day mortality of 29-44%; HRS-AKI causes 15-43% of AKI, hypovolemia 27-50%, ATN 14-35% (AASLD 2021)

Former Type 2 HRS: now falls under CKD: eGFR under 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for at least 3 months (AASLD 2021)

Precipitants: fluid losses, bacterial infections, hemodynamic instability, nephrotoxic agents, especially NSAIDs (AASLD 2021); GI bleeding and large-volume paracentesis without albumin (AASLD 2021)

DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (ICA-AKI 2015)

Required Criteria (AASLD 2021, Table 11):

  • Cirrhosis with ascites
  • AKI by ICA criteria: creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours, or 50% or more known or presumed within the prior 7 days (AASLD 2021)
  • No response after 2 consecutive days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin 1 g/kg/day (cap 100 g/day, AGA 2024)
  • No shock
  • No current or recent nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast)
  • No structural kidney injury: proteinuria over 500 mg/day, microhematuria over 50 RBC/hpf, or abnormal renal ultrasound

AKI Stage: 1: creatinine rise 0.3 mg/dL or more, up to 2-fold; 2: 2- to 3-fold; 3: over 3-fold, or over 4 mg/dL with an acute rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more, or RRT (AASLD 2021, Table 10)

Key Point: HRS-AKI is diagnosed after excluding hypovolemia, shock, nephrotoxins, and structural kidney damage; separating severe HRS-AKI from ATN is particularly hard (AASLD 2021)

Urine Studies:

  • Fractional excretion of sodium under 1% may suggest HRS; urine sediment and biomarkers may point to ATN (AASLD 2021, Figure 4)
  • Urine NGAL is the most promising biomarker for ATN (AUROC 0.80 or more), but it is not widely available (AASLD 2021)
  • Older criteria (creatinine over 1.5 mg/dL, urine sodium under 10, FENa under 1% as a requirement) are not part of the HRS-AKI definition (AASLD 2021, Table 11)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. General Measures (AASLD 2021):

  • Search for and treat precipitants quickly: infection, fluid losses, hemodynamic instability, nephrotoxins
  • Stop diuretics; consider holding NSBBs, especially if hypotensive; avoid indwelling bladder catheters
  • Hypovolemic AKI: fluid replacement (5% albumin or crystalloids, preferably balanced) and correction of the cause
  • Albumin 1 g/kg/day for 2 days (cap 100 g/day, AGA 2024) as the diagnostic challenge; albumin is the volume expander of choice for AKI with ascites (AGA 2024)
  • ICU or intermediate care if severe hepatic encephalopathy, multiorgan failure, or need for RRT

2. Vasoconstrictor plus Albumin (HRS-AKI only, not other AKI in cirrhosis; AGA 2024):

  • Terlipressin: preferred (AASLD 2021; AGA 2024); peripheral IV, no ICU required (AGA 2024)
    • Dose: 0.85 mg IV over 2 min every 6 h on days 1-3. Day 4: if creatinine fell 30% or more, continue; if less than 30%, may increase to 1.7 mg every 6 h; if at or above baseline, stop. Continue until 24 h after two creatinine values of 1.5 mg/dL or less at least 2 h apart, maximum 14 days (Terlivaz label, rev 06/2026)
    • Boxed warning: serious or fatal respiratory failure. Get baseline SpO2; do not start if SpO2 is under 90%; assess ACLF grade and volume status; avoid in ACLF grade 3. Contraindicated with hypoxia or ongoing coronary, peripheral, or mesenteric ischemia (Terlivaz label, rev 06/2026)
    • Creatinine over 5 mg/dL: benefit unlikely; MELD 35 or higher when listed for transplant: benefit may not outweigh risk (Terlivaz label, rev 06/2026; AGA 2024). CONFIRM: verified HRS reversal 29.1% vs 15.8% with placebo (Terlivaz label, rev 06/2026)
    • Albumin: 1 g/kg on day 1, then 40-50 g/day for the course (AASLD 2021); trial patients mostly received 20-40 g/day, and need beyond 1-2 days should be judged by volume status (AGA 2024); CONFIRM median 50 g/day (Terlivaz label, rev 06/2026)
  • Norepinephrine (if terlipressin unavailable; ICU): start 0.5 mg/h; increase by 0.5 mg/h every 4 h to a maximum of 3 mg/h, aiming for a MAP rise of at least 10 mm Hg or urine output over 200 mL/4 h; albumin to keep CVP 4-10 mm Hg (AASLD 2021). Fewer data; the largest RCT (120 patients) favored terlipressin (AGA 2024)
  • Midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin (only if neither is available): midodrine 5-15 mg PO every 8 h plus octreotide 100-200 mcg every 8 h or 50 mcg/h IV; low efficacy (AASLD 2021), unclear benefit over placebo (AGA 2024)
  • Watch for ischemic complications and pulmonary edema (AASLD 2021)

3. Response and Duration (AASLD 2021):

  • Response: creatinine under 1.5 mg/dL or back within 0.3 mg/dL of baseline, over a maximum of 14 days
  • May stop if creatinine stays at or above pretreatment after 4 days at maximum tolerated doses
  • Recurrence after stopping should be retreated; response rates 20-80% (about 50%) (AASLD 2021)
  • Start early: higher creatinine predicts lower response (AGA 2024)

4. TIPS: not recommended for HRS-AKI because of insufficient information (AASLD 2021)

5. Liver Transplantation: the ultimate therapy for HRS-AKI. Consider urgent transplant evaluation for all patients with cirrhosis and AKI, even responders; kidney recovery after transplant is not always predictable, and simultaneous liver-kidney transplant may be needed. Treatment lowers creatinine and MELD, which can lower transplant priority without a matching survival gain (AASLD 2021)

6. Renal Replacement Therapy: for transplant candidates with worsening kidney function, electrolyte disturbances, or rising volume overload despite vasoconstrictors; continuous RRT if hemodynamically unstable. In non-candidates, mortality on RRT is extremely high: start only with a clear endpoint, as a limited trial in selected patients (AASLD 2021). Decide with hepatology, nephrology, critical care, and transplant surgery (AASLD 2021)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Albumin challenge first: 1 g/kg/day for 2 days with diuretics stopped before diagnosing HRS-AKI (AASLD 2021; cap 100 g/day, AGA 2024)
  • Look for infection: bacterial infection is a key precipitant; albumin with antibiotics in SBP reduces HRS-AKI and improves survival (AASLD 2021)
  • Terlipressin is preferred (FDA-approved 2022) with albumin; check SpO2 first and avoid in ACLF grade 3 (AGA 2024; Terlivaz label, rev 06/2026)
  • FENa under 1% may suggest HRS but is not a diagnostic criterion (AASLD 2021)
  • Transplant is the ultimate therapy; evaluate urgently, even if creatinine responds (AASLD 2021)
  • RRT without a transplant option: mortality is extremely high; use only as a limited trial with a clear endpoint (AASLD 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Albumin, 💊 Octreotide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Urine Sodium/FENa, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated Ammonia
↑ Back to Table of Contents

323. DRUG-INDUCED LIVER INJURY (DILI)

Hepatotoxicity • R-Ratio Classification
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Presentation: asymptomatic liver test elevation to hepatocellular or cholestatic jaundice, liver failure, or chronic hepatitis (ACG 2021 DILI)

Symptoms (when present): fatigue, weakness, abdominal pain, nausea, dark urine, jaundice, pruritus; fever, rash, and eosinophilia point to immunoallergic injury (ACG 2021 DILI, Tables 5-6)

Patterns by R Value (at presentation; AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 15):

  • R = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN); ACG uses R over 5 and R under 2 as the cut points (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 3)
  • Hepatocellular (R ≥5): acetaminophen (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 4); isoniazid, nitrofurantoin, minocycline, diclofenac (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 6); statins, in most cases (LiverTox, Statins)
  • Mixed (R between 2 and 5): phenytoin, carbamazepine, allopurinol, often with fever, rash, eosinophilia (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 6); sulfonamides, variable but often mixed (LiverTox, Sulfonamides)
  • Cholestatic (R ≤2): amoxicillin-clavulanate (can be hepatocellular), androgen-containing steroids (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 6; LiverTox)
  • The pattern can change as the injury evolves, and one drug can cause more than one pattern; ACG lists trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as cholestatic or hepatocellular (AASLD 2023 DILI; ACG 2021 DILI, Table 6)

High-Risk Medications:

  • Antibiotics: amoxicillin-clavulanate (the most common cause of clinically apparent DILI in the US and Europe, LiverTox; the most common antimicrobial cause in adults, minocycline in children, ACG 2021 DILI), isoniazid, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, fluoroquinolones (top US DILIN agents; AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 2)
  • NSAIDs: diclofenac especially; hepatocellular with autoimmune features (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 6)
  • Anticonvulsants: phenytoin, carbamazepine (hypersensitivity syndrome); valproate (hyperammonemia, Reye-like microvesicular steatosis), far more common in children (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 6 and text)
  • Statins: transient aminotransferase rises are common; clinically significant injury is rare (1.8% of DILIN cases) and latency can exceed 6 months or reach several years (AASLD 2023 DILI; LiverTox, Statins)
  • Acetaminophen: dose-dependent (intrinsic); the leading cause of ALF in US adults (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 46); idiosyncratic DILI is second (ACG 2023 ALF)
  • Herbal/supplements: about 20% of US cases; anabolic steroids, green tea extract, multi-ingredient products (ACG 2021 DILI); ashwagandha, turmeric/curcumin, Garcinia cambogia, kratom (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 7); kava, a well-known cause (likelihood A) of liver injury including liver failure (LiverTox, Kava)
  • Immunotherapy: Checkpoint inhibitors (ipilimumab, nivolumab)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Key Principle: DILI is a diagnosis of exclusion (ACG 2021 DILI; AASLD 2023 DILI)

Clinically Significant DILI (any one; AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 13):

  • AST or ALT over 5× ULN, or ALP over 2× ULN (multiples of the pretreatment baseline if it was abnormal), on 2 occasions at least 24 h apart
  • Total bilirubin over 2.5 mg/dL with elevated AST, ALT, or ALP
  • INR over 1.5 with elevated AST, ALT, or ALP

Exposure History: every prescription drug and HDS product taken in the 180 days before onset, with start and stop dates; most injury starts within 6 months, but amoxicillin-clavulanate can present after the course ends (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 14)

Rule Out Other Causes:

  • Viral hepatitis: anti-HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV and HCV RNA (anti-HCV can be negative early in acute HCV) (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 1a, Table 5; AASLD 2023 DILI)
  • Anti-HEV IgM in selected cases: travel to an endemic area, atypical phenotype, no clear culprit, or older adults with very high aminotransferases; commercial assays are of uncertain reliability (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 1b; AASLD 2023 DILI)
  • CMV, EBV, HSV if classic viral hepatitis is excluded, or with atypical lymphocytosis or lymphadenopathy (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 1c)
  • Autoimmune hepatitis: ANA, ASMA, IgG levels
  • Imaging in all: abdominal ultrasound first; CT or MR cholangiography for vascular or pancreaticobiliary disease (AASLD 2023 DILI; ACG 2021 DILI, rec 2a)
  • Cholestatic DILI: AMA for PBC only if imaging shows no biliary pathology; ERCP only if MRI or EUS cannot exclude stones, PSC, or malignancy (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 2b-2c)
  • Wilson disease: ceruloplasmin, particularly under age 40; it is an acute-phase reactant and can be falsely normal in acute hepatitis (ACG 2021 DILI)
  • Ischemic hepatitis: recent hypotension, sepsis, or heart failure; rapid rise and fall of aminotransferases with normal or near-normal bilirubin (AASLD 2023 DILI)
  • Alcohol-associated hepatitis: AST over ALT, AST generally under 300 U/L; check CK in this setting (AASLD 2023 DILI)
  • Budd-Chiari syndrome when clinically appropriate (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 1d)

Causality Assessment:

  • RUCAM: scores timing, course after stopping the drug, risk factors, concomitant drugs, other causes, the drug's known hepatotoxicity, and rechallenge (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 7; AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 5)
  • Original RUCAM: over 8 highly probable; 6-8 probable; 3-5 possible; 1-2 unlikely; 0 or less excluded (ACG 2021 DILI)
  • Not a sole diagnostic tool (retest reliability 0.51); use it as a framework. Alternatives: RECAM (online, needs more validation) and DILIN expert opinion (ACG 2021 DILI; AASLD 2023 DILI, statements 24-28)

Hy's Law (all 3 criteria; ACG 2021 DILI, Table 3):

  • ALT or AST over 3× ULN, plus
  • Total bilirubin over 2× ULN without initial cholestasis (ALP not elevated), plus
  • No other cause, such as viral hepatitis or other acute or pre-existing liver disease
  • About 10% mortality (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 3). AASLD uses bilirubin over 2.5 mg/dL and ALP under 2× ULN, with PPV 8-20% for death or transplant; not for mixed or cholestatic injury (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 8)
  • 6-month mortality: ACG suggests a model of MELD, Charlson comorbidity index, and serum albumin (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 4)

Liver Biopsy: not required for diagnosis (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 19). Consider it if AIH remains possible and immunosuppression is planned; if tests keep rising or liver function worsens after stopping the drug; if ALT has not fallen by over 50% at 30-60 days (hepatocellular) or ALP by over 50% at 180 days (cholestatic); or if re-exposure is planned (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 3)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Stop Offending Agent: Most important intervention

2. Specific Antidotes:

  • Acetaminophen: IV NAC 150 mg/kg over 1 h, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, 100 mg/kg over 16 h (ACG 2023 ALF, Table 10); with liver injury, continue 6.25 mg/kg/h until ALT is falling and INR is under 2 (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 10). Full stop criteria: card 155 (Acute Liver Failure)
  • Valproate hepatotoxicity or hyperammonemia: stop valproate and give L-carnitine promptly, preferably IV (LiverTox, Valproate). Dose: 100 mg/kg IV over 30 min (less than 6 g), then 15 mg/kg every 4 h until clinical improvement (LiverTox, Valproate). AASLD lists 100 mg/kg load, then 50 mg/kg every 8 h (uncontrolled data, hospitalized children; AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9). Off-label: the FDA label covers inborn errors of metabolism and ESRD, at 50 mg/kg per dose given every 3 to 4 h and never less often than every 6 h (Carnitor label)
  • Amanita mushroom: call poison control; IV silibinin as soon as possible (not FDA approved); IV penicillin G only if silibinin is unavailable; IV NAC; gastric lavage within 1 h and activated charcoal early; IV fluids for urine output 100-200 mL/h (ACG 2023 ALF, rec 9 and text)
  • Leflunomide: stop it and give cholestyramine 8 g orally 3 times daily for 11 days, or activated charcoal 50 g every 12 h for 11 days (Arava label, section 5.3). AASLD lists 1 packet every 6-8 h for 14 days (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9). Give other drugs separately (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9); cholestyramine is contraindicated in complete biliary obstruction (cholestyramine label)

3. NAC for Non-Acetaminophen DILI with ALF (adults only):

  • IV NAC is suggested in adults with early-stage ALF, coma grade I-II (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 7; ACG 2023 ALF, rec 7; AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 40)
  • US trial: transplant-free survival 52% vs 30% in coma grade I-II; DILI subgroup (n = 42) 58% vs 27% (ACG 2021 DILI)
  • Dosing: the acetaminophen IV regimen, 72 h total in the trials, with cardiac monitoring (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9)
  • Not for children: survival was lower with IV NAC in pediatric non-acetaminophen ALF (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 8; AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 40)

4. Corticosteroids (no controlled trials; dose and duration not established; ACG 2021 DILI, rec 9; AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 41):

  • Severe hypersensitivity, DRESS, or AIH-like histology: prednisone 40-60 mg daily (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9)
  • Checkpoint inhibitor injury with ALT over 5× ULN: methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day equivalents (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9)
  • Checkpoint inhibitor grade 2 (ALT 3-5× ULN or bilirubin 1.5-3× ULN): hold the drug, consider prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day. Grade 3 or higher (ALT 5-20× ULN or bilirubin 3-10× ULN): stop it permanently, IV steroids 1-1.5 mg/kg/day. Steroid-refractory: mycophenolate or azathioprine (AASLD 2023 DILI)
  • Most courses can be tapered over 1-3 months (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9)

5. Ursodeoxycholic Acid: not an established DILI therapy, but presumably safe (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 42; efficacy not established, ACG 2021 DILI). For severe pruritus: 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses (AASLD 2023 DILI, Table 9; ursodiol labels express the dose per day, URSO label). Contraindicated in complete biliary obstruction (URSO label)

6. Transplant Center: transfer early once ALF develops (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy): spontaneous survival in DILI-related ALF is only about 25% (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 36). Refer progressive jaundice, with or without coagulopathy, to a tertiary center (ACG 2021 DILI)

Prognosis: about 80% recover fully within 6 months of onset after the drug is stopped (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 34); about 10% have ALF, transplant, or death within 6 months (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 35); 10-20% have chronic injury beyond 6-12 months, more often after cholestatic DILI (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 37). Higher bilirubin and INR and lower albumin at presentation predict worse outcomes (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 38)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • R value guides the workup: (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN) at presentation sorts hepatocellular, mixed, or cholestatic injury and the tests for other causes (AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 15)
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the most common cause of clinically apparent DILI in the US and Europe; acetaminophen is a separate, dose-dependent cause (LiverTox; AASLD 2023 DILI)
  • Hy's law = danger: hepatocellular injury plus jaundice with no other cause carries about 10% mortality (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 3)
  • Ask about supplements directly: they cause about 20% of US cases, and supplement injury can go unrecognized by patients and clinicians (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 10; AASLD 2023 DILI)
  • Latency: most idiosyncratic DILI appears 2-24 weeks after starting the drug; amoxicillin-clavulanate can appear days to weeks after the course ends (AASLD 2023 DILI; LiverTox); nitrofurantoin, minocycline, statins, and methotrexate can have long latency, over 90 days, sometimes years (ACG 2021 DILI, Table 6; LiverTox)
  • Do not re-expose: strong recommendation against re-exposure to a drug likely to have caused DILI, especially after ALT over 5× ULN, Hy's law, or jaundice; exception: a life-threatening condition with no suitable alternative (ACG 2021 DILI, rec 5; AASLD 2023 DILI, statement 44)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 N-Acetylcysteine, 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Ursodiol, 💊 Penicillin G
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated Bilirubin, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Low Albumin

324. AUTOIMMUNE HEPATITIS

Immune-Mediated Liver Inflammation • Steroid-Responsive
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Presentation: asymptomatic in 25%-34%; acute onset (under 30 days) in 25%-75%; ALF with encephalopathy in 3%-6% of North American and European patients; cirrhosis at presentation in 28%-33% of adults, especially age 60 or older (AASLD 2019 AIH)

Symptoms: fatigue (the main complaint in 85%), malaise, arthralgias, amenorrhea; jaundice may be present. Pruritus or hyperpigmentation is inconsistent with AIH; weight loss suggests a serious complication such as malignancy (AASLD 2019 AIH)

Demographics:

  • Women are 71%-95% of adult patients (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Early reports suggested onset peaks at 10-30 and 40-60 years, possibly from referral bias; onset after 60 is reported (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Concurrent autoimmune disease in 14%-44%; autoimmune thyroid disease is the most common in type 1 (10%-18%). Screen for celiac and thyroid disease at diagnosis; assess for rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and diabetes by symptoms (AASLD 2019 AIH, guidance statements)

Types:

  • AASLD 2019 (US): type 1: ANA and/or SMA (anti-actin), 96% of US adults, peripubertal and adult onset; type 2: anti-LKM1 (anti-LC1), usually without ANA or SMA, usually under age 14, 9%-12% of US children, acute onset in about 40%, remission off therapy rare (AASLD 2019 AIH, Table 3)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): no longer subclassifies AIH by autoantibody profile (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)

Overlap Syndromes:

  • AASLD 2019 (US): clinical descriptions, not validated entities; their value is identifying patients who may not respond to standard AIH therapy. AIH-PBC (Paris criteria): 2 of 3 PBC criteria (ALP at least 2× ULN or GGT at least 5× ULN; AMA; florid bile duct lesions), plus interface hepatitis with ALT at least 5× ULN and IgG at least 2× ULN or SMA. AIH-PSC: cholestatic labs, bile duct injury or loss on biopsy, and ulcerative colitis call for cholangiography. Consider adding UDCA to prednisone and azathioprine (AASLD 2019 AIH, guidance statements)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): MR cholangiography in adults with cholestatic features; treat the predominant component; AIH-PBC: standard immunosuppression combined with UDCA; AIH-PSC: immunosuppression with or without UDCA (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Simplified Diagnostic Criteria (IAIHG 2008; AASLD 2019 AIH, Supplementary Table 2; 6 or more points = probable, 7 or more = definite):

  • ANA or SMA: at least 1:40, 1 point; at least 1:80, 1 more point (AASLD 2019 AIH, Supplementary Table 2). The original table gives 2 points at 1:80 (Hennes 2008)
  • Anti-LKM1 at least 1:40, 2 points; anti-SLA positive, 2 points (AASLD 2019 AIH, Supplementary Table 2)
  • All autoantibodies together count for at most 2 points (Hennes 2008; the AASLD table does not state this cap)
  • IgG: above ULN, 1 point; above 1.1× ULN, 2 points (AASLD 2019 AIH, Supplementary Table 2)
  • Liver histology: compatible with AIH, 1 point; typical of AIH, 2 points. Negative viral markers: 2 points (AASLD 2019 AIH, Supplementary Table 2)
  • Use scores only to support clinical judgment in challenging cases. The simplified score is less sensitive than the revised original score (95% vs 100%) but more specific (90% vs 73%); rescore with the revised system if the simplified score is low (AASLD 2019 AIH). Revised original score before treatment: definite AIH over 15, probable 10-15 (AASLD 2019 AIH, Supplementary Table 2)

Serology and Labs:

  • Elevated AST and ALT, elevated IgG, and one or more characteristic autoantibodies (AASLD 2019 AIH, Table 2)
  • Initial testing: ANA and SMA in adults (add anti-LKM1 in children). Anti-LKM1 has 1% sensitivity in North American adults, so test it after ANA and SMA are negative (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Anti-SLA: present in 7%-22% of type 1 AIH and the only marker in 14%-20% of patients; linked to severe disease and relapse after withdrawal. Atypical pANCA is common in type 1 (50%-92%) but not specific (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Acute severe AIH: ANA is absent or weak in 29%-39% and IgG is normal in 25%-39% (AASLD 2019 AIH)

Liver Biopsy (required: AIH cannot be diagnosed without compatible histology; AASLD 2019 AIH):

  • Interface hepatitis is the hallmark; plasma cells in 66%, emperipolesis in 65%, lobular hepatitis in 47%, rosettes in 33%, centrilobular necrosis in 29%; no single feature is specific (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • NAFLD features are present in 17%-30% of adults with AIH and may affect response (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Elastography (VCTE) can identify advanced fibrosis but should wait at least 6 months after successful treatment; serum fibrosis panels should not be used (AASLD 2019 AIH, guidance statements)

Exclude: viral hepatitis, Wilson disease, hereditary hemochromatosis, and other hereditary, metabolic, cholestatic, and drug-induced disease (AASLD 2019 AIH). Checkpoint inhibitor hepatitis lacks the autoantibodies and histology of AIH and is not AIH (AASLD 2019 AIH; card 323)

Drug-Induced AIH-like Injury:

  • AASLD 2019 (US): latency 1-8 weeks to 3-12 months, over 12 months possible with nitrofurantoin and minocycline; anti-TNF agents also implicated. Stop the drug and monitor; give steroids if severe or not improving after withdrawal; a flare after steroid withdrawal suggests AIH (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): stop the suspected agent at once; a short predniso(lo)ne course if hepatitis is severe or does not improve within 30 days, tapered off within 1-2 months; course and treatment response separate it from AIH (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Who to Treat:

  • AASLD 2019 (US): all patients with AIH except those with inactive disease by clinical, laboratory, and histological assessment; absence of symptoms should not discourage treatment (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): all patients with active disease, including advanced fibrosis; elderly patients with at least moderate activity get standard therapy, but elderly asymptomatic patients with mild activity: watch and wait (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)

Before Treatment (AASLD 2019 AIH, guidance statements):

  • HBsAg and anti-HBc. Vaccinate susceptible patients against HAV and HBV, preferably before immunosuppression. HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive: periodic HBsAg and HBV DNA during therapy; consider preemptive antivirals with high-dose steroids or B cell-depleting agents
  • Consider TPMT testing before azathioprine (absent or near-absent activity in 0.3%-0.5%)
  • Bone density at baseline if osteoporosis risk factors, repeated every 2-3 years on steroids; 25-OH vitamin D at diagnosis and yearly; calcium 1,000-1,200 mg and vitamin D at least 400-800 IU daily while on steroids
  • Address adherence barriers at the start; monitor for depression and quality of life

Induction, AASLD 2019, US (no cirrhosis and not acute severe: budesonide + azathioprine or prednisone + azathioprine; AASLD 2019 AIH, recommendation 1):

  • Prednisone + azathioprine: prednisone 20-40 mg daily (prednisone alone: 40-60 mg daily); azathioprine usually 50-100 mg daily to start (US range 50-150 mg daily). Most centers start azathioprine about 2 weeks after prednisone to confirm steroid response, check TPMT, and exclude azathioprine hepatitis (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Budesonide + azathioprine: budesonide 3 mg three times daily (twice daily after remission) with azathioprine 1-2 mg/kg daily; remission at 6 months 60% vs 39%, steroid side effects 28% vs 53%, compared with prednisone + azathioprine (AASLD 2019 AIH). Not as rescue for steroid-refractory AIH (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Cirrhosis or acute severe AIH: no budesonide (AASLD 2019 AIH, recommendation 2); azathioprine is not recommended in decompensated cirrhosis or acute severe AIH (AASLD 2019 AIH, Table 8). Acute severe AIH: see below
  • Prednisone alone: when treatment is expected to last under 6 months (e.g., drug-induced AIH-like injury) or azathioprine is contraindicated (intolerance, complete TPMT deficiency) (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Taper: after biochemical remission, reduce prednisone to 20 mg daily with labs every 2 weeks, then by 2.5-5 mg every 2-4 weeks to 5-10 mg daily; it may then be stopped, leaving azathioprine. Avoid prolonged prednisone above 10 mg daily (AASLD 2019 AIH)

Induction, EASL 2025, non-US (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US):

  • Predniso(lo)ne at least 0.5 mg/kg/day, up to 1 mg/kg/day in more severe disease, plus azathioprine 50 mg/day rising to 1-2 mg/kg/day (started about 2 weeks after steroids) or MMF 1.5-2 g/day as first line
  • Budesonide is not recommended as first-line treatment and is contraindicated in cirrhosis; a switch to budesonide may be considered for steroid side effects in non-cirrhotic, prednisolone-dependent patients
  • Avoid azathioprine in acute severe AIH and decompensated cirrhosis

FDA Labels (AIH is off-label for azathioprine, budesonide, and MMF):

  • Azathioprine: CBC weekly for 1 month, twice monthly for months 2-3, then monthly; alternative therapy for homozygous TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency, reduced dose if heterozygous; with allopurinol give 1/3 to 1/4 of the usual dose; avoid febuxostat (Imuran label). Long term, AASLD advises cell counts at least every 6 months (AASLD 2019 AIH, Table 8)
  • Budesonide (labeled for Crohn disease): avoid in Child-Pugh C; consider 3 mg daily in Child-Pugh B (Entocort EC label)

Maintenance and Withdrawal (AASLD 2019 AIH, US, unless marked):

  • Long term: azathioprine adjusted up to 2 mg/kg daily as prednisone is reduced to the lowest dose or stopped. If azathioprine is not tolerated: MMF, or in adults prednisone alone at 7.5 mg daily or less
  • Consider withdrawal only after AST, ALT, and IgG have been normal for at least 2 years; pre-withdrawal biopsy is valuable but not mandatory in adults
  • After withdrawal: labs regularly for the first 12 months, then yearly for life; treatment-free remission is achieved in 19%-40%
  • Relapse: restart the original regimen until remission, then long-term maintenance; adults should stay on long-term therapy after a first relapse
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): consider withdrawal after at least 2 years of stable complete biochemical response on low-dose monotherapy; a pre-withdrawal biopsy is generally desirable in adults and children; reported relapse rates range from 25% to 100% (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)

Response Definitions (AASLD 2019 AIH, US, Table 2, unless marked):

  • Biochemical remission: normal AST, ALT, and IgG (IgG may stay high in cirrhosis). Aminotransferases should improve within 2 weeks; remission within 6 months lowers the risk of cirrhosis and transplant (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Histological remission: no inflammation on biopsy after treatment
  • Incomplete response: improvement short of remission. Treatment failure: worsening labs or histology despite adherence (7%-9% of adults; AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): complete biochemical response is normal aminotransferases and IgG no later than 6-12 months after starting treatment; insufficient response is no complete response by 6-12 months (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)

Second-Line:

  • AASLD 2019 (US): for treatment failure, incomplete response, or intolerance: MMF or tacrolimus (AASLD 2019 AIH, recommendation 3), MMF before tacrolimus (AASLD 2019 AIH, recommendation 4). With nonresponse, first recheck the diagnosis and adherence. Anti-TNF or anti-CD20 (rituximab) only after first- and second-line failure; data are limited. No MMF dose given (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): MMF 1.5-2 g/day; MMF is also a first-line alternative to azathioprine (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)

Pregnancy:

  • AASLD 2019 (US): aim for 1 year of remission before conception; continue maintenance glucocorticoids and/or azathioprine through pregnancy; MMF is contraindicated; monitor closely for 6 months postpartum (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): continue thiopurines (with or without corticosteroids) during pregnancy; stop MMF at least 3 months before conception (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)
  • FDA labels: azathioprine: avoid in pregnancy whenever possible (Imuran label); MMF: boxed warning for first-trimester loss and malformations (CellCept label)

Acute Severe AIH, ALF, and Liver Transplant:

  • AASLD 2019 (US): ALF (INR 2 or more with encephalopathy): evaluate directly for transplant; steroids have not improved survival in ALF and may harm with severe decompensation. Acute severe AIH (jaundice, INR over 1.5 and under 2, no encephalopathy): prednisone alone 0.5-1 mg/kg daily; evaluate for transplant if labs do not improve or the patient worsens within 1-2 weeks (AASLD 2019 AIH, Table 2 and guidance statements)
  • EASL 2025 (non-US): acute severe AIH: predniso(lo)ne 0.5-1 mg/kg/day or IV methylprednisolone at an equivalent dose; refer to a transplant centre if no improvement after 3-7 days. ALF or ACLF: direct transplant evaluation. Decompensated cirrhosis from AIH: evaluate for transplant (EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)
  • Recurrence after transplant: 8%-12% at 1 year, 36%-68% at 5 years (AASLD 2019 AIH)

Cirrhosis: HCC surveillance with ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months (AASLD 2019 AIH, guidance statement; same in EASL 2025 AIH, non-US)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Fast response is expected: aminotransferases should improve within 2 weeks; no response means recheck the diagnosis and adherence (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Normal IgG or negative ANA does not exclude AIH: in acute severe AIH, IgG is normal in 25%-39% and ANA absent or weak in 29%-39%; biopsy is required (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Pruritus points elsewhere: pruritus or hyperpigmentation is inconsistent with AIH (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Azathioprine spares steroids: prolonged prednisone above 10 mg daily causes frequent toxicity and should be avoided (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Relapse is common: 50%-87% of adults relapse after drug withdrawal, half within 3 months; almost all respond to retreatment (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • ALF: AIH with encephalopathy goes straight to transplant evaluation, not a prolonged steroid trial (AASLD 2019 AIH)
  • Always consider drug-induced AIH-like injury (nitrofurantoin, minocycline); checkpoint inhibitor hepatitis is not AIH (AASLD 2019 AIH)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone, 💊 Azathioprine, 💊 Mycophenolate, 💊 Tacrolimus
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 ANA, 🔬 Low Albumin, 🔬 Hepatitis Panel

325. BUDD-CHIARI SYNDROME

Hepatic Vein Outflow Obstruction
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Presentation: from asymptomatic (15%-20%, found incidentally) to acute liver failure, depending on how extensive and fast the obstruction is (AASLD 2021); from fulminant liver failure to subacute and chronic outflow obstruction, the most common presentation (ACG 2020)

Common Findings: ascites (83%), hepatomegaly (67%), abdominal pain (61%); esophageal varices in over 50%. Labs: raised bilirubin and aminotransferases, prolonged PT when severe; high-protein ascites. IVC obstruction: abdominal wall varices, leg edema or ulcers (AASLD 2021)

Causes of Primary BCS (endoluminal thrombus or web; a prothrombotic disorder in about 75%, more than one in at least 35%, none found in 15%-30%; AASLD 2021):

  • Myeloproliferative neoplasm: 41%, the most common cause in Western patients; JAK2 V617F in 86% of these, CALR much less often; often masked by hypersplenism (AASLD 2021, Table 7)
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome 10%; PNH 7% (AASLD 2021, Table 7)
  • Inherited thrombophilia: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C (5%), protein S (4%), and antithrombin (1%) deficiency (AASLD 2021, Table 7)
  • Oral contraceptives or recent pregnancy: 23% (AASLD 2021, Table 7); up to 74% of Western women with BCS used oral contraceptives (Elkrief 2023)
  • Other: Behcet disease (2%-3%; Mediterranean), celiac disease (AASLD 2021, Table 7); inflammatory bowel disease, vasculitis, sarcoidosis, connective tissue disease (ACG 2020, Table 6). Asian IVC-type BCS: few prothrombotic disorders; linked to low socioeconomic status and abdominal infection (AASLD 2021)

Key Point: test JAK2 V617F even when the blood count is normal; occult MPN is frequent (AASLD 2021, Table 8)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Doppler Ultrasound (first-line; AASLD 2021, guidance statement; ACG 2020, recommendation 16):

  • Sensitivity over 75% with an experienced operator (AASLD 2021)
  • Signs: thrombus; hepatic veins not seen or turned into a cord without flow; collateral veins; caudate lobe hypertrophy; caudate vein over 3 mm (AASLD 2021)

Contrast CT or MRI (confirms the diagnosis and plans intervention; first choice when no experienced ultrasound operator is available; AASLD 2021):

  • Also to define thrombus extent, rule out tumor thrombus, judge response to anticoagulation, and assess indeterminate nodules; get CT or MRI whenever suspicion stays high despite a negative or inconclusive Doppler (ACG 2020, recommendation 16)
  • Rapid contrast clearance from the caudate lobe and patchy enhancement from uneven portal perfusion (AASLD 2021); occluded hepatic veins and/or IVC, caudate hypertrophy (ACG 2020)
  • Nodules develop in about 40% during follow-up, mostly benign regenerative nodules; adenoma and HCC also occur (AASLD 2021)

Hepatic Venography: for uncertain cases; the typical sign is a "spider web" collateral pattern; rarely needed for diagnosis alone (AASLD 2021; ACG 2020, key concept 18)

Liver Biopsy: not needed unless small intrahepatic vein obstruction is suspected, where histology is the only way to the diagnosis (AASLD 2021)

Thrombophilia Workup (at diagnosis, with a hematologist; keep looking after one factor is found; AASLD 2021, guidance statement; ACG 2020, key concepts 16 and 19):

  • JAK2 V617F in all, even with a normal CBC; if negative, CALR, then bone marrow biopsy if MPN is still suspected (AASLD 2021, Tables 7-8)
  • Antiphospholipid: anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I IgG and IgM can be tested acutely; lupus anticoagulant not in the acute phase or on anticoagulation; APS needs persistence on repeat testing at 12 weeks or more (AASLD 2021, Table 8)
  • PNH: flow cytometry (AASLD 2021, Table 8)
  • Inherited thrombophilia: ACG tests inherited and acquired causes in all (ACG 2020, key concept 16). AASLD Table 8 does not routinely recommend it: results rarely change management, and protein C, protein S, and antithrombin fall in acute thrombosis and liver disease (AASLD 2021, Table 8)

HCC Surveillance: chronic BCS: ultrasound every 6 months with or without AFP (AASLD 2021, guidance statement); ultrasound and AFP every 6 months (ACG 2020, recommendation 18). Nodules: triphasic contrast CT or MRI (ACG 2020, key concept 27). HCC needs histology; LI-RADS does not apply in BCS (AASLD 2021)

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Stepwise Approach: least to most invasive by clinical response: anticoagulation, then angioplasty or TIPS, then transplant; refer early to a tertiary center (AASLD 2021, guidance statement; ACG 2020, recommendation 17)

1. Anticoagulation (All Patients):

  • Start at diagnosis in every patient, even when no prothrombotic disorder is found (AASLD 2021; ACG 2020)
  • Immediate LMWH, then a vitamin K antagonist; avoid long-term unfractionated heparin because of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (AASLD 2021). Target INR 2-3 (Elkrief 2023)
  • DOACs: data very limited (AASLD 2021); not studied in BCS (ACG 2020); not recommended with antiphospholipid syndrome (Elkrief 2023). Rivaroxaban label: avoid in Child-Pugh B or C or any liver disease with coagulopathy; not recommended in triple-positive APS (Xarelto label, 5.5, 5.10, 8.7)
  • Duration: long term in all patients; no clear basis to stop once BCS is stable and the cause treated (Elkrief 2023). AASLD and ACG give no duration beyond long-term warfarin use (ACG 2020)
  • Varices are not a contraindication; give primary or secondary variceal prophylaxis as indicated (ACG 2020, key concept 20). Major bleeding is common, mostly from procedures and portal hypertension (ACG 2020); consider a brief interruption before paracentesis (Elkrief 2023)

2. Treat the Underlying Cause:

  • Refer to hematology to evaluate and treat the prothrombotic disorder, including whether MPN-directed therapy will help (ACG 2020, key concept 19)
  • PNH: eculizumab may be considered (ACG 2020)

3. Portal Hypertension Complications:

  • Treat early (AASLD 2021); manage ascites, bleeding, infection, renal failure, and encephalopathy as in cirrhosis (Elkrief 2023)

4. Angioplasty, Stenting, Thrombolysis:

  • Angioplasty, with or without stenting, for short-segment stenosis of a hepatic vein or the suprahepatic IVC: about 10% of Western cases, over 80% in China; AASLD reserves stents for angioplasty failure (AASLD 2021). Long-term success is about one third (ACG 2020)
  • Thrombolysis: limited experience; local tPA, streptokinase, or urokinase with angioplasty in selected recent, incomplete thrombosis (AASLD 2021). Systemic or intra-arterial thrombolysis is ineffective; local infusion into the hepatic vein or IVC can work when combined with angioplasty; success is low because most BCS is chronic at presentation; may help acute occlusion of a hepatic vein stent or TIPS (ACG 2020)

5. TIPS:

  • Treatment of choice when medical therapy or angioplasty fails or is not feasible: TIPS, or DIPS (direct IVC-to-portal-vein puncture, needed in over 40%), with PTFE-covered stents, in expert centers (AASLD 2021, guidance statement)
  • Medical therapy has failed when liver or renal function worsens, or ascites or encephalopathy develops (ACG 2020, recommendation 17)
  • 5-year transplant-free survival 72% after TIPS for BCS unresponsive to medical therapy (AASLD 2021); pooled TIPS success 96.4%, 5-year survival 72.1% (ACG 2020)
  • Surgical shunts only when neither TIPS nor DIPS is possible (ACG 2020, key concept 24)

6. Liver Transplantation:

  • After less invasive steps fail (AASLD 2021); for TIPS failure or fulminant liver failure (ACG 2020, recommendation 17). In severe acute liver failure, transplant may be the first step; consider TIPS while waiting (AASLD 2021)
  • Needed in about 7% (AASLD 2021) or 10%-15% (ACG 2020); 5-year survival over 70%; prior TIPS does not worsen the outcome (AASLD 2021)
  • After transplant: thrombosis recurs in up to 20% (ACG 2020); keep treating the prothrombotic disorder (AASLD 2021) and consider long-term anticoagulation (ACG 2020, key concept 25)

Pregnancy: possible once BCS is controlled; switch a VKA to LMWH before week 6; no DOACs at any point in pregnancy; stop teratogenic MPN cytoreduction before conception; avoid estrogen contraceptives after delivery; breastfeeding is possible with warfarin but not with DOACs (Elkrief 2023, Table 3). Rivaroxaban label: not contraindicated in pregnancy, but dosing is not established, it carries a pregnancy-related hemorrhage warning, and it is detected in human milk (Xarelto label, 5.7, 8.1, 8.2)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • JAK2 in everyone: MPN is the leading cause (41%) and is often masked by hypersplenism, so test even with a normal CBC (AASLD 2021, Tables 7-8)
  • Caudate hypertrophy: well-drained segments hypertrophy while affected segments atrophy; a hypertrophied caudate can compress the IVC (AASLD 2021)
  • Step up by response: anticoagulation, then angioplasty or TIPS, then transplant (ACG 2020, recommendation 17)
  • Young woman with BCS: look for oral contraceptives or pregnancy (23%) and another prothrombotic factor, which is common (AASLD 2021, Table 7; Elkrief 2023)
  • Thrombolysis is not routine: most BCS is chronic at presentation; reserve it for selected recent, incomplete thrombosis, usually with angioplasty (AASLD 2021; ACG 2020)
  • Anticoagulate long term: recommended for all patients (Elkrief 2023); varices do not prevent it (ACG 2020)
  • Do not use LI-RADS in BCS: nodules are common and HCC needs histology (AASLD 2021)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Enoxaparin, 💊 Warfarin, 💊 Rivaroxaban
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated AST/ALT, 🔬 Elevated INR, 🔬 Elevated D-dimer, 🔬 Low Albumin
