326. HEPATOPULMONARY SYNDROME

Intrapulmonary Shunting in Liver Disease • Platypnea-Orthodeoxia
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: impaired gas exchange from intrapulmonary vascular dilatations (IPVDs) and right-to-left shunts, usually with cirrhosis and portal hypertension; also with acute or chronic liver disease without cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and abnormal liver-lung blood flow (cavopulmonary shunts, Abernethy malformation). Affects 10%-30% of patients evaluated for liver transplant; severity does not track the severity of liver disease (Raevens 2022)

Symptoms and Signs:

  • Often asymptomatic, so it is underdiagnosed; transplant candidates need active screening (Raevens 2022)
  • Platypnea: dyspnea worse when moving from supine to upright (Raevens 2022)
  • Orthodeoxia: PaO₂ falls by more than 5% or more than 4 mmHg from supine to upright; platypnea and orthodeoxia occur in only 18%-20% (Raevens 2022)
  • Exam: digital clubbing, cyanosis, diffuse telangiectasias (Raevens 2022); spider angiomas and other signs of chronic liver disease (Merck Manual)
  • Look for coexisting lung disease (COPD, asthma, pulmonary fibrosis), which worsens symptoms and gas exchange (Raevens 2022)

Pathophysiology:

  • Gas exchange fails through ventilation-perfusion mismatch, diffusion limitation, and direct arteriovenous communications (Raevens 2022)
  • Dilatations are more numerous at the lung bases, so dyspnea and hypoxemia worsen upright and improve lying down (Merck Manual)

Severity by Room-Air PaO₂ (Raevens 2022, Table 1):

  • Mild: PaO₂ ≥80 mmHg
  • Moderate: PaO₂ 60-79 mmHg
  • Severe: PaO₂ 50-59 mmHg
  • Very severe: PaO₂ <50 mmHg
DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA

Diagnostic Criteria (AASLD-AST 2025):

  • Liver disease and/or portal hypertension (Raevens 2022, Fig. 1)
  • IPVDs on bubble echocardiography: microbubbles in the left heart 3 or more cardiac cycles after they appear in the right heart, after 10 mL agitated saline in a peripheral arm vein (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • Alveolar-arterial gradient greater than 15 mmHg (greater than 20 mmHg if age over 64) (AASLD-AST 2025), on an ABG drawn sitting upright on room air (Raevens 2022)
  • No other explanation for the gas exchange defect (Raevens 2022)

Contrast (Bubble) Echocardiography (most sensitive screening test for IPVDs; AASLD-AST 2025):

  • Positive for IPVDs: microbubbles in the left heart 3 or more cycles after the right heart; the guideline sets no upper limit (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • Intracardiac shunt: microbubbles in the left atrium within 3 cycles (Raevens 2022)
  • A positive bubble study alone is not HPS; the A-a gradient criterion must also be met (AASLD-AST 2025)

99mTc-MAA Lung Perfusion Scan: an alternative to echocardiography but less well standardized; quantifies pulmonary and systemic (brain, kidney) uptake but cannot tell an intracardiac from an intrapulmonary shunt (Raevens 2022)

Screening and Workup:

  • Evaluate every liver transplant candidate for HPS. With dyspnea not explained by cardiac dysfunction, platypnea, or orthodeoxia, get pulse oximetry, an ABG, and bubble echocardiography (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • Bubble echocardiography is recommended for screening transplant candidates when available; centers that do not screen routinely should use it for pulmonary symptoms or oxygenation abnormalities (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • After a positive bubble study, pulse oximetry and ABG grade severity and transplant urgency (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • Pulse oximetry misses HPS: SaO₂ of 94% had 22.1% sensitivity for severe HPS; an ABG is mandatory (Raevens 2022)
  • Chest imaging in all transplant candidates (AASLD-AST 2025); the radiograph is usually normal or shows increased lower-lobe markings (Raevens 2022)
  • PFTs: not routine without lung disease or risk factors (AASLD-AST 2025); reduced DLCO is common in cirrhosis and nonspecific (Raevens 2022)
  • Transthoracic echo also screens for portopulmonary hypertension: RVSP over 45 mmHg or an abnormal right ventricle needs right heart catheterization (AASLD-AST 2025)
TREATMENT

No Effective Drug Therapy:

  • Methylene blue, inhaled L-NAME, pentoxifylline, norfloxacin, aspirin, somatostatin, indomethacin, garlic, and mycophenolate showed no clear benefit or contradictory results in case reports and small studies; low-dose sorafenib failed in a randomized pilot trial (Raevens 2022)

Supportive Care:

  • Continuous long-term low-flow oxygen for severe hypoxemia at rest; the only effective supportive therapy (Raevens 2022)
  • Not a transplant candidate and has arteriovenous malformations: coil embolization is a potential palliative treatment (Raevens 2022)

Liver Transplantation (Only Curative Treatment):

  • Refer for transplant evaluation: HPS and portopulmonary hypertension are listed among the events that warrant it (AASLD-AST 2025, Figure 1)
  • Complete resolution in about 95%, mostly within 6 to 12 months; 5-year survival 76%, similar to cirrhosis without HPS (Raevens 2022)
  • No PaO₂ cutoff: transplant is curative, and selected patients with PaO₂ under 50 mmHg have been transplanted successfully; ECMO can support oxygenation around transplant (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • Very severe HPS: older UNOS data showed worse outcomes at PaO₂ of 44 mmHg or less; in data through 2019, overall survival did not differ by PaO₂ group, and survival under 45 mmHg was lower but still good (median 11.5 years vs 14.1 years at 45 to under 50 mmHg); refer to a high-volume center (Raevens 2022)
  • Severe post-transplant hypoxemia (100% FiO₂ needed to keep saturation at 85% or more) occurs in 6%-21%, with 45% peri-transplant mortality; options include Trendelenburg position, inhaled epoprostenol, inhaled nitric oxide, IV methylene blue, embolization, and ECMO as a last resort (Raevens 2022)

MELD Exception:

  • All 4 required: ascites, varices, splenomegaly, or thrombocytopenia; a shunt on contrast echo or lung scan; PaO₂ under 60 mmHg on room air within 30 days before the request; no clinically significant primary lung disease (OPTN Policy 9.5.E)
  • Adult score: 3 points below the median MELD at transplant (MMaT). The exception lasts 90 days; each extension needs PaO₂ still under 60 mmHg within 30 days (OPTN Policy 9.4, 9.5.E)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Screen, do not wait for symptoms: HPS is often asymptomatic; platypnea and orthodeoxia occur in only 18%-20%, so their absence does not exclude HPS (Raevens 2022)
  • Bubble study plus ABG: HPS needs a delayed bubble study (3 or more cycles) and an A-a gradient over 15 mmHg (over 20 if older than 64) (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • Pulse oximetry is not enough: sitting SaO₂ in HPS averaged 96%, only 2% below patients without HPS; get an ABG (Raevens 2022)
  • HPS vs portopulmonary hypertension: HPS is vascular dilatation with hypoxemia; portopulmonary hypertension is vasoconstriction and remodeling, screened by RVSP over 45 mmHg on echo and confirmed by right heart catheterization (AASLD-AST 2025)
  • Transplant cures: no PaO₂ cutoff bars transplant (AASLD-AST 2025); PaO₂ under 60 mmHg qualifies for MELD exception points (OPTN Policy 9.5.E)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Methylene Blue

327. CONTRAST-INDUCED NEPHROPATHY (CIN)

Contrast-Associated AKI • Prevention is Key
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: AKI occurring within 48-72 hours of contrast exposure

  • Increase in serum creatinine ≥0.5 mg/dL OR ≥25% from baseline
  • Peak creatinine typically at 3-5 days
  • Usually recovers within 7-14 days

Risk Factors:

  • Pre-existing CKD (eGFR <60): Most important risk factor
  • Diabetes mellitus (especially with CKD)
  • Heart failure, hypotension
  • Volume depletion
  • Age >75
  • High contrast volume (>100-150 mL or >3× eGFR mL)
  • Multiple contrast exposures within 72 hours
  • Intra-arterial > IV contrast
  • High-osmolar > low-osmolar > iso-osmolar contrast

Clinical Course:

  • Usually non-oliguric
  • Creatinine peaks day 3-5, returns to baseline by day 7-14
  • Dialysis rarely needed (~1%)
  • May accelerate progression of underlying CKD
RISK ASSESSMENT

Mehran Risk Score (for PCI):

  • Hypotension: 5 points
  • IABP: 5 points
  • CHF: 5 points
  • Age >75: 4 points
  • Anemia: 3 points
  • Diabetes: 3 points
  • Contrast volume (1 point per 100 mL)
  • eGFR 40-60: 2 points; 20-40: 4 points; <20: 6 points

Risk Categories:

  • Low risk (≤5): CIN risk 7.5%
  • Moderate (6-10): CIN risk 14%
  • High (11-15): CIN risk 26%
  • Very high (≥16): CIN risk 57%
PREVENTION PROTOCOL

1. Volume Expansion (Most Important):

  • Isotonic saline: 1-1.5 mL/kg/hr for 6-12 hours before AND after contrast
  • Alternative: Sodium bicarbonate 154 mEq/L at 3 mL/kg/hr × 1 hour before, then 1 mL/kg/hr × 6 hours after
  • IV hydration superior to oral

2. Minimize Contrast Volume:

  • Use lowest effective dose
  • Target: contrast volume (mL) < 3× eGFR
  • Use iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast agents

3. Hold Nephrotoxins:

  • NSAIDs, aminoglycosides
  • Hold metformin (risk of lactic acidosis if AKI develops — restart after 48h if creatinine stable)

4. Interventions NOT Proven Beneficial:

  • N-acetylcysteine (NAC): No longer recommended (PRESERVE trial negative)
  • Prophylactic dialysis: Not beneficial
  • Fenoldopam, theophylline: Not effective

5. Special Considerations:

  • Emergency procedures: Don't delay for hydration if life-threatening indication
  • CKD + urgent CT: Benefit of diagnosis often outweighs CIN risk
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Hydration is prevention: IV saline before and after contrast is the most effective strategy
  • NAC doesn't work: PRESERVE trial showed no benefit — stop ordering it
  • Don't delay necessary imaging: Risk of missed diagnosis often exceeds CIN risk
  • Peaks day 3-5: If creatinine still rising at day 7, consider other causes
  • Metformin is a passenger: Hold it because of lactic acidosis risk IF CIN develops, not because it causes CIN
  • CIN vs atheroemboli: CIN improves by day 7-14; atheroemboli progressively worsens

328. ACUTE INTERSTITIAL NEPHRITIS (AIN)

Drug-Induced Tubulointerstitial Disease • Eosinophiluria
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Triad (Present in <10%): Fever, rash, eosinophilia

More Common: AKI without classic triad features

Symptoms:

  • Often asymptomatic except for rising creatinine
  • Flank pain, arthralgias, low-grade fever
  • Maculopapular rash (especially with beta-lactams)

Causes:

  • Drugs (70-75%):
    • Antibiotics: Beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, rifampin
    • NSAIDs: Can occur after months of use; often without systemic symptoms
    • PPIs: Increasingly recognized; latency can be months
    • Checkpoint inhibitors: Ipilimumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab
    • Others: Allopurinol, phenytoin, diuretics
  • Infections (15%): Legionella, Leptospira, CMV, EBV, Streptococcus
  • Autoimmune: Sarcoidosis, Sjögren's, TINU syndrome, SLE
  • Idiopathic

Latency Period:

  • Antibiotics: Days to weeks
  • NSAIDs: Weeks to months
  • PPIs: Weeks to months (median 10-11 weeks)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Urinalysis:

  • WBC casts (hallmark)
  • Sterile pyuria
  • Hematuria (usually microscopic)
  • Mild-moderate proteinuria (<1 g/day, unless NSAID-associated)

Eosinophiluria:

  • Urine eosinophils by Hansel stain (Wright stain less sensitive)
  • Sensitivity only 40-60% — ABSENCE does NOT rule out AIN
  • Not specific (also seen in UTI, prostatitis, GN, atheroemboli)

Labs:

  • Peripheral eosinophilia (present in ~35%)
  • Elevated IgE (sometimes)
  • FENa may be elevated (tubular dysfunction)

Kidney Biopsy (Gold Standard):

  • Interstitial edema and inflammatory infiltrate
  • Lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils
  • Tubulitis (inflammatory cells invading tubular epithelium)
  • Consider if diagnosis uncertain or no improvement with drug withdrawal

Gallium-67 Scan: Increased renal uptake; rarely used now

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

1. Remove Offending Agent:

  • Most important intervention
  • Review ALL medications including OTC and supplements

2. Supportive Care:

  • Avoid nephrotoxins
  • Monitor creatinine for improvement

3. Corticosteroids (Controversial):

  • Consider if: No improvement 3-7 days after drug withdrawal, severe AKI, biopsy-proven AIN
  • Regimen: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) × 2-4 weeks, then taper over 4-8 weeks
  • Earlier steroid initiation (<2 weeks) may improve outcomes
  • Benefit less clear with prolonged AKI or chronic changes on biopsy

4. Checkpoint Inhibitor AIN:

  • Higher dose steroids often needed
  • Prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day
  • May need to discontinue immunotherapy depending on severity

Prognosis:

  • Most recover with drug withdrawal ± steroids
  • ~40% have incomplete recovery (residual CKD)
  • Poor prognostic factors: Prolonged AKI, interstitial fibrosis on biopsy
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Classic triad is rare: Fever + rash + eosinophilia present in <10% — don't rely on it
  • Eosinophiluria is insensitive: Absence does NOT rule out AIN
  • PPIs are underrecognized: Can cause AIN after months of use; increasing reports
  • WBC casts are key: Suggest tubulointerstitial inflammation
  • Early steroids may help: Consider if no improvement within 3-7 days of drug withdrawal
  • NSAID-AIN is different: Often has nephrotic-range proteinuria and lacks systemic symptoms
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Prednisone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Urinalysis, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Proteinuria

329. CPPD (Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease)

Pseudogout • Chondrocalcinosis
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Clinical Phenotypes:

  • Acute CPP Crystal Arthritis (Pseudogout):
    • Acute monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis
    • Knee most common (>50%), also wrist, ankle, shoulder
    • Mimics gout or septic arthritis
  • Chronic CPP Crystal Inflammatory Arthritis:
    • Resembles rheumatoid arthritis
    • Symmetric polyarthritis, morning stiffness
  • Osteoarthritis with CPPD:
    • Accelerated OA in atypical joints (wrists, MCPs, shoulders)
  • Asymptomatic Chondrocalcinosis: Incidental radiographic finding

Triggers for Acute Attacks:

  • Surgery, illness, trauma
  • Similar triggers to gout flares

Associated Conditions (Screen if <55 years or polyarticular):

  • Hyperparathyroidism
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypophosphatasia
  • Familial/hereditary CPPD
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Synovial Fluid Analysis (Gold Standard):

  • CPP crystals: Rhomboid or rod-shaped
  • Weakly positive birefringence under polarized light (blue when parallel to compensator axis)
  • Inflammatory fluid: WBC 15,000-30,000/μL (can be higher)
  • Always rule out septic arthritis (can coexist!)

Imaging:

  • X-ray — Chondrocalcinosis:
    • Linear calcifications in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage
    • Best seen: Knee menisci, triangular fibrocartilage of wrist, pubic symphysis
  • Ultrasound: Hyperechoic deposits within cartilage
  • CT: More sensitive for calcifications

Metabolic Workup (if <55 or polyarticular):

  • Calcium, PTH (hyperparathyroidism)
  • Iron studies, ferritin (hemochromatosis)
  • Magnesium
  • Alkaline phosphatase (hypophosphatasia)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Acute Attack:

  • NSAIDs: First-line if no contraindications
  • Colchicine: 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg one hour later (same as gout dosing)
  • Intra-articular corticosteroids: Effective for monoarticular disease
  • Systemic corticosteroids: Prednisone 30-40 mg/day × 5-7 days if NSAIDs/colchicine contraindicated
  • IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra): For refractory cases

Prophylaxis:

  • Low-dose colchicine 0.6 mg daily or BID
  • Low-dose NSAIDs if tolerated

Key Differences from Gout:

  • NO urate-lowering therapy equivalent for CPPD
  • Cannot dissolve existing CPP crystite deposits
  • Focus on treating acute attacks and prophylaxis

Treat Underlying Metabolic Condition:

  • Parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism
  • Phlebotomy for hemochromatosis
  • Magnesium replacement
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Weakly positive birefringence: Blue when parallel (vs gout: strongly negative, yellow when parallel)
  • Knee and wrist: Most common joints (gout favors 1st MTP)
  • No "allopurinol equivalent": Can't dissolve CPP crystals; only treat attacks and prevent recurrence
  • Screen for metabolic causes: Especially if young (<55) or polyarticular — check PTH, iron, Mg
  • Chondrocalcinosis ≠ CPPD disease: Many patients with radiographic CC are asymptomatic
  • Can coexist with septic arthritis: Always send fluid for culture; crystals don't rule out infection
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Indomethacin, 💊 Colchicine, 💊 Prednisone
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Synovial Fluid Analysis, 🔬 Hypercalcemia, 🔬 Hypomagnesemia

330. ANGIOEDEMA

Bradykinin vs Histamine-Mediated • ACEi-Induced
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Localized, non-pitting edema of deep dermis, subcutaneous tissue, or submucosa

Locations:

  • Face (lips, eyelids, tongue)
  • Oropharynx, larynx (AIRWAY EMERGENCY)
  • Extremities, genitalia
  • GI tract (abdominal pain, nausea; can mimic a surgical abdomen)

Types (ED consensus 2014):

  • Histamine-Mediated (Mast Cell):
    • Often with urticaria; usually resolves within 24-48 h
    • Pruritic
    • Responds to antihistamines, epinephrine, corticosteroids
    • Causes: Allergic reactions (drugs, foods, latex, insect stings), chronic spontaneous urticaria; most idiopathic angioedema
  • Bradykinin-Mediated:
    • NO urticaria; firm, non-pruritic swelling; attacks typically last 2-5 days
    • No response to antihistamines or corticosteroids; poor response to epinephrine
    • Causes: ACE inhibitors (ARBs less often; JTF 2013), HAE (card 187), acquired C1-INH deficiency

ACE Inhibitor-Induced Angioedema:

  • 0.1%-0.7% of ACE inhibitor users (JTF 2013)
  • Higher risk: African American patients (substantially higher; JTF 2013); immunosuppressant use (ED consensus 2014)
  • Risk highest in the first 30 days, but persists beyond 1 year of use (ED consensus 2014)
  • Mostly lips and tongue (ED consensus 2014)

Hereditary and Acquired C1-INH Deficiency:

  • HAE type I (about 85%): low C1-INH antigen and function; type II (about 15%): normal or high antigen, low function (JTF 2013)
  • HAE with normal C1-INH: normal C4 and C1-INH; subtypes defined by mutation (US HAEA 2020)
  • HAE: family history in most (JTF 2013); half have attacks by age 10 (ED consensus 2014). Full management: card 187
  • Acquired C1-INH deficiency: not familial, usually after age 40; C1-INH consumed by a lymphoproliferative disorder and/or an anti-C1-INH antibody (ED consensus 2014)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Differentiation (ED consensus 2014):

Feature Histamine-Mediated Bradykinin-Mediated
Urticaria Often present Absent
Pruritus Yes No
Duration 24-48 h 2-5 days
Response to epinephrine Yes Poor
Response to antihistamines, corticosteroids Yes No

Labs: No ED test guides immediate treatment; draw C4 (HAE) and tryptase (anaphylaxis) during the attack for follow-up (ED consensus 2014)

  • C4, C1-INH antigen, C1-INH function: test together; HAE-C1INH = antigen or function <50% of normal plus low C4 (US HAEA 2020)
  • C1q: low in 80% of acquired C1-INH deficiency, rarely low in HAE (US HAEA 2020)
  • ACE inhibitor angioedema: C4 and C1-INH tests normal (WAO 2025)

Airway Assessment (ED consensus 2014): Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy, if immediately available, for any tongue involvement or upper airway complaints; neck imaging has limited utility and delays observation

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Airway Management (Priority; ED consensus 2014):

  • Assess for stridor, voice changes, tongue swelling; monitor oxygen saturation and cardiac status
  • Oxygen, nasal trumpet, bag-valve-mask: temporizing only, not a substitute for intubation if the airway is at risk
  • Decide on intubation from prior history, airway anatomy, comorbidities, and nasopharyngeal findings; call anesthesia and ENT early (Practical)
  • Before intubating: a rescue plan with alternative airway devices and the means to perform a cricothyrotomy

Histamine-Mediated Angioedema: H1 and H2 antagonists and corticosteroids; epinephrine for anaphylaxis or a life-threatening presentation (ED consensus 2014). Doses as on card 69:

  • Epinephrine 1 mg/mL IM, anterolateral thigh: 0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg (usual adult 0.3-0.5 mg) (JTF 2023)
  • H1: Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg IV (JTF 2015); label 10-50 mg IV, max 400 mg/day
  • H2: Famotidine 20 mg IV (label dose for GI indications; off-label here)
  • Corticosteroid: Methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg up to 125 mg IV (JTF 2015); label initial dose 10-40 mg IV

ACEi-Induced Angioedema:

  • Stop all ACE inhibitors (JTF 2013; ED consensus 2014); recurrence risk persists for at least 6 weeks (JTF 2013)
  • Standard therapy (epinephrine, antihistamines, corticosteroids): generally not effective but not contraindicated; give it when the cause is unknown (ED consensus 2014)
  • Icatibant: FDA-approved for HAE only (label). A small phase 2 RCT (27 patients) favored it (Bas 2015), but a multicenter RCT (121 patients) found it no better than placebo for at least moderately severe upper airway ACE inhibitor angioedema (Sinert 2017)
  • C1-INH concentrate, ecallantide: off-label; data limited for non-HAE patients (ED consensus 2014)
  • Fresh frozen plasma: the only readily available ED option; risks of viral transmission, allergic reaction, volume overload (ED consensus 2014)
  • ARBs afterward: modest risk of recurrence, but most patients can use ARBs safely (JTF 2013)

Hereditary Angioedema, Acute Attack (full dosing and prophylaxis: card 187):

  • Treat every attack early; first-line IV C1-INH, icatibant, or sebetralstat (WAO 2025)
  • Plasma-derived C1-INH (Berinert): 20 IU/kg IV (label)
  • Icatibant (Firazyr): 30 mg SC; adults 18 yr and older (label)
  • Sebetralstat (Ekterly): 600 mg PO; 12 yr and older (label)
  • Ecallantide (Kalbitor): 30 mg SC; healthcare professional only, BOXED WARNING for anaphylaxis (label)
  • Cinryze is labeled for routine prophylaxis, not for attacks (label)

HAE Prophylaxis: First-line SC pdC1-INH, lanadelumab, berotralstat, garadacimab, or donidalorsen (WAO 2025); danazol second-line; doses on card 187

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • No urticaria = think bradykinin: ACE inhibitor, HAE, or acquired C1-INH deficiency; poor response to standard allergic treatment (ED consensus 2014)
  • ACE inhibitor angioedema after years of use: risk is highest in the first 30 days but persists beyond 1 year (ED consensus 2014)
  • Cause unknown: give epinephrine, then H1 antagonists and corticosteroids; they are not contraindicated in bradykinin angioedema (ED consensus 2014)
  • Labs during the attack: C4 with C1-INH antigen and function (US HAEA 2020); tryptase if anaphylaxis is possible (ED consensus 2014)
  • Icatibant for ACE inhibitor angioedema: the larger RCT found no benefit over placebo (Sinert 2017); stop the drug and protect the airway
  • ARBs after ACE inhibitor angioedema: modest recurrence risk; most patients tolerate them (JTF 2013)
⚠️ ESCALATE TO ICU IF:
  • Lingual edema (Ishoo stage III) or laryngeal edema (stage IV) (ED consensus 2014)
  • Respiratory distress or any airway intervention needed (ED consensus 2014)
  • HAE attack involving the upper airway: on-demand therapy at once (WAO 2025; card 187)
✓ DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Face, lip, or soft palate edema only (Ishoo stage I or II), normal larynx on nasopharyngoscopy: home or observation (ED consensus 2014)
  • Not with edema at more than 3 of: lips, anterior tongue, floor of mouth, soft palate, base of tongue, larynx (ED consensus 2014)
  • Mild to moderate cases admitted to a ward can often go home within 24 h (ED consensus 2014)
  • ACE inhibitor stopped and recorded as an allergy; alternative antihypertensive arranged (Practical)
  • Follow-up with primary care or an angioedema specialist, with the C4 and tryptase results (ED consensus 2014)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Epinephrine, 💊 Diphenhydramine, 💊 Methylprednisolone, 💊 Famotidine

331. TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury)

Non-Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema • Antibody-Mediated
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Acute lung injury occurring within 6 hours of transfusion, not explained by other ALI risk factors

Symptoms:

  • Acute dyspnea, hypoxemia
  • Fever, chills (common)
  • Hypotension (more common than hypertension)
  • Typically occurs 1-2 hours into or after transfusion

Diagnostic Criteria:

  • Acute onset (within 6 hours of transfusion)
  • Hypoxemia: PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤300 OR SpO₂ <90% on room air
  • Bilateral infiltrates on CXR
  • No evidence of left atrial hypertension (PAOP ≤18 or no clinical evidence of volume overload)
  • No pre-existing ALI before transfusion

Pathophysiology:

  • Immune TRALI: Donor antibodies (anti-HLA or anti-HNA) react with recipient leukocytes
  • Non-immune TRALI: Bioactive lipids in stored blood products
  • Results in neutrophil activation and pulmonary capillary leak

High-Risk Products:

  • Products with high plasma content: FFP, platelets, whole blood
  • Risk reduced with male-only plasma donors (fewer HLA antibodies)
TREATMENT PROTOCOL

Immediate Actions:

  • Stop transfusion immediately
  • Supportive care with oxygen
  • Mechanical ventilation if needed (lung-protective strategy)

Supportive Care:

  • Oxygen supplementation
  • Intubation/mechanical ventilation for severe hypoxemia
  • Vasopressors for hypotension (not volume — avoid fluid overload)

NOT Beneficial:

  • Diuretics (not cardiogenic — may worsen hypotension)
  • Steroids (no proven benefit)

Prognosis:

  • Mortality 5-10% (lower than ARDS from other causes)
  • Most improve within 48-96 hours with supportive care
  • Usually no long-term pulmonary sequelae

Reporting:

  • Report to blood bank immediately
  • Donor testing for HLA/HNA antibodies
  • Implicated donor may be deferred from future donations
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Within 6 hours: TRALI occurs during or within 6 hours of transfusion
  • TRALI vs TACO: TRALI = hypotension, non-cardiogenic; TACO = hypertension, volume overload
  • No diuretics: Not cardiogenic edema — diuretics may worsen hypotension
  • Usually resolves: Most patients recover within 48-96 hours
  • Report to blood bank: Critical for donor management and future prevention
  • Plasma-rich products: Higher risk with FFP, platelets than PRBCs
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids
↑ Back to Table of Contents

332. TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload)

Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema from Volume Overload
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Acute pulmonary edema due to volume overload from transfusion

Symptoms:

  • Acute dyspnea, orthopnea
  • Hypertension (key differentiator from TRALI)
  • Tachycardia
  • Elevated JVP
  • Typically occurs during or within 6-12 hours of transfusion

Diagnostic Criteria:

  • Acute or worsening respiratory distress within 12 hours of transfusion
  • Evidence of positive fluid balance
  • Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP
  • Evidence of left heart failure (elevated PAOP, response to diuretics)
  • Bilateral infiltrates on CXR

Risk Factors:

  • Pre-existing heart failure
  • Renal insufficiency
  • Age >70
  • Low albumin
  • Rapid transfusion rate
  • Large transfusion volume
  • Positive fluid balance
DIFFERENTIATING TACO vs TRALI
Feature TACO TRALI
Blood pressure Hypertension Hypotension
JVP Elevated Normal/low
BNP Elevated (>1.5× baseline) Normal or mildly elevated
Response to diuretics Yes No
Fever Uncommon Common
Mechanism Volume overload Antibody-mediated
TREATMENT & PREVENTION

Immediate Treatment:

  • Stop or slow transfusion
  • Sit patient upright
  • IV diuretics: Furosemide 20-40 mg IV
  • Supplemental oxygen
  • Non-invasive ventilation if needed

Prevention Strategies:

  • Slower transfusion rate: 1-2 mL/kg/hr in high-risk patients
  • Smaller aliquots: Split units, transfuse over longer time
  • Prophylactic diuretics: Furosemide between units in high-risk patients
  • Restrictive transfusion: Transfuse only when necessary
  • Monitor fluid balance

Prognosis:

  • Usually resolves with diuresis within 12-24 hours
  • Mortality <5% with appropriate treatment
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • TACO is more common than TRALI: Most common cause of transfusion-related death
  • Hypertension = TACO: Key differentiator from TRALI (hypotensive)
  • Diuretics work: Unlike TRALI, TACO responds to diuresis
  • BNP helps differentiate: Elevated in TACO, normal/mildly elevated in TRALI
  • Prevention is key: Slow transfusion, prophylactic diuretics in high-risk patients
  • Can coexist: Some patients have features of both TACO and TRALI
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide
↑ Back to Table of Contents

333. ENDEMIC FUNGAL INFECTIONS

Histoplasmosis • Blastomycosis • Coccidioidomycosis
GEOGRAPHIC DISTRIBUTION

Histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum):

  • Ohio and Mississippi River valleys
  • Soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings
  • Cave exploration, demolition of old buildings

Blastomycosis (Blastomyces dermatitidis):

  • Great Lakes, Ohio/Mississippi River valleys, Southeast
  • Moist soil, decaying vegetation near waterways

Coccidioidomycosis (Coccidioides immitis/posadasii):

  • Southwestern US (Arizona, California Central Valley), Northern Mexico
  • "Valley fever"
  • Dust storms, construction, earthquakes
CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS

Histoplasmosis:

  • Acute pulmonary: Self-limited flu-like illness; may see hilar lymphadenopathy
  • Chronic cavitary: Upper lobe disease resembling TB; in patients with COPD
  • Progressive disseminated: Immunocompromised (AIDS, TNF inhibitors); hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, adrenal involvement

Blastomycosis:

  • Pulmonary: Pneumonia with mass-like lesions (can mimic malignancy)
  • Skin: Verrucous or ulcerative lesions (papulopustules → crusted nodules)
  • Bone: Osteomyelitis (vertebrae, ribs, long bones)
  • GU: Prostatitis, epididymitis
  • Can occur in immunocompetent hosts

Coccidioidomycosis:

  • Primary pulmonary: "Valley fever" — fever, cough, chest pain, arthralgias
  • Pulmonary nodules/cavities: Can be incidental findings
  • Disseminated: Skin, bones, meninges; higher risk in immunocompromised, pregnant women, Filipino/African American descent
  • Meningitis: Most serious complication; chronic basilar meningitis
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Histoplasmosis:

  • Urine/serum Histoplasma antigen: Sensitive for disseminated disease and acute pulmonary
  • Serology: Antibodies (complement fixation, immunodiffusion); less useful in immunocompromised
  • Culture/histopath: Small intracellular yeasts in macrophages

Blastomycosis:

  • Culture: Gold standard but slow (2-4 weeks)
  • Direct visualization: Broad-based budding yeast (8-15 μm)
  • Urine Blastomyces antigen: Cross-reacts with Histoplasma

Coccidioidomycosis:

  • Serology: IgM (early), IgG (complement fixation titers correlate with disease severity)
  • Culture: HAZARDOUS — alert lab (biosafety concern)
  • Direct visualization: Spherules with endospores
TREATMENT

Histoplasmosis:

  • Mild-moderate acute: Observation or itraconazole × 6-12 weeks
  • Moderate-severe/disseminated: Amphotericin B (liposomal) × 1-2 weeks → itraconazole × 12 months
  • AIDS patients: Lifelong suppression with itraconazole until immune reconstitution

Blastomycosis:

  • Mild-moderate pulmonary: Itraconazole × 6-12 months
  • Severe/disseminated/CNS: Amphotericin B → itraconazole × 12 months
  • Always treat (higher mortality than other endemic mycoses)

Coccidioidomycosis:

  • Primary pulmonary (mild): Observation in healthy hosts OR fluconazole if symptoms >2 months
  • Severe/disseminated: Fluconazole (high dose) or itraconazole; amphotericin B for severe
  • Meningitis: Fluconazole 400-1200 mg/day LIFELONG (relapse common)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Geography matters: Ask about travel/residence in endemic areas
  • Histoplasma antigen: Best test for disseminated disease; also useful for monitoring treatment
  • Blasto skin lesions: Verrucous/ulcerative — can mimic squamous cell carcinoma
  • Cocci meningitis = lifelong azole: Relapse is common; don't stop therapy
  • Broad-based budding: Classic for Blastomycosis (vs narrow-based in other yeasts)
  • Alert lab for Cocci: Highly infectious in culture — biosafety hazard
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Voriconazole, 💊 Fluconazole, 💊 Liposomal AmB
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Beta-D-Glucan, 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 LDH

334. PULMONARY HYPERTENSION

WHO Groups 1-5 • Right Heart Catheterization Required
DEFINITION & CLASSIFICATION

Definition: Mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) >20 mmHg at rest by right heart catheterization

Clinical Classification (7th WSPH 2024):

  • Group 1, Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH):
    • Idiopathic PAH (vasoreactivity responders and non-responders)
    • Heritable (BMPR2 mutations)
    • Drug/toxin-induced (methamphetamines, anorexigens)
    • Associated: CTD (scleroderma), HIV, portal hypertension, CHD, schistosomiasis
    • PAH with features of venous/capillary involvement (PVOD/PCH)
  • Group 2, Left Heart Disease: HFpEF, HFrEF, valvular disease
  • Group 3, Lung Disease/Hypoxia: COPD, ILD, OSA, high altitude
  • Group 4, Chronic Thromboembolic (CTEPH): Organized thrombi; potentially curable
  • Group 5, Multifactorial: Sarcoidosis, hematologic disorders, metabolic
  • Prevalence: Groups 2 and 3 account for 90-95% of PH worldwide

Hemodynamic Definitions (7th WSPH 2024; ESC/ERS 2022):

  • Pre-capillary PH: mPAP >20, PAWP ≤15, PVR >2 WU (Groups 1, 3, 4, 5)
  • Isolated post-capillary PH: mPAP >20, PAWP >15, PVR ≤2 WU (Group 2)
  • Combined post- and pre-capillary PH: mPAP >20, PAWP >15, PVR >2 WU
  • Exercise PH: Normal resting mPAP with an mPAP/cardiac output slope >3 mmHg/L/min
  • Borderline values (mPAP 20-25, PVR 2-3 WU): interpret with comorbidities; the PVR >2 WU threshold comes mainly from non-PAH cohorts (ALA-PHA 2025)
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Symptoms:

  • Dyspnea on exertion (most common, early)
  • Fatigue, weakness
  • Chest pain (RV ischemia)
  • Syncope, near-syncope (ominous; suggests severe disease)
  • Peripheral edema, ascites (right heart failure)

Physical Exam:

  • Loud P2, right-sided S4
  • Tricuspid regurgitation murmur
  • JVD, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema
  • Signs of underlying disease (scleroderma, COPD)
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Evaluation:

  • Echocardiogram: Estimates RVSP, RV function, left heart disease
  • PFTs: Assess for lung disease
  • V/Q scan: Screen for CTEPH; a negative V/Q scan excludes significant thromboembolic disease (7th WSPH 2024)
  • CT chest: Parenchymal lung disease, PA enlargement
  • 6-minute walk test: Functional assessment
  • BNP/NT-proBNP: Prognostic

Right Heart Catheterization (Required for Diagnosis):

  • Confirms diagnosis
  • Differentiates pre- vs post-capillary
  • Vasoreactivity testing: Only in idiopathic, heritable, or drug-associated PAH, at a PH center; inhaled nitric oxide or inhaled iloprost (IV epoprostenol if these are unavailable) (ESC/ERS 2022). ESC/ERS rejects adenosine; ALA-PHA 2025 does not recommend it but would not reject it outright
  • Positive: mPAP falls ≥10 mmHg to ≤40 mmHg with increased or unchanged cardiac output (ESC/ERS 2022)

Evaluate for Underlying Causes:

  • ANA, Scl-70 (scleroderma)
  • HIV testing
  • LFTs (portal hypertension)
  • Liver transplant candidates (AASLD-AST 2025, strong): RVSP >45 mmHg or abnormal RV structure or function on TTE requires RHC for portopulmonary hypertension; on optimized PH therapy, mPAP 45 mmHg with PVR >3 WU should be considered a contraindication to transplant
  • Sleep study (OSA)
TREATMENT

Hospitalized Patient with Acute Right Heart Failure (ESC/ERS 2022 unless stated):

  • Involve the PH center; treat triggers (infection, arrhythmia, anemia)
  • Most patients need a negative fluid balance to unload the RV
  • Low cardiac output: dobutamine or milrinone. Keep mean systemic BP >60 mmHg; norepinephrine or vasopressin for persistent hypotension
  • Avoid intubation whenever possible: high risk of hemodynamic deterioration and death
  • Monitor NT-proBNP, troponin, echocardiography; upper-body central line for central venous pressure and ScvO2
  • Never interrupt IV/SQ prostacyclin or make large sudden dose cuts: rebound PH can be life-threatening (labels; 7th WSPH 2024). Temporary peripheral IV is allowed until central access is restored (epoprostenol label)
  • Mechanical circulatory support as a bridge to transplant or recovery in selected patients; transfer if unavailable

General Measures (ESC/ERS 2022):

  • Diuretics for RV failure with fluid retention
  • Oxygen if PaO2 <60 mmHg (or SaO2 <92%) on two occasions, to keep PaO2 above 60 mmHg; nocturnal oxygen for sleep-related desaturation
  • Avoid pregnancy; counsel women of childbearing potential at diagnosis
  • Supervised exercise training
  • Vaccinate against influenza, pneumococcus, SARS-CoV-2; correct iron deficiency

Vasoreactivity-Positive Patients (ESC/ERS 2022):

  • High-dose calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, diltiazem, amlodipine) only after a positive test. Never start them without a test or after a negative test: severe hypotension, syncope, RV failure
  • Continue high-dose CCB only in WHO-FC I or II with marked hemodynamic improvement; otherwise add PAH therapy and consider continuing the CCB
  • Responders are a small minority of PAH (classically about 10%, Practical)

PAH-Specific Therapies:

  • Endothelin receptor antagonists: Ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan
  • PDE-5 inhibitors: Sildenafil, tadalafil
  • Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator: Riociguat
  • Prostacyclin pathway: Epoprostenol (IV), treprostinil (IV/SQ/inhaled/oral), iloprost (inhaled), selexipag (oral)
  • Activin signalling inhibitor: Sotatercept (SQ; FDA approved March 2024)

Initial Therapy and Escalation (7th WSPH 2024; ALA-PHA 2025):

  • Not high risk: ERA + PDE5i
  • High risk: ERA + PDE5i + IV/SQ prostacyclin; discuss lung transplant referral
  • Reassess at 3-4 months and often after. Intermediate-low risk: add sotatercept or an oral/inhaled prostacyclin pathway agent, or switch PDE5i to riociguat. Intermediate-high or high risk: add IV/SQ prostacyclin (do not delay it for sotatercept) or sotatercept
  • Sotatercept: Add-on, not first-line. Check hemoglobin and platelets for the first 5 doses and periodically; watch for bleeding and telangiectasia
  • Do not combine riociguat with a PDE5i (ESC/ERS 2022)

Group 2 (Left Heart): Treat the underlying heart disease; drugs approved for PAH are not recommended in PH due to left heart disease (ESC/ERS 2022)

Group 3 (Lung Disease): Optimize underlying disease; supplemental O₂. PH with ILD: inhaled treprostinil may be considered; ambrisentan is not recommended in PH with IPF, and riociguat is not recommended in PH with idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (ESC/ERS 2022)

Group 4 (CTEPH): Lifelong anticoagulation; review by a CTEPH team. Pulmonary endarterectomy is the treatment of choice; balloon pulmonary angioplasty or riociguat if inoperable or for residual PH after surgery (ESC/ERS 2022)

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • RHC is required: Echo suggests PH, but diagnosis requires right heart catheterization
  • Pre-capillary PH: mPAP >20, PAWP ≤15, PVR >2 WU (7th WSPH 2024)
  • Left heart disease: PAH drugs are not recommended in Group 2 (ESC/ERS 2022)
  • V/Q scan for CTEPH: A negative scan excludes significant thromboembolic disease; CTEPH is potentially curable with surgery
  • Acute RV failure: Diurese to a negative balance, support BP, avoid intubation, never stop IV prostacyclin
  • Syncope is ominous: Indicates severe disease with high mortality
  • Avoid pregnancy: Maternal mortality remains 11-25% in PAH (ESC/ERS 2022)
  • Combination therapy upfront: ERA + PDE5i; triple therapy with IV/SQ prostacyclin if high risk
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Sildenafil, 💊 Furosemide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP, 🔬 Low PaO2, 🔬 Elevated A-a Gradient, 🔬 Elevated D-dimer, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine
↑ Back to Table of Contents

335. OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA (OSA)

Sleep-Disordered Breathing • Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Classic Symptoms:

  • Loud snoring with witnessed apneas
  • Excessive daytime sleepiness
  • Morning headaches
  • Unrefreshing sleep, fatigue
  • Nocturia
  • Cognitive impairment, difficulty concentrating

Screening Tools (screen only; AASM 2017):

  • STOP-Bang: Snoring, Tired, Observed apnea, Pressure (HTN), BMI >35, Age >50, Neck >40 cm, male Gender; 1 point each
  • Score 0-2 low, 3-4 intermediate, 5-8 high risk of OSA (STOP-Bang developers, University Health Network)
  • Epworth Sleepiness Scale: Quantifies daytime sleepiness
  • Questionnaires and prediction tools do not diagnose OSA; confirm with PSG or HSAT (AASM 2017, strong)

Complications:

  • Resistant hypertension
  • Atrial fibrillation (meta-analysis odds ratio 1.71, possibly higher with more severe OSA; ACC/AHA 2023)
  • Stroke, cardiovascular disease
  • Type 2 diabetes
  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS)
  • Motor vehicle accidents

Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) (ATS 2019):

  • BMI >30 kg/m² + awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg at sea level) + sleep-disordered breathing, after excluding other causes of hypoventilation
  • Serum bicarbonate <27 mmol/L makes OHS unlikely when suspicion is not very high; measure arterial blood gases when OHS is strongly suspected
  • Higher mortality than OSA alone, with heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and hospitalization
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Polysomnography (Gold Standard):

  • In-laboratory overnight sleep study
  • Measures AHI, oxygen desaturation, sleep stages, arousals

Home Sleep Apnea Testing (HSAT) (AASM 2017):

  • PSG or HSAT (technically adequate device) for uncomplicated adults with signs and symptoms suggesting moderate to severe OSA
  • HSAT reports the respiratory event index (REI), counted per hour of recording rather than sleep, so it may underestimate severity
  • Negative, inconclusive, or technically inadequate HSAT: perform PSG
  • Use PSG, not HSAT, with significant cardiorespiratory disease, possible respiratory muscle weakness from neuromuscular disease, awake or suspected sleep-related hypoventilation, chronic opioid use, prior stroke, or severe insomnia

Diagnosis (ICSD-3, as stated in AASM 2017):

  • Obstructive events ≥5/hour with typical symptoms (sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, insomnia, waking gasping or choking, loud snoring, witnessed apneas), or ≥15/hour even without symptoms

Severity (AHI on PSG or REI on HSAT):

  • Mild: 5 to <15 events/hour
  • Moderate: 15 to <30 events/hour
  • Severe: ≥30 events/hour

Additional Workup:

  • Suspected OHS: serum bicarbonate; arterial blood gas if suspicion is high (ATS 2019)
  • TFTs if hypothyroidism is suspected; it can worsen OSA (Practical)
  • Echocardiogram if pulmonary hypertension is suspected
TREATMENT

Positive Airway Pressure (First-Line) (AASM 2019):

  • Who to treat: PAP for OSA with excessive sleepiness (strong); suggested with impaired sleep-related quality of life or with hypertension
  • CPAP or auto-titrating CPAP (APAP): Standard ongoing treatment; start with APAP at home or in-laboratory titration if no significant comorbidities
  • Bilevel PAP: Not for routine OSA (CPAP or APAP suggested over bilevel). Stable OHS with severe OSA also starts with CPAP; bilevel NIV after hospitalization for respiratory failure with suspected OHS (ATS 2019)
  • Education at PAP start (strong); behavioral, troubleshooting, and telemonitoring support early on
  • Follow-up testing: PSG or HSAT to confirm response to non-PAP treatments; consider after a 10-20% weight change (AASM 2021)

Alternatives (If PAP Not Tolerated or Declined):

  • Oral appliances: For PAP intolerance or preference for another therapy; custom, titratable device fitted by a qualified dentist; confirm efficacy with follow-up sleep testing (AASM 2015)
  • Positional therapy: Secondary or supplemental therapy for supine-predominant OSA (AASM 2006)
  • Hypoglossal nerve stimulation (Inspire): AHI 15-100 after PAP failure (AHI >15 despite PAP) or intolerance; no complete concentric collapse at the soft palate. Contraindicated if central plus mixed apneas exceed 25% of AHI. Safety and effectiveness data now extend to BMI 40, previously 32 (FDA 2023)

Surgical Referral (AASM 2021):

  • Discuss referral to a sleep surgeon if BMI <40 and PAP is not tolerated or not accepted (strong), or adherence is poor because of pressure side effects
  • Discuss referral to a bariatric surgeon if BMI ≥35 and PAP is not tolerated or not accepted (strong)
  • Major upper airway anatomic abnormality: try PAP first, before upper airway surgery
  • Procedures include upper airway surgery (e.g., uvulopalatopharyngoplasty), maxillomandibular advancement, hypoglossal nerve stimulation

Weight Loss and Lifestyle:

  • Dietary weight loss may lower the AHI in obesity; combine it with a primary OSA treatment (AASM 2006)
  • Avoid alcohol and sedatives before bed (Practical)
  • Sleep position optimization

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Tirzepatide (Zepbound): FDA approved December 2024 for moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity, with diet and physical activity. 2.5 mg SQ weekly for 4 weeks, then increase by 2.5 mg after at least 4 weeks; OSA maintenance 10 mg or 15 mg weekly (label)
  • SURMOUNT-OSA (NEJM 2024): AHI fell 20.0 and 23.8 events/hour more than placebo at 52 weeks (without and with PAP)
  • Contraindicated with personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2; stop when pregnancy is recognized; pulmonary aspiration reported with general anesthesia or deep sedation (label)

Inpatient Considerations (AASM 2025, medically hospitalized adults):

  • Continue home PAP unless contraindicated (aspiration risk, facial trauma); record device type, settings, and mask at admission; reassess settings and oxygen need if the acute illness changes breathing
  • At risk, no diagnosis: Screening (questionnaire or overnight oximetry) is suggested within a pathway to diagnosis and PAP; test once medically stable
  • New diagnosis, or known moderate to severe OSA off treatment: Inpatient PAP suggested
  • Lateral sleeping, head of bed elevation, judicious opioids and sedatives, especially if OSA is untreated
  • Discharge plan: postdischarge testing or sleep medicine follow-up
  • Respiratory failure with suspected OHS: Discharge on NIV until outpatient sleep study and PAP titration, ideally within 3 months of discharge (ATS 2019)
  • AASM 2025 does not cover patients needing NIV for respiratory failure or perioperative care. Perioperative: higher risk of difficult intubation; monitor after surgery (Practical)
CENTRAL SLEEP APNEA (CSA)

Treatment (AASM 2025):

  • Treat contributing conditions first (heart failure, opioids, other medical causes)
  • CPAP suggested. Other options: ASV; acetazolamide; low-flow oxygen in heart failure or at high altitude; bilevel PAP with a backup rate when CSA is not from heart failure. Avoid bilevel PAP without a backup rate
  • ASV in HFrEF: Only at experienced centers with close monitoring (SERVE-HF found harm; AASM pooled trials showed no mortality effect)
  • Transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation (primary or heart failure CSA): consider other treatments first
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Resistant HTN: OSA is a common secondary cause; screen and refer for PSG or HSAT. CPAP can lower BP in resistant HTN with moderate to severe OSA (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • CPAP and outcomes: CPAP treats symptoms and lowers BP, but data do not support it for preventing cardiovascular events or death (AHA/ACC 2025)
  • AF + OSA: Screening for OSA may be reasonable in AF; whether treatment helps maintain sinus rhythm is uncertain (ACC/AHA 2023, 2b)
  • OHS is worse: Awake hypercapnia; serum bicarbonate <27 mmol/L makes OHS unlikely when suspicion is low (ATS 2019)
  • Questionnaires screen, tests diagnose: STOP-Bang 5-8 is high risk, but diagnosis needs PSG or HSAT; a negative HSAT needs PSG (AASM 2017)
  • Continue PAP inpatient: Use the home device and record its settings (AASM 2025)
  • Weight loss: Tirzepatide is FDA approved for moderate to severe OSA with obesity; combine weight loss with a primary OSA treatment (label; AASM 2006)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Acetazolamide
↑ Back to Table of Contents

336. HYPERPARATHYROIDISM

Primary vs Secondary vs Tertiary • Hypercalcemia Workup
CLASSIFICATION

Primary Hyperparathyroidism:

  • Diagnosis: albumin-adjusted serum calcium elevated with intact PTH elevated or inappropriately normal, on two occasions at least 2 weeks apart (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Causes: single adenoma (85%), multigland disease (15%), carcinoma (<1%) (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Differential with high calcium and PTH: familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), thiazides, lithium, ectopic PTH (very rare) (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Normocalcemic PHPT: normal adjusted total and ionized calcium with elevated intact PTH on at least two occasions over 3-6 months, after secondary causes are excluded (5th Workshop 2022)

Secondary Hyperparathyroidism (Practical):

  • Appropriate PTH response to hypocalcemia
  • Causes: CKD (most common), vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption
  • Labs: ↓ or normal calcium, ↑ PTH

Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism (Practical):

  • Autonomous PTH after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism
  • Typically post-renal transplant
  • Labs: ↑ Calcium, ↑ PTH
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

"Stones, Bones, Groans, Thrones, and Psychiatric Overtones" (Practical):

  • Stones: Nephrolithiasis (calcium oxalate/phosphate), nephrocalcinosis
  • Bones: Osteoporosis, osteitis fibrosa cystica (brown tumors), fractures
  • Groans: Abdominal pain, constipation, pancreatitis, peptic ulcer
  • Thrones: Polyuria, polydipsia (nephrogenic DI from hypercalcemia)
  • Psychiatric: Depression, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, anxiety

Many Patients Asymptomatic: discovered on biochemical screening (5th Workshop 2022). No data support routine evaluation for neurocognitive, quality-of-life, or cardiovascular features (5th Workshop 2022)

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Evaluation (5th Workshop 2022):

  • Labs: albumin-adjusted total calcium (ionized if normocalcemic PHPT is considered), phosphorus (low or low-normal: reduced renal phosphate reabsorption), intact PTH, 25OHD, creatinine
  • Skeletal: three-site DXA (lumbar spine, hip, distal 1/3 radius); vertebral fracture assessment or spine X-ray; trabecular bone score if available
  • Renal: eGFR or, preferably, creatinine clearance; 24-hour urine calcium and stone risk factors; imaging for nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis. Urine calcium is unreliable on lithium or thiazides

Key Patterns:

  • Primary HPT: ↑ Ca, ↑ PTH (or inappropriately normal), ↓ phos, ↑ or normal urine Ca (Practical)
  • FHH: may be suspected in younger patients with a urinary calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 and/or a family history of hypercalcemia (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Malignancy: ↑ Ca, ↓ PTH, ↑ PTHrP (Practical; card 34)

Localization (Only If Surgery Is Planned; 5th Workshop 2022):

  • Imaging is not for diagnosis; it locates abnormal glands before surgery
  • High-resolution neck ultrasound, Tc-99m sestamibi subtraction scintigraphy, or contrast 4D-CT
  • 4D-CT after negative or discordant ultrasound and sestamibi (Practical)
TREATMENT

Surgery: recommended to cure asymptomatic PHPT (strong, high-quality evidence; biochemical cure 97.8%) and an option for all patients; by an experienced parathyroid surgeon (5th Workshop 2022)

Indications for Parathyroidectomy (5th Workshop 2022; any one):

  • Symptomatic disease (Practical)
  • Serum calcium >1 mg/dL (0.25 mmol/L) above the upper limit of normal
  • Vertebral fracture on VFA or X-ray, or T-score ≤-2.5 at any site
  • eGFR or creatinine clearance <60 mL/min
  • Nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis on imaging
  • Hypercalciuria (e.g., >250 mg/day in women, >300 mg/day in men)
  • Age <50 (sufficient alone)
  • Not to improve neurocognitive function, quality of life, or cardiovascular indices (evidence inconclusive) (5th Workshop 2022); the American Association of Endocrine Surgeons lists neurocognitive or psychiatric symptoms and cardiovascular disease as indications, on weak evidence (via OpenEvidence)

Surgical Options:

  • Selective (minimally invasive) parathyroidectomy after successful localization, with or without intraoperative PTH monitoring (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Bilateral neck exploration if localization fails or multigland disease (Practical)

Medical Management (If Surgery Not Pursued):

  • No surgical indication: may be followed without drug therapy (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Meets surgical criteria but no surgery (5th Workshop 2022): cinacalcet lowers serum calcium into the normal range (and lowers PTH) but does not improve BMD; alendronate or denosumab to increase BMD; combine with cinacalcet when both are needed
  • Vitamin D: replete to 25OHD >30 ng/mL and below the laboratory upper limit (e.g., <50 ng/mL) (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Adequate hydration, avoid thiazides (Practical)
  • Monitor: calcium and 25OHD yearly; creatinine clearance (preferred over eGFR) yearly; three-site DXA every 1-2 years (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Pregnancy: no bisphosphonates or denosumab; limited data on cinacalcet; consider second-trimester surgery if calcium >11.0 mg/dL (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Severe or symptomatic hypercalcemia: card 34 (Practical)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • PTH should be LOW in hypercalcemia: an elevated or inappropriately normal PTH with high calcium points to primary HPT (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Rule out FHH: calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 (FHH needs no surgery) (5th Workshop 2022; Practical)
  • Surgery is curative: biochemical cure in 97.8% of asymptomatic PHPT in the systematic review (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Hungry bone syndrome: post-parathyroidectomy hypocalcemia as bone takes up calcium (Practical; card 109)
  • Normocalcemic variant: defined above; limited data, so no surgical guidelines yet (5th Workshop 2022)
  • Genetic evaluation (MEN, card 219): consider if <30 years old, multigland disease, family history of hypercalcemia, or a syndromic disease (5th Workshop 2022)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Fluids, 💊 Zoledronic Acid, 💊 Alendronate, 💊 Denosumab
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hypercalcemia, 🔬 Elevated PTH, 🔬 Low eGFR, 🔬 Hypophosphatemia

337. HYPOPARATHYROIDISM

PTH Deficiency • Post-Surgical Hypocalcemia
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Symptoms of Hypocalcemia:

  • Neuromuscular: Paresthesias (perioral, fingertips), muscle cramps, tetany, seizures (Practical)
  • Cardiac: prolonged QT interval, arrhythmia, hypocalcemic heart failure (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Neuropsychiatric: Anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment (Practical)
  • Laryngospasm: Medical emergency (Practical)
  • Chronic complications: nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, renal insufficiency, cataracts, infections; higher all-cause mortality (International Best Practice 2025)

Physical Exam Signs (Practical):

  • Chvostek sign: Facial twitch when tapping facial nerve (anterior to ear)
  • Trousseau sign: Carpal spasm with BP cuff inflated above systolic for 3 minutes (more specific)

Etiology (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025):

  • Post-surgical (most common; about 75% of adult cases): after thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy, neck dissection; transient after removal of a single adenoma until the suppressed glands recover
  • Autoimmune: isolated, or APECED (APS-1, AIRE gene) with mucocutaneous candidiasis and adrenal insufficiency
  • Genetic: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion), GATA3 (HDR syndrome), CASR or GNA11 (autosomal dominant hypocalcemia), GCM2, PTH gene
  • Infiltrative or deposition: granulomatous disease, iron (hemochromatosis), copper (Wilson disease), metastatic disease
  • Radiation
  • Magnesium deficiency or excess (functional): low magnesium causes PTH resistance; high magnesium lowers PTH secretion
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Diagnosis (International Best Practice 2025): low albumin-corrected or ionized calcium with inappropriately normal or low intact PTH on two occasions at least 2 weeks apart. Post-surgical: chronic if present ≥12 months after neck surgery

After Total Thyroidectomy (International Best Practice 2025): PTH 12-24 h after surgery >10 pg/mL (1.05 pmol/L) makes permanent hypoparathyroidism unlikely. If lower, check calcium and PTH within the first week, earlier with symptoms or severe hypocalcemia

Labs (International Best Practice 2025):

  • Low calcium (albumin-corrected or ionized; albumin formulas are less reliable in CKD and severe acid-base disturbance)
  • Low or inappropriately normal PTH (stop biotin >5 mg/day for at least 3 days before testing: it can falsely lower PTH)
  • Supporting findings: elevated phosphorus, increased fractional excretion of calcium, low 1,25(OH)2D, low bone turnover markers. Routine 1,25(OH)2D measurement has limited value
  • 25(OH)D: check; correct low levels with parent vitamin D
  • Magnesium: check and correct if abnormal
  • Genetic testing: idiopathic (nonsurgical) disease, especially with a family history or age <40

ECG: 12-lead for QTc prolongation (International Best Practice 2025)

24-hour Urine Calcium and Creatinine: elevated urinary calcium supports the diagnosis; without PTH-mediated renal calcium reabsorption, hypercalciuria is common, especially once treatment raises the filtered calcium load (2nd International Workshop 2022; International Best Practice 2025)

TREATMENT

Acute Symptomatic Hypocalcemia (Emergency): IV calcium for cardiac, respiratory, or significant neurologic symptoms (2nd International Workshop 2022); at any calcium level for QTc >450 ms (men) or >470 ms (women), laryngospasm, bronchospasm, seizures or tetany; possibly for albumin-corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL (1.9 mmol/L), with no universally accepted threshold (International Best Practice 2025). The 2022 Workshop threshold is <7.0 mg/dL; card 109 shows both

  • IV Calcium gluconate: 1 g (90 mg elemental calcium) over 10 minutes, then 10 g calcium gluconate in 1 L D5W at 100 mL/h, titrated with cardiac monitoring (International Best Practice 2025). Label dilution and rate limits, the digoxin caution, and the 2022 Workshop regimen: card 109
  • Start oral calcium and active vitamin D at the same time (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Calcium chloride: more concentrated but irritating; central line (Practical; card 109)
  • Check albumin-corrected calcium, magnesium, and a 12-lead ECG; monitor for arrhythmia, laryngospasm, and tetany (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Correct magnesium (International Best Practice 2025)

Chronic Management (Conventional Therapy, First Line; International Best Practice 2025):

  • Calcium: carbonate or citrate with meals (also binds phosphate), in multiple daily doses; citrate with PPI use. Usual total 1-3 g/day elemental (Practical)
  • Active vitamin D: calcitriol, usually started at 0.25 mcg daily; 0.25-3 mcg/day total in divided doses (short half-life); higher after neck surgery with severe hypocalcemia (e.g., 0.25-0.5 mcg twice daily). Recheck calcium 2-3 days after a dose change
  • Parent vitamin D to keep 25(OH)D normal; magnesium kept normal
  • Targets: albumin-corrected calcium in the lower half of normal or slightly below; 24-h urine calcium <250 mg (women) or <300 mg (men); normal phosphorus and magnesium; relieve symptoms and avoid hypercalcemia
  • Hypercalciuria: thiazide (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide 25-100 mg/day, off label) with a low-sodium diet; monitor BP, potassium, magnesium, and renal function. Not with adrenal insufficiency or in pregnancy; caution in autosomal dominant hypocalcemia (International Best Practice 2025; 2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • Calcium >2 g/day or active vitamin D >2 mcg/day needed: consider PTH therapy (2nd International Workshop 2022)

PTH Replacement Therapy:

  • When: conventional therapy inadequate or not tolerated (International Best Practice 2025); inadequate control means symptomatic hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, renal insufficiency, hypercalciuria, or poor quality of life (2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • Palopegteriparatide (Yorvipath): indicated for hypoparathyroidism in adults; not studied for acute post-surgical hypoparathyroidism. Before the first dose: 25(OH)D normal and albumin-corrected calcium ≥7.8 mg/dL. Start 18 mcg SC once daily; adjust by 3 mcg, no more often than every 7 days (increase) or every 3 days (decrease); range 6-30 mcg once daily. No boxed warning; warnings include serious hypercalcemia and hypocalcemia, osteosarcoma risk, orthostatic hypotension, and digoxin toxicity if hypercalcemia develops (US label)
  • Natpara (rhPTH 1-84) is no longer available (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Teriparatide (PTH 1-34, approved for osteoporosis) is an off-label alternative if Yorvipath is unavailable (Practical)
  • Admitted patient on PTH therapy (sick day or missed dose): check calcium and albumin daily for 3-5 days. Palopegteriparatide: do not give the missed dose; check albumin-corrected calcium and give extra calcium carbonate or citrate 600 mg two to four times daily as needed (International Best Practice 2025)

Pregnancy and Lactation (International Best Practice 2025):

  • No safety data for PTH or PTH analogues: switch to conventional therapy; stop thiazides
  • Target low-normal to mid-normal calcium; measure albumin-corrected or ionized calcium (hemodilution lowers total calcium)
  • Check calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, and creatinine every 2-4 weeks, and 4-7 days after a dose change
  • Calcium and active vitamin D needs often rise when lactation stops

Monitoring (International Best Practice 2025):

  • Calcium, albumin, phosphorus, magnesium, creatinine/eGFR every 3-12 months by stability; recheck calcium within several days of a significant dose change
  • After discharge: weekly calcium for the first month (Practical; card 109)
  • 25(OH)D every 6-12 months once in range (about every 3 months until then)
  • 24-hour urine calcium and creatinine every 6-24 months
  • Renal ultrasound or other abdominal imaging for stones and nephrocalcinosis

Cautions:

  • Thiazides: used for hypercalciuria (see above); stop in pregnancy (International Best Practice 2025); not with adrenal insufficiency (2nd International Workshop 2022)
  • Loop diuretics (increase calcium excretion) (Practical)
  • Antiresorptives (e.g., denosumab) can cause hypocalcemia: use cautiously and expect to raise the active vitamin D dose (International Best Practice 2025; 2nd International Workshop 2022)
💎 HIGH-YIELD PEARLS
  • Active vitamin D is required: 1-alpha hydroxylation of 25(OH)D falls without PTH; still keep 25(OH)D normal with parent vitamin D (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Check magnesium: low magnesium causes PTH resistance; correct it (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Post-thyroidectomy: most common cause; PTH 12-24 h after total thyroidectomy >10 pg/mL makes permanent disease unlikely (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Target low-normal Ca: active vitamin D raises urine calcium and phosphorus; treat hypercalciuria with a thiazide (International Best Practice 2025)
  • Trousseau > Chvostek: Trousseau is more specific for hypocalcemia (Practical)
  • High phosphorus: Key differentiator from vitamin D deficiency (which has low phosphorus) (Practical)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Calcium Gluconate, 💊 Magnesium, 💊 Teriparatide
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hypocalcemia, 🔬 Low PTH, 🔬 Hyperphosphatemia, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine

338. TRICUSPID REGURGITATION

Right Heart Failure • Secondary vs Primary
ETIOLOGY

Etiologic Classification (2025 ACC TR ECDP Table 1; 2020 ACC/AHA Table 19):

  • Secondary TR (most cases), ventricular (V-STR): Pulmonary hypertension from LV dysfunction or left-sided valve disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, chronic lung disease, CTEPH, intracardiac shunt; dilated cardiomyopathy; RV volume overload
  • Secondary TR, atrial (A-STR): Atrial fibrillation, HFpEF; annular dilation with normal-appearing leaflets, LVEF >60%, PASP <50 mmHg, no left-sided valve disease. Lower mortality risk than V-STR
  • Primary TR: Degenerative (prolapse, flail), infective endocarditis, trauma (chest wall or leaflets; endomyocardial biopsy), Ebstein anomaly, carcinoid, mediastinal radiation, rheumatic disease, drugs (e.g., fenfluramine, methysergide)
  • CIED-related TR: Causative (lead directly interferes with leaflets or subvalvular apparatus) vs incidental (lead present but not the cause); best considered separately

Epidemiology: TR affects 4% of people age 75 and older; women outnumber men; AF is common (ECDP)

CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Symptoms (ECDP):

  • Mild to moderate TR: usually well tolerated, often clinically silent
  • Increasing severity: edema; dyspnea and fatigue from reduced forward output
  • Advanced (ominous): abdominal bloating, worsening edema, weight gain, anorexia

Physical Exam (TR is more often "seen" than "heard"):

  • JVP: Elevated with a prominent systolic cv wave and rapid y descent
  • Liver and congestion: Hepatomegaly with a pulsatile liver edge, ascites, edema, pleural effusions, sarcopenia; jaundice is a very late sign of hepatic failure
  • Murmur: Holosystolic, lower left sternal border; louder with inspiration (Carvallo sign), but may not increase when RA pressure is very high
  • RV heave: Parasternal lift
  • Exam is far less sensitive and specific than TTE; diuretics can mask signs; TR severity waxes and wanes with loading
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

TTE (COR 1, LOE C-LD): Presence, severity, and etiology of TR; right-sided chamber and IVC size; RV systolic function; PASP; associated left-sided disease. Look for leaflet abnormality, vegetation, and lead interaction

Stages (2020 ACC/AHA Table 20):

StageValve HemodynamicsConsequences / Symptoms
B: ProgressiveCentral jet <50% RA; VC <0.7 cm; ERO <0.40 cm²; RVol <45 mLNone
C: Asymptomatic severeCentral jet ≥50% RA; VC ≥0.7 cm; ERO ≥0.40 cm²; RVol ≥45 mL; dense triangular CW signal; hepatic vein systolic flow reversalDilated RV and RA; elevated venous pressure with c-V wave; no symptoms
D: Symptomatic severeSame as CSame plus dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, ascites, edema

Expanded Grading (ECDP Table 2; prognostic):

GradeVC (mm)PISA EROA (mm²)3D VCA (mm²)
Mild<3<20
Moderate3-6.920-39
Severe7-13.940-5975-94.9
Massive14-20.960-7995-114.9
Torrential≥21≥80≥115

RV Function: Normal: TAPSE >16 mm, tricuspid annular S' >10 cm/s, RV end-systolic area <20 cm² or fractional area change >35% (2020). CMR, CT, or 3D echo for more accurate RV assessment

PA Pressure Caveat: Severe TR or a weak TR signal can underestimate PASP; IVC-based RA pressure estimates are often inaccurate

Right Heart Catheterization (COR 2a, LOE C-LD): When clinical and noninvasive data are discordant or inadequate: cardiac index, right-sided pressures, PA pressures, PVR. Distinguishes pre- vs post-capillary PH. Use Fick, not thermodilution, cardiac output with severe TR

Labs: BNP, liver function tests

TREATMENT

Medical Management:

  • Diuretics (COR 2a, LOE C-EO): Right-sided HF from severe TR (Stages C/D). Loop diuretics typical, limited by worsening low-flow state; aldosterone antagonist may add benefit (hepatic congestion, secondary hyperaldosteronism). Low-salt diet, support stockings (2020)
  • Diuretic resistance (ECDP): Gut congestion impairs absorption: consider a higher-bioavailability oral loop (torsemide, bumetanide). Refractory to high-dose oral: IV loop bolus or infusion. Add thiazide (metolazone) for dual nephron blockade; acetazolamide or SGLT2 inhibitor may enhance decongestion
  • Treat the cause of secondary TR (COR 2a, LOE C-EO): Pulmonary vasodilators for elevated PA pressure, GDMT for HFrEF, rhythm control of AF

Tricuspid Valve Surgery (2020 ACC/AHA):

COR / LOEIndication
1 / B-NRSevere TR (Stage C or D) undergoing left-sided valve surgery
2a / B-NRProgressive TR (Stage B) at left-sided valve surgery with tricuspid annulus >4.0 cm (or >21 mm/m²) or prior right-sided HF
2a / B-NRRight-sided HF with severe primary TR (Stage D): isolated TV surgery
2a / B-NRRight-sided HF with severe isolated secondary TR from annular dilation (no PH or left-sided disease), poorly responsive to medical therapy: isolated TV surgery
2b / C-LDAsymptomatic severe primary TR (Stage C) with progressive RV dilation or systolic dysfunction
2b / B-NRRight-sided HF with severe TR after prior left-sided valve surgery, without severe PH or severe RV dysfunction: reoperation

ESC/EACTS 2025 differs: Concomitant repair for moderate TR (IIa, B) and for mild secondary TR with annulus ≥40 mm or >21 mm/m² (IIb, B); isolated surgery for symptomatic severe primary TR without severe RV dysfunction or severe PH is Class I (C)

Surgical Risk and Technique: Isolated TV surgery mortality up to 8-20% in older series (often after end-organ damage); reoperation after prior left-sided surgery 10-25%. Repair preferred; replacement for marked annular dilation or intrinsic leaflet disease. Severe RV dysfunction or irreversible PH risks postoperative RV failure. No randomized survival benefit of isolated surgery vs medical therapy

Transcatheter Therapy (ECDP 2025):

  • FDA-approved 2024 for symptomatic severe TR despite optimal medical therapy, selected by a multidisciplinary team, to improve health status: TriClip (transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) and EVOQUE (transcatheter valve replacement)
  • TRILUMINATE (TEER vs medical therapy, n=350): TR moderate or less at 30 days 87% vs 4.8%; KCCQ +12.3 vs +0.6 at 1 year; death or TV surgery (9.4% vs 10.6%) and HF hospitalization not different
  • TRISCEND II (TTVR vs medical therapy, n=400): TR mild or less in 95.3%; benefit driven by quality of life and NYHA class; 1-year mortality and HF hospitalization not different. 30-day mortality 3.5%, severe bleeding 10.4%, new pacemaker 24.7%
  • Benefit is symptomatic: No mortality or HF-hospitalization reduction shown. Precapillary PH predicts worse outcome after TEER
  • Device choice: TEER favored with coaptation gap ≤7 mm, anteroseptal jet, inability to take anticoagulation, advanced renal dysfunction. TTVR favored with gap >7 mm, severe leaflet tethering, CIED-related TR
  • ESC/EACTS 2025: Transcatheter TV treatment should be considered in high-risk symptomatic severe TR despite optimal medical therapy, without severe RV dysfunction or precapillary PH (Class IIa, A)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Secondary TR is most common: Treat the cause first: left heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, AF (rhythm control can reduce TR)
  • Seen more than heard: Look at the neck and liver: elevated JVP with a cv wave and rapid y descent, pulsatile liver edge (ECDP)
  • Carvallo sign: Murmur increases with inspiration, but may not when RA pressure is very high
  • IVDU + TR + fever: Think right-sided endocarditis
  • Carcinoid: Fibrous plaques on leaflets cause regurgitation and stenosis
  • Fix it during left heart surgery: Severe TR (Class 1); progressive TR with annulus >4.0 cm or prior right HF (2a). Reoperation later carries 10-25% mortality
  • CIED lead and TR: Distinguish lead-causative from incidental TR; it changes device and valve strategy
  • Transcatheter devices help symptoms, not survival: TriClip and EVOQUE improve quality of life; no mortality benefit shown
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Torsemide, 💊 Bumetanide, 💊 Metolazone, 💊 Spironolactone, 💊 Acetazolamide

339. LONG QT SYNDROME

QTc Prolongation • Torsades de Pointes Risk
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Congenital LQTS Diagnosis (ESC 2022; matches card 230): QTc ≥480 ms on repeated 12-lead ECGs or LQTS diagnostic score >3 (I, C); or a pathogenic variant regardless of QTc (I, C). QTc 460-479 ms with arrhythmic syncope and no secondary cause: consider LQTS (IIa, C)

Acquired QT Prolongation: Torsades risk rises when QTc >500 ms, especially with bradycardia (2025 AHA ALS)

Types:

  • Congenital LQTS: Rare variants in 17 genes reported, causality questioned for several; the undisputed genes cause LQT1-3. Genetic testing finds a variant in about 75%; 3 genes account for 90% of positives (ESC 2022)
    • LQT1: KCNQ1; exercise trigger (Practical: classically swimming)
    • LQT2: KCNH2; emotional stress trigger (Practical: auditory startle)
    • LQT3: SCN5A; events during sleep or rest
  • Acquired LQTS: Drugs, electrolytes, bradycardia, structural heart disease

Symptoms:

  • Syncope (from torsades)
  • Seizures (often misdiagnosed as epilepsy)
  • Sudden cardiac death
  • Palpitations
  • May be asymptomatic

Acquired Causes:

  • Drugs (CredibleMeds.org):
    • Antiarrhythmics: Sotalol, dofetilide, procainamide; amiodarone prolongs QT but TdP is infrequent (ESC 2022)
    • Antibiotics: Fluoroquinolones, macrolides, azoles
    • Antipsychotics: Haloperidol, ziprasidone, thioridazine
    • Antidepressants: TCAs, citalopram
    • Antiemetics: Ondansetron, droperidol
    • Others: Methadone, hydroxychloroquine
  • Electrolytes: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia
  • Bradycardia: Including high-grade AV block; long-short sequences initiate torsades (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS)
  • Structural: LVH, cardiomyopathy, myocardial ischemia
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

ECG:

  • Measure QTc on repeated 12-lead ECGs (Bazett: QTc = QT/√RR)
  • T-wave morphology (notched T waves in LQT2)
  • Look for TWA (T-wave alternans)
  • Torsades: Polymorphic VT with QT prolongation; QRS twists around the baseline. Polymorphic VT with a normal QT is usually ischemic and is managed differently

LQTS Diagnostic (Schwartz) Score: QTc, T-wave morphology, clinical history, family history. Score >3 is diagnostic (ESC 2022, I, C)

Additional Testing:

  • Electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca) and medication review (CredibleMeds.org)
  • Ambulatory ECG, ECG lying then immediately standing, and/or exercise testing for suspected LQTS (2a, B-NR)
  • Genetic counseling and testing for clinically diagnosed LQTS (1, B-NR; ESC I, C); a negative test does not exclude LQTS
  • Family: cascade genetic testing and clinical screening of first-degree relatives (ESC 2022, Class I)
  • Not recommended in LQTS: epinephrine challenge (III, C); invasive EP study (III, C)
TREATMENT

Acute Torsades de Pointes:

  • Sustained polymorphic VT or pulseless: Immediate unsynchronized shock (2025 AHA ALS, 1, B-NR); shock may not prevent recurrence
  • IV magnesium sulfate: Recurrent torsades with acquired QT prolongation (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, I, C-LD; ESC 2022, I, C, with potassium supplementation); effective even without hypomagnesemia. Usual dose 1-2 g IV (2017 text). 2025 ALS grades magnesium for torsades 2b, C-LD
  • Not for normal-QT polymorphic VT: Routine magnesium not recommended (ALS, 3: No Benefit); not beneficial for refractory VF unrelated to torsades (2017, 3: No Benefit, A)
  • Electrolytes (2017, I, C-LD): Replete potassium to ≥4.0 mmol/L and magnesium to normal (2017 text: some keep potassium 4.5-5.0)
  • Recurrent torsades with acquired QT prolongation and bradycardia despite magnesium (2017, I, B-NR; ESC, I, C): Increase heart rate with atrial or ventricular pacing or isoproterenol. These recommendations cover acquired LQTS only
  • Stop QT-prolonging drugs: QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics can promote torsades; in bradycardia- or pause-dependent torsades, acute beta-blockade can worsen bradycardia (ALS text)

Congenital LQTS, Long-Term (matches card 230):

  • For all: Avoid QT-prolonging drugs (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, 3: Harm, B-NR). ESC 2022 (I, C) adds: avoid and correct electrolyte abnormalities; avoid genotype-specific triggers
  • Beta-blocker: Recommended if resting QTc >470 ms (1, B-NR); reasonable if asymptomatic with QTc <470 ms (2a, B-NR). Propranolol, atenolol, or nadolol; metoprolol appears less effective. ESC 2022 prefers nonselective agents (nadolol or propranolol) (I, B). Event reduction: LQT1 >95%, LQT2 >75%, LQT3 women >60%
  • LQT3: Mexiletine indicated with prolonged QTc (ESC 2022, I, C)
  • Escalation (2017): High-risk symptomatic with beta-blocker failure or intolerance: genotype-guided drugs, left cardiac sympathetic denervation, and/or ICD (1, B-NR). Recurrent appropriate shocks on maximal beta-blocker: add drugs or denervation (1, B-NR). Asymptomatic with QTc >500 ms on beta-blocker: may consider the same (2b, B-NR)
  • ICD: Part of 2017 escalation for high-risk symptomatic LQTS, where high risk includes prior cardiac arrest (1, B-NR). ESC 2022: ICD in addition to beta-blocker after cardiac arrest (I, B); symptomatic despite beta-blocker and genotype-specific therapy (I, C)
  • Left cardiac sympathetic denervation: Part of 2017 escalation (1, B-NR). ESC 2022 (I, C): symptomatic LQTS when ICD is contraindicated or declined, or with multiple shocks or syncope despite ICD, beta-blocker, and genotype-specific therapy
  • High risk: QTc >500 ms, LQT2 or LQT3, women with LQT2 (especially 9 months postpartum), age <40, symptom onset <10 years, recurrent syncope

Acquired LQTS:

  • Withdraw the offending drug and avoid other QT-prolonging drugs (ESC 2022)
  • Correct potassium and magnesium
  • Treat the underlying condition (e.g., bradycardia or high-grade AV block)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Is the QT long? Polymorphic VT with a prolonged QT is torsades; with a normal QT it is usually ischemic and magnesium does not help
  • Magnesium for torsades: 1-2 g IV, effective even when the magnesium level is normal
  • Pace or isoproterenol only for acquired, pause-dependent torsades: Recurrent despite magnesium; recommendations do not cover congenital LQTS
  • Keep K ≥4.0 and Mg normal: In acquired QT prolongation with torsades (2017, I, C-LD); check CredibleMeds.org before adding any drug
  • LQT1 = exercise: Beta-blockers reduce events >95% (Practical: classically swimming)
  • LQT2 = emotional stress: Beta-blockers reduce events >75%; young women with QTc >500 ms are at increased risk, especially in the 9 months postpartum (Practical: auditory startle)
  • LQT3 = sleep: Mexiletine indicated with prolonged QTc (ESC, I, C); beta-blocker data limited in men
  • Not metoprolol: Metoprolol appears less effective; ESC prefers nadolol or propranolol
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Magnesium, 💊 Potassium Chloride, 💊 Atenolol
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Hyperkalemia, 🔬 Hypokalemia, 🔬 Hypomagnesemia, 🔬 Digoxin Level
