340. BRUGADA SYNDROME

Inherited Arrhythmia Syndrome • Coved ST Elevation
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Demographics: Predominantly young men, but reported at all ages (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS). Asymptomatic patients are the majority of new diagnoses (ESC 2022)

Presentation (ESC 2022):

  • About one-third present with syncope; unexplained syncope carries about 4 times the arrhythmic risk of asymptomatic patients
  • Cardiac arrest from polymorphic VT/VF; recurrent VF after cardiac arrest 48% at 10 years
  • Nocturnal agonal respiration
  • Asymptomatic: arrhythmic events about 0.5% per year

Triggers (2017; ESC 2022):

  • Fever (can unmask the type 1 pattern and trigger VF)
  • Vagotonic states
  • Drugs: sodium channel blockers, some psychotropics, anesthetic agents (brugadadrugs.org)
  • Cocaine, cannabis, excessive alcohol

Genetics: Yield about 20-30% in phenotype-positive patients, mostly SCN5A; 2-10% of healthy people carry a rare SCN5A variant, and a negative test does not exclude Brugada syndrome (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS). ESC 2022: yield about 20%; SCN5A is the only gene with evidence for clinical testing

ECG PATTERNS

Type 1 Pattern (the only diagnostic pattern):

  • Coved ST elevation with T-wave inversion in at least one right precordial lead, V1 or V2, placed in the 2nd, 3rd, or 4th intercostal space (matches card 230)
  • Spontaneous, or induced by a sodium channel blocker or fever
  • Exclude phenocopies (other causes of right precordial ST elevation)

ECG Tips:

  • High V1-V2 placement (2nd-3rd intercostal space) improves detection of type 1 (2017)
  • Pattern may be intermittent: present spontaneously, during fever or vagotonic states, or after a sodium channel blocker (2017)
  • Other markers associated with higher risk: early repolarization pattern, QRS fragmentation (ESC 2022)

Sodium Channel Blocker Challenge:

  • Indication (2017, 2a, B-NR): Suspected Brugada without a spontaneous type 1 pattern. Not recommended with a prior type 1 pattern (ESC, III, C); adds nothing in asymptomatic patients who already have type 1
  • Agents: Procainamide, flecainide, or ajmaline, in a monitored setting
  • Stop for: Ventricular arrhythmia, marked QRS widening, or type 1 pattern
  • Specificity: Drug- or fever-induced type 1 occurs in 2-4% of healthy people; an induced pattern alone needs supporting clinical features (ESC 2022)
DIAGNOSIS & RISK STRATIFICATION

Diagnosis (ESC 2022):

  • Spontaneous type 1 pattern, no other heart disease (I, C)
  • Cardiac arrest survivor from VF or polymorphic VT with type 1 induced by sodium channel blocker or fever (I, C)
  • Induced type 1 plus at least one of: arrhythmic syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration; family history of BrS; family history of sudden death <45 years with negative autopsy and suspicious circumstances (IIa, C)
  • Induced type 1 alone: may be considered (IIb, C)

Risk Stratification:

  • Highest risk: Spontaneous type 1 with prior cardiac arrest or syncope
  • Lowest risk: Asymptomatic with only a drug-induced type 1 pattern; family history of BrS or SCA is not a significant predictor (2017)
  • EP study: May be considered in asymptomatic spontaneous type 1 (2017, 2b, B-NR; ESC, IIb, B); inducibility is actionable only in that group
  • Unexplained syncope: Implantable loop recorder (ESC, IIa, C)

Genetic Testing and Family Screening: Suspected or established Brugada: genetic counseling and testing may be useful to facilitate cascade screening of relatives (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, 2b, C-EO); clinical screening of first-degree relatives. ESC 2022 goes further: SCN5A testing recommended for probands (I, C)

TREATMENT

All Patients (ESC 2022, I, C; 2017 text):

  • Avoid drugs that can induce right precordial ST elevation (brugadadrugs.org), including some psychotropics and anesthetic agents
  • Avoid cocaine, cannabis, and excessive alcohol
  • Treat fever early and aggressively with antipyretics

ICD:

  • 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS (1, B-NR): Spontaneous type 1 with cardiac arrest, sustained VA, or recent syncope presumed arrhythmic, if meaningful survival >1 year is expected
  • ESC 2022: Aborted cardiac arrest and/or documented spontaneous sustained VT (I, C); type 1 pattern with arrhythmic syncope (IIa, C); selected asymptomatic patients with VF inducible with up to 2 extrastimuli (IIb, C)
  • Asymptomatic with only a drug-induced type 1 pattern (2017, 1, B-NR): Observation without therapy; ICD has shown no benefit

Quinidine or Catheter Ablation:

  • Recurrent ICD shocks for polymorphic VT (2017, 1, B-NR): Add quinidine or catheter ablation. ESC 2022: quinidine (IIa, C); ablation of triggering PVCs and/or RVOT epicardial substrate when refractory to drugs (IIa, C)
  • Spontaneous type 1 with symptomatic VA, ICD declined or not possible (2017, 1, B-NR): Quinidine or catheter ablation (ESC: quinidine IIa, C)
  • Quinidine: Suppresses VF storm; adverse effects in up to 37% (2017 text)
  • Ablation: Eliminated the spontaneous type 1 pattern in >75% in small series; ICD still recommended after syncope or cardiac arrest. Not recommended in asymptomatic patients (ESC, III, C)

Electrical Storm: Isoproterenol infusion (ESC 2022, IIa, C); quinidine

🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Only coved type 1 is diagnostic: Coved ST elevation with T-wave inversion in V1 or V2 (2nd-4th intercostal space); exclude phenocopies
  • Fever unmasks Brugada: Fever can induce type 1 and trigger VF; treat it early with antipyretics
  • Drug-induced type 1, asymptomatic: Observe; no ICD (2017, Class 1). An induced pattern is positive in 2-4% of healthy people
  • Spontaneous type 1 plus arrhythmic syncope: ICD (2017 Class 1; ESC IIa)
  • Events at rest or sleep: Nocturnal agonal respiration counts as a clinical feature; unlike LQT1 (exercise)
  • High leads help: Record V1-V2 in the 2nd-3rd intercostal space when suspicion is high
  • Electrical storm: Isoproterenol infusion; quinidine
  • Check brugadadrugs.org before any new drug or anesthetic
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 IV Acetaminophen

341. VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED PNEUMONIA (VAP)

ICU-Acquired Pneumonia • Prevention Bundles
DEFINITION & EPIDEMIOLOGY

Definition: Pneumonia occurring >48 hours after endotracheal intubation

Incidence: 5-15% of mechanically ventilated patients; risk increases with duration of ventilation

Mortality: Attributable mortality 10-15%; increases ICU stay by 7-9 days

Risk Factors:

  • Prolonged mechanical ventilation
  • Supine positioning
  • Heavy sedation, paralysis
  • Reintubation
  • Prior antibiotic exposure
  • Aspiration
  • ARDS, COPD, immunosuppression

Pathogenesis: Microaspiration of oropharyngeal secretions around ETT cuff; biofilm on ETT

MICROBIOLOGY

Early VAP (<5 days):

  • S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, MSSA
  • Enteric gram-negatives

Late VAP (≥5 days):

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • MRSA
  • Acinetobacter
  • ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae
  • Stenotrophomonas maltophilia

MDR Risk Factors:

  • Prior IV antibiotics within 90 days
  • ≥5 days hospitalization before VAP
  • Septic shock at time of VAP
  • ARDS preceding VAP
  • Acute renal replacement therapy before VAP
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Clinical Suspicion (All Present):

  • New/progressive infiltrate on CXR
  • Fever (>38°C) or hypothermia
  • Leukocytosis or leukopenia
  • Purulent secretions
  • Decline in oxygenation

Respiratory Sampling (Before Antibiotics if Possible):

  • Endotracheal aspirate (ETA): Easier to obtain; semi-quantitative
  • Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): More specific; threshold ≥10⁴ CFU/mL
  • Protected specimen brush (PSB): Threshold ≥10³ CFU/mL

Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS):

  • Combines temperature, WBC, secretions, oxygenation, CXR, culture
  • Score >6 suggests VAP
  • Limited sensitivity/specificity; not routinely used for diagnosis

Blood Cultures: Obtain before antibiotics; positive in 10-25%

Biomarkers: Procalcitonin may help guide antibiotic duration (not diagnosis)

TREATMENT

Empiric Therapy — Low MDR Risk:

  • Piperacillin-tazobactam OR
  • Cefepime OR
  • Levofloxacin OR
  • Meropenem (if local ESBL prevalence high)

Empiric Therapy — High MDR Risk:

  • Anti-pseudomonal coverage (choose 2 from different classes):
    • Piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, carbapenem, aztreonam
    • PLUS fluoroquinolone (cipro/levo) OR aminoglycoside
  • Add MRSA coverage: Vancomycin or linezolid

De-escalation:

  • Narrow therapy based on culture results (typically within 48-72h)
  • Stop MRSA coverage if cultures negative

Duration:

  • 7 days for most VAP (non-fermenting GNRs may need longer)
  • Procalcitonin-guided discontinuation reduces antibiotic exposure
PREVENTION (VAP Bundle)
  • Head of bed elevation 30-45°
  • Daily sedation interruption ("sedation vacation")
  • Daily assessment of readiness to extubate
  • DVT prophylaxis
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis (though may increase VAP risk)
  • Oral care with chlorhexidine (0.12% twice daily)
  • Subglottic secretion drainage (specialized ETT)
  • Avoid unnecessary intubation/reintubation
  • Maintain ETT cuff pressure 20-30 cm H₂O
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Duration matters: Late VAP (≥5 days) needs broader MDR coverage
  • 7 days is enough: Shorter courses work for most VAP
  • De-escalate aggressively: Narrow to culture results within 48-72h
  • Bundle compliance: VAP prevention bundles reduce incidence by 50%+
  • Extubation is prevention: Every day on vent increases VAP risk
  • Don't overdiagnose: Many CXR infiltrates in ICU are not VAP (atelectasis, CHF, ARDS)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Pip-Tazo, 💊 Cefepime, 💊 Meropenem, 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Linezolid
🧫 ABX COMPANION Cunha Empiric Framework

342. FAT EMBOLISM SYNDROME

Post-Fracture Complication • Gurd Criteria
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: Multi-system dysfunction (pulmonary, neurologic, dermatologic) following fat emboli, typically after long bone fractures

Timeline:

  • Typically 24-72 h after injury; median 48.5 h after long bone injury
  • Rarely presents during surgery; fulminant FES (sudden large emboli with immediate coma and cardiopulmonary arrest) is rare

Classic Triad (not present in all patients):

  • Respiratory distress: Hypoxemia, tachypnea, ARDS-like picture; hypoxia is the most common finding (96%) and often the earliest
  • Neurologic changes: Confusion, agitation, altered consciousness, seizures, focal deficits; mental status changes in 59%
  • Petechial rash: Axillary or subconjunctival, torso; characteristic but seen in only 33% to about 50%, and often lasts under 24 h

Risk Factors:

  • Long bone fractures (femur > tibia)
  • Pelvic fractures
  • Multiple fractures
  • Orthopedic procedures: Intramedullary nailing, arthroplasty
  • Non-traumatic: Pancreatitis, liposuction, bone marrow transplant, sickle cell crisis (rare)

Pathophysiology:

  • Fat globules embolize to pulmonary circulation → inflammatory cascade
  • Mechanical obstruction + toxic free fatty acid effects
  • Systemic inflammation → multiorgan dysfunction
DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA

Gurd Criteria (most cited; none validated, no gold-standard test):

  • Diagnosis: 1 major + 4 minor (Gurd 1970). Gurd and Wilson 1974 also required fat macroglobulinemia; some reviews also accept 2 major (Kwiatt 2013)
  • Other scores (Lindeque, Schonfeld) exist; all are based on small samples

Major Criteria:

  • Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae
  • Hypoxemia with bilateral radiographic changes
  • Cerebral signs unrelated to head injury or any other condition

Minor Criteria:

  • Tachycardia (>110 bpm)
  • Pyrexia (>38.5°C)
  • Retinal emboli on fundoscopy
  • Fat in urine
  • Sudden drop in hematocrit or platelets
  • Rising ESR
  • Fat globules in sputum
  • The Gurd and Wilson 1974 list also includes jaundice and renal changes

Laboratory Findings (non-specific):

  • Anemia, thrombocytopenia, raised inflammatory markers
  • ABG: hypoxemia with an increased A-a gradient
  • Increased lipase and free fatty acids, which can cause hypocalcemia and hypoalbuminemia
  • Fat globules in blood, urine, sputum, or BAL are not specific (also seen in sepsis)

Imaging:

  • CXR: Bilateral non-specific patchy diffuse infiltrates
  • CT chest (preferred): Patchy ground-glass opacities with smooth septal thickening; small centrilobular nodules
  • MRI brain (if neurologic signs): Diffusion-weighted "starfield" pattern as early as 1 h; multiple T2 hyperintense lesions after about 4 h. Differential: thromboembolism, diffuse axonal injury

Differential Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism, bacterial pneumonia, sepsis, ARDS, COVID-19. FES is usually a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with risk factors

TREATMENT

Primarily Supportive (no specific therapy):

  • Refer for critical care review and ICU admission
  • Respiratory: Oxygen; 10-44% need NIV or intubation. Lung-protective ventilation as for ARDS (no FES-specific strategy); prone positioning, APRV, and ECMO have been reported
  • Hemodynamic: Resuscitate with IV fluids; vasoconstrictors, inotropes, and pulmonary vasodilators for cardiovascular instability
  • Neurologic: Brain-injury principles to limit secondary injury; consider seizure prophylaxis, and ICP monitoring if severe
  • Early definitive fracture fixation as soon as practical

Unproven Drug Therapies:

  • Corticosteroids: Prophylaxis meta-analysis (7 trials, 389 patients): FES risk reduced 78%, number needed to treat 8, no mortality difference; trials small, all but one over 20 years old. Routine use not advised (infection, delayed wound healing, osteonecrosis); most clinicians do not use them for established FES
  • Heparin: Treatment-dose heparin is not commonly used (bleeding risk after major trauma, unproven benefit). Therapeutic anticoagulation is for coexisting VTE, not FES itself (Practical)
  • Albumin: Lowers free fatty acids in animal models; role controversial because albumin raised mortality in traumatic brain injury

Prevention:

  • Expedite definitive fixation of long bone fractures; minimize movement at the fracture site before and during fixation
  • Urgent vs delayed (>24 h) fixation: ARDS 7% vs 39% in one study
  • Minimize intramedullary pressure during fixation
  • Prophylactic methylprednisolone: trial regimens ranged from 6 to 90 mg/kg total (Schonfeld 1983: 90 mg/kg over 72 h); not routine

Prognosis:

  • Mortality reported 7-36%; 7-10% in modern series with supportive care and early fixation
  • Even severe cases can be self-limiting, with complete neurologic and cardiovascular recovery
  • ARDS causes the most significant morbidity
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • 24-72 hour delay: FES usually presents 1-3 days after fracture (median 48.5 h); watch for it in the days after injury
  • Hypoxia first: Present in 96% and often the earliest sign; petechiae in only a third to a half
  • Think FES: Post-fracture patient with unexplained hypoxia, confusion, and petechiae, after excluding PE, pneumonia, and sepsis
  • Early fixation: Thought to reduce risk; fix long bone fractures as early as practical
  • No specific drug therapy: Steroid prophylaxis is not routine, and treatment-dose heparin is not used for FES itself
  • Thrombocytopenia is common: Unexplained platelet drop post-fracture should raise suspicion
  • Supportive care works: Most patients recover fully with appropriate respiratory support

343. ACUTE GASTROENTERITIS

Infectious Diarrhea • Inflammatory vs Non-inflammatory • Empiric Management • Extra-intestinal Manifestations
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition: 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours plus an enteric symptom (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or cramps, tenesmus, fecal urgency, or moderate to severe flatulence) (ACG 2016, Figure 1). Acute: less than 14 days; persistent: 14 to 30 days; chronic: more than a month (ACG 2016). IDSA uses acute less than 7 days, prolonged 7 to 13 days, persistent 14 to 29 days, chronic 30 days or longer (IDSA 2017)

Initial Characterization, Inflammatory vs Non-inflammatory (pathogen associations from IDSA 2017 Table 3):

Feature Non-inflammatory (Secretory) Inflammatory (Invasive)
Stool character Watery, no blood (Practical) Frequent scant stools with blood and mucus (dysentery) (IDSA 2017); small-volume stools with tenesmus in shigellosis (CDC)
Fever Not discriminatory: viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections can all cause fever; norovirus has low-grade fever in the first 24 hours in about 40% (IDSA 2017 Table 3) Higher temperatures suggest a bacterial cause or E. histolytica; STEC is usually afebrile at presentation (IDSA 2017 Table 3)
Fecal WBCs / lactoferrin Not recommended to establish the cause (IDSA 2017 rec 20) Not recommended to establish the cause (IDSA 2017 rec 20); imprecise and probably unnecessary for guiding further testing (ACG 2016)
Likely pathogens Norovirus, rotavirus, ETEC, S. aureus or B. cereus toxin, C. perfringens, Giardia, Cryptosporidium (IDSA 2017 Table 3; CDC; CDC Yellow Book 2026) Visible blood: STEC, Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. histolytica, noncholera Vibrio, Yersinia (IDSA 2017 Table 3). C. difficile is in the inflammatory group (IDSA 2017), but bloody stools are not expected (IDSA 2017 rec 8)
Role of antibiotics Not recommended for most acute watery diarrhea without recent international travel (IDSA 2017 rec 36); exceptions: traveler's diarrhea (ACG 2016 rec 9), Giardia (treatment below) Empiric therapy while awaiting results is not recommended in immunocompetent patients, with the exceptions below (IDSA 2017 rec 30). Avoid in STEC O157 and Shiga toxin 2 producers (IDSA 2017 rec 35)

⚠️ Extra-intestinal and Postinfectious Manifestations (evaluate for these: IDSA 2017 rec 7):

Finding Associated Pathogen(s) Clinical Pearl
Rising creatinine Dehydration (prerenal AKI) or HUS (STEC; Shigella dysenteriae type 1) (IDSA 2017 Table 4) Bloody diarrhea with rising creatinine and falling platelets: evaluate for HUS; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents (IDSA 2017 rec 35; CDC)
Seizures, encephalopathy Shigella (IDSA 2017 Table 4) Ekiri syndrome (lethal toxic encephalopathy) and/or seizures (IDSA 2017 Table 4); generalized seizures occasionally in young children, usually with high fever or abnormal electrolytes (CDC)
Reactive arthritis Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia; rarely Giardia and Cyclospora (IDSA 2017 Table 4) Starts 1 to 6 weeks after infection; joints (often knees and ankles, usually one side), eyes (conjunctivitis, uveitis), urinary tract; not everyone gets all three; HLA-B27 raises risk (NIAMS). About 2% after S. flexneri; after Yersinia, usually about 1 month after the diarrhea (CDC)
HUS (anemia, low platelets, kidney injury) STEC; Shigella dysenteriae type 1 (IDSA 2017 Table 4) Antibiotics may increase HUS risk: avoid in STEC (CDC; IDSA 2017 rec 35). Monitor hemoglobin, platelets, electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine; smear for red cell fragments when HUS is suspected (IDSA 2017 rec 23). Supportive care; may need dialysis and transfusions (CDC). Practical: urgent nephrology consult
Guillain-Barré syndrome Campylobacter (IDSA 2017 Table 4) 0.2 to 1.7 of every 1,000 Campylobacter illnesses lead to GBS; Campylobacter causes 5% to 41% of GBS; weakness usually starts in both legs, then the arms (CDC)
Bacteremia, aortitis, osteomyelitis Nontyphoidal Salmonella; Yersinia (IDSA 2017 Table 4) Invasive Salmonella in about 8% of laboratory-confirmed infections, mostly young children, older adults, and the immunocompromised (CDC). Hemoglobinopathy is a risk factor (IDSA 2017 Table 2). Blood cultures: see Laboratory Studies
Erythema nodosum Yersinia, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella (IDSA 2017 Table 4) After Yersinia, usually resolves within 1 month (CDC)
Postinfectious IBS Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, STEC, Giardia (IDSA 2017 Table 4) In 3% to 10% of adults after bacterial diarrhea; usually resolves within 1 year (IDSA 2017)
PATHOGEN DIFFERENTIAL

Non-inflammatory (watery diarrhea, absent or low-grade fever):

  • Norovirus: Leading cause of gastroenteritis outbreaks in all ages in the US; incubation 12 to 48 hours; acute vomiting and non-bloody diarrhea, sometimes low-grade fever; recovery in 1 to 3 days; outbreaks on cruise ships, camps, dormitories, long-term care facilities, hotels (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Infectious dose 10 to 100 virions (HICPAC 2011)
  • Rotavirus: Infants and young children most at risk; higher-risk adults: older adults, caregivers of infected children, the immunocompromised. Incubation about 2 days; vomiting and watery diarrhea for three to eight days; more common in winter and spring (CDC). Vaccinate all infants (IDSA 2017 rec 57)
  • Staphylococcus aureus (preformed toxin): Incubation 30 minutes to 8 hours; sudden nausea, vomiting, and cramps, most also have diarrhea; lasts 1 day; foods not cooked after handling (sliced meats, puddings, pastries, sandwiches) (FoodSafety.gov)
  • Bacillus cereus: Emetic form: incubation 30 minutes to 6 hours; diarrheal form: 6 to 15 hours; rice and leftovers, prepared foods left at room temperature; lasts about 24 hours (FoodSafety.gov)
  • Clostridium perfringens: Incubation 6 to 24 hours; diarrhea and cramps without fever or vomiting; usually less than 24 hours; beef, poultry, gravies, food held in steam tables or at room temperature (FoodSafety.gov)
  • ETEC (enterotoxigenic E. coli): Diarrheagenic E. coli, most prominently ETEC, are the most common pathogens identified in traveler's diarrhea (CDC Yellow Book 2026); treat by severity (Traveler's Diarrhea, below)
  • Giardia duodenalis (lamblia): Most likely parasite to cause persistent diarrhea; suspect with fatty stools, flatulence, or upper GI-predominant symptoms; waterborne (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Starts 1 to 2 weeks after exposure and typically lasts 2 to 6 weeks; fever is less common; weight loss and malabsorption can follow (CDC)
  • Cryptosporidium: Food and water, including recreational water; watery diarrhea, nausea, cramps; most infections asymptomatic or self-limited; more severe and prolonged in the immunocompromised (CDC Yellow Book 2026)

Inflammatory (bloody or mucoid diarrhea, fever, fecal WBCs):

  • Campylobacter jejuni: Highest reported incidence among the eight foodborne pathogens FoodNet tracks in 2023, followed by Salmonella and STEC (FoodNet 2023); mostly raw or undercooked poultry; incubation 2 to 5 days; diarrhea often bloody, abdominal pain, fever; fluoroquinolone resistance is common in the US (CDC); see ID Guide: Campylobacter
  • Salmonella (nontyphoidal): Poultry, eggs, other foods; reptiles, amphibians, baby chicks (FoodSafety.gov). Sudden diarrhea (may be bloody), cramps, fever usually present; invasive infection in about 8%; antibiotics generally do not shorten illness in healthy people: consider only for severe infection or risk of invasive disease (infants, age 50 or older with atherosclerosis, immunosuppression, heart disease, major joint disease) (CDC); see ID Guide: Salmonella
  • Shigella: Low infectious inoculum, among the most contagious enteric pathogens (ACG 2016); watery, bloody, or prolonged diarrhea, tenesmus, fever, small-volume stools; seizures, reported mainly in young children (CDC); Ekiri syndrome (IDSA 2017 Table 4); multidrug resistance is widespread: get susceptibility testing if treating (CDC); see ID Guide: Shigella
  • STEC (including O157:H7): Undercooked ground beef, raw milk and juice, leafy greens, sprouts; bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, usually little or no fever; HUS usually after about 1 week (FoodSafety.gov). About 65% of O157 patients have WBC over 10,000/µL (IDSA 2017); avoid antibiotics (IDSA 2017 rec 35); see ID Guide: STEC / HUS
  • Yersinia enterocolitica: Pork (including chitterlings) and dairy products (IDSA 2017); incubation 4 to 6 days (range 1 to 14); enterocolitis with fever and diarrhea that can be bloody and persist for weeks; mesenteric adenitis mimics appendicitis; reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum; higher risk with iron overload, including chelation (CDC)
  • C. difficile: Biggest risk factors: healthcare contact, age 65 or older, antibiotic use; community-associated cases are 35% to 48% of diagnoses; toxins A and B (ACG CDI 2021). With ileus, rectal swab PCR may help (ACG CDI 2021). Bloody stools are not expected (IDSA 2017 rec 8); see ID Guide: C. difficile
  • Entamoeba histolytica: Foodborne, waterborne, fecal-oral; mild diarrhea to dysentery; stool PCR, microscopy, or enzyme immunoassay (microscopy cannot tell it from E. dispar); antibody testing for extra-intestinal infection only; metronidazole, then an intraluminal agent (paromomycin or iodoquinol) (CDC Yellow Book 2026); see ID Guide: Amebiasis
  • Vibrio spp.: Raw or undercooked seafood, especially oysters; watery diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever. With liver disease: bloodstream infection with fever, hypotension, blistering skin lesions, sometimes death; about 1 in 5 with V. vulnificus die (CDC). Iron overload also raises risk (IDSA 2017)

Systemic Syndromes:

  • Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi (enteric fever): Consider in a febrile traveler from an endemic area (IDSA 2017 rec 4). Insidious onset; fever rises daily to 39 to 40°C by the third or fourth day; anorexia, headache, and malaise nearly universal; abdominal pain, constipation, and diarrhea common; hepatosplenomegaly; rose spots occasionally; complications in 10% to 15% of hospitalized patients after 2 to 3 weeks: GI hemorrhage, perforation, encephalopathy (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Blood culture is preferred; a single culture is positive in only about 50%, so draw several; stool culture usually negative in the first week (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Do not use serologic tests (IDSA 2017 rec 17). Treatment: see ID Guide: Salmonella
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Default: Most acute diarrhea in healthy, immunocompetent people is short, self-resolving, and viral or of unknown cause, so laboratory testing generally is not warranted (IDSA 2017)

Testing Indicated When:

  • Fever, bloody or mucoid stools, severe abdominal cramping or tenderness, or signs of sepsis: test for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile, and STEC (IDSA 2017 rec 8)
  • Dysentery, moderate to severe disease, or symptoms lasting more than 7 days (ACG 2016 rec 2)
  • Diarrhea after antibiotics or healthcare-associated diarrhea: consider C. difficile testing (IDSA 2017 rec 18)
  • Immunocompromised: broad testing (culture, viral studies, parasites) (IDSA 2017 rec 12)
  • Travelers: no testing for most uncomplicated traveler's diarrhea unless treatment is indicated; parasites if 14 days or longer; C. difficile if antibiotics in the preceding 8 to 12 weeks (IDSA 2017 rec 13)
  • Persistent abdominal pain or right lower quadrant pain mimicking appendicitis: test for Yersinia. Rice-water stools, brackish water, raw shellfish, or travel to a cholera-endemic area within 3 days before onset: test for Vibrio (IDSA 2017 rec 10)
  • Possible outbreak (shared meal, sudden cluster) or a patient at high risk of spreading disease: broader testing, coordinated with public health (IDSA 2017 rec 11; ACG 2016 rec 1)

Stool Studies:

  • GI multiplex PCR panel: FDA-approved culture-independent tests are recommended at least as an adjunct to traditional methods (ACG 2016 rec 3); e.g., BioFire FilmArray GI Panel, 22 pathogens in 1 to 2 hours (ACG 2016 Table 2). Detects DNA, not necessarily viable organisms (IDSA 2017 rec 14). Culture positive specimens when public health requires it or when susceptibility results would change care (IDSA 2017 rec 15); reflex culture for Salmonella found by PCR (CDC)
  • Stool culture: Routine culture identifies Campylobacter, Shigella, and Salmonella; Yersinia and Vibrio need special culture methods (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Use culture and culture-independent tests in parallel when practicable (ACG 2016)
  • C. difficile: Test only with 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours, on unformed stool (ACG CDI 2021). Multistep testing preferred: GDH or PCR first, then toxin A/B enzyme immunoassay (AGA 2026; ACG CDI 2021 Figure 1). One specimen; more do not increase yield (IDSA 2017 rec 18)
  • STEC: Culture for E. coli O157 and test for Shiga toxin (or its genes) at the same time; the toxin test finds non-O157 STEC (CDC; IDSA 2017 rec 8)
  • Ova and parasites: Travelers with diarrhea 14 days or longer (IDSA 2017 rec 13); serial specimens over 3 or more days for persistent diarrhea when parasites are suspected (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Giardia: EIA or NAAT; Cryptosporidium: direct fluorescent immunoassay, EIA, or NAAT (IDSA 2017 Table 5)
  • Entamoeba histolytica: Species-specific immunoassay or NAAT (IDSA 2017 Table 5); microscopy cannot tell E. histolytica from E. dispar (CDC Yellow Book 2026)

Laboratory Studies (Hospitalized / Moderate-Severe Illness):

  • CBC: Not for establishing the cause (IDSA 2017 rec 22). Neutrophilia is common with invasive bacteria; shigellosis can cause a leukemoid reaction; high WBC and neutrophil counts often occur in STEC O157 patients who go on to HUS; a falling platelet count during days 1 to 14 marks higher HUS risk (IDSA 2017)
  • BMP, BUN, creatinine: Assess dehydration (IDSA 2017 rec 5). STEC: frequent hemoglobin, platelets, electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine (IDSA 2017 rec 23)
  • Blood cultures: Signs of septicemia or systemic infection, suspected enteric fever, immunocompromise, high-risk conditions such as hemolytic anemia, infants under 3 months, or febrile illness after travel to (or contact with travelers from) enteric fever areas (IDSA 2017 rec 9)
  • Peripheral smear: Required when HUS is suspected, for red cell fragments (IDSA 2017 rec 23)
  • LFTs and HAV IgM: Practical: jaundice or suspected hepatitis A. No source read supports routine LFTs in acute gastroenteritis
  • Lactate: Practical: hemodynamic instability or suspected sepsis
  • HIV test: Practical: unexplained prolonged or severe course in a patient with risk factors. AIDS with persistent diarrhea: test for Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora, microsporidia, MAC, and CMV (IDSA 2017 rec 12)
INITIAL MANAGEMENT

Step 1: Rehydration and Supportive Care (All Patients):

  • Oral rehydration: Reduced-osmolarity ORS is first-line for mild to moderate dehydration (IDSA 2017 rec 39). Adults: 2 to 4 L of ORS, then replace ongoing losses, up to about 2 L/day (IDSA 2017 Table 7). Balanced ORS for older adults with severe diarrhea or travelers with cholera-like watery diarrhea; most others can keep up with water, juices, sports drinks, soups, and saltines (ACG 2016 rec 5). Sources differ on sports drinks: apple juice, Gatorade, and soft drinks are not for rehydration (IDSA 2017); any preferred liquid is fine in mild cases, but large amounts of sodas can cause osmotic diarrhea (CDC Yellow Book 2026)
  • IV fluids: Isotonic fluids such as lactated Ringer's or normal saline for severe dehydration, shock, or altered mental status with failure of ORS, or for ileus; the guideline states no preference between them (IDSA 2017 rec 41). Continue until pulse, perfusion, and mental status normalize, then finish with ORS (IDSA 2017 rec 42); adjust electrolytes by chemistry values (IDSA 2017 Table 7)
  • Diet: Resume the usual diet during or right after rehydration (IDSA 2017 rec 45). Data for the BRAT diet and avoiding dairy are limited; fasting for 24 hours does not appear useful (IDSA 2017)
  • Antiemetics: Can be considered once hydrated, never instead of fluids (IDSA 2017 rec 46); no recommendation for routine use in adults (IDSA 2017); useful adjuncts to rehydration in adults with norovirus (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Ondansetron is FDA-labeled only for chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and postoperative nausea, with no gastroenteritis dose (Practical: 4-8 mg IV or PO every 8 h as needed, as on card 102); QT prolongation: avoid in congenital long QT, ECG monitoring with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, or other QT-prolonging drugs; severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh 10 or more): no more than 8 mg/day (FDA label)
  • Loperamide: For immunocompetent adults with acute watery diarrhea (IDSA 2017 rec 47): 4 mg, then 2 mg after each unformed stool, maximum 16 mg/day; stop if no improvement in 48 hours (FDA label). Used alone, cap at 8 mg/day for no more than 48 hours (ACG 2016). Contraindicated in acute dysentery (blood in stool and high fever), invasive bacterial enterocolitis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter), and pseudomembranous colitis such as C. difficile (FDA label); avoid with fever or inflammatory diarrhea (IDSA 2017 rec 47) and in STEC (CDC). Boxed warning: torsades, cardiac arrest, and death above recommended doses (FDA label). Not for children under 18 (IDSA 2017 rec 47)
  • Bismuth subsalicylate: 30 mL (525 mg) liquid or two 263 mg tablets every 30 to 60 minutes, no more than 8 doses in 24 hours (ACG 2016 rec 7). Not for patients with IBD or HIV (risk of bismuth encephalopathy); the prophylactic dose should not be combined with other salicylates (ACG 2016)

Step 2: Antibiotics (Specific Indications Only):

⚠️ Antibiotics NOT routinely indicated for acute infectious diarrhea, except traveler's diarrhea (ACG 2016 rec 9); most community-acquired diarrhea is viral (ACG 2016 rec 10). Risks: prolonged Salmonella shedding (IDSA 2017), C. difficile (antibiotic use is a leading risk factor, ACG CDI 2021), and HUS with STEC (CDC).
  • Traveler's diarrhea: Mild (tolerable, does not interfere with plans): no antibiotic. Moderate (distressing or interferes with plans): antibiotics can be used. Severe (incapacitating; all dysentery is severe): azithromycin preferred (CDC Yellow Book 2026 Table 1.6.2)
    • Azithromycin 1,000 mg PO once (single or divided dose) or 500 mg PO daily for 3 days: preferred for dysentery or febrile diarrhea; first-line in Southeast Asia or where fluoroquinolone-resistant bacteria are suspected; after a single dose, if not better in 24 hours, continue daily for up to 3 days (CDC Yellow Book 2026 Table 1.6.1; ACG 2016 Table 4)
    • Rifaximin 200 mg PO TID for 3 days or rifamycin SV 388 mg PO BID for 3 days: noninvasive E. coli only; not with suspected Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, or other invasive diarrhea (CDC Yellow Book 2026 Table 1.6.1)
    • Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO once or 500 mg PO BID for 3 days; levofloxacin 500 mg PO daily for 1 to 3 days: resistance limits use in South and Southeast Asia; FDA boxed warning (aortic tears, hypoglycemia, mental health effects, tendinitis and tendon rupture) (CDC Yellow Book 2026)
    • Loperamide may be added: 4 mg, then 2 mg after each loose stool, maximum 16 mg in 24 hours (CDC Yellow Book 2026 Table 1.6.1; ACG 2016 rec 8)
  • Bloody diarrhea (immunocompetent): No empiric therapy while awaiting results, except: fever documented in a medical setting with abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and bacillary dysentery presumed to be Shigella; or recent international travel with temperature 38.5°C or higher or signs of sepsis (IDSA 2017 rec 30)
    • Adults: azithromycin or a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin, by local susceptibility and travel history (IDSA 2017 rec 31); azithromycin 500 mg PO daily for 3 days preferred for dysentery or febrile diarrhea (ACG 2016; CDC Yellow Book 2026)
    • Shigella: resistance to azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, and TMP-SMX is widespread; get susceptibility testing if treating (CDC); avoid fluoroquinolones if the ciprofloxacin MIC is 0.12 µg/mL or higher (IDSA 2017 Table 6)
    • Consider STEC in any bloody diarrhea, especially without fever, and do not give antibiotics while STEC is possible (IDSA 2017)
  • Immunocompromised host:
    • Consider empiric antibacterial treatment with severe illness and bloody diarrhea (IDSA 2017 rec 32); empiric therapy for acute watery diarrhea may be an exception to the no-treatment rule (IDSA 2017 rec 36). Blood cultures (IDSA 2017 rec 9); modify or stop antibiotics once an organism is identified (IDSA 2017 rec 38)
  • C. difficile, initial episode: Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID for 10 days preferred; vancomycin 125 mg PO QID for 10 days is an acceptable alternative (IDSA/SHEA 2021; AGA 2026). Metronidazole 500 mg PO TID for 10 to 14 days only for nonsevere CDI when neither is available (IDSA/SHEA 2021); not outside fulminant disease (AGA 2026). Fulminant (hypotension or shock, ileus, megacolon): vancomycin 500 mg PO or by NG tube QID plus IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h; add rectal vancomycin if ileus (IDSA/SHEA 2021)
  • Giardia: Tinidazole 2 g PO once with food, or nitazoxanide 500 mg PO q12h with food for 3 days (FDA label); both are first choices (IDSA 2017 Table 6); tinidazole is preferred over metronidazole for less frequent dosing and higher efficacy against some organisms (CDC Yellow Book 2026). Metronidazole is an alternative but not FDA-approved for giardiasis (IDSA 2017 Table 6); no metronidazole dose in the sources read. Tinidazole: boxed carcinogenicity warning; no alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after; not in the first trimester (FDA label)
  • Cryptosporidium: Most immunocompetent patients recover with rehydration alone; nitazoxanide for persistent symptoms (CDC Yellow Book 2026): 500 mg PO q12h with food for 3 days (FDA label). Not shown effective in HIV or immunodeficiency (FDA label); in HIV, effective ART with immune reconstitution may bring a response (IDSA 2017 Table 6)
🚫 STEC O157:H7 and Shiga toxin 2 producers: AVOID ANTIBIOTICS
Avoid antibiotics for STEC O157, STEC that make Shiga toxin 2, or when the toxin type is unknown (IDSA 2017 rec 35). In children under 10 with O157, antibiotics raised HUS risk (relative risk 17.3) (Wong 2000); a meta-analysis of 9 highly heterogeneous studies found no significant increase (pooled odds ratio 1.15, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.68) (Safdar 2002); the guideline advises avoidance because of evidence of harm (IDSA 2017). Suspect STEC with bloody diarrhea, abdominal tenderness, and no fever at first evaluation; leukocytosis does not exclude it (IDSA 2017). Avoid antimotility agents (CDC). Early IV fluids (within the first 4 days of diarrhea) may lower renal failure risk in children (CDC).

Pathogen-Directed Therapy → ID Guide:

  • 🦠 Campylobacter · 🦠 Salmonella · 🦠 Shigella · 🦠 STEC / HUS · 🦠 Norovirus · 🦠 Giardia · 🦠 C. difficile · 🦠 Amebiasis
ISOLATION AND PUBLIC HEALTH REPORTING
  • Contact precautions, C. difficile: Gowns and gloves; hand hygiene preferably with soap and water (ACG CDI 2021); alcohol sanitizers do not kill spores; disinfect high-touch areas with EPA-approved sporicidal agents such as bleach, 1 part to 9 parts water (AGA 2026)
  • Contact precautions, norovirus: For symptomatic patients; during outbreaks, continue at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve and use soap and water for hand hygiene (HICPAC 2011)
  • Food handlers and healthcare workers: Exclude when ill, until at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve (HICPAC 2011). Return to child care, work, or group settings may require serial stool cultures (Typhi, Paratyphi, STEC, Shigella, nontyphoidal Salmonella) per local health authorities (IDSA 2017 rec 26)
  • Reporting: Nationally notifiable in 2026 (routine notification): campylobacteriosis, cholera (Vibrio cholerae infection), cryptosporidiosis, cyclosporiasis, giardiasis, post-diarrheal HUS, listeriosis, salmonellosis, S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi infection, shigellosis, STEC, trichinellosis, vibriosis, foodborne and waterborne disease outbreaks; foodborne botulism is immediately notifiable, extremely urgent (NNDSS 2026). Report to the state or local health department and submit isolates when required (IDSA 2017 rec 60). Practical: state reportable lists differ; check yours
⚠️ ESCALATE / URGENT CONSULTATION IF:
  • HUS (STEC): Bloody diarrhea with rising creatinine, falling platelets, and red cell fragments: avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents (IDSA 2017 rec 35; CDC). Rising creatinine and blood pressure or volume overload: care in a center that can manage acute renal failure (IDSA 2017); may need dialysis and transfusions (CDC). Practical: urgent nephrology consult
  • Sepsis or shock: Blood cultures (IDSA 2017 rec 9); IV isotonic fluids (IDSA 2017 rec 41); suspected enteric fever with sepsis: broad-spectrum antibiotics after blood, stool, and urine cultures (IDSA 2017 rec 34). Practical: ICU
  • Fulminant C. difficile: Hypotension or shock, ileus, or megacolon (IDSA/SHEA 2021; AGA 2026); surgery for refractory severe or fulminant CDI, especially toxic megacolon, ischemia, or perforation (ACG CDI 2021). Antimotility agents are contraindicated in untreated or fulminant CDI and severe colonic IBD (AGA 2026). Toxic megacolon: transverse colon over 6 cm with loss of haustra, with systemic toxicity (AGA inpatient IBD 2026; card 181)
  • Invasive Salmonella or Yersinia in an older patient: Atherosclerosis, sustained fever or bacteremia despite therapy, or new chest, back, or abdominal pain: consider imaging for aortitis, mycotic aneurysm, or toxic megacolon (IDSA 2017 rec 25). Practical: vascular surgery consult if found
  • Severe electrolyte abnormalities: Practical: hypokalemia, hypernatremia, metabolic acidosis; adjust electrolytes by chemistry values (IDSA 2017 Table 7)
  • Altered mental status: IV isotonic fluids (IDSA 2017 rec 41); consider enteric fever encephalopathy (CDC Yellow Book 2026), HUS, and Shigella encephalopathy or seizures (IDSA 2017 Table 4)
✓ SAFE FOR DISCHARGE / DE-ESCALATE WHEN:
  • Practical: tolerating oral intake, stool frequency improving, hemodynamically stable, afebrile for 24 hours, creatinine at or near baseline
  • Organism identified: modify or stop antibiotics (IDSA 2017 rec 38)
  • HUS: daily labs can stop once the platelet count rises or stabilizes with resolving symptoms (IDSA 2017); Practical: nephrology follow-up
  • No routine follow-up stool testing after diarrhea resolves (IDSA 2017 rec 26). Giardia: retest if symptoms persist after treatment (CDC); Cryptosporidium: retest at least 1 week after the last nitazoxanide dose only if symptoms do not resolve (CDC); C. difficile: no test of cure (AGA 2026)
  • Counsel: no swimming, water activities, or sexual contact while symptomatic (IDSA 2017 rec 56); no swimming until two weeks after Cryptosporidium symptoms resolve (CDC); norovirus: do not prepare food for others while ill and for two days after (FoodSafety.gov); food workers stay out at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve (HICPAC 2011)
🔑 TEACHING PEARLS
  • Most acute diarrhea needs no stool testing and no antibiotics: usually viral or of unknown cause and self-limited (IDSA 2017; ACG 2016 rec 10)
  • Bloody diarrhea + rising creatinine + falling platelets = evaluate for HUS: smear for red cell fragments; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents (IDSA 2017 recs 23, 35; CDC). Practical: nephrology now
  • STEC: bloody diarrhea with little or no fever (FoodSafety.gov); leukocytosis does not exclude it: about 65% of O157 patients have WBC over 10,000/µL (IDSA 2017)
  • C. difficile: fidaxomicin preferred, vancomycin acceptable for the first episode (IDSA/SHEA 2021); no test of cure (AGA 2026)
  • Azithromycin for dysentery or febrile traveler's diarrhea: fluoroquinolone resistance limits use in South and Southeast Asia (CDC Yellow Book 2026); Campylobacter fluoroquinolone resistance is common in the US (CDC); US Campylobacter macrolide resistance is under 5% (IDSA 2017)
  • GI PCR detects DNA, not necessarily live organisms (IDSA 2017 rec 14); culture is still needed for susceptibility and public health (IDSA 2017 rec 15)
  • Loperamide: contraindicated in dysentery, invasive bacterial enterocolitis, and C. difficile colitis (FDA label); avoid in STEC (CDC)
  • Weakness after Campylobacter: one of the most common causes of GBS in the US; about 1 in every 1,000 people with Campylobacter infection gets GBS (CDC)
  • Norovirus: soap and water for at least 20 seconds; alcohol sanitizer is not a substitute; bleach or EPA-approved disinfectant (CDC Yellow Book 2026)
  • Salmonella risk groups: hemoglobinopathy (IDSA 2017 Table 2); consider antibiotics for severe illness, bloodstream infection, or risk of invasive disease (infants, age 50 or older with atherosclerosis, immunosuppression, heart disease, major joint disease) (CDC)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Azithromycin, 💊 Ciprofloxacin, 💊 Metronidazole, 💊 Vancomycin, 💊 Ondansetron, 💊 Fidaxomicin, 💊 Loperamide, 💊 Rifaximin
🔬 Lab Reference: 🔬 Leukocytosis, 🔬 Elevated Lactate, 🔬 Elevated Creatinine, 🔬 Blood Cultures

344. HEART FAILURE WITH PRESERVED EJECTION FRACTION (HFpEF)

LVEF ≥50% • Raised Filling Pressures • SGLT2i (US 2a; ESC I) • MRA incl. Finerenone (US 2b; ESC I)
CLINICAL PRESENTATION

Definition (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA; ESC 2026): Symptoms and/or signs of HF, LVEF ≥50% (never previously <50%; otherwise HF with improved EF), and objective evidence of structural or functional abnormalities consistent with diastolic dysfunction or raised LV filling pressures, supported by raised natriuretic peptides. Up to 50% of all HF

Contributors (2022):

  • Comorbidities: Hypertension, diabetes, obesity, CAD, CKD, AF
  • Specific causes to seek: Cardiac amyloidosis and other infiltrative or hypertrophic cardiomyopathies
  • Coronary microvascular dysfunction: Affects up to 80% of HFpEF; associated with worse prognosis (ESC 2026)

Symptoms and Signs: Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, peripheral edema, elevated JVP

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Natriuretic Peptides: HF unlikely if NT-proBNP <125 pg/mL or BNP <35 pg/mL (ESC); NT-proBNP rises with age. Obesity lowers natriuretic peptides, so a normal value does not exclude HFpEF in obese patients (ESC 2026)

Echo Criteria Supporting HFpEF (ESC 2026 Table 10): Probability rises with each abnormal parameter

  • LV hypertrophy: LV mass index ≥115 g/m² (men) or ≥95 g/m² (women), or relative wall thickness >0.42
  • LA dilation: LA volume index >34 mL/m² in sinus rhythm, >40 mL/m² in AF
  • Filling pressure: E/e′ >9 at rest (≥15 more specific, less sensitive; 2022 uses ≥15)
  • Pulmonary pressure: Estimated PASP >35 mmHg or TR velocity >2.8 m/s

H₂FPEF Score (Reddy, Circulation 2018, doi 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.118.034646): Heavy (BMI >30) 2; Hypertensive (≥2 antihypertensive drugs) 1; AF (paroxysmal or persistent) 3; Pulmonary hypertension (PASP >35 mmHg) 1; Elder (age >60) 1; Filling pressure (E/e′ >9) 1. Range 0-9. 0-1 low probability; 2-5 intermediate (exercise echo or catheterization); ≥6 high (2022). ESC 2026: use scores to raise suspicion, not to establish the diagnosis

Invasive Hemodynamics (gold standard; ESC 2026): PCWP ≥15 mmHg at rest or ≥25 mmHg with exercise, or LVEDP ≥16 mmHg at rest. Reserve for diagnostic uncertainty after noninvasive testing; CPET or exercise echo are alternatives

Exclude Specific Causes: Cardiac amyloidosis (bone scintigraphy plus serum and urine monoclonal protein testing; see card 227), HCM, constrictive pericarditis (septal bounce), significant valve disease, high-output states

TREATMENT PROTOCOL

SGLT2 Inhibitor: Empagliflozin 10 mg or dapagliflozin 10 mg daily. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA COR 2a, LOE B-R; ESC 2026 Class I, A (all symptomatic HF regardless of LVEF). EMPEROR-Preserved: 21% reduction in CV death or HF hospitalization, driven by HF hospitalization, no all-cause mortality benefit. DELIVER (doi 10.1056/NEJMoa2206286): CV death or worsening HF HR 0.82 (0.73-0.92). Benefit regardless of diabetes. Expect a mild initial eGFR dip; genital and urinary infections are the common adverse effects

Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonist: 2022: may be considered in selected patients, particularly LVEF toward 50% (COR 2b, LOE B-R). ESC 2026: steroidal or nonsteroidal MRA recommended in symptomatic HF regardless of LVEF (Class I, A). Finerenone FDA-approved July 2025 for HF with LVEF ≥40% (FINEARTS-HF: CV death or total HF events RR 0.84, 0.74-0.95); start 10-20 mg, target 20-40 mg daily by eGFR (ESC Table 11). Label: do not start if K >5.0 mEq/L; initiation not recommended with eGFR <25; hyperkalemia 9.7% vs 4.2%; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors contraindicated. Spironolactone: TOPCAT overall neutral; MRA meta-analysis positive for LVEF >40% (ESC)

Diuretics: Loop diuretic for fluid retention (2022, COR 1, LOE B-NR); dynamic dosing to volume status, lowest dose that maintains euvolemia (ESC 2026, I, A). Watch for hypotension, kidney function decline, and electrolyte disturbance

Blood Pressure: Titrate to guideline targets (2022, COR 1, LOE C-LD). 2025 AHA/ACC hypertension guideline: SBP <130 mmHg using RAAS inhibitors, especially MRA or ARNI (ARB if ARNI not feasible); beta-blockers are not for hypertension in HFpEF, only for specific comorbidities (arrhythmia, ACS)

ARB / ARNI / ACEi: 2022: ARB or ARNI may be considered in selected patients, particularly LVEF toward 50% (COR 2b, LOE B-R). ESC 2026: ACEi/ARB/ARNI may be considered (IIb, C)

Atrial Fibrillation: Managing AF can improve symptoms (2022, 2a, C-EO); catheter ablation can be useful for symptomatic AF in selected patients (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF, 2a, B-NR). Anticoagulate by stroke risk; DOAC preferred unless mechanical valve or moderate-severe rheumatic MS. Urgent cardioversion for decompensated HF with rapid rates and hemodynamic instability (ESC 2026, I, C)

Obesity: Semaglutide or tirzepatide should be considered with symptomatic HF, LVEF ≥45%, and BMI ≥30, regardless of diabetes, to reduce weight and improve exercise capacity and QoL (ESC 2026, IIa, B1); an HF-event benefit is suggested (SUMMIT) but not established

Exercise: Exercise training (2022, COR 1, LOE A); cardiac rehabilitation can be useful (2a, B-NR)

Not Effective: Routine nitrates or PDE-5 inhibitors to improve activity or QoL (2022, 3: No Benefit, B-R). IV iron: ESC 2026 recommendations cover HFrEF only

TEACHING PEARLS
  • HFpEF ≠ "normal heart": Structural or functional abnormality with raised filling pressures; always look for a specific cause such as amyloidosis
  • SGLT2i for most, MRA in selected patients: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA: SGLT2i COR 2a and MRA COR 2b (both B-R). ESC 2026 rates both Class I, A. Finerenone is now FDA-approved for LVEF ≥40%
  • Low BNP in obesity: Obesity lowers natriuretic peptides; a normal value does not exclude HFpEF
  • No reflexive beta-blockers: Not for hypertension in HFpEF; reserve for MI, symptomatic CAD, or AF rate control (chronotropic incompetence)
  • Diurese to euvolemia: Lowest effective dose; monitor BP, kidney function, and electrolytes
  • AF in HFpEF: Treat it; ablation can improve symptoms. Urgent cardioversion is for hemodynamic instability; otherwise follow AF card anticoagulation rules first
  • Think amyloid: Red flags include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar or cervical spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, QRS voltage discordant with LV wall thickness, conduction system disease or pacemaker (2023 ACC ECDP on cardiac amyloidosis, Table 1, doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2022.11.022; ESC 2026 Table 20 similar). Bone scintigraphy plus monoclonal protein testing (card 227)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Empagliflozin, 💊 Dapagliflozin, 💊 Finerenone, 💊 Spironolactone, 💊 Furosemide, 💊 Torsemide, 💊 Sacubitril/Valsartan, 💊 Semaglutide

345. ATRIAL FLUTTER

Macroreentrant Atrial Tachycardia • Atrial Rate 250-350 bpm • Often 2:1 Conduction • CTI Ablation (COR 1)
CLINICAL PRESENTATION & ECG

Definition (2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT): Macroreentrant atrial arrhythmia with a regular atrial rate and constant P-wave morphology. When the circuit uses the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) it is CTI-dependent flutter

Typical (CTI-dependent, counterclockwise):

  • ECG: Dominant negative "sawtooth" flutter waves in II, III, aVF; positive P wave in V1
  • Atrial rate: 250-350 bpm; slower with antiarrhythmic drugs, severe atrial disease, or after unsuccessful ablation
  • Ventricular rate: Depends on AV conduction ratio (Practical: 2:1 gives about 150 bpm; 3:1 or 4:1 slower); regular with a fixed ratio, irregular with variable block

Reverse typical (CTI-dependent, clockwise): Opposite pattern: positive flutter waves inferiorly, wide negative flutter waves in V1

Non-CTI-dependent (atypical) flutter: Other macroreentrant circuits, often after cardiac surgery or ablation; needs EP mapping

Diagnosis: If the atrial rate exceeds the ventricular rate, flutter or atrial tachycardia is usually present. Adenosine can unmask flutter waves but rarely terminates flutter; it may precipitate AF, which can conduct rapidly with pre-excitation, so have cardioversion available (2015). Practical: a regular narrow-complex rate near 150 bpm should prompt a search for flutter waves

Context: Same settings as AF; AF and flutter commonly coexist. Flutter can emerge during flecainide, propafenone, or amiodarone therapy for AF. Class IC drugs can slow the flutter cycle and allow rapid 1:1 AV conduction

Symptoms: Palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, lightheadedness; rapid rates sustained over time risk tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy (2015)

RATE vs RHYTHM CONTROL

Acute Rate Control (hemodynamically stable; 2015, COR 1, LOE B-R): IV or oral beta-blocker, diltiazem, or verapamil. Rate control is often harder than in AF (slower atrial rate, less concealed AV nodal conduction); higher doses or combinations may be needed

  • Esmolol (preferred IV beta-blocker, rapid onset): 500 mcg/kg IV over 1 min, then 50-300 mcg/kg/min
  • Metoprolol tartrate: 2.5-5 mg IV over 2 min; may repeat every 10 min, up to 3 doses
  • Diltiazem (preferred IV CCB): 0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 min, then 5-10 mg/h, up to 15 mg/h. Avoid diltiazem and verapamil in advanced HF, heart block or sinus node dysfunction without a pacemaker, and pre-excitation
  • Amiodarone (2015, COR 2a, LOE B-R): Systolic HF when beta-blockers are contraindicated or ineffective, no pre-excitation: 150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min for 18 h. May convert to sinus rhythm: consider anticoagulation status. Not for long-term rate control
  • Digoxin: 0.25-0.5 mg IV, may repeat 0.25 mg, maximum 1.0 mg in 24 h (2015 Table 6)
  • Pre-excited flutter: Avoid beta-blockers, diltiazem, and verapamil (risk of accelerated rates and VF)

Rhythm Control / Cardioversion:

  • Unstable (2015, COR 1, LOE B-NR): Synchronized cardioversion without delay (with anticoagulation considerations)
  • Energy (2025 AHA ALS, 2b, C-LD): Initial 200 J biphasic may be reasonable, increased if the shock fails; higher first-shock energy is preferable to lower settings
  • Elective cardioversion (2015, COR 1, LOE B-NR): Stable, well-tolerated flutter when pursuing rhythm control
  • Pharmacological cardioversion (2015, COR 1, LOE A): IV ibutilide or oral dofetilide; less effective than electrical cardioversion
  • Ibutilide: 1 mg IV over 10 min (0.01 mg/kg if <60 kg); repeat once if not terminated within 10 min. About 60% conversion. Contraindicated with QTc >440 ms; best avoided with LVEF ≤40% (2023 AF); keep potassium and magnesium in the normal range; magnesium pretreatment improves efficacy and safety; continuous ECG monitoring for at least 4 h
  • Dofetilide: Start in hospital; dose by renal function with QT monitoring
  • Rapid atrial pacing (2015, COR 1, LOE B-NR): When atrial wires or a device are in place; terminates flutter in >50%

Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm (if no ablation): Amiodarone, dofetilide, or sotalol (2015, COR 2a, LOE B-R). Flecainide or propafenone only without structural or ischemic heart disease (COR 2b, LOE B-R) and with an AV nodal blocker, because of 1:1 conduction risk

CATHETER ABLATION

CTI-Dependent Flutter (2015 ACC/AHA/HRS):

  • COR 1, LOE B-R: CTI ablation for flutter that is symptomatic or refractory to pharmacological rate control. Single-procedure success >90% with an excellent safety profile (2023 meta-analysis: 92% single, 97% multiple procedures); long-term sinus rhythm more likely than with drugs
  • COR 2a, LOE B-NR: CTI ablation for flutter arising during flecainide, propafenone, or amiodarone therapy for AF (continue the drug for AF)
  • COR 2a, LOE C-LD: CTI ablation during AF ablation when CTI-dependent flutter is documented or induced
  • COR 2b, LOE C-LD: Ablation may be reasonable for asymptomatic recurrent flutter

Non-CTI-Dependent Flutter: Ablation after failure of at least 1 antiarrhythmic (COR 1, LOE C-LD) or as primary therapy after weighing risks (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). Flutter in the first 3 months after ablation or cardiac surgery often resolves; ablation can be deferred

AF After CTI Ablation (2023 AF): 34% over 14 months in a meta-analysis (reported range 16-82%); 53% with AF before ablation vs 23% without at 16-18 months. Predictors: LA enlargement, inducible AF, prolonged interatrial conduction time or HV interval, COPD, obstructive sleep apnea, HATCH score. Post-ablation anticoagulation: see Anticoagulation

ANTICOAGULATION

Same rules as AF (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF Section 6.8.6, COR 1, LOE B-NR; 2015 SVT concordant): Typical flutter without AF: stroke 4.1% vs 1.2% in a matched population. Thromboembolism after flutter cardioversion 0-6%, highest 1-2 days after

  • Long-term OAC (2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF): Recommended at annual risk ≥2% (e.g., CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 men, ≥3 women) (1, A); reasonable at 1% to <2% (score 1 men, 2 women) (2a, A). Aspirin (with or without clopidogrel) instead of OAC: 3: Harm
  • Agent: DOAC over warfarin unless moderate-severe rheumatic MS or a mechanical valve (1, A)
  • Cardioversion, flutter ≥48 h or unknown (1, B-R): 3 weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation or imaging to exclude thrombus first
  • All cardioversions (1, B-NR): Therapeutic anticoagulation established before cardioversion and continued at least 4 weeks after
  • <48 h, not anticoagulated, CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (2b, C-LD): Precardioversion imaging may be considered. Score 0-1 and <12 h: benefit of imaging or anticoagulation uncertain (2b, C-LD)
  • Rules apply to both electrical and pharmacological cardioversion

After CTI Ablation of Typical Flutter (2023 AF):

  • 1, C-LD: Continue anticoagulation at least 4 weeks after successful cardioversion or ablation
  • 1, A: AF detected before ablation: ongoing OAC as indicated for AF
  • 1, B-NR: No prior AF, high thromboembolic risk, not on OAC: close follow-up and arrhythmia monitoring for silent AF
  • 2b, B-NR: No prior AF but high AF risk (LA enlargement, inducible AF, COPD, HF) and stroke risk >2% per year: long-term OAC may be reasonable
  • Left-sided flutter or atrial tachycardia after AF ablation: anticoagulate and manage like AF
FLUTTER vs AF DISTINCTION
FeatureAtrial FlutterAtrial Fibrillation
Atrial activitySawtooth flutter waves; typical CTI flutter 250-350 bpmIrregular atrial activity; no distinct P waves
Ventricular rhythmRegular, or irregular with variable AV conductionIrregular R-R intervals
Rate controlOften more difficult than AF (less concealed AV nodal conduction); higher doses or combinationsSee AF card
Initial cardioversion energy (2025 ALS, biphasic)200 J (2b, C-LD)≥200 J (2a, B-R)
AblationCTI ablation (1, B-R); single-procedure success >90%See AF card
AnticoagulationSame as AF (1, B-NR)2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline
TEACHING PEARLS
  • Regular rate near 150 = look for flutter (Practical): Adenosine can unmask flutter waves but rarely terminates flutter, and it can precipitate AF
  • Flecainide or propafenone needs an AV nodal blocker: Give a beta-blocker or nondihydropyridine CCB at least 30 min before to prevent 1:1 AV conduction (2023 AF)
  • Ibutilide: Contraindicated when QTc >440 ms; continuous ECG during infusion and at least 4 h after; magnesium pretreatment raises efficacy and lowers TdP risk; best avoided with LVEF ≤40% (2023 AF); keep potassium and magnesium normal
  • Cardiovert high, not low: Initial 200 J biphasic (2025 ALS, 2b, C-LD); success approaches 100% at 200 J vs 50-75% at 50 J
  • Pre-excited flutter: Avoid beta-blockers, diltiazem, and verapamil (risk of accelerated ventricular rate and VF)
  • CTI ablation does not settle anticoagulation: >90% success, but AF follows in about a third; OAC after ablation follows prior AF and stroke risk, not ablation success
  • Anticoagulate like AF: Same stroke risk scores, DOAC preference, and cardioversion rules
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Esmolol, 💊 Metoprolol, 💊 Diltiazem, 💊 Digoxin, 💊 Amiodarone, 💊 Ibutilide, 💊 Dofetilide, 💊 Apixaban

346. POST-CARDIAC ARREST CARE / TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT

ROSC Management • Temperature Control 32–37.5°C ≥36 h • Neuroprognostication • Multimodal Assessment
IMMEDIATE POST-ROSC MANAGEMENT

First 1 Hour Goals (the "Bundle"):

  • Airway/Ventilation: Intubate if not already; 100% FiO₂ until SpO₂ or PaO₂ can be reliably measured (COR 1, B-R), then titrate FiO₂ to SpO₂ 90–98% / PaO₂ 60–105 mmHg, avoiding hypoxemia and hyperoxemia (COR 2a, B-R); pulse oximetry can mask hypoxemia in darker skin (AHA 2025); Practical: confirm with ABG; pCO₂ 35–45 mmHg (avoid hyperventilation → cerebral vasoconstriction)
  • Hemodynamics: Minimum MAP ≥65 mmHg (COR 1, B-R). Four RCTs (>1000 OHCA patients) found no survival or neurologic benefit from higher MAP targets; benefit of 80–100 in selected patients is unknown. The SBP target was removed. Vasopressor: insufficient evidence for a specific agent (COR 2b, B-NR); norepinephrine is suggested first-line in cardiogenic and septic shock, but unproven in undifferentiated post-arrest shock. Temporary MCS for post-arrest cardiogenic shock: not routine (COR 3: No Benefit, B-R); may be considered in highly selected refractory cases (COR 2b, B-NR). (AHA 2025)
  • 12-lead EKG: Immediately after ROSC; persistent ST elevation with suspected cardiac cause → emergent cath lab activation regardless of consciousness; do NOT delay for neurologic exam. ECGs in the first ~8 min after ROSC have higher false-positive STEMI rates (AHA 2025); Practical: repeat the ECG if equivocal
  • Glucose: Avoid hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) and hyperglycemia (>180 mg/dL) (COR 2b, B-NR) (AHA 2025)
  • Find the cause: 12-lead ECG as soon as feasible (COR 1); head-to-pelvis CT for etiology and resuscitation injury (2b); echo or POCUS for diagnoses needing intervention (2b) (AHA 2025)
  • Other therapies: Prophylactic antibiotics: uncertain benefit (2b; lower early pneumonia in one RCT, no survival or neurologic difference). Steroids for post-arrest shock: uncertain value (2b). Neuroprotective agents: uncertain (2b). (AHA 2025)
  • Seizures: Prompt EEG in anyone not following commands (COR 1, C-LD); repeated or continuous EEG reasonable (2a). Treat clinically apparent seizures (COR 1) and EEG-only seizures (2a) with the same ASMs used for other causes, e.g. levetiracetam, valproate, lacosamide; benzodiazepines for status (2b). Ictal-interictal continuum: a trial of a nonsedating ASM may be reasonable (2b, C-EO). NO routine seizure prophylaxis (COR 3: No Benefit, B-R). Myoclonus: get EEG promptly (COR 1); do NOT treat myoclonus that has no EEG correlate (COR 3: No Benefit). (AHA 2025)
TEMPERATURE CONTROL (formerly TTM)

Who: all adults unresponsive to verbal commands after ROSC, any arrest location or rhythm: deliberate, protocolized temperature control (COR 1, B-R). Target: maintain 32–37.5°C (COR 1, B-R). Duration: at least 36 h total, counting any hypothermic phase plus the fever-prevention phase (COR 2a, B-R). (AHA 2025 Post-Cardiac Arrest Care)

TrialFindingImplication
HACA 200233°C ↓ death and neurologic disability vs normothermia in VFCAEstablished TTM as standard of care
TTM 201333°C vs 36°C: no difference in mortality or neurologic outcome36°C acceptable; both are "TTM" (not just hypothermia)
TTM2 2021Hypothermia (33°C) vs normothermia (37.5°C): no difference in 6-month mortality or neurologic outcomeStrict fever prevention (≤37.5°C) equivalent to active cooling; but both groups received careful temperature control

Choosing a target (post-TTM2): Pooled RCTs show no survival difference between 32–34°C and 36°C/normothermia, but CIs do not exclude benefit from colder targets and no trial showed harm from lower targets; benefit of a specific target in higher-severity subgroups is unclear (COR 2b). 36 h is the shortest recommended duration; the TTM and TTM2 trials used 72 h total. Active control with surface or intravascular devices. Rewarming: avoid faster than 0.5°C/h, both after hypothermic control and in spontaneous post-ROSC hypothermia (COR 2b, B-R). Prehospital rapid cold IV fluids: not recommended (COR 3: No Benefit). (AHA 2025)

Cautions with hypothermic targets (Practical, not in AHA 2025): Pre-existing coagulopathy or active bleeding (relative); severe hemodynamic instability. Do not delay PCI to start cooling.

Monitoring during temperature control (Practical, not in AHA 2025): Continuous core temp, ECG (bradycardia, QT prolongation), electrolytes (K shifts during rewarming), blood glucose, coagulation, shivering (treat with meperidine, buspirone, magnesium, or neuromuscular blockade if refractory).

CORONARY ANGIOGRAPHY TIMING
  • Persistent ST elevation, suspected cardiac cause: Emergent angiography regardless of coma (COR 1, B-NR); do NOT let GCS guide this decision
  • No ST elevation BUT cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias, or significant ongoing ischemia: Emergency angiography is reasonable, regardless of coma (COR 2a, B-NR)
  • No ST elevation, none of the above (comatose): Emergency angiography NOT recommended over a delayed or selective strategy (COR 3: No Benefit, B-R). Basis: COACT (NEJM 2019, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1816897) and TOMAHAWK (NEJM 2021, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2101909), no survival benefit from immediate angiography
  • Before discharge: Angiography recommended in survivors with suspected cardiac cause, particularly initial shockable rhythm, unexplained LV systolic dysfunction, or severe myocardial ischemia (COR 1, B-NR)
  • Multivessel CAD with post-arrest shock: Culprit-only first; immediate non-culprit PCI not recommended (COR 3: No Benefit, B-R). (AHA 2025)
NEUROPROGNOSTICATION

Timing: Consolidate the multimodal assessment no earlier than 72 h after normothermia AND discontinuation of sedatives (COR 2a, B-NR); typically ≥5 days after ROSC if hypothermic temperature control was used. Each test has its own optimal window (below). Sedatives and neuromuscular blockers clear slowly after arrest. (AHA 2025)

Multimodal Assessment (AHA 2025): every finding counts only together with other tests

TestSupports UNFAVORABLE outcomeSupports FAVORABLE outcome
Pupillary light reflexBilaterally absent at ≥72 h (2b)Preserved reflex NOT useful (3: No Benefit)
Quantitative pupillometryAbnormal at ≥72 h (2b)Usefulness not well established (2b)
Corneal reflexBilaterally absent at ≥72 h (2b)Preserved reflex NOT useful (3: No Benefit)
Motor responseAbsent or extensor upper-extremity response: usefulness uncertain (2b)Withdrawal or better (2b)
MyoclonusUndifferentiated myoclonus, even within 72 h: usefulness uncertain (2b)–
SSEP (N20)Bilaterally absent cortical N20 at ≥48 h (2b)N20 amplitude: not well established (2b)
EEGBurst suppression off sedation at ≥72 h (2b); status epilepticus continuing ≥72 h (2b). Do NOT use absent EEG reactivity within 72 h (3: No Benefit). Seizures, rhythmic/periodic discharges: uncertain (2b)Continuous background without discharges within 72 h (2b)
Brain CTReduced gray-white ratio (2b); optimal threshold and timing not establishedNot well established (2b)
Brain MRIExtensive restricted diffusion / reduced ADC at 2–7 d (2b)No restricted diffusion at 2–7 d (2b)
Serum NSE / NfLHigh NSE or NfL within 72 h (2b); no universal cutoff (lab-specific, hemolysis raises NSE). ERC/ESICM 2021 used NSE >60 μg/L at 48 and/or 72 hNormal NSE within 72 h (2b)

Rule: Multimodal, never based on a single finding (COR 1, B-NR). The ERC/ESICM 2021 algorithm requires ≥2 concordant predictors of poor outcome. Hold early, regular, transparent multidisciplinary discussions with surrogates about the timeline and its uncertainty (COR 1, C-EO). Prognostication in isolation by any single test or examiner is inappropriate. Invasive neuromonitoring (ICP, brain O2, SjvO2): usefulness not established (2b).

BEFORE DISCHARGE
  • Emotional distress: Structured assessment and treatment or referral for survivors AND caregivers, after medical stabilization (COR 1, B-R)
  • Rehabilitation: Multimodal assessment and treatment for cognitive, physical, neurological, and cardiopulmonary impairments (COR 1, C-LD)
  • Discharge planning: Multidisciplinary, including medical and rehab recommendations and return to activity/work expectations (COR 1, C-LD). (AHA 2025)
TEACHING PEARLS
  • Persistent ST elevation + cardiac arrest = emergent angiography regardless of GCS: Do NOT withhold cath based on "futility" before 72h prognostication window
  • TTM2 does not mean "do nothing": Normothermia is an actively controlled target (≤37.5°C), not passive permissiveness; keep control going for at least 36 h total (AHA 2025)
  • Sedation confounds neurologic exam: Wait at least 72 h after normothermia and sedative discontinuation (AHA 2025); document all sedatives/opioids; consider drug levels before prognostication
  • SSEP is the most reliable single prognostic test: Bilateral absence of N20 cortical response has FPR ~1%; but still requires multimodal confirmation
  • Avoid hyperoxia once measurable: Start at 100% FiO₂, then titrate to SpO₂ 90–98% as soon as saturation is reliable; also avoid hyperventilation (PaCO₂ 35–45, COR 1) (AHA 2025)
  • Post-arrest myocardial stunning: Shock often starts as low-output cardiogenic shock from post-arrest myocardial dysfunction and evolves into vasodilatory shock (AHA 2025). Practical: LV dysfunction is often transient over 24–48 h even without coronary occlusion; may need inotropes
  • Seizures are not a stand-alone death sentence: Prognostic value of seizures is uncertain (2b); only status epilepticus persisting ≥72 h supports a poor prognosis, and only with other tests. Myoclonic jerks (especially Lance-Adams syndrome) may be non-epileptic; EEG correlation is essential before treating (AHA 2025)
📖 Drug Reference: 💊 Norepinephrine, 💊 Levetiracetam, 💊 Valproic Acid, 💊 Lacosamide, 💊 Meperidine, 💊 Magnesium

347. INPATIENT PAIN MANAGEMENT

WHO Analgesic Ladder • Multimodal Analgesia • Opioid Stewardship • Equianalgesic Dosing
ASSESSMENT & GENERAL PRINCIPLES

Assessment: NRS 0–10 or CPOT (Critical Care Pain Observation Tool) for non-verbal/intubated patients. Document pain quality, location, radiation, aggravating/relieving factors, functional impact.

WHO Analgesic Ladder (modified for inpatient):

  1. Step 1 (mild, NRS 1–3): Non-opioid monotherapy — acetaminophen ± NSAID ± adjuvant
  2. Step 2 (moderate, NRS 4–6): Weak opioid (tramadol, low-dose oxycodone) + non-opioid ± adjuvant
  3. Step 3 (severe, NRS 7–10): Strong opioid (morphine, hydromorphone, oxycodone) + non-opioid ± adjuvant

Multimodal Analgesia (preferred strategy): Combine agents with different mechanisms to maximize analgesia, minimize opioid doses, and reduce adverse effects. "Opioid-sparing" is the goal in all patients.

NON-OPIOID ANALGESICS
AgentDoseKey Notes
Acetaminophen650–1000 mg PO/IV q6h (max 4g/day; 2g if liver disease or heavy alcohol)Backbone of multimodal; underused IV; no GI/renal/platelet effects. Watch cumulative dosing in combo products (Percocet, Vicodin)
Ibuprofen / KetorolacIbuprofen 400–800 mg PO q6–8h; Ketorolac 15–30 mg IV/IM q6h (max 5 days)Avoid if CrCl <30, GI ulcer history, anticoagulation, post-cardiac surgery, pregnancy. NSAIDs often outperform opioids for bone/renal colic/inflammatory pain
Gabapentin / PregabalinGabapentin 300 mg TID (titrate); Pregabalin 75–150 mg BIDNeuropathic pain, post-op analgesia (opioid-sparing); dose-reduce in renal failure; sedation additive with opioids
Lidocaine (IV)1–1.5 mg/kg IV bolus, then 1–2 mg/kg/hr infusionPost-op and abdominal pain; opioid-sparing; monitor for arrhythmia and CNS toxicity (tinnitus, perioral numbness)
Ketamine (low-dose)0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV bolus; 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/hr infusionNMDA antagonist; excellent for opioid-tolerant/hyperalgesia patients; preserves airway; can cause dysphoria/hallucinations (co-administer midazolam 1mg if needed)
Methocarbamol / CyclobenzaprineMethocarbamol 750–1500 mg PO QID; Cyclobenzaprine 5–10 mg TIDMusculoskeletal/spasm component; avoid cyclobenzaprine in elderly (anticholinergic; Beers list)
OPIOID ANALGESICS

Equianalgesic Conversion Table (oral morphine equivalents, OME):

OpioidPO EquianalgesicIV EquianalgesicNotes
Morphine30 mg10 mgReference standard; active metabolite (M6G) accumulates in renal failure → respiratory depression; histamine release
Hydromorphone7.5 mg1.5 mgPreferred in renal failure (no active metabolite accumulation relative to morphine); 5× more potent than morphine IV
Oxycodone20 mgN/A (PO only)1.5× more potent than PO morphine; no IV form in US; CYP2D6 metabolism
FentanylN/A (patch)0.1 mg (100 mcg)100× more potent than morphine. Patch: 25 mcg/hr ≈ 60 mg PO morphine/day. Safe in renal failure (no active metabolites); preferred in ICU
MethadoneComplex (non-linear)—QT prolongation; drug interactions; long/variable half-life. Pain management: pain specialist consultation. OUD maintenance: only through certified program
Tramadol300 mg—Weak opioid + serotonin/NE reuptake inhibitor; lowers seizure threshold; avoid in seizure disorder or SSRI/SNRI (serotonin syndrome risk)

Opioid Dosing Strategy:

  • Opioid-naive: Start low (morphine 2–4 mg IV q4h PRN or oxycodone 5 mg PO q4h PRN)
  • Opioid-tolerant: Convert prior 24h opioid use to OME, then give 50–100% of total as scheduled long-acting + 10–15% of total q4h PRN breakthrough
  • PCA: Hydromorphone 0.2 mg IV demand q10min (no basal unless opioid-tolerant or cancer pain) — patient-controlled reduces total opioid use vs nurse-administered PRN
  • Route: PO preferred when feasible; IV for acute severe pain or NPO; avoid IM (unpredictable absorption, painful)
SPECIAL POPULATIONS & ADVERSE EFFECTS
SituationRecommendation
Renal failureAvoid morphine (M6G accumulation); use hydromorphone or fentanyl. Avoid NSAIDs, tramadol, codeine
Hepatic failureReduce acetaminophen to max 2g/day; reduce opioid doses and frequency; tramadol CI in severe hepatic failure
Elderly (>65)Start 25–50% lower opioid doses; avoid diphenhydramine, meperidine, ketorolac >5 days, cyclobenzaprine (Beers criteria); fall risk assessment
OUD / on MOUDContinue buprenorphine perioperatively (do NOT abruptly d/c) — partial agonist at mu receptor reduces opioid effect but maintains baseline analgesia; use multimodal maximally; opioids still work but higher doses needed
Opioid-induced constipationProphylactic bowel regimen for ALL patients on opioids: senna + docusate. Refractory: methylnaltrexone (peripheral mu antagonist; does not reverse central analgesia)
Respiratory depressionRR <8 or SpO₂ <90 with pinpoint pupils: naloxone 0.04–0.1 mg IV q2–3min (titrate to adequate respirations — NOT to full reversal, which precipitates acute withdrawal and pain crisis). Repeat dosing or infusion if long-acting opioid
TEACHING PEARLS
  • Acetaminophen is underused: Scheduled IV/PO APAP reduces opioid consumption by ~20% — add it to every pain regimen without renal/hepatic contraindication
  • NSAIDs often outperform opioids for renal colic, bone pain, and inflammatory pain — try before escalating opioids
  • Morphine in renal failure = M6G accumulation: Can cause delayed respiratory depression 12–24h after dosing in CKD/ESRD; use hydromorphone or fentanyl instead
  • Never divide the daily opioid dose to convert: When converting between opioids (rotation), reduce by 25–50% from calculated equianalgesic dose to account for incomplete cross-tolerance and individual variation
  • Don't stop buprenorphine perioperatively: Abrupt discontinuation → withdrawal; buprenorphine can continue perioperatively with supplemental opioids as needed (they still work at higher doses)
  • Low-dose ketamine for opioid-tolerant patients: NMDA antagonism treats opioid-induced hyperalgesia and reduces total opioid requirements; effective in sickle cell, chronic opioid use, post-op spine surgery patients
  • Naloxone dose — titrate, don't reverse completely: 0.04 mg increments to restore respirations — full reversal precipitates acute pain crisis, withdrawal, and potential pulmonary edema
