348. PALLIATIVE CARE & GOALS OF CARE

Goals-of-Care Conversations • Code Status • Symptom Management • Hospice
GOALS-OF-CARE CONVERSATIONS

Core Principle: Goals of care = aligning medical care with what matters most to the patient. Not about "giving up" — about choosing the right care for the right goals.

REMAP Framework (for serious illness):

  1. Reframe why you're having this conversation: "Your illness has become more serious. I want to make sure we're doing the right things for you."
  2. Expect emotion — respond empathically before continuing: "This is a lot to take in. What's going through your mind?"
  3. Map the patient's values/priorities: "What do you understand about your illness?" → "What matters most to you?" → "What are you hoping for?"
  4. Align with their goals: "Given what you've told me, I want to make sure all of your care is aimed at [goal]."
  5. Plan medical treatments that match: Propose, ask, revise treatment options that match their goals.

SPIKES Protocol (breaking bad news): Setting (private, seated) → Perception (what does patient know?) → Invitation (ask permission to share) → Knowledge (share information in plain language) → Empathy (respond to emotion) → Summarize & Strategize.

Serious Illness Conversation Guide (Ariadne Labs): Evidence-based; use the phrase: "I want to make sure that if things change with your illness, you get the care you want. Is this something we could talk about?"

CODE STATUS & ADVANCE DIRECTIVES

Code Status Options:

StatusMeaningNotes
Full CodeAll resuscitative measures including CPR, intubation, defibrillation, ACLS drugsDefault if no documented preference
DNR onlyNo CPR; all other interventions continue (pressors, antibiotics, intubation for respiratory failure)Most common intermediate status; does NOT mean "do not treat"
DNR/DNINo CPR, no mechanical ventilationPatient may still want aggressive non-intubation treatment; clarify what IS desired
Comfort-Focused / CMOGoal is comfort; no interventions to prolong life; symptom management onlyDiscontinue non-comfort medications (statins, antihypertensives); continue opioids, anxiolytics, APAP; may or may not include artificial nutrition

Surrogate Decision-Making Hierarchy (when patient lacks capacity): Healthcare proxy/POA > legal guardian > spouse > adult children (unanimous or majority) > parents > siblings > next of kin. Standard = substituted judgment ("What would the patient want?") not best interests alone.

POLST/MOLST Forms: Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment — portable, actionable medical orders that cross care settings (hospital → SNF → home). Different from advance directives (which are patient documents, not orders).

SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT AT END OF LIFE
SymptomFirst-Line TreatmentNotes
DyspneaOpioids (morphine 2–4 mg IV/SC q4h); low-dose anxiolytic (lorazepam 0.5–1 mg) if anxiety component; fan/cool air; positioningOpioids are the most effective treatment for dyspnea at end of life; do NOT withhold for fear of "hastening death" — evidence does not support this concern
PainScheduled opioids + PRN breakthrough; maximize non-opioid adjuvants; avoid IM routeAnticipate and treat proactively; reassess q4h minimum
Secretions ("death rattle")Glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg SC/IV q4h; hyoscine (scopolamine) patchReassure family that patient is not distressed by secretions; repositioning and oropharyngeal suctioning
Agitation / deliriumHaloperidol 0.5–2 mg IV/SC q4–6h PRN; lorazepam 0.5–1 mg q4h if benzodiazepine refractory agitationTerminal restlessness — differentiate from pain (treat with opioid) and delirium; rule out urinary retention, fecal impaction, uncontrolled pain
NauseaOndansetron 4–8 mg IV q6–8h; prochlorperazine 10 mg PO/IV; haloperidol 0.5–1 mg IV (opioid-induced nausea)D/c contributing medications if comfort-focused (opioid-sparing not priority in CMO)
Palliative sedationMidazolam continuous infusion (refractory symptoms); requires ethics/palliative consultation; family meeting documentationEthical principle of double effect; intent = relieve suffering (not hasten death); distinct from euthanasia
HOSPICE & PROGNOSTICATION

Hospice Eligibility (Medicare Hospice Benefit):

  • Physician certification that life expectancy ≤6 months if disease runs its natural course
  • Patient elects comfort-focused care (foregoes curative treatment for terminal illness)
  • Does NOT require active withdrawal; patient can continue non-curative treatments (e.g., transfusions for QoL)

Disease-Specific Prognosis Criteria:

  • Cancer: Multiple metastases, performance status deteriorating, KPS <50, serum albumin <2.5, weight loss >10% in 6 months
  • Heart failure: NYHA IV despite optimal therapy, recurrent hospitalizations, LVEF <20%, dependence on inotropes/IABP
  • COPD: FEV₁ <30% predicted, cor pulmonale, hypoxemia at rest, repeated hospitalizations, age >70
  • Dementia: Stage 7 FAST (non-ambulatory, minimal verbal ability, incontinent), recurrent infections/fevers, aspiration pneumonia
  • Renal failure: eGFR <15 declining, refusing/not candidate for dialysis, malnutrition, recurrent hospitalizations

Surprise Question: "Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next year?" — if NO, initiate goals-of-care conversation and consider palliative referral.

TEACHING PEARLS
  • DNR ≠ "do not treat": DNR means no CPR; patient still gets antibiotics, pressors, procedures, IVF. Clarify what IS desired
  • Opioids do not hasten death at comfort doses: Evidence consistently shows appropriate opioid dosing for dyspnea/pain does not accelerate dying — withholding causes unnecessary suffering
  • Early palliative care improves survival: Temel 2010 (NEJM): Early palliative care + oncology vs oncology alone in metastatic NSCLC → early palliative group lived 2.7 months longer, with less aggressive end-of-life care and better QoL
  • Capacity vs competence: Capacity is a clinical determination (can patient understand, appreciate, reason, and communicate a choice?) — assessed by the treating physician. Competence is a legal term. A patient can have capacity for some decisions but not others (decision-specific)
  • Surrogate standard = substituted judgment: "What would the patient want?" not "What do you think is best?" — surrogates represent the patient's values, not their own preferences
  • Code status is reversible: DNR/DNI can be changed at any time by a capacitated patient or if clinical situation changes; document conversations thoroughly
  • Palliative sedation ≠ euthanasia: Intent, agent, and legality differ — palliative sedation is ethical, legal, and appropriate for refractory suffering; euthanasia requires explicit intent to end life
